explanation: Pure replication of Haushofer & Shapiro (2016) using the authors' cleaned dataset, re-coded in different software: 'We produced the exact same results for means, coefficients and standard errors as reported in Table II for all eight indices in all five columns' (p.12). Headline treatment effects (Table 2, p.12; N=940 households, 1,474 individuals for psychological well-being): non-land assets +301.51 USD PPP (SE 27.25), non-durable expenditure +35.66 (5.85), monthly revenue +16.15 (5.88), food security index +0.26 SD (0.06), psychological well-being +0.26 SD (0.05), all FWER p<=0.02; health, education and female empowerment indices null. Original design: 120 villages in Rarieda, Kenya; 1,440 households (503 treatment / 505 spillover / 432 pure control). Caveats from the replication's extensions: FWER-adjusted p-values differ slightly (different re-ranking algorithm); the food security and psychological well-being main effects lose significance once village-x-treatment interactions are added (Table 11, p.24); PCA returns multiple factors for the food security, health and psych well-being indices; the index-construction formulas were absent from the authors' code and the original authors did not respond to requests. Overall verdict (p.i): 'Our pure replication results are consistent with the findings published in the original study.'

explanation: The replication found a statistically significant difference in percent body fat between 'poor' and 'full, good or fair' outcome groups (22% vs. 27%, p < 0.035, Cohen's d = 1.10), directly supporting the original finding. explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion (p.516): 'The present study replicated and validated previous findings documenting reduced global cortical volume and reduced gyrification in the lateral frontal, temporal, and postcentral cortices bilaterally in women with acute AN.' Table 3 shows highly significant LGI reductions across 6 large bilateral clusters (all corrected CWP = 0.0002, cluster sizes ranging from 780-4424 mm²), closely matching the widespread gyrification reductions reported by Bernardoni et al. replication_authors: Jenni Leppanen; Felicity Sedgewick; Valentina Cardi; Janet Treasure; Kate Tchanturia

explanation: The authors explicitly state (p.516): 'The present finding did not replicate previous work that has documented widespread reduction in cortical thickness and regional increases in cortical curvature,' naming King et al. (2015) and Bernardoni et al. (2016) as key sources. While King et al. reported global cortical thinning affecting up to 85% of the cortex, the present study found only small, localised clusters of reduced thickness (Table 2: cluster sizes 130-189 mm², corrected CWP 0.007-0.042) in the occipital and parietal cortices, and no group differences in cortical curvature. The authors attribute the failure to replicate partly to the older age of their sample.

Contrary to the null finding by Miles et al., the present study found significant reductions in cortical surface area in three left-hemisphere clusters (Table 4: superior frontal cortex CWP=0.006, inferior temporal cortex CWP=0.028, superior temporal cortex CWP=0.049). It is classified as a close extension because the study added escape extinction, tested in-person and telehealth delivery formats, included more participants and younger ages, and extended to face shields — deliberately testing the effect in expanded conditions beyond the original.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our CFA replicated the previously reported observation of three latent dimensions in the ADOS algorithm reflecting RRBs, Basic Social-Communication behaviors and Interaction Quality.' replication_title: Inhibition of CD203c membrane up-regulation in human basophils by high dilutions of histamine: a controlled replication study
explanation: The paper's title explicitly calls this 'a controlled replication study.' The Discussion (p.762) states: 'In this work we were able to reproduce evidence for the effects of high histamine dilutions on anti-IgE-triggered basophil activation.' Statistical results are unambiguous: Friedman test P = 0.012 for high dilutions overall; individual Wilcoxon tests show significant inhibition at 12C (P = 0.047), 14C (P = 0.003), 15C (P = 0.036), 16C (P = 0.009), while water controls showed no effect (Friedman P = 0.590). The primary original study is Belon et al. 2004, the European multicentre trial establishing that histamine dilutions modulate basophil activation. The replication type is 'close extension' because the paper introduces a new polychromatic flow cytometry protocol with CD203c as primary marker (rather than optical microscopy or CD63 used in prior studies) and a novel standardized mechanical succussion procedure, while testing the same biological phenomenon in the same general in vitro basophil model. PDF review confirmed all details.

explanation: The authors replicated an unspecified fraction of the 85 SNPs selected from the Icelandic deCODE GWAS (3 promising + 82 sub-promising), with an average replication rate of ~25–27% across all three GWASs combined. The authors conclude 'this study showed promise for replication of some initial genome-wide association signals,' indicating partial rather than full replication.

explanation: The authors replicated a subset of the 36 SNPs selected from the UK-NL GWAS (2 promising + 34 sub-promising), with notably strong replication for rs3736228 in LRP5 (combined p=5.3×10⁻¹²) but an overall replication rate of ~25–27% across all three GWASs combined. replication_title: Relationships among peri-traumatic circulating endocannabinoids and long-term, negative outcomes following traumatic injury
explanation: The authors report that 2-AG was positively associated with PTSD severity in the current cohort but this relationship 'did not survive correction for multiple comparisons,' and the AEA-PTSD link was 'not replicated in this cohort.' The discussion describes the PTSD finding as showing 'some evidence' of replication with qualified language, making the overall result inconclusive.

replication_title: Relationships among peri-traumatic circulating endocannabinoids and long-term, negative outcomes following traumatic injury
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our previous study found that higher concentrations of 2-AG predicted greater depression 6-9 months post-injury, this was not seen in the current cohort,' and the overall conclusion confirms 'associations between 2-AG concentrations and depression...were not replicated in this cohort.'

replication_title: Relationships among peri-traumatic circulating endocannabinoids and long-term, negative outcomes following traumatic injury
explanation: The authors state: 'In accordance with results in the previous cohort (Trevino et al. 2022), we identified a significant positive association between peri-traumatic serum 2-AG concentrations and severity of pain 6-10 months later.' The Discussion also confirms that 'The conclusions of the initial study that circulating 2-AG concentrations in the peri-traumatic period were positively associated with...chronic pain were replicated in the current cohort.'

replication_title: Regional specificity of the cingulate cortex thickness association with the intensity of psilocybin experience: a replication study
explanation: The replication found a comparable effect size in the same direction (β = 0.523 vs. original range 0.324-0.572) but failed to reach statistical significance (p = 0.297), likely due to lower statistical power (N = 25 vs. N = 55). Authors describe this as 'a partial replication where effect direction and magnitude align with the original study, though significance was not reached.'

replication_title: Bats, Bacteria, and Bat Smell V.2.0: Repeatable Sex-Specific Differences in Scent Organ Microbiota
explanation: The authors explicitly frame this as a conceptual replication and conclude: 'our findings are consistent with the original study: wing-sac microbiota of S. bilineata exhibit sex-specific differences. In line with the original study, microbial richness is lower in wing sacs of males than wing sac rudiments of females.' Both key findings (lower richness and different composition in males) were confirmed using 16S rRNA sequencing instead of culture-dependent methods.

replication_title: Association of common variants in KIF21B and ankylosing spondylitis in a Chinese Han population: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we first replicated the association of the KIF21B 1q32 locus and AS in a Chinese Han population,' finding two SNPs (rs502658 and rs10494829) significantly associated with AS. The replication extends the original European ancestry finding to a Chinese Han population using the same case-control SNP genotyping approach.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We successfully showed decreased uptake of Gd-EOB-DTPA into liver parenchyma in the severe or uncontrolled diabetic group,' confirming the same effect found in the original mouse study in a human clinical population. The replication is a close extension because it tests the same hypothesis using a similar MRI contrast enhancement paradigm but in humans rather than mice.

replication_journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience
explanation: The authors explicitly state they aimed to 'replicate previous findings' from Grabe et al. using the same instruments (HOCI-S and DES), and conclude that 'consistent with two previous studies [12][14], our results provide further evidence for a significant link between the checking dimension and dissociation in OCD,' characterizing the study as 'both replicating and extending earlier research.'

replication_title: Exploration of irony appreciation in schizophrenia
replication_journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience
explanation: The paper's subtitle is explicitly 'A replication study on an Italian sample.' The core Marjoram et al. finding—impaired ToM joke comprehension vs. physical jokes—was clearly replicated (t=6.55, df=19, p<0.0005), and the response time pattern also aligned ('Similar results are reported by Marjoram et al.'). However, the symptom correlation findings diverged: this study found ToM performance correlated with PANSS positive symptoms, whereas Marjoram et al. found correlations with negative symptoms. The authors state this is 'in disagreement with Marjoram et al. results' but consistent with other literature [3,4]. Result classified as inconclusive because the primary ToM deficit replicated but the key symptom-specificity finding did not.

[36] in a well-characterized clinical sample' and 'our replication study supports the reproducibility of the findings by Mann et al. [36].' They found a significant interaction between VS activation and naltrexone treatment on relapse risk (HR = 7.406, p = 0.033), mirroring the original study's findings.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the current investigation provides the first independent replication of the findings from this previous smaller cohort study,' and confirm in the Conclusion: 'This study has identified an association between polymorphisms in the PTK2 gene and VL muscle specific force, thus providing an independent replication of previous research.' The same genotype-phenotype associations were found in the larger replication sample.

explanation: The authors used the identical apparatus, stimuli, and procedure from the original study but tested expert musicians rather than non-musicians. They explicitly report: 'Our results widely replicated those of [15]' and 'we replicated and extended the findings of [15],' with the key finding confirmed—the strongest SMARC effect emerged when pitch-height and brightness varied coherently (effect size d ≈ 0.7, BF10 = 1821).

description: Presenting numbers in the context of a clockface (where small numbers are on the right and large numbers on the left) reverses the typical SNARC effect, producing faster right-hand responses to small numbers and faster left-hand responses to large numbers

replication_title: It’s SNARC o’ clock: manipulating the salience of the context in a conceptual replication of Bächtold et al.’s (1998) clockface study
explanation: The authors explicitly label their Experiment 4 as 'the closest replication of Bächtold et al.'s (1998) clockface condition' and state that 'the results from the original experiment were conceptually replicated.' Experiment 4 using a clockface-position task (high salience condition) showed a significant reversed SNARC effect (regression weights t(29) = 1.78, p < .05, d = 0.32), consistent with the original finding, though the task instructions differed (visuospatial vs. semantic), hence the conceptual classification.

description: Adult male dyslexics show less gray matter volume than controls in left temporal lobe regions (inferior, middle, and superior gyri) as measured by voxel-based morphometry

replication_authors: Evans TM; Flowers DL; Napoliello EM; Eden GF
replication_title: Sex-specific gray matter volume differences in females with developmental dyslexia
explanation: The paper explicitly states it conducted 'a replication study of men' and the Conclusion confirms: 'In pure male samples, we replicated previous findings of relatively less GMV in left middle/inferior temporal gyri and right postcentral gyrus in men with dyslexia.' The key adult male finding (less GMV in left middle/inferior temporal gyri, Z=4.23, 91 voxels) survived FWE correction (p<0.05). This directly replicates Brown et al. (2001) who found less GMV in left temporal lobe (inferior, middle and superior gyri) in 16 male dyslexics vs 14 male controls, and Vinckenbosch et al. (2005) who found less GMV in left middle and inferior temporal gyri. Although multiple prior studies are cited, the replication claim is unambiguous and the statistical evidence is robust. Reviewed PDF Discussion, Conclusion, and Table 2 to confirm.

explanation: The paper specifically names Eckert et al. as being replicated: 'Boys with dyslexia compared to their male pediatric control group had relatively less GMV in left supramarginal/angular gyri, again replicating prior work in male children [18].' The original study [18] found less GMV in dyslexic boys in left supramarginal gyrus, which was confirmed in the replication.

explanation: The authors explicitly designed the study as a replication and confirm in the Discussion: 'This appears to consolidate our previous findings on beta topography for the same task comparison with fewer components and electrodes but larger sample [8].' Both key findings were confirmed: inter-subject similarity was significantly lower than inter-session similarity (all t-tests p < 0.003), and inter-task similarity was very high (overall R² ≈ 0.92, >92% of components explained by complementary task).

The authors conclude: 'the results from Experiment 2 corroborate the initial findings that the Landolt paradigm per se evokes higher levels of activation in the right IPS,' confirming that right parietal activation occurs even in the absence of targets.

In Stage 2 (N=5,192), HR for OS was 1.0 (0.8-1.2) for heterozygotes and 1.0 (0.7-1.3) for minor allele homozygotes (p=0.820), compared to significant associations in Stage 1.

replication_title: Replication study for reported SNP associations with breast cancer survival

explanation: The authors note that 'another SNP (COMT rs4680) also had generally consistent results between the two study stages for OS; however, the primary Stage 1 finding was for a recessive association for DFS, which was not replicated in Stage 2.' replication_title: Replication study of three functional polymorphisms associated with bone mineral density in a cohort of Spanish women
replication_journal: Journal of Bone and Mineral Metabolism
explanation: The replication found no statistically significant association between rs4876869 and BMD at any skeletal site. Table 3 shows FN-sBMD P = 0.090 and LS-sBMD P = 0.504 (unadjusted), both non-significant after Bonferroni correction (threshold P < 0.0083). Table 4 (covariate-adjusted) shows FN-sBMD P = 0.178. Table 5 shows non-significant osteoporosis risk: FN adjusted OR = 1.67 (95% CI 0.77-3.62, P = 0.192), LS adjusted OR = 1.36 (95% CI 0.88-2.10, P = 0.170). The original paper (Vidal et al.) found rs4876869 significant only within a haplotype (P = 0.01), not independently. The authors note this negative result 'is in agreement with previous results in which no association was detected between this SNP and BMD when analyzed independently.' Classified as failure because the replication paper's stated aim was to test this functional polymorphism's association with BMD and no significant association was found.

explanation: The replication found no association between rs12503796 in the FGFBP1 gene and any bone phenotype. Table 3 shows completely non-significant P values: FN-sBMD P = 0.416 (recessive model), LS-sBMD P = 0.427 (dominant model). The SNP was dropped from further adjusted analysis due to its lack of association. The authors note: 'Although Hoppman et al. Classified as failure because the paper explicitly aimed to replicate this BMD association and found none in their women-only cohort, even though the null result is expected given the original study's sex-stratified finding (men only).

explanation: The study found a statistically significant association of rs7588550 in ERBB4 with diabetic nephropathy in Japanese type 2 diabetes patients, but in the opposite direction to the original (p=0.0126, OR=0.79, 95% CI: 0.65-0.95): 'the G allele of rs7588550, which showed a protective effect in the original report, increased the risk of diabetic nephropathy.' The authors conclude this was 'not replicated' due to the inconsistent effect direction.

replication_authors: Marcello Passarelli; Michele Masini; Carlo Chiorri; Alessandro Nurcis; Roberta Daini; Fabrizio Bracco
replication_title: Implicit evidence on the dissociation of identity and emotion recognition
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The Invisible Expression effect was successfully replicated (F(2, 38.18) = 16.24, p < 0.001)'. The replication followed Laeng et al.'s procedure but used different stimuli (Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces database) and tested an Italian population, making it a close extension.

description: When a wh-phrase indicates parallelism between an upcoming wh-clause and a preceding clause, the parser predictively constructs the wh-clause (gender mismatch effects at the reflexive occur only in wh-NP conditions, but not when a preposition undermines parallelism in wh-PP conditions), suggesting prediction is a parallelism-driven process
original_authors: Masaya Yoshida; Michael Walsh Dickey; Patrick Sturt
original_title: Predictive processing of syntactic structure: sluicing and ellipsis in real-time sentence processing
replication_authors: Hiroki Fujita
replication_title: Predictive structure building in language comprehension: a large sample study on incremental licensing and parallelism
explanation: The present study used the same 24 experimental materials from Yoshida et al. but employed a lexicality maze task (rather than self-paced reading) and 324 participants (rather than 40). The authors report the findings are 'partially inconsistent with Yoshida et al.': gender mismatch effects were found in both wh-NP and wh-PP conditions (no wh-type × gender interaction), contradicting the original's finding that prediction is parallelism-driven (only in wh-NP conditions). However, the core finding of predictive structure building was confirmed and even extended, and garden-path effects (absent in the original) were observed.

description: Female relatives (mothers, grandmothers, aunts) of androphilic Samoan males (fa'afafine) exhibit elevated reproductive output compared to those of gynephilic men, consistent with the sexually antagonistic gene hypothesis
original_authors: Doug P. VanderLaan; Deanna L. Forrester; Lanna J. Petterson; Paul L. Vasey
original_title: Offspring production among the extended relatives of Samoan men and fa'afafine
replication_authors: Scott W. Semenyna; Lanna J. Petterson; Doug P. VanderLaan; Paul L. Vasey
replication_title: A Comparison of the Reproductive Output Among the Relatives of Samoan Androphilic Fa’afafine and Gynephilic Men
explanation: The replication found that mothers and maternal grandmothers of fa'afafine had significantly elevated reproductive output (consistent with the original), but failed to replicate the paternal grandmother effect found by VanderLaan et al. (2012). The authors concluded support for the SAGH is 'equivocal' because no maternal aunt effect was found, which would represent the 'gold standard' evidence for the hypothesis.

description: Men who perform mate retention (mate guarding) behavior less frequently produce higher-quality ejaculates, suggesting that humans deploy mate retention behavior and ejaculate quality investment as compensatory anti-cuckoldry tactics
original_authors: Samantha Leivers; Gillian Rhodes; Leigh W. Simmons
original_title: Sperm competition in humans: Mate guarding behavior negatively correlates with ejaculate quality
replication_authors: Tara DeLecce; Todd K. Shackelford; Virgil Zeigler-Hill; Bernhard Fink; Mohaned G. Abed
replication_title: Mate Retention Behavior and Ejaculate Quality in Humans
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'this conceptual replication was not successful because we did not identify statistically significant associations between the deployment of mate retention behavior (overall or along the domains of benefit-provisioning or cost-inflicting) and (most assessments of) ejaculate quality.' The study used a different operationalization of ejaculate quality (4 principal components from 17 parameters) and the MRI-SF instrument, constituting a conceptual rather than direct replication.

description: Men produce more sperm in ejaculates when they have spent less time together with their partner since the couple's last copulation, indicating ejaculate adjustment in response to sperm competition risk
original_authors: R.Robin Baker; Mark A. Bellis
original_title: Human sperm competition: Ejaculate adjustment by males and the function of masturbation
replication_authors: Tara DeLecce; Gavin S. Vance; Virgil Zeigler-Hill; Lisa L. M. Welling; Todd K. Shackelford
replication_title: Ejaculate Adjustment in Response to Sperm Competition Risk in Humans
explanation: The paper explicitly labels itself a 'conceptual replication' of Baker & Bellis, using additional measures of sperm competition risk and updated technology. The main finding of Baker & Bellis — that time spent apart predicts ejaculate quality — was not replicated: 'time spent together since the couple's last copulation was not associated with any of the several indicators of ejaculate quality in the present study.'

description: Fitness landscapes in unit test generation are dominated by neutral regions (plateaus), with ruggedness and neutrality properties measurably affecting search algorithm effectiveness in covering branches

original_journal: Proceedings of the 2020 Genetic and Evolutionary Computation Conference
replication_authors: Omur Sahin; Man Zhang; Andrea Arcuri
replication_title: Causes and effects of fitness landscapes in system test generation: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly replicate Albunian et al.'s (2020) fitness landscape analysis methodology (same six metrics, same random walk approach, same 1000 steps and 30 runs) but apply it to system-level test generation with EvoMaster rather than unit-level testing with EvoSuite. The Conclusions state: 'Our results confirm the existing results reported in the literature for unit testing, albeit with some differences,' with notable differences in the DBI metric between system-level and unit-level testing.

explanation: The replication found that the fetal genotype of rs4769612 was associated with preeclampsia risk in Iranian women under the recessive model (Table 3, P=0.0048), but the C/C genotype was protective (OR=0.34) rather than risk-increasing as reported in the original. The Discussion confirms: 'Steinthorsdottir et al. reported...the C allele increased the risk of PE,' whereas in the replication 'the fetal C/C genotype lowered the risk of PE.' The same genome (fetal) shows association but with reversed effect direction. The authors acknowledge 'discrepancies with previous studies.' Classified as inconclusive because the fetal association was found but with opposite directionality.

explanation: The replication found that the maternal genotype of rs1421085 showed no association with preeclampsia in Iranian women (Table 4: all maternal P-values >0.05), directly contradicting the original finding. The Discussion confirms: 'Steinthorsdottir et al. showed for the first time that rs1421085 is significantly associated with PE risk through the maternal genome.' Instead, the fetal genotype was associated under dominant (OR=1.87, P=0.031) and over-dominant (OR=2.01, P=0.034) models. The specific original claim about maternal genome association was not replicated; association was found only through fetal genome. Classified as inconclusive because the variant-disease association exists but through a different biological mechanism (fetal vs. maternal genome).

description: Cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS) symptoms show strong internal and structural validity relative to ADHD-inattention symptoms, with invariance of CDS symptom loadings and thresholds across mother and father ratings of the same child, and CDS showing stronger associations than ADHD-IN with anxiety and depression
original_authors: Sáez B.; Servera M.; Becker SP; Burns GL
original_title: Optimal items for assessing sluggish cognitive tempo in children across mother, father, and teacher ratings
original_journal: Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology
replication_authors: Belinati G.; Moura M.; Becker SP; Burns GL
replication_title: Validity of Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome with Mother and Father Ratings of Brazilian Children: Replication of Northern Hemisphere Findings in South America
explanation: The paper's title explicitly frames it as 'Replication of Northern Hemisphere Findings in South America.' The PDF confirms all key findings replicate: (1) CDS symptoms had substantial loadings on CDS factor (mothers M=0.78, fathers M=0.71) with near-zero cross-loadings on ADHD-IN, matching prior studies; (2) 14 of 15 CDS symptoms showed invariance across mother/father ratings, described as 'almost identical' to Sáez et al. [8,9]; (3) CDS factor means did not differ across parents (d=-0.06), matching Sáez et al. (d=0.01); (4) external validity pattern replicated — ADHD-IN stronger with ADHD-HI, CDS stronger with anxiety/depression across all source analyses. The Discussion states results were 'highly consistent with the findings from studies in the five earlier studies.' The one minor deviation (CDS and ADHD-IN similarly associated with academic impairment, whereas prior studies found ADHD-IN stronger) is explicitly noted by the authors but does not undermine the overall successful replication pattern.

description: First-grade Norwegian students who experienced COVID-19 emergency remote instruction scored lower on writing quality, handwriting fluency, and attitude toward writing than a pre-pandemic cohort of first-graders in the same schools
original_authors: Gustaf Bernhard Uno Skar; Steve Graham; Alan Huebner
original_title: Learning loss during the COVID-19 pandemic and emergency remote instruction first grade students' writing: A natural experiment
replication_authors: Gustaf B. Skar; Steve Graham; Alan Huebner
replication_title: The Long-Term Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Children’s Writing: a Follow-up Replication Study
explanation: The authors replicated the same methodology with the same cohort one year later (as second-graders) and found no significant differences between the Before and During COVID-19 cohorts on any of the three writing measures. As stated in the Discussion: 'Contrary to our prediction, we did not find statistically significant differences between the Before COVID-19 cohort and the During COVID-19 cohort on any of the three writing measures: writing quality, handwriting fluency, or attitude toward writing.' The COVID-19 learning loss effect observed in first grade did not persist to second grade.

description: MORLOT (Many-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Online Testing), which combines RL and many-objective search, outperforms random testing and search-based techniques for online testing of Deep Neural Network-enabled Autonomous Driving Systems in terms of safety requirements violations exposed within a given time budget
original_authors: Haq, Fitash Ul; Shin, Donghwan; Briand, Lionel
original_title: Many-objective reinforcement learning for online testing of DNN-enabled systems
original_journal: IEEE/ACM 45th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE)
replication_authors: Luca Giamattei; Matteo Biagiola; Roberto Pietrantuono; Stefano Russo; Paolo Tonella
replication_title: Reinforcement learning for online testing of autonomous driving systems: a replication and extension study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The replication does not confirm the finding that many-objective Reinforcement Learning, specifically MORLOT, outperforms the random baseline in ADS testing.' They found that when the random baseline is run under the same detection conditions as MORLOT (correcting a confounding factor), MORLOT and random are 'statistically indistinguishable' in both effectiveness and efficiency across all three test routes.

explanation: The replication found no clear winner among the three feedbackDirectedSampling settings, which 'reaffirmed the same conclusions as in the original study' — thus the original finding (that no configuration is clearly dominant) was successfully replicated across a larger set of SUTs and a newer tool version.

explanation: The replication confirmed that the value of 5 for maxSQLInitActionsPerMissingData was the most effective, consistent with the original study: 'We found that a configuration of 5 for maxSQLInitActionsPerMissingData is indeed the most effective' across line coverage, branch coverage, and fault detection metrics.

description: A value of 0.5 for probOfApplySQLActionToCreateResources is the most effective setting for maximizing code coverage in EvoMaster REST API testing

original_journal: International Symposium on Search Based Software Engineering
replication_authors: Amid Golmohammadi; Man Zhang; Andrea Arcuri
replication_title: Tools and benchmarks evolve: what is their impact on parameter tuning in SBSE experiments?
explanation: The replication confirmed the original finding. Table 10 shows Vargha-Delaney effect sizes comparing 0.5 vs other settings are all near 0.50 (no significant difference favoring alternatives), with 0.5 slightly ahead on average for line and branch coverage (Â=0.51-0.53). The authors explicitly conclude: 'Evaluating the collective data from all 15 REST APIs, we determined that a 0.5 setting consistently provided the best overall performance, aligning with the conclusions of the original study.' While individual SUTs showed variation (e.g., proxy-print and scout-api favored different values), the aggregate finding clearly replicates. Verified against PDF Tables 9-10 and RQ1 findings summary.

explanation: The replication found that 0.8 outperformed the original optimal value of 0.5 for probOfRandomSampling, contradicting the original study. The replication paper summarizes: 'Contrary to the original articles that found 0.5 to be the optimum, here we discovered that 0.8 performed better across multiple case studies' — indicating the original recommendation does not hold in the updated tool version.

replication_title: Improved Diagnostic Validity of the ADOS Revised Algorithms: A Replication Study in an Independent Sample
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'our overall finding that the diagnostic validity of the revised algorithms is better than that of the original algorithms.' The improvement was most apparent for autism cases, with less consistent improvement for non-autism ASD. The paper's title itself describes it as 'A Replication Study' of Gotham et al.'s revised algorithms.

original_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders

replication_title: Improved Diagnostic Validity of the ADOS Revised Algorithms: A Replication Study in an Independent Sample
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
explanation: The authors confirm: 'We confirmed the factor structure proposed by [Gotham et al. 2007], and the revised algorithms were minimally influenced by age.' The two-factor model fit well (CFI 0.96-1.00, RMSEA 0.04-0.08) in cells A, B, C, with only slightly unsatisfactory fit in cell D. replication_journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
explanation: PDF Tables 2-4 and Discussion reviewed. The four European GWAS-derived SNPs (from Aston et al. 2010, per Table 2 header) showed no significant association with collective male infertility in Japanese men (Table 2: p=0.98, 0.18, 0.36, 0.18 for the four SNPs). However, subgroup analysis found rs11204546 in OR2W3 was significantly associated with oligospermia (Table 4: p=0.0037, OR=1.74). The Discussion frames this as partial support: OR2W3 may be 'a common risk factor in infertile men across widely different ethnicities' but the other three loci did not replicate. Classified as inconclusive because the primary analysis (collective male infertility) failed while one of four SNPs was significant only in the smaller oligospermia subgroup (n=70).

explanation: Study 1 (lab, n=127) and Study 2 (gambling venue, n=124) both found pop-up/dynamic messages were recalled significantly more frequently and accurately than static messages. Study 1: free recall accuracy χ²(2, N=127) = 13.65, p < .001; Study 2: free recall accuracy χ²(2, N=124) = 22.72, p < .0001. Pop-up messages also had significantly greater self-reported impact on within-session thoughts and behaviors in both studies. The Discussion (p. 85) explicitly states: 'The results replicate and extend previous research findings. Similar to previous empirical laboratory studies (Cloutier et al. 2006; Floyd et al. 2006; Ladouceur and Sevigny 2003) pop-up messages appear to be superior to static signs in enhancing message recall and influencing thoughts.' The abstract also calls this a 'qualitative replication study.' This is a self-replication (same authors as [39]) that extends the original by adding message content variables (informative vs. self-appraisal vs. control) and testing in a real gambling venue (Study 2). PDF review confirmed unambiguous replication success across all measures of the dynamic vs. static comparison.

However, the specifics diverge substantially: (1) the significant effect appeared in the YOUNG subgroup (≤74 years; p=0.045, OR=0.428) rather than the OLD subgroup as in Rodriguez-Rodriguez and Burgess; (2) the T-allele direction was protective, explicitly described as 'inconsistent with the Spanish in Rodriguez-Rodriguez et al. study.' The authors attribute these paradoxical findings to ethnic differences in T-allele frequency (75% in Asians vs. 25% in Caucasians vs. 54% in African-Americans). Reviewed PDF Tables 3 and 4: total sample showed no association (p=0.651 adjusted), old subgroup showed no association (p=0.286-0.957), only the young subgroup dominant model was significant (p=0.045).

replication_journal: International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction
explanation: The replication used identical audit methodology on 50 online gambling operators (32 overlapping with the original, 18 replaced due to closures). Table 2 provides a direct head-to-head comparison across 15 RG criteria. Improvements were found on 11 of 15 metrics (e.g., no promotional material on RG page: 12%→92%; cooling off: 72%→96%; self-exclusion: 86%→96%; CS communication re limits: 60%→86%). Four metrics were roughly unchanged. The core finding from the original — that operators have variable and often insufficient RG practices — was confirmed, with the replication additionally documenting improvements attributable to increased regulatory pressure. The authors conclude 'RG practices in the present study appear to have increased' while noting 'there are still some areas that need to be improved.' Classified as success because the replication confirms the original methodology and core descriptive finding that RG practices remain inconsistent across operators and insufficient in key areas. This is a descriptive audit study with no inferential statistics.

replication_title: The Influence of Genetic Variation on Social Disposition, Romantic Relationships and Social Networks: a Replication Study
explanation: Testing the same 24 SNPs and social measures in a subclinical Caucasian sample (N=140 with history of mental illness), chi-squared tests found no significant differences in the frequency of significant associations across any of the six neurochemicals between the original and subclinical samples. The authors conclude: 'broad agreement exists' and that findings are 'quite robust' in this new population.

description: Receptor gene variants for different neurochemicals (oxytocin, β-endorphin, dopamine, vasopressin, serotonin, testosterone) are each associated with distinct domains of human sociality (social disposition, romantic/dyadic relationships, and wider social networks) in a healthy Caucasian sample
original_authors: Pearce, E.; Wlodarski, R.; Machin, A.; Dunbar, R.
original_title: Variation in the β-endorphin, oxytocin, and dopamine receptor genes is associated with different dimensions of human sociality
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Eiluned Pearce; Rafael Wlodarski; Anna Machin; Robin I. M. Dunbar
replication_title: The Influence of Genetic Variation on Social Disposition, Romantic Relationships and Social Networks: a Replication Study
explanation: Testing the same 24 SNPs and social measures in a non-Caucasian sample (N=66), chi-squared tests found no significant differences for five of six neurochemicals, but the oxytocin system showed a significant difference (χ²=10.572, df=2, p=0.005), driven by a lack of associations with dyadic sexual relationships in this sample — a key finding of the original. Only one SNP-level replication was confirmed (OXTR rs237897 and anxious attachment).

description: In a bonus-version of the gift-exchange game, the introduction of an unobservable random shock to worker effort significantly reduces welfare compared to a no-shock condition
original_authors: Jared Rubin; Roman M. Sheremeta
original_title: Principal-agent settings with random shocks
replication_authors: Brent J. Davis; Rudolf Kerschbamer; Regine Oexl
replication_title: Is reciprocity really outcome-based? A second look at gift-exchange with random shocks
replication_journal: Journal of the Economic Science Association
explanation: The replication authors explicitly state: 'We largely reproduce RS16's finding (1)' that introducing an unobservable shock significantly reduces welfare, confirmed with MWU test p=0.05 in the replication.

description: Informing the principal about the size of the random shock does not restore gift-exchange — welfare in the observable-shock condition remains as low as in the unobservable-shock condition
original_authors: Jared Rubin; Roman M. Sheremeta
original_title: Principal-agent settings with random shocks
replication_authors: Brent J. Davis; Rudolf Kerschbamer; Regine Oexl
replication_title: Is reciprocity really outcome-based? A second look at gift-exchange with random shocks
replication_journal: Journal of the Economic Science Association
explanation: The replication explicitly states 'we fail to confirm finding (2)': unlike RS16, they find welfare is statistically indistinguishable between the no-shock and observable-shock treatments (MWU p=0.96), and significantly higher in observable-shock than unobservable-shock (p=0.04), indicating that observable shocks do restore gift-exchange.

description: A 6-item revision of the ORTO-15 questionnaire (ORTO-R) has an acceptable confirmatory factor structure for assessing orthorexia nervosa tendencies as a continuous scale
original_authors: Radosław Rogoza; Lorenzo M. Donini
original_title: Introducing ORTO-R: a revision of ORTO-15 based on the re-assessment of original data

replication_title: Orthorexia nervosa: replication and validation of the ORTO questionnaires translated into Greek in a survey of 848 Greek individuals
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'replicate the findings of the factorial structure of ORTO-R' using a Greek-translated version of the questionnaire in a Greek sample of 848 adults, and concluded: 'The ORTO-R questionnaire has been validated in this Greek sample, and its factorial structure has been fully replicated in the present analysis.'

description: Exposure to losses disguised as wins (LDWs) in electronic gambling machines causes participants to overestimate the number of genuine wins that occurred during a gambling session
original_authors: Candice Graydon; Mike J. Dixon; Jeffrey Gutierrez; Madison Stange; Chanel J. Larche; Tyler B. Kruger
original_title: Do losses disguised as wins create a "sweet spot" for win overestimates in multiline slots play?
replication_authors: Dan Myles; Daniel Bennett; Adrian Carter; Murat Yücel; Lucy Albertella; Cassandra de Lacy-Vawdon; Charles Livingstone
replication_title: “Losses disguised as wins” in electronic gambling machines contribute to win overestimation in a large online sample
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our primary results unambiguously replicated the LDW triggered over-estimation effect. Consistent with previous studies (Graydon et al., 2021).' The Introduction identifies Graydon et al. (2021) as the primary body of work: 'previous studies investigating the LDW triggered overestimation effect had been predominately conducted by researchers at the Gambling Research Lab at the University of Waterloo (Graydon et al., 2021).' The replication used a similar video-based paradigm online with an Australian sample (n=940), finding d=0.44, p<.001. The study was pre-registered and the result is unambiguous. PDF review confirmed all details.

description: Genetic variants in mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation genes (assessed via a weighted genetic risk score of 11 SNPs in 9 genes) are associated with increased risk of abruptio placentae
original_authors: Tsegaselassie Workalemahu; Daniel A. Enquobahrie; Amy Moore; Sixto E. Sánchez; Cande V. Ananth; Percy Pacora; Liming Liang; Manuel Salazar; Michelle A. Williams
original_title: Genome-wide and candidate gene association studies of placental abruption
original_journal: International Journal of Molecular Epidemiology and Genetics
replication_authors: Tsegaselassie Workalemahu; Daniel A. Enquobahrie; Bizu Gelaye; Timothy A. Thornton; Fasil Tekola-Ayele; Sixto E. Sanchez; Pedro J. Garcia; Henry G. Palomino; Anjum Hajat; Roberto Romero; Cande V. Ananth; Michelle A. Williams
replication_title: Abruptio placentae risk and genetic variations in mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation: replication of a candidate gene association study
replication_journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the associations of maternal MB/OP wGRS that we reported before with risk of AP' using the same 11 SNPs and methodology in an independent cohort (PAGE study). The highest quartile of wGRS was associated with 1.75-fold (95% CI 1.27-2.42; P=7.0E-04) higher odds of AP, consistent with the original finding.

description: States that have passed medical marijuana laws (MMLs) have higher rates of adolescent past-month marijuana use and lower perceived riskiness of monthly marijuana use compared to states without such laws
original_authors: Melanie M. Wall; Ernest Poh; Magdalena Cerdá; Katherine M. Keyes; Sandro Galea; Deborah S. Hasin
original_title: Adolescent marijuana use from 2002 to 2008: higher in states with medical marijuana laws, cause still unclear
replication_authors: Sam Harper; Erin C. Strumpf; Jay S. Kaufman
replication_title: Do Medical Marijuana Laws Increase Marijuana Use? Replication Study and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated the findings of Wall et al. that marijuana use was higher in states that have passed MMLs.' They reproduced nearly identical prevalence estimates using the same dataset (NSDUH 2002-2009) and confirmed higher monthly marijuana use in MML states (8.68%) versus non-MML states (6.94%), with a prevalence difference of 1.74% (95% CI: 1.4%-2.4%). The extension using difference-in-differences methodology suggests the association is likely due to confounding, not a causal effect of MMLs.

description: Specific candidate SNPs (including PRDM14 rs16936667 and other gene variants) are associated with the development of new-onset diabetes after kidney transplantation (NODAT)
original_authors: Jennifer A. McCaughan; Amy Jayne McKnight; Alexander P. Maxwell
original_title: Genetics of new-onset diabetes after transplantation
original_journal: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology
replication_authors: Chand S.; McKnight AJ; Shabir S.; Chan W.; McCaughan JA; Maxwell AP; Harper L.; Borrows R.
replication_title: Analysis of single nucleotide polymorphisms implicate mTOR signalling in the development of new-onset diabetes after transplantation
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself a 'replication study of candidate SNPs associated with developing NODAT' (abstract and conclusion). It validates SNPs from the Belfast GWAS [ref 1] in an independent Birmingham cohort. Only 5 of 37 tested SNPs were significantly associated with NODAT in the adjusted model, including PRDM14 (rs16936667) from the original GWAS. The authors state 'the current study therefore replicates these findings' for the 5 significant SNPs. However, 32/37 SNPs were not significant, and the authors acknowledge only 60% power to detect OR of 2 with 20% MAF, stating 'the 5 identified SNPs in this study requires further validation in another cohort.' The very wide confidence intervals (e.g., OR 10.6, CI 1.8-63.0) and small sample size (18 NODAT vs 50 controls) further indicate inconclusive results. PDF review confirmed all details; three original study authors (McKnight, McCaughan, Maxwell) are co-authors on this replication.

description: Spatially contiguous cocaine-related cues bias concurrent monetary choices toward the cocaine-cued option selectively among individuals with cocaine use history
original_authors: Strickland, Justin C.; Marks, Kathleen R.; Beckmann, Joshua S.; Lile, Joshua A.; Rush, Craig R.; Stoops, William W.
original_title: Contribution of cocaine-related cues to concurrent monetary choice in humans
replication_authors: Justin C. Strickland; Cecilia L. Bergeria
replication_title: Contribution of alcohol- and cigarette-related cues to concurrent reinforcer choice in humans
explanation: The authors explicitly designed these experiments as 'conceptual replications of this prior work' and concluded in the General Discussion: 'we replicate the finding that spatially contiguous drug-related cues can bias decisions involving concurrently presented nondrug reinforcers.' Both Experiment 1 (alcohol cues; hazardous drinkers: t=3.04, p=.004, d=0.51) and Experiment 2 (cigarette cues; smokers: t=2.39, p=.02, d=0.22) demonstrated the same selective cue-induced choice bias pattern.

description: Spatially contiguous cannabis-related cues bias concurrent monetary choices toward the cannabis-cued option selectively among individuals with cannabis use history
original_authors: Strickland, Justin C.; Lile, Joshua A.; Stoops, William W.
original_title: Contribution of cannabis-related cues to concurrent reinforcer choice in humans
replication_authors: Justin C. Strickland; Cecilia L. Bergeria
replication_title: Contribution of alcohol- and cigarette-related cues to concurrent reinforcer choice in humans
explanation: The authors explicitly designed these experiments as 'conceptual replications of this prior work' and confirmed that 'these associations, as reported previously, were specific to an individual's substance use history and related to substance use variables.' Experiment 2 (cigarette cues, N=256) demonstrated a significant cue-choice bias in smokers (t=2.39, p=.02, d=0.22), consistent with the cannabis cue-bias pattern of the original.

description: Negative emotion differentiation (NED) moderates the relationship between rumination and frequency of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) in borderline personality disorder, such that rumination predicts greater NSSI only among low differentiators
original_authors: Landon F. Zaki; Karin G. Coifman; Eshkol Rafaeli; Kathy R. Berenson; Geraldine Downey
original_title: Emotion differentiation as a protective factor against nonsuicidal self-injury in borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Seah THS; Aurora P.; Coifman KG
replication_title: Emotion Differentiation as a Protective Factor Against the Behavioral Consequences of Rumination: A Conceptual Replication and Extension in the Context of Social Anxiety
explanation: The authors explicitly frame the paper as a 'conceptual replication' of Zaki et al. (2013), testing whether NED moderates rumination → maladaptive behavior in social anxiety (rather than BPD and NSSI). Study 1 (clinical SAD sample) found NED significantly moderated the rumination–social avoidance relationship (interaction B = -.78, p = .010), consistent with the original finding, leading the authors to conclude 'the results of Study 1 replicated and extended [78]'s findings.'

description: Negative emotion differentiation (NED) moderates the relationship between rumination and frequency of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) in borderline personality disorder, such that rumination predicts greater NSSI only among low differentiators
original_authors: Landon F. Zaki; Karin G. Coifman; Eshkol Rafaeli; Kathy R. Berenson; Geraldine Downey
original_title: Emotion differentiation as a protective factor against nonsuicidal self-injury in borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Seah THS; Aurora P.; Coifman KG
replication_title: Emotion Differentiation as a Protective Factor Against the Behavioral Consequences of Rumination: A Conceptual Replication and Extension in the Context of Social Anxiety
explanation: Study 2 (non-clinical socially anxious college students) also found NED significantly moderated the rumination–social avoidance relationship (interaction B = -.14, p = .009), replicating both Zaki et al. (2013) and Study 1. The authors conclude 'our results replicate and expand upon previous findings reported by [78],' describing unanimity across both studies.

description: Time of year (season) and time of day interact such that participants recorded in fall mornings show less relative left frontal EEG activity than participants recorded in spring mornings
original_authors: Carly K. Peterson; Eddie Harmon-Jones
original_title: Circadian and seasonal variability of resting frontal EEG asymmetry
replication_authors: Jamie R. Velo; Jennifer L. Stewart; Brant P. Hasler; David N. Towers; John J.B. Allen
replication_title: Should it matter when we record? Time of year and time of day as factors influencing frontal EEG asymmetry
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The present study failed to replicated [44] using seasonal coding' and note that 'contrary to previous findings, no simple time of year by time of day interaction was found.' Additionally, the seasonal main effect that was found ran in the opposite direction from Peterson & Harmon-Jones.

description: Frontocentral spindling excessive beta (SEB) is associated with greater impulse control problems in patients with ADHD or sleep problems
original_authors: Martijn Arns; Ron J. Swatzyna; Jay Gunkelman; Sebastian Olbrich
original_title: Sleep maintenance, spindling excessive beta and impulse control: An RDoC arousal and regulatory systems approach?
replication_authors: Noralie Krepel; Hanneke van Dijk; Alexander T. Sack; Ronald J. Swatzyna; Martijn Arns
replication_title: To spindle or not to spindle: A replication study into spindling excessive beta as a transdiagnostic EEG feature associated with impulse control
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current results replicate and extend on the earlier report,' with a significant main effect of SEB on the impulse control (IMP) scale (F(1,72) = 15.899, p < .001, d = 0.87) and on false positive errors on the CPT (d = 0.55), both replicating the original finding. The IMP scale was operationalized identically to the original study.

description: Frontocentral spindling excessive beta (SEB) is associated with greater sleep maintenance problems in patients with ADHD or sleep problems
original_authors: Martijn Arns; Ron J. Swatzyna; Jay Gunkelman; Sebastian Olbrich
original_title: Sleep maintenance, spindling excessive beta and impulse control: An RDoC arousal and regulatory systems approach?
replication_authors: Noralie Krepel; Hanneke van Dijk; Alexander T. Sack; Ronald J. Swatzyna; Martijn Arns
replication_title: To spindle or not to spindle: A replication study into spindling excessive beta as a transdiagnostic EEG feature associated with impulse control
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the association between SEB and sleep maintenance problems could not be conceptually replicated.' The closest measure (PSQI sleep disturbances) showed a null result in the opposite direction (F(1,71) = 1.131, p = .291, d = -0.20). The authors note an accurate replication could not be performed because the questionnaire items did not identically match those in the original study.

description: Preoperative Trail Making Test B (TMT-B) performance is associated with the risk of developing postoperative delirium in surgical patients
original_authors: Nathaniel H. Greene; Deborah K. Attix; B. Craig Weldon; Patrick J. Smith; David L. McDonagh; Terri G. Monk
original_title: Measures of executive function and depression identify patients at risk for postoperative delirium
replication_authors: Marinus Fislage; Insa Feinkohl; Friedrich Borchers; Maria Heinrich; Tobias Pischon; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen; Arjen J.C. Slooter; Claudia D. Spies; Georg Winterer; Norman Zacharias
replication_title: Trail making test B in postoperative delirium: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We consider this replication study a success,' finding OR 1.06 (95% CI 1.02–1.09), p=0.001. The sensitivity analysis using Greene et al.'s covariates yielded OR 1.05 (95% CI 1.01–1.09), p=0.02, confirming the association. The BioCog study used a different, larger population across two centres and broader surgery types than Greene et al.'s single-centre, 91%-male, preliminary sample.

description: Preoperative Trail Making Test B (TMT-B) performance is associated with postoperative delirium incidence in older noncardiac surgical patients
original_authors: Heidi Lindroth; Lisa Bratzke; Sara Twadell; Paul Rowley; Janie Kildow; Mara Danner; Lily Turner; Brandon Hernandez; Roger Brown; Robert D. Sanders
original_title: Predicting postoperative delirium severity in older adults: the role of surgical risk and executive function
replication_authors: Marinus Fislage; Insa Feinkohl; Friedrich Borchers; Maria Heinrich; Tobias Pischon; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen; Arjen J.C. Slooter; Claudia D. Spies; Georg Winterer; Norman Zacharias
replication_title: Trail making test B in postoperative delirium: a replication study
explanation: The replication confirmed the core finding that TMT-B performance is associated with postoperative delirium (OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.02–1.09, p=0.001). The authors' Conclusion explicitly states 'this effect replicates the effect found by three prior studies,' counting Lindroth among them. Lindroth's higher AUROC of 0.81 came from a multivariate model including NSQIP-SC as a covariate (not TMT-B alone), and the authors could not test that specific model due to lacking the NSQIP-SC variable. However, the replicated claim is the association between TMT-B and POD, which was confirmed. Reviewed PDF Discussion (p.8) and Conclusion (p.9) to verify authors' own assessment.

description: Preoperative Trail Making Test B (TMT-B) performance (standardised z-score) is independently associated with reported delirium symptoms after controlling for age, sex, comorbidities, depression, frailty, and number of drugs taken
original_authors: Christian Mychajliw; Matthias L. Herrmann; Ulrike Suenkel; Katharina Brand; Anna-Katharina von Thaler; Isabel Wurster; Rezzak Yilmaz; Gerhard W. Eschweiler; Florian G. Metzger
original_title: Impaired executive function and depression as independent risk factors for reported delirium symptoms: an observational cohort study over 8 years
replication_authors: Marinus Fislage; Insa Feinkohl; Friedrich Borchers; Maria Heinrich; Tobias Pischon; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen; Arjen J.C. Slooter; Claudia D. Spies; Georg Winterer; Norman Zacharias
replication_title: Trail making test B in postoperative delirium: a replication study
explanation: The sensitivity analysis using Mychajliw et al.'s covariates (age, sex, GDS, Charlson Comorbidity Index, frailty, sum of drugs) found OR 1.03 per 10-s increment (95% CI 0.999–1.07), p=0.10 — a non-significant result. The authors acknowledge 'we were unable to replicate their results,' noting substantial methodological differences (Mychajliw used retrospective delirium symptom reporting and only 69% of cases were attributed to surgery).

description: Common genetic variants near HLA-DQA2 (rs3916765) are associated with increased risk of cytogenetically normal acute myeloid leukemia
original_authors: Lin, W.; Fordham, S.; Hungate, E.
original_title: Genome-wide association study identifies susceptibility loci for acute myeloid leukemia
replication_authors: Rose Laflamme; Véronique Lisi; Josée Hébert; Guy Sauvageau; Sébastien Lemieux; Vincent-Philippe Lavallée; Guillaume Lettre
replication_title: Replication of a GWAS signal near HLA-DQA2 with AML using a disease-only cohort and external population-based controls
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the association between HLA-DQA2-rs3916765 and CN-AML (G-allele odds ratio [OR], 1.96; P = .0031)', confirming the original GWAS finding in an independent cohort of French Canadian AML patients using a different genotyping platform (low-pass WGS).

description: An evaluative conditioning (EC) procedure pairing own body pictures with smiling faces increases body satisfaction and general self-esteem, especially in women with relatively high body concern
original_authors: Carolien Martijn; Marlies Vanderlinden; Anne Roefs; Jorg Huijding; Anita Jansen
original_title: Increasing body satisfaction of body concerned women through evaluative conditioning using social stimuli
replication_authors: Klaske A. Glashouwer; Irina Masselman; Peter J. de Jong
replication_title: Reducing body dissatisfaction by means of an evaluative conditioning procedure in undergraduate women: A replication study
explanation: The authors conducted an explicit 'exact replication' of the Martijn et al. (2010) study in a well-powered sample (N=129) and found no significant effect of the EC procedure on body satisfaction indices (VAS body satisfaction: Condition × Time F(1,125) = 0.75, p = .39; appearance SSES: F(1,125) = 1.81, p = .18). The conclusion states: 'Our study did not provide evidence for the effectiveness of an EC procedure developed by [Martijn et al.] as a tool to enhance body satisfaction in undergraduate women.'

description: A single 20-minute session of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the left prefrontal cortex immediately after gastric bypass surgery reduces postoperative patient-controlled morphine use by approximately 40%
original_authors: Jeffrey J. Borckardt; Mitchel Weinstein; Scott T. Reeves; F. Andrew Kozel; Ziad Nahas; Arthur R. Smith; T. Karl Byrne; Katherine Morgan; Mark S. George
original_title: Post-operative left prefrontal repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation reduces patient-controlled analgesia use
replication_authors: Borckardt JJ; Reeves ST; Weinstein M.; Smith AR; Shelley N.; Kozel FA; Nahas Z.; Byrne KT; Morgan K.; George MS
replication_title: Significant analgesic effects of one session of postoperative left prefrontal cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This study replicates and extends the findings from the previous study by Borckardt et al. that a single 20-minute postoperative prefrontal rTMS session in gastric bypass surgery patients may significantly reduce patient-administered morphine usage.' The replication found a significant effect of TMS condition on morphine use (P < .01), with real TMS patients using 35% less morphine than sham patients.

description: Quadripulse stimulation with 5 ms inter-pulse intervals (QPS-5) induces facilitation of motor evoked potentials (LTP-like plasticity) in human motor cortex
original_authors: Masashi Hamada; Yasuo Terao; Ritsuko Hanajima; Yuichiro Shirota; Setsu Nakatani-Enomoto; Toshiaki Furubayashi; Hideyuki Matsumoto; Yoshikazu Ugawa
original_title: Bidirectional long-term motor cortical plasticity and metaplasticity induced by quadripulse transcranial magnetic stimulation
replication_authors: Sara Simeoni; Ricci Hannah; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami; John Rothwell; Sara Simeoni; Gian Luigi Gigli; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami
replication_title: Effects of Quadripulse Stimulation on Human Motor Cortex Excitability: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors found a main effect of time for QPS-5 (p = 0.024), indicating facilitation of MEPs compared to baseline, consistent with the original Japanese studies. They conclude 'QPS-5 induced overall facilitation of corticospinal excitability as reported by Ugawa and colleagues.'

description: Quadripulse stimulation with 50 ms inter-pulse intervals (QPS-50) induces suppression of motor evoked potentials (LTD-like plasticity) in human motor cortex
original_authors: Masashi Hamada; Yasuo Terao; Ritsuko Hanajima; Yuichiro Shirota; Setsu Nakatani-Enomoto; Toshiaki Furubayashi; Hideyuki Matsumoto; Yoshikazu Ugawa
original_title: Bidirectional long-term motor cortical plasticity and metaplasticity induced by quadripulse transcranial magnetic stimulation
replication_authors: Sara Simeoni; Ricci Hannah; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami; John Rothwell; Sara Simeoni; Gian Luigi Gigli; Daisuke Sato; Michiyuki Kawakami
replication_title: Effects of Quadripulse Stimulation on Human Motor Cortex Excitability: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors found no significant effect of time for QPS-50 (p = 0.461), indicating no inhibition of MEPs occurred in the Caucasian sample. They note 'there was no significant suppression after QPS-50' and discuss that the inhibitory effect 'was more difficult to reproduce in the present study.'

description: D-cycloserine (NMDA receptor partial agonist) enhances 10-Hz rTMS-induced motor cortex plasticity as measured by motor-evoked potential (MEP) amplitudes in healthy adults
original_authors: Joshua C. Brown; William H. DeVries; Jeffrey E. Korte; Gregory L. Sahlem; Leonardo Bonilha; E. Baron Short; Mark S. George
original_title: NMDA receptor partial agonist, d-cycloserine, enhances 10 Hz rTMS-induced motor plasticity, suggesting long-term potentiation (LTP) as underlying mechanism
replication_authors: Jamie Kweon; Megan Vigne; Rich Jones; Mark S. George; Linda L. Carpenter; Joshua C. Brown
replication_title: A replication study of NMDA receptor agonism sufficiency to enhance 10-Hz rTMS-induced motor cortex plasticity
explanation: The replication found a trend-level but non-significant effect on the primary measure (MEP single-pulse time course: F=2.19, p=.12), while a secondary measure (recruitment curve intercept change) showed significant DCS-enhanced facilitation (p=.04). The authors state the results 'did not reach significance' for the primary measure and explicitly attribute this to insufficient power, while still describing findings as 'consistent with results published previously.'

description: The readiness potential (RP) precedes the conscious intention to act by approximately 350 ms and the actual voluntary movement by approximately 500 ms, implying that neural preparation for voluntary acts begins prior to conscious awareness of the intention
original_authors: Benjamin Libet; Curtis A. Gleason; Elwood W. Wright; Dennis K. Pearl
original_title: Time of conscious intention to act in relation to onset of cerebral activity (readiness-potential): The unconscious initiation of a freely voluntary act
replication_authors: Ceci Verbaarschot; Jason Farquhar; Pim Haselager
replication_title: Lost in time...
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were able to replicate the results found by [Libet et al.]: the RP we measured preceded the intention to act by 544 ms and the button press by 700 ms on average.' The study used a similar paradigm with slight modifications (bilateral button presses instead of right-hand only), and confirmed the core temporal ordering across all analysis methods at the group level.

description: Individual differences in cortico-striatal tract strength (right pre-SMA to right striatum) positively correlate with individual differences in control over speed and accuracy in a perceptual decision making paradigm
original_authors: Birte U. Forstmann; Alfred Anwander; Andreas Schäfer; Jane Neumann; Scott Brown; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Rafal Bogacz; Robert Turner
original_title: Cortico-striatal connections predict control over speed and accuracy in perceptual decision making
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations
explanation: No positive correlation between pre-SMA-to-striatum tract strength and LBA flexibility. Values are the corrected ones from the Keuken et al. 2017 corrigendum, 10.1016/j.cortex.2017.03.007 (DWI post-processing error): n=32, r=-.08, BF01=6.09 (moderate evidence for H0), one-sided p=.67; the original 2015 report had n=31, r=.03, BF01=3.90, p=.431. Conclusion unchanged: failed replication.

description: Real-world social network size (SNS) is positively correlated with grey matter volume in the right amygdala
original_authors: Ryota Kanai; B. Bahrami; R. Roylance; G. Rees
original_title: Online social network size is reflected in human brain structure
replication_authors: Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations
explanation: Boekel et al. 2015 Table 3: r_orig=.26 (n=65), r_rep=.30 (n=33); confirmatory BF01=.57 (anecdotal evidence for H1), exploratory replication BF0r=.27 (moderate evidence for the proponent's hypothesis), one-sided p=.041. The only one of the 17 effects whose p-value the authors say indicates a successful replication, with an effect size similar to the original. Converted from a study-level Kanai 2012 row; the five FBN effects of the same study are FReD's rows (fred:1901-1905).

description: Individual differences in aspects of attention (executive control and alerting) as measured by the Attention Network Test are negatively correlated with cortical thickness in multiple brain regions including anterior cingulate cortex, superior temporal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and superior parietal lobe
original_authors: Lars T. Westlye; Håkon Grydeland; Kristine B. Walhovd; Anders M. Fjell
original_title: Associations between regional cortical thickness and attentional networks as measured by the attention network test
replication_authors: Wouter Boekel; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Luam Belay; Josine Verhagen; Scott Brown; Birte U. Forstmann
replication_title: A purely confirmatory replication study of structural brain-behavior correlations
explanation: All 4 hypothesized effects showed support for the null hypothesis (BF01 ranging from 1.60 to 8.58), and all p-values indicated failed replications. The authors explicitly stated 'all p-values indicate failed replications' for this study.

description: Excitatory high-frequency rTMS applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex increases reward responsiveness as measured by response bias on the probabilistic learning task
original_authors: Hyeon Min Ahn; Sang Eun Kim; Sang Hee Kim
original_title: The effects of high-frequency rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex on reward responsiveness
replication_authors: Hadden LM; Penny H.; Jones AL; Partridge AM; Lancaster TM; Allen C.
replication_title: Pre-frontal stimulation does not reliably increase reward responsiveness
explanation: The authors conclude they 'failed to replicate Ahn et al., (2013) and Duprat et al., (2016)'s key findings that active stimulation would positively modulate reward responsiveness.' For Ahn et al.'s primary interaction (Stimulation × Block), the Bayes Factor was .243 providing evidence towards the null, and the primary 1df test yielded BF = .696 with the mean difference in the opposite direction to that predicted.

description: Negative social judgments (compared to positive judgments) lead to more aggressive behavior in adults using the Social Network Aggression Task (SNAT), where participants can blast loud noises at judging peers

replication_authors: Ilse C. van Wijk; Bianca G. van den Bulk; Saskia Euser; Marian J. Bakermans-Kranenburg; Marinus H. van IJzendoorn; Renske Huffmeijer
replication_title: Social judgments, frontal asymmetry, and aggressive behavior in young children: A replication study using EEG
explanation: The paper has 'replication study' in its title and the Discussion explicitly states: 'By replicating these behavioral results in young children, we have shown that the SNAT-EC is an age appropriate task to examine the behavioral response to social judgments in early childhood.' The SNAT-EC is an adapted version of the SNAT from Achterberg et al. (2016), modified for 4-6 year olds (cuddly animal rejection instead of personal rejection, button press destroying balloons instead of noise blast). The behavioral effect was significant in all three independent samples (pilot: b=794.02, p<.01; test 1: b=802.28, p<.01; test 2: b=828.78, p<.01) with a large meta-analytic combined effect size (r=.42, 95% CI: .29-.54, p<.01). The Discussion notes smaller effect sizes in early childhood (omega-squared 0.12-0.15) vs adults (omega-squared=0.41; Achterberg et al. 2016), but the effect clearly replicates. PDF reviewed for Discussion, Results, and meta-analysis table.

The Discussion states this study found 'a comparable effect of social judgment on aggressive behavior in adults (Achterberg et al., 2016) and older children (Achterberg et al., 2017)' and that it is 'replicating these behavioral results in young children.' The effect was significant in all three samples with a large meta-analytic combined effect size (r=.42, 95% CI: .29-.54, p<.01). The Discussion notes smaller effect sizes in early childhood (omega-squared 0.12-0.15) vs 7-10 year olds (omega-squared 0.30-0.46; Achterberg et al. 2017). PDF reviewed for Discussion, Results, and meta-analysis table.

Although the HACE1 polymorphisms from the same Diskin et al. 2012 paper were not confirmed, this entry focuses specifically on the LIN28B finding, which was clearly replicated.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Limitations/Conclusion section: 'we successfully replicated several associations between HLA alleles and immune responses after two doses of measles vaccine.' Key antibody associations (B*3503, DQA1*0201, DQB1*0303, DQB1*0602, DRB1*0701, and B7 supertype) showed consistent findings across both cohorts, and statistically more associations replicated than expected by chance (p=0.0001).

description: HLA class I and class II alleles (including B*0801, DRB1*0301, C*0802, DPA1*0202, and DRB1*1303) are associated with measles vaccine-induced cellular immune responses (IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-10 cytokine secretion) in schoolchildren
original_authors: Ovsyannikova, Irina G.; Jacobson, Robert M.; Ryan, Jill E.; Vierkant, Robert A.; Pankratz, V. Shane; Jacobsen, Steven J.; Poland, Gregory A.

replication_authors: Ovsyannikova IG; Pankratz VS; Vierkant RA; Jacobson RM; Poland GA
replication_title: Consistency of HLA associations between two independent measles vaccine cohorts: A replication study
explanation: The PDF confirms consistent directional associations across both cohorts for all key cytokine-HLA allele pairs: B*0801 with lower IFN-γ (cohort 1 p=0.04, cohort 2 p=0.03), DRB1*0301 with lower IFN-γ (p=0.05, p=0.08), C*0802 with higher IL-2 (p=0.06, p=0.06), DPA1*0202 with lower IL-2 (p=0.09, p=0.06), and DRB1*1301 with IL-10 variation (p=0.06, p=0.04). The Discussion states: 'Consistent associations were found between the B*0801 and DRB1*0301 alleles and lower production of a major Th1-like cytokine-IFN-γ.' The Conclusion confirms: 'the association of B*0801, C*0802, DRB1 (*0301, *1303), and DPA1*0202 alleles with MV-specific cytokine levels was found in both cohorts.' Despite different cell culture conditions across cohorts, directional consistency and suggestive/significant p-values support the authors' claim of successful replication.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the protective association with RA (OR~0.5) was not confirmed (combined OR = 0.87[0.67-1.14]).' The paper is subtitled a 'genetic replication study' and used four independent cohorts of RA cases and controls, finding no compelling evidence for either a risk or protective association.

replication_authors: Roman Kessler; Kristin M. Rusch; Kim C. Wende; Verena Schuster; Andreas Jansen
replication_title: Revisiting the effective connectivity within the distributed cortical network for face perception
explanation: Using four fMRI datasets and contemporary DCM methods, the authors found a fully interconnected model with significant backward and lateral connections — directly contradicting the original's feed-forward-only model. The Discussion explicitly states: 'While we successfully reproduced some aspects of the original model, the revised model was distinct in terms of some other major aspects,' and the Conclusion describes 'a revised model more complex than the originally proposed model.'

description: The medial temporal lobe shows increased activation for true old stimuli (both hits and misses) compared to new stimuli, regardless of the participant's subjective experience or behavioral response

replication_authors: Van J.; Nielsen SE; Kirwan CB
replication_title: Evidence for a single rather than a triple dissociation in the medial temporal lobe: An fMRI recognition memory replication study
explanation: The authors replicated a significant main effect of true oldness but found this activation was driven primarily by correct 'old' decisions (hits) rather than all true old stimuli, contradicting the original claim that MTL distinguishes old from new independently of subjective experience. They state: 'in our sample the MTL response depended on both the true oldness of the stimulus and the participants' reported conscious experience and was driven by correct 'old' decisions, i.e., hits.'

replication_authors: Van J.; Nielsen SE; Kirwan CB
replication_title: Evidence for a single rather than a triple dissociation in the medial temporal lobe: An fMRI recognition memory replication study
explanation: The replication found recollection and familiarity signals consistent with the original, but found no novelty signal in any a priori ROI or even at liberal voxel-wise thresholds. The authors explicitly state: 'the present study fails to replicate a triple dissociation in the MTL' and 'we conclusively fail to replicate a triple dissociation in the MTL.'

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusions: 'The current study serves as a replication and extension of our previous study, observing that multiple diffusion MRI metrics...could reliably classify between incarcerated individuals with and without self-reported history of chronic TBI.' FA achieved an AUC of 82.50% in the replication (vs. 75.50% in the original), confirming the classification approach works in the new sample.

explanation: The authors describe their second family study as 'a replication study of familial OCD using similar methodology in an independent sample' of their first study. The replication found 'less robust support for familial OCD' — no significant differences in rates of definite OCD were found at any diagnostic threshold without proband informant data, and only partial evidence emerged with broader diagnostic thresholds and proband informant data included. The authors conclude 'our own inconsistent results suggest that OCD may be heterogeneous with regard to familial transmission.'

replication_authors: Zimmerman M.; Chelminski I.
replication_title: A scale to screen for DSM-IV Axis I disorders in psychiatric out-patients: performance of the Psychiatric Diagnostic Screening Questionnaire
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the results were highly consistent with the original report.' AUCs were nearly identical (mean 0.83 vs. 0.85), sensitivity was comparable (85% vs. 88%), and NPV was identical (97% vs. 97%), with recommended cut-off scores remaining the same for 9 of 13 subscales.

replication_title: Genetic and environmental influences on gambling disorder liability: a replication and combined analysis of two twin studies
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The findings of a previous Australian twin study [34] were replicated in an independent Australian twin cohort.' Heritability estimates in the replication (60%) were comparable to the original (49%), with no significant shared environmental contributions or sex differences in either study, and the two cohorts did not statistically differ in parameter estimates.

The replication used the same variables (DSM-5 symptoms and CRP) but a different dataset (NESDA, N=2321) and network analysis methodology rather than the original's approach.
