description: Higher levels of Vg% (percent of vague responses) on the Rorschach R-PAS are inversely associated with average fixation durations, reflecting shallower and more superficial cognitive processing strategies
original_authors: Francesca Ales; Luciano Giromini; Alessandro Zennaro
original_title: Complexity and cognitive engagement in the rorschach task: An eye-tracking study
replication_authors: Barry Dauphin; Harold H. Greene; Mindee Juve; Mellisa Boyle; Ellen Day; Emily Bemis
replication_title: Expanding the Interpretive Potential of Eye Tracking for the Rorschach: Replication and Extension of the Findings of Ales et al. (2020)
explanation: The authors report 'Vg% was also significantly correlated with Fixation Duration in [1], so their finding on this variable was replicated in the present study of approximately the same magnitude (r = -0.266 in Ales et al., 2020 and r = -0.259 in the present study).' The Discussion confirms the replication and extension of this finding.

description: Pornography consumption predicts heterosexual U.S. adult men's support for same-sex marriage, with this association moderated by education (stronger among less educated men), via sexual liberalism scripts
original_authors: Wright, Paul; Randall, Ashley
original_title: Pornography consumption, education, and support for same-sex marriage among adult U.S. males
replication_authors: Paul J. Wright; Robert S. Tokunaga
replication_title: U.S. Adults’ Attitudes toward Gay Individuals’ Civil Liberties, Moral Judgments of Homosexuality, Support for Same-sex Marriage, and Pornography Consumption, Revisited
explanation: The main effect of pornography on same-sex marriage support was successfully replicated (same direction, significant, CI contained original point-estimate), but the interaction with education was not replicated (b = .01, p = .76 vs. original b = -.17, p < .05). The authors describe the results as mixed, with some effects replicated and others not.

description: Pornography consumption predicts heterosexual U.S. adults' attitudes toward homosexuality (composite index of moral acceptance and same-sex marriage support), with the association moderated by sex and ethnicity
original_authors: Wright, Paul; Bae, Soyoung
original_title: Pornography consumption and attitudes toward homosexuality: A national longitudinal study
replication_authors: Paul J. Wright; Robert S. Tokunaga
replication_title: U.S. Adults’ Attitudes toward Gay Individuals’ Civil Liberties, Moral Judgments of Homosexuality, Support for Same-sex Marriage, and Pornography Consumption, Revisited
explanation: The main effect of pornography on homosexuality attitudes was replicated (deemed replicated because the 95% CI contained the original point-estimate and the replication result was significant), but the interaction effects of pornography with sex and ethnicity were not replicated (not significant, original point-estimates fell outside 95% CIs). The authors describe these results as partially replicated.

description: Pornography use directly and indirectly (through nontraditional sexual attitudes) predicts heterosexual U.S. adults' moral acceptance of homosexuality, support for same-sex marriage, and positive attitudes toward civil liberties for gay persons
original_authors: Wright, Paul; Tokunaga, Robert; Bae, Soyoung
original_title: Pornography consumption and U.S. adults' attitudes toward gay individuals' civil liberties, moral judgments of homosexuality, and support for same-sex marriage: Mediating and moderating factors
replication_authors: Paul J. Wright; Robert S. Tokunaga
replication_title: U.S. Adults’ Attitudes toward Gay Individuals’ Civil Liberties, Moral Judgments of Homosexuality, Support for Same-sex Marriage, and Pornography Consumption, Revisited
explanation: Direct and indirect effects of pornography on moral acceptance of homosexuality and same-sex marriage support were replicated (significant effects with CIs containing original point-estimates), but direct and indirect effects on civil liberties for gay persons were not replicated (non-significant). The authors conclude: 'pornography use was neither directly nor indirectly related to attitudes toward civil liberties for gay persons in the more recent data.'

description: Exposing participants to an economic justice manipulation (being told that a master's degree will not pay off financially) increases secondary victimization (derogation) of innocent victims
original_authors: Isabel Correia; Jorge Vala
original_title: When will a victim be secondarily victimized? The effect of observer's belief in a just world, victim's innocence and persistence of suffering
replication_authors: Sean M. Laurent; Jun-Yeob Kim
replication_title: Do Injustice and Mortality Salience Impact Secondary Victimization Through the Need to Believe in a Just World?
explanation: Authors explicitly state: 'Experiment 1 was a conceptual, but relatively close, replication of the experimental conditions in [10] (Study 2)... each of the hypothesized effects was very small, and for some, the direction of findings was opposite from our prediction.' Effect sizes on all secondary victimization measures were near zero (d = 0.01 to 0.11).

description: Innocent assault victims are blamed more for their victimization when the perpetrator is not caught compared to when the perpetrator is caught and will be punished
original_authors: Annemarie Loseman; Kees van den Bos
original_title: A self-regulation hypothesis of coping with an unjust world: Ego-depletion and self-affirmation as underlying aspects of blaming of innocent victims
replication_authors: Sean M. Laurent; Jun-Yeob Kim
replication_title: Do Injustice and Mortality Salience Impact Secondary Victimization Through the Need to Believe in a Just World?
explanation: Authors state that 'effects were again very small (respectively, ds = 0.09, 0.16, and 0.04) and in mixed directions,' compared to the original d = 0.72. They conclude that 'the effects of exposure to a just-world manipulation were mixed, depending on measure' and that they 'did not consistently emerge, particularly compared with the findings on which the experiment was based.'

description: Mortality salience induction leads participants to engage in secondary victimization (blaming) of innocent victims compared to an anxiety control condition
original_authors: Gilad Hirschberger
original_title: Terror management and attributions of blame to innocent victims: Reconciling compassionate and defensive responses
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Sean M. Laurent; Jun-Yeob Kim
replication_title: Do Injustice and Mortality Salience Impact Secondary Victimization Through the Need to Believe in a Just World?
explanation: Authors report 'effects of the salience condition on variables measuring SV were small (respectively for victim blaming, perceived fairness of the outcome, and the suffering of the victim, ds = 0.09, 0.09, and 0.24)' and state that 'measures of secondary victimization also failed to reveal any substantive effects, with effect sizes much smaller than those previously reported, regardless of their direction,' compared to d = 0.40–1.02 in the original.

description: Savoring (self-perceived ability to experience positive experiences) moderates the association between cannabis use frequency and cannabis-associated consequences, such that higher savoring weakens the link between more frequent use and more problems
original_authors: Rachel R. Luba; Mitch Earleywine; Benedict Melse; Elana B. Gordis
original_title: Savoring moderates the link between marijuana use and marijuana problems
replication_authors: Catherine D. Trinh; Melissa R. Schick; Blaine Lynch-Gadaleta; Anika Martz; Tessa Nalven; Nichea S. Spillane
replication_title: The Role of Savoring in Young Adult Cannabis Use and Associated Consequences: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'results from the present study did not replicate previous findings [22][24].' The interaction between cannabis use frequency and savoring on cannabis-associated consequences was not significant (b = 0.0004, p = .91), failing to replicate the moderating effect found in Luba et al. (2020). Reviewer note: the citation_sentence uses bracketed reference numbers [22] and [24], which correspond to Luba et al. (2020) and Mian et al. (2021) respectively in the reference list. The PDF Introduction (p. 3) explicitly names these authors: 'the goal of the present study was to replicate the work of Luba et al. (2020) and Mian et al. (2021).' No citation mismatch exists.

description: Savoring is negatively associated with cannabis-associated consequences even after controlling for gender, accounting for significant variance (β = -.30) in cannabis-associated consequences
original_authors: Maha N. Mian; Brianna R. Altman; Luna F. Ueno; Mitch Earleywine
original_title: Confirming savoring's link to fewer cannabis problems
replication_authors: Catherine D. Trinh; Melissa R. Schick; Blaine Lynch-Gadaleta; Anika Martz; Tessa Nalven; Nichea S. Spillane
replication_title: The Role of Savoring in Young Adult Cannabis Use and Associated Consequences: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'results from the present study did not replicate previous findings [22][24],' grouping both Luba et al. (2020) and Mian et al. (2021) as non-replicated. The key finding from Mian et al. (2021) was that savoring accounted for significant variance (β = -.30) in cannabis-associated consequences after controlling for gender. In the present study, after controlling for gender and cannabis use frequency, savoring was not significantly associated with consequences (b = -0.05, p = .16). The authors note: 'This finding contrasts with previous research which found that savoring accounted for a significant portion of the variance (β = -.30) in cannabis-associated consequences, even after controlling for gender [24].' While the bivariate correlation between savoring and consequences was replicated (r = -.20, p < .05), this does not constitute replication of the core finding (savoring's unique predictive value after controlling for covariates). Result changed from 'inconclusive' to 'failure' and confidence upgraded from 'medium' to 'high' based on the authors' explicit non-replication statement. Reviewer note on citation: the bracketed [24] in the citation_sentence corresponds to Mian et al. (2021) in the reference list; the PDF Introduction names them explicitly.

description: Figural reasoning and visualization are unique positive predictors of computational thinking in secondary school students, whereas arithmetic is not significantly related to CT, and boys outperform girls on the CT test
original_authors: Román-González, Marcos; Pérez-González, Juan-Carlos; Jiménez-Fernández, Carmen
original_title: Which cognitive abilities underlie computational thinking? criterion validity of the computational thinking test
replication_authors: Sabrina Finke; Ferenc Kemény; Markus Sommer; Vesna Krnjic; Martin Arendasy; Wolfgang Slany; Karin Landerl
replication_title: Unravelling the numerical and spatial underpinnings of computational thinking: a pre-registered replication study
explanation: The replication successfully reproduced the positive associations between CT and figural reasoning (r = .47) and visualization (r = .48), as well as the gender effect (d = .44, p = .014). However, the null finding for arithmetic did not replicate: contrary to the original, the replication found a small but significant positive association between mental arithmetic and CT (r = .33, p < .01). The authors note: 'our results support the view that CT is underpinned by reasoning... and spatial abilities... However, in contrast to the original study, we also found a significant association between CT and mental arithmetic.'

description: No significant suppression-induced forgetting (SIF) effect is observed when the Think/No-Think paradigm is implemented in an online setting, replicating Wiechert et al.'s (2023) null finding for online TNT implementations
original_authors: Sera Wiechert; Leonie Loewy; Ineke Wessel; Jonathan M. Fawcett; Gershon Ben-Shakhar; Yoni Pertzov; Bruno Verschuere
original_title: Suppression-induced forgetting: a pre-registered replication of the think/no-think paradigm
replication_authors: Ineke Wessel; Robyn Lehmann; Sera Wiechert
replication_title: Two replications of Wiechert et al.'s (2023) online Think/No-Think study in undergraduate students
explanation: Reviewer verified: The thesis by Kuipers (2024) explicitly replicates Wiechert et al. (2023), reference [22] in the paper. Wiechert et al. found no SIF effect in their online TNT implementation (N=150). This thesis's online condition (N=41) likewise found no SIF effect: t(40) = -0.77, p = .222, d = -0.12, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.04]. The Discussion states unambiguously: 'This aligns the results of Wiechert et al.'s (2023) which also did not [find] a significant result in the online implementation of the TNT-task.' Result classified as 'success' because the replication target is Wiechert et al.'s null finding for the online condition, and this thesis obtains the same null result. The thesis additionally tested an in-person condition (N=49, where SIF was significant, d = -0.45, p = .001), but this extends beyond the Wiechert replication scope. Replication type is 'close extension' because the thesis used the same TNT paradigm and materials but with a Dutch student sample rather than English-speaking participants, and added the in-person condition. The citation mismatch flag was a false alarm: the body.md uses bracketed reference numbers ([22]) rather than author-year format, but [22] correctly maps to Wiechert et al. (2023) in references.json. Confidence upgraded to high based on the explicit alignment statement in the Discussion and unambiguous statistical results.

description: Performing eye movements while recalling an aversive autobiographical memory reduces the experienced vividness and emotionality of that memory compared to recall only (no dual task)
original_authors: Kevin van Schie; Suzanne C. van Veen; Iris M. Engelhard; Irene Klugkist; Marcel A. van den Hout
original_title: Blurring emotional memories using eye movements: Individual differences and speed of eye movements
replication_authors: Meckling HI; Nauta MH; van Hout WJPJ; Wessel I.
replication_title: The effects of eye movements on the content and characteristics of unpleasant autobiographical memories: an extended replication study
explanation: Experiment 1 (N=97) partially replicated the target effect: vividness was significantly reduced in the EM condition versus recall-only (F(1,95)=6.65, p=.01, partial η²=.065), but the emotionality reduction did not reach significance (F(1,95)=1.16, p=.28, partial η²=.01). The authors note the sample may have lacked power to detect the smaller emotionality effect (sensitivity d=0.72), and describe the emotionality result as inconclusive.

description: Performing eye movements while recalling an aversive autobiographical memory reduces the experienced vividness and emotionality of that memory compared to recall only (no dual task)
original_authors: Kevin van Schie; Suzanne C. van Veen; Iris M. Engelhard; Irene Klugkist; Marcel A. van den Hout
original_title: Blurring emotional memories using eye movements: Individual differences and speed of eye movements
replication_authors: Meckling HI; Nauta MH; van Hout WJPJ; Wessel I.
replication_title: The effects of eye movements on the content and characteristics of unpleasant autobiographical memories: an extended replication study
explanation: Experiment 2 (N=250, pre-registered) successfully replicated both target effects: EM produced a significantly larger reduction in vividness (F(1,249)=15.77, p<.001, partial η²=.06) and emotionality (F(1,249)=9.24, p=.003, partial η²=.04) compared to recall only. The authors conclude: 'eye movements reduced the vividness and emotionality of the most aversive image of participants' unpleasant autobiographical memories.'

description: Pre-military, military, and post-military trauma exposures are indirectly associated with eating disorder symptoms via PTSD symptoms among men and via shape/weight overvaluation among women in a veteran sample
original_authors: Rachel L. Zelkowitz; Megan E. Sienkiewicz; Dawne S. Vogt; Brian N. Smith; Karen S. Mitchell
original_title: Gender differences in direct and indirect associations of trauma types with disordered eating in a national U.S. veteran sample
replication_authors: Kelsey N. Serier; Whitney S. Livingston; Rachel L. Zelkowitz; Shannon Kehle-Forbes; Brian N. Smith; Karen S. Mitchell
replication_title: Examining posttraumatic cognitions as a pathway linking trauma exposure and eating disorder symptoms in veteran men and women: A replication and extension study
explanation: The replication was partial: the shape/weight overvaluation pathway was replicated for women (consistent with Zelkowitz et al. 2023), but the PTSD pathway for men did not replicate. The authors note: 'Among men, we only found support for shape/weight overvaluation as a potential mechanism, whereas Zelkowitz and colleagues (2023) identified both PTSD and shape/weight overvaluation as pathways connecting trauma with ED symptoms.'

description: Playing an online fake news role-playing game (exposing participants to deception techniques used by fake news producers) significantly reduces participants' susceptibility to fake news (broad-spectrum inoculation effect)
original_authors: Jon Roozenbeek; Sander van der Linden
original_title: The fake news game: Actively inoculating against the risk of misinformation
replication_authors: Catherine Mei Ling Wong; Yuanyuan Wu
replication_title: Limits to inoculating against the risk of fake news: a replication study in Singapore during COVID-19
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to replicate the positive inoculation effects against fake news in this study' (F(1, 112) = 0.09, p = 0.76), and in their conclusion: 'our failure to replicate the inoculation effects of Roosenbeek and van der Linden's original study'. Neither narrow-spectrum nor broad-spectrum effects were found.

description: Listening to a verbal description of a traumatic event (field perspective audio report) induces a significant number of intrusive images in the following week
original_authors: Julie Krans; Gérard Näring; Emily A. Holmes; Eni S. Becker
original_title: Intrusive images from listening to a traumatic verbal report
replication_authors: Judith K. Daniels; Jonathan Thielemann; Charmaine Borg
replication_title: Can Listening to a Verbal Trauma Report Induce Intrusions? – Replication of a Randomized Trial
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Summary: 'We successfully replicated the finding that intrusions can develop from a purely verbal description of a traumatic event.' The verbal report induced intrusions in participants as measured by the diary, the intrusion provocation task, and the IES-R.

description: Engaging in a visuospatial interference task (modeling clay objects) concurrently while listening to a verbal trauma report results in significantly fewer intrusions in the subsequent week compared to a control group with no concurrent task
original_authors: Julie Krans; Gérard Näring; Emily A. Holmes; Eni S. Becker
original_title: Intrusive images from listening to a traumatic verbal report
replication_authors: Judith K. Daniels; Jonathan Thielemann; Charmaine Borg
replication_title: Can Listening to a Verbal Trauma Report Induce Intrusions? – Replication of a Randomized Trial
explanation: The authors report only partially replicating this effect: 'we were only partially able to replicate the effect of the visuospatial interference task.' The primary diary measure showed significantly fewer intrusions in the experimental group (partial eta-squared = .05, small effect), but the IES-R intrusion subscale showed no significant difference between groups, and the IPT showed significantly *more* intrusions in the experimental group — contradicting the original finding.

description: Word class effect in the picture-word interference paradigm is modulated by naming context: naming latencies are slower for noun distractors than adverb distractors only in sentence frame naming, with no word class effect in bare noun naming (null result in bare noun condition supporting a lexical-syntactic origin of the effect)
original_authors: Thomas Pechmann; Dieter Zerbst
original_title: The activation of word class information during speech production
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Niels Janssen; Alissa Melinger; Bradford Z. Mahon; Matthew Finkbeiner; Alfonso Caramazza
replication_title: The word class effect in the picture–word interference paradigm
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our failure to replicate the null result in the bare noun naming condition confirms the unreliability of this effect reported by [Pechmann & Zerbst].' While the sentence frame word class effect did replicate, the critical null result in the bare noun naming condition — which was the key evidence supporting a lexical-syntactic interpretation — did not replicate, and the authors frame this as a Type II error in the original study.

description: Recognition memory performance for stimuli associated with rewards follows adaptive scaling: memory is better for contextually higher reward outcomes than lower outcomes, independently of absolute reward value
original_authors: Nico Bunzeck; Peter Dayan; Raymond J. Dolan; Emrah Duzel
original_title: A common mechanism for adaptive scaling of reward and novelty
replication_authors: Alice Mason; Casimir Ludwig; Simon Farrell
replication_title: Adaptive scaling of reward in episodic memory: a replication study
explanation: The replication found a statistically significant effect of reward outcome on memory but in the opposite direction: lower outcomes led to better memory than higher outcomes (t(39) = 3.08, p = .004). The authors explicitly state: 'Our results indicate that lower outcomes lead to better memory performance than higher outcomes. This pattern is the opposite of the findings in the original study.'

description: Providing choice within a cluster of water and energy conservation behavioral recommendations reduces freedom threat and psychological reactance, while including a high descriptive norm increases perceived descriptive norm and behavioral intention without elevating reactance
original_authors: Tobias Reynolds-Tylus; Andrea Martinez Gonzalez; Brian L. Quick
original_title: The role of choice clustering and descriptive norms in attenuating psychological reactance to water and energy conservation messages
replication_authors: Andrea Martinez Gonzalez; Tobias Reynolds-Tylus; Sam R. Wilson
replication_title: The Role of Choice and Descriptive Norms in Attenuating Reactance to BPA Risk Messages: A Conceptual Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we conceptually replicated previous work by Reynolds-Tylus and colleagues (2019) in a novel context,' and in the Conclusion: 'These results conceptually replicated previous work by Reynolds-Tylus and colleagues (2019).' All five hypotheses were confirmed, showing consistent patterns with the original study — choice reduced freedom threat and reactance, and a high descriptive norm increased perceived descriptive norm and behavioral intention without elevating reactance.

description: School districts randomized to receive recommendation lists identifying the most instructionally effective and experienced teachers recruit more effective and experienced clinical mentors, and pre-service teachers assigned to those mentors report feeling significantly more ready to teach at the end of their clinical placements
original_authors: Matthew Ronfeldt; Emanuele Bardelli; Matthew Truwit; Hannah Mullman; Kevin Schaaf; Julie C. Baker
original_title: Improving preservice teachers' feelings of preparedness to teach through recruitment of instructionally effective and experienced cooperating teachers: A randomized experiment
replication_authors: Matthew Ronfeldt; Emanuele Bardelli; Matthew Truwit; Kevin Schaaf; Julie Baker
replication_title: Mentors Matter Recruitment Replication & Extension: Investigating Effects Across Implementation Years
replication_journal: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication: 'the replication study is a direct experimental replication with the goal of assessing estimate stability over similar re-implementation conditions.' The replication successfully reproduced the core finding that recommendation lists produced large contrasts in CM instructional effectiveness (d=0.654 for observation ratings, p<.001) and experience (d=0.645, p<.001), consistent with Cohort 1 results. The replication also extended outcomes beyond the original's self-report measures to include clinical assessment scores, which were significantly higher for treatment PSTs.

description: School districts randomized to receive recommendation lists identifying the most instructionally effective and experienced teachers recruit more effective and experienced clinical mentors, and pre-service teachers assigned to those mentors report feeling significantly more ready to teach at the end of their clinical placements
original_authors: Matthew Ronfeldt; Emanuele Bardelli; Matthew Truwit; Hannah Mullman; Kevin Schaaf; Julie C. Baker
original_title: Improving preservice teachers' feelings of preparedness to teach through recruitment of instructionally effective and experienced cooperating teachers: A randomized experiment
replication_authors: Matthew Ronfeldt; Emanuele Bardelli; Matthew Truwit; Kevin Schaaf; Julie Baker
replication_title: Mentors Matter Recruitment Replication & Extension: Investigating Effects Across Implementation Years
replication_journal: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
explanation: The extension study used an interrupted time series (quasi-experimental) design with three new educator preparation programs under minimal research oversight — a broader generalization test than the original RCT. It successfully found that receiving recommendation lists significantly increased CM observation ratings by 0.226 standard deviations (p<.01) compared to prior years, consistent with the original experiment's findings. The authors conclude the initiative 'has promise across various types of program contexts and with less support from research and policy partners.'

description: Optimized 10-item (PANSS10) and 20-item (PANSS20) short forms of the PANSS show strong reliability, criterion validity, treatment sensitivity, and calibration compared with the full 30-item PANSS for pediatric schizophrenia trials
original_authors: Robert L. Findling; Eric A. Youngstrom; Jon M. McClellan; Jean A. Frazier; Linmarie Sikich; David Gordon Daniel; Joan Busner
original_title: An optimized version of the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale (PANSS) for pediatric trials
original_journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
replication_authors: Joshua A. Langfus; Eric A. Youngstrom; David Daniel; Joan Busner; Robert L. Findling
replication_title: Extension and Further Replication of the Reliability, Criterion Validity, and Treatment Sensitivity of the PANSS10 and PANSS20 for Pediatric Trials
replication_journal: Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychopharmacology
explanation: The paper explicitly states it is replicating findings from the original development study [4] using data from an independent clinical trial: 'Overall, these results support three previous studies showing that the PANSS10 and PANSS20 compare favorably to the 30-item PANSS in terms of content coverage, reliability, validity, and calibration.' The Discussion confirms: 'These independent replications have consistently shown that the optimized PANSS forms demonstrate good reliability and validity and are well calibrated compared with the full-length PANSS.'

description: Marriages beginning with online dating (vs. offline) are less satisfying and less stable, mediated by reduced network support from friends and family
original_authors: Liesel L. Sharabi; Elizabeth Dorrance-Hall
original_title: The online dating effect: Where a couple meets predicts the quality of their marriage
replication_authors: Junwen M. Hu; Rui Zhu; Yue Zhang
replication_title: Does Online Dating Make Relationships More Successful? Replication and Extension of a Previous Study
explanation: The authors found a marginally significant negative association between online dating and marital relationship success (p = 0.065), leading them to conclude they 'largely confirmed' the original finding, but the result did not reach conventional significance thresholds. As they state: 'we largely confirmed Sharabi and Dorrance-Hall's finding on the potentially negative impact of online dating on marital relationships... though the association merely approached marginal significance (p = 0.065).'

description: Perceived uncontrollable mortality risk (PUMR) negatively predicts health effort, and mediates the positive relationship between subjective socioeconomic position and health effort (approximately 90% of the total effect mediated by PUMR)
original_authors: Gillian V. Pepper; Daniel Nettle
original_title: Perceived extrinsic mortality risk and reported effort in looking after health
replication_authors: Richard Brown; Gillian Pepper
replication_title: The Relationship Between Perceived Uncontrollable Mortality Risk and Health Effort: Replication, Secondary Analysis, and Mini Meta-analysis
explanation: The authors explicitly declare a successful replication: 'this result provides a successful replication of Pepper and Nettle [17].' PUMR negatively predicted health effort (β = -0.23, p < .001) and mediated 24% of the effect of subjective socioeconomic position, consistent with the original direction but with weaker effect sizes than the original study's ~90% mediation.

description: The Mindfulness-Based Social Work and Self-Care (MBSWSC) programme delivered by two facilitators significantly improves mindfulness, attention regulation, non-attachment, non-aversion, acceptance, and self-compassion in social workers
original_authors: Alan Maddock; Karen McGuigan; Pearse McCusker
original_title: A randomised trial of mindfulness-based social work and self-care with social workers
replication_authors: Alan Maddock; Karen McGuigan; Pearse McCusker
replication_title: Mindfulness-Based Social Work and Self-Care with Social Work Professionals: Replication and Expansion of a Randomised Controlled Trial
replication_journal: The British Journal of Social Work
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our results confirm the effect of the MBSWSC programme on mindfulness, attention regulation, nonattachment, non-aversion, acceptance and self-compassion when delivered by a single rather than two facilitators as the changes found in this study are in line with Maddock et al. (2023, 2024a, b).' The Conclusion also states: 'This mixed methods paper replicates previous research which highlighted the positive effects that engagement with the MBSWSC programme has on the development of mindfulness, attention regulation skills, non-attachment, non-aversion, acceptance and self-compassion.' The original study (Maddock et al., 2023) was the first RCT of the MBSWSC programme; the current paper tests a single-facilitator delivery model (n=27) against the prior two-facilitator results (combined n=121 across two RCTs).

description: Adults rate a child undergoing a medical procedure as experiencing more pain when the child is described as a boy compared to a girl, despite identical clinical circumstances and identical pain behavior across conditions
original_authors: Lindsey L. Cohen; Jean Cobb; Sarah R. Martin
original_title: Gender biases in adult ratings of pediatric pain
replication_authors: Brian D. Earp; Joshua T. Monrad; Marianne LaFrance; John A. Bargh; Lindsey L. Cohen; Jennifer A. Richeson
replication_title: Featured Article: Gender Bias in Pediatric Pain Assessment
explanation: The authors conducted a pre-registered direct replication of Cohen et al. (2014) and found the same directional effect: 'the Boy was rated as experiencing more pain than the Girl.' In the General Discussion they state: 'We therefore replicated the findings of [9], while providing a plausible explanation for their results.' The effect was smaller (d=.21 vs d=.31) and only significant one-tailed (p=.043), but the authors considered this a successful replication given a larger and more demographically diverse sample.

description: Groups that allowed members to reward cooperators and punish defectors (sanctioning institutions) outgrow and outperform groups without a peer-sanctioning institution in a public goods game with voluntary institutional choice
original_authors: Özgür Gürerk; Bernd Irlenbusch; Bettina Rockenbach
original_title: The competitive advantage of sanctioning institutions
replication_authors: Sergio Lo Iacono; Wojtek Przepiorka; Vincent Buskens; Rense Corten; Marcel van Assen; Arnout van de Rijt
replication_title: The competitive advantage of sanctioning institutions revisited: A multilab replication
explanation: The authors conducted an exact multilab replication across 7 labs and conclude: 'This exact multilab replication study shows that the emergence and persistence of peer-sanctioning institutions in experimental public goods settings is a robust phenomenon.' All three preregistered replication criteria were jointly met in 5 of 7 labs, with the remaining 2 labs showing weaker but still pro-sanctioning results.

description: Greater left amygdala activation when viewing ambiguous vs clear threat-gaze pairs (direct fear and averted anger vs averted fear and direct anger) using sustained (2s) presentations of facial expressions
original_authors: Reginald B. Adams; Heather L. Gordon; Abigail A. Baird; Nalini Ambady; Robert E. Kleck
original_title: Effects of gaze on amygdala sensitivity to anger and fear faces
replication_authors: Reginald B. Adams; Robert G. Franklin; Kestutis Kveraga; Nalini Ambady; Robert E. Kleck; Paul J. Whalen; Nouchine Hadjikhani; Anthony J. Nelson
replication_title: Amygdala responses to avertedvsdirect gaze fear vary as a function of presentation speed
explanation: Study 1 used 1s sustained presentations of fear faces and found greater left amygdala activation to direct vs averted gaze fear, which the authors explicitly describe as 'replicating Adams et al. (2003); the original pattern of findings.' The discussion confirms: 'Study 1 revealed greater left amygdala activation to direct vs averted fear using 1 s presentation durations, replicating Adams et al.'s (2003) original pattern of findings.'

description: Greater amygdala activation in response to averted vs direct gaze fear faces when stimuli are presented rapidly (300 ms), reflecting a reflexive threat response to congruent cues
original_authors: Nouchine Hadjikhani; Rick Hoge; Josh Snyder; Beatrice de Gelder
original_title: Pointing with the eyes: the role of gaze in communicating danger
replication_authors: Reginald B. Adams; Robert G. Franklin; Kestutis Kveraga; Nalini Ambady; Robert E. Kleck; Paul J. Whalen; Nouchine Hadjikhani; Anthony J. Nelson
replication_title: Amygdala responses to avertedvsdirect gaze fear vary as a function of presentation speed
explanation: Study 2 used the same 300 ms stimulus presentation paradigm as Hadjikhani et al. (2008) (an 'identical design varying only in stimulus presentation duration') and found greater amygdala response to averted vs direct gaze fear in bilateral dorsal amygdalae/SI. The Discussion confirms: 'Using these same stimuli, we also replicated the reverse pattern of activation in Study 2 using 300 ms stimulus durations (see [31]).'

description: All closed head injured postcoma patients show some degree of linguistic impairment, with the population dividing into three roughly equal groups: classical aphasia, dysarthria accompanied by linguistic deficits, and subclinical aphasic deficits
original_authors: Sarno, Martha Taylor
original_title: The nature of verbal impairment after closed head injury
original_journal: Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
replication_authors: Martha Taylor Sarno
replication_title: Verbal Impairment after Closed Head Injury Report of a Replication Study
replication_journal: The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a direct replication using an identical protocol: 'inasmuch as we have used an identical protocol, this report is a replication of our earlier study.' The conclusion confirms success: 'verbal changes...are consistent across samples, i.e., replication.'

description: The Denial Rating Scale (DRS) demonstrates reliability, validity, and heuristic utility in assessing alcoholic denial, with a positive relationship between clinical change in denial during treatment and program completion
original_authors: Goldsmith, Richard J.; Green, Barry L.
original_title: A rating scale for alcoholic denial
original_journal: Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
replication_authors: Richard D. Newsome; Thomas Ditzler
replication_title: Assessing Alcoholic Denial Further Examination of the Denial Rating Scale
replication_journal: The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
explanation: The authors explicitly frame this as a replication study and report: 'The same strong relationship between clinical change and program completion as found by Goldsmith and Green is identified.' The replication was conducted in a different inpatient military treatment setting (TRISARF, Tripler Army Medical Center) with a substantially larger sample (N=647), confirming the core findings while also extending the original work with additional predictive validity analyses.

description: Syntactic conflict from garden-path sentences enhances cognitive control, as reflected in improved performance on subsequent non-syntactic Stroop trials (congruency sequence effect across domains)
original_authors: Irene P. Kan; Susan Teubner-Rhodes; Anna B. Drummey; Lauren Nutile; Lauren Krupa; Jared M. Novick
original_title: To adapt or not to adapt: the question of domain-general cognitive control
replication_authors: Balazs Aczel; Marton Kovacs; Miklos Bognar; Bence Palfi; Andree Hartanto; Sandersan Onie; Lucas E. Tiong; Thomas Rhys Evans
replication_title: Is there evidence for cross-domain congruency sequence effect? A replication of Kan et al . (2013)
explanation: Results were mixed: the RT analysis yielded inconclusive evidence (B=0.37, p=0.56), while the accuracy analysis provided support for the effect (B=10.60, p=0.01). The authors describe 'partial support' for the original finding and conclude that 'with only a single exception, we could not replicate the original findings.'

description: Perceptual conflict from viewing a bistable Necker cube enhances cognitive control on subsequent verbal Stroop trials (cross-domain congruency sequence effect from perceptual to verbal domain)
original_authors: Irene P. Kan; Susan Teubner-Rhodes; Anna B. Drummey; Lauren Nutile; Lauren Krupa; Jared M. Novick
original_title: To adapt or not to adapt: the question of domain-general cognitive control
replication_authors: Balazs Aczel; Marton Kovacs; Miklos Bognar; Bence Palfi; Andree Hartanto; Sandersan Onie; Lucas E. Tiong; Thomas Rhys Evans
replication_title: Is there evidence for cross-domain congruency sequence effect? A replication of Kan et al . (2013)
explanation: Both the RT analysis (B=1.81, p=0.09) and accuracy analysis (B=0.50, p=0.92) yielded inconclusive results. The three-way interaction with reversal group in the RT analysis showed evidence for no effect (B=0.28). The authors describe the results as 'inconclusive for both the RT and the accuracy tests of the congruency sequence effect.'

description: Externally controlled (non-internally conflicted) Necker cube reversals do not produce cross-domain congruency sequence effects on subsequent Stroop trials, demonstrating that internal conflict experience is necessary for the effect
original_authors: Irene P. Kan; Susan Teubner-Rhodes; Anna B. Drummey; Lauren Nutile; Lauren Krupa; Jared M. Novick
original_title: To adapt or not to adapt: the question of domain-general cognitive control
replication_authors: Balazs Aczel; Marton Kovacs; Miklos Bognar; Bence Palfi; Andree Hartanto; Sandersan Onie; Lucas E. Tiong; Thomas Rhys Evans
replication_title: Is there evidence for cross-domain congruency sequence effect? A replication of Kan et al . (2013)
explanation: Both the RT analysis (B=0.36, p=0.87) and accuracy analysis (B=1.63, p=0.23) yielded inconclusive results, with RT nearly reaching the threshold for evidence of no effect. The authors conclude 'the analyses drove inconclusive results' and that 'this experiment adds relatively little to our primary aims' given no effect was found in Experiment 2 either.

description: Emotional (threatening and positive) stimuli are prioritized in iconic memory — both selected at higher accuracy than neutral stimuli (emotional selection effect) and threatening stimuli exhibit slower decay of information over time (longevity effect)
original_authors: Christof Kuhbandner; Bernhard Spitzer; Reinhard Pekrun
original_title: Readout of emotional information from iconic memory: the longevity of threatening stimuli
replication_authors: Florian Kattner; Alexandra Clausen
replication_title: Revisiting the prioritization of emotional information in iconic memory
explanation: Experiment 1 replicated the main emotional selection effect (emotional targets recalled at higher accuracy than neutral targets, p < .001), but failed to replicate the decay/longevity effect for threatening stimuli: 'in contrast to what has been reported previously [12], we were not able to demonstrate that the decay of information that was initially available in iconic memory was prolonged for negative targets.' The authors call it a successful replication of the selection effect but note the mixed outcome regarding temporal dynamics.

description: Emotional (threatening and positive) stimuli are prioritized in iconic memory — both selected at higher accuracy than neutral stimuli, using a verbal recall task in an adapted Sperling partial-report paradigm
original_authors: Christof Kuhbandner; Bernhard Spitzer; Reinhard Pekrun
original_title: Readout of emotional information from iconic memory: the longevity of threatening stimuli
replication_authors: Florian Kattner; Alexandra Clausen
replication_title: Revisiting the prioritization of emotional information in iconic memory
explanation: Experiment 2 replaced verbal recall with visual recognition (a methodological and context change) and successfully replicated the emotional prioritization effect. The authors state: 'Experiment 2 successfully replicated the basic effects of emotional targets and distractors using a visual recognition task,' with significant effects of target valence (F(2,104) = 43.44, p < .001) and distractor valence (F(2,104) = 6.68, p = .002).

description: Seventeen-month-old infants track an agent's false belief when interpreting her referential communicative act, choosing the non-referred box in the false belief condition and the referred box in the true belief condition
original_authors: Victoria Southgate; Coralie Chevallier; Gergely Csibra
original_title: Seventeen-month-olds appeal to false beliefs to interpret others' referential communication
replication_authors: Lisa Wenzel; Sebastian Dörrenberg; Marina Proft; Ulf Liszkowski; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Actions do not speak louder than words in an interactive false belief task
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the central original finding that infants respond differently in FB and TB condition could not be replicated.' In Study 1, 17-month-olds chose both boxes at chance levels in both conditions (FB: 15/24 = 62% chose referred box, binomial p = 0.307; TB: 16/24 = 67%, binomial p = 0.152; no difference between conditions, Fisher's exact p = 1).

description: Seventeen-month-old infants track an agent's false belief when interpreting her referential communicative act, choosing the non-referred box in the false belief condition and the referred box in the true belief condition
original_authors: Victoria Southgate; Coralie Chevallier; Gergely Csibra
original_title: Seventeen-month-olds appeal to false beliefs to interpret others' referential communication
replication_authors: Lisa Wenzel; Sebastian Dörrenberg; Marina Proft; Ulf Liszkowski; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Actions do not speak louder than words in an interactive false belief task
explanation: Studies 2a and 2b were conceptual replications with pragmatically modified Sefo task versions tested with 2-year-olds. The authors conclude: 'In studies 2a and 2b, we did not find any evidence that 2-year-olds take an agent's belief into account when interpreting her referential communicative act.' In all modified versions, children predominantly chose the referred box regardless of the agent's true or false belief.

description: 25-month-old infants anticipate an agent's action on the basis of the agent's false belief, as measured by anticipatory looking in an eye-tracking paradigm
original_authors: Southgate V.; Senju A.; Csibra G.
original_title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds
replication_authors: Kampis D.; Kármán P.; Csibra G.; Southgate V.; Hernik M.
replication_title: A two-lab direct replication attempt of Southgate, Senju and Csibra (2007)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were unable to replicate the original finding of Southgate et al.' and conclude 'the effect reported by Southgate et al. [2] is not reliable and should not be used as evidence for false-belief attribution in children of this age.' Only 45% of included infants (22/49) anticipated correctly, which did not differ from chance (p = 0.568).

description: Reading syntactically ambiguous (garden-path) sentences results in conflict adaptation effects in subsequent Stroop trials, indicating that conflict monitoring operates in a domain-general manner across linguistic and non-linguistic tasks
original_authors: Irene P. Kan; Susan Teubner-Rhodes; Anna B. Drummey; Lauren Nutile; Lauren Krupa; Jared M. Novick
original_title: To adapt or not to adapt: the question of domain-general cognitive control
replication_authors: Carolin Dudschig
replication_title: Are control processes domain-general? A replication of ‘To adapt or not to adapt? The question of domain-general cognitive control’ (Kan et al. 2013)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of the current experiment do not provide additional support for this finding' and 'the present study did not replicate the cross-domain CSE effect reported in Experiment 1 of Kan et al.' The critical interaction (Previous Sentence Congruency × Current Stroop Congruency) was non-significant for error rates and was significant in the opposite direction for RT, with no converging evidence across any subset analyses.

description: Reading syntactically ambiguous (garden-path) sentences results in conflict adaptation effects in subsequent Stroop trials, indicating that conflict monitoring operates in a domain-general manner across linguistic and non-linguistic tasks
original_authors: Irene P. Kan; Susan Teubner-Rhodes; Anna B. Drummey; Lauren Nutile; Lauren Krupa; Jared M. Novick
original_title: To adapt or not to adapt: the question of domain-general cognitive control
replication_authors: Carolin Dudschig
replication_title: Are control processes domain-general? A replication of ‘To adapt or not to adapt? The question of domain-general cognitive control’ (Kan et al. 2013)
explanation: The authors conclude: 'The core findings of Experiment 2 offer little to support the result reported by Kan et al.' Using a response-based (rather than stimulus-based) Stroop task with larger conflict, the critical interaction was non-significant for both RT (F=3.12, p=0.081) and ER (F=1.69, p=0.197), and the combined analysis across both experiments was also non-significant.

description: Observing others' actions produces perceptual biases toward expected efficient trajectories: inefficient straight reaches toward an obstacle are perceived as higher than they are, and inefficient arched reaches over empty space are perceived as lower, with biases increasing when participants explicitly process environmental constraints or predict efficient trajectories
original_authors: Matthew Hudson; Katrina L. McDonough; Rhys Edwards; Patric Bach
original_title: Perceptual teleology: expectations of action efficiency bias social perception
original_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
replication_authors: Katrina L. McDonough; Patric Bach
replication_title: Expectations of efficient actions bias social perception: a pre-registered online replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The analysis fully replicated the prior study' and in the Discussion: 'The current study fully replicated the findings of Hudson et al. [37] in a modified procedure adapted to online testing.' All key effects were significant and in the predicted direction, including the crucial Reach Trajectory × Reach Efficiency interaction (F(1,130) = 60.1, p < 0.001, η²p = 0.316) and the three-way interaction with Task (F(1,130) = 9.28, p < 0.001).

description: An evolutionary agent-based simulation model showing that incentives for publication productivity cause scientific populations to evolve toward lower research effort, higher false-positive rates, and higher false-discovery rates — termed 'the natural selection of bad science'
original_authors: Paul E. Smaldino; Richard McElreath
original_title: The natural selection of bad science
replication_authors: Florian Kohrt; Paul E. Smaldino; Richard McElreath; Felix Schönbrodt
replication_title: Replication of the natural selection of bad science
explanation: Four of five figures from the original study were successfully replicated based on the 'relational equivalence' criterion (figs. 3, 4, 6, 7), with figs. 3 and 4 showing near-numeric identity (relative error <1%). However, fig. 5 (showing coevolution of effort and replication rate) yielded inconsistent results, which the authors traced to a coding error in the original implementation. The core conclusion that low effort and high false-discovery rates evolve was upheld, but the specific evolutionary dynamics for the replication rate variable differed.

description: In word list learning, spontaneous strategy use (especially manipulation strategies such as grouping, visualization, and association) predicts better objective task performance compared to maintenance strategies or no strategy
original_authors: Otto Waris; Daniel Fellman; Jussi Jylkkä; Matti Laine
original_title: Stimulus novelty, task demands, and strategy use in episodic memory
replication_authors: Matti Laine; Daniel Fellman; Tilda Eräste; Liisa Ritakallio; Juha Salmi
replication_title: Strategy use and its evolvement in word list learning: a replication study
explanation: The authors state: 'the analyses described above replicated the finding by Waris et al. [11] that the use of a Manipulation strategy is associated with superior Word List Learning performance. However, their finding on a performance difference between Maintenance strategy and No strategy users was not replicated.' Thus the first finding was only partly replicated.

description: The proportion of participants changing their memory strategy between task blocks decreases (stabilizes) as the word list learning task progresses, with more strategy changes occurring in the first block transition than in subsequent transitions
original_authors: Otto Waris; Daniel Fellman; Jussi Jylkkä; Matti Laine
original_title: Stimulus novelty, task demands, and strategy use in episodic memory
replication_authors: Matti Laine; Daniel Fellman; Tilda Eräste; Liisa Ritakallio; Juha Salmi
replication_title: Strategy use and its evolvement in word list learning: a replication study
explanation: The authors confirm: 'the finding of a decreased rate of strategy changers across the task blocks was replicated.' A Bayesian binomial test provided positive evidence for the hypothesis (BF₁₀ = 5.96), with 54 participants changing strategy in the first but not second transition vs. 29 showing the opposite pattern.

description: Self-reported strategy use increases during the first two task blocks of a word list learning task, reflecting task-initial strategy generation and adjustment
original_authors: Otto Waris; Daniel Fellman; Jussi Jylkkä; Matti Laine
original_title: Stimulus novelty, task demands, and strategy use in episodic memory
replication_authors: Matti Laine; Daniel Fellman; Tilda Eräste; Liisa Ritakallio; Juha Salmi
replication_title: Strategy use and its evolvement in word list learning: a replication study
explanation: The replication found no evidence for an increase in strategy use across the first two blocks (BF₀₁ = 2.00). A post-hoc re-analysis of the original data also showed only weak support (BF₁₀ = 1.45) when restricted to the real word condition, leading the authors to conclude: 'The third finding turned out to be misguided as far as only the real word learning task is concerned.'

description: Morally good changes in others are more likely to be attributed to a person's true-self than morally bad or neutral changes (Study 1)
original_authors: George E. Newman; Paul Bloom; Joshua Knobe
original_title: Value judgments and the true self
replication_authors: Shuk Ching Lee; Gilad Feldman
replication_title: Revisiting the link between true-self and morality: Replication and extension Registered Report of Newman, Bloom, and Knobe (2014) Studies 1 and 2
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully replicated the results for all the chosen studies with Cohen's d condition comparison effects larger than those reported in the original.' For Study 1, they concluded 'support for Hypothesis 1 that morally good change is more likely to reveal the true-self than morally bad or neutral changes,' with a significant main effect (F(2,1602) = 199.6, p < 0.001, η²p = .20), comparable to the original's η² = 0.39.

description: Political views moderate true-self attributions such that liberals rate liberal-aligned changes as more reflective of true-self, while conservatives rate conservative-aligned changes as more reflective of true-self (Study 2)
original_authors: George E. Newman; Paul Bloom; Joshua Knobe
original_title: Value judgments and the true self
replication_authors: Shuk Ching Lee; Gilad Feldman
replication_title: Revisiting the link between true-self and morality: Replication and extension Registered Report of Newman, Bloom, and Knobe (2014) Studies 1 and 2
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We concluded support for Hypothesis 2 that true-self ratings for change depend on alignment with political views.' The replication found a significant interaction (F(1,630) = 340.93, p < 0.001, η²p = .35, 95% CI [0.29, 0.41]), larger than the original's η² = 0.04. Post-hoc comparisons also showed significant effects in both liberal and conservative participants.

description: Hemispheric specialization of functional brain networks, as measured by the autonomy index, shows that language and attention networks are specialized to the left and right hemispheres respectively, with dual-specialization of the frontoparietal control/executive control network
original_authors: Danhong Wang; Randy L. Buckner; Hesheng Liu
original_title: Functional specialization in the human brain estimated by intrinsic hemispheric interaction
replication_authors: Madeline Peterson; Dorothea L. Floris; Jared A. Nielsen
replication_title: Parsing Brain Network Specialization: A Replication and Expansion of Wang et al. (2014)
explanation: The authors explicitly state their intent to replicate Wang et al. (2014) in new datasets. In the Results section they conclude: 'This pattern of specialized networks replicates that found by [60],' confirming the core finding of left-specialized default and frontoparietal control networks and right-specialized frontoparietal control, dorsal attention, and ventral attention networks.

description: The Family Game intervention improves parenting strategies (giving clear instructions, reinforcing cooperation, correcting non-cooperation) during role-play situations in parents with intellectual disability, but fails to generalise to real-life settings
original_authors: Munazza Tahir; Colleen Sword; Maurice Feldman
original_title: Evaluation of a game-based parent education intervention to increase positive parent-child interactions in parents with learning difficulties
replication_authors: Joany Tremblay; Elise Douard; Marc J. Lanovaz
replication_title: The Family Game to support parents with intellectual disability in managing challenging behaviours: A replication
replication_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'These results are nearly identical to those reported by Tahir et al. (2015) wherein parents displayed the strategies during the game, but failed to show generalisation during in-situ probes.' The replication followed the same multiple baseline design and procedures, but extended to a French-speaking family with a 3-year-old child (vs. children aged 10+ in the original), making it a close extension.

description: Preen oil composition of pied flycatchers differs between sexes (females have higher volatility and slightly higher chemical diversity than males) during the nestling-rearing period
original_authors: Marc Gilles; Rienk W. Fokkema; Peter Korsten; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll
original_title: Preen oil composition of pied flycatchers is similar between partners but differs between sexes and breeding stages
replication_authors: Laurence Jeanjean; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll; Marc Gilles
replication_title: Chemical signatures in the preen oil of pied flycatchers: testing reproducibility and exploring ontogeny
explanation: The replication found no sex difference in overall preen oil composition (PERMANOVA p=0.17), chemical richness, diversity, or volatility during nestling-rearing. The authors conclude: 'Our failure to reproduce the original result thus suggests that it was a false positive rather than the result of true among-year differences in the degree of sexual dimorphism.'

description: Preen oil composition of pied flycatcher breeding partners is more similar to each other than to other individuals (pair chemical signature), including in chemical richness and diversity
original_authors: Marc Gilles; Rienk W. Fokkema; Peter Korsten; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll
original_title: Preen oil composition of pied flycatchers is similar between partners but differs between sexes and breeding stages
replication_authors: Laurence Jeanjean; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll; Marc Gilles
replication_title: Chemical signatures in the preen oil of pied flycatchers: testing reproducibility and exploring ontogeny
explanation: The PERMANOVA showed borderline significance (p=0.05) for overall composition similarity between partners, but chemical richness and diversity pair effects from the original could not be reproduced. The authors conclude: 'these results hint toward a very subtle (or even potentially absent) breeding pair similarity in preen oil composition.'

description: Preen oil composition of individual female pied flycatchers changes systematically between breeding stages (incubation vs. nestling-rearing), including increased volatility during incubation
original_authors: Marc Gilles; Rienk W. Fokkema; Peter Korsten; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll
original_title: Preen oil composition of pied flycatchers is similar between partners but differs between sexes and breeding stages
replication_authors: Laurence Jeanjean; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll; Marc Gilles
replication_title: Chemical signatures in the preen oil of pied flycatchers: testing reproducibility and exploring ontogeny
explanation: Both the original study and the replication found that preen oil composition changes between incubation and nestling-rearing within individual females. The replication found even stronger effects (also significant changes in richness, diversity, and volatility), leading the authors to state: 'our replication results reinforce the suggestions from Gilles et al. (2024a) regarding the potential functions associated with the changes in preen oil across breeding stages in females.'

description: Individual female pied flycatchers do not show repeatable (individual) chemical signatures in preen oil composition across breeding stages
original_authors: Marc Gilles; Rienk W. Fokkema; Peter Korsten; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll
original_title: Preen oil composition of pied flycatchers is similar between partners but differs between sexes and breeding stages
replication_authors: Laurence Jeanjean; Barbara A. Caspers; Tim Schmoll; Marc Gilles
replication_title: Chemical signatures in the preen oil of pied flycatchers: testing reproducibility and exploring ontogeny
explanation: The replication reproduced the original null finding of no individual repeatability in preen oil within females across breeding stages (PERMANOVA p=0.22; repeatability for richness, diversity, and volatility all with 95% CI including 0). The authors confirm: 'as in the original study' no individual signature was detected, and all effect size estimates fell within the original study's confidence intervals.

description: Employed males in their 20s–40s misinterpret the attitudes of other male employees toward paternity leave as more negative than they actually are (pluralistic ignorance exists)
original_authors: Takeru Miyajima; Hiroyuki Yamaguchi
original_title: I want to but I won't: Pluralistic ignorance inhibits intentions to take paternity leave in Japan
replication_authors: Yuta Kawamura; Kanatsu Totake
replication_title: Pluralistic Ignorance did not Prevent Paternity Leave in Japan in December 2021: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication found that estimated attitudes of others (M = 3.55) were significantly lower than participants' actual attitudes (M = 4.64; F(1, 213) = 220.99, p < .001, η² = .51), replicating the original finding of pluralistic ignorance about paternity leave. The authors state this result 'supports Hypothesis 1.'

description: Employed males who experience pluralistic ignorance (self-other discrepancy group) show similar desire but significantly lower willingness to take paternity leave compared to those with positive attitudes, indicating that pluralistic ignorance inhibits paternity leave intentions
original_authors: Takeru Miyajima; Hiroyuki Yamaguchi
original_title: I want to but I won't: Pluralistic ignorance inhibits intentions to take paternity leave in Japan
replication_authors: Yuta Kawamura; Kanatsu Totake
replication_title: Pluralistic Ignorance did not Prevent Paternity Leave in Japan in December 2021: A Replication Study
explanation: The interaction between attitude group and behavioral intention type was not significant (F(2, 204) = 0.06, p = .944, η² < .01), failing to replicate the original finding. The authors explicitly state: 'Unlike Miyajima and Yamaguchi's (2017) work, pluralistic ignorance did not inhibit participants' willingness to take paternity leave' and 'Hypothesis 2 was not supported.'

description: Higher intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is associated with greater threat generalization (reduced discrimination between a conditioned threat cue and perceptually similar safety cues) during acquisition training, and with delayed extinction learning, as measured by SCR and uneasiness ratings
original_authors: Jayne Morriss; Birthe Macdonald; Carien M. van Reekum
original_title: What is going on around here? Intolerance of uncertainty predicts threat generalization
replication_authors: Elizabeth A. Bauer; Annmarie MacNamara; Aislinn Sandre; Tina B. Lonsdorf; Anna Weinberg; Jayne Morriss; Carien M. van Reekum
replication_title: Intolerance of uncertainty and threat generalization: A replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state the direct replication 'failed': 'In the direct replication, we not only failed to replicate the interactions involving IU that Morriss and colleagues (2016a) reported, but we also observed additional findings that are hard to reconcile with the original study.' Notably, in the SCR data, higher IU participants showed GREATER discrimination (opposite direction), constituting a reversal of the original finding.

description: Higher intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is associated with greater threat generalization (reduced discrimination between a conditioned threat cue and perceptually similar safety cues) during acquisition training, and with delayed extinction learning, as measured by SCR and uneasiness ratings
original_authors: Jayne Morriss; Birthe Macdonald; Carien M. van Reekum
original_title: What is going on around here? Intolerance of uncertainty predicts threat generalization
replication_authors: Elizabeth A. Bauer; Annmarie MacNamara; Aislinn Sandre; Tina B. Lonsdorf; Anna Weinberg; Jayne Morriss; Carien M. van Reekum
replication_title: Intolerance of uncertainty and threat generalization: A replication and extension
explanation: Conceptual replication 1 (McGill University) found partial support: higher IU was associated with less differentiation between acquisition and extinction phases as measured by SCR (supporting delayed learning), but the three-way phase × stimulus × IU interaction only approached significance (p=.05). The authors note 'overall, we found support at the conceptual level for increased threat generalization among higher IU individuals using SCR,' but the full pattern of results did not consistently align with the original.

description: Higher intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is associated with greater threat generalization (reduced discrimination between a conditioned threat cue and perceptually similar safety cues) during acquisition training, and with delayed extinction learning, as measured by SCR and uneasiness ratings
original_authors: Jayne Morriss; Birthe Macdonald; Carien M. van Reekum
original_title: What is going on around here? Intolerance of uncertainty predicts threat generalization
replication_authors: Elizabeth A. Bauer; Annmarie MacNamara; Aislinn Sandre; Tina B. Lonsdorf; Anna Weinberg; Jayne Morriss; Carien M. van Reekum
replication_title: Intolerance of uncertainty and threat generalization: A replication and extension
explanation: Conceptual replication 2 (Texas A&M University) found partial support via SCR: higher IU participants showed greater threat generalization across both training phases (stimulus × IU interaction, p=.02), but this differed from the original in that the effect was not phase-specific. Using the LPP (ERP), the study replicated the finding of increased threat differentiation during extinction for higher IU individuals (phase × stimulus × IU interaction, p=.02). The authors conclude 'overall, we found support at the conceptual level,' but with notable differences from the original pattern.

description: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) enhances the invigoration of effort (speed of ramping up button-press frequency) during an effort allocation task for monetary and food rewards
original_authors: Monja P. Neuser; Vanessa Teckentrup; Anne Kühnel; Manfred Hallschmid; Martin Walter; Nils B. Kroemer
original_title: Vagus nerve stimulation boosts the drive to work for rewards
replication_authors: Federica Lucchi; Beth Lloyd; Sander Nieuwenhuis
replication_title: Non‐invasive vagus nerve stimulation and the motivation to work for rewards: A replication of Neuser et al. (2020, Nature Communications)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were not able to replicate their key finding: taVNS did not increase the strength of invigoration, regardless of reward type, reward magnitude, and trial difficulty. The data were five times more likely (BF₁₀ = 0.19) under the null hypothesis than under the alternative hypothesis that taVNS modulates invigoration.' The study was pre-registered as a direct replication using the original analysis scripts provided by Neuser et al.

description: Cochlear-implant users demonstrate perceptual restoration benefits (better speech understanding with noise-burst interrupted sentences than silent-gap interrupted sentences) under certain conditions, particularly at a 75% duty cycle across all SNRs tested
original_authors: Pranesh Bhargava; Etienne Gaudrain; Deniz Başkent
original_title: Top-down restoration of speech in cochlear-implant users
replication_authors: Brittany N. Jaekel; Sarah Weinstein; Rochelle S. Newman; Matthew J. Goupell
replication_title: Impacts of signal processing factors on perceptual restoration in cochlear-implant users
replication_journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that 'we found that we were unable to replicate the +4.6 RAU restoration benefit reported in the original study by [7], despite utilizing the same interruption parameters and similar experimental procedures.' The replication found a -0.9 RAU restoration effect compared to the original +4.6 RAU, with no significant difference between conditions [t(12)=0.26, p=0.802].

description: A lightweight testing checklist intervention helps students write higher-quality unit tests (in terms of coverage and mutation testing scores) compared to a code coverage tool, and is particularly beneficial to students with lower prior knowledge in unit testing
original_authors: Gina R. Bai; Kai Presler-Marshall; Thomas W. Price; Kathryn T. Stolee
original_title: Check it off: Exploring the impact of a checklist intervention on the quality of student-written unit tests
original_journal: 27th ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education
replication_authors: Gina R. Bai; Zuoxuan Jiang; Thomas W. Price; Kathryn T. Stolee
replication_title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Testing Checklist Intervention in CS2: An Quasi-experimental Replication Study
replication_journal: Proceedings of the 2024 ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research - Volume 1
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results confirm the initial findings of Bai et al. [9][11] that the testing checklists could significantly improve the quality of student-authored tests.' Students who received the checklist achieved significantly higher mutation coverage (rrb=0.258, p=3.4e-05) and line coverage (rrb=0.260, p=2.0e-05) than control group students.

description: English lower secondary students (aged 11-13) show hierarchical levels of fractional understanding, with most able to label simple fractions but few able to perform complex fraction computations, and word/diagram problems generally easier than computation tasks
original_authors: Hart, K.; Brown, M.; Kerslake, D.; Küchemann, D.; Ruddock, G.
original_title: Diagnostic mathematics tests: teacher's guide (fractions 1)
replication_authors: Julie Vangsøe Færch; Jeremy Hodgen
replication_title: Danish Students’ Understanding of Fractions: A Replication Study
replication_journal: Implementation and Replication Studies in Mathematics Education
explanation: The authors conclude that 'many of the findings of the original study broadly hold true, but there are some significant differences.' Danish students were slightly stronger on labelling/word problems but weaker on computation tasks, and the original level 2/3 hierarchy collapsed in the new data, indicating partial but not full replication of the original findings.

description: Responses to a pointing direction estimation task are repulsively biased away from the previous trial's stimulus, but this repulsive bias switches to an attractive bias when an unrelated Stroop task is introduced during the delay period; response trajectories show repulsion throughout most of the response execution period regardless of condition
original_authors: Kuo-Wei Chen; Gi-Yeul Bae
original_title: Working memory flips the direction of serial bias through memory-based decision
replication_authors: Juni B. Akselberg; Sara B. Cardona; Mikkel Dybvad; Lise Martine Karlstad; Malin Langemyr; Ingrid A. Mellingsæter-Jokic; Mats K. K. Moe; Amalie C. Solvang; Andrey Chetverikov
replication_title: Between repulsion and attraction in serial biases: Replication of Chen and Bae (2024)
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we were able to replicate the main findings of Chen and Bae (2024a), which showed repulsive biases in the delayed pointing direction estimation task and a shift to attraction with the addition of an extra task during the delay period.' All three key findings (repulsive bias, switch to attraction in Stroop condition, and repulsive response trajectories) were confirmed.

description: An interdisciplinary behavioral program (involving a behavior analyst, dentists, and medical professionals) increases cooperation during routine dental exams in adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities who have a history of receiving sedation, anesthesia, or protective stabilization
original_authors: John C. Berens; Loukia Tsami; Dorothea C. Lerman; Marissa Matteucci; David F. Fray; Ben F. Warner; Laura A. Keehan; Kristen A. Staggers; Cynthia Peacock
original_title: Preliminary results of an interdisciplinary behavioral program to improve access to preventative dental care for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities
replication_authors: Emily Exline; Kristina McGinnis; Serena R. Garza; Stephanie Gerow; Tracey N. Sulak; Monserrat Austin
replication_title: Progressive Functional Analysis and Function-Based Intervention Via Telehealth: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The purpose of this study was to replicate and extend the interdisciplinary model described by [Berens et al.],' and in the Discussion conclude 'This replicates the preliminary results of [Berens et al.] with experimenter-implemented interventions in the clinic.' The core finding—that the majority of adults with IDD with a history of SAS did not require behavioral intervention and completed dental exams—was reproduced. The current study modified the original by having caregivers (rather than experimenters) implement mock exams and interventions via telehealth at home, constituting a close extension.

description: Prosecutors and defense attorneys differ in perceptions of defendant guilt, probability of winning at trial, and plea-bargaining decisions when evaluating eyewitness evidence; attorneys show some sensitivity to witnessing conditions (familiarity and cross-race) in plea-related decisions
original_authors: Kathy Pezdek; Matthew O'Brien
original_title: Plea bargaining and appraisals of eyewitness evidence by prosecutors and defense attorneys
replication_authors: Angela M. Jones; Sean Patrick Roche
replication_title: The Pragmatic American Revisited: A Direct Replication of Pickett and Baker (2014)
replication_journal: International Journal of Offender Therapy and Comparative Criminology
explanation: The replication produced mixed results: 'Replicating Pezdek and O'Brien (2014), prosecutors were more likely to view the defendant as guilty, more likely to offer a plea, and sought harsher sentences than defense attorneys.' However, other findings did not replicate — there was no difference in probability of winning (Hypothesis 3 not supported), and sensitivity to eyewitness procedures was absent across all hypotheses (5, 6, 7). The overall pattern is mixed, with the authors using both 'replicating' and 'in contrast to [44]' language across different findings.

description: Patients admitted to a psychiatric emergency department after a suicide attempt have a significantly stronger implicit association between self and death/suicide (higher S-IAT scores) than patients admitted for other psychiatric reasons
original_authors: Matthew K. Nock; Jennifer M. Park; Christine T. Finn; Tara L. Deliberto; Halina J. Dour; Mahzarin R. Banaji
original_title: Measuring the suicidal mind: Implicit cognition predicts suicidal behavior
replication_authors: Nina Tello; Ghina Harika-Germaneau; Wilfried Serra; Nematollah Jaafari; Armand Chatard
replication_title: Forecasting a Fatal Decision: Direct Replication of the Predictive Validity of the Suicide–Implicit Association Test
explanation: The replication found no significant difference in S-IAT scores between suicide attempters and controls: t(160)=0.14, p=.889, d=0.024 (original: d=0.44, p=.015). The authors state: 'we did not replicate Nock et al.'s (2010)' first key finding, attributing the failure partly to the high prevalence of prior suicide attempts in the control group.

description: Among patients with a history of suicide attempts, higher S-IAT scores at baseline prospectively predict making a new suicide attempt within 6 months, over and beyond other clinical predictors (depressive disorder, multiple suicide attempts, suicidal ideation, clinician and patient predictions)
original_authors: Matthew K. Nock; Jennifer M. Park; Christine T. Finn; Tara L. Deliberto; Halina J. Dour; Mahzarin R. Banaji
original_title: Measuring the suicidal mind: Implicit cognition predicts suicidal behavior
replication_authors: Nina Tello; Ghina Harika-Germaneau; Wilfried Serra; Nematollah Jaafari; Armand Chatard
replication_title: Forecasting a Fatal Decision: Direct Replication of the Predictive Validity of the Suicide–Implicit Association Test
explanation: The replication found that S-IAT scores significantly predicted future suicide attempts at 6-month follow-up (OR=5.28, 95% CI [1.41, 19.77] for continuous scores; OR=9.72 [2.50, 37.73] for dichotomous scores), consistent with the original (OR=30.68 [1.18, 795.12]). The authors conclude: 'the present direct and independent replication is reassuring, as it confirms the predictive validity of the Suicide-Implicit Association Test.'

description: The surveillance task produces evaluative conditioning (EC) effects — specifically, preferences for a conditioned stimulus (CS) paired with positive stimuli over one paired with negative stimuli — even among participants who are unaware of the CS-US contingency pairings
original_authors: Olson, Michael A.; Fazio, Russell H.
original_title: Implicit attitude formation through classical conditioning
replication_authors: Tal Moran; Sean Hughes; Ian Hussey; Miguel A. Vadillo; Michael A. Olson; Frederik Aust; Karoline Bading; Robert Balas; Taylor Benedict; Olivier Corneille; Samantha B. Douglas; Melissa J. Ferguson; Katherine A. Fritzlen; Anne Gast; Bertram Gawronski; Tamara Giménez-Fernández; Krzysztof Hanusz; Tobias Heycke; Fabia Högden; Mandy Hütter; Benedek Kurdi; Adrien Mierop; Jasmin Richter; Justyna Sarzyńska-Wawer; Colin Tucker Smith; Christoph Stahl; Philine Thomasius; Christian Unkelbach; Jan De Houwer
replication_title: Incidental Attitude Formation via the Surveillance Task: A Preregistered Replication of the Olson and Fazio (2001) Study
