explanation: The primary analysis using the original authors' awareness criterion found a small but significant EC effect (g = 0.12, p = .002), and the authors state 'when the original authors' awareness exclusion criterion was employed, their original effect was replicated.' However, all three secondary (preregistered) awareness criteria yielded non-significant effects, leading the authors to conclude: 'the failure to find significant effects with the three secondary criteria...creates considerable uncertainty regarding the robustness of any unaware EC effect.'

description: Individuals who use reappraisal more during uncontrollable versus controllable situations in daily life (better strategy-situation fit) have greater well-being beyond their habitual reappraisal use, as measured via ecological momentary assessment
original_authors: Simon J. Haines; John Gleeson; Peter Kuppens; Tom Hollenstein; Joseph Ciarrochi; Izelle Labuschagne; Caitlin Grace; Peter Koval
original_title: The wisdom to know the difference: Strategy-situation fit in emotion regulation in daily life is associated with well-being
replication_authors: Emily C. Willroth; Gerald Young; Brett Q. Ford; Allison Troy; Dorota Swierzewicz; Iris B. Mauss
replication_title: Preregistered Direct Replication and Extension of “The Wisdom to Know the Difference: Strategy-Situation Fit in Emotion Regulation in Daily Life Is Associated With Well-Being”
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The current preregistered direct replication study did not replicate the original finding that strategy-situation fit in daily life is associated with better well-being.' The focal parameter (β11) was statistically nonsignificant in all six well-being models in the replication study (N=285), versus all significant in the original (N=74).

description: Entrepreneurs make more intuitive decisions than hired managers (as measured by the Contemplative Index), while showing no significant difference from nonmanagerial employees
original_authors: Martin Koudstaal; Randolph Sloof; Mirjam van Praag
original_title: Entrepreneurs: intuitive or contemplative decision-makers?
replication_authors: Frank M. Fossen; Levent Neyse
replication_title: Entrepreneurship, Management, and Cognitive Reflection: A Preregistered Replication Study With Extensions
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We confirm the main results from their analysis.' The replication found that hired managers scored significantly higher on the CRT than entrepreneurs (manager coefficient 0.221, SE=0.069, p=.001), while entrepreneurs did not differ significantly from nonmanagerial employees (p=.817), matching Koudstaal et al.'s pattern. Effect sizes were 'remarkably similar' to the original.

description: Adding page-by-page interactive questions to digitally presented study information (interactive condition) improves participant retention of that information compared to standard information presentation (control condition)
original_authors: Caitlin Geier; Robyn B. Adams; Katharine M. Mitchell; Bree E. Holtz
original_title: Informed consent for online research - is anybody reading?: Assessing comprehension and individual differences in readings of digital consent forms
original_journal: Journal of Empirical Research on Human Research Ethics
replication_authors: Marije aan het Rot; Ineke Wessel
replication_title: How Making Consent Procedures More Interactive can Improve Informed Consent: An Experimental Study and Replication
replication_journal: Journal of Empirical Research on Human Research Ethics
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our interactive condition showed a higher overall retention score than our control condition (Hypothesis 1)' and that 'The interactive and control conditions in our research were comparable to the conditions in [Geier et al., 2021].' Study 1 produced a significant effect (t(110)=5.84, p<.0001, d=1.11), successfully replicating the original finding.

description: Adding page-by-page interactive questions to digitally presented study information (interactive condition) improves participant retention of that information compared to standard information presentation (control condition)
original_authors: Caitlin Geier; Robyn B. Adams; Katharine M. Mitchell; Bree E. Holtz
original_title: Informed consent for online research - is anybody reading?: Assessing comprehension and individual differences in readings of digital consent forms
original_journal: Journal of Empirical Research on Human Research Ethics
replication_authors: Marije aan het Rot; Ineke Wessel
replication_title: How Making Consent Procedures More Interactive can Improve Informed Consent: An Experimental Study and Replication
replication_journal: Journal of Empirical Research on Human Research Ethics
explanation: Study 2 was 'purposely conducted earlier in the year' to assess robustness and 'results were comparable across the two studies.' Study 2 produced a significant effect (t(124)=7.20, p<.0001, d=1.29), replicating both the original Geier et al. (2021) finding and Study 1.

description: Viewing recession-related images primes adults who reported a less affluent childhood to prefer smaller-sooner rewards on a delay discounting task, compared with those who reported more affluent childhoods
original_authors: Vladas Griskevicius; Joshua M. Ackerman; Stephanie M. Cantú; Andrew W. Delton; Theresa E. Robertson; Jeffry A. Simpson; Melissa Emery Thompson; Joshua M. Tybur
original_title: When the economy falters, do people spend or save? responses to resource scarcity depend on childhood environments
replication_authors: Richard J. Tunney; Jodie N. Raybould
replication_title: Thinking about neither death nor poverty affects delay discounting, but episodic foresight does: Three replications of the effects of priming on time preferences
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we did not replicate either effect' (the priming effect and the childhood SES interaction). Despite testing with n=238, neither main effects of prime type nor the key interaction between childhood SES and prime type were replicated.

description: Asking participants to think and write about their own death (mortality salience) significantly reduces delay discounting compared to a control group asked to think about dental pain
original_authors: Nicholas J. Kelley; Brandon J. Schmeichel
original_title: Thinking about death reduces delay discounting
replication_authors: Richard J. Tunney; Jodie N. Raybould
replication_title: Thinking about neither death nor poverty affects delay discounting, but episodic foresight does: Three replications of the effects of priming on time preferences
explanation: The authors state: 'Despite having a sufficient sample size, and a very close method including using the same items, we were unable to replicate their effect.' The t-test showed no significant difference between Mortality Salience and Dental Pain conditions (t187 = -1.714, p = .088).

description: Cuing participants to imagine positive or negative future events (episodic foresight) reduces delay discounting compared to a neutral cue condition
original_authors: Adam Bulley; Beyon Miloyan; Gillian V. Pepper; Matthew J. Gullo; Julie D. Henry; Thomas Suddendorf
original_title: Cuing both positive and negative episodic foresight reduces delay discounting but does not affect risk-taking
replication_authors: Richard J. Tunney; Jodie N. Raybould
replication_title: Thinking about neither death nor poverty affects delay discounting, but episodic foresight does: Three replications of the effects of priming on time preferences
explanation: The authors state: 'we were able to replicate this result very closely. All three experiments were conducted online.' The replication found significant main effects of both Positive vs. Neutral (β = -0.252, t = -3.826, p < .001) and Negative vs. Neutral (β = -0.274, t = -4.169, p < .001) conditions, closely matching the original study's pattern of results.

description: Need for Cognition (NFC) is negatively associated with the burnout subscale reduced personal efficacy in student teachers, mediated by higher habitual use of reappraisal (but not by suppression or self-control)
original_authors: Grass, J.; Strobel, J.; Strobel, A.
original_title: The joy of thinking as the key to success? The importance of Need for Cognition for subjective experience and achievement in academic studies
replication_authors: Josephine Zerna; Nicole Engelmann; Anja Strobel; Alexander Strobel
replication_title: Need for cognition and burnout in teachers – A replication and extension study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we could neither replicate the effect of NFC on reappraisal (β = 0.12, p = 0.105), nor the indirect effect of NFC on reduced personal efficacy via reappraisal (β = −0.02, p = 0.153).' The central mediation via reappraisal — the key finding of the original study — was not confirmed. The Discussion concludes that 'differences between [31] and the present analysis suggest that burnout is being mediated by different factors in student teachers than in teachers.'

description: Children aged 5-6 rarely spontaneously verbalize during a memory task, while verbalization increases substantially in 7-8 and 10-11 year-old children, confirming the production deficiency hypothesis that verbal rehearsal emerges around age 7
original_authors: John H. Flavell; David R. Beach; Jack M. Chinsky

replication_authors: Emily M. Elliott; Candice C. Morey; Angela M. AuBuchon; Nelson Cowan; Chris Jarrold; Eryn J. Adams; Meg Attwood; Büşra Bayram; Stefen Beeler-Duden; Taran Y. replication_title: Multilab Direct Replication of Flavell, Beach, and Chinsky (1966): Spontaneous Verbal Rehearsal in a Memory Task as a Function of Age
replication_journal: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
explanation: The replication confirmed the general developmental trend (χ² = 87.47, p < 0.01), and the 5 vs. 7 and 5 vs. 10 age-group differences were replicated, but the critical finding that 5-year-olds rarely verbalize was not reproduced (76% of 5-year-olds verbalized in the replication vs. 10% in the original). The authors described the outcome as replicating 'the spirit' of the original while noting substantial discrepancies: 'it was clear from this much larger sample of children that even the youngest children exhibited more speech behavior than would have been expected based on the original work.'

description: A Visual Attention Model (VAM)-based approach using neural networks and SVM can classify Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) vs. typically developing individuals from eye-tracking fixation patterns, achieving an average AUC of 0.82 without requiring manual region-of-interest demarcation.

replication_title: Computer-aided autism diagnosis using visual attention models and eye-tracking: replication and improvement proposal
replication_journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
explanation: The authors retrained the VAMs using the same hyperparameters and methodology as Oliveira et al. (2021) but with a new stimulus and new sample (n=77). The replication achieved an average AUC of 0.71 vs. the original 0.82, a statistically significant drop (p=0.012). While authors describe results as 'satisfactory' and indicative of the approach's 'robustness', they also explicitly note the inferior performance, making the overall outcome inconclusive.

description: Black Hispanic individuals' health behaviors (e.g., drinking) mirror those of white Hispanic individuals, while their health service outcomes (e.g., having a usual source of care, having seen a doctor in the past year) align more closely with non-Hispanic Black individuals, with health status reflecting a mix of both groups' profiles
original_authors: Thomas Alexis LaVeist-Ramos; Jessica Galarraga; Roland J. Thorpe; Caryn N. Bell; Chermeia J. Austin

original_journal: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
replication_authors: Mariana Rodrigues; Emma Risner; Brennan Rhodes-Bratton; Stephanie H. Cook; Adolfo Cuevas
replication_title: Intersectionality matters for Hispanic health: A replication study using the All of Us Research Program
replication_journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
explanation: The authors explicitly contrast their findings with the original: 'In contrast to the results reported by LaVeist-Ramos and colleagues [10], where ethnicity (Hispanic) appeared to play a predominant role in health behaviors, our findings indicate that race (identifying as Black) plays a more dominant influence on health behaviors and health-related outcomes.' The replication used the All of Us Research Program dataset instead of the NHIS, testing a different but larger and more diverse cohort.

description: Kappa agreement between LUCIE (Lund University Checklist for Incipient Exhaustion) and KEDS (Karolinska Exhaustion Disorder Scale) is fair to moderate in a highly educated and healthy population sample drawn from the general population
original_authors: Roger Persson; Kai Österberg; Njördur Viborg; Peter Jönsson; Artur Tenenbaum

replication_authors: Roger Persson; Kai Österberg; Jonas Björk
replication_title: The concurrent validity of the Lund University Checklist for Incipient Exhaustion and the Karolinska Exhaustion Disorder Scale: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to 'replicate our previous observations by comparing KEDS and LUCIE in a new study sample' (school principals), and the Discussion and Conclusions both confirm: 'the pattern of Kappa estimates between LUCIE and KEDS in the present sample...can be said to replicate our previous observations' and 'The present results essentially replicate our previous observations among highly educated and healthy individuals drawn from the general population.'

original_authors: Bonny Chang; Carla Sharp; Carolyn Ha

replication_authors: Tess Gecha; Veronica McLaren; Carla Sharp
replication_title: Clinical cut-off scores for the Borderline Personality Features Scale for Children to differentiate among adolescents with Borderline Personality Disorder, other psychopathology, and no psychopathology: a replication study
replication_journal: Borderline Personality Disorder and Emotion Dysregulation
explanation: The authors explicitly state the study aimed to 'replicate the Chang et al. study establishing cutoff scores, correcting for its limitations.' The replication confirmed that the BPFS-C and BPFS-P can discriminate adolescents with BPD from psychiatric controls with moderate diagnostic accuracy, though the specific optimal cut-off scores differed (75 vs. 66 for BPFS-C; 74 vs. 72 for BPFS-P), with the authors attributing the discrepancy to the small sample size in the original study.

description: CV targets are named faster when preceded by CV primes than CVG primes, and CVG targets are named faster when preceded by CVG primes than CV primes (crossover syllable priming interaction) in Mandarin Chinese masked word naming
original_authors: Jenn-Yeu Chen; Wei-Chun Lin; L. Ferrand
original_title: Masked priming of the syllable in Mandarin Chinese speech production
replication_authors: Wenping You; Qingfang Zhang; Rinus G. Verdonschot
replication_title: Masked Syllable Priming Effects in Word and Picture Naming in Chinese
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'a direct replication of Chen et al.'s [10] third experiment' using 'identical stimuli and experimental design.' The Discussion confirms: 'Experiment 1 replicated the masked syllable priming effect reported in Chen et al. [10]. The important cross-over interaction between the Prime Type and the Target Type was also observed.'

description: CV targets are named faster when preceded by CV primes than CVN primes, and CVN targets are named faster when preceded by CVN primes than CV primes (crossover syllable priming interaction) in Mandarin Chinese masked word naming, extending the effect to CVN syllable types
original_authors: Jenn-Yeu Chen; Wei-Chun Lin; L. Ferrand
original_title: Masked priming of the syllable in Mandarin Chinese speech production
replication_authors: Wenping You; Qingfang Zhang; Rinus G. Verdonschot
replication_title: Masked Syllable Priming Effects in Word and Picture Naming in Chinese
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. Experiment 2 extends Chen et al. (2003) to CVN syllable types in a word naming task. The critical crossover interaction between Target Type and Prime Type was highly significant (F1(2,32) = 15.62, p<.001; F2(2,76) = 8.44, p<.001). The Discussion explicitly states: 'Similar to Experiment 1, we obtained the critical interaction between the Target Type and Prime Type in naming latencies. The results show a syllable priming effect, not the segmental overlap effect.' The General Discussion confirms: 'Four experiments consistently found that CV targets were named faster when preceded by CV primes.' Clear successful extension of the syllable priming effect to new syllable types.

description: Crossover syllable priming interaction (CV targets named faster with CV primes, CVN targets named faster with CVN primes) in Mandarin Chinese, extended from word naming to picture naming task with CV and CVN syllable types
original_authors: Jenn-Yeu Chen; Wei-Chun Lin; L. Ferrand
original_title: Masked priming of the syllable in Mandarin Chinese speech production
replication_authors: Wenping You; Qingfang Zhang; Rinus G. Verdonschot
replication_title: Masked Syllable Priming Effects in Word and Picture Naming in Chinese
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. Experiment 3 tests whether the syllable priming effect from Chen et al. (2003) replicates using picture naming instead of word naming, with CV and CVN syllables. The critical crossover interaction was highly significant (F1(2,30) = 10.80, p<.001; F2(2,76) = 12.09, p<.001). The Discussion explicitly states: 'We replicated the syllable priming effect using a picture naming task. The critical interaction between the Prime Type and the Target Type was again found.' The General Discussion further confirms the result was 'consistent across different stimuli and different tasks (word and picture naming).' The paper's Introduction makes clear this experiment targets the same Chen et al. [10] effect: 'As Chen et al. [10] only used word naming task in their study... Experiment 3 tested whether or not the masked syllable priming effect can be replicated using a picture naming task.'

description: Individual differences in analytic thinking (measured by the CRT) negatively correlate with religious beliefs such that more analytic thinkers endorse less religious belief
original_authors: Will M. Gervais; Ara Norenzayan
original_title: Analytic thinking promotes religious disbelief
replication_authors: Anna J. Finley; David Tang; Brandon J. Schmeichel
replication_title: Revisiting the Relationship between Individual Differences in Analytic Thinking and Religious Belief: Evidence That Measurement Order Moderates Their Inverse Correlation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These results directly replicated Gervais and Norenzayan (Study 1)' after finding significant negative correlations between CRT scores and religious beliefs (r = -.17 to -.23, all p < .05) in the analytic-first condition, using the same CRT and religiosity measures as the original.

description: Adults given privileged information about an object's true location overestimate the likelihood that a protagonist holding a false belief will search in the correct (true) location — a 'curse of knowledge' effect in false belief reasoning
original_authors: Susan A.J. Birch; Paul Bloom
original_title: The curse of knowledge in reasoning about false beliefs
replication_authors: Benjamin G. Farrar; Ljerka Ostojić
replication_title: Does social distance modulate adults’ egocentric biases when reasoning about false beliefs?
explanation: Across three experiments and an internal meta-analysis (total N=1,308), the curse of knowledge effect was reliably replicated. The authors state: 'the modified false belief task does seem to reliably elicit egocentric biases in false belief reasoning when participants of white Western European descent mentalise about an in-group protagonist.' Effect sizes across the in-group conditions (d=0.407–0.507) were directly in line with the original (d=0.469).

description: Social distance modulates egocentric biases in false belief reasoning: adults show a curse of knowledge effect for in-group protagonists but not for out-group protagonists (social distance effect)
original_authors: Andrew R. Todd; Karlene Hanko; Adam D. Galinsky; Thomas Mussweiler
original_title: When focusing on differences leads to similar perspectives
replication_authors: Benjamin G. Farrar; Ljerka Ostojić
replication_title: Does social distance modulate adults’ egocentric biases when reasoning about false beliefs?
explanation: Across three experiments and an internal meta-analysis (N=872 across conspecific conditions), no significant social distance effect (Knowledge x Protagonist interaction) was found. The authors conclude: 'the present data do not support the hypothesis that social distance modulates adults' egocentric biases when reasoning about false beliefs.' The social distance interaction only became significant when Todd et al.'s own data were pooled in, suggesting the current study's independent experiments failed to replicate this effect.

description: Priming participants with cooperative (vs. competitive) words increases cooperative behavioral intentions in a Prisoner's Dilemma game, with the effect amplified when participants explicitly construe the situation before deciding
original_authors: Aaron C. Kay; Lee Ross
original_title: The perceptual push: The interplay of implicit cues and explicit situational construals on behavioral intentions in the Prisoner's Dilemma
replication_authors: Anabel Belaus; Cecilia Reyna; Esteban Freidin
replication_title: Testing the effect of cooperative/competitive priming on the Prisoner’s Dilemma. A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'could not reproduce their findings in the present close replication.' All effects — priming on name ratings, beliefs about others' intentions, and own behavioral intentions — were non-significant across both the full sample (N=346) and a reduced sample (N=200), with very small effect sizes (η²p ranging from <.000 to .011).

description: Reinstating a simple background color during retrieval (compared to a changed background color) improves free recall of words encoded with that color context
original_authors: Takeo Isarida; Toshiko K. Isarida
original_title: Environmental context effects of background color in free recall
replication_authors: Michel Juhani Wälti; Daniel Graham Woolley; Nicole Wenderoth
replication_title: Reinstating verbal memories with virtual contexts: Myth or reality?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we could not replicate Isarida and Isarida [23] and found no experimental support for a context dependent memory effect when using simple color context cues in Study 1.' The Bayesian analysis provided strong evidence for the null hypothesis (BF01 = 12.5).

description: Sleep protects newly learned word pairs against retroactive interference from subsequently learned overlapping word pairs, such that interference learning is much less detrimental to memory following a night of sleep compared to a day of wakefulness (significant Sleep/Wake x Interference/No-Interference interaction)
original_authors: Jeffrey M. Ellenbogen; Justin C. Hulbert; Ying Jiang; Robert Stickgold
original_title: The sleeping brain's influence on verbal memory: boosting resistance to interference
replication_authors: Carrie Bailes; Mary Caldwell; Erin J. Wamsley; Matthew A. Tucker
replication_title: Does sleep protect memories against interference? A failure to replicate
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we did not replicate Ellenbogen et al.'s observation of a large effect of sleep in protecting memories against interference learning.' The critical Sleep x Interference interaction was non-significant (F(1,95) = 0.38, p = 0.54, η²p = 0.004), compared to the original η²p = 0.0985, with the original effect size falling outside the 90% confidence interval of the replication effect.

description: Sexualized women are processed in an object-like way, as evidenced by a stronger body inversion effect (recognition impairment for upside-down photos) for sexualized male than female targets in an inverted body recognition task
original_authors: Philippe Bernard; Sarah J. Gervais; Jill Allen; Sophie Campomizzi; Olivier Klein
original_title: Integrating sexual objectification with object versus person recognition: the sexualized-body-inversion hypothesis
replication_authors: Cristina Zogmaister; Federica Durante; Silvia Mari; Franca Crippa; Chiara Volpato
replication_title: Measuring objectification through the Body Inversion Paradigm: Methodological issues
explanation: The authors explicitly conducted a direct replication of Bernard et al. (2012) using the same stimulus materials with counterbalanced stimuli. The Discussion confirms: 'Using the same stimulus materials of Bernard and colleagues [4], we replicated the stronger inversion effects for sexualized men as compared to women (H1).' Bayesian analysis yielded BF10 = 5.39, interpreted as moderate evidence in favor of a successful replication.

description: Sexualized women are processed in an object-like way, as evidenced by a stronger body inversion effect (recognition impairment for upside-down photos) for sexualized male than female targets in an inverted body recognition task
original_authors: Philippe Bernard; Sarah J. Gervais; Jill Allen; Sophie Campomizzi; Olivier Klein
original_title: Integrating sexual objectification with object versus person recognition: the sexualized-body-inversion hypothesis
replication_authors: Cristina Zogmaister; Federica Durante; Silvia Mari; Franca Crippa; Chiara Volpato
replication_title: Measuring objectification through the Body Inversion Paradigm: Methodological issues
explanation: Using different sexualized stimuli, the authors found no significant difference in the inversion effect for male versus female targets. They explicitly state 'H1 was not replicated. If anything, the effect of target sex was in the opposite direction.' Bayesian analysis yielded BF01 = 5.26, interpreted as moderate evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.

description: People of both sexes react more positively to female-favoring than male-favoring sex differences, with no significant difference between men and women in the strength of this effect
original_authors: Steve Stewart-Williams; Chern Yi Marybeth Chang; Xiu Ling Wong; Jesse D. Blackburn; Andrew G. Thomas
original_title: Reactions to male-favoring vs. female-favoring sex differences: A pre-registered experiment and Southeast Asian replication
replication_authors: Steve Stewart-Williams; Xiu Ling Wong; Chern Yi Marybeth Chang; Andrew G. Thomas
replication_title: People react more positively to female- than to male-favoring sex differences: A direct replication of a counterintuitive finding
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the present study replicated almost all the findings of our original one, using a comparable sample and identical materials.' The main effect of Sex Favored was clearly replicated (F(1,299) = 24.48, p < .001, d = 0.58), consistent with the original finding.

description: Both men and women greatly overestimate own-sex favoritism in their predictions about how the average man and woman would react to male- vs. female-favoring sex differences
original_authors: Steve Stewart-Williams; Chern Yi Marybeth Chang; Xiu Ling Wong; Jesse D. Blackburn; Andrew G. Thomas
original_title: Reactions to male-favoring vs. female-favoring sex differences: A pre-registered experiment and Southeast Asian replication
replication_authors: Steve Stewart-Williams; Xiu Ling Wong; Chern Yi Marybeth Chang; Andrew G. Thomas
replication_title: People react more positively to female- than to male-favoring sex differences: A direct replication of a counterintuitive finding
explanation: The authors report that participants' predictions about average-man and average-woman reactions replicated the original study: both sexes predicted strong own-sex favoritism, and the average woman's own-sex favoritism was greatly exaggerated (predicted d = 2.38 vs. actual d = 0.66, a 361% overestimate), consistent with the original findings.

description: Participants randomly assigned to spend money on others (prosocial condition) report greater happiness than those assigned to spend money on themselves (personal condition)
original_authors: Elizabeth W. Dunn; Lara B. Aknin; Michael I. Norton
original_title: Spending money on others promotes happiness
replication_authors: Garam Kim; Ingrid Adams; Malik Diaw; Mira Celly; Leif D. Nelson; Minah H. Jung
replication_title: Prosocial spending encourages happiness: A replication of the only experiment reported in Dunn, Aknin, and Norton (2008)
explanation: The primary analysis using the original specification (11-item composite happiness measure) yielded a non-significant result (F(1,130) = .35, p = .557), but an additional exploratory 1-item measure of immediate post-spending happiness showed a significant effect in the expected direction (t(131) = 2.27, p = .025). The authors conclude: 'We sought to replicate a key experiment from Dunn et al. [3] and observed mixed results. We did not replicate the result using the original measures and specifications. However, our exploratory measure...did find some support for the original analysis.'

description: Not sharing research data is associated with a higher prevalence of statistical consistency errors in published psychology papers
original_authors: Jelte M. Wicherts; Marjan Bakker; Dylan Molenaar
original_title: Willingness to share research data is related to the strength of the evidence and the quality of reporting of statistical results
replication_authors: Aline Claesen; Wolf Vanpaemel; Anne-Sofie Maerten; Thomas Verliefde; Francis Tuerlinckx; Tom Heyman
replication_title: Data sharing upon request and statistical consistency errors in psychology: A replication of Wicherts, Bakker and Molenaar (2011)
explanation: The replication found no statistically significant relation between data sharing and consistency errors (β = -0.18, z = -0.78, p = 0.43), and the Discussion states: 'Our replication results did not support the original findings: We have found no evidence for a relation between data sharing and (consistency or decision) errors.'

description: Not sharing research data is associated with a higher prevalence of statistical decision errors (gross inconsistencies that change the accept/reject conclusion) in published psychology papers
original_authors: Jelte M. Wicherts; Marjan Bakker; Dylan Molenaar
original_title: Willingness to share research data is related to the strength of the evidence and the quality of reporting of statistical results
replication_authors: Aline Claesen; Wolf Vanpaemel; Anne-Sofie Maerten; Thomas Verliefde; Francis Tuerlinckx; Tom Heyman
replication_title: Data sharing upon request and statistical consistency errors in psychology: A replication of Wicherts, Bakker and Molenaar (2011)
explanation: The replication found no statistically significant relation between data sharing and decision errors (p = 0.816, Fisher's exact test), whereas the original found a significant relationship (p = .015). The Discussion concludes: 'Our replication results did not support the original findings.'

description: Recombinant VSTM1-v2 induces Th17 cell differentiation and activation when added to CD4+ T cells stimulated with anti-CD3, anti-CD28, and a Th17 polarizing cytokine cocktail
original_authors: Xiaohuan Guo; Yanfei Zhang; Pingzhang Wang; Ting Li; Weiwei Fu; Xiaoning Mo; Taiping Shi; Zhixin Zhang; Yingyu Chen; Dalong Ma; Wenling Han
original_title: VSTM1-v2, a novel soluble glycoprotein, promotes the differentiation and activation of Th17 cells
replication_authors: Helen J. von Richthofen; Florianne M. J. Hafkamp; Anouk van Haperen; Esther C. de Jong; Linde Meyaard
replication_title: VSTM1-v2 does not drive human Th17 cell differentiation: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly used the same experimental setup as Guo et al. (CD4+ T cells with anti-CD3, anti-CD28, and Th17 polarizing cytokine mix, same VSTM1-v2 concentrations) and found no effect: 'the Th17 polarizing mix increased the percentage of IL-17+ cells, but there was no effect of VSTM1-v2.' The Discussion states: 'we did not find any effect of VSTM1-v2 on Th17 cell differentiation and activation, unlike the results by Guo et al.'

description: Recombinant VSTM1-v2 promotes Th17 cell differentiation and activation of CD4+ T cells (as a proposed Th17 polarizing cytokine)
original_authors: Xiaohuan Guo; Yanfei Zhang; Pingzhang Wang; Ting Li; Weiwei Fu; Xiaoning Mo; Taiping Shi; Zhixin Zhang; Yingyu Chen; Dalong Ma; Wenling Han
original_title: VSTM1-v2, a novel soluble glycoprotein, promotes the differentiation and activation of Th17 cells
replication_authors: Helen J. von Richthofen; Florianne M. J. Hafkamp; Anouk van Haperen; Esther C. de Jong; Linde Meyaard
replication_title: VSTM1-v2 does not drive human Th17 cell differentiation: A replication study
explanation: The authors tested whether VSTM1-v2 affects Th17 cell differentiation in a DC-driven system (with neutrophils and Candida albicans-activated monocyte-derived DCs), an extended context not used by Guo et al. Both naive and memory CD4+ T cells showed no increase in IL-17+ cells upon VSTM1-v2 addition. The Discussion concludes: 'our results do not support a role for VSTM1-v2 in Th17 cell differentiation.'

description: Approximately 35% of naive subjects conform to an obviously incorrect group judgment in a line-length matching task when surrounded by confederates who give wrong answers
original_authors: Asch, Solomon E.
original_title: Opinions and social pressure
replication_authors: Axel Franzen; Sebastian Mader
replication_title: The power of social influence: A replication and extension of the Asch experiment
explanation: The authors report an average error rate of 33% in the non-incentivized group, which they call 'a perfect replication of Asch's (1955) original 36.8% result (two sample two-sided T-test, t(16) = 0.59, p = 0.57)', indicating no significant difference from the original.

description: Group social pressure causes subjects to conform to the group's stated political opinions at a rate roughly 40 percentage points higher than individual judgment conditions
original_authors: Crutchfield, Richard S.
original_title: Conformity and Character
replication_authors: Axel Franzen; Sebastian Mader
replication_title: The power of social influence: A replication and extension of the Asch experiment
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. The authors find an average conformity rate difference of 38 percentage points across 5 political opinion questions (all 5 statistically significant at p < 0.001, shown in Fig 2), closely matching Crutchfield's (1955) finding of approximately 36-40 percentage point differences. The conclusion explicitly states: 'our study suggests that group pressure is not only influential in the simple line task but also when it comes to political opinions... This result is in line with former evidence by Crutchfield [8].' Classified as 'close extension' rather than 'direct' because the specific political questions differ (Swiss political statements vs. Crutchfield's American 'free speech' statement) and responses were public rather than anonymous. The quantitative correspondence (38% vs ~40%) and clear statistical significance across all 5 items provide unambiguous evidence of a successful replication of the core finding that group pressure generalizes from perceptual judgments to political opinions.

description: Biased search engine results rankings shift the opinions and voting preferences of undecided voters toward the favored candidate
original_authors: Robert Epstein; Ronald E. Robertson
original_title: The search engine manipulation effect (SEME) and its possible impact on the outcomes of elections
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Robert Epstein; Ji Li
replication_title: Can biased search results change people’s opinions about anything at all? a close replication of the Search Engine Manipulation Effect (SEME)
explanation: The authors describe this as a 'close replication of the Search Engine Manipulation Effect (SEME)' using the same Kadoodle mock search engine paradigm and pre/post design, extended to the non-electoral topic of artificial intelligence. The experiment found a significant Manipulation Power of 25.0% (p < 0.001), confirming the SEME effect generalizes beyond voting preferences.

description: Biased search engine results rankings shift the opinions and voting preferences of undecided voters toward the favored candidate
original_authors: Robert Epstein; Ronald E. Robertson
original_title: The search engine manipulation effect (SEME) and its possible impact on the outcomes of elections
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Robert Epstein; Ji Li
replication_title: Can biased search results change people’s opinions about anything at all? a close replication of the Search Engine Manipulation Effect (SEME)
explanation: Using the same Kadoodle mock search engine paradigm and pre/post design extended to the non-electoral topic of fracking, Experiment 2 found a significant Manipulation Power of 30.9% (p < 0.001), successfully replicating the core SEME effect in a new topic domain.

description: Biased search engine results rankings shift the opinions and voting preferences of undecided voters toward the favored candidate
original_authors: Robert Epstein; Ronald E. Robertson
original_title: The search engine manipulation effect (SEME) and its possible impact on the outcomes of elections
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Robert Epstein; Ji Li
replication_title: Can biased search results change people’s opinions about anything at all? a close replication of the Search Engine Manipulation Effect (SEME)
explanation: Using the same Kadoodle mock search engine paradigm and pre/post design extended to the non-electoral topic of sexual orientation (born gay vs. choose to be gay), Experiment 3 found a significant Manipulation Power of 17.8% (p < 0.001), further confirming the SEME effect generalizes beyond voting preferences.

description: Experimentally manipulating status (via a social comparison ladder task) causes individuals assigned to the high-status condition to report higher subjective well-being than those assigned to the low-status condition
original_authors: Cameron Anderson; Michael W. Kraus; Adam D. Galinsky; Dacher Keltner
original_title: The local-ladder effect
replication_authors: Cameron Anderson; John Angus D. Hildreth
replication_title: Status and subjective well-being: A conceptual replication and extension of Anderson et al. (2012)
explanation: The authors explicitly call this 'a conceptual replication of [3]' using a different status manipulation (false group feedback rather than a comparison ladder). Study 1 found a significant main effect of own status on SWB, F(1,222)=24.91, p<.001, η²=.101, and the Discussion states 'This finding provides a conceptual replication of [3]'.

description: Experimentally manipulating status (via a social comparison ladder task) causes individuals assigned to the high-status condition to report higher subjective well-being than those assigned to the low-status condition
original_authors: Cameron Anderson; Michael W. Kraus; Adam D. Galinsky; Dacher Keltner
original_title: The local-ladder effect
replication_authors: Cameron Anderson; John Angus D. Hildreth
replication_title: Status and subjective well-being: A conceptual replication and extension of Anderson et al. (2012)
explanation: Study 2 (preregistered) replicated the same conceptual finding: 'in the control condition, participants again had higher subjective well-being when they had higher rather than lower status, F(1,200)=12.63, p<.001, η²=.059'. The Discussion confirms 'Two studies, one preregistered, found that individuals' status had a causal effect on their subjective well-being. This finding provides a conceptual replication of [3]'.

description: Individuals depicted holding everyday objects with incidentally lethal affordances (e.g., a kitchen knife) are perceived as higher in state anger, more anger-prone, and more socially unpleasant than those holding contextually equivalent non-lethal objects
original_authors: Colin Holbrook; Andrew Galperin; Daniel M. T. Fessler; Kerri L. Johnson; Gregory A. Bryant; Martie G. Haselton
original_title: If looks could kill: anger attributions are intensified by affordances for doing harm
replication_authors: Cody Moser; Richard Ellk; Ayonna Jones; Colin Holbrook
replication_title: Possessing potential weapons (still) heightens anger perception: Replicating and extending a test of error management theory
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion: 'we successfully replicated previously documented shifts in attributions of state anger and related antisocial traits (i.e., anger-proneness, social unpleasantness) caused by manipulation of a highly subtle contextual determinant.' State anger, trait anger, and trait unpleasantness all showed significant effects in the expected direction, though trait fear, disgust, and dishonesty did not replicate.

description: Gender differences in vocational interests (preferences) are the dominant factor explaining sex segregation in college major choices in Germany, accounting for approximately 37% of the gender gap, while constraints such as relative math grades and peer approval play only minor roles
original_authors: Fabian Ochsenfeld
original_title: Preferences, constraints, and the process of sex segregation in college majors: A choice analysis
replication_authors: Alexander Patzina; Carina Toussaint
replication_title: Assessing the Importance of Sample Choice and Selectivity for Sex Segregation in College Majors: A Replication of Ochsenfeld (2016)
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm their replication validates the original findings: 'The most important result from our replication study is that [Ochsenfeld 2016] findings are not biased by the two forms of collider bias studied here. Therefore, gender differences in preference (i.e., vocational interests) are the most important factors in explaining sex segregation in higher education.' The explanatory power of the model even increases slightly when using panel data (52.8% vs. 46% in original).

description: Interpersonal facet ratings of the PCL-R are positively and uniquely associated with cocaine dependence symptom counts in incarcerated men, over and above the other facets of psychopathy
original_authors: Zach Walsh; Lindsay C. Allen; David S. Kosson
original_title: Beyond social deviance: Substance use disorders and the dimensions of psychopathy
replication_authors: Chelsea L. Brieman; William J. McGarrigle; Lora M. Cope; Kent A. Kiehl; David S. Kosson
replication_title: Clarifying Relations Between Core Features of Psychopathy and Substance (Mis)use: A Replication and Extension in Two Large Independent Samples
explanation: The paper explicitly states its first aim was 'to replicate previously reported relations between the interpersonal traits of psychopathy and the (mis)use of cocaine (Coid et al., 2009a, Coid et al., 2009b; Walsh et al., 2007).' The Discussion confirms: 'Both studies replicated findings from previous research (Coid et al., 2009a, 2009b; Walsh et al., 2007) linking interpersonal facet ratings to cocaine outcomes.' In Study One, interpersonal traits were positively associated with cocaine dependence symptom counts (Rate Ratio = 1.06, p = .030), and this remained significant after controlling for the other three PCL-R facets (RR = 1.08, p = .024). In Study Two, interpersonal traits predicted greater likelihood of cocaine use (OR = 0.79 for abstinence, p < .001), also surviving facet-level controls (OR = 0.82, p = .011). The authors note consistency across five independent samples. Walsh et al. (2007) is cited alongside Coid et al. (2009a, 2009b) as the replication targets; Walsh et al. is the primary four-facet-model study reporting this specific interpersonal-cocaine link.

description: Affective facet ratings of the PCL-R are negatively (protectively) associated with substance use disorder outcomes in incarcerated men, reflecting reduced risk for substance misuse among those high in affective psychopathy features
original_authors: Zach Walsh; Lindsay C. Allen; David S. Kosson
original_title: Beyond social deviance: Substance use disorders and the dimensions of psychopathy
replication_authors: Chelsea L. Brieman; William J. McGarrigle; Lora M. Cope; Kent A. Kiehl; David S. Kosson
replication_title: Clarifying Relations Between Core Features of Psychopathy and Substance (Mis)use: A Replication and Extension in Two Large Independent Samples
explanation: Reviewer assessment: 'medium' confidence and 'inconclusive' result are retained because the ambiguity is genuine. The paper found unique negative (protective) associations between affective facet ratings and substance dependence severity in both samples, but the effects were inconsistent in which substance class was affected: Study One showed a unique negative relation only with illicit substance severity (RR = 0.94, p = .015 at Step Two), while Study Two showed a robust negative relation with alcohol dependence severity (RR = 0.97, p = .032; RR = 0.95, p = .010 at Step Two) but not illicit substance severity. Across both studies, only 3 of 8 regressions yielded significant unique negative relations. The authors themselves describe the prior evidence as 'mixed' and frame this aim as exploratory ('we explored the possibility'). The Discussion states there 'may be some robustness to these relationships' and notes the appearance of effects 'for different substance classes (alcohol vs. illicit substances) in the two samples raises the possibility that... affective features may be more related to a general reduction in severity of dependence than to reduced dependence on a specific kind of substance.' This is cautiously supportive but not a clear-cut replication. Walsh et al. (2007) is one of three studies cited as reporting the protective effect (alongside Reardon et al., 2002 [41] and Schulz et al., 2016 [44]); Walsh et al. is the primary four-facet-model study reporting this specific negative affective-SUD link.

description: Adolescents seeking treatment at a gender identity unit display levels of general identity development (measured with AIDA) similar to those of same-aged population peers, with about a third showing signs of identity diffusion
original_authors: Nina Haid-Stecher; Martin Fuchs; Nora Ortner; Kathrin Sevecke
original_title: TransIdentität - die Entwicklung der Identität bei transidenten Jugendlichen
replication_authors: Rasa Barkauskienė; Carla Sharp; Sophie Kerr; Elena Gaudiešiūtė; Kirstin Goth; Gabrielė Skabeikytė-Norkienė
replication_title: Examining the Validity of the Levels of Personality Functioning Questionnaire for Adolescents Aged 12-18 (LOPF-Q 12-18): A Replication and Extension With a Sample of Lithuanian Adolescents
explanation: The Finnish study used the same AIDA tool and identical design (GD adolescents vs. general population) as the Austrian Haid-Stecher et al. (2020) study in a new country context. The authors explicitly state: 'Finnish adolescents with features of GD in our study showed no marked pathological identity development as a group, which concurs with the results of the only study on the subject so far, conducted on Austrian youth.'

description: Public sector managers and professionals are susceptible to framing bias when evaluating performance information, particularly when metrics are presented with negative framing
original_authors: Javier Fuenzalida; Gregg G. Van Ryzin; Asmus Leth Olsen
original_title: Are managers susceptible to framing effects? An experimental study of professional judgment of performance metrics
replication_authors: Minrui Zhu; Gilad Feldman
replication_title: Revisiting the Links Between Numeracy and Decision Making: Replication Registered Report of Peters et al. (2006) With an Extension Examining Confidence
explanation: The replication confirmed that Brazilian public servants are susceptible to framing bias overall (hypothesis not rejected), but found a different pattern from the original: this study found stronger bias in POSITIVE scenarios (83% in scenario 3), whereas Fuenzalida et al. (2020) found effects particularly in negative scenarios. The authors explicitly note: 'Resultado diferente da encontrada nesta pesquisa, uma vez que o grau de suscetibilidade ao viés de enquadramento foi superior nos cenários positivos.'

description: Both syntactic violations in language and harmonic inconsistencies in music elicit the P600 ERP component with similar amplitude and scalp distribution, suggesting shared neural processing resources
original_authors: Aniruddh D. Patel; Edward Gibson; Jennifer Ratner; Mireille Besson; Phillip J. Holcomb
original_title: Processing syntactic relations in language and music: an event-related potential study
replication_authors: Joshua De Leeuw
replication_title: Similar event-related potentials to structural violations in music and language
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract that 'the results of our replication are largely consistent with the conclusions of the original study,' finding P600 responses to violations in both language and music. While some minor differences emerged (e.g., no P600 at occipital sites for music, RATN not replicated), the core finding of similar ERP components for structural violations in both domains was supported.

description: Supporters of the Iraq War in online discussion forums display greater external focus and more simplistic thinking style (lower cognitive complexity), while opponents display greater internal focus, cognitive processing, and use of negative emotion words
original_authors: Jo Ann A. Abe
original_title: Cognitive-affective styles associated with position on war
original_journal: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Kayla N. Jordan; Erin M. Buchanan; William E. Padfield
replication_title: The Language of War: A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013)
explanation: The authors tested Abe's (2012) hypotheses about internal/external attentional focus and cognitive complexity in Congressional speeches. Results were inconsistent: H2 (internal focus for war opponents) was 'supported' only in the Kosovo Senate study and explicitly described as 'failing to replicate [2]' in the General Discussion. H1 (external focus for supporters) was only weakly supported in some contexts. The authors concluded 'Hypothesis 2 received the weakest, most inconsistent support of any of our hypotheses with strong evidence for the effect found only in the Senate debate of the Kosovo resolution failing to replicate [2].'

description: Speeches by world and political group leaders preceding violent acts of aggression show greater external focus (more first person plural pronouns), less internal focus (fewer first person singular pronouns), and lower cognitive complexity compared to speeches preceding nonviolent acts of resistance
original_authors: David Matsumoto; Hyisung C. Hwang
original_title: The language of political aggression
original_journal: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Kayla N. Jordan; Erin M. Buchanan; William E. Padfield
replication_title: The Language of War: A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Abe (2012) and Matsumoto and Hwang (2013)
explanation: The authors found consistent support for H3 (lower cognitive complexity among war supporters), explicitly stating 'we found consistent evidence that supporters of war measures show less cognitive complexity in their speeches than those on the opposing side (Hypothesis 3) replicating part of the Matsumoto and Hwang (2013) study.' However, H1 (external focus) was strongly supported only for the Iraq War debate, and inconsistently so for Kosovo and Libya. The word 'part' and the inconsistencies across conflicts indicate an inconclusive overall result.

description: White Americans perceive that Whites are now the victims of discrimination more than Blacks are, rating anti-White bias as a bigger societal problem than anti-Black bias in the United States today
original_authors: Norton, Michael; Sommers, Samuel
original_title: Whites see racism as a zero-sum game that they are now losing
replication_authors: Lawrence James Zigerell
replication_title: Perceived Discrimination against Black Americans and White Americans
explanation: Study 1 found that only 10% of non-Hispanic Whites rated discrimination against Whites greater than against Blacks in the ANES 2012 data, while 54% rated discrimination against Blacks as greater — directly contradicting Norton & Sommers' conclusion that 'Whites have now come to view anti-White bias as a bigger societal problem than anti-Black bias.'

description: White Americans perceive that Whites are now the victims of discrimination more than Blacks are, rating anti-White bias as a bigger societal problem than anti-Black bias in the United States today
original_authors: Norton, Michael; Sommers, Samuel
original_title: Whites see racism as a zero-sum game that they are now losing
replication_authors: Lawrence James Zigerell
replication_title: Perceived Discrimination against Black Americans and White Americans
explanation: Study 2 (preregistered) found that only 7% of non-Hispanic Whites in the ANES 2016 data reported greater perceived discrimination against Whites than against Blacks, while 66% reported the reverse, with confidence intervals non-overlapping — failing to replicate Norton & Sommers' finding that Whites perceive more anti-White than anti-Black discrimination.

description: White Americans perceive that Whites are now the victims of discrimination more than Blacks are, rating anti-White bias as a bigger societal problem than anti-Black bias in the United States today
original_authors: Norton, Michael; Sommers, Samuel
original_title: Whites see racism as a zero-sum game that they are now losing
replication_authors: Lawrence James Zigerell
replication_title: Perceived Discrimination against Black Americans and White Americans
explanation: Study 3 (preregistered YouGov 2017 survey) found that only 12% of non-Hispanic Whites selected White Americans as more often the victim of discrimination, while 43% selected Black Americans, with p < .001 — directly contradicting the Norton & Sommers finding and consistent with the failures in Studies 1 and 2.

description: Mortality salience (death reminders via essay-writing task) increases preference for national patriotic values as measured by evaluation of pro- vs. anti-patriotic essays
original_authors: Abram Rosenblatt; Jeff Greenberg; Sheldon Solomon; Tom Pyszczynski; Deborah Lyon
original_title: Evidence for terror management theory: I. The effects of mortality salience on reactions to those who violate or uphold cultural values
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Bjørn Sætrevik; Hallgeir Sjåstad
replication_title: Mortality salience effects fail to replicate in traditional and novel measures
explanation: Experiment 1 (N = 101 Norwegian lab participants) used the traditional MS essay paradigm from Rosenblatt et al. (1989) but added Stroop tasks and novel essays. The key hypothesis E1H3 was not supported: 'E1H3 showed no significant main effect of MS on the rating of patriotic essays' (p = .58, d = .04).

description: Mortality salience (death reminders via essay-writing task followed by a mood delay task) increases preference for national patriotic values as measured by evaluation of pro- vs. anti-patriotic essays
original_authors: Jeff Greenberg; Tom Pyszczynski; Sheldon Solomon; Linda Simon; Michael Breus
original_title: Role of consciousness and accessibility of death-related thoughts in mortality salience effects
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Bjørn Sætrevik; Hallgeir Sjåstad
replication_title: Mortality salience effects fail to replicate in traditional and novel measures
explanation: Experiment 2 (N = 784 US online participants) is described as 'a direct replication of the prototypical MS study (see e.g. [24])'. E2H2 was not supported: 'there was no significant difference between the MS and control group on the focal outcome measure of national patriotism' (p = .91, d = 0.01).

description: Mortality salience increases ingroup identification (with one's national group) in an Italian sample
original_authors: Emanuele Castano; Vincent Yzerbyt; Maria-Paola Paladino; Simona Sacchi
original_title: I belong, therefore, I exist: Ingroup identification, ingroup entitativity, and ingroup bias
replication_authors: Bjørn Sætrevik; Hallgeir Sjåstad
replication_title: Mortality salience effects fail to replicate in traditional and novel measures
explanation: Experiment 2 tested whether MS increases American ingroup identification (E2H1) and the Discussion states this 'constitutes a failed replication of the results from a previous study in Italy, using similar measures [12]'. The result was not significant (p = .46, d = 0.05).

description: Children's engagement in book reading (initiations, responses, passive engagement) does not consistently vary based on whether the book's protagonist shares the child's race, but children show a preference for books featuring same-race protagonists
original_authors: Jessica K. Hardy; Robert Pennington; Renea Griffin; Jill Jacobi-Vessels
original_title: Comparing the effects of protagonist race on preschoolers' engagement in book reading
replication_authors: Jessica Hardy; Robert Pennington; Abigail Black; Tianhong Yao
replication_title: Impact of Protagonist Race on Preschoolers’ Engagement and Preferences in Book Reading: A Systematic Replication
replication_journal: Single Case in the Social Sciences
explanation: The replication (conducted by the same author team) found the same pattern as the original: no consistent differences in engagement based on protagonist race, and a same-race preference for book selection. The Discussion states 'children's engagement did not differ based on whether the book protagonist appeared to share the same race as the child' and 'all [four children with sufficient preference data] demonstrated a marked preference for books with a same-race protagonist,' consistent with the original findings.

description: Vulnerable narcissism is positively associated with hostile attribution bias (measured via HSNS and AQ Hostility Scale), such that higher vulnerable narcissism predicts greater tendency to attribute hostile intentions to others
original_authors: Ashley A. Hansen-Brown; Stephanie D. Freis
original_title: Assuming the worst: hostile attribution bias in vulnerable narcissists
replication_authors: Dörr, Johanna Marie; Röseler, Lukas
replication_title: Überprüfung des Zusammenhangs von vulnerablem Narzissmus und dem feindseligen Attributionsstil: Eine präregistrierte, originalgetreue Replikation der Studie von Hansen-Brown & Freis (2019)
explanation: The replication found r(82) = .50, 95% CI [.325, .649], p < .001, confirming the positive association between vulnerable narcissism and hostile attribution bias found in the original (r = .61). The authors state: 'Der Befund der Originalstudie, dass vulnerabler Narzissmus und der feindselige Attributionsstil positiv zusammenhängen, konnte bestätigt werden' (The finding of the original study that vulnerable narcissism and hostile attribution bias are positively related was confirmed).

description: Grandiose narcissism is not associated with hostile attribution bias (measured via NPI and AQ Hostility Scale), in contrast to vulnerable narcissism
original_authors: Ashley A. Hansen-Brown; Stephanie D. Freis
original_title: Assuming the worst: hostile attribution bias in vulnerable narcissists
replication_authors: Dörr, Johanna Marie; Röseler, Lukas
replication_title: Überprüfung des Zusammenhangs von vulnerablem Narzissmus und dem feindseligen Attributionsstil: Eine präregistrierte, originalgetreue Replikation der Studie von Hansen-Brown & Freis (2019)
explanation: The replication found r(82) = -.08, p = .482 (non-significant), consistent with the original direction, but the equivalence test failed to rule out a meaningful association (90% CI [-.255, .104] exceeded the SESOI of .10 in both directions). The authors conclude: 'Die Hypothese 2...konnte in der vorliegenden Replikation nicht bestätigt werden' (Hypothesis 2 could not be confirmed in this replication), citing insufficient power due to small sample size.

description: People are willing to accept a longer drive (30 minutes) to receive a tax-related discount (8% tax-free) at a farther store rather than a slightly larger tax-unrelated discount (9% regular discount) at the same farther store
original_authors: Sussman, Abigail; Olivola, Christopher
original_title: Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs
replication_authors: Brandt, Mark; Kogler, Christoph; Kirchler, Erich; Dezső, Linda; Olsen, Jerome
replication_title: Registered Report for Replication of Sussman and Olivola (2011)
explanation: The replication found no significant difference between conditions in the USA (rΦ=.02, 95% CI [-.06, .10], p=.685). The authors state: 'replication results of Experiment 1 for both the US and the UK sample were informative of failed replications.'

description: People are willing to accept a longer drive (30 minutes) to receive a tax-related discount (8% tax-free) at a farther store rather than a slightly larger tax-unrelated discount (9% regular discount) at the same farther store, tested in the UK value added tax system
original_authors: Sussman, Abigail; Olivola, Christopher
original_title: Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs
replication_authors: Brandt, Mark; Kogler, Christoph; Kirchler, Erich; Dezső, Linda; Olsen, Jerome
replication_title: Registered Report for Replication of Sussman and Olivola (2011)
explanation: The UK replication of Experiment 1 found no significant difference between conditions (rΦ=.01, 95% CI [-.07, .09], p=.823). The authors state that 'replication results of Experiment 1 for both the US and the UK sample were informative of failed replications.'

description: People are willing to wait longer in line to receive a tax-related discount ('axe-the-tax' sale) than an equivalent tax-unrelated discount ('customer rewards' sale)
original_authors: Sussman, Abigail; Olivola, Christopher
original_title: Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs
replication_authors: Brandt, Mark; Kogler, Christoph; Kirchler, Erich; Dezső, Linda; Olsen, Jerome
replication_title: Registered Report for Replication of Sussman and Olivola (2011)
explanation: The US replication of Experiment 2 found a significant effect in the expected direction (r=.09, 95% CI [.01, .16], p=.012). The authors conclude: 'replication results of Experiment 2 were successful in the USA.'

description: People are willing to wait longer in line to receive a tax-related discount ('axe-the-tax' sale) than an equivalent tax-unrelated discount ('customer rewards' sale), tested in the UK value added tax system
original_authors: Sussman, Abigail; Olivola, Christopher
original_title: Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs
replication_authors: Brandt, Mark; Kogler, Christoph; Kirchler, Erich; Dezső, Linda; Olsen, Jerome
replication_title: Registered Report for Replication of Sussman and Olivola (2011)
explanation: The UK replication of Experiment 2 did not find a significant effect (r=.03, 95% CI [-.04, .11], p=.197), but the effect was also not significantly smaller than what would be detectable with the original sample size. The authors conclude: 'replication results of Experiment 2 were successful in the USA but inconclusive in the UK.'

description: Sentiment in political Twitter messages is positively associated with retweet quantity, negatively associated with retweet time lag (emotionally charged content spreads faster), and the negative sentiment moderates these relationships more strongly than positive sentiment
original_authors: Stefan Stieglitz; Linh Dang-Xuan
original_title: Emotions and information diffusion in social media - sentiment of microblogs and sharing behavior
replication_authors: Linus Hagemann; Olga Abramova
replication_title: Emotions and Information Diffusion on Social Media: A Replication in the Context of Political Communication on Twitter
explanation: The methodological replication (using SentiStrength) supported H1 (sentiment positively linked to retweet quantity, b=0.139, p<0.001) but failed to support H2 (sentiment insignificant for retweet speed) and H3 (negativity moderation insignificant). The authors conclude results are 'only partially consistent with the initial findings.'

description: Sentiment in political Twitter messages is positively associated with retweet quantity, negatively associated with retweet time lag (emotionally charged content spreads faster), and the negative sentiment moderates these relationships more strongly than positive sentiment
original_authors: Stefan Stieglitz; Linh Dang-Xuan
original_title: Emotions and information diffusion in social media - sentiment of microblogs and sharing behavior
replication_authors: Linus Hagemann; Olga Abramova
replication_title: Emotions and Information Diffusion on Social Media: A Replication in the Context of Political Communication on Twitter
explanation: The conceptual replication using LIWC for sentiment assessment found the opposite of H1 — overall sentiment was significantly negatively related to retweet quantity (b=-0.011, p=0.003), while H2 and H3 were also not supported. The authors note LIWC 'yielded a different conclusion on H1, suggesting that more neutral content receives more retweets.'

description: Dynamic capabilities (resources, processes, and values) positively affect digital platform capacity and firm performance in the newspaper industry facing digital disruption, with digital platform capacity mediating the relationship between dynamic capabilities and the number of digital products/services offered
original_authors: Jahangir Karimi; Zhiping Walter
original_title: The role of dynamic capabilities in responding to digital disruption: A factor-based study of the newspaper industry
replication_authors: Angélica Pigola; Priscila Rezende da Costa; Evandro Luis Lopes
replication_title: On Behalf of Digital Innovation: A Replication Study on International and National Executive Search Consultancy Firms
explanation: The authors explicitly describe their findings as consistent with the original: 'These findings are in line with [39] results demonstrating that DC is a strong predictor of performance for firms.' All four hypotheses from the original model were supported with significant path coefficients, and the authors describe 'similar results to those shown by [39]'.

description: Parental self-esteem influences children's depression, autonomy, and career consciousness through the mediating effects of parenting behaviors (respecting children's thoughts and positive responsiveness), based on triad data from junior high school students and their parents
original_authors: Jalalizadeh M.; Roesch HRM; Korkes F.; Dien-Trinh Q.; Reis LO
original_title: The effects of parents' self-esteem on children's depression, autonomy, and career consciousness: Focusing on the mediating effect of parenting behaviors
original_journal: Bulletin of the Graduate School of Education
replication_authors: Yukiko Nishimura; Haruka Shimizu; Ken’ichiro Nakashima
replication_title: Effects of parental self-esteem on depression, autonomy, and career consciousness among children: A replication study focusing on the mediation of parenting behaviors
replication_journal: THE JAPANESE JOURNAL OF EXPERIMENTAL SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'this study did not validate the model obtained by [Nishimura et al. (2022)]' and note in the Discussion that the full mediation model was not replicated. They characterized the study as a conceptual replication due to using a different autonomy scale (JEAS) from the original, and confirmed only partial overlap in the mediation paths.

description: Empathy is positively associated with individualizing moral foundations (care, fairness), need for closure is positively associated with binding moral foundations (loyalty, authority, purity), and both indirectly affect political conservatism and system justification through moral foundations
original_authors: Michael Strupp-Levitsky; Sharareh Noorbaloochi; Andrew Shipley; John T. Jost
original_title: Moral "foundations" as the product of motivated social cognition: Empathy and other psychological underpinnings of ideological divergence
replication_authors: Goun Park; Keiko Ishii
replication_title: Empathy and need for closure are linked to moral foundations and political orientation: A replication study in Japan
replication_journal: THE JAPANESE JOURNAL OF EXPERIMENTAL SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY
explanation: The paper replicates core findings of Strupp-Levitsky et al. (2020, Study 2) in a Japanese sample using identical measures. Key paths (empathy → individualizing foundations, need for closure → binding foundations, mediation of political orientation) were replicated, but contrary findings also emerged: empathy was additionally positively associated with binding foundations and need for closure with individualizing foundations — both absent in the original. The authors describe results as partially consistent and partially contrary.

description: The 'healing attempt' brief digital music-based mindfulness intervention decreases state anxiety with high feasibility and acceptability in Black Americans with elevated race-based anxiety
original_authors: Grant Jones; Felipe Herrmann; Matthew K. Nock
original_title: A digital music-based mindfulness intervention for Black Americans with elevated race-based anxiety: a multiple-baseline pilot study
replication_authors: Grant Jones; Franchesca Castro-Ramirez; Maha Al-Suwaidi; Taylor McGuire; Felipe Herrmann
replication_title: A Brief, Digital Music-Based Mindfulness Intervention for Black Americans With Elevated Race-Based Anxiety and Little-to-No Meditation Experience (“healing attempt"): Replication and Extension Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'These results are in line with our prior 2 feasibility studies of 'healing attempt,' which also found the intervention to decrease state anxiety and increase mindfulness/self-compassion with high feasibility and acceptability.' All Tau-U values for state anxiety were negative and significant (P<.001), replicating the anxiety-reduction finding.

description: The 'healing attempt' intervention decreases state anxiety and simultaneously increases mindfulness and self-compassion with high feasibility and acceptability in Black Americans with elevated race-based anxiety
original_authors: Jones, G.; Castro-Ramirez, F.; Mcguire, T.; Al-Suwaidi, M.; Herrmann, F.; Nock, M.
original_title: "healing attempt": a digital music-based mindfulness intervention for race-based anxiety in Black American adults (a replication and extension)
replication_authors: Grant Jones; Franchesca Castro-Ramirez; Maha Al-Suwaidi; Taylor McGuire; Felipe Herrmann
replication_title: A Brief, Digital Music-Based Mindfulness Intervention for Black Americans With Elevated Race-Based Anxiety and Little-to-No Meditation Experience (“healing attempt"): Replication and Extension Study
explanation: The current study replicates all key findings from the second prior study: state anxiety decreased (Tau-U range: -0.93 to -0.66; P<.001) and mindfulness/self-compassion increased (Tau-U range: 0.57-0.86; P<.001), with high feasibility scores. Authors conclude: 'This study adds to the evidence that 'healing attempt' may be a feasible intervention for race-based anxiety in the Black community.'

description: Task difficulty moderates the effect of audience presence on cockroach performance: audience presence facilitates performance on a simple runway task but impairs performance on a complex maze task (Audience × Task Difficulty interaction)
original_authors: Robert B. Zajonc; Alexander Heingartner; Edward M. Herman
original_title: Social enhancement and impairment of performance in the cockroach
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Halfmann, Emma; Bredehöft, Janne; Häusser, Jan Alexander
replication_title: Halfmann_OpenPracticesDisclosure_rev – Supplemental material for Replicating Roaches: A Preregistered Direct Replication of Zajonc, Heingartner, and Herman’s (1969) Social-Facilitation Study
explanation: The replication found no evidence for the critical Audience × Task Difficulty interaction (F(1,116)=0.02, p=.882, ηp²=.00, BF01=3.88), and audience presence produced inhibition in both simple and complex tasks. The authors conclude: 'there was no evidence for a social-facilitation effect' and describe 'robust evidence against the social-facilitation hypothesis.'

description: Myocardial infarction patients in a coronary care unit perceive technical/competency-related nurse behaviors (e.g., 'knows how to handle equipment') as the most important caring behaviors, as measured by the Caring Behaviors Assessment (CBA)
original_authors: Sherill Nones Cronin; Bobbi Harrison
original_title: Importance of nurse caring behaviors as perceived by patients after myocardial infarction
replication_authors: Ward, Larae McClellan
replication_title: Importance of nurse caring behaviors as perceived by patients after myocardial infarction: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The design and methodology of the study was unchanged from the original study' and conclude that 'the findings of this study supported the findings of the original study.' Comparison tables (Tables 15-17) show substantial consistency in CBA item rankings and subscale scores between the two studies, including an identical mean score of 3.80 for the 'Expression of positive/negative feelings' subscale.

description: Gender of the respondent, gender of the child, and response of the child (encouraging, passive, or resistant) affect attributions of responsibility to both the child victim and the adult offender in child sexual abuse scenarios
original_authors: Sylvia D. Broussard; William G. Wagner
original_title: Child sexual abuse: Who is to blame?
replication_authors: Busà R.; Iannolo G.; Douradinha B.; Pagano D.; Gallina A.; Cappello G.; La Rocca A.; Gruttadauria S.; Conaldi PG; Badami E.
replication_title: The attribution of responsibility for child sexual abuse in a New Zealand setting : a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the present results only partially replicate the findings of Broussard and Wagner (1988).' Some effects were replicated (child response significantly affecting responsibility attributed to the child; no significant effects of child gender or adult gender), while several other effects were not (contrary to Broussard and Wagner, respondent gender significantly affected attribution to the adult; no significant interactive effects were found in this study whereas several were found in the original).

description: Phone respondents have higher rates of item non-substantive response (e.g., 'Don't know', 'Prefer not to answer') compared to web/email respondents in surveys of residential energy efficiency program participants, even when controlling for demographic and background factors.
original_authors: Michael Soszynski; Ryan Bliss
original_title: Does survey administration mode relate to non-substantive responses? A comparison of email versus phone administration of a residential utility-sponsored energy efficiency program survey
replication_authors: Michael Soszynski; Ryan Bliss
replication_title: Survey Mode and Item Non-Substantive Response: Insights from a Replication Study and Other Recent Trials
explanation: The replication produced mixed results: the logistic regression on whether respondents had 'at least one non-substantive response' was not statistically significant (p=0.49), failing to replicate the original finding; however, the linear regression on 'average portion of survey with non-substantive responses' did show a significant difference (phone 9% vs web 4%, p<0.01). The authors note that 'All three of our studies have found evidence that phone respondents had more item non-substantive response than web respondents, though the level and type of evidence has varied.'

description: Keeping a listening log motivates ESL learners toward autonomous learning by raising their metacognitive awareness and encouraging self-monitoring of listening performance
original_authors: Kemp, Jenny
original_title: The listening log: Motivating autonomous learning
replication_authors: Bozorgian, Hossein; Muhammadpour, Meysam; Qara, Raheleh
replication_title: EFL Listening Log: A Conceptual Replication of Kemps (2010) Study on Motivating Autonomous Learning
replication_journal: Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research
explanation: The authors explicitly state their findings 'are in total alignment with those of [27] study' and conclude that 'the findings of [27] study were found to be robust and transferable to other contexts and populations.' The same six-factor evidence framework was applied, with comparable positive outcomes across all six categories.

description: Individuals with sequential motor processing deficits (as measured by slower alternating than repetitive diadochokinesis) show corresponding deficits in other tasks requiring high sequential processing loads (nonword imitation, nonword reading/decoding, spelling, verbal processing) but not in tasks with low sequential processing loads, in a multigenerational family with childhood apraxia of speech
original_authors: Beate Peter; Le Button; Carol Stoel-Gammon; Kathy Chapman; Wendy H. Raskind
original_title: Deficits in sequential processing manifest in motor and linguistic tasks in a multigenerational family with childhood apraxia of speech
replication_authors: Le Button; Beate Peter; Carol Stoel-Gammon; Wendy H. Raskind
replication_title: Associations among measures of sequential processing in motor and linguistics tasks in adults with and without a family history of childhood apraxia of speech: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results from the present study replicate the findings in the companion study' and 'The qualitative error analyses from the real word and nonword imitation tasks replicate the patterns described in the companion study (Peter et al., in press) to a very close extent.' The paper is also explicitly titled 'A replication study.' In both studies, affected participants scored lower on high-sequential-processing tasks but not low-sequential-processing tasks, and produced more phoneme sequencing errors during imitation tasks.
