replication_authors: Black DS; Sussman S.; Johnson CA; Milam J.
replication_title: Psychometric Assessment of the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) Among Chinese Adolescents
explanation: Independent review confirms 'success' classification with high confidence. The paper (Black et al., 2012) explicitly and unambiguously replicates the 15-item unidimensional factor structure of the MAAS from Brown & Ryan (2003) among Chinese adolescents (N=5,287). The Discussion states: 'The 15-item single-dimension structure of the MAAS as reported by Brown and Ryan (2003) had adequate fit, and all measured indicators loaded significantly on the MAAS latent factor.' CFA fit indices meet conventional thresholds (CFI=.93, TLI=.93, RMSEA=.07, SRMR=.04 at Time 1), and the structure was replicated at Time 2. Reliability was strong (Cronbach's α=.89-.93). Convergent/discriminant, nomological, and incremental validity all supported the original findings. The authors conclude the MAAS is 'a psychometrically sound measure of trait mindfulness among the typical adolescents residing in China.' Subdiscipline corrected from 'psychophysiology' to 'psychometrics' as this is a measurement validation study. Classified as 'close' replication because the same instrument was used in a new population (Chinese adolescents vs. original US adults) with a Chinese translation.

description: 5-HTTLPR genotype interacts with childhood trauma to produce biased information processing (e.g., memory bias) as an intermediate phenotype for depression in remitted depressed patients
original_authors: Vrijsen JN; van Oostrom I.; Arias-Vásquez A.; Franke B.; Becker ES; Speckens A.
original_title: Association between genes, stressful childhood events and processing bias in depression vulnerable individuals

replication_title: Automatic approach-avoidance tendencies as a candidate intermediate phenotype for depression: Associations with childhood trauma and the 5-HTTLPR transporter polymorphism
explanation: Reviewer verified: The paper describes itself as a 'conceptual replication' of earlier G x E intermediate phenotype findings (refs 10,11,14,16-22), extending from memory/attention bias to approach-avoidance tendencies. Vrijsen et al. 2014 (ref 20) is retained as the primary replication target because it is the most closely related study — same research group, same 'Info in Genes' sample, same gene (5-HTTLPR) x childhood trauma design — though the paper frames itself as replicating a body of work rather than one specific study. The citation sentence does not name a single original study because the replication targets the general G x E pattern across multiple studies. Result: 'inconclusive' is appropriate because the authors themselves describe results as 'partly support[ing]' earlier findings. The key three-way interaction (Genotype x Childhood trauma x Facial expression) was significant (p=.034, eta-sq=.042), showing S/Lg-carriers with childhood trauma avoided sad faces more than LaLa homozygotes with trauma. However, multiple hypothesized patterns were absent or contradicted: (1) no main effect of childhood trauma (contrary to expectation and ref 9), (2) unexpected avoidance in LaLa homozygotes WITHOUT trauma, (3) no avoidance of angry faces (expected based on ref 42), and (4) S/Lg-carriers with trauma did not differ from those without trauma. The authors repeatedly describe results as 'preliminary,' 'tentative,' and 'explorative,' stating 'replications are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.' Confidence remains medium because the ambiguity is genuine — the paper itself does not resolve whether this is a successful or failed replication.

description: Models using perceived ideology, status, and choice of target groups can predict the direction and magnitude of the ideology-prejudice association across multiple target groups, with ideology-only and ideology+status+choice models being most accurate (lowest MSE), while status-only and choice-only models perform no better than a null model

replication_title: Enhanced recall of disgusting relative to frightening photographs is not due to organisation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Replicating previous results [8][63](van Hooff, van Buuringen, M'rabet, de Gier, & van Zalingen, 2014), participants were slower to indicate the location of the line when it co-occurred with a disgust photograph compared to a fear photograph (t[29] = p = 0.007, d_z = 0.53)'. Reference [63] is Van Hooff, Devue, Vieweg, & Theeuwes (2013), which specifically demonstrated that disgust-evoking images hold attention more than fear-evoking images, the finding directly replicated here.

description: Six semantic and experiential variables (familiarity, AoA, SER, imageability, semantic transparency, and lexeme meaning dominance) predict English compound word processing times in lexical decision and word naming tasks
original_authors: Barbara J. Juhasz; Yun-Hsuan Lai; Michelle L. Woodcock
original_title: A database of 629 English compound words: Ratings of familiarity, lexeme meaning dominance, semantic transparency, age-of-acquisition, imageability, and sensory experience
replication_authors: Barbara J. Juhasz
replication_title: Experience with compound words influences their processing: An eye movement investigation with English compound words
explanation: The current study tested the same six variables from Juhasz et al. (2015) on eye movement fixation durations during reading (rather than lexical decision/naming). Familiarity and AoA significantly predicted fixation durations (replicating those effects), and SER showed a significant early effect; however, imageability, semantic transparency, and LMD did not significantly influence reading times, yielding mixed results across the six variables.

description: Movie review-based language tasks improve learner motivation and perceived L2 production in EFL classroom settings, as measured by a five-question participant survey
original_authors: Masaaki Oki
original_title: Implementing lessons based on movie reviews
replication_authors: Kent David Bradley; Michael Jones
replication_title: Using Smartphones to Create and Deliver Learner-Generated Video Content for Tasks
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were able to successfully replicate Oki's study and found the same results (2011b) in the Korean context.' The survey results mirrored those of the original Oki (2011b) study, with participants similarly reporting the movie review class as useful and enjoyable for language learning.

description: Relationships between Schwartz's value priorities and Wulff's religious attitude types (Orthodoxy, External Critique, Relativism, Second Naiveté) can be reduced to two theoretically derived value patterns: Transcendence/Mutual Care (TC) and Social Order/Uncertainty Avoidance (SU)
original_authors: Johnny Fontaine; Patrick Luyten; Jozef Corveleyn
original_title: Tell me what you believe and I'll tell you what you want: Empirical evidence for discriminating value patterns of five types of religiosity
original_journal: International Journal for the Psychology of Religion
replication_authors: Jacek Śliwak; Beata Zarzycka
replication_title: Is It Possible to Discriminate the Value Patterns of Wulff's Approaches to Religion in a Polish Sample?
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'The present study replicates the systematic patterns of association found by [9] only partially.' While the TC pattern was confirmed for Orthodoxy and Second Naiveté, the SU pattern was only supported for Orthodoxy, and Relativism and External Critique were mainly explained by the inverse TC pattern alone.

description: Positive mood induction increases willingness to make utilitarian moral judgments in the trolley problem
original_authors: Piercarlo Valdesolo; David DeSteno
original_title: Manipulations of emotional context shape moral judgment
replication_authors: Aaron A. Duke; Laurent Bègue
replication_title: The drunk utilitarian: Blood alcohol concentration predicts utilitarian responses in moral dilemmas
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We also failed to replicate previous findings linking positive mood to increased utilitarian responding (Strohminger et al., 2011; Valdesolo & DeSteno, 2006).' In Study 2, self-reported positive mood showed essentially zero correlation with utilitarian preference (r = .01). Upgraded to high confidence because the authors use the word 'replicate' directly and the null result is unambiguous.

description: Foreign aid does not have a positive and statistically significant effect on economic growth when combining evidence across 68 aid-growth studies via meta-analysis (and the variation in reported effects is attributable to study characteristics)
original_authors: Hristos Doucouliagos; Martin Paldam
original_title: Aid effectiveness on growth: a meta study
replication_authors: Tseday Jemaneh Mekasha; Finn Tarp
replication_title: Aid and Growth: What Meta-Analysis Reveals
explanation: The authors explicitly re-examine DP08's core meta-analytic result using the same 68 underlying studies but with corrected data and methodologically superior approaches (random effects model, standard errors as precision weights). They conclude that 'the DP08 findings paint an erroneous picture' and find a positive and statistically significant impact of aid on growth (magnitude ~0.14), directly reversing DP08's conclusion that the aid effectiveness literature has 'failed to show that the effect of development aid on growth is positive and statistically significant.'

description: Using propensity score matching on Bangladesh microfinance data, Duvendack and Palmer-Jones claimed to fail to confirm Pitt and Khandker's positive microfinance effects, finding that microfinance participants spend 0.4–6.5% less than control village individuals
original_authors: Duvendack, Maren; Palmer-Jones, Richard
original_title: High noon for microfinance impact evaluations: reinvestigating the evidence from Bangladesh
replication_authors: Mark M. Pitt
replication_title: Gunfight at the Not OK Corral: Reply to ‘High Noon for Microfinance’
explanation: Pitt re-ran DPJ's propensity score matching code on the same Bangladesh microfinance data and documented 18 serious methodological errors and code misrepresentations, concluding 'I can only conclude that the DJP results are entirely spurious' and that their work 'completely lacks credibility' — thus DPJ's claimed finding that microfinance has no positive effect cannot be replicated from their own code.

description: Presenting men in front of a red background enhances their perceived attractiveness in the eyes of female observers (Experiment 1)
original_authors: Andrew J. Elliot; Daniela Niesta Kayser; Tobias Greitemeyer; Stephanie Lichtenfeld; Richard H. Gramzow; Markus A. Maier; Huijun Liu
original_title: Red, rank, and romance in women viewing men
replication_authors: Vera M. Hesslinger; Lisa Goldbach; Claus-Christian Carbon
replication_title: Men in red: A reexamination of the red-attractiveness effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Neither of our replications yielded a statistically significant effect of the color red on the dependent variables (Experiment 1: perceived attractiveness...).' In Experiment 1, the difference in attractiveness ratings between red and white conditions was non-significant: t(87)=0.92, p=0.360, and also non-significant for the female subsample: t(70)=0.24, p=0.810.

description: Presenting men in front of a red background enhances their perceived attractiveness and perceived status in the eyes of female observers
original_authors: Andrew J. Elliot; Daniela Niesta Kayser; Tobias Greitemeyer; Stephanie Lichtenfeld; Richard H. Gramzow; Markus A. Maier; Huijun Liu
original_title: Red, rank, and romance in women viewing men
replication_authors: Vera M. Hesslinger; Lisa Goldbach; Claus-Christian Carbon
replication_title: Men in red: A reexamination of the red-attractiveness effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Neither of our replications yielded a statistically significant effect of the color red on the dependent variables (...Experiment 2: perceived attractiveness and perceived status).' Experiment 2 extended the paradigm with multiple stimuli of different men and added apparel style as a factor, but still found no significant red effect (all Fs < 1.8, ps ≥ 0.193 for color condition).

description: A community-based, multicomponent HIV prevention intervention for rural Zimbabwean youth (ages 18-22) does not significantly reduce the prevalence of HIV or HSV-2, though it modestly improves knowledge and attitudes
original_authors: Frances M. Cowan; Sophie JS Pascoe; Lisa F. Langhaug; Webster Mavhu; Samson Chidiya; Shabbar Jaffar; Michael T. Mbizvo; Judith M. Stephenson; Anne M. Johnson; Robert M. Power; Godfrey Woelk; Richard J. Hayes
original_title: The Regai Dzive Shiri Project: results of a randomised trial of an HIV prevention intervention for Zimbabwean youth
replication_authors: Fang Yu; Nicholas A Hein; Danstan S Bagenda
replication_title: Preventing HIV and HSV-2 through improving knowledge and attitudes: a replication study of a multicomponent intervention in Zimbabwe
explanation: The replication authors explicitly state: 'we reproduced the original results with only minor discrepancies' and 'we were able to replicate the original findings with minor discrepancies.' The pure replication confirmed the null effect of the intervention on HIV and HSV-2 prevalence, and confirmed modest improvements in knowledge and attitudes, matching the original findings with only minor coding-related differences that did not change significance levels or conclusions.

description: A cluster-randomized controlled trial comparing the effectiveness of cash, food vouchers, and in-kind food transfers versus a control condition on food consumption, dietary diversity, food security, and caloric intake among vulnerable households in northern Ecuador
original_authors: Melissa Hidrobo; John Hoddinott; Amber Peterman; Amy Margolies; Vanessa Moreira
original_title: Cash, food, or vouchers? Evidence from a randomized experiment in northern Ecuador
replication_authors: Stefan K Lhachimi; Till Seuring
replication_title: Thou shalt be given... but how? A replication study of a randomized experiment on food assistance in northern Ecuador
explanation: The authors conducted a pure replication using the original study's own data and code, and explicitly conclude: 'we find that the results of the original paper are fully replicable. We do not find any meaningful differences in the reported results or the interpretation of the results.' They were able to replicate all main result tables (OP-Tables 2-5 and 7) using both the provided Stata code and independently reconstructed R code.

description: Using a randomized controlled trial in Niger, the Zap mobile money transfer intervention had a greater positive impact on household food diversity, diet diversity score, and intra-household dynamics compared to cash or mobile-only transfer mechanisms
original_authors: Jenny C. Aker; Rachid Boumnijel; Amanda McClelland; Niall Tierney
original_title: Payment mechanisms and antipoverty programs: evidence from a mobile money cash transfer experiment in Niger
replication_authors: Jean Pierre Meneses; Edgar Ventura; Oliver Elorreaga; César Huaroto; Giovanna Aguilar; Edmundo Beteta
replication_title: Mobile money and its impact on improving living conditions in Niger: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The pure replication section, our independent reproduction of findings, confirmed the comparability of our results to the original authors'. They found no major differences from the original published results: 'We did not find any major differences in relation to the results shown in the published paper and its complementary corrigendum. The minor observations we identified do not affect the relevant results established by the original paper.'

description: M-PESA mobile money adoption enables Kenyan households to better smooth consumption in response to negative income shocks, by reducing transaction costs and facilitating informal risk-sharing through remittances
original_authors: William Jack; Tavneet Suri
original_title: Risk sharing and transactions costs: evidence from Kenya's mobile money revolution
replication_authors: Nazila Alinaghi; W Robert Reed
replication_title: Risk sharing and transaction costs: a replication study of evidence from Kenya's mobile money revolution
explanation: Pure replication by independent re-coding of Jack & Suri (2014) from the AER replication data. Table A7 (p.43) reproduces the original Table 4A exactly: the headline DiD interaction (M-PESA user x negative shock) on log per-capita consumption is 0.0917 (SE 0.0506, p~0.07) in OLS, rising to 0.1483 (SE 0.0599, p<0.05) in the preferred specification; N=4,562 household-period observations (2,282 households x 2 rounds). The author's verdict (p.38): 'I was able to reproduce all of the main findings from the original paper, although I discovered some minor differences in the code and tables. Accordingly, my pure and push-button replication is categorised as comparable but incomplete.' Notable finding (p.5): the original's first column claims robust SEs but uses conventional OLS SEs - with heteroskedasticity-robust SEs the headline coefficient loses significance (SE 0.0717, p=0.201). Some original tables could not be replicated for lack of data (Table 2 Panel B; Table 7A falsification test - proprietary data), and the replication found the ROSCA and SACCO estimates switched in the original's Table 8A. Row enriched and n corrected 2026-08-08 (4,562 was previously attributed to the replication side only; it is the original's regression N, exactly reproduced).

description: Biometrically authenticated Smartcard payment infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh, India reduced the time NREGS beneficiaries spent collecting payments and modestly reduced leakage of funds, without hindering access to the NREGS and SSP welfare programs
original_authors: Karthik Muralidharan; Paul Niehaus; Sandip Sukhtankar
original_title: Building state capacity: evidence from biometric smartcards in India
replication_authors: Akinwande A Atanda
replication_title: Biometric smartcards and payment disbursement: a replication study of a state capacity-building experiment in India
explanation: The replication (line-by-line audit of the original Stata do-files re-run in Stata 14.1, plus MEA robustness checks) exactly reproduces Muralidharan et al. (2016). Effect stored here: Smartcards reduced NREGS beneficiaries' time to collect payments by 22 minutes (cluster-robust SE 9.2, p=0.019, N=10,191 individuals; control mean 112 min; Table A2 p.16 - p-values computed by the replicator, absent from the original). Other reproduced results: NREGS payment lag -10 days (p=0.005); NREGS survey payments +35 Rs (p=0.026); leakage -24 to -25 Rs, marginal (p=0.054-0.067) and driven by the over-reporting channel (-0.082, p=0.014; ghost households and bribes null); NREGS participation +0.072 (p=0.03). SSP effects are null throughout (time to collect p=0.24-0.52; no SSP participation estimate exists in the paper). Verdict (p.13): 'Our replication is exactly comparable to the findings of Muralidharan and colleagues (2016)... we are able to confirm the original findings', with robustness 'comparable in 90 percent of the cases'; one documented contradiction (footnote 13, p.9): the replicator's TOT decomposition finds a significant Smartcard/non-Smartcard difference in time-to-collect where the original's Table A7 equality test found none. Description corrected 2026-08-08 (previously claimed improved participation in NREGS AND SSP and unqualified time savings; the SSP effects are null).

description: Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) reduces the risk of genetically linked HIV-1 transmission to uninfected partners among serodiscordant couples by 96% compared with delayed therapy
original_authors: Myron S. Cohen; Ying Q. Chen; Marybeth McCauley; Theresa Gamble; Mina C. Hosseinipour; Nagalingeswaran Kumarasamy; James G. Hakim; Johnstone Kumwenda; Beatriz Grinsztejn; Jose H.S. Pilotto; Sheela V. Godbole; Sanjay Mehendale; Suwat Chariyalertsak; Breno R. Santos; Kenneth H. Mayer; Irving F. Hoffman; Susan H. Eshleman; Estelle Piwowar-Manning; Lei Wang; Joseph Makhema; Lisa A. Mills; Guy de Bruyn; Ian Sanne; Joseph Eron; Joel Gallant; Diane Havlir; Susan Swindells; Heather Ribaudo; Vanessa Elharrar; David Burns; Taha E. Taha; Karin Nielsen-Saines; David Celentano; Max Essex; Thomas R. Fleming
original_title: Prevention of HIV-1 infection with early antiretroviral therapy
replication_authors: Eric W Djimeu; Eleanor G Dickens
replication_title: Treatment as prevention: a replication study on early antiretroviral therapy initiation and HIV-1 transmission
explanation: Pure replication using the original authors' data and methods reproduced the main results: linked-transmission HR 0.04 (95% CI 0.01-0.27), identical to the original (Table 3, p.12; multivariate Cox 0.04 [0.01-0.28], Table 4, p.16) - a 96% relative reduction; any-transmission HR 0.11 (89% reduction) and composite clinical events also reproduced. The replication does not print a separate p-value for the primary outcome; replication_p<0.001 mirrors the original's printed value (the CI excludes 1, and the only printed replication p is <0.01 for the African-subgroup MEA re-estimate, p.18). Conclusion (p.40): 'In general - except for Figure 2 in the original paper, where we found a major difference with our replication - the pure replication confirmed the main findings of the original paper.' The Figure 2 discrepancy concerns the numbers-at-risk tables (replication starts with 1,718 uninfected / 1,754 infected vs the original's 1,775 / 1,763, due to missing duration values); the authors write that if confirmed 'an errata should be submitted to the New England Journal of Medicine' (p.39). The original authors declined to share male-circumcision and ART-adherence data. Row enriched 2026-08-08.

description: A universal test-and-treat (TasP) intervention providing ART to all HIV-positive individuals regardless of CD4 count did not reduce HIV incidence at the population level in rural South Africa (adjusted HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87-1.17)
original_authors: Collins C. Iwuji; Joanna Orne-Gliemann; Joseph Larmarange; Eric Balestre; Rodolphe Thiebaut; Frank Tanser; Nonhlanhla Okesola; Thembisa Makowa; Jaco Dreyer; Kobus Herbst; Nuala McGrath; Till Bärnighausen; Sylvie Boyer; Tulio De Oliveira; Claire Rekacewicz; Brigitte Bazin; Marie-Louise Newell; Deenan Pillay; François Dabis; Till Bärnighausen; Kobus Herbst; Collins Iwuji; Thembisa Makowa; Kevi Naidu; Marie-Louise Newell; Nonhlanhla Okesola; Tulio De Oliveira; Deenan Pillay; Tamsen Rochat; Frank Tanser; Johannes Viljoen; Thembelihle Zuma; Nuala McGrath; Eric Balestre; François Dabis; Sophie Karcher; Joanna Orne-Gliemann; Melanie Plazy; Mélanie Prague; Rodolphe Thiébaut; Thierry Tiendrebeogo; Sylvie Boyer; Hermann Donfouet; Andrea Gosset; Laura March; Camelia Protopopescu; Bruno Spire; Alexandra Calmy; Joseph Larmarange; Maxime Inghels; Hassimiou Diallo; Vincent Calvez; Anne Derache; Anne-Geneviève Marcelin; Rosemary Dray-Spira; France Lert; Kamal El Farouki; Richard Lessells; Kenneth Freedberg; John Imrie; Marie-Laure Chaix; Colin Newell; Jan Hontelez; Brigitte Bazin; Claire Rekacewicz
original_title: Universal test and treat and the HIV epidemic in rural South Africa: a phase 4, open-label, community cluster randomised trial
replication_authors: Sridevi K Prasad; Douglas M Glandon
replication_title: Treatment as prevention: a replication study on a universal test and treat cluster-randomized trial in South Africa from 2012–2016
explanation: The original ANRS 12249 TasP trial found a null result: adjusted HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.87-1.17, p=0.89) for HIV incidence in intervention vs control clusters (augmented GEE, the trial's primary model). The replication's matched augmented-GEE estimate (using the original authors' code) was HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.71-1.37, p=0.89); their non-augmented GEE gave HR 0.93 (0.74-1.18, p=0.57) vs the original's 0.95 (0.75-1.20, p=0.68) (Table 5, p.13). The push-button replication reproduced Tables 1-4 and S7A with no differences. The authors state: 'We did not find any major discrepancies that affected either point estimates or the main conclusion of this study' and 'Overall, we found that the results were fairly robust, and we were able to replicate the original analyses.' result=success records a CONFIRMED NULL. n=14,223 is the HIV-incidence analysis sub-sample (>=2 dried-blood-spot samples, first test HIV-negative); 28,419 individuals were enrolled at baseline. Row corrected 2026-08-08: the previous description asserted the intervention 'reduces HIV incidence' (the trial's aim, not its result), and the previous p-values paired the original's augmented model (0.89) with the replication's non-augmented model (0.57).

description: A cash transfer programme for schooling (both conditional and unconditional) reduces HIV and HSV-2 prevalence among never-married school-enrolled girls aged 13–22 in Malawi
original_authors: Baird, Sarah J.; Garfein, Richard S.; McIntosh, Craig T.; Özler, Berk
original_title: Effect of a cash transfer programme for schooling on prevalence of HIV and herpes simplex type 2 in Malawi: a cluster randomised trial
replication_authors: Lynette M Smith; Nicholas A Hein; Danstan S Bagenda
replication_title: Cash transfers and HIV/HSV-2 prevalence: a replication of a cluster randomized trial in Malawi
explanation: The pure replication successfully reproduced the original results ('the original results were replicated in the pure replication portion of the study'), with adjusted OR for HIV = 0.36 (95% CI 0.14–0.92). However, the measurement and estimation analysis showed the HIV prevalence finding was sensitive to model choice: using a generalized linear mixed model, the OR increased from 0.36 to 0.54 and the 95% CI widened to 0.19–1.54 (non-significant), and permutation testing also failed to retain significance for HIV. The Conclusions note that 'it is recommended that additional research is performed in assessing the effectiveness of cash transfer programs in reducing HIV.'

description: PEPFAR funding to focus countries in Africa was associated with a statistically significant reduction in all-cause adult mortality between 2004 and 2008, as measured by a difference-in-difference analysis comparing 9 PEPFAR focus countries to 18 non-focus African countries
original_authors: Eran Bendavid; Charles B. Holmes; Jay Bhattacharya; Grant Miller
original_title: HIV development assistance and adult mortality in Africa
replication_authors: Nicholas A Hein; Danstan S Bagenda; Jiangtao Luo
replication_title: PEPFAR and adult mortality: a replication study of HIV development assistance effects in Sub-Saharan African countries
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our replication study supports the findings of Bendavid and colleagues' and 'we cautiously agree with the Bendavid and colleagues' findings that PEPFAR is associated with a reduction in all-cause adult mortality in focus countries.' The pure replication replicated the primary result (OR 0.84, CI 0.72–0.97, p=0.02 vs. original OR 0.84, CI 0.72–0.99, p=0.03) with only minor rounding differences that did not change the substantive conclusions.

description: Land titling (assigning property rights to poor urban squatters) substantially increases housing investment and generates social impacts including reduced household size and increased child education, operating through a slow channel of physical and human capital investment rather than expanded credit access
original_authors: Sebastian Galiani; Ernesto Schargrodsky
original_title: Property rights for the poor: effects of land titling
replication_authors: Drew Cameron; Edward Whitney; Paul Winters
replication_title: The effects of land titling on the urban poor: a replication of property rights for the poor
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we are able to satisfactorily replicate all results reported in the original paper. Aside from incidental rounding inconsistences, we note no difference between the output for the pure replication and that of the original paper.' The Discussion section further confirms: 'Not only did our analysis replicate the authors' approach, but robustness checks using alternative estimates of impact also confirmed the results. In sum, we judge the outcomes presented in the original paper to be reasonable.'

description: The TOMM40 polyT polymorphism (rs10524523) very long allele is associated with earlier age at onset of late-onset Alzheimer's disease in APOE ε3/ε3 and ε3/ε4 carriers
original_authors: A. Roses; M. W. Lutz; M. W. Lutz; H. Amrine-Madsen; Ann M. Saunders; Ann M. Saunders; Donna G. Crenshaw; Donna G. Crenshaw; S. Sundseth; S. Sundseth; M. Huentelman; Kathleen A. Welsh-Bohmer; Kathleen A. Welsh-Bohmer; E. Reiman; E. Reiman
original_title: A TOMM40 variable-length polymorphism predicts the age of late-onset Alzheimer's disease
replication_authors: Cruchaga C.; Nowotny P.; Kauwe JS; Ridge PG; Mayo K.; Bertelsen S.; Hinrichs A.; Fagan AM; Holtzman DM; Morris JC; Goate AM
replication_title: Association and Expression Analyses With Single-Nucleotide Polymorphisms in <emph type="ital">TOMM40</emph> in Alzheimer Disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Although we did not replicate the earlier association between the APOE3-TOMM40 haplotypes and age at onset.' In the APOE ε3/ε3 stratum, the polyT repeat showed no association with AAO (P=.19) despite a much larger sample (N=1594 cases vs original N=34).

description: The TOMM40 polyT polymorphism (rs10524523) very long allele is associated with increased risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease in APOE ε3/ε3 homozygotes
original_authors: A. Roses; M. W. Lutz; M. W. Lutz; H. Amrine-Madsen; Ann M. Saunders; Ann M. Saunders; Donna G. Crenshaw; Donna G. Crenshaw; S. Sundseth; S. Sundseth; M. Huentelman; Kathleen A. Welsh-Bohmer; Kathleen A. Welsh-Bohmer; E. Reiman; E. Reiman
original_title: A TOMM40 variable-length polymorphism predicts the age of late-onset Alzheimer's disease
replication_authors: Cruchaga C.; Nowotny P.; Kauwe JS; Ridge PG; Mayo K.; Bertelsen S.; Hinrichs A.; Fagan AM; Holtzman DM; Morris JC; Goate AM
replication_title: Association and Expression Analyses With Single-Nucleotide Polymorphisms in <emph type="ital">TOMM40</emph> in Alzheimer Disease
explanation: The authors found a significant association between the polyT repeat and risk of LOAD in APOE ε3/ε3 homozygotes (P=.004, OR=0.78), but in the opposite direction: the very long allele was underrepresented in cases vs controls (0.41 vs 0.48), contrary to Roses et al.'s report of increased risk. The authors state: 'we observed an association between the polyT repeat and risk of disease but in the opposite direction as that reported previously.'

description: The TGFB1 gene coding SNP rs1800470 (codon 10 polymorphism, proline to leucine) is associated with high myopia, with allele C being more frequent in cases than controls
original_authors: Lin, H.; Wan, L.; Tsai, Y.
original_title: The TGFB1 gene codon 10 polymorphism contributes to the genetic predisposition to high myopia
replication_authors: Yi Zha
replication_title: TGFB1 as a Susceptibility Gene for High Myopia
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the present study successfully replicated the Taiwanese study, and added further strength to the significance role of TGFB1 as a susceptibility gene for high myopia.' The replication found the same direction of association for rs1800470 in a Hong Kong Chinese sample (OR=0.55 for allele T with C as reference, equivalent to the original OR of 1.83 for allele C).

description: IL1A rs17561 (Ser114Ala) polymorphism is associated with susceptibility to nasal polyposis in a Turkish population
original_authors: Erbek SS; Yurtcu E.; Erbek S.; Atac FB; Sahin FI; Cakmak O.
original_title: Proinflammatory cytokine single nucleotide polymorphisms in nasal polyposis
replication_authors: Mfuna Endam L.; Cormier C.; Bossé Y.; Filali-Mouhim A.; Desrosiers M.
replication_title: Association of IL1A, IL1B, and TNF Gene Polymorphisms With Chronic Rhinosinusitis With and Without Nasal Polyposis
replication_journal: Archives of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
explanation: The authors confirm in their conclusion: 'we confirm the association between IL1A rs17561 and CRS and extend these results by identifying 3 additional IL1A SNPs associated with CRS.' The replication used a Canadian rather than Turkish population, making it a close extension testing generalizability.

description: IL1B rs16944 (-511CC) polymorphism is associated with susceptibility to nasal polyposis in a Turkish population
original_authors: Selim S. Erbek; Erkan Yurtçu; Seyra Erbek; Fatma Belgin Ataç; Feride İffet Şahin; Özcan Çakmak
original_title: Proinflammatory cytokine single nucleotide polymorphisms in nasal polyposis

replication_title: Association of IL1A, IL1B, and TNF Gene Polymorphisms With Chronic Rhinosinusitis With and Without Nasal Polyposis
replication_journal: Archives of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
explanation: The authors state: 'we did not replicate previously reported associations of IL1B and TNF polymorphisms with CRS.' For IL1B rs16944, the OR was 0.99 (p = .94), showing no association.

description: TNF polymorphisms (-238AA [rs361525] and -308GA [rs1800629]) are associated with susceptibility to nasal polyposis in a Turkish population
original_authors: Selim S. Erbek; Erkan Yurtçu; Seyra Erbek; Fatma Belgin Ataç; Feride İffet Şahin; Özcan Çakmak
original_title: Proinflammatory cytokine single nucleotide polymorphisms in nasal polyposis
replication_authors: Mfuna Endam L.; Cormier C.; Bossé Y.; Filali-Mouhim A.; Desrosiers M.
replication_title: Association of IL1A, IL1B, and TNF Gene Polymorphisms With Chronic Rhinosinusitis With and Without Nasal Polyposis
replication_journal: Archives of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
explanation: The authors state: 'we did not replicate previously reported associations of IL1B and TNF polymorphisms with CRS.' TNF rs1800629 showed OR of 1.01 (p = .98), and the AA genotype for rs361525 was not even found in the Canadian population.

description: Adult schizophrenics perform more poorly than normal adults on Piaget-based cognitive tasks (measuring conjunctive class formation, seriation, and logical reasoning), with performance patterns similar to those of normal developing children, indicating schizophrenic thought disturbance reflects developmental aberrations
original_authors: Thomas L. Trunnell
original_title: Thought disturbance in schizophrenia
replication_authors: Trunnell TL
replication_title: Thought Disturbance in Schizophrenia
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'This paper reports a replication study' of the pilot study (Trunnell 1964). The Results section confirms 'the hypotheses advanced tend to be confirmed,' and the summary states that '24 adult schizophrenics was distinguished from a population of 24 adult controls.' Only the letter identification test failed to distinguish groups, which the authors noted was compatible with other reports. The overall replication was judged successful.

description: Approximately one third of alcoholic suicides had experienced loss of a close interpersonal relationship within six weeks or less of their death, with events significantly skewed toward the final weeks of the subject's life
original_authors: Murphy, G.; Robins, E.
original_title: Social factors in suicide
replication_authors: Murphy GE; Armstrong JW Jr; Hermele SL; Fischer JR; Clendenin WW
replication_title: Suicide and Alcoholism
explanation: The authors explicitly state replication success: 'Thus, the original finding of a close temporal relationship between affectional loss and suicide in alcoholics is replicated.' The replication found 26% of 50 alcoholic suicides experienced interpersonal loss within six weeks (vs. 32% in the original N=31), with both results statistically significant at P < .01.

description: Psychostimulant medication (methylphenidate) produces significant therapeutic improvement in adults with attention deficit disorder (minimal brain dysfunction), with approximately 60% showing favorable response
original_authors: Wood, D.; Reimherr, F.; Wender, P.
original_title: Diagnosis and treatment of minimal brain dysfunction in adults: A preliminary report

In the replication, phenelzine response rate was 83% vs. imipramine 50% vs. placebo 19% at 6 weeks, closely matching original rates of 75%, 54%, and 28%.

The authors conclude that 'a history of panic was probably not relevant in predicting drug effects in this population.'

Type 2 risk was 6-fold higher in sons with type 2 genetic background (OR=5.8, 95% CI 2.3-14.7), and severe type 1 risk was 4-fold higher in men with both genetic and severe environmental risk (OR=4.2, 95% CI 1.3-13.5), replicating the original findings.

The authors state that 'by using improved materials...and sound statistical analysis (correcting for overcontrol), the data replicate the long-established relationship between playing violent video games and aggressive behavior,' effectively demonstrating that the original null finding was a methodological artifact.

replication_title: Two methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase gene (MTHFR) polymorphisms, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder: An association study
replication_journal: American Journal of Medical Genetics Part B: Neuropsychiatric Genetics
explanation: REVIEWER VERIFIED. The authors explicitly state: 'no significant association was found between two functional MTHFR gene polymorphisms and schizophrenia...in the present Scandinavian samples' and 'The present Scandinavian results do not verify previous associations.' All chi-square tests for C677T and A1298C genotype/allele comparisons between schizophrenia patients and controls were non-significant across all three countries (Denmark P=0.91, Norway P=0.45, Sweden P=0.61 for C677T genotypes). Result classification as 'failure' is unambiguous. Replication type 'close extension' is appropriate because the study tests the same polymorphisms using the same case-control design but in new Scandinavian populations (Denmark, Norway, Sweden), testing generalizability of meta-analytic findings. Confidence remains 'medium' because: (1) the 'original' being replicated is a meta-analytic pooled finding from four meta-analyses (Lewis et al. 2005; Muntjewerff et al. 2006; Zintzaras 2006; Gilbody et al. 2007), not a single study — Gilbody et al. 2007 was selected as representative but multiple could serve; (2) the authors' own updated meta-analysis including their new data still shows significant association (OR=1.12, 95% CI 1.05-1.19 for C677T), creating nuance around whether this is truly a 'failure' at the meta-analytic level even though the individual Scandinavian samples clearly failed to replicate.

explanation: REVIEWER VERIFIED. The authors explicitly state: 'We also did not find any significant association between the two MTHFR polymorphisms and bipolar disorder in the relatively small Norwegian sample.' The abstract confirms results 'do not verify previous associations between the putative functional MTHFR gene polymorphisms and schizophrenia or bipolar disorder.' Statistics confirm: C677T genotype distribution χ²=1.30, df=2, P=0.52; allele distribution χ²=1.10, df=1, P=0.29. A1298C genotype χ²=0.86, df=1, P=0.65; allele χ²=0.74, df=1, P=0.39. Result classification as 'failure' is unambiguous. Confidence remains 'medium' because: (1) the original is a meta-analytic finding (Gilbody et al. 2007 is the only meta-analysis cited for bipolar, making attribution cleaner than the schizophrenia entry); (2) the bipolar sample is relatively small (117 patients + 177 controls = 294 total), which the authors themselves acknowledge, limiting power; (3) the authors' updated meta-analysis still supports association with bipolar disorder (OR=1.20, 95% CI 1.04-1.39 for C677T T vs C alleles), so the null finding may reflect low power rather than true absence of effect.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in their discussion: 'these findings provide clear support for previous reports of increased FA associated with ASC [Hammond et al., 2008; Ozgen et al., 2011], and replicated the direction of autism-specific asymmetry observed by Hammond et al. [2008].' Significantly greater depth-wise FA was found in ASC children vs. TD children (F(1, 140) = 4.87, P = 0.029).

explanation: The authors state: 'We were not able to replicate the association between CLOPD and VACTERL in offspring in our primary analysis,' but the crude OR pointed in the same direction (OR 2.2 [1.0-4.9]) and a sensitivity analysis including medication use yielded aOR 2.1 [1.0-4.4], making the result inconclusive rather than a clear failure.

They conclude: 'The increased risk for pregestational diabetes mellitus observed in the European study could not be replicated or refuted due to a lack of case mothers with pregestational diabetes mellitus.'

description: Exposure of murine L929 fibroblast cells to TDMA digital cellular telephone signal (840 MHz, burst modulated at 50 Hz, 33% duty cycle) at SAR 2.5 W/kg for 8 h increases ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) activity by approximately 40%, with the effect being modulation-specific (not seen with continuous wave signals)
original_authors: L. Miguel Penafiel; Theodore Litovitz; David Krause; Abiy Desta; J. Michael Mullins
original_title: Role of modulation on the effect of microwaves on ornithine decarboxylase activity in L929 cells
replication_authors: Höytö A.; Juutilainen J.; Naarala J.
replication_title: Ornithine decarboxylase activity of L929 cells after exposure to continuous wave or 50 Hz modulated radiofrequency radiation—a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We were unable to confirm the induction of cellular ODC activity in L929 cells after exposure to DAMPS modulated radiofrequency radiation carried out in a Crawford chamber,' and the abstract concludes 'The results did not confirm findings of previous studies reporting increased ODC activity in RF-exposed cells.' While the waveguide exposure system showed an increase in one condition (8h, 6 W/kg), the primary replication using a Crawford chamber similar to the original protocol failed to confirm the ODC increase, and this anomalous waveguide finding was attributed to uncertain mechanisms requiring further investigation.

description: Long-term low-level microwave RF exposure (2375 MHz, 5 W/m2, 7 h/day) causes formation of antibodies against brain tissue antigens in rats, indicating an autoimmune response
original_authors: Vinogradov, G.; Dumansky, Y.
original_title: Change of antigenic properties of fabrics and autoallergic processes at influence of MW-energy
original_journal: Bulletin of Experimental Biology and Medicine
replication_authors: Yury G. Grigoriev; Oleg A. Grigoriev; Alexander A. Ivanov; Antonina M. Lyaginskaya; Anton V. Merkulov; Natalia B. Shagina; Vyacheslav N. Maltsev; Philippe Lévêque; Alla M. Ulanova; Vyacheslav A. Osipov; Alexander V. Shafirkin
replication_title: Confirmation studies of Soviet research on immunological effects of microwaves: Russian immunology results
explanation: The authors report that results 'partly confirmed the findings of the early studies,' showing a statistically significant increase in antibodies against brain antigens in RF-exposed vs. Sham-exposed rats on day 14 (p < 0.01), but the effect was smaller in magnitude than in the original studies. The ELISA test provided additional supporting evidence for oxidative stress.

description: Injection of blood serum from RF-exposed rats into intact pregnant rats causes high embryo mortality (28%) and increased offspring mortality compared to controls, indicating adverse effects of RF-exposed serum on fetal and postnatal development
original_authors: Shandala, M.; Vinogradov, G.
original_title: Autoallergic effects of electromagnetic energy of the MW-range exposure and their influence on a foetus and posterity
original_journal: The Bulletin of the Academy of Medical Sciences of the USSR
replication_authors: Yury G. Grigoriev; Oleg A. Grigoriev; Alexander A. Ivanov; Antonina M. Lyaginskaya; Anton V. Merkulov; Natalia B. Shagina; Vyacheslav N. Maltsev; Philippe Lévêque; Alla M. Ulanova; Vyacheslav A. Osipov; Alexander V. Shafirkin
replication_title: Confirmation studies of Soviet research on immunological effects of microwaves: Russian immunology results
explanation: The authors report that results 'showed the same general trends as the earlier study,' with statistically significantly higher in utero mortality in the RF-exposed serum group (55.6%) vs. sham-serum group (11.7%) and biological controls (4.3%). However, the authors explicitly call this a 'pilot study' noting high variability, problems with the animal model, and incomplete information in the original publications, classifying the result as inconclusive for regulatory purposes.

description: Exposure to combined 60-Hz electric (9 kV/m) and magnetic (20 µT) fields in humans causes statistically significant slowing of heart rate, changes in late components of event-related brain potentials, and decreased errors on a choice reaction-time task
original_authors: Graham, C.; Cohen, H.D.; Cook, M.R.; Phelps, J.W.; Gerkovich, M.M.; Fotopoulos, S.S.
original_title: A double-blind evaluation of 60-Hz field effects on human performance, physiology, and subjective state
original_journal: Interaction of Biological Systems with Static and ELF Electric and Magnetic Fields
replication_authors: Mary R. Cook; Charles Graham; Harvey D. Cohen; Mary M. Gerkovich
replication_title: A replication study of human exposure to 60‐Hz fields: Effects on neurobehavioral measures
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'The major neurobehavioral findings of the previous screening study were repeated,' with field-related slowing of heart rate, P300 amplitude changes, and fewer CRT errors all confirmed in the replication (though heart rate slowing was only statistically significant for the nonsequential-order group). The study used the same field conditions (9 kV/m, 20 µT), same double-blind protocol, and same measures, but with a larger sample and added capability to collect physiological data during exposure.

description: Exposure of female Suffolk lambs to 60 Hz electric and magnetic fields from a 500 kV transmission line for 10 months does not affect serum melatonin patterns or onset of puberty
original_authors: Lee JM Jr; Stormshak F.; Thompson JM; Thinesen P.; Painter LJ; Olenchek EG; Hess DL; Forbes R.; Foster DL
original_title: Melatonin secretion and puberty in female lambs exposed to environmental electric and magnetic fields
replication_authors: Lee JM Jr; Stormshak F.; Thompson JM; Hess DL; Foster DL
replication_title: Melatonin and puberty in female lambs exposed to EMF: A replicate study
explanation: The authors explicitly state that this is a replicate experiment of their own prior study [Lee et al., 1993] with increased sample size (15 vs 10 per group), using the same 500 kV line, same protocol, and same primary hypothesis. The abstract states 'The replicate produced essentially the same results as our previous study,' with no significant differences found in melatonin duration (P=.97), amplitude (P=.78), phase (P=.19), or age at puberty (244.9 vs. 244.5 days).

description: Multiple object tracking (MOT) engages a network of occipitotemporal, parietal, and frontal cortical areas as measured by fMRI, with frontal activations in the dorsolateral frontal cortex (DLFC)
original_authors: Jody C. Culham; Stephan A. Brandt; Patrick Cavanagh; Nancy G. Kanwisher; Anders M. Dale; Roger B. H. Tootell
original_title: Cortical fMRI activation produced by attentive tracking of moving targets
replication_authors: Silke Atmaca; Waltraud Stadler; Anne Keitel; Derek V. M. Ott; Jöran Lepsien; Wolfgang Prinz
replication_title: Prediction processes during multiple object tracking (<scp>MOT</scp>): involvement of dorsal and ventral premotor cortices
explanation: REVIEWED. The authors make an explicit, unhedged replication claim in the Summary: 'we replicated previous results (Culham et al. 1998, 2001; Jovicich et al. 2001; Howe et al. 2009), revealing activations in occipitotemporal, parietal, and frontal areas.' Table 1 confirms the activation network (occipitotemporal, parietal, frontal) matches prior findings. The replication used the same MOT paradigm under fMRI but with deliberate methodological improvements (LUM control instead of passive viewing, FEF localizer mask), fitting 'close experiment.' Result 'success' is unambiguous — the authors treat the replication of the basic activation network as a clear, settled finding before advancing their novel prediction-process interpretation of the frontal activations.

description: GPR50 polymorphisms (rs13440581 and D502-505/rs561077) are associated with increased risk of major depressive disorder specifically in women
original_authors: Thomson PA; Wray NR; Thomson AM; Dunbar DR; Grassie MA; Condie A.; Walker MT; Smith DJ; Pulford DJ; Muir W.; Blackwood DH; Porteous DJ
original_title: Sex-specific association between bipolar affective disorder in women and GPR50, an X-linked orphan G protein-coupled receptor
replication_authors: Joanne Ryan; Isabelle Carrière; Karen Ritchie; Marie-Laure Ancelin
replication_title: Involvement of <scp>GPR</scp>50 polymorphisms in depression: independent replication in a prospective elderly cohort
explanation: The authors found weak support for GPR50 associations with depression in women, with some variants reaching significance but failing Bonferroni correction, and inconsistent findings across outcomes. The Discussion states: 'Our results thus provide only weak support for the involvement of GPR50 variants in late-life depression' and 'despite our relatively large sample size, this suggests little support for GPR50 as a good candidate gene for late-life depression.'

description: Sorafenib treatment for advanced hepatocellular cancer produces an overall survival of approximately 11.2 months (as found in the RCT comparator arm)
original_authors: Ann-Lii Cheng; Yoon-Koo Kang; Deng-Yn Lin; Joong-Won Park; Masatoshi Kudo; Shukui Qin; Hyun-Cheol Chung; Xiangqun Song; Jianming Xu; Guido Poggi; Masao Omata; Susan Pitman Lowenthal; Silvana Lanzalone; Liqiang Yang; Maria Jose Lechuga; Eric Raymond
original_title: Sunitinib versus sorafenib in advanced hepatocellular cancer: results of a randomized phase III trial
replication_authors: Thomas Jemielita; Linnea Widman; Claire Fox; Stina Salomonsson; Kai‐Li Liaw; Andreas Pettersson
replication_title: Replication of Oncology Randomized Trial Results using Swedish Registry Real World‐Data: A Feasibility Study
explanation: The replication partially succeeded: TTD was similar between RWD and RCT (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.16), but OS was substantially shorter in RWD (8.0 months) vs. RCT (11.2 months; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.63-0.87). The authors conclude 'OS was shorter in the RWD, whereas TTD was similar,' indicating a mixed result.

description: Melphalan, prednisone, and thalidomide (MPT-T) treatment for untreated multiple myeloma produces an overall survival of approximately 52.6 months (as found in the RCT comparator arm)
original_authors: Stewart AK; Jacobus S.; Fonseca R.; Weiss M.; Callander NS; Chanan-Khan AA; Rajkumar SV
original_title: Melphalan, prednisone, and thalidomide vs melphalan, prednisone, and lenalidomide (ECOG E1A06) in untreated multiple myeloma
replication_authors: Thomas Jemielita; Linnea Widman; Claire Fox; Stina Salomonsson; Kai‐Li Liaw; Andreas Pettersson
replication_title: Replication of Oncology Randomized Trial Results using Swedish Registry Real World‐Data: A Feasibility Study
explanation: The replication partially succeeded: TTD was similar between RWD and RCT (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.74-1.06), but OS was substantially shorter in the RWD (36.9 months) vs. RCT (52.6 months; HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.51-0.87). The authors conclude 'OS was shorter in the RWD, whereas TTD was similar,' indicating a mixed result.

description: COMT Met/Met carriers diagnosed with PTSD exhibit increased fear-potentiated startle responses to safety signals (CS-) during extinction compared to Met/Met carriers without PTSD
original_authors: Seth Davin Norrholm; Tanja Jovanovic; Alicia K. Smith; Elisabeth Binder; Torsten Klengel; Karen Conneely; Kristina B. Mercer; Jennifer S. Davis; Kimberly Kerley; Jennifer Winkler; Charles F. Gillespie; Bekh Bradley; Kerry J. Ressler
original_title: Differential genetic and epigenetic regulation of catechol-O-methyltransferase is associated with impaired fear inhibition in posttraumatic stress disorder
replication_authors: Jessica Deslauriers; Dean T. Acheson; Adam X. Maihofer; Caroline M. Nievergelt; Dewleen G. Baker; Mark A. Geyer; Victoria B. Risbrough
replication_title: COMT val158met polymorphism links to altered fear conditioning and extinction are modulated by PTSD and childhood trauma
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'These results replicate previous findings that Met/Met carriers with PTSD exhibit increased responses to safety signals compared to Met/Met carriers without PTSD (Norrholm et al., 2013).' The replication found a significant genotype × PTSD interaction on CS- FPS (F 2,701 = 3.21, p < 0.05) consistent with the original. The study is classified as close extension because it used the same fear-potentiated startle paradigm but tested a different population (active-duty Marines vs. civilians) and added new moderating variables (childhood trauma, combat trauma).

description: Infants show an asymmetrical pattern of categorization of happy versus fearful facial expressions: they demonstrate a novelty preference for fear after habituation to happy, but not a novelty preference for happy after habituation to fearful expressions
original_authors: Pamela M. Ludemann; Charles A. Nelson
original_title: Categorical representation of facial expressions by 7-month-old infants
replication_authors: Kristina Safar; Margaret C. Moulson
replication_title: Recognizing facial expressions of emotion in infancy: A replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated previous results showing an asymmetrical pattern of categorization of happy versus fearful facial expressions,' and indeed infants in the unfamiliar group showed a significant novelty preference in the happy condition (d=1.71, p=.008) but not the fearful condition (d=0.25, p=.659), replicating the asymmetrical categorization pattern. The study extended prior work by also testing familiar (caregiver) faces.

description: Seven-month-old infants show a spontaneous visual preference for fearful over happy facial expressions
original_authors: Mikko J. Peltola; Jukka M. Leppänen; Silja Mäki; Jari K. Hietanen
original_title: Emergence of enhanced attention to fearful faces between 5 and 7 months of age
replication_authors: Kristina Safar; Margaret C. Moulson
replication_title: Recognizing facial expressions of emotion in infancy: A replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated previous results showing... a spontaneous preference for fearful over happy facial expressions (Peltola et al., 2008, 2009).' Infants in the unfamiliar group showed a significant fear preference (d=0.85, p=.003) and infants in the familiar group also showed a significant fear preference (d=1.09, p<.001), extending the replication to familiar faces.

description: Phoneme discrimination (PD) training (6 hours, 11 phoneme contrasts) produces significant improvements in phonological awareness (rhyme and spoonerisms) in mainstream school children compared with a no-intervention control group
original_authors: David R. Moore; Joy F. Rosenberg; John S. Coleman
original_title: Discrimination training of phonemic contrasts enhances phonological processing in mainstream school children
replication_authors: Lorna F. Halliday
replication_title: A Tale of Two Studies on Auditory Training in Children: A Response to the Claim that ‘Discrimination Training of Phonemic Contrasts Enhances Phonological Processing in Mainstream School Children’ by Moore, Rosenberg and Coleman (2005)
explanation: The replication (Halliday et al., 2012) used an almost identical training programme but found no significant group differences on any phonological awareness measure (Rhyme: F(1,41)=0.93, p=0.341; Spoonerisms: F(1,41)=0.05, p=0.829). The current paper explicitly states 'we failed to replicate this finding' and attributes the discrepancy to design differences (randomization, blinding, differential treatment of groups).

description: Long-term recovered bulimia nervosa subjects, compared to non-eating-disordered controls, show elevated levels of pathological eating behaviors, body dissatisfaction, ineffectiveness, decreased interoceptive awareness, greater eating-related and general obsessionality, and elevated levels of perfectionism, depression, and anxiety
original_authors: Kaye WH; Greeno CG; Moss H.; Fernstrom J.; Fernstrom M.; Lilenfeld LR; Weltzin TE; Mann JJ
original_title: Alterations in serotonin activity and psychiatric symptomatology after recovery from bulimia nervosa
replication_authors: Stein D.; Kaye WH; Matsunaga H.; Orbach I.; Har-Even D.; Frank G.; McConaha CW; Rao R.
replication_title: Eating‐related concerns, mood, and personality traits in recovered bulimia nervosa subjects: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These data replicate previous findings (Kaye et al., 1998) that showed persistent elevations of eating and weight-related concerns, ineffectiveness, perfectionism, depression, and trait anxiety in women who were long-term RBN.' All key comparisons were statistically significant, with elevated EDI-2 subscales, BDI, STAI trait scores, and MPQ Stress Reaction/Negative Emotionality in recovered BN women relative to healthy controls.

description: Temperature at birth is positively associated with restrictive eating attitudes (EDI Drive for Thinness) among non-clinical teenage females born during warmer months
original_authors: Glenn Waller; Caroline Meyer; Laurence van Hanswijck de Jonge
original_title: Early environmental influences on restrictive eating pathology among non-clinical females: The role of temperature at birth
replication_authors: Laurence van Hanswijck de Jonge; Caroline Meyer; Kelly Smith; Glenn Waller
replication_title: Environmental temperature during pregnancy and eating attitudes during teenage years: A replication and extension study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This paper has only partially replicated that effect because the correlation for the equivalent group in this study (r = .14) was in the predicted direction but was not as large as in the previous study (rho = .22), failing to achieve significance.' The effect was directionally consistent but did not reach significance in the matched older female group.

description: A six-session school-based life-skills promotion program for Grade 6 girls failed to significantly improve body image satisfaction or reduce eating problem scores compared to controls, with both groups improving similarly over time
original_authors: Gail L. McVey; Ron Davis
original_title: A program to promote positive body image: A one-year follow-up evaluation
replication_authors: Gail L. McVey; Ron Davis; Stacey Tweed; Brian F. Shaw
replication_title: Evaluation of a school‐based program designed to improve body image satisfaction, global self‐esteem, and eating attitudes and behaviors: A replication study
explanation: The replication found significant short-term improvements in body image satisfaction, global self-esteem, and dieting scores at post-intervention, a different outcome from McVey and Davis (2002) who found no significant intervention effect. However, as the authors note: 'the gains were not maintained at the 12-month follow-up,' and 'Despite the similarity in intervention, this intervention had the positive influence of lowering participants' dieting scores (albeit short-term); a different outcome than that reported by McVey and Davis (2002).' The results are thus mixed — short-term success but no sustained long-term benefit.

description: The three-way interaction among perfectionism, perceived overweight, and low self-esteem predicts increases in bulimic symptoms over a 9-month period among female undergraduates
original_authors: Kathleen D. Vohs; Anna M. Bardone; Thomas E. Joiner; Lyn Y. Abramson
original_title: Perfectionism, perceived weight status, and self-esteem interact to predict bulimic symptoms: A model of bulimic symptom development
replication_authors: Heather E. Shaw; Eric Stice; David W. Springer
replication_title: Perfectionism, body dissatisfaction, and self‐esteem in predicting bulimic symptomatology: Lack of replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our findings did not provide support for this model, even though we focused on a developmental period when bulimic pathology more often increases, used more sensitive structured interviews to assess bulimic pathology, followed participants for a longer period of time, and used a larger sample.' The three-way interaction was non-significant (B = .020, 95% CI: [-.084, .123], r = .02, p = .706).

description: The three-way interaction among perfectionism, body dissatisfaction, and low self-esteem predicts increases in bulimic symptoms over a 5-week period among female undergraduates
original_authors: Kathleen D. Vohs; Zachary R. Voelz; Jeremy W. Pettit; Anna M. Bardone; Jennifer Katz; Lyn Y. Abramson; Todd F. Heatherton; Thomas E. Joiner
original_title: Perfectionism, body dissatisfaction, and self-esteem: An interactive model of bulimic symptom development
original_journal: Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Heather E. Shaw; Eric Stice; David W. Springer
replication_title: Perfectionism, body dissatisfaction, and self‐esteem in predicting bulimic symptomatology: Lack of replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state the study was an 'independent replication' that aimed to provide 'a more sensitive test' of the Vohs et al. model, but 'the three-way interaction did not predict subsequent increases in bulimic symptoms.' The Discussion confirms: 'our findings did not provide support for this model.'

description: Family, peer, and media influences on body dissatisfaction and eating disturbances are linked through internalization of media ideals and appearance comparison as mediators, forming the tripartite influence model
original_authors: Van Den Berg, P.; Thompson, J.; Brandon, K.; Coovert, M.
original_title: A preliminary test of the tripartite influence model of body image and eating disturbance
replication_authors: Yamamiya Y.; Shroff H.; Thompson JK
replication_title: The tripartite influence model of body image and eating disturbance: A replication with a Japanese sample
explanation: The authors found moderate fit for a modified version of the tripartite model, with several key paths supported. However, they explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'Although the model did not fully replicate the van den Berg findings, the changes made to that model were minimal, and the primary relations found for that model...were supported.' This partial support with necessary model modifications warrants an inconclusive classification.

description: An eight-SNP haplotype at the ESR1 gene and three individual SNPs (rs726281, rs2295193, rs3798577) are associated with anorexia nervosa and/or eating disorders
original_authors: Audrey Versini; Nicolas Ramoz; Yann Le Strat; Susann Scherag; Stefan Ehrlich; Claudette Boni; Anke Hinney; Johannes Hebebrand; Lucia Romo; Julien-Daniel Guelfi; Philip Gorwood
original_title: Estrogen receptor 1 gene (ESR1) is associated with restrictive anorexia nervosa
replication_authors: Slof-Op 't Landt MC; van Furth EF; Meulenbelt I.; Bartels M.; Hottenga JJ; Slagboom PE; Boomsma DI
replication_title: Association study of the estrogen receptor I gene (ESR1) in anorexia nervosa and eating disorders: No replication found
explanation: The authors state explicitly in the Discussion: 'we could not confirm the previous findings' and 'The current study failed to replicate previously reported associations between the ESR1 gene and AN.' None of the haplotype or individual SNP associations were statistically significant in the replication sample.

description: Obstetric complications (OCs), particularly pregnancy, delivery, hypoxic, and dysmaturity complications, are significantly associated with increased risk of developing anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa
original_authors: Angela Favaro; Elena Tenconi; Paolo Santonastaso
original_title: Perinatal factors and the risk of developing anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa
replication_authors: Elena Tenconi; Paolo Santonastaso; Francesco Monaco; Angela Favaro
replication_title: Obstetric complications and eating disorders: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state that their replication sample 'confirmed the association between the risk of developing AN or BN and the occurrence and number of OCs' and that 're-analysis of the whole sample substantially confirmed the findings of our previous study.' While a few specific complications (anemia, diabetes, age-of-onset relationship) did not replicate, the core findings about OCs as risk factors for eating disorders were confirmed.

description: AFLP fragments at outlier locus EM74.7 show higher frequencies in moist habitat types than in rock/scree or nutrient-rich habitats in Arabis alpina, indicating habitat-mediated selection
original_authors: Dominique Buehler; Bénédicte N. Poncet; Rolf Holderegger; Stéphanie Manel; Pierre Taberlet; Felix Gugerli
original_title: An outlier locus relevant in habitat-mediated selection in an alpine plant across independent regional replicates
replication_authors: Dominique Buehler; Rolf Holderegger; Sabine Brodbeck; Elvira Schnyder; Felix Gugerli
replication_title: Validation of outlier loci through replication in independent data sets: a test on Arabis alpina
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We therefore failed to validate the allele distribution model at EM74.7 found in the original study in the validation dataset of the Swiss Alps.' The general linear model showed no significant effect of habitat type on haplotype frequencies (P = 0.191), contrary to the original finding.

description: Egg rejection in American robins is determined by background color, maculation, and size, with rejection only triggered when a model egg differs from the robin's own egg appearance by at least two features (not one feature alone)
original_authors: Stephen I. Rothstein
original_title: Mechanisms of avian egg recognition: Which egg parameters elicit responses by rejecter species?
replication_authors: Alec B. Luro; Branislav Igic; Rebecca Croston; Analía V. López; Matthew D. Shawkey; Mark E. Hauber
replication_title: Which egg features predict egg rejection responses in American robins? Replicating Rothstein's (1982) study
explanation: The paper confirmed most of Rothstein's (1982) findings — that background color, maculation, and size all influence egg rejection, with color being the strongest predictor — but found a key discrepancy: unlike Rothstein, who concluded that two or more feature differences are required to evoke rejection responses, this study found that robins do reject model eggs differing by a single feature alone (e.g., 37% rejection for large beige eggs, 68% for maculated eggs, 16% for small-sized eggs). The authors state 'In contrast with [38] conclusion that American robin egg recognition is not specifically tuned toward rejection of brown-headed cowbird eggs, we argue that our results and those of other recent studies of robin egg rejection suggest a discrimination bias toward rejection of cowbird eggs.'

explanation: The authors explicitly claim replication: 'We could replicate previous findings of a significant positive correlation between TS of the RIII-reflex and TS of pain intensity in NCC (c.f., Marouf et al. 2015).' The zero-order Spearman correlation was significant (rs=0.50, p=0.02). However, confidence remains medium because the partial correlation controlling for stimulus intensity rendered this non-significant (rs=0.37, p=0.10), with the authors noting 'the significant association between TS at the reflex and perceptual levels of pain in NCC is largely explained by their mutual dependence on stimulus intensity.' This introduces genuine ambiguity about whether the underlying effect truly replicated or is confounded. The n=21 for NCC reflects 3 participants with missing EMG data due to technical problems.

explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: The authors explicitly state in both the Abstract and Conclusions: 'we replicated our previous finding of syntactic effects during the off-line phase [Lee et al., 2008].' The current study used the same stimuli (conjoined-active and object-relative sentences) and the same paradigm (5-s sentence presentation, 6-s delay, then comprehension probe) as Lee et al. 2008, with the addition of a distance manipulation. The ROIs were directly derived from the Lee et al. 2008 data. Statistical results in the current study strongly support the replication claim: Table IV shows significant syntactic complexity effects during the probe phase in BA 44 (F=9.02, p<0.01) and BA 22 (F=8.97, p<0.01), the same regions where the original study found off-line syntactic effects. Result classification 'success' and replication type 'close experiment' are both correct. Confidence upgraded from 'low' to 'medium': the replication claim is explicit and statistically supported in this paper, but the original is an unpublished conference presentation (not peer-reviewed), no direct quantitative comparison with original effect sizes is reported, and the replication is a self-replication by the same lab (Newman is senior author on both). These factors introduce genuine uncertainty about the strength of the evidence, preventing a 'high' confidence rating.

explanation: Independent review confirms 'success' classification. The authors explicitly state they 'replicated three patterns underlying the three specific forms of memory judgment' (abstract). Conjunction analyses showed significant overlap for the Temporal task (precuneus/angular gyrus, p-corr = 0.011/< 0.001) and Spatial task (bilateral superior parietal cortex, multiple clusters at p-corr < 0.05). For the Object task, MFC/hippocampus overlap reached significance only at uncorrected thresholds. However, three lines of evidence resolve this ambiguity: (1) the formal between-study interaction test showed NO significant difference in these regions (Supporting Information Table 2), meaning the two datasets do not significantly differ; (2) small-volume correction using the LTM hippocampal clusters revealed significant effects in both Exp 1 (p-FWE < 0.001) and Exp 2 (p-FWE = 0.004); (3) the authors attribute the weaker whole-brain conjunction to a sensitivity limitation of univariate methods. The conclusion states 'delay-independent functional correspondence of the judgment specific patterns.' Replication type is correctly 'close extension' because the study tests whether the tripartite dissociation generalizes from 24h to ~2s retention delays — a context/generalizability question (scale-invariance), not a methodology change. Upgraded to high confidence because the authors' own targeted analyses directly resolve the Object task ambiguity.

Classified as 'close extension' because the authors expanded beyond prior work's intra-hemispheric cortical-only connectivity to include inter-hemispheric and cortical-subcortical connections, and added corrections for ROI volume and spatial autocorrelation not used in prior studies.

description: Patients with hippocampal damage show a selective impairment in rejecting re-paired stimuli (novel combinations of previously encountered components) compared to single-repeat or novel stimuli, supporting the hypothesis that the hippocampus is specifically needed for associative/conjunctive memory but not single-item memory

explanation: This was an explicit direct replication using the exact same stimuli and protocol as Kroll et al. (1996). The authors found hippocampal patients were impaired across all trial types, not selectively on Re-paired (associative) trials: 'the patients with hippocampal damage exhibited impaired recognition memory performance. Critically, the impairment was not limited to, or even disproportionately weighted towards the Re-paired trials, but extended relatively evenly across all trial types.'

The replication used the same paired-stimulus preference assessment procedure with adults with dementia, but in a different country (Wales, UK vs. Spain) and with a different population subset (those with intact vocal-verbal repertoires and moderate impairment).

replication_title: Preference for leisure items over edible items in individuals with dementia: A replication
explanation: For 4 of 6 participants who completed the engagement analysis, the highest-ranked stimulus produced the longest engagement duration, consistent with Raetz et al. (2013) where 5 of 7 showed this pattern. However, for Julia and Maria the middle-ranked stimulus produced longer engagement, and the authors do not explicitly label this replication as successful or unsuccessful. The Discussion states 'Presentation of the highest-ranked stimulus resulted in higher durations of engagement' but also notes important caveats (rankings were relative to leisure items only, and even 'lowest' ranked items were selected in 65%+ of trials). The overall pattern is broadly consistent with the original, but the 2/6 exceptions and lack of explicit author verdict warrant medium confidence.

description: Quizzes improve exam performance and some academic behaviors (participation, studying) in college students enrolled in residential courses

replication_authors: Kathryn R. Glodowski; Yusuke Hayashi
replication_title: Toward cross‐disciplinary translation of the testing effect: A systematic replication
explanation: Independent review confirms: the primary hypothesis (testing effect on exam performance) was clearly replicated — authors explicitly state 'successfully replicating the testing effect in the behavior-analytic context,' with F(1.19, 15.44) = 14.53, p = .001, η²p = .528. However, the secondary outcomes were mixed: attendance was NOT replicated (p = .108, ns), and authors explicitly state 'the present study failed to replicate previous research showing that quizzes improve attendance.' Participation showed a significant omnibus effect (p = .021) but post hoc NQ-vs-quiz comparisons were not significant. Reading (10+ min) showed a significant omnibus effect (p = .022) but post hoc NQ-vs-quiz comparisons were all non-significant. Studying (practicing quiz questions) was significantly improved (p < .001). The 'success' classification is appropriate for the primary exam-performance hypothesis, which is what the authors themselves call a replication success. Confidence remains medium because the original paper's scope included all four academic behaviors (attendance, participation, reading, studying), and the present study only partially reproduced those secondary findings — reasonable analysts could weight the mixed secondary outcomes differently.

explanation: Upgraded to high confidence after independent review. The paper's results are unambiguous: F1 progeny from Pst-inoculated 2-week-old seedlings showed statistically significant reductions in Pst::LUX colonization compared to untreated and mock-treated controls (Figure 1b; Welch's ANOVA, Games-Howell post-hoc, α=.05, n>110), directly confirming Luna et al. (2022)'s failed reproduction and used optimized conditions (seedling inoculations at 2 weeks, 100% RH) that represent deliberate methodological improvements — same core paradigm (pathogen-expose parents, test F1 resistance) with modified protocol, hence 'close experiment'. The authors also demonstrated that h-IR strength correlates with parental disease severity, and identified epigenetic markers (DDM1, MET1, CMT3 repression) maintained across generations. The Discussion unequivocally states the results confirm h-IR reproducibility under sufficient parental stress.
