Owen; Lon R. Cardon; Mark Walker; Graham A. Hitman; Colin N. A. Palmer; Alex S. F. Doney; Andrew D. Morris; George Davey Smith; Andrew T. Hattersley; Mark I. McCarthy
original_title: A common variant in the FTO gene is associated with body mass index and predisposes to childhood and adult obesity
replication_authors: Gaifen Liu; Haidong Zhu; Yanbin Dong; Robert H. Podolsky; Frank A. Treiber; Harold Snieder
replication_title: Influence of common variants in FTO and near INSIG2 and MC4R on growth curves for adiposity in African– and European–American youth
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated the effect of FTO rs9939609 on levels of BMI (increasing with 2.1% per A-allele), weight (increasing with 1.9% per A-allele) and waist circumference (increasing with 1.2% per A-allele) in the meta-analysis.' All three associations were statistically significant (P = 0.01, 0.04, 0.04 respectively).

description: Common variants near MC4R (rs17782313, rs17700633) are associated with fat mass, weight, and BMI in both children and adults
original_authors: Loos RJ; Lindgren CM; Li S.; Wheeler E.; Zhao JH; Prokopenko I.; Inouye M.; Freathy RM; Attwood AP; Beckmann JS; Berndt SI; Jacobs KB; Chanock SJ; Hayes RB; Bergmann S.; Bennett AJ; Bingham SA; Bochud M.; Brown M.; Cauchi S.; Connell JM; Cooper C.; Smith GD; Day I.; Dina C.; De S.; Dermitzakis ET; Doney AS; Elliott KS; Elliott P.; Evans DM; Sadaf Farooqi I.; Froguel P.; Ghori J.; Groves CJ; Gwilliam R.; Hadley D.; Hall AS; Hattersley AT; Hebebrand J.; Heid IM; Lamina C.; Gieger C.; Illig T.; Meitinger T.; Wichmann HE; Herrera B.; Hinney A.; Hunt SE; Jarvelin MR; Johnson T.; Jolley JD; Karpe F.; Keniry A.; Khaw KT; Luben RN; Mangino M.; Marchini J.; McArdle WL; McGinnis R.; Meyre D.; Munroe PB; Morris AD; Ness AR; Neville MJ; Nica AC; Ong KK; O'Rahilly S.; Owen KR; Palmer CN; Papadakis K.; Potter S.; Pouta A.; Qi L.; Randall JC; Rayner NW; Ring SM; Sandhu MS; Scherag A.; Sims MA; Song K.; Soranzo N.; Speliotes EK; Syddall HE; Teichmann SA; Timpson NJ; Tobias JH; Uda M.; Vogel CI; Wallace C.; Waterworth DM; Weedon MN; Willer CJ; Wraight; Yuan X.; Zeggini E.; Hirschhorn JN; Strachan DP; Ouwehand WH; Caulfield MJ; Samani NJ; Frayling TM; Vollenweider P.; Waeber G.; Mooser V.; Deloukas P.; McCarthy MI; Wareham NJ; Barroso I.; Jacobs KB; Chanock SJ; Hayes RB; Lamina C.; Gieger C.; Illig T.; Meitinger T.; Wichmann HE; Kraft P.; Hankinson SE; Hunter DJ; Hu FB; Lyon HN; Voight BF; Ridderstrale M.; Groop L.; Scheet P.; Sanna S.; Abecasis GR; Albai G.; Nagaraja R.; Schlessinger D.; Jackson AU; Tuomilehto J.; Collins FS; Boehnke M.; Mohlke KL
original_title: Common variants near MC4R are associated with fat mass, weight and risk of obesity
replication_authors: Gaifen Liu; Haidong Zhu; Yanbin Dong; Robert H. Podolsky; Frank A. Treiber; Harold Snieder
replication_title: Influence of common variants in FTO and near INSIG2 and MC4R on growth curves for adiposity in African– and European–American youth
explanation: The paper states it 'replicated the effect of...common variants near MC4R on general and central adiposity,' but the primary MC4R associations (weight, BMI, waist circumference for rs17782313) did not reach statistical significance; only the triceps skinfold association was significant (P = 0.02), representing only partial replication of the original findings.

description: Logging practices in open-source C/C++ server-side software projects exhibit ten characteristic patterns, including log density averaging one line per 30 lines of code, bug reports with log messages resolving faster, and majority of log updates being consistent updates co-occurring with feature changes
original_authors: Ding Yuan; Soyeon Park; Yuanyuan Zhou
original_title: Characterizing logging practices in open-source software
original_journal: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE '12)
replication_authors: Boyuan Chen; Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang
replication_title: Characterizing logging practices in Java-based open source software projects – a replication study in Apache Software Foundation
explanation: The authors tested the same ten findings from Yuan et al. (2012) in Java-based Apache projects, finding that some results were similar (e.g., logging pervasiveness and code churn) while others were contradicted (e.g., bug resolution time was longer rather than shorter for bug reports with log messages, and after-thought updates were far more common than consistent updates). The conclusion states: 'Similar to the original study, we have found that logging is pervasive in most of the software projects and the logging code is actively maintained. Different from the original study, the median BRT of bug reports containing log messages is longer than bug reports without log messages.'

description: Technical leverage (ratio of borrowed FOSS code to own code) in the Maven (Java) ecosystem enables faster software releases while increasing the risk of vulnerability exposure by ~60% for high-leverage libraries
original_authors: Fabio Massacci; Ivan Pashchenko
original_title: Technical leverage in a software ecosystem: Development opportunities and security risks
original_journal: IEEE/ACM 43rd International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE)
replication_authors: Haya Samaana; Diego Elias Costa; Ahmad Abdellatif; Emad Shihab
replication_title: Opportunities and security risks of technical leverage: A replication study on the NPM ecosystem
explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicate Massacci and Pashchenko [46] in the NPM ecosystem, finding that the same qualitative trade-off holds: high technical leverage is associated with faster releases but significantly higher vulnerability risk. The authors conclude: 'our study shows that technical leverage is associated with opportunities for shipping more code in less time, but comes at the cost of a higher risk of vulnerabilities. Both the opportunities and risks are magnified in NPM, compared to the Maven ecosystem.' The direction of all key findings was confirmed, though magnitudes differed substantially.

description: A repeated four-person public goods game with and without peer punishment (within-subjects design, 10 periods each condition) shows characteristic cooperation dynamics and primarily prosocial punishment patterns across diverse societies
original_authors: Benedikt Herrmann; Christian Thöni; Simon Gächter
original_title: Antisocial punishment across societies
replication_authors: Antonio A. Arechar; Simon Gächter; Lucas Molleman
replication_title: Conducting interactive experiments online
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'basic behavioral patterns of cooperation and punishment in the laboratory are replicable online' and conclude that 'established results from the laboratory can be replicated online.' While cooperation levels differed in absolute terms (higher on MTurk), the key patterns — cooperation decay without punishment, cooperation increase with punishment, and prosocial punishment — were replicated in both the laboratory and online samples.

description: Ingroup identity (established via shared online chat and puzzle-solving) leads to higher average effort in a minimum-effort coordination game compared to outgroup matching, enabling more efficient coordination
original_authors: Roy Chen; Yan Chen
original_title: The potential of social identity for equilibrium selection
replication_authors: Roy Chen; Yan Chen; Yohanes E. Riyanto
replication_title: Best practices in replication: a case study of common information in coordination games
explanation: The authors ran new experiments at NUS and NTU (Singapore) following the original UM protocol with common information (oral instructions). Pooled results show a significant ingroup effect (coefficient = 18.45, p < 0.001), leading them to conclude: 'The pooled result is consistent with the main result obtained in the original study (Chen and Chen 2011).' The replication demonstrates that the earlier Camerer et al. (2016) failure was due to a protocol deviation (removing common information), not because the original effect was false.

description: Students exposed to oral performance assessment as a novel high-stakes intervention associate oral assessment with conceptual understanding, report higher anxiety than for written exams, change their study habits toward deeper engagement, and perceive oral assessment as a better learning experience than traditional written exams
original_authors: Paola Iannone; Christoph Czichowsky; Johannes Ruf
original_title: The impact of high stakes oral performance assessment on students' approaches to learning: A case study
replication_authors: Paola Iannone; Naďa Vondrová
replication_title: The Novelty Effect on Assessment Interventions: a Qualitative Replication Study of Oral Performance Assessment in Undergraduate Mathematics
replication_journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'many of the findings reported in the previous study are still relevant' and state 'the findings of the current study appear to be comparable to those of the original study.' Key findings replicated include students associating oral assessment with conceptual understanding, written assessment with procedures, higher anxiety for oral exams, and perceiving oral assessment as a better learning experience.

description: PEERS® for Young Adults social skills intervention improves social skills, social skills knowledge, empathy, loneliness, and direct social interactions among young adults with autism spectrum disorder
original_authors: Alexander Gantman; Steven K. Kapp; Kaely Orenski; Elizabeth A. Laugeson
original_title: Social skills training for young adults with high-functioning autism spectrum disorders: A randomized controlled pilot study
original_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
replication_authors: Alana J. McVey; Bridget K. Dolan; Kirsten S. Willar; Sheryl Pleiss; Jeffrey S. Karst; Christina L. Casnar; Christina Caiozzo; Elisabeth M. Vogt; Nakia S. Gordon; Amy Vaughan Van Hecke
replication_title: A Replication and Extension of the PEERS® for Young Adults Social Skills Intervention: Examining Effects on Social Skills and Social Anxiety in Young Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
explanation: The majority of Aim 1 (replication) hypotheses were supported — social skills, PEERS knowledge, empathy, and social interactions all improved significantly — but the loneliness hypothesis was not supported, yielding mixed results. The authors characterize the overall outcome as providing 'further empirical support' while acknowledging that 'five out of eleven outcome measures showed significant improvement,' indicating partial rather than full replication success.

description: Big Five personality traits (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability) are associated with ASD characteristics in adults, and correspond to differential social function and well-being
original_authors: Benjamin C. Schwartzman; Jeffrey J. Wood; Steven K. Kapp
original_title: Can the five factor model of personality account for the variability of autism symptom expression? Multivariate approaches to behavioral phenotyping in adult autism spectrum disorder
original_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
replication_authors: Jonathan D. Rodgers; Jennifer Lodi-Smith; Patrick L. Hill; Seth M. Spain; Christopher Lopata; Marcus L. Thomeer
replication_title: Brief Report: Personality Mediates the Relationship between Autism Quotient and Well-Being: A Conceptual Replication using Self-Report
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
explanation: The paper's title explicitly states 'conceptual replication' and the Discussion (p.201 body.md) states verbatim: 'We also successfully replicated results demonstrating that personality is associated with ASD characteristics in adulthood (Austin 2005; Berna et al. 2016; ... Schwartzman et al. 2016; ...). Specifically, higher ASD characteristics were associated with lower openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability, and self-concept clarity.' The replication type (conceptual) and result (success) are unambiguous — the authors state both directly. The study used self-report online survey with a general population sample (n=253) rather than the clinical sample of the original, testing the same personality-ASD relationship with partially different measures. Confidence upgraded from medium to high because the key classification questions are resolved by explicit author statements, not inference.

description: Autistic traits are significantly associated with current gender dysphoric feelings and recalled cross-gender behaviour, and mentalising ability is significantly associated with gender dysphoric feelings, in a general population sample of cisgender individuals
original_authors: Kallitsounaki, Aimilia; Williams, David
original_title: Mentalising moderates the link between autism traits and current gender dysphoric features in primarily non-autistic, cisgender individuals
original_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
replication_authors: Aimilia Kallitsounaki; David M. Williams; Sophie E. Lind
replication_title: Links Between Autistic Traits, Feelings of Gender Dysphoria, and Mentalising Ability: Replication and Extension of Previous Findings from the General Population
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted a direct replication using identical materials and a new sample. The Discussion concludes: 'the current study successfully reproduced (a) the link between autistic traits and current gender dysphoric feelings/recalled cross-gender behaviour and (b) the relation between mentalising and current gender dysphoric feelings, reported by Kallitsounaki and Williams (2020).'

description: The Disruptive Behavior Stress Inventory (DBSI) reliably differentiates primary caregivers of children with ADHD from those without, with significantly higher Stress Experience and Stress Degree scores in the ADHD group and large effect sizes for both subscales
original_authors: James H. Johnson; Steven K. Reader
original_title: Assessing stress in families of children with ADHD: Preliminary development of the Disruptive Behavior Stress Inventory (DBSI)
original_journal: Journal of Clinical Psychology in Medical Settings
replication_authors: Steven K. Reader; Lindsay M. Stewart; James H. Johnson
replication_title: Assessing ADHD-related Family Stressors with the Disruptive Behavior Stress Inventory (DBSI): A Replication and Extension
replication_journal: Journal of Clinical Psychology in Medical Settings
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These results replicated those from the original Johnson and Reader (2002) study' and 'Overall, the results of this study are consistent with the major findings of the original study by Johnson and Reader (2002) in providing additional support for the adequacy of the DBSI Stress Experience and Stress Degree scales.' Both DBSI subscale scores were significantly higher for the ADHD group with large effect sizes (Cohen's f = .84 and .77), matching the pattern found in the original.

description: Engaging in the Noticing Nature Intervention (NNI) — noticing and photographing everyday nature over two weeks — significantly enhances well-being (positive affect, connectedness) and is not moderated by trait connectedness to nature nor by increased time spent in nature
original_authors: Holli-Anne Passmore; Mark D. Holder
original_title: Noticing nature: Individual and social benefits of a two-week intervention
replication_authors: Holli-Anne Passmore; Ying Yang; Sarena Sabine
replication_title: An Extended Replication Study of the Well-Being Intervention, the Noticing Nature Intervention (NNI)
explanation: The authors explicitly classify this as a 'conceptual replication study' and their conclusion states: 'The current study replicated Passmore and Holder's (2017) findings regarding the overall efficacy of the Noticing Nature Intervention (NNI) to enhance well-being.' Key findings on well-being, moderation by nature connectedness, and time in nature all replicated, though elevation did not (attributed to measurement issues).

description: A large-scale survey of Miranda warnings across 560 American jurisdictions found striking heterogeneity in length, content, and reading comprehension levels of Miranda warnings used across the United States
original_authors: Richard Rogers; Kimberly S. Harrison; Daniel W. Shuman; Kenneth W. Sewell; Lisa L. Hazelwood
original_title: An analysis of Miranda warnings and waivers: Comprehension and coverage
replication_authors: Richard Rogers; Lisa L. Hazelwood; Kenneth W. Sewell; Kimberly S. Harrison; Daniel W. Shuman
replication_title: The language of Miranda warnings in American jurisdictions: A replication and vocabulary analysis.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their abstract that 'most of the original findings were confirmed,' and their Discussion opens with 'This replication confirms the perplexing patchwork of Miranda warnings.' Effect sizes across nearly all comparisons are negligible to small (M d = 0.09), indicating close correspondence between original and replication surveys.

description: Youth participation in hazards education programs is associated with increased hazard-related knowledge, more realistic risk perceptions, lower child and parental fear, and adoption of more household hazard adjustments, with family discussions as a predictor of increased benefits
original_authors: Ronan, Kevin R.; Johnston, David M.
original_title: Correlates of hazards education programs for youth
replication_authors: Kevin R. Ronan; Kylie Crellin; David Johnston
replication_title: Correlates of hazards education for youth: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to 'replicate and extend previous findings (Ronan and Johnston 2001)' using a separate sample in a different region with different hazard profiles. The Discussion concludes: 'the findings of the current study support the value of hazards education programs for youth, replicating as well as extending features of previous research,' with the core findings on knowledge, hazard adjustments, and predictors (program recency, parent interaction) mirroring the original.

description: Increases in women's positive communication following PREP training are paradoxically associated with higher (not lower) risk for marital distress over time
original_authors: Elizabeth A. Schilling; Donald H. Baucom; Charles K. Burnett; Elizabeth Sandin Allen; Lynelle Ragland
original_title: Altering the course of marriage: the effect of PREP communication skills acquisition on couples' risk of becoming maritally distressed
replication_authors: Stanley SM; Rhoades GK; Olmos-Gallo PA; Markman HJ
replication_title: Mechanisms of Change in a Cognitive Behavioral Couples Prevention Program: Does Being Naughty or Nice Matter?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'in direct tests for replication, we did not find evidence for the paradoxical finding of Schilling et al. in either of our two samples.' The Discussion concludes: 'In summary, we did not replicate the paradoxical findings of Schilling et al.'

description: QLQ-C30 cutoff scores can discriminate between cancer patients with and without unmet needs as identified by the SCNS-SF34, with six specific QLQ-C30 domains achieving AUC ≥ 0.70
original_authors: Claire F. Snyder; Amanda L. Blackford; Julie R. Brahmer; Michael A. Carducci; Roberto Pili; Vered Stearns; Antonio C. Wolff; Sydney M. Dy; Albert W. Wu
original_title: Needs assessments can identify scores on HRQOL questionnaires that represent problems for patients: an illustration with the Supportive Care Needs Survey and the QLQ-C30
replication_authors: Claire F. Snyder; Amanda L. Blackford; Toru Okuyama; Tatsuo Akechi; Hiroko Yamashita; Tatsuya Toyama; Michael A. Carducci; Albert W. Wu
replication_title: Using the EORTC-QLQ-C30 in clinical practice for patient management: identifying scores requiring a clinician’s attention
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The findings from our original analysis were supported. The same six domains with AUC ≥ 0.70 in the original analysis had AUC ≥ 0.70 in this new sample,' and conclude 'given the substantial concordance between this replication sample and our original sample, we believe there is adequate evidence to support implementing these cutoffs in PatientViewpoint.' The replication used a larger sample (n=408 vs. n=117) of Japanese breast cancer patients, testing generalizability across cultural/linguistic contexts.

description: Latent class analysis of US cancer patients' function, symptoms, and supportive care needs identifies two-class (high vs. low) models, with class assignment made by level of burden rather than type of symptom cluster
original_authors: Claire F. Snyder; Elizabeth Garrett-Mayer; Amanda L. Blackford; Julie R. Brahmer; Michael A. Carducci; Roberto Pili; Vered Stearns; Antonio C. Wolff; Sydney M. Dy; Albert W. Wu
original_title: Concordance of cancer patients' function, symptoms, and supportive care needs
replication_authors: Jennifer Barsky Reese; Amanda Blackford; Jonathan Sussman; Toru Okuyama; Tatsuo Akechi; Daryl Bainbridge; Doris Howell; Claire F. Snyder
replication_title: Cancer patients’ function, symptoms and supportive care needs: a latent class analysis across cultures
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the results of the Japanese and Canadian data analyses were generally consistent with the US findings in that patients were classified based on their level of burden in each of the three outcomes' and in the Conclusion: 'this analysis supported the findings of our original study that the levels of deficits patients experience in their symptoms, functioning, and supportive care needs are the key factors in classification.'

description: Adults with ASD report worse mental and physical health-related quality of life (HRQoL) compared to neurotypical counterparts, with sex differences such that physical HRQoL is reduced specifically in women with ASD
original_authors: Laura Graham Holmes; Casey J. Zampella; Caitlin Clements; Joseph P. McCleery; Brenna B. Maddox; Julia Parish‐Morris; Manisha D. Udhnani; Robert T. Schultz; Judith S. Miller
original_title: A lifespan approach to patient-reported outcomes and quality of life for people on the autism spectrum
replication_authors: Braden BB; Pagni BA; Monahan L.; Walsh MJM; Dixon MV; Delaney S.; Ballard L.; Ware JE Jr
replication_title: Quality of life in adults with autism spectrum disorder: influence of age, sex, and a controlled, randomized mindfulness-based stress reduction pilot intervention
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Study 1 conclusions: 'We replicated previous findings that mental HRQoL is worse in both men and women with ASD, compared to their NT counterparts, but that physical HRQoL is only reduced in women with ASD.' Graham Holmes et al. [10] was the specific study used for power calculations (effect sizes) and is cited alongside Mason et al. [4] for the sex-by-diagnosis finding. The replication used the SF-36 in a new independent sample of US adults with ASD and NT controls.

description: Participants endowed with an item exhibit exchange asymmetry (under-trading, well below the 50% expected rate) even with familiar goods like mugs and pens, consistent with endowment effect theory
original_authors: Charles R. Plott; Kathryn Zeiler
original_title: Exchange asymmetries incorrectly interpreted as evidence of endowment effect theory and prospect theory?
replication_authors: Christina McGranaghan; Steven G. Otto
replication_title: Choice uncertainty and the endowment effect
explanation: The follow-up experiment EP2 explicitly replicates the 'Baseline' procedure of PZ2007 and successfully finds an exchange asymmetry in the control condition (13% trade rate, well below 50%), consistent with the original finding. The authors state: 'Experiment EP2 thus successfully replicates the full dissipation of the exchange asymmetries in the treated groups.'

description: In the baseline 'KKT Replication' condition (following Kahneman et al. 1990), participants endowed with an item report higher WTA than non-endowed participants report WTP, producing a sizable WTA/WTP valuation asymmetry
original_authors: Charles R. Plott; Kathryn Zeiler
original_title: The willingness to pay-willingness to accept gap, the 'endowment effect', subject misconceptions, and experimental procedures for eliciting valuations
replication_authors: Christina McGranaghan; Steven G. Otto
replication_title: Choice uncertainty and the endowment effect
explanation: The follow-up experiment VP2 explicitly replicates the 'KKT Replication' baseline design of PZ2005 but failed to produce a sizable endowment effect: the WTA/WTP ratio in the control condition was only 1.31, compared to 3.47 in the authors' own primary study (VP1). The authors attribute this to COVID-related precautions that altered the experimental conditions.

description: General TCP techniques (ARPJacMaxMin, ARPManMaxMin, FixedWeights, Stoop) applied to model-based test suites show no best performer overall, but characteristics of failing test cases (size, branch traversal) significantly affect technique performance, while model layout alone does not
original_authors: João Felipe Silva Ouriques; Emanuela Gadelha Cartaxo; Patrícia Duarte Lima Machado
original_title: Revealing influence of model structure and test case profile on the prioritization of test cases in the context of model-based testing
original_journal: Journal of Software Engineering Research and Development
replication_authors: João Felipe S. Ouriques; Emanuela G. Cartaxo; Patrícia D. L. Machado
replication_title: Test case prioritization techniques for model-based testing: a replicated study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The results presented here provide more evidence favoring the previous ones, since the conclusions point to the same direction.' Both key findings replicate: (1) no clear best performer among TCP techniques, and (2) characteristics of failing test cases affect technique performance.

description: The 2005 German accounting enforcement reforms had weak but consistently positive effects on earnings quality, stock liquidity, and market valuation of affected companies
original_authors: Jürgen Ernstberger; Michael Stich; Oliver Vogler
original_title: Economic consequences of accounting enforcement reforms: the case of Germany
replication_authors: Marius Gros; Alexander Nevrela
replication_title: Revisiting the effectiveness of the German accounting enforcement reforms: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion that 'we cannot substantiate a weak but consistently positive effect of the reforms on accounting quality and capital market properties.' While some stock liquidity results partially align with ESV (2012), the replication fails to confirm the original's earnings quality and market valuation findings, and the authors reject hypotheses H1 and H3 for both periods.

description: Aging in C57BL/6 mice is associated with reduced use of the running wheel and increased fragmentation of locomotor activity under stable light:dark conditions
original_authors: Verónica S. Valentinuzzi; Kathryn Scarbrough; Joseph S. Takahashi; Fred W. Turek
original_title: Effects of aging on the circadian rhythm of wheel-running activity in C57BL/6 mice
replication_authors: Leise TL; Harrington ME; Molyneux PC; Song I.; Queenan H.; Zimmerman E.; Lall GS; Biello SM
replication_title: Voluntary exercise can strengthen the circadian system in aged mice
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated previous reports that aging is associated with reduced use of the running wheel, fragmentation of activity under a stable LD cycle, and slowed phase resetting following a shift in the LD cycle.' The Results section also confirms: 'Both the reduced overall activity and increased fragmentation of activity for aged mice are consistent with previous findings (Valentinuzzi et al. 1997).'

description: Older C57BL/6 mice show increased locomotor activity in the late portion of the dark phase (a 'sundowning'-like effect), analogous to agitation and worsened dementia symptoms seen in Alzheimer's patients in the late afternoon
original_authors: Tracy A. Bedrosian; Kamillya L. Herring; Zachary M. Weil; Randy J. Nelson
original_title: Altered temporal patterns of anxiety in aged and amyloid precursor protein (APP) transgenic mice
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Leise TL; Harrington ME; Molyneux PC; Song I.; Queenan H.; Zimmerman E.; Lall GS; Biello SM
replication_title: Voluntary exercise can strengthen the circadian system in aged mice
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Whereas a prior study reported that older mice showed increased locomotor activity in the late portion of the dark phase... (Bedrosian et al. 2011), we failed to replicate this effect.' The current study used the same C57BL/6 strain but tested mice at 18-20 months rather than 29 months and under LD 12:12 rather than 14:10.

description: Chicago's CeaseFire program (a public health approach using street outreach workers to mediate conflicts and change norms) was associated with significant reductions in shootings and retaliatory homicides in four of seven intervention neighborhoods studied
original_authors: Skogan, Wesley G.; Hartnett, Susan M.; Bump, Natalie; Dubois, Jill
original_title: Evaluation of CeaseFire-Chicago
replication_authors: Daniel W. Webster; Jennifer Mendel Whitehill; Jon S. Vernick; Frank C. Curriero
replication_title: Effects of Baltimore’s Safe Streets Program on Gun Violence: A Replication of Chicago’s CeaseFire Program
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself 'A Replication of Chicago's CeaseFire Program' and tests the same program model in Baltimore. Results were mixed across four sites: Cherry Hill showed large reductions (56% homicide, 34% NFS), one East Baltimore site reduced NFS only, another reduced homicides only, and Madison-Eastend showed increased homicides alongside decreased NFS. The authors conclude: 'the magnitude and consistency of the effects vary and some program sites did not experience program-related reductions in gun violence.'

description: Morbidly obese patients presenting for bariatric surgery show significant elevations on multiple MMPI-2 scales compared to a normal distribution
original_authors: Salvatore R. Maddi; Deborah M. Khoshaba; Michelle Persico; Felicia Bleecker; Gregory VanArsdall
original_title: Psychosocial correlates of psychopathology in a national sample of the morbidly obese
replication_authors: Kinder BN; Walfish S.; Scott Young M.; Fairweather A.
replication_title: MMPI-2 Profiles of Bariatric Surgery Patients: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of the present study generally confirm the findings of Maddi et al.' and 'Our present data are very consistent with those reported by Maddi et al., with both sets of data indicating a high proportion of bariatric surgery candidates reporting significantly elevated MMPI-2 patterns.' Only 2 of 10+ MMPI-2 scales showed statistically significant differences between the original and replication samples.

description: An 8-week Mindfulness-Based Resilience Training (MBRT) program for police officers reduces perceived stress, sleep disturbances, anxiety, and burnout
original_authors: Christopher, Michael; Goerling, Richard J.; Rogers, Brant S.; Hunsinger, Matthew; Baron, Greg; Bergman, Aaron L.; Zava, David T.
original_title: A pilot study evaluating the effectiveness of a mindfulness-based intervention on cortisol awakening response and health outcomes among law enforcement officers
original_journal: Journal of Police and Criminal Psychology
replication_authors: Daniel W. Grupe; Chad McGehee; Chris Smith; Andrew D. Francis; Jeanette A. Mumford; Richard J. Davidson
replication_title: Mindfulness Training Reduces PTSD Symptoms and Improves Stress-Related Health Outcomes in Police Officers
replication_journal: Journal of Police and Criminal Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated some but not all of the previously reported improvements in stress-related health outcomes noted by Christopher et al. (2016).' They confirmed reductions in perceived stress, sleep quality (PSQI), anxiety, and exhaustion, but found no effects on physical health outcomes (pain, physical functioning, CRP) that the original study reported.

description: Perioperative mean arterial blood pressure (MAP) is a major predictor of neuromotor recovery outcome in rats with spinal cord injury, discovered using topological data analysis on single-center MASCIS data
original_authors: Nielson JL; Paquette J.; Liu AW; Guandique CF; Tovar CA; Inoue T.; Irvine KA; Gensel JC; Kloke J.; Petrossian TC; Lum PY; Carlsson GE; Manley GT; Young W.; Beattie MS; Bresnahan JC; Ferguson AR
original_title: Topological data analysis for discovery in preclinical spinal cord injury and traumatic brain injury
replication_authors: Almeida CA; Torres-Espin A.; Huie JR; Sun D.; Noble-Haeusslein LJ; Young W.; Beattie MS; Bresnahan JC; Nielson JL; Ferguson AR
replication_title: Excavating FAIR Data: the Case of the Multicenter Animal Spinal Cord Injury Study (MASCIS), Blood Pressure, and Neuro-Recovery
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In the current confirmatory study, we recovered legacy data from 1125 rats to independently replicate the results from Nielson et al. (2015).' The results confirmed the interaction between perioperative blood pressure, injury severity, and neuromotor recovery, with the Discussion concluding that 'these findings confirm and expand prior results that a narrow window of blood-pressure control optimizes outcome.'

description: Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) deposition is positively associated with heart weight in post-mortem cases across normal, ischemic, and hypertrophic hearts
original_authors: Domenico Corradi; Roberta Maestri; Sergio Callegari; Paolo Pastori; Matteo Goldoni; Tu Vinh Luong; Cesare Bordi
original_title: The ventricular epicardial fat is related to the myocardial mass in normal, ischemic and hypertrophic hearts
replication_authors: Aitken-Buck HM; Moore MK; Bingham KT; Coffey S.; Tse RD; Lamberts RR
replication_title: Association of epicardial adipose tissue volume with heart weight in post-mortem cases
explanation: Independent review confirms this is a clear replication success. The authors explicitly framed the study as attempting to 'replicate or provide explanations for the contrary findings' of Peczkowski et al. (2022), who had failed to find the positive EAT-heart weight relationship established by Corradi et al. (2004). The replication result (r = 0.60, p < 0.0001, N=87) directly confirms the positive association Corradi et al. found (r = 0.68). The Conclusion section explicitly states: 'These findings confirm that individuals with normal heart weights have predictable EAT deposition, as established previously [Corradi et al., Silaghi et al., Womack].' The nuance that the relationship breaks down in hypertrophic hearts does not undermine the success classification — the paper uses this finding to explain why Peczkowski et al. failed (their sample was predominantly hypertrophic), thereby validating rather than contradicting Corradi et al. Upgraded from medium to high: the evidence is specific, quantitative, directly cited by the authors, and unambiguous in interpretation.

description: College students report matrilateral biases (maternal relatives invest more than paternal) and sex biases (aunts invest more than uncles) in the investment of aunts and uncles, interpreted as a consequence of paternity uncertainty
original_authors: Steven J. C. Gaulin; Donald H. McBurney; Stephanie L. Brakeman-Wartell
original_title: Matrilateral biases in the investment of aunts and uncles
replication_authors: Donald H. McBurney; Jessica Simon; Steven J. C. Gaulin; Allan Geliebter
replication_title: Matrilateral biases in the investment of aunts and uncles
explanation: The authors used the identical questionnaire from the original study but tested it in a new population (Orthodox Jewish college students) presumed to have higher paternity certainty. The replication confirmed both the matrilateral and sex biases: 'the present study replicated the results of our earlier study in finding both a matrilateral and a sex bias in investment by aunts and uncles in an Orthodox Jewish population.'

description: Negative fantasies about a romantic interest predict obsessive preoccupation and intentions to pursue romantic closeness
original_authors: Timothy J. Valshtein; Elizabeth R. Mutter; Gabriele Oettingen; Peter M. Gollwitzer
original_title: Relatedness needs and negative fantasies as the origins of obsessive thinking in romantic relationships
replication_authors: Timothy J. Valshtein; Elizabeth R. Mutter; Peter M. Gollwitzer; Gabriele Oettingen
replication_title: I’ve been thinkin’ bout you: socially distant relationship pursuit during COVID-19
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our results replicate work (Valshtein et al., 2020) finding that people more prone to negative fantasies are also more prone to preoccupation with a romantic interest.' The main effect of negative fantasies on presumptuous romantic intentions was found in Study 1 (b=0.41, p=0.004) and at the between-person level in Study 2 (b=0.19, p=0.01).

description: In the presence of an aroused relatedness need, negative fantasies intensify obsessive thinking and pursuit intentions toward a romantic interest (interaction between relatedness threat and negative fantasies)
original_authors: Timothy J. Valshtein; Elizabeth R. Mutter; Gabriele Oettingen; Peter M. Gollwitzer
original_title: Relatedness needs and negative fantasies as the origins of obsessive thinking in romantic relationships
replication_authors: Timothy J. Valshtein; Elizabeth R. Mutter; Peter M. Gollwitzer; Gabriele Oettingen
replication_title: I’ve been thinkin’ bout you: socially distant relationship pursuit during COVID-19
explanation: The authors report 'Conceptually replicating the pattern found by Valshtein and colleagues (2020)' at the between-person level (negative fantasies more strongly predicted intentions when relatedness frustration was higher), but the within-person interaction went in the opposite direction (higher daily frustration paired with negative fantasies predicted lower intentions). The authors describe these as 'modest interactions' with a 'novel' within-person opposite pattern.

description: Hospital nurses' engagement in social learning activities (ESLA) after errors is mediated by the estimated relevance of the error to learning (transmitting error strain) and by the tendency to cover up errors (transmitting safe team climate perceptions)
original_authors: Johannes Bauer; Regina H. Mulder
original_title: Engagement in learning after errors at work: enabling conditions and types of engagement
replication_authors: Veronika Leicher; Regina H. Mulder; Johannes Bauer
replication_title: Learning from Errors at Work: A Replication Study in Elder Care Nursing
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'The results from our study entirely corroborate the mediation model of ESLA proposed by the earlier study' and that the findings 'entirely cross-validate the exploratory findings of Bauer and Mulder (2011) on hospital nurses' ESLA and show that they generalise to the domain of elder care nursing.' All hypothesised effects were statistically significant and in expected directions.

description: Latent profile analysis of college students' FFMQ mindfulness scores identifies four distinct mindfulness profiles: high mindfulness, low mindfulness, judgmentally observing, and non-judgmentally aware groups with differentially adaptive psychological health outcomes
original_authors: Pearson MR; Lawless AK; Brown DB; Bravo AJ
original_title: Mindfulness and emotional outcomes: identifying subgroups of college students using latent profile analysis
replication_authors: Adrian J. Bravo; Matthew R. Pearson; Michelle L. Kelley
replication_title: Mindfulness and Psychological Health Outcomes: a Latent Profile Analysis Among Military Personnel and College Students
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract 'In the subsample of college students, we replicated previous research and found four distinct mindfulness profiles,' and in the Introduction they describe the goal as replicating 'the four-class solution reported previously (Bravo et al. 2016; Kimmes et al. 2017; Pearson et al. 2015b) in an independent sample.' The same four classes with similar profiles were found in a new college student sample, with the high mindfulness group again showing the most adaptive psychological outcomes.

description: Chronic stress is negatively associated with mindful acceptance skills (but not attention monitoring), and acceptance moderates the association between attention monitoring and chronic stress
original_authors: Francesco Saldarini; Mark Cropley
original_title: Chronic stress is associated with reduced mindful acceptance skills but not with mindful attention monitoring: A cross-sectional study
original_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
replication_authors: Francesco Saldarini; Kaho Yamasaki; Hiromitsu Miyata
replication_title: Associations Between Chronic Stress, Attention, Working Memory, and Mindful Acceptance in the Context of Monitor and Acceptance Theory: A Direct Replication and Exploratory Cross-Sectional Study
explanation: The authors state 'Our results almost exactly replicated the findings of the original study' and in the Discussion confirm that the significant negative associations between chronic stress and acceptance, and the null associations with monitoring, both replicated. The study was conducted in a Japanese sample (vs. original British sample), justifying close extension classification.

description: A brief online socio-cognitive mindfulness intervention ('notice new things' and other tasks) substantially improves performance on cognitive-bias tasks
original_authors: Philip Z. Maymin; Ellen J. Langer
original_title: Cognitive biases and mindfulness
replication_authors: Phillip Thiedmann; Florence Dejardin; Leonhard Reiter; Ulrich S. Tran
replication_title: Brief Online Socio-Cognitive Mindfulness Interventions Neither Improve Socio-Cognitive Mindfulness nor Cognitive Biases: A Two-Study Conceptual Replication and Reanalysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
explanation: Study 1 tested the isolated 'notice new things' component of the original intervention with a much larger sample (n=479). The intervention and control groups did not differ in cognitive-bias scores (d = -0.04, p = 0.70), and equivalence testing confirmed the effect was smaller than a minimally meaningful threshold. The authors conclude 'no relevant or significant mean difference in cognitive-bias scores favoring the intervention over the control group could be observed.'

description: A brief online socio-cognitive mindfulness intervention ('notice new things' and other tasks) substantially improves performance on cognitive-bias tasks
original_authors: Philip Z. Maymin; Ellen J. Langer
original_title: Cognitive biases and mindfulness
replication_authors: Phillip Thiedmann; Florence Dejardin; Leonhard Reiter; Ulrich S. Tran
replication_title: Brief Online Socio-Cognitive Mindfulness Interventions Neither Improve Socio-Cognitive Mindfulness nor Cognitive Biases: A Two-Study Conceptual Replication and Reanalysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
explanation: Study 2 tested the full intervention (all four components) with n=299 participants and also included a manipulation check for socio-cognitive mindfulness. Neither cognitive-bias scores (d = -0.15, p = 0.17) nor the manipulation check for socio-cognitive mindfulness (d = -0.13, p = 0.27) showed significant group differences. The authors conclude 'no relevant or significant mean difference in cognitive-bias scores favoring the intervention over the control group could be observed in Study 2.'

description: Gene expression levels of individual genes and gene networks in peripheral blood monocytes (including oxidative-stress-related genes such as KEAP1) correlate with neurocognitive functioning in HIV+ adults
original_authors: Andrew J. Levine; Steve Horvath; Eric N. Miller; Elyse J. Singer; Paul Shapshak; Gayle C. Baldwin; Otoniel Martínez-Maza; Mallory D. Witt; Peter Langfelder
original_title: Transcriptome analysis of HIV-infected peripheral blood monocytes: gene transcripts and networks associated with neurocognitive functioning
replication_authors: Austin Quach; Steve Horvath; Natasha Nemanim; Dimitrios Vatakis; Mallory D. Witt; Eric N. Miller; Roger Detels; Peter Langfelder; Paul Shapshak; Elyse J. Singer; Andrew J. Levine
replication_title: No reliable gene expression biomarkers of current or impending neurocognitive impairment in peripheral blood monocytes of persons living with HIV
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Contrary to our hypotheses, we were unable to replicate the findings from our earlier study (Levine et al. 2013), which had implicated several genes involved in anti-oxidant response.' The procedures were identical to the original study and none of the top genes identified previously were validated in the independent HIV+ group.

original_authors: Deborah Nejman; Ilana Livyatan; Garold Fuks; Nancy Gavert; Yaara Zwang; Leore T. Geller; Aviva Rotter-Maskowitz; Roi Weiser; Giuseppe Mallel; Elinor Gigi; Arnon Meltser; Gavin M. Douglas; Iris Kamer; Vancheswaran Gopalakrishnan; Tali Dadosh; Smadar Levin-Zaidman; Sofia Avnet; Tehila Atlan; Zachary A. Cooper; Reetakshi Arora; Alexandria P. Cogdill; Md Abdul Wadud Khan; Gabriel Ologun; Yuval Bussi; Adina Weinberger; Maya Lotan-Pompan; Ofra Golani; Gili Perry; Merav Rokah; Keren Bahar-Shany; Elisa A. Rozeman; Christian U. Blank; Anat Ronai; Ron Shaoul; Amnon Amit; Tatiana Dorfman; Ran Kremer; Zvi R. Cohen; Sagi Harnof; Tali Siegal; Einav Yehuda-Shnaidman; Einav Nili Gal-Yam; Hagit Shapira; Nicola Baldini; Morgan G. I. Langille; Alon Ben-Nun; Bella Kaufman; Aviram Nissan; Talia Golan; Maya Dadiani; Keren Levanon; Jair Bar; Shlomit Yust-Katz; Iris Barshack; Daniel S. Peeper; Dan J. Raz; Eran Segal; Jennifer A. Wargo; Judith Sandbank; Noam Shental; Ravid Straussman
original_title: The human tumor microbiome is composed of tumor type-specific intracellular bacteria
replication_authors: Noel F. C. C. de Miranda; Vincent T. H. B. M. Smit; Manon van der Ploeg; Jelle Wesseling; Jacques Neefjes
replication_title: Absence of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) expression in breast cancer cells
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the failure to replicate the detection of LPS in breast cancer cells.' Using the same antibody clone (WN1 222-5) as the original study, LPS expression was never detected in cancer cells across 129 breast cancer samples; it was only found in macrophages and ducts as expected from normal biology.

description: Current use of oral fluoroquinolones is associated with a 4.5-fold increased risk of retinal detachment compared with non-users
original_authors: M. Etminan; F. Forooghian; J. Brophy; Steven T. Bird; D. Maberley
original_title: Oral fluoroquinolones and the risk of retinal detachment
replication_authors: Daniel Fife; Vivienne Zhu; Erica Voss; Grace Levy-Clarke; Patrick Ryan
replication_title: Exposure to Oral Fluoroquinolones and the Risk of Retinal Detachment: Retrospective Analyses of Two Large Healthcare Databases
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'the present study does not confirm the recent Canadian study's finding of a strong relationship between RD and current exposure to fluoroquinolones.' Across all analyses in two large US databases, adjusted ORs for current exposure were mostly around 1.0-1.3 (not statistically significant), far below the original 4.5-fold risk (OR 4.50, 95% CI 3.56-5.70), and the SCCS analysis showed no significant association at all.

description: An enhanced stimulus-stimulus pairing (SSP) procedure — pairing target vocalizations with high-preference items, with interspersed target/nontarget trials, an observing response, and motherese speech — produces substantial increases in target vocalizations in children with autism
original_authors: Barbara E. Esch; James E. Carr; Laura L. Grow
original_title: Evaluation of an enhanced stimulus-stimulus pairing procedure to increase early vocalizations of children with autism
replication_authors: Lisa Rader; Tina M. Sidener; Kenneth F. Reeve; David W. Sidener; Lara Delmolino; Adriane Miliotis; Vincent Carbone
replication_title: Stimulus-Stimulus Pairing of Vocalizations: A Systematic Replication
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Systematic Replication' of Esch et al. (2009) and follows the same protocol. Results were mixed: 2 of 3 participants showed substantial increases in target vocalizations (replicating the original), but the third (Paul) showed only minimal and non-differential increases, unlike the original where all 3 participants responded. The authors frame the overall outcome as partial support: 'Results showed substantial increases in target vocalizations above baseline levels and above nontarget vocalizations for two of three participants.'

description: Listener-speaker multiple exemplar instruction (MEI) with rotating response operants (match, point, tact) establishes incidental bidirectional naming (Inc-BiN) in preschoolers with developmental disabilities
original_authors: Emma Hawkins; Sheri Kingsdorf; Jackie Charnock; Mariann Szabo; Grant Gautreaux
original_title: Effects of multiple exemplar instruction on naming
replication_authors: Yoon JS; Greer RD; Virk M.; Fienup DM
replication_title: The Establishment of Incidental Bidirectional Naming through Multiple Exemplar Instruction: a Systematic Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our findings are consistent with the findings of Hawkins et al.'s (2009) study' and found listener-speaker MEI with added echoics was effective in establishing Inc-BiN for 3 of 4 participants. The study is described as a systematic replication with procedural modifications (adding echoics), new instructors, and new participants.

description: Opt-out (negative) framing with an unchecked box as default produces higher enrollment/participation rates than opt-in (positive) framing arrangements
original_authors: Eric J. Johnson; Steven Bellman; Gerald L. Lohse
original_title: Defaults, framing and privacy: Why opting in-opting out
replication_authors: Fernanda S. Oda; Robert S. LeComte; Derek D. Reed
replication_title: Do NOT Read this Article: the Effects of Autoclitics and Nudge on Choosing
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We were surprised to replicate Johnson et al.' (2002) results on having the negative framing with unchecked box producing the highest enrollment.' Both studies found that the negative frame with unchecked box produced the highest enrollment rates (97.7% in Study 1; 100% in Study 2), consistent with the original findings.

description: Child choice of putative reinforcers confers advantage over experimenter choice during skill acquisition for children with autism
original_authors: Karen A. Toussaint; Tiffany Kodak; Jason C. Vladescu
original_title: An evaluation of choice on instructional efficacy and individual preference for children with autism
replication_authors: Jessie Northgrave; Jason C. Vladescu; Ruth M. DeBar; Karen A. Toussaint; Lauren K. Schnell
replication_title: Reinforcer Choice on Skill Acquisition for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: a Systematic Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'our findings did not replicate those of Toussaint et al. (2016),' finding that the experimenter-choice condition was more efficient than child choice for both participants — the opposite of Toussaint et al.'s finding that child choice conferred advantage.

description: An interview-informed functional analysis followed by functional communication training and delay/denial tolerance training produces meaningful reductions in problem behavior and increases in functional communication responses in children with autism
original_authors: Hanley GP; Jin CS; Vanselow NR; Hanratty LA
original_title: Producing meaningful improvements in problem behavior of children with autism via synthesized analyses and treatments
replication_authors: Lauren Beaulieu; Meghan E. Van Nostrand; Ashley L. Williams; Brandon Herscovitch
replication_title: Incorporating Interview-Informed Functional Analyses into Practice
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the results of Hanley et al. (2014), Santiago et al. (2016), and Jessel et al. (2018), which further support the generality of the assessment and treatment model.' They demonstrated successful treatment effects with one participant in a home-based service setting with limited supervision, extending generality across novel stimuli, settings, people, and time.

description: Prompting and reinforcement procedures effectively teach gaze-shifting skills for requesting and joint attention (responding and initiating) to toddlers with autism spectrum disorder, with generalization across related social communication skills
original_authors: Krstovska-Guerrero, Ivana; Jones, Emily A.
original_title: Social-communication intervention for toddlers with autism spectrum disorder: Eye gaze in the context of requesting and joint attention
original_journal: Journal of Developmental and Physical Disabilities
replication_authors: Holly R. Weisberg; Emily A. Jones
replication_title: Individualizing Intervention to Teach Joint Attention, Requesting, and Social Referencing to Children with Autism
explanation: The authors state 'Results replicated previous literature by demonstrating that, in general, prompting and reinforcement resulted in acquisition of RR, SR, RJA, and IJA for two children with ASD.' However, they also note 'these results contrast with previous research in which all children responded to the same intervention procedures (Krstovska-Guerrero & Jones, 2016)' and found substantially less generalization than the original study, with not all children acquiring each skill and all requiring individualized modifications.

description: Prompting and reinforcement procedures effectively teach gaze-shifting skills for requesting and initiating joint attention to toddlers with autism spectrum disorder, with generalization to interactions with the mother
original_authors: Madiha S. Muzammal; Emily A. Jones
original_title: Social-communication intervention for toddlers with autism spectrum disorder: Effects on initiating joint attention and interactions with mother
original_journal: Journal of Developmental and Physical Disabilities
replication_authors: Holly R. Weisberg; Emily A. Jones
replication_title: Individualizing Intervention to Teach Joint Attention, Requesting, and Social Referencing to Children with Autism
explanation: The replication partially succeeded — two of three children acquired skills — but diverged from Muzammal and Jones (2017) in important ways: not all children responded to the same intervention procedures, less generalization was observed across social communication skills and with mothers, and all children required individualized modifications unlike the original study.

description: Open-ended caregiver interview responses for practical functional assessment (PFA) show only moderate reliability and moderate to weak correspondence with analog functional analyses
original_authors: Saini V.; Ubdegrove K.; Biran S.; Duncan R.
original_title: A preliminary evaluation of interrater reliability and concurrent validity of open-ended indirect assessment
replication_authors: Adithyan Rajaraman; Gregory P. Hanley; Holly C. Gover; Kelsey W. Ruppel; Robin K. Landa
replication_title: On the Reliability and Treatment Utility of the Practical Functional Assessment Process
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated and extended Saini et al.' by evaluating PFA reliability across two independent processes and assessing treatment utility. The Discussion notes 'The findings of the current study add to and extend Saini et al. (2019),' finding high categorical reliability (97% vs. Saini's 75%) but lower specific-level reliability (57%), and demonstrating robust treatment utility across all four cases — a finding that extends and broadly supports Saini et al.'s cautions while showing treatment utility remains strong regardless of reliability level.

description: Synthesized reinforcement contingent on participant-selected successive food-related behaviors (a stepwise approach with choice and assent) reduces food selectivity and challenging mealtime behavior in individuals with autism
original_authors: Holly C. Gover; Gregory P. Hanley; Kelsey W. Ruppel; Robin K. Landa; Juliana Marcus
original_title: Prioritizing choice and assent in the assessment and treatment of food selectivity
replication_authors: Vanderzell ML; Gover HC; Badger SA; Hanson JL; Smith YM
replication_title: Treating Food Selectivity in Adolescents and Adults with Autism: A Systematic Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated and extended Gover et al. (2023)' using the same intervention procedures in a congregate care setting with adolescents and adults. The Discussion confirms efficacy: 'These results of the current study demonstrate the efficacy and extension of an intervention package for food selectivity for an adolescent and adult population living in a congregate care setting.'

description: Cultural consequences (differential feedback) reduce variability in the aggregate products (meeting locations) produced by pairs of participants cooperating in a chess knight task (experiment 2)
original_authors: Vasconcelos, Isis Gomes; Todorov, João Claudio
original_title: Experimental analysis of the behavior of persons in groups: Selection of an aggregate product in a metacontingency
replication_authors: João Claudio Todorov; João Guilherme S. Casalecchi; João Vianney B. C. Severo; Marina S. Mendes; Sofia V. Nishiyama; Elenice S. Hanna
replication_title: Effects of Metacontingencies on Cooperative Behavior: A Systematic Replication Using Innovative Procedures during Isolation
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results replicate previous studies (Vasconcelos & Todorov, 2015-experiment 2; Carvalho et al., 2017-experiment 1)' and confirm decreased AP variability in shaping conditions compared to baseline, replicating the original finding with the extension to an online environment.

description: Cultural consequences reduce variability in aggregate products produced by cooperating dyads in a chess knight paradigm (experiment 1)
original_authors: Lucas Couto de Carvalho; Kalliu Carvalho Couto; Nayara de Souza Gois; Ingunn Sandaker; João Claudio Todorov
original_title: Evaluating effects of cultural consequences on the variability of interlocking behavioral contingencies and their aggregate products

replication_title: Effects of Metacontingencies on Cooperative Behavior: A Systematic Replication Using Innovative Procedures during Isolation
explanation: The authors explicitly report that 'results of groups 1 and 2 showed a clear replication and extension of Vasconcelos and Todorov (2015) and Carvalho et al. (2017) regardless of communication,' confirming the original finding of decreased AP variability under shaping conditions.

description: Men and women differ in preferences for long-term marriage partners, with women valuing earning potential and older age more, and men valuing physical attractiveness and younger age more, as assessed via willingness-to-marry ratings on 12 traits in a nationally representative U.S. sample
original_authors: Susan Sprecher; Quintin Sullivan; Elaine Hatfield
original_title: Mate selection preferences: sex differences examined in a national sample
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Jens Bech-Sørensen; Thomas V. Pollet
replication_title: Sex Differences in Mate Preferences: a Replication Study, 20 Years Later
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The replication was largely successful' and 'Our results largely replicated the findings by Sprecher et al. (1994) showing that in 9 out of 12 tests, the direction of the effect was the same.' They used the same 12-item willingness-to-marry questionnaire but collected data via an online crowdsourced sample (CrowdFlower) 20 years later, testing a different population context and time period, hence classified as close extension.

description: Framing a bribery game in social context (as petty corruption between citizens and officials) reduces bribery behaviour compared to a neutral abstract presentation of the same game
original_authors: Barr, Abigail; Serra, Danila
original_title: The effects of externalities and framing on bribery in a petty corruption experiment
replication_authors: Alessio Gaggero; Simon Appleton; Lina Song
replication_title: Framing effects on bribery behaviour: experimental evidence from China and Uganda
replication_journal: Journal of the Economic Science Association
explanation: The Uganda replication found strong and significant framing effects: students exposed to the framed version were significantly less likely to offer or accept bribes. The authors state: 'The results for Uganda are consistent with those obtained by Barr and Serra (2009).'

description: Framing a bribery game in social context (as petty corruption between citizens and officials) reduces bribery behaviour compared to a neutral abstract presentation of the same game
original_authors: Barr, Abigail; Serra, Danila
original_title: The effects of externalities and framing on bribery in a petty corruption experiment
replication_authors: Alessio Gaggero; Simon Appleton; Lina Song
replication_title: Framing effects on bribery behaviour: experimental evidence from China and Uganda
replication_journal: Journal of the Economic Science Association
explanation: In the Chinese sample, framing had virtually no effect on bribery behaviour — an average of 4.6 successful bribes per session occurred regardless of treatment. The authors conclude: 'we do not find any significant effects of framing on bribery behaviour in China.'

description: Distributional properties of facial emotion stimuli shift participants' emotion category boundaries (i.e., exposure to a shifted distribution of face stimuli causes the category threshold for labeling an expression as 'upset' to shift accordingly)
original_authors: Rista C. Plate; Adrienne Wood; Kristina Woodard; Seth D. Pollak
original_title: Probabilistic learning of emotion categories
replication_authors: Kristina Woodard; Rista C. Plate; Michele Morningstar; Adrienne Wood; Seth D. Pollak
replication_title: Categorization of Vocal Emotion Cues Depends on Distributions of Input
explanation: Independent review confirms this is a clear successful extension. The current paper applies the same distributional-learning paradigm from Plate et al. (2019) — which used facial stimuli — to vocal (auditory) stimuli in both adults and children. Both verbal (χ²(2) = 489.07, p < .001) and nonverbal (χ²(2) = 707.84, p < .001) conditions showed strong, unambiguous distributional shift effects. The calm shifted and upset shifted conditions produced significant effects in the predicted directions in both cases (all individual contrasts p < .001). The General Discussion explicitly states: 'In combination with prior research on the categorization of facial cues meant to represent anger (Plate et al., 2019), these results provide evidence for a general learning mechanism.' No ambiguity remains — the effect replicated strongly in a new modality with a large N (n=171) and essentially 100% power. Upgrading to high confidence.

description: Distributional learning of emotion categories generalizes beyond a single prototypical cue, with exposure to shifted distributions across multiple emotions shifting category boundaries (as tested in Experiments 2 and 3 of the original study)
original_authors: Rista C. Plate; Adrienne Wood; Kristina Woodard; Seth D. Pollak
original_title: Probabilistic learning of emotion categories
replication_authors: Kristina Woodard; Rista C. Plate; Michele Morningstar; Adrienne Wood; Seth D. Pollak
replication_title: Categorization of Vocal Emotion Cues Depends on Distributions of Input
explanation: Independent review confirms medium confidence is appropriate. Experiment 2 (n=40) found an overall significant shift effect across multiple emotions/speakers: χ²(2) = 25.92, p < .001. The Discussion of Experiment 2 states 'We replicated and extended the findings of Experiment 1.' However, there is a genuine asymmetry: the upset shifted condition was clearly significant (b = -1.29, z = -3.47, p < .001), but the calm shifted condition only reached marginal significance (b = 0.83, z = 1.76, p = .078). The authors also acknowledge: 'the current data cannot determine how much individuals were adjusting to different speakers versus different emotions.' The overall result is consistent with replication success, but the one-sided marginal effect and interpretive ambiguity (speaker adaptation vs. emotion learning) justify retaining medium confidence rather than upgrading.

description: Novel categories of aliens are learned faster when participants are provided with nonsense labels during feedback (word-enhancement effect on category learning)
original_authors: Gary Lupyan; David H. Rakison; James L. McClelland
original_title: Language is not just for talking: Redundant labels facilitate learning of novel categories
replication_authors: Katie Hoemann; Maria Gendron; Lisa Feldman Barrett
replication_title: Assessing the Power of Words to Facilitate Emotion Category Learning
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we were unable to conceptually replicate this effect with novel emotion categories.' The Bayesian analysis provided strong support for the null hypothesis (BF₀₁ = 31.12), with no facilitation of categorization by labels across all five studies.

description: Emotion-induced blindness (tendency for emotional stimuli to impair attention to subsequent stimuli) correlates positively with repetitive negative thinking (rumination and worry), with r = .34
original_authors: Sandersan Onie; Steven B. Most
original_title: Two roads diverged: Distinct mechanisms of attentional bias differentially predict negative affect and persistent negative thought
replication_authors: Ella K. Moeck; Jessica Mortlock; Sandersan Onie; Steven B. Most; Peter Koval
replication_title: Blinded by and Stuck in Negative Emotions: Is Psychological Inflexibility Across Different Domains Related?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'These findings suggest independence between emotion-induced blindness and all aspects of repetitive negative thinking, failing to replicate Onie and Most's (2017) findings.' All correlations were non-significant with Bayes factors of 0.09–0.15, indicating strong-to-substantial evidence for the null hypothesis.

description: Negative affect inertia (measured via film-task autoregressive slopes) correlates positively with rumination, r = .19
original_authors: Peter Koval; Stefan Sütterlin; Peter Kuppens
original_title: Emotional inertia is associated with lower well-being when controlling for differences in emotional context
replication_authors: Ella K. Moeck; Jessica Mortlock; Sandersan Onie; Steven B. Most; Peter Koval
replication_title: Blinded by and Stuck in Negative Emotions: Is Psychological Inflexibility Across Different Domains Related?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Contrary to H2, we found no evidence that repetitive negative thinking, rumination, or worry predicted negative affect inertia... Therefore, we failed to replicate Koval et al. (2016).' The Bayes factor was 0.017 for all three models, indicating very strong support for the null hypothesis.

description: People can infer which of two individuals a displayed heart rate belongs to (the 'other-HR task') by simply looking at them, at above-chance accuracy
original_authors: Alejandro Galvez-Pol; Salome Antoine; Charlotte Li; James M. Kilner
original_title: People can identify the likely owner of heartbeats by looking at individuals' faces
replication_authors: Irena Arslanova; Alejandro Galvez-Pol; James Kilner; Gianluca Finotti; Manos Tsakiris
replication_title: Seeing Through Each Other’s Hearts: Inferring Others’ Heart Rate as a Function of Own Heart Rate Perception and Perceived Social Intelligence
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated the finding of Galvez-Pol et al. (2022) — people can infer the HR of others in an online experimental context above a chance level.' Performance was significantly above chance (t(142) = 11.2, p < .001, d = .94), closely following the original task protocol.

description: The integral of magnitudes of spatial vectors during initial abnormal QRS depolarization, measured by computerized spatial vectorcardiography, can significantly estimate the percent volume of myocardial infarction
original_authors: Marie J. Cowan; Dennis D. Reichenbach; Robert A. Bruce; Lloyd Fisher
original_title: Estimation of myocardial infarct size by digital computer analysis of the VCG
replication_authors: Marie J. Cowan; Robert A. Bruce; Dennis D. Reichenbach
replication_title: Validation of a computerized QRS criterion for estimating myocardial infarction size and correlation with quantitative morphologic measurements
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the criterion...was determined in a learner set, and was validated on another independent sample using the same computerized electrocardiographic and pathologic method in this study. There was not a significant difference between the 2 straight-line regression equations or the correlation coefficients from the learning and test studies.' The replication achieved r = 0.94 versus r = 0.90 in the original, with no statistically significant difference between the two regression models.

description: Classical conditioning of meaning: pairing nonsense syllable trigrams with evaluatively-valenced words causes the trigrams to acquire corresponding evaluative meaning
original_authors: Carolyn K. Staats; Arthur W. Staats
original_title: Meaning established by classical conditioning
replication_authors: Scott D. Cicero; Warren W. Tryron
replication_title: Classical conditioning of meaning—II. A replication and triplet associative extension
replication_journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'language conditioning did occur to the CSl trigram under the first phase of the triplet conditioning arrangement, thereby replicating Staats and Staats' (1957) finding.' The Meaning × Syllable interaction was significant (F(1,34)=15.64, p<.0004), with significant conditioning at CS1 (Q(2,34)=3.51, p<.05).

description: CVC trigrams (nonsense syllables) paired with positive or negative evaluative words as unconditioned stimuli acquire corresponding evaluative meaning, demonstrating classical conditioning of meaning
original_authors: Carolyn K. Staats; Arthur W. Staats
original_title: Meaning established by classical conditioning
replication_authors: Warren W. Tryon; Scott D. Cicero
replication_title: Classical conditioning of meaning—I. A replication and higher-order extension
replication_journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm replication success in the Discussion: 'First, language conditioning did occur to the CSl trigram, thus replicating the finding of Staats and Staats (1957).' The Tukey HSD test showed a significant positive vs. negative difference at CS1 (Q(2,33) = 3.71, p < .05). The study adds a second-order conditioning link (CS2→CS1) as an extension — though the extension failed, the original one-link conditioning was successfully replicated.

description: Training parents of aggressive boys using social learning procedures (group sessions, programmed text, home observation) reduces deviant child behavior as measured by home observations and parent-reported problem behavior
original_authors: Patterson, G. R.; Cobb, J. A.; Ray, R. S.
original_title: A behavioral technology for retraining the families of aggressive boys
replication_authors: Patterson GR; Reid JB
replication_title: Intervention for families of aggressive boys: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly designed the current study 'to replicate, as closely as possible, the sample and procedures used in the 1969 study.' The Discussion confirms: 'The results of the present study closely approximated those of the 1969 study; in fact, the present findings were a bit stronger.' Targeted deviant behavior was reduced by 61% from baseline (F = 3.77, df = 2, 20; p < 0.05), paralleling the original study's findings.

description: The BAROMAS scales can reliably detect variation in subjective stress among medical students across time, with stress highest at entry and before major exams and lowest at the start of the second year
original_authors: Ted L. Rosenthal; Neil B. Edwards; Bette J. Ackerman
original_title: Students' self-ratings of subjective stress across 30 months of medical school
replication_authors: Ted L. Rosenthal; Renate H. Rosenthal; Neil B. Edwards
replication_title: Students' self-ratings of stress in medical school: a replication across 20 months
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the present results replicated the robustness and practical value of the BAROMAS,' confirming that the same pattern of stress variation across medical school phases was found in a new sample. The abstract also states 'We replicated the essential results of a prior study.'

description: Behaviour therapy (desensitization in vivo) eliminates attentional bias for spider-related words in spider phobics as measured by a Stroop colour-naming task
original_authors: Fraser N. Watts; Frank P. McKenna; Robert Sharrock; Lorna Trezise
original_title: Colour naming of phobia-related words
replication_authors: Edith Lavy; Marcel van den Hout; Arnoud Arntz
replication_title: Attentional bias and spider phobia: Conceptual and clinical issues
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'These findings are an encouraging replication of the Foa and McNally (1986) and Watts et al. (1986) studies.' The spider interference index decreased significantly after one-session exposure treatment [t(35) = 2.44, P = 0.02], and the decrease in the phobic group was significantly larger than in the control group [F(1,64) = 5.46, P = 0.02].

description: Behaviour therapy (imaginal flooding plus exposure in vivo with response prevention) eliminates attentional bias for threat-relevant stimuli in obsessive-compulsive patients
original_authors: Edna B. Foa; Richard J. McNally
original_title: Sensitivity to feared stimuli in obsessive-compulsives: a dichotic listening analysis
replication_authors: Edith Lavy; Marcel van den Hout; Arnoud Arntz
replication_title: Attentional bias and spider phobia: Conceptual and clinical issues
explanation: Independent review confirms result=success: the Discussion states attentional bias was 'reduced, but not completely eliminated' and the statistics are clear [t(35)=2.44, P=0.02; F(1,64)=5.46, P=0.02]. replication_type=conceptual is correct — this used spider phobics with Stroop colour-naming vs. Foa & McNally's OCD patients with dichotic listening. Medium confidence is retained because the paper bundles Foa & McNally (1986) and Watts et al. (1986) together as joint motivation ('an encouraging replication of the Foa and McNally (1986) and Watts et al. (1986) studies') without targeting either finding separately. The study design (spider phobia, Stroop, one-session exposure in vivo) is virtually identical to Watts et al., so the Foa & McNally claim is an incidental conceptual parallel rather than the primary replication target. The ambiguity about whether this entry is genuinely a separate replication attempt of Foa & McNally (vs. being subsumed by the Watts et al. entry) is real.

description: Use of broad SCOR scoring criteria (1-5 sec latency window, 3-trial habituation criterion) confounds spontaneous skin conductance activity with orienting responses, producing spuriously high nonhabituation rates in schizophrenics compared to more restrictive scoring criteria
original_authors: Levinson DF; Robert Edelberg; Bridger Wh
original_title: The orienting response in schizophrenia: Proposed resolution of a controversy
replication_authors: Douglas F. Levinson; Robert Edelberg; Hildegard R. Maricq
replication_title: The skin conductance orienting response in neuroleptic-free schizophrenics: Replication of the scoring criteria effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We report here the replication of these findings in unmedicated patients' and their Discussion confirms 'The major predictions were confirmed, with scoring methods yielding significantly different habituation score distributions.' The key findings replicated: broad criteria produced significantly different habituation scores than restrictive criteria, Method 1 scored 20% of patients as nonhabituators while Method 3 scored none.

description: Dexamethasone nonsuppression and reduced REM latency occur at higher incidence in endogenous depression compared to nonendogenous depression, validating the endogenous/nonendogenous classification over primary/secondary classification
original_authors: Rush, A.J.; Schlesser, M.A.; Giles, D.E.; Crowley, G.T.; Fairchild, C.J.; Altshuler, K.Z.
original_title: Polysomnographic and dexamethasone suppression test findings in endogenous and nonendogenous depression
replication_authors: Donna E. Giles; Michael A. Schlesser; A.John Rush; Paul J. Orsulak; Carl L. Fulton; Howard P. Roffwarg
replication_title: Polysomnographic findings and dexamethasone nonsuppression in unipolar depression: A replication and extension
explanation: The Discussion explicitly states: 'The first is that the essential findings of our original study (Rush et al. 1982) were replicated and confirmed. Those patients with endogenous depression show higher incidences of both reduced REM latency and dexamethasone nonsuppression compared to the nonendogenous group.' The primary/secondary distinction again showed no differences as in the original.

description: Familial pure depressive disease (FPDD) subgroup shows higher incidence of DST nonsuppression, and the sporadic depressive disorder (SDD) subgroup produces more Stage 4 sleep, relative to other family history subtypes
original_authors: Rush, A.J.; Schlesser, M.A.; Giles, D.E.; Crowley, G.T.; Fairchild, C.J.; Altshuler, K.Z.
original_title: Polysomnographic and dexamethasone suppression test findings in endogenous and nonendogenous depression
replication_authors: Donna E. Giles; Michael A. Schlesser; A.John Rush; Paul J. Orsulak; Carl L. Fulton; Howard P. Roffwarg
