replication_title: Polysomnographic findings and dexamethasone nonsuppression in unipolar depression: A replication and extension
explanation: Independent review confirms failure classification. The paper's Results section (body.md line 132) uses the authors' own words: 'Family history comparisons in the 1982 series indicated that the FPDD subgroup had a higher incidence of DST nonsuppression, and the SDD subgroup produced more Stage 4 sleep. These findings were not replicated in this study; patients in the SDD group had a higher incidence of dexamethasone nonsuppression and no differences were found in Stage 4 sleep.' The failure is doubly clear: (1) the authors use the phrase 'not replicated' explicitly, and (2) the direction of the DST nonsuppression effect reversed — in the original it was FPDD with higher nonsuppression, but in the replication it was SDD. Table 3 data corroborate this (DST rates: FPDD 25.8%, SDD 38.1%, p=0.05 — SDD is highest, opposite to the original finding). Upgraded from medium to high confidence because the paper's conclusion is unambiguous and the reversal is documented in both text and table data.

description: Kraepelinian schizophrenic patients (chronically hospitalized or fully dependent for 5+ years) show greater diagnostic consistency across criteria, less haloperidol response, greater morbid risk for schizophrenia spectrum disorders in first-degree relatives, greater left-to-right lateral ventricular asymmetry, and more severe formal thought disorder than other chronic schizophrenic patients, while not differing in positive symptom severity
original_authors: Ede Frecska; Miklos Losonczy; Richard S.E. Keefe; J. M. Silverman; Michael Davidson; Keith L. Davis
original_title: Characteristics of very poor outcome schizophrenia
replication_title: Characteristics of kraepelinian schizophrenia: Independent replication study
explanation: Independent review confirms result=success is correct. The abstract explicitly titles itself 'Independent Replication Study' and states it 'supports most of the findings reported on the first cohort.' Key findings were replicated: 100% diagnostic consistency across RDC/DSM-III/ICD-9, more severe formal thought disorder (p<0.001), and greater morbid risk for schizophrenia spectrum disorders in first-degree relatives (p<0.001). The CT finding partially differed — left frontal horn enlargement was found rather than left-to-right ventricular asymmetry, but the authors treat this as broadly confirmatory. Confidence remains LOW because the original study cannot be identified from this document: the abstract only references 'previous studies from our center' with no explicit citation, and references.json is empty. The original_authors and original_title fields are educated guesses based on the overlapping Mount Sinai authorship (Keefe, Losonczy, Davis appear on both the replication and the likely original), but cannot be confirmed from this source. The citation mismatch flagged in review is real and unresolvable from available materials.

description: Nocturnal penile tumescence (NPT) and penile rigidity are diminished in depressed men compared to healthy controls
original_authors: Michael E. Thase; Charles F. Reynolds; J.Richard Jennings; Ellen Frank; Joseph R. Howell; Patricia R. Houck; Susan Berman; David J. Kupfer
original_title: Nocturnal penile tumescence is diminished in depressed men
replication_authors: Michael E. Thase; Charles F. Reynolds; J.Richard Jennings; Ellen Frank; Gregory L. Garamoni; Eric A. Nofzinger; Amy L. Fascizka; David J. Kupfer
replication_title: Diminished nocturnal penile tumescence in depression: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as an 'internal replication study' and conclude: 'The results of this internal replication study provide further evidence that depressed men manifest alterations of erectile neurophysiology.' The new sample of 51 depressed men showed highly significant reductions in all polygraphic measures of NPT compared to controls (ps < 0.001), consistent with the 1988 findings.

description: Melancholic patients show an abnormal flash visual evoked response (FVER) with a statistically significant negative deviation in the 150-300 msec poststimulus latency range, particularly in the midparietal and occipital regions, compared with age-matched controls
original_authors: Russell G. Vasile; Frank H. Duffy; Gloria McAnulty; David Bear; John J. Mooney; Kerry Bloomingdale; Leslie K. Serchuck; Joseph J. Schildkraut
original_title: Abnormal visual evoked response in melancholia
replication_authors: Russell G. Vasile; Frank H. Duffy; Gloria McAnulty; John J. Mooney; Kerry Bloomingdale; Joseph J. Schildkraut
replication_title: Abnormal flash visual evoked response in melancholia: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm the findings of the original pilot study: 'the findings of our initial pilot study (Figure 1) are broadly confirmed' using the identical computer-based quantified neurophysiological technique with topographic mapping on two independently collected new groups of melancholic patients, both showing statistically significant (p < 0.01) FVER abnormalities in the 224-300 msec poststimulus epoch in the centroparietal region.

description: Oral administration of the serotonergic agonist mCPP causes acute exacerbation of OCD symptoms as well as significant anxiety and other behavioral responses in OCD patients compared to healthy controls
original_authors: Zohar, J.; Mueller, E.A.; Insel, T.R.; Zohar-Kadouch, R.C.; Murphy, D.L.
original_title: Serotonergic responsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder: comparison of patients and healthy controls
replication_authors: Teresa A. Pigott; James L. Hill; Tana A. Grady; Francine L'Heureux; Suzanne Bernstein; Cheryl S. Rubenstein; Dennis L. Murphy
replication_title: A comparison of the behavioral effects of oral versus intravenous mCPP administration in OCD patients and the effect of metergoline prior to IV mCPP
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'replicate the behavioral effects, particularly OCD symptom changes, previously reported to be associated with oral mCPP administration in OCD patients.' The replication failed: 'Our results with oral mCPP in the OCD patients and controls, are in contrast to earlier reports (Zohar et al 1987; Hollander et al 1988, 1992).' Oral mCPP did not produce significant OCD exacerbation, and there was no difference in behavioral responses between OCD patients and controls.

description: Intravenously administered mCPP produces anxiety but no OCD symptom exacerbation in patients with OCD
original_authors: Charney, D.S.; Goodman, W.K.; Price, L.H.; Woods, S.W.; Rasmussen, S.A.; Henninger, G.R.
original_title: Serotonin function in obsessive-compulsive disorder: a comparison of the effects of tryptophan and m-CPP in patients and healthy subjects
replication_authors: Teresa A. Pigott; James L. Hill; Tana A. Grady; Francine L'Heureux; Suzanne Bernstein; Cheryl S. Rubenstein; Dennis L. Murphy
replication_title: A comparison of the behavioral effects of oral versus intravenous mCPP administration in OCD patients and the effect of metergoline prior to IV mCPP
explanation: Reviewer confirmed: The paper explicitly states 'The OCD patients had significant exacerbations in OCD symptoms after IV mCPP administration. This finding is in contrast to the only previous report of mCPP administered intravenously to OCD patients (Charney et al 1988).' The authors also confirm agreement on the anxiety component: current study 'is in agreement with the one previous study reporting anxiogenic and other behavioral responses to IV mCPP in OCD patients and in volunteers (Charney et al 1988).' So Charney 1988 found anxiety but no OCD exacerbation; the current study found both — a direct reversal on the OCD-specific symptom claim. The reversal classification is unambiguous and explicitly stated by the authors. Methodological differences (90-sec bolus vs. 20-min infusion; rating obtained at 30 min vs. 90 min post-infusion) are clearly documented and provide specific mechanistic explanation for the discrepancy, but do not undermine the classification. Confidence upgraded to high because the contrast is stated unambiguously in the paper.

description: Schizophrenic patients show a reversal of the normal planum temporale asymmetry (left larger than right), such that right PT surface area is larger than left in schizophrenia
original_authors: Pearlson, G.; Barta, P.
original_title: Reversed planum temporale asymmetry in schizophrenia
replication_authors: Godfrey D. Pearlson; Patrick E. Barta; Ann E. Pulver; Richard E. Powers; Manuel Casanova; Sophia Frangou; Richard Petty
replication_title: Reversed planum temporale asymmetry in schizophrenia — Replication study
explanation: Independent review confirms the result classification and original author identification. The paper (abstract #470, 'Reversed Planum Temporale Asymmetry in Schizophrenia — A Replication Study') explicitly states: 'As previously (AJP 1995), there was striking reversal of normal PT asymmetry for surface area in male and female schizophrenic subjects' and 'This study confirms our prior finding of a reversal of expected asymmetry of PT surface area in schizophrenia.' The citation '(AJP 1995)' refers to Pearlson and Barta's own prior AJP 1995 publication — confirmed by the first-person 'our prior finding' and the fact that Pearlson and Barta are lead authors on both studies. The original authors field is correctly identified despite their names not being spelled out in the citation sentence. Confidence upgraded to high: result is unambiguously stated as a confirmation, replication type is correctly close extension (original sample included plus larger group, same MRI methodology, plus new measures of GM volume and thickness).

description: Narcoleptic canines exhibit altered regional concentrations of catecholamines and their metabolites (especially DA and DOPAC) in specific brain regions compared to control canines
original_authors: Ivan N. Mefford; Theodore L. Baker; Richard Boehme; Arthur S. Foutz; Roland D. Ciaranello; Jack D. Barchas; William C. Dement
original_title: Narcolepsy: biogenic amine deficits in an animal model
replication_authors: Miller JD; Faull KF; Bowersox SS; Dement WC
replication_title: CNS monoamines and their metabolites in canine narcolepsy: a replication study
explanation: The authors replicated several key findings (elevated DA and DOPAC in amygdala, DOPAC in reticularis parvicellularis, NE changes), but the abstract explicitly states that 'previously observed differences between narcoleptic and control canines in DOPAC levels in the caudate and reticularis oralis failed to replicate,' making the overall result mixed/inconclusive.

description: A 32-item Resident Applicant Scale (RAS) can discriminate between applicants who are accepted versus rejected for psychiatric residencies, with specific items related to creativity, curiosity, general range of knowledge, and intellectual grasp of psychiatry being the most discriminating
original_authors: Plutchik, Robert; Conte, Hope; Kandler, Henry
original_title: Variables related to the selection of psychiatric residents
replication_authors: Robert Plutchik; Hope Conte; Henry Kandler
replication_title: Variables related to the selection of psychiatric residents. II. A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The results of the present investigation are in accord with those obtained in the previous study of the selection of psychiatric residents. The RAS again successfully discriminated between applicants who were accepted for residencies and those who were rejected.' The same RAS instrument was applied to the following year's applicants at the same institution, and similar items (curiosity, creativity, general range of knowledge) again showed high discriminating power.

description: The Personality Diagnostic Questionnaire-Revised (PDQ-R) shows high sensitivity and moderate specificity for detecting DSM-III-R personality disorders when compared to structured clinical interviews (SCID-II and PDE) in an inpatient psychiatric sample
original_authors: Andrew E. Skodol; H. D. Kellman; John M. Oldham; L. Rosnick; Steven E. Hyler
original_title: Validity of personality diagnostic questionnaire-revised: comparison with two structured interviews
replication_authors: Hyler SE; Skodol AE; Oldham JM; Kellman HD; Doidge N.
replication_title: Validity of the Personality Diagnostic Questionnaire-Revised: A replication in an outpatient sample
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The findings of this study replicate those of our prior report on the validity of the PDQ-R' and 'The results of this study replicate those of the previous study in that the PDQ-R showed excellent sensitivity in detecting the majority of personality disorders.' The same methodology was used but in an outpatient rather than inpatient sample to test generalizability.

description: Auditory evoked potentials recorded from temporal-to-vertex leads show hemispheric amplitude asymmetries as a function of verbal vs. musical task performance, with higher amplitude AEPs from the hemisphere most involved in the ongoing task
original_authors: Shucard DW; Shucard JL; Thomas DG
original_title: Auditory evoked potentials as probes of hemispheric differences in cognitive processing
replication_authors: Shucard DW; Cummins KR; Thomas DG; Shucard JL
replication_title: Evoked potentials to auditory probes as indices of cerebral specialization of function—replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state the study was conducted 'to replicate the findings of our previous experiment' and conclude that 'Significant AEP amplitude asymmetries were obtained as a function of the ongoing tasks, replicating our previous findings.' The condition × placement × hemisphere interaction was highly significant (F[2,28]=6.2, p<0.006), confirming the original finding. The study also extended the original by adding mastoid-referenced placements and examining sex differences.

description: Infants show an inverted-U relation between limb activity suppression and level of stimulus complexity/predictability, with suppression of both limb and sucking activity to visual stimulation
original_authors: Marshall M. Haith; William Kessen; Doris Collins
original_title: Response of the human infants to level of complexity of intermittent visual movement
replication_authors: Doris Collins; William Kessen; Marshall Haith
replication_title: Note on an attempt to replicate a relation between stimulus unpredictability and infant attention
explanation: The authors describe their results as providing only 'marginal support' for the key inverted-U relation (A×C interaction: F(2,72) = 2.95, p < .10), while noting that other findings (general suppression of limb and sucking activity) did replicate. They explicitly state the study was 'disappointing' in some respects but that 'several of these findings replicated those of an earlier study.'

description: Principal component analysis of the 52-item Illness Behaviour Questionnaire in 100 pain clinic patients yields seven interpretable factors: General Hypochondriasis, Disease Conviction, Psychological vs Somatic Focusing, Affective Inhibition, Affective Disturbance, Denial, and Irritability
original_authors: Pilowsky, I.; Spence, N.D.
original_title: Patterns of illness behaviour with intractable pain
replication_authors: Pilowsky I.
replication_title: Dimensions of illness behaviour as measured by the illness behaviour questionnaire: A replication study
explanation: The paper explicitly titles itself 'A Replication Study' and uses a much larger sample (N=1578) to test the robustness of the original seven IBQ factors. The conclusion notes that 'the most robust IBQ factors are Affective Inhibition, Affective Disturbance, Denial and Irritability,' while 'Psychological vs Somatic Focusing was far less robust, appearing recognizably only in the original analysis,' indicating only partial replication of the original factor structure.

description: Preterm birth, intrauterine growth retardation, and neonatal acidemia are each independently associated with increased rates of neonatal neurological abnormality in a birth cohort
original_authors: Jurgens-van der Zee AD; Bierman-van Eendenburg ME; Fidler VJ; Olinga AA; Visch JH; Touwen BC; Huisjes HJ
original_title: Preterm birth, growth retardation and acidemia in relation to abnormality of the newborn
replication_authors: Huisjes HJ; Touwen BC; Hoekstra J.; van Woerden-Blanksma JT; Bierman-van Eendenburg ME; Jurgens-van der Zee AD; Fidler VJ; Olinga AA
replication_title: Obstetrical-neonatal neurological relationship. A replication study
replication_journal: European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The results of this study show that the findings of the previous investigation (Jurgens-van der Zee et al., 1979) are reproducible.' All three relationships (neurological abnormality with growth retardation, acidemia, and preterm birth) were confirmed in the second cohort using the same neurological examination technique but with different examiners.

description: Left-handed persons are more field-dependent (less field-independent) than right-handed persons, as measured by the Rod and Frame Test and Embedded Figures Test
original_authors: Albert J. Silverman; Greta Adevai; W.Edward McGough
original_title: Some relationships between handedness and perception
replication_authors: G.Anthony Newland
replication_title: Left-handedness and field-independence
explanation: The paper explicitly states it is a replication attempt of Silverman et al. (1966) and found the opposite result: 'Contrary to the findings of Culver et al. and Silverman et al., left- compared to right-handers were found to be significantly more field-independent' (F(1,184)=35.29, p<0.001). The result was statistically significant in the opposite direction.

description: Left-handed persons tend to be more field-dependent than right-handed persons, based on a sample where three of four left-handers scored as field-dependent
original_authors: Albert J. Silverman; Greta Adevai; W.Edward McGough
original_title: Some relationships between handedness and perception
replication_authors: G.Anthony Newland
replication_title: Left-handedness and field-independence
explanation: The present paper explicitly names Culver et al. (1963) alongside Silverman et al. as sources whose findings were contradicted: 'Contrary to the findings of Culver et al. and Silverman et al., left- compared to right-handers were found to be significantly more field-independent' (F(1,184)=35.29, p<0.001). The reversal classification is correct. Medium confidence is retained because Culver et al.'s original 'finding' was an incidental observation — 3 of 4 left-handers scored as field-dependent in a study of isolation response, with no formal statistical test of the handedness-field-dependence relationship. Calling the present paper's result a 'reversal' of Culver et al. requires treating that informal observation as an original finding, which is a reasonable but not unambiguous interpretive judgment. The present paper itself frames its primary replication target as Silverman et al. (1966), which was the first formal test. Ambiguity is genuine.

description: Individual rhesus monkeys show consistent hand preferences across three different tasks (simple reaching, visual discrimination, and food retrieval from a row), indicating that hand preference tends to be consistent within and across activities
original_authors: Ralph A.W. Lehman
original_title: The handedness of rhesus monkeys. III. Consistency within and across activities
replication_authors: Ralph A.W. Lehman
replication_title: Hand preferences of rhesus monkeys on differing tasks
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication study and state in the Discussion: 'The present replication study not only confirmed the tendency for monkeys to prefer the same hand for different tasks, but the level of confirmation was statistically significant.' The new study used 31 subjects following the same three-task ABBCA sequence as the original study of 39 animals.

description: Administration of 33% nitrous oxide combined with altered expectations of enhanced creativity and sensitivity yields lower (not higher) pain thresholds, reversing the expected analgesic effect
original_authors: Samuel F. Dworkin; Andrew C. N. Chen; Linda LeResche; Daniel W. Clark
original_title: Cognitive reversal of expected nitrous oxide analgesia for acute pain
replication_authors: Dworkin SF; Schubert M.; Chen AC; Clark DW
replication_title: Psychological preparation influences nitrous oxide analgesia: Replication of laboratory findings in a clinical setting
replication_journal: Oral Surgery, Oral Medicine, Oral Pathology
explanation: The authors explicitly state this study 'experimentally confirms prior laboratory pain research, namely, that the planned psychological preparation of the subject prior to administration of nitrous oxide in conventional dental doses can significantly modify the perception of tooth pulp pain.' Both PTH and PTO changes were statistically significant (t=2.05, p<0.05 and t=2.37, p<0.05 respectively), confirming the key finding from the original laboratory study in a clinical dental setting.

description: Compulsory admissions to psychiatric hospitals across six countries (Brazil, Denmark, Egypt, Swaziland, Switzerland, Thailand) share common characteristics, including that the majority of patients were admitted from home and were already known to the mental health system
original_authors: Soothill KL; Harding TW; Adserballe H.; Bernheim J.; Erné S.; Magdi S.; Panpreecha C.; Reinhold F.
original_title: Compulsory admissions to mental hospitals in six countries
original_journal: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry
replication_authors: Keith Soothill; Pisamai Kupituksa; Dinesh Badiani; Fiona Macmillan
replication_title: Compulsory admissions to mental hospitals: A replication study
replication_journal: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the results support the value of the earlier WHO study which only considered one hospital in each country,' with similarities noted in sources of admission, evidence of previous psychiatric treatment, diagnoses, alcohol abuse, treatment patterns, and length of stay. The replication extended the original WHO study to England (not included in the original) using identical questions.

description: Reaction time (RT) using Hick's paradigm correlates negatively with psychometric intelligence (g), with the Hick slope (regression of median RT on bits of information) correlating significantly with IQ, and RT-IQ correlations increasing as the number of choice alternatives increases
original_authors: Hanes DW; Clouston SAP
original_title: Reaction time and psychometric g
replication_authors: Paul Barrett; H. J. Eysenck; S. Lucking
replication_title: Reaction time and intelligence: A replicated study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our data support a general speed-IQ paradigm (Eysenck, 1967), but not the particular form given to it by Jensen and the Erlangen school. Their version requires two deductions to be verified which we fail to replicate, namely the slope-IQ correlations, and the increase in correlation between RT and IQ as number of bits increases.' General negative RT-IQ direction was preserved, and the variability-IQ relationship was replicated, but the specific key claims (slope-IQ correlation, increasing RT-IQ with bits) failed to replicate.

description: Study 1: Peripheral nerve conduction velocity (NCV) along the median nerve correlates positively with IQ (r = .42) in a mixed-sex sample of undergraduates
original_authors: Philip A. Vernon; Monica Mori
original_title: Intelligence, reaction times, and peripheral nerve conduction velocity
replication_authors: John C. Wickett; Philip A. Vernon
replication_title: Peripheral nerve conduction velocity, reaction time, and intelligence: An attempt to replicate Vernon and Mori (1992)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In direct contrast to the findings of Vernon and Mori (1992), the present study failed to find a significant relationship between NCV and IQ.' NCV correlations with GIQ were r = -.12 and .02 (both n.s.) in the replication sample of 38 females.

description: Study 2: Peripheral nerve conduction velocity (wrist-to-finger NCV) correlates positively with IQ (r = .48) in a mixed-sex sample of undergraduates
original_authors: Philip A. Vernon; Monica Mori
original_title: Intelligence, reaction times, and peripheral nerve conduction velocity
replication_authors: John C. Wickett; Philip A. Vernon
replication_title: Peripheral nerve conduction velocity, reaction time, and intelligence: An attempt to replicate Vernon and Mori (1992)
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that the replication 'failed to find a significant relationship between NCV and IQ,' consistent with a failure of both Study 1 and Study 2 of Vernon & Mori (1992). Neither wrist-to-finger nor wrist-to-elbow NCV correlated significantly with any IQ measure.

description: Principal component analysis of symptom ratings in depressed patients yields three interpretable factors: a general severity factor, a bipolar factor contrasting endogenous and neurotic depression, and a bipolar factor contrasting anxiety and depressive symptoms
original_authors: Eugene S. Paykel; Brigitte Prusoff; Gerald L. Klerman
original_title: The endogenous-neurotic continuum in depression: rater independence and factor distributions
replication_authors: Rassaby E.; Paykel ES
replication_title: Factor patterns in depression
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'The findings of the new principal component analysis show virtually identical replication of the severity factor, and good replication of the endogenous-neurotic factor with minor differences in loadings. The third factor replicated less well but still showed a moderate amount of overlap.' Congruency coefficients were 0.96, 0.73, and 0.46 for the three factors respectively, using a new UK sample different from the original US sample.

description: Depressed patients report significantly more life events (particularly exits from the social field, undesirable events, and events not under the subjects' control) in the 6 months before illness onset compared to matched normal controls
original_authors: Paykel, E.S.; Myers, J.K.; Dienelt, M.N.; Klerman, G.L.; Lindenthal, J.J.; Pepper, M.P.
original_title: Life events and depression
replication_authors: Fava GA; Munari F.; Pavan L.; Kellner R.
replication_title: Life events and depression
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'A fairly close replication of the results occurred' and found the same pattern of significantly more exits, undesirable events, and uncontrolled events in depressives vs. controls as in the original. The study was conducted in a different cultural setting (Northern Italy vs. US), making it a close extension.

description: The majority of patients with panic disorder with agoraphobia experience prodromal symptoms (agoraphobic avoidance, generalized anxiety, and hypochondriacal fears and beliefs) before the first panic attack
original_authors: Giovanni A. Fava; Silvana Grandi; Renzo Canestrari
original_title: Prodromal symptoms in panic disorder with agoraphobia
replication_authors: Giovanni A. Fava; Silvana Grandi; Chiara Rafanelli; Renzo Canestrari
replication_title: Prodromal symptoms in panic disorder with agoraphobia: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of this study confirmed the presence of prodromal symptoms (agoraphobia, hypochondriasis, generalized anxiety) before the first panic attack and fairly replicated our previous investigation (Fava et al., 1988).' The replication used the same semi-structured interview procedure, the same N=20 patients, and found nearly identical rates of prodromal symptoms (18/20 phobic anxiety, 17/20 hypochondriasis, 16/20 phobic avoidance) as the original study.

description: Bipolar/manic-depressive patients show decreased fluidity (increased polarization) in the hydrocarbon core of the erythrocyte membrane compared to controls, as measured by fluorescent probe polarization spectroscopy using 12(9)-anthroyl stearate
original_authors: Jay Wesley Pettegrew; John Stephen Nichols; Nancy Jean Minshew; Augustus John Rush; Robert Malcolm Stewart
original_title: Membrane biophysical studies of lymphocytes and erythrocytes in manic-depressive illness
replication_authors: John Nurnberger; Marvin Miller; Elizabeth Bowman; John Sullivan; Harry Brittain; Dawn Lawrence; Carolyn York
replication_title: Erythrocyte membrane structure in bipolar affective disorder: A non-replication
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'a non-replication' and reports no significant differences between 15 bipolar patients and 16 controls on any of the three fluorescent probe polarization measures. The Discussion confirms: 'The probability that we missed a real difference of the magnitude reported by Pettegrew et al., (Type II error) is < 0.01,' indicating the null result is robust.

description: The ratio of the 'melancholic type' to the 'manic type' of premorbid personality drops systematically from unipolar depressives through bipolar II, bipolar I, and 'unipolar' manics, with the two extreme groups showing a reversal in the predominant personality type
original_authors: Detlev von Zerssen; Josef Pössl
original_title: The premorbid personality of patients with different subtypes of an affective illness: statistical analysis of blind assignment of case history data to clinical diagnoses
replication_authors: Detlev von Zerssen; Rudolf Tauscher; Josef Pössl
replication_title: The relationship of premorbid personality to subtypes of an affective illness. A replication study by means of an operationalized procedure for the diagnosis of personality structures
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of this study prove that an operationalized assessment of premorbid personality structures from case history data reveals similar relationships between these structures and subtypes of an affective illness as the original global assessment.' The paper's title itself declares it 'A replication study', and the replication used a larger sample (n=80 vs. n=42) with an operationalized procedure rather than global expert rating.

description: Panic disorder patients show an increased maximal rate of platelet serotonin uptake (Vmax) compared to healthy controls
original_authors: Trevor R. Norman; Fiona K. Judd; Margaret Gregory; Robyn H. James; Nigel M. Kimber; Iain M. McIntyre; Graham D. Burrows
original_title: Platelet serotonin uptake in panic disorder
replication_authors: Trevor R. Norman; Fiona K. Judd; Graham D. Burrows; Iain M. McIntyre
replication_title: Platelet serotonin uptake in panic disorder patients: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm: 'The present data confirm our previous reports of an increased rate of 5HT uptake by the blood platelets of patients with panic disorder (Norman et al., 1986).' The replication found significantly elevated Vmax in panic patients (65 ± 22 pmol/10^8 platelets/min) vs. controls (44 ± 13 pmol/10^8 platelets/min), p < 0.0005.

description: Steeper slope of the amplitude/stimulus-intensity function (ASF slope) of the N1/P2 component of auditory evoked potentials characterizes responders to prophylactic lithium medication compared with nonresponders
original_authors: Hegerl U.; Ulrich G.; Müller-Oerlinghausen B.
original_title: Auditory evoked potentials and response to lithium prophylaxis
replication_authors: Ulrich Hegert; Hilde Wuff; Bruno Müller-Oerlinghausen
replication_title: Intensity dependence of auditory evoked potentials and clinical response to prophylactic lithium medication: A replication study
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Replication Study' and directly replicates the pilot study by Hegerl et al. (1987). The Discussion states: 'Our findings confirm the hypothesis that a steep ASF slope is related to favorable response to prophylactic lithium medication,' with responders showing significantly steeper ASF slopes than nonresponders (F=4.72; df=1,32; p<0.05).

description: Patients with major depressive disorder have a blunted cortisol response to intramuscular desipramine (75 mg) compared to normal control subjects, suggesting norepinephrine deficit or alpha-1-adrenergic receptor insensitivity
original_authors: Gregory M. Asnis; Uriel Halbreich; Harry Rabinovich; Neal D. Ryan; Edward J. Sachar; Beverly Nelson; Joaquim Puig-Antich; Hanna Novacenko
original_title: The cortisol response to desipramine in endogenous depressives and normal control subjects: Preliminary findings
replication_authors: Gregory M. Asnis; William C. Sanderson; Herman M. van Praag
replication_title: Cortisol response to intramuscular desipramine in patients with major depression and normal control subjects: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This double-blind, placebo-controlled study with age- and sex-matched groups of depressed and control subjects replicated earlier preliminary reports by Asnis et al. (1985, 1986) which found that patients with MDD had a blunted cortisol response to i.m. desipramine in comparison with normal control subjects.' The placebo-corrected group effect was statistically significant (F = 5.8, df = 1, 38, p = 0.02).

description: New immigrants' need for catharsis (deprivation of emotional support and sympathy) directly increases their rate of physician utilization, independently of actual illness
original_authors: Shuval, Judith T.; Antonovsky, Aaron; Davis, A. Michael
original_title: Social functions of medical practice
replication_authors: Tikvah Honig-Parnass
replication_title: The effects of latent social needs on physician utilization by immigrants: A replication study
explanation: The replication found the need for catharsis has a negligible effect on physician utilization (-0.005), far below the original positive association. The authors conclude: 'the former immigrants seem to have abandoned the previously customary mode of gratifying the need for catharsis by turning to the health services. Hence, even the respondents with a keen experience of that need tended to refrain from turning to physicians in the absence of concrete symptoms.'

description: Individual specific response (ISR), stimulus specific response (SSR), and motivation specific response (MSR) patterns account for substantial proportions of variance in physiological and psychological variables during stress conditions
original_authors: Foerster F.; Schneider HJ; Walschburger P.
original_title: The differentiation of individual-specific, stimulus-specific, and motivation-specific response patterns in activation processes: An inquiry investigating their stability and possible importance in psychophysiology
replication_authors: Friedrich Foerster
replication_title: Psychophysiological response specificities: A replication over a 12-month period
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the results of the analyses of psychophysiological response specificity within a single experimental period had already been sufficiently replicated in our earlier studies' and 'the proportion of subjects exhibiting a stable ISR tendency over several weeks could be fully replicated.' The variance components for ISR, SSR, and MSR closely match those from the earlier study.

description: The permutation (sequence) of stress conditions is significantly related to subjects' stable individual specific response (ISR) tendency
original_authors: Foerster, F.; Schneider, H.J.; Walschburger, P.
original_title: Psychophysiologische Reaktionsmuster. Zur Theorie und Methodik der Analyse individualspezifischer, stimulusspezifischer und motivationsspezifischer Reaktionsmuster in Aktivierungsprozessen
replication_authors: Friedrich Foerster
replication_title: Psychophysiological response specificities: A replication over a 12-month period
explanation: The paper explicitly tests this finding from Foerster et al. (1983b) and confirms it: 'Of the six subjects exhibiting stable ISR tendency over all four experimental periods (12 months) five subjects were examined with the favorable permutation (p < 0.04, one-tailed). Thus, it must be taken into account that different sequences of stress conditions have some effect on the stability of ISR tendency.'

description: Subjects with stable ISR tendencies show significantly higher scores on the 'compensation' and 'distraction' scales of the Stressverarbeitungsfragebogen (SVF) coping behavior questionnaire
original_authors: Foerster, F.; Schneider, H.J.; Walschburger, P.
original_title: Psychophysiologische Reaktionsmuster. Zur Theorie und Methodik der Analyse individualspezifischer, stimulusspezifischer und motivationsspezifischer Reaktionsmuster in Aktivierungsprozessen
replication_authors: Friedrich Foerster
replication_title: Psychophysiological response specificities: A replication over a 12-month period
explanation: The original finding (Foerster et al., 1983b) was that stable ISR subjects scored significantly higher on BOTH the 'compensation' and 'distraction' SVF scales (both p < 0.05, two-tailed). The replication confirmed the 'distraction' scale (p < 0.025, one-tailed) but did NOT confirm the 'compensation' scale — it is not reported as significant and is explicitly absent from the results. Section 3.6 states: 'This was also confirmed in the present study with respect to the distraction scale (p < 0.025, one-tailed t-test)' — the omission of 'compensation' is unambiguous. Additional coping scales (self-guilt, self-pity, medication intake, self-esteem) reached significance, but these were not part of the original claim. Since the original description names two specific scales and only one replicated, the result is inconclusive: partially supported but not a clean replication of the stated finding.

description: Cognitive task load (as manipulated by a visual scanning task with varying light complexity) increases the correlation dimensionality (D_c) of the EEG attractor, reflecting greater brain dynamic complexity under more demanding tasks
original_authors: Robert A.M. Gregson; L.Anna Britton; Edward A. Campbell; G.Richard Gates
original_title: Comparisons of the nonlinear dynamics of electroencephalograms under various task loading conditions: a preliminary report
replication_authors: Robert A.M. Gregson; Edward A. Campbell; G.Richard Gates
replication_title: Cognitive load as a determinant of the dimensionality of the electroencephalogram: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe the study as 'partially replicating and extending' the 1990 study, and report that D_c 'was shown to change in the expected direction, increasing as the task became more complicated.' The Discussion confirms: 'Taken with the preliminary study we reported, it is deducible that small fluctuations in the average D_c values can be induced with different task loadings.'

description: Exposure of Chinese hamster ovary cells to high-intensity pulsed ultrasound (2.5 MHz, nominal 2500 W/cm2) causes a small but statistically significant increase in sister chromatid exchanges
original_authors: Barnett SB; Miller MW; Cox C.; Carstensen EL
original_title: Increased sister chromatid exchanges in Chinese hamster ovary cells exposed to high intensity pulsed ultrasound
replication_authors: Morton W. Miller; Mitra Azadniv; Susanne E. Pettit; Charles C. Church; Edwin L. Carstensen; Diane Hoffman
replication_title: Sister chromatid exchanges in Chinese hamster ovary cells exposed to high intensity pulsed ultrasound: Inability to confirm previous positive results
explanation: The authors explicitly describe regimen (4) as 'an exact replication of the Barnett et al. (1988) procedure' and the title states 'inability to confirm previous positive results.' The one-sided p-value for the exact replication condition was 0.22 (not significant), and the Discussion states 'there is obvious disagreement between the results of the present investigation and those of the Barnett et al. (1988) report.'

description: Doxapram is a potent and specific panicogenic agent that triggers panic attacks in approximately 80% of patients with panic disorder and 20% of controls, and produces an exaggerated ventilatory response in patients
original_authors: Yue-Joe Lee; George C. Curtis; John G. Weg; James L. Abelson; Jack G. Modell; Kelly M. Campbell
original_title: Panic attacks induced by doxapram
replication_authors: James L. Abelson; John G. Weg; Randolph M. Nesse; George C. Curtis
replication_title: Neuroendocrine responses to laboratory panic: Cognitive intervention in the doxapram model
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We conducted a replication study to confirm doxapram's panicogenic activity' and report that under standard conditions panic attacks occurred in 75% of patients (vs. ~80% in the original), confirming doxapram's panicogenic effects. The paper also extended the original by adding a cognitive intervention condition and measuring neuroendocrine responses.

description: Male social drinkers who believed they had consumed alcohol (expectancy) showed reduced physiological arousal and self-reported anxiety compared to those who believed they consumed a nonalcoholic drink, irrespective of actual drink content
original_authors: G. Terence Wilson; David Abrams
original_title: Effects of alcohol on social anxiety and physiological arousal: Cognitive versus pharmacological processes
replication_authors: Mieke C. De Boer; Gerard M. Schippers; Cees P.F. van der Staak
replication_title: Alcohol and social anxiety in women and men: Pharmacological and expectancy effects
explanation: The replication found no significant expectancy effect in men (consistent with the original pattern but not a clear confirmation), and also found a pharmacological anxiety-reducing effect that was not found in the original study. The authors describe being 'partially able to replicate' the results, with key differences in the pharmacological effects and some procedural differences.

description: Women who believed they had consumed alcohol (expectancy) showed increased physiological arousal and were rated as more uncomfortable (more anxious) compared to women who believed they consumed a nonalcoholic drink, with no pharmacological effect of alcohol on self-reported anxiety
original_authors: David B. Abrams; Guyanne Wilson
original_title: Effects of alcohol on social anxiety in women: Cognitive versus physiological processes
replication_authors: Mieke C. De Boer; Gerard M. Schippers; Cees P.F. van der Staak
replication_title: Alcohol and social anxiety in women and men: Pharmacological and expectancy effects
explanation: The replication found that women who believed they had consumed alcohol were significantly LESS anxious (not more anxious as in the original), with t(1,30) = 2.14, p < .05. The authors explicitly state: 'As compared with Abrams and Wilson (1979) and Sutker et al. (1982), this is an effect in the opposite direction.' A pharmacological anxiety-reducing effect was also found, in contrast to the original's null pharmacological effect.

description: Chicks tested in pairs in an open field take longer to begin distress calling and ambulating than chicks tested individually, due to reduced social reinstatement motivation
original_authors: Gordon G. Gallup; Susan D. Suarez
original_title: An ethological analysis of open-field behaviour in chickens
replication_authors: Suarez SD; Gallup GG Jr
replication_title: Open-field behaviour in chickens: A replication revisited
explanation: Experiment 1 successfully replicated the pair-testing effect when conducted in a novel open-field environment (p < .001 for distress calls, p < .005 for ambulation), demonstrating that Jones' failure to replicate was due to using a familiar home-cage-like environment rather than a novel open field.

description: Chicks housed in isolation for two days prior to testing take longer to begin distress calling and ambulating in an open field than those reared in groups
original_authors: Gordon G. Gallup; Susan D. Suarez
original_title: An ethological analysis of open-field behaviour in chickens
replication_authors: Suarez SD; Gallup GG Jr
replication_title: Open-field behaviour in chickens: A replication revisited
explanation: Experiment 2, using chicks isolated from hatching (following Jones' procedure rather than the original), found no significant difference between isolation and group-reared chicks in either distress call or ambulation latency (F < 1 for both), failing to replicate the original isolation effect.

description: Chicks housed in isolation for two days prior to testing take longer to begin distress calling and ambulating in an open field than those reared in groups
original_authors: Gordon G. Gallup; Susan D. Suarez
original_title: An ethological analysis of open-field behaviour in chickens
replication_authors: Suarez SD; Gallup GG Jr
replication_title: Open-field behaviour in chickens: A replication revisited
explanation: Experiment 3 used the original procedure (group rearing followed by 2-day isolation before testing) and successfully replicated the isolation effect, with isolated chicks showing significantly longer latencies to distress call (p < .025) and ambulate (p < .01) than group-housed chicks.

description: Seven MMPI items that appear specific to alcoholism discriminate alcoholic patients from psychiatric and normal groups better than other MMPI alcoholism scales
original_authors: Conley, J.J.; Kammeier, M.L.
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Hoffmann NG; Lumry AE; Harrison PA; Lessard RJ
replication_title: Brief Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory scales to screen for substance abuse
explanation: REVIEWED. The paper explicitly calls itself 'a replication attempt' and finds that 4 of the 7 Conley-Kammeier items replicated in the 13-item scale, while 3 (items 156, 251, 378) did not emerge. This partial item-level replication supports 'inconclusive' over 'success.' However, there is a complication: when the 7-item Conley-Kammeier scale is directly applied to the new sample (Table I), it performs strongly (89-90% specificity, 91-93% sensitivity at cut score 2-3), outperforming MacAndrew and Holmes — which would suggest the original *performance* claim replicated. The ambiguity arises from the different populations (job applicants vs. original psychiatric/normal groups) and different comparison groups, which the authors themselves flag as limiting comparability. The Discussion concludes positively ('suggests definite screening potential') but with explicit cautions. 'Inconclusive' is the honest classification given partial item-level replication and methodological differences, even though scale-level performance was strong. Medium confidence is retained because reasonable analysts could classify this as 'success' based on the direct scale performance data in Table I.

description: A group active treatment program (involving structured activities, staff training, monitoring, and feedback) implemented in residential living units reduces nonadaptive client behavior during group leisure periods
original_authors: Marsha B. Parsons; Victoria B. Cash; Dennis H. Reid
original_title: Improving residential treatment services: Implementation and norm-referenced evaluation of a comprehensive management system
replication_authors: Marsha B. Parsons; Dennis H. Reid
replication_title: Evaluating and improving residential treatment during group leisure situations: A program replication and refinement
explanation: The authors explicitly report this as a 'systematic replication' of Parsons et al. (1989) and note that 'the average amount of decrease (23%) across both units from baseline to the program condition was the same average (23%) decrease across the five living units in the initial study,' concluding that 'such a systematic replication suggests the program can be effective when initiated from a consultant model in addition to when initiated by direct supervisory personnel.'

description: Older chronic alcoholic patients show greater cortical sulcal and ventricular CSF volume enlargement for their age than younger alcoholic patients, suggesting greater vulnerability of the aging brain to alcohol
original_authors: Adolf Pfefferbaum; Margaret Rosenbloom; Kathryn Crusan; Terry L. Jernigan
original_title: Brain CT changes in alcoholics: The effects of age and alcohol consumption
replication_authors: Adolf Pfefferbaum; Edith V. Sullivan; Margaret J. Rosenbloom; Paula K. Shear; Daniel H. Mathalon; Kelvin O. Lim
replication_title: Increase in brain cerebrospinal fluid volume is greater in older than in younger alcoholic patients: A replication study and CT/MRI comparison
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This study replicated our findings that alcoholic patients, as a group, show abnormally enlarged cortical sulcal and ventricular CSF volumes as compared with normal control subjects, and furthermore that older alcoholic patients show greater CSF volume increases for their age than do younger alcoholic patients.' The replication used a different scanner model, acquisition parameters, and ROI definitions with a new head-size correction procedure, but retained the same general CT-based paradigm.

description: Older chronic alcoholic patients show greater cortical sulcal and ventricular CSF volume enlargement for their age than younger alcoholic patients, as measured by CT brain scanning
original_authors: Zipursky RB; Kelvin O. Lim; Margaret J. Rosenbloom; A. Pfefferbaum
original_title: Differing effects of duration of illness on CT findings in alcoholism and schizophrenia
replication_authors: Adolf Pfefferbaum; Edith V. Sullivan; Margaret J. Rosenbloom; Paula K. Shear; Daniel H. Mathalon; Kelvin O. Lim
replication_title: Increase in brain cerebrospinal fluid volume is greater in older than in younger alcoholic patients: A replication study and CT/MRI comparison
explanation: Independent review confirms 'success' classification but medium confidence is appropriate for two reasons. First, Zipursky et al. 1988 is always cited jointly with Pfefferbaum et al. 1988a; the paper says it aimed to replicate both together, making it difficult to cleanly attribute specific findings to Zipursky alone. Second, the Discussion explicitly carves out one exception specific to Zipursky et al.: 'The sole exception was that the age effect was not present in the Sylvian fissure in the earlier CT study (Zipursky et al., 1988).' The present study did find the age effect in Sylvian fissures (r=0.50, significant), meaning this constitutes a partial failure for the Zipursky replication specifically. Nonetheless, the broader claim — that older alcoholic patients show greater CSF volume increases for their age — was confirmed across most ROIs, supporting overall 'success.' The exception is minor relative to the whole, but the dual-citation structure makes it genuinely ambiguous how much of the success belongs to Zipursky et al. specifically. Medium confidence is the honest answer.

description: Frequency of anabolic steroid use among ninth grade adolescents is associated with poly drug use (cocaine, injectable drugs, alcohol, marijuana, cigarettes, smokeless tobacco), and these substances are the best predictors of anabolic steroid use frequency in a multiple regression model
original_authors: Durant, R.H.; Rickert, V.I.; Ashworth, C.S.
original_title: Multiple substance use associated with anabolic steroid use among adolescents
replication_authors: Robert H. Durant; Carolyn Seymore Ashworth; Cheryl Newman; Vaughn I. Rickert
replication_title: Stability of the relationships between anabolic steroid use and multiple substance use among adolescents
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The regression model from the initial study was replicated in this sample of students' and 'In confirmation of the initial study, we found significant associations between anabolic steroid use and the use of marijuana, cocaine, cigarettes, smokeless tobacco, and alcohol.' The same four variables remained the best predictors, and the relationships were stable over a 4-month period.

description: In a divided visual field paradigm, word pairs presented to the left visual field (right hemisphere) show a match effect — faster semantic-relatedness judgments when a word pair's vertical arrangement matches the canonical spatial relationship of its referents — but no such match effect is observed in the right visual field
original_authors: Rolf A. Zwaan; Richard H. Yaxley
original_title: Hemispheric differences in semantic-relatedness judgments
replication_authors: Eduard Berndt; Carolin Dudschig; Jeff Miller; Barbara Kaup
replication_title: A replication attempt of hemispheric differences in semantic-relatedness judgments (Zwaan & Yaxley, 2003)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to replicate the hemispheric asymmetry found by Zwaan and Yaxley (2003b), despite sufficient power.' Instead of finding the interaction between visual field and match, they found only a main effect of match and a Simon effect (VF × response side interaction), with no VF × match interaction.

description: Using a red pen (versus blue pen) causes participants to complete more word stems with words associated with failure and errors
original_authors: Abraham M. Rutchick; Michael L. Slepian; Bennett D. Ferris
original_title: The pen is mightier than the word: Object priming of evaluative standards
replication_authors: Fikrlova J.; Cechova L.; Lebedova T.; Pycha P.; Sesulkova A.; Prochazka J.; Vaculik M.
replication_title: The power of red: The influence of colour on evaluation and failure – A replication
explanation: The authors found that red pen users completed significantly more failure-related word stems than blue pen users (d=0.42, p=.004), directly supporting H1. The Discussion states: 'Our findings and results are thus in line with the results of Rutchick et al. (2010).'

description: Using a red pen (versus blue pen) causes participants to mark more mistakes when correcting a text written by others
original_authors: Abraham M. Rutchick; Michael L. Slepian; Bennett D. Ferris
original_title: The pen is mightier than the word: Object priming of evaluative standards
replication_authors: Fikrlova J.; Cechova L.; Lebedova T.; Pycha P.; Sesulkova A.; Prochazka J.; Vaculik M.
replication_title: The power of red: The influence of colour on evaluation and failure – A replication
explanation: Red pen users marked significantly more mistakes than blue pen users (d=0.41, p=.004), directly supporting H2. The authors conclude their findings 'support the findings of the original study' by Rutchick et al. (2010).

description: Four distinct cluster subtypes (Classic, Early, Progressing, and Disengaged) exist within the Contemplation stage of change among smokers, identifiable via cluster analysis of Pros, Cons, and Situational Temptations measures
original_authors: Gregory J. Norman; Wayne F. Velicer; Joseph L. Fava; James O. Prochaska
original_title: Cluster subtypes within stage of change in a representative sample of smokers
replication_authors: Anatchkova MD; Velicer WF; Prochaska JO
replication_title: Replication of subtypes for smoking cessation within the contemplation stage of change
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The major result of this study is that it successfully replicated the cluster subtypes within the Contemplation stage previously reported by Norman et al. (2000) and Velicer et al. (1995).' Four consistent cluster subtypes were found and replicated across all four independent random subsamples.

description: Cluster analysis of smokers within stages of change (using Pros, Cons, and Situational Temptations) reveals distinct subgroup profiles within each stage, including the Preparation stage, externally validated using Processes of Change
original_authors: Gregory J. Norman; Wayne F. Velicer; Joseph L. Fava; James O. Prochaska
original_title: Cluster subtypes within stage of change in a representative sample of smokers
replication_authors: Milena D. Anatchkova; Wayne F. Velicer; James O. Prochaska
replication_title: Replication of subtypes for smoking cessation within the Preparation stage of change
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The major result of this study is the successful replication of previously reported cluster subtypes within the Preparation stage.' Four distinct cluster subtypes (Classic, Progressing, Early Preparation, and Disengaged) were found and replicated across two random sub-samples, matching the profiles from Norman et al. (2000).

description: Cluster analysis of smokers in the Precontemplation stage reveals distinct subtype profiles (Immotive, Progressing, and Disengaged) based on the Pros, Cons, and Situational Temptations measures from the Transtheoretical Model
original_authors: Gregory J. Norman; Wayne F. Velicer; Joseph L. Fava; James O. Prochaska
original_title: Cluster subtypes within stage of change in a representative sample of smokers
replication_authors: Milena D. Anatchkova; Wayne F. Velicer; James O. Prochaska
replication_title: Replication of subtypes for smoking cessation within the precontemplation stage of change
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The main finding of this study is the replication of cluster subtypes within the Precontemplation stage of change reported by Norman et al. (2000).' The Discussion confirms that all four cluster profiles and external validation patterns closely replicated the earlier findings, including similar Processes of Change and smoking behavior differences.

description: Young adolescents (aged 12-14) are more strongly influenced by the opinions of teenagers than by adults when re-rating the riskiness of everyday situations, whereas children and adults are more influenced by adults
original_authors: Knoll, Lisa J.; Magis-Weinberg, Lucía; Speekenbrink, Maarten; Blakemore, Sarah-Jayne
original_title: Social influence on risk perception during adolescence
replication_authors: Lisa J. Knoll; Jovita T. Leung; Lucy Foulkes; Sarah‐Jayne Blakemore
replication_title: Age‐related differences in social influence on risk perception depend on the direction of influence
explanation: The authors explicitly state the replication was partial: 'The current study partially replicated the previous findings in three ways.' While they replicated the general social influence effect and age-related decrease, the key original finding — that young adolescents (12-14 year olds) are specifically more influenced by teenagers than adults — did not reach significance in the direct comparison (t(6499) = -0.65, p = 0.5), though the interaction between this age group and young adults was significant.

description: Homozygosity for the THBS-4 1186C (CC genotype) variant is a sex-dependent risk factor for myocardial infarction, specifically in women from the genetically isolated Newfoundland population
original_authors: Jianxun Cui; Edward Randell; James Renouf; Guang Sun; Fei-Yu Han; Banfield Younghusband; Ya-Gang Xie
original_title: Gender dependent association of thrombospondin-4 A387P polymorphism with myocardial infarction
replication_authors: Jianxun Cui; Edward Randell; James Renouf; Guang Sun; Roger Green; Fei-Yu Han; Ya-Gang Xie
replication_title: Thrombospondin-4 1186G>C (A387P) is a sex-dependent risk factor for myocardial infarction: A large replication study with increased sample size from the same population
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we validated our previous case-control study for the THBS-4 1186G N C variant' and 'the sex-dependent association of the CC genotype with MI reported in our initial study was confirmed in this study.' While the validation cohort alone did not reach statistical significance (OR 1.53, P=.307), the combined cohort confirmed the finding (OR 2.14, P=.009), and the authors conclude the original association is validated.

description: rs2071473 is an eQTL for TAP2 in mid-secretory-phase endometrium and is significantly associated with fecundability (time to pregnancy) in Hutterite women
original_authors: Courtney K. Burrows; Gülüm Kosova; Catherine Herman; Kristen Patterson; Katherine E. Hartmann; Digna R. Velez Edwards; Mary D. Stephenson; Vincent J. Lynch; Carole Ober
original_title: Expression quantitative trait locus mapping studies in mid-secretory phase endometrial cells identifies HLA-F and TAP2 as fecundability-associated genes
replication_authors: Mika KM; Lynch VJ
replication_title: An Ancient Fecundability-Associated Polymorphism Switches a Repressor into an Enhancer of Endometrial TAP2 Expression
replication_journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was 'to replicate this observation in an independent cohort and in additional tissues' using GTEx data. They found rs2071473 is an eQTL for TAP2 in GTEx uterus samples (n=70, β=-1.1, p=9.1×10⁻¹¹), consistent with their previous finding.

description: Higher circulating levels of glycocholenate sulfate (a secondary bile acid) are associated with increased risk of incident atrial fibrillation in Black adults
original_authors: Alvaro Alonso; Bing Yu; Waqas T. Qureshi; Morgan E. Grams; Elizabeth Selvin; Elsayed Z. Soliman; Laura R. Loehr; Lin Y. Chen; Sunil K. Agarwal; Danny Alexander; Eric Boerwinkle
original_title: Metabolomics and incidence of atrial fibrillation in African Americans: the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study
replication_authors: Alvaro Alonso; Bing Yu; Yan V. Sun; Lin Y. Chen; Laura R. Loehr; Wesley T. O'Neal; Elsayed Z. Soliman; Eric Boerwinkle
replication_title: Serum Metabolomics and Incidence of Atrial Fibrillation (from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study)
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated a previously described association of glycocholenate sulfate, a secondary bile acid, with the incidence of AF.' The replication sample (N=2,003) showed HR 1.10 (95% CI 1.00, 1.21) in the adjusted model, consistent with the original finding of HR 1.20 (95% CI 1.08, 1.33) in the derivation sample.

description: Higher circulating levels of glycolithocholate sulfate (a secondary bile acid) are associated with increased risk of incident atrial fibrillation in Black adults
original_authors: Alvaro Alonso; Bing Yu; Waqas T. Qureshi; Morgan E. Grams; Elizabeth Selvin; Elsayed Z. Soliman; Laura R. Loehr; Lin Y. Chen; Sunil K. Agarwal; Danny Alexander; Eric Boerwinkle
original_title: Metabolomics and incidence of atrial fibrillation in African Americans: the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study
replication_authors: Alvaro Alonso; Bing Yu; Yan V. Sun; Lin Y. Chen; Laura R. Loehr; Wesley T. O'Neal; Elsayed Z. Soliman; Eric Boerwinkle
replication_title: Serum Metabolomics and Incidence of Atrial Fibrillation (from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The previously described association of another secondary bile acid, glycolithocholate sulfate, with AF was not replicated in this new analysis.' The replication sample showed HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.92, 1.13, p=0.69), compared with HR 1.21 (95% CI 1.11, 1.31) in the original sample.

description: ADRB2 genotypes or haplotypes at positions 16 and 27 have no effect on bronchial hyperresponsiveness to methacholine in patients with asthma
original_authors: Wilson AM; Gray RD; Hall IP; Lipworth BJ
original_title: The effect of β2-adrenoceptor haplotypes on bronchial hyper-responsiveness in patients with asthma
replication_authors: Arvind Manoharan; William J. Anderson; Brian J. Lipworth
replication_title: Influence of β2-adrenergic receptor polymorphism on methacholine hyperresponsiveness in asthmatic patients
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'have confirmed in this replication study of a larger cohort of patients that ADRB2 genotype and haplotype 16/27 does not have an effect on BHR in methacholine-responsive patients with asthma.' No significant differences in methacholine PC20 were found across any genotype, haplotype, or BHR severity subgroup.

description: Fertilization by proxy occurs in Tribolium castaneum: males remove rival sperm from females and translocate it to new females during subsequent matings, occurring in 22% of sequential matings with ~53% of offspring sired by translocated sperm
original_authors: Eric Haubruge; L. Arnaud; J. Mignon; Mjg. Gage
original_title: Fertilization by proxy: rival sperm removal and translocation in a beetle
original_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, Series B
replication_authors: Natasha Tigreros; Adam South; Tatyana Fedina; Sara Lewis
replication_title: Does fertilization by proxy occur in Tribolium beetles? A replicated study of a novel mechanism of sperm transfer
explanation: The authors found zero evidence of sperm translocation in 84 successful trials, directly contradicting Haubruge et al. (1999): 'Our results indicate that fertilization by proxy is not a common phenomenon in T. castaneum, as we found no evidence that viable sperm were translocated between females by mating males. This directly contradicts results obtained by Haubruge et al. (1999).'

description: Chimpanzees respond negatively to inequitable outcomes (receiving less preferred food than a partner for completing the same exchange task), with responses varying by social group membership
original_authors: Sarah F. Brosnan; Hillary C. Schiff; Frans B. M. de Waal
original_title: Tolerance for inequity may increase with social closeness in chimpanzees
original_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
replication_authors: Sarah F. Brosnan; Catherine Talbot; Megan Ahlgren; Susan P. Lambeth; Steven J. Schapiro
replication_title: Mechanisms underlying responses to inequitable outcomes in chimpanzees, Pan troglodytes
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to replicate the Brosnan et al. (2005) methodology with new subjects from stable, long-term social groups. While chimpanzees again responded to inequity (replicating the general finding), the current study found a sex difference not previously reported, and — contrary to the original — stable long-term groups DID respond in this study (males did). The Discussion notes: 'Unlike in previous studies, we found a sex difference in the response to inequity' and the authors frame the results as extending rather than cleanly replicating the prior findings.

description: Premorbid psychopathology in early to mid-adulthood predicts later diagnosis of CFS/ME in the 1946 British birth cohort
original_authors: Samuel B. Harvey; Michael Wadsworth; Simon Wessely; Matthew Hotopf
original_title: The relationship between prior psychiatric disorder and chronic fatigue: evidence from a national birth cohort study
replication_authors: Laura Goodwin; Peter D. White; Matthew Hotopf; Stephen A. Stansfeld; Charlotte Clark
replication_title: Psychopathology and Physical Activity as Predictors of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in the 1958 British Birth Cohort: A Replication Study of the 1946 and 1970 Birth Cohorts
explanation: The 1958 cohort data supported the 1946 cohort finding: premorbid psychopathology at ages 23 (OR=1.85, 95% CI=1.06-3.22, p=0.03) and 33 years (OR=2.81, 95% CI=1.28-6.18, p=0.01) significantly increased the odds of CFS/ME, with the authors explicitly concluding this 'supported the 1946 cohort findings.'

description: Persistent physical activity in early to mid-adulthood increases the risk of CFS/ME in the 1946 British birth cohort
original_authors: Samuel B. Harvey; Michael Wadsworth; Simon Wessely; Matthew Hotopf
original_title: Etiology of chronic fatigue syndrome: testing popular hypotheses using a national birth cohort study
replication_authors: Laura Goodwin; Peter D. White; Matthew Hotopf; Stephen A. Stansfeld; Charlotte Clark
replication_title: Psychopathology and Physical Activity as Predictors of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in the 1958 British Birth Cohort: A Replication Study of the 1946 and 1970 Birth Cohorts
explanation: The 1958 cohort found no association between persistent physical activity at ages 23 and 33 years and CFS/ME (OR=1.12, 95% CI=0.57-2.19, p=0.83), in contrast to the 1946 cohort finding of a 10.80-fold increase in odds. The authors explicitly state: 'the data did not support previous findings regarding extremes of physical activity.'

description: Childhood participation in sports during spare time at age 10 is associated with reduced risk of CFS/ME in adulthood in the 1970 British birth cohort
original_authors: Russell Viner; Matthew Hotopf
original_title: Childhood predictors of self reported chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis in adults: national birth cohort study
replication_authors: Laura Goodwin; Peter D. White; Matthew Hotopf; Stephen A. Stansfeld; Charlotte Clark
replication_title: Psychopathology and Physical Activity as Predictors of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in the 1958 British Birth Cohort: A Replication Study of the 1946 and 1970 Birth Cohorts
explanation: The 1958 cohort found no evidence that playing sports in spare time at age 11 was associated with CFS/ME (OR=0.96, p=0.93 for 'sometimes'; OR=0.85, p=0.72 for 'most days'), providing 'no support for the 1970 cohort findings.'

description: High scores on the Malaise Inventory (psychopathology) at the time of CFS/ME diagnosis are cross-sectionally associated with CFS/ME in the 1970 British birth cohort
original_authors: Russell Viner; Matthew Hotopf
original_title: Childhood predictors of self reported chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis in adults: national birth cohort study
replication_authors: Laura Goodwin; Peter D. White; Matthew Hotopf; Stephen A. Stansfeld; Charlotte Clark
replication_title: Psychopathology and Physical Activity as Predictors of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in the 1958 British Birth Cohort: A Replication Study of the 1946 and 1970 Birth Cohorts
explanation: Reviewer confirmed: Table 2 (body.md) presents both cohorts' data explicitly — 1958 cohort OR=5.56 (95% CI 3.15-9.82, p<0.001) vs 1970 cohort OR=2.6 (95% CI 1.6-4.3, p<0.001), both using the Malaise Inventory measured concurrently with CFS/ME self-report. The Discussion states unambiguously: 'There was also support across the cohorts for a cross-sectional association between CFS/ME and psychopathology (10), in agreement with previous research.' Both the numerical evidence and the authors' explicit conclusion confirm this is a clear replication success. The cross-sectional nature (Malaise assessed at same wave as CFS/ME self-report, not premorbid) is reflected in the entry description and does not introduce ambiguity about the result classification.

description: A Brain Injury Coping Skills (BICS) treatment group improves perceived self-efficacy (PSE) in persons with brain injury and their caregivers
original_authors: Backhaus, Samantha
replication_authors: Anne M. Moessner; Samantha Backhaus; Summer Ibarra; Devan Parrot; Daniel W. Klyce; Sysan Lepore; James F. Malec
replication_title: Poster 164: Brain Injury Coping Skills Group: A Replication Study
replication_journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
explanation: Reviewer confirmed: The paper is explicitly titled 'Brain Injury Coping Skills Group: A Replication Study' (Poster 164). Authors state: 'this study demonstrated a significant treatment effect for the BICS group in improving PSE, replicating previous findings for the BICS group treatment.' Primary endpoint replicated: significant PSE improvement on BICSQ (F=18.41, P=.001) and significant group difference immediately post-treatment (t=-2.35, P=.044). Close extension typing is correct — conducted in a separate setting with different facilitators to test generalizability. Medium confidence is retained because: (1) the original Backhaus et al. (2010) paper is not characterized in detail within this abstract, so original effect sizes/N are unavailable for quantitative comparison; (2) at 3-month follow-up, PSE converged between groups (BICS=95.13, control=98.5, no significant difference), raising genuine questions about durability that the authors acknowledge; (3) N=16 total is very small. Result='success' is correct for the primary outcome, but the null follow-up result introduces real ambiguity about the overall picture.

description: An extended dual pathway model of overeating in which the relation between negative affect and overeating is mediated by lack of interoceptive awareness and emotional eating (beyond Stice's original restrained eating and negative affect pathways)
original_authors: Tatjana Van Strien; Rutger C. M. E. Engels; Jan Van Leeuwe; Harriëtte M. Snoek
original_title: The Stice model of overeating: tests in clinical and non-clinical samples
replication_authors: Ouwens MA; van Strien T.; van Leeuwe JF; van der Staak CP
replication_title: The dual pathway model of overeating. Replication and extension with actual food consumption
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'the present study confirms the extended model that van Strien et al. (2005) constructed from Stice's dual pathway model for overeating in a sample of female college students.' The extended model fit the data well and the key finding — that negative affect relates to food consumption via lack of interoceptive awareness and emotional eating — was replicated.

description: Short-term restriction of a palatable snack food increases preschool children's intake, selection, and behavioral response (comments, requests, physical attempts to access) to the restricted food when it becomes available
original_authors: Jennifer Orlet Fisher; Leann Lipps Birch
original_title: Restricting access to palatable foods affects children's behavioral response, food selection, and intake
replication_authors: Rollins BY; Loken E.; Savage JS; Birch LL
replication_title: Effects of restriction on children’s intake differ by child temperament, food reinforcement, and parent’s chronic use of restriction
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we found that a short-term restriction increased children's intake and behavioral response immediately after the food was restricted, thereby replicating Fisher and Birch's (1999b).' The replication used the same preschool snack paradigm, same session duration, and same behavioral observation checklist as the original study.

description: Sensory sensitivity fully mediates the relationship between anxiety and picky eating in children ages 5-10
original_authors: Claire V. Farrow; Helen Coulthard
original_title: Relationships between sensory sensitivity, anxiety and selective eating in children
replication_authors: Hana F. Zickgraf; Anjeli Elkins
replication_title: Sensory sensitivity mediates the relationship between anxiety and picky eating in children/ adolescents ages 8–17, and in college undergraduates: A replication and age-upward extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study replicates, and extends into a new age group and larger sample, Farrow and Coulthard's 2012 finding that sensory sensitivity mediates the relationship between picky eating and anxiety in childhood.' The mediation was significant in the child/adolescent sample (n=158, ages 8-17, clinical anxiety/OCD population).

description: Sensory sensitivity fully mediates the relationship between anxiety and picky eating in children ages 5-10
original_authors: Claire V. Farrow; Helen Coulthard
original_title: Relationships between sensory sensitivity, anxiety and selective eating in children
replication_authors: Hana F. Zickgraf; Anjeli Elkins
replication_title: Sensory sensitivity mediates the relationship between anxiety and picky eating in children/ adolescents ages 8–17, and in college undergraduates: A replication and age-upward extension
explanation: The abstract states 'We replicated this finding... in 813 young adult college students.' Mediation analyses confirmed sensory sensitivity mediated the anxiety–picky eating relationship in undergraduates (Step 2: R²=0.04, F(2,812)=12.09, p<.001), extending the original child finding to young adults.

description: Recalling a meal consumed earlier in the day (today's lunch) leads to reduced subsequent snack intake compared to recalling a meal from the previous day (yesterday's lunch)
original_authors: Higgs S.
original_title: Memory for recent eating and its influence on subsequent food intake
replication_authors: Joanna Szypula; Amy Ahern; Lucy Cheke
replication_title: The role of memory ability, depth and mode of recall in the impact of memory on later consumption
explanation: The authors explicitly report replicating the meal-recall effect in the written, unguided condition (as in Higgs, 2002), finding significantly fewer biscuits eaten after recalling today's vs. yesterday's meal (F(1,15)=6.07, p=.026, η²=.288). The Discussion states: 'This study replicated the previous finding that written, unguided recall of an earlier meal, immediately before a snacking session, significantly reduced biscuit intake compared to recalling a meal from the previous day.' The effect was smaller than in the original (d_z=0.62 vs. d=1.57 in original Experiment 2).

description: Mink housed in non-enriched cages show greater interest in diverse stimuli (higher exploration/orientation/contact) compared to those in enriched enclosures, consistent with a boredom-like state
original_authors: Rebecca K. Meagher; Georgia J. Mason
original_title: Environmental enrichment reduces signs of boredom in caged mink
replication_authors: Rebecca K. Meagher; Dana L.M. Campbell; Georgia J. Mason
replication_title: Boredom-like states in mink and their behavioural correlates: A replicate study
explanation: The authors state 'we did successfully replicate the original finding of increased exploratory behaviour by mink in non-enriched housing.' Non-enriched mink again explored stimuli more than enriched mink, with statistically significant effects for time in contact (F1,4=22.8, p=0.004) and for aversive stimulus categories.

description: Time spent lying still but awake (inert with eyes open) positively correlates with interest in diverse stimuli as an indicator of boredom-like states in mink
original_authors: Rebecca K. Meagher; Georgia J. Mason
original_title: Environmental enrichment reduces signs of boredom in caged mink
replication_authors: Rebecca K. Meagher; Dana L.M. Campbell; Georgia J. Mason
replication_title: Boredom-like states in mink and their behavioural correlates: A replicate study
explanation: The lying-still-but-awake correlation was partially replicated: in enriched mink, lying awake correlated positively with orientation and contact time (p=0.008, p=0.002), but housing treatment no longer significantly elevated lying awake in non-enriched mink. The authors describe this as showing 'some of the expected relationships' rather than a full replication.

description: Locomotor stereotypic behaviour (pacing, head-twirling) negatively correlates with interest in diverse stimuli, suggesting it may alleviate boredom-like states in mink
original_authors: Rebecca K. Meagher; Georgia J. Mason
