replication_title: Neural entrainment to speech and nonspeech in dyslexia: Conceptual replication and extension of previous investigations
explanation: The authors explicitly call this a 'closer conceptual replication' of Lehongre et al. (2011). Table 2 shows the SNR replication at 30 Hz in LH failed: t(37)=0.87, p=0.39, d=0.28. The authors state: 'we failed to replicate previous results suggesting a group difference in the delta, theta and gamma ranges, whether measured using SNR, PLV, IHPS or coherence.'

description: Carrying out a demanding rhythmic task with the hands selectively impairs working memory for arm-related action words (e.g., clap), while carrying out the same task with the feet selectively impairs memory for leg-related action words (e.g., kick), producing a double dissociation that implicates the motor system in keeping action verbs in working memory
original_authors: Zubaida Shebani; Friedemann Pulvermüller

replication_authors: Guillermo Montero-Melis; Jeroen van Paridon; Markus Ostarek; Emanuel Bylund
replication_title: No evidence for embodiment: The motor system is not needed to keep action verbs in working memory
explanation: The authors conducted a fully pre-registered direct replication with N=77 (over 5x the original sample size of 15) and found very strong Bayesian evidence against the hypothesized effector-specific interference effect (BF01=91). They explicitly conclude: 'We have found very strong evidence that the motor system is not needed to keep action verbs in working memory.'

description: Touching the face of upper-limb amputees evokes phantom hand sensations (referred sensations), reflecting cortical remapping in primary somatosensory cortex following amputation (the 'perceptual remapping hypothesis')
original_authors: Ramachandran VS; Rogers-Ramachandran D.; Stewart M.
original_title: Perceptual correlates of massive cortical reorganization
replication_authors: Elena Amoruso; Devin B. Terhune; Maria Kromm; Stephen Kirker; Dollyane Muret; Tamar R. Makin
replication_title: Reassessing referral of touch following peripheral deafferentation: The role of contextual bias
explanation: REVIEWER UPGRADE: The paper provides clear, multi-pronged evidence against the perceptual remapping hypothesis. Behaviourally, all three groups (amputees N=18, congenital one-handers N=19, two-handers N=22) reported referred sensations at comparable rates — the overall proportion did not differ across groups (χ²=.338, p=.845), with amputees reporting no more than controls (both U<220, p>.550, BF10<.355). Amputees were not more likely to lateralise referred sensations to the phantom hand than controls were to their missing/non-dominant hand. Neuroimaging (fMRI RSA) found no increased face-to-phantom-hand representational similarity in amputees' missing hand region versus two-handed controls (F(1,36)=.372, p=.546; BF10=.483). The Discussion explicitly states: 'these findings weaken the interpretation of referred sensations as a perceptual correlate of S1 plasticity.' There is marginal evidence (p=.058, BF10=2.215) that amputees lateralise face-evoked sensations toward the phantom hand, but this did not reach significance across groups and was not supported by the neural data. The failure of both the amputee-specificity claim and the cortical remapping interpretation is unambiguous and warrants high confidence.

description: Vibrotactile stimulation of the face and other body parts evokes referred sensations specifically in upper-limb amputees, and the pattern of referred sensations reflects cortical reorganization
original_authors: Knecht S.; Henningsen H.; Elbert T.; Flor H.; Höhling C.; Pantev C.; Taub E.
original_title: Reorganizational and perceptional changes after amputation
replication_authors: Elena Amoruso; Devin B. Terhune; Maria Kromm; Stephen Kirker; Dollyane Muret; Tamar R. Makin
replication_title: Reassessing referral of touch following peripheral deafferentation: The role of contextual bias
explanation: REVIEWER UPGRADE: Using the same vibrotactile stimulation paradigm and the same 10 body-parts reported in Knecht et al. (1996), the replication found that referred sensations were not specific to amputees. The overall proportion of reported referred sensations did not differ across the three groups (χ²=.338, p=.845; Kruskal-Wallis), and amputees (N=18) did not report more referred sensations than one-handers (N=19) or two-handers (N=22) (both U<220, p>.550, BF10<.355). Amputees showed no greater lateralisation of sensations toward the phantom hand compared with controls. The specificity claim from Knecht et al. — that vibrotactile stimulation evokes referred sensations specifically in amputees and that these patterns reflect cortical reorganisation — is directly and clearly contradicted. The authors explicitly attribute prior findings to demand characteristics: referred sensations were similarly enhanced by expectancy suggestion across all three groups, including congenital one-handers who had never experienced touch on their 'missing' hand. The failure is unambiguous and clearly reported, warranting high confidence.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to confirm the previously reported large effects of homeopathic histamine dilutions on basophil function of the examined donor.' The paper directly adapted methods from Sainte-Laudy and Belon (1996) and found no significant effect of highly diluted histamine under rigorously blinded and randomised conditions.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to confirm the previously reported large effects of homeopathic histamine dilutions on basophil function of the examined donor.' Methods were adapted from Brown and Ennis (2001), and under rigorously blinded and randomised experimental conditions, no large inhibitory effects of highly diluted histamine were found.

The 10-metabolite panel achieved an AUC of only 0.609 in the replication compared to 0.96 in the original.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We successfully replicated our previous finding that 14-month-old infants exhibit an N400 effect when another person in their presence could have thought that a label did not match an object.' The replication used identical procedure but tested Hungarian infants in Budapest rather than French infants in Paris, making it a close extension testing cross-linguistic/cross-lab generalizability.

(2020).' The replication was pre-registered and found a significant positive association (r = 0.302, p = 0.026).

(2015), who did not find a significant relationship between hardiness and sport engagement but did find a comparable small effect between resiliency and sport engagement.'

The absence of quantitative similarity metrics is a limitation of the abstract format, but does not create genuine ambiguity about the result direction.

explanation: Upgraded from medium: The paper's Conclusions section explicitly states 'We replicated prior studies that a baseline PSA value at age 40-69 yr can be used to stratify a man's risk of dying from prostate cancer within the next 15-20 yr.' The Discussion directly compares the Norwegian NPCC results (C-index 0.807 for PCa death) to the Malmö Diet and Cancer cohort (C-indices 0.86, 0.85, 0.84) and describes them as 'consistent.' The lower Norwegian C-index is explicitly explained by the authors as predictable ascertainment bias: in Norway, men with higher PSA underwent opportunistic screening and received treatment, reducing the PSA-mortality association. This mechanistic explanation removes ambiguity — the quantitative difference is expected and understood, and the authors unambiguously characterize the finding as a replication. The citation sentence and original vs. replication effect sizes are accurately recorded. No genuine ambiguity remains.

explanation: Upgraded from medium: The paper's Conclusions section explicitly states 'We replicated prior studies that a baseline PSA value at age 40-69 yr can be used to stratify a man's risk of dying from prostate cancer within the next 15-20 yr.' Overall, our findings were consistent with the Malmö and Västerbotten studies.' The Norwegian NPCC overall C-index (0.807) is lower than the Västerbotten age-specific C-indices (0.859, 0.840), but the authors explicitly explain this as predictable: Norway's opportunistic PSA screening meant men with higher PSA were treated, attenuating the PSA-mortality association. The authors' own language — 'consistent,' 'replicated' — is unambiguous. The extension aspect is appropriate: the Norwegian cohort used clinically-obtained PSA (not retrospectively-frozen samples) in a population with opportunistic rather than zero screening. No genuine ambiguity remains.

description: A three-month telephone-based tailored risk-factor reduction program (CHOICE) significantly lowers coronary risk factors in ACS survivors not accessing cardiac rehabilitation at one and four years
original_authors: Redfern J.; Briffa T.; Ellis E.; Freedman SB
original_title: Choice of secondary prevention improves risk factors after acute coronary syndrome: 1-year follow-up of the CHOICE (Choice of Health Options In prevention of Cardiovascular Events) randomised controlled trial
replication_authors: Lis Neubeck; Nicole Lowres; Ben Freedman; Tom Briffa; Adrian Bauman; Kris Rogers; Julie Redfern
replication_title: Two Year Outcomes of the Choice of Health Options in Prevention of Cardiovascular Events (CHOICE) Replication Study
explanation: Reviewer reassessment: This is a conference abstract reporting a multi-site replication of the original CHOICE RCT (Redfern et al. 2009, Heart). Results are genuinely mixed at 2 years. Lipid profiles (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL) improved significantly and the composite ≥3 risk factors above target improved significantly (52.9% → 39.8%). However, systolic blood pressure worsened significantly (130.3 → 136.3 mmHg, mean diff +5.91, 95%CI 2.82–9.0). BMI, depression scores, and smoking rates showed no significant change. The authors' conclusion ('significantly improved coronary risk profile') is selectively optimistic and not fully supported by the data. Additionally, this is a close extension (adds a CHOICE-plus 2-year arm and tests multi-site generalizability) rather than a direct replication. The result is inconclusive: some outcomes replicate the original's positive findings, others do not, and the study is an underpowered conference abstract without a full reference list. Confidence remains low because: (1) the paper is a brief abstract with no formal reference list, (2) the mixed results preclude a clear success/failure verdict, and (3) no comparison to the original's effect sizes is possible from this abstract alone. The original study was identified as Redfern et al. 2009 (Heart 95:468-475, DOI 10.1136/hrt.2008.150870) based on the citation sentence and the known CHOICE literature.

(2022), which introduced the MDI in a US pre-birth cohort — co-author Carina Venter appears on both papers. Confidence upgraded to high: the result is unambiguous, the original reference is now identified, and the replication framing is explicit in the paper title ('a replication study from Sweden').

Confidence upgraded to high: the non-significance is unambiguous, the original reference is now identified, and the failure classification is clear.

description: Modafinil can be used as adjunctive therapy in depressed outpatients without inducing mood switching (mania/hypomania), tolerance, or abuse in affective disorder patients

explanation: Independent review confirms the original extraction. The paper explicitly self-identifies as a replication in its title ('A replication study') and conclusions state: 'This study confirms previous results of generally well-tolerated use of modafinil in affective disorder patients with little abuse, tolerance or mood switch.' The lead author (Nasr) is replicating his own 2004 study using the same retrospective chart review methodology in a larger patient sample (191 patients). Results are unambiguous: 0 patients in any group switched to mania/hypomania, dose stability was maintained after the first 10 months, and no abuse was detected. Close extension rather than direct replication because the sample is larger and adds a substance abuse history subgroup analysis. Result = success is clearly supported. Confidence upgraded to high because the result classification, replication type, and outcome are all unambiguous from the paper text — the only missing field is original_n (not reported in this paper), which does not create genuine ambiguity about the classification.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our study did not confirm the findings of Barber and Muenz (1996).' The key moderation interactions (treatment by AVPD and treatment by OCPD) were all non-significant in both HAM-D and IDS-SR analyses.

explanation: The replication found a statistically significant effect in the opposite direction: non-remitters had HIGHER FA than remitters (p=0.02 and 0.01 for left and right amygdala respectively), whereas the original found lower FA in non-remitters. The authors explicitly state: 'we found the opposite pattern; rather than positively correlating with symptom improvement, fractional anisotropy (FA) in the tracts between the raphe nucleus (RN) and amygdala positively correlated with symptom worsening, and non-remitters had higher FA between the raphe and amygdala than remitters' and conclude 'these findings can be taken as negative on a clinical level, and do not replicate previous results.'

replication_title: Data mining algorithm predicts a range of adverse outcomes in major depression
explanation: The authors applied their previously developed prediction model to two independent test samples from different populations (USA and Netherlands) and found consistent prediction performance (AUC 0.68-0.73) comparable to the training sample AUC (~0.75), with overlapping confidence intervals. They conclude: 'Our prediction model consistently predicted a range of adverse outcomes in MD across two independent test samples derived from studies in different subpopulations, countries, using different measurement procedures.'

The replication used the same paradigm (fMRI faces/shapes task) but in an elderly population (60+) rather than the younger adult males in the original.

original_title: Common variants at 7p21 are associated with frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 inclusions
replication_authors: Stuart Pickering-Brown
replication_title: P1‐103: Genome wide association in frontotemporal lobar degeneration: A replication study
explanation: REVIEWER UPDATE: Fixed DOI typo — original entry had ng.566; correct DOI is 10.1038/ng.536 (confirmed via web search: 'Common variants at 7p21 are associated with frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 inclusions', Nature Genetics). The citation_sentence says 'Van Deerlin et al. Nature Genetics - In Press' (no year given because the paper was in press at time of submission), which correctly identifies the Van Deerlin et al. target study. The extracted authors/title are correct. DOI mismatch was a typo, not a metadata error. Result classification: genuinely inconclusive. The replication (330 FTLD cases, 258 controls, Manchester cohort) tested all SNPs from the Van Deerlin GWAS. TMEM106B — the primary genome-wide significant finding — failed to replicate ('No TMEM106B SNPs was associated with FTLD in the Manchester cohort'). Loci on chr 1, 8, and 10 also failed. One chr11 SNP (rs2015747; p=0.009, OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33-0.85) replicated, and chr9p SNPs replicated in FTLD+ALS subgroup only. Authors offer two explanations for TMEM106B failure: cohort composition (~45% FTLD-tau cases masking a TDP-specific signal) or type 1 error in the original. This mixed pattern — primary finding fails, secondary loci partially replicate — is genuinely ambiguous. 'Inconclusive' is the most defensible classification. Medium confidence is appropriate: the paper itself is clear about the results, but whether this constitutes a failure or partial replication is interpretively ambiguous.

explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication study conducted with a different lead investigator and research site using the same design, methods, and formulation. They conclude: 'These results support similar, statistically significant findings from a prior study' with significant placebo-adjusted reductions in LDL cholesterol (-4.3%), non-HDL cholesterol (-4.1%), and total cholesterol (-3.5%), consistent with the original study's significant reductions.

(2016)' and in the Conclusion: 'this replication study using a single sprint approach and reference force plate data confirms the initial validation study (Samozino et al., 2016).' The replication found good agreement between the simple method and force platform data (grand average bias of 4.71%).

The authors explicitly state: 'This experiment replicated earlier findings on dissociation and memory fragmentation.'

description: State dissociation during exposure to an aversive film is related to subjective memory fragmentation but not to objective memory performance (sequential memory task)

For the third time in a row, state dissociation was not related to objective memory fragmentation, but it was related to the subjective experience of memory fragmentation.'

replication_title: Interpretation bias for uncertain threat: A replication and extension
replication_journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly state this was a replication: 'Our findings provide an important replication of prior research demonstrating that individuals high in IU display elevated concern over ambiguous scenarios (Dugas et al., 2005; Koerner & Dugas, 2008).' IU significantly predicted elevated concern over ambiguous scenarios (b = .43, p < .001) even after controlling for negative affect.

description: Imagining a non-consensual kiss from an immoral man evokes greater feelings of mental contamination than imagining a consensual kiss from a moral man, using a 2×2 between-subjects design manipulating morality and consent

original_title: Analyses of mental contamination: Part I, experimental manipulations of morality
replication_authors: Tan Tang; Zhongfang Fu; Jianping Wang
replication_title: Mental contamination among people in China: A replication of a moral manipulation experiment
replication_journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
explanation: The replication partially confirmed the original findings — the main effect of kiss desirability (consensual vs. non-consensual) replicated, but key differences emerged: in China, even a consensual kiss with a moral man evoked strong mental contamination (unlike the original), and immoral pre-kiss information intensified contamination in the non-consensual condition (unlike the original). The authors conclude: 'our results show that among people in China, feelings of mental contamination could be induced by the same experimental conditions as in the precedent study' but also identify 'results in contrast to Elliott and Radomsky's (2009)' that they attribute to cultural differences.

A high fidelity score of 0.95 was achieved for the methods domain.

description: Adults show an asymmetry between low-match classification and low-match inference tasks, relying on category labels (treating them as category markers) more in inference than in classification when labels conflict with perceptual similarity

original_title: Inference using categories
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Deng W.; Sloutsky VM
replication_title: The role of linguistic labels in inductive generalization
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The goal of Experiment 1 was to (a) replicate Yamauchi and Markman's (2000) paradigm with adults.' Across all experiments (1A, 1B, 2A, 2B, 3), adults consistently replicated the predicted asymmetry: significantly more category-consistent responding in low-match inference than in low-match classification (all interactions significant at p=.001), confirming adults treat labels as category markers. The authors conclude 'similar to Yamauchi and Markman's study, adults treated labels differently from other features.'

description: Adults show an asymmetry between low-match classification and low-match inference tasks, relying on category labels (treating them as category markers) more in inference than in classification when labels conflict with perceptual similarity

original_title: Category learning by inference and classification
replication_authors: Deng W.; Sloutsky VM
replication_title: The role of linguistic labels in inductive generalization
explanation: Independent review confirms medium confidence. The abstract names both Yamauchi & Markman (1998) and (2000) as replication targets ('we replicated Yamauchi and Markman's findings with adults... Journal of Memory and Language, 1998...'). However, the body text consistently identifies the 2000 paper as the explicit replication target ('we replicated Yamauchi and Markman's (2000) findings with adults'; 'The goal of Experiment 1 was to replicate Yamauchi and Markman's (2000) paradigm'). The 1998 paper is cited in the body primarily as a co-originator of the paradigm and for inference/classification learning differences, not as the specific experimental target. The result (success) is unambiguous — adults did show the asymmetry — but whether this paper is best characterized as replicating the 1998 study specifically (vs. the 2000 study) is genuinely unclear. Medium confidence is appropriate and honest.

The replication succeeded with a significant effect of condition on ANS accuracy (F(1, 36) = 13.78, p = .001, η²p = .28), with Easy-First children outperforming Hard-First children (76.84% vs. 66.80% correct).

The replication found no significant performance advantage for the Duplo false belief task (58%) over the standard false belief task (41%), and the joint DTB×DFB probability (.45) was significantly below the original's value of .73.

Replication Experiment 1 found F(2,178)=0.27, p=.77, with d=-0.12 (heat vs. cold) and d=-0.02 (heat vs. neutral), far below the original effect.

However, the effect was absent when non-compliant participants were included (d=0.15, p>0.250), making the overall result dependent on analytical choices. The Discussion notes 'the replicability of the effect...hinges on the degree to which noncompliant participants are included in analyses,' indicating genuine ambiguity about success.

description: Willingness to change, generational involvement, and perceived technological opportunities positively predict corporate entrepreneurship in family firms, with strategic planning moderating these relationships

The authors conclude: 'the replication was able to confirm the external validity of the original study's result in most parts' but 'the moderating effect of strategic planning proposed in the original study cannot be transferred to the replication's sample.'

description: Concepts with many semantic features (high number-of-features) are responded to more quickly than concepts with few semantic features in a lexical decision task
original_authors: Penny M. Pexman; Stephen J. Lupker; Yasushi Hino
original_title: The impact of feedback semantics in visual word recognition: Number-of-features effects in lexical decision and naming tasks
replication_authors: Ray Grondin; Stephen J. Lupker; Ken McRae
replication_title: Shared features dominate semantic richness effects for concrete concepts
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated Pexman et al.'s (2002) NoF effect in the lexical decision task' after finding 30 ms shorter latencies for high NoF concepts (t1(16)=7.37, p<.00001), using a larger and better-controlled item set from McRae et al. (2005) norms.

description: Concepts with many semantic features (high number-of-features) are responded to more quickly than concepts with few semantic features in a concreteness decision task
original_authors: Penny M. Pexman; Gregory G. Holyk; Marie-H. Monfils
original_title: Number-of-features effects and semantic processing
replication_authors: Ray Grondin; Stephen J. Lupker; Ken McRae
replication_title: Shared features dominate semantic richness effects for concrete concepts
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Study 1B replicated the NoF effect using a concreteness decision task with an extremely tightly controlled and large set of items,' finding 29 ms shorter latencies for high NoF concepts (t1(16)=4.27, p<.0001) using an improved stimulus set.

description: Semantic preview benefit in English reading occurs for synonym previews but not for semantically associated previews when target words are embedded in neutral sentence contexts
original_authors: Elizabeth R. Schotter
original_title: Synonyms provide semantic preview benefit in English
replication_authors: Elizabeth R. Schotter; Michelle Lee; Michael Reiderman; Keith Rayner
replication_title: The effect of contextual constraint on parafoveal processing in reading
explanation: The authors explicitly label their neutral-sentence conditions in Experiment 2 as a 'replication of Schotter (2013)' and confirm the result: 'these data confirm the preview benefit effects for identical and synonym previews and non-significant preview benefit for semantically related previews reported by Schotter (2013) for words in neutral sentences.' They used the same stimuli, paradigm (boundary paradigm), and measures as the original study.

description: Adult chiropractic users are significantly more likely than nonusers to receive seasonal influenza vaccination, based on 2007 NHIS data
original_authors: Lawrence Jones; Christopher Sciamanna; Erik Lehman
original_title: Are those who use specific complementary and alternative medicine therapies less likely to be immunized?
replication_authors: Monica Smith; Matthew A. Davis
replication_title: Immunization Status of Adult Chiropractic Patients in Analyses of National Health Interview Survey
replication_journal: Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics
explanation: The authors explicitly attempted to replicate Jones et al.'s methodology using the same 2007 NHIS dataset and found divergent results: 'we found no significant difference between chiropractic users and nonusers relative to having received the seasonal flu vaccine,' contradicting Jones et al.'s finding of a significant positive association. The authors conclude that 'methodological differences in previous studies that investigated the association between chiropractic care and adult vaccination likely explain divergent findings reported in the literature.'

description: IL6 rs1800795 (-174G>C) gene polymorphism is associated with risk of hip osteoarthritis
original_authors: Pola E.; Papaleo P.; Pola R.; Gaetani E.; Tamburelli FC; Aulisa L.; Logroscino CA
original_title: Interleukin-6 gene polymorphism and risk of osteoarthritis of the hip: a case-control study
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In IL6, rs1800797 (marker for rs1800795, -174G>C) did not associate with hip OA as previously reported in Pola et al.' and conclude 'We did not find statistically significant evidence at the 0.05 level to support the reported associations with OA... in any of the 12 studied genes.'

description: ADAM12 SNP rs3740199 (Gly48Arg) is associated with female knee osteoarthritis
original_authors: Ana M. Valdes; Deborah J. Hart; Karen A. Jones; Gabriela Surdulescu; Peter Swarbrick; David V. Doyle; Alan J. Schafer; Tim D. Spector
original_title: Association study of candidate genes for the prevalence and progression of knee osteoarthritis
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'ADAM12 SNP rs3740199 (Gly48Arg) was not associated with female knee OA as reported in Valdes et al.' and the overall conclusion states no significant evidence was found for any of the 12 studied genes.

description: COL2A1 SNP rs1635550 (and haplotype with rs2070739) is associated with male knee osteoarthritis
original_authors: Ana M. Valdes; John Loughlin; Mark Van Oene; Kay Chapman; Gabriela L. Surdulescu; Michael Doherty; Tim D. Spector
original_title: Sex and ethnic differences in the association of ASPN, CALM1, COL2A1, COMP, and FRZB with genetic susceptibility to osteoarthritis of the knee

replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'COL2A1 SNP rs1635550 was not associated with male knee OA as a single SNP or in a haplotype with rs2070739 as reported in Valdes et al.' and the overall conclusion supports failure to replicate.

description: The 194 bp allele of the IGF1 CA repeat promoter polymorphism is associated with osteoarthritis in subjects under 65 years
original_authors: Meulenbelt I.; Bijkerk C.; Miedema HS; Breedveld FC; Hofman A.; Valkenburg HA; Pols HA; Slagboom PE; van Duijn CM
original_title: A genetic association of the IGF-1 gene and radiological osteoarthritis in a population-based cohort study (the Rotterdam study)
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors state 'comparison of the frequency of the 194 bp allele of the CA repeat to the other alleles in subjects under 65 years old did not detect the association reported by Meulenbelt et al. with neither OA, hip OA nor knee OA.'

description: IL1B SNPs (rs1143634 and rs16944) and IL1RN VNTR haplotype are associated with hip osteoarthritis
original_authors: Meulenbelt I.; Seymour AB; Nieuwland M.; Huizinga TW; van Duijn CM; Slagboom PE
original_title: Association of the interleukin-1 gene cluster with radiographic signs of osteoarthritis of the hip
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors state 'The associations between IL1B SNPs (rs1143634 and rs16944) and the IL1RN VNTR... and hip OA in Meulenbelt et al. were not significantly replicated here' and 'A haplotype comprised of rs16944 (IL1B), rs1143634 (IL1B) and rs419598 (marker SNP for IL1RN VNTR) was not associated with hip OA as previously reported.'

description: IL1A SNP rs1800587 (-889T>C) is associated with knee osteoarthritis
original_authors: John Loughlin; Barbara Dowling; Zehra Mustafa; Kay Chapman
original_title: Association of the interleukin-1 gene cluster on chromosome 2q13 with knee osteoarthritis
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors state 'The association between IL1A SNP rs17561 (marker for rs1800587, -889T>C) and knee OA reported by Loughlin et al. was not significantly replicated.'

description: IL4R variants rs1805013 and rs1805016 are associated with hip osteoarthritis in females
original_authors: Tracy Forster; Kay Chapman; John Loughlin
original_title: Common variants within the interleukin 4 receptor alpha gene (IL4R) are associated with susceptibility to osteoarthritis
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In IL4R, rs1805013 and rs1805016 were not associated with hip OA in females as reported by Forster et al.' and the overall conclusion confirms failure to replicate all investigated associations.

description: TGFB1 rs1982073 (Leu10Pro) polymorphism is associated with osteoarthritis in females
original_authors: Yoshiji Yamada; Hiroyasu Okuizumi; Akimitsu Miyauchi; Yasuyuki Takagi; Kyoji Ikeda; Atsushi Harada
original_title: Association of transforming growth factor beta1 genotype with spinal osteophytosis in Japanese women
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors state 'rs1982073 (Leu10Pro) in TGFB1 was not associated with OA in females as reported in Yamada et al.' and note that the previous association was actually with spinal osteophytosis, not large-joint OA tested here.

description: VDR rs731236 (Taq I RFLP) polymorphism is associated with knee osteoarthritis in females
original_authors: Keen RW; Hart DJ; Lanchbury JS; Spector TD
original_title: Association of early osteoarthritis of the knee with a Taq I polymorphism of the vitamin D receptor gene
replication_authors: Limer KL; Tosh K.; Bujac SR; McConnell R.; Doherty S.; Nyberg F.; Zhang W.; Doherty M.; Muir KR; Maciewicz RA
replication_title: Attempt to replicate published genetic associations in a large, well-defined osteoarthritis case–control population (the GOAL study)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In VDR, rs731236 was not associated with knee OA in females as reported by Keen et al.' and the overall conclusion confirms failure to replicate all investigated associations.

description: A 4-day concentrated exposure and response prevention (Bergen 4-Day Treatment, B4DT) for adolescents with OCD yields large reductions in OCD symptoms, with high rates of response (91%) and remission (73%) at post-treatment
original_authors: Eili N. Riise; Gerd Kvale; Lars-Göran Öst; Solvei Harila Skjold; Hans Hansen; Bjarne Hansen
original_title: Concentrated exposure and response prevention for adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder: An effectiveness study
original_journal: Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
replication_authors: Eili N. Riise; Gerd Kvale; Lars-Göran Öst; Solvei Harila Skjold; Bjarne Hansen
replication_title: Concentrated exposure and response prevention for adolescents with obsessive-compulsive disorder: A replication study
replication_journal: Journal of Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The present study replicated the results from the first effectiveness study on the B4DT for adolescents (Riise et al., 2016).' No significant differences in OCD severity, response rates, or remission rates were found between the present and original sample at post-treatment or follow-up.

description: Recalling positive autobiographical memories prior to making intertemporal choices reduces temporal discounting (increases preference for larger, delayed rewards)
original_authors: Lempert, Karolina M.; Speer, Megan E.; Delgado, Mauricio R.; Phelps, Elizabeth A.
original_title: Positive autobiographical memory retrieval reduces temporal discounting
replication_authors: Karolina M. Lempert; Trishala Parthasarathi; Samantha Linhares; Natalia Ruh; Joseph W. Kable
replication_title: Positive autobiographical memory recall does not influence temporal discounting: An internal meta-analysis of experimental studies
explanation: Experiments 4-7 were direct and close replications of Lempert et al. (2017). The authors explicitly state in the abstract: 'we failed to replicate these findings.' The overall meta-analytic effect was Cohen's d_z = 0.079 (95% CI: [-0.008, 0.166]), not significantly different from zero, and publication status analysis showed the original published experiments (Exps 1-3) had significantly larger effects than the unpublished replications.

description: Inducing feelings of gratitude through a writing task reduces temporal discounting (increases preference for larger, delayed monetary rewards)
original_authors: DeSteno, David; Li, Ye; Dickens, Leah; Lerner, Jennifer S.
original_title: Gratitude: a tool for reducing economic impatience
replication_authors: Karolina M. Lempert; Trishala Parthasarathi; Samantha Linhares; Natalia Ruh; Joseph W. Kable
replication_title: Positive autobiographical memory recall does not influence temporal discounting: An internal meta-analysis of experimental studies
explanation: Experiments 8-12 attempted to replicate DeSteno et al. (2014) using a within-subjects gratitude writing task design. The authors explicitly state they 'failed to replicate these findings.' Gratitude was not a significant moderator of temporal discounting (β = -0.121, 95% CI: [-0.286, 0.043], z = -1.44; p = 0.149), even when controlling for publication status.

description: Inducing feelings of nostalgia through a writing task about past nostalgic events makes participants more patient in intertemporal choices (increases preference for larger, delayed rewards)
original_authors: Huang, Xun (Irene); Huang, Zhongqiang (Tak); Wyer, Robert S.
original_title: Slowing down in the good old days: the effect of nostalgia on consumer patience
replication_authors: Karolina M. Lempert; Trishala Parthasarathi; Samantha Linhares; Natalia Ruh; Joseph W. Kable
replication_title: Positive autobiographical memory recall does not influence temporal discounting: An internal meta-analysis of experimental studies
explanation: Experiments 13-14 attempted to replicate Huang et al. (2016) using a within-subjects nostalgia writing task design with a hyperbolic discount rate task. The authors explicitly state they 'failed to replicate these findings.' Nostalgia was not a significant moderator of temporal discounting (β = -0.008, 95% CI: [-0.250, 0.235], z = -0.06; p = 0.951).

description: Estimated ventilatory dead space indices (Harris-Benedict dead space fraction, ventilatory ratio, end-tidal-to-arterial PaCO2 ratio) are not independently associated with 28-day mortality in COVID-19 ARDS patients after adjustment for conventional risk factors
original_authors: Luis Morales-Quinteros; Ary Serpa Neto; Antonio Artigas; Lluis Blanch; Michela Botta; David A. Kaufman; Marcus J. Schultz; Anissa M. Tsonas; Frederique Paulus; Lieuwe D. Bos
original_title: Dead space estimates may not be independently associated with 28-day mortality in COVID-19 ARDS
replication_authors: Lada Lijović; Harm Jan de Grooth; Patrick Thoral; Lieuwe Bos; Zheng Feng; Tomislav Radočaj; Paul Elbers
replication_title: Preparing for future pandemics: Automated intensive care electronic health record data extraction to accelerate clinical insights
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'our results confirm that estimates of dead space fraction increased over time and were higher in non-survivors than survivors. We also confirmed the absence of a significant association between Vd/Vt and 28-day mortality after controlling for potential confounding factors.' The replication used automated EHR data extraction rather than manual abstraction but followed the same protocol and largely overlapping patient cohort.

description: A population approach intervention using a standing back extension exercise ('One Stretch') based on the McKenzie method improves or prevents low back pain and reduces medical consultations among Japanese care workers
original_authors: Ko Matsudaira; Miho Hiroe; Masatomo Kikkawa; Takayuki Sawada; Mari Suzuki; Tatsuya Isomura; Hiroyuki Oka; Kou Hiroe; Ken Hiroe
original_title: Can standing back extension exercise improve or prevent low back pain in Japanese care workers?
original_journal: Journal of Manual and Manipulative Therapy
replication_authors: Tonosu J.; Matsudaira K.; Oka H.; Okazaki H.; Oshio T.; Hanaoka I.; Muraoka Y.; Midorikawa M.; Wakabayashi K.; Tanaka S.
replication_title: A population approach to analyze the effectiveness of a back extension exercise “One Stretch” in patients with low back pain: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that 'This result is similar to what the previously trial on this exercise [4],' and all primary outcomes (subjective LBP improvement, fewer medical consultations, better exercise compliance, and lower ODI disability rates) showed statistically significant differences in favor of the intervention group, replicating the original findings in a different study center and delivered by someone outside the original development team.

description: Patients with chronic nonmalignant pain taking opioids at admission to a pain rehabilitation program show significant improvement in pain severity, disability, and depression comparable to patients not taking opioids, following an interdisciplinary cognitive-behavioral program with opioid withdrawal.
original_authors: Rome, J.D.; et al.
replication_authors: Judith Scheman; Stephen M. Smith; C. Van Keuren; Edward C. Covington
replication_title: Chronic nonmalignant pain rehabilitation with opioid withdrawal: A replication study of treatment outcomes
explanation: Upgraded from medium to high after independent review of the paper. The abstract (entry 737 in the conference proceedings) is titled 'Chronic nonmalignant pain rehabilitation with opioid withdrawal: A replication study of treatment outcomes' — it explicitly identifies itself as a replication in the title. The first sentence states 'The current study replicates a recent study at the Mayo Comprehensive Pain Rehabilitation Center.' The conclusion states 'this study confirms the previous finding that patients who experience severe and disabling pain while taking opioid therapy can experience significant improvement in physical and emotional functioning while participating in a pain rehabilitation program that incorporates opioid withdrawal.' All outcome measures (pain severity, disability, depression) showed significant improvement consistent with the original. The citation to Rome et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 2004 is explicit. There is no ambiguity: the authors use the words 'replicates' and 'confirms,' the results aligned across all measures, and the study design closely mirrors the original at a different institution (close extension). Result = success is clearly correct.

description: Naturally occurring headache impairs performance on multiple attention tasks (flanker, n-back, cued switching, dual task) compared to a headache-free condition
original_authors: David J. Moore; Edmund Keogh; Christopher Eccleston
original_title: Headache impairs attentional performance
replication_authors: Nina Attridge; Christopher Eccleston; Donna Noonan; Elaine Wainwright; Edmund Keogh
replication_title: Headache Impairs Attentional Performance: A Conceptual Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a conceptual replication and extension of Moore et al. (2013). Both studies found attentional disruption from headache, confirming the general effect, although the specific task-by-task patterns differed: 'Although both studies showed attentional disruption, the specific effects differed.' The conclusion states 'pain has consistently disrupted attention in multiple studies.'

description: OCD patients show significantly larger P3b (temporo-basal dipole) amplitudes than healthy controls, reflecting cortical hyperactivity in temporo-parietal and hippocampal regions, with no difference in P3a amplitude
original_authors: Paraskevi Mavrogiorgou; Georg Juckel; Thomas Frodl; Jürgen Gallinat; Walter Hauke; Michael Zaudig; Gerhard Dammann; Hans-Jürgen Möller; Ulrich Hegerl
original_title: P300 subcomponents in obsessive-compulsive disorder
replication_authors: Doris Gohle; Georg Juckel; Paraskevi Mavrogiorgou; Oliver Pogarell; Christoph Mulert; Dan Rujescu; Ina Giegling; Michael Zaudig; Ulrich Hegerl
replication_title: Electrophysiological evidence for cortical abnormalities in obsessive–compulsive disorder – A replication study using auditory event-related P300 subcomponents
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The present study replicates the negative finding concerning the amplitude of the P3a and the positive finding of enhanced P3b amplitude from our pilot study.' The replication used a larger sample (n=63 vs n=21) of acutely ill, unmedicated OCD patients rather than the stabilized patients at end of therapy used in the original pilot study.

description: Individuals carrying the Met allele of the BDNF Val66Met polymorphism who had been exposed to childhood abuse report more positive psychotic-like experiences than those with the Val/Val genotype in a non-clinical general population sample
original_authors: Silvia Alemany; Bárbara Arias; Mari Aguilera; Helena Villa; Jorge Moya; Manuel I. Ibáñez; Helen Vossen; Cristobal Gastó; Generós Ortet; Lourdes Fañanás
original_title: Childhood abuse, the BDNF-Val66Met polymorphism and adult psychotic-like experiences
replication_authors: Marta de Castro-Catala; Martine van Nierop; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Paula Cristóbal-Narváez; Tamara Sheinbaum; Thomas R. Kwapil; Elionora Peña; Nele Jacobs; Catherine Derom; Evert Thiery; Jim van Os; Ruud van Winkel; Araceli Rosa
replication_title: Childhood trauma, BDNF Val66Met and subclinical psychotic experiences. Attempt at replication in two independent samples
explanation: The authors state their study 'partially replicates previous findings' and that results 'do not provide conclusive results.' Across two independent samples, results were discordant in terms of risk allele: Sample 1 showed Val/Val (not Met) carriers were more vulnerable to childhood trauma effects on positive PEs (opposite direction to original), while Sample 2 showed Met carriers presented higher positive PE scores with childhood trauma exposure (consistent with original). The mixed and contradictory direction of findings across samples renders the replication inconclusive.

description: A multilocus genetic profile score (MGPS) capturing additive risk from five serotonin-linked polymorphisms moderates the association between major interpersonal stressful life events and depression
original_authors: Suzanne Vrshek-Schallhorn; Catherine B. Stroud; Susan Mineka; Richard E. Zinbarg; Emma K. Adam; Eva E. Redei; Constance Hammen; Michelle G. Craske
original_title: Additive genetic risk from five serotonin system polymorphisms interacts with interpersonal stress to predict depression
replication_authors: Lisa R. Starr; Suzanne Vrshek-Schallhorn; Catherine B. Stroud
replication_title: Serotonergic multilocus genetic variation moderates the association between major interpersonal stress and adolescent depressive symptoms: Replication and candidate environment specification
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we provide a critical replication, showing that a serotonergic MGPS interacts with major interpersonal stress to predict depressive symptoms.' The interaction accounted for 4% of variance in the replication, comparable to the original's 3% (R-squared).

description: Lower-level personality trait measures (Achievement, Understanding, Play from the Personality Research Form) predict undergraduate academic performance better than broad Big Five factor scores derived from those traits
original_authors: Paunonen, Sampo V.; Ashton, Michael C.
original_title: Big five predictors of academic achievement
replication_authors: Sampo V. Paunonen; Michael C. Ashton
replication_title: On the prediction of academic performance with personality traits: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Conclusions: 'The results of that earlier study were closely replicated with the present data set.' They used the same predictor instrument (PRF), same criterion (final course grade in the same course taught by the same professor), and a new large independent sample (N=652 vs. original N=717). Table 1 shows near-identical correlations across both studies, with none of the differences reaching statistical significance.

description: Situational and stable social hierarchy negatively predict expressive suppression use, and hierarchy moderates the relationship between situational suppression and well-being (with suppression being less maladaptive when people feel lower in social hierarchy)
original_authors: Arman Daniel Catterson; Lameese Eldesouky; Oliver P. John
original_title: An experience sampling approach to emotion regulation: situational suppression use and social hierarchy
replication_authors: Pilch, Irena; Baran, Lidia; Bolek-Kochanowska, Magdalena; Bożek, Maciej; Friedrich, Wiola; Hyla, Magdalena; Sikora, Jagoda
replication_title: Situational suppression use and social hierarchy in non-individualistic and hierarchic society: A replication study
explanation: The replication yielded mixed results: within-person variation in suppression and the negative extraversion-suppression relationship replicated, but the hierarchy-suppression relationship was positive (contrary to the original), stable suppression positively (not negatively) predicted well-being, and the hierarchy × suppression interaction on well-being failed to replicate. The authors state: 'only a negative association of suppression and extraversion was replicated in our sample' and 'This study failed to replicate the third finding of the original study according to which when people felt lower in social hierarchy, the negative effects of suppression on well-being could be reduced.'

description: Distinct latent personality profiles (based on Big Three dimensions) can be identified among adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders, and these profiles differ meaningfully on key functioning variables such as substance use, parent-child relationship quality, academic engagement, and comorbid psychological disorders
original_authors: Sylia Wilson; Christopher J. Hopwood; Matt McGue; William G. Iacono
original_title: Personality heterogeneity in adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders
replication_authors: Geneviève Rivard; Yann Le Corff; Michèle Déry; Vincent Bégin; Mélanie Lapalme
replication_title: Personality heterogeneity in adolescents with disruptive behavior disorders: A conceptual replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly characterize this as a partial replication: 'Our results therefore partially replicated those reported by Wilson et al. (2019).' While personality heterogeneity was confirmed and some similarities in profile-outcome associations were found, the present study obtained fewer profiles (2-3 vs. 4) using a different personality model (Big Five vs. Big Three), and the profiles did not perfectly replicate Wilson et al.'s four-profile solution.

description: Self-reported mental toughness is positively associated with behavioural perseverance (as indexed by 20-m multistage shuttle run test performance) in adolescent Australian footballers
original_authors: Daniel F. Gucciardi; Peter Peeling; Kagan J. Ducker; Brian Dawson
original_title: When the going gets tough: mental toughness and its relationship with behavioural perseverance
original_journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
replication_authors: Brandon Giles; Paul S.R. Goods; Dylan R. Warner; Dale Quain; Peter Peeling; Kagan J. Ducker; Brian Dawson; Daniel F. Gucciardi
replication_title: Mental toughness and behavioural perseverance: A conceptual replication and extension
replication_journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
explanation: The authors explicitly designed the study as a 'conceptual replication' of Gucciardi et al. (2016). Under typical (non-fatigued) circumstances, mental toughness was a credible Bayesian predictor of MST performance (β = .22; 95% CI = .10, .35), consistent with the original finding (β = .24).

description: Self-reported mental toughness is positively associated with behavioural perseverance (20-m multistage shuttle run test performance) in Australian footballers, extending to physically fatigued conditions
original_authors: Daniel F. Gucciardi; Peter Peeling; Kagan J. Ducker; Brian Dawson
original_title: When the going gets tough: mental toughness and its relationship with behavioural perseverance
original_journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
replication_authors: Brandon Giles; Paul S.R. Goods; Dylan R. Warner; Dale Quain; Peter Peeling; Kagan J. Ducker; Brian Dawson; Daniel F. Gucciardi
replication_title: Mental toughness and behavioural perseverance: A conceptual replication and extension
replication_journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
explanation: The extension tested whether the mental toughness–behavioural perseverance association holds when participants are physically fatigued. Mental toughness was not a credible predictor when fatigued (β = .08; 95% CI = -.08, .24), with the CI crossing zero. The authors conclude 'the positive association between mental toughness and behavioural perseverance did not generalise to a performance context in which participants were fatigued.'

description: A single 20-minute computer-delivered (e-SBI) brief intervention for drug use among postpartum women reduces self-reported drug use at follow-up
original_authors: Steven J. Ondersma; Dace S. Svikis; Charles R. Schuster
original_title: Computer-based brief intervention a randomized trial with postpartum women
replication_authors: Steven J. Ondersma; Dace S. Svikis; Leroy R. Thacker; Jessica R. Beatty; Nancy Lockhart
replication_title: Computer-delivered screening and brief intervention (e-SBI) for postpartum drug use: A randomized trial
explanation: The authors report mixed results: the 3-month primary outcome was significant (OR=3.3, p=.01), replicating the original finding, but 6-month abstinence was not significant and days-of-drug-use outcomes failed to reach significance. As the abstract states: 'This result replicates previous findings but fails to show durable effects.'

description: Quality (but not quantity) of coping skills acquired during CBT4CBT treatment mediates the effect of the program on duration of abstinence following treatment in outpatient substance users
original_authors: Kiluk, B.; Nich, C.; Babuscio, T.; Carroll, K.
original_title: Quantity vs. quality: Acquisition of coping skills following computerized cognitive behavioral therapy for substance use disorders
replication_authors: Brian D. Kiluk; Elise E. DeVito; Matthew B. Buck; Karen Hunkele; Charla Nich; Kathleen M. Carroll
replication_title: Effect of computerized cognitive behavioral therapy on acquisition of coping skills among cocaine-dependent individuals enrolled in methadone maintenance
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study failed to replicate the quality of coping skills as a mediator of CBT4CBT's effect on reducing drug use previously shown in a mixed outpatient substance use sample.' The mediation analysis found no significant indirect effect (95% CI -0.17, 0.07, which included zero), indicating failure to replicate.

description: Code change complexity, author experience, and build history are statistically influential factors explaining CI build failures in Java open-source projects, as identified through univariate models
original_authors: Thomas Rausch; Waldemar Hummer; Philipp Leitner; Stefan Schulte
original_title: An empirical analysis of build failures in the continuous integration workflows of java-based opensource software
original_journal: IEEE/ACM 14th International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR)
replication_authors: Amine Barrak; Ellis E. Eghan; Bram Adams; Foutse Khomh
replication_title: Why do builds fail?—A conceptual replication study
explanation: The authors confirm most but not all of Rausch et al.'s findings. Table 6 shows 4 out of 7 key findings confirmed as 'Yes', 1 as 'Partially', and 2 as 'No' — including a reversal that pushed changes (not PRs) cause more failures. The paper states 'Our results confirm most of Rausch et al.'s findings,' indicating mixed/partial replication.

description: Build runtime environments and operating systems significantly affect CI build outcomes, with 77% of builds succeeding across all environment versions and a minority of builds fluctuating based on the chosen environment
original_authors: Mahdis Zolfagharinia; Bram Adams; Yann-Gael Guehenuc
original_title: Do not trust build results at face value: An empirical study of 30 million CPAN builds
original_journal: 2017 IEEE/ACM 14th International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR)

All results remained significant after covariate adjustment. The study had 99.9% statistical power for the T2D analysis (n=1513). The Discussion explicitly states: 'we found that ENPP1 rs1044498 was linked with T2D and T2D/obesity-related metabolic traits such as waist circumference and fasting glucose.' The result classification and direction of effect are clear and unambiguous, warranting upgrade from medium to high confidence.

The Discussion explicitly states 'our analyses did not significantly implicate ENPP1 rs1044498 in the risk of obesity (BMI ≥ 27).' However, a key limitation undermines confidence in classifying this as a definitive failure: the authors report only 56.7% statistical power to detect an obesity association (vs. 99.9% for T2D), and explicitly flag 'insufficient sample size of obese cases' as the study's main weakness. At 56.7% power, a false negative is nearly as likely as a true null result. The failure classification is correct given the observed data, but the low power means this could be a false negative rather than a genuine replication failure, justifying retention of medium confidence.
