explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were unable to provide evidence for the proposed association between general intelligence and functional brain network efficiency, as was demonstrated by van den Heuvel et al. (2009)'. Across all eight network definition schemes, no significant associations were found (all p > .05), with a maximal R² of 0.01.

description: CRFR1 activation within the central amygdala increases miniature inhibitory postsynaptic current (mIPSC) frequency without changing mIPSC amplitude in adult male rodents
original_authors: Marisa Roberto; Maureen T. Cruz; Nicholas W. Gilpin; Valentina Sabino; Paul Schweitzer; Michal Bajo; Pietro Cottone; Samuel G. Madamba; David G. Stouffer; Eric P. Zorrilla; George F. Koob; George R. Siggins; Loren H. Parsons
original_title: Corticotropin releasing factor-induced amygdala gamma-aminobutyric acid release plays a key role in alcohol dependence
replication_authors: Siara Kate Rouzer; Marvin R. Diaz
replication_title: Factors of sex and age dictate the regulation of GABAergic activity by corticotropin-releasing factor receptor 1 in the medial sub-nucleus of the central amygdala
explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicated prior findings: 'As previously established in adult males (Herman et al., 2013b; Roberto et al., 2010), we found that CRFR1 activation significantly increased mIPSC frequency at the 1 μM concentration of Stressin-1.' The replication is a close extension because the authors used the same whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology paradigm in the same brain region but extended the investigation to include adolescent males and both sexes.

description: Incongruent object-scene pairs (simultaneous presentation) elicit an early frontocentral negativity (N300) in the 200-300 ms time window, reflecting contextual processing prior to full object identification
original_authors: Liad Mudrik; Dominique Lamy; Leon Y. Deouell
original_title: ERP evidence for context congruity effects during simultaneous object-scene processing
replication_authors: Liad Mudrik; Shani Shalgi; Dominique Lamy; Leon Y. Deouell
replication_title: Synchronous contextual irregularities affect early scene processing: Replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The findings of this study provide a clear replication of our previous results [81]; see also [115] showing even earlier contextual processing.' The N300 congruency effect was again found in the 200-300 ms time window (starting ~210 ms), confirming the original finding with a new group of subjects.

description: STN deep brain stimulation using clinically-determined parameters in Parkinson's disease patients improves reactive inhibitory control of impulsive actions while also inducing greater susceptibility to impulsive response capture (poorer proactive impulse control) compared to DBS-off state
original_authors: Wylie SA; Ridderinkhof KR; Elias WJ; Frysinger RC; Bashore TR; Downs KE; van Wouwe NC; van den Wildenberg WP
original_title: Subthalamic nucleus stimulation influences expression and suppression of impulsive behaviour in Parkinson's disease
replication_authors: van Wouwe NC; Pallavaram S.; Phibbs FT; Martinez-Ramirez D.; Neimat JS; Dawant BM; D'Haese PF; Kanoff KE; van den Wildenberg WPM; Okun MS; Wylie SA
replication_title: Focused stimulation of dorsal subthalamic nucleus improves reactive inhibitory control of action impulses
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results that the improvement in reactive inhibitory control with STN DBS 'replicates prior findings in dopamine medicated Parkinson's disease patients,' and in the Discussion: 'We replicated and extended previous findings by demonstrating that DBS applied using clinical settings improves reactive inhibitory control of response impulses in Parkinson's disease patients withdrawn from the influence of dopamine medications.' The replication used the same Simon task and DPAS framework but with patients off dopaminergic medications (original used medicated patients), making it a close extension.

description: Adults with traumatic brain injury score significantly lower than uninjured adults on a video-based theory of mind task (VSIT), with larger group differences under higher working memory load conditions
original_authors: Lyn S. Turkstra
original_title: Conversation-based assessment of social cognition in adults with traumatic brain injury
replication_authors: Turkstra LS; Norman RS; Mutlu B.; Duff MC
replication_title: Impaired theory of mind in adults with traumatic brain injury: A replication and extension of findings
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are conducting a 'replication and extension' of the prior study. In the Discussion they confirm: 'Adults with TBI had lower scores overall than healthy comparison peers across all item types, replicating previous findings and extending these to a novel and larger group.' The main effect of group was significant (F(1,360) = 21.03, p < .001), consistent with the original finding.

description: A distributed network including the anterior insula and mid-frontal cortex (including ACC) is activated when participants update their conscious perceptual representations during a gradually morphing picture task, with activations occurring before and at the moment of perceptual change
original_authors: Elisabeth Stöttinger; Alex Filipowicz; Derick Valadao; Jody C. Culham; Melvyn A. Goodale; Britt Anderson; James Danckert
original_title: A cortical network that marks the moment when conscious representations are updated
replication_authors: Elisabeth Stöttinger; Markus Aichhorn; Britt Anderson; James Danckert
replication_title: The neural systems for perceptual updating
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we were able to replicate our earlier results' despite using fewer picture sets (10 vs. 20) and different analysis software (SPM12 vs. Brain Voyager). They found the same key activations: 'Again we found that the anterior insula and mid frontal/ACC region was active before participants reported a change.'

description: Threatening visual stimuli used as stop signals improve behavioral response inhibition (decreased SSRT) and enhance the N2-P3 ERP complex compared to neutral stimuli in a stop-signal task
original_authors: Magdalena Senderecka
original_title: Threatening visual stimuli influence response inhibition and error monitoring: An event-related potential study
replication_authors: Magdalena Senderecka; Magdalena Matyjek; Bartłomiej Kroczek; Michał Ociepka
replication_title: Socially Induced Negative Emotions Elicit Neural Activity in the Mentalizing Network in a Subsequent Inhibitory Task
explanation: The authors explicitly designed the study as a 'conceptual replication of previous works [64][65][66]' and found that behavioral inhibitory performance (SSRT) was comparable across all conditions, opposing the enhancement found in the original: 'These findings stand in opposition to those reported in many previous studies [64][65].' The P3 was also found to decrease (rather than increase) for negative stimuli.

description: Aversive auditory stop signals improve response inhibition (decreased SSRT) and elicit a larger P3 amplitude compared to neutral tones in a stop-signal task
original_authors: Magdalena Senderecka
original_title: Emotional enhancement of error detection-The role of perceptual processing and inhibition monitoring in failed auditory stop trials
replication_authors: Magdalena Senderecka; Magdalena Matyjek; Bartłomiej Kroczek; Michał Ociepka
replication_title: Socially Induced Negative Emotions Elicit Neural Activity in the Mentalizing Network in a Subsequent Inhibitory Task
explanation: The current study found no improvement in behavioral SSRT (failure to replicate the facilitation effect) and found a decreased P3 for negative stimuli, which 'stands in opposition to our predictions and to the results of our previous study [65], in which aversive auditory stop signals elicited a larger P3 relative to neutral tones.'

description: Affective stimuli do not elicit an emotional facilitation effect on inhibitory performance (SSRT) compared to the neutral condition in a stop-signal paradigm
original_authors: Magdalena Senderecka; Michał Ociepka; Magdalena Matyjek; Bartłomiej Kroczek
original_title: Post-error brain activity correlates with incidental memory for negative words
replication_authors: Magdalena Senderecka; Magdalena Matyjek; Bartłomiej Kroczek; Michał Ociepka
replication_title: Socially Induced Negative Emotions Elicit Neural Activity in the Mentalizing Network in a Subsequent Inhibitory Task
explanation: Independent review confirms success classification. The paper explicitly states: 'The SSRT did not differ significantly between the three stop-signal conditions, F(2,62) = 0.56, p = ns, indicating that inhibitory performance was comparable in the negative, positive and neutral stop-signal trials.' The Discussion further states the behavioral findings 'are in line with the results of other studies, however much less numerous, in which the presentation of affective stimuli did not elicit an emotional facilitation effect on inhibitory performance as compared to the neutral condition [62][4][66]' — explicitly naming ref [66] as the study whose null finding is replicated. Ref [66] (Senderecka et al., 2018, Front Hum Neurosci) is specifically cited as finding no facilitation, and the current null SSRT result (p = ns) directly replicates that finding. Although [66] is grouped with [64][65] in the citation sentence describing the study as a 'conceptual replication,' the behavioral result clearly aligns with [66] specifically. Confidence upgraded to high based on explicit author statement linking results to [66] and unambiguous statistical outcome.

description: Four distinct biotypes of depression can be identified by combining resting-state fMRI connectivity and clinical symptom data via canonical correlation analysis and hierarchical clustering, with these biotypes showing different clinical profiles and being predictive of TMS treatment response
original_authors: Drysdale AT; Grosenick L.; Downar J.; Dunlop K.; Mansouri F.; Meng Y.; Fetcho RN; Zebley B.; Oathes DJ; Etkin A.; Schatzberg AF; Sudheimer K.; Keller J.; Mayberg HS; Gunning FM; Alexopoulos GS; Fox MD; Pascual-Leone A.; Voss HU; Casey BJ; Dubin MJ; Liston C.
original_title: Resting-state connectivity biomarkers define neurophysiological subtypes of depression
replication_authors: Richard Dinga; Lianne Schmaal; Brenda W.J.H. Penninx; Marie Jose van Tol; Dick J. Veltman; Laura van Velzen; Maarten Mennes; Nic J.A. van der Wee; Andre F. Marquand
replication_title: Evaluating the evidence for biotypes of depression: Methodological replication and extension of
explanation: The authors followed the original pipeline as closely as possible in a different clinical population (depression and anxiety, n=187) and found high canonical correlations (0.99, 0.97) and a 3-cluster solution, but these were not statistically significant using permutation tests (p=0.64 and p=0.99). The conclusion states: 'we did not find stable or statistically significant biotypes of depression and anxiety in an independent sample from a different clinical population.'

description: Practiced and novel task rules rely on rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (RLPFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in a reversal pattern: novel rules are encoded by DLPFC and integrated by RLPFC during performance, while practiced rules show the opposite temporal dynamics
original_authors: Michael W. Cole; Anto Bagic; Robert Kass; Walter Schneider
original_title: Prefrontal dynamics underlying rapid instructed task learning reverse with practice
replication_authors: Joseph M. Orr; Jesus Lopez; Michael J. Imburgio; Andrea Pelletier-Baldelli; Jessica A. Bernard; Vijay A. Mittal
replication_title: Adolescents at clinical high risk for psychosis show qualitatively altered patterns of activation during rule learning
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'largely failed to replicate this pattern in healthy controls.' In an ROI analysis, the 3-way Region × Period × Condition interaction that would replicate the prefrontal dynamics of Cole et al. (2010) showed strong evidence for the null (BF_incl = 0.067), and no statistically significant differences were found for novel vs. practiced task contrasts.

description: QEEG-informed neurofeedback (assigning patients to SMR, TBR, or SCP protocols based on individual EEG characteristics) is effective in reducing ADHD symptoms, with a response rate of 76% (≥50% symptom reduction) and large effect sizes for inattention and hyperactivity
original_authors: Arns M.; Drinkenburg W.; Leon Kenemans J.
original_title: The effects of QEEG-informed neurofeedback in ADHD: an open-label pilot study
replication_authors: Noralie Krepel; Tommy Egtberts; Alexander T. Sack; Hartmut Heinrich; Mark Ryan; Martijn Arns
replication_title: A multicenter effectiveness trial of QEEG-informed neurofeedback in ADHD: Replication and treatment prediction
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Clinical effectiveness of QEEG-informed neurofeedback was replicated, meaning that the current response and remission rates were not significantly different from those reported in 2012.' The R50 response rate comparison was non-significant (χ²(1) = 1.428, p = 0.232), confirming equivalence between the 2012 original and the current 114-patient replication sample.

description: OCD symptoms (measured continuously) are negatively correlated with drift rate (evidence integration rate) during a perceptual dot-motion decision task, with larger impairments for easier (higher coherence) decisions
original_authors: Paula Banca; Martin D. Vestergaard; Vladan Rankov; Kwangyeol Baek; Simon Mitchell; Tatyana Lapa; Miguel Castelo-Branco; Valerie Voon
original_title: Evidence accumulation in obsessive-compulsive disorder: the role of uncertainty and monetary reward on perceptual decision making thresholds
replication_authors: Alec Solway; Isabella Schneider; Yuqing Lei
replication_title: The relationships between subclinical OCD symptoms, beta/gamma-band power, and the rate of evidence integration during perceptual decision making
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Replicating prior work [2]Erhan et al., 2017;[19][25], OCD score was negatively associated with drift rate during easier decisions, with significantly larger effects for easier compared to harder conditions.' The Discussion confirms: 'Consistent with previous work, we found a negative relationship between OCD symptoms and drift rate, and this effect was larger for easier decisions.'

description: Gamma-band and beta-band power ramp up during perceptual decision making in proportion to evidence strength, reflecting the evidence integration process described by the drift-diffusion model
original_authors: Tobias H. Donner; Markus Siegel; Pascal Fries; Andreas K. Engel
original_title: Buildup of choice-predictive activity in human motor cortex during perceptual decision making
replication_authors: Alec Solway; Isabella Schneider; Yuqing Lei
replication_title: The relationships between subclinical OCD symptoms, beta/gamma-band power, and the rate of evidence integration during perceptual decision making
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In line with previous EEG and MEG work [8][35], and remarkably similar to the pattern seen in the firing rate of neurons in animal studies [17], the aggregate measure for both bands gradually increased during decision making.' The rate of increase was higher for higher coherence trials, consistent with the original findings.

description: EEG-measured gamma-band power ramps up during perceptual decision making analogously to an evidence integration model, and beta-band power negatively correlates with evidence integration during decision making
original_authors: Rafael Polanía; Ian Krajbich; Marcus Grueschow; Christian C. Ruff
original_title: Neural oscillations and synchronization differentially support evidence accumulation in perceptual and value-based decision making
replication_authors: Alec Solway; Isabella Schneider; Yuqing Lei
replication_title: The relationships between subclinical OCD symptoms, beta/gamma-band power, and the rate of evidence integration during perceptual decision making
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In line with previous EEG and MEG work [8][35]... the aggregate measure for both bands gradually increased during decision making. The rate of increase was higher for higher coherence (easier) trials.' Additionally, 'Drift rate was independently correlated with the slope of the aggregate measure for gamma power in all conditions, and for beta power in five out of six conditions.'

description: A single ~3-minute fMRI run using population receptive field (pRF) modelling accurately characterizes ophthalmic evaluations of visual function (static automatic perimetry) in patients with choroideremia
original_authors: Edward H. Silson; Tomas S. Aleman; Aimee Willett; Leona W. Serrano; Denise J. Pearson; Andreas M. Rauschecker; Albert M. Maguire; Chris I. Baker; Jean Bennett; Manzar Ashtari
original_title: Comparing clinical perimetry and population receptive field measures in patients with choroideremia
replication_authors: Edward H. Silson; Chris I. Baker; Tomas S. Aleman; Albert M. Maguire; Jean Bennett; Manzar Ashtari
replication_title: Motion-selective areas V5/MT and MST appear resistant to deterioration in choroideremia
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Consistent with our previous report, a single ~ 3 min fMRI run accurately characterized ophthalmic evaluations of visual function in most CHM subjects,' with 21 out of 24 comparisons (~87.5%) showing significant positive correlations between SAP and pRF measures. The paper replicates the same methodology in a new cohort of gene therapy trial participants, qualifying as a close extension.

description: Younger people with multiple sclerosis (mean age ~37 years) exhibit elevated thalamic iron concentrations (increased susceptibility) compared to healthy controls, as measured by quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM)
original_authors: David A. Rudko; Igor Solovey; Joseph S. Gati; Marcelo Kremenchutzky; Ravi S. Menon
original_title: Multiple sclerosis: improved identification of disease-relevant changes in gray and white matter by using susceptibility-based MR imaging
replication_authors: Fahad Salman; Niels Bergsland; Michael G. Dwyer; Jack A. Reeves; Abhisri Ramesh; Dejan Jakimovski; Bianca Weinstock-Guttman; Robert Zivadinov; Ferdinand Schweser
replication_title: Thalamic iron in multiple sclerosis: Waning support for the early-rise late-decline hypothesis
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our study did not replicate previous reports of increased thalamic susceptibility in young people with MS.' Instead, they found significantly lower thalamic susceptibility in younger pwMS compared to controls across all 196 QSM pipeline configurations (effect sizes -0.35 to -0.91), contradicting the original finding of elevated thalamic iron.

description: Older people with multiple sclerosis (mean age ~47 years) exhibit decreased thalamic iron concentrations (reduced susceptibility) compared to healthy controls, as measured by QSM
original_authors: Adam Pudlac; Andrea Burgetova; Petr Dusek; Petra Nytrova; Manuela Vaneckova; Dana Horakova; Jan Krasensky; Lukas Lambert
original_title: Deep gray matter iron content in neuromyelitis optica and multiple sclerosis
replication_authors: Fahad Salman; Niels Bergsland; Michael G. Dwyer; Jack A. Reeves; Abhisri Ramesh; Dejan Jakimovski; Bianca Weinstock-Guttman; Robert Zivadinov; Ferdinand Schweser
replication_title: Thalamic iron in multiple sclerosis: Waning support for the early-rise late-decline hypothesis
explanation: Both pipelines showed significantly lower thalamic susceptibility in older pwMS compared to controls (P < 0.05), which the authors note was 'consistent with the original study's findings' of reduced thalamic susceptibility in older MS cohorts.

description: Presenting an isolated retrieval trial of a previously reinforced CS+ followed by Extinction Training within the reconsolidation window prevents the return of fear (reinstatement and spontaneous recovery) as measured by skin conductance
original_authors: Daniela Schiller; Marie-H. Monfils; Candace M. Raio; David C. Johnson; Joseph E. LeDoux; Elizabeth A. Phelps
original_title: Preventing the return of fear in humans using reconsolidation update mechanisms
replication_authors: Victor Taylor Warren; Kemp M. Anderson; Cliffe Kwon; Lauren Bosshardt; Tanja Jovanovic; Bekh Bradley; Seth Davin Norrholm
replication_title: Human fear extinction and return of fear using reconsolidation update mechanisms: The contribution of on-line expectancy ratings
explanation: The present study attempted to replicate the Schiller et al. (2010) retrieval + extinction reconsolidation update paradigm using fear-potentiated startle (instead of skin conductance) with and without on-line US-expectancy measures. Results were mixed: all groups showed spontaneous recovery, and only the Retrieval/Keypad group failed to show reinstatement of fear-potentiated startle — but this was not specific to the reactivated cue. The authors conclude the results are complex and do not clearly replicate the original finding of retrieval + extinction blocking fear return.

description: The common SNP rs2292832 in MIR149 is significantly associated with age at onset and severity of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A in Korean patients
original_authors: Soo Hyun Nam; Sumaira Kanwal; Da Eun Nam; Min Hee Lee; Tae Hoon Kang; Sung-Chul Jung; Byung-Ok Choi; Ki Wha Chung
original_title: Association of miR-149 polymorphism with onset age and severity in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A
replication_authors: Feifei Tao; Stephan Züchner
replication_title: Replication studies of MIR149 association in Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1A in a European population
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our evidence did not support MIR149 as a genetic modifier of CMT1A in an independent European cohort.' All p-values for association of rs2292832 with AAO, CMTNS, and MNCV were non-significant in both additive and dominant models.

description: SNP rs2292832 in MIR149 is significantly associated with age at onset and severity of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A in Korean patients
original_authors: Soo Hyun Nam; Sumaira Kanwal; Da Eun Nam; Min Hee Lee; Tae Hoon Kang; Sung-Chul Jung; Byung-Ok Choi; Ki Wha Chung
original_title: Association of miR-149 polymorphism with onset age and severity in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A
replication_authors: Byung-Ok Choi; Soo Hyun Nam; Ki Wha Chung
replication_title: Replication studies of MIR149 association in Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1A in a European population - response
explanation: The replication authors explicitly state 'our evidence did not support MIR149 as a genetic modifier of CMT1A in an independent European cohort.' All p-values across additive and dominant models for all three phenotypes (AAO, CMTNS, MNCV) were non-significant, and binary stratified analyses also yielded null results.

description: 5-HT1A receptor binding potential is reduced in the mesiotemporal cortex and raphe in unmedicated depressives with primary recurrent familial mood disorders relative to healthy controls, as measured by PET and [carbonyl-11C]WAY-100635
original_authors: Wayne C. Drevets; Ellen Frank; Julie C. Price; David J. Kupfer; Daniel Holt; Phil J. Greer; Yiyun Huang; Clara Gautier; Chester Mathis
original_title: PET imaging of serotonin 1A receptor binding in depression
replication_authors: Wayne C. Drevets; Michael E. Thase; Eydie L. Moses-Kolko; Julie Price; Ellen Frank; David J. Kupfer; Chester Mathis
replication_title: Serotonin-1A receptor imaging in recurrent depression: replication and literature review
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In this independent-subjects sample, the mean 5-HT1AR BP was reduced by 26% in the MTC (P<.005) and by 43% in the raphe (P<.001) in depressives versus controls, replicating the findings in our original sample, which showed BP being reduced by 27% in the MTC (P<.025) and by 42% in the raphe (P<.02) in depressives versus controls.' The replication used the same PET radioligand, same scanner protocol, same ROI definitions, and the same patient selection criteria, with an entirely independent sample.

description: Policy uncertainty is significantly and negatively associated with M&A activities in the subsequent year among US firms
original_authors: Alice Bonaime; Huseyin Gulen; Mihai Ion
original_title: Does policy uncertainty affect mergers and acquisitions?
replication_authors: James Borthwick; Searat Ali; Xiaofei Pan
replication_title: Does policy uncertainty influence mergers and acquisitions activities in China? A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion: 'Using a similar dataset and methodology, we confirm their findings of the negative effect of policy uncertainty on subsequent year M&As for US firms.' The logistic regression results confirm that the overall EPU index and all sub-components are negatively and significantly associated with M&A activity, though coefficient magnitudes are smaller than in the original.

description: Policy uncertainty is significantly and negatively associated with M&A activities in the subsequent year among US firms
original_authors: Alice Bonaime; Huseyin Gulen; Mihai Ion
original_title: Does policy uncertainty affect mergers and acquisitions?
replication_authors: James Borthwick; Searat Ali; Xiaofei Pan
replication_title: Does policy uncertainty influence mergers and acquisitions activities in China? A replication study
explanation: The authors extend the original US findings to Chinese firms (2003-2017) and find that 'subsequent year M&A likelihood is decreasing in economic policy uncertainty' in China as well. The conclusion states: 'we find that economic policy uncertainty significantly reduces firm M&A activities in both countries,' confirming the original effect generalizes to an emerging market context.

description: Positive affect (PA) and broad-minded coping reciprocally and prospectively predict one another over time, initiating upward spirals toward increasing emotional well-being
original_authors: Barbara L. Fredrickson; Thomas Joiner
original_title: Positive emotions trigger upward spirals toward emotional well-being
replication_authors: Burns AB; Brown JS; Sachs-Ericsson N.; Plant EA; Curtis JT; Fredrickson BL; Joiner TE
replication_title: Upward spirals of positive emotion and coping: Replication, extension, and initial exploration of neurochemical substrates
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'our findings replicated those reported by [Fredrickson & Joiner (2002)]' — PA predicted improved positive coping over time and vice versa, with evidence of partial mediation consistent with the upward spiral hypothesis. Construct specificity (no similar pattern for NA) was also replicated.

description: Personality traits (Big Five and Dark Triad) are systematically associated with individual differences in the perception of situations as measured by the DIAMONDS framework, with neuroticism linked to threat avoidance, extraversion and Dark Triad linked to engagement with the world, and Big Five traits having a wider range of situational perception associations than Dark Triad traits
original_authors: Peter K. Jonason; Ryne A. Sherman
original_title: Personality and the perception of situations: The Big Five and Dark Triad traits
replication_authors: Marcin Zajenkowski; Peter K. Jonason; Maria Leniarska; Zuzanna Kozakiewicz
replication_title: Who complies with the restrictions to reduce the spread of COVID-19?: Personality and perceptions of the COVID-19 situation
explanation: The authors explicitly state their secondary aim was to 'replicate and extend previous findings [8][20]' about personality-situation perception associations, and in the Discussion confirm: 'we replicated and extended what is known about the associations between personality and individual differences in the perception of situations.' The replication was conducted in a concrete COVID-19 situation (rather than hypothetical/ambiguous situations) with a Polish (non-American) sample, using longer and multidimensional measures of Dark Triad traits.

description: Personality traits are associated with individual differences in how people perceive situations, with neuroticism linked to threat-avoidance perceptions and Dark Triad and extraversion linked to approach-oriented perceptions of situations
original_authors: David G. Serfass; Ryne A. Sherman
original_title: Personality and the perceptions of situations from the Thematic Apperception Test
replication_authors: Marcin Zajenkowski; Peter K. Jonason; Maria Leniarska; Zuzanna Kozakiewicz
replication_title: Who complies with the restrictions to reduce the spread of COVID-19?: Personality and perceptions of the COVID-19 situation
explanation: The authors bundle Serfass & Sherman (2013) with Jonason & Sherman (2020) as prior work they aim to 'replicate and extend' (cited together as [8][20]), and the Discussion confirms 'we replicated and extended what is known about the associations between personality and individual differences in the perception of situations.' However, the paper never disentangles which specific findings from each prior work were replicated — the replication claim is made for both together. This creates genuine ambiguity: Jonason & Sherman (2020) also used the DIAMONDS framework and is a closer methodological match, so the replication claim may primarily reflect that study. Serfass & Sherman (2013) used the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) rather than the DIAMONDS/S8* framework, making this a conceptual replication at best. The bundled citation and lack of differentiation in the paper's claims is a genuine source of ambiguity, not a resolvable one — medium confidence is appropriate.

description: The glycine allele of the DRD3 gene (312G>A polymorphism) is associated with risk for essential tremor, and glycine homozygosity is associated with earlier age of onset and more severe tremor
original_authors: Freddy Jeanneteau; Benoît Funalot; Joseph Jankovic; Hao Deng; Jean-Pierre Lagarde; Gérard Lucotte; Pierre Sokoloff
original_title: A functional variant of the dopamine D3 receptor is associated with risk and age-at-onset of essential tremor
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Marcia A. Blair; Shaochun Ma; Fenna Phibbs; John Y. Fang; Michael K. Cooper; Thomas L. Davis; Peter Hedera
replication_title: Reappraisal of the role of the DRD3 gene in essential tremor
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our findings were unable to replicate the previously reported role of the glycine and serine forms of the DRD3 gene.' They found no significant allele frequency differences between ET patients and controls, no preferential transmission of the glycine allele (TDT), obligatory recombinants in linkage analysis, and 'We also failed to replicate the relationship between glycine homozygosity and an earlier age of onset or more severe tremor course.'

description: The HAP1 T441M polymorphism (M441 allele) is associated with delayed age at onset in Huntington's disease, with MM homozygotes showing an approximately 8-year delay in onset compared to TT/TM patients
original_authors: Metzger S.; Rong J.; Nguyen HP; Cape A.; Tomiuk J.; Soehn AS; Propping P.; Freudenberg-Hua Y.; Freudenberg J.; Tong L.; Li SH; Li XJ; Riess O.
original_title: Huntingtin-associated protein-1 is a modifier of the age-at-onset of Huntington's disease
replication_authors: Georgia Karadima; Christina Dimovasili; Georgios Koutsis; Demetris Vassilopoulos; Marios Panas
replication_title: Age at onset in Huntington's disease: Replication study on the association of HAP1
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'this is the second independent study that has failed to confirm the findings of Metzger et al. on the association of the HAP1 T441M polymorphism with the AAO of HD.' Multivariate analysis found no significant association between HAP1 T441M genotypes and residual variance in AAO, and age at onset was 'almost identical' across genotype groups.

description: Adult-onset binge-drinking in male C57BL/6J mice produces anxiety-like behavior in early withdrawal, while in adolescent-onset binge-drinkers, negative affect incubates during protracted withdrawal (age-of-onset × withdrawal interaction using multi-bottle-choice Drinking-in-the-Dark procedures)
original_authors: Kaziya M. Lee; Michal A. Coehlo; Noah R. Solton; Karen K. Szumlinski
original_title: Negative affect and excessive alcohol intake incubate during protracted withdrawal from binge-drinking in adolescent, but not, adult mice
replication_authors: Karen K. Szumlinski; Michal A. Coelho; Kaziya M. Lee; Tori Tran; Kimberly R. Sern; Alexandria Bernal; Tod E. Kippin
replication_title: DID it or DIDn't it? Exploration of a failure to replicate binge-like alcohol-drinking in C57BL/6J mice
explanation: The authors explicitly state this was designed to replicate the age-of-onset × withdrawal interaction on negative affect from their prior work (Lee et al., 2017b). Experiment 1 failed: 'Experiment 1 failed to replicate binge-levels of alcohol intake' and 'the results of the light-dark shuttle-box test represent a failure to replicate an alcohol withdrawal-induced increase in anxiety-related behavior, as well as the age-related differences therein.' Notably, some behaviors were in the opposite direction from prior findings.

description: SNP rs1424954 in the ACVR2A gene is associated with susceptibility to preeclampsia in Australian/New Zealand families
original_authors: Moses EK; Fitzpatrick E.; Freed KA; Dyer TD; Forrest S.; Elliott K.; Johnson MP; Blangero J.; Brennecke SP
original_title: Objective prioritization of positional candidate genes at a quantitative trait locus for pre-eclampsia on 2q22
replication_authors: Ferreira LC; Gomes CE; Araújo AC; Bezerra PF; Duggal P.; Jeronimo SM
replication_title: Association between ACVR2A and early-onset preeclampsia: Replication study in a Northeastern Brazilian population
explanation: The authors tested SNP rs1424954 (originally identified by Moses et al. 2006) in a Brazilian population and found no overall association with preeclampsia, but did find significant association specifically with early-onset preeclampsia (OR=1.86; 95% CI, 1.25-2.78; p=0.002). The authors state they 'successfully validated the association' but only when stratifying by gestational age — a subgroup analysis not performed in the original study.

description: SNPs rs2161983, rs1014064, rs1424941, and rs3768687 in the ACVR2A gene are associated with preeclampsia in a large Norwegian population-based study
original_authors: Roten, Linda T.; Johnson, Matthew P.; Forsmo, Siri; Fitzpatrick, Elizabeth; Dyer, Thomas D.; Brennecke, Shaun; Blangero, John; Moses, Eric; Austgulen, Rigmor
original_title: Association between the candidate susceptibility gene ACVR2A on chromosome 2q22 and pre-eclampsia in a large Norwegian population-based study (the HUNT study)
original_journal: European Journal of Human Genetics : EJHG
replication_authors: Ferreira LC; Gomes CE; Araújo AC; Bezerra PF; Duggal P.; Jeronimo SM
replication_title: Association between ACVR2A and early-onset preeclampsia: Replication study in a Northeastern Brazilian population
explanation: The authors tested four SNPs from Roten et al. (2008) in a Brazilian population and found no overall association with preeclampsia, but did find significant associations with early-onset preeclampsia for rs1014064 (OR=1.77; p=0.004) and rs2161983 (OR=1.70; p=0.008). The original study did not stratify by early vs. late onset, making the partial replication in only an early-onset subgroup inconclusive regarding the original claim.

description: The Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) shows acceptable interrater reliability, discriminant validity (significant differences in scores between rest and noxious procedures), and criterion validity (significant correlation between CPOT scores and patient self-report) when used to assess pain in critically ill cardiac surgery patients

original_title: Validation of the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool in adult patients
replication_authors: Kathleen Marie Keane
replication_title: Validity and Reliability of the Critical Care Pain Observation Tool: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication found that discriminant validity and interrater reliability were supported ('This replication study supports the DV and IRR of the CPOT instrument...and supports the reproducibility of the findings of the Gelinas reference study'), but criterion validity was not replicated — a weak nonsignificant Spearman correlation of 0.26 (P < .312) was found, whereas the original found significant moderate correlations. The authors attributed the CV failure to an underpowered sample, yielding mixed overall results.

description: The BDNF 270 C/T polymorphism is associated with schizophrenia, with the T-allele occurring at higher frequency in schizophrenic patients than controls
original_authors: S. Nanko; H. Kunugi; H. Hirasawa; N. Kato; T. Nabika; Shotai Kobayashi

replication_authors: Erik G. Jönsson; Bodil Edman-Ahlbom; Anna Sillén; Agneta Gunnar; Bettina Kulle; Arnoldo Frigessi; Maria Vares; Birgit Ekholm; Birgitta Wode-Helgodt; Johannes Schumacher; Sven Cichon; Ingrid Agartz; Göran C. Sedvall; Håkan Hall; Lars Terenius
replication_title: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor gene (BDNF) variants and schizophrenia: An association study
replication_journal: Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry
explanation: The Swedish replication (n=187 patients, n=275 controls) found no significant differences in 270 C/T allele, genotype, or haplotype frequencies between schizophrenic patients and controls. The authors explicitly state: 'the present Swedish results do not verify previous associations between putative functional BDNF gene polymorphisms and schizophrenia.' A subgroup finding among women showed an association in the *opposite direction* to the original (lower T-allele frequency in female patients vs. controls). A meta-analysis pooling this study with prior data (>2300 subjects) did show a significant T-allele association, but the direct replication itself clearly failed. The failure classification is well-supported by explicit authorial statement and negative primary statistics.

description: The BDNF Val66Met polymorphism is associated with schizophrenia and with favourable response to clozapine treatment
original_authors: Chen-Jee Hong; Younger W.-Y Yu; Ching-Hua Lin; Shih-Jen Tsai
original_title: An association study of a brain-derived neurotrophic factor Val66Met polymorphism and clozapine response of schizophrenic patients
replication_authors: Erik G. Jönsson; Bodil Edman-Ahlbom; Anna Sillén; Agneta Gunnar; Bettina Kulle; Arnoldo Frigessi; Maria Vares; Birgit Ekholm; Birgitta Wode-Helgodt; Johannes Schumacher; Sven Cichon; Ingrid Agartz; Göran C. Sedvall; Håkan Hall; Lars Terenius
replication_title: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor gene (BDNF) variants and schizophrenia: An association study
replication_journal: Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry
explanation: The Swedish replication (n=187 patients, n=275 controls) found no significant association between Val66Met and schizophrenia. The authors state they 'did not find any significant evidence for association between the Val66Met polymorphism and schizophrenia' and explicitly frame their inability to reproduce the Val66Val/favourable-clozapine-response finding as a non-replication: 'Our inability to reproduce the association between the Val66Val genotype and favourable response to antipsychotic drugs may depend on differences in methodology.' The authors note the study was retrospective and primarily used typical antipsychotics vs. the original prospective clozapine study, and invoke ethnic/LD differences as possible explanations. Meta-analysis across 11 studies (6217 subjects) did find a homozygous-state association, but the direct replication clearly failed. The failure classification is unambiguous.

description: HSV-1 seropositivity is associated with cognitive deficits (particularly impaired immediate memory) in patients with bipolar disorder
original_authors: Faith B. Dickerson; John J. Boronow; Cassie Stallings; Andrea E. Origoni; Sara Cole; Bogdana Krivogorsky; Robert H. Yolken

replication_authors: Sonja I. Gerber; Ute J. Krienke; Nane-Christine Biedermann; Heinz Grunze; Robert H. Yolken; Sandra Dittmann; Jens M. Langosch
replication_title: Impaired functioning in euthymic patients with bipolar disorder — HSV-1 as a predictor
replication_journal: Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The US based study of Dickerson et al. showed a relationship between HSV-1 and cognitive impairment in bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. This main finding could be replicated here for a sample of German patients with bipolar disorder.' The same direction of association was confirmed, with HSV-1 antibody prevalence serving as an independent predictor of neuropsychological impairment in bipolar patients.

description: PD-MCI patients show reduced bilateral CA1 hippocampal subfield volumes relative to cognitively normal PD patients, and cognitive status (but not CSF Abeta-42) is associated with hippocampal subfield volumes, while CSF t-tau is associated with hippocampal subfield volumes and cognition
original_authors: Sara Becker; Oliver Granert; Maarten Timmers; Andrea Pilotto; Luc Van Nueten; Benjamin Roeben; Giacomo Salvadore; Wendy R. Galpern; Johannes Streffer; Klaus Scheffler; Walter Maetzler; Daniela Berg; Inga Liepelt-Scarfone
original_title: Association of hippocampal subfields, CSF biomarkers, and cognition in patients with Parkinson disease without dementia
replication_authors: Erik Erhardt; Anna Horner; Nicholas Shaff; Chris Wertz; Stephanie Nitschke; Andrei Vakhtin; Andrew Mayer; John Adair; Janice Knoefel; Gary Rosenberg; Kathleen Poston; Gerson Suarez Cedeno; Amanda Deligtisch; Sarah Pirio Richardson; Sephira Ryman
replication_title: Longitudinal hippocampal subfields, CSF biomarkers, and cognition in patients with Parkinson disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated prior reports that PD-MCI exhibited reduced bilateral CA1 volumes relative to PD-NC,' and in the Conclusion: 'our results replicated prior findings that reduced bilateral CA1 volumes are associated with cognitive changes in a de novo PD cohort.' The same hippocampal subfield segmentation methodology (Freesurfer) and cognitive classification approach (MoCA-based PD-MCI criteria) were used, but in an independent de novo PD cohort from PPMI.

description: Enjoyment, social benefit, economic benefit, and sustainability determine consumer satisfaction and future intention to use peer-to-peer (P2P) accommodation services (Airbnb) in a developed market context
original_authors: Tussyadiah, Iis P.
original_title: Factors of satisfaction and intention to use peer-to-peer accommodation
replication_authors: Adhi Setyo Santoso; Liza Agustina Maureen Nelloh
replication_title: User Satisfaction and Intention to Use Peer-to-Peer Online Transportation: A Replication Study
explanation: Independent review: result changed from 'inconclusive' to 'failure'. The paper reports clear, definitive statistical results — this is not a case of ambiguity warranting 'inconclusive'. Of the 8 hypothesized paths tested, only 3 are supported (enjoyment→satisfaction, economic benefit→satisfaction, satisfaction→future intention); 5 fail (social benefit→satisfaction, social benefit→future intention, enjoyment→future intention, economic benefit→future intention, sustainability→both). The original study's key finding that antecedents directly predict future intention does not replicate at all. Authors frame results charitably ('some findings can be generalized') but the empirical pattern is predominantly non-replication. 'Inconclusive' is reserved for cases where results are statistically underpowered or ambiguous; here the results are unambiguous — most relationships do not hold in the new context (P2P motorcycle transport in Indonesia vs. Airbnb accommodation in developed markets).

description: Using appreciative inquiry to examine a nursing program's community of interest's priorities and attitudes about nursing education, including stakeholders' visions of the best of the past, future vision, and roles in realizing the vision
original_authors: Marie Farrell; Dianna Douglas; Susan Siltanen
original_title: Exploring and developing a college's community of interest: an appreciative inquiry
replication_authors: Marie Farrell; Nancy C. Wallis; Marci Tyler Evans
replication_title: A Replication Study of Priorities and Attitudes of Two Nursing Programs' Communities of Interest: An Appreciative Inquiry
explanation: The authors explicitly designed this as a replication study using the exact same AI interview protocol, codebook, and coding scheme from the original study, applied to a new western university context. The Conclusion states that 'both communities of interest share similar visions for their respective nursing program,' indicating the methodology successfully produced comparable findings in the new setting.

description: Using fine art museum visits and music listening training improves observational and auscultative perceptual skills in graduate-entry nursing students
original_authors: Linda Honan Pellico; Kristopher Fennie; Stephanie Tillman; Thomas C. Duffy; Linda Friedlaender; Gillian Graham
original_title: Artwork and music: Innovative approaches to physical assessment instruction and learning
replication_authors: Linda Honan; Sarah Shealy; Kristopher Fennie; Thomas C. Duffy; Linda Friedlaender; Megan Del Vecchio
replication_title: Looking Is Not Seeing and Listening Is Not Hearing: A Replication Study With Accelerated BSN Students
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as 'replication of our work with accelerated nursing students,' testing the same combined art-and-music pedagogy in a BSN (bachelor's-level) population instead of the original graduate-entry nursing students. Results confirmed improved perceptual skills: heart sound interpretation improved by 263%, lung sounds by 109%, and bowel sounds by 52%, while observational scores also increased significantly.

description: Adolescents and young adults with adolescent-onset alcohol use disorder show significantly smaller bilateral hippocampal volumes than case-matched controls, with no differences in overall cerebral, cortical gray/white matter, corpus callosum, or amygdala volumes
original_authors: Michael D. De Bellis; Duncan B. Clark; Sue R. Beers; Paul H. Soloff; Amy M. Boring; Julie Hall; Adam Kersh; Matcheri S. Keshavan

replication_authors: Bonnie J. Nagel; Alecia D. Schweinsburg; Vinh Phan; Susan F. Tapert
replication_title: Reduced hippocampal volume among adolescents with alcohol use disorders without psychiatric comorbidity
explanation: The current study replicated the finding of reduced left hippocampal volume in adolescents with AUD (t = 2.90, p < 0.01, d = 1.08), but failed to replicate the original study's finding of reduced right hippocampal volume. As the authors state: 'Unlike the first study to examine structural neuropathology in teens with AUD [8], the current study did not demonstrate smaller volumes of the right hippocampus among adolescents with AUD.' The original bilateral effect was only partially reproduced.

description: Patients with schizophrenia show a significant volume reduction in the left mediodorsal thalamic nucleus compared to normal control subjects
original_authors: Peter Danos; Bruno Baumann; Andrea Krämer; Hans-Gert Bernstein; Renate Stauch; Dieter Krell; Peter Falkai; Bernhard Bogerts

replication_title: Volume and neuron number of the mediodorsal thalamic nucleus in schizophrenia: A replication study
explanation: The replication found only a near-significant trend for left MD volume reduction (ANOVA F1,34=3.65, p=0.06 with whole brain volume as covariate), which became non-significant (p=0.15) after also covarying for postmortem interval. The authors note this is 'consistent with our previous study' but the effect does not reach conventional significance thresholds.

description: Suicide attempters show increased orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) response to angry faces compared to patient controls without suicidal history
original_authors: Fabrice Jollant; Natalia S. Lawrence; Vincent Giampietro; Michael J. Brammer; Miguel A. Fullana; Dominique Drapier; Philippe Courtet; Mary L. Phillips
original_title: Orbitofrontal cortex response to angry faces in men with histories of suicide attempts

replication_title: Processing of decision-making and social threat in patients with history of suicidal attempt: A neuroimaging replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm replication of this finding: 'we confirm the higher response of OFC (and VLPFC) to angry faces in SA vs. PC, a finding that did not apply to sad or happy faces suggesting a specific sensitivity to anger.' The same paradigm (emotional faces viewing task) was used but in a different sample (French males with mixed mood disorders).

original_authors: Fabrice Jollant; Natalia S. Lawrence; Emilie Olie; Owen G. O' Daly; Alain Malafosse; Philippe Courtet; Mary L. Phillips
original_title: Decreased activation of lateral orbitofrontal cortex during risky choices under uncertainty is associated with disadvantageous decision-making and suicidal behavior
replication_authors: Emilie Olié; Yang Ding; Emmanuelle Le Bars; Nicolas Menjot de Champfleur; Thibault Mura; Alain Bonafé; Philippe Courtet; Fabrice Jollant
replication_title: Processing of decision-making and social threat in patients with history of suicidal attempt: A neuroimaging replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state failure to replicate: 'we cannot confirm the role of the same region in deficient risk processing in SA.' They found decreased activation in the left DPFC (not OFC) during risky vs. safe choices, a region not previously investigated, while failing to confirm the OFC finding from the original study.

replication_title: Gulf War illness associated with abnormal auditory P1 event-related potential: Evidence of impaired cholinergic processing replicated in a national sample
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'The present study...replicated a pattern of early auditory P1 component differences across various Haley syndrome groups found in a prior study of male veterans from a single naval construction battalion (Tillman et al., 2012): Syndromes 2 and 3 exhibited significantly higher and Syndrome 1 significantly lower P1 amplitudes.' The same hyperarousal pattern was also replicated.

original_authors: Takuya Saito; Feifei Guan; Demitri F. Papolos; Stephanie Lau; Marjorie H. Klein; Cathy S.J. Fann; Herbert M. Lachman

replication_authors: Pavla Stopkova; Jan Vevera; Ivo Paclt; Ilja Zukov; Herbert M. Lachman
replication_title: Analysis of SYNJ1, a candidate gene for 21q22 linked bipolar disorder: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'although we did not replicate the original finding' — none of the three rare SYNJ1 variants were detected in the Czech BPD sample, and the intron 12 polymorphism result was not significant (p=0.69). The replication was conducted in a different population (Czech Republic vs. US Caucasians), qualifying it as a close extension.

description: Patients with schizophrenia (unmedicated) show a significantly weaker loudness dependence of auditory evoked potentials (LDAEP) compared to healthy controls, indicating higher central serotonergic activity in schizophrenia
original_authors: Georg Juckel; Jürgen Gallinat; Michael Riedel; Safet Sokullu; Carl Schulz; Hans-Jürgen Möller; Norbert Müller; Ulrich Hegerl

replication_title: Loudness dependence of the auditory evoked N1/P2 component as an indicator of serotonergic dysfunction in patients with schizophrenia — A replication study
explanation: The replication only partially reproduced the original findings. The paper explicitly states 'The present study only replicated parts of the previous study' — a significant difference in LDAEP was found for the left hemisphere but not the right, whereas the original found bilateral differences. The use of medicated (rather than unmedicated) patients also extends the population studied.

description: The marker D15S122, located at the 5' end of UBE3A, is significantly associated with autism, with preferential maternal transmission of the 155-bp allele

replication_title: Role of UBE3A and ATP10A genes in autism susceptibility region 15q11-q13 in an Italian population: A positive replication for UBE3A
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the association of D15S122, in UBE3A, with autism originally reported by [34]' and 'We replicate in an Italian sample the original positive finding of D15S122 by [34] in a North American population.' They found significant under-transmission of the 222-bp allele (p = 0.005, corrected p = 0.05), confirming the original finding.

replication_title: Anticipatory vs. consummatory pleasure: What is the nature of hedonic deficits in schizophrenia?
explanation: The authors explicitly state they failed to replicate the core finding: 'we were unable to replicate several of the critical findings presented by [13][14] and other studies...We found that individuals with SZ differed from controls in their ratings of consummatory but not anticipatory pleasure—the opposite of the pattern previously reported.' They also failed to replicate several correlational findings from the original study.

replication_title: Replication analysis for composition of the Delirium Motor Subtype Scale (DMSS) in a referral cohort from Northern India
explanation: The authors explicitly state they aimed to 'replicate and extend the validation analyses for the original development of the DMSS' in a different population. In the Discussion they conclude: 'This replication study performed in a population that contrasted both clinically and socioculturally to the original development study of the DMSS supports its coherence in measuring motor activity,' and describe 'remarkable similarity in DMSS composition between the studies.'

description: Female individuals with a history of depression are hypomethylated in the first exon/intron region of the MAOA gene compared to controls, as measured in saliva DNA
original_authors: Philippe A. Melas; Yabin Wei; Chloe C. Y. Wong; Louise K. Sjöholm; Elin Åberg; Jonathan Mill; Martin Schalling; Yvonne Forsell; Catharina Lavebratt
original_title: Genetic and epigenetic associations of MAOA and NR3C1 with depression and childhood adversities
replication_authors: Philippe A. Melas; Yvonne Forsell
replication_title: Hypomethylation of MAOA׳s first exon region in depression: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we demonstrate a replication of our initial data,' finding that depressed females were hypomethylated compared to controls (standardized coefficient β=0.516, p=0.007) using the same EpiTYPER platform on the same MAOA region from the same PART cohort.

original_authors: Menachem Fromer; Andrew J. Pocklington; David H. Kavanagh; Hywel J. Williams; Sarah Dwyer; Padhraig Gormley; Lyudmila Georgieva; Elliott Rees; Priit Palta; Douglas M. replication_authors: Sakae Takahashi; Masahiro Suzuki; Makoto Uchiyama; Tomohiro Nakayama
replication_title: Replication study of de novo mutations of TAF13 in schizophrenia
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We did not find de novo LoF mutations of TAF13 in schizophrenia' after sequencing 1401 subjects from 474 schizophrenia trios across Chinese, Japanese, and Taiwanese cohorts — a different population from the original Bulgarian cohort.

description: Patients with schizophrenia show greater metacognitive deficits than patients with bipolar disorder and healthy community controls, as measured by the Metacognition Assessment Scale
original_authors: Raffaele Popolo; Elizabeth Smith; Paul H. Lysaker; Krizia Lestingi; Francesca Cavallo; Luisa Melchiorre; Cristina Santone; Giancarlo Dimaggio
original_title: Metacognitive profiles in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder: Comparisons with healthy controls and correlations with negative symptoms
replication_authors: Paul H. Lysaker; Leonor Irarrázaval; Emily C. Gagen; Ivan Armijo; Massimo Ballerini; Milena Mancini; Giovanni Stanghellini
replication_title: Metacognition in schizophrenia disorders: Comparisons with community controls and bipolar disorder: Replication with a Spanish language Chilean sample
explanation: Independent review resolves the ambiguity. The core claim being replicated — that schizophrenia patients have greater metacognitive deficits than BOTH bipolar patients AND healthy controls — is clearly confirmed: schizophrenia group had significantly lower MAS-A total and subscale scores than both other groups (F=35.72, p≤0.001), consistent with the authors' stated prediction and their framing ('Consistent with initial predictions, we found that the MAS-A profiles of the schizophrenia patients suggested significantly poorer metacognitive function than the other two groups'). The 'unexpected finding' flagged in the original extraction — that bipolar group showed metacognitive abilities similar to controls — is a secondary observation about a comparison not central to the Popolo 2017 claim. The description's claim that schizophrenia > bipolar AND schizophrenia > controls is robustly replicated. The result should be 'success', not 'inconclusive'.

description: Metacognitive capacity is uniquely associated with negative and cognitive symptoms in schizophrenia, and this relationship is independent of other social cognitive abilities such as trait-level empathy
original_authors: Lysaker PH; Gumley A.; Luedtke B.; Buck KD; Ringer JM; Olesek K.; Kukla M.; Leonhardt BL; Popolo R.; Dimaggio G.
original_title: Social cognition and metacognition in schizophrenia: Evidence of their independence and linkage with outcomes
replication_authors: Paul H. Lysaker; Leonor Irarrázaval; Emily C. Gagen; Ivan Armijo; Massimo Ballerini; Milena Mancini; Giovanni Stanghellini
replication_title: Metacognition in schizophrenia disorders: Comparisons with community controls and bipolar disorder: Replication with a Spanish language Chilean sample
explanation: Independent review confirms success with high confidence. The paper provides two lines of clear evidence: (1) cognitive and negative PANSS symptoms were broadly correlated with MAS-A scores in the schizophrenia group (Table 3); (2) stepwise regression showed that after IRI empathy subscales (Personal Distress and Perspective Taking) already accounted for 41% of variance in negative symptoms, MAS-A subscales accounted for a further significant 36% (F(3,22)=10.21, p<0.001), directly demonstrating independence from trait empathy. The authors explicitly frame this as a replication: 'Finding thus replicate previously North American [30] ... findings as well as Italian, Danish, Chinese, Turkish and Hebrew language studies suggesting metacognitive deficits are related to psychopathology in schizophrenia cross-culturally and can be separated from other social cognitive abilities.' Both the correlation and independence components of the original claim are confirmed. Medium confidence was unwarranted given the explicit replication statement and significant statistical results.

description: Patients with paranoid schizophrenia show impaired cognitive empathy but preserved emotional empathy as measured by the Multifaceted Empathy Test (MET)
original_authors: Anja Lehmann; Katja Bahçesular; Eva-Maria Brockmann; Sarah-Elisabeth Biederbick; Isabel Dziobek; Jürgen Gallinat; Christiane Montag
original_title: Subjective experience of emotions and emotional empathy in paranoid schizophrenia
replication_authors: Philipp Berger; Florian Bitsch; Babette Jakobi; Arne Nagels; Benjamin Straube; Irina Falkenberg
replication_title: Cognitive and emotional empathy in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders: A replication and extension study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In this independent replication study, we corroborate findings by [Lehmann et al., 2014], demonstrating impaired cognitive, but preserved emotional empathy in patients with SSD within both behavioural and self-report measures.' The study extended the original by including the broader schizophrenia spectrum (not just paranoid schizophrenia) and adding social anhedonia analyses.

description: CHR individuals with a family history of psychosis (FHR) show very few clinical differences from CHR individuals without FHR in positive/negative symptoms, social and role functioning, IQ, cannabis use, and trauma, and FHR does not differentially predict transition to psychosis
original_authors: Grace Georgopoulos; Jacqueline Stowkowy; Lu Liu; Kristin S. Cadenhead; Tyrone D. Cannon; Barbara A. Cornblatt; Thomas H. McGlashan; Diana O. Perkins; Larry J. Seidman; Ming T. Tsuang; Elaine F. Walker; Scott W. Woods; Carrie E. Bearden; Daniel H. Mathalon; Jean Addington
original_title: The role of a family history of psychosis for youth at clinical high risk of psychosis
replication_authors: Olga Santesteban-Echarri; Danah Sandel; Lu Liu; Carrie E. Bearden; Kristin S. Cadenhead; Tyrone D. Cannon; Barbara A. Cornblatt; Matcheri Keshavan; Daniel H. Mathalon; Thomas H. McGlashan; Diana O. Perkins; Larry J. Seidman; William S. Stone; Ming T. Tsuang; Elaine F. Walker; Scott W. Woods; Jean Addington
replication_title: Family history of psychosis in youth at clinical high risk: A replication study
explanation: The abstract states the study 'supports some of the already reported differences in trauma, physical and psychological abuse between CHR individuals with and without FHR,' while the Discussion notes key discrepancies: NAPLS-3 found significant differences in positive/negative symptoms and IQ that NAPLS-2 did not, though both found no differences in functioning, cannabis use, or transition rates. This mixed pattern of partial replication warrants an inconclusive classification.

description: Behavioral regulations (identified regulation), explicit attitudes, and social desirability moderate implicit-explicit discrepancies (IEDs) between automatic associations and explicit exercise motives related to health and appearance outcomes in adults
original_authors: Tanya R. Berry; Wendy M. Rodgers; David Markland; Craig R. Hall
original_title: Moderators of implicit-explicit exercise cognition concordance
replication_authors: Tanya R. Berry; Parvaneh Taymoori; Kohestan Shirzadi; Tahereh Pashaei; Afshin Bahamani
replication_title: Testing attitudes, social desirability and behavioral regulations as moderators of implicit-explicit exercise discrepancies: A replication study in Iranian students
explanation: The current study explicitly describes itself as a replication of Berry et al. (2016) in a new population (Iranian adolescents). Results were mixed: attitudes moderated health-related IEDs as in the original, but introjected regulations and social desirability showed different or contrary patterns, leading the authors to note several findings were 'inconsistent with other research' [4].

description: Falls in the general hospital are associated with delirium, with a large proportion (96%) of patients who fell displaying evidence of delirium, most of which was undiagnosed

replication_title: Falls in A Tertiary Care Hospital—Association With Delirium: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication confirmed the general relationship between delirium and falls (73% of patients who fell had evidence or diagnosis of delirium), but the delirium rate was notably lower than the original (73% vs. 96%). The Discussion acknowledges 'notable differences between the two studies' including lower delirium rates, while also stating the results 'further confirmed that delirium is associated with a majority of falls.'

description: Intranasal oxytocin administration (24IU) improves performance on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET), enhancing the ability to infer others' mental states from the eye region in healthy males

explanation: Oxytocin did not improve RMET performance overall (t(23)=.465, p=.64), nor for any item subcategory (difficulty, valence, intensity, sex of poser). The authors explicitly state: 'Our main result deviates from generally enhanced mind-reading after oxytocin administration [8][12],' confirming the replication failed.

description: Acute systemic injection of MK212 (a selective 5-HT2C receptor agonist) dose-dependently disrupts active components of rat maternal behavior, particularly pup retrieval
original_authors: Weihai Chen; Qi Zhang; Wenxin Su; Haorong Zhang; Yu Yang; Jing Qiao; Nan Sui; Ming Li

replication_authors: Ruiyong Wu; Jun Gao; Shinnyi Chou; Collin Davis; Ming Li
replication_title: Behavioral, pharmacological and neuroanatomical analysis of serotonin 2C receptor agonism on maternal behavior in rats
explanation: Independent review confirms all fields. The authors use unambiguous replication language in two places: (1) 'In agreement with our previous report [12], acute MK212 injection severely disrupted various active components of maternal behavior' (Results, Experiment 1); (2) 'we replicated the acute disruptive effect of MK212 on pup retrieval' (Results, Experiment 4). The original study (Chen et al. 2014, Pharmacol Biochem Behav 117:25-33, ref [12]) is the direct target — same drug (MK212 2.0 mg/kg SC), same behavioral paradigm, same species/strain. Result=success is unambiguous: all key maternal behavior measures (pup retrieval number and latency, nursing, licking, nest building) showed significant disruption (p<0.001). Replication_type=close extension is correct: the current paper uses the identical core paradigm but adds novel mechanistic arms (pup separation manipulation, SB242084 pharmacological reversal, microinjection into NAs/MPOA/mPFC, c-Fos immunohistochemistry), going well beyond a direct replication. Replication n=31 (16 MK212 + 15 VEH in Experiment 1) and p<0.001 are both directly stated. No genuine ambiguity remains; confidence upgraded from medium to high.

description: Individuals with the GG genotype of OXTR rs53576 have higher levels of empathy than those with the A allele, as measured by self-report questionnaire
original_authors: Sarina M. Rodrigues; Laura R. Saslow; Natalia Garcia; Oliver P. John; Dacher Keltner

original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Pingyuan Gong; Huiyong Fan; Jinting Liu; Xing Yang; Kejin Zhang; Xiaolin Zhou
replication_title: Revisiting the impact of OXTR rs53576 on empathy: A population-based study and a meta-analysis
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the association of OXTR rs53576 with empathy in a relatively large population' (Discussion). In the replication study (N=1830 Chinese Han students), GG genotype individuals scored significantly higher on IRI total score (β = .058, p = .010 uncorrected, Bonferroni-adjusted p = .050). A significant linear trend was also found (F(1,1829) = 6.431, p = .011). Additionally, a meta-analysis pooling 13 independent samples (N=6,631) confirmed the association with Cohen's d = 0.148–0.152 (p < .01). The Bonferroni-adjusted p is exactly at threshold (.050), and only 1 of 4 IRI subscales (Fantasy) reached significance individually; however, the primary outcome (total IRI) is significant, the authors frame it as a successful replication without qualification, and the meta-analysis provides strong corroborating evidence. This is a close extension (not direct replication) because it tests the same SNP and measure in a different population (Chinese/Asian vs. original Western sample), explicitly examining cross-cultural generalizability. Confidence upgraded from medium to high based on clear authorial framing, significant primary outcome, and meta-analytic support.

The replication used the same imitation-inhibition paradigm but tested two doses (20 IU and 40 IU) in a different population (older males, not undergraduates) at a later time point post-administration (135 min).

explanation: The authors conducted a two-stage association analysis of TRAR4 haplotype-tagging SNPs in Japanese schizophrenia patients and concluded: 'we could not replicate the association of TRAR4 and SCZ using a Japanese population.' One marker showed nominally significant association in the first-set analysis but this did not survive correction for multiple testing, and was not confirmed in the independent second-set analysis.

No significant associations were found in any allele-, genotype-, or haplotype-wise analyses in their Japanese population sample.

explanation: The paper's conclusion explicitly states: 'our gene-based analysis of GAD1 showed no association between this gene and AOS in the Japanese population.' AOS (adult onset schizophrenia) is precisely what Straub et al. studied, and the introduction identifies Straub (reference [14]) as the study reporting 'a significant association between GAD1 and schizophrenia in two independent adult onset schizophrenia (AOS) samples.' All 14 tagging SNPs showed non-significant p-values in allele-, genotype-, and haplotype-wise analyses. The null result is unambiguous and the paper's language directly addresses the AOS claim made by Straub et al.

replication_title: Smoking initiation and schizophrenia: A replication study in a Chinese Han population
explanation: Independent review confirms high confidence. The paper explicitly frames itself as a replication of three prior studies (US, Spain, US) and the Results/Discussion are unambiguous. The Chinese sample (N=1336) showed significantly higher prevalence of ever smoking daily (79.7% vs 63.0%, p<0.001), current daily smoking (75.8% vs 53.9%, p<0.001), and a significantly higher cumulative hazard curve after age 20 (stratified log-rank p<0.001), all controlling for education. The Discussion concludes: 'This Chinese replication of three prior studies in the USA and Spain suggests that vulnerability to schizophrenia may be associated with vulnerability to smoking.' This directly replicates the original US study's finding of higher post-age-20 smoking initiation in schizophrenic patients. No ambiguity remains.

description: Schizophrenic patients in Spain have higher rates of smoking initiation and initiate daily smoking at higher rates after age 20 compared to controls, as shown by survival analysis of age of smoking onset

replication_title: Smoking initiation and schizophrenia: A replication study in a Chinese Han population
explanation: Independent review confirms high confidence. The paper explicitly states it was 'designed to replicate these associations between age at onset of daily smoking (AODS)' including the Spanish study's finding. Results are unambiguous: the cumulative hazard curve for schizophrenic patients was significantly different from controls (chi-sq=21.4, p<0.001), and after controlling for education (chi-sq=15.6, p<0.001), with significantly higher smoking initiation rates after age 20. The Discussion states results are 'consistent with previous studies in the USA and Spain,' directly confirming replication of the Spanish sample's findings. No ambiguity remains.

description: The association between schizophrenia and smoking initiation rates (higher after age 20) cannot be explained by the illness itself or the prodromal period, as demonstrated by excluding patients who started smoking within 5 years of illness onset

replication_authors: Xiang Yang Zhang; Cun Bao Li; Min Li; You Lan Zheng; Chong Xi Zhang; Quan Zhi Yan; Wen Zhong Liu; Yi Min Kang; Fan Wang; Da Chun Chen; Mei Hong Xiu; Thomas R. Kosten
replication_title: Smoking initiation and schizophrenia: A replication study in a Chinese Han population
explanation: Independent review confirms high confidence. The paper explicitly tests the same claim as Diaz et al. (2008) using the identical methodological approach: excluding schizophrenic patients who started smoking within 5 years before illness onset, then comparing cumulative hazard curves. Results are unambiguous: after this exclusion (N=377 patients vs N=353 ever-smoked controls), the schizophrenic hazard curve was still significantly higher (chi-sq=38.3, p<0.001; after education adjustment chi-sq=14.5, p<0.001). The Discussion's second explicit main conclusion states: 'The age for starting to smoke daily even among those schizophrenic patients who start smoking at least 5 years before illness onset suggests that the association between starting to smoke and schizophrenia cannot be explained by the illness itself or its prodromal period.' This is an exact replication of Diaz et al.'s central claim. No ambiguity remains.
