replication_title: Inspirational Stimuli Improve Idea Fluency during Ideation: A Replication and Extension Study with Eye-Tracking
explanation: The authors conclude that 'Preliminary results presented here corroborates the original study's results, inspirational stimuli influence idea output and questionnaire ratings.' The key finding — that near and far inspirational stimuli increased idea fluency over time (Wordset2: F(2,46)=10.316, p<0.001, η²=0.310) — was replicated, though there were some differences in specific contrasts (e.g., Far-Control contrast was not significant in this study).

description: Genetic factors explain a large share (67–89%) of the correlation between extraversion and political participation and interest, as well as political efficacy, in a sample of Swedish twins
original_authors: Dawes, Christopher T.; Cesarini, David; Fowler, James H.; Johannesson, Magnus; Magnusson, Patrik K.E.; Oskarsson, Sven
original_title: The relationship between genes, psychological traits, and political participation
replication_authors: Aaron Weinschenk; Christopher Dawes; Robert Klemmensen; Stig Hebbelstrup Rye Rasmussen
replication_title: Genes, personality, and political behavior
explanation: The original Swedish study found genetic factors explain 67–89% of extraversion–participation correlations, ~58% of extraversion–interest, 64% of extraversion–external efficacy, and 71% of extraversion–internal efficacy. The Danish replication finds genetic factors account for 79% of the extraversion–communication (participation) correlation and 69% of the extraversion–interest correlation — both consistent with the original's participation and interest findings. However, the efficacy finding clearly does not replicate: Danish heritability for political efficacy is near zero and non-significant, with common environmental (not genetic) factors dominating. The paper explicitly notes: 'it is somewhat surprising that the heritability estimate is not significant in our sample and that our measure of efficacy is instead influenced by shared and unique environmental factors.' This is a genuine partial result — participation and interest replicate, efficacy does not — making 'inconclusive' the appropriate classification. Medium confidence is retained because the original's bundled findings (participation + interest + efficacy) produce clearly mixed results, not a clean success or failure.

description: Genetic factors account for 49% to 72% of the correlation between political interest and four Big Five personality traits (extraversion, conscientiousness, emotional stability, and openness) in U.S. twin samples
original_authors: Weinschenk, Aaron C.; Dawes, Christopher T.
original_title: The relationship between genes, personality traits, and political interest
replication_authors: Aaron Weinschenk; Christopher Dawes; Robert Klemmensen; Stig Hebbelstrup Rye Rasmussen
replication_title: Genes, personality, and political behavior
explanation: The original U.S. study found genetic factors explain 49–72% of the interest–personality correlation across four Big Five traits (extraversion, conscientiousness, emotional stability, openness). The Danish replication finds 69% for extraversion–interest and 70% for openness–interest — both within or slightly above the original's 49–72% range and directionally consistent. The paper states: 'This finding is similar to what has been reported in several previous studies.' However, only two of the original's four personality traits (extraversion and openness) are examined in the Danish bivariate analysis; conscientiousness and emotional stability are excluded because their phenotypic correlations with political behavior were too small to decompose reliably. This partial coverage means the full original claim cannot be assessed, warranting medium rather than high confidence. Within the traits that were tested, results replicate.

description: Genetic factors account for 67% of the correlation between openness and political participation, and 63% of the correlation between openness and political interest, in a sample of German twins
original_authors: Weinschenk, Aaron C.; Dawes, Christopher T.; Kandler, Christian; Bell, Edward; Riemann, Rainer
original_title: New evidence on the link between genes, psychological traits, and political participation
replication_authors: Aaron Weinschenk; Christopher Dawes; Robert Klemmensen; Stig Hebbelstrup Rye Rasmussen
replication_title: Genes, personality, and political behavior
explanation: The original German study found genetic factors explain 67% of the openness–participation correlation and 63% of the openness–interest correlation. The Danish replication finds 86% for openness–communication (participation) and 70% for openness–interest. Both are in the same direction and the interest finding (70% vs. 63%) is numerically close. The participation finding (86% vs. 67%) is directionally consistent but notably higher in magnitude. The paper characterizes both as 'similar to what has been reported in previous studies.' Medium confidence is retained because the participation measure differs (Danish 'communication' index vs. broader German participation measure), the magnitudes diverge more on participation, and the original tested additional personality traits that the Danish study does not examine in the bivariate models. Within openness specifically, the results are consistent.

description: The AGECAT computerized diagnostic system shows high concordance with psychiatrists' diagnoses (kappa ~0.74 overall) when applied to Geriatric Mental State interview data from community-dwelling elderly subjects
original_authors: Copeland JR; Dewey ME; Griffiths-Jones HM
original_title: Computerized psychiatric diagnostic system and case nomenclature for elderly subjects: GMS and AGECAT
replication_authors: Copeland JR; Dewey ME; Henderson AS; Kay DW; Neal CD; Harrison MA; McWilliam C.; Forshaw D.; Shiwach R.
replication_title: The Geriatric Mental State (GMS) used in the community: replication studies of the computerized diagnosis AGECAT
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the results of the replication studies reported here are satisfactory. Concordance rates between AGECAT and psychiatric diagnosis are at least as good as in the previous studies.' The overall kappa was 0.71 across three community samples (N=647), closely matching the original kappa of 0.74 for the community sample in Copeland et al. (1986).

description: Dements and depressives can be differentiated on barbiturate sedation threshold measures and psychological test scores, with dements scoring significantly lower than depressives
original_authors: Robert H. Cawley; Felix Post; Antonia Whitehead
original_title: Barbiturate tolerance and psychological functioning in elderly depressed patients
replication_authors: Davies G.; Hamilton S.; Hendrickson DE; Levy R.; Post F.
replication_title: Psychological test performance and sedation thresholds of elderly dements, depressives and depressives with incipient brain change
explanation: The replication confirmed that dements (organics) scored significantly below depressives (functionals) on psychological tests and had much lower sedation thresholds, consistent with the original 1973 findings. The Discussion states: 'The replication study has confirmed that in psychiatric hospital patients over the age of 60 an admission diagnosis of either depression or dementia is highly likely to be confirmed some 6 months after the completion of treatment.'

description: Depressives responding to treatment show significant increases in both sedation threshold values and psychological test scores following clinical improvement
original_authors: Robert H. Cawley; Felix Post; Antonia Whitehead
original_title: Barbiturate tolerance and psychological functioning in elderly depressed patients
replication_authors: Davies G.; Hamilton S.; Hendrickson DE; Levy R.; Post F.
replication_title: Psychological test performance and sedation thresholds of elderly dements, depressives and depressives with incipient brain change
explanation: The replication found no significant increase in psychological scores (except psychomotor speed) or sedation threshold values after treatment. The Discussion explicitly states: 'A more serious failure to replicate related to the finding that there were, in contrast to the 1973 results, no significant proportionate increases of psychological scores (except for those on the psychomotor speed measure) and of sedation threshold readings in the case of those depressives who improved clinically.'

description: Cerebral age changes short of those in dementia facilitate the occurrence of depression in late life, as evidenced by a significant negative correlation between age at first depressive episode and sedation thresholds and psychological test scores
original_authors: Robert H. Cawley; Felix Post; Antonia Whitehead
original_title: Barbiturate tolerance and psychological functioning in elderly depressed patients
replication_authors: Davies G.; Hamilton S.; Hendrickson DE; Levy R.; Post F.
replication_title: Psychological test performance and sedation thresholds of elderly dements, depressives and depressives with incipient brain change
explanation: The replication found a negative relationship between age at first attack and sedation threshold level, but it was not statistically significant. The abstract states: 'Evidence obtained from the earlier investigations to the effect that cerebral age changes short of those occurring in dementia may facilitate the occurrence of depression in late life was only weakly confirmed by the replication study.'

description: The Mental Adjustment to Cancer (MAC) scale, developed on a British cancer patient population, demonstrates acceptable internal consistency reliability, construct validity, and a five-factor structure
original_authors: Watson M.; Greer S.; Young J.; Inayat Q.; Burgess C.; Robertson B.
original_title: Development of a questionnaire measure of adjustment to cancer; the MAC scale
replication_authors: Carolyn E. Schwartz; Lawren H. Daltroy; Ursula Brandt; Richard Friedman; Leo Stolbach
replication_title: A psychometric analysis of the Mental Adjustment to Cancer Scale
explanation: The replication successfully reproduced internal consistency reliability and construct validity of the MAC subscales in a USA cancer population, but found a different factor structure (four factors rather than five). The authors conclude: 'This psychometric analysis of the MAC revealed similar internal consistency reliability and construct validity in a USA population as Watson et al.'s (1988) findings on a British population. The factor structure that emerged from the present sample was different, however.'

description: CBT, person-centred therapy, and psychodynamic therapy show equivalently positive outcomes when delivered in routine UK NHS primary-care settings (the psychotherapy equivalence paradox / Dodo verdict)
original_authors: William B. Stiles; Michael Barkham; Elspeth Twigg; John Mellor-Clark; Mick Cooper
original_title: Effectiveness of cognitive-behavioural, person-centred, and psychodynamic therapies as practiced in UK National Health Service settings
replication_authors: William B. Stiles; Michael Barkham; John Mellor-Clark; Janice Connell
replication_title: Effectiveness of cognitive-behavioural, person-centred, and psychodynamic therapies in UK primary-care routine practice: replication in a larger sample
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Replicating the earlier results, the theoretically different approaches tended to have equivalent outcomes.' The replication used the same CORE-OM methodology and NHS setting but with a non-overlapping sample 4x larger (n=5613 vs. 1309) restricted to primary-care services only.

description: Patients with major depressive disorder recall fewer specific autobiographical memories and more categorical memories than healthy controls when presented with emotionally valenced cue words
original_authors: James Williams; Jan Scott
original_title: Autobiographical memory in depression
replication_authors: Young KD; Erickson K.; Nugent AC; Fromm SJ; Mallinger AG; Furey ML; Drevets WC
replication_title: Functional anatomy of autobiographical memory recall deficits in depression
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated earlier behavioral findings [54] showing that subjects with MDD recall fewer specific and more categorical memories than controls.' The behavioral results clearly support success: MDD subjects recalled fewer specific memories (p=0.013) and more categorical memories (p<0.001) than controls. However, a genuine citation ambiguity warrants keeping confidence at medium: the Discussion cites reference [54] (Van Vreeswijk & De Wilde, 2004 meta-analysis) as the replicated finding, not the primary empirical study. Reference [57] (Williams & Scott, 1988) is the original study establishing this effect and is cited in the Introduction alongside [54] as the source of the phenomenon. The entry attributes the replication to Williams & Scott (1988) by tracing back through the meta-analysis, but the authors themselves say they replicated [54]. This is a genuine ambiguity: the 'original' could reasonably be identified as either the 1988 empirical paper or the 2004 meta-analysis that consolidated it. The result classification as 'success' and 'close extension' (fMRI added to behavioral paradigm) are both well-supported.

description: Familial resemblance for drug abuse in sibling pairs is inversely related to age difference between siblings, such that siblings closer in age have higher concordance for drug abuse
original_authors: Kenneth S. Kendler; Henrik Ohlsson; Kristina Sundquist; Jan Sundquist
original_title: Within-family environmental transmission of drug abuse: a Swedish national study
replication_authors: Kendler KS; Ohlsson H.; Sundquist K.; Sundquist J.
replication_title: Environmental influences on familial resemblance for drug abuse in first-cousin pairs: a Swedish national study
explanation: The authors explicitly sought to replicate the age-difference effect from sibling pairs in cousin pairs, and found a significant inverse association between age differences and DA resemblance in cousin pairs (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.98–0.997, p = 0.004), consistent with prior sibling results, though the effect was weaker.

description: Risk for drug abuse is greater when a drug-abusing sibling is older rather than younger (older-to-younger transmission is stronger than younger-to-older transmission)
original_authors: Kenneth S. Kendler; Henrik Ohlsson; Kristina Sundquist; Jan Sundquist
original_title: Within-family environmental transmission of drug abuse: a Swedish national study
replication_authors: Kendler KS; Ohlsson H.; Sundquist K.; Sundquist J.
replication_title: Environmental influences on familial resemblance for drug abuse in first-cousin pairs: a Swedish national study
explanation: The authors replicated the older-to-younger transmission effect in cousin pairs: the hazard ratio for DA in the cousin was significantly greater when the proband was older than younger (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.37–1.47), consistent with prior sibling results. The authors note 'we replicated in our cousin pairs prior results from full siblings.'

description: Without explicit instructions, healthy adults slow their responses when stop-signal probability increases (proactive inhibition effect in the stop-signal anticipation task)
original_authors: Bram B. Zandbelt; Matthijs Vink
original_title: On the role of the striatum in response inhibition
replication_authors: Branko M. van Hulst; Patrick de Zeeuw; Chantal Vlaskamp; Yvonne Rijks; Bram B. Zandbelt; Sarah Durston
replication_title: Children with ADHD symptoms show deficits in reactive but not proactive inhibition, irrespective of their formal diagnosis
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Here, we replicated this finding in children' referring to Zandbelt & Vink's (2010) finding that adults show proactive response slowing with increasing stop-signal probability. The replication confirmed this effect in a child sample (F(2.71,271) = 57.92, p < 0.001).

description: The Climate Schools: Alcohol and Cannabis web-based prevention program is more effective than standard AOD education in increasing alcohol and cannabis knowledge, reducing alcohol use and heavy episodic drinking, and reducing cannabis use frequency among secondary school students
original_authors: Katrina E. Champion; Nicola C. Newton; Lexine Stapinski; Tim Slade; Emma L. Barrett; Maree Teesson
original_title: A cross-validation trial of an internet-based prevention program for alcohol and cannabis: Preliminary results from a cluster randomised controlled trial
original_journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
replication_authors: Nicola C. Newton; Cath Chapman; Tim Slade; Louise Birrell; Annalise Healy; Marius Mather; Nyanda McBride; Leanne Hides; Steve Allsop; Louise Mewton; Gavin Andrews; Maree Teesson
replication_title: A national effectiveness trial of an eHealth program to prevent alcohol and cannabis misuse: responding to the replication crisis
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim was 'to conduct a national effectiveness trial to replicate the research of the Climate Schools: Alcohol and Cannabis course.' Results provided partial replication: knowledge and alcohol use outcomes were replicated (SMD ~0.51, p < .001; OR 0.62, p = .014) but cannabis use (OR 0.57, p = .22) and alcohol harms (OR 0.73, p = .17) effects were not significant. The Discussion notes 'support for the effectiveness and feasibility of the course with respect to knowledge outcomes and alcohol uptake, but not with respect to cannabis use or alcohol harms.'

description: The Climate Schools: Alcohol and Cannabis web-based prevention program is more effective than standard AOD education in increasing alcohol and cannabis knowledge and reducing alcohol use and risky drinking among secondary school students in New South Wales
original_authors: Nicola C. Newton; Laura E. Vogl; Maree Teesson; Gavin Andrews
original_title: CLIMATE schools: Alcohol module: Cross-validation of a school-based prevention programme for alcohol misuse
original_journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
replication_authors: Nicola C. Newton; Cath Chapman; Tim Slade; Louise Birrell; Annalise Healy; Marius Mather; Nyanda McBride; Leanne Hides; Steve Allsop; Louise Mewton; Gavin Andrews; Maree Teesson
replication_title: A national effectiveness trial of an eHealth program to prevent alcohol and cannabis misuse: responding to the replication crisis
explanation: Independent review confirms medium confidence is appropriate. The current study explicitly aimed to replicate both prior Climate Schools trials together (Champion et al. 2015 and Newton et al. 2009), treating them as a unified evidence base without disaggregating which outcomes correspond to which original. Newton 2009 was specifically the alcohol-only module ('CLIMATE Schools: Alcohol module'), yet the current study's replication target is the combined Alcohol and Cannabis course — meaning some outcomes (cannabis knowledge, cannabis use) are not directly traceable to Newton 2009 as an original. The mixed results (alcohol knowledge and alcohol use replicated; cannabis use p=.22 and alcohol harms p=.17 not significant) are clearly stated in the Discussion, supporting the 'inconclusive' classification. Confidence remains medium because: the paper never disaggregates which prior trial's findings are being replicated by which outcome, making it inherently ambiguous which results can be attributed specifically to Newton 2009 vs. Champion 2015.

description: Transgender women have significantly lower fractional anisotropy (FA) in the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) compared to cisgender men, irrespective of sexual orientation, suggesting sex-atypical white-matter microstructure specific to gender identity
original_authors: Sarah M. Burke; Amir H. Manzouri; Ivanka Savic
original_title: Structural connections in the brain in relation to gender identity and sexual orientation
replication_authors: Jason van Heesewijk; Martijn D. Steenwijk; Baudewijntje P. C. Kreukels; Dick J. Veltman; Julie Bakker; Sarah M. Burke
replication_title: Alterations in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus – a specific neural correlate of gender incongruence?
explanation: The authors explicitly used 'identical analysis settings' as the original study (Burke et al., 2017) and concluded: 'we replicated the finding of lower FA in the IFOF of post-pubescent transgender girls and women, which suggests this to be a salient neural correlate of gender incongruence.' The current study confirmed transgender adolescent girls had significantly lower FA in the left IFOF compared to adolescent cisgender boys, consistent with the original adult finding.

description: Attention bias to reward is concurrently associated with greater externalizing and attention problems, and lower parent-reported effortful control, in school-age children
original_authors: Santiago Morales; Koraly Pérez‐Edgar; Kristin Buss
original_title: Longitudinal relations among exuberance, externalizing behaviors, and attentional bias to reward: The mediating role of effortful control
replication_authors: Santiago Morales; Natalie V. Miller; Sonya V. Troller-Renfree; Lauren K. White; Kathryn A. Degnan; Heather A. Henderson; Nathan A. Fox
replication_title: Attention bias to reward predicts behavioral problems and moderates early risk to externalizing and attention problems
explanation: The authors explicitly state they aimed to 'replicate the concurrent relations between attention bias to reward, externalizing problems and attention problems, and parent-reported effortful control.' The Discussion confirms: 'These findings replicate previous studies that find that attention bias to reward is related to greater externalizing and attention problems…and lower parent-reported effortful control.' Both effects were significant in the expected direction.

description: Cross-sectional associations between psychopathology/personality features (impulsivity, externalizing, prodromal schizophrenia symptoms, fun seeking) and alcohol sipping in 9-10-year-olds in the ABCD cohort at baseline
original_authors: Ashley L. Watts; Phillip K. Wood; Kristina M. Jackson; Krista M. Lisdahl; Mary M. Heitzeg; Raul Gonzalez; Susan F. Tapert; Deanna M. Barch; Kenneth J. Sher
original_title: Incipient alcohol use in childhood: Early alcohol sipping and its relations with psychopathology and personality
replication_authors: Ashley L. Watts; Mark I. Doss; Donte L. Bernard; Kenneth J. Sher
replication_title: Psychopathology as dynamic markers of alcohol initiation across development: A three-year longitudinal examination
explanation: The authors explicitly state the Watts et al. (2020) baseline examination of cross-sectional correlates of sipping was 'the primary target for our replication effort.' In the Conclusion they state: 'We replicated and extended [39] examination of the concurrent associations between alcohol sipping...and a wide array of psychopathology and personality variables,' noting that aspects of externalizing, reward sensitivity, and prodromal schizophrenia symptoms emerged as the strongest predictors as in the original.

description: Executive functioning (EF) predicts performance on the Pillbox Test beyond processing speed (PS), but not beyond the combination of language, attention, visuospatial, and memory domains
original_authors: Logue, E.; Marceaux, J.; Balldin, V.; Hilsabeck, R.
original_title: Pillbox test performance in a mixed clinical neuropsychology sample
replication_authors: Frances M. Bozsik; Timothy J. Arentsen; Brad L. Roper; Jessica M. Fett; Marcy C. Adler; Jennifer L. Jacobson; Charlotte Bayer
replication_title: 16 Validation of the Pillbox Test in a Veteran Sample: A Replication Study.
replication_journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
explanation: Independent review resolved the ambiguity. The original entry called this 'inconclusive' because the authors say 'partially replicated,' but close reading shows both core EF findings from Logue et al. (2015) replicated cleanly: (1) EF predicted PT performance beyond PS (∆R²=.02, p=.044 — replicates), and (2) EF did NOT predict beyond the combined domain model (∆R²=.00, p=.863 — replicates). The authors' 'partial' qualifier refers to a secondary finding in a separate forced-entry regression — visuospatial performance was significant in the original but not here. That is a different analysis from the primary hierarchical regression used to test the original EF claim. The primary replication target is clearly supported. Result upgraded to 'success' with one noted divergence on the secondary visuospatial finding.

description: APOE-ε4 presence impacts brain structure (grey matter volume) and cognitive function in healthy older adults, as examined via voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)
original_authors: Honea, Robyn A.; Vidoni, Eric; Harsha, Amith; Burns, Jeffrey M.
original_title: Impact of APOE on the healthy aging brain: a voxel-based MRI and DTI study
replication_authors: Colleen Lacey; Jodie Gawryluk; Theone Paterson
replication_title: 4 Impact of APOE-ε Alleles on Brain Structure and Function in Healthy Older Adults: A VBM and DTI Replication Study
replication_journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current study replicated and extended previous findings.' Consistent with Honea et al. (2009), no statistically significant differences were found at corrected thresholds (p>0.05), and trend-level results (p<0.2) were consistent with the original, suggesting subtle neurostructural differences in APOE-ε4 carriers.

description: When deaf ASL-English bilinguals read English words, they activate the phonological forms of their ASL sign translations, as evidenced by slower reaction times for semantically unrelated English word pairs whose ASL translations are phonologically related, compared to phonologically unrelated ASL translations
original_authors: Jill P. Morford; Erin Wilkinson; Agnes Villwock; Pilar Piñar; Judith F. Kroll
original_title: When deaf signers read English: Do written words activate their sign translations
replication_authors: Jill P. Morford; Corrine Occhino-Kehoe; Pilar Piñar; Erin Wilkinson; Judith F. Kroll
replication_title: The time course of cross-language activation in deaf ASL–English bilinguals
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated prior findings of cross-language activation between English print and ASL signs despite the introduction of a much faster rate of presentation.' The same semantic similarity judgment paradigm was used, and the interaction of Phonology × Group was significant (F1(2,93)=6.07, p<.01 for unrelated condition; F1(2,93)=14.14, p<.001 for related condition), replicating the core cross-language activation effects of Morford et al. (2011).

description: Cross-language phonological similarity between English written words and their ASL sign translations enhances performance (faster reaction times) for semantically related English word pairs in deaf sign-print bilinguals
original_authors: Jill P. Morford; Judith F. Kroll; Pilar Piñar; Erin Wilkinson
original_title: Bilingual word recognition in deaf and hearing signers: Effects of proficiency and language dominance on cross-language activation
replication_authors: Jill P. Morford; Corrine Occhino-Kehoe; Pilar Piñar; Erin Wilkinson; Judith F. Kroll
replication_title: The time course of cross-language activation in deaf ASL–English bilinguals
explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicated 'prior studies that have found that cross-language phonological similarity can enhance performance in sign-print bilinguals [30][29]'. The significant Phonology × Group interaction (F1(2,93)=14.14, p<.001, η²P=.23) for semantically related items confirms replication of the facilitatory cross-language phonological effect found in Morford et al. (2014).

description: Bilingual French-English readers more accurately identify target words in syntactically grammatical mixed-language sentences than in ungrammatical ones (bilingual sentence superiority effect), attributed to rapid cross-linguistic parsing of shared syntactic representations
original_authors: Mathieu Declerck; Yun Wen; Joshua Snell; Gabriela Meade; Jonathan Grainger
original_title: Unified syntax in the bilingual mind
replication_authors: Portia N. Washington; Robert W. Wiley
replication_title: The contributions of proficiency and semantics to the bilingual sentence superiority effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Experiment 1 did replicate the bilingual SSE, in a heterogenous population of individuals who speak both Spanish and English,' finding a comparable effect size (8.4% accuracy advantage for grammatical sentences vs. 7.3% in the original). The replication used the same RPVP paradigm but adapted stimuli from French-English to Spanish-English bilinguals, constituting a close extension to a new population/language pair.

description: Depressed patients assigned to placebo in antidepressant clinical trials are not at greater risk for suicide or suicide attempts than patients assigned to active drug treatment
original_authors: Arif Khan; Heather A. Warner; Walter A. Brown
original_title: Symptom reduction and suicide risk in patients treated with placebo in antidepressant clinical trials: an analysis of the Food and Drug Administration database
replication_authors: Arif Khan; Shirin R. Khan; Robyn M. Leventhal; Walter A. Brown
replication_title: Symptom reduction and suicide risk in patients treated with placebo in antidepressant clinical trials: a replication analysis of the Food and Drug Administration Database
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our aim was to follow-up our previous findings [5] in a new sample of patients' and confirm that 'The small differences in rates of suicide and attempted suicide among those assigned to antidepressants compared to those assigned to placebo did not approach statistical significance,' consistent with the original finding.

description: Depressed patients assigned to placebo in antidepressant clinical trials experience substantial reduction in depressive symptoms (as measured by the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale)
original_authors: Arif Khan; Heather A. Warner; Walter A. Brown
original_title: Symptom reduction and suicide risk in patients treated with placebo in antidepressant clinical trials: an analysis of the Food and Drug Administration database
replication_authors: Arif Khan; Shirin R. Khan; Robyn M. Leventhal; Walter A. Brown
replication_title: Symptom reduction and suicide risk in patients treated with placebo in antidepressant clinical trials: a replication analysis of the Food and Drug Administration Database
explanation: The authors confirm 'patients who were assigned to placebo treatment experienced substantial symptom reduction, although not of the magnitude experienced by those assigned to antidepressants. These results are similar to those from our earlier analysis,' with a 35.5% symptom reduction in placebo-treated patients.

description: A health education and exercise programme for older adults with osteoarthritis of the knee reduces physical therapy visits and improves OA knowledge, pain, and self-efficacy
original_authors: Hopman-Rock, M.; Westhoff, M.
original_title: The effects of a health educational and exercise programme for older adults with osteoarthritis of the hip or knee
replication_authors: Reinhard de Jong; Erwin Tak; Niek Klazinga; Marijke Hopman-Rock
replication_title: The impact on health services utilization in a replication study of two self-management programmes for osteoarthritis of the knee and hip
explanation: The authors explicitly conducted a 'replication study' of both RCTs in real-life conditions (by primary healthcare providers) rather than controlled research settings. They conclude: 'Both programmes produced similar outcomes in real-life conditions compared to their RCTs.' For the Knee programme, physical therapy use and OA medication use both decreased significantly, consistent with the original RCT findings.

description: An exercise programme (hip muscle strengthening with ergonomic advice) for older adults with osteoarthritis of the hip improves pain and hip function
original_authors: Tak, E.; Staats, P.; Hespen Van, A.; Hopman-Rock, M.
original_title: The effects of an exercise programme for older adults with osteoarthritis of the hip
replication_authors: Reinhard de Jong; Erwin Tak; Niek Klazinga; Marijke Hopman-Rock
replication_title: The impact on health services utilization in a replication study of two self-management programmes for osteoarthritis of the knee and hip
explanation: The authors conclude 'Both programmes produced similar outcomes in real-life conditions compared to their RCTs.' However, this paper measures only health services utilization and expenditure — NOT the pain/hip function outcomes that were the original Hip RCT's findings. The original Hip RCT (Tak et al., 2005) explicitly did not measure health services utilization. The authors themselves state in the Limitations: 'For the Hip programme such a conclusion cannot be drawn, since health services utilization was not measured in the RCT.' The pain/hip function replication is reported separately in Jong [11] (not this paper). Within this paper, the Hip programme showed significant reductions in physical therapy visits, medical specialist visits, and OA medication use — but these outcomes have no RCT baseline for comparison. The 'success' classification reflects the overall positive trajectory and the authors' collective conclusion, but direct comparison to the original Hip RCT's measured outcomes is not possible from this paper alone. Confidence kept at medium because the basis for calling this a replication success is genuinely limited for the Hip programme.

description: Distraction (unconscious thought) leads to better decision making than conscious deliberation in multi-attribute choice tasks (unconscious thought advantage), and that this advantage may be gender-specific with female participants benefiting more from distraction
original_authors: Mark Nieuwenstein; Hedderik van Rijn
original_title: The unconscious thought advantage: Further replication failures from a search for confirmatory evidence
replication_authors: Mark R. Nieuwenstein; Tjardie Wierenga; Richard D. Morey; Jelte M. Wicherts; Tesse N. Blom; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Hedderik van Rijn
replication_title: On making the right choice: A meta-analysis and large-scale replication attempt of the unconscious thought advantage
explanation: The large-scale replication (N=399) of Nieuwenstein and Van Rijn's Experiment 1 found no significant UTA (58.2% vs. 61.9% correct choices for deliberation vs. distraction), with a Bayes factor of 7.83 in favor of the null hypothesis, and also failed to replicate the gender interaction. The authors explicitly conclude: 'the results of the current study lead us to conclude that the claim that distraction leads to better decision making than deliberation in a multi-attribute choice task has no reliable support.'

description: Making the opportunity cost of the smaller-but-sooner (SS) option explicit (SS zero frame) increases patience in intertemporal choice, while making the opportunity cost of the larger-but-later (LL) option explicit has no effect — the asymmetric subjective opportunity cost (ASOC) effect
original_authors: Daniel Read; Christopher Y. Olivola; David J. Hardisty
original_title: The value of nothing: asymmetric attention to opportunity costs drives intertemporal decision making
replication_authors: Si-Chu Shen; Yuan-Na Huang; Cheng-Ming Jiang; Shu Li
replication_title: Can asymmetric subjective opportunity cost effect explain impatience in intertemporal choice? A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the replication was successful: 'The results indicated that participants were more patient in the SS zero frame than in the Hidden zero frame (41.61% vs. 31.11%, t(870) = 6.10, p < .001, d = .41)' and 'The results of the present study supported the ASOC effect of [11] in their original condition.' The effect size was comparable to the original (ηp² = .05 in original vs. .033 in replication), and no LL zero effect was found, consistent with the ASOC prediction.

description: Expressing numerical information in a currency unit with lower value makes the perceived relative difference between options smaller, leading people to be less patient in intertemporal choice (unit effect)
original_authors: Mario Pandelaere; Barbara Briers; Christophe Lembregts
original_title: How to make a 29% increase look bigger: the unit effect in option comparisons
replication_authors: Si-Chu Shen; Yuan-Na Huang; Cheng-Ming Jiang; Shu Li
replication_title: Can asymmetric subjective opportunity cost effect explain impatience in intertemporal choice? A replication study
explanation: Independent review confirms success. The paper reports clear, significant evidence: participants were less patient in the Money Unit condition vs. the original baseline (26.88% vs. 31.11% LL choice, t(444) = -3.70, p < .001, d = .25, 95% CI [0.115, 0.380]). Item-level analysis showed 11/15 choice items (73%) shifted in the expected direction with significant McNemar χ² values. Authors explicitly state 'unit effect was also demonstrated to be able to prompt people to select more SS options' and 'The unit effect was successfully replicated.' The unit effect is tested as a byproduct verification (the primary goal was to use it to generate a lower-patience baseline), but the authors treat this as a genuine replication. The only noted limitation is that Thai Baht may have been less familiar to Chinese participants (requiring double currency conversion), which the authors acknowledge may have weakened the effect relative to what it might have been — but the effect itself is clearly present and significant.

description: Removing zero complements of risky options in gain/loss framing tasks eliminates the framing effect, while removing non-zero complements enlarges it, supporting fuzzy-trace theory over prospect theory
original_authors: Anton Kühberger; Carmen Tanner
original_title: Risky choice framing: Task versions and a comparison of prospect theory and fuzzy-trace theory
replication_authors: Lei Zhou; Nan Liu; Ya-Qiong Liao; Ai-Mei Li
replication_title: Risky choice framing with various problem descriptions: A replication and extension study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we successfully replicated the study in [22] using a Chinese sample.' The replication interaction effect (η² = .088) was consistent with the original (η² = .107), and the signal detection evaluation confirmed 'a signal was detected, and the ES was consistent with the original study.'

description: Removing zero complements of risky options in gain/loss framing tasks eliminates the framing effect, while removing non-zero complements enlarges it, supporting fuzzy-trace theory over prospect theory
original_authors: Anton Kühberger; Carmen Tanner
original_title: Risky choice framing: Task versions and a comparison of prospect theory and fuzzy-trace theory
replication_authors: Lei Zhou; Nan Liu; Ya-Qiong Liao; Ai-Mei Li
replication_title: Risky choice framing with various problem descriptions: A replication and extension study
explanation: The authors conclude: 'varying the probability did not change the original findings, with significant interactions found between task type and frame for all probability conditions.' The interaction effect (η² = .104) was consistent with the original (η² = .107), confirming robust replication across small, medium, and large probability conditions.

description: Removing zero complements of risky options in gain/loss framing tasks eliminates the framing effect, while removing non-zero complements enlarges it, supporting fuzzy-trace theory over prospect theory
original_authors: Anton Kühberger; Carmen Tanner
original_title: Risky choice framing: Task versions and a comparison of prospect theory and fuzzy-trace theory
replication_authors: Lei Zhou; Nan Liu; Ya-Qiong Liao; Ai-Mei Li
replication_title: Risky choice framing with various problem descriptions: A replication and extension study
explanation: The authors conclude: 'the original finding that framing effects vary across task type was replicated in all three EV ratio conditions.' The interaction effect (η² = .106) was consistent with the original (η² = .107), and the evaluation confirmed the signal was detected and effect size was consistent with the original.

description: Children with ADHD exhibit significantly slower stop signal reaction times than normal comparison children on the stop task, with an effect size of approximately d = 0.64
original_authors: Jaap Oosterlaan; Gordon D. Logan; Joseph A. Sergeant
original_title: Response inhibition in ADHD, CD, comorbid ADHD + CD, anxious, and normal children: A meta-analysis of studies with the stop task
original_journal: Journal of Child Psychiatry and Psychology
replication_authors: Nigg JT
replication_title: The ADHD response-inhibition deficit as measured by the stop task: replication with DSM-IV combined type, extension, and qualification.
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm in the Discussion: 'the results show that the new tracking procedure yields the same findings for response inhibition as in prior studies.' The effect size for boys (d = .64) matched the prior literature benchmark (d ~ .6), and the overall effect was even larger (d = .88), confirming the ADHD response inhibition deficit with DSM-IV criteria, inclusion of girls, and the new tracking procedure.

description: Number of risk factors (prior camp experience, hospitalizations, missing school, no formal schooling, negative feelings toward American father, hostile stepfather relationship, low family income, conduct disorder symptoms, not living with mother) linearly predicts symptoms of anxiety and depression among Vietnamese Amerasian youth
original_authors: McKelvey, Robert; Mao, Angela; Webb, John
original_title: A risk profile predicting psychological distress in Vietnamese Amerasian youth
original_journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
replication_authors: Webb JA; McKelvey RS; Strobel R.
replication_title: Replication and extension of a risk profile for Amerasian youth.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'results of the analyses provide support for the validity of the risk profile developed on an earlier cohort of Vietnamese Amerasians,' with statistically significant linear trends for all three distress measures (p < .001) in the independent 1993 cohort.

description: A research induction group procedure (four sessions of information and discussion about experimental conditions and research procedures) results in informed decision-making, high recruitment rates, low attrition from services and research, and high client satisfaction in a mental health clinical trial
original_authors: Robert E. Drake; Deborah R. Becker; William A. Anthony
original_title: A research induction group for clients entering a mental health research project
replication_authors: Bebout RR; Becker DR; Drake RE
replication_title: A research induction group for clients entering a mental health research project: a replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study replicated the success of the research induction group procedure in our earlier New Hampshire study. As in the earlier study, recruitment goals were fully met; clients were satisfied that they were informed and prepared for the study; participation rates both in services and research were high; and clients demonstrated that they were ready for vocational services.' The replication used the same paradigm in a different setting (inner-city Washington D.C. vs. rural New Hampshire) with a different population (predominantly African-American, dually diagnosed, recently homeless clients).

description: Lower scores on the Multnomah Community Ability Scale (MCAS) predict subsequent involuntary psychiatric hospitalization in clients with severe mental illness
original_authors: Sela Barker; Nancy Barron; Bentson H. McFarland; Douglas A. Bigelow; Terry Carnahan
original_title: A community ability scale for chronically mentally ill consumers: Part II. Applications
replication_authors: Zani B.; McFarland B.; Wachal M.; Barker S.; Barron N.
replication_title: Statewide replication of predictive validation for the Multnomah Community Ability Scale.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study replicated the predictive validation of a level of functioning measure' and found the statewide test for trend was highly significant (chi-squared=42.46, p<.0001), with regression coefficients not significantly different from the original study (heterogeneity chi-squared=0.59, p=NS), confirming a successful replication.

description: Stochastic dependence in multidimensional source memory retrieval is not an artifact of aggregating over participants with different memory strengths, but reflects genuine binding of context features
original_authors: Meiser, Thorsten; Sattler, Christine; Weisser, Katharina
original_title: Binding of multidimensional context information as a distinctive characteristic of remember judgments
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Arnold NR; Heck DW; Bröder A.; Meiser T.; Boywitt CD
replication_title: Testing Hypotheses About Binding in Context Memory With a 					Hierarchical Multinomial Modeling Approach
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated the findings by [15] and [2] and showed that stochastic dependency in source memory is not merely an artifact of the aggregation of response frequencies over participants.' Binding parameters were significantly larger than zero in both experimental conditions (separate-categorization: M=.14, 95% BCI [.07, .23]; simultaneous-categorization: M=.19, 95% BCI [.10, .27]).

description: Positive affect high in approach motivational intensity (induced by pictures of desserts) narrows attentional breadth, improving local processing and impairing global processing in a Navon letter task compared to neutral conditions
original_authors: Philip A. Gable; Eddie Harmon-Jones
original_title: Approach-motivated positive affect reduces breadth of attention
replication_authors: Alberto De Luca; Stephan Verschoor; Bernhard Hommel
replication_title: No Correlation Between Mood or Motivation and the Processing of                     Global and Local Information
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we again failed to replicate the main results of Gable and Harmon-Jones (2008, Experiment 2)' across two well-powered online experiments (1A and 2A), finding no significant interaction of affective condition with attentional level on RTs in either experiment.

description: Positive stimuli high in approach motivational intensity (relative to low-motivational or neutral stimuli) impair global processing in a within-subjects 3-condition Navon letter task design
original_authors: Irena Domachowska; Christina Heitmann; Roland Deutsch; Thomas Goschke; Stefan Scherbaum; Annette Bolte
original_title: Approach-motivated positive affect reduces breadth of attention: Registered replication report of Gable and Harmon-Jones
replication_authors: Alberto De Luca; Stephan Verschoor; Bernhard Hommel
replication_title: No Correlation Between Mood or Motivation and the Processing of                     Global and Local Information
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we again failed to replicate the main results of... Domachowska et al. (2016, Experiments 1 and 2)'. Experiments 1B and 2B found no significant interaction of affective condition with attentional level on RTs or PEs, with Bayesian analyses providing substantial to strong evidence against any interaction effect.

description: Emotion and group membership of face primes interactively influence automatic evaluative responses in the evaluative priming task, such that happy ingroup and fearful outgroup faces facilitate reactions to positive targets while fearful ingroup and happy outgroup faces facilitate reactions to negative targets
original_authors: Max Weisbuch; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Affective divergence: Automatic responses to others' emotions depend on group membership
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Emre Gurbuz; Michaela Rohr; Dirk Wentura
replication_title: Independent Effects of Emotional Expression and Group Membership in the Evaluative Priming Task
explanation: Experiment 1 found only independent effects of emotion and group membership (main effects) with no significant interaction (F(1,87)=0.69, p=.410, η²p=0.008, d_Z=0.09), failing to replicate the interactive pattern reported by Weisbuch and Ambady. The authors conclude: 'Experiment 2 confirmed that the effects of emotion and ethnicity remain independent, indicating that increased task relevance did not yield the integrated processing of emotion and ethnicity as initially hypothesized.'

description: Emotion and group membership of face primes interactively influence automatic evaluative responses in the evaluative priming task, such that happy ingroup and fearful outgroup faces facilitate reactions to positive targets while fearful ingroup and happy outgroup faces facilitate reactions to negative targets
original_authors: Max Weisbuch; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Affective divergence: Automatic responses to others' emotions depend on group membership
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Emre Gurbuz; Michaela Rohr; Dirk Wentura
replication_title: Independent Effects of Emotional Expression and Group Membership in the Evaluative Priming Task
explanation: Experiment 2 (n=122, pre-registered with sequential Bayes testing) found no interaction between emotion and group membership (F(1,121)=0.01, p=.941, d_Z=0.01), providing clear evidence against the interactive effect from Weisbuch & Ambady (2008). Authors conclude: 'The results are clear: the prediction of a main effect of ethnicity was supported, indicating that ingroup primes elicited higher priming scores for both happy and fearful expressions compared to outgroup primes. There was no support for the SMA.'

description: The San Andreas fault slip rate at Wallace Creek in the Carrizo Plain is 33.9 ± 2.9 mm/year over the past ~3,700 years, based on measurement of channel offset and conventional radiocarbon dating
original_authors: Kerry E. Sieh; Richard H. Jahns
original_title: Holocene activity of the San Andreas fault at Wallace Creek, California
replication_authors: Ludwig, Lisa Grant; Akciz, Sinan; Arrowsmith, Ramon; Salisbury, J. Barrett
replication_title: Reproducibility of San Andreas Fault Slip Rate Measurements at Wallace Creek in the Carrizo Plain, CA
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Within the error of measurement, the slip rate is the same as 33.9 ± 2.9 mm/year reported by S&J84' and conclude 'the late Holocene slip rate of the SAF, a key indicator of seismic hazard, is reproducible within measurement uncertainty.' Their measurement of 36 ± 1 mm/year overlaps with the original within measurement uncertainty.

description: Psychomotor disturbance (PMD) as measured by the CORE measure is the primary distinguishing feature between melancholic and non-melancholic depression, while endogeneity symptoms lack class specificity, supporting a hierarchical model for distinguishing psychotic, melancholic, and non-melancholic depression classes
original_authors: Gordon Parker; Kay Wilhelm; Philip B. Mitchell; Kay Roy; Dušan Hadži-Pavlović
original_title: Sub-typing depression testing algorithms and identification of a tiered model
original_journal: Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
replication_authors: Parker G.; Roy K.; Hadzi-Pavlovic D.; Mitchell P.; Wilhelm K.; Menkes DB; Snowdon J.; Loo C.; Schweitzer I.
replication_title: Subtyping depression by clinical features:the Australasian database
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'The data from this and our two preceding studies again support a hierarchical or tiered model for distinguishing three substantive depressive classes on the basis of clinical features alone.' The replication used a broader sample of 27 non-MDU Australasian psychiatrists to rule out potential observer bias, finding that CORE-rated PMD achieved a kappa of 0.73 in distinguishing melancholic from non-melancholic depression, while endogeneity symptoms produced kappas of only 0.00 to 0.09.

description: Manic symptoms, psychotic symptoms, and impaired global functioning are significantly positively correlated with homicidal ideation and intent among patients with schizophrenia
original_authors: Robert C. Schwartz; Suni Petersen; Jobie L. Skaggs
original_title: Predictors of homicidal ideation and intent in schizophrenia: An empirical study
replication_authors: Robert C. Schwartz; Cynthia A. Reynolds; James F. Austin; Suni Petersen
replication_title: Homicidality in schizophrenia: A replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Results found in this study support earlier findings by Schwartz et al. (2001).' Manic symptoms and impaired global functioning were confirmed as significant predictors of homicidality, and additionally substance abuse and male gender were found significant.

description: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) reduces relapse/recurrence rates in recovered recurrently depressed patients with three or more previous episodes of major depression compared to treatment as usual
original_authors: John D. Teasdale; Zindel V. Segal; James Williams; Valerie Ridgeway; Judith M. Soulsby; Mark A. Lau
original_title: Prevention of relapse/recurrence in major depression by mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Ma SH; Teasdale JD
replication_title: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Depression: Replication and Exploration of Differential Relapse Prevention Effects.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study replicated both the positive and negative outcome findings of Teasdale et al.'s (2000) clinical trial.' For patients with 3+ episodes, MBCT reduced relapse from 78% (TAU) to 36% (MBCT), with p=.001, a large effect size (h=0.88), even larger than the original study's effect.

description: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) does not reduce relapse/recurrence in recovered depressed patients with only two (recent) previous episodes of major depression
original_authors: John D. Teasdale; Zindel V. Segal; James Williams; Valerie Ridgeway; Judith M. Soulsby; Mark A. Lau
original_title: Prevention of relapse/recurrence in major depression by mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Ma SH; Teasdale JD
replication_title: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Depression: Replication and Exploration of Differential Relapse Prevention Effects.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The earlier finding that a group of patients with two previous episodes of depression...showed no evidence of benefit from MBCT was also replicated.' In the 2-episode group, 50% of MBCT participants relapsed vs 20% of TAU participants, with no significant difference (Wald p=.231), matching the original's null finding.

description: Undetected changes in the orientation of visual stimuli influence subsequent orientation judgments (implicit change detection congruency effect), even after correcting for the spatial link confound identified by Mitroff et al.
original_authors: Diego Fernandez-Duque; Ian M. Thornton
original_title: Explicit mechanisms do not account for implicit localization and identification of change: an empirical reply to Mitroff et al.
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Cédric Laloyaux; Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
replication_title:
Implicit change identification: A replication of Fernandez-Duque and
                        Thornton (2003).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors explicitly call their study a 'conceptual replication' and conclude: 'Our results therefore replicate Fernandez-Duque and Thornton's (2003) findings and are thus congruent with the notion that changes in visual displays can be processed unconsciously.' They found a significant congruency effect for both aware and unaware trials on accuracy (F(1,20)=14.32, p<.001) and RT (F(1,20)=8.40, p<.008).

description: Participants trained on a serial reaction time task with 0 ms RSI cannot intentionally control the expression of their sequence knowledge, as shown by equivalent generation rates under inclusion and exclusion instructions (I = E) and above-baseline generation even under exclusion (E > B)
original_authors: Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
original_title: Can sequence learning be implicit? New evidence with the process dissociation procedure
replication_authors: Leonora Wilkinson; David R. Shanks
replication_title: Intentional Control and Implicit Sequence Learning.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: The authors explicitly describe Experiment 1 as an attempt to replicate Destrebecqz and Cleeremans's findings but with a between-participants design and an added probabilistic condition. The replication failed: participants showed I > E (capable of withholding sequence knowledge) and E = B (exclusion did not exceed baseline), directly contradicting D&C's claim that sequence knowledge in the no-RSI condition was outside intentional control.

description: Participants trained on a deterministic serial reaction time sequence with 0 ms RSI for 15 blocks (including a transfer block) cannot intentionally suppress the trained sequence during free-generation under exclusion instructions (E = I and E > B)
original_authors: Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
original_title: Can sequence learning be implicit? New evidence with the process dissociation procedure
replication_authors: Leonora Wilkinson; David R. Shanks
replication_title: Intentional Control and Implicit Sequence Learning.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 2 is described as 'a more exact replication of Destrebecqz and Cleeremans's study' using 15 training blocks with a transfer block and the same within-participants inclusion-then-exclusion design. The replication failed: participants showed I > E and E = B, which the authors describe as 'a direct failure to replicate the findings reported by Destrebecqz and Cleeremans.'

description: Participants trained on a serial reaction time task with 0 ms RSI cannot intentionally control the expression of their sequence knowledge, as shown by equivalent generation rates under inclusion and exclusion instructions (I = E) and above-baseline generation even under exclusion (E > B)
original_authors: Arnaud Destrebecqz; Axel Cleeremans
original_title: Can sequence learning be implicit? New evidence with the process dissociation procedure
replication_authors: Leonora Wilkinson; David R. Shanks
replication_title: Intentional Control and Implicit Sequence Learning.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 3 used a novel trial-by-trial generation procedure (rather than the original free-generation test) and extended training (15 or 45 blocks of probabilistic sequences), conceptually testing D&C's claim that sequence knowledge cannot be brought under intentional control. Again the claim failed to replicate: participants showed I > E and E = B under both training lengths, consistent with the findings in Experiments 1 and 2.

description: Disorientation (induced by spinning in place) results in a decrease in the precision of people's estimates of the relative directions to objects in their environment (the 'disorientation effect')
original_authors: Ranxiao Frances Wang; Elizabeth S. Spelke
original_title: Updating egocentric representations in human navigation
replication_authors: David Waller; Eric Hodgson
replication_title: Transient and enduring spatial representations under disorientation and self-rotation.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Variable error for egocentric pointing increased significantly as a result of disorientation, replicating the effect found by [Wang & Spelke].' Both Experiments 1 and 2 contain replication conditions following Wang & Spelke's procedure closely (same chamber, objects in same configuration, same measures), and the disorientation effect was reliably observed, though with smaller effect sizes (d ≈ 0.45–0.50) than the original (d ≈ 1.08).

description: Cluster analysis of alcohol-dependent veterans on the URICA identifies two motivational subtypes (precontemplators and contemplation-action), with theoretically consistent differences between groups on clinical dependent variables
original_authors: Frederick W. Willoughby; John F. Edens
original_title: Construct validity and predictive utility of the stages of change scale for alcoholics
replication_authors: John F. Edens; Frederick W. Willoughby
replication_title: Motivational patterns of alcohol dependent patients: A replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'Findings from Willoughby and Edens's (1996) study were partially replicated' — the two-cluster solution and some dependent variable differences (Guilt/Worry, Receptive to Help, Mood Management) replicated, but expected differences on Social Improvement and BDI did not replicate. The paper also reports a new finding (cluster differences in treatment completion) not found in the original.

description: Childhood cancer diagnosis has negative effects on parental distress and family environment, with mothers of children with cancer showing more psychological symptoms and family dysfunction than mothers of healthy comparison children
original_authors: Robert B. Noll; Andre Hawkins; Kathryn Vannatta; Maria A. Gartstein; W. Hobart Davies; William M. Bukowski
original_title: Comparing parental distress for families with children who have cancer and matched comparison families without children with cancer
replication_authors: Cynthia A. Gerhardt; Joeanne Gutzwiller; Kristine A. Huiet; Stephanie Fischer; Robert B. Noll; Kathryn Vannatta
replication_title: Parental adjustment to childhood cancer: A replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We completed a direct replication of an earlier study [35] to clarify the robustness and reliability of findings among a contemporary cohort of families of children with cancer.' Using identical inclusion criteria, procedures, and measures, 94% of effect sizes were replicated (45/48), compared to only 67% agreement by significance testing alone.

description: Wearing a heavy backpack (1/5 to 1/6 of body weight) causes participants to verbally estimate target distances as significantly farther away than participants not wearing a backpack
original_authors: Dennis R. Proffitt; Jeanine Stefanucci; Tom Banton; William Epstein
original_title: The role of effort in perceived distance
replication_authors: Adam J. Woods; John W. Philbeck; Jerome V. Danoff
replication_title: The various perceptions of distance: An alternative view of how effort affects distance judgments.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors conducted 'a strict methodological replication of Proffitt et al.'s (2003) backpack experiment' closely matching targets, setting, instructions, stimuli, design, trial numbers, and subjects. They found no effect of backpack condition (F(1,20) = 0.07, p = .79), concluding that effort-related effects 'occur under a relatively limited set of circumstances' and adding to literature suggesting some of Proffitt's effort-related findings 'may be more fragile than has been heretofore appreciated.'

description: Participants who toss a heavy ball verbally estimate target distances as significantly farther away than participants who toss a lighter ball
original_authors: Jessica K. Witt; Dennis R. Proffitt; William Epstein
original_title: Perceiving distance: A role of effort and intent
replication_authors: Adam J. Woods; John W. Philbeck; Jerome V. Danoff
replication_title: The various perceptions of distance: An alternative view of how effort affects distance judgments.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: In Experiments 2, 3, and 4 — spanning different conditions (no intention, intention to act, indoor, outdoor) — the authors found no significant effect of ball weight on verbal distance estimates (e.g., Experiment 2: F(1,20) = 1.3, p = .26; Experiment 3: F(1,20) = 0.44, p = .52; Experiment 4: F(1,20) = 0.06, p = .8). The general discussion concludes that 'our results from 96 participants in Experiments 1-4, in whom we found no effort-related effects' add to literature suggesting Proffitt/Witt effort-related findings 'may be more fragile than has been heretofore appreciated.'

description: Couples who cohabited before engagement (rather than after engagement or not at all before marriage) report lower marital quality and higher divorce risk
original_authors: Kline GH; Stanley SM; Markman HJ; Olmos-Gallo PA; St Peters M.; Whitton SW; Prado LM
original_title: Timing is everything: Pre-engagement cohabitation and increased risk for poor marital outcomes
replication_authors: Galena K. Rhoades; Scott M. Stanley; Howard J. Markman
replication_title: The pre-engagement cohabitation effect: A replication and extension of previous findings.
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'sought to replicate these findings' and conclude that 'the basic findings are in line with previous research,' though effect sizes were smaller than in the original convenience sample. Those who cohabited before engagement reported significantly lower marital satisfaction, dedication, confidence, and more negative communication than those who cohabited after engagement or not at all.

description: Study 1 (homogeneous case): Fisher-z and Pearson-r estimators and tests in fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis of correlations perform similarly under homogeneous correlation parameters, with specific bias and rejection rate patterns
original_authors: Andy P. Field
original_title: Meta-analysis of correlation coefficients: A Monte Carlo comparison of fixed- and random-effects models
replication_authors: Adam R. Hafdahl; Michelle A. Williams
replication_title: Meta-analysis of correlations revisited: Attempted replication and extension of Field's (2001) simulation studies.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Nearly all of Field's results under homogeneity (Study 1) were replicable.' The paper's abstract also confirms 'Field's results under homogeneity were mostly replicable.'

description: Study 2 (heterogeneous case): Fisher-z estimators exhibit substantial positive bias (over .1 and up to .2) for the mean Pearson-r correlation and specific rejection rate patterns when correlation parameters are heterogeneous
original_authors: Andy P. Field
original_title: Meta-analysis of correlation coefficients: A Monte Carlo comparison of fixed- and random-effects models
replication_authors: Adam R. Hafdahl; Michelle A. Williams
replication_title: Meta-analysis of correlations revisited: Attempted replication and extension of Field's (2001) simulation studies.
explanation: The authors state in the Discussion: 'most of those under heterogeneity (Study 2) were not [replicable]; in many conditions the latter discrepancies were both statistically and practically significant.' They conclude that 'Field's (2001) bias values are quite inflated, by up to over .17' and that results 'substantially under- and overstate rejection probabilities for tests of the mean correlation (up to over .60 too low) and homogeneity (up to over .65 too high), respectively.'

description: Recovery of conditioned responding to a target cue in a stimulus relative validity design when the reinforced companion cue is extinguished (retrospective revaluation)
original_authors: Robert P. Cole; Robert C. Barnet; Ralph R. Miller
original_title: Effect of relative stimulus validity: Learning or performance deficit?
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes
replication_authors: Bridget L. McConnell; Kouji Urushihara; Ralph R. Miller
replication_title: Contrasting predictions of extended comparator hypothesis and acquisition-focused models of learning concerning retrospective revaluation.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The current series of experiments replicated the retrospective revaluation effect and extended the findings to show that recovery of responding was specific to the target that had been trained with the revalued excitatory companion stimulus.' All three experiments demonstrated the retrospective revaluation effect consistent with the original finding.

description: Patients with schizophrenia show a specific context-processing deficit on the dot pattern expectancy (DPX) task, evidenced by making more BX errors relative to AY errors compared to healthy controls
original_authors: MacDonald, Angus W. III; Goghari, Vina M.; Hicks, Brian M.; Flory, Janine D.; Carter, Cameron S.; Manuck, Stephen B.
original_title: A convergent-divergent approach to context processing, general intellectual functioning, and the genetic liability to schizophrenia
replication_authors: Jessica A. H. Jones; Scott R. Sponheim; Angus W. MacDonald
replication_title: The dot pattern expectancy task: Reliability and replication of deficits in schizophrenia.
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'aimed to replicate these results in Study 3' and concluded: 'This study reported the first replication of a specific deficit in context processing in patients with schizophrenia as measured by the full version of the DPX.' The replication found a significant BX-AY error difference score (t(93) = 1.871, p = .033, d = 0.383) and significantly higher d'-context in controls vs. patients (t(87) = -2.409, p = .009, d = 0.511), consistent with the original findings.

description: Individuals with borderline personality disorder (BPD) show lower FFM trait stability (differential, mean-level, individual-level, and ipsative) compared to those with other personality disorders, particularly on neuroticism and conscientiousness, over a 6-year period
original_authors: Hopwood CJ; Newman DA; Donnellan MB; Markowitz JC; Grilo CM; Sanislow CA; Ansell EB; McGlashan TH; Skodol AE; Shea MT; Gunderson JG; Zanarini MC; Morey LC
original_title: The stability of personality traits in individuals with borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Christopher J. Hopwood; Mary C. Zanarini
replication_title: Five-factor trait instability in borderline relative to other personality disorders.
replication_journal: Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment
explanation: The replication partially succeeded: lower rank-order stability for conscientiousness, greater mean-level neuroticism decline for BPD, and greater individual-level conscientiousness instability were replicated. However, neuroticism differential and individual-level stability differences did not replicate, nor did mean-level conscientiousness differences. The authors state: 'whereas several specific effects replicated across CLPS and MSAD samples, some did not.'

description: Kindergarten math skills are the strongest predictor of later academic achievement, literacy and attention skills also predict later achievement, but socioemotional behaviors do not significantly predict later school achievement
original_authors: Greg J. Duncan; Chantelle J. Dowsett; Amy Claessens; Katherine Magnuson; Aletha C. Huston; Pamela Klebanov; Linda S. Pagani; Leon Feinstein; Mimi Engel; Jeanne Brooks-Gunn; Holly Sexton; Kathryn Duckworth; Crista Japel
original_title: School readiness and later achievement
replication_authors: Elisa Romano; Lyzon Babchishin; Linda S. Pagani; Dafna Kohen
replication_title: School readiness and later achievement: Replication and extension using a nationwide Canadian survey.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'NLSCY results were consistent with the general conclusions drawn from the six studies included in [Duncan et al.] in showing that better developed kindergarten math, reading, and attention skills significantly predicted better third-grade math and reading achievement, but kindergarten socioemotional behaviors generally were insignificant predictors.' The core findings of Duncan et al. were replicated using a new nationwide Canadian dataset (NLSCY, N=1,521), though new analyses using multiple imputation revealed some socioemotional effects not found in the original.

description: An integrated model combining ICF constructs (impairment) and theory of planned behavior constructs (PBC, intention) explains activity limitation better than either a biomedical (ICF) or behavioral (TPB) model alone in orthopedic patients awaiting joint replacement surgery
original_authors: Diane Dixon; Marie Johnston; David Rowley; Beth Pollard
original_title: Using the ICF and psychological models of behaviour to predict mobility limitations
replication_authors: Francis Quinn; Marie Johnston; Diane Dixon; Derek W. Johnston; Beth Pollard; David I. Rowley
replication_title: Testing the integration of ICF and behavioral models of disability in orthopedic patients: Replication and extension.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our findings clearly replicate those of Dixon et al. (2008) for orthopedic patients before surgery.' Before surgery, the integrated model fitted better and accounted for more variance (59%) than either the ICF model alone (35%) or the TPB model alone (48%), consistent with the original study's findings.

description: An integrated model combining ICF constructs (impairment) and theory of planned behavior constructs (PBC, intention) explains activity limitation better than either a biomedical (ICF) or behavioral (TPB) model alone in orthopedic patients awaiting joint replacement surgery
original_authors: Diane Dixon; Marie Johnston; David Rowley; Beth Pollard
original_title: Using the ICF and psychological models of behaviour to predict mobility limitations
replication_authors: Francis Quinn; Marie Johnston; Diane Dixon; Derek W. Johnston; Beth Pollard; David I. Rowley
replication_title: Testing the integration of ICF and behavioral models of disability in orthopedic patients: Replication and extension.
explanation: The authors extended Dixon et al.'s (2008) study by testing the same models 1 year post-surgery, a novel time point not tested in the original. Results showed even stronger model fit post-surgery: the integrated model accounted for 82% of the variance in activity limitation, and the authors state 'Our findings clearly replicate those of Dixon et al. (2008)...as well as after a surgical change in body structure and function.'

description: A scene preview session (viewing scenes before searching) does not facilitate later visual search efficiency — memory acquired during non-search tasks does not transfer to guide attention during subsequent search
original_authors: Vö, Melissa L.-H.; Wolfe, Jeremy M.
original_title: When does repeated search in scenes involve memory? Looking at versus looking for objects in scenes
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Andrew Hollingworth
replication_title: Task specificity and the influence of memory on visual search: Comment on Võ and Wolfe (2012).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The original Võ & Wolfe (2012b) found NO significant preview effect (preview did not improve search times). The replication, using a within-subjects design, found a robust preview benefit: 'elapsed time to target fixation was reliably shorter when the scene had been previewed (1475 ms) than when it had not (1578 ms), F(1, 46) = 12.0, p < .001'. The authors conclude 'visual memory representations formed in the context of a nonsearch task reliably transferred to visual search', directly refuting the original null result.

description: Repeated search across blocks — the second search for a particular target object is faster than the first, reflecting memory for target location
original_authors: Vö, Melissa L.-H.; Wolfe, Jeremy M.
original_title: When does repeated search in scenes involve memory? Looking at versus looking for objects in scenes
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Andrew Hollingworth
replication_title: Task specificity and the influence of memory on visual search: Comment on Võ and Wolfe (2012).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'There was a reliable effect of block, indicating that the second searches for the objects were more efficient than the first searches, F(1, 46) = 480, p < .001, ηp² = .91. This replicates repeated search effects in Vo and Wolfe (2012b).'

description: Multiple searches within a scene produce decreasing search times (distractor memory effect) — searching for multiple objects sequentially in the same scene facilitates later searches for other objects in that scene
original_authors: Vö, Melissa L.-H.; Wolfe, Jeremy M.
original_title: When does repeated search in scenes involve memory? Looking at versus looking for objects in scenes
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Andrew Hollingworth
replication_title: Task specificity and the influence of memory on visual search: Comment on Võ and Wolfe (2012).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The replication found a reliable linear effect of epoch in Block 1: 'F(1, 46) = 6.98, p = .01, ηp² = .13, indicating that search times decreased as searches progressed through the set of 12. This replicates the effects of multiple searches reported by Vö & Wolfe (2012a, 2012b).' The numerical magnitude was similar to the original (~87 ms vs ~91 ms).

description: An unconscious (masked) no-go prime slows go response times in a go/no-go task, indicating that response inhibition can be triggered unconsciously
original_authors: Simon van Gaal; K. Richard Ridderinkhof; H. Steven Scholte; Victor A. F. Lamme
original_title: Unconscious activation of the prefrontal no-go network
