replication_authors: Yu-Chin Chiu; Adam R. Aron
replication_title: Unconsciously triggered response inhibition requires an executive setting.
explanation: The authors explicitly adopted Van Gaal et al.'s (2010) go/no-go masked priming paradigm and state in the Discussion: 'Using the masked prime paradigm of van Gaal et al. (2010), we replicated their finding of RT slowing following no-go primes in a go/no-go task.' In Experiment 1, the post hoc t-test confirmed significantly longer RTs following no-go primes than go primes in the go/no-go condition, t(15) = -4.52, p < .01.

description: An unconscious (masked) no-go prime slows go response times in a go/no-go task, indicating that response inhibition can be triggered unconsciously
original_authors: Simon van Gaal; K. Richard Ridderinkhof; H. Steven Scholte; Victor A. F. Lamme
original_title: Unconscious activation of the prefrontal no-go network
replication_authors: Yu-Chin Chiu; Adam R. Aron
replication_title: Unconsciously triggered response inhibition requires an executive setting.
explanation: Experiment 2 replicated the go/no-go RT slowing effect with a larger sample and additional controls for learning and attention. The significant two-way interaction between executive setting and prime type, F(1,17) = 11.39, p < .01, confirmed the original finding, and post hoc t-tests showed significant RT slowing in the go/no-go task for both trial sets.

description: Universal preventive interventions implemented during early adolescence reduce young adult substance misuse (drunkenness, alcohol-related problems, cigarette use, illicit drug use) indirectly through delaying adolescent substance initiation
original_authors: Spoth, Richard; Trudeau, Linda; Guyll, Max; Shin, Chungyeol; Redmond, Cleve
original_title: Universal intervention effects on substance use among young adults mediated by delayed adolescent substance initiation
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Richard Spoth; Linda Trudeau; Cleve Redmond; Chungyeol Shin
replication_title: Replication RCT of early universal prevention effects on young adult substance misuse.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'there was general support for the replication and extension of the proposed developmental model of positive effects on reduced substance misuse in young adulthood through delayed initiation in adolescence.' Significant indirect intervention effects were found on all four young adult outcomes, consistent with the original model, though the current study used a different multicomponent intervention and added risk-moderation analyses.

description: People who engage in nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) have stronger implicit associations between self-injury and the self, as measured by the IAT, compared to those with no history of NSSI
original_authors: Nock, Matthew K.; Banaji, Mahzarin R.
original_title: Assessment of self-injurious thoughts using a behavioral test
replication_authors: Glenn JJ; Werntz AJ; Slama SJ; Steinman SA; Teachman BA; Nock MK
replication_title: Suicide and self-injury-related implicit cognition: A large-scale examination and replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results not only replicate prior laboratory and hospital studies demonstrating similar group differences for NSSI (Nock & Banaji, 2007a),' confirming successful replication of the NSSI IAT group differences in a large online community sample.

description: Adolescents with a history of suicide attempt have stronger implicit associations between suicide/death and the self, as measured by the IAT, compared to those with no history of suicide attempt
original_authors: Nock, Matthew K.; Banaji, Mahzarin R.
original_title: Prediction of suicide ideation and attempts among adolescents using a brief performance-based test
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Glenn JJ; Werntz AJ; Slama SJ; Steinman SA; Teachman BA; Nock MK
replication_title: Suicide and self-injury-related implicit cognition: A large-scale examination and replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results not only replicate prior laboratory and hospital studies demonstrating similar group differences for NSSI (Nock & Banaji, 2007a) and suicide attempt (Nock & Banaji, 2007b; Nock et al., 2010),' confirming successful replication of the suicide attempt IAT group differences in a large online community sample.

description: Individuals with a history of suicide attempt have stronger implicit associations between suicide/death and the self, as measured by the IAT, and these associations predict future suicidal behavior above and beyond other known risk factors
original_authors: Nock, Matthew K.; Park, Jane M.; Finn, Christine T.; Deliberto, Tara L.; Dour, Halina J.; Banaji, Mahzarin R.
original_title: Measuring the suicidal mind: Implicit cognition predicts suicidal behavior
replication_authors: Glenn JJ; Werntz AJ; Slama SJ; Steinman SA; Teachman BA; Nock MK
replication_title: Suicide and self-injury-related implicit cognition: A large-scale examination and replication.
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the current study replicated prior studies including Nock et al. (2010) showing group differences in IAT scores for suicide attempt history, with the Suicide IAT producing the largest effect size (d = 0.54) in the suicide attempter vs. control comparison in the initial sample.

description: Patients with schizophrenia show a preferential impairment in anticipatory (representational) goal-directed responding relative to consummatory (evoked) responding on the Anticipatory and Consummatory Pleasure (ACP) task, as well as a link between emotion-behaviour coupling and working memory function
original_authors: Erin A. Heerey; James M. Gold
original_title: Patients with schizophrenia demonstrate dissociation between affective experience and motivated behavior
replication_authors: Joyce Yuen Ting Lam; Marcus Hoi Fung Ng; Po Yee Ivy Cheng; Maritta Välimäki; Benjamin K. Yee
replication_title: Coexpression of anticipatory and consummatory volitional deficits in schizophrenia and their association with memory impairment.
replication_journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science
explanation: The replication confirmed robust deficits in both anticipatory and consummatory responding in schizophrenia ('consolidated the presence of robust impairment in both types of response'), but explicitly challenged the key original finding of a preferential anticipatory impairment: 'the majority of ACP studies failed to substantiate the hypothesis that schizophrenia selectively undermines willed actions incentivized by anticipatory emotional reinforcement.' The working memory correlation was also clarified — it was unique to the SZ group only, differing from the pooled-sample finding of Heerey and Gold (2007).

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 1 (overt study/test instructions) replicated the core age-related deficit in lure discrimination from the original study. The authors state: 'Consistent with our previous findings, post hoc t tests revealed a decrease in the LDI for aging adults compared to young (t(100) = 4.5, 95% CI [.09, .29]), but no difference in REC between groups.' The study used participants from the original Stark et al. (2013) study as a comparison group.

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 2 (continuous self-paced recognition paradigm) replicated the age-related deficit in lure discrimination. The authors conclude: 'Despite this change in task design, from a study/test format to a continuous recognition test with no response deadline, the aging impairment on the LDI remained.' Statistics show a significant main effect of age group, F(1,42)=8.1, p<.01, and a significant interaction F(1,42)=12.6, p<.01.

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 3 (old/new response format with confidence ratings) replicated the age-related bias toward old responses for lure items. Using d' signal detection analysis, older adults showed a greater disparity between the lure and foil distributions than younger adults (F(1,88)=4.3, p<.05, interaction), consistent with the original finding. The authors conclude: 'again reinforcing the greater overlap in the distribution between lures and repeats for older adults.'

description: Older adults show age-related declines in lure discrimination (LDI) in the Mnemonic Similarity Task, identifying similar lures as old items at a greater rate than young adults, while recognition memory for repeated items remains intact
original_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Michael A. Yassa; Joyce W. Lacy; Craig E.L. Stark
original_title: A task to assess behavioral pattern separation (BPS) in humans: Data from healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
replication_authors: Shauna M. Stark; Rebecca Stevenson; Claudia Wu; Samantha Rutledge; Craig E. L. Stark
replication_title: Stability of age-related deficits in the mnemonic similarity task across task variations.
explanation: Experiment 4 (gist/veridical instructions) replicated the age-related deficit under veridical instructions. Even when instructed to respond 'new' to lures, older adults continued to endorse lures as old items. The authors conclude: 'Whereas the younger adults were able to modify their responses based on task instructions, the aging adults were unable to overcome their impairment in lure discrimination to improve their performance in the veridical condition.'

description: Inducing empathy via perspective-taking instructions increases altruistic helping (volunteering) even when social evaluation is low, supporting the empathy-altruism hypothesis
original_authors: Fultz J.; Batson CD; Fortenbach VA; McCarthy PM; Varney LL
original_title: Social evaluation and the empathy-altruism hypothesis
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Thomas G. McCauley; William H. B. McAuliffe; Michael E. McCullough
replication_title: Does empathy promote helping by activating altruistic motivation or concern about social evaluation? A direct replication of Fultz et al. (1986).
explanation: The supplemental material explicitly labels Prediction 3 as 'the focal hypothesis from Fultz et al., 1986' and reports that neither the empathy manipulation (b = 0.09, p = .699), social evaluation manipulation (b = -0.00, p = .987), nor their interaction (b = -0.03, p = .934) significantly predicted volunteering (Table S2). The failure is confirmed across multiple analyses: the original pre-registration model also showed null results for all three predictors (empathy: b = 0.17, p = .705; Table S7), and exploratory sex (Tables S8-9) and race (Tables S10-12) subgroup analyses likewise showed null empathy effects in every subgroup. The available file is the supplemental material only; no main paper body is present. However, this does not create ambiguity about the result — the statistics are explicit, the authors themselves identify Prediction 3 as the focal Fultz et al. hypothesis, and the null outcome is consistent across every analysis conducted. The replication type is 'close experiment' rather than 'direct' because the authors note several protocol differences from Fultz et al. (1986): only one communicator note vs. two, different note content, both-sex vs. female-only sample, different note-disposal procedure, different volunteering scale (11-point vs. 5-point), additional individual-differences measures, and a different analytic strategy (negative binomial regression vs. 2x2 ANOVA).

description: Couples can be classified into distinct typologies (Validators, Volatiles, Avoiders, Hostile, and Hostile-Detached) based on their observed conflict communication behavior, with typologies predicting relationship satisfaction
original_authors: John M. Gottman
original_title: The roles of conflict engagement, escalation, and avoidance in marital interaction: A longitudinal view of five types of couples
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology

explanation: The authors explicitly state that their five-class solution is 'largely concordant with previous findings' and that results should 'increase the field's confidence in groups found with smaller, homogeneous samples (e.g., Fitzpatrick, 1988; Gottman, 1993).' The five typologies identified mirror Gottman's (1993) groups, confirming the generalizability of his original typology in a much larger, diverse multi-site sample.

description: Couples can be classified into three communication typologies (Traditional, Independent, and Separate) based on their interaction patterns and levels of independence

replication_title: Testing the generalizability of couple communication typologies: A multisite replication and extension study.
explanation: Reviewer confirmed medium confidence is appropriate. The paper's Discussion states the five-class solution is 'largely concordant with previous findings' and increases confidence in groups from Fitzpatrick (1988) and Gottman (1993). Four of the five groups are said to 'resemble typologies identified by Gottman (1993) and Fitzpatrick (1988).' However, the paper never explicitly maps its five groups to Fitzpatrick's three-category scheme (Traditional, Independent, Separate), the methodologies differ fundamentally (observational RMICS coding vs. Fitzpatrick's self-report), and the number of categories differs (five vs. three). The authors note 'some of our findings differ from existing typologies' and describe three specific divergences. The success classification is defensible given the authors' stated concordance, but the Fitzpatrick-specific mapping is genuinely ambiguous. Ambiguity is real and confidence is appropriately medium.

explanation: The replication successfully reproduced the finding that premorbid adjustment and manifest distress predict improvement (overall R = .57 vs. original .59, both significant), but failed to replicate the finding for negative expectations: 'In this study we were unable to replicate the previously observed relationship between negative expectations regarding psychotherapy...and poor outcome in such a hospital setting.'

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated the finding that the effect of word frequency can be accommodated entirely by changes in the drift rate (Ratcliff et al., 2004).' The same diffusion model paradigm and word frequency manipulation were used with a different (preclinical AD risk) population.

description: Family history of Alzheimer's disease confers cognitive deficits (composite measures of processing speed, memory and executive functioning) in otherwise cognitively healthy individuals even after controlling for APOE genotype

original_journal: The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry

replication_title: A diffusion model analysis of episodic recognition in preclinical individuals with a family history for Alzheimer’s disease: The adult children study.
explanation: The Introduction explicitly cites Donix et al. (2012) as needing replication due to small sample size (n=42), and the current paper's results support the core finding that family history confers cognitive deficits independent of APOE genotype. Across both experiments, family history+ individuals showed significantly lower drift rates (Exp 1: p=.04, eta2=.043; Exp 2: p=.02, eta2=.03). The General Discussion confirms 'subtle but detectable cognitive deficits relative to family history- controls.' However, medium confidence is retained because: (1) the operationalization differs substantially — the original used composite neuropsychological measures (processing speed, memory, executive functioning), while the replication uses diffusion model drift rate; (2) crucially, the current paper found that standard neuropsychological tests did NOT show the family history effect, with drift rate predicting group membership above and beyond those tests — making this a partial or reformulated replication rather than a direct confirmation of the original composite-measure finding; (3) the accuracy effect only reached significance in Experiment 1 (not Experiment 2, p=.08). The finding supports the directional claim that FH confers cognitive risk, but the specific measures through which this manifests differ from the original.

explanation: The authors explicitly state they are replicating McGee Ng et al. (2016) using an analog simulation design instead of a known-groups criterion design. Results confirmed the original finding: the MANOVA was highly significant (Pillai's trace = 0.79, F(10,442) = 28.80, p < .001, η² = .40), with medium-to-large effect sizes for mean differences across response style conditions, and the authors conclude that 'there are now results from both simulation and criterion design studies that converge on the same finding, suggesting that these results are robustly replicable.'

The replication found t(60) = -0.21, p = .83, d = 0.05, with Bayesian analyses providing 'substantial evidence in favor of the null hypothesis' (BF0 = 4.49).

replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: The DAM's basic predictive validity was replicated (it was positively correlated with attitudes in all 14 instances across Studies 1–3), partially supporting Hypothesis 1 from H&A 2013. However, the incremental validity of the DAM beyond the established NOSQ was not supported — the DAM did not consistently explain unique variance in attitudes after controlling for the NOSQ ('The utility of the DAM…is greatly diminished by the inclusion of the NOSQ'). The authors conclude the DAM and NOSQ assess the same underlying construct, which limits the novelty of H&A's claim.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The present study replicated the results of the Orth et al. (2008) study in a notable manner, in regard to the comparability of the coefficients, and therefore, corroborates the vulnerability model (and not the scar or the common-factor model).' Cross-lagged paths from self-esteem to depression were significant (-.23 and -.24, ps < .001), closely matching the original averaged coefficient of -.21, while paths from depression to self-esteem were non-significant as in the original.

replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 1 is described as 'a direct replication of previous cross-cultural research on the religiosity-adjustment relation' (Discussion section). The paper's abstract states 'Our results fully and firmly replicated and extended prior evidence for cross-cultural differences in religious adjustment benefits.' The cross-level interaction between personal and country-level religiosity was replicated (PE = .04 [.03, .05]), and the pattern (strong religiosity-esteem relation in religious countries, weak in secular countries) fully matched RASV predictions.

It again showed no effect of order on probability estimates (F<1), with means in the opposite direction to Vosgerau's findings. A Bayesian meta-analysis across Experiments 2, 3, and 4 showed 6.08:1 evidence in favor of the null hypothesis over the SLH.

description: Study 1: Participants provide higher probability estimates for future events when answering on bright pink paper (assumed to increase arousal) compared to grey paper (assumed not to evoke arousal)
original_authors: Joachim Vosgerau
original_title: How prevalent is wishful thinking? Misattribution of arousal causes optimism and pessimism in subjective probabilities
replication_authors: Laura de Molière; Adam J. L. Harris
replication_title: Conceptual and direct replications fail to support the stake-likelihood hypothesis as an explanation for the interdependence of utility and likelihood judgments.
explanation: Experiment 5 closely followed Vosgerau's Study 1 procedure (same paper color manipulation, same probability scale, similar participant recruitment), but used updated questions relevant to UK participants in 2014. Color did not significantly impact probability estimates: F(1,169)=1.05, p=.31, η²=.01. The authors concluded: 'we observed no evidence for an increase in probability estimates when participants provided their estimates on pink ('arousing') compared to grey ('unarousing') paper in Experiment 5.'

description: The action-sentence compatibility effect (ACE): processing sentences implying movement toward or away from the body facilitates congruent motor responses and interferes with incongruent responses, indicating that language comprehension is grounded in bodily action
original_authors: Arthur M. Glenberg; Michael P. Kaschak
original_title: Grounding language in action
replication_authors: Megan H. Papesh
replication_title: Just out of reach: On the reliability of the action-sentence compatibility effect.
explanation: Across 8 experiments using mouse-movement and button-press paradigms (including experiments using the original stimuli from Glenberg & Kaschak), the ACE could not be replicated. The conclusion states: 'the ACE, a key finding supporting the embodiment hypothesis for language comprehension, could not be replicated. It did not emerge in a mouse-movement paradigm with new sentences, or with the original sentences from Glenberg and Kaschak (2002), nor did it emerge in a paradigm that closely matched the original study.'

description: The action-sentence compatibility effect (ACE): processing sentences implying movement toward or away from the body facilitates congruent motor responses and interferes with incongruent responses, using original stimuli and near-identical response apparatus (button-press response box)
original_authors: Arthur M. Glenberg; Michael P. Kaschak
original_title: Grounding language in action
replication_authors: Megan H. Papesh
replication_title: Just out of reach: On the reliability of the action-sentence compatibility effect.
explanation: Experiments 7 and 8 used the original stimuli from Glenberg & Kaschak (2002) and keyboards modified to closely approximate the original response box. Neither experiment produced the ACE: in Experiment 7, the ACE interaction was not reliable (F(1,58)=3.68, p=.06), and in Experiment 8, no ACE interaction was observed (F(1,85)=0.14, p=.71). The author concludes the effect 'did not emerge in a paradigm that closely matched the original study.'

description: Concurrent spatial working memory load reduces distractor interference in a spatial Stroop-like task (Experiment 3b)
original_authors: So-Yeon Kim; Min-Shik Kim; Marvin M. Chun
original_title: Concurrent working memory load can reduce distraction
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño; Franca Stablum; Carlo Umiltà
replication_title: Can concurrent memory load reduce distraction? A replication study and beyond.
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate Kim et al.'s results' for Experiment 1, which added a neutral condition and more trials to the original Experiment 3b paradigm. The interaction between load and congruency was not significant (F < 1), in contrast to the significant beneficial WM load effect found by Kim et al.

description: Concurrent spatial working memory load reduces distractor interference in a spatial Stroop-like task (Experiment 3b) — exact replication without neutral condition
original_authors: So-Yeon Kim; Min-Shik Kim; Marvin M. Chun
original_title: Concurrent working memory load can reduce distraction
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño; Franca Stablum; Carlo Umiltà
replication_title: Can concurrent memory load reduce distraction? A replication study and beyond.
explanation: Experiment 2 was an exact replication of Kim et al.'s Experiment 3b (same two conditions, same stimulus sizes). The authors state: 'Once again, we have not replicated Kim et al.'s (2005, Experiment 3b) results.' The interaction was significant but in the opposite direction — larger congruency effects under WM load (63 ms) vs. SSL-only (37 ms), the reverse of Kim et al.'s finding.

description: Concurrent spatial working memory load reduces distractor interference in a spatial Stroop-like task (Experiment 3b) — tested with directional arrow WM task to maximize WM-distractor overlap
original_authors: So-Yeon Kim; Min-Shik Kim; Marvin M. Chun
original_title: Concurrent working memory load can reduce distraction
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño; Franca Stablum; Carlo Umiltà
replication_title: Can concurrent memory load reduce distraction? A replication study and beyond.
explanation: Experiment 3 modified the WM task to use arrows (same directional information as distractors) to maximize WM-distractor overlap per Kim et al.'s hypothesis, and used an easier WM task to achieve comparable accuracy (0.88 vs. Kim et al.'s ~0.85). The authors state: 'Once more, we have failed to replicate Kim et al.'s (2005) results.' No reduction in congruency effects under WM load was found; instead, interference increased under WM + SSL for RTs.

description: Participants are less trusting of consequentialist others than deontological others in trust game social dilemmas, based on knowing the moral judgment those others made on a trolley dilemma
original_authors: Everett JA; Pizarro DA; Crockett MJ
original_title: Inference of trustworthiness from intuitive moral judgments
replication_authors: Dries H. Bostyn; Arne Roets
replication_title: Trust, trolleys and social dilemmas: A replication study.
explanation: Study 1 used a different multi-phase methodology but found the same core effect: participants were more trusting of deontological others (M=4.21) than consequentialist others (M=3.68), t(207)=5.29, p<.001, d=0.52. The authors state: 'these results constitute a strong replication of the findings of Everett et al. (2016).'

description: Participants are less trusting of consequentialist others than deontological others in trust game social dilemmas, based on knowing the moral judgment those others made on a trolley dilemma
original_authors: Everett JA; Pizarro DA; Crockett MJ
original_title: Inference of trustworthiness from intuitive moral judgments
replication_authors: Dries H. Bostyn; Arne Roets
replication_title: Trust, trolleys and social dilemmas: A replication study.
explanation: Study 2 extended the effect to a public goods game context (instead of trust games), finding that subjects were more trusting of deontological others (M=3.63) than consequentialist others (M=3.39), t(98)=3.43, p<.001, d=.41. The authors conclude 'results of the second study corroborate the key finding of Everett et al. (2016) once more.'

description: Extensive (3-day) instrumental training leads to habit formation in humans, as evidenced by greater insensitivity to outcome devaluation (food satiation) compared to briefly (1-day) trained participants
original_authors: Elizabeth Tricomi; Bernard W. Balleine; John P. O’Doherty
original_title: A specific role for posterior dorsolateral striatum in human habit learning
replication_authors: Sanne de Wit; Merel Kindt; Sarah L. Knot; Aukje A. C. Verhoeven; Trevor W. Robbins; Julia Gasull-Camos; Michael Evans; Hira Mirza; Claire M. Gillan
replication_title: Shifting the balance between goals and habits: Five failures in experimental habit induction.
explanation: Experiment 3A (NYU) explicitly aimed to replicate Tricomi et al. (2009) as closely as possible. The authors found no Group × Value interaction (F < 1, Bayes factor = 3.96 in favor of null), concluding: 'In contrast to Tricomi et al., (2009), we did not find any evidence for habit induction as a consequence of overtraining.'

description: Extensive (3-day) instrumental training leads to habit formation in humans, as evidenced by greater insensitivity to outcome devaluation (food satiation) compared to briefly (1-day) trained participants
original_authors: Elizabeth Tricomi; Bernard W. Balleine; John P. O’Doherty
original_title: A specific role for posterior dorsolateral striatum in human habit learning
replication_authors: Sanne de Wit; Merel Kindt; Sarah L. Knot; Aukje A. C. Verhoeven; Trevor W. Robbins; Julia Gasull-Camos; Michael Evans; Hira Mirza; Claire M. Gillan
replication_title: Shifting the balance between goals and habits: Five failures in experimental habit induction.
explanation: Experiment 3B (University of Amsterdam) independently attempted to replicate Tricomi et al. (2009) and also failed. The Group × Value interaction was non-significant (F < 1, Bayes factor = 3.71 against interaction), with both 1-day and 3-day groups showing equal sensitivity to outcome devaluation. The authors concluded: 'Experiment 3B (like Experiment 3A) failed to replicate the previously reported effect of overtraining on outcome devaluation sensitivity (Tricomi et al., 2009).'

description: Despite instructions to respond randomly to a trivia quiz, participants answer significantly more easy questions correctly than hard questions, demonstrating that knowledge automatically influences responding without participants' awareness (sense of agency is disrupted: estimates of accuracy are far below actual accuracy)
original_authors: Daniel M. Wegner; Valerie A. Fuller; Betsy Sparrow
original_title: Clever hands: Uncontrolled intelligence in facilitated communication
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Vince Polito; Amanda J. Barnier; Michael H. Connors
replication_title: Hypnotic clever hands: Agency and automatic responding.
explanation: The Discussion section heading reads 'Quiz One: Replicating Wegner's Clever Hands' and explicitly states: 'As in Wegner et al.'s (2003) original study, participants in quiz one produced significantly more correct responses for easy questions than for hard questions, indicating that, despite the instruction to respond randomly, knowledge of the correct answers strongly influenced their responses.'

description: Sound-shape association (SSA) — congruence between auditory pitch and visual shape (spiky vs. smooth) — modulates multisensory temporal resolution as measured by a temporal order judgment (TOJ) task
original_authors: Parise, Cesare V.; Spence, Charles
original_title: When birds of a feather flock together: Synesthetic correspondences modulate audiovisual integration in non-synesthetes
replication_authors: Suddha Sourav; Brigitte Röder; Franka Ambsdorf; Andromachi Melissari; Miketa Arvaniti; Argiro Vatakis
replication_title: No evidence that sound–shape associations influence temporal resolution in humans: Five nonreplications of Parise and Spence (2009) and meta-analyses.
explanation: Independent review confirms this is an unambiguous failure to replicate. The paper title itself states 'Five Non-Replications of Parise and Spence (2009).' The supplemental material (S2) states explicitly: 'We found no evidence that SSA modulated temporal resolution, irrespective of visual stimulus size' (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p = .610). The supplemental S3 heading is 'No Evidence That SSA Modulates Reaction Times in a Temporal Order Judgement Task' (HGAM, p = .989). The key experiment (preregistered Experiment 3) directly targeted the SSA-TOJ effect from Parise and Spence (2009) Experiment 2. Multiple converging null results across primary (JND) and secondary (RT) measures, preregistered design, and the authors' own framing as non-replications all support a clear failure classification with high confidence.

description: Gender differences in salary negotiation are mediated by women's anticipated backlash and attenuated when negotiating on behalf of others (other-advocacy), such that women request lower salaries than men only when negotiating for themselves
original_authors: Amanatullah, Emily T.; Morris, Michael W.
original_title: Negotiating gender roles: Gender differences in assertive negotiating are mediated by women's fear of backlash and attenuated when negotiating on behalf of others
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Jens Mazei; Julia B. Bear; Rebecca Schaumberg; Joachim Hüffmeier
replication_title: Explaining gender differences in negotiation: A close replication of Amanatullah and Morris (2010).
explanation: The available file is the Online Supplement only; the main manuscript is not in the folder. The supplement repeatedly defers to the main manuscript for primary results, which limits full classification. However, the supplement provides clear evidence on the central test: the moderated mediation — the effect of gender on salary requests through anticipated backlash, moderated by advocacy condition — was not significant (index of moderated mediation = 809.30, 95% CI [-19,189.63; 18,148.09]). This CI is enormous and clearly spans zero, constituting a definitive failure to replicate the original's headline finding (that the gender-backlash-salary mediation is attenuated in other-advocacy). The b-path (anticipated backlash predicting salary requests) did replicate (p < .001). An additional analysis found that backlash mediated the gender effect on salary requests within the self-advocacy condition alone (indirect effect = -1,711.97, 95% CI [-3,285.97; -304.97]), suggesting partial support for the mediation mechanism but only when the moderation is stripped away. The supplement also references significant gender effects on backlash and salary requests in the main manuscript. Overall: the core moderated mediation (the original's distinctive contribution) failed; a simpler, partial version of the mediation (within self-advocacy only) was supported. Classified as failure because the original paper's central claim — that the gender gap is specifically attenuated under other-advocacy — did not replicate. Confidence remains medium due to the absence of the main manuscript's Discussion/Conclusion.

description: Subliminal primes (masked) and supraliminal primes have opposite effects on reaction times: congruent supraliminal primes speed responses while congruent subliminal primes slow responses (masked inhibition effect / negative compatibility effect)
original_authors: Martin Eimer; Friederike Schlaghecken
original_title: Effects of masked stimuli on motor activation: Behavioral and electrophysiological evidence
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Theresa Wildegger; Nicholas E. Myers; Glyn Humphreys; Anna C. Nobre
replication_title: Supraliminal but not subliminal distracters bias working memory recall.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the expected pattern of speeded RTs following congruent supraliminal primes and slowed RTs following congruent subliminal primes (Eimer & Schlaghecken, 1998, 2002)' and in the Discussion: 'The results replicated previous findings (Eimer & Schlaghecken, 1998, 2002).' The replication was successful in both Experiments 1a and 1b with new orientation stimuli replacing the original arrow stimuli.

description: Abruptly changing surface features (color/luminance) of moving objects disrupts or reverses the object-specific preview benefit in the object-reviewing paradigm
original_authors: Cathleen M. Moore; Teresa Stephens; Elisabeth Hein
original_title: Features, as well as space and time, guide object persistence
replication_authors: Anja Fiedler; Cathleen M. Moore
replication_title: Illumination frame of reference in the object-reviewing paradigm: A case of luminance and lightness.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results of Experiment 1: 'There was a significantly reversed OSPB when disks moved on a plain gray background. This replicates previous findings showing that OSBPs are disrupted and can even reverse when surface features change abruptly (Moore, Stephens, & Hein, 2010).' The reversed OSPB was statistically significant (t(15) = 2.37, p = .031), consistent with Moore et al.'s (2010) findings.

description: Subjects who are overall more confident in their thought probe responses show a greater distinction in response time variability between reports of on-task and mind wandering (between-subjects moderating effect of confidence on thought-report validity)
original_authors: Paul Seli; Tanya R. Jonker; James Allan Cheyne; Kassandra Cortes; Daniel Smilek
original_title: Can research participants comment authoritatively on the validity of their self-reports of mind wandering and task engagement?
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Matt E. Meier
replication_title: Can research participants comment authoritatively on the validity of their self-reports of mind wandering and task engagement? A replication and extension of Seli, Jonker, Cheyne, Cortes, and Smilek (2015).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The replication found no evidence for the between-subjects moderating effect: confidence did not moderate the relation between mind wandering propensity and response time variability (F(1,287) = 0.06, p = .80, ΔR² = .0002), and a Bayesian model comparison favored the null by a factor of 4.5. The author concludes: 'I found no evidence that mean confidence moderates the report type and response time variability relation.'

description: When subjects report low confidence on individual thought probe responses, reports of mind wandering and on-task are not distinguished by response time variability (within-subjects effect of confidence on thought-report validity)
original_authors: Paul Seli; Tanya R. Jonker; James Allan Cheyne; Kassandra Cortes; Daniel Smilek
original_title: Can research participants comment authoritatively on the validity of their self-reports of mind wandering and task engagement?
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Matt E. Meier
replication_title: Can research participants comment authoritatively on the validity of their self-reports of mind wandering and task engagement? A replication and extension of Seli, Jonker, Cheyne, Cortes, and Smilek (2015).
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: Results were mixed across analyses: the ANOVA with complete cases showed no significant interaction (F(2,120) = 1.90, p = .15, η²p = .03 vs. original η²p = .20), while the ANOVA with imputed data showed a significant interaction (F(2,580) = 5.31, p = .005, η²p = .02 vs. original η²p = .07). The author concludes these within-subjects effects are 'not robust,' citing the modest effect sizes and Bayesian analyses showing the data do not discriminate between models with and without the interaction.

description: Placing hands near a to-be-remembered array decreased visual working memory for color but increased memory for orientation, reflecting differential effects of hand proximity on magnocellular vs. parvocellular visual processing
original_authors: Kelly, Shane P.; Brockmole, James R.
original_title: Hand proximity differentially affects visual working memory for color and orientation in a binding task
replication_authors: Tomer Sahar; Tal Makovski
replication_title: Grab that face, hammer, or line: No effect of hands position on visual memory.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. Sahar & Makovski (2019) ran 7 experiments; Experiment 7 was an explicit direct replication following Kelly & Brockmole (2014) original analyses. The paper title ('No Effect of Hands Position on Visual Memory') states the conclusion unambiguously. Bayesian analysis (Table S-4) across all experiments consistently favors the null: Exp 7 overall BF = 3.3 in favor of null; Exp 7 Orientation BF = 6.9 in favor of null; Exp 7 M-P hypothesis BF = 20.7 against for color and 7.07 against for orientation. The one ambiguous signal — Exp 7 Color null BF = 0.833 (only weak support for null) — does not undermine the failure classification: the d' values for color in Exp 7 show near-hands numerically *better* than far (1.45 vs. 1.326), i.e., opposite to Kelly & Brockmole's direction (near should decrease color memory), making this a failure in direction as well as in significance. No experiment across the 7 reported a replication of the near-hands effect on visual working memory.

description: Semantically richer (pre-modified) words yield an encoding cost (slower reading during encoding) and a subsequent retrieval benefit (faster reading times on the retrieval-triggering verb) relative to unmodified words during language comprehension
original_authors: Karimi, Hossein; Diaz, Michele; Wittenberg, Evelyn
original_title: Expectation, attention & memory retrieval during sentence processing
replication_authors: Hossein Karimi; Jaden Zinn
replication_title: The facilitatory effect of modifications (semantic richness) on subsequent retrieval during language comprehension is age-invariant, but depends on level of engagement with task.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: The encoding cost of modification was clearly replicated ('we replicated the modification (semantic richness) effect for pre-modified words during encoding'; Discussion). The retrieval benefit was also replicated, but only for the Low Engagement group — it was absent for the High Engagement group. The authors explicitly frame this as a successful replication with a newly-identified moderator variable (task engagement), not as a failure. The re-analysis of the independent Karimi et al. (2023) dataset (N=333) confirmed the same engagement-dependent pattern. The authors' own conclusion is that the modification-induced retrieval benefit does replicate under the appropriate engagement conditions, and the engagement moderation itself is presented as a positive new finding consistent with 'resolution-without-retrieval' theory. Confidence remains medium because the conditional nature of the retrieval replication — present only for ~50% of participants — means reasonable reviewers could classify this as 'inconclusive' rather than 'success'. The 'success' classification follows the authors' framing and the fact that the effect replicated in the theoretically predicted direction for the subgroup where it was expected to emerge.

description: Narratively coherent event pairs (events that can be meaningfully integrated into a single narrative) are recalled in greater detail than unrelated event pairs (events sharing a recurring character but no meaningful narrative link)
original_authors: Brendan I. Cohn-Sheehy; Angelique I. Delarazan; Jordan E. Crivelli-Decker; Zachariah M. Reagh; Nidhi S. Mundada; Andrew P. Yonelinas; Jeffrey M. Zacks; Charan Ranganath
original_title: Narratives bridge the divide between distant events in episodic memory
replication_authors: Angelique I. Delarazan; Elena Bosak; Brendan I. Cohn-Sheehy; Veronica Foureaux-Lee; Jeffrey M. Zacks; Zachariah M. Reagh
replication_title: Narrative coherence warps the timeline of recalled naturalistic events.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Experiment 1 replicated the finding that narrative coherence increases the likelihood that events are remembered (Cohn-Sheehy, Delarazan, et al. 2022)' and in the General Discussion: 'We replicated and extended prior work (Cohn-Sheehy, Delarazan, et al. 2022) demonstrating that narrative coherence enhanced recall.' The coherence effect was significant in all experiments (Exp 1A: F(1,38)=37.06, p<.001; Exp 1B: F(1,35)=16.90, p<.001; Exp 2: F(1,38)=33.53, p<.001).

description: Exposure to post-event misleading information causes participants to misremember details of a previously witnessed event (the misinformation effect)
original_authors: Loftus, Elizabeth F.; Miller, David G.; Burns, Helen J.
original_title: Semantic integration of verbal information into a visual memory
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory
replication_authors: Sera Wiechert; Amelie Verschueren; Gershon Ben-Shakhar; Yoni Pertzov; Elizabeth F. Loftus; Bruno Verschuere
replication_title: The misinformation effect: A contemporary replication and extension of Loftus et al. (1978) to investigate its underlying mechanisms.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Independent review confirms: the PDF filed under this DOI (10.1037/xlm0001529) is exclusively a 3-page Open Practices Disclosure form — not the actual article. The form reveals the full manuscript title ('The misinformation effect: A contemporary replication and extension of Loftus et al. (1978) to investigate its underlying mechanisms') and authors (Wiechert, Verschueren, Ben-Shakhar, Pertzov, Loftus, Verschuere), confirming this is a replication/extension of the classic misinformation effect. The form also shows the study was preregistered (OSF: osf.io/6c2dn for original replication, osf.io/5f387 betting form study, osf.io/y75c8 reversed order study), the plan was registered prior to data collection, and no changes were made to the preregistered analysis. However, there is no Methods, Results, or Discussion content available in any of the extracted files (abstract.md and body.md are also just the same disclosure form). The 'close extension' classification is reasonable given 'replication and extension' in the title. Result must remain 'inconclusive' — no paper content exists in the available files to determine whether the misinformation effect was replicated. Low confidence is warranted; this is a file ingestion problem, not genuine ambiguity in the paper's conclusions.

description: Interphase cells derived from the muscle of newborn dystrophic chickens have greatly diminished cytoplasmic microtubule complexes, suggesting a specific defect in the microtubule-organising centres
original_authors: Shay, J.; Fuseler, J.
original_title: Diminished cytoplasmic microtubule complexes in interphase cells derived from the muscle of newborn dystrophic chickens
replication_authors: Peiris JS; Porterfield JS
replication_title: Antibody-mediated enhancement of Flavivirus replication in macrophage-like cell lines
explanation: Independent review confirms a clear replication failure. The replicating paper (Connolly, Kalnins & Barber, 1979) states explicitly: 'Unlike Shay and Fuseler, we find no lack of a microtubular network in cells derived from cardiac or skeletal muscle of chickens carrying the dystrophic gene (am). Furthermore, our examination of fibroblasts from persons with DMD revealed a similar extensive network of microtubules in each case.' This is an unambiguous failure to replicate in both the original chicken model and in the extended DMD fibroblast context. The citation sentence correctly identifies Shay and Fuseler as reference 5 in the paper (cited as 'recently' reported, consistent with ~1979). The year 1979 cannot be independently confirmed from the available reference list (the PDF's reference list for this article was not captured), but the in-text description as 'recent' and the publication date of the replicating paper (November 1979) make this highly plausible. Confidence is set to high on the result classification; the year field remains a best estimate.

description: A 5-SNP set (4 SNPs identified via 10K microarray plus 1 brain-expressed gene SNP) is associated with general cognitive ability (g) in children from the Twins Early Development Study (TEDS), explaining 0.86% of variance in g
original_authors: Lee M. Butcher; Emma Meaburn; Jo Knight; Pak C. Sham; Leonard C. Schalkwyk; Ian W. Craig; Robert Plomin
original_title: SNPs, microarrays and pooled DNA: identification of four loci associated with mild mental impairment in a sample of 6000 children
replication_authors: Michelle Luciano; Penelope A. Lind; Ian J. Deary; Antony Payton; Danielle Posthuma; Lee M. Butcher; Zoltan Bochdanovits; Lawrence J. Whalley; Peter M. Visscher; Sarah E. Harris; Tinca J. C. Polderman; Oliver S. P. Davis; Margaret J. Wright; John M. Starr; Eco J. C. de Geus; Timothy C. Bates; Grant W. Montgomery; Dorret I. Boomsma; Nicholas G. Martin; Robert Plomin
replication_title: Testing replication of a 5-SNP set for general cognitive ability in six population samples
explanation: The meta-analysis of six independent population samples yielded a non-significant correlation of r = -0.01 (P = 0.57), and the authors concluded 'the SNP set was not correlated with g' and that 'the SNP set was not related to general cognitive ability in the cohorts we tested.' While one sample (ABC1936 at 64 years) showed a significant positive association, one showed a significant negative association, and the overall meta-analytic result was clearly null.

description: The rs1858830 C allele in the MET gene promoter region is significantly overtransmitted to autistic offspring (associated with autism susceptibility)
original_authors: Daniel B. Campbell; James S. Sutcliffe; Philip J. Ebert; Roberto Militerni; Carmela Bravaccio; Simona Trillo; Maurizio Elia; Cindy Schneider; Raun Melmed; Roberto Sacco; Antonio M. Persico; Pat Levitt
original_title: A genetic variant that disrupts MET transcription is associated with autism
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Inês Sousa; Taane G. Clark; Claudio Toma; Kazuhiro Kobayashi; Maja Choma; Richard Holt; Nuala H. Sykes; Janine A. Lamb; Anthony J. Bailey; Agatino Battaglia; Elena Maestrini; Anthony P. Monaco
replication_title: MET and autism susceptibility: family and case–control studies
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the earlier reported genetic association of the common C allele of rs1858830 in the promoter region failed to replicate in this study.' TDT analysis found p=0.555 for rs1858830 in the main IMGSAC family sample, and p=0.067 in the Italian trios — neither significant.

description: Variants in the UGT1A1 gene (rs11891311, rs887829, rs6742078, rs4148323) are associated with serum bilirubin levels in a Korean population
original_authors: Tae-Wook Kang; Hee-Jin Kim; Hyoungseok Ju; Jeong-Hwan Kim; Yeo-Jin Jeon; Han-Chul Lee; Ka-Kyung Kim; Jong-Won Kim; Siwoo Lee; Jong Yeol Kim; Seon-Young Kim; Yong Sung Kim
original_title: Genome-wide association of serum bilirubin levels in Korean population
replication_authors: Guanjie Chen; Edward Ramos; Adebowale Adeyemo; Daniel Shriner; Jie Zhou; Ayo P. Doumatey; Hanxia Huang; Michael R. Erdos; Norman P. Gerry; Alan Herbert; Amy R. Bentley; Huichun Xu; Bashira A. Charles; Michael F. Christman; Charles N. Rotimi
replication_title: UGT1A1 is a major locus influencing bilirubin levels in African Americans
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'successfully replicated all four previously reported UGT1A1 variants from GWAS of serum bilirubin in European- or East-Asian-ancestry populations' and directly replicated rs11891311 (the top scoring SNP from the Korean GWAS). The replication used the same GWAS approach but in a different ancestry population (African Americans vs. Koreans).

description: Variants in the UGT1A1 gene are associated with serum bilirubin levels in European-ancestry populations, with rs6742078 and rs887829 among the top associations
original_authors: Johnson AD; Kavousi M.; Smith AV; Chen MH; Dehghan A.; Aspelund T.; Lin JP; van Duijn CM; Harris TB; Cupples LA; Uitterlinden AG; Launer L.; Hofman A.; Rivadeneira F.; Stricker B.; Yang Q.; O'Donnell CJ; Gudnason V.; Witteman JC
original_title: Genome-wide association meta-analysis for total serum bilirubin levels
replication_authors: Guanjie Chen; Edward Ramos; Adebowale Adeyemo; Daniel Shriner; Jie Zhou; Ayo P. Doumatey; Hanxia Huang; Michael R. Erdos; Norman P. Gerry; Alan Herbert; Amy R. Bentley; Huichun Xu; Bashira A. Charles; Michael F. Christman; Charles N. Rotimi
replication_title: UGT1A1 is a major locus influencing bilirubin levels in African Americans
explanation: The authors successfully replicated UGT1A1 variants (rs6742078 and rs887829) reported in Johnson et al. explanation: REVIEWER UPGRADED from medium to high. The paper reports direct quantitative comparison between smartphone-collected gaze heatmaps and the OSIE desktop eye-tracker dataset (Xu et al. 2014, EyeLink 1000): pixel-level r=0.74 and object-level r=0.90 (Table 1), both far above a shuffled-desktop baseline (r=0.11 pixel-level, r=0.59 object-level). The Discussion explicitly states they 'validate our methodology by reproducing the key findings from previous eye movement research on oculomotor tasks and saliency analyses for natural images obtained using bulky, expensive desktop eye trackers.' The result classification as success is unambiguous: the authors' own framing, the quantitative correlations, and the comparison-to-baseline all confirm the smartphone replicates the desktop saliency pattern. No original ES was reported in the Xu et al. paper, so direct effect-size comparison is not possible, but the replication outcome is clear.

replication_title: Accelerating eye movement research via accurate and affordable smartphone eye tracking
explanation: REVIEWER UPGRADED from medium to high. The paper reports clear quantitative results on smartphones replicating classic visual search effects: (1) target saliency significantly reduced fixations to find the target (F(3,63)=37.36, p<10^-5); (2) the set-size × saliency interaction was replicated — low saliency targets showed positive set-size slope (slope=0.17, F(2,40)=3.52, p=0.04), medium-high saliency showed no set-size effect (F(2,40)=0.85, p=0.44), and very high saliency showed a negative set-size slope (slope=-0.06, F(2,40)=4.39, p=0.02). The authors explicitly state 'These findings are consistent with previous work on desktops 47-50' (which includes Wolfe 1998) and the Discussion confirms they 'replicated the key findings on oculomotor tasks such as prosaccade, smooth pursuit and visual search tasks using our smartphone eye tracker.' The directional pattern of set-size slopes matches precisely what Wolfe 1998 described. No original ES to compare numerically, but the qualitative and directional replication is unambiguous.

description: Gaze patterns during viewing of natural images are affected by the task being performed: gaze is more dispersed during free viewing and more focused on task-relevant regions during visual search

replication_title: Accelerating eye movement research via accurate and affordable smartphone eye tracking
explanation: REVIEWER KEPT at medium (upgraded from low). The smartphone data strongly supports the Yarbus task-dependency finding: gaze entropy was significantly higher for free viewing than visual search (16.94 vs. 16.39, t(119)=11.14, p=10^-23), and qualitative inspection (Fig. 5) confirms gaze is more focused on task-relevant regions during search. The paper states this is 'known since the classic eye tracking experiments by Yarbus in 1967.' However, confidence remains medium rather than high because: (1) Yarbus 1967 is a book-length monograph reporting qualitative demonstrations, not a paper with specific quantitative effect sizes to compare against; (2) the 'original' finding is more of a foundational qualitative observation (task affects gaze) than a testable numerical claim, making it impossible to assess whether the replication matches the original effect magnitude; (3) Wolfe 1998 and OSIE (entries 0 and 1) cite single papers with more specific claims, whereas Yarbus is cited as a historical touchstone for a general principle. The result direction is unambiguous, but the nature of the original precludes high confidence.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated our previous finding that dams with a history of maltreatment mistreat their own offspring.' The replication confirmed the effect: post-hoc analyses showed maltreated-vehicle dams performed significantly more adverse behaviors toward offspring than nurturing-care vehicle dams (t(29) = 2.315, p = 0.0279).

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In the present study, we replicated this beneficial effect of an odor cue,' and found effect sizes (d = 0.61–1.22) comparable to or larger than Rasch et al.'s d ≈ 0.6, demonstrating that the odor cueing effect generalizes to a real-life school setting with continuous whole-night stimulation.

replication_title: Risk of sudden cardiac arrest and ventricular arrhythmia with sulfonylureas: An experience with conceptual replication in two independent populations
explanation: The authors extended their prior Medicaid analysis (Leonard et al. 2018, 1999-2010 data) to 1999-2012 Medicaid data using similar methods. They report 'results were generally consistent with the current Medicaid study containing two more years of data, with only two minor differences,' indicating a successful close extension with essentially the same findings.

replication_title: Risk of sudden cardiac arrest and ventricular arrhythmia with sulfonylureas: An experience with conceptual replication in two independent populations
explanation: The authors conducted a conceptual replication using a different database (Optum commercial insurance) and population. The paper explicitly states this is a 'conceptual replication' and found 'dataset-specific associations with SCA/VA for both glimepiride and glyburide (vs. glipizide) were on opposite sides of and could not exclude the null,' demonstrating that results are sensitive to the specific data source used and no clear replication was achieved.

description: Two visual working memory representations (not just one) can simultaneously capture attention and interfere with concurrent visual search

replication_authors: Michael J. King; Brooke N. Macnamara

explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted 'an exact replication of Chen and Du's Experiment 2' and conclude in the Discussion: 'In the first experiment, we replicated Chen and Du's experiment demonstrating that not one, but two items held in visual working memory can capture attention.' All key statistical patterns matched, including M1 and M2 distractors producing significantly longer RTs than New and None conditions, and the combined MCI for M1+M2 being significantly larger than for a single cued item.

replication_title: Electronic nicotine delivery systems exhibit reduced bronchial epithelial cells toxicity compared to cigarette: the Replica Project
explanation: The authors confirmed the cytotoxicity findings (VP constituted ~88% of total toxicity, consistent with the original's ~89%), but the inflammatory and remodeling marker data differed significantly: 'our data on inflammatory and remodeling activity triggered by smoke differed significantly from those in the original reports.' The paper explicitly concludes: 'results on inflammatory and remodeling markers were not reproduced.'

They conclude this 'replication study can allay doubts about the results and proper execution' of the Azzopardi et al. (2016) study.

explanation: The authors confirmed the substantially reduced cytotoxicity of THP aerosol versus cigarette smoke: cell viability was 93.34% with IQOS and 95.04% with glo PRO versus only 26.45% with cigarette smoke exposure, consistent with Jaunky et al.'s finding of >87% viability. The paper concludes this study 'can allay doubts about the results and proper execution' of the Jaunky et al. (2018) study.

description: Undergraduates with a history of mild traumatic brain injury (hmTBI) perform significantly worse than controls on visual working memory tasks (change detection with colored patches)

replication_authors: Hector Arciniega; Jorja Shires; Sarah Furlong; Alexandrea Kilgore-Gomez; Adelle Cerreta; Nicholas G. Murray; Marian E. Berryhill
replication_title: Impaired visual working memory and reduced connectivity in undergraduates with a history of mild traumatic brain injury
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated our previous finding showing visual WM deficits in those with a hmTBI' in the Discussion. In Experiment 1A, an independent sample t-test showed significantly less visual WM accuracy in the hmTBI group: t(48) = 2.25, p = 0.03, d = 0.58.

description: Undergraduates with a history of mild traumatic brain injury (hmTBI) show persistent visual working memory deficits across multiple experiments manipulating encoding, maintenance, retrieval demands, and feedback
original_authors: Arciniega, H.; Kilgore-Gomez, A.; Mcnerney, W.; Lane, S.; Berryhill, M.

original_journal: Journal of Clinical and Translational Research
replication_authors: Hector Arciniega; Jorja Shires; Sarah Furlong; Alexandrea Kilgore-Gomez; Adelle Cerreta; Nicholas G. Murray; Marian E. Berryhill
replication_title: Impaired visual working memory and reduced connectivity in undergraduates with a history of mild traumatic brain injury
explanation: The authors state 'We replicated our previous finding showing visual WM deficits in those with a hmTBI' citing both [47] (Arciniega 2019) and [48] (Arciniega 2020) together in a single bundled statement, without distinguishing which study's findings are being specifically replicated. The identical citation sentence and replication statistics (Exp 1A: t(48)=2.25, p=0.03, d=0.58) are shared between both entries. Arciniega 2020 established the finding across six experiments with parameter manipulations (encoding, maintenance, retrieval, feedback); the current paper replicates only the basic visual WM deficit from a change detection paradigm and extends with neuroimaging and SR-mTBI comparison. The close extension classification is appropriate but confidence remains medium because the replication evidence cannot be cleanly attributed to [48] specifically vs. [47] — the authors treat them as a joint prior body of work.

replication_authors: Mihai Dricu; Sina Ladina Jossen; Tatjana Aue

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated previous findings with an entirely different set of stimuli while also adding two new levels of complexity.' The social optimism bias for warm characters and social pessimism bias for cold-incompetent characters from the original study were both successfully replicated.

description: Rhythmic complexity (syncopation) produces an inverted U-shaped relationship with groove (urge to move and enjoyment), such that moderate syncopation maximizes groove
original_authors: Maria A. G. Witek; Eric F. Clarke; Mikkel Wallentin; Morten L. Kringelbach; Peter Vuust
original_title: Syncopation, body-movement and pleasure in groove music
replication_authors: Connor Spiech; George Sioros; Tor Endestad; Anne Danielsen; Bruno Laeng
replication_title: Pupil drift rate indexes groove ratings
explanation: Independent review confirms clear success. The authors explicitly state in both Discussion and Conclusions: 'We replicated the inverted U-shaped relationship between rhythmic complexity and groove' and 'Here we replicate the canonical inverted U-shaped relationship between rhythmic complexity and groove ratings.' Statistical evidence is unambiguous: significant negative quadratic trends for both Urge to Move (χ²(1)=14.643, p<0.001) and Enjoyment (χ²(1)=20.774, p<0.001). The replication type as close extension is also confirmed: the core paradigm from Witek et al. (2014) is preserved (drumbeats varying in syncopation, rated for urge to move/enjoyment), but the study adds novel elements — pupillometry as a neurophysiological measure, orthogonal distinction between pickups and syncopations as a new manipulation, and rigorously controlled stimuli. These extensions go clearly beyond the original without changing the core question. No genuine ambiguity remains.

description: Facial mimicry responses (particularly corrugator muscle activity mirroring sad expressions) are less predictive of emotion recognition accuracy in individuals with higher autistic trait levels
original_authors: Julia Folz; Rüya Akdağ; Milica Nikolić; Henk van Steenbergen; Mariska E. Kret

replication_authors: Julia Folz; Milica Nikolić; Mariska E. Kret

explanation: The current Experiment 2 explicitly tested the finding from Folz et al. (2023) that facial mimicry is less predictive of emotion recognition with higher autistic trait levels, but failed to replicate it. The authors state: 'Facial muscle responses were not less predictive of Emotion recognition accuracy with higher autistic trait levels as found in a previous study' and 'In contrast to a previous study, facial muscle responses were not predictive of accurately recognizing specific emotional expressions, and the relation between facial muscle responses and emotion recognition accuracy was not altered by an individual's autistic trait levels in the current lab study.'

description: Task-evoked pupil response amplitude is negatively correlated with choice bias during challenging perceptual detection decisions, such that larger task-evoked pupil dilation predicts reduced bias
original_authors: Jan Willem de Gee; Olympia Colizoli; Niels A. Kloosterman; Tomas Knapen; Sander Nieuwenhuis; Tobias H. Donner

replication_title: Task-irrelevant stimuli reliably boost phasic pupil-linked arousal but do not affect decision formation
explanation: The authors explicitly state in both the abstract and Discussion that 'we replicated a negative correlation between task-evoked pupil responses and bias' using the same contrast detection task as the original. In Experiments 1 and 2, significant negative correlations were found (Exp 1: r = -0.211, p = 0.001; Exp 2: r = -0.297, p < 0.001).

description: European Americans are more strongly associated with the concept of 'American' than Asian Americans on the Implicit Association Test (IAT), revealing an American = White/Foreign = Asian implicit stereotype
original_authors: Thierry Devos; Mahzarin R. Banaji

original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Kirsten N. Morehouse; Tessa E. S. Charlesworth; Thierry Devos; Mahzarin R. Banaji
replication_title: Who is American? A comprehensive analysis of the American = White/Foreign = Asian stereotype (2007–2023)
explanation: The paper explicitly states it 'replicates, extends, and challenges previously reported results' and confirms a robust American = White effect in the largest sample to date (N = 666,623): implicit d = 0.50 and explicit d = 0.51. However, the finding that East Asian respondents also show the implicit American = White association (originally found in small convenience samples) was not replicated — East Asians showed no implicit bias (d = 0.02), challenging one sub-finding of the original.

description: Implicit American = White stereotype trends reversed course and began increasing in the three weeks following the proliferation of the term 'Chinese virus' on Twitter (March 9 to April 1, 2020), indicating that COVID-19 reversed implicit stereotype trends as early as March 2020
original_authors: Sean Darling-Hammond; Eli K. Michaels; Amani M. Allen; David H. Chae; Marilyn D. Thomas; Thu T. Nguyen; Mahasin M. Mujahid; Rucker C. Johnson
original_title: After 'the China virus' went viral: Racially charged coronavirus coverage and trends in bias against Asian Americans
replication_authors: Kirsten N. Morehouse; Tessa E. S. Charlesworth; Thierry Devos; Mahzarin R. Banaji
replication_title: Who is American? A comprehensive analysis of the American = White/Foreign = Asian stereotype (2007–2023)
explanation: Independent review confirms failure classification. The current paper uses the same Project Implicit dataset over a longer period (2007-2023) and applies segmented regression to identify the COVID-19 breakpoint. Darling-Hammond (2020) specifically claimed the implicit stereotype trend reversed course in the three weeks following the 'Chinese virus' Twitter proliferation (March 9–April 1, 2020). The current paper finds the breakpoint was August 2021 — 17 months later, coinciding with Delta variant dominance — not March 2020. The paper explicitly states: 'the results do appear to challenge previous findings that COVID-19 reversed implicit stereotype trends in March 2020.' The core causal claim (March 2020 reversal tied to xenophobic Twitter language) is directly contradicted by a different dataset analysis identifying August 2021 as the inflection point. Confidence upgraded to high because the paper provides an unambiguous directional conclusion with a specific alternative breakpoint, despite hedged framing ('appear to challenge') and a caveat that pandemic trends fall within predicted 95% CIs — the latter concerns the magnitude of disruption, not the timing claim being evaluated.

description: AI chatbots outperform human participants in originality (semantic distance and subjective ratings) in the Alternate Uses Task, a divergent thinking measure, when using the original task instructions emphasizing quality over quantity with a 30-second time limit

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Study 1 replicated the approach of Koivisto and Grassini as closely as possible' and found that 'AI scored higher than the human participants - both for the original and the modified approaches' for mean scores, and AI significantly outperformed humans in maximum scores under the original approach, consistent with the original findings.

description: AI chatbots outperform human participants in originality (semantic distance and subjective ratings) in the Alternate Uses Task, a divergent thinking measure, when using the original task instructions emphasizing quality over quantity with a 30-second time limit

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Both our initial results and subsequent meta-analysis replicated the earlier GWAS showing a genetic association between the SNP rs11098403 with schizophrenia in the Han Chinese.' The association was replicated in two independent Han Chinese samples and confirmed by meta-analysis (OR=0.70, 95% CI: 0.61-0.79, Z=5.56, P<0.001), though the G allele acts protectively in Han Chinese vs. as a risk allele in Caucasians.

No significant differences were found in individual SNP marker genotypes or allele distributions between the BD and control groups in either stage 1 or stage 2.

description: Stuttering frequency in adult male dextral stuttering speakers is correlated with cerebral blood flow increases in speech-motor regions (particularly right anterior insula) and decreases in auditory regions (right BA 21/22), as identified by PET performance correlation analysis
original_authors: Fox, Peter T.; Ingham, Roger J.; Ingham, Janis C.; Zamarripa, Frank; Xiong, Jinhu; Lancaster, Jack
original_title: Brain correlates of stuttering and syllable production: A PET performance-correlation analysis
replication_authors: Ingham RJ; Fox PT; Ingham JC; Xiong J.; Zamarripa F.; Hardies LJ; Lancaster JL
replication_title: Brain Correlates of Stuttering and Syllable Production
replication_journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal is a 'gender replication study' of Fox et al. (2000). In the Discussion they confirm: 'The present study and its companion study (Fox et al., 2000) offer added support to the suggestion that developmental stuttering is functionally related to abnormalities within the speech planning/production and auditory systems during speech. The principal findings have now been replicated in a different population using an identical methodology.' The same key regions (R anterior insula positive correlate, R BA 21/22 and L GFi negative correlates) were found in females, with some gender-specific differences.

description: Some adults with right hemisphere brain damage (RHD) generate but do not maintain predictive inferences over time, exhibiting a recency effect such that inference maintenance is lower in the RHD group than in no-brain-damage controls
original_authors: Margaret T. Lehman-Blake; Connie A. Tompkins

replication_authors: Margaret Lehman Blake
replication_title: Inferencing Processes After Right Hemisphere Brain Damage: Maintenance of Inferences
replication_journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The replication was partially successful: Although inference generation results were replicated, patterns of results for inference maintenance differed.' The original found that only 58% of RHD participants maintained inferences compared to 83% of NBD participants, but the replication found that ~85% of RHD and ~86% of NBD participants maintained inferences, failing to replicate the group difference in maintenance.

description: A composite measure based on age, MLU, and lexical diversity (D) yields high sensitivity and specificity (>90%) for differentiating Cantonese-speaking 4-year-old children with specific language impairment (SLI) from typically developing peers

replication_title: Differentiating Cantonese-Speaking Preschool Children With and Without SLI Using MLU and Lexical Diversity (D)
replication_journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Results from this study did not replicate the high sensitivity, high specificity, high LR+, and low LR- reported in the original Klee et al. (2004) study.' Sensitivity dropped from >90% in the original to 73.3%, and specificity dropped to 57.1%, both below the 80% threshold for acceptable clinical utility.

description: Tense and agreement productivity (TAP) growth from 21 to 30 months of age in typically developing toddlers is best characterized by a no-intercept quadratic growth model, with significant linear growth at 21 months and accelerating growth over time

explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'direct comparison of the two cohorts revealed compelling evidence of replication. In both cohorts, a no-intercept quadratic model best fit the data, with significant linear growth at 21 months and overall acceleration.' The combined cohort model showed no significant difference between cohorts in linear or quadratic growth parameters.

description: Verb Network Strengthening Treatment (VNeST) targeting verbs and thematic roles improves lexical retrieval in sentence production and generalizes to untrained words and discourse in persons with aphasia

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The current group study showed significant improvement on production of sentences containing trained and untrained semantically related stimuli, replicating previous findings.' The current study extends the single-subject design of the 2009 study to a larger group (n=11) with standardized dosage, confirming the core VNeST treatment effect.

description: Verb Network Strengthening Treatment (VNeST) improves lexical retrieval and sentence production in persons with moderate-to-severe aphasia, with generalization to untrained words and discourse measures

explanation: The Discussion explicitly states 'The current group study showed significant improvement on production of sentences containing trained and untrained semantically related stimuli, replicating previous findings' from both prior VNeST studies. The current study extends to a larger group with standardized dosage, confirming the treatment effect observed in Edmonds & Babb (2011).

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Findings from this study replicate findings from previous cross-linguistic LDS studies of Greek, Korean, and Italian.' Cross-linguistic vocabulary patterns (age/gender effects, vocabulary concordance Q~.50, noun predominance, and late talker similarity to younger vocabulary-matched peers) were all replicated in Portuguese.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Prior positive outcomes for CD service delivery have been replicated in a less restrictive approach to participant recruitment' and 'in large part, this study replicated the findings of the original Humes et al. (2017) study for the CD service delivery model on a more heterogenous unscreened sample.' The primary outcome measure (PHABglobal) did not differ significantly between the original and follow-up cohorts, though one secondary outcome (CST benefit) showed a significant difference explained by different baseline unaided performance.

description: LSVT LOUD treatment produces significant improvement in vowel articulation (as measured by F2i/F2u ratio) and perceptual ratings of speech clarity in individuals with Parkinson's disease
