explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'partial replication' of Sapir et al. (2007). The significant main effect of treatment was replicated (POST tokens rated more clearly, p=.01), and a significant correlation between acoustic and perceptual measures was reproduced (r=.62 vs. r~.60 in original). However, the authors note: 'our online rating tasks did not include data from two other groups in the original study,' limiting the scope of the replication to only the treatment group finding.

description: LSVT LOUD treatment significantly improves voice quality (as measured acoustically by the AVQI) in people with Parkinson's disease, with a significant group-by-time interaction showing improvement from pre- to posttreatment that is maintained at 6-month follow-up, while other groups (LSVT ARTIC, untreated PD) do not show the same pattern of improvement

This study corroborated Moya-Galé et al.'s results for the LSVT LOUD group, finding a significant change in perceptually rated voice quality from pre- to posttreatment that remained significant at the 6-month follow-up time point.' The significant group × session interaction (β = 1.4, SE = 0.43, p < .001) with LSVT LOUD being the only group showing significant improvement directly replicates the original finding.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study demonstrated successful replication and extension of the CRI treatment study (Devanga et al., 2021)' and dedicate a Discussion section titled 'Successful Replication of Treatment Effects on Naming.' The omnibus TauU of 0.87 (p < .0001) replicates the original TauU of 0.92 (p < .0001), with all three participants showing significant positive treatment effects.

The paper is even titled 'A Direct Replication of Sussman, McCaffrey, and Matthews.'

explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'This replication study found striking similarities to the results of Prutting et al., thus supporting the occurrence of a typical pattern of interaction between clinicians and children in treatment settings across geographic areas, personalities, and clinical education.' The original study's author also confirmed the close correspondence in a published reply.

description: A modified version of milieu teaching facilitates increases in intentional prelinguistic requesting by young children with developmental delays in intervention sessions with staff members
original_authors: Steven F. Warren; Paul J. Yoder; Gail E. Gazdag; Kyoungran Kim; Hazel A. Jones

replication_journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
explanation: The Discussion explicitly states: 'The results of this experiment replicated the Warren et al. (1993) finding that a modified milieu teaching approach is an effective method for facilitating intentional, prelinguistic requesting in young children with mental retardation in their interactions with teachers.' All four subjects showed clear increases in intentional requesting with the onset of intervention, mirroring the four-subject pattern in the original study.

description: Strong positive allergic patch test reactions cause increased intensity of reactions in adjacent skin ('spill-over effect'), demonstrating localized skin hyperreactivity around a positive patch test site
original_authors: Bruynzeel DP; Nieboer C.; Boorsma DM; Scheper RJ; van Ketel WG
original_title: Allergic reactions, 'spill-over' reactions, and T-cell subsets
replication_authors: Memon AA; Friedmann PS
replication_title: Angry back syndrome': a non-reproducible phenomenon
explanation: Independent review confirms a clear replication failure. The paper explicitly states in the Discussion: 'there was no evidence of so-called spill-over effects; a phenomenon described by Bruynzeel et al. in which the intensity of reactions increases adjacent to a positive reaction.' The Results section reports that in 10 of 18 nickel-sensitive subjects responses to all five threshold challenges were identical regardless of distance from a strong positive reaction, with no consistent trend. The Conclusion states: 'one strong positive reaction does not generally influence the skin reactivity as it neither increased the local reactivity of the skin nor caused a general shift in the reaction pattern.' The citation mismatch flag was a false alarm: the extracted original reference (Bruynzeel DP, Nieboer C, Boorsma DM et al., Arch Dermatol Res 1983; 275: 89-95, reference 6 in the paper) is correct — it is the paper that specifically reported the spill-over effect using SLS at a fixed distance, matching the citation sentence exactly. Year 1983 confirmed from reference list.

description: Staff nurses in the US preferred head nurse responses that were similar to what they perceived their head nurse would make, with a high percentage preferring non-exploratory (NON-EXP) responses (i.e., head nurses not including staff nurses in the problem-solving process)
original_authors: Schmieding, Norma Jean

replication_title: The need for and process of collaborative international research: a replication study of Japanese staff nurse perceptions of head nurses' actions
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The authors concluded that there was marked similarity in what actions both Japanese and US staff nurses preferred from their head nurse and what they thought their head nurse would make,' and note 'Data comparison of the two studies indicated marked similarities between the staff nurses in these two countries.' The replication was conducted in Japan using a translated version of the same questionnaire with a new cultural population.

description: A national survey of UK ophthalmic units found inadequate numbers of nurses holding relevant ophthalmic qualifications (37.6% in 1994) and severely limited provision and access to post-registration ophthalmic nurse education
original_authors: Waterman H.; Hope KW; Beed P.; Clayton E.; McQueen L.; Owen C.; Stott M.; Studley M.

replication_authors: Heather Waterman; Christine Waterman
replication_title: Trends in ophthalmology services, nursing skill‐mix and education: 2nd national survey
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'a replication study of the first national survey' (Waterman et al. 1995), using a modified version of the same questionnaire on the same population 3 years later. Results were mixed: some measures showed significant change (rise in day surgery, fall in C/G/I grade nurses, rise in institutions offering ophthalmic nurse education), but the primary measure — rise in nurses holding ophthalmic qualifications from 37.6% to 49.4% — did not reach statistical significance (P=0.2).

description: The Childbirth Self-Efficacy Inventory (CBSEI) is a valid and reliable tool for measuring women's confidence in their ability to cope with labour, with good internal consistency and ability to differentiate between outcome expectancies and self-efficacy expectancies
original_authors: Nancy K. Lowe
original_title: Maternal confidence for labor: development of the Childbirth Self-Efficacy Inventory
replication_authors: Marlene Sinclair; Colm O’Boyle
replication_title: The Childbirth Self‐Efficacy Inventory: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study has successfully replicated the use of the CBSEI with intrapartum women in Northern Ireland.' The reliability estimates (Cronbach alpha coefficients) compare favourably with Lowe's (1993) original results, and the instrument successfully differentiated between outcome and self-efficacy expectancies, confirming the tool's validity in a new cultural setting.

description: Patients with underwater seal chest drains post-thoracotomy have unmet information needs and inadequate pain control, with all patients experiencing moderate to severe pain while the drain is in situ

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Overall the findings of this study corroborated the results of Owen & Gould (1997)' and conclude that 'Replication of this study has now confirmed that the issues of patient information and adequate pain control that emerged were not local phenomena.' The same key findings (discomfort, pain, sleep disturbance, inadequate information) were found in a second hospital 2 years later using a constructive replication approach.

description: Novel information is better recognized than familiar information in a yes/no recognition task, with the superiority of novel items appearing in both hit rates and false-alarm rates (a mirror effect), as measured by an interaction of familiarity on hits and false alarms

The key interaction was significant: F(1,39) = 195.56, p = 0.0001. The study replication used Swedish materials and 40 participants vs. the original's 4, constituting a close extension.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'none of the results obtained by us supported the hypothesis that the loci implicated by Zhong et al. (1996) are involved in the genetic aetiology of CD.' All 11 microsatellite markers at the implicated loci yielded negative two-point lod scores, and neither MLINK, MFLINK, nor multipoint analysis provided evidence in favour of linkage.

explanation: The Danish replication found no significant difference in Small allele frequencies between centenarians and controls (p=0.176), in contrast to the original Italian finding (p=0.002). The authors conclude: 'The data in Table 1 indicated that the 3'APOB-VNTR polymorphism is not associated with longevity in Danes.'

explanation: The demographic-genetic approach (Yashin et al. 2000) applied to Danish data confirmed Small alleles are not risk factors for longevity in Denmark (r.r.=0.952), failing to replicate the Italian cohort finding. replication_title: Genetic Modifiers of Lung Disease in Cystic Fibrosis
explanation: The authors explicitly designed an initial study to test TGFβ1 among other candidate modifier genes, finding significant association of TGFβ1 codon 10 CC and -509 TT genotypes with severe lung disease (p=0.0002 and p=0.002 in logistic regression). They then conducted a separate replication study confirming this finding. The discussion states: 'the replication study clearly confirmed that the TGFβ1 codon 10 CC genotype acted as an adverse modifier of lung disease in cystic fibrosis. Moreover, the magnitude of the effect (odds ratio, approximately 2.2) was similar to that in the initial study.'

description: Polymorphisms in ACE, IL10, TGFβ1, and TNFα genes are associated with end-organ dysfunction and disease severity in cystic fibrosis patients
original_authors: Arkwright PD; Pravica V.; Geraghty PJ; Super M.; Webb AK; Schwarz M.; Hutchinson IV

Darrah; Ruslan Dorfman; Andrew J. Sandford; Mary Corey; Julian Zielenski; Peter Durie; Katrina Goddard; James R. Yankaskas; Fred A. Wright; Michael R. Knowles
replication_title: Genetic Modifiers of Lung Disease in Cystic Fibrosis
explanation: Independent reviewer update: The previous classification of 'inconclusive' was too generous. The paper gives unambiguous results. Table 2 shows that ACE, IL10, and TNFα polymorphisms were all non-significant in the initial study (n=808). The Discussion explicitly states: 'Of these candidates, only TGFβ1 variants were strongly associated with pulmonary phenotypes that are predictive of the long-term outcome.' The Arkwright 2003 paper's central claim was that ACE and cytokine gene polymorphisms (IL10, TGFβ1, TNFα) collectively associate with end-organ dysfunction — only TGFβ1 was confirmed here. The bundled multi-gene claim failed: 3 of 4 genes showed no significant association, and the paper's own authors characterize it as only TGFβ1 being confirmed. TGFβ1 confirming does not rescue the overall claim, especially since Arkwright 2003's distinctive contribution was the ACE and cytokine associations. This is a clear failure to replicate the original multi-gene association claim. Confidence upgraded to high because the paper's conclusions are explicit and leave no ambiguity.

description: The GN version (Germanisches Nationalmuseum) is the principal portrait by Rembrandt himself and the Mh version (Mauritshuis) is a contemporary studio copy, based on technical examination including IRR underdrawing evidence showing the Mh version was copied from the GN version
original_authors: Buijsen, E.

replication_title: The attribution of two portraits of Rembrandt revisited: a replication study in art history
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'The reproduction and conceptual replication corroborated the conclusions of the initial study.' Both the reproduction and conceptual replication confirmed the original attribution findings: the GN version is by Rembrandt and the Mh version is a studio copy. The authors explicitly selected Buijsen (1999) and Wadum (2000) as 'the main sources for our replication study.'

description: The GN version is the principal Rembrandt self-portrait and the Mh version is a studio copy, supported by IRR, X-Ray, and dendrochronological evidence, including the hypothesis that blotchiness in IRR images indicates Rembrandt's unique undermodelling technique
original_authors: Jørgen Wadum
original_title: Rembrandt under the skin. The Mauritshuis "Portrait of Rembrandt with Gorget" in retrospect
replication_authors: Charlotte C. S. Rulkens; Rik Peels; Maartje Stols-Witlox; Sabrina Meloni; Iris M. Lechner; Lex Bouter
replication_title: The attribution of two portraits of Rembrandt revisited: a replication study in art history
explanation: Independent review confirms the result classification and replication type are well-supported. The Findings section (line 113) states explicitly: 'Both the reproduction and the conceptual replication corroborated the attributions made in the initial study, including the principality of the GN painting.' The reproduction findings (line 123) further confirm: 'The reproduction corroborated the initial findings that the GN is the principal version on which the Mh version was directly based, and confirmed the initial conclusion that the GN was painted by Rembrandt, identifying the Mh version as a contemporary studio copy by another hand.' The conceptual replication found all four experts unanimous in attributing GN to Rembrandt, de-attributing Mh, and agreeing on GN as principal (average 94% certainty). The dendrochronology reproduction found minor dating discrepancies but these did not affect the attribution conclusions. The 'close extension' replication type is confirmed by the paper's own description of the conceptual replication as 'a repetition that used an improved study protocol including new technical research methods' (Ma-XRF, higher-resolution IRR, expert meeting protocol). Upgrading to high confidence because the paper's own language unambiguously confirms success on all main research questions.

description: Per-dependent ultradian ~60-second cycles in the interpulse interval (IPI) of male Drosophila melanogaster courtship song, with perL mutants (long 29-h circadian cycles) singing with longer ~80-s song cycles compared to wild-type ~55-s cycles

explanation: The authors manually re-examined Stern's raw primary song recordings using Stern's own FlySongSegmenter platform and found highly significant per-dependent song cycle differences: 'Statistical analysis revealed a highly significant genotype effect (F1,111 = 31.2, P~0)' with perL mean periods of 87.6s (cosinor) versus wild-type 60.8s. description: The steppe pastoralist migration into central Europe after 5,000 years ago was sex-biased, with X-chromosome ancestry (36.6%) substantially lower than autosomal ancestry (61.8%), implying a ratio of 5–14 steppe males for every female

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we do not find less SP ancestry on the X chromosome' using qpAdm, obtaining 67.5 ± 17% SP ancestry on X vs. 61.4 ± 2.9% on autosomes. They further demonstrate the original finding was driven by estimation bias in supervised ADMIXTURE, concluding that 'bias in the estimation of admixture proportions, rather than sex bias in the steppe migration, drives the findings of ref. 1.'

description: Drift rate in a dot motion perceptual decision-making task is reduced as a function of OCD symptom severity, with larger impairments for easier (higher coherence) trials
original_authors: Paula Banca; Martin D. Vestergaard; Vladan Rankov; Kwangyeol Baek; Simon Mitchell; Tatyana Lapa; Miguel Castelo-Branco; Valerie Voon
original_title: Evidence accumulation in obsessive-compulsive disorder: The role of uncertainty and monetary reward on perceptual decision-making thresholds
replication_authors: Alec Solway; Zhen Lin; Ekansh Vinaik
replication_title: Transfer of information across repeated decisions in general and in obsessive–compulsive disorder
replication_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
explanation: Review confirms clear replication success. The paper states replication in three places: (1) Abstract: 'we replicated previous work demonstrating impairments in baseline decision-making as a function of self-reported OCD symptoms'; (2) Results (body.md ~line 101): 'In both datasets, we replicated previous work showing that drift rate during a new decision (the first decision episode) is reduced as a function of OCD severity, and that this effect is larger for easier trials' — directly confirming the coherence-level interaction in the description; (3) Discussion: 'we replicated previous work showing that baseline drift rate (for the first decision episode) is reduced (21-24)' with Banca et al. 2015 as ref 21. Replication held across both Experiment 1 (n=175, AMT) and Experiment 2 (n=213, AMT). The online AMT design versus Banca et al.'s lab paradigm makes this a close extension. Confidence upgraded to high because the replication success is unambiguous, confirmed across both datasets, and the specific description detail (larger effect for easier/higher-coherence trials) is explicitly stated in the Results.

description: In repeated public goods games with constant ('partner') groups, when players are told after the final round that they will play again, cooperation briefly increases — the 'restart effect'
original_authors: Andreoni, James
original_title: Why free ride - strategies and learning in public-goods experiments
replication_authors: Maxwell N. Burton-Chellew
replication_title: The restart effect in social dilemmas shows humans are self-interested not altruistic
replication_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'we replicated the standard restart effect in our Classic Replay treatment (Fig. 2),' with mean contributions increasing significantly from 25% to 42% (LMM: +17.2 ±3.36%, t=5.1, df=80, P<0.001). The result is unambiguously a success. Confidence remains medium because the paper treats the restart effect as a shared canonical result across multiple studies, citing refs 36 (Andreoni 1988), 48 (Croson 1996), and 51 (Andreoni & Croson 2008) as co-equal sources in the Classic Replay description. The paper does not frame this as a replication of Andreoni (1988) specifically — all three are cited identically. Assigning Andreoni (1988) as the sole original is an editorial choice; the other two cited studies have equal claim. The success classification and effect size are not in doubt, only the attribution to a single original paper.

The paper finds partial similarities (proportions of replication types are comparable) but also differences (much lower overall rate of 0.06% vs 1.07% in psychology), and the authors frame the results as exploratory rather than claiming success or failure of replication.

Results show similar patterns (no explicit rejection, majority with no stated position) but lower explicit acceptance (0.8% vs 6% in neuroscience); the discussion notes the similarities but concludes there is an 'absence of reference to replication' in TIS journals rather than a clear positive or negative bias.

replication_title: Information Reduces Corruption and Improves Enrolment (But Not Schooling): A Replication Study of a Newspaper Campaign in Uganda
explanation: The replication confirms the core finding that the newspaper campaign reduced elite capture of public funds. The authors state in their Discussion: 'This replication study confirms the key finding of RS (2005): that the newspaper campaign launched in Uganda in 1997 reduced the capture of government capitation grants transferred to schools by increasing information and awareness among head teachers.' The pure replication exactly reproduced the original summary statistics and first-stage estimates.

description: Reduced capture of capitation grants due to the newspaper campaign had a positive effect on school enrolment
original_authors: Ritva Reinikka; Jakob Svensson
original_title: Fighting corruption to improve schooling: Evidence from a newspaper campaign in Uganda
original_journal: Journal of the European Economic Association
replication_authors: Maria Kuecken; Marie-Anne Valfort
replication_title: Information Reduces Corruption and Improves Enrolment (But Not Schooling): A Replication Study of a Newspaper Campaign in Uganda
explanation: The pure replication of RS (2005)'s enrolment result (using total enrolment reported by head teachers) fails to hold once 10 schools with enrolment declines are reintegrated. The result only becomes robust when using the improved P7 enrolment measure from the later RS (2011) paper. The authors write: 'we endorse the conclusion that the receipt of capitation grants increased enrolment, although this result emerges only if we rely on a more accurate enrolment measure introduced in RS (2011). It fails to hold when we replicate RS (2005).'

description: Reduced capture of capitation grants due to the newspaper campaign had a positive effect on student learning outcomes (PLE test scores)
original_authors: Ritva Reinikka; Jakob Svensson
original_title: Fighting corruption to improve schooling: Evidence from a newspaper campaign in Uganda
original_journal: Journal of the European Economic Association
replication_authors: Maria Kuecken; Marie-Anne Valfort
replication_title: Information Reduces Corruption and Improves Enrolment (But Not Schooling): A Replication Study of a Newspaper Campaign in Uganda
explanation: The replication cannot support the claim that lower capture improved student learning. The authors report: 'We cannot, however, support the authors' conclusion that lower capture enhanced learning.' The second-stage IV estimate of the effect of grant share on PLE scores is far from significant (p = 0.885 in column 1 of Table 11), and once competing channels (local development/remoteness) are controlled, the coefficient remains insignificant.

description: Providing community-level health service delivery information and guidance on community-based monitoring improved provider behaviour, health care utilisation, and health outcomes in Uganda
original_authors: Martina Björkman; Jakob Svensson
original_title: Power to the people: Evidence from a randomized field experiment on community-based monitoring in Uganda
replication_authors: Katherine Donato; Adrian Garcia Mosqueira
replication_title: Information Improves Provider Behaviour: A Replication Study of a Community-Based Monitoring Programme in Uganda
explanation: The authors describe a 'pure replication' and confirm: 'we have been able to closely verify all of the results' for provider behaviour, utilisation, and health outcomes. However, extended analyses raised important doubts about immunisation impacts (baseline imbalances suggest the effect was pre-existing) and health outcome robustness (effects on weight-for-age z-scores lost significance when controlling for prior CBO presence), leading the abstract to conclude that 'results surrounding the programme's impact on health outcomes appear less robust.'

description: Male circumcision reduces HIV acquisition by approximately 60 per cent in young men in Kisumu, Kenya, with no evidence of behavioural risk compensation following circumcision
original_authors: Robert C. Bailey; Stephen Moses; Corette B. Parker; Kawango Agot; Ian Maclean; John N. Krieger; Carolyn FM Williams; Richard T. Campbell; Jeckoniah O. Ndinya-Achola
original_title: Male circumcision for HIV prevention in young men in Kisumu, Kenya: a randomised controlled trial
replication_authors: Jeffrey E. Korte; Eric W. Djimeu; Flor A. Calvo
replication_title: Evidence of Behavioural Compensation in Internal Replication Study of Male Circumcision Trial to Reduce HIV Acquisition in Kisumu, Kenya
explanation: The replication confirmed the primary finding — a ~60% protective effect of circumcision against HIV acquisition — across both epidemiological and econometric approaches ('Both approaches confirmed the 60 per cent protective effect of circumcision reported in the original paper'). However, contrary to the original, this replication found statistically significant evidence of behavioural risk compensation (circumcised men less likely to stay abstinent, more likely to have unprotected intercourse), yielding mixed overall results relative to the original study.

description: The Make a Sentence Test (MAST) scoring categories show consistent personality correlates (e.g., correlations with personality inventory subtests) across different populations, as originally demonstrated in college male and female samples
original_authors: Borgatta, Edgar F.
original_title: The coincidence of subtests in four personality inventories
replication_authors: Edgar F. Borgatta
replication_title: The make a Sentence Test (Mast): A Replication Study
explanation: Independent review confirmed: The Summary and Conclusions (body.md lines 2701-2741) present a genuinely mixed picture. The authors state 'considerable consistency' for 5 of ~11 MAST variables (Paranoid, Hostile, Conventional, Depressive/GZ, Optimistic) across college vs. high-variance samples. The statistical recurrence argument is notable — in the male data, 11 relationships coincided with the original study when even 1 recurring had p<.05 by chance; for females, 4 coincided when p<.02. This suggests above-chance replication for many relationships. However, 'the apparent lack of consistency between the other MAST variables' is explicitly acknowledged and left unresolved, with speculative explanations (language meaning differences across populations, range restriction). The paper does not clearly claim overall replication success or failure — it is a partial replication with both confirming and disconfirming evidence. 'Inconclusive' is retained as the most accurate classification for the overall claim, though 'success' could be argued for the 5 consistently-defined variables specifically. Confidence kept at medium because the paper itself presents mixed results with no clear overall verdict.

description: Daily hassles (undesirable daily events) are better predictors of physical health/somatic symptomatology than major life events, while uplifts (desirable events) do not contribute significantly to health outcomes
original_authors: Anita DeLongis; James C. Coyne; Gayle Dakof; Susan Folkman; Richard S. Lazarus
original_title: Relationship of daily hassles, uplifts, and major life events to health status
replication_authors: Lina Jandorf; Esther Deblinger; John M. Neale; Arthur A. Stone
replication_title: Daily Versus Major Life Events as Predictors of Symptom Frequency: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the results of the present study are remarkably similar to the findings reported by DeLongis et al. (1982).' Undesirable daily events accounted for 17-19% of variance in symptomatic days, while major life events did not significantly add predictive power — replicating DeLongis et al.'s core finding that hassles outperform major life events in predicting somatic symptoms.

description: Children discover conservation of mass, weight, and volume in a regular age-related order: mass at ages 7-8, weight at ages 9-10, and volume at ages 11-12
original_authors: Piaget, J.; Inhelder, B.
original_title: Le développement des quantités chez l'enfant
replication_authors: David Elkind
replication_title: Children's Discovery of the Conservation of Mass, Weight, and Volume: Piaget Replication Study II
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'The results of the present study agreed with Piaget's findings regarding the ages at which children discover the conservation of mass, weight, and volume. In both studies: the conservation of mass did not usually appear before the ages 7-8; the conservation of weight did not usually appear before the ages 9-10; and the conservation of volume did not in most cases appear before the age of 11.'

description: Children show three age-related stages in the ability to additively compose classes (include partial classes within a total class), demonstrated via the 'wooden beads' experiment and a control test asking whether there are more boys/girls or more children in a classroom
original_authors: Piaget, Jean
original_title: The child's conception of number
replication_authors: David Elkind
replication_title: The Development of the Additive Composition of Classes in the Child: Piaget Replication Study III
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of the present study were in agreement with Piaget's finding of three age related stages in the development of the child's ability to additively compose classes.' The chi-square analysis (χ² = 12.59, p < .05) confirmed that stages were significantly related to age.

description: Children's conceptions of right and left develop through three age-related stages, with right-left tests discriminating between age groups across ages 5-11
original_authors: Piaget, Jean
original_title: The child's conception of the world
replication_authors: David Elkind
replication_title: Children's Conceptions of Right and Left: Piaget Replication Study IV
explanation: The Discussion section explicitly states: 'The results of this replication study were in close agreement with Piaget's original findings regarding: (a) the ages at which particular tests were passed, and (b) the three stages in the development of right-left conceptions.' Table 2 shows no more than a one-year discrepancy between original and replication age-level placements.

description: Children's conceptions of brother and sister develop through three stages, with tests discriminating between age groups showing that Swiss children pass specific relational and class conception tests at predictable ages between 5 and 12
original_authors: Piaget, Jean
original_title: The child's conception of the world
replication_authors: David Elkind
replication_title: Children's Conceptions of Brother and Sister: Piaget Replication Study V
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'there was generally good agreement between original and replication studies regarding the ages at which tests were passed' with no more than a one-year discrepancy on five of six tests. The one large discrepancy (Test 1) was explained by a known confounding factor (family size differences).

description: Children develop the ability to discriminate, seriate, and numerate size differences in three stages: a global perceptual stage (age 4), an intuitive representation stage (age 5), and an operational conceptual stage (ages 6-7), with discrimination mastered earliest and numeration latest
original_authors: Piaget, Jean
original_title: The child's conception of number
replication_authors: David Elkind
replication_title: Discrimination, Seriation, and Numeration of Size and Dimensional Differences in Young Children: Piaget Replication Study VI
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Summary that 'The results are in agreement with those secured by Piaget,' and the Discussion confirms 'the author presented quantitative and qualitative evidence that is in general agreement with Piaget's observation on the development of the concepts of series and number.' All major predictions derived from Piaget's observations (age differences, test difficulty ordering, influence of dimensionality) were confirmed at the .01 significance level.

description: Traditional-Jewish boys, compared to Anglo-Saxon Protestant boys, show greater field-dependence (less psychological differentiation) on measures including the Embedded Figures Test, Human Figure Drawing, and Verbal Disembedding Test
original_authors: Dershowitz, Zecharia
original_title: Influences of cultural patterns on the thinking of children in certain ethnic groups: A study of the effect of Jewish subculture on the field-dependence-independence dimension of cognition
original_journal: Unpublished Doctoral Dissertation, New York University
replication_authors: Zecharia Dershowitz
replication_title: Jewish Culture and Psychological Differentiation—Partial Replication
explanation: The paper is titled 'partial replication' and confirms the original finding only for the EFT (p < .05), while the Figure Drawing and Verbal Disembedding tests did not confirm the hypothesis — with Figure Drawing actually showing a reversed direction (TJ group more differentiated). The authors state: 'Despite the small sample size, the results supported the hypothesis with regard to the EFT. The results on the other two tests did not confirm a difference between the two sample groups.'

description: Factor analysis of leisure attitude items identifies five relatively independent dimensions in the leisure domain: affinity for leisure, society's role in leisure planning, self-definition through leisure or work, amount of perceived leisure, and amount of work or vacation desired
original_authors: Neulinger, John; Breit, Miranda
original_title: Attitude dimensions of leisure
replication_authors: John Neulinger; Miranda Breit
replication_title: Attitude Dimensions of Leisure: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'The most striking result of this study is the surprising similarity of factors in this and the previous study. There remains little doubt that the factors identified represent some very real dimensions in the leisure domain.' The same five factors with the same labels emerged from the replication, with only two of 27 items loading on different factors than in the original.

description: Early memory (EM) thematic codes can be used to distinguish delinquent from nondelinquent adolescents, correctly identifying 80% of delinquents and 100% of nondelinquents
original_authors: Bruhn, Arnold R.; Davidow, Sharon
original_title: Earliest memories and the dynamics of delinquency
replication_authors: Sharon Davidow; Arnold R. Bruhn
replication_title: Earliest Memories and the Dynamics of Delinquency: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We showed that when the EM variables were combined, they were able to distinguish the overwhelming majority of delinquents from nondelinquents, thus replicating the results of Bruhn and Davidow (1983).' The replication achieved 81.7% correct classification of delinquents and 95.8% of nondelinquents, closely mirroring the original study's 80% and 100%, and the abstract notes the study 'effectively validates the use of the EM scoring system for this population.'

description: The Dutch paper-and-pencil version of the Impact Message Inventory-Circumplex (IMI-C) approaches circumplex structure, with three Submissive octant items causing distortion
original_authors: Anton Hafkenscheid; Danny Rouckhout
original_title: Circumplex structure of the Impact Message Inventory (IMI-C): An empirical test with the Dutch version
replication_authors: Anton Hafkenscheid; Danny Rouckhout
replication_title: The Impact Message Inventory–Circumplex (IMI–C): A Replication Study of Its Circumplex Structure in a Dutch Sample
explanation: The authors found that the computer-delivered Dutch IMI-C approached circumplexity with the same three Submissive items being problematic as in the original, and concluded that 'The circumplex structure of the computer-delivered IMI-C was found to be equivalent to the paper-and-pencil IMI-C (Hafkenscheid & Rouckhout, 2009),' with a Procrustes congruence of 0.998 between the two versions.

description: A majority of attorneys and law students endorse providing clients with information about MMPI-2 validity scales prior to forensic psychological testing, and most believe they should generally prepare clients for psychological evaluations
original_authors: Martha W. Wetter; Susan K. Corrigan
original_title: Providing information to clients about psychological tests: A survey of attorneys' and law students' attitudes
replication_authors: Paul M. Spengler; Nathan T. Walters; Eric Bryan; Brandon S. Millspaugh
replication_title: Attorneys’ Attitudes Toward Coaching Forensic Clients on the MMPI–2: Replication and Extension of Attorney Survey by Wetter and Corrigan (1995)
explanation: The replication found similar rates for general preparation advice (73.2% vs. 70.9%, z = -0.519, p = .604, d = .05 — no significant difference), but a statistically significantly lower rate for validity scale coaching (52.7% vs. 62.7%, z = 2.096, p = .036, d = -.20). The authors describe the overall pattern as mirroring Wetter and Corrigan's numbers while acknowledging the significant decline on the key coaching question, stating the change 'might reflect a change in attorney attitudes' or 'could be an artifact of differences in the surveys.'

description: The CASES instrument validly assesses three domains of empathy (cognitive, affective, somatic) and two valences (positive, negative) with concurrent, convergent, and discriminant validity in youth, and shows sex differences with females scoring higher
original_authors: Raine, Adrian; Chen, Frances
original_title: The cognitive, affective, and somatic empathy scales (CASES) for children
original_journal: Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology
replication_authors: Frances R. Chen; Annis Lai Chu Fung; Adrian Raine
replication_title: The cognitive, affective, and somatic empathy scales (CASES): Cross-cultural replication and specificity to different forms of aggression and victimization
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated most of the concurrent, convergent, and discriminant validity findings in the original development of CASES.' The Discussion confirms: 'Consistent with the original development of CASES in the US (Raine & Chen, 2018), we found support for the distinction between cognitive, affective and somatic empathy, the distinction between positive and negative empathy.' Cross-study correlations were strong for key associations (CU traits r=.80, proactive aggression r=.78), though some validity findings (reactive aggression, parent-report CU) replicated less strongly.

description: Subliminally presented sexual pictures (primes) facilitate recognition of subsequent sexual targets in men, providing evidence for nonconscious activation of implicit sexual memory
original_authors: Mark Spiering; Walter Everaerd; Erick Janssen
original_title: Priming the sexual system: implicit versus explicit activation
replication_authors: Mark Spiering; Walter Everaerd; Petra Karsdorp; Stephanie Both; Marieke Brauer
replication_title: Nonconscious processing of sexual information: A generalization to women
explanation: The authors explicitly called Experiment 1 'a direct replication, in women, of the male study (Experiment 1, Spiering et al., 2003).' The conclusion states: 'A direct replication failed, however (Experiment 1).' No significant Prime × Target interaction was found (F(1, 29) = 2.01, p = .17), unlike the original male study.

description: Subliminally presented sexual pictures (primes) facilitate recognition of subsequent sexual targets in men, providing evidence for nonconscious activation of implicit sexual memory
original_authors: Mark Spiering; Walter Everaerd; Erick Janssen
original_title: Priming the sexual system: implicit versus explicit activation
replication_authors: Mark Spiering; Walter Everaerd; Petra Karsdorp; Stephanie Both; Marieke Brauer
replication_title: Nonconscious processing of sexual information: A generalization to women
explanation: Experiment 2 extended the original paradigm by adding female-oriented sexual pictures, baby stimuli, and testing across three menstrual cycle phases in women. Only male-oriented sexual primes produced a significant facilitation effect (during the midluteal phase), while female-oriented sexual primes did not. The authors conclude 'our data provide preliminary support for the role of implicit processes in the female sexual system' — a partial and qualified result.

description: Comparing two self-report measures of sexual perpetration (SES-SFP vs. SSS) in men reveals significant discrepancies in prevalence rates, with poor agreement (60.6% agreement, kappa = .25) between questionnaires assessing the same construct
original_authors: Emily Strang; Zoë D. Peterson; Yvette N. Hill; Julia R. Heiman
original_title: Discrepant responding across self-report measures of men's coercive and aggressive sexual strategies
replication_authors: RaeAnn E. Anderson; Douglas L. Delahanty
replication_title: Discrepant Responding across Measures of College Students’ Sexual Victimization Experiences: Conceptual Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to 'conceptually replicate Strang et al. (2013)' by comparing victimization (rather than perpetration) versions of the same questionnaires. The Discussion confirms replication success: 'Consistent with Hypotheses 1, 2, and prior research, we found significant discrepancies in reported rates of sexual victimization between the two measures,' with the same pattern of higher detection rates for the PRSPS-type measure and especially pronounced gender differences in concordance.

description: Accuracy of judging unposed emotional behavior in a natural setting using sound-on-film recordings, including effects of sex differences, emotional valence (pleasant vs. unpleasant), and communication mode (audio-visual, audio, visual, transcript) on judgment accuracy
original_authors: E. Clay Jorgensen; Robert J. Howell
original_title: Judging unposed emotional behavior
replication_authors: Howell RJ; Jorgensen EC
replication_title: Accuracy of Judging Unposed Emotional Behavior in a Natural Setting: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The present study is a replication of the first' and use the same stimuli and paradigm. All three main findings from the original study were confirmed: no sex differences in accuracy, pleasant emotions judged more accurately than unpleasant ones (65% vs 50%, p < .001), and transcript mode inferior to other modes (46% vs 61% mean correct, p < .01). The change from semantic differential to dichotomous judgments is the main methodological modification.

description: Students who enroll in psychology courses (especially abnormal psychology) are more maladjusted than students who enroll in other university courses, with maladjustment increasing as course content becomes more morbid
original_authors: Leon M. Wise
original_title: Abnormal psychology as a selective factor: A confirmation and extension
replication_authors: Blair R. Swanson; Robert J. Howell
replication_title: The Relationship between Specific Psychology Classes and Maladjustment—a Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state the results do not confirm Wise's findings: 'the results do not confirm those of Wise.' The ANOVA yielded F = 0.99, df 4/147, p > .05, showing no significant differences in maladjustment across psychology and non-psychology course enrollees.

description: European Americans (vs. East Asians) strongly prefer uncommon pen colors when selecting a pen as a gift, reflecting cultural differences in the tendency to opt for originality versus majority-based choices
original_authors: Heejung Kim; Hazel Rose Markus
original_title: Deviance or uniqueness, harmony or conformity? A cultural analysis
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Tobias Otterbring; Roopali Bhatnagar; Michał Folwarczny
replication_title: Selecting the special or choosing the common? A high-powered conceptual replication of Kim and Markus’ (1999) pen study
explanation: The replication found a statistically significant effect in the same direction (US vs. Chinese participants, V=.12, p=.001), but the effect was significantly weaker than the original (V=.52), with non-overlapping 95% CIs. The authors describe it as a conceptual replication that 'replicates...overall results' but with an effect size 'significantly weaker than that of the original study.'

description: Laypeople's definitions of empathy cluster into four factors (Prosocial Emotional Response, Interpersonal Perceptiveness, Other Perspective, and Anxious Reactivity), with women endorsing the Other Perspective and Prosocial Emotional Response definitions more than men
original_authors: Judith A. Hall; Rachel Schwartz; Fred Duong
original_title: How do laypeople define empathy
replication_authors: Johanna K. Blomster Lyshol; Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos; Peder Mortvedt Isager; Magnus H. Blystad
replication_title: What is empathy for laypeople? – A replication study of Hall, Schwartz, and Duong (2021)
explanation: The pre-registered confirmatory factor analysis (H1) failed to replicate the original four-factor structure (χ²(2848) = 10031.41, CFI = 0.807, not meeting cutoff criteria). However, exploratory graph analyses revealed a conceptually similar five-factor structure. The authors conclude: 'we consider this to be a successful partial replication of Hall et al.'s (2021) findings.'

description: Anxiety sensitivity and attentional control interact such that individuals with high anxiety sensitivity and low attentional control experience the greatest posttraumatic stress symptoms
original_authors: Joseph R. Bardeen; Thomas A. Fergus
original_title: Emotional distress intolerance, experiential avoidance, and anxiety sensitivity: The buffering effect of attentional control on associations with posttraumatic stress symptoms
original_journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment
replication_authors: Brian J. Albanese; Richard J. Macatee; Nicholas P. Allan; Nicole A. Short; Aaron M. Norr; Norman B. Schmidt
replication_title: Interactive Effects of Anxiety Sensitivity and Attentional Control on Posttraumatic Stress in Community and Clinical Populations
explanation: The authors explicitly state they designed Study 1 'to replicate the findings by Bardeen and Fergus (2016)' and found a significant AS×AC interaction (β = -.07, p = .01) predicting PTSS, extending and confirming the marginally significant interaction reported in the original study. The Discussion describes the current findings as extending prior research by Bardeen and Fergus (2016).

description: Size of family of orientation is positively associated with preferred family size, and this relationship is moderated by birth order, religion, happiness of family of orientation, and lifestyle stability, when examined via multiple classification analysis
original_authors: Stokes, C. Shannon; Johnson, Nan E.
original_title: Birth order, size of family of orientation, and desired family size
replication_authors: Raymond J. Adamek; Marvin R. Koller
replication_title: Size of Family of Orientation and Family Size Preference: A Replication
explanation: Independent review confirms success classification. The paper reports a clear gamma = .26 positive association between family of orientation size and preferred family size (Table 1), and the Conclusion explicitly states as finding #1: 'There is a modest, positive association between size of family of orientation and family size preference, which has been demonstrated in large, probability sample studies and in smaller, non-probability sample studies.' The multiple classification analysis (Table 3) shows parental family size is among the top predictors for both males and females. Birth order has no independent effect for females (beta = .09), directly matching Stokes and Johnson's (1977) finding that 'birth order had no independent effect on desired family size.' The authors acknowledge their sample (n=379 college students, non-probability) limits generalizability, but this does not create ambiguity about the result direction — the positive association is confirmed unambiguously. Upgraded from medium to high confidence because the conclusion is explicit, the key statistic (gamma = .26) is clearly reported, and the comparison to Stokes & Johnson (1977) is direct and unambiguous.

description: A 30-minute online computer-based intervention (RISE) reduces internalized homonegativity (IH) in gay and same-sex attracted men compared to a control condition
original_authors: Yen-Jui Lin; Tania Israel
original_title: A computer-based intervention to reduce internalized heterosexism in men
replication_authors: Tania Israel; Joshua A. Goodman; Caitlin R. S. Merrill; Yen-Jui Lin; Krishna G. Kary; Em Matsuno; Andrew Young Choi
replication_title: Reducing Internalized Homonegativity: Refinement and Replication of an Online Intervention for Gay Men
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Results supported our first two hypotheses. The refined IH intervention was efficacious with a small effect size' and 'our findings reflect a similar magnitude of effect as reported in Lin and Israel (2012).' Effect sizes were nearly identical across all three outcomes (e.g., d = 0.21 vs. 0.18 for IHNI sum score).

description: Prolonged exposure to a 50-Hz, 100-µT alternating magnetic field promotes the development and growth of mammary tumors in DMBA-treated female Sprague-Dawley rats
original_authors: Anke Baum; Meike Mevissen; Kenji Kamino; Ulrich Mohr; Wolfgang Löscher
original_title: A histopathological study on alterations in DMBA-induced mammary carcinogenesis in rats with 50 Hz, 100 µT magnetic field exposure
replication_authors: Meike Mevissen Monika Haussler Alex
replication_title: ACCELERATION OF MAMMARY TUMORIGENESIS BY EXPOSURE OF 7,12-DIMETHYLBENZ\[a]ANTHRACENE-TREATED FEMALE RATS IN A 50-Hz, 100-muT MAGNETIC FIELD: REPLICATION STUDY
replication_journal: Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health, Part A
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'One main finding of the present study is that the tumor (co)promoting effect of MF exposure in the DMBA breast cancer model is reproducible when the same experiment is repeated in the same laboratory.' The replication found 83% tumor incidence in MF-exposed vs. 62% in sham-exposed rats (p < .0004 by Mantel-Cox test), closely mirroring the original findings.

description: The borderline of comfort and discomfort (BCD), a subjective measure of glare sensitivity, can be predicted from glare source size, angular position above the observer's line of sight, and background luminance for roadway lighting conditions
original_authors: Corwin A. Bennett
original_title: Discomfort glare: Concentrated sources-parametric study of angularly small sources
replication_authors: Corwin A. Bennett; R. Michael Rubison; Balaji C. V. Ramaro
replication_title: Discomfort Glare: Luminance Range-Limited Replication Study of Angularly Small Sources
replication_journal: Journal of the Illuminating Engineering Society
explanation: The authors explicitly run a new experiment replicating the 1977 study with a restricted luminance range to account for range effects, using the same BCD paradigm but with modified conditions. The conclusion states 'a new experiment has provided more appropriate data for applying discomfort glare to roadways' and the regression analysis yielded compatible results with higher predictability (R²=0.94 vs 0.82), indicating a successful replication with improvement.

description: The prolactin receptor gene intron C/T polymorphism (rs37389) is associated with recurrent miscarriage, with women with recurrent miscarriage having an excess of heterozygotes compared to controls
original_authors: Courtney W. Hanna; Karla L. Bretherick; Chi-Chao Liu; Mary D. Stephenson; Wendy P. Robinson
original_title: Genetic variation within the hypothalamus-pituitary-ovarian axis in women with recurrent miscarriage
replication_authors: Jin Ju Kim; Young Min Choi; Sung Ki Lee; Kwang Moon Yang; Eun Chan Paik; Hyeon Jeong Jeong; Jong Kwan Jun; Ae Ra Han; Kyu Ri Hwang; Min A. Hong
replication_title: Prolactin receptor gene polymorphism and the risk of recurrent pregnancy loss: a case-control study
explanation: The replication found no significant difference in genotype distribution between RPL patients and controls (p = .587), in contrast to the original study's finding (p = .028). The authors explicitly state: 'Although we could not identify PRL-R gene polymorphism as a candidate gene for RPL, which differs from the results of Hanna et al.'s previous study.'

description: Higher compassion satisfaction (CS) and lower compassion fatigue (CF) predict lower burnout among mental health-care providers, with CS, CF, and years of experience as significant predictors of burnout
original_authors: Susan L. Ray; Carol Wong; Dawn White; Kimberly Heaslip
original_title: Compassion satisfaction, compassion fatigue, work life conditions, and burnout among frontline mental health care professionals
replication_authors: Jonathan Singer; Caroline Cummings; Danielle Boekankamp; Ryan Hisaka; Lorraine T. Benuto
replication_title: Compassion Satisfaction, Compassion Fatigue, and Burnout: A Replication Study with Victim Advocates
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Using victim advocates, we replicated Ray et al.'s (2013) study and found similar results, particularly that CS and CF were highly predictive of burnout.' While some differences emerged (CS and CF explained more variance, years of experience was not significant), the main finding of CS and CF predicting burnout was replicated.

description: The Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery (LNNB) can identify neuropsychological deficits in epilepsy patients with high accuracy, achieving overall hit rates of 82.5% (77.3% for idiopathic epilepsy and 88.9% for symptomatic epilepsy)
original_authors: Richard A. Berg; Charles J. Golden
original_title: Identification of neuropsychological deficits in epilepsy using the Luria-Nebraska Neuropsychological Battery
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Bruce P. Hermann; Michelle Melyn
replication_title: Identification of neuropsychological deficits in epilepsy using the Luria-Nebraska neuropsychological battery: A replication attempt
replication_journal: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Neuropsychology
explanation: The replication obtained an overall hit rate of only 41% (47% for idiopathic, 30% for symptomatic epilepsy), dramatically lower than the original 82.5%. The authors explicitly state: 'Our results are, therefore, at odds with those of Berg and Golden' and devote the Discussion to explaining the methodological reasons for the discrepant findings.

description: Learning design factors (teaching materials, assessment strategies, workload) and long-term goals of learners are strong predictors of overall satisfaction among students in undergraduate blended and online modules at the Open University UK
original_authors: Li, Nai; Marsh, Vicky; Rienties, Bart
original_title: Modeling and managing learner satisfaction: use of learner feedback to enhance blended and online learning experience
original_journal: Decision Sciences Journal of Innovative Education
replication_authors: Nai Li; Vicky Marsh; Bart Rienties; Denise Whitelock
replication_title: Online learning experiences of new versus continuing learners: a large-scale replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'large scale replication study' of Li, Marsh, and Rienties (2016), and the Discussion confirms: 'While most of the key drivers for learning satisfaction across the 2014 and 2015 cohort were similar, thereby verifying the initial study of Li, Marsh, and Rienties (2016).' The same key drivers (teaching materials, assessment, career relevance) were found to predict learner satisfaction, supporting the original findings.

description: An evidence module explicitly teaching 'concepts of evidence' improves pre-service primary teachers' content knowledge of scientific evidence, their ability to conduct open-ended investigations, and their ability to question evidence behind scientific claims
original_authors: Gott, R.; Roberts, R.
original_title: Concepts of evidence and their role in open-ended practical investigations and scientific literacy; background to published papers
replication_authors: Ros Roberts; Esin Sahin-Pekmez
replication_title: Scientific evidence as content knowledge: a replication study with English and Turkish pre-service primary teachers
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'This replication study has demonstrated that the intervention, originally designed in the English context, has resulted in very significant increases in the content knowledge of the Turkish cohort of student teachers, despite the cohorts having different characteristics. We have replicated the increases found in the English cohort in the Turkish cohort.' The same evidence module and instruments were used but in a new national/cultural context (Turkey instead of England).

description: High letter confusability eliminates the facilitatory effect of large orthographic neighbourhood size (N size) on word naming performance in letter-by-letter (LBL) dyslexia, indicating that residual parallel letter processing is blocked by visual letter similarity
original_authors: Martin Arguin; Stéphanie Fiset; Daniel Bub
original_title: Sequential and parallel letter processing in letter-by-letter dyslexia
replication_authors: Martin Arguin; Daniel Bub
replication_title: Parallel processing blocked by letter similarity in letter by letter dyslexia: A replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'The observations of Experiment 2 provide a complete replication of the previous findings of Arguin et al. (2002) with IH regarding the joint effects of N size and letter confusability.' The Conclusion reaffirms: 'The present report replicates, in three LBL dyslexics, the previous findings of Arguin et al. (2002) in patient IH.' All three new patients showed the identical pattern.

description: Verifying verbal statements about object-property relations (e.g., 'cat-whiskers?') activates the left fusiform gyrus, a modality-specific visual region, indicating that perceptual knowledge is represented in a modality-specific manner
original_authors: Irene P. Kan; Lawrence W. Barsalou; Karen Olseth Solomon; Jeris K. Minor; Sharon L. Thompson-Schill
original_title: Role of mental imagery in a property verification task: fMRI evidence for perceptual representations of conceptual knowledge
replication_authors: Edward E. Smith; Nicholas Myers; Umrao Sethi; Spiro Pantazatos; Ted Yanagihara; Joy Hirsch
replication_title: Conceptual representations of perceptual knowledge
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated Kan et al.'s activation in the left fusiform gyrus' using the identical task and items, but with more participants and an event-related design. The ROI analysis confirmed marginally significant fusiform activation (t(12) = 1.74, p = .054, one-tailed). The authors also extended the findings by identifying additional amodal areas not found by Kan et al.

description: Intuitive eating is positively associated with body image satisfaction and negatively associated with disordered eating and depressive symptomology in postpartum women, with body image dissatisfaction predicting intuitive eating scores
original_authors: Megan F. Lee; Susan L. Williams; Karena J. Burke
original_title: Striving for the thin ideal post-pregnancy: a cross-sectional study of intuitive eating in postpartum women
original_journal: Journal of Reproductive and Infant Psychology
replication_authors: Megan F. Lee; Charlotte Target; Caitlin Liddelow; Karena J. Burke
replication_title: Bouncing back with bliss: nurturing body image and embracing intuitive eating in the postpartum: a cross-sectional replication study
replication_journal: Journal of Reproductive and Infant Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current study aims to replicate the data collection and analysis in M. F. Lee et al. (2020)' and confirm in the Discussion that body image dissatisfaction, postpartum depression, and disordered eating were negatively correlated with intuitive eating, replicating the key findings of the original study.

description: A survey of lay public respondents reveals widespread misconceptions about brain injury, including beliefs about memory deficits, coma and unconsciousness, and recovery processes
original_authors: Wm. Drew Gouvier; Perry H. Prestholdt; Mark Warner
original_title: A survey of common misconceptions about head injury and recovery
replication_authors: Karen Hux; Charisse Deuel Schram; Tracy Goeken
replication_title: Misconceptions about brain injury: A survey replication study
explanation: The current study used a modified version of Gouvier et al.'s original questionnaire (17 of 25 items) administered to a new sample. Results were mixed: some misconceptions declined over 20 years (improved general brain injury knowledge), while others increased (e.g., coma awareness decreased 27.62%, belief in possibility of complete recovery from severe injury worsened dramatically). The authors conclude: 'improved understanding of brain injury in general has not extended to issues relating to coma and unconsciousness, memory deficits and the brain injury recovery process.'

description: The Violence Risk Appraisal Guide (VRAG) predicts violent recidivism among male offenders with a previous violent or hands-on sex offence, yielding a ROC area of 0.76 in a Canadian maximum-security sample over a 7-year follow-up period
original_authors: Grant T. Harris; Marnie E. Rice; Vernon L. Quinsey
original_title: Violent recidivism of mentally disordered offenders: The development of a statistical prediction instrument
replication_authors: Frank Urbaniok; Thomas Noll; Sonja Grunewald; Jennifer Steinbach; Jérôme Endrass
replication_title: Prediction of violent and sexual offences: A replication study of the VRAG in Switzerland
explanation: The authors explicitly designed the study to test VRAG predictive accuracy in a German-speaking Swiss population. The replication yielded a ROC area of .73 (95% CI: 0.62–0.83), which the authors describe as 'satisfying predictive accuracy' and 'comparable with the effect sizes reached in previous validation studies,' including the original.

description: A single session of reading literary fiction improves mentalising performance (as measured by the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test) relative to reading non-fiction
original_authors: Kidd, David Comer; Castano, Emanuele
original_title: Reading literary fiction improves theory of mind
replication_authors: Dalya Samur; Mattie Tops; Sander L. Koole
replication_title: Does a single session of reading literary fiction prime enhanced mentalising performance? Four replication experiments of Kidd and Castano (2013)
explanation: Experiment 1 used the same texts and RMET task as Kidd & Castano's Experiment 1 (literary fiction vs. non-fiction, Amazon Mechanical Turk) with twice the sample size. The effect was not significant: F(1, 153) = .56, p = .45, η²p = .00. Authors conclude there was 'no evidence to support Kidd and Castano's (2013) finding.'

description: A single session of reading literary fiction improves mentalising performance (as measured by the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test) relative to reading popular fiction or non-fiction
original_authors: Kidd, David Comer; Castano, Emanuele
original_title: Reading literary fiction improves theory of mind
replication_authors: Dalya Samur; Mattie Tops; Sander L. Koole
replication_title: Does a single session of reading literary fiction prime enhanced mentalising performance? Four replication experiments of Kidd and Castano (2013)
explanation: Experiment 2 added a popular fiction condition to the design with different texts than those used in Experiment 1. The main effect of condition was not significant (F(2, 227) = 2.53, p = .08, η²p = .02), and pairwise comparisons showed no advantage for literary fiction over popular fiction or non-fiction. Authors report no support for Kidd & Castano's finding.

description: A single session of reading literary fiction improves mentalising performance (as measured by the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test) relative to reading popular fiction, non-fiction, or no text
original_authors: Kidd, David Comer; Castano, Emanuele
original_title: Reading literary fiction improves theory of mind
replication_authors: Dalya Samur; Mattie Tops; Sander L. Koole
replication_title: Does a single session of reading literary fiction prime enhanced mentalising performance? Four replication experiments of Kidd and Castano (2013)
explanation: Experiment 3 used the same paradigm with a pre/post RMET design and added a no-text control condition. The critical condition × time interaction was not significant (F(3, 320) = .32, p = .81, η²p = .00), and the main effect of condition on post-manipulation RMET (controlling for pre-RMET) was also not significant (F(3, 316) = .31, p = .82, η²p = .00). Authors conclude no significant effects of reading literary fiction on mentalising.

description: A single session of reading literary fiction improves mentalising performance (as measured by the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test) relative to reading popular fiction (Experiment 3 of Kidd & Castano)
original_authors: Kidd, David Comer; Castano, Emanuele
original_title: Reading literary fiction improves theory of mind
replication_authors: Dalya Samur; Mattie Tops; Sander L. Koole
replication_title: Does a single session of reading literary fiction prime enhanced mentalising performance? Four replication experiments of Kidd and Castano (2013)
explanation: Experiment 4 was a pre-registered direct replication of Kidd & Castano's Experiment 3. The main effect of condition was not significant (F(3, 289) = 1.43, p = .24, η²p = .02). The authors explicitly state in the General Discussion that 'the present findings fail to confirm the notion that a single session of reading literary fiction can prime enhanced mentalising performance.'

description: Facial age cues affect emotion recognition speed through evaluative associations, such that happiness is detected faster than sadness on young but not old male faces (dual-valence context)
original_authors: Belinda M. Craig; Ottmar V. Lipp
original_title: Facial age cues and emotional expression interact asymmetrically: Age cues moderate emotion categorisation
replication_authors: Gijsbert Bijlstra; Désirée Kleverwal; Tjits van Lent; Rob W. Holland
replication_title: Evaluations versus stereotypes in emotion recognition: a replication and extension of Craig and Lipp’s (2018) study on facial age cues
explanation: The authors ran a pre-registered direct replication of Craig and Lipp (2018a)'s dual-valence context study. They found a significant interaction between emotion and age-groups, F(1,28) = 16.04, p < .001, η² = .36, consistent with the original findings, and explicitly state: 'The results of Study 1 revealed a clear and straightforward replication of Craig and Lipp's (2018a) findings.'

description: Gustatory unconditioned stimuli (tastes) produce evaluative conditioning effects for olfactory conditioned stimuli (smells) but not for color conditioned stimuli, suggesting modality-specific preparedness in flavor-flavor conditioning
original_authors: Frank Baeyens; Paul Eelen; Omer Van den Bergh; Geert Crombez
original_title: Flavor-flavor and color-flavor conditioning in humans
replication_authors: Borys Ruszpel; Anne Gast
replication_title: Memory and preparedness in evaluative conditioning in a smell-taste paradigm. A registered report
explanation: The authors explicitly label Experiment 1 as 'a conceptual replication of the study by Baeyens et al. (1990)'. They found an overall EC effect (p = .049) but no significant interaction of US valence × CS type (p = .581), meaning they did not replicate the modality-specific finding that smell-taste (but not color-taste) pairings produce EC. The discussion notes the result 'tentatively supports the evidence for the effectiveness of gustatory USs to condition olfactory CSs' but the key modality-specificity finding was not replicated.

description: A computational model captures momentary subjective well-being fluctuations during a gambling task, with reward prediction errors (RPE) exerting a greater influence on SWB than expected value (EV)
original_authors: Robb B. Rutledge; Nikolina Skandali; Peter Dayan; Raymond J. Dolan
original_title: A computational and neural model of momentary subjective well-being
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Niels Vanhasbroeck; Levi Devos; Sebastiaan Pessers; Peter Kuppens; Wolf Vanpaemel; Agnes Moors; Francis Tuerlinckx
replication_title: Testing a computational model of subjective well-being: a preregistered replication of Rutledge et al. (2014)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'this study can be considered a successful replication': model fit (R²=0.54±0.21 vs original 0.47±0.21), all model weights were significantly greater than 0, and RPE weight was significantly greater than EV weight (t(49)=4.92, p<.001). Both the individual and hierarchical analyses confirmed all three preregistered criteria.

description: Model M1 (the full computational model with CR, EV, and RPE terms) outperforms eight competing models in describing momentary subjective well-being data
original_authors: Robb B. Rutledge; Nikolina Skandali; Peter Dayan; Raymond J. Dolan
original_title: A computational and neural model of momentary subjective well-being
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Niels Vanhasbroeck; Levi Devos; Sebastiaan Pessers; Peter Kuppens; Wolf Vanpaemel; Agnes Moors; Francis Tuerlinckx
replication_title: Testing a computational model of subjective well-being: a preregistered replication of Rutledge et al. (2014)
explanation: The authors report they 'cannot conclude that we successfully replicated the model comparison results of Rutledge et al. (2014)': models M4 and M9 slightly outperformed M1 on both R² and BIC, and several models showed similar performance rather than M1 clearly dominating.

description: Participants choose reappraisal over distraction more often when viewing low-intensity compared to high-intensity negative images
original_authors: Gal Sheppes; Susanne Scheibe; Gaurav Suri; Peter Radu; Jens Blechert; James J. Gross
original_title: Emotion regulation choice: A conceptual framework and supporting evidence
replication_authors: Catherine N. M. Ortner; Allister Grapes; Maria Stoney
replication_title: The effect of temporal goals on emotion regulation choice: a replication and extension
explanation: The authors state 'We replicated the effect of intensity: participants chose reappraisal more often when intensity was low than high' with a comparable effect size (η²p = .71 in the replication vs. η²p = .89 in the original).

description: Participants choose reappraisal over distraction more often when given a long-term emotion regulation goal (expecting to re-encounter the stimuli) compared to an immediate goal
original_authors: Gal Sheppes; Susanne Scheibe; Gaurav Suri; Peter Radu; Jens Blechert; James J. Gross
original_title: Emotion regulation choice: A conceptual framework and supporting evidence
replication_authors: Catherine N. M. Ortner; Allister Grapes; Maria Stoney
replication_title: The effect of temporal goals on emotion regulation choice: a replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We did not replicate the effect of temporal goal on reappraisal choice' (Ft(1, 70.80) = 1.21, p = .28), and describe 'our failure to replicate' in the Discussion, citing the original large effect (Hedges' g = 1.1) as likely overestimated due to the small original sample (N = 22).

description: A cross-age tutoring program improves academic performance and social behavior for both emotionally disturbed adolescent tutors and educable mentally retarded child tutees in an urban public school setting
original_authors: Charles A. Maher
original_title: Handicapped adolescents as cross-age tutors: Program description and evaluation
replication_authors: Charles A. Maher
replication_title: Direct Replication of a Cross-Age Tutoring Program Involving Handicapped Adolescents and Children
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The investigation presented above can be considered a direct replication of the one conducted by Maher (1984).' Results were described as 'very similar to those of the prior study, both for program implementation and program outcome results,' with tutors and tutees both improving on academic and social measures in the same pattern as the original.

description: Older adults preferentially remember positive images over negative and neutral ones (positivity effect), whereas young adults show the reverse pattern (negativity bias), in a standard emotional memory paradigm
original_authors: Susan Turk Charles; Mara Mather; Laura L. Carstensen
original_title: Aging and emotional memory: The forgettable nature of negative images for older adults
replication_authors: Clémence Joubert; Patrick S. R. Davidson; Hanna Chainay
replication_title: When Do Older Adults Show a Positivity Effect in Emotional Memory?
explanation: The authors explicitly describe their study as 'a close replication of Charles et al.'s study' using the original stimuli and a very similar procedure. The conclusion states: 'older adults showed a positivity effect in memory under similar conditions to Charles et al. (2003)', and the abstract states 'The finding of a positivity effect in older but not young adults replicates the original report from [Charles et al., 2003].'

description: Parental guidance of children's television viewing falls into three distinct dimensions (restrictive, evaluative, and unfocused), and parental beliefs about television's negative effects predict greater use of restrictive and evaluative guidance methods
original_authors: Carl R. Bybee; Danny Robinson; Joseph Turow
original_title: Determinants of parental guidance of children's television viewing for a special subgroup: Mass media scholars
replication_authors: Tom H. A. van der Voort; Peter Nikken; Jan E. van Lil
replication_title: Replication: Determinants of parental guidance of children's television viewing: A Dutch replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'Despite cultural differences between the two countries and the different populations surveyed, the results of the present study and those of Bybee et al. (1982) are in marked agreement on the major points. All of the four main hypotheses that were derived from Bybee et al.'s study (Hypotheses 1-4) have been confirmed.'

description: The underpinning and ownership stages of an active learning model for knowledge construction in e-learning positively and significantly contribute to the engaging stage where actual knowledge construction takes place
original_authors: Koohang, A.; Paliszkiewicz, J.; Nord, J.; Ramim, M.
original_title: Advancing a theoretical model for knowledge construction in e-learning
original_journal: The Online Journal of Applied Knowledge Management
replication_authors: Alex Koohang; Joanna Paliszkiewicz; Jerzy Gołuchowski; Jeretta Horn Nord
replication_title: Active Learning for Knowledge Construction in E-Learning: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The results of the present study are consistent with Koohang et al. [28]', with both hypotheses accepted at p < 0.001 in both studies. The replication used the same instrument and methodology as the original but with a different population sample from a different geographic area (Midwest USA vs Southeast USA).

description: Social networking site success model: content quality, system quality, and trust influence social capital and user satisfaction, which in turn drive continued-use intention among US Facebook users
original_authors: Aaron M. French; Jung P. Shim; Robert F. Otondo; Gary F. Templeton
original_title: An empirical study evaluating social networking continuance and success
replication_authors: Aaron M. French; Andrew William Green
replication_title: Social Networking Continuance and Success: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication used the same survey instrument and methods (methodological replication) but tested the model with South Korean SNS users. Most hypotheses were supported in both samples, but two differed: H2b (System Quality → User Satisfaction) was not supported in South Korea, and H4b (Social Capital → Continued Use Intention) was significant in South Korea but not in the US original. The authors conclude that 'generalizability is limited by significant differences between the original study results and our results.'

description: Students attending institutions with a social norms marketing (SNM) campaign had a lower relative risk of alcohol consumption than students attending control group institutions
original_authors: William DeJong; Shari Kessel Schneider; Laura Gomberg Towvim; Melissa J. Murphy; Emily E. Doerr; Neal R. Simonsen; Karen E. Mason; Richard A. Scribner
original_title: A multisite randomized trial of social norms marketing campaigns to reduce college student drinking
replication_authors: William DeJong; Shari Kessel Schneider; Laura Gomberg Towvim; Melissa J. Murphy; Emily E. Doerr; Neal R. Simonsen; Karen E. Mason; Richard A. Scribner
replication_title: A Multisite Randomized Trial of Social Norms Marketing Campaigns to Reduce College Student Drinking: A Replication Failure
explanation: The paper's title explicitly calls this a 'Replication Failure,' and the abstract states 'This study failed to replicate a previous multisite randomized trial of SNM campaigns.' The Discussion confirms: 'students attending institutions that implemented a social norms marketing (SNM) campaign did not have a lower risk of alcohol consumption relative to students attending control group institutions.'

description: A community-based, social cognitive theory-driven weight loss treatment emphasizing physical activity self-regulation generalized to eating self-regulation (phase 1) can induce weight loss over 6 months and maintain that loss through 24 months in women with obesity
original_authors: James J. Annesi; Ping H. Johnson; Gisèle A. Tennant; Kandice J. Porter; Kristin L. McEwen
original_title: Weight loss and the prevention of weight regain: evaluation of a treatment model of exercise self-regulation generalizing to controlled eating
replication_authors: James J. Annesi; Jennifer L. Unruh-Rewkowski; Nicole Mareno
replication_title: Replication and Extension of the Weight Loss For Life Community-Based Treatment Protocol
explanation: The authors explicitly state the purpose was 'to replicate the initial trial of the phase 1 treatment' and in the Discussion confirm: 'Significant improvements in self-regulatory skills usage, fruit/vegetable consumption, and physical activity outputs were similarly found in both the phase 1 and phase 2 treatment versions, along with a loss of between 6% and 6.5% of initial body weight over 6 months.
