description: Changes in discrimination indexes during operant discrimination training are largely a function of cumulative time in SΔ (the extinction component), not the number of reinforcers earned in S+
original_authors: J. Gilmour Sherman; Frederick W. Hegge; Rosemary Pierrel
original_title: Discrimination formation as related to the amount of SΔ training
replication_authors: Matthew E. Andrzejewski; Curtis D. Ryals; Sean Higgins; Jennifer Sulkowski; Janice Doney; Ann E. Kelley; Philip J. Bersh
replication_title: Is extinction the hallmark of operant discrimination?: Reinforcement and SΔ effects
explanation: Experiment 1 explicitly states 'the invariance that was observed in the present experiment involved cumulative time spent in SΔ, thereby replicating the experiment conducted by Sherman et al. (1964).' The proportion of responding in SD as a function of cumulative SΔ exposure was equivalent across groups at each level of reinforcement, confirming Sherman et al.'s (1964) finding.

description: Changes in discrimination indexes during operant discrimination training are largely a function of cumulative time in SΔ (the extinction component), not the number of reinforcers earned in S+
original_authors: J. Gilmour Sherman; Frederick W. Hegge; Rosemary Pierrel
original_title: Discrimination formation as related to the amount of SΔ training
replication_authors: Matthew E. Andrzejewski; Curtis D. Ryals; Sean Higgins; Jennifer Sulkowski; Janice Doney; Ann E. Kelley; Philip J. Bersh
replication_title: Is extinction the hallmark of operant discrimination?: Reinforcement and SΔ effects
explanation: Experiment 3 explicitly sought to 'replicate that finding within-subject' (the invariant relation between cumulative SΔ exposure and proportion of responding in SD). Results were mixed across individual rats: some showed the invariant relation (S09, S10), some showed similar terminal levels but different rates (S13, S14), some showed early equivalence then divergence (S11, S12), and some showed consistently better performance in the 4-min condition (S15, S16). Authors describe the results as 'equivocal on this matter.'

description: Agreeableness (and Neuroticism) scores can be predicted from resting-state EEG spectral power using support vector regression (SVR) multivariate pattern analysis, with Agreeableness showing a negative correlation at 8–11 Hz at posterior channels and a positive relationship at 11.5–19 Hz for parietal and frontal channels
original_authors: Hayley K. Jach; Daniel Feuerriegel; Luke D. Smillie
original_title: Decoding personality trait measures from resting EEG: An exploratory report
replication_authors: Christoph Fruehlinger; Katharina Paul; Jan Wacker
replication_title: Can personality traits be predicted from resting-state EEG oscillations? A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract: 'We were not able to replicate the findings for Agreeableness.' In the conclusion: 'we could not replicate them for Agreeableness and other personality traits based on our thresholds.' The decoding performance did not reach the pre-defined threshold of r = .20 in any frequency bin, and Spearman correlations for predefined electrode-frequency clusters were rho = .06 (non-significant), with Bayes factors providing positive evidence for the null hypothesis.

description: Community-wide implementation of the Triple P parenting and family support program reduces county-wide rates of substantiated child maltreatment cases
original_authors: Prinz, Ronald J.; Sanders, Matthew R.; Shapiro, Cheri J.; Whitaker, Daniel J.; Lutzker, John R.
original_title: Population-based prevention of child maltreatment: the U.S. Triple P system population trial
replication_authors: Ronald J. Prinz
replication_title: Assessing child maltreatment prevention via administrative data systems: A case example of reproducibility
explanation: The author re-queried the same administrative database a decade later for the same time period and re-ran the identical ANCOVA analyses. Results were reproducible: the reproduced analyses showed significant intervention effects for substantiated CM in the same direction with even higher effect sizes (Cohen's d = 1.61 and 1.34) compared to the originals (Cohen's d = 1.30 and 1.04), and the author concludes that 'data patterns and statistical inferences were essentially reproducible with only modest alteration after a lapse of ten years.'

description: Community-wide implementation of the Triple P parenting and family support program reduces county-wide rates of out-of-home placements for children
original_authors: Prinz, Ronald J.; Sanders, Matthew R.; Shapiro, Cheri J.; Whitaker, Daniel J.; Lutzker, John R.
original_title: Population-based prevention of child maltreatment: the U.S. Triple P system population trial
replication_authors: Ronald J. Prinz
replication_title: Assessing child maltreatment prevention via administrative data systems: A case example of reproducibility
explanation: The author re-queried the same administrative database a decade later and re-ran identical ANCOVA analyses for out-of-home placements. The reproduced analyses produced comparable effect sizes (Cohen's d = 1.06 and 1.10) to the original analyses (Cohen's d = 0.87 and 1.10), with the same pattern of means (control counties increased, intervention counties decreased), leading to the conclusion that the data patterns and statistical effects were reproducible.

description: Latent class analysis (LCA) of child maltreatment (CM) exposure identifying four unique classes: nonmaltreated, episodic single-type neglect, episodic single-type abuse, and chronic multi-type
original_authors: Warmingham, Jennifer M.; Handley, Elizabeth D.; Rogosch, Fred A.; Manly, Jody Todd; Cicchetti, Dante
original_title: Identifying Maltreatment Subgroups with Patterns of Maltreatment Subtype and Chronicity: A Latent Class Analysis Approach
replication_authors: Justin Russotti; Jennifer Warmingham; Elizabeth D. Handley; Jody Todd Manly; Dante Cicchetti
replication_title: Common patterns of maltreatment exposure: A replication study using confirmatory latent class analysis
explanation: Reviewer update: The original study being replicated is Warmingham et al. (2019), which used exploratory LCA to identify four CM latent classes. The current study (Russotti et al., 2025, n=566) used Confirmatory LCA (CLCA) in a new, independent sample to test whether the same four-class structure replicates. The abstract explicitly states: 'Results provide evidence for the replication of four unique latent classes of CM exposure.' This is a clear successful direct replication — same construct, same four-class structure, different sample. Confidence upgraded to high because the original study is now identified and the result classification is unambiguous from the abstract. Several of the same senior authors (Warmingham, Handley, Manly, Cicchetti) appear on both papers.

description: Total sentence reading times do not differ across Chinese, Finnish, and English readers, and basic lexical properties (word frequency, word length) account for common variance in eye movements across these three typologically different orthographies, reflecting universal aspects of reading
original_authors: Simon P. Liversedge; Denis Drieghe; Xin Li; Guoli Yan; Xuejun Bai; Jukka Hyönä
original_title: Universality in eye movements and reading: A trilingual investigation
replication_authors: Simon P. Liversedge; Henri Olkoniemi; Chuanli Zang; Xin Li; Guoli Yan; Xuejun Bai; Jukka Hyönä
replication_title: Universality in eye movements and reading: A replication with increased power
explanation: The replication failed to reproduce the central finding (no language differences in total sentence reading time) — Chinese readers were significantly faster than Finnish and English readers (BF = 4453.71 against the null). However, many other findings replicated: effects of word frequency, number of words, and visual complexity on eye movements across languages. The authors conclude: 'it is certainly the case that one particular, quite central, aspect of our study was not replicated – total sentence reading time differences emerged across languages' while also noting 'many aspects of the results of the current study did replicate those of the original study.'

description: A single-session equine-assisted psychotherapy incorporating horses (PIH) resiliency intervention for healthcare workers improves psychological flexibility (as measured by AAQ-II) with no adverse events
original_authors: Marchand, William R.; Sullivan-Sakaeda, Laurie
original_title: A pilot observational study of a psychotherapy incorporating equines resiliency intervention for staff at a large medical center
replication_authors: William R. Marchand; Laurie Sullivan-Sakaeda; Ryan Lackner; Dylan Taplin; Elena Nazarenko
replication_title: A replication study of a psychotherapy incorporating horses resiliency intervention for healthcare workers
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The first aim of this pilot observational study was to replicate a previous study of a resiliency psychotherapy incorporating horses (PIH) intervention for healthcare workers.' In the Discussion they confirm: 'This finding is consistent with our previous study of a similar equine-assisted PIH resilience intervention for healthcare workers' — specifically referring to the replication of the primary outcome (improved psychological flexibility on the AAQ-II, p = .022).

description: Radiomics-based machine learning models (Rad-score and complex model) using PET/CT imaging can predict PD-L1 expression status in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with AUCs of 0.761 and 0.769 respectively
original_authors: Zhao, et al.
original_title: Predicting PD-L1 expression status in patients with non-small cell lung cancer using [18F]FDG PET/CT radiomics
replication_authors: Anna Theresa Stüber; Maurice M. Heimer; Johanna Ta; Matthias P. Fabritius; Boj F. Hoppe; Gabriel Sheikh; Matthias Brendel; Lena Unterrainer; Philip Jurmeister; Amanda Tufman; Jens Ricke; Clemens C. Cyran; Michael Ingrisch
replication_title: Replication study of PD-L1 status prediction in NSCLC using PET/CT radiomics
explanation: The replication result is unambiguous. The abstract explicitly states 'Our study failed to replicate original findings, suggesting poor model performance and questioning predictive value of radiomics features in classifying PD-L1 expression from PET/CT imaging.' All three models performed significantly below Zhao et al.'s reported AUCs: Rad-score AUC 0.573–0.593 vs. original 0.761; complex model AUC 0.505–0.519 vs. original 0.769; clinical model AUC 0.555 vs. original 0.640. A benchmark study across four ML pipelines also showed consistently low performance. Confidence upgraded to high after independent web search confirmed the full citation for Zhao et al. (EJNMMI Research, 2023) and verified that the AUC values reported in the replication paper match the original study's validation-group results exactly.

description: E-cigarettes tested at 5.0 V produce 5–15-fold higher levels of formaldehyde emissions compared to tobacco cigarettes
original_authors: Jensen, R. Paul; Luo, Wentai; Pankow, James F.; Strongin, Robert M.; Peyton, David H.
original_title: Hidden formaldehyde in e-cigarette aerosols
replication_authors: Konstantinos E. Farsalinos; Vassilis Voudris; Alketa Spyrou; Konstantinos Poulas
replication_title: E-cigarettes emit very high formaldehyde levels only in conditions that are aversive to users: A replication study under verified realistic use conditions
explanation: Independent review confirms a clear replication failure. The paper explicitly states 'We set to replicate this study using the same e-cigarette equipment and e-liquid' and concludes: 'The high levels of formaldehyde emissions that were reported in a previous study were caused by unrealistic use conditions that create the unpleasant taste of dry puffs to e-cigarette users and are thus avoided.' Jensen et al. (2015) found 5–15-fold higher formaldehyde at 5.0 V; this replication confirms high formaldehyde at 5.0 V (718.2 μg/10 puffs) but adds dry-puff detection showing that 5.0 V is unrealistic — 88% of users detected dry puffs at ≤4.2 V. Under realistic conditions (≤4.0 V), formaldehyde was 32% lower than from tobacco cigarettes, the opposite of the original alarm. The citation mismatch flag was a false positive: the abstract says 'a study' without naming Jensen et al. by name, but the described finding (5–15-fold higher at 5.0 V, 2015, same equipment) uniquely identifies Jensen et al. (NEJM 2015, doi:10.1056/NEJMc1414754) as the target. All fields are confirmed correct.

description: The morphing technique (gradually morphing human and robot/animal images) reliably elicits the uncanny valley effect, such that morphed intermediate images are rated as less likable than either endpoint (pure human or pure robot)
original_authors: Anne E. Ferrey; Tyler J. Burleigh; Mark J. Fenske
original_title: Stimulus-category competition, inhibition, and affective devaluation: a novel account of the uncanny valley
replication_authors: Jussi Palomäki; Anton Kunnari; Marianna Drosinou; Mika Koverola; Noora Lehtonen; Juho Halonen; Marko Repo; Michael Laakasuo
replication_title: Evaluating the replicability of the uncanny valley effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion: 'we could not replicate the effects for the stimuli generated with a morphing technique (Ferrey et al., 2015).' Studies 1 and 2 used a between-subjects design with a subset of Ferrey's CGI stimuli in a Finnish population, and while some marginal effects were found, none survived multiple comparisons correction, and the typical UV markers (likability, creepiness) were not reliably elicited.

description: Pre-categorized robot pictures of varying levels of uncanniness reliably elicit the uncanny valley effect, with the most uncanny robot rated as less pleasant, likable, and friendly and more creepy, repulsive, and disgusting than both non-uncanny robots and human images
original_authors: Astrid M. Rosenthal-von der Pütten; Nicole C. Krämer
original_title: How design characteristics of robots determine evaluation and uncanny valley related responses
replication_authors: Jussi Palomäki; Anton Kunnari; Marianna Drosinou; Mika Koverola; Noora Lehtonen; Juho Halonen; Marko Repo; Michael Laakasuo
replication_title: Evaluating the replicability of the uncanny valley effect
explanation: The authors report that Studies 3a and 3b successfully found the UV effect using Rosenthal-von der Pütten and Krämer's (2014) pre-categorized stimuli: 'In Studies 3a and 3b, unlike Studies 1 and 2, we observed the UV effect for both positive ("likable" and "friendly", "pleasant") and negative ("creepy", "repulsive") attributes.' All contrasts were highly significant (all p < .001 in Study 3b) and robust to multiple comparisons correction.

description: Nurses' clinical judgment (rated on a visual analogue scale) more closely agrees with expert panel opinion on pressure ulcer risk than formal risk assessment scales (Norton, Braden, and Waterlow), and some patients are more difficult to assess than others
original_authors: Dinah Gould; Daniel Kelly; Len Goldstone; John Gammon
original_title: Examining the validity of pressure ulcer risk assessment scales: developing and using illustrated patient simulations to collect the data
replication_authors: Dinah Gould; Len Goldstone; Daniel Kelly; John Gammon
replication_title: Examining the validity of pressure ulcer risk assessment scales: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the results of replication accord with the original study findings' for both Patients C and D, and conclude: 'Replication supported the original study findings' — nurses' VAS clinical judgement again more closely matched expert opinion than the Waterlow Score.

description: Organizational/managerial support for nursing has a pronounced effect on nurses' job dissatisfaction, burnout, and quality of care across Western countries (the International Hospital Outcomes Study)
original_authors: Aiken, Linda H.; Clarke, Sean P.; Sloane, Douglas M.
original_title: Hospital staffing, organization, and quality of care: cross-national findings
replication_authors: Chanyeong Kwak; Bok Yae Chung; Yu Xu; Cho Eun-Jung
replication_title: Relationship of job satisfaction with perceived organizational support and quality of care among South Korean nurses: A questionnaire survey
explanation: This study explicitly describes itself as 'a replication study of the IHOS using the same method and instruments.' Results largely confirmed the association of burnout and organizational support with job satisfaction, but South Korean nurses showed higher job satisfaction (68.8%) and lower burnout (35.7%) than IHOS counterparts despite far higher patient-to-nurse ratios — a counter-intuitive divergence the authors attribute to cultural differences. The study uses the same instruments (Pennsylvania Registered Nurse Survey) and methods but applies them in a non-Western (South Korean) context.

description: Motor cortex excitability (as measured by paired-pulse TMS cMEP/uMEP ratios) is positively correlated with neuroticism scores from the NEO personality inventory, particularly in men
original_authors: Eric M. Wassermann; Benjamin D. Greenberg; Margaret B. Nguyen; Dennis L. Murphy
original_title: Motor cortex excitability correlates with an anxiety-related personality trait
replication_authors: Martin Schecklmann; Michael Landgrebe; Elmar Frank; Philipp G. Sand; Peter Eichhammer; Göran Hajak; Berthold Langguth
replication_title: Is motor cortex excitability associated with personality factors? A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We tried, but failed to replicate these findings in a sample almost twice as large as the former sample.' No systematic significant correlations between NEO personality factors and TMS measures were found, and the overall number of significant correlations was below chance level.

description: Olfactory event-related potentials (N1 and P2) to hydrogen sulfide stimuli in schizophrenia patients, as characterized by CSD-PCA methodology, show a distinct N1 sink over lateral frontotemporal sites and P2 source over centroparietal sites with monotonic amplitude increases as a function of odor intensity
original_authors: Jürgen Kayser; Craig E. Tenke; Dolores Malaspina; Christopher J. Kroppmann; Jennifer D. Schaller; Andrew Deptula; Nathan A. Gates; Jill M. Harkavy-Friedman; Roberto Gil; Gerard E. Bruder
original_title: Neuronal generator patterns of olfactory event-related brain potentials in schizophrenia
replication_authors: Jürgen Kayser; Craig E. Tenke; Christopher J. Kroppmann; Daniel M. Alschuler; Shelly Ben-David; Shiva Fekri; Gerard E. Bruder; Cheryl M. Corcoran
replication_title: Olfaction in the psychosis prodrome: Electrophysiological and behavioral measures of odor detection
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusions: 'The present study soundly replicates our previous olfactory ERP findings using a combined CSD-PCA approach (Kayser et al., 2010).' The same H2S odor detection paradigm with CSD-PCA methodology was used, and the same N1 sink and P2 source morphology with monotonic intensity-dependent increases were confirmed, though now tested in a clinical high-risk (CHR) adolescent/young adult population rather than diagnosed schizophrenia patients.

description: The transdiagnostic compulsivity dimension (compulsive behaviour and intrusive thought) is associated with reduced goal-directed learning in a two-step reinforcement learning task
original_authors: Claire M. Gillan; Michal Kosinski; Robert Whelan; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Nathaniel D. Daw
original_title: Characterizing a psychiatric symptom dimension related to deficits in goal-directed control
replication_authors: Seow TXF; Benoit E.; Dempsey C.; Jennings M.; Maxwell A.; McDonough M.; Gillan CM
replication_title: A dimensional investigation of error-related negativity (ERN) and self-reported psychiatric symptoms
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated this finding (β = −0.07, SE = 0.04, p < 0.05)' in section 3.4, and further confirm it in the Discussion noting 'two replications with respect to the specific association between compulsive behaviour and intrusive thought scores and goal-directed planning; one observed in the present study.'

description: Female and male participants show clear sexual dichotomy in pupil dilation when viewing images of different interest value (e.g., females dilate more to images of mother and baby, males dilate more to images of a partially nude female)
original_authors: Eckhard H. Hess; James M. Polt
original_title: Pupil size as related to interest value of visual stimuli
replication_authors: de Winter JCF; Petermeijer SM; Kooijman L.; Dodou D.
replication_title: Replicating five pupillometry studies of Eckhard Hess
explanation: The authors explicitly state in Table 8: 'Failure to replicate, as only 2 of the 15 statistical tests showed a significant gender difference in pupil dilation (one consistent with and the other in the opposite direction to Hess and Polt, 1960).' The Discussion confirms: 'we did not obtain support for the hypothesis of gender differences in pupil dilation.'

description: Solving more difficult multiplication problems is associated with greater pupil dilation than solving easier problems
original_authors: Eckhard H. Hess; James M. Polt
original_title: Pupil size in relation to mental activity during simple problem-solving
replication_authors: de Winter JCF; Petermeijer SM; Kooijman L.; Dodou D.
replication_title: Replicating five pupillometry studies of Eckhard Hess
explanation: Table 8 explicitly states 'Successful replication. However, a nuance is provided: we found larger dilation for easier multiplications and more prolonged dilation for more difficult multiplications.' The within-subject linear contrast for PC[ans-2.5,ans] was significant: F(1,178) = 15.5, p < 0.001.

description: Participants show pupil mimicry (dilation in response to larger depicted pupils) specifically for images of two schematic eyes (as opposed to one or three), reflecting an evolutionarily innate pupil-to-pupil communication response
original_authors: Eckhard H. Hess
original_title: The role of pupil size in communication
replication_authors: de Winter JCF; Petermeijer SM; Kooijman L.; Dodou D.
replication_title: Replicating five pupillometry studies of Eckhard Hess
explanation: Table 8 explicitly states: 'Failure to replicate, as we found statistically significant pupillary mimicry for one-eyed images, not for two-eyed and three-eyed images.' The one-way ANOVA showed no significant effect for two-eyed stimuli (F(2,292) = 0.81, p = 0.446), which directly contradicts Hess's specific claim about two-eyed stimuli.

description: When watching a scene from a Western TV series where a male hero tries to escape a crowd, men's pupils dilate more than women's, reflecting fundamental gender differences in emotional engagement with the scene
original_authors: Hess, E.
original_title: The tell-tale eye: how your eyes reveal hidden thoughts and emotions
original_journal: The Tell-tale Eye. How Your Eyes Reveal Hidden Thoughts and Emotions
replication_authors: de Winter JCF; Petermeijer SM; Kooijman L.; Dodou D.
replication_title: Replicating five pupillometry studies of Eckhard Hess
explanation: The Discussion states: 'In our replication, we did not find this gender-specific pattern.' The repeated-measures ANOVA showed no significant effect of gender (F(1,145) = 0.03, p = 0.864) and no significant time × gender interaction (F(2,290) = 2.25, p = 0.107). Table 8 describes 'Different overall pattern than that described in Hess (1975b).'

description: Arousing words (e.g., 'nude', 'flay') cause greater pupil dilation than non-arousing words in male and female participants
original_authors: James M. Polt; Eckhard H. Hess
original_title: Changes in pupil size to visually presented words
replication_authors: de Winter JCF; Petermeijer SM; Kooijman L.; Dodou D.
replication_title: Replicating five pupillometry studies of Eckhard Hess
explanation: Table 8 explicitly states 'Successful replication: Arousing words caused greater dilation than non-arousing words.' The ANOVA showed a significant effect of arousal (F(1,146) = 5.27, p = 0.023). The Discussion notes: 'Our findings are consistent with this hypothesis: just as the line drawings of nudes caused pupil dilation, so did the presentation of the words 'nude' and 'flirt' cause a larger pupil dilation than neutral stimuli.'

description: Expert meditators show larger MMN amplitude during focused attention (FA) meditation compared to a control condition and novice practitioners, with an interaction between meditation expertise and meditation styles on auditory mismatch negativity (MMN) amplitude
original_authors: Fucci E.; Abdoun O.; Caclin A.; Francis A.; Dunne JD; Ricard M.; Davidson RJ; Lutz A.
original_title: Differential effects of non-dual and focused attention meditations on the formation of automatic perceptual habits in expert practitioners
replication_authors: Enrico Fucci; Arnaud Poublan-Couzardot; Oussama Abdoun; Antoine Lutz
replication_title: No effect of focused attention and open monitoring meditation on EEG auditory mismatch negativity in expert and novice practitioners
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'non replication of meditation states and expertise effects on MMN amplitude.' They found no significant interaction between group and state (F(2) = 0.51; p = 0.6), with Bayesian analysis providing strong evidence against the interaction effect (BF01 = 11.0).

description: Increased alpha oscillatory power (8-12 Hz) during focused attention (FA) and open presence (OP) meditation practices compared to a control condition in both expert and novice practitioners
original_authors: Fucci E.; Abdoun O.; Caclin A.; Francis A.; Dunne JD; Ricard M.; Davidson RJ; Lutz A.
original_title: Differential effects of non-dual and focused attention meditations on the formation of automatic perceptual habits in expert practitioners
replication_authors: Enrico Fucci; Arnaud Poublan-Couzardot; Oussama Abdoun; Antoine Lutz
replication_title: No effect of focused attention and open monitoring meditation on EEG auditory mismatch negativity in expert and novice practitioners
explanation: The authors state in the Discussion: 'This partially replicates findings on oscillatory power from Fucci et al. (2018).' They found a significant main effect of state on alpha power (frontal ROI: F(2) = 35.9, p < .001), with post-hoc tests confirming higher alpha during FA and OP compared to the video control condition.

description: Distributive justice, procedural justice, and interactional justice are the major determinants of satisfaction with complaint handling (SATCOM) in business-to-consumer service contexts, with distributive justice having the strongest effect
original_authors: Orsingher, Chiara; Valentini, Sara; de Angelis, Matteo
original_title: A meta-analysis of satisfaction with complaint handling in services
original_journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
replication_authors: Christian Brock; Markus Blut; Heiner Evanschitzky; Peter Kenning
replication_title: Satisfaction with complaint handling: A replication study on its determinants in a business-to-business context
replication_journal: International Journal of Research in Marketing
explanation: The authors replicate the justice model of complaint satisfaction in a B2B industrial context and find mixed results: distributive justice replicates with similar effect sizes (βB2B=.47 vs. βB2C=.45, n.s. difference), procedural justice is significantly stronger in B2B (βB2B=.49 vs. βB2C=.09, p<.01), and interactional justice fails to replicate in B2B (βB2B=.09, non-significant, vs. βB2C=.25, p<.01). The authors conclude the justice model partially generalizes to B2B but with important differences.

description: 33-month-old children succeed at above-chance rates in a false belief task when inhibitory control and response generation demands are reduced
original_authors: Peipei Setoh; Rose M. Scott; Renée Baillargeon
original_title: Two-and-a-half-year-olds succeed at a traditional false-belief task with reduced processing demands
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Stella S. Grosso; Tobias Schuwerk; Larissa J. Kaltefleiter; Beate Sodian
replication_title: 33-month-old children succeed in a false belief task with reduced processing demands: A replication of Setoh et al. (2016)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In this study, we successfully replicated the finding by Setoh et al. (2016) that 33-month-olds succeed in a false belief task with reduced processing demands.' They found 74% correct responding (43/58), closely matching the original >70% success rate.

description: About one-third of 2-year-old children pass a representational change false belief task involving a deceptive picture book, demonstrating nascent false belief understanding in toddlers
original_authors: Claire Hughes; Rosie Ensor
original_title: Executive function and theory of mind: Predictive relations from ages 2 to 4
replication_authors: Stella S. Grosso; Tobias Schuwerk; Larissa J. Kaltefleiter; Beate Sodian
replication_title: 33-month-old children succeed in a false belief task with reduced processing demands: A replication of Setoh et al. (2016)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we did not replicate Hughes and Ensor (2007) finding in a representational change false belief task, but obtained floor effects.' Only 4.8% (2/42) passed both belief questions, compared to the expected ~33% from the original study (M=0.65, SD=0.77, N=122 in original vs. M=0.26, SD=0.54, N=42 in replication).

description: Nine-month-old infants encode the identity of novel objects preferentially in communicative contexts and their location preferentially in non-communicative contexts, producing a double dissociation in memory biases
original_authors: Jennifer M. D. Yoon; Mark H. Johnson; Gergely Csibra
original_title: Communication-induced memory biases in preverbal infants
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Priya Silverstein; Teodora Gliga; Gert Westermann; Eugenio Parise
replication_title: Probing communication-induced memory biases in preverbal infants: Two replication attempts of Yoon, Johnson and Csibra (2008)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results do not replicate the finding by Yoon et al. (2008) that infants show a memory bias for identity information after viewing communicative scenes, and a memory bias for location information after viewing non-communicative scenes.' No significant interaction between action and outcome was found.

description: Nine-month-old infants encode the identity of novel objects preferentially in communicative contexts and their location preferentially in non-communicative contexts, producing a double dissociation in memory biases
original_authors: Jennifer M. D. Yoon; Mark H. Johnson; Gergely Csibra
original_title: Communication-induced memory biases in preverbal infants
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Priya Silverstein; Teodora Gliga; Gert Westermann; Eugenio Parise
replication_title: Probing communication-induced memory biases in preverbal infants: Two replication attempts of Yoon, Johnson and Csibra (2008)
explanation: The authors conclude that 'Neither experiment replicated the results of the original study' and the Bayes Factor Analysis for Experiment 2 yielded BF01=4.12, constituting moderate evidence for the null hypothesis of no memory biases.

description: 11-month-old infants flexibly anticipate the goal of a grasping action (anticipating that a hand grasps the same object even when its position is swapped), indicating goal-based rather than path-based action prediction
original_authors: Erin N. Cannon; Amanda L. Woodward
original_title: Infants generate goal-based action predictions
replication_authors: Kerstin Ganglmayer; Manja Attig; Moritz M. Daum; Markus Paulus
replication_title: Infants’ perception of goal-directed actions: A multi-lab replication reveals that infants anticipate paths and not goals
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'While the previous experiments 1-4 represent conceptual replications of the study by Cannon and Woodward (2012).' In Experiment 1, infants showed significantly more location-related than identity-related anticipations (z = -2.14, p = .03), failing to replicate the goal-based prediction finding.

description: 11-month-old infants flexibly anticipate the goal of a grasping action (anticipating that a hand grasps the same object even when its position is swapped), indicating goal-based rather than path-based action prediction
original_authors: Erin N. Cannon; Amanda L. Woodward
original_title: Infants generate goal-based action predictions
replication_authors: Kerstin Ganglmayer; Manja Attig; Moritz M. Daum; Markus Paulus
replication_title: Infants’ perception of goal-directed actions: A multi-lab replication reveals that infants anticipate paths and not goals
explanation: Experiment 2 removed the occluder and changed movement direction to horizontal (as in Cannon & Woodward 2012), but infants showed chance performance: neither significant identity- nor location-related anticipations in the additional analysis using Cannon and Woodward's criteria (t(23) = -0.72, p = .482, d = 0.15).

description: 11-month-old infants flexibly anticipate the goal of a grasping action (anticipating that a hand grasps the same object even when its position is swapped), indicating goal-based rather than path-based action prediction
original_authors: Erin N. Cannon; Amanda L. Woodward
original_title: Infants generate goal-based action predictions
replication_authors: Kerstin Ganglmayer; Manja Attig; Moritz M. Daum; Markus Paulus
replication_title: Infants’ perception of goal-directed actions: A multi-lab replication reveals that infants anticipate paths and not goals
explanation: Experiment 3 replaced the animated fish with a human hand (as in Cannon & Woodward 2012) but retained other differences. Using Cannon & Woodward's analysis criteria, infants showed chance performance (t(31) = -1.53, p = .137, d = 0.27), failing to replicate goal-based anticipations.

description: 11-month-old infants flexibly anticipate the goal of a grasping action (anticipating that a hand grasps the same object even when its position is swapped), indicating goal-based rather than path-based action prediction
original_authors: Erin N. Cannon; Amanda L. Woodward
original_title: Infants generate goal-based action predictions
replication_authors: Kerstin Ganglmayer; Manja Attig; Moritz M. Daum; Markus Paulus
replication_title: Infants’ perception of goal-directed actions: A multi-lab replication reveals that infants anticipate paths and not goals
explanation: Experiment 4 adapted timing and presentation to closely match Cannon & Woodward (2012) while still using animated targets. Infants showed a significant preference for the location over the goal (t(31) = -4.05, p < .001, d = 0.72), the opposite of the original finding, indicating a clear failure to replicate goal-based anticipations.

description: 11-month-old infants flexibly anticipate the goal of a grasping action (anticipating that a hand grasps the same object even when its position is swapped), indicating goal-based rather than path-based action prediction
original_authors: Erin N. Cannon; Amanda L. Woodward
original_title: Infants generate goal-based action predictions
replication_authors: Kerstin Ganglmayer; Manja Attig; Moritz M. Daum; Markus Paulus
replication_title: Infants’ perception of goal-directed actions: A multi-lab replication reveals that infants anticipate paths and not goals
explanation: The authors explicitly label Experiment 5 as the direct replication: 'Experiment 5 represents a direct replication.' New videos were filmed to match the original stimuli as closely as possible. Using Cannon & Woodward's analysis criteria, infants showed chance performance (t(30) = -0.92, p = .363, d = 0.17), failing to replicate goal-based anticipations.

description: 11-month-old infants flexibly anticipate the goal of a grasping action (anticipating that a hand grasps the same object even when its position is swapped), indicating goal-based rather than path-based action prediction
original_authors: Erin N. Cannon; Amanda L. Woodward
original_title: Infants generate goal-based action predictions
replication_authors: Kerstin Ganglmayer; Manja Attig; Moritz M. Daum; Markus Paulus
replication_title: Infants’ perception of goal-directed actions: A multi-lab replication reveals that infants anticipate paths and not goals
explanation: Study 2's hand-paradigm (conducted in a second lab) was based on Cannon & Woodward (2012) with deliberate modifications (within-subjects design, 5 learning trials instead of 3, 3 consecutive test trials instead of 1, introductory movie added). 11-month-olds showed chance performance on the First Fixation Score (t(33) = -0.88, p = .39, d = -0.15), failing to replicate goal-directed anticipations.

description: Developers care about code smells: most professional software developers are aware of and concerned about code smells, and the top three most popular code smells are Duplicated Code, Long Method, and Accidental Complexity
original_authors: Aiko Yamashita; Leon Moonen
original_title: Do developers care about code smells? An exploratory survey
original_journal: Proceedings of the 20th Working Conference on Reverse Engineering
replication_authors: Davide Taibi; Andrea Janes; Valentina Lenarduzzi
replication_title: How developers perceive smells in source code: A replicated study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'externally replicated the study [8]' by Yamashita and Moonen. The conclusion states 'This study confirms and extends the results obtained in [8].' The Discussion (Section 5.1) finds comparable respondent profiles and that developers became even more aware and concerned about code smells in the three years since the original.

description: Developers can recognize code smells as design problems in source code: showing 34 developers code fragments from open-source projects infected with code smells, most smells were perceived as harmful, with Long Class, Cyclomatic Complexity, and Long Method most often identified as harmful
original_authors: Fabio Palomba; Gabriele Bavota; Massimiliano Di Penta; Rocco Oliveto; Andrea De Lucia
original_title: Do they really smell bad? A study on developers' perception of bad code smells
original_journal: Proceedings of the 2014 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
replication_authors: Davide Taibi; Andrea Janes; Valentina Lenarduzzi
replication_title: How developers perceive smells in source code: A replicated study
explanation: The authors 'externally replicated the study [25]' by Palomba et al., extending it to 23 code smells (vs. 12 in the original) and using more professional developers. Section 5.2 reports 'large differences' between the studies for several smells (e.g., Class Data Should Be Private perceived as harmful by 93% vs. 11% in the original), which the authors attribute to the more professional participant pool. The conclusion says 'confirms and extends' both studies but the large discrepancies for specific smells make the result inconclusive.

description: Group cognitive behavioural therapy enhanced for older adults (CBT-OA) significantly reduces depression, anxiety, and improves quality of life in older adults with late-life depressive and anxiety disorders
original_authors: Ursuliak, Z.; Cassidy, K.-L.; Eskes, G.; Burke, D.
original_title: An observational study of the effectiveness of group cognitive behavioral therapy for late-life depressive and anxiety disorders
replication_authors: Anna Skosireva; Linda Gobessi; Gail Eskes; Keri-Leigh Cassidy
replication_title: Effectiveness of enhanced group cognitive behaviour therapy for older adults (CBT-OA) with depression and anxiety: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This is the first replication study of the CBT-OA intervention for late-life depression or anxiety. We found significant statistical and clinical benefits of Cassidy's manualized CBT-OA program on measures of depression, anxiety, and quality of life, replicating the findings of Ursuliak et al.' The study used the same protocol and measures but was conducted at a different centre (Ottawa vs. Halifax) with a larger and somewhat different sample.

description: ASSIP (Attempted Suicide Short Intervention Program) add-on therapy to treatment as usual (TAU) reduces suicidal behavior (suicide attempts and suicide deaths) by approximately 80% compared to TAU alone in patients with a recent suicide attempt
original_authors: Anja Gysin-Maillart; Simon Schwab; Leila Soravia; Millie Megert; Konrad Michel
original_title: A novel brief therapy for patients who attempt suicide: a 24-months follow-up randomized controlled study of the attempted suicide short intervention program (ASSIP)
replication_authors: Anna Monn; Tania Villar de Araujo; Annia Rüesch; Golo Kronenberg; Christoph Hörmann; Atalìa Adank; Zachary Roman; Georgios Schoretsanitis; Michael Rufer; Erich Seifritz; Birgit Kleim; Sebastian Olbrich
replication_title: Randomized controlled trial for the Attempted Suicide Short Intervention Program (ASSIP): An independent non-replication study
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself an 'independent non-replication study' and concludes: 'Contrary to the original findings, this non-replication study suggests that ASSIP combined with TAU does not significantly reduce suicidal behavior compared to TAU alone.' The ITT analysis found OR = 2.55 (95% CI: 0.88–8.10, p = .093), directionally opposite to the original 80% risk reduction.

description: Readers slow down at the disambiguation region when a temporarily ambiguous sentence resolves toward the dispreferred sentential complement structure, with this garden-path effect modulated by the verb's distributional bias (DO-biased vs. SC-biased verbs)
original_authors: Susan M. Garnsey; Neal J. Pearlmutter; Elizabeth Myers; Melanie A. Lotocky
original_title: The contributions of verb bias and plausibility to the comprehension of temporarily ambiguous sentences
replication_authors: Ariel N. James; Scott H. Fraundorf; Eun-Kyung Lee; Duane G. Watson
replication_title: Individual differences in syntactic processing: Is there evidence for reader-text interactions?
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'these findings replicate the verb bias effect in the literature,' reporting a significant ambiguity effect (β = 0.074, p < 0.001) and significant ambiguity × verb bias interaction (β = 0.099, p < 0.001), using 80 stimuli drawn from Lee et al. (2013) which employed the Garnsey et al. (1997) paradigm.

description: Object-extracted relative clauses (ORCs) are read more slowly and comprehended less accurately than subject-extracted relative clauses (SRCs) in English
original_authors: Edward Gibson; Timothy Desmet; Daniel Grodner; Duane Watson; Kara Ko
original_title: Reading relative clauses in English
replication_authors: Ariel N. James; Scott H. Fraundorf; Eun-Kyung Lee; Duane G. Watson
replication_title: Individual differences in syntactic processing: Is there evidence for reader-text interactions?
explanation: Using Gibson et al.'s (2005) original 32 items, the authors report reading times were significantly longer in ORC sentences relative to SRC sentences (β = 0.222, SE = 0.050, p < 0.001), explicitly stating this 'replicate[s] the standard finding in the literature.'

description: English readers exhibit a low-attachment preference for globally ambiguous relative clauses (e.g., 'The maid of the princess who scratched herself'), and lower verbal working memory capacity is associated with stronger high-attachment preference due to prosodic chunking strategies
original_authors: Benjamin Swets; Timothy Desmet; David Z. Hambrick; Fernanda Ferreira
original_title: The role of working memory in syntactic ambiguity resolution: A psychometric approach
replication_authors: Ariel N. James; Scott H. Fraundorf; Eun-Kyung Lee; Duane G. Watson
replication_title: Individual differences in syntactic processing: Is there evidence for reader-text interactions?
explanation: Using Swets et al.'s (2007) original 20 items, the authors replicate both the low-attachment preference (β = 2.246, p < 0.001) and the finding that lower verbal working memory is associated with stronger high-attachment preference (Low Attach. × VWM: β = 0.937, p = 0.001), described as 'consistent with Swets et al. (2007).'

description: Ranking antidepressants by clinical acceptability using filled prescription sequences (continuation/failure ratio), with escitalopram as the most acceptable first-line option
original_authors: Romain Olekhnovitch; Nicolas Hoertel; Frédéric Limosin; Carlos Blanco; Mark Olfson; Anne Fagot-Campagna; Philippe Fossati; Emmanuel Haffen; Marcel Goldberg; Marie Zins; Cédric Lemogne
original_title: Using filled prescription sequences to rank antidepressants according to their acceptability in the general population: The Constances cohort
replication_authors: Charles Ouazana-Vedrines; Thomas Lesuffleur; Pierre Denis; Nicolas Hoertel; Frédéric Limosin; Antoine Rachas; Philippe Tuppin; Cédric Lemogne
replication_title: Using filled prescription sequences to rank antidepressants: A nationwide replication study
explanation: The abstract explicitly states this study 'aimed to replicate the results of a proof-of-concept study ranking anti-depressants according to the proportion of filled prescription sequences consistent with a continuation of the first treatment versus those consistent with a change.' The proof-of-concept study is Ouazana-Vedrines et al. (2020), which used the Constances cohort (~64,467 individuals). The replication extends this to a much larger nationwide French cohort (SNDS, ~1.2 million new antidepressant users in 2011), constituting a close extension into a different, larger dataset using the same methodology. The result is a clear success: 'Escitalopram again was the most acceptable option, and the five following antidepressants were the same as in the replication sample of the proof-of-concept study' (Fluoxetine, Paroxetine, Sertraline, Citalopram, Venlafaxine). The original study reference was confirmed via PubMed (PMID 32036076) and ScienceDirect (DOI 10.1016/j.jpsychires.2020.01.017). Confidence upgraded from low to high after identifying the original study.

description: Optimism (total LOT and unipolar optimism scores) is associated with a warm-dominant interpersonal style, and unipolar pessimism is associated with a hostile-submissive interpersonal style, as measured by regression on IPC affiliation and control dimensions
original_authors: Alexandra L. Terrill; John M. Ruiz; John P. Garofalo
original_title: Look on the bright side: Do the benefits of optimism depend on the social nature of the stressor
replication_authors: Timothy W. Smith; John M. Ruiz; Jenny M. Cundiff; Kelly G. Baron; Jill B. Nealey-Moore
replication_title: Optimism and pessimism in social context: An interpersonal perspective on resilience and risk
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim was to 'replicate these IPC analyses of dispositional optimism across multiple samples,' and in the Results section report: 'As in prior research (Terrill, Ruiz, & Garofalo, 2010), total LOT-R scores and unipolar optimism scores were associated with a friendly-dominant interpersonal style, whereas unipolar pessimism scores were associated with a hostile-submissive style,' confirming a successful replication across four undergraduate samples using a different but equivalent IPC measure.

description: SNP rs2057178 (near WT1 on chromosome 11p13) is associated with susceptibility to tuberculosis in a Ghana-Gambia cohort, with the A allele being protective (OR 0.62)
original_authors: Thorsten Thye; Ellis Owusu-Dabo; Fredrik O. Vannberg; Reinout van Crevel; James Curtis; Edhyana Sahiratmadja; Yanina Balabanova; Christa Ehmen; Birgit Muntau; Gerd Ruge; Jürgen Sievertsen; John Gyapong; Vladyslav Nikolayevskyy; Philip C. Hill; Giorgio Sirugo; Francis Drobniewski; Esther van de Vosse; Melanie Newport; Bachti Alisjahbana; Sergey Nejentsev; Tom H. M. Ottenhoff; Adrian V. S. Hill; Rolf D. Horstmann; Christian G. Meyer
original_title: Common variants at 11p13 are associated with susceptibility to tuberculosis
replication_authors: Anuradha Gautam; Ahana Dasgupta; Suvamita Rout; Samsiddhi Bhattacharjee; Bhaswati Pandit
replication_title: Genetic association of missense (rs2919643), intergenic (rs2057178) and a 3’UTR (rs1009170) variant with tuberculosis: A replication study from India
explanation: The authors explicitly replicated the association of rs2057178 with TB in an Indian cohort, finding the A allele protective against TB (OR 0.7133, p=0.04188), consistent with the original finding in a Ghana-Gambia population (OR 0.62, p=3.00E-06). The Discussion states: 'rs2057178-A was found to be protective against TB susceptibility.'

description: SNP rs1009170 (3' UTR variant on chromosome 14) is associated with susceptibility to tuberculosis in an Indian case-household contact cohort from West Bengal
original_authors: Chandrika Bhattacharyya; Partha Pratim Majumder; Bhaswati Pandit
original_title: An exome wide association study of pulmonary tuberculosis patients and their asymptomatic household contacts
replication_authors: Anuradha Gautam; Ahana Dasgupta; Suvamita Rout; Samsiddhi Bhattacharjee; Bhaswati Pandit
replication_title: Genetic association of missense (rs2919643), intergenic (rs2057178) and a 3’UTR (rs1009170) variant with tuberculosis: A replication study from India
explanation: The authors (same group) explicitly validated their own prior finding: 'Association of rs1009170; previously reported by us with TB was also replicated in the new set of samples (p=0.0359).' The genotypic model was significantly associated with TB (p=0.0359) in the replication cohort.

description: SNP rs61104666 (synonymous variant in linkage disequilibrium with rs2919643 on chromosome 18) is associated with susceptibility to tuberculosis in an Indian case-household contact cohort, implicating the SIGLEC15/EPG5 genomic locus
original_authors: Chandrika Bhattacharyya; Partha Pratim Majumder; Bhaswati Pandit
original_title: An exome wide association study of pulmonary tuberculosis patients and their asymptomatic household contacts
replication_authors: Anuradha Gautam; Ahana Dasgupta; Suvamita Rout; Samsiddhi Bhattacharjee; Bhaswati Pandit
replication_title: Genetic association of missense (rs2919643), intergenic (rs2057178) and a 3’UTR (rs1009170) variant with tuberculosis: A replication study from India
explanation: Upgraded from medium after independent review. The prior agent flagged ambiguity because rs2919643 is a different SNP from the original hit rs61104666. However, the paper's Introduction explicitly states this was a deliberate design choice: 'In our replication study we have included rs2919643 which is in high LD with one of the top hits of the previous study: rs61104666... rs61104666 is a synonymous variant while, rs2919643 is a missense polymorphism of SIGLEC15.' The authors chose the proxy because it is more biologically interpretable (missense vs. synonymous). The Discussion and Conclusion (p0165) explicitly count rs2919643 among 'three replicated variants' and frame the study as a successful replication. The association is strong (p=8.81E-5, OR 1.653). The LD-proxy approach is a principled design decision that resolves rather than introduces ambiguity: the locus is unambiguously replicated in the authors' framing and the data. 'close experiment' type is correct — same Indian household-contact design as original, different specific SNP (proxy in LD), same chromosomal locus.

description: 13 SNPs identified in a whole-genome association study are associated with susceptibility to Parkinson disease
original_authors: Maraganore DM; de Andrade M.; Lesnick TG; Strain KJ; Farrer MJ; Rocca WA; Pant PV; Frazer KA; Cox DR; Ballinger DG
original_title: High-resolution whole-genome association study of Parkinson disease
replication_authors: Manu Sharma; Peter Lichtner; Rejko Kruger; Daniela Berg; Claudia Schulte; Thomas Illig; Olaf Riess; Thomas Gasser
replication_title: Further delineation of the association signal on chromosome 5 from the first whole genome association study in Parkinson's disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our study did not lend support to the finding that the reported SNPs are directly influencing the susceptibility to sporadic form of PD at least in our population.' After correcting for multiple testing by permutation procedure, none of the 11 successfully genotyped SNPs showed significant association.

description: Masked repetition priming during recognition memory tests increases familiarity-based ('Know') responses and is associated with posterior N400 ERP effects that are topographically distinct from frontal FN400 potentials linked to familiarity for studied words
original_authors: Anna M. Woollams; Jason R. Taylor; Frini Karayanidis; Richard N. Henson
original_title: Event-related potentials associated with masked priming of test cues reveal multiple potential contributions to recognition memory
replication_authors: Heather D. Lucas; Jason R. Taylor; Richard N. Henson; Ken A. Paller
replication_title: Many roads lead to recognition: Electrophysiological correlates of familiarity derived from short-term masked repetition priming
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Experiment 1 Discussion: 'In addition to replicating the behavioral Jacoby-Whitehouse masked priming effect, we replicated two key ERP findings from Woollams et al. (2008). First, MP-same words were associated with more positive posterior N400 potentials relative to MP-different words. Second, these N400 effects were topographically distinct from frontal potentials found in the contrast between K hits and misses.' Some secondary findings differed (absence of 150-250ms central effect; masked priming not selective to 'Know' responses), but the primary ERP and behavioral findings were successfully replicated.

description: White matter integrity (DTI indices) mediates adult age differences in cognitive performance including RT components derived from the diffusion model (drift rate and non-decision time)
original_authors: David J. Madden; Julia Spaniol; Matthew C. Costello; Barbara Bucur; Leonard E. White; Roberto Cabeza; Simon W. Davis; Nancy A. Dennis; James M. Provenzale; Scott A. Huettel
original_title: Cerebral white matter integrity mediates adult age differences in cognitive performance
replication_authors: Yiqin Yang; Andrew R. Bender; Naftali Raz
replication_title: Age related differences in reaction time components and diffusion properties of normal-appearing white matter in healthy adults
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Changed from 'inconclusive' to 'failure' and upgraded confidence to 'high'. The paper is unambiguous: after Bonferroni correction, the only significant WM-RT association was DR in corpus callosum body with non-decision time. The authors state 'we found little evidence of association between diffusion properties of the normal appearing white matter and reaction time parameters' and conclude 'age differences in NAWM diffusion properties are not a major contributor to age differences in RT components.' This directly contradicts Madden et al.'s (2009b) finding that WM integrity mediates age differences in cognitive performance/RT components. The authors designed the study specifically to address Madden et al.'s limitations (simplified EZ model, extreme age groups only, no WMH exclusion) and the broader mediation claim was not supported. The one surviving association (DR in CCb → non-decision time) is far more limited than the original mediation finding, making this a failure rather than inconclusive.

description: Advanced age is associated with lower drift rate (slower information accumulation), greater response conservativeness, and longer non-decision time in a letter discrimination task using the Ratcliff diffusion model
original_authors: Anjali Thapar; Roger Ratcliff; Gail McKoon
original_title: A diffusion model analysis of the effects of aging on letter discrimination
replication_authors: Yiqin Yang; Andrew R. Bender; Naftali Raz
replication_title: Age related differences in reaction time components and diffusion properties of normal-appearing white matter in healthy adults
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Upgraded confidence to 'high'. The authors explicitly state they 'replicated all major extant findings pertaining to age differences in RT components.' All three diffusion model parameters showed significant age effects: drift rate F(1,87)=34.31, p<0.001; response conservativeness F(1,87)=5.32, p<0.05; non-decision time F(1,87)=31.57, p<0.001. The authors specifically cite Thapar et al. (2003) among the studies whose findings they extend 'to an adult life-span sample.' This is a close extension because the current study uses the same letter discrimination task but with a broader age range (18-82 continuous rather than extreme age groups) and the full Ratcliff diffusion model rather than the simplified EZ version.

description: Behavioral CO2 reactivity (specifically rearing and ambulation during flush-out phases) predicts long-term fear extinction memory in rats
original_authors: Monfils MH; Lee HJ; Keller NE; Roquet RF; Quevedo S.; Agee L.; Cofresi R.; Shumake J.
original_title: Predicting extinction phenotype to optimize fear reduction
replication_authors: Raskin M.; Keller NE; Agee LA; Malone CA; Quevedo S.; Hilz EN; Roquet RF; Shumake J.; Smits JAJ; Telch MJ; Otto MW; Lee HJ; Monfils MH
replication_title: Associations of CO2 reactivity and orexin activity with extinction memory to fear and reward cues: results from a large sample of male rats across multiple studies
explanation: Reviewer verified: genuinely inconclusive (partial replication). For CO2 session 1 (n=110), the exploratory best-subset analysis selected the null model — no overall predictive effect in the combined sample. However, a directed regression confirmed ambulation during flush out 1 negatively predicts fear extinction LTM (R²=-.15, p=.002), consistent with Monfils et al. 2019. For the fear-only sample in session 2, a new predictor emerged (ambulation during 25% hold, R²=0.21) rather than the original flush-out predictors. Authors state they 'confirm previous findings suggesting that fear and appetitive extinction memory can both be predicted with CO2 reactivity but have distinct predictors.' The general concept (CO2 reactivity predicts extinction) is supported, but the specific original predictors only partially hold, and the best-performing predictor in the larger combined fear sample is a newly identified variable. This genuine partial-replication pattern warrants medium confidence — reasonable people could classify this as success or inconclusive.

description: CO2-induced orexin activity (c-Fos+orexin co-labeled cells) is associated with long-term fear extinction memory in rats
original_authors: Monfils MH; Lee HJ; Keller NE; Roquet RF; Quevedo S.; Agee L.; Cofresi R.; Shumake J.
original_title: Predicting extinction phenotype to optimize fear reduction
replication_authors: Raskin M.; Keller NE; Agee LA; Malone CA; Quevedo S.; Hilz EN; Roquet RF; Shumake J.; Smits JAJ; Telch MJ; Otto MW; Lee HJ; Monfils MH
replication_title: Associations of CO2 reactivity and orexin activity with extinction memory to fear and reward cues: results from a large sample of male rats across multiple studies
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we did not replicate our previous finding that CO2-induced orexin activity is associated with extinction memory in either the fear or appetitive samples (Monfils et al., 2019).' In the combined sample analysis (n=77), the full sample R² was 0, and neither CO2 reactivity nor orexin activity significantly predicted long-term extinction memory.

description: Ideal L2 self and discrepancy between current and ideal L2 self predict intended English learning effort, and suppressed self-authenticity (authenticity gap) has a negative relationship with school effort among Swedish learners of English
original_authors: Alastair Henry; Christina Cliffordson
original_title: The impact of out-of-school factors on motivation to learn English: Self-discrepancies, beliefs, and experiences of self-authenticity
replication_authors: Sara A. Smith; Matthew E. Foster; Jessica Briggs Baffoe-Djan; Zhengjie Li; Sun Yu
replication_title: Unifying the current self, ideal self, attributions, self-authenticity, and intended effort: A partial replication study among Chinese university English learners
explanation: The authors partially replicated Henry and Cliffordson (2017) in a rural Chinese context. Hypotheses 1a and 1b (ideal L2 self scores and correlation with effort) replicated, but the discrepancy model (H1c) could not be replicated, attribution findings differed in direction, and the self-authenticity null finding was reversed (significant positive relationship in the current study, though not significant in the comprehensive SEM). The conclusion notes 'discrepancies between our findings and those of Henry and Cliffordson (2017).'

description: The HOBSCOTCH (HOme Based Self-management and COgnitive Training CHanges Lives) program improves quality of life and cognitive functioning (attention) in adults with epilepsy in a randomized controlled trial
original_authors: Tracie A. Caller; Robert J. Ferguson; Robert M. Roth; Karen L. Secore; Faith P. Alexandre; Wenyan Zhao; Tor Devin Tosteson; Patricia L. Henegan; Kimberly Birney; Barbara C. Jobst
original_title: A cognitive behavioral intervention (HOBSCOTCH) improves quality of life and attention in epilepsy
replication_authors: Cam Escoffery; Archna Patel; Katie L. Bullinger; Robin E. McGee; Jerik Leung; Taylor Shade; Shreya Shankar; Erica K. Johnson; Barbara C. Jobst; Elaine T. Kiriakopoulos
replication_title: Replication of an evidence-based epilepsy self-management program in Georgia (USA): The HOBSCOTCH trial
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'The present findings are consistent with previous HOBSCOTCH RCT reporting of improved QOL and cognition' and that the study replicated 'the findings noted by our Dartmouth colleagues but in a separate and distinct population.' Significant improvements were found for QOLIE-31 (beta=6.34, SE=2.75), Neuro-QOL (beta=7.34, SE=2.99), and AESMMI-65 (beta=0.29, SE=0.11).

description: Patients with schizophrenia show impairments in facial emotion recognition compared to healthy controls, including misidentification of neutral cues as threatening or unpleasant
original_authors: Leppänen JM; Niehaus DJ; Koen L.; Du Toit E.; Schoeman R.; Emsley R.
original_title: Emotional face processing deficit in schizophrenia: a replication study in a South African Xhosa population
replication_authors: Soyoung Lee; Hyo-Deog Rim; Y.W. Park; J.J. Lee; Seoyoung Jang; Jincheol Woo; Hyeyoung Jo; K.U. Lee
replication_title: P.3.e.001 Facial emotion recognition deficit in schizophrenia: a replication study in Korean subjects
explanation: Independent review confirms result and replication_type. The paper's title explicitly says 'a replication study in Korean subjects.' The authors tested facial emotion recognition deficits in schizophrenia in a Korean sample with Korean facial stimuli, extending prior work (including Leppanen et al. 2006 in South African Xhosa subjects) to a new cultural context — fitting 'close extension' exactly. Korean patients showed significant impairments in recognition of sad [F(1,114)=6.26, p=0.014], fearful [F(1,114)=6.18, p=0.014], and angry faces [F(1,114)=9.28, p=0.003]. The conclusion states: 'These findings are consistent with previous studies carried out in different ethnic groups, suggesting the cross-cultural similarities in the impairments of facial recognition in schizophrenia.' Happy face recognition was unimpaired, but the authors interpret the overall pattern as supporting the original finding. replication_title: Implication of European-derived adiposity loci in African Americans
explanation: INDEPENDENT REVIEW: This paper tested 46 SNPs across 19 European GWAS-identified adiposity loci in 4992 African Americans across six cohorts. The result is genuinely mixed. Seven SNPs at 4 loci (NEGR1, TMEM18, SH2B1/ATP2A1, MC4R) showed nominal significance (0.005 < P < 0.05) with consistent direction of effect, and the authors' own Conclusion states 'We replicated the association of variants at four loci.' However, no SNP survived Bonferroni correction (threshold P < 0.0011), FTO — one of the strongest European signals — was not replicated, and 15/19 loci showed no significant association. The Discussion explicitly attributes non-replication to power limitations (sample too small to detect effects of 0.03-0.05 s.d. units). This is a genuine ambiguity: partial nominal replication at 4/19 loci, zero loci surviving multiple-testing correction, and the paper's own framing alternates between claiming replication (4 loci, consistent direction) and acknowledging the overall failure to transfer (15 loci null, no Bonferroni-significant findings). 'Inconclusive' is appropriate for the bundle-level claim (do European GWAS loci transfer to African Americans?). Medium confidence is retained because the paper itself is genuinely unclear — the authors use the word 'replicated' while the data show mostly non-replication.

description: Testing after initial exposure to learning content (post-testing) enhances long-term retention relative to restudying, with a meta-analytic mean effect size of g = 0.69 in between-subject experiments
original_authors: Christopher A. Rowland

replication_authors: Alice Latimier; Arnaud Riegert; Hugo Peyre; Son Thierry Ly; Roberto Casati; Franck Ramus
replication_title: Does pre-testing promote better retention than post-testing?
explanation: The paper directly and unambiguously replicates the post-testing effect. The Discussion states: 'Regarding the post-testing effect, we replicated the same large effect size (d = 0.62 across question types) as found by Rowland in his meta-analysis of between-subject experiments (g = 0.69).' Post-testing produced a highly significant advantage over re-reading for trained questions (d = 0.74, 95% CI [0.44, 1.04], p < 0.0001) and for untrained questions (d = 0.36, p = 0.028). Note: the paper reports d = 0.74 for trained questions and d = 0.62 across all question types when explicitly comparing to Rowland's g = 0.69; the replication_es here reflects the trained-questions figure. The abstract, results, and discussion all converge unambiguously on a successful replication. Upgraded from medium to high confidence based on the explicit and consistent replication language throughout the paper.

description: Taking a test before being exposed to learning content (pre-testing) enhances retention compared with no retrieval practice, even when participants answer most pre-test questions incorrectly
original_authors: Lindsey E. Richland; Nate Kornell; Liche Sean Kao
original_title: The pretesting effect: do unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance learning?
replication_authors: Alice Latimier; Arnaud Riegert; Hugo Peyre; Son Thierry Ly; Roberto Casati; Franck Ramus
replication_title: Does pre-testing promote better retention than post-testing?
explanation: The paper unambiguously replicates the core pre-testing effect. The abstract states: 'We replicated both post-testing (d = 0.74) and pre-testing effects (d = 0.35).' The Discussion confirms a 'smaller but significant effect on trained questions (d = 0.35, p = 0.013)' for pre-testing vs. re-reading. The basic Richland et al. claim — that pre-testing (even with mostly incorrect answers) improves retention relative to a control — is confirmed. The replication found a smaller effect than Richland et al. (where ~95% of answers were wrong, giving more room for improvement vs. 40% correct in this study), and the pre-testing effect did not extend to untrained questions (d = -0.01, p = 0.95), which the authors discuss as a nuanced finding. However, the core effect for trained questions is clear and statistically significant. Upgraded from medium to high confidence: the paper explicitly uses the word 'replicated' for this effect, the statistics are unambiguous, and the smaller effect size in this study vs. Richland et al. is fully explained by the higher pre-test baseline performance.

replication_title: Genotypic variability enhances the reproducibility of an ecological study
explanation: Reviewed independently. The replication type is correctly 'conceptual': the original Richter et al. 2011 study tested CSV (controlled systematic variability) in mouse behavior, while this study tests the same hypothesis in a completely different domain — ecological plant microcosm experiments across 14 European labs. The 'inconclusive' result classification is appropriate and reflects genuine ambiguity: genotypic CSV reduced among-laboratory variability by 18% in growth chambers (supporting the hypothesis), but had no significant effect in glasshouses, and environmental CSV had little effect overall. The authors themselves use hedged language, describing the findings as 'supporting evidence for the hypothesis' rather than confirmation, and their conclusion states CSV 'may turn out to be a simple solution' (emphasis on 'may'). The mixed results across experimental setups mean the hypothesis is partially supported under stringently controlled conditions but not under more variable ones. This genuine conditionality in the findings makes 'inconclusive' the most accurate classification — upgrading to 'success' would overstate the evidence, while 'failure' would understate the growth chamber results. Confidence remains 'medium' because the ambiguity is inherent in the paper's findings, not due to unclear reporting.

Three converging analyses (regression, equivalence testing, bootstrap P-curve) all support this null finding, with EF P-value distributions indistinguishable from random data. Confidence remains medium because (1) the paper targets a broad literature claim rather than specifically replicating Martin-Rhee & Bialystok (2008), and (2) the authors list caveats that the null may be age-, task-, or population-specific.

explanation: Independent review confirms: the result classification (success) and all other fields are correct. Study 1 (n=28 sighted individuals) was explicitly designed to replicate the finding that RSFC between visual and non-visual regions is higher during eyes-closed than eyes-open rest. The authors state unambiguously in the Results: 'The results of Study 1 replicated those of recent reports showing that RSFC between visual and somatosensory cortical regions, as well as between visual and auditory cortical regions, is increased in both sighted adolescents and sighted adults.' The Discussion opens with the same confirmation. Table 1 provides clear statistical support: visual-somatosensory FC instances showed FDR-corrected significant effects (t = 3.67, 4.22, 3.86, 3.10) and visual-auditory also significant (t = 2.29, 4.52). The authors further note the effect held despite a substantially different parcellation scheme. The original medium confidence was due to the fact that the replication targets a cluster of prior studies (refs 16, 18, 21, 25, 26) rather than a single paper; Agcaoglu et al. (2019) is ref 16, the most recently published and explicitly named in the confirmation statement. This is a valid attribution choice: the result direction is unambiguous, the word 'replicated' is used explicitly, and the statistical evidence is clear. Upgraded to high.

The Conclusion repeats this: 'we also replicated prior work showing that members of East Asian societies predominantly attribute moral transgressions to situational factors, whereas members of Western societies tend to attribute transgressions to the intrinsic dispositions of transgressors.' The effect is very large across all six transgression scenarios (ηp² = 0.24–0.71, all p < 0.001), with Seoul participants consistently rating transgressions as more situationally caused than Los Angeles participants. The replication is a close extension (Korean rather than Chinese participants, different scenarios, additional moral parochialism component), and the original agent's 'medium' rating appears unwarranted given the unambiguous and repeated explicit replication language and overwhelming statistical support. Upgraded to high.
