explanation: The authors conducted a preregistered replication across 41 samples in 36 countries (vs. 31 in the original) and explicitly state: 'we replicated each of the country-level relationships from the study by Van Doesum and colleagues [11]' and 'we first directly replicated past work [11] in a novel sample with a greater variety of countries.' The key relationship — higher EPI associated with more socially mindful choices — was confirmed (β = 0.61, p < .001).

description: Odor cueing during learning, sleep, and testing (LST condition) provides the largest memory performance benefit for vocabulary learning compared to cueing during learning+sleep only, learning+testing only, or no odor control
original_authors: Franziska Neumann; Vitus Oberhauser; Jürgen Kornmeier
original_title: How odor cues help to optimize learning during sleep in a real life-setting
replication_authors: Jessica Knötzele; Dieter Riemann; Lukas Frase; Bernd Feige; Ludger Tebartz van Elst; Jürgen Kornmeier
replication_title: Presenting rose odor during learning, sleep and retrieval helps to improve memory consolidation: a real-life study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated our previous findings of better memory performance in the LST Condition than in the LT Condition,' and the LST group learned 8.5% more vocabulary words than other groups overall. The replication used adult online participants rather than school children, hence close extension.

description: Odor cueing during learning and subsequent slow-wave sleep (LS condition) enhances declarative memory consolidation compared to a no-odor control condition
original_authors: Björn Rasch; Christian Büchel; Steffen Gais; Jan Born
original_title: Odor cues during slow-wave sleep prompt declarative memory consolidation
replication_authors: Jessica Knötzele; Dieter Riemann; Lukas Frase; Bernd Feige; Ludger Tebartz van Elst; Jürgen Kornmeier
replication_title: Presenting rose odor during learning, sleep and retrieval helps to improve memory consolidation: a real-life study
explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The authors are unambiguous: they explicitly call this a 'replication failure' (Discussion, 'Possible reasons for only partial replication of previous TMR findings' section) and state 'We did not replicate this finding' and 'We did not find statistically significant differences between our LS Condition on one hand and the LT Condition and the N Condition.' The LS condition (odor during learning + sleep only) failed to show the expected memory enhancement over control. The authors speculate this may be due to testing effects pushing participants near learning capacity limits, but they do not dispute the failure. Classification as close extension is correct: the original used lab-based object-location tasks during SWS; this study used online vocabulary learning with whole-night odor exposure in adult participants.

description: Pressing a button (Enter key) in response to a cue leads to cue-independent forgetting on an independent probe test, comparable to that produced by retrieval suppression, supporting a recovery interference account
original_authors: Tracy D. Tomlinson; David E. Huber; Cory A. Rieth; Eddy J. Davelaar
original_title: An interference account of cue-independent forgetting in the no-think paradigm
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Kevin van Schie; Jonathan M. Fawcett; Michael C. Anderson
replication_title: On the role of inhibition in suppression-induced forgetting
explanation: In Experiment 1, using a between-subjects design (but retaining the trial-and-error task-set learning procedure), the authors explicitly state 'we replicated the button-press forgetting effect' when tasks were uncued, observing below-baseline forgetting regardless of whether participants suppressed retrieval or pressed the spacebar (F(1,60)=11.963, p=.001). The replication thus confirmed the original finding under this modified condition.

description: Pressing a button (Enter key) in response to a cue leads to cue-independent forgetting on an independent probe test, comparable to that produced by retrieval suppression, supporting a recovery interference account
original_authors: Tracy D. Tomlinson; David E. Huber; Cory A. Rieth; Eddy J. Davelaar
original_title: An interference account of cue-independent forgetting in the no-think paradigm
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Kevin van Schie; Jonathan M. Fawcett; Michael C. Anderson
replication_title: On the role of inhibition in suppression-induced forgetting
explanation: In Experiment 2, using a between-subjects design AND color-coded explicit task cues (as is standard in the TNT paradigm), pressing the spacebar produced no below-baseline forgetting (F(1,30)=1.116, p=.299, BF_exclusion=3.18), while suppression-induced forgetting remained robust. The authors conclude 'simply pressing spacebar in response to a cue is not enough to induce forgetting, contrary to prior conclusions.'

description: First-yes-counts instructions in sequential lineups do not affect eyewitness culprit detection but decrease the probability of guessing-based selections compared to sequential lineups without such instructions
original_authors: Ruth Horry; Ryan J. Fitzgerald; Jamal K. Mansour
original_title: Only your first yes will count": the impact of pre-lineup instructions on sequential lineup decisions
replication_authors: Kristina Winter; Nicola Marie Menne; Raoul Bell; Axel Buchner
replication_title: Evaluating the impact of first-yes-counts instructions on eyewitness performance using the two-high threshold eyewitness identification model
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of this conceptual replication of the sequential-lineup conditions of Horry et al. nicely fit with the results of the original study.' The culprit-presence-detection parameter dP did not differ significantly between conditions (ΔG²(1) = 0.01, p = 0.936), and guessing-based selection g was significantly lower with first-yes-counts instructions (ΔG²(1) = 21.16, p < 0.001), confirming both of the original study's core conclusions.

description: Contextual dependency of memory is lower for emotional (negative) compared to neutral memories, and correct recognition is higher when tested in the original encoding context than in a different context
original_authors: Vanessa A. van Ast; Sandra Cornelisse; Martijn Meeter; Marian Joëls; Merel Kindt
original_title: Time-dependent effects of cortisol on the contextualization of emotional memories
replication_authors: Wouter R. Cox; Mandy Woelk; Olivier T. de Vries; Angelos-Miltiadis Krypotos; Merel Kindt; Iris M. Engelhard; Dieuwke Sevenster; Vanessa A. van Ast
replication_title: Context reexposure to bolster contextual dependency of emotional episodic memory
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These findings replicate earlier studies [4–6], and show that our basic manipulations were successful.' In the Results they note that contextual dependency was at least trend-significantly lower for emotional than neutral memories (Contextualization Similar Context: t54 = 2.09, p = 0.04, d = 0.56), and describe these as 'largely replicate earlier studies showing context-dependent memory and smaller contextual dependency for emotional versus neutral memories.'

description: Contextual dependency of memory is lower for emotional (negative) compared to neutral memories, and correct recognition is higher when tested in the original encoding context than in a different context
original_authors: Vanessa A. van Ast; Sandra Cornelisse; Martijn Meeter; Merel Kindt
original_title: Cortisol mediates the effects of stress on the contextual dependency of memories
replication_authors: Wouter R. Cox; Mandy Woelk; Olivier T. de Vries; Angelos-Miltiadis Krypotos; Merel Kindt; Iris M. Engelhard; Dieuwke Sevenster; Vanessa A. van Ast
replication_title: Context reexposure to bolster contextual dependency of emotional episodic memory
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These findings replicate earlier studies [4–6], and show that our basic manipulations were successful.' In the Results they note that contextual dependency was at least trend-significantly lower for emotional than neutral memories, and describe these as 'largely replicate earlier studies showing context-dependent memory and smaller contextual dependency for emotional versus neutral memories.'

description: Contextual dependency of memory is lower for emotional (negative) compared to neutral memories, and correct recognition is higher when tested in the original encoding context than in a different context
original_authors: Wouter R. Cox; Martijn Meeter; Merel Kindt; Vanessa A. van Ast
original_title: Time-dependent emotional memory transformation: Divergent pathways of item memory and contextual dependency
replication_authors: Wouter R. Cox; Mandy Woelk; Olivier T. de Vries; Angelos-Miltiadis Krypotos; Merel Kindt; Iris M. Engelhard; Dieuwke Sevenster; Vanessa A. van Ast
replication_title: Context reexposure to bolster contextual dependency of emotional episodic memory
explanation: REVIEW: The authors explicitly state 'These findings replicate earlier studies [4–6]' and 'these results largely replicate earlier studies showing context-dependent memory 1,2,4–6, and smaller contextual dependency for emotional versus neutral memories 4–6.' Cox et al. 2023 (ref 6) is one of three studies cited as replicated. Result classified as 'success' because the authors claim replication. Confidence remains medium for two reasons: (1) the statistical evidence is mixed — Contextualization Similar Context reached p=0.04 (d=0.56) but Contextualization Original Context only reached p=0.08 (d=0.48), and Bayes factors were 'anecdotal' (BF10=1.62 and 0.99), leading the authors to use the qualifier 'largely replicate' and 'at least trend significantly'; (2) this is a manipulation check confirming the basic paradigm works, not the primary hypothesis of the paper (which produced null results). The ambiguity is genuine — the replication is partial rather than clean.

description: Reward conditioning on items from one semantic category (animals or tools) retroactively enhances recognition memory for items from the same category that were encoded before the conditioning phase (category-specific retrospective memory enhancement)
original_authors: Anuya Patil; Vishnu P. Murty; Joseph E. Dunsmoor; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Lila Davachi
original_title: Reward retroactively enhances memory consolidation for related items
replication_authors: Priyanka Sukumaran; Nina Kazanina; Conor Houghton
replication_title: Reward conditioning may not have an effect on category-specific memory
explanation: Experiment 1 used a more complex word-image associative learning paradigm based on the same reward conditioning protocol as Patil et al. (2017). No consistent evidence for category-specific memory enhancement was found; any effect in the conditioning phase was inconsistent across memory measures (significant for corrected recognition but not d-primes) and there was no retrospective enhancement in the pre-conditioning phase.

description: Reward conditioning on items from one semantic category (animals or tools) retroactively enhances recognition memory for items from the same category that were encoded before the conditioning phase (category-specific retrospective memory enhancement)
original_authors: Anuya Patil; Vishnu P. Murty; Joseph E. Dunsmoor; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Lila Davachi
original_title: Reward retroactively enhances memory consolidation for related items
replication_authors: Priyanka Sukumaran; Nina Kazanina; Conor Houghton
replication_title: Reward conditioning may not have an effect on category-specific memory
explanation: Experiment 2a closely replicated Patil et al.'s design using their original stimulus set and the same reward paradigm, but found no consistent memory advantage for items from the high-reward category; effects observed with corrected recognition were in the opposite (low-reward) direction and absent with d-primes and higher-certainty analyses. The authors conclude: 'We did not find a consistent memory advantage for items belonging to the high-reward category in Experiment 2a.'

description: Reward conditioning on items from one semantic category (animals or tools) retroactively enhances recognition memory for items from the same category that were encoded before the conditioning phase (category-specific retrospective memory enhancement)
original_authors: Anuya Patil; Vishnu P. Murty; Joseph E. Dunsmoor; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Lila Davachi
original_title: Reward retroactively enhances memory consolidation for related items
replication_authors: Priyanka Sukumaran; Nina Kazanina; Conor Houghton
replication_title: Reward conditioning may not have an effect on category-specific memory
explanation: Experiment 3 was an explicitly high-powered pre-registered replication of Experiment 2a (itself a close replication of Patil et al.). With n=170 participants, no significant effect was found: 'We did not find a significant memory advantage for items belonging to the high-reward semantic category in Experiment 3 despite the higher sample size used in this experiment.'

description: Parametric manipulation of distractor incompatibility in a flanker task (three levels: no-conflict, low-conflict, high-conflict) affects sequential congruency effects, with changes in conflict level triggering conflict adaptation, with mixed results suggesting both conflict monitoring and repetition expectancy accounts
original_authors: Mengke Zhang; Qing LI; Shouhang Yin; Antao Chen
original_title: Changes in the level of conflict trigger conflict adaptation
replication_authors: Miklos Bognar; Zsuzsa Szekely; Marton A. Varga; Kinga Nagy; Giacomo Spinelli; Andree Hartanto; Nadyanna M. Majeed; Nicole Rui Ying Chen; Mate Gyurkovics; Balazs Aczel
replication_title: Cognitive control adjustments are dependent on the level of conflict
explanation: The authors state they 'did not fully reproduce the result pattern observed in the original study that was interpreted as providing evidence for the repetition expectancy theory,' but did find that 'changes in the level of conflict lead to decreases in congruency effects.' The replication found monotonic patterns supporting conflict monitoring theory, while the original found non-monotonic patterns favouring repetition expectancy, constituting a partial but not complete replication.

description: Spider-fearful individuals show speeded attentional capture (faster detection of spider targets) and increased distraction (slower search when spiders are distractors) in a visual search task compared to non-fearful individuals
original_authors: Mike Rinck; Andrea Reinecke; Thomas Ellwart; Kathrin Heuer; Eni S. Becker
original_title: Speeded detection and increased distraction in fear of spiders: Evidence from eye movements
replication_authors: Miriam Becker; Nikolaus F. Troje; Filipp Schmidt; Anke Haberkamp
replication_title: Moving spiders do not boost visual search in spider fear
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we did not replicate earlier findings of a faster search for static spider targets by spider-fearful individuals [9,17,18,21], adding to previous studies that failed to observe this effect.' Spider distraction was replicated (spiders as distractors slowed search), but the key finding of spider-fearful individuals showing faster target detection was not — and the study found spider targets actually slowed search.

description: Snakes are detected faster than neutral targets (attentional capture) and snake distractors slow down visual search (prolonged disengagement) in a visual search paradigm
original_authors: Arne Öhman; Anders Flykt; Francisco Esteves
original_title: Emotion drives attention: Detecting the snake in the grass
replication_authors: Miriam Becker; Nikolaus F. Troje; Filipp Schmidt; Anke Haberkamp
replication_title: Moving spiders do not boost visual search in spider fear
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'snake targets elicited faster reaction times than neutral targets' and 'snake and spider distractors slowed down search compared to neutral distractors', concluding that 'snake targets sped search up... replicating earlier findings with static snake stimuli [23,26,27].'

description: Assaultive adolescent offenders report less overall drug consumption than non-assaultive controls, alcohol is the drug most frequently involved in violent crimes, cannabis is underrepresented in violent crimes relative to its use frequency, and secobarbital is overrepresented in violent crimes
original_authors: Tinklenberg, J.R.; Murphy, P.L.; Darley, C.F.; Roth, W.T.; Kopell, B.S.
original_title: Drug involvement in criminal assaults by adolescents
replication_authors: Jared R. Tinklenberg; Peggy Murphy; Patricia L. Murphy; Adolf Pfefferbaum
replication_title: Drugs and Criminal Assaults by Adolescents: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly list which findings replicated and which did not: alcohol's predominance in violent crime (predictions 2, 5), cannabis being underrepresented (predictions 3, 6), secobarbital selected as most aggression-promoting drug (prediction 7), and cannabis as most aggression-reducing drug (prediction 8) were all confirmed. However, prediction 1 (assaultive offenders reporting less overall drug use than controls) was not confirmed, and prediction 4 (secobarbital overrepresented in physically assaultive crime) was also not confirmed: 'This result was a lower representation than our 1971-72 findings and contrary to our fourth prediction.'

description: Genetic factors account for substantial heritability (57%) of forced expiratory volume (FEV) in middle-aged and older Swedish twins, with nonshared environmental factors accounting for the remainder and shared environmental factors playing no significant role
original_authors: Gerald E. McClearn; Magnus Svartengren; Nancy L. Pedersen; Debra A. Heller; Robert Plomin
original_title: Genetic and environmental influences on pulmonary function in aging Swedish twins
replication_authors: Keith E. Whitfield, Julie Grant, Inna Rav
replication_title: Genetic and Environmental Influences on Forced Expiratory Volume in Midlife: A Cross-Cultural Replication
explanation: The replication found that shared environmental effects (47%) dominated FEV variance in Russian twins, while genetic effects (28%) could be dropped from the model without significant decrease in fit. This directly contradicts the Swedish study's finding of 57% heritability and no significant shared environmental contribution. The authors explicitly state: 'Results from the Russian sample differ in several ways from those obtained in the study of Swedish twins.'

description: Non-right-handers have significantly higher Behavioural Inhibition System (BIS) scores than right-handers, with left-handed females showing the highest BIS scores
original_authors: Lynn Wright; Scott M. Hardie; Karen Wilson
original_title: Handedness and behavioural inhibition: left handed females show most inhibition as measured by BIS/BAS self-report
replication_authors: Alan A. Beaton; Imogen H. Kaack; Philip J. Corr
replication_title: Handedness and behavioural inhibition system/behavioural activation system (BIS/BAS) scores: A replication and extension of Wright, Hardie, and Wilson (2009)
replication_journal: Laterality: Asymmetries of Body, Brain and Cognition
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results replicate those of Wright et al. (2009) and Hardie and Wright (2014) that left-handers have higher BIS scores than right-handers.' Non-right-handers had significantly higher mean BIS scores (M=21.69) than right-handers (M=20.08), F(1,84)=4.50, p=0.037, partial eta²=0.051. The authors note it is 'not an exact replication' because different handedness questionnaires were used (Peters 1998 vs. Briggs-Nebes modification of AHPQ), and explicitly label it a 'conceptual replication.'

description: People with MCI are significantly more disabled in everyday technology (ET) use compared to older adults without cognitive impairment, and less disabled than people with dementia, as measured by the Everyday Technology Use Questionnaire (ETUQ)
original_authors: Lena Rosenberg; Anders Kottorp; Bengt Winblad; Louise Nygård
original_title: Perceived difficulty in everyday technology use among older adults with or without cognitive deficits
replication_authors: Louise Nygård; Monica Pantzar; Brittmari Uppgard; Anders Kottorp
replication_title: Detection of activity limitations in older adults with MCI or Alzheimer's disease through evaluation of perceived difficulty in use of everyday technology: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'The significant differences found between all three groups in terms of perceived difficulty in ET use are a confirmation of earlier findings (Rosenberg, Kottorp, et al., 2009),' confirming the original study's finding that the ETUQ sensitively differentiates MCI, AD, and control groups. The replication used a revised version of ETUQ with stricter design and improved scale, while testing the same core hypothesis with the same population types.

description: Children's gender shapes the motifs and materials they use to express their God concept in creative collage tasks, with boys using manufactured objects and girls using natural phenomena, and boys using hard materials more than girls and soft materials less than girls
original_authors: Szagun, A.-K.
original_title: Dem sprachlosen sprache verleihen. rostocker langzeitstudie zu gottesverständnis und gottesbeziehung von kindern, die in mehrheitlich konfessionslosem kontext aufwachsen
replication_authors: Kathrin Kaiser; Ulrich Riegel
replication_title: Differences in children’s concepts of god. A replication study based on creative tasks with different materials
explanation: The authors replicated Szagun's (2006) Rostock collage method with n=51 children in a culturally Catholic German region. Two of three hypotheses were confirmed (manufactured objects/natural phenomena: p=.002; soft materials: p=.009), but the hard materials hypothesis was not significant (p=.111). The Discussion states 'This study confirms two aspects of gender-typical effects' while noting the hard materials finding 'does not reveal gender-typical behaviour,' yielding a mixed/partial replication.

description: Pre-K Mathematics curriculum intervention significantly improved mathematics outcomes for low-SES children at the end of their pre-kindergarten year, compared to business-as-usual control
original_authors: Alice Klein; Prentice Starkey; Douglas Clements; Julie Sarama; Roopa Iyer
original_title: Effects of a pre-kindergarten mathematics intervention: A randomized experiment
original_journal: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
replication_authors: Prentice Starkey; Alice Klein; Ben Clarke; Scott Baker; Jaime Thomas
replication_title: Effects of early mathematics intervention for low-SES pre-kindergarten and kindergarten students: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The main child outcomes were replicated. Both the original efficacy study and the replication study found significant, positive child outcomes in mathematics at the end of PK.' Effect sizes were similar (d = 0.55 in original vs. d = 0.52 in replication). The authors note the study 'can be considered a close rather than a direct replication' due to differences in setting (urban vs. agricultural regions) and participant demographics (different racial/ethnic composition, lower teacher education in replication).

description: Firearm availability is associated only with firearm suicide rates but not with total or non-firearm suicide rates across 194 nations, suggesting firearms influence the method of suicide but not overall suicide numbers
original_authors: Gary Kleck
original_title: The cross-national association of gun ownership rates and suicide rates: An analysis of 194 nations
replication_authors: Tyler J. Lane
replication_title: Associations Between Firearm and Suicide Rates: A Replication of Kleck (2021)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The main result in Kleck (2021) failed to reproduce, finding a significant association between firearm availability and suicide rates.' The replication using the same OLS methods and Small Arms Survey data found a significant positive association between firearm availability and total suicide rates (p = 0.006), contradicting Kleck's null finding (p = 0.618).

description: Reaction times in hybrid search increase linearly with visual set size and logarithmically with memory set size in younger adults
original_authors: Jeremy M. Wolfe
original_title: Saved by a log: How do humans perform hybrid visual and memory search
replication_authors: Iris Wiegand; Jeremy M. Wolfe
replication_title: Age doesn’t matter much: hybrid visual and memory search is preserved in older adults
explanation: The authors explicitly used the 10 younger adult participants from Wolfe (2012), followed the same procedure, and confirmed the same linear RT × visual set size and logarithmic RT × memory set size functions in both younger and older adults. They state: 'First, we replicated the pattern of linear RT × visual set size and logarithmic RT × memory set size functions in a sample of OA.'

description: Younger adults do not rely on item familiarity in hybrid search — distractor familiarity (frequency-matched to targets) does not impair search performance
original_authors: Jeremy M. Wolfe; Sage E. P. Boettcher; Emilie L. Josephs; Corbin A. Cunningham; Trafton Drew
original_title: You look familiar, but I don't care: Lure rejection in hybrid visual and memory search is not based on familiarity
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Iris Wiegand; Jeremy M. Wolfe
replication_title: Age doesn’t matter much: hybrid visual and memory search is preserved in older adults
explanation: The authors used 12 YA from Wolfe et al. (2015) and compared them to new OA data using the same procedure, confirming that neither age group relied on familiarity cues. They state: 'In Experiment 2, we replicated the findings of Experiment 1, demonstrating no evidence for qualitative age-related changes in hybrid search over and above an overall slowing with age. Importantly, we further showed that OA, similar to YA (Wolfe et al., 2015), did not rely on item familiarity alone in hybrid search.'

description: Partitioning memory sets into context-associated groups (requiring retrieval of target-context associations) increases search RT costs in younger adults during hybrid search
original_authors: Sage E. P. Boettcher; Trafton Drew; Jeremy M. Wolfe
original_title: Lost in the supermarket: Quantifying the cost of partitioning memory sets in hybrid search
replication_authors: Iris Wiegand; Jeremy M. Wolfe
replication_title: Age doesn’t matter much: hybrid visual and memory search is preserved in older adults
explanation: The authors used 18 YA from Boettcher et al. (2018, Experiment 1a) and tested new older adult data using the same task. The core effect (RT cost of partitioning memory sets) was replicated, and older adults showed a comparable pattern to younger adults. The discussion states that the results 'did not provide evidence that a general associative memory deficit in older age severely affected hybrid search performance in OA.'

description: Approximately half of the words spoken by deaf adolescents in Norwegian schools for the deaf were understood by normal-hearing adults, with large individual variation in intelligibility
original_authors: Kvam, Marit Hoem
original_title: Blir døves tale forstått? (do we understand the speech of the deaf?)
original_journal: Institute of Special Education, University of Oslo
replication_authors: Marit Hoem Kvam, Unni J. Bredal
replication_title: Do we understand the speech of deaf adolescents?: An evaluation and comparison of the intelligibility in two similar research projects from 1979 and 1995
explanation: The authors explicitly conducted a replication of the 1979 study and found nearly identical results: 50.4% of words understood in 1979 vs 51.4% in 1995. The paper states: 'The main conclusion of the comparison is that the speech of deaf adolescents in schools for the deaf is as easy-or as difficult-to understand today as it was in 1979.'

description: Infants in the high distress group during the Strange Situation Procedure are more likely to be carriers of the short form of the serotonin transporter gene (5HTT VNTR) than infants in the low distress group
original_authors: Raby KL; Cicchetti D.; Carlson EA; Cutuli JJ; Englund MM; Egeland B.
original_title: Genetic and caregiving contributions to infant attachment: Unique associations with distress reactivity and attachment security
replication_authors: Glenn I. Roisman; Cathryn Booth-Laforce; Jay Belsky; Keith B. Burt; Ashley M. Groh
replication_title: Molecular-genetic correlates of infant attachment: A cautionary tale
explanation: The authors explicitly state they found 'little consistent evidence to support the finding of Raby et al. (2012) that high-distress infants were more likely to be carriers of the short form of the serotonin transporter gene.' In fact, in the White sub-sample they found a small but significant effect in the opposite direction (r[431] = -.12, p < .05), and a non-significant trend in the opposite direction for non-White infants.

description: Undergraduates whose parents experienced the loss of a family member within two years of their birth scored significantly higher on Tellegen's Absorption Scale than those without such parental loss
original_authors: Hesse, E.; Van IJzendoorn, M.
original_title: Parental loss of close family members and propensities towards absorption in offspring
replication_authors: Naomi I. Gribneau Bahm; Robbie Duschinsky; Erik Hesse
replication_title: Parental loss of family members within two years of offspring birth predicts elevated absorption scores in college
explanation: The authors explicitly state the replication succeeded: 't(925) = -2.323; p = .010 (one-tailed), which fully replicates Hesse and van IJzendoorn's (1998) findings.' The Conclusions section also affirms: 'we were able to fully replicate Hesse and van IJzendoorn's (1998) finding of elevated absorption scores in adolescence for individuals born within a 24 month period of reported parents' important loss experiences.'

description: Leadership in public sector networks (emergency management) differs from leadership in single-agency structures, with people-oriented behaviors being more prominent in network settings compared to task-oriented behaviors in hierarchical single agencies
original_authors: Chris Silvia; Michael McGuire
original_title: Leading public sector networks: an empirical examination of integrative leadership behaviors
replication_authors: Denita Cepiku; Marco Mastrodascio
replication_title: Leadership behaviours in local government networks: an empirical replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our research confirms findings of the original study, nonetheless, to a different extent.' They replicated the core finding that leadership in networks differs from single-agency structures with people-oriented behaviors more prominent in networks, though the magnitude of differences was smaller in the Italian local government context than in the original US emergency management context.

description: Secondary school students prefer school-based counselling (over external), individual counselling (over group), and a female counsellor, with this preference for female counsellors being especially strong among female students
original_authors: Mick Cooper
original_title: Scottish secondary school students' preferences for location, format of counselling and sex of counsellor
replication_authors: Philip Quinn; Stephanie Chan
replication_title: Secondary school students' preferences for location, format of counselling and gender of counsellor: A replication study based in Northern Ireland
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'These findings replicate those of Cooper (2004, 2006), providing strong support for the generalisability of this data.' Results closely matched the original across all three measures (location, format, and gender preference).

description: Students' intuitive models of multiplication (as repeated addition) and division (as partitive/quotative) constrain their ability to solve word problems, such that problems violating these intuitive models (e.g., non-integer multipliers) yield lower rates of correct answers
original_authors: Efraim Fischbein; Maria Deri; Maria Sainat Nello; Maria Sciolis Marino
original_title: The role of implicit models in solving verbal problems in multiplication and division
original_journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education
replication_authors: Clelia Cascella; Chiara Giberti; Andrea Maffia
replication_title: Percentages versus Rasch estimates: alternative methodological strategies for replication studies in mathematics education
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm replication success: 'we can state that our study confirms the results of the original one, because the effects of the intuitive model described in the original study are still predictive of the relative difficulty of the tasks.' Both percentage-based and Rasch-based analyses were consistent with the original findings.

description: IBM employees from different countries differ systematically on five cultural dimensions (power distance, individualism, masculinity, uncertainty avoidance, and long-term orientation), with each country having a stable characteristic score on each dimension
original_authors: Hofstede, Geert
original_title: Culture's consequences: Comparing values, behaviors, institutions, and organizations across nations
replication_authors: Klaes Eringa; Laura N. Caudron; Kathrin Rieck; Fei Xie; Tobias Gerhardt
replication_title: How relevant are Hofstede's dimensions for inter-cultural studies? A replication of Hofstede's research among current international business students
explanation: The paper finds that absolute country scores differ significantly from Hofstede's original values on most dimensions (particularly Power Distance and Long-Term Orientation for all countries), but the relative rankings of countries are largely preserved. The authors conclude: 'Our results confirm many of Hofstede's original findings with regard to the ranking of the countries against each other, not necessarily in the absolute scores we obtained.'

description: Rhesus (Rh) blood group incompatibility between mother and fetus increases risk of schizophrenia in male offspring
original_authors: Hollister JM; Laing P.; Mednick SA
original_title: Rhesus incompatibility as a risk factor for schizophrenia in male adults
replication_authors: Palmer CG; Turunen JA; Sinsheimer JS; Minassian S.; Paunio T.; Lönnqvist J.; Peltonen L.; Woodward JA
replication_title: RHD Maternal-Fetal Genotype Incompatibility Increases Schizophrenia Susceptibility
replication_journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
explanation: Independent review confirms result=success and replication_type=conceptual. The authors explicitly state 'These results replicate previous findings that implicate the RHD locus in schizophrenia' and find significant evidence for RHD maternal-fetal genotype incompatibility (χ²=3.72, p=.027 one-sided, M=2.6), consistent with Hollister et al.'s (1996) relative risk of 2.78. The Discussion notes the M=2.6 estimate is consistent with the meta-analytic OR of 2.0 and the Hollister-derived estimate of 1.8 across different populations, which the authors call 'remarkable.' explanation: The paper tested 7 SNPs across 6 candidate gene loci (F5, CYP1B1, ESR1, AMHR2, HSDB1, APOE) in 6510 African-American women. Table 2 shows that 6 of the 7 SNPs showed no significant association (p-values ranging from 0.05 to 0.79). Only rs2002555 at AMHR2 reached nominal significance (p=0.006), but this does not survive Bonferroni correction for 7 tests (threshold ~0.007). Critically, the Discussion notes that 'A recent study in a large number of women with European ancestry did not replicate any of these genes' (citing ref 33, which is He et al. 2010 itself — meaning subsequent large European studies also failed). The authors' own framing is that 'of these genes, we only found rs2002555 at AMHR2 to be significantly associated,' with no claim that the original candidate gene findings are validated. The medium confidence is retained because the AMHR2 result is close to the Bonferroni threshold (0.006 vs. 0.007) and the authors do provide biological rationale for AMHR2, leaving marginal ambiguity about whether AMHR2 represents a true positive exception within an otherwise failed replication.

explanation: The authors state that 'Analysis of models without CS information (RD4 and RD9) revealed that the number of variables and the relative importance of the six feature categories largely corroborated the discoveries in the reference,' and that 'These findings validated the reproducibility of the models.' While adding chromatin state information improved general redundancy (RD9) predictions but slightly reduced extreme redundancy (RD4) predictions, the core replication of the original models was confirmed.

description: Later replicating regions of the (primate) genome have higher rates of neutral mutation/divergence and nucleotide diversity than regions replicating earlier during S-phase
original_authors: John A. Stamatoyannopoulos; Ivan Adzhubei; Robert E. Thurman; Gregory V. Kryukov; Sergei M. Mirkin; Shamil R. Sunyaev
original_title: Human mutation rate associated with DNA replication timing
replication_authors: Pink CJ; Hurst LD
replication_title: Timing of Replication Is a Determinant of Neutral Substitution Rates but Does Not Explain Slow Y Chromosome Evolution in Rodents
explanation: The authors explicitly state they aimed to replicate the primate finding in rodents and confirm it: 'Confirming the previously reported trend, seen in primates (Stamatoyannopoulos et al. 2009), in rodents, there is a significant relationship between timing of replication and intronic substitution rates.' The Discussion further states 'replication timing appears to be an important determinant of substitution rates both in rodents (as shown here) and in primates.'

original_authors: Hakwan C. Lau; Richard E. Passingham
original_title: Relative blindsight in normal observers and the neural correlate of visual consciousness
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Brian Maniscalco; Hakwan Lau
replication_title: The signal processing architecture underlying subjective reports of sensory awareness
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results section: 'We replicated previous findings that objective task performance and subjective ratings of stimulus visibility can dissociate in the metacontrast masking paradigm (Lau & Passingham, 2006).' They used the same metacontrast masking paradigm with ring-of-stimuli presentation (a deliberate modification from foveal presentation in the original) rather than single-stimulus foveal presentation, but confirmed the same U-shaped dissociation effect.

original_authors: Loukola A.; Broms U.; Maunu H.; Widén E.; Heikkilä K.; Siivola M.; Salo A.; Pergadia ML; Nyman E.; Sammalisto S.; Perola M.; Agrawal A.; Heath AC; Martin NG; Madden PA; Peltonen L.; Kaprio J.

replication_title: Chromosome 20 Shows Linkage With DSM-IV Nicotine Dependence in Finnish Adult Smokers
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim was to 'replicate the linkage signal between chromosome 20 markers and ND (Study 1).' Study 1 found significant linkage with DSM-IV ND at 20p11.21 with MLOD score of 3.8, exceeding the original LOD score of 2.36, and in Discussion they state: 'We replicated earlier findings that chromosome 20 harbors a genetic element influencing ND.'

replication_authors: Keskitalo-Vuokko K.; Hällfors J.; Broms U.; Pergadia ML; Saccone SF; Loukola A.; Madden PA; Kaprio J.
replication_title: Chromosome 20 Shows Linkage With DSM-IV Nicotine Dependence in Finnish Adult Smokers
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Essentially, we did not replicate our MaxCigs24 finding (Saccone et al., 2007), which suggests that the original finding was either a false positive or, among other possible explanations, the variance or patterns of transmission for MaxCigs24 was different in consequential ways once subjects were added to the linkage families.' No significant linkage was observed with MaxCigs24 in either Study 1 or Study 2.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We robustly replicated the modest effect reported earlier in 2010' and 'we can confirm that the replication was successful in this smaller but genetically more homogeneous sample of Finns.' The replication effect size (OR = 1.07) closely matched the original (OR = 1.06).

description: Physicians tend to misunderstand the FDA's Breakthrough Therapy designation, overestimating the evidentiary standard required and strongly preferring drugs labeled as 'FDA-designated breakthrough' over drugs described with the actual definition of the designation
original_authors: Kesselheim, Aaron S.; Woloshin, Steven; Eddings, Wesley; Franklin, Jessica M.; Ross, Karen M.; Schwartz, Lisa M.
original_title: Physicians' knowledge about FDA approval standards and perceptions of the 'breakthrough therapy' designation
replication_authors: Ryan S. Paquin; Vanessa Boudewyns; Amie C. O’Donoghue; Kathryn J. Aikin
replication_title: Physician Perceptions of the FDA’s Breakthrough Therapy Designation: An Update
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated three questions asked by Kesselheim et al' and their Discussion confirms 'Physicians tend to misunderstand the BT designation,' supporting the original finding. The core finding of persistent misunderstanding was confirmed, though some metrics showed improvement (e.g., 65% now correct on evidence level vs. 45% originally; 59% preferring 'breakthrough' label vs. 94% originally), making this a partial replication with the original direction of effects maintained.

description: Higher levels of Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) symptoms are negatively associated with striatal (caudate) volume in healthy young male individuals
original_authors: Xinqi Zhou; Renjing Wu; Congcong Liu; Juan Kou; Yuanshu Chen; Halley M. Pontes; Dezhong Yao; Keith M. Kendrick; Benjamin Becker; Christian Montag
original_title: Higher levels of (Internet) Gaming Disorder symptoms according to the WHO and APA frameworks associate with lower striatal volume
replication_authors: Benjamin Klugah-Brown; Xinqi Zhou; Lan Wang; Xianyang Gan; Ran Zhang; Xiqin Liu; Xinwei Song; Weihua Zhao; Bharat B. Biswal; Fangwen Yu; Christian Montag; Benjamin Becker
replication_title: Associations between levels of Internet Gaming Disorder symptoms and striatal morphology–replication and associations with social anxiety
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In line with the findings in the discovery study, we observed a negative association between IGD and volumes of the bilateral caudate.' The independent replication sample (n=157) confirmed the negative association between IGD symptom load and bilateral caudate volume, successfully replicating the original finding while also extending it to include female participants.

description: Hand splints reduce stereotypic hand-wringing behavior and increase purposeful hand movements (e.g., for eating and playing) in girls with Rett syndrome
original_authors: Gay M. Naganuma; Felix F. Billingsley
original_title: Effect of hand splints on stereotypic hand behavior of three girls with Rett syndrome
replication_authors: Helen Tuten; James Miedaner
replication_title: Effect of Hand Splints on Stereotypic Hand Behavior of Girls with Rett Syndrome: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Unlike the previous study, we did not observe a consistent decrease in stereotypic hand behavior following intervention with the hand splints.' The conclusion confirms: 'The stereotypic hand behavior of the girls in our study did not decrease as in the previous study following the introduction of the hand splints.'

description: A functional haplotype of the PADI4 gene (padi4_104 SNP and related polymorphisms) is associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis, conferring an odds ratio of approximately 2 in homozygous carriers in the Japanese population
original_authors: Akari Suzuki; Ryo Yamada; Xiaotian Chang; Shinya Tokuhiro; Tetsuji Sawada; Masakatsu Suzuki; Miyuki Nagasaki; Makiko Nakayama-Hamada; Reimi Kawaida; Mitsuru Ono; Masahiko Ohtsuki; Hidehiko Furukawa; Shinichi Yoshino; Masao Yukioka; Shigeto Tohma; Tsukasa Matsubara; Shigeyuki Wakitani; Ryota Teshima; Yuichi Nishioka; Akihiro Sekine; Aritoshi Iida; Atsushi Takahashi; Tatsuhiko Tsunoda; Yusuke Nakamura; Kazuhiko Yamamoto

replication_title: PADI4 polymorphisms are not associated with rheumatoid arthritis in the Spanish population
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were unable to confirm the association reported in the Japanese population between the less frequent allele of the padi4_104 polymorphism and susceptibility to RA.' No statistically significant difference was found (P=0.46, OR=1.15, 95% CI 0.78-1.71), consistent with the original claim of OR≈2.

description: Six microsatellite markers (D3S0186i, D6S0014i, D6S0032i, 536G12A, D12S0645i, D22S0104i) are significantly associated with Behcet's disease susceptibility in a Japanese population genome-wide association study

replication_authors: Horie Y.; Meguro A.; Kitaichi N.; Lee EB; Kanda A.; Noda K.; Song YW; Park KS; Namba K.; Ota M.; Inoko H.; Mizuki N.; Ishida S.; Ohno S.
replication_title: Replication of a microsatellite genome-wide association study of Behcet's disease in a Korean population
explanation: Only 1 of the 6 microsatellite markers (D6S0032i, located near HLA-B) showed significant association in the Korean replication (P=0.028), while the other 5 markers did not replicate. The authors describe this as partially confirming the original: 'we determined the reproducibility of the recent Japanese GWAS results and successfully found the new disease susceptibility gene,' but note that 5 markers were non-significant in this population.

original_authors: Liu Y.; Aryee MJ; Padyukov L.; Fallin MD; Hesselberg E.; Runarsson A.; Reinius L.; Acevedo N.; Taub M.; Ronninger M.; Shchetynsky K.; Scheynius A.; Kere J.; Alfredsson L.; Klareskog L.; Ekström TJ; Feinberg AP

replication_authors: Hanna W. van Steenbergen; René Luijk; Robert Shoemaker; Bastiaan T. Heijmans; Tom W. J. Huizinga; Annette H. M. van der Helm-van Mil
replication_title: Differential methylation within the major histocompatibility complex region in rheumatoid arthritis: a replication study
explanation: The replication found support for one of the ten DMPs (cg21325723 in the MHC region, combined P=0.026), with comparable effect sizes for four others but no statistical significance, and no replication of the GSTA2 locus outside the MHC. The authors conclude: 'the present data support the finding that at least one DMP in the MHC region (cg21325723) is associated with RA' — a mixed, partially-supportive result.

description: Social cognitive capacity (SCC) is associated with objective social isolation but not loneliness, while social cognitive bias (SCB) is linked to both objective and perceived social isolation in nonclinical individuals
original_authors: Łukasz Okruszek; Aleksandra Piejka; Małgorzata Krawczyk; Anna Schudy; Marcelina Wiśniewska; Karolina Żurek; Amy E. Pinkham
original_title: Owner of a lonely mind? Social cognitive capacity is associated with objective, but not perceived social isolation in healthy individuals
replication_authors: Szymon Mąka; Marcelina Wiśniewska; Aleksandra Piejka; Marta Chrustowicz; Łukasz Okruszek
replication_title: Investigating trajectories linking social cognitive capacity, bias, and social isolation using computational modeling
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we corroborated our initial findings by showing that loneliness is linked to SCB, but not to SCC, both in the novel replication sample of 271 nonclinical individuals.' The key findings were reproduced: SCB predicted both PSI (beta=0.56, p<.001) and OSI (beta=0.31, p<.001), while SCC predicted only OSI (beta=-0.26, p<.001) and not PSI. This is a close extension because the same protocol was used in a new sample while also adding computational DDM modeling.

description: Oxytocin increases communal orientation (warmth, kindness, understanding) especially for avoidantly attached individuals who typically lack communion
original_authors: Jennifer A. Bartz; John E. Lydon; Alexander Kolevzon; Jamil Zaki; Eric Hollander; Natasha Ludwig; Niall Bolger
original_title: Differential effects of oxytocin on agency and communion for anxiously and avoidantly attached individuals
replication_authors: Jennifer A. Bartz; Willis Klein; Amy J. P. Gregory
replication_title: Effects of Oxytocin on Agency in Anxiously Attached Individuals, a Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated these effects, with additional nuance' and in the Conclusion: 'we replicate two previously reported interaction effects of oxytocin—namely, that oxytocin augments communion for more avoidantly attached individuals.' The three-way interaction (attachment anxiety × attachment avoidance × oxytocin) was significant (P < .001), replicating the original effect, though with additional nuance showing the effect was specific to fearful avoidants rather than all avoidants.

description: Oxytocin selectively decreases agency (self-confidence, independence, empowerment) in anxiously attached individuals
original_authors: Jennifer A. Bartz; John E. Lydon; Alexander Kolevzon; Jamil Zaki; Eric Hollander; Natasha Ludwig; Niall Bolger
original_title: Differential effects of oxytocin on agency and communion for anxiously and avoidantly attached individuals
replication_authors: Jennifer A. Bartz; Willis Klein; Amy J. P. Gregory
replication_title: Effects of Oxytocin on Agency in Anxiously Attached Individuals, a Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the oxytocin-anxiety-agency effect (P = .014)' in the abstract and 'We also replicated the oxytocin-attachment anxiety-agency effect, again with additional nuance' in the Discussion. The three-way interaction (attachment anxiety × attachment avoidance × oxytocin) predicting agency was significant (t(220) = 2.47, P = .014) and the two-way interaction (attachment anxiety × oxytocin) was also significant (t(219) = -2.95, P = .004).

description: Inducing negative affect via derogatory performance feedback enhances ERN amplitude (error-related negativity), indicating increased early error-detection processes
original_authors: Daniel Wiswede; Thomas F. Münte; Jascha Rüsseler
original_title: Negative affect induced by derogatory verbal feedback modulates the neural signature of error detection
replication_authors: Peter E. Clayson; Ann Clawson; Michael J. Larson
replication_title: The effects of induced state negative affect on performance monitoring processes
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we fail to replicate any portion of the Wiswede et al. findings.' No significant group differences were found for ERN, Pe, or N2 amplitudes between encouraging and derogatory feedback groups, contrary to the original findings of enhanced ERN with induced negative affect.

description: Completing the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) before a moral dilemma (inducing reflection) leads to more utilitarian judgments, and answering more CRT questions correctly correlates with more utilitarian responses to deontological-intuitive moral dilemmas
original_authors: Jonas Herec; Jaroslav Sykora; Kamil Brahmi; David Vondracek; Oldriska Dobesova; Martin Smelik; Martin Vaculik; Jakub Prochazka
original_title: Reflection and reasoning in moral judgment
replication_authors: Joseph M. Paxton; Tommaso Bruni; Joshua D. Greene
replication_title: Are ‘counter-intuitive’ deontological judgments really counter-intuitive? An empirical reply to Kahaneet al.(2012)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated both of the main findings from Paxton et al. (2011) using the DI dilemma (Sophie's Choice).' The condition effect was significant for subjects who answered at least one CRT question correctly (t(15) = 2.2, p = .04), and the correlation between CRT performance and utilitarian judgment was significant (r = 0.44, p = 0.006).

description: Completing the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) before a moral dilemma (inducing reflection) leads to more utilitarian judgments, and answering more CRT questions correctly correlates with more utilitarian responses to deontological-intuitive moral dilemmas
original_authors: Jonas Herec; Jaroslav Sykora; Kamil Brahmi; David Vondracek; Oldriska Dobesova; Martin Smelik; Martin Vaculik; Jakub Prochazka
original_title: Reflection and reasoning in moral judgment
replication_authors: Joseph M. Paxton; Tommaso Bruni; Joshua D. Greene
replication_title: Are ‘counter-intuitive’ deontological judgments really counter-intuitive? An empirical reply to Kahaneet al.(2012)
explanation: The extension to a 'Utilitarian Intuitive' (UI) dilemma (White Lie 2) found no significant condition effect (p = 0.59 for successful CRT performers; p = 0.73 for all subjects), but the correlational test was significant (r = 0.45, p = 0.02). The authors interpret this as consistent with the original theory but acknowledge the condition effect was non-significant, possibly due to a ceiling effect.

description: Retaliatory aggression is associated with greater ventral striatum activity, and this striatal activity positively correlates with both actual retaliatory behavior and self-reported tendencies to improve mood through aggression
original_authors: Chester DS; DeWall CN
original_title: The pleasure of revenge: retaliatory aggression arises from a neural imbalance toward reward
replication_authors: Chester DS; Lynam DR; Milich R.; DeWall CN
replication_title: Neural mechanisms of the rejection–aggression link
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Seeking to replicate previous work (Chester and DeWall, 2016)' in their Present Study section, and in the Discussion confirm 'we also replicated the association between activity in the ventral striatum during retaliatory aggression and the extent of actual retaliation' and 'we replicated the correlation between such striatal activity and participants' self-reported tendencies to react aggressively in order to improve their mood (as in Chester and DeWall, 2016).' The replication succeeded with similar correlations (r = 0.342, p = 0.007 for striatum-aggression; r = 0.33, p = 0.010 for striatum-AMII).

description: Three neurobiologically distinct psychosis Biotypes (Biotype-1: low neural response magnitudes; Biotype-2: overactive neural responses and poor sensory-motor inhibition; Biotype-3: near-normal bio-factors) can be identified in psychosis patients using k-means clustering of brain-based biomarkers (cognition, saccades, stop-signal, and EEG/ERP measures)

replication_title: Psychosis Biotypes: Replication and Validation from the B-SNIP Consortium
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'a promising demonstration, replication, cross-validation, and construct validation within psychosis.' The replication sample (N=717 psychosis, N=198 healthy) yielded three virtually identical Biotypes to the original B-SNIP1 sample, with bio-factor pattern ICC=0.95 and cross-validation similarity of 88.5%-89%.

description: The PANSS-Autism-Severity-Score (PAUSS) demonstrates good internal consistency, convergent validity with the ADOS, and valid cut-offs for distinguishing autistic phenotypes in schizophrenia spectrum disorder populations
original_authors: Anne Kästner; Martin Begemann; Tanja Maria Michel; Sarah Everts; Beata Stepniak; Christiane Bach; Luise Poustka; Joachim Becker; Tobias Banaschewski; Matthias Dose; Hannelore Ehrenreich
original_title: Autism beyond diagnostic categories: characterization of autistic phenotypes in schizophrenia
replication_authors: Katharine Chisholm; Frederike Schirmbeck; Amy E. Pinkham; Noah J. Sasson; Claudia J. P. Simons; Lieuwe de Haan; Philip D. Harvey; David L. Penn; Tim Ziermans
replication_title: A Cross-sectional Conceptual Replication and Longitudinal Evaluation of the PANSS-Autism-Severity-Score Measure Suggests it Does Not Capture Autistic Traits in Individuals With Psychosis
explanation: The authors explicitly state their results 'differed in important ways from the original validation,' with the PAUSS showing lower internal consistency (α=.76 vs original .86 in SSD, and unacceptable consistency in ASC and TC), a very low rate of ASC participants classified as PAUSS-Autistic, and the conclusion that 'the PAUSS does not appear appropriate for assessing autism.'

description: Positive, negative, and disorganized schizotypy dimensions are differentially associated with mean levels of psychotic-like, suspicious, negative, and disorganized schizotypic experiences in daily life as assessed by experience sampling methodology
original_authors: Thomas R. Kwapil; Kathryn C. Kemp; Alyssa Mielock; Sarah H. Sperry; Charlotte A. Chun; Georgina M. Gross; Neus Barrantes-Vidal
original_title: Association of multidimensional schizotypy with psychotic-like experiences, affect, and social functioning in daily life: comparable findings across samples and schizotypy measures
replication_authors: Kathryn C. Kemp; Sarah H. Sperry; Laura Hernández; Neus Barrantes-Vidal; Thomas R. Kwapil
replication_title: Association of Positive, Negative, and Disorganized Schizotypy With the Temporal Dynamics of Schizotypic Experiences in Daily Life
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Goals section that 'The first aim was to replicate prior findings regarding the expression of mean levels of daily-life schizotypic experiences' from Kwapil et al. (2020). In the Discussion they confirm: 'We replicated associations of trait schizotypy dimensions with ESM-assessed mean levels of psychotic-like, suspicious, negative, and disorganized schizotypic experiences.' The replication uses a substantially larger combined sample (n=693 vs. the original ~191 from that study) with two additional cohorts assessed in 2019-2022.

description: Deficit syndrome schizophrenia patients show selective neuropsychological impairments on frontal lobe measures (Stroop Color-Word Interference and Trails B) and parietal lobe measure (Mooney Faces Closure) relative to nondeficit patients
original_authors: Robert W. Buchanan; Milton E. Strauss; Brian Kirkpatrick; C. Holstein; Alan Breier; William T. Carpenter
original_title: Neuropsychological impairments in deficit vs nondeficit forms of schizophrenia
replication_authors: Cohen AS; Saperstein AM; Gold JM; Kirkpatrick B.; Carpenter WT Jr; Buchanan RW
replication_title: Neuropsychology of the Deficit Syndrome: New Data and Meta-analysis of Findings To Date
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of the new empirical study failed to replicate the findings from our original investigation of the neuropsychology of the deficit syndrome.' Study I found no significant differences between deficit and nondeficit patients on frontal or parietal domain scores, and the group-by-domain interaction was not significant (F3,450 = 1.13, P > .05).

description: Altered DLPFC-hippocampus functional connectivity during working memory is present in healthy unaffected first-degree relatives of schizophrenia patients, indicating it is an intermediate phenotype for schizophrenia genetic risk
original_authors: Roberta Rasetti; F. Sambataro; Qiang Chen; J. Callicott; V. Mattay; D. Weinberger
original_title: Altered cortical network dynamics: a potential intermediate phenotype for schizophrenia and association with ZNF804A
replication_authors: Michael Schneider; Henrik Walter; Carolin Moessnang; Axel Schäfer; Susanne Erk; Sebastian Mohnke; Lydia Romund; Maria Garbusow; Luanna Dixson; Andreas Heinz; Nina Romanczuk-Seiferth; Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg; Heike Tost
replication_title: Altered DLPFC–Hippocampus Connectivity During Working Memory: Independent Replication and Disorder Specificity of a Putative Genetic Risk Phenotype for Schizophrenia
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This observation provides an independent replication of Rasetti et al. and supports the contention that this phenotype is indeed related to genetic risk for the disorder.' They found significantly stronger negative DLPFC-hippocampus functional connectivity in SCZ relatives compared to controls (P_FWE = .001), closely matching the original finding.

description: Individuals with schizophrenia display decreased willingness to exert cognitive effort for rewards compared to healthy controls on the Deck Choice Effort Task, as indexed by a group-by-reward-level interaction
original_authors: Reddy LF; Horan WP; Barch DM; Buchanan RW; Dunayevich E.; Gold JM; Lyons N.; Marder SR; Treadway MT; Wynn JK; Young JW; Green MF
original_title: Effort-based decision-making paradigms for clinical trials in schizophrenia: part 1-psychometric characteristics of 5 paradigms
replication_authors: Reddy LF; Horan WP; Barch DM; Buchanan RW; Gold JM; Marder SR; Wynn JK; Young J.; Green MF
replication_title: Understanding the Association Between Negative Symptoms and Performance on Effort-Based Decision-Making Tasks: The Importance of Defeatist Performance Beliefs
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In the current study, we replicated the finding of a significant interaction between group and reward level in an independent replication sample on the Deck Choice Effort Task.' Effect sizes were consistent across studies (original Cohen's d = .37; replication Cohen's d = .49).

original_authors: Dunham, H. Warren; Knauer, Mary E.
original_title: The juvenile court in its relationship to adult criminality
replication_authors: Mildred R. Chaitin; H. Warren Dunham
replication_title: The Juvenile Court in Its Relationship to Adult Criminality: A Replicated Study
explanation: Within the replication period (1941-1952), the null hypothesis was confirmed (critical ratio of 1.43, not significant), supporting Knauer's prediction of constant rates. However, when comparing total percentages across both periods, the difference (30.6% vs 40.2%) yielded a critical ratio of 3.31 (p = .00097), indicating a significant upward trend — leading the authors to conclude both that rates were constant within the replication period AND that an upward trend occurred over the full 1920-1952 span.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These results confirm the factor structure and extend the possible utility of the SWAI in a siesta culture,' having replicated 5 of 6 original SWAI factors using a Spanish translation administered to 722 Mexican college students. Although one factor did not replicate, the authors frame this as a broad confirmation of the instrument's cross-cultural validity.

description: Spatial attention modulates the earliest C1 component of the visual evoked potential, reflecting initial afferent activity in human primary visual cortex (V1), in a spatially cued ring-detection task

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the C1 effect was also present individually in experiment 1, thereby replicating the original study (Kelly et al. 2008).' A significant main effect of attention on the C1 was found (F(1,14)=10.64, P=0.0057), and no significant difference in the magnitude or onset latency of the attention modulation was found when directly comparing original and replication datasets.

explanation: Experiment 2 used a different target stimulus (orthogonal Gabor instead of ring), different cueing (block-level rather than trial-by-trial), and different stimulus size/eccentricity, yet still found a significant main effect of attention on the C1 (P=0.02). Authors describe this as 'a second reproduction of the C1's modulation by spatial attention in a task condition that differed in several ways.'

description: Spatial attention modulates the earliest C1 component of the visual evoked potential, reflecting initial afferent activity in human primary visual cortex (V1), in a spatially cued ring-detection task

replication_title: Modulation of the Earliest Component of the Human VEP by Spatial Attention: An Investigation of Task Demands
explanation: Experiment 3 found no overall C1 modulation by attention (P=0.85), and in fact found unexpected suppression of C1 in one condition (upper visual field, Gabor target, no CSD). Authors note 'this experiment does not support the core hypothesis' but conclude 'it is difficult to draw a strong conclusion on this question based on this experiment,' rendering the result inconclusive rather than a clear failure.

replication_authors: Jessica A. Bernard; Hannah K. Ballard; Trevor Bryan Jackson
replication_title: Cerebellar Dentate Connectivity across Adulthood: A Large-Scale Resting State Functional Connectivity Investigation
explanation: Under the 'Dentate Dissociation Replication' section of the Discussion, the authors explicitly state that 'consistent with our prior work...we further demonstrated that the dorsal dentate region is more robustly correlated with motor cortical regions, whereas the ventral dentate is more robustly correlated with prefrontal and association cortices.' The replication used the same seed coordinates as the original but with standard whole-brain (CONN toolbox) analysis approaches rather than cerebellar-specific methods, in a much larger sample (n=590).

description: Developmental fMRI study showing that core oculomotor brain regions (FEF, IPS/SPL) are engaged during antisaccades in children as well as adults, with activity in frontoparietal regions increasing with age
original_authors: Beatriz Luna; Keith R. Thulborn; Douglas P. Munoz; Elisha P. Merriam; Krista E. Garver; Nancy J. Minshew; Matcheri S. Keshavan; Christopher R. Genovese; William F. Eddy; John A. Sweeney

replication_authors: Alia Afyouni; Franziska Geringswald; Bruno Nazarian; Marie-Helene Grosbras
replication_title: Brain Activity During Antisaccades to Faces in Adolescence
explanation: The abstract explicitly states 'We replicate the finding of the engagement of the core oculomotor and face perception brain regions in all age-groups, with increased involvement of frontoparietal oculomotor regions.' The Discussion (body.md lines 244, 256) confirms: 'the level of antisaccade-specific activity in these regions increases with age consistent with previous reports (Luna et al. 2001...)' and notes the current study uses the same anti- vs. prosaccade contrast as Luna et al. 2001, which is why both find the developmental increase. The success result is unambiguous and directly stated by the authors. Upgraded from medium to high confidence based on multiple explicit confirmatory statements in both abstract and Discussion.

description: Adult fMRI study showing that antisaccade-related brain activity is modulated by social stimulus category (faces vs. cars), with increased activity in the superior frontal sulcus and posterior face-sensitive regions for faces
original_authors: Émilie Salvia; Monika Harvey; Bruno Nazarian; Marie‐Hélène Grosbras
original_title: Social perception drives eye-movement related brain activity: evidence from pro-and anti-saccades to faces
replication_authors: Alia Afyouni; Franziska Geringswald; Bruno Nazarian; Marie-Helene Grosbras
replication_title: Brain Activity During Antisaccades to Faces in Adolescence
explanation: The paper explicitly aimed to replicate Salvia et al. (2020)'s finding of face-specific modulation of antisaccade brain activity in adults, but the replication attempt in adults was only partially consistent. The Discussion states: 'in adults, a task-stimulus interaction could be observed only without correction for multiple comparisons, but in different regions, including the superior frontal sulcus (as in Salvia et al. 2020).' The superior frontal sulcus overlap is suggestive of partial replication, but the failure to survive multiple-comparisons correction and the shift to largely different regions means the original finding was not robustly reproduced. The main significant task-stimulus interaction was found only in adolescents (not adults), in different brain regions (postcentral gyrus, STG, fusiform, LOC). The ambiguity is genuine: there is partial directional agreement (trend in adults in similar regions) but no corrected significant effect, justifying inconclusive. Confidence remains medium because the paper's own framing acknowledges the adult result did not survive correction, making it unclear whether this constitutes a replication failure or simply an underpowered attempt in adults (n=19).

description: Four autosomal SNP loci (rs12097821 near PRMT6, rs2477686 near PEX10, rs10842262 near SOX5, and rs6080550 at SIRPA-AIRPG) are associated with risk of nonobstructive azoospermia in Chinese men

The authors conclude that 'insufficient statistical power may explain why no significant associations between the SNPs and NOA were detected' and call for 'further replication studies with larger sample sizes.'

description: Learning style, as measured by the Learning Style Inventory, can be associated with choice of a particular medical field, with students choosing primary care tending to be concrete types (accommodators and divergers) and academic medicine/pathology being chosen more by assimilators

replication_authors: Wunderlich R.; Gjerde CL
replication_title: Another look at learning style inventory and medical career choice
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The results do not support Plovnick's claim that different types of medical careers become associated with certain predictable learning styles' and 'Plovnick's conclusions could not be supported in this study.' Using the same instrument (LSI) with a different and larger sample (practicing physicians and medical students in Connecticut vs. Boston University students), this study found no meaningful association between learning style and medical career choice.

The authors conclude: 'Job stress was a significant predictor of job satisfaction, and this finding supports the theorized conceptual relationship between job stress and job satisfaction as described in the anticipated turnover model.'
