replication_authors: Priyanka Nandakumar; Alanna C. Morrison; Megan L. Grove; Eric Boerwinkle; Aravinda Chakravarti
replication_title: Contributions of rare coding variants in hypotension syndrome genes to population blood pressure variation
explanation: The authors failed to replicate the blood pressure-lowering effect when applying Ji et al.'s methods to their own ARIC exome sequencing data (SBP: -0.745 mm Hg, P=.36; DBP: +1.177 mm Hg, P=.83), but successfully replicated the effect when restricting to the subset of specific variants identified in the original FHS study (SBP: -6.888 mm Hg, P=.02; DBP: -3.120 mm Hg, P=.11). The authors state: 'Although we failed to replicate the previous findings when applying their methods to the ARIC study data, we observed a similar effect when we restricted analyses to the subset of variants they observed.'

description: SLC6A20 polymorphisms are associated with susceptibility to Hirschsprung disease, as identified by a genome-wide association study
original_authors: Jeong-Hyun Kim; Hyun Sub Cheong; Jae Hoon Sul; Jeong-Meen Seo; Dae-Yeon Kim; Jung-Tak Oh; Kwi-Won Park; Hyun-Young Kim; Soo-Min Jung; Kyuwhan Jung; Min Jeng Cho; Joon Seol Bae; Hyoung Doo Shin
original_title: A genome-wide association study identifies potential susceptibility loci for Hirschsprung disease
replication_authors: Jin Sol Lee; Jung-Tak Oh; Jeong-Hyun Kim; Jeong-Meen Seo; Dae-Yeon Kim; Kwi-Won Park; Hyun-Young Kim; Kyuwhan Jung; Byung Lae Park; InSong Koh; Hyoung Doo Shin
replication_title: Association Analysis of SLC6A20 Polymorphisms With Hirschsprung Disease
replication_journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
explanation: The authors explicitly state they performed 'a replication study for the association of SLC6A20 polymorphisms with HSCR' based on their own prior GWAS (Kim et al. 2014, ref 16). The imputed meta-analysis confirmed that 13 SLC6A20 SNPs were significantly associated with HSCR even after FDR correction (minimum P_FDR = 0.005), supporting the original finding.

description: Nurses in a salary-wage model unit have a significantly higher perception of the professional practice environment (PPE) compared with nurses in an hourly-wage model unit
original_authors: Hickey, Rosa G.; Buchko, Barbara L.; Coe, Paula F.; Woods, Anne B.
original_title: A comparison of the salary wage and hourly wage acute care nursing units. A pilot study
replication_authors: Rosa G. Hickey; Barbara L. Buchko; Paula F. Coe; Anne B. Woods
replication_title: Effect of the Salary Model on Sustainability of a Professional Practice Environment
replication_journal: JONA: The Journal of Nursing Administration
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a replication/sustainability study of their pilot study, and results confirm the original finding: salary-wage nurses had significantly higher total RPPE scores than hourly-wage nurses (t = -3.02, p = .005, Cohen's d = 1.13). The conclusion states the study 'supports the statistically significant and persistent effect of a salary wage model on RN perceptions of the PPE during a 2-year period.'

description: Visual Perception (VP) and Motor Coordination (MC) supplemental tests provide clinically meaningful information beyond the VMI test alone, such that children who perform within normal limits on the VMI may still show deficits in VP and/or MC, warranting individual evaluation of each area
original_authors: Marjean Taylor Kulp; and Jennifer Mazzola Sortor
original_title: Clinical value of the Beery visual-motor integration supplemental tests of visual perception and motor coordination
replication_authors: Tamara Avi‐Itzhak; Doris Richard Obler
replication_title: Clinical Value of the VMI Supplemental Tests: A Modified Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Overall, findings were similar to those reported in the replicated study attesting to the clinical value of the supplemental tests and their conclusion that each area (VMI, VP, and MC) should be individually evaluated during a visual-perceptual assessment of children regardless of performance on the VMI.' The key clinical conclusion was replicated, though minor differences were found (only VP was significant in the regression model, not MC as in the original).

description: FOXP2 rs10447760 minor allele T is associated with schizophrenia risk in the Chinese Han population (allele frequency differences between 1135 cases and 1135 controls, P = 0.00069)
original_authors: Tao Li; Zhen Zeng; Qian Zhao; Ti Wang; Ke Huang; Junyan Li; You Li; Jie Liu; Zhiyun Wei; Yang Wang; Guoyin Feng; Lin He; Yongyong Shi
original_title: FoxP2 is significantly associated with schizophrenia and major depression in the Chinese Han population
replication_authors: Jiajun Yin; Ningren Jia; Yansong Liu; Chunhui Jin; Fuquan Zhang; Shui Yu; Jun Wang; Jianmin Yuan
replication_title: No association between FOXP2 rs10447760 and schizophrenia in a replication study of the Chinese Han population
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the case-control study in an independent Han Chinese population' and conclude 'no statistically significant association between FOXP2 rs10447760 and SCZ was discovered in a Chinese Han population.' The replication found OR = 0.772 (95% CI: 0.429–1.389), P = 0.387, compared to the original's P = 0.00069.

description: Chimpanzees fail to cover both tube openings to prepare for mutually exclusive future outcomes (where a grape would drop from one of two parallel tubes), suggesting they lack the capacity to represent and prepare for mutually exclusive futures
original_authors: Thomas Suddendorf; Jessica Crimston; Jonathan Redshaw
original_title: Preparatory responses to socially determined, mutually exclusive possibilities in chimpanzees and children
replication_authors: Megan L. Lambert; Mathias Osvath
replication_title: Comparing chimpanzees' preparatory responses to known and unknown future outcomes
explanation: The uncertain outcome condition replicated the same behavioral pattern as the original (none covered both tubes on trial 1; subjects rarely used both hands), but the authors added a certain outcome control in which subjects also failed to cover both tubes — undermining the task's validity. The authors conclude: 'the original task does not adequately rule out alternative explanations for the apes' failures... it is premature to argue that apes fail to show evidence for the ability to prepare for two alternative outcomes based on their performance in this task.'

description: Sibling relatedness (having only half/step-siblings or no siblings vs. full siblings) predicts earlier age at menarche, while father absence does not predict age at menarche when sibling relatedness is accounted for, in the UK ALSPAC cohort
original_authors: Daniel Smith
original_title: O brother, where art thou? Investment in siblings for inclusive fitness benefits, not father absence, predicts earlier age at menarche
replication_authors: Peter Lenárt; Filip Zlámal; Lubomír Kukla; Jiří Jarkovský; Julie Bienertová-Vašků
replication_title: Sibling relatedness rather than father absence predicts earlier age at menarche in ELSPAC cohort
explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicated Smith's (2017) results using the Czech ELSPAC cohort, which used identical questionnaires to ALSPAC but in a geographically and socioeconomically distinct population. The Discussion confirms: 'as these findings are in accordance with results previously achieved using the UK ALSPAC cohort, our results thus show that this association exists in geographically distinct populations.'

description: Exposure to a 500 µT static magnetic field enhances cryptochrome-dependent responses in Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings, including inhibition of hypocotyl elongation (~30% reduction), increased anthocyanin accumulation (~40%), and reduced Cry2 levels under blue-light irradiation
original_authors: Margaret Ahmad; Paul Galland; Thorsten Ritz; Roswitha Wiltschko; Wolfgang Wiltschko
original_title: Magnetic intensity affects cryptochrome-dependent responses in Arabidopsis thaliana
replication_authors: Harris SR; Henbest KB; Maeda K.; Pannell JR; Timmel CR; Hore PJ; Okamoto H.
replication_title: Effect of magnetic fields on cryptochrome-dependent responses in Arabidopsis thaliana
replication_journal: Journal of The Royal Society Interface
explanation: The authors explicitly attempted 'the gold standard of independent replication' with experimental conditions chosen to match those of the original study. They found 'In no case were consistent, statistically significant magnetic field responses detected,' with p=0.396 for hypocotyl growth (11 replicates) and p=0.531 for anthocyanin accumulation, in contrast to the original's reported ~30% reduction in hypocotyl lengths and ~40% increase in anthocyanin production.

description: Implicit religious priming (scrambled sentence task with religious words) increases Dictator Game transfers to anonymous strangers compared to unprimed or neutral prime conditions
original_authors: Azim F. Shariff; Ara Norenzayan
original_title: God is watching you: priming God concepts increases prosocial behavior in an anonymous economic game
replication_authors: Joseph Billingsley; Cristina M. Gomes; Michael E. McCullough
replication_title: Implicit and explicit influences of religious cognition on Dictator Game transfers
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'both experiments provided evidence that implicit religious priming does not increase monetary transfers in the DG,' and Bayesian analyses in Experiment 1 were 'anywhere from 6 to 16 times more likely under the null hypothesis than under the research hypothesis.' The implicit priming effect was g = -0.05 (not significant), directly failing to replicate the original positive finding.

description: Implicit religious priming (scrambled sentence task with religious words) increases Dictator Game transfers to anonymous strangers compared to unprimed or neutral prime conditions
original_authors: Azim F. Shariff; Ara Norenzayan
original_title: God is watching you: priming God concepts increases prosocial behavior in an anonymous economic game
replication_authors: Joseph Billingsley; Cristina M. Gomes; Michael E. McCullough
replication_title: Implicit and explicit influences of religious cognition on Dictator Game transfers
explanation: Experiment 2 used a modified Dictator Game with a 'taking' option to allow higher baseline selfishness, yet again found strong evidence against implicit religious priming: 'the data were anywhere from 7.5 to 20 times more likely under the null than under the priming hypothesis.' The implicit priming effect was g = -0.09 (not significant).

description: Prosocial individuals (compared to proselfs) score higher on attachment security and lower on attachment anxiety and avoidance, suggesting Social Value Orientation is rooted in early attachment experiences
original_authors: Paul A. M. van Lange; Ellen M. N. De Bruin; Wilma Otten; Jeffrey A. Joireman
original_title: Development of prosocial, individualistic, and competitive orientations: theory and preliminary evidence
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Hans IJzerman; Jaap J. A. Denissen
replication_title: Social value orientation and attachment: a replication and extension of Van Langeet al. (1997)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate the effect' in the abstract, and in the Discussion: 'we found no relationship between social value orientation and attachment, and we could thus not replicate Van Lange et al. [1]'. The replication used improved attachment measures with a larger sample (N=879 vs. N=573), yet all comparisons on security, anxiety, and avoidance were non-significant.

description: Aged Barbary macaques (Macaca sylvanus) show diminished interest in novel non-social stimuli (food-baited objects) but maintain social interest with increasing age
original_authors: Laura Almeling; Kurt Hammerschmidt; Holger Sennhenn-Reulen; Alexandra M. Freund; Julia Fischer
original_title: Motivational shifts in aging monkeys and the origins of social selectivity
replication_authors: Eliza Bliss-Moreau; Mark G. Baxter
replication_title: Interest in non-social novel stimuli as a function of age in rhesus monkeys
explanation: The authors explicitly identify this as a 'conceptual replication' of Almeling et al. (2016) and find no support for the original finding: 'Contrary to the findings of Almeling et al. [11], there were no effects of age on exploration' across all measures (p-values ranging from 0.25 to 0.92). In the Discussion, they conclude 'we found no indication that monkeys lost interest in the non-social environment with increased age.'

description: Adults show anticipatory looking towards an agent's believed object location in implicit false belief removal conditions (FB1/FB2), evidencing automatic Theory of Mind
original_authors: Southgate V.; Senju A.; Csibra G.
original_title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds
replication_authors: Louisa Kulke; Marieke Wübker; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Is implicit Theory of Mind real but hard to detect? Testing adults with different stimulus materials
explanation: The authors ran two preregistered studies with modified stimuli as conceptual replications of the Southgate et al. [17] paradigm. Results were mixed: FB1 was partially replicated in Study 1 (looking time only, not first saccades) but not in Study 2; FB2 was consistently at chance. Authors state: 'In terms of replication, the present findings thus only partially replicate the results of previous studies' and conclude the situation 'remains inconclusive.'

description: Adults show differential anticipatory looking in transfer false belief conditions (FB vs. TB), with increased looking to the empty box where the agent falsely believes the object to be, evidencing automatic Theory of Mind via transfer task
original_authors: Luca Surian; Alessandra Geraci
original_title: Where will the triangle look for it? Attributing false beliefs to a geometric shape at 17 months
replication_authors: Louisa Kulke; Marieke Wübker; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Is implicit Theory of Mind real but hard to detect? Testing adults with different stimulus materials
explanation: Across both Study 1 and Study 2, the critical interaction (differential looking to empty location in FB vs. TB conditions) was not found. The authors state: 'In the transfer conditions, there was no replication of the main findings (i.e. the interaction effect due to increased looking to the empty location in the FB condition). Only the TB but not the FB condition was replicated, which was originally designed as a baseline condition and is therefore not informative by itself.'

description: Alerting signals at varying foreperiod lengths produce a U-shaped preparation function for reaction time and a speed-accuracy trade-off in a spatial localization task
original_authors: Michael I. Posner; Raymond Klein; Jeffery Summers; Stephen Buggie
original_title: On the selection of signals
replication_authors: McCormick CR; Redden RS; Hurst AJ; Klein RM
replication_title: On the selection of endogenous and exogenous signals
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'this experiment successfully replicated the seminal results of Posner et al.' They observed both the expected U-shaped RT function (minimum at 250 ms SOA) and the inverted U-shaped error rate function matching the original findings, with minor differences attributed to the 45-year gap between studies.

description: Purely endogenous alerting signals (isointense, contingent) produce genuine performance improvements in both reaction time and accuracy, while combined (intense, contingent) alerting signals produce a speed-accuracy trade-off
original_authors: Michael A. Lawrence; Raymond M. Klein
original_title: Isolating exogenous and endogenous modes of temporal attention
replication_authors: McCormick CR; Redden RS; Hurst AJ; Klein RM
replication_title: On the selection of endogenous and exogenous signals
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'there was a failure to reproduce the effects on performance that would be expected by Lawrence & Klein.' The purely endogenous condition produced a near-identical SAT function to the combined condition rather than the expected genuine improvement in both speed and accuracy.

description: Differences in retrospective estimates of accumulated amounts of deliberate practice (practice alone) correspond completely to each skill level of student violinists, such that individual differences in ultimate performance can largely be accounted for by differential amounts of past and current practice
original_authors: K. Ericsson; R. Krampe; Clemens Tesch-Romer; Catherine Ashworth; G. Carey; R. Crutcher; Janet Grassia; R. Hastie; Stefanie Heizmann; Charles M. Judd; Ronald T. Kellogg; R. Levin; C. Lewis; William Oliver; Peter G. Poison; Robert Rehder; K. Schlesinger; V. Schneider; James Wilson
original_title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
replication_authors: Brooke N. Macnamara; Megha Maitra
replication_title: The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer (1993)
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'the main result from Ericsson et al. [1] — that there was complete correspondence between accumulated amount of practice alone and skill level on the violin among elite performers — was not replicated.' The replication found an overall group effect (η²=0.26 vs original η²=0.48) but crucially found no significant difference in accumulated practice between the best and good violinists, contradicting the original's claim of 'complete correspondence.'

description: Manipulating participants' belief in free will (via an anti-free will text) reduces post-error slowing in a Simon task, suggesting that weakened free will beliefs impair cognitive control adjustments after errors
original_authors: Davide Rigoni; Hélène Wilquin; Marcel Brass; Boris Burle
original_title: When errors do not matter: weakening belief in intentional control impairs cognitive reaction to errors
replication_authors: Charlotte Eben; Zhang Chen; Emiel Cracco; Marcel Brass; Joël Billieux; Frederick Verbruggen
replication_title: Are post-error adjustments influenced by beliefs in free will? A failure to replicate Rigoni, Wilquin, Brass and Burle, 2013
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were not able to reproduce the finding that reduced belief in free will leads to reduced PES' and 'we were not able to replicate the central finding that the Crick manipulation of belief in free will influences post-error adjustment behaviour.' The Bayesian t-test showed substantial evidence for the null hypothesis (BF10 = 0.139). The study was conducted online with a much larger sample (N=400) compared to the original, which is why it is classified as close extension rather than direct.

description: Winners of pairwise competitions are more likely than others to steal money in subsequent games of chance against different opponents, possibly because of an enhanced sense of entitlement among competition winners
original_authors: Amos Schurr; Ilana Ritov
original_title: Winning a competition predicts dishonest behavior
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Andrew M. Colman; Briony D. Pulford; Caren A. Frosch; Marta Mangiarulo; Jeremy N. V. Miles
replication_title: Does competitive winning increase subsequent cheating?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our study 1 replicated Schurr and Ritov's study as closely as possible with adequate power and random assignment to experimental and control conditions. We observed significant levels of cheating in both experimental and control conditions but failed to replicate Schurr and Ritov's basic finding of higher cheating by winners.' The ANOVA found no significant difference between conditions (F(2,256)=0.546, p=0.580).

description: Winners of pairwise competitions are more likely than others to steal money in subsequent games of chance against different opponents, possibly because of an enhanced sense of entitlement among competition winners
original_authors: Amos Schurr; Ilana Ritov
original_title: Winning a competition predicts dishonest behavior
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Andrew M. Colman; Briony D. Pulford; Caren A. Frosch; Marta Mangiarulo; Jeremy N. V. Miles
replication_title: Does competitive winning increase subsequent cheating?
explanation: Study 2 was an online replication using a coin-flip task instead of dice, and also failed to replicate the basic finding. Authors state: 'Once again, we observed significant levels of cheating in all treatment conditions but found no evidence to support the hypotheses that either winning or losing is associated with subsequent cheating.' The ANOVA across conditions was non-significant (F(3,267)=1.743, p=0.159).

description: High state anxiety (induced via 7.5% CO2 inhalation) reduces global emotion recognition accuracy compared to low state anxiety
original_authors: Angela S. Attwood; Kayleigh E. Easey; Michael N. Dalili; Andrew L. Skinner; Andy Woods; Lana Crick; Elizabeth Ilett; Ian S. Penton-Voak; Marcus R. Munafò
original_title: State anxiety and emotional face recognition in healthy volunteers
replication_authors: Maddy L. Dyer; Angela S. Attwood; Ian S. Penton-Voak; Marcus R. Munafò
replication_title: The role of state and trait anxiety in the processing of facial expressions of emotion
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Conclusion: 'Replicating previous research [39], state anxiety reduced emotion recognition accuracy globally', confirming successful replication of this primary effect. The replication found F(1,44)=6.89, p=0.01, η²p=0.14, consistent with the original study's finding (dz=0.69).

description: High state anxiety (induced via 7.5% CO2 inhalation) increases interpretation bias towards perceiving anger in ambiguous angry-happy facial morphs
original_authors: Angela S. Attwood; Kayleigh E. Easey; Michael N. Dalili; Andrew L. Skinner; Andy Woods; Lana Crick; Elizabeth Ilett; Ian S. Penton-Voak; Marcus R. Munafò
original_title: State anxiety and emotional face recognition in healthy volunteers
replication_authors: Maddy L. Dyer; Angela S. Attwood; Ian S. Penton-Voak; Marcus R. Munafò
replication_title: The role of state and trait anxiety in the processing of facial expressions of emotion
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Conclusion: 'We failed to replicate the main effect of state anxiety on interpretation bias towards perceiving anger.' The replication found no significant effect (F(1,44)=1.87, p=0.18, η²p=0.04), and the authors note 'the robustness of our earlier finding is questionable.'

description: Domestic cats have smaller cranial volumes than European wildcats (Felis silvestris) and African wildcats (Felis lybica), with African wildcats intermediate between European wildcats and domestic cats
original_authors: Hemmer H.
original_title: Hirngrössenvariation im Felis silvestris-Kreis
replication_authors: Lesch R.; Kitchener AC; Hantke G.; Kotrschal K.; Fitch WT
replication_title: Cranial volume and palate length of cats, Felis spp., under domestication, hybridization and in wild populations
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In this paper, we replicated results regarding cranial volumes in domestic cats and wildcats first presented by Schauenberg [2] and Hemmer [1]. Our data support their findings that domestic cats have significantly smaller cranial volumes than those of both European wildcats (F. silvestris) and African wildcats (F. lybica).' The new data fully verify Hemmer's findings.

description: Domestic cats (Felis catus) have smaller cranial volumes relative to skull length than European wildcats (Felis silvestris), as measured by the cranial index (greatest skull length divided by cranial volume)
original_authors: Schauenberg, P.
original_title: L'identification du chat forestier d'Europe Felis s. silvestris Schreber 1777 par une méthode ostéométrique
original_journal: Revue Suisse de Zoologie; Annales de La Societe Zoologique Suisse et Du Museum D'histoire Naturelle de Geneve
replication_authors: Lesch R.; Kitchener AC; Hantke G.; Kotrschal K.; Fitch WT
replication_title: Cranial volume and palate length of cats, Felis spp., under domestication, hybridization and in wild populations
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In this paper, we replicated results regarding cranial volumes in domestic cats and wildcats first presented by Schauenberg [2] and Hemmer [1]. Our data support their findings that domestic cats have significantly smaller cranial volumes than those of both European wildcats (F. silvestris) and African wildcats (F. lybica).' The replication directly digitized Schauenberg's data to enable comparison.

description: Social judgements of faces can be summarized by two orthogonal underlying dimensions — trustworthiness (valence) and dominance — as revealed by principal component analysis of ratings on 14 trait dimensions
original_authors: Nikolaas N. Oosterhof; Alexander Todorov
original_title: The functional basis of face evaluation
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Eva Tzschaschel; Kevin R. Brooks; Ian D. Stephen
replication_title: The valence-dominance model applies to body perception
explanation: The authors applied Oosterhof & Todorov's 14-trait rating paradigm and PCA/EFA analyses to bodies instead of faces. Results were mixed: PCA produced three components (not the two in the original), while EFA produced two factors matching valence and dominance. The authors conclude 'The hypothesis was supported by the EFA but was not supported in the PCA,' making the overall replication inconclusive.

description: Trait-based dehumanization of criminals (denying them uniquely human animalistic and mechanistic traits) predicts the severity of punishment endorsed for them
original_authors: Brock Bastian; Thomas F. Denson; Nick Haslam
original_title: The roles of dehumanization and moral outrage in retributive justice
replication_authors: Robert A. Brennan; Florence E. Enock; Harriet Over
replication_title: Attribution of undesirable character traits, rather than trait-based dehumanization, predicts punishment decisions
explanation: Studies 1A (violent crime) and 1B (theft) used a similar but not identical paradigm to Bastian et al. (2013) and found that both animalistic and mechanistic dehumanization significantly predicted harsher punishment endorsement. The authors explicitly state: 'we successfully replicated previous findings, demonstrating that our paradigm was sensitive to finding predictive relationships between trait-based dehumanization and harm should they occur.'

description: Trait-based dehumanization of criminals (denying them uniquely human animalistic and mechanistic traits) predicts the severity of punishment endorsed for them, even when controlling for social desirability of those traits
original_authors: Brock Bastian; Thomas F. Denson; Nick Haslam
original_title: The roles of dehumanization and moral outrage in retributive justice
replication_authors: Robert A. Brennan; Florence E. Enock; Harriet Over
replication_title: Attribution of undesirable character traits, rather than trait-based dehumanization, predicts punishment decisions
explanation: Studies 2A and 2B incorporated socially undesirable human traits into the stimulus set to test whether dehumanization independently predicts punishment. When desirability was controlled, the previously reported relationships between animalistic and mechanistic dehumanization and punishment were no longer significant. The authors conclude that 'apparent evidence for the relationship between trait-based dehumanization and punishment is better explained by the extent to which participants attribute socially desirable attributes to criminals rather than the extent to which they attribute uniquely human attributes.'

description: Trait-based dehumanization of criminals (denying them uniquely human character traits) causally increases willingness to endorse harsh punishment for them
original_authors: Brock Bastian; Thomas F. Denson; Nick Haslam
original_title: The roles of dehumanization and moral outrage in retributive justice
replication_authors: Robert A. Brennan; Florence E. Enock; Harriet Over
replication_title: Attribution of undesirable character traits, rather than trait-based dehumanization, predicts punishment decisions
explanation: Studies 3A and 3B used an experimental design manipulating both trait humanness (uniquely human vs. shared) and trait desirability in criminal vignettes to directly test the causal relationship. Trait desirability strongly predicted parole decisions, but trait humanness had no consistent independent effect. The authors conclude: 'There was no evidence for the hypothesis that criminals described with uniquely human terms would be more likely to be granted parole.'

description: Typical faces (closer to the average) are detected faster than distinctive faces (further from the average) in a face detection task
original_authors: Jonathan E. Prunty; Rob Jenkins; Rana Qarooni; Markus Bindemann
original_title: Ingroup and outgroup differences in face detection
replication_authors: Linda Ficco; Meike Ramon; Anna Schroeger; Jürgen M. Kaufmann; Stefan R. Schweinberger
replication_title: The role of expansion and adaptability of face-space for individual differences in face identity processing
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors unambiguously confirm successful replication of the typicality detection advantage in four separate locations: the abstract ('We replicate previous results indicating a detection advantage for typical, as compared with distinctive faces'), Discussion §4.1, §4.2 ('Our result that typical faces are detected faster than distinctive ones dovetails with previous studies'), and Conclusions §5 ('We replicated detection advantages for typical faces'). The effect is highly significant (t(51) = 4.078, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.09 [0.05-0.14]). While the effect size is described as 'negligible' and smaller than prior studies, the authors attribute this to methodological differences (go/no-go with 3D stimuli vs. visual search paradigm) and explicitly treat it as a successful replication. There is no ambiguity in the authors' interpretation. Classified as 'close experiment' because the paradigm differs from Prunty et al.'s visual search approach while testing the same core typicality detection advantage.

description: Adding superfluous neuroscience information (SNI) to bad explanations boosts their quality ratings among novices and students, but not among neuroscience experts
original_authors: Deena Skolnick Weisberg; Frank C. Keil; Joshua Goodstein; Elizabeth Rawson; Jeremy R. Gray
original_title: The seductive allure of neuroscience explanations
replication_authors: Pearl Amber Väth; Jakob von Petersdorff; Christof Neumann; Roger Mundry; Julia Fischer
replication_title: Replicating the ‘seductive allure of neuroscience explanations’ effect in a classroom experiment and an online study
explanation: The classroom experiment (Study 1) found the opposite ordering from the original: good explanations without SNI received the highest ratings. The authors attribute variation between cohorts to stochastic effects, and note that the observed pattern 'deviated from the one described in the original study,' but caution against firm conclusions given the small per-cohort sample sizes.

description: Adding superfluous neuroscience information (SNI) to bad explanations boosts their quality ratings among novices and students, but not among neuroscience experts
original_authors: Deena Skolnick Weisberg; Frank C. Keil; Joshua Goodstein; Elizabeth Rawson; Jeremy R. Gray
original_title: The seductive allure of neuroscience explanations
replication_authors: Pearl Amber Väth; Jakob von Petersdorff; Christof Neumann; Roger Mundry; Julia Fischer
replication_title: Replicating the ‘seductive allure of neuroscience explanations’ effect in a classroom experiment and an online study
explanation: The online study (Study 2, n=430) found a significant interaction between SNI and expertise level (p < 0.001), corroborating the moderation finding. However, good explanations were rated higher than bad ones irrespective of SNI across all expertise levels — the straightforward SANE boosting effect was not clearly reproduced. The authors describe results as 'corroborating previous findings' for the expertise moderation, but the differences were 'surprisingly small' and variation was high, leaving the overall replication status mixed.

description: Detour performance in white leghorn chickens is impaired (longer latency) when faced with vertical-bar barriers compared to horizontal-bar barriers, supporting the ecological-niche hypothesis that barrier type affects response inhibition based on species-specific perceptual ecology
original_authors: Lucia Regolin; Giorgio Vallortigara; Mario Zanforlin
original_title: Perceptual and motivational aspects of detour behaviour in young chicks
replication_authors: Anneleen Dewulf; Clara Garcia-Co; Wendt Müller; Joah Robert Madden; An Martel; Luc Lens; Frederick Verbruggen
replication_title: Do ecological valid stop signals aid detour performance? A comparison of four bird species
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate this earlier work, as RI was not significantly improved when the barrier type supposedly matched the ecological niche of the species (Prediction 1)' and 'our findings do not support the ecological-niche hypothesis as proposed by Regolin et al. [9] and Zucca et al. [12].'

description: Detour performance differs between species (quails, gulls, canaries) based on barrier type (vertical vs. horizontal bars), with the direction of the effect depending on each species' ecological niche, supporting the ecological-niche hypothesis for species-specific stop-signal detection in response inhibition
original_authors: Paolo Zucca; Fabrizio Antonelli; Giorgio Vallortigara
original_title: Detour behaviour in three species of birds: quails (Coturnix sp.), herring gulls (Larus cachinnans) and canaries (Serinus canaria)
replication_authors: Anneleen Dewulf; Clara Garcia-Co; Wendt Müller; Joah Robert Madden; An Martel; Luc Lens; Frederick Verbruggen
replication_title: Do ecological valid stop signals aid detour performance? A comparison of four bird species
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'failed to replicate this earlier work' and that 'our findings do not support the ecological-niche hypothesis as proposed by Regolin et al. [9] and Zucca et al. [12]', with the Species × Barrier interaction (Prediction 1) being non-significant.

description: Exposure to a near-zero magnetic field created by μ-metal shielding reduces stress-induced analgesia in C57 mice

replication_title: Shielding, but not zeroing of the ambient magnetic field reduces stress-induced analgesia in mice
replication_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B: Biological Sciences
explanation: Experiment 1 (Pisa, Italy) used a different mouse strain (Swiss CD1 instead of C57) and a different geographical location, replicating the original finding of reduced SIA under μ-metal shielding. The authors confirmed: 'there was a significant reduction from the pre- to the post-latency of the mice held in the μ-metal box' and stated the effect 'confirms and extends previous results with C57 mice (Del Seppia et al. 2000).'

description: Exposure to a near-zero magnetic field created by μ-metal shielding reduces stress-induced analgesia in C57 mice

replication_title: Shielding, but not zeroing of the ambient magnetic field reduces stress-induced analgesia in mice
replication_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B: Biological Sciences
explanation: Experiment 2 (London, Ontario, Canada) replicated the μ-metal shielding effect on SIA with CD1 mice in a different geographical location, using two different μ-metal boxes. Post-latencies of μ-metal groups were significantly lower than control groups (p = 0.0001), confirming the original finding.

description: Exposure to a near-zero magnetic field created by μ-metal shielding reduces stress-induced analgesia in C57 mice

replication_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B: Biological Sciences
explanation: Experiment 3 (London, Ontario, Canada) again replicated the core finding with CD1 mice, while additionally ruling out electric field shielding as the mechanism. The μ-metal box II group showed significantly lower post-latency compared to control (p = 0.0002), confirming the SIA suppression effect of magnetic shielding.

description: Exposure to a near-zero magnetic field created by μ-metal shielding reduces stress-induced analgesia in C57 mice
original_authors: Cristina Del Seppia; Paolo Luschi; Sergio Ghione; Elena Crosio; Elena Choleris; Floriano Papi

replication_title: Shielding, but not zeroing of the ambient magnetic field reduces stress-induced analgesia in mice

explanation: Experiment 4 confirmed that a 2-hour (but not 30-minute) stay in the μ-metal box eliminated SIA, replicating and extending the core finding: 'the results of experiment 4 confirm those of experiment 2 obtained with the μ-metal box shipped to Canada from Italy, showing that a 2 h stay in the μ-metal box eliminated SIA.'

description: Grapheme-colour synaesthetes are better able to detect an embedded shape (e.g., a triangle of 2s) among distractor graphemes (e.g., 5s) because their synaesthetic colour experiences allow the shape to 'pop out' pre-attentively
original_authors: Ramachandran VS; Hubbard EM
original_title: Psychophysical investigations into the neural basis of synaesthesia
original_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London B
replication_authors: Jamie Ward; Clare Jonas; Zoltan Dienes; Anil Seth
replication_title: Grapheme-colour synaesthesia improves detection of embedded shapes, but without pre-attentive ‘pop-out’ of synaesthetic colour
replication_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
explanation: The replication found a significant synaesthete advantage over controls (t(70) = 3.04, p < 0.005, Cohen's d = 0.68), consistent with the original finding. The Discussion states 'Our results demonstrate that synaesthetes, on the whole, do significantly outperform controls on this task, consistent with Ramachandran & Hubbard (2001a).' However, the study challenges the pop-out interpretation — the basic effect replicates but the mechanism explanation does not.

description: Sighted players in a rock-paper-scissors game imitate the gestures of their blindfolded opponents, resulting in a higher proportion of draws in the sighted-blind condition than in the blind-blind condition, as evidence of automatic (unconscious) imitation
original_authors: Richard Cook; Geoffrey Bird; Gabriele Lünser; Steffen Huck; Cecilia Heyes
original_title: Automatic imitation in a strategic context: players of rock-paper-scissors imitate opponents' gestures
original_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
replication_authors: Balazs Aczel; Bence Bago; Andrei Foldes
replication_title: Is there evidence for automatic imitation in a strategic context?
replication_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
explanation: The replication found no significant difference in the proportion of draws between the sighted-blind and blind-blind conditions (t₃₃ = −1.02, p = 0.32, two-tailed), with draws actually numerically higher in the blind-blind condition. The authors conclude: 'Thorough examination of the methods and the data did not support the original claims, but rather suggested alternative interpretations.'

description: Scattering cross-section of silicon carbide rectangular cylinder nanoparticles at resonance wavelengths for different aspect ratios, computed using a 2D boundary element method
original_authors: Carsten Rockstuhl; Martin G. Salt; Hans P. Herzig
original_title: Analysis of the phonon-polariton response of silicon carbide microparticles and nanoparticles by use of the boundary element method
original_journal: Journal of the Optical Society of America B
replication_authors: Clementi NC; Barba LA
replication_title: Reproducible validation and replication studies in nanoscale physics
replication_journal: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences
explanation: The authors report in the Discussion: 'We were successful at replicating the strong peaks reported by Rockstuhl et al. at wavelengths 10.42 µm and 10.7 µm, when the electric field E is parallel to the short side of the rectangle, and 10.42 µm and 10.82 µm when E is parallel to the long side.' The replication uses a 3D boundary element with the electrostatic approximation versus the original 2D boundary element with full Maxwell equations — a different methodology — qualifying this as a conceptual replication.

description: Wavenumber position of the lower-frequency resonance mode (E‖100) as a function of aspect ratio for SiC nanopillars, computed using finite-element simulations in COMSOL (figure S4 of supplementary materials)
original_authors: Chase T. Ellis; Joseph G. Tischler; Orest J. Glembocki; Francisco J. Bezares; Alexander J. Giles; Richard Kasica; Loretta Shirey; Jeffrey C. Owrutsky; Dmitry N. Chigrin; Joshua D. Caldwell
original_title: Aspect-ratio driven evolution of high-order resonant modes and near-field distributions in localized surface phonon polariton nanostructures
replication_authors: Clementi NC; Barba LA
replication_title: Reproducible validation and replication studies in nanoscale physics
replication_journal: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences
explanation: The authors report in the Discussion: 'Figure 8 shows the results for this replication, where the relative errors between our computations and theirs is always smaller than 2%.' The replication used a 3D boundary element method with quasi-static approximation rather than COMSOL's finite-element solver with full Maxwell equations and periodic boundary conditions, constituting a conceptual replication.

description: Reflectance as a function of wavenumber for SiC pillar arrays with aspect ratio AR=4 showing multiple resonance mode positions, computed using COMSOL finite-element simulations (fig. 2a)
original_authors: Chase T. Ellis; Joseph G. Tischler; Orest J. Glembocki; Francisco J. Bezares; Alexander J. Giles; Richard Kasica; Loretta Shirey; Jeffrey C. Owrutsky; Dmitry N. Chigrin; Joshua D. Caldwell

replication_authors: Clementi NC; Barba LA
replication_title: Reproducible validation and replication studies in nanoscale physics
replication_journal: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences
explanation: The abstract states 'The results partially replicate: the wavenumber position of some modes match, but for other modes they differ.' The Discussion confirms that after applying a first-order correction for coupling effects, the dominant mode and two additional peaks match well, but the second peak (longitudinal mode L000) and a fifth peak show discrepancies that the authors attribute to their simulations lacking a substrate and not modeling coupling effects.

description: Young children (approximately 4–6 years old) show low rates of tool innovation (bending a pipecleaner into a hook) even after scaffolding demonstrations, with most children under age 6 failing to solve the task even with support
original_authors: Nicola Cutting; Ian A. Apperly; Jackie Chappell; Sarah R. Beck
original_title: The puzzling difficulty of tool innovation: why can't children piece their knowledge together?
replication_authors: Kimberly M. Sheridan; Abigail W. Konopasky; Sophie Kirkwood; Margaret A. Defeyter
replication_title: The effects of environment and ownership on children's innovation of tools and tool material selection
replication_journal: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
explanation: Study 1 replicated Cutting et al.'s (2014) hook innovation task in a children's museum environment. The youngest (3–4 year old) group performed comparably to Cutting et al., but the older groups (4–7 years) showed notably higher innovation rates, especially at Stage 2 (e.g., 50% vs. 25% for the 4–5 year age range). The authors conclude that 'children in the 3–4-year-old age group performed similarly to prior studies, but older groups performed notably better,' attributing differences to the enriched museum context.

description: Grasp aperture when reaching for a disc embedded in an Ebbinghaus display is largely refractory to the disc's misperceived size (perception-action dissociation), even though perceived size is affected by the illusion
original_authors: Salvatore Aglioti; Joseph F.X. DeSouza; Melvyn A. Goodale
original_title: Size-contrast illusions deceive the eye but not the hand
replication_authors: Robert L. Whitwell; Mehul A. Garach; Melvyn A. Goodale; Irene Sperandio
replication_title: Looking at the Ebbinghaus illusion: differences in neurocomputational requirements, not gaze-mediated attention, explain a classic perception-action dissociation
replication_journal: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
explanation: The authors explicitly state in both the abstract and discussion that they 'replicated the classic dissociation: grasp aperture was refractory to the measured illusory effect on perceived size, while judgments and manual estimates of disc size were not.' They used the original dual display paradigm while adding eye-tracking and additional tasks to test the attention account.

description: The combined allele size of the tandem repeat near APOC1 gene is significantly expanded in Alzheimer's disease patients compared to controls, with longer alleles associated with increased AD risk
original_authors: Michael H. Guo; Wan-Ping Lee; Badri Vardarajan; Gerard D. Schellenberg; Jennifer Phillips-Cremins
original_title: Polygenic burden of short tandem repeat expansions promote risk for Alzheimer's disease
replication_authors: Niccoló Tesi; Alex Salazar; Yaran Zhang; Sven van der Lee; Marc Hulsman; Lydian Knoop; Sanduni Wijesekera; Jana Krizova; Anne-Fleur Schneider; Maartje Pennings; Kristel Sleegers; Erik-Jan Kamsteeg; Marcel Reinders; Henne Holstege
replication_title: Characterizing tandem repeat complexities across long-read sequencing platforms with TREAT and otter
explanation: The authors successfully replicated the APOC1 TR association with AD (beta=0.38, P=2.63×10⁻⁹), reporting that 'the direction of effect of these TRs was in line with the original studies.' The replication used long-read sequencing (PacBio Sequel II) on an independent cohort, whereas the original used short-read sequencing.

description: The short allele of the tandem repeat within SPI1 gene is significantly contracted in Alzheimer's disease patients compared to controls, associating with reduced AD risk
original_authors: Hui Wang; Beth A. Dombroski; Po‐Liang Cheng; Albert Tucci; Yaqin Si; John J. Farrell; Jung‐Ying Tzeng; Yuk Yee Leung; John Malamon; The Alzheimer’s Disease Sequencing Project; Li-San Wang; Badri N. Vardarajan; Lindsay A. Farrer; Gerard D. Schellenberg; Wan-Ping Lee
original_title: Structural variation detection and association analysis of whole-genome-sequence data from 16,905 Alzheimer's diseases sequencing project subjects
replication_authors: Niccoló Tesi; Alex Salazar; Yaran Zhang; Sven van der Lee; Marc Hulsman; Lydian Knoop; Sanduni Wijesekera; Jana Krizova; Anne-Fleur Schneider; Maartje Pennings; Kristel Sleegers; Erik-Jan Kamsteeg; Marcel Reinders; Henne Holstege
replication_title: Characterizing tandem repeat complexities across long-read sequencing platforms with TREAT and otter
explanation: The authors replicated the SPI1 TR association with AD (beta=-0.03, P=6.5×10⁻³), and noted that 'the direction of effect of these TRs was in line with the original studies.' The replication used long-read sequencing on an independent cohort while the original used short-read sequencing.

description: The joint allele size of the tandem repeat within FERMT2 gene is significantly associated with Alzheimer's disease risk
original_authors: Hui Wang; Beth A. Dombroski; Po‐Liang Cheng; Albert Tucci; Yaqin Si; John J. Farrell; Jung‐Ying Tzeng; Yuk Yee Leung; John Malamon; The Alzheimer’s Disease Sequencing Project; Li-San Wang; Badri N. Vardarajan; Lindsay A. Farrer; Gerard D. Schellenberg; Wan-Ping Lee
original_title: Structural variation detection and association analysis of whole-genome-sequence data from 16,905 Alzheimer's diseases sequencing project subjects
replication_authors: Niccoló Tesi; Alex Salazar; Yaran Zhang; Sven van der Lee; Marc Hulsman; Lydian Knoop; Sanduni Wijesekera; Jana Krizova; Anne-Fleur Schneider; Maartje Pennings; Kristel Sleegers; Erik-Jan Kamsteeg; Marcel Reinders; Henne Holstege
replication_title: Characterizing tandem repeat complexities across long-read sequencing platforms with TREAT and otter
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'could not replicate the association of the TR within FERMT2 (beta=0.01, P=0.27, short allele),' indicating a clear failure to replicate this specific association.

description: Individuals carrying intronic tandem repeat alleles in ABCA7 gene exceeding 5720 bp have a 4.5-fold increased risk of Alzheimer's disease
original_authors: Arne De Roeck; Lena Duchateau; Jasper Van Dongen; Rita Cacace; Maria Bjerke; Tobi Van den Bossche; Patrick Cras; Rik Vandenberghe; Peter P. De Deyn; Sebastiaan Engelborghs; Christine Van Broeckhoven; Kristel Sleegers
original_title: An intronic VNTR affects splicing of ABCA7 and increases risk of Alzheimer's disease
replication_authors: Niccoló Tesi; Alex Salazar; Yaran Zhang; Sven van der Lee; Marc Hulsman; Lydian Knoop; Sanduni Wijesekera; Jana Krizova; Anne-Fleur Schneider; Maartje Pennings; Kristel Sleegers; Erik-Jan Kamsteeg; Marcel Reinders; Henne Holstege
replication_title: Characterizing tandem repeat complexities across long-read sequencing platforms with TREAT and otter
explanation: The authors replicated the ABCA7 TR association with AD (beta=8.63×10⁻⁵, P=0.04), observing 'that individuals carrying larger allele-sequences were significantly associated with AD,' and confirmed the direction was consistent with the original 4.5-fold odds ratio finding, though the effect was mainly driven by centenarians having protective shorter alleles. The original used Southern blot assay; this replication used long-read sequencing.

description: Spending a 10-minute retention interval in quiet wakefulness in a dimly lit room after learning leads to better long-term memory retention than engaging in unrelated cognitive tasks during the same interval
original_authors: Dewar, Michaela; Cowan, Nelson; Sala, Sergio Della
original_title: Forgetting due to retroactive interference: a fusion of Müller and Pilzecker's (1900) early insights into everyday forgetting and recent research on anterograde amnesia
replication_authors: Daisy Arkell; Isabelle Groves; Emma R. Wood; Oliver Hardt
replication_title: The Black Box effect: sensory stimulation after learning interferes with the retention of long-term object location memory in rats
explanation: Independent review confirms 'success' and 'conceptual' classifications. The authors explicitly state they 'replicated in rats the basic effect that quiet wakefulness promotes memory retention as previously observed in humans.' The within-group Wilcoxon test for the Black Box condition is significant (W=36, p=0.008, rb=1.0). However, confidence remains 'medium' because genuine ambiguity exists: the critical between-group comparison (Black Box vs. Home Cage) was NOT significant (t(9.391)=1.749, p=0.11, d=0.88), and the authors acknowledge the study was underpowered (1-β=0.37). Experiments 2 and 3 replicate the pattern with larger samples and within-subjects designs (Dark Box: p<0.0001; alone vs. cage mate: p=0.0009), strengthening the overall conclusion, but these used modified procedures. Replication type is correctly 'conceptual': the original studied humans with verbal material over 10-minute intervals, while this study uses rats with spatial object location memory over 1-hour intervals — same theoretical principle, entirely different species and paradigm.

description: Reactivating previously learned vocabulary words during sleep (TMR) improves memory performance compared with non-reactivated control words in a Dutch-German vocabulary task
original_authors: Thomas Schreiner; Björn Rasch
original_title: Boosting vocabulary learning by verbal cueing during sleep
replication_authors: Anna Wick; Björn Rasch
replication_title: Targeted memory reactivation during slow-wave sleep vs. sleep stage N2: no significant differences in a vocabulary task
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The fact that we could not replicate the memory-enhancing effect of TMR independently of sleep stages was unexpected. We used exactly the same task and procedures as reported in our previous studies.' The overall ANOVA was not significant (F(1.64,32.80)=0.98, P=0.37), and the authors conclude they 'failed to find an overall memory benefit of reactivated over nonreactivated words.'

description: Successful memory reactivation during sleep is associated with increased theta oscillations (5–7 Hz) in the 500–800 msec window after cue onset for later-remembered versus non-remembered words
original_authors: Thomas Schreiner; Maurice Göldi; Björn Rasch
original_title: Cueing vocabulary during sleep increases theta activity during later recognition testing
replication_authors: Anna Wick; Björn Rasch
replication_title: Targeted memory reactivation during slow-wave sleep vs. sleep stage N2: no significant differences in a vocabulary task
explanation: The authors explicitly report: 'In contrast to previous findings, we were not able to detect significant clusters within this particular time window independent of the sleep stage (P>0.05),' referring to theta power increases for remembered vs. non-remembered words as described by Schreiner et al. (2015a).

description: Accurate forced-choice recognition without awareness (implicit recognition): guess responses in a forced-choice recognition test with perceptually similar target-foil pairs (kaleidoscope images) are highly accurate (82%) despite subjects reporting no memory retrieval awareness, especially following divided-attention encoding
original_authors: Voss, Joel L.; Baym, Carol L.; Paller, Ken A.
original_title: Accurate forced-choice recognition without awareness of memory retrieval
replication_authors: Joel L. Voss; Ken A. Paller
replication_title: What makes recognition without awareness appear to be elusive? Strategic factors that influence the accuracy of guesses
explanation: The authors explicitly state their new experiment replicated the key conditions from Voss et al. (2008). When guessing was encouraged, guess accuracy reached 77.7% (vs. 82% in the original), significantly above chance (t(23) = 4.9, p < .0001), and the Discussion states 'our results supported the veracity of implicit recognition.' The same U-shaped accuracy pattern (guess ≈ recollection > familiarity) reported in Voss and Paller (2009) was also replicated under the guessing-encouraged condition.

description: Post-session infusions of anisomycin into the core of the nucleus accumbens impair the acquisition of free-operant instrumental responding in rats
original_authors: Pepe J. Hernandez; Kenneth Sadeghian; Ann E. Kelley
original_title: Early consolidation of instrumental learning requires protein synthesis in the nucleus accumbens
replication_authors: Sietse Jonkman; Barry J. Everitt
replication_title: Dorsal and ventral striatal protein synthesis inhibition affect reinforcer valuation but not the consolidation of instrumental learning
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of the first experiment replicate the reported finding that intra-NAcc infusions of anisomycin after free-operant instrumental conditioning sessions in rats impaired instrumental acquisition (Hernandez et al. 2002).' The replication found a significant Drug × Session interaction (F(1,13)=4.1, P=0.027) with anisomycin-treated rats pressing significantly less in sessions 4, 5, and 6.

description: Short-delay extinction (extinction conducted shortly after acquisition) is context-independent in rodents, suggesting extinction can erase fear memory rather than just suppress it
original_authors: Karyn M. Myers; Kerry J. Ressler; Michael Davis
original_title: Different mechanisms of fear extinction dependent on length of time since fear acquisition
replication_authors: Ruben P. Alvarez; Linda Johnson; Christian Grillon
replication_title: Contextual-specificity of short-delay extinction in humans: Renewal of fear-potentiated startle in a virtual environment
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to replicate Myers et al. (2006) in humans using the same fear-potentiated startle measure and ABA renewal design, but found clear context-dependent extinction even with immediate extinction: 'These data do not support the view that extinction conducted shortly after acquisition is context independent.' The renewal effect was robust across startle, skin conductance, and verbal report measures.

description: Brief perfusion with cGMP analog (8-Br-cGMP) combined with weak tetanic stimulation produces activity-dependent long-lasting potentiation in hippocampal CA1 slices
original_authors: Min Zhuo; Yinghe Hu; Carsten Schultz; Eric R. Kandel; Robert D. Hawkins
original_title: Role of guanylyl cyclase and cGMP-dependent protein kinase in long-term potentiation
replication_authors: Hyeon Son; Yun-Fei Lu; Min Zhuo; Ottavio Arancio; Eric R. Kandel; Robert D. Hawkins
replication_title: The Specific Role of cGMP in Hippocampal LTP
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Replicating the results of Zhuo et al. (1994a), we found that perfusion of slices of guinea pig hippocampus with the membrane-permeable analog 8-Br-cGMP (100 µM) for 5 min before weak tetanic stimulation resulted in rapid potentiation... that lasted for at least 1 hr.' The Discussion confirms 'We first replicated the finding of Zhuo et al. (1994a) that perfusion with either 8-Br-cGMP or 8-pCPT-cGMP plus weak tetanic stimulation produces long-lasting potentiation.'

description: Inhibitors of cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG) block the induction of hippocampal LTP produced by strong tetanic stimulation
original_authors: Min Zhuo; Yinghe Hu; Carsten Schultz; Eric R. Kandel; Robert D. Hawkins
original_title: Role of guanylyl cyclase and cGMP-dependent protein kinase in long-term potentiation
replication_authors: Hyeon Son; Yun-Fei Lu; Min Zhuo; Ottavio Arancio; Eric R. Kandel; Robert D. Hawkins
replication_title: The Specific Role of cGMP in Hippocampal LTP
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Replicating the results of Zhuo et al. (1994a) in guinea pigs and Blitzer et al. (1995) in rats, Rp-8-Br-cGMPS (100 µM) significantly reduced LTP in s. radiatum in mice.' They used more specific inhibitors (Rp-8-Br-cGMPS and KT5823) in a different species (mice) and also tested anatomical specificity (s. radiatum vs. s. oriens), which constitutes deliberate methodological modifications.

description: CREB-deficient mice show impaired spatial learning and memory in the Morris water maze when given two trials per day with a 1-min intertrial interval
original_authors: Jeffrey H. Kogan; Paul W. Frankland; Julie A. Blendy; Jodi Coblentz; Zachary Marowitz; Günther Schütz; Alcino J. Silva
original_title: Spaced training induces normal long-term memory in CREB mutant mice
replication_authors: Elaine K. Hebda-Bauer; Stanley J. Watson; Huda Akil
replication_title: Cognitive performance is highly sensitive to prior experience in mice with a learning and memory deficit: Failure leads to more failure
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In Experiment 1, we replicated the learning and memory deficit initially reported in CREB-deficient mice (Bourtchuladze et al. 1994; Kogan et al. 1997).' The replication used the same MWM2 protocol (two trials per day with 1-min ITI) and confirmed significant spatial learning impairment in CREB homozygous-deficient mice.

description: Physics students outperform nonphysics (psychology) students on graph slope and area-under-a-curve problems in physics and finance contexts, and all students perform better on slope problems than area problems, as revealed by test scores and eye-tracking data
original_authors: Ana Susac; Andreja Bubic; Elizabeta Kazotti; Maja Planinic; Marijan Palmovic
original_title: Student understanding of graph slope and area under a graph: A comparison of physics and nonphysics students
replication_authors: Pascal Klein; Stefan Küchemann; Sebastian Brückner; Olga Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia; Jochen Kühn
replication_title: Student understanding of graph slope and area under a curve: A replication study comparing first-year physics and economics students
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the findings from Susac et al. [7] with another nonphysics comparison group, viz., economics students' and that 'the findings broadly confirm the results of Susac et al.; that is, physics students perform better than nonphysics students.' Some eye-tracking differences were found (total viewing time did not differ between groups, unlike the original), but the key performance findings were replicated.

description: Relationship value in business markets can be operationalised as a higher-order formative construct where relationship benefits (particularly service support and personal interaction) are more important than relationship costs as key differentiators when choosing a main supplier
original_authors: Wolfgang Ulaga; Andreas Eggert
original_title: Value-based differentiation in business relationships: gaining and sustaining key supplier status
replication_authors: Nektarios Tzempelikos
replication_title: Relationship value in business-to-business markets: a replication and extension of Ulaga and Eggert’s (2006) study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'the findings of the replication study provide support for Ulaga and Eggert's (2006a) conceptualisation of relationship value as a higher-order construct.' Both H1 (relationship value as a higher-order formative construct) and H2 (relationship benefits more important than costs) are supported, with results closely matching the original study's pattern, though with some quantitative differences in variance explained by benefits vs. costs (91%/9% vs. 81%/20% in the original).

description: Providing social information about other donors' contribution amounts (at the 85th and 90th percentile of prior donations) increases individual donations to public radio, with the effect strongest for new donors
original_authors: Jen Shang; Rachel Croson
original_title: A field experiment in charitable contribution: the impact of social information on the voluntary provision of public goods
replication_authors: James J. Murphy; Nomin Batmunkh; Benjamin Nilsson; Samantha Ray
replication_title: The Impact of Social Information on the Voluntary Provision of Public Goods: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors found no significant effect of social information on donation decisions in any condition. They explicitly state: 'We found no evidence that donations were responsive to comparison amounts.' The joint test that all three social information coefficients equal zero could not be rejected (p=0.654), failing to replicate the original finding.

description: Java programs use inheritance widely, with roughly three-quarters of Java types using some form of inheritance, and global metrics (DUI and IF) following approximately normal distributions across systems
original_authors: Tempero, Ewan; Noble, James; Melton, Hayden
original_title: How do Java programs use inheritance? an empirical study of inheritance in Java software
original_journal: Proceedings of the 22nd European Conference on Object-Oriented Programming (ECOOP '08)
replication_authors: Matteo Orru; Ewan Tempero; Michele Marchesi; Roberto Tonelli
replication_title: How Do Python Programs Use Inheritance? A Replication Study
explanation: The replication finds broadly similar distributional patterns (e.g., roughly power-law-like local metrics, normally distributed global metrics) but statistically significant differences in values: Python's median DUI (55%) is lower than Java's (74%) and Python's median IF (22%) is higher than Java's (17%), with Mann-Whitney tests showing significant differences at p < 0.01. The authors conclude 'inheritance is used differently in different languages,' indicating a partial/mixed outcome.

description: Time of day when visual field tests are conducted influences AGIS metric scores, with early glaucoma patients performing significantly better in the early morning compared with the rest of the day, while the effect is less pronounced in moderate/severe glaucoma
original_authors: Francisco G. Junoy Montolio; Christiaan Wesselink; Marijke Gordijn; Nomdo M. Jansonius
original_title: Factors that influence standard automated perimetry test results in glaucoma: test reliability, technician experience, time of day, and season
replication_authors: Steve Counsell; Stephen Swift; Allan Tucker
replication_title: The AGIS Metric and Time of Test: A Replication Study
replication_journal: 2016 IEEE 29th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We found support for the earlier study when contrasting the AGIS metric scores for patients with early and patients with advanced onset of glaucoma' and 'We would concur with the results in [4].' The replication used the same four time-period analysis framework on a substantially larger dataset (2468 patients vs. 160) from a different institution (Moorfields Eye Hospital).

description: Patients with early glaucoma perform significantly better on the AGIS metric in the early morning compared with the rest of the day, while the effect of time of day is less pronounced in moderate/severe glaucoma patients
original_authors: Francisco G. Junoy Montolio; Christiaan Wesselink; Marijke Gordijn; Nomdo M. Jansonius
original_title: Factors that influence standard automated perimetry test results in glaucoma: test reliability, technician experience, time of day, and season
replication_authors: Steve Counsell; Stephen Swift; Allan Tucker
replication_title: A Deconstructed Replication of a Time of Test Study Using the AGIS Metric
replication_journal: 2017 IEEE 30th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS)
explanation: Reviewer verification: The authors explicitly conclude 'we found broad support for the results in [5]' (Montolio et al.). Both key findings replicated: (1) for early glaucoma (AGIS 1-5), median AGIS scores rise in later time periods (from 2 to 3), consistent with Montolio's finding that early glaucoma patients perform worse later in the day; (2) for moderate/severe glaucoma (AGIS 6-17), median AGIS stayed at 10 across all four time periods, confirming less time-of-day variation. The novel extension is deconstructing by individual eye (left vs right separately), which revealed discrepancies between eyes in later periods for early glaucoma — a methodological caveat about using single-eye data, not a failure to replicate the original finding. 'Close extension' is correct: same AGIS metric and dataset as the authors' prior replication [2], but decomposed by individual eye rather than combined. Result upgraded to 'high' confidence because the authors' conclusion is unambiguous and the data clearly supports it. Year 2012 added for Montolio et al. (IOVS Vol. 53).

description: Students struggle to correctly implement the Rainfall Problem, a benchmark programming task requiring plan composition (sentinel, loop, averaging), with most novice programmers failing to correctly integrate all required components

replication_authors: Rita Garcia; Rebecca Vivian; Katrina Falkner
replication_title: Understanding Problems through Assignment Presentation: A Replication Study
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from 'inconclusive' to 'success': The original finding was that novice programmers struggle with plan composition in the Rainfall Problem. This replication, using a new scaffolded presentation in a different university/language (Processing.js, University of Adelaide), confirms that core finding — Sentinel (70%, comparable to Ebrahimi's 71-77%) and DivZero (43%) remain challenging due to plan composition difficulty. While scaffolding improved isolated tasks (Negative 95%, Sum 94%), the fundamental struggle with integrating multiple plans persists. Confidence kept at medium because the authors frame results as both a replication of Rainfall Problem difficulties (which succeeds) and a test of scaffolding effectiveness (which is mixed), creating some ambiguity in what exactly is being replicated. Subdiscipline corrected from 'special education' to 'other' (CS education has no matching subdiscipline in ontology).

Results show partial overlap (crash/functional error as top symptoms, inconsistency and type confusion bugs common to both) but significant differences (logic error dominates PyTorch at 25% vs. processing in TensorFlow at 22%; different bug location distributions), yielding a mixed picture that the authors present as complementary rather than confirmatory.

As stated in the conclusion: 'The general findings could be validated...However, previously found differences regarding simulator sickness could not be confirmed.'

Both studies found that the error abstraction and classification process significantly improved effectiveness, people errors were the major source of faults, and human cognition research made a meaningful contribution.

explanation: The authors state 'We replicated some of the observations made in the original study' — confirming high correlation between linguistic features and CFP, similar CFP distribution properties, and moderate classification performance — but found notable differences (features #2 and #4 behaved differently) and tested on a different type of requirements (use cases vs. generic requirements), with the overall classification performance remaining moderate but sensitive to language and requirement type.

description: Fault-prone software components can be identified using an approach combining Principal Components Analysis (PCA) with stepwise non-parametric discriminant analysis on software metrics data
original_authors: Taghi M. Khoshgoftaar; Edward B. Allen; Kalai Kalaichelvan; Nishith Goel
original_title: Early Quality Prediction: A Case Study in Telecommunications
replication_authors: Magnus C. Ohlsson; Per Runeson
replication_title: Experience from replicating empirical studies on prediction models
replication_journal: Proceedings Eighth IEEE Symposium on Software Metrics
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Corrected original_title, original_authors, original_journal, and original_pages — the previous entry cited a non-existent paper title ('Detection of software modules with high debug code churn...') that does not match any of the three Khoshgoftaar et al. studies [14][15][16] replicated. Now references [14] as the primary original study. The paper replicates three related Khoshgoftaar et al. studies [14][15][16] at the 'statistical method replication' level (their level 4 — only the statistical method is reused, not metrics or parametrised model), using a different dataset (28 SDL-design components from a telecom system with design metrics, vs. the originals' code metrics from different systems). The authors' explicit purpose is to illustrate methodological challenges in replication, not to validate or refute the original findings. They state: 'The purpose of this study is not to evaluate and find the best classification method. Rather the purpose is to illustrate the differences between different approaches and variants.' They conclude that 'results are very divergent depending on how different parameters are chosen,' demonstrating that poor documentation makes meaningful replication impossible. Result remains 'inconclusive' because the study was deliberately designed not to render a success/failure verdict. Confidence remains 'medium' because the paper functions more as a methodological commentary using a replication as illustration rather than a straightforward replication study — reasonable people could debate whether this qualifies as a replication at all.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated our EASE2020 work with the best approach for automatically identifying decisions from the Hibernate developer mailing list.' The different performance numbers compared to EASE2020 are explicitly attributed to using a different evaluation method (10-fold cross-validation vs. 90/10 split), not to replication failure.

explanation: The replication found mixed results: it replicated the original's non-significant finding for time (no significant difference in fixing time for cloned vs. non-cloned bugs), but diverged for correctness — finding it was significantly more difficult to correctly fix cloned bugs (p < 0.01), which the original did not find. The authors confirm the laws remain effective, noting 'effect sizes were smaller, as expected' but possession/purchase, ZT, use and lose laws all remained significantly associated with reduced underage drinking-driver fatal crash ratios (e.g., possession/purchase -12.6%, p < 0.001; ZT -2.5%, p < 0.001; use and lose -3.7%, p < 0.001).
