The replication confirmed positive Self-Transcendence and negative Conservation effects, but found opposite signs for Openness to Change (negative instead of positive) and Self-Enhancement (positive instead of ambiguous/negative), and found that value effects were stronger in less democratic countries rather than more democratic ones as in the original.

description: Priming Hong Kong college students with cultural icons (Chinese vs. Western) activates different cultural meaning systems, leading to different attribution styles — more external attributions after Chinese priming and more internal attributions after Western priming
original_authors: Ying-yi Hong; Michael W. Morris; Chi-yue Chiu; Verónica Benet-Martínez
original_title: Multicultural minds: A dynamic constructivist approach to culture and cognition
replication_authors: Yi‐meng Wang; Feng‐yan Wang; Thomas Talhelm; Yi‐qun Chen
replication_title: New evidence finds young people in Mainland China are now bicultural
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The internal attribution pattern replicated the findings of Hong et al. (1997, 2000)' and the General Discussion confirms 'our results replicated the findings of...studies of bicultural identity (Hong et al., 1997, 2000) over 20 years later.' Study 1 found F(2,104)=20.23, p<.001, with American-primed participants giving significantly more internal attributions than Chinese-primed participants (d=1.479).

description: Priming Hong Kong college students with cultural icons (Chinese vs. Western) activates different cultural meaning systems, leading to different attribution styles — more external attributions after Chinese priming and more internal attributions after Western priming
original_authors: Ying-yi Hong; Michael W. Morris; Chi-yue Chiu; Verónica Benet-Martínez
original_title: Multicultural minds: A dynamic constructivist approach to culture and cognition
replication_authors: Yi‐meng Wang; Feng‐yan Wang; Thomas Talhelm; Yi‐qun Chen
replication_title: New evidence finds young people in Mainland China are now bicultural
explanation: Study 2 extended the Hong Kong biculturalism paradigm to Mainland Chinese college students and found the same pattern: 'Studies 1 and 2 replicated the finding that college students in Mainland China are bicultural, similar to earlier studies of college students in Hong Kong (Hong et al., 2000).' Cultural priming significantly affected internal attributions, F(2,269)=26.15, p<.001, with American-primed students giving more internal attributions than Chinese-primed students (d=1.062).

description: Experience-sharing (simulation) leads to higher empathic accuracy than mentalizing (theorization) when inferring the emotional states of others
original_authors: Haotian Zhou; Elizabeth A. Majka; Nicholas Epley
original_title: Inferring perspective versus getting perspective: Underestimating the value of being in another person's shoes
replication_authors: Rose Turner; Frédéric Vallée‐Tourangeau
replication_title: Challenges of measuring empathic accuracy: A mentalizing versus experience‐sharing paradigm
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'using absolute difference scores yielded a nonsignificant effect of inferencing process, indicating that the average error was similar in magnitude across the two conditions' and 'we failed to replicate Zhou et al.'s first finding.' While an exploratory analysis using raw scores found directional differences supporting the original conclusion, the pre-specified main analysis (absolute scores) did not replicate the accuracy advantage of simulation over theorization.

description: Participants undervalue experience-sharing (simulation) and overvalue mentalizing (theorization) as effective strategies for empathic accuracy, preferring theorization despite simulation being more effective
original_authors: Haotian Zhou; Elizabeth A. Majka; Nicholas Epley
original_title: Inferring perspective versus getting perspective: Underestimating the value of being in another person's shoes
replication_authors: Rose Turner; Frédéric Vallée‐Tourangeau
replication_title: Challenges of measuring empathic accuracy: A mentalizing versus experience‐sharing paradigm
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated Zhou et al.'s finding that participants tended to show a preference for the theorization condition' and that 'participants remained significantly more likely to value the theorization condition in general, which replicated Zhou et al.' The chi-square test showed a statistically significant association between process group and retroactive group preference, χ²(1) = 34.30, p < .001.

description: Institutional trust mediates the relationship between precarity (economic hardship) and endorsement of conspiracy beliefs, such that higher precarity is associated with lower institutional trust, which in turn predicts stronger conspiracy belief endorsement
original_authors: Jais Adam‐Troian; Maria Chayinska; Maria Paola Paladino; Özden Melis Uluğ; Jeroen Vaes; Pascal Wagner‐Egger
original_title: Of precarity and conspiracy: Introducing a socio-functional model of conspiracy beliefs
replication_authors: Magdalena Adamus; Eva Ballová Mikušková; Pavol Kačmár; Martin Guzi; Matuš Adamkovič; Maria Chayinska; Jais Adam‐Troian
replication_title: The mediating effect of institutional trust in the relationship between precarity and conspiracy beliefs: A conceptual replication of Adam‐Troian et al. (2023)
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'Across four studies, we found that the original theoretical model was replicated consistently, thus suggesting its generalizability despite altered operationalization of the constructs and across different populations and cultural contexts.' The mini meta-analysis (N = 50,340) also confirmed the indirect effect of precarity on conspiracy beliefs via trust.

description: A dysregulated fear (DF) profile — characterized by high fear in low-threat situations — can be identified in a distinct subgroup (~10%) of toddlers at 24 months
original_authors: Buss, Kristin A.
original_title: Which fearful toddlers should we worry about? Context, fear regulation, and anxiety risk
replication_authors: Kristin A. Buss; Elizabeth L. Davis; Nilam Ram; Michael Coccia
replication_title: Dysregulated Fear, Social Inhibition, and Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we were able to replicate the identification of children with DF in this new sample' (Discussion). The replication used a new oversampled cohort (n=124) following the same laboratory paradigm and coding procedures as Buss (2011), confirming the DF pattern in a second cohort.

description: Dysregulated fear (DF) in toddlers is associated with greater social withdrawal throughout preschool years compared to a normative fear profile
original_authors: Buss, Kristin A.
original_title: Which fearful toddlers should we worry about? Context, fear regulation, and anxiety risk
replication_authors: Kristin A. Buss; Elizabeth L. Davis; Nilam Ram; Michael Coccia
replication_title: Dysregulated Fear, Social Inhibition, and Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors confirm 'Consistent with our previous studies (Buss, 2011; Buss et al., 2013) and the hypotheses of the current study, a pattern of DF was associated with parent reports of higher inhibition (inhibition to novelty and social inhibition) concurrently and at 1 and 2 years after the laboratory visit.' Results showed significant associations at all three time points (24, 36, 48 months).

description: High quantities of hours in center-based care predict increased externalizing behavior problems in young children (ages 2 and 4.5 years), particularly when assessed by caregiver/teacher reports
original_authors: NICHD Early Child Care Research Network
original_title: Does amount of time spent in child care predict socioemotional adjustment during the transition to kindergarten?
replication_authors: Catalina Rey-Guerra; Henrik D. Zachrisson; Eric Dearing; Daniel Berry; Susanne Kuger; Margaret R. Burchinal; Ane Nærde; Thomas van Huizen; Sylvana M. Côté
replication_title: Do more hours in center-based care cause more externalizing problems? A cross-national replication study
explanation: Across seven longitudinal studies in five countries (N=10,105), the authors found no association between hours in center-based care and externalizing problems (meta-analytic r=.00, p=.88). The Discussion states: 'our results were unequivocal: we found little evidence that time spent in center care relates to more externalizing behavior problems.' The citation sentence references 'NICHD ECCRN, 2003, 2004' — NICHD ECCRN is the standard abbreviation for NICHD Early Child Care Research Network, confirming the original study is correctly identified.

description: Children who attended center-based care showed more behavior problems as reported by teachers up through sixth grade
original_authors: Belsky J.; Vandell DL; Burchinal M.; Clarke-Stewart KA; McCartney K.; Owen MT
original_title: Are there long-term effects of early child care?
replication_authors: Catalina Rey-Guerra; Henrik D. Zachrisson; Eric Dearing; Daniel Berry; Susanne Kuger; Margaret R. Burchinal; Ane Nærde; Thomas van Huizen; Sylvana M. Côté
replication_title: Do more hours in center-based care cause more externalizing problems? A cross-national replication study
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. The paper explicitly tests and fails to replicate the Belsky et al. (2007) finding that center-based care predicts more teacher-reported behavior problems. Across seven longitudinal studies in five countries (N=10,105), the meta-analytic correlation was r=.00 (p=.88), and none of the seven fixed-effects estimates reached significance. The authors state unambiguously: 'our results were unequivocal: we found little evidence that time spent in center care relates to more externalizing behavior problems.' The Conclusion reinforces: 'we found no evidence that more time spent in center-based child care poses a risk for developing behavior problems in early childhood.' No SES moderation was found either. The result classification as 'failure' and the effect size (r=.00) are well-supported.

description: Preschoolers (3- and 4-year-olds) successfully comprehend novel verbs in the prepositional dative frame but perform at chance with novel verbs in the double object dative frame
original_authors: Rowland, Caroline; Noble, Claire
original_title: The role of syntactic structure in children's sentence comprehension: Evidence from the dative
replication_authors: Sudha Arunachalam
replication_title: Preschoolers' Acquisition of Novel Verbs in the Double Object Dative
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This work makes three contributions. First, we provide a replication of Rowland and Noble (2010)... Like them, we found that DO datives containing novel verbs are extremely challenging for young learners.' Experiment 1 confirmed children succeeded with PP frames (69% correct, p < .01) but performed at chance with DO frames (53% correct, p = .74), replicating Rowland and Noble's key finding. Subdiscipline changed from 'second language acquisition' to 'applied linguistics' because this is a first language (L1) acquisition study with children learning their native language.

description: Younger children (3-year-olds and young 4-year-olds) fail to comprehend novel verbs in the double object dative frame, replicating the younger children's data from Rowland et al. (2014)
original_authors: Rowland, Caroline; Noble, Claire; Chan, Angela
original_title: Competition all the way down: How children learn word order cues to sentence meaning
original_journal: Competing Motivations in Grammar and Usage
replication_authors: Sudha Arunachalam
replication_title: Preschoolers' Acquisition of Novel Verbs in the Double Object Dative
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Confidence kept at medium. The authors explicitly state they replicate 'the younger children's data from Rowland et al. (2014)' — this is a partial replication. Rowland et al. (2014) reported two findings: (1) 3-year-olds fail with DO datives, and (2) older 4-year-olds (mean 4;9) succeed. The current study's Experiment 1 children (mean age 4;2, with 4-year-olds averaging 4;5) performed at chance with DO (53%, p = .74), replicating only the younger children's failure. The older 4-year-olds' success was NOT tested because the sample was too young. The authors note: 'Rowland et al. (2014), however, did find successful comprehension of novel verbs in the DO frame with 4 year olds, who were on average older than the 4 year olds in our study.' Result classification of 'success' is correct — the component they aimed to replicate (younger children's failure) was confirmed. Medium confidence retained because this is an explicitly partial replication. Description corrected to reflect what was actually replicated. Subdiscipline changed from 'second language acquisition' to 'applied linguistics' — this is an L1 acquisition study.

description: Participants trained on a repeating 10-item button-press sequence show faster reaction times over training compared to participants trained on a random sequence, suggesting implicit sequence learning
original_authors: Mary Jo Nissen; Peter Bullemer
original_title: Attentional requirements of learning: evidence from performance measures
replication_authors: Roy de Kleijn; George Kachergis; Bernhard Hommel
replication_title: Predictive Movements and Human Reinforcement Learning of Sequential Action
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the overall Nissen and Bullemer (1987) RT results' using a mouse-trajectory adaptation of the SRT task. The Discussion confirms: 'Experiment 1 replicated the speed-up results from the Nissen and Bullemer (1987) serial button-pressing task with a mouse-trajectory version of the task,' with significant condition × block interaction (F(7,210) = 14.7, p < .01).

description: Gesture-speech synchrony is maintained (not disrupted) when speech is perturbed by delayed auditory feedback (DAF) during spontaneous narrative gesturing
original_authors: McNeill, David
original_title: Hand and mind: What gestures reveal about thought
replication_authors: Wim Pouw; James A. Dixon
replication_title: Entrainment and Modulation of Gesture–Speech Synchrony Under Delayed Auditory Feedback
explanation: The authors explicitly state they aim to 'conceptually replicate McNeill's (1992) classic setup' and the Discussion confirms: 'Our results indicating that gesture-speech synchrony is present under DAF leads us to conclude that gesture and speech are indeed bi-directionally coupled (discounting the ballistic model). This supports McNeill's (1992) pioneering descriptive work.' The core finding — that gesture-speech synchrony is maintained under DAF — was confirmed, and the study further extended McNeill's findings with quantitative evidence of coupling strength and entrainment effects.

description: Top-down linguistic information (lexical-semantic coherence and phonological similarity) influences speaker discrimination, with listeners more likely to judge two words as spoken by the same speaker when they form lexical compounds or rhymes
original_authors: Chandan R. Narayan; Lorinda Mak; Ellen Bialystok
original_title: Words get in the way: linguistic effects on talker discrimination
replication_authors: Ashley Quinto; Sandy Abu El Adas; Susannah V. Levi
replication_title: Re‐Examining the Effect of Top‐Down Linguistic Information on Speaker‐Voice Discrimination
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'modified replication' of Narayan et al. (2017) and conclude: 'Our results confirmed that how you process speaker information is not only based on the signal, but on how words are related in the mental lexicon, as the relationship between words affected performance.' The key finding that top-down linguistic information influences speaker discrimination was replicated, with performance on same-speaker trials directly replicating the original study's graded condition effects.

description: Under semantic strain, verb meanings are more likely to be adjusted than noun meanings during sentence paraphrasing, and this verb mutability effect increases with the degree of semantic strain
original_authors: Dedre Gentner; Ilene M. France
original_title: The verb mutability effect: Studies of the combinatorial semantics of nouns and verbs
replication_authors: Daniel King; Dedre Gentner
replication_title: Verb Metaphoric Extension Under Semantic Strain
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The results of Experiment 1 demonstrate a verb mutability effect, replicating Gentner and France's (1988) original findings.' Both key results were confirmed: (a) verbs changed significantly more than nouns overall, and (b) verb change increased with semantic strain while noun change remained flat.

description: Learners exposed to input where objects (features) precede labels (FL condition) learn the discriminating features of categories better than learners exposed to input where labels precede objects (LF condition)
original_authors: Michael Ramscar; Daniel Yarlett; Melody Dye; Katie Denny; Kirsten Thorpe
original_title: The effects of feature-label order and their implications for symbolic learning
replication_authors: Eva Viviani; Michael Ramscar; Elizabeth Wonnacott
replication_title: The Effects of Linear Order in Category Learning: Some Replications of Ramscar et al. (2010) and Their Implications for Replicating Training Studies
explanation: Results were mixed across the two AFC test types. The four pictures task showed trends in the predicted direction (ambiguous Bayes Factors leaning toward H1), while the four labels task showed evidence for the null hypothesis. As the authors conclude, 'overall, this experiment does not confirm the key findings of Ramscar et al. (2010),' though the effect was partially observed in the four pictures test, and combined exploratory analyses across both experiments did show substantial evidence for H1 in the four pictures task.

description: Toddlers who hear a novel verb in a transitive frame while concurrently viewing a contact event (e.g., patting) will map the verb to the contact scene compared to those hearing the verb in an intransitive frame
original_authors: Letitia G. Naigles; Edward T. Kako
original_title: First contact in verb acquisition: Defining a role for syntax
replication_authors: Sudha Arunachalam; Shaun Dennis
replication_title: Semantic detail in the developing verb lexicon: An extension of Naigles and Kako (1993)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated Naigles and Kako's finding that toddlers can use transitive syntax as an indicator of a contact scene referent.' Experiment 1 used the same paradigm and found a significant effect of syntactic condition (t=2.33, p<0.05 Pre-Delay; t=2.79, p<0.05 Post-Delay). The study used new materials with separate side-by-side scenes rather than the original's simultaneous combined scenes.

description: 7-month-old bilingual infants outperform monolingual infants on a visual switch task, showing better ability to update their anticipatory looking behavior when a reward switches sides after an auditory pattern cue (AAB or ABB) signals the switch
original_authors: Ágnes Melinda Kovács; Jacques Mehler
original_title: Cognitive gains in 7-month-old bilingual infants
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Sybren Spit; Andreea Geambașu; Daan van Renswoude; Elma Blom; Paula Fikkert; Sabine Hunnius; Caroline Junge; Josje Verhagen; Ingmar Visser; Frank Wijnen; Clara C. Levelt
replication_title: Robustness of the cognitive gains in 7‐month‐old bilingual infants: A close multi‐center replication of Kovács and Mehler (2009)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our results did not replicate the original findings: although anticipatory looks increased slightly during post-switch trials for both groups, bilingual infants were not better switchers than monolingual infants.' All three analytical approaches (original ANOVAs, Bayesian mixed-effects models, and cluster-based permutation analyses) consistently showed no significant group difference.

description: Children aged 17-31 months show a shape bias when generalizing novel nouns (selecting shape-match over material-match test objects), and this bias is positively related to the size of their productive noun vocabulary
original_authors: Samuelson, Larissa K.; Smith, Linda B.
original_title: Early noun vocabularies: Do ontology, category structure and syntax correspond?
replication_authors: Milena Bakopoulou; Megan G. Lorenz; Samuel H. Forbes; Rachel Tremlin; Jessica Bates; Larissa K. Samuelson
replication_title: Vocabulary and automatic attention: The relation between novel words and gaze dynamics in noun generalization
explanation: REVIEW: Upgraded to high confidence. The authors explicitly state 'We replicated prior findings that attention to shape increased with the number of nouns in children's productive vocabularies' (Discussion, first paragraph). Both key findings are statistically significant: overall shape bias (intercept t(51)=7.41, p<.001) and vocabulary-shape relationship (t(51)=2.60, p=.011). The paradigm used the same stimuli (from Samuelson 2002, using Samuelson & Smith 1999 novel words: Zup, Fum, Mip, Kiv), same age range (17-31 months), and same NNG task structure (exemplar + shape-match + material-match, novel naming, forced choice). The addition of frame-by-frame gaze coding via GoPro is a methodological enhancement that does not alter what is being tested. UK population (vs. US original) uses the Oxford CDI instead of MacArthur CDI, but the population shift appears incidental to the study's primary aim of examining gaze dynamics, not a deliberate generalizability test. Classified as close experiment rather than close extension because the core paradigm and context are essentially the same.

original_title: Twelve type 2 diabetes susceptibility loci identified through large-scale association analysis
replication_authors: Zia A.; Wang X.; Bhatti A.; Demirci FY; Zhao W.; Rasheed A.; Samuel M.; Kiani AK; Ismail M.; Zafar J.; John P.; Saleheen D.; Kamboh MI
replication_title: A replication study of 49 Type 2 diabetes risk variants in a Punjabi Pakistani population
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Confirmed 'inconclusive' and 'medium' confidence after independent review. 8 of 49 GWAS SNPs replicated (P<0.05 after FDR correction) in Pakistani Punjabis, with TCF7L2/rs7903146 the strongest (P=3.54E-06, OR=1.383). However, 41/49 did not replicate, and KCNQ1 and KLF14 showed opposite allelic effects. The authors' own conclusion uses hedged language: 'some Type 2 diabetes susceptibility loci are shared between Europeans and Punjabis living in Pakistan.' This partial replication pattern (16% of tested loci) with mixed directionality fits the 'inconclusive' classification per the schema's 'conditional success' criterion. The ambiguity is genuine and inherent in the data — upgrading confidence is not warranted because reasonable analysts could disagree on whether 8/49 constitutes meaningful replication or predominant failure. Replication type 'close extension' is correct: same SNPs and phenotype but tested in a genetically distinct population (Punjabi Pakistanis vs. Europeans/East Asians), constituting a change in both methodological context and population.

description: PD patients exhibit greater beneficial effects of reward motivation on task-switching than healthy controls, with the magnitude correlating positively with dopamine cell loss in the dorsal striatum
original_authors: Esther Aarts; Rick C. Helmich; Marcel J. R. Janssen; Wim J. G. Oyen; Bastiaan R. Bloem; Roshan Cools
original_title: Aberrant reward processing in Parkinson's disease is associated with dopamine cell loss
replication_authors: Monique H.M. Timmer; Esther Aarts; Rianne A.J. Esselink; Roshan Cools
replication_title: Enhanced motivation of cognitive control in Parkinson's disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The finding that reward motivation has contrasting effects on task-switching in patients with PD and healthy controls is a direct replication of our previous study with the exact same paradigm (Aarts et al., 2011).' The key three-way interaction (TRIAL-TYPE × REWARD × GROUP) was significant (F(2,65) = 5.11, p = .009, η²p = 0.136), replicating the original finding.

description: Rhythmic fluctuations in visuospatial attentional performance (at ~4 Hz) are detectable at validly cued locations in a modified Egly-Driver task
original_authors: Randolph F. Helfrich; Ian C. Fiebelkorn; Sara M. Szczepanski; Jack J. Lin; Josef Parvizi; Robert T. Knight; Sabine Kastner
original_title: Neural mechanisms of sustained attention are rhythmic
replication_authors: Olof J. van der Werf; Sanne Ten Oever; Teresa Schuhmann; Alexander T. Sack
replication_title: No evidence of rhythmic visuospatial attention at cued locations in a spatial cuing paradigm, regardless of their behavioural relevance
explanation: The authors explicitly designed their moderately informative cue condition to 'directly replicate the behavioural findings of Helfrich and colleagues' using nearly identical task parameters and analysis. The abstract and conclusion both state 'we did not find evidence of rhythmic sampling at cued locations, failing to replicate earlier studies', with Bayesian analyses providing moderate-to-strong evidence for the null hypothesis (BF01 = 7.20 at 4 Hz, BF01 = 17.35 at 8 Hz).

description: Adults with Lesch-Nyhan disease and its variants show reduced total intracranial, cortical grey matter, subcortical grey matter, and white matter volumes relative to healthy controls
original_authors: Schretlen DJ; Varvaris M.; Ho TE; Vannorsdall TD; Gordon B.; Harris JC; Jinnah HA
original_title: Regional brain volume abnormalities in Lesch-Nyhan disease and its variants: A cross-sectional study
replication_authors: Victor A. Del Bene; Jeffrey L. Crawford; Ainara Gómez‐Gastiasoro; Tracy D. Vannorsdall; Alison Buchholz; Natalia Ojeda; James C. Harris; Hyder A. Jinnah; David J. Schretlen
replication_title: Microstructural white matter abnormalities in Lesch–Nyhan disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'using a different volumetric segmentation methodology from our prior study in a subset of participants who were all scanned on a single 3 Tesla machine, we replicated our previous findings of reduced total intracranial, cortical and subcortical GM, and WM volumes in patients with LND and LNV (Schretlen et al., 2013).' The same direction of findings (reduced brain volumes in LND/LNV vs. healthy controls) was confirmed with large Hedges' g effect sizes (e.g., WMV LND vs. HC: g = 2.83).

description: OurRelationship and ePREP online programs produce greater improvements in relationship functioning (satisfaction, communication conflict, emotional intimacy, breakup potential, and IPV) compared to a waitlist control group in low-income couples
original_authors: Doss BD; Knopp K.; Roddy MK; Rothman K.; Hatch SG; Rhoades GK
original_title: Online programs improve relationship functioning for distressed low-income couples: Results from a nationwide randomized controlled trial
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Hatch SG; Knopp K.; Le Y.; Allen MOT; Rothman K.; Rhoades GK; Doss BD
replication_title: Online relationship education for help‐seeking low‐income couples: A Bayesian replication and extension of the OurRelationship and ePREP programs
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the medium-sized effects of OurRelationship and ePREP on these relationship outcomes were similar to those found in the Doss et al. (2020) study, providing strong evidence for the reproducibility of these effects in low-income couples.' The replication succeeded on four of five outcomes (relationship satisfaction, communication conflict, emotional intimacy, and breakup potential), with IPV effects not replicating — however, the authors frame the overall result as a successful replication.

description: OurRelationship produces significantly greater reductions in communication conflict than ePREP among low-income couples
original_authors: Doss BD; Knopp K.; Roddy MK; Rothman K.; Hatch SG; Rhoades GK
original_title: Online programs improve relationship functioning for distressed low-income couples: Results from a nationwide randomized controlled trial
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Hatch SG; Knopp K.; Le Y.; Allen MOT; Rothman K.; Rhoades GK; Doss BD
replication_title: Online relationship education for help‐seeking low‐income couples: A Bayesian replication and extension of the OurRelationship and ePREP programs
explanation: In the current study, traditional null hypothesis testing found no reliable differences between OurRelationship and ePREP on communication conflict, unlike Doss et al. (2020) which found OurRelationship superior. However, Bayesian analysis narrowly replicated the original between-group difference (d = -0.175, 95% CI [-.348, .002]). The authors state 'more research is needed before confidently claiming program superiority on this outcome,' indicating mixed results.

description: COMT val158met genotype modulates the effects of d-amphetamine on executive functioning, such that met/met individuals are impaired while val/val individuals are improved on tasks including the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task and N-back working memory task

replication_title: Evidence for Linkage between Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy–Related Idiopathic Generalized Epilepsy and 6p11‐12 in Dutch Families
explanation: Independent review confirms 'success' classification. The paper explicitly describes itself as a 'replication linkage study' using 'an independent data set to replicate the proposed linkage of JME to 6p.' Results clearly meet the authors' pre-specified replication threshold (p < 0.01): LOD scores of 2.07 (narrow) and 2.53 (broad phenotype), NPL p-values of 0.0013 and 0.0010. The authors conclude 'Our findings support previous work (10-13).' Replication type 'close extension' is appropriate: the core linkage question is replicated in a new population (Dutch vs. Belize/LA/Mexico families), and the study extends prior work by adding a novel broad phenotype definition (JME/IGE-plus-fast EEG background activity). Confidence remains medium because: (1) the study targets multiple prior studies collectively (refs 10-13) rather than a single original, making Liu et al. 1995 a representative but not sole target; (2) LOD scores of 2.07-2.53 provide 'suggestive' rather than 'significant' evidence by Lander & Kruglyak genome-wide criteria, though the authors apply the less stringent replication threshold of p < 0.01 which is met. Discipline changed from medical fields/psychiatry to biology/genetics as this is fundamentally a genetic linkage analysis study and epilepsy is a neurological (not psychiatric) condition.
