The results were highly significant (Pc = 0.0002; Pexp = 0.0006), confirming the original finding.

description: IL10 gene polymorphisms are associated with increased risk of inhibitor (antibody) development in haemophilia A patients receiving factor VIII treatment
original_authors: Astermark, Jan; Oldenburg, Johannes; Pavlova, Anna; Berntorp, Erik; Lefvert, Ann-Kari; For The Mibs Study Group
original_title: Polymorphisms in the IL10 but not in the IL1beta and IL4 genes are associated with inhibitor development in patients with hemophilia A
replication_authors: Lozier JN; Rosenberg PS; Goedert JJ; Menashe I.
replication_title: A case-control study reveals immunoregulatory gene haplotypes that influence inhibitor risk in severe haemophilia A
explanation: The paper has a dedicated Results subsection titled 'Replication of association between IL10 polymorphisms and inhibitor development', and the Discussion explicitly states 'Our case-control study replicates the association of FVIII inhibitors with polymorphisms in the IL10 promoter region seen in family studies [6].' The replication found a significant IL10 haplotype effect (OR = 1.23, P = 0.04), confirming the original association.

description: A patient-centred nursing approach during hospital admission alleviates stress and improves emotional and physiological welfare in elective surgical patients
original_authors: Georing, P. N.
original_title: The Effects of Varied Nursing Approaches on Patients' Self-Report of Emotional Welfare
replication_authors: Julia Wong
replication_title: An exploration of a patient‐centred nursing approach in the admission of selected surgical patients: a replicated study
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: The paper explicitly calls itself 'the replication of a necessarily circumscribed descriptive study' but never names the original study by author or title. Contextual evidence (shared measurement tools — the WI and WS developed by Wolfer for Georing 1971, and the methodological comparison 'Unlike the original study in which the subjects were unaware...') points to Georing (1971) as the most likely original, but this identification is inferential, not stated. Result changed from 'success' to 'inconclusive': while the Findings section reports 'positive differences' in physiological welfare and 'a noticeable difference' in emotional welfare, no statistical tests or p-values are reported anywhere in the paper. The study is purely descriptive (pre-post with no control group). Critically, the authors' own Conclusions section emphasizes 'many difficulties in the methods used' rather than claiming the findings confirm the original. The absence of inferential statistics and the authors' cautious framing make 'success' an overstatement. Confidence remains 'low' because (1) the original study cannot be definitively identified, (2) no formal statistical evaluation of results is provided, and (3) the authors do not clearly state whether their findings replicate the original.

description: Self-care agency scores (measured by the ESCA) and self-concept scores (measured by the SCI) in East German adults, with self-care agency positively related to overall self-concept scores
original_authors: William R. Whetstone
original_title: Perceptions of self-care in East Germany: a cross-cultural empirical investigation
replication_authors: William R. Whetstone; Anne‐Marie Olow Hansson
replication_title: Perceptions of self‐care in Sweden: a cross‐cultural replication
explanation: The paper explicitly states its purpose was 'through replication, it examines cross-cultural perceptions and capabilities of participants to be involved in their own self-care.' The Swedish mean ESCA score (112.5) was comparable to the East German mean (113.6), and differences between Swedish and East German groups on both self-care and self-concept were not statistically significant, confirming the cross-cultural generalizability of the original findings.

description: Nursing students' valuing of altruism declines over the course of their training programme, and students enter nursing with relatively high altruistic orientation
original_authors: Johnson, M.
original_title: Nurses' values and nurse training: a pilot survey of the values of student nurses
original_journal: MSc Thesis, Department of Nursing, University of Manchester
replication_authors: Martin Johnson; Carol Haigh; Natalie Yates‐Bolton
replication_title: Valuing of altruism and honesty in nursing students: a two‐decade replication study
explanation: The 2005 replication found that modern students started from a lower altruism baseline (median 13.79 vs. 15.82 in year 1) and no longer showed a statistically significant decline over the programme, while the original 1983 study found a significant decline (p=0.001). Honesty valuing increased significantly in 2005 vs. 1983 (p<0.001), a new finding not central to the original study's claims. The authors describe important changes rather than a straightforward confirmation or failure.

description: Healthcare professionals rate their skills in advising patients about physical rehabilitation higher than their skills in advising on psychosocial rehabilitation following burn injury
original_authors: Alex Clarke; Clare Cooper
original_title: Psychological rehabilitation after disfiguring injury investigating the training needs of specialist nurses
replication_authors: Jeanne Reeve; Frances James; Rob McNeill
replication_title: Providing psychosocial and physical rehabilitation advice for patients with burns
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a replication study and confirm: 'Consistent with the UK results, New Zealand healthcare professionals rated their skills in advising patients about physical items of burn rehabilitation higher than their skills for psychosocial items.' The same questionnaire (Nurses Skills Questionnaire) was used but the study was conducted in New Zealand rather than the UK, making it a close extension testing generalizability to a different country/population.

description: The quality of life (QOL) construct has both etic (universal) and emic (culture-bound) properties across respondent groups (consumers, professionals, parents) and geographical groupings
original_authors: Schalock, R.; Verdugo, M.A.; Jenaro, C.; Wang, M.; Wehmeyer, M.; Xu, J.; Lachapelle, Y.
original_title: A cross-cultural study of core quality of life domains and indicators
replication_authors: Jenaro C.; Verdugo MA; Caballo C.; Balboni G.; Lachapelle Y.; Otrebski W.; Schalock RL
replication_title: Cross‐cultural study of person‐centred quality of life domains and indicators: a replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The present study replicated the major finding of the previous study (Schalock et al.) that the QOL construct has both etic and emic properties.' The same survey instrument and procedure were used, but the replication extended to new geographical groups (European countries: France, Belgium, Italy, Poland) rather than the original groupings (Spain, Latin America, Canada, China, USA).

description: A City nurse intervention (employing clinical experts to work with ward staff) significantly reduced conflict and containment behaviours on two acute psychiatric wards
original_authors: Bowers, L.; Flood, C.; Brennan, G.
original_title: A trial to reduce conflict and containment on acute psychiatric wards: city nurses
original_journal: Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing
replication_authors: Bowers L.; Flood C.; Brennan G.; Allan T.
replication_title: A replication study of the City nurse intervention: reducing conflict and containment on three acute psychiatric wards
replication_journal: Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing
explanation: The paper explicitly labels itself a replication study. The more rigorous controlled analysis found no significant effect ('no effect of the intervention was found'), while the simpler before-and-after analysis showed significant reductions. The authors concluded: 'The results were therefore ambiguous, and neither confirm nor contradict the efficacy of the intervention.'

description: 40% of nursing staff working at a medium-secure psychiatric unit in the UK were unable to break away from a simulated life-threatening situation within 10 seconds using taught breakaway techniques (60% success rate)
original_authors: Paul Rogers; Peter Ghroum; Richard Benson; Lavinia Forward; Kevin Gournay
original_title: Is breakaway training effective? An audit of one medium secure unit
original_journal: Journal of Forensic Psychiatry and Psychology
replication_authors: Dickens G.; Rogers G.; Rooney C.; Mc Guinness A.; Doyle D.
replication_title: An audit of the use of breakaway techniques in a large psychiatric hospital: a replication study
replication_journal: Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing
explanation: The replication produced markedly different results from the original (14% used taught techniques correctly vs. 60% success rate at the original site), with the authors stating results 'compared very unfavourably' with the Caswell study. The broad conclusion — that breakaway training effectiveness must be questioned — is consistent with the original, but the specific performance figures differ dramatically; the authors attribute this to differences in setting, training duration, and staff mix, making the result inconclusive rather than a clear failure or success.

description: Genome-wide linkage scan identified suggestive evidence for an asthma susceptibility locus on chromosome Xp11 in a Danish population
original_authors: Haagerup A.; Bjerke T.; Schiøtz PO; Binderup HG; Dahl R.; Kruse TA
original_title: Asthma and atopy - a total genome scan for susceptibility genes
replication_authors: Brasch-Andersen C.; Møller MU; Haagerup A.; Vestbo J.; Kruse TA
replication_title: Evidence for an asthma risk locus on chromosome Xp: a replication linkage study
explanation: The replication study found strong suggestive evidence for linkage to chromosome Xp21 (MLS = 2.92), confirming the candidate region identified in the original genome scan. The authors conclude: 'our results provide suggestive evidence for linkage to asthma to chromosome Xp21 in a replication study. The fact that the same locus was suggested by two independent studies in the Danish population shows strong evidence for an asthma gene on chromosome Xp21.'

description: Genome-wide linkage scan identified suggestive evidence for an asthma susceptibility locus on chromosome 1p36 in a Danish population
original_authors: Haagerup A.; Bjerke T.; Schiøtz PO; Binderup HG; Dahl R.; Kruse TA
original_title: Asthma and atopy - a total genome scan for susceptibility genes
replication_authors: Brasch-Andersen C.; Møller MU; Haagerup A.; Vestbo J.; Kruse TA
replication_title: Evidence for an asthma risk locus on chromosome Xp: a replication linkage study
explanation: The replication study found no evidence for linkage to chromosome 1p36.31-p36.21 (peak MLS near 0), failing to replicate the original genome scan finding. The authors state: 'We did not find evidence to support the linkage suggested in the genome-wide scan on chromosome 1p36.31-p36.21.'

description: Genome-wide linkage scan identified suggestive evidence for an asthma susceptibility locus on chromosome 5q15-q23.2 in a Danish population
original_authors: Haagerup A.; Bjerke T.; Schiøtz PO; Binderup HG; Dahl R.; Kruse TA
original_title: Asthma and atopy - a total genome scan for susceptibility genes
replication_authors: Brasch-Andersen C.; Møller MU; Haagerup A.; Vestbo J.; Kruse TA
replication_title: Evidence for an asthma risk locus on chromosome Xp: a replication linkage study
explanation: The replication study found no evidence for linkage to chromosome 5q15-q23.2 (peak MLS < 0.15), failing to replicate the original genome scan finding. The authors state: 'We did not find evidence to support the linkage suggested in the genome-wide scan...on chromosome 5q21.3-q23.2.'

description: Genome-wide linkage scan identified suggestive evidence for an asthma susceptibility locus on chromosome 6p24.3-p22.3 in a Danish population
original_authors: Haagerup A.; Bjerke T.; Schiøtz PO; Binderup HG; Dahl R.; Kruse TA
original_title: Asthma and atopy - a total genome scan for susceptibility genes
replication_authors: Brasch-Andersen C.; Møller MU; Haagerup A.; Vestbo J.; Kruse TA
replication_title: Evidence for an asthma risk locus on chromosome Xp: a replication linkage study
explanation: The replication study found no evidence for linkage to chromosome 6p24.3-p22.3 (peak MLS < 1.0), failing to replicate the original genome scan finding. The authors state: 'We did not find evidence to support the linkage suggested in the genome-wide scan...nor on chromosome 6p24-p21.3.'

description: Six-month-old infants can discriminate temporal intervals that differ by a 1:2 ratio but not a 2:3 ratio, demonstrating ratio-dependent temporal discrimination consistent with scalar variability
original_authors: Kristy VanMarle; Karen Wynn
original_title: Six-month-old infants use analog magnitudes to represent duration
replication_authors: Elizabeth M. Brannon; Sumarga Suanda; Klaus Libertus
replication_title: Temporal discrimination increases in precision over development and parallels the development of numerosity discrimination
explanation: The authors state 'The goal of the first study was to replicate the finding by vanMarle and Wynn (2006) that 6-month-old infants succeed at discriminating a 1:2 ratio in temporal intervals.' The replication succeeded: infants looked significantly longer at novel test trials (8.6 s vs 5.8 s, t(15) = 3.48, p < .01), consistent with the original findings.

description: Infants preferentially attend to continuous properties (contour length) rather than number when discriminating small sets of 2 versus 3 items
original_authors: Melissa Wechsler Clearfield; Kelly S. Mix
original_title: Number versus contour length in infants' discrimination of small visual sets
replication_authors: Sara Cordes; Elizabeth M. Brannon
replication_title: The relative salience of discrete and continuous quantity in young infants
explanation: The authors explicitly state their Experiment 1 results 'differ from those of Clearfield & Mix (1999)': whereas the original found infants preferred the change in contour over number, the replication found infants dishabituated to both changes with no preference for contour over number. The core claim — that continuous extent is more salient than number — was not replicated.

description: Interaction between CYP1A2 genotype (rs762551 CC slow metabolizer) and coffee consumption increases the inverse association between coffee and Parkinson's disease risk
original_authors: Popat RA; Van Den Eeden SK; Tanner CM; Kamel F.; Umbach DM; Marder K.; Mayeux R.; Ritz B.; Ross GW; Petrovitch H.; Topol B.; McGuire V.; Costello S.; Manthripragada AD; Southwick A.; Myers RM; Nelson LM
original_title: Coffee, ADORA2A, and CYP1A2: the caffeine connection in Parkinson's disease
replication_authors: Hill-Burns EM; Hamza TH; Zabetian CP; Factor SA; Payami H.
replication_title: An attempt to replicate interaction between coffee andCYP1A2gene in connection to Parkinson’s disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Unfortunately, we did not replicate the reported interactions under any of the models nor did we find a stronger PD-coffee association amongst slow metabolizers.' All SNP*coffee interaction p-values in the replication were far from significance (0.46–0.81) compared to the original (0.04–0.07).

description: Genetic variants in the Chr17q25 locus (SNPs including rs3744028 and rs1055129) are independently associated with white matter hyperintensity burden in subjects of European descent
original_authors: Fornage M.; Debette S.; Bis JC; Schmidt H.; Ikram MA; Dufouil C.; Sigurdsson S.; Lumley T.; DeStefano AL; Fazekas F.; Vrooman HA; Shibata DK; Maillard P.; Zijdenbos A.; Smith AV; Gudnason H.; de Boer R.; Cushman M.; Mazoyer B.; Heiss G.; Vernooij MW; Enzinger C.; Glazer NL; Beiser A.; Knopman DS; Cavalieri M.; Niessen WJ; Harris TB; Petrovic K.; Lopez OL; Au R.; Lambert JC; Hofman A.; Gottesman RF; Garcia M.; Heckbert SR; Atwood LD; Catellier DJ; Uitterlinden AG; Yang Q.; Smith NL; Aspelund T.; Romero JR; Rice K.; Taylor KD; Nalls MA; Rotter JI; Sharrett R.; van Duijn CM; Amouyel P.; Wolf PA; Gudnason V.; van der Lugt A.; Boerwinkle E.; Psaty BM; Seshadri S.; Tzourio C.; Breteler MM; Mosley TH; Schmidt R.; Longstreth WT; DeCarli C.; Launer LJ
original_title: Genome-wide association studies of cerebral white matter lesion burden: the CHARGE consortium
replication_authors: Tabara Y.; Igase M.; Okada Y.; Nagai T.; Uetani E.; Kido T.; Ochi N.; Takita R.; Yamamoto M.; Kohara K.; Miki T.
replication_title: Association of <scp>C</scp>hr17q25 with cerebral white matter hyperintensities and cognitive impairment: the <scp>J</scp>‐<scp>SHIPP</scp> study
explanation: The authors explicitly frame this as the first replication in non-European subjects, and conclude: 'this is the first study to report this association in subjects of non-European origin, suggesting that the susceptibility of the 17q25 locus may be conserved beyond ethnic differences.' rs3744028 was significantly associated with DSWMH grade (P=0.015) in 1190 Japanese participants.

description: Mere exposure to stimuli enhances positive evaluation (liking), and this effect is driven by exposure frequency rather than stimulus recognition
original_authors: Richard L. Moreland; Robert B. Zajonc
original_title: Is stimulus recognition a necessary condition for the occurrence of exposure effects?
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Keiko Ishii
replication_title: Does mere exposure enhance positive evaluation, independent of stimulus recognition? A replication study in Japan and the USA<sup>1</sup>
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the current study successfully replicated the previous results on the mere exposure effect, obtained mainly in the USA, in a different culture (i.e., Japan).' They adopted the regression procedure of Moreland & Zajonc (1977) and found the same pattern: exposure frequency predicted liking (β = 0.35, p < 0.05) but recognition did not (β = 0.09, ns).

description: The CALHM1 P86L polymorphism (rs2986017) is associated with increased Aβ levels and elevated risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, with an allele-specific odds ratio of 1.44
original_authors: Dreses-Werringloer U.; Lambert JC; Vingtdeux V.; Zhao H.; Vais H.; Siebert A.; Jain A.; Koppel J.; Rovelet-Lecrux A.; Hannequin D.; Pasquier F.; Galimberti D.; Scarpini E.; Mann D.; Lendon C.; Campion D.; Amouyel P.; Davies P.; Foskett JK; Campagne F.; Marambaud P.
original_title: A polymorphism in CALHM1 influences Ca2+ homeostasis, Aβ levels, and Alzheimer's disease risk
replication_authors: Gary W. Beecham; Nathalie Schnetz‐Boutaud; Jonathan L. Haines; Margaret A. Pericak-Vance
replication_title: CALHM1 Polymorphism is not Associated with Late‐onset Alzheimer Disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results do not confirm the risk of LOAD associated with this CALHM1 polymorphism' and suggest the original finding 'may be a false positive.' The replication found no significant association (p = 0.63; OR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.86–1.27) despite having 95% power to detect the originally reported effect sizes.

description: The Gly972Arg variant (rs1801278) of the IRS1 gene is associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus in the Mexican population
original_authors: Ana I. Burguete-Garcia; Miguel Cruz-Lopez; Vicente Madrid-Marina; Ruy Lopez-Ridaura; Mauricio Hernández-Ávila; Bernardo Cortina; Rosa E. Gómez; Eduardo Velasco-Mondragón
original_title: Association of Gly972Arg polymorphism of IRS-1 gene with type 2 diabetes mellitus in lean participants of a national health survey in Mexico: a candidate gene study
replication_authors: Laura E. Martínez-Gómez; Miguel Cruz; Gabriela A. Martínez-Nava; Vicente Madrid-Marina; Esteban Parra; Jaime García-Mena; Mónica Espinoza-Rojo; Barbara I. Estrada-Velasco; Luis F. Piza-Roman; Penelope Aguilera; Ana I. Burguete-García
replication_title: A Replication Study of the IRS1, CAPN10, TCF7L2, and PPARG Gene Polymorphisms Associated with Type 2 Diabetes in Two Different Populations of Mexico
explanation: The replication found that heterozygosity for Gly972Arg of IRS1 was significantly associated with T2D in both Guerrero (OR = 2.43, 95% CI 1.12-5.26) and Mexico City (OR = 2.64, 95% CI 1.37-5.10), consistent with the original OR of 2.80. The authors state: 'The replication study of the Gly972Arg variant of IRS1 showed the strongest effect for T2D, as previously reported by Burguete-Garcia et al.'

description: Polymorphisms rs7903146 and rs12255372 in the TCF7L2 gene are associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes in Mexico City
original_authors: Parra EJ; Cameron E.; Simmonds L.; Valladares A.; McKeigue P.; Shriver M.; Wacher N.; Kumate J.; Kittles R.; Cruz M.
original_title: Association of TCF7L2 polymorphisms with type 2 diabetes in Mexico City
replication_authors: Laura E. Martínez-Gómez; Miguel Cruz; Gabriela A. Martínez-Nava; Vicente Madrid-Marina; Esteban Parra; Jaime García-Mena; Mónica Espinoza-Rojo; Barbara I. Estrada-Velasco; Luis F. Piza-Roman; Penelope Aguilera; Ana I. Burguete-García
replication_title: A Replication Study of the IRS1, CAPN10, TCF7L2, and PPARG Gene Polymorphisms Associated with Type 2 Diabetes in Two Different Populations of Mexico
explanation: The replication confirmed associations of both TCF7L2 SNPs (rs7903146 and rs12255372) with T2D in two Mexican populations (Guerrero and Mexico City), with ORs ranging from 1.78 to 1.98. The authors state: 'Our results for IRS1 and the two polymorphisms of TCF7L2 are in agreement with previous studies in other population groups' including Parra et al. (2007).

description: A bioecological gene-by-environment interaction exists between reading disability heritability and parental education, such that reading disability is more heritable in higher-education environments
original_authors: Bruce F. Pennington; Lauren M. McGrath; Jenni Rosenberg; Holly Barnard; Shelley D. Smith; Erik G. Willcutt; Angela Friend; John C. DeFries; Richard K. Olson
original_title: Gene × environment interactions in reading disability and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
replication_authors: Jenni Rosenberg; Bruce F. Pennington; Erik G. Willcutt; Richard K. Olson
replication_title: Gene by environment interactions influencing reading disability and the inattentive symptom dimension of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
replication_journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'replicate opposite G·E interactions with parental education in RD and ADHD-I.' They successfully found a significant bioecological G×E interaction for RD (B=0.249, p=.008), consistent with Pennington et al. (2009), and conclude that 'opposite G·E interactions are robust in RD and ADHD-I.'

description: A diathesis-stress gene-by-environment interaction exists between ADHD inattentive symptom heritability and parental education, such that ADHD-I is more heritable in lower-education (risk) environments
original_authors: Bruce F. Pennington; Lauren M. McGrath; Jenni Rosenberg; Holly Barnard; Shelley D. Smith; Erik G. Willcutt; Angela Friend; John C. DeFries; Richard K. Olson
original_title: Gene × environment interactions in reading disability and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
replication_authors: Jenni Rosenberg; Bruce F. Pennington; Erik G. Willcutt; Richard K. Olson
replication_title: Gene by environment interactions influencing reading disability and the inattentive symptom dimension of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
replication_journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'replicate opposite G·E interactions with parental education in RD and ADHD-I.' They successfully found a significant diathesis-stress G×E interaction for ADHD-I (B=−0.345, p=.023), consistent with Pennington et al. (2009), and the Discussion confirms these interactions as 'robust.'

description: Individual differences in cardiovascular responses (heart rate, blood pressure, stroke volume, preejection period) to a standardized PC-based cognitive task protocol show high test-retest reliability (≥.80) when aggregated across tasks and sessions in predominantly white male samples
original_authors: Kamarck TW; Jennings JR; Debski TT; Glickman-Weiss E.; Johnson PS; Eddy MJ; Manuck SB
original_title: Reliable measures of behaviorally-evoked cardiovascular reactivity from a PC-based test battery: Results from student and community samples
replication_authors: Kamarck TW; Jennings JR; Stewart CJ; Eddy MJ
replication_title: Reliable responses to a cardiovascular reactivity protocol: A replication study in a biracial female sample
explanation: The Discussion section explicitly states 'This study replicates previous findings, showing that a standardized multitask laboratory protocol for assessing cardiovascular reactivity yields test-retest results meeting conventional psychometric standards for reliability.' The replication extended the original findings to a biracial female community sample tested in a mobile laboratory, with session-pooled reliability coefficients ≥.85 for heart rate, systolic, and diastolic blood pressure, and ≥.70 for preejection period and stroke volume.

description: Resting EEG asymmetry consists of approximately 60% trait variance and 40% occasion-specific (state) variance, as decomposed using latent state-trait structural equation modeling
original_authors: Dirk Hagemann; Ewald Naumann; Julian F. Thayer; Dieter Bartussek
original_title: Does resting EEG asymmetry reflect a trait? An application of latent state-trait theory
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Dirk Hagemann; Johannes Hewig; Jan Seifert; Ewald Naumann; Dieter Bartussek
replication_title: The latent state‐trait structure of resting EEG asymmetry: Replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the present finding is a close replication of the results from Hagemann et al. (2002) in an independent sample,' with the replication finding approximately 40-50% occasion specificity and 60% trait specificity for anterior EEG asymmetry measures, closely matching the original's findings.

description: Pragmatic violations evoke a robust N400 effect and morphosyntactic violations evoke a robust P600 effect on midsentence critical verbs during sentence comprehension
original_authors: Gina R. Kuperberg; Tatiana Sitnikova; David Caplan; Phillip J. Holcomb
original_title: Electrophysiological distinctions in processing conceptual relationships within simple sentences
replication_authors: Tali Ditman; Phillip J. Holcomb; Gina R. Kuperberg
replication_title: An investigation of concurrent ERP and self‐paced reading methodologies
explanation: Upgraded to high after independent review. The authors make an explicit, unhedged replication claim in the Discussion: 'the results of the current study replicated both previous ERP and behavioral findings: Pragmatic violations evoked a robust N400 effect and syntactic violations evoked a robust P600 effect on the midsentence critical verbs (for similar findings using these stimuli, see Kuperberg et al., 2003, 2006).' The replication is further confirmed later in the Discussion where they state 'in overall analyses we replicated previous findings of a larger N400 amplitude to semantically/pragmatically violated critical words and a larger P600 amplitude to morphosyntactic violations.' The study used the same stimuli from Kuperberg et al. (2003) but with a novel concurrent self-paced reading + ERP methodology (rather than traditional RSVP), making this a close extension. Both ERP and behavioral results were statistically significant (p<.001). The paper's primary goal was methodological validation, and successful replication of known effects was the key evidence that the new technique works.

description: The α2C-Del322-325 adrenoceptor polymorphism exhibits reduced signalling (inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity) compared to the wild-type receptor when expressed in CHO cells
original_authors: Kersten M. Small; Susan L. Forbes; Fahema F. Rahman; Kari M. Bridges; Stephen B. Liggett
original_title: A four amino acid deletion polymorphism in the third intracellular loop of the human alpha 2C-adrenergic receptor confers impaired coupling to multiple effectors
replication_authors: Montgomery MD; Bylund DB
replication_title: Lack of effect of the α<sub>2C</sub>‐adrenoceptor Del322‐325 polymorphism on inhibition of cyclic AMP production in HEK293 cells
explanation: The authors explicitly attempted to replicate the reduced signalling of the Del322-325 receptor reported by Small et al. (2000) in CHO cells, but using HEK293 cells instead. They found no difference in efficacy or potency between WT and Del322-325 receptors, and state: 'our failure to show reduced function in HEK293 cells compared with the decreased function reported previously in CHO cells adds to the complexities of the phenotypic consequences of the α2C-adrenoceptor Del322-325 genetic polymorphism.'

description: The Headache-Specific Locus of Control scale (HSLC) has satisfactory psychometric properties (factor structure and internal reliability) when administered to a university student population
original_authors: Nancy J. Martin; Kenneth A. Holroyd; Donald B. Penzien
original_title: The headache-specific locus of control scale: adaptation to recurrent headaches
replication_authors: Larry VandeCreek; Min Deng; Francis O’Donnell
replication_title: Psychometric Characteristics of the Headache‐Specific Locus of Control Scale
replication_journal: Headache: The Journal of Head and Face Pain
explanation: The authors explicitly call this 'a replication study' and conclude: 'This study suggests that the psychometric characteristics of the HSLC remain similar to those reported by Martin when it is used with a more diverse sample... Factor analysis and alpha coefficients remain satisfactory.' The same instrument was applied to a clinical headache patient population and comparison sample rather than the original university students.

description: A susceptibility locus (EGI) for common subtypes of idiopathic generalized epilepsy maps to chromosomal region 8q24
original_authors: Zara F.; Bianchi A.; Avanzini G.; Di Donato S.; Castellotti B.; Patel PI; Pandolfo M.
original_title: Mapping of genes predisposing to idiopathic generalized epilepsy
replication_authors: Thomas Sander; Rebekka Kretz; Herbert Schulz; Ulrike Sailer; Gerhard Bauer; Alejandro Scaramelli; Jörg T. Epplen; Olaf Riess; Dieter Janz
replication_title: Replication Analysis of a Putative Susceptibility Locus (EGI) for Idiopathic Generalized Epilepsy on Chromosome 8q24
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We failed to replicate evidence favoring a major locus for common IGE syndromes in the region 8q24' and 'our present parametric linkage results provide evidence against linkage across the region under a broad range of genetic models.'

description: Neuronal complexity loss (L*) extracted from interictal intracranial EEG recordings using intrahippocampal depth and subdural strip electrodes correctly lateralizes the primary epileptogenic area in patients with unilateral mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
original_authors: Lehnertz K.; Elger CE
original_title: Spatio-temporal dynamics of the primary epileptogenic area in temporal lobe epilepsy characterized by neuronal complexity loss
replication_authors: Weber B.; Lehnertz K.; Elger CE; Wieser HG
replication_title: Neuronal Complexity Loss in Interictal EEG Recorded with Foramen Ovale Electrodes Predicts Side of Primary Epileptogenic Area in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This result replicates the previous findings of Lehnertz and Elger (10).' The replication correctly lateralized seizure onset in 16/19 patients using the same neuronal complexity loss analysis but with semi-invasive foramen ovale electrodes instead of intrahippocampal depth electrodes, and the key ANOVA interaction was highly significant (F=27.8, p<0.0001).

description: Individuals who began drinking by age 14 and experienced past-year life stressors had higher alcohol consumption than early drinkers without stressors and later-onset drinkers (interaction between drinking onset age and stressful life events on alcohol consumption)
original_authors: Deborah A. Dawson; Bridget F. Grant; Ting‐Kai Li
original_title: Impact of age at first drink on stress-reactive drinking
replication_authors: Lewina O. Lee; Kelly C. Young Wolff; Kenneth S. Kendler; Carol A. Prescott
replication_title: The Effects of Age at Drinking Onset and Stressful Life Events on Alcohol Use in Adulthood: A Replication and Extension Using a Population‐Based Twin Sample
explanation: The authors found that 'the pattern of our findings is consistent with the interaction reported by Dawson and colleagues (2007),' but the interaction explained ≤1% of variance and was not statistically significant for total SLE. The authors conclude they found 'limited evidence supporting a replication for higher stress-related drinking among early-onset drinkers,' with some sex-specific effects (significant for dependent SLE in women and independent SLE in men). The replication used a different population (twins), different SLE measures, and added moderators.

description: Earlier age of drinking onset is associated with higher adult alcohol consumption (main effect of drinking onset on past-year alcohol intake)
original_authors: Deborah A. Dawson; Bridget F. Grant; Ting‐Kai Li
original_title: Impact of age at first drink on stress-reactive drinking
replication_authors: Lewina O. Lee; Kelly C. Young Wolff; Kenneth S. Kendler; Carol A. Prescott
replication_title: The Effects of Age at Drinking Onset and Stressful Life Events on Alcohol Use in Adulthood: A Replication and Extension Using a Population‐Based Twin Sample
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the prior finding of a main effect of higher alcohol consumption among individuals reporting earlier drinking onset.' Drinking onset accounted for 3–6% of variance in past-year drinking density in both men and women, and the association was statistically significant.

description: The Functional Assessment Inventory (FAI) can reliably distinguish among elderly subjects in different service settings (nursing homes, adult congregate living facilities, adult day care programs, and senior centers) based on their functional status
original_authors: Pfeiffer E.; Johnson TM; Chiofolo RC
original_title: Functional assessment of elderly subjects in four service settings
original_journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
replication_authors: Barbara A. Pfeiffer; Tina McClelland; Joan Lawson
replication_title: Use of the Functional Assessment Inventory to Distinguish Among the Rural Elderly in Five Service Settings
replication_journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This replication study further supports the hypothesis that the FAI can reliably distinguish between the elderly in different service settings.' The FAI successfully discriminated among five service setting groups in rural Ohio, consistent with the original South Florida findings.

description: Three different approaches to measuring social class in a small town community (subjective self-ratings, reputational ratings, and objective status indicators) correspond to a moderate degree, with rank-order correlations ranging from .51 to .68
original_authors: Rennie, Douglas; Hilgendorf, Robert
original_title: Stratification in a Small Town
replication_authors: Gary M. Maranell
replication_title: Stratification in a Small Town: An Attempt to Replicate
explanation: The replication found substantially lower correlations than the original across all three pairs of stratification measures (e.g., .48 vs .68 for reputational-objective; .196 vs .56 for reputational-subjective; .25 vs .51 for objective-subjective). The authors explicitly conclude: 'we cannot conclude, as they did, that all three approaches correspond to a moderate degree in the classifications they yield, but rather we must observe that the correspondence is astonishingly low in some cases.'

description: Five gene variants (PALLD rs12510359, ROS1 rs619203, TAS2R50 rs1376251, OR13G1 rs1151640, ZNF627 rs4804611) are associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction
original_authors: Dov Shiffman; Stephen G. Ellis; Charles M. Rowland; Mary J. Malloy; May M. Luke; Olga A. Iakoubova; Clive R. Pullinger; June Cassano; Bradley E. Aouizerat; Raymond G. Fenwick; Richard E. Reitz; Joseph J. Catanese; Diane U. Leong; Christian Zellner; John J. Sninsky; Eric J. Topol; James J. Devlin; John P. Kane
original_title: Identification of four gene variants associated with myocardial infarction
replication_authors: Zee RY; Michaud SE; Hegener HH; Diehl KA; Ridker PM
replication_title: A prospective replication study of five gene variants previously associated with risk of myocardial infarction
explanation: The authors replicated the association of ROS1 rs619203 with MI risk (crude OR=2.50, 95% CI 1.12-5.57, P=0.03), consistent with Shiffman et al., but found no significant association for the other four variants. The conclusion states: 'our prospective investigation replicates an association of the ROS1 rs619203 polymorphism...with increased risk of incident MI' while acknowledging failure for the remaining four variants.

description: A 45-item Continuity and Discontinuity of Self Scale (CDSS) administered to stroke survivors produces a two-factor solution distinguishing discontinuity of self from continuity of self
original_authors: Janet S. Secrest; Richard Zeller
original_title: Measuring continuity and discontinuity following stroke
replication_authors: Janet Secrest; Richard Zeller
replication_title: Replication and Extension of the Continuity and Discontinuity of Self Scale (CDSS)
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'a principal components analysis of the additional 50 cases provides a robust replication of the 55 cases in Secrest and Zeller (2003),' and the two-factor structure (discontinuity and continuity) was reproduced with similar Cronbach's alpha coefficients using identical procedures.

description: CSF/serum albumin ratios are increased in violent offenders compared to healthy controls, indicating increased blood-brain barrier permeability
original_authors: Soderstrom H.; Blennow K.; Manhem A.; Forsman A.
original_title: CSF studies in violent offenders. II. Blood-brain barrier dysfunction without concurrent inflammation or structure degeneration
replication_authors: Anckarsäter H.; Forsman A.; Blennow K.
replication_title: Increased CSF/serum albumin ratio: a recurrent finding in violent offenders
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a replication study and conclude that 'The CSF/serum albumin ratio was thus increased also in our second study group of violent offenders.' The replication found a statistically significant increase (mean 6.2 vs 4.6, P=0.012) in the same direction as the original.

description: Parental couples with a schizophrenic offspring communicate less efficiently than matched control couples in a standardized communication conflict situation, but not in a simple communication situation
original_authors: Helge Arnulf Sølvberg; Rolv Mikkel Blakar
original_title: Communication efficiency in couples with and without a schizophrenic offspring
replication_authors: Blakar RM; Paulsen OG; Sølvberg HA
replication_title: Schizophrenia and communication efficiency
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The main findings of the original study are reproduced' and found that Group S (schizophrenic offspring) couples showed significantly less efficient communication than Group N (normal) couples (Fisher's P = 0.01 for the combined sample). The replication was conducted in a rural sample rather than the original urban (Oslo) sample, making this a close extension testing generalizability across ecological backgrounds.

description: Interrater reliability coefficients of the standardized and expanded Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS-E), with the 10-item psychotic disintegration scale and BPRS-18 global scores meeting acceptable reliability standards, but not the anxiety-depression subscale
original_authors: Anton Hafkenscheid
original_title: Psychometric evaluation of a standardized and expanded Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale
replication_authors: Hafkenscheid A.
replication_title: Reliability of a standardized and expanded Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The replication findings largely support the conclusions of the 1991 psychometric evaluation,' and the core finding that the psychotic disintegration scale and BPRS-18 global scale meet acceptable interrater reliability standards was confirmed. A notable difference was that the anxiety-depression subscale met acceptable reliability in the replication but not in the 1991 study, which the authors treat as an additional positive finding.

description: Preadult onset MDD (before age 18) in STAR*D participants is more common in women and is associated with a more chronic, severe, and disabling course of depression, more comorbidity, higher suicidality, and lower educational and marital rates compared to adult onset MDD
original_authors: Zisook S.; Rush AJ; Albala A.; Alpert J.; Balasubramani GK; Fava M.; Husain M.; Sackeim H.; Trivedi M.; Wisniewski S.
original_title: Factors that differentiate early vs. later onset of major depression disorder
replication_authors: Zisook S.; Rush AJ; Lesser I.; Wisniewski SR; Trivedi M.; Husain MM; Balasubramani GK; Alpert JE; Fava M.
replication_title: Preadult onset vs. adult onset of major depressive disorder: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Overall, this study only partially replicated our earlier, preliminary study' and note 'The failure to more fully replicate our preliminary findings should serve as a reminder of how important it is to have replication before accepting the results of any single study.' Some findings were replicated (female predominance, family history of MDD, elevated suicidality), while many others were not (severity, episodes, comorbidity, psychosocial functioning).

description: Past-year prevalence of pathological gambling in the Swiss population was estimated at 0.2% and problem gambling at 1.0% using the South Oaks Gambling Screen (SOGS) telephone survey
original_authors: Bondolfi G.; Osiek C.; Ferrero F.
original_title: Prevalence estimates of pathological gambling in Switzerland
replication_authors: Bondolfi G.; Jermann F.; Ferrero F.; Zullino D.; Osiek C.
replication_title: Prevalence of pathological gambling in Switzerland after the opening of casinos and the introduction of new preventive legislation
explanation: The authors explicitly conducted this as a replication of their 1998 baseline study using identical methods, finding stable prevalence rates: 'the past-year prevalence of disordered gambling did not change between 1998 and 2005' (all χ² < 1.34; all P > 0.25), confirming the original estimates.

description: Scottish dentists show systematic variation in restorative treatment decisions and diagnostic thresholds when evaluating interproximal caries on bitewing radiographs, as measured by ROC analysis and sensitivity/specificity of caries detection
original_authors: Elizabeth Jane Kay; Robin Knill‐Jones
original_title: Variation in restorative decisions: application of receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) analysis
replication_authors: Kay EJ; Locker D.
replication_title: Variations in restorative treatment decisions: an international comparison
explanation: Reviewer verification: The original study (ref 5 in the paper, Kay & Knill-Jones 1992) examined Scottish dentists' restorative decision-making using ROC analysis on bitewing radiographs. The Canadian replication (ref 15, Lewis et al., in press) used the same methodology in a different country/healthcare system. The core finding — overall discriminatory ability — was similar (ROC area 0.76 Canadian vs 0.73 Scottish), supporting replication. However, Canadian dentists showed meaningfully higher sensitivity (49% vs 26% at T1; 65% vs 55% at T2) and lower specificity, indicating different action thresholds. The authors explicitly state 'the data from the study need to be interpreted with caution' due to small, non-random samples, and note that within-group variation exceeded between-group variation. No statistical tests were performed. The ambiguity is genuine: the overall ROC ability replicated but threshold differences and methodological caveats prevent a clear success or failure classification. Confidence remains medium — this reflects the paper's own stated limitations, not reviewer uncertainty.

description: Six SNPs identified by genome-wide association study in UK Caucasians are associated with chronic lymphocytic leukemia risk
original_authors: Maria Chiara Di Bernardo; Dalemari Crowther-Swanepoel; Peter Broderick; Emily Webb; Gabrielle Sellick; Ruth Wild; Kate Sullivan; Jayaram Vijayakrishnan; Yufei Wang; Alan M. Pittman; Nicola J. Sunter; Andrew G. Hall; Martin J. S. Dyer; Estella Matutes; Claire Dearden; Tryfonia Mainou-Fowler; Graham H. Jackson; Geoffrey Summerfield; Robert J. Harris; Andrew R. Pettitt; Peter Hillmen; David J. Allsup; James R. Bailey; Guy Pratt; Chris Pepper; Chris Fegan; James M. Allan; Daniel Catovsky; Richard S. Houlston
original_title: A genome-wide association study identifies six susceptibility loci for chronic lymphocytic leukemia
replication_authors: Lan Q.; Au WY; Chanock S.; Tse J.; Wong KF; Shen M.; Siu LP; Yuenger J.; Yeager M.; Hosgood HD 3rd; Purdue MP; Liang R.; Rothman N.
replication_title: Genetic susceptibility for chronic lymphocytic leukemia among Chinese in Hong Kong
explanation: Only 3 of the 6 SNPs from the original UK GWAS showed statistically significant associations in the Hong Kong Chinese population (IRF4 rs872071, SP140 rs13397985, ACOXL rs17483466), while 2 did not replicate and 1 had near-zero MAF making it untestable. The authors note 'statistically significant associations were still present for three of the six SNPs' and call for further study in larger samples.

description: CRISPLD2, a gene near marker D16S3037 on chromosome 16q24.1, is linked and associated with non-syndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate in Caucasian multiplex families
original_authors: Brett Chiquet; Andrew C. Lidral; Samuel Stal; John B. Mulliken; Lina M. Moreno; Mauricio Arco-Burgos; Consuelo Valencia-Ramirez; Susan H. Blanton; Jacqueline T. Hecht
original_title: CRISPLD2: a novel NSCLP candidate gene
replication_authors: Ambra Girardi; Marcella Martinelli; Francesco Carinci; Paolo G. Morselli; Elisabetta Caramelli; Luca Scapoli
replication_title: No evidence for a role ofCRISPLD2in non‐syndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate in an Italian population
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim was a replication study to confirm CRISPLD2's role in NSCLP, and conclude: 'these results failed to replicate evidence of a role for the 16q24 genomic region, and thus for CRISPLD2, which had been previously obtained with an analysis of familial cases.' No evidence of linkage or association was found in the Italian population.

description: Common variants of the latrophilin 3 (LPHN3) gene are associated with ADHD susceptibility across multiple populations
original_authors: Arcos-Burgos M.; Jain M.; Acosta MT; Shively S.; Stanescu H.; Wallis D.; Domené S.; Vélez JI; Karkera JD; Balog J.; Berg K.; Kleta R.; Gahl WA; Roessler E.; Long R.; Lie J.; Pineda D.; Londoño AC; Palacio JD; Arbelaez A.; Lopera F.; Elia J.; Hakonarson H.; Johansson S.; Knappskog PM; Haavik J.; Ribases M.; Cormand B.; Bayes M.; Casas M.; Ramos-Quiroga JA; Hervas A.; Maher BS; Faraone SV; Seitz C.; Freitag CM; Palmason H.; Meyer J.; Romanos M.; Walitza S.; Hemminger U.; Warnke A.; Romanos J.; Renner T.; Jacob C.; Lesch KP; Swanson J.; Vortmeyer A.; Bailey-Wilson JE; Castellanos FX; Muenke M.
original_title: A common variant of the latrophilin 3 gene, LPHN3, confers susceptibility to ADHD and predicts effectiveness of stimulant medication
replication_authors: Ribasés M.; Ramos-Quiroga JA; Sánchez-Mora C.; Bosch R.; Richarte V.; Palomar G.; Gastaminza X.; Bielsa A.; Arcos-Burgos M.; Muenke M.; Castellanos FX; Cormand B.; Bayés M.; Casas M.
replication_title: Contribution of LPHN3 to the genetic susceptibility to ADHD in adulthood: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In this study, we replicated the recently described association between LPHN3 and ADHD, supporting the involvement of this gene in the susceptibility to this psychiatric disorder in adults.' A significant association was found with combined type ADHD after correction for multiple testing (P = 0.0019, OR = 1.82), and a strongly associated risk haplotype was identified (P = 5.1e-05, OR = 2.25).

description: Individuals carrying the low-expressing 's' allele of the 5-HTTLPR polymorphism are more vulnerable to depression following stressful life events than those carrying the higher-expressing 'l' allele, demonstrating a gene-by-environment interaction
original_authors: Avshalom Caspi; Karen Sugden; Terrie E. Moffitt; Alan Taylor; Ian W. Craig; HonaLee Harrington; Joseph McClay; Jonathan Mill; Judy Martin; Antony Braithwaite; Richie Poulton
original_title: Influence of life stress on depression: moderation by a polymorphism in the 5-HTT gene
replication_authors: Muller JM; Morelli E.; Ansorge M.; Gingrich JA
replication_title: Serotonin transporter deficient mice are vulnerable to escape deficits following inescapable shocks
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to test the Caspi et al. (2003) gene-by-environment interaction in a mouse model, and confirmed the hypothesis: 'Confirming a gene by environment interaction, we found that stress increases escape latencies in a gene-dose dependent manner (5-htt−/− > 5-htt+/− > 5-htt+/+), whereas there were no differences among the genotypes in the unstressed condition.' The replication used a fundamentally different paradigm (mouse genetics + inescapable shock behavior rather than human epidemiological study).

description: Affective processes in couples' newlywed interactions (including men's rejection of influence, men's de-escalation of partner's negative affect, women's negative start-up, and negative/positive affect composites) predict relationship stability and satisfaction 6 years later
original_authors: John M. Gottman; James Coan; Sybil Carrere; Catherine Swanson
original_title: Predicting marital happiness and stability from newlywed interactions
original_journal: Journal of Marriage and the Family
replication_authors: Hyoun K. Kim; Deborah M. Capaldi; Lynn Crosby
replication_title: Generalizability of Gottman and Colleagues’ Affective Process Models of Couples’ Relationship Outcomes
explanation: The abstract explicitly states 'The major findings of Gottman et al. failed to replicate,' and the Discussion confirms: 'One of the major findings of the current study is the failure to provide consistent evidence that [the affective process models hold].' The same paradigm (SPAFF coding, problem-solving interaction) was used but with a community at-risk sample rather than the original's newlywed middle-class sample.

description: Neutral pictures paired with genital vibrostimulation (unconditional stimulus) during an acquisition phase produce conditioned genital arousal responses (higher vaginal pulse amplitude to CS+ than CS-) during extinction in women
original_authors: Stephanie Both; Ellen Laan; Mark Spiering; Tove Nilsson; Sanne Oomens; Walter Everaerd
original_title: Appetitive and aversive classical conditioning of female sexual response
replication_authors: Stephanie Both; Marieke Brauer; Ellen Laan
replication_title: Classical Conditioning of Sexual Response in Women: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion: 'This replication of our previous study confirms the effectiveness of our conditioning procedure.' The replication successfully observed conditioned genital arousal (VPA higher for CS+ than CS- during extinction, F(1,31)=9.51, p<0.005), consistent with the original study's findings.

description: Physicians perceive distinct incentives for collaborating with nurse practitioners, ranked in order: accessibility to health care, physician satisfaction, economic incentives, and quality of care, with significant differences between all four incentive groups
original_authors: John E. Bezjak
original_title: Physician-perceived incentives for association with nurse practitioners
original_journal: Nurse Practitioner: American Journal of Primary Health Care
replication_authors: Alice Running; Lisa Hoffman; Victoria Mercer
replication_title: Physician perceptions of nurse practitioners: A replication study
replication_journal: Journal of the American Academy of Nurse Practitioners
explanation: The replication used the same instrument and analysis procedures as the original. Rankings were broadly consistent (accessibility ranked highest), but while the original found significant differences between all four incentive groups, the replication found that accessibility and quality of care collapsed into one group, and physician satisfaction and economic incentives collapsed into another — the abstract notes 'the original study demonstrated a much clearer distinction among the four groups of incentives.'

description: The 'Reducing the Risk' sexuality education curriculum delays initiation of sexual intercourse, increases contraceptive use among sexually active students, and improves parent-child communication about sexual issues among secondary school students
original_authors: Douglas Kirby; Richard P. Barth; Nancy Leland; Joyce V. Fetro
original_title: Reducing the risk: a new curriculum to prevent sexual risk-taking
replication_authors: Betty M. Hubbard; Mark L. Giese; Jacquie Rainey
replication_title: A Replication Study of Reducing the Risk, a Theory‐Based Sexuality Curriculum for Adolescents
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a replication study and conclude: 'Results suggest the curriculum produced several programmatically and statistically significant effects. Many effects were consistent with previous research.' The main findings — delay in initiating intercourse and increased STD/pregnancy prevention use — were successfully replicated in a new southern, rural setting (Arkansas).

description: Rural nurse practitioners in Minnesota perceive significant barriers to practice, including lack of public knowledge of NP roles, peer network deficits, physician resistance, and insurance reimbursement problems, and rate the overall rural practice climate as somewhat restrictive
original_authors: Linda L. Lindeke; Theresa R. Bly; Rachel A. Wilcox
original_title: Perceived barriers to rural nurse practitioner practice
replication_authors: Linda Lindeke; Angela Jukkala; Mary Tanner
replication_title: Perceived Barriers to Nurse Practitioner Practice in Rural Settings
explanation: The 2001 replication found mixed results compared to the 1996 survey: some barriers persisted (public knowledge of NP role) while others changed significantly (lack of peer network decreased, p < .01; physician resistance and insurance reimbursement problems dropped from top 5). New barriers (low salary, limited space) emerged. The practice climate restrictiveness score remained essentially unchanged (3.64 in 1996 vs. 3.65 in 2001, no significant difference by Student's t test), representing a partial replication with meaningful shifts in specific barrier rankings.

description: Couple therapy as practiced in German and Austrian marital counseling agencies significantly alleviates relationship distress (as measured by the Global Distress Scale) and individual depression (as measured by the CES-D) in real-world effectiveness settings
original_authors: Kurt Hahlweg; Notker Klann
original_title: The effectiveness of marital counseling in Germany: A contribution to health services research
replication_authors: Notker Klann; Kurt Hahlweg; Donald H. Baucom; Christine Kroeger
replication_title: The Effectiveness of couple therapy in Germany: A Replication Study
replication_journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to 'replicate the Hahlweg and Klann (1997) findings, following almost identical procedures in the same German marriage counseling settings.' The Discussion concludes: 'What is striking is that the findings are remarkably consistent across the two effectiveness investigations when considering all three areas,' with no statistically significant differences in effect sizes between the two studies.

description: The Brinemark osseointegrated titanium implant system for rehabilitation of the edentulous mandible achieves high long-term fixture survival rates with minimal marginal bone loss after the initial adaptation period
original_authors: Adell R.; Lekholm U.; Rockler B.; Brånemark PI
original_title: A 15 year study of osseointegrated implants in the treatment of the edentulous jaw
replication_authors: Henry PJ; Adler EA; Wall CD
replication_title: Osseointegrated dental implants: 2 year follow‐up replication study*
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'These results replicate and endorse the validity of the Brinemark reports.' All 15 patients successfully wore their prostheses at the 2-year follow-up with no fixture loss (vs. 9-10% loss reported in Brinemark's work), and 1.5 mm marginal bone loss consistent with Brinemark's data.

description: Disturbed adolescents perceive significantly lower family satisfaction and family effectiveness compared to their normal siblings and normal control children
original_authors: Novak, Arthur L.; van der Veen, Ferdinand
original_title: Family concepts and emotional disturbance in the families of disturbed adolescents with normal siblings
replication_authors: Ferdinand van der Veen; Arthur L. Novak
replication_title: The family concept of the disturbed child: A replication study.
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We may conclude, therefore, that the findings for the hypotheses replicate the results of the 1970 study.' Both hypotheses were confirmed — disturbed children showed lower family satisfaction and effectiveness than siblings and controls, while siblings and controls did not differ from each other.

description: People with psychosis construe their voices as omnipotent and omniscient, with affective and behavioural responses (engagement with benevolent, resistance to malevolent voices) closely corresponding to beliefs about the voices' malevolence or benevolence
original_authors: Chadwick, P.; Birchwood, M.
original_title: The omnipotence of voices: A cognitive approach to auditory hallucinations
replication_authors: Helen Close; Philippa Garety
replication_title: Cognitive assessment of voices: Further developments in understanding the emotional impact of voices
explanation: The authors found 'both similarities and differences' compared to the original study. The replication sample was significantly less likely to believe in voices' omnipotence and omniscience, and showed far fewer positive affective responses to benevolent voices, but showed similar behavioural response patterns and similarly high negative affect to malevolent voices. The Discussion explicitly frames this as a mixed picture requiring further investigation.

description: Subjects high on the lie scale of the Maudsley Personality Inventory tend to be less susceptible to hypnosis, and the most susceptible subjects predominate in the stable extravert and neurotic introvert personality quadrants
original_authors: Furneaux WD; Gibson HB
original_title: The Maudsley Personality Inventory as a predictor of susceptibility to hypnosis
original_journal: International Journal of Clinical and Experimental Hypnosis
replication_authors: Gibson HB; Curran JD
replication_title: HYPNOTIC SUSCEPTIBILITY AND PERSONALITY: A REPLICATION STUDY
explanation: The authors explicitly state they designed the study to replicate the Maudsley study and conclude: 'At the level of empirical findings the present investigation offers support for the findings of the Maudsley study rather than the Stanford study.' The key prediction from the Maudsley study — that susceptible subjects predominate in the SE and NI quadrants — was confirmed.

description: Poor mental health is associated with simplified (assembly-line) jobs, but only for employees who perceive low skill utilization and simultaneously report high levels of cognitive failure (a three-way ordinal interaction)
original_authors: Chris Clegg; Toby Wall; Nigel KEMP
original_title: Women on the assembly-line: A comparison of main and interactive explanations of job satisfaction, absence and mental health
replication_authors: Chris Clegg; Toby Wall
replication_title: The relationship between simplified jobs and mental health: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe a 'constructive replication' of Clegg, Wall & Kemp (1987) and conclude 'we can however claim that these findings replicate our earlier study.' The predicted three-way ordinal interaction was fully confirmed in sample 2 (p < .002) and the pattern was consistent in sample 1 despite some additional main effects, using two new samples in a different factory setting.

description: Decreases in desirable events and increases in undesirable events occur in the three- to five-day period preceding the onset of upper respiratory illness episodes
original_authors: Arthur A. Stone; Bruce R. Reed; John M. Neale
original_title: Changes in daily event frequency precede episodes of physical symptoms
replication_authors: Arthur A. Stone; Laura S. Porter; John M. Neale
replication_title: Daily events and mood prior to the onset of respiratory illness episodes: A non‐replication of the 3–5 day ‘desirability dip’
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Despite the similarity of this study to those of Stone et al. (1987), Evans et al. (1988) and Evans & Edgerton (1991), we were unable to replicate the previous results.' No significant effects were found in any of the repeated measures ANOVAs using Stone et al.'s methodology (e.g., desirable events F(1,22) = .50, p = .49; undesirable events F(1,22) = .25, p = .62).

description: Desirable events are less frequent than expected in the four-day period preceding illness onset, replicating the lagged relationship between daily life events and upper respiratory illness episodes
original_authors: Philip D. Evans; Marian K. Pitts; Kath Smith
original_title: Minor infection, minor life events and the four day desirability dip
replication_authors: Arthur A. Stone; Laura S. Porter; John M. Neale
replication_title: Daily events and mood prior to the onset of respiratory illness episodes: A non‐replication of the 3–5 day ‘desirability dip’
explanation: The authors adopted Evans et al.'s (1988) analytic method and found no significant results: 'None of the interactions were significant' and 'Repeated measures ANOVA was used... No significant results were obtained.' The discussion explicitly states inability to replicate previous findings.

description: Decreases in desirable events and increases in angry, tensed up, and sceptical mood during the four-day period preceding cold episode onsets relative to control days
original_authors: Philip D. Evans; Nick Edgerton
original_title: Life events and mood as predictors of the common cold
replication_authors: Arthur A. Stone; Laura S. Porter; John M. Neale
replication_title: Daily events and mood prior to the onset of respiratory illness episodes: A non‐replication of the 3–5 day ‘desirability dip’
explanation: Using Evans & Edgerton's (1991) analytic approach (comparing days -7 to -5 versus days -4 to -1 adjusted for control levels), no significant differences were found for mood or events (e.g., negative affect F(1,40) = .05, p = .82). The authors conclude they 'were unable to replicate the previous results.'

description: Using an in situ repeated-measures methodology, traffic congestion, time urgency, perceived control, and trait driver stress predict state driver stress during highway commutes, with no gender differences in state driver stress
original_authors: Dwight A. Hennessy; David L. Wiesenthal
original_title: The relationship between traffic congestion, driver stress and direct versus indirect coping behaviours
replication_authors: Christine M. Wickens; David L. Wiesenthal; James E. W. Roseborough
replication_title: In Situ Methodology for Studying State Driver Stress: A Between‐Subjects Design Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Results of the current study replicated those of the previous research, demonstrating the strength and utility of the in situ methodology regardless of the research design.' All five hypotheses (time urgency, perceived control, congestion, trait stress, and no gender difference) were confirmed.

description: Children with an intellectual disability who lack 'key skills' (as measured by the Essential Eight questionnaire) are at substantially higher risk of displaying challenging behaviour, with those scoring lowest having a 93% probability of challenging behaviour and those with all skills present having only a 13% probability
original_authors: Armstrong, H.; Denne, L.; Bailey, T.
original_title: The role of key skills as a risk marker for the development of challenging behaviour in children and young people who have an intellectual disability
original_journal: International Journal of Positive Behavioural Support
replication_authors: Heather Armstrong; Claire McDowell; Gerard Leavey; Louise D. Denne
replication_title: ‘Key skills’ building in schools as a possible approach to reducing and preventing challenging behaviour
replication_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our findings are similar. We found that pupils with the lowest skill level on the E8 (a score of 1 on at least one skill) were most likely to have challenging behaviour (94%), while those with the highest scores (a score of 4 on all the skills) were least likely (6%). Armstrong et al. (2021) found these were 93% and 13%, respectively. This adds additional support to the hypothesis that the lack of these 'key skills' may be an important risk marker for the development of challenging behaviour.'

description: The Questionnaire Epistemic Trust (QET) has a 4-factor structure (Hypervigilance, Curiosity/Openness, Expectation of help, Openness to help) with good to excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's alphas 0.80–0.90) in community and clinical populations
original_authors: Saskia Knapen; Wilma E. Swildens; Wendy Mensink; Adriaan Hoogendoorn; Joost Hutsebaut; Aartjan T. F. Beekman
original_title: The development and psychometric evaluation of the questionnaire epistemic trust (QET): a self-report assessment of epistemic trust
replication_authors: Suzanne D. M. Derks; Annelies de Bildt; Veerle M. M. Andries; Saskia Knapen; Paula S. Sterkenburg
replication_title: Psychometric Properties of the Questionnaire Epistemic Trust in People With Mild to Moderate Intellectual Disabilities or Borderline Intellectual Functioning
replication_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Contrary to our expectations, the underlying structure of the original QET was not fully replicated' — the 4-factor structure was replicated (with four items excluded), but the Hypervigilance subscale showed poor internal consistency (α=0.58–0.61 vs. original α=0.88), and test-retest reliability for that subscale was poor (ICC=0.461–0.504), while the other three subscales showed acceptable to good reliability approaching original levels.

description: NRG1 SNPs rs16879552 and rs7835688 are significantly associated with susceptibility to Hirschsprung's disease
original_authors: Maria-Mercè Garcia-Barcelo; Clara Sze-Man Tang; Elly Sau-Wai Ngan; Vincent Chi-Hang Lui; Yan Chen; Man-Ting So; Thomas Yuk-yu Leon; Xiao-ping Miao; Cathy Ka-yee Shum; Feng-qin Liu; Ming-yiu Yeung; Zhen-wei Yuan; Wei-hong Guo; Lei Liu; Xiao-bing Sun; Liu-ming Huang; Jin-fa Tou; You-Qiang Song; Danny Chan; Kenneth M. C. Cheung; Kenneth Kak-Yuen Wong; Stacey S. Cherny; Pak-Chung Sham; Paul Kwong-Hang Tam

replication_authors: Yan Zhang; Xiaoli Xie; Jixiao Zeng; Qiang Wu; Ruizhong Zhang; Deli Zhu; Huimin Xia
replication_title: Association of NRG1 and AUTS2 genetic polymorphisms with Hirschsprung disease in a South Chinese population
replication_journal: Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The association of NRG1 was further replicated in our study.' Both SNPs rs16879552 (P = 1.05E-04, OR = 1.23) and rs7835688 (P = 1.19E-07, OR = 1.43) were significantly associated in the same direction as the original GWAS, confirming the original findings.

original_authors: Maria-Mercè Garcia-Barcelo; Clara Sze-Man Tang; Elly Sau-Wai Ngan; Vincent Chi-Hang Lui; Yan Chen; Man-Ting So; Thomas Yuk-yu Leon; Xiao-ping Miao; Cathy Ka-yee Shum; Feng-qin Liu; Ming-yiu Yeung; Zhen-wei Yuan; Wei-hong Guo; Lei Liu; Xiao-bing Sun; Liu-ming Huang; Jin-fa Tou; You-Qiang Song; Danny Chan; Kenneth M. original_title: Genome-wide association study identifies NRG1 as a susceptibility locus for Hirschsprung's disease
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

replication_title: Association of NRG1 and AUTS2 genetic polymorphisms with Hirschsprung disease in a South Chinese population
replication_journal: Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We failed to further support the individual association of AUTS2 with disease.' The SNP rs7785360 failed to reach significance (P = 0.149, OR = 1.14), with only a marginal recessive model effect (P = 0.089).

description: A variant in the glycosyltransferase gene GLT6D1 (rs1537415) is associated with increased susceptibility to aggressive periodontitis in a European (German/Dutch) population
original_authors: Arne S. Schaefer; Gesa M. Richter; Michael Nothnagel; Thomas Manke; Henrik Dommisch; Gunnar Jacobs; Alexander Arlt; Philip Rosenstiel; Barbara Noack; Birte Groessner-Schreiber; Søren Jepsen; Bruno G. Loos; Stefan Schreiber
