replication_authors: Nada T. Hashim; Gerard J. Linden; Muntasir E. Ibrahim; Bakri G. Gismalla; Fionnuala T. Lundy; Francis J. Hughes; Ikhlas A. El Karim
replication_title: Replication of the association of <scp>GLT</scp>6<scp>D</scp>1 with aggressive periodontitis in a <scp>S</scp>udanese population
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The finding independently replicated the identification of rs1537415 as a candidate genetic variant in one of the few GWAS of AgP (Schaefer et al. 2010) reported to date.' The replication found OR=1.56 (95% CI 1.15-2.16, p=0.0042; p=0.013 after Bonferroni correction) in a Sudanese population, compared to the original OR=1.59 (95% CI 1.36-1.86).

description: Prenatal maternal depressive symptoms moderate the association between postnatal maternal depressive symptoms and child emotional problems in a sex-dependent fashion, such that girls (but not boys) show greater vulnerability to postnatal depression when prenatal depression was low (mismatch effect)
original_authors: Jonathan Hill; Andrew Pickles; Nicola Wright; John P. Quinn; Chris Murgatroyd; Helen Sharp
original_title: Mismatched prenatal and postnatal maternal depressive symptoms and child behaviours: A sex-dependent role for NR3C1 DNA methylation in the Wirral Child Health and Development Study
replication_authors: Elizabeth C. Braithwaite; Andrew Pickles; Nicola Wright; Helen Sharp; Jonathan Hill
replication_title: Sex differences in foetal origins of child emotional symptoms: a test of evolutionary hypotheses in a large, general population cohort
replication_journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated the previous finding that the association between postnatal maternal depressive symptoms and child emotional symptoms is moderated by the level of prenatal depressive symptoms in a sex-dependent manner.' The three-way interaction was statistically significant in the replication (coeff = .042, 95% CI = 0.015 to 0.068, p = .002), consistent with the original WCHADS findings. However, the specific pattern differed: in ALSPAC the sex difference was driven mainly by a protective effect of low prenatal depression in boys, while in WCHADS it arose from greater vulnerability of girls.

description: A multivariable demographic risk calculator using childhood clinical and demographic variables (sex, IQ, maltreatment, disruptive disorder, ADHD symptoms, family social class, mother's depression, single-parent family) accurately predicts ADHD diagnosis in young adulthood
original_authors: Caye A.; Agnew-Blais J.; Arseneault L.; Gonçalves H.; Kieling C.; Langley K.; Menezes AMB; Moffitt TE; Passos IC; Rocha TB; Sibley MH; Swanson JM; Thapar A.; Wehrmeister F.; Rohde LA
original_title: A risk calculator to predict adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: generation and external validation in three birth cohorts and one clinical sample
replication_authors: Cezar H. Lorenzi; Douglas Teixeira Leffa; Rodrigo Bressan; Sintia Belangero; Ary Gadelha; Marcos L. Santoro; Giovanni A. Salum; Luis Augusto Rohde; Arthur Caye
replication_title:
Replication of a predictive model for youth
                    <scp>ADHD</scp>
                    in an independent sample from a developing country
replication_journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
explanation: The authors successfully validated the original ADHD predictive model in a new Brazilian community cohort (BHRCS), obtaining an AUC of 0.76 (95% CI 0.70–0.82), which is comparable to the external validation AUCs of 0.75 and 0.76 achieved in the original study's other external samples. The Discussion concludes: 'we found a good predictive performance (AUC of .75) of a previously developed predictive model for youth in a completely diverse cultural context, thus expanding its external validity.'

description: Clinicians learning Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFT) report positive professional and personal outcomes, including more effective therapy and improved personal relationships, with difficulty transitioning to the model being a notable theme
original_authors: Jonathan G. Sandberg; Andrea Knestel
original_title: The experience of learning emotionally focused couples therapy
original_journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy
replication_authors: Jonathan G. Sandberg; Martiño Rodríguez‐González; Sergio Pereyra; Ragan Lybbert; Leo Perez; Kwin Willis
replication_title: The Experience of Learning <scp>EFT</scp> in Spanish‐speaking Countries: A Multi‐National Replication Study
replication_journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy
explanation: The authors explicitly designed the study as a replication of Sandberg and Knestel (2011) using the same translated survey, finding that 'a comparison of results across the two studies revealed more similarities than differences.' Core themes (positive professional and personal change from EFT training) replicated, with notable cultural variations (Spanish-speaking therapists showed greater appreciation for emotional focus and less reported difficulty learning the model).

description: Genetic polymorphisms (SNPs in TAC1, FOXC1, ITGA1, ACYP2, DLEU7, BTG4, CAMK2N1, and FARS2 gene loci) are associated with severe chronic oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neurotoxicity in colon cancer patients
original_authors: Hong-Hee Won; Jeeyun Lee; Joon Oh Park; Young Suk Park; Ho Yeong Lim; Won Ki Kang; Jong-Won Kim; Soo‐Youn Lee; Se Hoon Park
original_title: Polymorphic markers associated with severe oxaliplatin-induced, chronic peripheral neuropathy in colon cancer patients
replication_authors: Salvatore Terrazzino; Andreas A. Argyriou; Sarah Cargnin; Anna G. Antonacopoulou; Chiara Briani; Jordi Bruna; Roser Velasco; Paola Alberti; Marta Campagnolo; Sara Lonardi; Diego Cortinovis; Marina Cazzaniga; Cristina Santos; Haralabos P. Kalofonos; Pier Luigi Canonico; Armando A. Genazzani; Guido Cavaletti
replication_title: Genetic determinants of chronic oxaliplatin‐induced peripheral neurotoxicity: a genome‐wide study replication and meta‐analysis
replication_journal: Journal of the Peripheral Nervous System
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we failed to confirm the role of the genetic variants previously identified by a GWAS study as determinants of chronic OXAIPN when assessed by NCI-CTC criteria (Won et al., 2012).' None of the 8 polymorphisms investigated was associated with grade ≥2 chronic OXAIPN using the same NCI-CTC criteria as the original GWAS.

description: Nurses hold less positive attitudes and emotions toward caring for adults with intellectual disability versus physical disability, with mainstream nurses holding less positive attitudes than specialist intellectual disability nurses, and nurses' beliefs about quality of life predicting attitudes toward caring for adults with intellectual disability
original_authors: Melissa L. Desroches; Kristen A. Sethares; Carol Curtin; Joohyun Chung
original_title: Nurses' attitudes and emotions toward caring for adults with intellectual disabilities: Results of a cross-sectional, correlational-predictive research study
original_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities
replication_authors: Melissa L. Desroches; Virginia A. Howie; Nathan J. Wilson; Peter Lewis
replication_title: Nurses’ attitudes and emotions toward caring for adults with intellectual disability: An international replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The purpose of this study was to replicate the study of Desroches et al. (2019) with an Australian sample' and conclude that 'this replication study produced consistent key findings across Australia and the USA,' with the main findings on attitude differences, emotion differences between specialist and mainstream nurses, and quality of life beliefs as a predictor all replicated.

description: The Gagging Problem Assessment (GPA) instrument is reliable and valid for estimating the severity of dental gagging and for distinguishing patients who suffer from dental gagging
original_authors: Van Linden van den Heuvell GF; Ter Pelkwijk BJ; Stegenga B.
original_title: Development of the Gagging Problem Assessment: a pilot study
replication_authors: Van Linden van den Heuvell GF; de Boer B.; Ter Pelkwijk BJ; Bildt MM; Stegenga B.
replication_title: Gagging Problem Assessment: a re‐evaluation
explanation: The replication found mixed results: the patient part (GPA-R-pa) showed adequate stability and distinguished gagging patients from controls, but the dentist part (GPA-R-de) had insufficient internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.66) and stability (ICC = 0.65). The authors state 'the GPA-R failed to meet our expectations' and that the dentist part results 'are in contrast with former results.'

description: Global sex differences in personality, measured multivariately using Mahalanobis' D on 15 primary 16PF factors in a demographically representative U.S. sample, are surprisingly large (D = 2.71), suggesting far greater male-female personality separation than previously assumed from univariate approaches
original_authors: Del Giudice, Marco; Booth, Tom; Irwing, Paul
original_title: The distance between Mars and Venus: Measuring global sex differences in personality
replication_authors: Tim Kaiser; Marco Del Giudice; Tom Booth
replication_title: Global sex differences in personality: Replication with an open online dataset
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'set out to replicate the analysis by Del Giudice and colleagues (2012)' using the same MG-CMSA methodology on an equivalent IPIP-based 16PF. They found a large global sex difference (D = 2.06), consistent in direction and pattern with the original (univariate correlation r = .95), supporting the original finding that global sex differences in personality are substantially larger than previously assumed, though 24% smaller in absolute magnitude, which the authors attribute to differences in sample and questionnaire version.

description: Short scales of subclinical psychopathy and everyday sadism show a jangle fallacy: their latent factors are almost perfectly correlated, their nomological networks are nearly identical, and core criteria of one construct are often more strongly related to the other construct's scale
original_authors: Christian Blötner; Andreas Mokros
original_title: The next distinction without a difference: do psychopathy and sadism scales assess the same construct?
replication_authors: Christian Blötner; Sandy S. Spormann; Miriam J. Hofmann; Andreas Mokros
replication_title: Measures of Subclinical Psychopathy and Everyday Sadism are Still Redundant: A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Blötner and Mokros (2023)
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'in line with the evidence from short scales by Blötner and Mokros (2023), we suggest that measures of (subclinical) psychopathy and everyday sadism reflect a jangle fallacy.' The latent psychopathy-sadism correlations (ρs ≥ 0.94) even exceeded those in the original study (ρ = 0.88), and nomological networks were similarly overlapping, confirming the main finding across long as well as short scales.

description: Hypocrites (who condemn wrongdoing then commit it) are evaluated more negatively than both liars (who deny wrongdoing then commit it) and control transgressors (who commit wrongdoing without prior comment), because hypocrites send false moral signals
original_authors: Jillian J. Jordan; Roseanna Sommers; Paul Bloom; David G. Rand
original_title: Why do we hate hypocrites? Evidence for a theory of false signaling
replication_authors: Xinyu Zhao; Eiichiro Watamura
replication_title: Cultural Generalizability of the False Signaling Theory: A Replication Study Using a Japanese Sample
explanation: The replication confirmed that Japanese participants evaluated hypocrites more negatively than transgressors (consistent with original), but unlike the original study, liars were evaluated as negatively as hypocrites, suggesting Japanese participants view lying as equally a false signal. Authors conclude results 'generally support the false signaling theory' but with cultural differences in the definition of false signals.

description: Hypocrites receive harsher moral evaluations than both honest hypocrites (who admit wrongdoing while condemning it) and control transgressors, because removal of the false signal (honest admission) mitigates negative evaluation
original_authors: Jillian J. Jordan; Roseanna Sommers; Paul Bloom; David G. Rand
original_title: Why do we hate hypocrites? Evidence for a theory of false signaling
replication_authors: Xinyu Zhao; Eiichiro Watamura
replication_title: Cultural Generalizability of the False Signaling Theory: A Replication Study Using a Japanese Sample
explanation: The key finding that hypocrites were evaluated more negatively than both transgressors and honest hypocrites was replicated. However, unlike the original study, Japanese participants also evaluated honest hypocrites significantly more positively than regular transgressors — a difference not found in the original. Authors report 'some results were the same as those of the original experiment' while noting others differed.

description: Frequent nightmare recallers produce more perseveration errors on a verbal fluency task than control participants, indicating executive inhibitory dysfunction, while not differing in overall verbal fluency
original_authors: Péter Simor; Péter Pajkossy; Klára Horváth; Róbert Bódizs
original_title: Impaired executive functions in subjects with frequent nightmares as reflected by performance in different neuropsychological tasks
replication_authors: Michelle Carr; Kadia Saint‐Onge; Cloé Blanchette‐Carrière; Tyna Paquette; Tore Nielsen
replication_title: Elevated perseveration errors on a verbal fluency task in frequent nightmare recallers: a replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The present results replicate this finding of increased perseveration errors on a VFT in frequent NM recallers compared to CTLs. In fact, our values constitute a clear—almost exact—replication of the Simor et al. (2012) results.' The replication found the same pattern: no group difference in fluency (P = 0.97) but significantly higher perseveration in the nightmare group (P = 0.03, d = 0.745), closely matching the original effect size (d = 0.790).

description: Dreaming about a virtual maze navigation task during a daytime nap strongly predicts subsequent performance improvements, suggesting that dream content reflects memory reactivation and consolidation during sleep
original_authors: Wamsley, Erin J.; Tucker, Matthew A.; Payne, Jessica D.; Benavides, Joseph A.; Stickgold, Robert
original_title: Dreaming of a learning task is associated with enhanced sleep-dependent memory consolidation
replication_authors: Erin J. Wamsley; Robert Stickgold
replication_title: Dreaming of a learning task is associated with enhanced memory consolidation: Replication in an overnight sleep study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'this observation exactly replicates the findings of our previously published nap study (Wamsley, Tucker, Payne, Benavides, et al., 2010), using the same criteria for direct task incorporation, the same learning task, and the same methods of assessing performance improvement.' Incorporators showed significantly greater overnight improvement in Completion Time (t15=2.38, p=0.03, d=1.16) and Distance Travelled (t15=2.27, p=0.04, d=1.10).

description: Linkage analysis of TFPI plasma levels identifies a locus on chromosome 2q as the highest genome-wide peak, implicating the chromosome 2q region in TFPI plasma level variability
original_authors: Almasy L.; Soria JM; Souto JC; Warren DM; Buil A.; Borrell M.; Muñoz X.; Sala N.; Lathrop M.; Fontcuberta J.; Blangero J.
original_title: A locus on chromosome 2 influences levels of tissue factor pathway inhibitor: results from the GAIT study
replication_authors: Dennis J.; Truong V.; Aïssi D.; Medina-Rivera A.; Blankenberg S.; Germain M.; Lemire M.; Antounians L.; Civelek M.; Schnabel R.; Wells P.; Wilson MD; Morange PE; Trégouët DA; Gagnon F.
replication_title: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in an intergenic chromosome 2q region associated with tissue factor pathway inhibitor plasma levels and venous thromboembolism
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated the finding of the chromosome 2q linkage to TFPI plasma levels originally reported in the GAIT Study.' The replication achieved a LOD score of 3.06 in the F5L Family Study, exceeding the threshold for candidate region significance, and further identified rs62187992 as a putative causal SNP contributing to the linkage peak.

description: Repetition of multiword units in reading-while-listening input has a large positive effect on the incidental learning of collocations, with 15 repetitions yielding the highest learning gains among university students
original_authors: Webb, S.; Newton, J.; Chang, A.
original_title: Incidental learning of collocation
replication_authors: Elke Peters; Eva Puimège; Paweł Szudarski
replication_title: Repetition and Incidental Learning of Multiword Units: A Conceptual Multisite Replication Study of Webb, Newton, and Chang (2013)
explanation: The authors confirmed a positive effect of repetition on incidental learning of MWUs (consistent with the original), but found smaller learning gains and different thresholds: 'Webb et al.'s effect of repetition could be replicated in the present study, even though the effect was smaller and the number of repetitions needed was different.' The large effect found in the original (partial eta squared = .28; Cohen's d = 4.15 for 15 repetitions) was not corroborated, and significant differences were only found between 1 exposure and 5, 10, or 15 exposures, not between the higher repetition conditions.

description: Prompts facilitate acquisition of rule-based regular English past tense forms more than recasts, while both recasts and prompts equally facilitate learning of exemplar-based irregular past tense forms in a Chinese EFL university context
original_authors: Yingli Yang; Roy Lyster
original_title: Effects of form-focused practice and feedback on Chinese EFL learners' acquisition of regular and irregular past tense forms
replication_authors: Nadia Mifka‐Profozic; Jennifer Behney; Susan M. Gass; Marijana Macis; Gaia Chiuchiù; Giulia Bovolenta
replication_title: Effects of Form‐Focused Practice and Feedback: A Multisite Replication Study of Yang and Lyster (2010)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the findings from our study did not fully align with the YL results' and found no group effect for either written or oral data at either site: 'We found no effect of group and no evidence of the superiority of either prompts or recasts in either written or oral data in either Bosnia or Italy.' The key original finding — that prompts outperform recasts for regular verbs — was not replicated.

description: ERP paradigms (LDT, SEMREL, GJT) can elicit N400, P600, and anterior negativities as indices of form-, meaning-, and use-related L2 vocabulary knowledge in laboratory and longitudinal settings
original_authors: Bert Vandenberghe; Maribel Montero Perez; Bert Reynvoet; Piet Desmet
original_title: The role of event-related potentials (ERPs) as sensitive measures in L2 vocabulary acquisition research
original_journal: Journal of the European Second Language Association
replication_authors: Bert Vandenberghe; Maribel Montero Perez; Bert Reynvoet; Piet Desmet
replication_title: Second Language Vocabulary Learning through Ecologically Valid Classroom Practice Can Be Indexed by Event‐Related Potentials (ERPs). A Conceptual Replication Study
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Keeping confidence at medium. The authors explicitly call this a 'conceptual replication study' and conclude success. N400 was elicited for LDT (form) and SEMREL (meaning), and P600 was elicited for GJT (use) — all in a classroom setting rather than a laboratory. However, all three components showed distributional and/or latency deviations from canonical patterns (more anterior N400 and P600, delayed N400 at 400-600ms instead of 300-500ms), and the anterior negativity (AN) component for target words in GJT did not reach significance. The authors interpret these deviations as consistent with 'newly established or emerging L2 word knowledge' citing prior literature, which is a reasonable but interpretive framing. The result is classified as 'success' because the authors explicitly conclude replication, but confidence remains medium because the non-significant AN and distributional shifts mean the replication is partial rather than complete.

description: Intermittent fasting (8 hours per day, 3 days per week) improves starvation resistance in Canton-S x w118 F1 Drosophila melanogaster
original_authors: Sharon Zhang; Eric Ratliff; Brandon Molina; Nadja El-Mecharrafie; Jessica Mastroianni; Roxanne Kotzebue; Madhulika Achal; Ruth Mauntz; Arysa Gonzalez; Ayeh Barekat; William Bray; Andrew Macias; Daniel Daugherty; Greg Harris; Robert Edwards; Kim Finley
original_title: Aging and intermittent fasting impact on transcriptional regulation and physiological responses of adult Drosophila neuronal and muscle tissues
replication_authors: Benedict A. Lenhart; Ayesha Ahsan; Margaret McHaty; Alan O. Bergland
replication_title: Improvement of starvation resistance via periodic fasting is genetically variable in Drosophila melanogaster
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated a previously published fasting assay described in Zhang et al. 2018' and confirm the replication in the Discussion: 'We replicated previously reported results (Zhang et al. 2018) of increased starvation resistance following periodic fasting of adult flies.' Male fasted flies showed significantly higher starvation resistance than controls (log rank test, χ²=5.21, df=1, p=0.02), and females showed even stronger improvement (χ²=23.51, df=1, p=1.2e-06).

description: Heart rate during the encoding phase of intrusive film sequences is lower than during non-intrusive sequences when viewing a trauma film
original_authors: Emily A. Holmes; Chris R. Brewin; Richard G. Hennessy
original_title: Trauma films, information processing, and intrusive memory development
replication_authors: Chia‐Ying Chou; Roberto La Marca; Andrew Steptoe; Chris R. Brewin
replication_title: Heart rate, startle response, and intrusive trauma memories
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our data provide the first replication of an important previous finding (Holmes et al., 2004)—HR during the encoding phase of the intrusive film sequences is lower than it is during the nonintrusive sequences.' The replication used the same trauma film paradigm with an added startle probe at the start.

description: Overall perifilm heart rate change (relative to baseline) predicts the frequency of intrusive memories following trauma film viewing
original_authors: Emily A. Holmes; Chris R. Brewin; Richard G. Hennessy
original_title: Trauma films, information processing, and intrusive memory development
replication_authors: Chia‐Ying Chou; Roberto La Marca; Andrew Steptoe; Chris R. Brewin
replication_title: Heart rate, startle response, and intrusive trauma memories
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The current study failed to replicate Holmes et al.'s (2004) finding of a significant relationship between overall perifilm HR change and intrusion frequency.' The overall perifilm HR change did not show any significant correlations with memory measures.

description: Error-related negativity (ERN) recorded during different experimental paradigms (flanker, Stroop, Go/no-go tasks) shows convergent and divergent validity, with ERNs across tasks correlating with each other more than with other ERPs recorded during the same task
original_authors: Anja Riesel; Anna Weinberg; Tanja Endrass; Alexandria Meyer; Greg Hajcak
original_title: The ERN is the ERN is the ERN? Convergent validity of error-related brain activity across different tasks
replication_authors: Peter E. Clayson; Julia B. Mcdonald; Bohyun Park; Amanda Holbrook; Scott A. Baldwin; Anja Riesel; Michael J. Larson
replication_title:
Registered replication report of the construct validity of the error‐related negativity (
                    <scp>ERN</scp>
                    ): A multi‐site study of task‐specific
                    <scp>ERN</scp>
                    correlations with internalizing and externalizing symptoms
explanation: The authors report that convergent and divergent validity of error-trial ERN, Pe, and ∆Pe were successfully replicated, but convergent validity of ∆ERN was not replicated: 'The present registered report directly replicated the findings of convergent and divergent validity of ERN, Pe, and ∆Pe recorded during the flanker, Stroop, and Go/no-go tasks, but failed to replicate convergent validity of ∆ERN.' Because not all pre-specified criteria were met, the overall replication is classified as inconclusive.

description: Deceptive (vs. truthful) responding to target words is accompanied by increased MFN/N2 (conflict monitoring) and increased LPC/P3b (sustained attention) ERP components, and behavioral costs such as slower reaction times and more errors
original_authors: Henning Gibbons; Robert Schnuerch; Christina Wittinghofer; Anne‐Simone Armbrecht; Jutta Stahl
original_title: Detection of deception: Event-related potential markers of attention and cognitive control during intentional false responses
replication_authors: Robert Schnuerch; Jonas Schmuck; Henning Gibbons
replication_title: Cortical oscillations and event‐related brain potentials during the preparation and execution of deceptive behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly replicated the LPC effect (increased sustained attention for lie vs. truth targets), confirming 'an enhanced posterior positivity such as the LPC (Gibbons et al., 2018).' However, the predicted MFN/conflict monitoring component was not observed at frontal sites; instead a posterior N400 was found, which the authors attributed to the novel cue-based paradigm design. Behavioral effects (RT, errors) were robustly replicated. The authors describe the overall result as a replication-and-extension, but the failure to observe the MFN (a key predicted component) makes this inconclusive.

description: Children with ADHD make more omission errors (but not more commission errors) than typically developing children on a response time computer task
original_authors: Stuart J. Johnstone; Daniel Galletta
original_title: Event-rate effects in the flanker task: ERPs and task performance in children with and without AD/HD
replication_authors: Katherine E. Christensen; Rebecca A. Lundwall
replication_title: Errors on a computer task and subclinical symptoms of attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (<scp>ADHD</scp>)
explanation: Study 1 explicitly failed to replicate: 'Our attempt to replicate the study conducted by Johnstone and Galletta (2013) did not demonstrate a significant difference in the overall frequency of commission or omission errors based on ADHD symptoms.' The key difference is using a dimensional (continuous) measure of ADHD symptoms in a general population rather than a categorical ADHD-diagnosed vs. control design, extending the context of the original study.

description: Children with ADHD show less post-error RT slowing (reduced error monitoring) compared to typically developing children on a response time computer task
original_authors: Keri Shiels; Leanne Tamm; Jeffery N. Epstein
original_title: Deficient post-error slowing in children with ADHD is limited to the inattentive subtype
original_journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
replication_authors: Katherine E. Christensen; Rebecca A. Lundwall
replication_title: Errors on a computer task and subclinical symptoms of attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (<scp>ADHD</scp>)
explanation: Study 2 explicitly succeeded: 'We successfully replicated the study by Shiels et al. (2012). As ADHD symptoms increased, RT slowing following an error became less likely.' The authors extended the finding to a general population using a dimensional measure of ADHD symptoms rather than a categorical diagnosis.

description: Higher levels of conscientiousness are positively associated with more positive attitudes toward vaccination (confidence in vaccine safety)
original_authors: Carol H.J. Lee; Isabelle M. Duck; Chris G. Sibley
original_title: Personality and demographic correlates of New Zealanders' confidence in the safety of childhood vaccinations
replication_authors: Heng Li
replication_title: To vaccinate or not: The relationship between conscientiousness and individual attitudes toward vaccination in real‐life contexts
explanation: Independent review confirms result classification. The abstract states Study 1 'fully replicated prior findings' and the General Discussion explicitly says 'Such findings replicated previous research showing that high degrees of self-reported conscientiousness are demonstrably related to positive perceptions toward vaccination in non-WEIRD populations.' The effect is clear and significant (r = 0.46, 95% CI [0.3614, 0.5484], p < 0.001). Authors are unambiguous that this is a successful replication. Classified as 'close extension' because the replication used a Chinese student sample (vs. New Zealand adults in Lee et al. 2017) and examined COVID-19 vaccination intention (vs. childhood vaccine confidence), while testing the same core relationship between conscientiousness and pro-vaccination attitudes. Lee et al. (2017) is the primary original study cited in the introduction as establishing the Big Five–vaccination link.

description: Anhedonia is associated with both suicide risk and past suicide attempts in a student sample, even when controlling for other depressive symptoms
original_authors: Winer ES; Drapeau CW; Veilleux JC; Nadorff MR
original_title: The association between anhedonia, suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts in a large student sample
replication_authors: Ahmad Daghigh; Vahid Daghigh; Mohsen Niazi; Michael R. Nadorff

explanation: Reviewer assessment: The direct replication in an independent European Caucasian population found NO evidence of association for any of the three CD247 SNPs (rs1052237, rs2056626, rs864537) with RA or anti-CCP status — a clear failure at the replication level. However, a subsequent meta-analysis combining the replication data with previously published GWAS data for rs864537 yielded genome-wide significant association with anti-CCP+ RA (OR 0.90, p=2.1e-10). The authors frame their conclusion positively, stating they 'described for first time at GWAS-level the association of this CD247 variant and RA risk.' This creates genuine ambiguity: the independent replication failed, but the pooled meta-analysis succeeded. 'Inconclusive' is appropriate because the replication itself did not support the original finding, yet the combined evidence (including the original data) did. Note: the effect size and p-value reported below are from the META-ANALYSIS, not from the replication cohort alone (the replication alone showed null results). Confidence remains medium due to this inherent ambiguity. Original title corrected from an incorrect title to the actual Zhernakova et al. 2011 PLoS Genet paper on RA/CeD GWAS meta-analysis.

description: mtDNA haplogroups (particularly haplogroup T and cluster TJ) significantly influence radiographic progression of knee osteoarthritis in patients from the OAI (Osteoarthritis Initiative) cohort, with haplogroup T carriers showing lower risk of K&L grade progression

replication_authors: Angel Soto-Hermida; M. Fernández-Moreno; M.E. Vázquez-Mosquera; E. Cortés-Pereira; S. Relaño-Fernández; Juan Fernández‐Tajes; N. Oreiro-Villar; C. Fernández-López; Francisco J. Blanco; Ignacio Rego-Pérez
replication_title: THU0009 Role of the Mtdna Haplogroups on the Radiographic Progression of Knee Osteoarthritis in Patients of the Check Cohort: A Replication Study of the OAI Data
explanation: Reviewer note: This is a self-replication — the same research group validates their own prior OAI findings (Soto-Hermida et al., PLOS ONE 2014) in the independent CHECK cohort. The original OAI study is not formally cited by reference number in this conference abstract; it is only described indirectly in the Objectives and Conclusions. The CHECK cohort results replicate the key finding: haplogroup T associated with lower risk of radiographic KOA progression (OR=0.467, p=0.015), and cluster TJ also protective (OR=0.586, p=0.025). The conclusion states 'As noted in KOA patients of the OAI cohort' confirming directional consistency. Result classified as 'success' — the same association was found in both cohorts with statistical significance. Replication type changed from 'close extension' to 'close experiment': this is validation of the same hypothesis in a new independent cohort (CHECK vs OAI, European vs US population) using the same outcome measure (K&L grade progression), with no novel extension of the original finding. Confidence kept at 'medium' because: (1) this is a brief conference abstract with limited methodological detail, (2) the original OAI study is not formally cited making exact comparison of effect sizes difficult, and (3) we cannot verify whether all originally reported associations were replicated or only a subset.

original_authors: Patricia Irigoyen; Annette T. Lee; Mark H. Wener; Wentian Li; Marlena Kern; Franak Batliwalla; Raymond F. Lum; Elena Massarotti; Michael Weisman; Claire Bombardier; Elaine F. Remmers; Daniel L. Kastner; Michael F. Seldin; Lindsey A. Criswell; Peter K. Gregersen

explanation: REVIEWER: The entry bundles three separate gene-CCP associations into one replication. Two clearly replicated: HLA-SE→CCP+ (OR 3.05, p=2.9e-9) and PTPN22→CCP+ (OR 1.81, p=0.006). One clearly did not: CTLA4→CCP+ (OR 1.04, p=0.30). The authors state: 'We replicated association of HLA-SE, and PTPN22 with CCP+ RA...but were unable to demonstrate any associations for CTLA-4.' They note the CTLA4 null result may reflect limited power (published CTLA4 susceptibility OR is only 1.2, vs 1.75 for PTPN22 and 3.0 for HLA-SE). 'Inconclusive' is a defensible classification for this mixed result (2/3 replicated, 1/3 null possibly due to power). Ideally this would be split into separate entries but the authors framed it as a single replication attempt across three genes. Keeping medium confidence because the ambiguity is genuine: reasonable reviewers could classify this as 'success' (majority replicated) or split the entry.

explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Mixed results across loci attributable to this original study. CELSR2/PSRC1/SORT1 was strongly replicated for LDL cholesterol in Japanese (p < 3.1×10^-11, effect size 4.7 mg/dl comparable to 5.48 mg/dl in Europeans). However, MVK/MMAB (rs2338104) showed no significant association with HDL cholesterol, and NCAN/CILP2/PBX4 (rs16996148) showed no significant association with LDL cholesterol or triglycerides. The authors attribute non-replication to ethnic differences in LD patterns (e.g., rs16996148 and rs2228603 are in tight LD in Europeans r²>0.8 but r²~0 in Japanese HapMap JPT panel). With 1 of 3 testable loci replicated, 'inconclusive' is appropriate — the partial success reflects genuine biological heterogeneity across populations rather than clear confirmation or disconfirmation. Confidence remains medium because the bundled multi-locus structure prevents a clean single classification.

explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Mixed results — majority of loci from this study replicated in Japanese but two did not. Replicated: TRIB1 for triglycerides (p < 4.6×10^-6) and LDL cholesterol (p < 1.2×10^-5); GALNT2 for triglycerides (p < 5.1×10^-5); ANGPTL3 for triglycerides (p < 3.7×10^-6); CELSR2/PSRC1/SORT1 for LDL cholesterol (p < 3.1×10^-11). Not replicated: NCAN/CILP2/PBX4 and MVK/MMAB showed no significant associations. The authors conclude 'associations between the novel loci and plasma lipid concentrations were generally conserved in the Japanese population, with the exception of NCAN/CILP2/PBX4 and MVK/MMAB' and state 'we successfully replicated associations between five newly identified loci.' While the authors frame this positively (4-5 of 6-7 loci replicated), the two non-replicated loci represent genuine failures, not marginal results — making 'inconclusive' the appropriate classification for this bundled entry per schema guidelines (partial support = inconclusive). Confidence remains medium because the mixed pattern is real and the bundled structure prevents a clean single classification.

description: A computational model (PreSS) using three factors — programming self-efficacy, mathematical ability, and hours per week playing computer games — can predict student success in introductory programming (CS1) with approximately 77.5% accuracy at a very early stage in the module
original_authors: Susan Bergin; Ronan Reilly
original_title: Predicting introductory programming performance: A multi-institutional multivariate study
replication_authors: Keith Quille; Susan Bergin
replication_title: Programming: predicting student success early in CS1. a re-validation and replication study
replication_journal: Proceedings of the 23rd Annual ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education
explanation: The authors replicated the PreSS model 12 years later on a much larger, more diverse, multi-institutional dataset (n=692 from 11 institutions in 2 countries vs. n=102 originally). Accuracy declined from 77% to 67% and sensitivity from 85% to 78%, but the authors frame this as still meaningful: 'PreSS is still able to predict with a high accuracy (for two out of every three students), twelve years on.' The decline (10 percentage points) is substantial enough that the replication is best characterized as inconclusive — partial success with degraded performance.

description: A survey of a representative sample of American adults estimates the prevalence of ransomware victimization in the US general population (2-3% per year) and characterizes attack types, payment methods, and behavioral responses
original_authors: Simoiu, Camelia; Bonneau, Joseph; Gates, Christopher; Goel, Sharad
original_title: "I was told to buy a software or lose my computer. I ignored it": A study of ransomware
original_journal: Fifteenth Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS 2019)
replication_authors: Anna-Marie Ortloff; Maike Vossen; Christian Tiefenau
replication_title: Replicating a Study of Ransomware in Germany
replication_journal: Proceedings of the 2021 European Symposium on Usable Security
explanation: The authors conducted a close extension of Simoiu et al. (2019) with a representative German sample, finding some similarities (ransom amounts, behavioral changes) but also notable differences (payment methods, ways of dealing with ransomware). The conclusion states: 'we found some differences between the German and American populations, e.g., concerning the payment method and the participants' way of dealing with the ransomware... Other aspects, such as the amounts of ransom demanded and the behavioral changes after a ransomware attack, were largely similar.'

description: CS students who experience discrimination perceive the gender gap more strongly, and women are more aware of gender gap issues than men across social, academic, and professional dimensions
original_authors: Alicia Garcia Holgado; Carina S. Gonzalez-Gonzalez; Francisco Jose Garcia-Penalvo
original_title: Gender gap perceptions of computing students: A case study in two Spanish universities
original_journal: Proceedings - 10th International Conference on Virtual Campus, JICV 2020
replication_authors: Carmen Lacave; Ana I. Molina; Alicia García-Holgado; Carina S. González-González
replication_title: Delving into gender gap perceptions of computing students: A replication study.
replication_journal: Ninth International Conference on Technological Ecosystems for Enhancing Multiculturality (TEEM'21)
explanation: Reviewer assessment: The paper presents genuinely mixed results. Core gender-difference findings replicated — women were significantly more aware of the gender gap across all three dimensions (social, academic, professional), and perceived differential treatment by teachers (QA1_I, p=0.028) and peers (QA5, p=0.014), confirming the original. However, the discrimination variable analysis diverged substantially: only 3 of the original 12 items showed significant differences by discrimination status (QA1_I, QA5, QS2), versus 12 in the original. The authors explicitly state 'some of the statistically significant differences found in the original study have not been confirmed, especially those related to the discrimination variable.' They attribute this to 'potential bias or influences of uncontrollable environmental factors.' The paper does not declare overall replication success or failure — it presents partial confirmation alongside notable non-confirmations. This genuine ambiguity warrants 'inconclusive' with medium confidence. Subdiscipline corrected from 'special education' (which refers to disability education) to empty, as the paper concerns computing/CS education and no matching subdiscipline exists in the ontology.

description: Implementation of an Episodic Organizational Change (EOC) in the Project Leaders sector of a matrix software company, including its motivations, action plan, critical success and failure factors, positive and negative impacts, and sustainability over time
original_authors: Lima, Rayfran Rocha; Pascareli, Luis; Ayres, Marcelo; Roberto, Suelen; Oran, Ana C.; França, César
original_title: Understanding an organizational change and development intervention applied in a global software industry
original_journal: XXXVII Brazilian Symposium on Software Engineering (SBES 2023)
replication_authors: Rayfran Rocha Lima; Margefson Barros; Miguel Castro; Ana Carolina Oran Rocha; Williamson Silva; César FrançA
replication_title: Improving test team performance through an Episodic Organizational Change implementation: A case study replication and extension
replication_journal: Proceedings of the XXII Brazilian Symposium on Software Quality
explanation: The authors explicitly replicate Lima et al. [26] using the same methodology (nine-step case study, same research questions, same units of analysis) but in a different sector (Testing sector vs. Project Leaders sector). The abstract states results 'corroborate with the motivations, goals, action plan implementation approach, and positive results' but 'diverge from generated negative results,' indicating partial success with notable differences — a mixed/inconclusive outcome.

description: LAMNER (combining a character language model and named entity recognition) outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on code comment generation across BLEU-1-4, ROUGE-L, METEOR, and CIDEr metrics on a Java dataset
original_authors: Sharma, Rishab; Chen, Fuxiang; Fard, Fatemeh
original_title: LAMNER: code comment generation using character language model and named entity recognition
replication_authors: Eray Erer; Turgay Aytac; Aysun Bozanta; Ayse Basar
replication_title: Insights into the Generalizability and Robustness of AI-Driven Code Comment Generation: A Replication Study
replication_journal: Proceedings of the 33rd ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering
explanation: The replication found that LAMNER performs below the results reported in the original study across all metrics, and CodeBERT outperforms LAMNER as the best model overall — contradicting the original study's main finding. The authors conclude that 'our findings reveal variations in performance when tested on an alternative dataset and evaluated using a different method' and note 'discrepancies highlight the challenges of reproducing AI model outcomes.'

description: A gamification plugin for IntelliJ IDEA (IntelliGame) with achievement-based rewards improves software testing behavior, test suite quality, and developer experience in a controlled experiment
original_authors: Straubinger, Philipp; Fraser, Gordon
original_title: Improving testing behavior by gamifying IntelliJ
original_journal: Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM 46th International Conference on Software Engineering
replication_authors: Philipp Straubinger; Tommaso Fulcini; Giacomo Garaccione; Luca Ardito; Gordon Fraser
replication_title: Gamifying Testing in IntelliJ: A Replicability Study
replication_journal: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In summary, we successfully replicated the original study on a gamification plugin with achievement features in the integrated development environment, largely confirming its results.' Most core findings (testing behavior, number of tests, achievement correlations, developer experience) replicated, though coverage and mutation score differences did not reach significance in the new context.

description: Faculty believe that the inherent nature of the physiology discipline (rather than instruction or student factors) is the primary source of student difficulty in learning physiology
original_authors: Joel Michael
original_title: What makes physiology hard for students to learn? Results of a faculty survey
replication_authors: Tara Slominski; Sarah Grindberg; Jennifer Momsen
replication_title: Physiology is hard: a replication study of students’ perceived learning difficulties
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted a 'direct replication' of Michael (2007), using the same survey. Faculty in the replication showed a statistically significant rank-order correlation with Michael's faculty rankings (τ = 0.588, p < 0.01), with both populations agreeing most strongly that discipline-inherent factors drive student difficulty.

description: Undergraduate students in human anatomy and physiology attribute their learning difficulties primarily to the inherent nature of the discipline rather than to instruction or their own learning approaches
original_authors: Diana Sturges; Trent Mauner
original_title: Allied health students' perceptions of class difficulty: the case of undergraduate human anatomy and physiology
original_journal: Internet J Allied Health Sci Pract
replication_authors: Tara Slominski; Sarah Grindberg; Jennifer Momsen
replication_title: Physiology is hard: a replication study of students’ perceived learning difficulties
explanation: The authors administered the same survey from Sturges and Maurer to new populations across four institutions. There was a statistically significant rank-order correlation between the pooled student rankings and those of Sturges and Maurer (τ = 0.725, p < 0.001), and the authors conclude that 'our findings thus reinforce the results of Sturges and Maurer.'

description: The arterio-mixed venous oxygen content difference increases linearly (not in an S-shaped manner) as a function of percentage of maximal oxygen consumption during incremental exercise testing
original_authors: Stringer WW; Hansen JE; Wasserman K.
original_title: Cardiac output estimated noninvasively from oxygen uptake during exercise
replication_authors: Holger Burchert; Fabian Klimpel
replication_title: Revisiting cardiac output estimated noninvasively from oxygen uptake during exercise: an exploratory hypothesis-generating replication study
replication_journal: American Journal of Physiology-Heart and Circulatory Physiology
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as an 'exploratory replication study' aimed at reanalyzing the data from Stringer et al. (1997). They digitized the published data from the original figure and fitted a third-order polynomial model, finding it fit significantly better than the linear model [F(2,101) = 9.5, P < 0.001], contradicting the original claim of linearity. They conclude that 'the increase in C(a-v̄DO2) during incremental exercise testing...was significantly better fitted by an S-shaped model than a linear one.'

description: Medium spiny neurons (MSNs) within the nucleus accumbens core of obesity-prone rats are more excitable (fire more action potentials) than MSNs from obesity-resistant rats at baseline, before any diet manipulation
original_authors: Max F. Oginsky; Joel D. Maust; John T. Corthell; Carrie R. Ferrario
original_title: Enhanced cocaine-induced locomotor sensitization and intrinsic excitability of NAc medium spiny neurons in adult but not in adolescent rats susceptible to diet-induced obesity
replication_authors: Max F. Oginsky; Carrie R. Ferrario
replication_title: Eating “junk food” has opposite effects on intrinsic excitability of nucleus accumbens core neurons in obesity-susceptible versus -resistant rats
explanation: The abstract explicitly states 'We replicated our initial finding that basal excitability is enhanced in obesity-prone versus obesity-resistant rats.' The Discussion confirms: 'Consistent with previous findings (Oginsky et al. 2016b), MSNs within the NAc core from OP rats fired more action potentials in response to current injection than MSNs from OR rats.'

description: Older adults show less spontaneous recovery of force-field motor adaptation than younger adults, indicating age-related impairments in short-term retention of implicit motor memory
original_authors: Trewartha KM; Garcia A.; Wolpert DM; Flanagan JR
original_title: Fast but fleeting: adaptive motor learning processes associated with aging and cognitive decline
replication_authors: Pauline Hermans; Koen Vandevoorde; Jean-Jacques Orban de Xivry
replication_title: Not fleeting but lasting: limited influence of aging on implicit adaptative motor learning and its short-term retention
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we failed to replicate the observation of Trewartha and colleagues' and conclude 'our conceptual replication failed to reproduce the result of Trewartha et al.' No difference in spontaneous recovery was found between young and older adults (Cohen's d = 0.036, P = 0.73), and Bayesian analysis provided moderate support (BF = 4.44) for the null hypothesis.

description: After learning to reach in a velocity-dependent force field in one region of the workspace, subjects generalize their learned dynamics to a new posture (shoulder rotation) in a manner consistent with intrinsic, joint-based coordinate representation
original_authors: Shadmehr R.; Mussa-Ivaldi FA
original_title: Adaptive representation of dynamics during learning of a motor task
replication_authors: Berniker M.; Franklin DW; Flanagan JR; Wolpert DM; Kording K.
replication_title: Motor learning of novel dynamics is not represented in a single global coordinate system: evaluation of mixed coordinate representations and local learning
explanation: Experiment 1 extended the original by testing generalization across shoulder, elbow, and wrist configurations. The authors state: 'we did not obtain clear evidence supporting previous work suggesting that dynamics are encoded in intrinsic coordinates (Malfait et al. 2002; Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi 1994).' No single coordinate frame accounted for generalization.

description: After learning to reach in a velocity-dependent force field in one region of the workspace, subjects generalize their learned dynamics to a new posture (shoulder rotation) in a manner consistent with intrinsic, joint-based coordinate representation
original_authors: Shadmehr R.; Mussa-Ivaldi FA
original_title: Adaptive representation of dynamics during learning of a motor task
replication_authors: Berniker M.; Franklin DW; Flanagan JR; Wolpert DM; Kording K.
replication_title: Motor learning of novel dynamics is not represented in a single global coordinate system: evaluation of mixed coordinate representations and local learning
explanation: Experiment 2 was an explicit reproduction of Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi (1994). The authors state: 'we were unable to replicate the original generalization results. We found no signs of a clear generalization pattern in intrinsic coordinates.' The repeated-measures ANOVA found no significant effect of group or force field on generalization performance.

description: Approximately half of dorsal spinocerebellar tract (DSCT) neurons in cats encode hindlimb paw position in extrinsic (hip-to-paw vector) coordinates rather than intrinsic joint angles, as evidenced by invariant tuning direction across two joint-covariance conditions (elastic vs. knee-fixed)
original_authors: Bosco G.; Poppele RE; Eian J.
original_title: Reference frames for spinal proprioception: limb endpoint based or joint-level based?
replication_authors: Raeed H. Chowdhury; Matthew C. Tresch; Lee E. Miller
replication_title: Musculoskeletal geometry accounts for apparent extrinsic representation of paw position in dorsal spinocerebellar tract
explanation: The authors used a simulation with randomly weighted muscle-length inputs to replicate two key findings from Bosco et al. (2000): (1) the bimodal distribution of neural tuning directions along the limb axis, and (2) small changes in tuning direction between constraint conditions (median |ΔθG| ~20° in simulation vs. 23° in original). They conclude: 'limb biomechanics and a simple linear convergence of muscle length inputs can replicate the apparent extrinsic representation of limb state by DSCT neurons,' though they offer a reinterpretation that musculoskeletal geometry — not neural computation — explains the phenomenon.

description: Anodal cerebellar transcranial direct current stimulation (ctDCS) leads to faster visuomotor adaptation relative to sham tDCS or motor cortex tDCS
original_authors: Galea JM; Vazquez A.; Pasricha N.; de Xivry JJ; Celnik P.
original_title: Dissociating the roles of the cerebellum and motor cortex during adaptive learning: the motor cortex retains what the cerebellum learns
replication_authors: Jalali R.; Miall RC; Galea JM
replication_title: No consistent effect of cerebellar transcranial direct current stimulation on visuomotor adaptation
explanation: In Experiment 1, using a slightly different setup (Polhemus sensor on finger vs. digitizing pen, no goggles), the authors showed anodal ctDCS led to significantly greater adaptation relative to sham (t(26)=2.9, P=0.007, d=1.17), successfully replicating the core finding of Galea et al. (2011).

description: Anodal cerebellar transcranial direct current stimulation (ctDCS) leads to faster visuomotor adaptation relative to sham tDCS or motor cortex tDCS
original_authors: Galea JM; Vazquez A.; Pasricha N.; de Xivry JJ; Celnik P.

replication_authors: Jalali R.; Miall RC; Galea JM
replication_title: No consistent effect of cerebellar transcranial direct current stimulation on visuomotor adaptation
explanation: Experiment 7 was a validation of Experiment 1 (which had succeeded) with a new set of naive participants using identical protocol; it found no significant difference between anodal and sham ctDCS groups during adaptation (t(24)=-2.5, P=0.8, d=0.1), failing to replicate the positive effect.

description: Whole-body Krtcap3 knockout female rats on a high-fat diet show increased body weight, food intake, and fat mass compared to wild-type controls
original_authors: Alexandria M. Szalanczy; Emily Goff; Osborne Seshie; Aaron Deal; Michael Grzybowski; Jason Klotz; Chia-Chi Chuang Key; Aron M. Geurts; Leah C. Solberg Woods
original_title: Keratinocyte-associated protein 3 plays a role in body weight and adiposity with differential effects in males and females
replication_authors: Alexandria M. Szalanczy; Gina Giorgio; Emily Goff; Osborne Seshie; Michael Grzybowski; Jason Klotz; Aron M. Geurts; Eva E. Redei; Leah C. Solberg Woods
replication_title: Changes in environmental stress over COVID-19 pandemic likely contributed to failure to replicate adiposity phenotype associated with Krtcap3
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Surprisingly, we failed to replicate the adiposity difference we had previously seen in the female rats, as there were no longer any significant differences in body weight, food intake, or fat mass between WT and KO females.' The Discussion confirms: 'In the current study, there were no differences in the adiposity measures between WT and KO females, contradicting our previous results.'

description: SNPs in RANKL (rs7984870) and OPG (rs2073618) are associated with risk of aromatase inhibitor-induced musculoskeletal adverse events, with the minor G allele of rs7984870 being protective in a Chinese Han breast cancer cohort
original_authors: Jingxuan Wang; Kangping Lu; Ying Song; Shu Zhao; Wenjie Ma; Qijia Xuan; Dabei Tang; Hong Zhao; Lei Liu; Qingyuan Zhang
original_title: RANKL and OPG polymorphisms are associated with aromatase inhibitor-related musculoskeletal adverse events in Chinese Han breast cancer patients
replication_authors: Dempsey JM; Xi J.; Henry NL; Rae JM; Hertz DL
replication_title: Attempted replication of SNPs in RANKL and OPG with musculoskeletal adverse events during aromatase inhibitor treatment for breast cancer
explanation: The primary phenotype (change in MS-AE from baseline to 3 months) was not replicated for either SNP. However, in a secondary analysis, rs7984870 (RANKL) showed a nominal association with protection from MS-AE-related AI discontinuation consistent with Wang et al.'s original direction, though lacking statistical correction. The authors state: 'Previously reported associations were not replicated with our primary hypothesis' while noting partial consistency for rs7984870 in secondary analyses.

description: A genetic variant in the OPG gene (rs2073618) is associated with aromatase inhibitor-related musculoskeletal toxicity in breast cancer patients, with the heterozygous group (CG) showing the highest risk of MS-AEs
original_authors: Lintermans A.; Van Asten K.; Jongen L.; Van Brussel T.; Laenen A.; Verhaeghe J.; Vanderschueren D.; Lambrechts D.; Neven P.
original_title: Genetic variant in the osteoprotegerin gene is associated with aromatase inhibitor-related musculoskeletal toxicity in breast cancer patients
replication_authors: Dempsey JM; Xi J.; Henry NL; Rae JM; Hertz DL
replication_title: Attempted replication of SNPs in RANKL and OPG with musculoskeletal adverse events during aromatase inhibitor treatment for breast cancer
explanation: The rs2073618 (OPG) SNP was not significantly associated with the primary phenotype (change in MS symptom cluster) or any secondary phenotypes in this study (all P > 0.05). The authors explicitly state 'Previously reported associations were not replicated with our primary hypothesis,' and no secondary association was detected for this SNP.

description: Six specific SNPs in the PON gene cluster (rs854549, rs3917564, rs2269829, rs854566, rs854572, rs3917510) predict PON1 arylesterase (AREase) activity beyond the four known functional PON1 SNPs

replication_title: Additional Common Polymorphisms in thePONGene Cluster Predict PON1 Activity but Not Vascular Disease
explanation: The authors explicitly tested the 6 SNPs identified by Carlson et al. in a non-overlapping sample of 523 subjects and found that only 2 of the 6 SNPs were replicated (rs854566/rs854567 and rs3917510), while 4 SNPs failed to replicate. The authors state: 'two of the six Carlson et al. findings were replicated,' and 'failing to replicate four (Table 5) in nonoverlapping data.'

original_title: DNA methyl transferase (DNMT) gene polymorphisms could be a primary event in epigenetic susceptibility to schizophrenia
replication_authors: Saxena S.; Maroju PA; Choudhury S.; Voina VC; Naik P.; Gowdhaman K.; Kkani P.; Chennoju K.; Ganesh Kumar S.; Ramasubramanian C.; Prasad Rao G.; Jamma T.; Narayan KP; Mohan KN

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we performed a replication study to validate the association of the two DNMT1 minor alleles using an independent collection of 310 controls and 304 patients' and confirmed the association of homozygous minor allele genotypes with schizophrenia (P=0.04 for rs2114724 and P=0.007 for rs2228611). description: Delay discounting moderates the relationship between low income and high food insecurity, such that low-income individuals with higher delay discounting experience greater food insecurity
original_authors: Leonard H. Epstein; Noelle Jankowiak; Henry Lin; Rocco Paluch; Mikhail N. Koffarnus; Warren K. Bickel
original_title: No food for thought: moderating effects of delay discounting and future time perspective on the relation between income and food insecurity
original_journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
replication_authors: Leonard H. Epstein; Ashfique Rizwan; Rocco A. Paluch; Jennifer L. Temple
replication_title: Delay Discounting and the Income-Food Insecurity-Obesity Paradox in Mothers
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated the finding that income is related to food insecurity and that DD moderates the relation between low income and high food insecurity [11].' The moderation was statistically significant (F(2,305) = 4.89, p = 0.008) in the same direction as the original.

description: Prevalence rates of problem and probable pathological gambling (lifetime and current) in Washington State adult population, as measured by the South Oaks Gambling Screen
original_authors: Rachel A. Volberg
original_title: Gambling and problem gambling in Washington State
original_journal: Report to the Washington State Lottery
replication_authors: Rachel A. Volberg; William L. Moore
replication_title: Gambling and problem gambling in Washington State : a replication study, 1992 to 1998, report to the Washington State Lottery
explanation: Independent review confirms success classification. The 1998 study is an explicit replication of the 1992 baseline using identical methodology (SOGS instrument, telephone survey, same research team, n=1502 vs n=1501). Table 16 shows no statistically significant changes in prevalence: lifetime combined 5.1%→5.0% (p=0.50), current combined 2.8%→2.3% (p=0.21). Only current probable pathological gambling showed a decrease (0.9%→0.5%) and only at the weak 90% confidence level (p=0.10). The authors state unambiguously: 'both the lifetime and current prevalence of problem and probable pathological gambling in Washington State have remained stable between 1992 and 1998.' The Summary section reinforces: 'The decline in gambling participation in Washington State between 1992 and 1998 has been accompanied by a stabilization in the prevalence of problem gambling.' Upgraded from medium to high because multiple lines of evidence (Table 16 p-values, explicit author conclusions, title framing as 'replication study') all converge on the same clear result.

description: The prevalence of disordered gambling (problem and probable pathological) among adults in Oregon, estimated at 3.3% combined rate using the South Oaks Gambling Screen (SOGS) in a telephone survey
original_authors: Rachel A. Volberg
original_title: Gambling and problem gambling in Oregon
replication_authors: Moore, Thomas L.
replication_title: The Prevalence of Disordered Gambling among Adults in Oregon: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state that their 2006 study 'providing an excellent replication of the 2001 and 1997 studies.' The design and methodology were consistent with the original 1997 baseline study, using the same randomized telephone survey approach with SOGS and NODS instruments on Oregon adults.

description: A five-factor model of 16 theory-based survey items measuring psychosocial correlates of colorectal cancer screening (salience-coherence, cancer worries, perceived susceptibility, response efficacy, and social influence) demonstrates factorial validity and invariance across African American and Caucasian U.S. populations

replication_title: Factorial Validity and Invariance of a Survey Measuring Psychosocial Correlates of Colorectal Cancer Screening in Ontario, Canada—A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are 'replicating previous survey validation work' by Tiro et al. (2005) and 'replicated the analytic processes used by Tiro et al.' in a Canadian population. The results show partial success: the five-factor model provided good fit for both males and females, but 'Tests for factorial invariance between sexes...found mixed results,' with the authors concluding 'partial factorial invariance' — supporting the factor structure but failing to fully confirm cross-sex invariance.

original_title: Multiple newly identified loci associated with prostate cancer susceptibility

explanation: The authors replicated 2 of 7 SNPs at nominal significance (rs10993994 at P=0.022 and rs5945619 at P=0.035), with rs10993994 reaching study-wide significance in the early-onset subset (P<0.0001). explanation: The IL4R 503P association was not significant in the replication study alone (p=0.41), but approached significance in the combined joint analysis (OR=2.1; 95% CI=1.1-3.8; p=0.03; Pcorr=0.09). The authors note that 'the magnitude and direction of this association were similar to the results reported in our original study' but it did not survive correction for multiple testing.

description: The ADRB2 27E variant is associated with increased risk of large vessel stroke in children with sickle cell anemia
original_authors: Hoppe, Carolyn; Klitz, William; Cheng, Suzanne; Apple, Ray; Steiner, Lori; Robles, Lara; Girard, Tom; Vichinsky, Elliott; Styles, Lori; The Csscd Investigators
original_title: Gene interactions and stroke risk in children with sickle cell anemia
replication_authors: Carolyn Hoppe; William Klitz; Katherine D’Harlingue; Suzanne Cheng; Michael Grow; Lori Steiner; Janelle Noble; Robert Adams; Lori Styles
replication_title: Confirmation of an Association Between the TNF(−308) Promoter Polymorphism and Stroke Risk in Children With Sickle Cell Anemia
explanation: The ADRB2 27 Q/E association was not replicated: genotype frequencies were nearly identical between cases and controls in the replication population (p=0.65), and the association was not significant in the combined analysis either (p=0.25). The authors do not discuss this as a confirmed finding.

description: Six single nucleotide polymorphisms on chromosome 17q25 are significantly associated with cerebral white matter lesion burden at genome-wide significance levels
original_authors: Fornage M.; Debette S.; Bis JC; Schmidt H.; Ikram MA; Dufouil C.; Sigurdsson S.; Lumley T.; DeStefano AL; Fazekas F.; Vrooman HA; Shibata DK; Maillard P.; Zijdenbos A.; Smith AV; Gudnason H.; de Boer R.; Cushman M.; Mazoyer B.; Heiss G.; Vernooij MW; Enzinger C.; Glazer NL; Beiser A.; Knopman DS; Cavalieri M.; Niessen WJ; Harris TB; Petrovic K.; Lopez OL; Au R.; Lambert JC; Hofman A.; Gottesman RF; Garcia M.; Heckbert SR; Atwood LD; Catellier DJ; Uitterlinden AG; Yang Q.; Smith NL; Aspelund T.; Romero JR; Rice K.; Taylor KD; Nalls MA; Rotter JI; Sharrett R.; van Duijn CM; Amouyel P.; Wolf PA; Gudnason V.; van der Lugt A.; Boerwinkle E.; Psaty BM; Seshadri S.; Tzourio C.; Breteler MM; Mosley TH; Schmidt R.; Longstreth WT; DeCarli C.; Launer LJ
original_title: Genome-wide association studies of cerebral white matter lesion burden: the CHARGE consortium
replication_authors: Verhaaren BF; de Boer R.; Vernooij MW; Rivadeneira F.; Uitterlinden AG; Hofman A.; Krestin GP; van der Lugt A.; Niessen WJ; Breteler MM; Ikram MA
replication_title: Replication Study of Chr17q25 With Cerebral White Matter Lesion Volume
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we successfully replicated the association between a locus on chromosome 17q25 and WML volume.' All 6 SNPs were significantly associated with WML volume (P=1.1×10⁻³ for the lead SNP rs3744028), and a meta-analysis combining this replication with the discovery data yielded P=5.3×10⁻¹⁷.

description: A sustained left-lateralized slow negativity (contingent negative variation, CNV) is elicited following the first stimulus word in a visual rhyme judgment task in hearing adults
original_authors: Michael D. Rugg
original_title: Event-related potentials in phonological matching tasks
replication_authors: Mairéad MacSweeney; Usha Goswami; Helen Neville
replication_title: The Neurobiology of Rhyme Judgment by Deaf and Hearing Adults: An ERP Study
explanation: Reviewer verification: The authors unambiguously state 'we replicated the two well-established ERP effects observed during a written word rhyme task (Rugg, 1984b).' The CNV was significantly more negative over left than right hemisphere (F(1,8) = 12.13, p < .01), consistent with the original finding. The authors note the anterior/posterior factor 'just failed to reach significance' due to small sample size, but the core left-lateralization effect was clearly replicated. The authors explicitly characterize this as a successful replication and use it as validation of their paradigm. Classified as 'close experiment' because the same visual rhyme judgment paradigm and ERP measures were used but with different stimuli and participants, embedded in a larger deaf-vs-hearing comparison study.

description: Enhanced negativity (N450) at around 450ms in response to non-rhyming compared to rhyming written words during a visual rhyme judgment task in hearing adults, largest over right temporo-parietal sites
original_authors: Michael D. Rugg
original_title: Event-related potentials in phonological matching tasks
replication_authors: Mairéad MacSweeney; Usha Goswami; Helen Neville
replication_title: The Neurobiology of Rhyme Judgment by Deaf and Hearing Adults: An ERP Study
explanation: Reviewer verification: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the two well-established ERP effects observed during a written word rhyme task (Rugg, 1984b).' The N450 showed significantly greater negativity to non-rhyming targets, largest over right, medial, parietal sites (rhyme × hemisphere interaction F(1,8) = 20.72, p < .005). The authors state 'Replication of these two rhyme-related ERP components in hearing participants suggests that our rhyming paradigm and stimuli were valid.' The effect direction, scalp distribution, and statistical significance all confirm successful replication. Classified as 'close experiment' because the same paradigm and measures were used with different stimuli and participants.

description: Previously reward-associated sounds involuntarily capture attention and interfere with goal-directed auditory processing (both voluntary prioritization of high-value targets in training and involuntary attentional capture by high-value distractors in test phase)
original_authors: Andy J. Kim; David S. Lee; Brian A. Anderson
original_title: Previously reward-associated sounds interfere with goal-directed auditory processing
replication_authors: Andy J. Kim; Laurent Grégoire; Brian A. Anderson
replication_title: Value-Biased Competition in the Auditory System of the Brain
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated behavioral evidence of two forms of value-based attentional biases in the auditory domain (Kim et al., 2021).' Both the voluntary prioritization effect in training (F(2,60)=17.73, p<.001) and the involuntary attentional capture in test (F(2,60)=3.69, p=.031) were successfully replicated. The paradigm was conducted in an fMRI scanner context but otherwise exactly matched the original.

description: Delaying the presentation of a verb in a role-reversed sentence (by inserting a neutral phrase such as 'that evening') prevents the N400 semantic illusion, such that the verb elicits a larger N400 amplitude relative to a non-role-reversed control sentence
original_authors: Wing-Yee Chow; Ellen Lau; Suiping Wang; Colin Phillips
original_title: Wait a second! Delayed impact of argument roles on on-line verb prediction
replication_authors: Kate Stone; Milena Rabovsky
replication_title: The Role of Syntactic and Semantic Cues in Preventing Temporary Illusions of Plausibility
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed 'to replicate Chow et al.'s (2018) Experiment 3' and found results directionally consistent with the delay preventing the illusion in German, but the Bayes factor was 0.46 (inconclusive), and the authors themselves concluded tentatively, stating 'the interaction effect size is likely too small to yield conclusive evidence for an interaction at the current sample size.' The meta-analytic estimate combining both studies was also inconclusive (BF10 = 0.55).

description: Hearing adult skilled readers show a left-lateralized hierarchical structure in the visual word form system (VWFS), with word selectivity gradients progressing from posterior to anterior along the left ventral visual stream, and no such gradient in the right hemisphere
original_authors: Olulade OA; Flowers DL; Napoliello EM; Eden GF
original_title: Developmental differences for word processing in the ventral stream
replication_authors: Laurie S. Glezer; Stephen McCullough; Brennan Terhune-Cotter; Karen Emmorey
replication_title: Bilateral Word Selectivity Gradients in the Visual Word Form System in Skilled Deaf Readers
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our results replicate previous findings for typical adult readers (Olulade et al., 2013, 2015; Vinckier et al., 2007).' For hearing readers, they confirmed the left-lateralized hierarchical gradient with word selectivity increasing from posterior to anterior ROIs, and no significant gradient in the right hemisphere.

description: Typical hearing adult readers show a left-lateralized hierarchical structure in the visual word form system with word selectivity gradients in the left but not right ventral visual stream
original_authors: Olulade OA; Flowers DL; Napoliello EM; Eden GF
original_title: Dyslexic children lack word selectivity gradients in occipito-temporal and inferior frontal cortex
replication_authors: Laurie S. Glezer; Stephen McCullough; Brennan Terhune-Cotter; Karen Emmorey
replication_title: Bilateral Word Selectivity Gradients in the Visual Word Form System in Skilled Deaf Readers
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results replicate previous findings for typical adult readers (Olulade et al., 2013, 2015; Vinckier et al., 2007).' For hearing readers, the expected left-lateralized hierarchical gradient was confirmed, with significant differences between conditions (RW vs CS, PW vs CS) in the three most anterior left hemisphere ROIs but not in the right hemisphere.

description: Hearing adult skilled readers show a left-lateralized hierarchical gradient of sensitivity to visual word forms (consonant strings, pseudowords, real words) in the ventral visual stream, with increasing word selectivity from posterior to anterior regions in the left hemisphere only
original_authors: Fabien Vinckier; Stanislas Dehaene; Antoinette Jobert; Jean Philippe Dubus; Mariano Sigman; Laurent Cohen
original_title: Hierarchical coding of letter strings in the ventral stream: Dissecting the inner organization of the visual word-form system
replication_authors: Laurie S. Glezer; Stephen McCullough; Brennan Terhune-Cotter; Karen Emmorey
replication_title: Bilateral Word Selectivity Gradients in the Visual Word Form System in Skilled Deaf Readers
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results replicate previous findings for typical adult readers (Olulade et al., 2013, 2015; Vinckier et al., 2007).' They used the same stimuli (consonant strings, pseudowords, real words) and same gradient mapping analysis as Vinckier et al. (2007), confirming the left-lateralized hierarchical gradient in hearing readers.

description: Mid-frontal theta power (4-8 Hz) increases for semantically related distractors relative to congruent or unrelated distractors during a picture-word interference task, reflecting top-down interference control in resolving competition between processing streams during word production
original_authors: Vitória Piai; Ardi Roelofs; Ole Jensen; Jan-Mathijs Schoffelen; Mathilde Bonnefond
original_title: Distinct patterns of brain activity characterise lexical activation and competition in spoken word production
replication_authors: Xiaochen Y. Zheng; Vitória Piai
replication_title: Neural Oscillations in the Aging Brain Associated With Interference Control in Word Production
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated the behavioral Stroop-like interference and semantic interference effects...but not the corresponding theta modulation on the neural level.' The primary claim of the original study — that mid-frontal theta oscillations serve as the neural underpinning of interference control in word production — was not observed in the older adult group; instead, beta power decreases were found in a different spatial-temporal pattern.

description: Prediction-mismatching words elicit a phonological mismatch negativity (PMN), a frontocentral negativity with a distinct scalp distribution that precedes the N400, reflecting phonological prediction mismatch detection independent of semantic processing
original_authors: John F. Connolly; Natalie A. Phillips
original_title: Event-related potential components reflect phonological and semantic processing of the terminal word of spoken sentences
replication_authors: Victoria R. Poulton; Mante S. Nieuwland
replication_title: Can You Hear What’s Coming? Failure to Replicate ERP Evidence for Phonological Prediction
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'Our study was an attempt to replicate the PMN effect associated with phonological prediction (Connolly & Phillips, 1994)... our results do not support the hypothesis that unpredictable words generated a PMN (or N200) effect'. Bayesian analyses yielded moderate evidence against the critical ROI × Time interaction (BF = 6.5 in favor of the additive model), and preregistered analyses found no significant distributional difference between the early and late time windows.

description: The N200 effect in spoken sentence comprehension has a distinct scalp distribution (more frontal/uniform) compared to the N400 effect (more posterior), as evidenced by a significant ROI × Time interaction when comparing early and late time windows
original_authors: Daniëlle van den Brink; Colin M. Brown; Peter Hagoort
original_title: Electrophysiological evidence for early contextual influences during spoken-word recognition: N200 versus N400 effects
replication_authors: Victoria R. Poulton; Mante S. Nieuwland
replication_title: Can You Hear What’s Coming? Failure to Replicate ERP Evidence for Phonological Prediction
explanation: Following the exact analysis procedure of Van den Brink et al. (2001), the authors found no significant ROI × Time interaction (F(1, 1724) = 1.438, p = 0.231), contrasting with the significant interaction reported by Van den Brink et al. (2001). The authors note: 'These results are in contrast to Van den Brink et al. (2001), but not Van den Brink and Hagoort (2004).'

description: Silently articulated speech (engaging motor-phonological processes) generates greater activity in auditory cortex than imagined speech (engaging only lexical-level processes), reflecting forward predictive signals even without auditory input.
original_authors: Kayoko Okada; William Matchin; Gregory Hickok
original_title: Neural evidence for predictive coding in auditory cortex during speech production
replication_authors: Alex Teghipco; Kayoko Okada; Emma Murphy; Gregory Hickok
replication_title: Predictive Coding and Internal Error Correction in Speech Production
