explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully replicated this effect, showing that auditory cortex does seem to receive predictive signals during speech production.' The group-level contrast and ROI analysis confirmed the forward prediction effect in bilateral Heschl's gyrus.

description: Tongue twisters biased toward nonword errors generate greater left posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG) activity than those biased toward word errors (lexicality effect), reflecting internal error detection and correction even on accurately produced trials.
original_authors: Kayoko Okada; William Matchin; Gregory Hickok
original_title: Neural evidence for predictive coding in auditory cortex during speech production
replication_authors: Alex Teghipco; Kayoko Okada; Emma Murphy; Gregory Hickok
replication_title: Predictive Coding and Internal Error Correction in Speech Production
explanation: The authors explicitly report: 'Because we failed to replicate the lexicality effect reported in previous work (i.e., no effect was observed at the group-level)...' No significant differences in brain response were found at any statistical threshold, including within the pMTG ROI (left hemisphere: t(33) = 0.56, p = 0.58; right hemisphere: t(33) = -1.35, p = 0.19).

description: Acoustic features of songs reliably predict their behavioral contexts (dance, lullaby, healing, love), with dance songs and lullabies classified most accurately and healing and love songs classified with lower accuracy
original_authors: Mehr SA; Singh M.; Knox D.; Ketter DM; Pickens-Jones D.; Atwood S.; Lucas C.; Jacoby N.; Egner AA; Hopkins EJ; Howard RM; Hartshorne JK; Jennings MV; Simson J.; Bainbridge CM; Pinker S.; O'Donnell TJ; Krasnow MM; Glowacki L.
original_title: Universality and diversity in human song
replication_authors: Bertolo M.; Snarskis M.; Kyritsis T.; Yurdum L.; Bainbridge CM; Atwood S.; Hilton CB; Keomurjian A.; Lee JS; Mackiel A.; Mak V.; Shin M.; Bitran A.; Shilton D.; Delasanta L.; Do HH; Lang J.; Irani T.; Kangatharan J.; Lafleur K.; Malko N.; Atkinson QD; Singh M.; Mehr SA
replication_title: The Expanded Natural History of Song Discography, A Global Corpus of Vocal Music
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The replication was successful': the LASSO ensemble model classified song behavioral contexts above chance (47.2% accuracy vs. ~42% in the original) and showed an 'identical' pattern across song types (dance and lullaby highest, healing and love lowest). They also explicitly label this 'a direct replication of prior results (see Figure 5B in Mehr et al., 2019).'

description: Human listeners across many cultures and languages classify love songs with lower accuracy compared to other behavioral contexts such as dance songs and lullabies
original_authors: Lidya Yurdum; Manvir Singh; Luke Glowacki; Thomas Vardy; Quentin D. Atkinson; Courtney B. Hilton; Disa Sauter; Max M. Krasnow; Samuel A. Mehr
original_title: Universal interpretations of vocal music
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Bertolo M.; Snarskis M.; Kyritsis T.; Yurdum L.; Bainbridge CM; Atwood S.; Hilton CB; Keomurjian A.; Lee JS; Mackiel A.; Mak V.; Shin M.; Bitran A.; Shilton D.; Delasanta L.; Do HH; Lang J.; Irani T.; Kangatharan J.; Lafleur K.; Malko N.; Atkinson QD; Singh M.; Mehr SA
replication_title: The Expanded Natural History of Song Discography, A Global Corpus of Vocal Music
explanation: The authors explicitly state the machine LASSO model 'only weakly detects love songs, conceptually replicating prior work on human classification of love songs (Yurdum et al., 2023).' Love songs were classified at chance level (p = 0.25), confirming the original finding that love songs are harder to identify than other song types. The replication is conceptual because it uses a machine classifier on acoustic features rather than human listeners, a fundamentally different methodology testing the same claim.

description: Bitter tastants (caffeine and coffee) correspond with lower musical pitches compared to other tastants, and trombone/clarinet instrument classes are more often paired with bitter tastes
original_authors: Crisinel AS; Spence C.
original_title: As bitter as a trombone: synesthetic correspondences in nonsynesthetes between tastes/flavors and musical notes
replication_authors: Quentin J. Watson; Karen L. Gunther
replication_title: Trombones Elicit Bitter More Strongly Than Do Clarinets: a Partial Replication of Three Studies of Crisinel and Spence
explanation: The authors state in the Discussion: 'We successfully replicated Crisinel and Spence's (2009, 2010a, b) findings of a low-pitch/bitter crossmodal correspondence when using trombone pitches and sometimes when using clarinet pitches.' The trombone result was significant (F(3,135) = 7.574, p < 0.001, η² = 0.144) and the average across instruments was also significant (F(3,135) = 4.269, p = 0.006), though the clarinet result alone was not (p = 0.065).

description: Taster status (sensitivity to bitter compounds) is not correlated with the strength of the low-pitch/bitter implicit association
original_authors: Anne-Sylvie Crisinel; Charles Spence
original_title: Implicit association between basic tastes and pitch
replication_authors: Quentin J. Watson; Karen L. Gunther
replication_title: Trombones Elicit Bitter More Strongly Than Do Clarinets: a Partial Replication of Three Studies of Crisinel and Spence
explanation: Crisinel and Spence (2009) found no correlation between taster status and the low-pitch/bitter IAT correspondence. The current replication found a significant positive Pearson's correlation (r(44) = 0.389, p = 0.007) between bitter perception of PTC strips and associated pitch, directly contradicting the 2009 finding. The authors note: 'contrary to the findings of Crisinel and Spence (2009) that pitch and taster status were uncorrelated, when our participants were asked to rate both the bitterness of the PTC strip and the corresponding pitch, we found a significant positive Pearson's correlation.'

description: Students' difficulty with partitive division word problems is governed by a primitive model: the dividend must be greater than the divisor, such that problems violating this model (divisor larger than dividend) lead to dramatically lower correct answer rates among grade 7 students
original_authors: Efraim Fischbein; Maria Deri; Maria Sainat Nello; Maria Sciolis Marino
original_title: The role of implicit models in solving verbal problems in multiplication and division
original_journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education
replication_authors: Chiara Giberti; Andrea Maffia
replication_title: Primitive Model of Partitive Division: A Replication of the Fischbein et al. Study
replication_journal: Implementation and Replication Studies in Mathematics Education
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm the original findings: 'Our study confirms Fischbein's results' and the abstract states 'the main results of the original study are confirmed.' The ~90% correct rate for standard items and the dramatic drop to ~16-19% for items violating the primitive model both replicate the original pattern (original: 24-30% for violating items).

description: Early childhood lung function (FEV1 at ages 6-8) predicts adolescent lung function in cystic fibrosis patients regardless of early Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection status
original_authors: Pittman, J.E.
original_title: Acquisition of Pseudomonas aeruginosa before age 5 is associated with severe lung disease in adolescence in cystic fibrosis
replication_authors: Jessica E. Pittman; Hannah H. Noah; Elizabeth H. Calloway; Stephanie D. Davis; Scott D. Sagel; Frank J. Accurso; Michael R. Knowles; Marci K. Sontag
replication_title: Early Infection With Pseudomonas Aeruginosa Does Not Explain Differences In Lung Function In Early Childhood That Persist Into Adolescence In Subjects With Cystic Fibrosis: A Replication Study
explanation: Reviewer note: The paper explicitly calls itself 'A Replication Study' in the title and states in Conclusions 'We have confirmed an association between early childhood lung function and adolescent lung function in subjects with CF.' This supports a 'success' classification per Step 1 of Result Classification (authors' explicit statement). However, confidence remains 'medium' for two reasons: (1) The original study (Pittman, Ped Pulm, in press) is cited only as 'in press' with no references list available, making it impossible to verify exact original claims or obtain full bibliographic details. (2) The relationship between the original's primary claim (Pa acquisition → severe disease) and what was actually replicated here (lung function tracking independent of Pa) is ambiguous — the replication confirmed the secondary observation from the Gene Modifier dataset (Figure 1) that early FEV1 differences persist regardless of Pa status, while the original's headline finding about Pa causing severe disease was effectively not supported (Pa status was not associated with adolescent lung function in the replication). Updated description to reflect the finding actually replicated rather than the original's headline claim.

description: Identical optic flow patterns generated by observer ego-motion are perceived differently than those generated by object motion, with ego-motion signals causing the visual system to prefer the percept of a stationary object (the 'stationarity prior')
original_authors: Mark Wexler; Francesco Panerai; Ivan Lamouret; Jacques Droulez
original_title: Self-motion and the perception of stationary objects
replication_authors: Jain A.; Backus BT
replication_title: Experience affects the use of ego-motion signals during 3D shape perception
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Experiment 1 replicated the study of Wexler, Panerai et al. (2001)' and in the Discussion confirm: 'In Experiment 1, we replicated Wexler, Panerai et al. (2001) finding that the perceptual interpretation of optic flow generated by observer motion favors objects that are stationary in the allocentric frame of reference.' Figure 2 caption also notes 'Data replicate of those of Wexler, Panerai et al. (2001).'

description: Double training with motion direction discrimination along one direction and dot number discrimination along the opposite direction produces complete transfer of motion discrimination learning to the dot number trained direction
original_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Yu-Xiang Yang
original_title: Perceptual learning of motion direction discrimination transfers to an opposite direction with TPE training
replication_authors: Ju Liang; Yifeng Zhou; Manfred Fahle; Zili Liu
replication_title: Specificity of motion discrimination learning even with double training and staircase
explanation: In Experiment 1 (China lab, n=6), the authors found a significant Time×Direction interaction F(1,5)=8.55, p<.05 showing that transfer to the dot number trained direction (18.7% MPI) was significantly less than learning along the motion trained direction (34.9% MPI), and was no greater than transfer to untrained control directions (9.7%). The authors explicitly state: 'we could not even replicate the original result in J. Y. Zhang and Yang (2014) with the first seven sessions of data, despite our effort to replicate the experiment as faithfully as possible.'

description: Double training with motion direction discrimination along one direction and dot number discrimination along the opposite direction produces complete transfer of motion discrimination learning to the dot number trained direction
original_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Yu-Xiang Yang
original_title: Perceptual learning of motion direction discrimination transfers to an opposite direction with TPE training
replication_authors: Ju Liang; Yifeng Zhou; Manfred Fahle; Zili Liu
replication_title: Specificity of motion discrimination learning even with double training and staircase
explanation: In Experiment 2 (UCLA lab, n=3), transfer indices to the dot number trained direction (-0.26, 0.25, 0.05) were far below the 1.2 reported in Zhang & Yang (2014) and were not higher on average than transfer to untrained control directions (0.33, 0.21, 0.45). The authors conclude this result 'does not support complete transfer as found in J. Y. Zhang and Yang (2014).'

description: Narrowband noise in the range of 1-5 cycles per degree (cpd) drastically reduces the perceived brightness differences in White's illusion, while noise at lower or higher frequencies has little or no effect
original_authors: Viljami R. Salmela; Pentti I. Laurinen
original_title: Low-level features determine brightness in White's and Benary's illusions
replication_authors: Torsten Betz; Robert Shapley; Felix A. Wichmann; Marianne Maertens
replication_title: Noise masking of White's illusion exposes the weakness of current spatial filtering models of lightness perception
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the main findings of Salmela and Laurinen (2009),' confirming that noise between 1 and 5 cpd had the largest masking effect on White's illusion and that the most effective noise frequency did not scale proportionally with grating frequency. The experiment used the same paradigm but with modifications including three different grating frequencies and adjusted presentation times.

description: Shape and texture of single objects can be processed independently using the Garner speeded-classification paradigm (i.e., observers can attend to shape while ignoring texture changes, and vice versa)
original_authors: Jonathan S. Cant; Mary-Ellen Large; Lindsay McCall; Melvyn A. Goodale
original_title: Independent processing of form, colour, and texture in object perception
replication_authors: Jonathan S. Cant; Sol Z. Sun; Yaoda Xu
replication_title: Distinct cognitive mechanisms involved in the processing of single objects and object ensembles
explanation: Across all five experiments that included single-object conditions (Experiments 1–5), the authors consistently found no significant interference between shape and texture processing in single-object perception, replicating Cant et al. (2008). The General Discussion explicitly states: 'Our findings replicate these results but expand upon them by demonstrating that these features can be processed independently not only when shape is defined as differences in the aspect ratio of rectangles (i.e., Cant et al., 2008) but also when shape is defined as differences in outline contour.'

description: Holistic processing measured by the Vanderbilt Holistic Face Processing Test (VHPT-F) is not significantly correlated with face recognition ability measured by the Cambridge Face Memory Test (CFMT)
original_authors: Richler JJ; Floyd RJ; Gauthier I.
original_title: The Vanderbilt Holistic Face Processing Test: A short and reliable measure of holistic face processing
replication_authors: Richler JJ; Floyd RJ; Gauthier I.
replication_title: About-face on face recognition ability and holistic processing
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Experiment 1 replicated the previous finding that holistic processing measured in the VHPT-F is not correlated with face recognition ability measured by the CFMT (Richler et al., 2014).' They used a modified version of the VHPT-F with a modified set of conditions, replicating the null correlation (r = 0.042, p = 0.67, n = 109) originally found in Richler et al. (2014).

description: Adapting to a set of female faces causes a previously gender-neutral face to appear male (and vice versa), demonstrating that face adaptation produces shifts in categorical boundaries for facial properties such as gender and ethnicity
original_authors: Michael A. Webster; Daniel Kaping; Yoko Mizokami; Paul Duhamel
original_title: Adaptation to natural facial categories
replication_authors: Minna Ng; Geoffrey M. Boynton; Ione Fine
replication_title: Face adaptation does not improve performance on search or discrimination tasks
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated this experiment to demonstrate that adaptation causes a shift in categorical perception' (Experiment 1). They found significant adaptation effects for all subjects under all three adaptation conditions (local, remote, contingent), with t-tests all p < .0001, confirming the original finding of categorical boundary shifts.

description: A genome-wide linkage scan in a large four-generation Caucasian pedigree identified a novel keratoconus susceptibility locus on chromosome 5q14.3-q21.1 (LOD = 3.53)
original_authors: Yongming G. Tang; Yaron S. Rabinowitz; Kent D. Taylor; Xiaohui Li; Mingshu Hu; Yoana Picornell; Huiying Yang
original_title: Genomewide linkage scan in a multigeneration Caucasian pedigree identifies a novel locus for keratoconus on chromosome 5q14.3-q21.1
original_journal: Genetics in Medicine : Official Journal of the American College of Medical Genetics
replication_authors: Luigi Bisceglia; Patrizia De Bonis; Costantina Pizzicoli; Lucia Fischetti; Antonio Laborante; Michele Di Perna; Francesco Giuliani; Nicola Delle Noci; Luca Buzzonetti; Leopoldo Zelante
replication_title: Linkage Analysis in Keratoconus: Replication of Locus 5q21.2 and Identification of Other Suggestive Loci
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results provide the first evidence of linkage replication on the 5q21.2 region,' identifying overlapping linkage peaks (NPL = 2.73, p = 0.003669) with the original Tang et al. locus. The paper's title itself announces 'Replication of Locus 5q21.2.'

description: SNP rs6885224 in the noncoding region of CTNND2 is associated with high myopia, with the minor allele C acting as a risk allele
original_authors: Yi-Ju Li; Liang Goh; Chiea-Chuen Khor; Qiao Fan; Miao Yu; Siyu Han; Xueling Sim; Rick Twee-Hee Ong; Tien-Yin Wong; Eranga Nishanthie Vithana; Eric Yap; Hideo Nakanishi; Fumihiko Matsuda; Kyoko Ohno-Matsui; Nagahisa Yoshimura; Mark Seielstad; E.-Shyong Tai; Terri L. Young; Seang-Mei Saw
original_title: Genome-wide association studies reveal genetic variants in CTNND2 for high myopia in Singapore Chinese
replication_authors: Boyu Lu; Dan Jiang; Panfeng Wang; Yang Gao; Wenmin Sun; Xueshan Xiao; Shiqiang Li; Xiaoyun Jia; Xiangming Guo; Qingjiong Zhang
replication_title: Replication Study SupportsCTNND2as a Susceptibility Gene for High Myopia
explanation: The replication confirmed a statistically significant association between rs6885224 and high myopia (allele P = 5.29E-6), but the direction was opposite: the minor allele C was protective in this study, whereas it was a risk allele in the original. The authors explicitly state: 'the effect direction of the minor allele at rs6885224 was in the opposite direction compared with the original study.'

description: SNP rs12716080 in the noncoding region of CTNND2 is associated with high myopia in Singapore Chinese
original_authors: Yi-Ju Li; Liang Goh; Chiea-Chuen Khor; Qiao Fan; Miao Yu; Siyu Han; Xueling Sim; Rick Twee-Hee Ong; Tien-Yin Wong; Eranga Nishanthie Vithana; Eric Yap; Hideo Nakanishi; Fumihiko Matsuda; Kyoko Ohno-Matsui; Nagahisa Yoshimura; Mark Seielstad; E.-Shyong Tai; Terri L. Young; Seang-Mei Saw
original_title: Genome-wide association studies reveal genetic variants in CTNND2 for high myopia in Singapore Chinese
replication_authors: Boyu Lu; Dan Jiang; Panfeng Wang; Yang Gao; Wenmin Sun; Xueshan Xiao; Shiqiang Li; Xiaoyun Jia; Xiangming Guo; Qingjiong Zhang
replication_title: Replication Study SupportsCTNND2as a Susceptibility Gene for High Myopia
explanation: The replication found no significant association between rs12716080 and either high myopia or moderate myopia (allele P = 0.366 for high myopia vs. controls). The authors report: 'The other SNP, rs12716080, showed no significant differences either between high myopia and controls or between moderate myopia and controls.'

description: Specific SNP associations (including rs476141 and rs10521145) identified in a genome-wide association study meta-analysis are associated with severe diabetic retinopathy in Caucasian type 1 diabetic subjects
original_authors: Grassi MA; Tikhomirov A.; Ramalingam S.; Below JE; Cox NJ; Nicolae DL
original_title: Genome-wide meta-analysis for severe diabetic retinopathy
replication_authors: Grassi MA; Tikhomirov A.; Ramalingam S.; Lee KE; Hosseini SM; Klein BE; Klein R.; Lussier YA; Cox NJ; Nicolae DL
replication_title: Replication Analysis for Severe Diabetic Retinopathy
explanation: The paper explicitly states it attempts to 'replicate the top SNP associations from a previous GWAS.' No associations reached genome-wide significance (threshold 5×10⁻⁸), the top prior association (rs476141) had an OR in the opposite direction in the replication cohort, and rs10521145 'failed to replicate (P = 0.631)'.

description: Multiple SNPs (particularly rs1073203 in the AKT3-ZNF238 region) are significantly associated with severe diabetic retinopathy in type 1 diabetes patients
original_authors: Grassi MA; Tikhomirov A.; Ramalingam S.; Below JE; Cox NJ; Nicolae DL
original_title: Genome-wide meta-analysis for severe diabetic retinopathy
replication_authors: Annie K. McAuley; Jie Jin Wang; Mohamed Dirani; Paul P. Connell; Ecosse Lamoureux; Alex W. Hewitt
replication_title: Replication of Genetic Loci Implicated in Diabetic Retinopathy
explanation: The authors found nominal allelic and dominant genotypic association for rs1073203 with DR (p=0.012 and p=0.005 respectively), and explicitly state 'Our study has replicated two loci (rs1073203 and rs4838605) that are nominally associated with the advance stages of DR.' However, no variant survived Bonferroni correction (threshold p=0.002), and the authors themselves describe the associations as 'nominal' and conclude 'some ongoing research may be warranted.'

description: Multiple SNPs across five loci (MYSM1, PLXDC2, ARHGAP22, HS6ST3, and C5orf36) are significantly associated with diabetic retinopathy in an Asian-Taiwanese cohort with type 2 diabetes, with rs4838605 in ARHGAP22 associated specifically with proliferative DR
original_authors: Yu-Chuen Huang; Jane-Ming Lin; Hui-Ju Lin; Ching-Chu Chen; Shih-Yin Chen; Chang-Hai Tsai; Fuu-Jen Tsai
original_title: Genome-wide association study of diabetic retinopathy in a Taiwanese population
replication_authors: Annie K. McAuley; Jie Jin Wang; Mohamed Dirani; Paul P. Connell; Ecosse Lamoureux; Alex W. Hewitt
replication_title: Replication of Genetic Loci Implicated in Diabetic Retinopathy
explanation: The authors found a nominal additive genotypic association for rs4838605 with DR (p=0.047, OR=1.650), and state 'Our study confirmed an association for rs4838605 with DR as identified previously in the Taiwanese DR study.' However, this did not survive Bonferroni correction, and the authors use hedging language noting that ongoing research 'may be warranted' for the nominally significant loci.

description: Genome-wide association study identifying multiple SNPs and genes (including GJD2, RASGRF1, BICC1, KCNQ5, BMP3, PRSS56, LAMA2, TOX, RDH5, and others) significantly associated with refractive error and myopia across Caucasian and Asian populations
original_authors: Verhoeven VJ; Hysi PG; Wojciechowski R.; Fan Q.; Guggenheim JA; Höhn R.; Macgregor S.; Hewitt AW; Nag A.; Cheng CY; Yonova-Doing E.; Zhou X.; Ikram MK; Buitendijk GH; McMahon G.; Kemp JP; Pourcain BS; Simpson CL; Mäkelä KM; Lehtimäki T.; Kähönen M.; Paterson AD; Hosseini SM; Wong HS; Xu L.; Jonas JB; Pärssinen O.; Wedenoja J.; Yip SP; Ho DW; Pang CP; Chen LJ; Burdon KP; Craig JE; Klein BE; Klein R.; Haller T.; Metspalu A.; Khor CC; Tai ES; Aung T.; Vithana E.; Tay WT; Barathi VA; Chen P.; Li R.; Liao J.; Zheng Y.; Ong RT; Döring A.; Evans DM; Timpson NJ; Verkerk AJ; Meitinger T.; Raitakari O.; Hawthorne F.; Spector TD; Karssen LC; Pirastu M.; Murgia F.; Ang W.; Mishra A.; Montgomery GW; Pennell CE; Cumberland PM; Cotlarciuc I.; Mitchell P.; Wang JJ; Schache M.; Janmahasatian S.; Igo RP Jr; Lass JH; Chew E.; Iyengar SK; Gorgels TG; Rudan I.; Hayward C.; Wright AF; Polasek O.; Vatavuk Z.; Wilson JF; Fleck B.; Zeller T.; Mirshahi A.; Müller C.; Uitterlinden AG; Rivadeneira F.; Vingerling JR; Hofman A.; Oostra BA; Amin N.; Bergen AA; Teo YY; Rahi JS; Vitart V.; Williams C.; Baird PN; Wong TY; Oexle K.; Pfeiffer N.; Mackey DA; Young TL; van Duijn CM; Saw SM; Bailey-Wilson JE; Stambolian D.; Klaver CC; Hammond CJ
original_title: Genome-wide meta-analyses of multiancestry cohorts identify multiple new susceptibility loci for refractive error and myopia
replication_authors: Munemitsu Yoshikawa; Kenji Yamashiro; Masahiro Miyake; Maho Oishi; Yumiko Akagi-Kurashige; Kyoko Kumagai; Isao Nakata; Hideo Nakanishi; Akio Oishi; Norimoto Gotoh; Ryo Yamada; Fumihiko Matsuda; Nagahisa Yoshimura
replication_title: Comprehensive Replication of the Relationship Between Myopia-Related Genes and Refractive Errors in a Large Japanese Cohort
explanation: The authors replicated the CREAM GWAS findings (Verhoeven et al. 2013) in a Japanese cohort. Of the 51 genes examined, 15 showed significant associations, including all key CREAM-reported genes like GJD2, RASGRF1, BICC1, and KCNQ5. However, 4 genes (PRSS56, LAMA2, TOX, RDH5) that 'consistently showed significant associations throughout the two previous GWASs' could not be replicated, making the overall result mixed.

description: Genome-wide association study using survival analysis for age of myopia onset in Caucasians, identifying genes including LRRC4C, B4GALNT2, QKI, BMP4, SFRP1, SH3GL2, EHBP1L1, and PRSS56 as associated with myopia
original_authors: Amy K. Kiefer; Joyce Y. Tung; Chuong B. Do; David A. Hinds; Joanna L. Mountain; Uta Francke; Nicholas Eriksson
original_title: Genome-wide analysis points to roles for extracellular matrix remodeling, the visual cycle, and neuronal development in myopia
replication_authors: Munemitsu Yoshikawa; Kenji Yamashiro; Masahiro Miyake; Maho Oishi; Yumiko Akagi-Kurashige; Kyoko Kumagai; Isao Nakata; Hideo Nakanishi; Akio Oishi; Norimoto Gotoh; Ryo Yamada; Fumihiko Matsuda; Nagahisa Yoshimura
replication_title: Comprehensive Replication of the Relationship Between Myopia-Related Genes and Refractive Errors in a Large Japanese Cohort
explanation: The authors replicated the 23andMe GWAS (Kiefer et al. 2013) findings in a Japanese cohort. Among the 22 genes identified only in the 23andMe dataset and not yet examined in Asian samples, 7 were replicated (LRRC4C, QKI, BMP4, SFRP1, SH3GL2, B4GALNT2, EHBP1L1). However, several other 23andMe-identified genes including PRSS56 could not be replicated, and the original study used Caucasian subjects only, making this a cross-ethnic extension with mixed results.

description: Perceived facial similarity and kinship judgments of child face pairs encapsulate the same information — similarity ratings are little more than a graded kin recognition signal
original_authors: Laurence T. Maloney; Maria F. Dal Martello
original_title: Kin recognition and the perceived facial similarity of children
replication_authors: Florian Hansen; Lisa M. DeBruine; Iris J. Holzleitner; Anthony J. Lee; Kieran J. O'Shea; Vanessa Fasolt
replication_title: Kin recognition and perceived facial similarity
explanation: The authors conclude 'we replicated Maloney and Dal Martello's (2006) finding that kinship and similarity ratings are highly correlated,' finding a comparable correlation coefficient of r=0.93 (vs. r=0.92 in the original) and no significant difference in task accuracy between the kinship and similarity tasks.

description: Kinship judgments are more accurate than similarity ratings for discriminating adult siblings of different sex, because similarity judgments of opposite-sex adult pairs are partly driven by sex difference cues unrelated to kinship
original_authors: DeBruine LM; Smith FG; Jones BC; Roberts SC; Petrie M.; Spector TD
original_title: Kin recognition signals in adult faces
replication_authors: Florian Hansen; Lisa M. DeBruine; Iris J. Holzleitner; Anthony J. Lee; Kieran J. O'Shea; Vanessa Fasolt
replication_title: Kin recognition and perceived facial similarity
explanation: The current study found no significant difference in task accuracy between similarity and kinship tasks, and found that sex differences affected both tasks equally — directly contrary to DeBruine et al.'s (2009) key finding. The authors explicitly state 'we found that the effect of sex was the same on similarity and on kinship judgments, contrary to DeBruine et al (2009).'

description: Observers freely viewing hundreds of complex scenes show large and consistent individual differences in fixation tendencies towards objects from semantic categories (faces, text, motion, taste, touched), which are stable across images and time
original_authors: de Haas B.; Iakovidis AL; Schwarzkopf DS; Gegenfurtner KR
original_title: Individual differences in visual salience vary along semantic dimensions
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Marcel Linka; Benjamin de Haas
replication_title: OSIEshort: A small stimulus set can reliably estimate individual differences in semantic salience
explanation: The abstract explicitly states 'The first session replicated the large and consistent individual differences along five semantic dimensions observed in the original study.' The Discussion confirms: 'they corroborate the finding of reliable individual differences in gaze behavior reported by de Haas et al. (2019). Individual differences in visual exploration and systematic fixation biases towards a set of semantic features replicated for both, dwell time and first fixations.'

description: Perception of the Kanizsa illusory triangle elicits both enhanced neural activity in early visual cortex neurons with receptive fields overlapping the illusory shape, and suppressed neural activity in neurons whose receptive fields overlap with the Pac-Men inducers
original_authors: Peter Kok; Floris P. de Lange
original_title: Shape perception simultaneously up-and downregulates neural activity in the primary visual cortex
replication_authors: Chuyao Yan; Alexis Pérez-Bellido; Floris P. de Lange
replication_title: Amodal completion instead of predictive coding can explain activity suppression of early visual cortex during illusory shape perception
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In the circles condition, we replicated earlier findings (Kok & de Lange, 2014; Utzerath et al., 2019), that is, enhanced early visual activity in neurons that have their receptive field overlapping with the illusory shape, and suppressed activity in the neurons that had receptive fields overlapping with the inducers during illusion perception.' The replication used a modified version of the original paradigm with an added circles/no-circles manipulation but preserved the core fMRI Kanizsa illusion design.

description: Observers averaging motion directions in skewed feature distributions show systematic biases toward the mode, consistent with robust averaging (rather than arithmetic averaging), with biases growing as mode-mean distance increases
original_authors: Tianyuan Teng; Sheng Li; Hang Zhang
original_title: The virtual loss function in the summary perception of motion and its limited adjustability
replication_authors: Aleksei U. Iakovlev; Igor S. Utochkin
replication_title: Ensemble averaging: What can we learn from skewed feature distributions?
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated systematic skew-related biases in another feature domain, namely, orientation averaging' and 'we replicated the systematic biases toward the mode in all of our experiments.' Experiment 1 (lab, n=12) found a significant positive slope of the bias-skew function (slope = 0.09, t(11) = 5.04, p < 0.001), consistent with Teng et al. (2021)'s motion averaging finding, though in a different feature domain (orientation instead of motion direction).

description: Observers averaging motion directions in skewed feature distributions show systematic biases toward the mode, consistent with robust averaging, with biases growing as mode-mean distance increases
original_authors: Tianyuan Teng; Sheng Li; Hang Zhang
original_title: The virtual loss function in the summary perception of motion and its limited adjustability
replication_authors: Aleksei U. Iakovlev; Igor S. Utochkin
replication_title: Ensemble averaging: What can we learn from skewed feature distributions?
explanation: Experiment 2 was an online replication of Experiment 1 (itself a conceptual replication of Teng et al. in orientation domain) with naive observers. A significant positive slope was found (slope = 0.05, t(48) = 2.65, p < 0.01), confirming the mode-bias effect. The authors conclude 'we again observed a bias toward the mode increasing with the mode-mean distance.'

description: Observers averaging motion directions in skewed feature distributions show systematic biases toward the mode, consistent with robust averaging, with biases growing as mode-mean distance increases
original_authors: Tianyuan Teng; Sheng Li; Hang Zhang
original_title: The virtual loss function in the summary perception of motion and its limited adjustability
replication_authors: Aleksei U. Iakovlev; Igor S. Utochkin
replication_title: Ensemble averaging: What can we learn from skewed feature distributions?
explanation: Experiment 3 tested orientation averaging with differently shaped distributions than Experiments 1 and 2, but the same mode-mean distances as Teng et al. (2021). A significant positive slope was found (slope = 0.16, t(45) = 4.54, p < 0.001), and crucially the slope was steeper with the new distributions, confirming the distribution-shape dependence of the mode bias.

description: Observers averaging motion directions in skewed feature distributions show systematic biases toward the mode, consistent with robust averaging, with biases growing as mode-mean distance increases
original_authors: Tianyuan Teng; Sheng Li; Hang Zhang
original_title: The virtual loss function in the summary perception of motion and its limited adjustability
replication_authors: Aleksei U. Iakovlev; Igor S. Utochkin
replication_title: Ensemble averaging: What can we learn from skewed feature distributions?
explanation: Experiment 4 used a novel paradigm where observers matched the mean of a sample distribution using a probe distribution (rather than a single item), with both having skewed or symmetric distributions. The bias grew significantly as a function of test-sample mode distance (slope = 0.11, t(44) = 3.94, p < 0.001), consistent with the mode-bias effect reported by Teng et al. (2021).

description: Increasing blank duration between a prime and probe stimulus reduces the strength of flash suppression (i.e., shorter blank durations produce stronger flash suppression effects)
original_authors: Jeremy M. Wolfe
original_title: Reversing ocular dominance and suppression in a single flash
replication_authors: Lisa Beckmann; Thomas Schenk; Karin Ludwig
replication_title: When contexts collide: Spatial context prevails over temporal context in binocular rivalry
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'These results are in line with findings by Wolfe (1984).' In Experiment 1 baseline, they confirm that shorter blank durations result in stronger flash suppression effects, as evidenced by a significantly better model fit including blank duration, χ²(3) = 119.27, p < 0.001.

description: Decreasing probe duration (test flash duration) reduces the strength of flash suppression, similar to the effect of decreasing blank duration
original_authors: Jeremy M. Wolfe
original_title: Reversing ocular dominance and suppression in a single flash
replication_authors: Lisa Beckmann; Thomas Schenk; Karin Ludwig
replication_title: When contexts collide: Spatial context prevails over temporal context in binocular rivalry
explanation: The authors report: 'Surprisingly, the probe duration model did not provide a significantly better fit, LRT: χ²(3) = 6.21, p = 0.102,' and conclude 'we could not replicate the effect of probe duration on the participants' perception.' Percepts in line with flash suppression were similarly frequent across all probe duration conditions.

description: The surrounding spatial context (annulus) biases binocular rivalry toward the non-matching grating, and this surround inhibition effect is stronger when the surrounding annulus has higher contrast
original_authors: Lisa Beckmann; Thomas Schenk; Karin Ludwig
original_title: Measuring the influence of contrast, ambiguity, and side of spatial context on perceptual dominance during binocular rivalry
replication_authors: Lisa Beckmann; Thomas Schenk; Karin Ludwig
replication_title: When contexts collide: Spatial context prevails over temporal context in binocular rivalry
explanation: The authors successfully replicate their own prior finding across both experiments. In Experiment 1, the surround contrast effect was significant (χ²(1) = 72.63, p < 0.001), and in Experiment 2 it was again significant (χ²(1) = 116.33, p < 0.001, R²McFadden = 0.101), with the authors stating 'we could replicate the SI baseline results from Experiment 1 and previous research (Beckmann et al., 2025; Paffen et al., 2006).'

description: Societies with more corporate political strategies (broader political participation) are more resilient to catastrophic climate-related disasters, while societal tightness (strong social norms) does not predict resilience to such disasters
original_authors: Peregrine, Peter N.
original_title: Social resilience to climate-related disasters in ancient societies: A test of two hypotheses
replication_authors: Peter N. Peregrine
replication_title: Social Resilience to Climate Change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age: A Replication Study
explanation: The author explicitly states 'this study does appear to be a successful replication,' finding support for Hypothesis 1 (corporate political strategies correlate with resilience, SCI r=0.465, p<0.020) and rejection of Hypothesis 2 (societal tightness), consistent with the original study, using a new sample of 20 societies that experienced the Late Antique Little Ice Age.

description: MMPI scales (LRS-F for women, LRS-M for men) can accurately predict antidepressant response to lithium in depressed patients
original_authors: Edward F. Donnelly; Frederick K. Goodwin; Ivan N. Waldman
original_title: Prediction of antidepressant response to lithium
replication_title: Replication of "Prediction of antidepressant response to lithium": problems in generalizing to a clinical setting
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the LRS-M and the LRS-F did not successfully predict antidepressant response and nonresponse.' All four replication conditions showed proportions of accurate predictions far below significance thresholds, and the paper's title itself announces failure to replicate.

description: Chronic schizophrenic patients exhibit lower frontal/posterior ratios and lower absolute frontal rates of cerebral glucose metabolism compared to normal control subjects as measured by PET
original_authors: T. Farkas; A. Wolf; J. Jaeger; J. Brodie; D. Christman; J. Fowler; R. Macgregor; M. deLeon; P. Defina; Alan I. Goldman; Y. Yonekura; A. Brill; Melvin S. Schwartz; J. Logan; R. Cancro
original_title: Regional brain glucose metabolism in chronic schizophrenia
replication_title: Low frontal glucose utilization in chronic schizophrenia: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These data replicate our earlier findings (1, 2) that schizophrenic subjects have lower frontal/posterior ratios and lower absolute frontal rates of glucose metabolism.' The frontal/posterior ratios were significantly lower in schizophrenic patients (p=0.02 left, p=0.03 right), and the methods were described as 'identical to those described earlier (1, 2)'.

description: Chronic schizophrenic patients exhibit lower frontal/posterior ratios and lower absolute frontal rates of cerebral glucose metabolism compared to normal control subjects as measured by PET
original_authors: Adam Wolkin; Judith Jaeger; Jonathan D. Brodie; A. Wolf; Joanna S. Fowler; John Rotrosen; F. Gomez-Mont; Robert Cancro
original_title: Persistence of cerebral metabolic abnormalities in chronic schizophrenia as determined by positron emission tomography
replication_title: Low frontal glucose utilization in chronic schizophrenia: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These data replicate our earlier findings (1, 2) that schizophrenic subjects have lower frontal/posterior ratios and lower absolute frontal rates of glucose metabolism. The average frontal/posterior ratios in the normal and the schizophrenic subjects were quite similar to those in our earlier report (2).' Methods were described as identical to the earlier studies.

description: High levels of expressed emotion (particularly family criticism) predict higher rates of relapse in depressed patients
original_authors: Jill M. Hooley; John Orley; John D. Teasdale
original_title: Levels of expressed emotion and relapse in depressed patients
replication_title: Expressed emotion, perceived criticism, and relapse in depression: a replication in an Egyptian community
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our results also replicate the earlier finding that the more a family is critical of the patient, the higher the risk of relapse.' The family criticism-relapse association was statistically significant (p<0.0003), confirming the core finding, though the optimal cutoff score (7) was higher than in Western studies (2-3).

description: Patient perception of family criticism (perceived criticism) predicts relapse in unipolar depressed patients
original_authors: Jill M. Hooley; John D. Teasdale
original_title: Predictors of relapse in unipolar depressives: expressed emotion, marital distress and perceived criticism
replication_title: Expressed emotion, perceived criticism, and relapse in depression: a replication in an Egyptian community
explanation: The authors clearly state 'our expectation about the utility of perception of criticism as a predictor of relapse was not supported' and 'no association between perceived criticism and relapse was detected.' The perceived criticism scale showed no statistically significant association with relapse, leading to a clear failure to replicate this specific effect.

description: Symptoms of complicated grief are distinct from symptoms of bereavement-related depression and anxiety, forming a separable dimension of emotional distress in elderly bereaved spouses
original_authors: Prigerson, Holly G.; Frank, Ellen; Kasl, Stanislav V.; Reynolds, Charles F. III; Anderson, Barbara; Zubenko, George S.; Houck, Patricia R.; George, Charles J.; Kupfer, David J.
original_title: Complicated grief and bereavement-related depression as distinct disorders: preliminary empirical validation in elderly bereaved spouses
replication_title: Complicated grief as a disorder distinct from bereavement-related depression and anxiety: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were able to replicate in a larger, independent, community-based group of mid- to late-life widowed individuals the coexistence of three distinct symptom dimensions—complicated grief, bereavement-related depression, and bereavement-related anxiety.' All complicated grief items loaded highly on the complicated grief factor and very poorly on the depression and anxiety factors, replicating the original pattern.

description: Gradual discontinuation of lithium treatment (over 2-4 weeks) results in a much longer time to recurrence of affective symptoms compared to rapid discontinuation (under 2 weeks) in patients with bipolar disorder
original_authors: Faedda, G.; Tondo, L.; Baldessarini, R.; Suppes, T.; Tohen, M.
original_title: Outcome after rapid vs gradual discontinuation of lithium treatment in bipolar mood disorders
replication_title: Reduced morbidity after gradual discontinuation of lithium treatment for bipolar I and II disorders: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The present findings with a new group of patients replicate initial observations suggesting that rapid and gradual discontinuation of lithium are followed by clinically significant, and somewhat predictable, differences in morbidity.' The replication found a 5.6:1 ratio of median survival times (gradual vs. rapid), consistent with the original's 4.7:1 ratio.

description: Thalamic N-acetylaspartate (NAA) concentrations are significantly reduced in patients with schizophrenia relative to healthy controls, and there is a significant positive correlation between left and right thalamic NAA measures in schizophrenic patients
original_authors: Raymond F. Deicken; Camilla Johnson; Yael Eliaz; Norbert Schuff
original_title: Reduced concentrations of thalamic N-acetylaspartate in male patients with schizophrenia
replication_authors: Gabriele Ende; Dieter F. Braus; Sigrid Walter; Fritz A. Henn
replication_title: Lower Concentration of Thalamic N-Acetylaspartate in Patients With Schizophrenia: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we have corroborated the finding of lower NAA concentrations in carefully selected voxels of the mediodorsal region of the thalamus in schizophrenic patients' and 'We also replicated the second finding reported by Deicken et al. (3) of a significant correlation between right and left thalamic NAA measures in patients with schizophrenia.' The NAA group difference was significant (F=19.5, df=1, 28, p < 0.001).

description: Concentrations of choline-containing compounds are significantly lower in the thalamus of patients with schizophrenia compared to healthy subjects
original_authors: Masao Omori; Tetsuhito Murata; Hirohiko Kimura; Yoshio Koshimoto; Hirotsugu Kado; Yoshiyuki Ishimori; Harumi Ito; Yuji Wada
original_title: Thalamic abnormalities in patients with schizophrenia revealed by proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy
replication_authors: Gabriele Ende; Dieter F. Braus; Sigrid Walter; Fritz A. Henn
replication_title: Lower Concentration of Thalamic N-Acetylaspartate in Patients With Schizophrenia: A Replication Study
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Result 'success' is well-supported — the present study found significantly lower thalamic choline concentrations in schizophrenia (F=8.6, p=0.007), consistent with Omori et al.'s finding. However, replication_type changed from 'direct' to 'close experiment' because Omori et al. used choline/creatine ratios while this study used absolute choline concentrations (corrected for coil loading), a meaningfully different quantification approach. Confidence kept at medium: the paper cites Omori et al.'s choline finding in the Introduction and measures choline as a planned outcome, but the Discussion does not explicitly frame this as a replication of Omori et al. — it presents the choline result as an additional finding ('These results are accompanied by...') rather than a targeted replication. The replication relationship is implicit but not strongly stated by the authors.

description: The prevalence of somatic depression (major depression with appetite disturbance, sleep disturbance, and fatigue) is much higher among women than men, while pure depression (without those somatic symptoms) shows much smaller gender differences
original_authors: Brett Silverstein
original_title: Gender difference in the prevalence of clinical depression: the role played by depression associated with somatic symptoms
replication_authors: Brett Silverstein
replication_title: Gender Differences in the Prevalence of Somatic Versus Pure Depression: A Replication
explanation: The replication successfully reproduced the key findings using a different large U.S. survey dataset (ECA vs. National Comorbidity Survey). The authors explicitly state: 'As in the earlier analysis of the National Comorbidity Survey, female respondents had twice the prevalence of somatic depression as male respondents (2.8% versus 1.4%) but a much smaller difference in prevalence in pure depression,' and the Discussion notes 'This is the fifth sample... in which the gender difference in depression was found to result primarily from a difference in somatic depression.'

description: The short allele of the 5-HTTLPR serotonin transporter gene moderates the influence of childhood maltreatment and stressful life events on risk of depression (gene-environment interaction)
original_authors: Caspi, Avshalom; Sugden, Karen; Moffitt, Terrie E.; Taylor, Alan; Craig, Ian W.; Harrington, HonaLee; McClay, Joseph; Mill, Jonathan; Martin, Judy; Braithwaite, Antony; Poulton, Richie
original_title: Influence of life stress on depression: moderation by a polymorphism in the 5-HTT gene
replication_authors: Thiago Botter-Maio Rocha; Mara H. Hutz; Angélica Salatino-Oliveira; Júlia P. Genro; Guilherme V. Polanczyk; João Ricardo Sato; Fernando C. Wehrmeister; Fernando C. Barros; Ana M.B. Menezes; Luis Augusto Rohde; Luciana Anselmi; Christian Kieling
replication_title: Gene-Environment Interaction in Youth Depression: Replication of the 5-HTTLPR Moderation in a Diverse Setting
explanation: The supplementary material explicitly states 'our analysis followed the multiplicative model adopted by Caspi et al. in 2003, and further corroborated the existence of an interaction,' and further notes that 'we therefore identified evidence of GxE on both multiplicative and additive scales in our sample.' The replication was conducted in a diverse Brazilian youth cohort (n=2,392), a different population and setting from the original.

description: Panic disorder patients with depersonalization/derealization (PD+) show a paradoxical increase of delta rhythms in temporal lobe EEG during olfactory stimulation, while panic patients without temporal lobe symptomatology (PD-) show stable or decreased slow activities like normal subjects
original_authors: Locatelli, Marco; Bellodi, Laura; Perna, Giampaolo; Scarone, Silvio
original_title: EEG power modifications in panic disorder during a temporolimbic activation task: relationships with temporal lobe clinical symptomatology
original_journal: Journal of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences
replication_title: Temporal lobe involvement in panic disorder: results of a replication study
replication_journal: The Journal of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Present data cannot support the hypothesis, suggested by our previous findings, of a temporal lobe involvement in a homogeneous subgroup of panic patients who share clinical symptoms and temporal lobe EEG pattern of response to specific conditions.' The replication found no statistically significant differences in EEG modifications during olfactory stimulation across the three groups, in contrast to the original finding of differential delta rhythm responses.

description: Staff injury rates and characteristics resulting from inpatient patient violence at a state psychiatric hospital, including injury rates by staff category and patterns by time of day and body location
original_authors: Harold Carmel; Mel Hunter
original_title: Staff injuries from inpatient violence
replication_authors: Ronald H. Hanson; Jonathan A. Balk
replication_title: A Replication Study of Staff Injuries in a State Hospital
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This study replicated the one by Carmel and Hunter,' using the same OSHA injury definition and staff category framework. Results were mixed: some findings were 'remarkably similar' (e.g., registered nurse injury rates, head injury patterns, weekday patterns) while others differed notably (senior technician injury rates were twice as high at AMRTC, time-of-day patterns for containment injuries differed, and injured staff at AMRTC had longer tenure unlike the Carmel and Hunter finding of recently-hired staff).

description: Converting a rehabilitative day treatment program to a supported employment program improves competitive employment rates among clients with severe mental disorders, particularly among former day treatment attendees, without adverse effects
original_authors: Robert E. Drake; Deborah R. Becker; Jeremy C. Biesanz; William C. Torrey; Gregory J. McHugo; Philip F. Wyzik
original_title: Rehabilitative day treatment vs supported employment: I. Vocational outcomes
replication_title: Day treatment versus supported employment for persons with severe mental illness: a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This replication of our earlier study provides further evidence that converting a rehabilitative day treatment program to an assertive supported employment program can improve vocational adjustment without increasing negative outcomes among clients with severe mental disorders.' The replication occurred in a different city with a lower employment rate and lower baseline employment among clients, but findings were similar to the original.

description: A brief CBT-based guided self-help (CBT-GSH) intervention significantly improved binge eating abstinence and eating pathology outcomes compared to usual care in female HMO members
original_authors: Striegel-Moore RH; Wilson GT; DeBar L.; Perrin N.; Lynch F.; Rosselli F.; Kraemer HC
original_title: Cognitive behavioral guided self-help for the treatment of recurrent binge eating
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: DeBar LL; Striegel-Moore RH; Wilson GT; Perrin N.; Yarborough BJ; Dickerson J.; Lynch F.; Rosselli F.; Kraemer HC
replication_title: Guided Self-Help Treatment for Recurrent Binge Eating: Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'this study replicated and extended the findings from our earlier study (23)' and 'Replication of the pattern of previous findings suggests that CBT-GSH is a robust treatment for patients with recurrent binge eating.' Effect sizes were comparable to or larger than the original, with the same directional pattern of results.

description: A test-retest factorial validity study of the Piers-Harris Children's Self Concept Scale reveals factorial instability across two administrations and strong evidence of unidimensionality rather than multidimensionality
original_authors: Marvin R. Platten; Larry R. Williams
original_title: A comparative analysis of the factorial structures of two administrations of the Piers-Harris Children's Self Concept Scale to one group of elementary school children
replication_authors: Marvin R. Platten; Larry R. Williams
replication_title: Replication of a Test-Retest Factorial Validity Study with the Piers-Harris Children's Self Concept Scale
explanation: The abstract explicitly states 'This study largely replicates the findings of a previous study reported by the authors (Platten and Williams, 1979).' The Discussion confirms both key findings were replicated: evidence of factorial instability and unidimensionality, with the authors noting 'Inasmuch as this finding was a replication of the 1979 study, this hypothesis becomes even more plausible.'

description: Intermittent progress monitoring schedules (e.g., two probes every 2 weeks, three probes every 3–6 weeks) are similarly accurate and timely as weekly CBM progress monitoring schedules for identifying students with adequate or inadequate reading growth
original_authors: Joseph Jenkins; Margaret Schulze; Allison Marti; Allen G. Harbaugh
original_title: Curriculum-based measurement of reading growth: Weekly versus intermittent progress monitoring
replication_authors: Samantha A. Gesel; Christopher J. Lemons
replication_title: Comparing Schedules of Progress Monitoring Using Curriculum-Based Measurement in Reading: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly frame this as a conceptual replication and conclude that it replicated the core finding: 'results demonstrated that intermittent PM schedules had greater accuracy and better timeliness compared with weekly PM schedules in almost all incidences, replicating the conclusions asserted by Jenkins et al.' While absolute accuracy rates were lower and it took longer to reach thresholds (9–12 weeks vs. 4–6 weeks), the central conclusion that intermittent schedules are viable alternatives to weekly monitoring was replicated.

description: Ward size and individualization of treatment affect self-rejection stigma among psychiatric inpatients, with smaller wards and peer group involvement reducing self-rejection
original_authors: Mieke Verhaeghe; Piet Bracke
original_title: Ward features affecting stigma experiences in contemporary psychiatric hospitals: A multilevel study
replication_authors: Justine Schneider; Chris Beeley; Kezia Scales; Simon Bailey; Mieke Verhaeghe; Piet Bracke
replication_title: Ward features and stigma experiences of mental health service users in Belgium and England: A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the failure to replicate this finding is likely to be due to the large difference in time spent as inpatients in each country' and 'the failure of this study to replicate the Belgian findings may be explained by differences in treatment approaches between the two countries.' Neither ward size nor individualized care proved significant in the English sample.

description: Hofstede's four indexes of national culture (Individualism-Collectivism, Power Distance, Masculinity-Femininity, Uncertainty Avoidance) derived from IBM employee surveys differentiate countries on stable cultural dimensions
original_authors: Geert Hofstede
original_title: Culture's consequences: International differences in work-related values
replication_authors: Ashleigh Merritt
replication_title: Culture in the Cockpit
explanation: The direct replication using Hofstede's exact items and formulae found significant correlations for Power Distance (r=.74) and Individualism-Collectivism (r=.67), but not for Masculinity-Femininity (r=.23) or Uncertainty Avoidance (r=.31), representing partial replication success.

description: Hofstede's four indexes of national culture (Individualism-Collectivism, Power Distance, Masculinity-Femininity, Uncertainty Avoidance) derived from IBM employee surveys differentiate countries on stable cultural dimensions
original_authors: Geert Hofstede
original_title: Culture's consequences: International differences in work-related values
replication_authors: Ashleigh Merritt
replication_title: Culture in the Cockpit
explanation: The conceptual replication removing item equivalence constraints found significant correlations for all four indexes (IND .96, PD .87, MAS .75, UA .68), and the paper's conclusion states 'the study confirms that the effects of national culture can be seen over and above the professional pilot culture.'

description: College students classified as learning disabled (LD) who received course substitutions for the foreign language requirement show few significant cognitive and achievement differences when grouped by levels of IQ-achievement discrepancy, FL aptitude (MLAT), phonological/orthographic processing, and FL course performance
original_authors: Sparks, Richard L.; Philips, Lois; Ganschow, Leonore; Javorsky, James
original_title: Students classified as learning disabled and the college foreign language requirement: A quantitative analysis
replication_authors: Richard L. Sparks; Lois G. Philips; James Javorsky
replication_title: Students Classified as LD Who Received Course Substitutions for the College Foreign Language Requirement
explanation: The authors explicitly state they were 'replicating those previous studies as closely as possible' using a new cohort. The Discussion confirms 'In this study, a large majority of the comparisons also resulted in nonsignificant group differences,' mirroring the pattern in Sparks, Philips, et al. (1999a). Demographic and standardized test profiles were similarly comparable across both studies.

description: Students classified as learning disabled who petitioned for course substitutions for the college foreign language requirement have lower IQ scores, more severe academic achievement difficulties, or different demographic profiles than LD students who fulfilled the FL requirement by passing FL courses
original_authors: Richard L. Sparks; Lois Philips; Leonore Ganschow; James Javorsky
original_title: Comparison of students classified as learning disabled who petitioned for or fulfilled the college foreign language requirement
replication_authors: Richard L. Sparks; Lois Philips; James Javorsky
replication_title: Students Classified as LD Who Petitioned for or Fulfilled the College Foreign Language Requirement—Are They Different?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study was designed to replicate a smaller study at the same university conducted by Sparks et al. (1999a).' In the Discussion, they confirm: 'these results replicate those obtained by Sparks et al. (1999a) with a smaller population of petition and nonpetition students at the same university,' finding no significant differences between petition and nonpetition groups on cognitive and achievement measures (with IQ as covariate).

description: Three independent neuropsychological subtypes of dyslexia can be empirically identified: a primary linguistic type, an articulo-graphomotor type, and a visuo-perceptual type
original_authors: Steven Mattis; Joseph H. French; Isabelle Rapin
original_title: Dyslexia in children and young adults: three independent neuropsychological syndromes
replication_authors: Otfried Spreen; Robert G. Haaf
replication_title: Empirically Derived Learning Disability Subtypes: A Replication Attempt and Longitudinal Patterns Over 15 Years
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The main purpose of this study, a replication of previously described types of LD, was partially successful.' All three Mattis et al. subtypes were identified in two separate cluster analyses of children aged 8–12, but the linguistic subtype was absent in the adult follow-up sample, yielding a mixed rather than fully confirmatory result.

description: The ACID subtype of learning disability, characterized by low scores on WISC Arithmetic, Coding, Information, and Digit Span subtests with other scores relatively unimpaired, represents a distinct and persistent sequencing disorder
original_authors: Rourke, B.P.; Strang, J.D.
original_title: Subtypes of reading and arithmetical disabilities: a neuropsychological analysis
replication_authors: Otfried Spreen; Robert G. Haaf
replication_title: Empirically Derived Learning Disability Subtypes: A Replication Attempt and Longitudinal Patterns Over 15 Years
explanation: Reviewed. The ACID subtype was found at referral age (19% of sample in a clear ACID cluster) and one corresponding adult cluster was identified (12.4% of sample). However, longitudinal tracing showed only 4 of 17 (23.5%) childhood ACID subjects entered the adult ACID cluster, and a second adult ACID-like cluster consisted largely (75.9%) of control subjects (average learners). The authors explicitly conclude the ACID subtype 'may not persist into adulthood and is specific to middle childhood; alternatively, this subtype may be viewed as common among adults without specific LD history.' This genuine ambiguity — partial cross-sectional replication but poor longitudinal persistence and confounding with non-LD adults — warrants inconclusive with medium confidence.

description: A Forced Choice Recognition (FCR) trial added to the Rey Complex Figure Test (RCFT) can accurately classify valid versus invalid performance in healthy (non-clinical) participants using an experimental malingering paradigm, with high specificity at cutoffs of ≤16 and ≤17
original_authors: Jaspreet K. Rai; Kelly Y. An; Jordan Charles; Sami Ali; Laszlo A. Erdodi
original_title: Introducing a forced choice recognition trial to the Rey Complex Figure Test
replication_authors: Kaitlyn Abeare; Kristoffer Romero; Laura Cutler; Christina D. Sirianni; Laszlo A. Erdodi
replication_title: Flipping the Script: Measuring Both Performance Validity and Cognitive Ability with the Forced Choice Recognition Trial of the RCFT
explanation: The authors conclude that 'the RCFT FCR maintained the same classification accuracy in our clinical sample as had been reported by Rai et al. (2019) in the experimental malingering paradigm,' with comparable specificity (.81-.97 vs .88-.89) and sensitivity (.52-.92 vs .58-.72) at the ≤18 cutoff, and essentially the same AUC (.83) against the WCT. The replication extends the original to a clinical patient population rather than an experimental malingering paradigm.

description: Mixed-handed (MH) individuals outperform consistent right-handers (cRH) in incidental word recognition after semantic (deep) encoding but not after phonemic (shallow) encoding, reflecting a handedness-related advantage tied to level of processing
original_authors: Stephen D. Christman; Michael Butler
original_title: Mixed-handedness advantages in episodic memory obtained under conditions of intentional learning extend to incidental learning
replication_authors: Henriette Johansen; Emilie H. Rusten; René Westerhausen
replication_title: No Incidental Memory Advantage for Mixed Handed vs. Consistent Right Handed Participants: Conflicting Results From Earlier Research
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our study failed to replicate the findings by Christman and Butler (2011).' In both independent samples, the predicted Handedness Group × Encoding Condition interaction was non-significant (all η p² < .03), and using the more appropriate d' measure in the combined sample (N=114) yielded negligible effect sizes (η p² = .005), allowing confident exclusion of substantial population effects.

description: People who first comply with a small request (answering soap-related questions) are more likely to comply with a subsequent large request (allowing workers to inventory household products) than those who received no initial request (foot-in-the-door effect)
original_authors: Jonathan L. Freedman; Scott C. Fraser
original_title: Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Malgorzata Gamian-Wilk; Dariusz Dolinski
replication_title: The Foot-in-the-Door Phenomenon 40 and 50 Years Later: A Direct Replication of the Original Freedman and Fraser Study in Poland and in Ukraine
explanation: In Ukraine in 2003, the FITD was effective: 53.3% compliance in FITD condition vs. 3.3% in control (χ² = 18.47, p < .001, d = 1.33, r = .55), closely reproducing the Freedman & Fraser finding. Authors confirm: 'we showed that the FITD proved effective following the original procedure only in a context similar to the original (thus in Ukraine).'

description: People who first comply with a small request (answering soap-related questions) are more likely to comply with a subsequent large request (allowing workers to inventory household products) than those who received no initial request (foot-in-the-door effect)
original_authors: Jonathan L. Freedman; Scott C. Fraser
original_title: Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Malgorzata Gamian-Wilk; Dariusz Dolinski
replication_title: The Foot-in-the-Door Phenomenon 40 and 50 Years Later: A Direct Replication of the Original Freedman and Fraser Study in Poland and in Ukraine
explanation: In Poland in 2003, the FITD effect was not significant: 5/30 (16.7%) vs. 2/30 (6.7%) in control (χ² = 1.46, p = .2, d = .32, r = .16). Authors state 'the FITD was not effective when the context was different from the original one (thus in Poland).'

description: People who first comply with a small request (answering soap-related questions) are more likely to comply with a subsequent large request (allowing workers to inventory household products) than those who received no initial request (foot-in-the-door effect)
original_authors: Jonathan L. Freedman; Scott C. Fraser
original_title: Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Malgorzata Gamian-Wilk; Dariusz Dolinski
replication_title: The Foot-in-the-Door Phenomenon 40 and 50 Years Later: A Direct Replication of the Original Freedman and Fraser Study in Poland and in Ukraine
explanation: In Ukraine in 2013, zero participants in either condition agreed to perform the target request, producing no FITD effect (χ² = 0). Authors conclude: 'the originally used sequence of requests and the FITD procedure are no longer effective, neither in Poland nor in Ukraine.'

description: People who first comply with a small request (answering soap-related questions) are more likely to comply with a subsequent large request (allowing workers to inventory household products) than those who received no initial request (foot-in-the-door effect)
original_authors: Jonathan L. Freedman; Scott C. Fraser
original_title: Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Malgorzata Gamian-Wilk; Dariusz Dolinski
replication_title: The Foot-in-the-Door Phenomenon 40 and 50 Years Later: A Direct Replication of the Original Freedman and Fraser Study in Poland and in Ukraine
explanation: In Poland in 2013, only 1/30 agreed to target request in FITD condition and 0/30 in control (χ² = 1.02, p = .31, d = .26, r = .13), a non-significant result. Authors confirm the FITD procedure was no longer effective in Poland in 2013.

description: Reflecting on one's interdependence with the natural environment (vs. disconnection) increases environmental commitment
original_authors: Jody L. Davis; Jeffrey D. Green; Allison Reed
original_title: Interdependence with the environment: Commitment, interconnectedness, and environmental behavior
replication_authors: Eric D. Wesselmann; Shane W. Boyd; Jordan A. Arellanes; Alexander Driskell; Matthew S. Hesson-McInnis
replication_title: Manipulating Environmental Commitment: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated Davis et al.'s (2009) basic finding that encouraging individuals to reflect upon their interdependence with the environment increases subsequent commitment.' Study 1 found a significant condition effect on commitment (p = .001, η²p = .08) with N = 139 college students.

description: Reflecting on one's interdependence with the natural environment increases environmental behavioral intentions
original_authors: Jody L. Davis; Jeffrey D. Green; Allison Reed
original_title: Interdependence with the environment: Commitment, interconnectedness, and environmental behavior
replication_authors: Eric D. Wesselmann; Shane W. Boyd; Jordan A. Arellanes; Alexander Driskell; Matthew S. Hesson-McInnis
replication_title: Manipulating Environmental Commitment: A Replication and Extension
explanation: Study 1 found no significant effect on behavioral intentions (p = .721, η²p < .01). The authors explicitly state 'we did not replicate the finding that the interdependence manipulation momentarily increases environmental behavioral intentions.'

description: Reflecting on one's interdependence with the natural environment (vs. disconnection) increases environmental commitment
original_authors: Jody L. Davis; Jeffrey D. Green; Allison Reed
original_title: Interdependence with the environment: Commitment, interconnectedness, and environmental behavior
replication_authors: Eric D. Wesselmann; Shane W. Boyd; Jordan A. Arellanes; Alexander Driskell; Matthew S. Hesson-McInnis
replication_title: Manipulating Environmental Commitment: A Replication and Extension
explanation: In Study 2 with a more diverse online MTURK sample, the authors again replicated the commitment effect: 'Participants in the high condition reported higher commitment than participants in the low condition, p < .001, η²p = .08. Thus, we again replicated the commitment effect in a new sample.'

description: Reflecting on one's interdependence with the natural environment increases environmental behavioral intentions
original_authors: Jody L. Davis; Jeffrey D. Green; Allison Reed
original_title: Interdependence with the environment: Commitment, interconnectedness, and environmental behavior
replication_authors: Eric D. Wesselmann; Shane W. Boyd; Jordan A. Arellanes; Alexander Driskell; Matthew S. Hesson-McInnis
replication_title: Manipulating Environmental Commitment: A Replication and Extension
explanation: In Study 2, the behavioral intentions effect was not statistically significant (p = .051, η²p = .02), and the authors state 'We again failed to replicate the manipulation's effect on behavioral intentions.' The marginal p-value was discussed primarily as a power issue.

description: Inequality in children's reading and math scores grows substantially between the start of kindergarten and end of first grade, with gap growth faster during summer vacations than school years
original_authors: Downey, Douglas B.; von Hippel, Paul T.; Broh, Beckett A.
original_title: Are schools the great equalizer? Cognitive inequality during the summer months and the school year
replication_authors: Paul T. von Hippel; Joseph Workman; Douglas B. Downey
replication_title: Inequality in Reading and Math Skills Forms Mainly before Kindergarten: A Replication, and Partial Correction, of “Are Schools the Great Equalizer?”
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Replication, and Partial Correction' of the 2004 Great Equalizer study. The authors find that the original's key conclusion — that inequality grows substantially after kindergarten — was an artifact of non-interval scale scores. With better-scaled IRT ability scores, inequality actually shrinks rather than grows. However, some seasonal patterns do replicate: total variance grows during most summers and shrinks during most school years, consistent with the original's finding that schools reduce inequality relative to summers. The authors describe this as a partial replication: 'Which conclusions of the original Great Equalizer study stood up to replication and which collapsed?'

description: A two-class latent structure (an 'addicted' group and a 'non-addicted' group) exists for multiple addictions among U.S. alternative high school youth, with highest prevalence on behavioral addictions (Internet, love, exercise) rather than substance addictions
original_authors: Steve Sussman; Thalida Em Arpawong; Ping Sun; Jennifer Tsai; Louise A. Rohrbach; Donna Spruijt-Metz
original_title: Prevalence and co-occurrence of addictive behaviors among former alternative high school youth
replication_authors: Jennifer Tsai; Jimi Huh; Bulat Idrisov; Artur Galimov; Jose P. Espada; María T. Gonzálvez; Steve Sussman
replication_title: Prevalence and Co-Occurrence of Addictive Behaviors Among Russian and Spanish Youth
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The last 30-day prevalence of addictions for Russia and Spain adolescents reported in this study replicated results of the Sussman et al. (2014) study.' The same two-class LCA solution was confirmed in the Russian sample (n=715), with the same 'Work hard, play hard' addicted group pattern (32.2% of the Russian sample), and highest prevalence on Internet, exercise, and love.

description: A two-class latent structure (an 'addicted' group and a 'non-addicted' group) exists for multiple addictions among U.S. alternative high school youth, with highest prevalence on behavioral addictions (Internet, love, exercise) rather than substance addictions
original_authors: Steve Sussman; Thalida Em Arpawong; Ping Sun; Jennifer Tsai; Louise A. Rohrbach; Donna Spruijt-Metz
original_title: Prevalence and co-occurrence of addictive behaviors among former alternative high school youth
replication_authors: Jennifer Tsai; Jimi Huh; Bulat Idrisov; Artur Galimov; Jose P. Espada; María T. Gonzálvez; Steve Sussman
replication_title: Prevalence and Co-Occurrence of Addictive Behaviors Among Russian and Spanish Youth
explanation: The Spanish sample (n=811) also confirmed the two-class LCA solution, with 28.6% classified in the 'Work hard, play hard' addicted group showing the same pattern of highest prevalence on Internet use, love, and exercise. The authors state 'the same two-class solution found in U.S. former continuation high school youth was replicated using LCA in both the Russian and Spanish populations.'

description: Students in Basic Helping Skills courses show improved empathic communication skills rated by independent observers, while Internship students show only increased self-reported confidence but not observable skill improvement
original_authors: Jennifer Katz; Melinda DuBois; Sara Wigderson
original_title: Learning by helping? Undergraduate communication outcomes associated with training or service-learning experiences
replication_authors: Catherine M. Reich; Lara J. LaCaille; Katherine E. Axford; Natalina R. Slaughter
replication_title: Empathic Communication Skills Across Applied Undergraduate Psychology Courses: A Replication Study
explanation: The Discussion explicitly states: 'The current study replicated the method and findings of Katz and colleagues (2014) with a larger sample.' Students in Basic Helping Skills showed significant empathic skill improvement (d = 1.53, p < .001) while Internship students did not (d = -0.04, p = .74), consistent with the original finding.

description: Women's jealousy is more strongly provoked by an attractive rival than men's, while men's jealousy is more strongly provoked by a dominant rival than women's (Gender × Attractiveness and Gender × Dominance interactions on jealousy ratings in a vignette paradigm)
original_authors: Pieternel Dijkstra; Bram P. Buunk
original_title: Jealousy as a function of rival characteristics: An evolutionary perspective
replication_authors: Thomas V. Pollet; Tamsin K. Saxton
replication_title: Jealousy as a Function of Rival Characteristics: Two Large Replication Studies and Meta-Analyses Support Gender Differences in Reactions to Rival Attractiveness But Not Dominance
explanation: Study 1 (N=339) found support for the Gender × Attractiveness interaction (p=.011, η²g=.02) but not the Gender × Dominance interaction (p=.231). Study 2 (N=456) found no support for either interaction. The authors concluded that 'we replicated the first but not the second of these two-way interactions' in Study 1, but Study 2 failed to replicate even the attractiveness effect, yielding mixed results overall.

description: In a three-person coalition game with unequal resources (weighted majority game), the strongest bargainer (Player A with highest weight) is disproportionately excluded from coalitions, with weak players forming coalitions against the strong one (the Strength-is-Weakness effect)
original_authors: W. Edgar Vinacke; Abe Arkoff
original_title: An experimental study of coalitions in the triad
replication_authors: Joeri Wissink; Ilja van Beest; Tila Pronk; Niels van de Ven
replication_title: Strength Is Still a Weakness in Coalition Formation: Replicating and Understanding the Strength-Is-Weakness Effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion of Study 1: 'we replicated the Strength-is-Weakness effect; the smallest BC-coalition was formed substantially more often than both the AB- and AC-coalitions.'
