description: Children with autism spectrum disorder show reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) specifically in the right inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF) but not in other white matter tracts, when controlling for head motion and data quality
original_authors: Kami Koldewyn; Anastasia Yendiki; Sarah Weigelt; Hyowon Gweon; Joshua Julian; Hilary Richardson; Caitlin Malloy; Rebecca Saxe; Bruce Fischl; Nancy Kanwisher
original_title: Differences in the right inferior longitudinal fasciculus but no general disruption of white matter tracts in children with autism spectrum disorder
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Bart Boets; Lien Van Eylen; Kevin Sitek; Pieter Moors; Ilse Noens; Jean Steyaert; Stefan Sunaert; Johan Wagemans
replication_title: Alterations in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus in autism and associations with visual processing: a diffusion-weighted MRI study
explanation: The authors conclude: 'our results replicate the findings of Koldewyn and colleagues [16] and support the growing evidence for altered structural connectivity along the right ILF in ASD.' Bayesian statistics (replication BF = 11.56) provided strong evidence for replication, with a large effect size (d = -0.82 vs. original d = -0.68). The study used an identical analysis approach in adolescents (rather than school-aged children), making it a close extension.

description: Participants implicitly confuse disconnected visual parts for their potential wholes in a Go/No Go target detection paradigm — they false-alarm more to pairs of Tetris-style pieces that could combine into a target than to pairs that could not
original_authors: Chenxiao Guan; Chaz Firestone
original_title: Seeing what's possible: disconnected visual parts are confused for their potential wholes
replication_authors: Nazia Jassim; Brónagh McCoy; Esther Wing-Chi Yip; Carrie Allison; Simon Baron-Cohen; Rebecca P. Lawson
replication_title: The “Tetris effect”: autistic and non-autistic people share an implicit drive for perceptual cohesion
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the findings from the original study [22] in the Target Detection task', finding that participants made significantly more false alarms to potential No Go trials than no potential trials (t(584.17) = 4.70, p < 0.001), consistent with the original study's finding.

description: Participants respond faster to a colour identification target when the preceding prime stimulus consists of Tetris-style pieces that could potentially combine into that target shape (potential condition) compared to unrelated pieces (no potential condition)
original_authors: Chenxiao Guan; Chaz Firestone
original_title: Seeing what's possible: disconnected visual parts are confused for their potential wholes
replication_authors: Nazia Jassim; Brónagh McCoy; Esther Wing-Chi Yip; Carrie Allison; Simon Baron-Cohen; Rebecca P. Lawson
replication_title: The “Tetris effect”: autistic and non-autistic people share an implicit drive for perceptual cohesion
explanation: The authors state participants 'responded more quickly to potential conditions... again replicating the results from the original study [22]', finding a significant main effect of condition on reaction time (b = -2.07, t = -2.45, p = 0.042).

description: XX mice have more GH than XY mice in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, regardless of gonadal sex
original_authors: Melisande L. Addison; Emilie F. Rissman
original_title: Sexual dimorphism of growth hormone in the hypothalamus: regulation by estradiol
replication_authors: Kayla M. Quinnies; Paul J. Bonthuis; Erin P. Harris; Savera RJ Shetty; Emilie F. Rissman
replication_title: Neural growth hormone: regional regulation by estradiol and/or sex chromosome complement in male and female mice
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated our previous finding that XX mice have more GH than XY mice in the arcuate, regardless of gonadal sex.' In the arcuate nucleus, XX mice had significantly higher GH protein than XY mice (F₁,₂₀ = 5.45, P < 0.04), consistent with the prior study.

description: Estradiol increases Gh mRNA levels in the hippocampus (originally demonstrated in rats)
original_authors: Christine P. Donahue; Kenneth S. Kosik; Tracey J. Shors
original_title: Growth hormone is produced within the hippocampus where it responds to age, sex, and stress
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Kayla M. Quinnies; Paul J. Bonthuis; Erin P. Harris; Savera RJ Shetty; Emilie F. Rissman
replication_title: Neural growth hormone: regional regulation by estradiol and/or sex chromosome complement in male and female mice
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. The authors explicitly state 'Confirming previous results in rats [15]' with a significant effect (F₁,₅₂ = 5.78, P < 0.03). The Discussion reinforces this: 'Consistent with observations in rat, our data in mice show that Gh is expressed in the hippocampus in a hormone-dependent manner.' The Conclusions section reaffirms: 'We have shown that Gh gene expression is influenced by estradiol in the cerebellum and hippocampus.' The original finding was in rats (Donahue et al. 2006); this study extends it to mice using the FCG model, making 'close extension' correct. No ambiguity — authors explicitly confirm the replication with clear statistical support and no caveats.

description: Dispersing an ambient chocolate scent in a bookstore increases total product sales and the likelihood of purchasing congruent-category books over incongruent-category books
original_authors: Lieve Doucé; Karolien Poels; Wim Janssens; Charlotte De Backer
original_title: Smelling the books: the effect of chocolate scent in purchase-related behavior in a bookstore
replication_authors: Mary C. McGrath; Peter M. Aronow; Vivien Shotwell
replication_title: Chocolate scents and product sales: a randomized controlled trial in a Canadian bookstore and café
explanation: The authors conducted a 31-day randomized controlled trial in a bookstore with adjoining café and found no statistically significant effects of chocolate scent on any outcome measure. They explicitly conclude: 'we find no effect of an ambient chocolate scent on sales,' with none of the treatment effects reaching the p < .10 threshold.

description: Retrieval practice produces a larger testing effect when final test cues are semantic mediators (words strongly associated with the original cue) than when they are weakly related cue words, supporting the semantic mediator hypothesis
original_authors: Shana K. Carpenter
original_title: Semantic information activated during retrieval contributes to later retention: Support for the mediator effectiveness hypothesis of the testing effect
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Leonora C. Coppens; Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen; Samantha Bouwmeester; Remy M. J. P. Rikers
replication_title: The testing effect for mediator final test cues and related final test cues in online and laboratory experiments
explanation: Experiment 1 was a conceptual replication using new stimuli to test an alternative account of Carpenter's (2011) results. The authors conclude: 'the findings from Experiment 1 are also inconsistent with the semantic mediator hypothesis. According to this hypothesis mediator final test cues ought to produce a larger testing effect than related final test cues both in the strong mediator-cue association list and in the no mediator-cue association list.' No significant Learning Condition × Final Test Cue interaction was found in either stimuli list.

description: Retrieval practice produces a larger testing effect when final test cues are semantic mediators (words strongly associated with the original cue) than when they are weakly related cue words, supporting the semantic mediator hypothesis
original_authors: Shana K. Carpenter
original_title: Semantic information activated during retrieval contributes to later retention: Support for the mediator effectiveness hypothesis of the testing effect
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Leonora C. Coppens; Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen; Samantha Bouwmeester; Remy M. J. P. Rikers
replication_title: The testing effect for mediator final test cues and related final test cues in online and laboratory experiments
explanation: Experiment 2 was a direct replication of Carpenter's (2011) Experiment 2 using the same word pairs and procedure but with MTurk participants. The authors state: 'the results from our Experiment 2 are inconsistent with Carpenter's [11] second experiment.' The Learning Condition × Final Test Cue interaction was very small and nonsignificant (F(1,137) = 0.067, p = .796, η²p < .001), and contrary to Carpenter, the testing effect for mediator cues was numerically smaller than for related cues.

description: Retrieval practice produces a larger testing effect when final test cues are semantic mediators (words strongly associated with the original cue) than when they are weakly related cue words, supporting the semantic mediator hypothesis
original_authors: Shana K. Carpenter
original_title: Semantic information activated during retrieval contributes to later retention: Support for the mediator effectiveness hypothesis of the testing effect
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Leonora C. Coppens; Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen; Samantha Bouwmeester; Remy M. J. P. Rikers
replication_title: The testing effect for mediator final test cues and related final test cues in online and laboratory experiments
explanation: Experiment 3 was a second direct replication of Carpenter's (2011) Experiment 2, and the authors state it 'clearly reinforced Carpenter's findings.' A significant Learning Condition × Final Test Cue interaction was found (F(1,80) = 6.606, p = .012, η²p = .076), indicating a larger testing effect for mediator cues than related cues, consistent with Carpenter's pattern, though the mediator testing effect advantage was smaller (about 26 percentage points vs. 23 in Carpenter's original).

description: Incidentally induced anger (compared to sadness or neutral emotion) creates automatic intergroup bias in a minimal group paradigm, as measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT)
original_authors: David DeSteno; Nilanjana Dasgupta; Monica Y. Bartlett; Aida Cajdric
original_title: Prejudice from thin air: the effect of emotion on automatic intergroup attitudes
replication_authors: Junhua Dang; Zeynep E. Ekim; Sarah Ohlsson; Helgi B. Schiöth
replication_title: Is there prejudice from thin air? Replicating the effect of emotion on automatic intergroup attitudes
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the current experiment failed to replicate DeSteno et al.'s results showing that anger, rather than sadness, created automatic intergroup bias as measured by the IAT task.' The IAT analyses showed no significant main effect of condition (F(2,96)=0.61, p=.548), no main effect of block (F(1,96)=0.11, p=.742), and no interaction (F(2,96)=0.89, p=.413), with Bayes factors supporting the null hypothesis in all emotion conditions.

description: Walking through doorways in a virtual 3D environment causes forgetting, reflected by reduced hit rates for objects carried or recently set down (the 'doorway effect' or 'location updating effect')
original_authors: Gabriel A. Radvansky; David E. Copeland
original_title: Walking through doorways causes forgetting: situation models and experienced space
replication_authors: Jessica McFadyen; Christopher Nolan; Ellen Pinocy; David Buteri; Oliver Baumann
replication_title: Doorways do not always cause forgetting: a multimodal investigation
explanation: Experiments 1 and 2 conceptually replicated Radvansky & Copeland (2006) using immersive VR. Experiment 1 found null results with Bayesian evidence for no doorway effect. Experiment 2 found a significant effect under working memory load, but only as increased false alarms (not reduced hit rates as in the original), which the authors state is 'inconsistent with the location updating effect as it has previously been reported.'

description: Walking through doorways in real-life environments causes forgetting, with the effect persisting across different types of boundaries and when returning to the original encoding location
original_authors: Gabriel A. Radvansky; Sabine A. Krawietz; Andrea K. Tamplin
original_title: Walking through doorways causes forgetting: further explorations
replication_authors: Jessica McFadyen; Christopher Nolan; Ellen Pinocy; David Buteri; Oliver Baumann
replication_title: Doorways do not always cause forgetting: a multimodal investigation
explanation: Experiments 3 and 4 aimed to replicate the doorway effect in real-life environments (passive video viewing and active navigation), but found null results in both: 'crossing event boundaries, either imaginatively through watching a video or by actually moving in a real-life environment, did not influence memory,' with Bayesian evidence favoring the null (BF10 = 0.281 and 0.290 respectively).

description: Humans have an immediate memory span of approximately 7 ± 2 items (the 'magical number seven')
original_authors: George A. Miller
original_title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: some limits on our capacity for processing information
replication_authors: Abdulrazaq A. Imam
replication_title: Remarkably reproducible psychological (memory) phenomena in the classroom: some evidence for generality from small-N research
explanation: The authors found that across 11 classroom sections, all showed students remembering mostly 5–9 items, confirming Miller's memory span. They state '11 of 11 (100% of the sections) successful replications of this effect' and that these results 'established the validity of the outcomes of historically important psychological findings on memory span.'

description: Attaching meaningful chunks (recoding) to information improves recall, allowing people to remember more items by grouping them into larger meaningful units
original_authors: George A. Miller
original_title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: some limits on our capacity for processing information
replication_authors: Abdulrazaq A. Imam
replication_title: Remarkably reproducible psychological (memory) phenomena in the classroom: some evidence for generality from small-N research
explanation: Students remembered more digits of π after hearing a meaningful story attached to the digits than before in all 11 sections where comparisons were possible (86% showed rightward shifts in recall). The authors state 'Altogether, then, there were 14 rightward shifts and peaks at the 20th digit in students recall of π; that represents 14 replications of the positive effects of attaching meaningful story to the 20 digits of π.'

description: Elaborative (deep) rehearsal leads to better memory retention than maintenance (shallow) rehearsal, as predicted by the levels of processing theory of memory
original_authors: Fergus I.M. Craik; Robert S. Lockhart
original_title: Levels of processing: a framework for memory research
replication_authors: Abdulrazaq A. Imam
replication_title: Remarkably reproducible psychological (memory) phenomena in the classroom: some evidence for generality from small-N research
explanation: Across all 17 classroom sections, students remembered more words following elaborative rehearsal than maintenance rehearsal. The authors state 'There were 17 sections showing the effect, representing 17 successful replications (i.e., 100%)' and that these results 'established the validity of the outcomes of historically important psychological findings on...depth of processing.'

description: High-power poses (vs. low-power poses) increase testosterone, decrease cortisol, increase feelings of power, and increase risk tolerance
original_authors: Dana R. Carney; Amy J.C. Cuddy; Andy J. Yap
original_title: Power posing: Brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance
replication_authors: Efrat Barel; Shosh Shahrabani; Lila Mahagna; Refaat Massalha; Raul Colodner; Orna Tzischinsky
replication_title: The effects of power posing on neuroendocrine levels and risk-taking
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we too failed to replicate the effect of power posing on testosterone and risk-taking' and 'did not show any effect of power posing on feelings of power'; however, they 'did partially replicate an effect of changes in cortisol levels on risk-taking,' finding that a decrease in cortisol during high-power poses was associated with risk tolerance. Overall result is inconclusive given the mixed pattern.

description: Smiling (happy expressions) makes young faces look older than neutral expressions when judging face ages
original_authors: Tzvi Ganel
original_title: Smiling makes you look older
replication_authors: Luyan Ji; Senrong Liao; William G. Hayward
replication_title: The effect of emotional expression on age estimates is modulated by face age and participant age
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In Experiment 1, we replicated the previous findings that smiling makes young faces look older relative to neutral faces [16, 17].' The replication succeeded with young Asian participants estimating White faces (t(87) = 4.00, p < .001, d = 0.23), confirming the original effect. The study extends the original by testing with Asian (rather than Western) participants.

description: Smiling makes young faces look older relative to neutral expressions, while older faces are not perceived differently when smiling vs. neutral
original_authors: Tzvi Ganel; Melvyn A. Goodale
original_title: The effect of smiling on the perceived age of male and female faces across the lifespan
replication_authors: Luyan Ji; Senrong Liao; William G. Hayward
replication_title: The effect of emotional expression on age estimates is modulated by face age and participant age
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to replicate findings from Ganel & Goodale (2021) [20]: 'In Experiment 1, we aimed to replicate the previous findings that smiles make young faces look older [16, 20].' The results were consistent: 'These results were consistent with previous evidence [20] using similar White face stimuli perceived by young White participants.' The aging effect of smiling for young faces was replicated (d = 0.23, p < .001) and no effect was found for older faces. The study extends the original by using Asian rather than White participants as observers.

description: Gene-based associations between GRN, TMEM106B, ABCC9, and KCNMB2 genes and hippocampal sclerosis of aging neuropathology, with Bonferroni-corrected significant associations for ABCC9 (recessive MOI) and nominally significant associations for GRN, TMEM106B, and KCNMB2
original_authors: Yuriko Katsumata; Peter T. Nelson; Sally R. Ellingson; David W. Fardo
original_title: Gene-based association study of genes linked to hippocampal sclerosis of aging neuropathology: GRN, TMEM106B, ABCC9, and KCNMB2
replication_authors: Adam J. Dugan; Peter T. Nelson; Yuriko Katsumata; Lincoln M. P. Shade; Kevin L. Boehme; Merilee A. Teylan; Matthew D. Cykowski; Shubhabrata Mukherjee; John S. K. Kauwe; Timothy J. Hohman; Julie A. Schneider; David W. Fardo
replication_title: Analysis of genes (TMEM106B, GRN, ABCC9, KCNMB2, and APOE) implicated in risk for LATE-NC and hippocampal sclerosis provides pathogenetic insights: a retrospective genetic association study
explanation: The paper explicitly excluded prior study participants and used a 'true replication cohort' to retest these gene-based associations. Results were mixed: TMEM106B, GRN, and APOE showed significant gene-based associations with both HS and LATE-NC, and ABCC9 showed significant associations with HS only, but KCNMB2 did not replicate. The authors note 'We found no evidence to support the hypothesis that KCNMB2 is a risk gene for either LATE-NC or HS pathologies.'

description: ABCC9 gene polymorphism (rs704178/rs704180) is associated with hippocampal sclerosis of aging risk in a genome-wide association study
original_authors: Peter T. Nelson; Steven Estus; Erin L. Abner; Ishita Parikh; Manasi Malik; Janna H. Neltner; Eseosa Ighodaro; Wang-Xia Wang; Bernard R. Wilfred; Li-San Wang; Walter A. Kukull; Kannabiran Nandakumar; Mark L. Farman; Wayne W. Poon; Maria M. Corrada; Claudia H. Kawas; David H. Cribbs; David A. Bennett; Julie A. Schneider; Eric B. Larson; Paul K. Crane; Otto Valladares; Frederick A. Schmitt; Richard J. Kryscio; Gregory A. Jicha; Charles D. Smith; Stephen W. Scheff; Joshua A. Sonnen; Jonathan L. Haines; Margaret A. Pericak-Vance; Richard Mayeux; Lindsay A. Farrer; Linda J. Van Eldik; Craig Horbinski; Robert C. Green; Marla Gearing; Leonard W. Poon; Patricia L. Kramer; Randall L. Woltjer; Thomas J. Montine; Amanda B. Partch; Alexander J. Rajic; KatieRose Richmire; Sarah E. Monsell; Gerard D. Schellenberg; David W. Fardo
original_title: ABCC9 gene polymorphism is associated with hippocampal sclerosis of aging pathology
replication_authors: Adam J. Dugan; Peter T. Nelson; Yuriko Katsumata; Lincoln M. P. Shade; Kevin L. Boehme; Merilee A. Teylan; Matthew D. Cykowski; Shubhabrata Mukherjee; John S. K. Kauwe; Timothy J. Hohman; Julie A. Schneider; David W. Fardo
replication_title: Analysis of genes (TMEM106B, GRN, ABCC9, KCNMB2, and APOE) implicated in risk for LATE-NC and hippocampal sclerosis provides pathogenetic insights: a retrospective genetic association study
explanation: The current study explicitly excluded participants from the Nelson et al. 2014 GWAS and used a new cohort as a replication. The Discussion confirms: 'We replicated significant gene-based associations between HS and the TMEM106B, ABCC9, GRN, and APOE genes.' ABCC9 showed significant gene-based association with HS (additive p=0.036, recessive p=0.006), with rs1914361 having the strongest association (recessive MOI meta-analytic OR=2.12, p<0.001).

description: Patients with BPD show dysregulated emotion sequences compared to healthy controls, including increased persistence of anxiety and sadness, more frequent switches between anxiety, sadness, and anger, and less frequent activation of joy and interest
original_authors: Reisch T.; Ebner-Priemer UW; Tschacher W.; Bohus M.; Linehan MM
original_title: Sequences of emotions in patients with borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Tobias D. Kockler; Wolfgang Tschacher; Philip S. Santangelo; Matthias F. Limberger; Ulrich W. Ebner-Priemer
replication_title: Specificity of emotion sequences in borderline personality disorder compared to posttraumatic stress disorder, bulimia nervosa, and healthy controls: an e-diary study
replication_journal: Borderline Personality Disorder and Emotion Dysregulation
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'By confirming, in large part, the findings of Reisch et al. [10], we conducted a successful replication study.' Five of the seven hypothesized dysregulated emotion sequences were replicated (persistence of anxiety, persistence of sadness, switches from anxiety to sadness and vice versa, and switch from anxiety to anger), while two (activation of joy and interest) were not replicated after Bonferroni correction.

description: Wielding a gun (compared to holding a neutral object) increases the signal detection bias (B") to perceive others as also holding a gun
original_authors: Jessica K. Witt; James R. Brockmole
original_title: Action alters object identification: Wielding a gun increases the bias to see guns
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Jessica K. Witt; Jamie E. Parnes; Nathan L. Tenhundfeld
replication_title: Wielding a gun increases judgments of others as holding guns: a randomized controlled trial
explanation: The authors found a 'clear failure to replicate this effect' for the original B″ bias measure (t(146)=0.95, p=0.34, dz=0.08), but found significant gun embodiment effects in reaction time (dz=0.26, p=0.001) and accuracy (dz=0.26, p=0.003). The General Discussion states 'The effect was replicated, albeit in accuracy and speed rather than a specific measure of bias,' making the overall result inconclusive.

description: Interpolated testing (periodic in-lecture tests) reduces task-unrelated thoughts (mind wandering) during a video lecture compared to a no-test or restudy control condition
original_authors: Karl K. Szpunar; Novall Y. Khan; Daniel L. Schacter
original_title: Interpolated memory tests reduce mind wandering and improve learning of online lectures
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, USA
replication_authors: Matthew S. Welhaf; Natalie E. Phillips; Bridget A. Smeekens; Akira Miyake; Michael J. Kane
replication_title: Interpolated testing and content pretesting as interventions to reduce task-unrelated thoughts during a video lecture
explanation: The authors found a statistically significant reduction in TUT rates for interpolated testing vs. restudy (d = -0.29, p = 0.046), but explicitly qualify the outcome: 'conceptually replicating previous findings—but with a small effect size and no supporting Bayes-factor evidence.' The BF was 0.99 (inconclusive), the effect was much smaller than the original d ≈ 1.0, and they note it was 'just-significant.'

description: Interpolated testing (compared to restudy) reduces task-unrelated thoughts (TUTs) during a video lecture (Experiment 2), while also increasing lecture-related off-task thought
original_authors: Helen G. Jing; Karl K. Szpunar; Daniel L. Schacter
original_title: Interpolated testing influences focused attention and improves integrations of information during a video-recorded lecture
replication_authors: Matthew S. Welhaf; Natalie E. Phillips; Bridget A. Smeekens; Akira Miyake; Michael J. Kane
replication_title: Interpolated testing and content pretesting as interventions to reduce task-unrelated thoughts during a video lecture
explanation: The interpolated testing effect on TUT rate was significantly replicated (d = -0.29, p = 0.046) but the BF = 0.99 provided no supporting evidence, and the effect was far smaller than Jing et al.'s Experiment 2 (d ≈ 0.90). The authors also 'failed to conceptually replicate the significant interpolated-testing effect on lecture-related off-task thoughts,' which was a key finding of Jing et al. Experiment 2.

description: Pretesting students on lecture material (before the video) reduces attention failures/mind wandering during a subsequent video lecture compared to a no-pretest control
original_authors: Steven C. Pan; Alexandra G. Schmitt; Elizabeth Ligon Bjork; Faria Sana
original_title: Pretesting reduces mind wandering and enhances learning during online lectures
original_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
replication_authors: Matthew S. Welhaf; Natalie E. Phillips; Bridget A. Smeekens; Akira Miyake; Michael J. Kane
replication_title: Interpolated testing and content pretesting as interventions to reduce task-unrelated thoughts during a video lecture
explanation: The present study found no significant effect of content-matched pretesting on TUT rates (F < 1, d = 0.08, BF = 0.18, providing modest evidence for the null). However, the design differed from Pan et al. (2020) in using a content-mismatched pretest as the control rather than an unrelated task (algebra problems), potentially explaining the null result.

description: TUT rates during a video lecture are negatively correlated with posttest performance and situational interest, while lecture-related off-task thoughts are positively correlated with posttest performance and situational interest
original_authors: Michael J. Kane; Bridget A. Smeekens; Claudia C. von Bastian; John H. Lurquin; Nicholas P. Carruth; Akira Miyake
original_title: A combined experimental and individual-differences investigation into mind wandering during a video lecture
replication_authors: Matthew S. Welhaf; Natalie E. Phillips; Bridget A. Smeekens; Akira Miyake; Michael J. Kane
replication_title: Interpolated testing and content pretesting as interventions to reduce task-unrelated thoughts during a video lecture
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we conclude that the present study replicated the primary correlational results from Kane et al. (2017)': the strong negative correlations between TUT rates and posttest performance (r = -.39 vs. -.48) and situational interest (r = -.47 vs. -.56), and the modest positive correlations between lecture-related off-task thoughts and posttest performance (r = .15 vs. .26) and situational interest (r = .20 vs. .26). All replication correlations fell within the original 95% CIs.

description: Face mask type and background noise level (SNR) affect listeners' speech recognition accuracy, with cloth masks and N95 respirators impairing recognition more at low SNRs, while surgical masks have little to no effect
original_authors: Joseph C. Toscano; Cheyenne M. Toscano
original_title: Effects of face masks on speech recognition in multi-talker babble noise
replication_authors: Anne Marie Crinnion; Joseph C. Toscano; Cheyenne M. Toscano
replication_title: Effects of experience on recognition of speech produced with a face mask
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated differences in speech recognition based on talker...and SNR...Speech recognition also varied as function of mask type, with the two homemade cloth masks affecting performance the most, and no statistically significant effect of the surgical mask.' They used the same stimuli recordings and identical procedure as T&T, with only minor additions (mask experience survey questions), confirming the core effects.

description: Greater attention to the peripheral visual field (vs. central visual field) during vection is negatively correlated with self-reported general motion sickness susceptibility (MSSQ-Short)
original_authors: Yue Wei; Jiayue Zheng; Richard H. Y. So
original_title: Allocating less attention to central vision during vection is correlated with less motion sickness
replication_authors: Sai Ho Yip; Jeffrey Allen Saunders
replication_title: Restricting the distribution of visual attention reduces cybersickness
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to replicate the results reported by Wei et al. (2018). We did not observe a significant relationship between the attention allocation scores and self-reported motion sickness susceptibility.' In Experiment 1, the correlation between attention allocation (ΔRT) and MSSQ-Short total was r(14) = .052, p = .848, compared to the original r = -.479.

description: Greater attention to the peripheral visual field (vs. central visual field) during vection is negatively correlated with self-reported general motion sickness susceptibility (MSSQ-Short)
original_authors: Yue Wei; Jiayue Zheng; Richard H. Y. So
original_title: Allocating less attention to central vision during vection is correlated with less motion sickness
replication_authors: Sai Ho Yip; Jeffrey Allen Saunders
replication_title: Restricting the distribution of visual attention reduces cybersickness
explanation: Experiment 2 was described as 'a closer replication' using the same ΔRTnorm measure as Wei et al. (2018) with a well-powered sample (N=40). The authors state: 'In Experiment 2, we were still unable to replicate the findings of Wei et al. (2018) despite using the same measures and a larger sample size that had sufficient power.' The ΔRTnorm correlation with MSSQ total was r(38) = .211, p = .192, opposite in direction to the original r = -.479.

description: Self-relevance facilitates the processing of unfamiliar faces associated with the self-label compared to those associated with other labels, as measured by faster and more accurate responses in a perceptual matching task
original_authors: Mateusz Woźniak; Günther Knoblich
original_title: Self-prioritization of fully unfamiliar stimuli
replication_authors: Tuo Liu; Jie Sui; Andrea Hildebrandt
replication_title: To see or not to see: the parallel processing of self-relevance and facial expressions
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our results successfully replicated the effect of self-relevance on face processing reported in previous studies (Woźniak & Knoblich, 2019).' Participants responded more accurately and quickly to faces associated with their self-label in matching trials, and Bayesian analyses confirmed the evidence (BF01 < 0.01 for all fixed factors).

description: Sentence unscrambling of expository texts (generation condition) produces better learning outcomes than simply reading the same texts (the genre-by-generation task interaction)
original_authors: Mark A. McDaniel; Gilles O. Einstein; Paul K. Dunay; Ronald E. Cobb
original_title: Encoding difficulty and memory: Toward a unifying theory
replication_authors: Julia Schindler; Tobias Richter
replication_title: Does text generation improve learning from expository text? A conceptual replication attempt
explanation: Across seven experiments testing the text generation effect for sentence unscrambling in expository texts, the authors found no positive generation effect in any experiment for prompted recall, and actually found a significant learning disadvantage for the generation condition in four experiments. Only one experiment (Experiment 6) showed a generation effect, and only for the MC-test. The authors conclude: 'the generation effect was not replicated in the present study except for one of the learning measures in just one of seven experiments.'

description: Social sensitivity (measured with Reading the Mind in the Eyes test) positively predicts collective intelligence in groups, over and above individual intelligence
original_authors: Woolley, Anita; Chabris, Christopher; Pentland, Alex; Hashmi, Nada; Malone, Thomas
original_title: Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
replication_authors: Matthew D. Blanchard; Eugene Aidman; Lazar Stankov; Sabina Kleitman
replication_title: A recipe for dyadic collective intelligence for well-structured tasks: mix equal parts cognitive ability and confidence plus a pinch of social sensitivity
explanation: The authors state: 'Consistent with Woolley et al. (2010), higher social sensitivity was associated with higher CI.' Social sensitivity (measured with a different instrument, the Composite Emotions Task) significantly predicted CI (β = 0.22, p < .01) in the final regression block.

description: Equality of conversational turn-taking (lower variance in speaking turns) positively predicts collective intelligence in groups
original_authors: Woolley, Anita; Chabris, Christopher; Pentland, Alex; Hashmi, Nada; Malone, Thomas
original_title: Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
replication_authors: Matthew D. Blanchard; Eugene Aidman; Lazar Stankov; Sabina Kleitman
replication_title: A recipe for dyadic collective intelligence for well-structured tasks: mix equal parts cognitive ability and confidence plus a pinch of social sensitivity
explanation: The authors state that 'we did not replicate the findings for equality of turn-taking.' Equality of turn-taking (labelled inequality of turn-taking in this study) did not significantly predict CI (β = 0.08, p = .24) in the final regression block.

description: Higher proportion of female group members positively predicts collective intelligence (fully mediated by social sensitivity)
original_authors: Woolley, Anita; Chabris, Christopher; Pentland, Alex; Hashmi, Nada; Malone, Thomas
original_title: Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
replication_authors: Matthew D. Blanchard; Eugene Aidman; Lazar Stankov; Sabina Kleitman
replication_title: A recipe for dyadic collective intelligence for well-structured tasks: mix equal parts cognitive ability and confidence plus a pinch of social sensitivity
explanation: The authors state they 'did not replicate the findings for...gender composition.' While a positive indirect effect through social sensitivity was found (consistent with mediation), there was also a strong negative direct effect of female dyads on CI (β = -0.54, p = .01), and the total effect was non-significant (p = .11). This contrasts with Woolley's finding of a fully mediated positive relationship.

description: Family history of schizophrenia is the strongest individual risk factor for schizophrenia, and urban birth and winter/spring season of birth also independently increase risk of schizophrenia
original_authors: Preben Bo Mortensen; Carsten Bøcker Pedersen; Tine Westergaard; Jan Wohlfahrt; Henrik Ewald; Ole Mors; Per Kragh Andersen; Mads Melbye
original_title: Effects of family history and place and season of birth on the risk of schizophrenia
replication_authors: Carsten Bøcker Pedersen; Preben Bo Mortensen
replication_title: Family history, place and season of birth as risk factors for schizophrenia in Denmark: A replication and reanalysis
explanation: The paper explicitly identifies itself as 'a replication and reanalysis' in its title. The Discussion section concludes that results are 'invariant with regard to diagnostic system, inclusion of out-patient information and bias in selecting the study population,' and the authors state their findings are consistent with Mortensen et al. (1999) across all four study populations tested.

description: The PAS-ADD Checklist has acceptable psychometric properties (internal consistency, factor structure, sensitivity, and specificity) for detecting psychiatric disorders in adults with intellectual disabilities
original_authors: Moss S.; Prosser H.; Costello H.; Simpson N.; Patel P.; Rowe S.; Turner S.; Hatton C.
original_title: Reliability and validity of the PAS-ADD checklist for detecting psychiatric disorders in adults with intellectual disability
replication_authors: Peter Sturmey; Jonathon Timothy Newton; Amy Cowley; Nick Bouras; Geraldine Holt
replication_title: The PAS–ADD Checklist: independent replication of its psychometric properties in a community sample
explanation: The replication found similar internal consistency and factor structure to the original (Moss et al., 1998), but lower sensitivity (66% vs. 78%) and higher false positive rate (15% vs. 8%), leading the authors to conclude the Checklist should not be used as the sole screening method. The results are partially consistent with the original but with notable discrepancies in sensitivity and specificity.

description: Low-activity MAOA genotype moderates the association between childhood maltreatment and antisocial behaviour, such that maltreated males with low-activity MAOA are significantly more likely to develop antisocial outcomes
original_authors: Avshalom Caspi; Joseph McClay; Terrie E. Moffitt; Jonathan Mill; Judy Martin; Ian W. Craig; Alan Taylor; Richie Poulton
original_title: Role of genotype in the cycle of violence in maltreated children
replication_authors: Fergusson DM; Boden JM; Horwood LJ; Miller AL; Kennedy MA
replication_title: MAOA, abuse exposure and antisocial behaviour: 30-year longitudinal study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The findings of this analysis provided replication and support for the original research. Specifically, we were able to show significant G×E interactions between MAOA and childhood maltreatment for a series of outcomes spanning adolescence to adulthood.' Significant interactions were found for 4 of 5 outcome measures.

description: A structured psychoeducational group intervention for patients with primary malignant melanoma decreases psychological distress and improves coping capacity at 6 months and enhances survival at 6 years post-intervention
original_authors: F. Fawzy; N. Fawzy; Christine S. Hyun; R. Elashoff; D. Guthrie; J. Fahey; D. Morton
original_title: Malignant melanoma: Effects of an early structured psychiatric intervention, coping, and affective state on recurrence and survival 6 years later
replication_authors: Ellen H. Boesen; Lone Ross; Kirsten Frederiksen; Birthe L. Thomsen; Karin Dahlstrøm; Grethe Schmidt; Jesper Næsted; Christen Krag; Christoffer Johansen
replication_title: Psychoeducational Intervention for Patients With Cutaneous Malignant Melanoma: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion: 'The findings of this study support the results of an earlier intervention study among patients with malignant melanoma and indicate that a psychoeducational group intervention for such patients can decrease psychological distress and enhance effective coping.' Significant improvements in total mood disturbance (p=.04), vigor (p=.003), fatigue (p=.04), active-behavioral coping (p=.0007), and active-cognitive coping (p=.0002) were found at 6-month follow-up, consistent with the original findings.

description: A structured psychoeducational intervention for patients with early-stage malignant melanoma improves recurrence and survival outcomes 6 years after the intervention
original_authors: F. Fawzy; N. Fawzy; Christine S. Hyun; R. Elashoff; D. Guthrie; J. Fahey; D. Morton
original_title: Malignant melanoma: effects of an early structured psychiatric intervention, coping, and affective state on recurrence and survival 6 years later
replication_authors: Ellen H. Boesen; Sidsel H. Boesen; Kirsten Frederiksen; Lone Ross; Karin Dahlstrøm; Grethe Schmidt; Jesper Næsted; Christen Krag; Christoffer Johansen
replication_title: Survival After a Psychoeducational Intervention for Patients With Cutaneous Malignant Melanoma: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'our findings are not consistent with the improvement in survival reported in the study by Fawzy et al.' The replication found no significant effect of psychoeducation on survival (HR=1.30, 95% CI 0.5-3.5) or recurrence (HR=0.73, 95% CI 0.3-1.9), with both CIs spanning 1.0.

description: Check & Connect, a sustained school engagement program, significantly increased school enrollment, persistence, and on-track graduation rates for middle school students with learning and emotional/behavioral disabilities compared to a control group
original_authors: Mary F. Sinclair; Sandra L. Christenson; David L. Evelo; Christine M. Hurley
original_title: Dropout prevention for high risk youth with disabilities: Efficacy of a sustained school engagement procedure
replication_authors: Camilla A. Lehr; Mary F. Sinclair; Sandra L. Christenson
replication_title: Addressing Student Engagement and Truancy Prevention During the Elementary School Years: A Replication Study of the Check & Connect Model
replication_journal: Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk (JESPAR)
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as 'one of three longitudinal replication studies' of the Check & Connect model. Results showed significant improvements in attendance for elementary students (average attendance improved from 87.24% to 89.37%, p < .05), and the Discussion concludes that 'Study findings provide evidence that elementary school-age youth placed at high risk for truancy and dropping out can be reengaged in school,' affirming the program's effectiveness in this new population.

description: The Neuropsychiatric Hospital Suicide Potential Scale (NPHSPS) can accurately predict suicide risk among neuropsychiatric hospital patients at the time of release from the hospital
original_authors: Farberow, Norman L.; MacKinnon, Douglas
original_title: A suicide prediction schedule for neuropsychiatric hospital patients
original_journal: Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease
replication_authors: Norman L. Farberow; Douglas MacKinnon
replication_title: Prediction of Suicide: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly report that 'comparing the results of this replication study with the results of the first validation study, the scale has functioned better than expected,' with 81.7% overall accuracy and 95.2% accuracy for the high risk group, consistent with the original study's findings.

description: Type A students, as identified by the Jenkins Activity Survey-Student Form (JAS-T), achieve and desire higher grade point averages than Type B students
original_authors: Christine A. Ovcharchyn; Homer H. Johnson; Thomas P. Petzel
original_title: Type A behavior, academic aspirations, and academic success
replication_authors: David W. Rainey
replication_title: The JAS-T and Type A in Students: A Replication Note
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'it does replicate earlier results that Type A students desire and obtain higher grades than Type Bs,' with effect sizes (rs of .24 and .29) consistent with those reported by Ovcharchyn et al. (1981). Significant main effects were found for JAS-T status on both actual GPA (F(1,68)=5.37, p<.05) and desired GPA (F(1,68)=7.61, p<.05).

description: Type A students show gender differences in the manifestation of Type A status, particularly in involvement in extracurricular activities
original_authors: Ingrid Waldron; Ann Hickey; Cathy McPherson; Arthur Butensky; Leslie Gruss; Karen Overall; Angela Schmader; David Wohlmuth
original_title: Type A behavior pattern: Relationship to variation in blood pressure, parental characteristics, and academic and social activities of students
replication_authors: David W. Rainey
replication_title: The JAS-T and Type A in Students: A Replication Note
explanation: Reviewer upgrade: The authors state this study 'expand[s] upon the gender differences found by Waldron et al. (1980)' — positive framing with no hedging. The significant JAS-T status × Gender interaction (F(1,68)=9.39, p<.05) confirms gender differences in Type A manifestation: male Type As spent significantly more time in extracurriculars than male Type Bs (20.0 vs 9.6 hrs/wk), while female Type As and Bs did not differ (14.2 vs 15.1 hrs/wk). The original extractor classified this as 'inconclusive' reasoning that the focus on extracurriculars rather than the full range of activities made support partial, but the authors themselves frame the finding unambiguously as expanding upon the original gender difference pattern. Per classification rules, when authors make an explicit positive statement with a significant effect in the expected direction, the result is 'success'.

description: A 10-factor solution best represents the factor structure of the DOTS-R (Revised Dimensions of Temperament Survey) adult form in a young adult sample, with high congruity across factors
original_authors: Windle, Michael; Lerner, Richard M.
original_title: Reassessing the dimensions of temperamental individuality across the life span: the revised dimensions of temperament survey (DOTS-R)
replication_authors: Michael Windle
replication_title: A Factorial Replication Study of the Adult Revised Dimensions of Temperament Survey
explanation: The authors conducted a cross-validation of the DOTS-R factor structure with a new sample of 264 young adults and found that 8 of 10 factors showed high congruity with the original sample (indicating support), but two factors — Rhythmicity-Daily Habits and Persistence — did not replicate well. The study is classified as inconclusive because the replication was only partially successful (8 of 10 factors), with 2 factors showing insufficient factorial similarity.

description: Test interaction styles (how patients approach the Rorschach and MMPI-2 in terms of defensive constriction vs. openness/dilation) moderate cross-method convergent validity, such that conceptually aligned Rorschach and MMPI-2 constructs correlate substantially when patients have similar styles on both tests and negatively when patients have opposing styles, but are uncorrelated when test interaction styles are ignored
original_authors: Meyer, Gregory J.
original_title: On the integration of personality assessment methods: The Rorschach and MMPI-2
replication_authors: Gregory J. Meyer; Robert J. Riethmiller; Regina D. Brooks; William A. Benoit; Leonard Handler
replication_title: A Replication of Rorschach and MMPI-2 Convergent Validity
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are replicating Meyer (1997b, 1999a) with an independent Tennessee sample and that 'results supported our hypotheses and paralleled the prior findings.' The Discussion confirms: 'Our general findings nicely replicate and extend the results of previous research,' with mean convergent validity correlations of r ≈ .42 for similar-style patients, closely matching prior findings.

description: First-factor related test-interaction styles moderate convergence between the Rorschach and MMPI-2, such that patients with similar test-interaction styles show positive intermethod correlations on conceptually related scales while those with discordant styles show negative correlations
original_authors: Gregory J. Meyer; Robert J. Riethmiller; Regina D. Brooks; William A. Benoit; Leonard Handler
original_title: A replication of Rorschach and MMPI-2 convergent validity
replication_authors: Thomas Lindgren; Anna Maria Carlsson
replication_title: Relationship Between the Rorschach and the MMPI-2 in a Swedish Population: A Replication Study of the Effects of First-Factor Related Test-Interaction Styles
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results are compatible with the findings of Meyer (1997, 1999) and Meyer et al. (2000).' The main hypothesis (H2) was confirmed, with a significant difference between concordant and discordant test-interaction style groups found in two of the three functional areas investigated.

description: A factor-analytic rating system (Child Behavior Characteristics Form) yields stable, interpretable cluster scores describing behavioral and personality dimensions of children known to psychiatric out-patient clinics
original_authors: Borgatta, E. F.; Fanshel, D.
original_title: Behavioral Characteristics of Children Known to Psychiatric Out-Patient Clinics (with special attention to adoption status, sex, and age groupings)
replication_authors: Edgar F. Borgatta; Patricia W. Cautley
replication_title: Behavioral Characteristics Of Children : Replication Studies With Foster Children
explanation: The authors explicitly frame the study as 'a replication and extension of previous research' and conclude that 'the Behavior Characteristics Cluster Scores have demonstrated consistency of factorial structures over several studies and over different sets of observers,' confirming successful replication of the factor structure with a new population (foster children) rated by two new observer types (foster mothers and social workers).

description: Factor analysis of a 68-item Symptom Check List administered to anxious neurotic outpatients yields a stable, interpretable factor structure of symptom distress (including factors for Neurotic Feelings, Somatization, Performance Difficulty, Fear-Anxiety, and two Depression factors)
original_authors: Nils Mattsson; Hayley Williams; Karl Rickels; Ronald S. Lipman; E. H. Uhlenhuth
original_title: Dimensions of symptom distress in anxious neurotic outpatients
replication_authors: Henrietta V. Williams; Ronald S. Lipman; Karl Rickels; Lino Covi; Eberhard H. Uhlenhuth; Nils B. Mattsson
replication_title: Replication Of Symptom Distress Factors In Anxious Neurotic Outpatients
explanation: The authors used the same 68-item SCL instrument, the same factor-analytic procedure, and an independent but clinically similar sample. They conclude: 'Four of our five factors replicate those reported by Mattsson et al. so clearly that no new interpretations of these factors are made.' The minor discrepancy (one combined Depression factor versus two in the original) is discussed as a potential artifact of sample differences.

description: Individual differences in semantic differential scale usage are substantial, such that a scale serving as a factor marker for Evaluation for one individual could mark a totally different factor (e.g., Potency or Activity) for another individual
original_authors: Wiggins, N.; Fishbein, M.
original_title: Dimensions of semantic space: A problem of individual differences
replication_authors: Richard Shikiar; Martin Fishbein; Nancy Wiggins
replication_title: INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES IN SEMANTIC SPACE: A REPLICATION AND EXTENSION
explanation: The authors explicitly state they set out 'to replicate Wiggins and Fishbein's earlier findings' and concluded that the results were 'consistent with the previous findings of Wiggins and Fishbein (1969).' The group average E, P, A structure was replicated (correlations between dimension loadings of .993, .986, and .996), and individual differences in scale usage were again found.

description: Children's callous/unemotional (C/U) traits moderate the association between ineffective parenting and children's externalizing problems, such that poor parenting predicts externalizing behavior for children low in C/U traits but not for children high in C/U traits
original_authors: Jane M. Wootton; Paul J. Frick; Karen K. Shelton; Persephanie Silverthorn
original_title: Ineffective parenting and childhood conduct problems: The moderating role of callous-unemotional traits
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Mary Oxford; Timothy A. Cavell; Jan N. Hughes
replication_title: Callous/Unemotional Traits Moderate the Relation Between Ineffective Parenting and Child Externalizing Problems: A Partial Replication and Extension
replication_journal: Journal of Clinical Child & Adolescent Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'partial replication.' Using the original dichotomous C/U scoring, they found 'we did not directly replicate their findings,' as the interaction was only significant for peer-rated aggression (not the composite or parent/teacher scores used by the original). However, using the revised continuous C/U scoring, they found significant moderation effects for teacher and peer ratings — providing 'at least partial support' for the original finding.

description: Carriers of the -71G allele in the HSD17B5 gene promoter display increased polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) risk (OR = 1.66) and a trend toward higher testosterone levels in homozygous carriers
original_authors: Kenan Qin; David A. Ehrmann; Nancy Cox; Samuel Refetoff; Robert L. Rosenfield
original_title: Identification of a functional polymorphism of the human type 5 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase gene associated with polycystic ovary syndrome
original_journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
replication_authors: Mark O. Goodarzi; Michelle R. Jones; Heath J. Antoine; Marita Pall; Yii-Der I. Chen; Ricardo Azziz
replication_title: Nonreplication of the Type 5 17β-Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase Gene Association with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
replication_journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In this replication study, we were unable to demonstrate association between polymorphisms in the HSD17B5 gene region and PCOS risk or phenotypic markers of PCOS as had been previously reported.' The promoter SNP -71 was not associated with PCOS risk (p = 0.78) or testosterone levels.

replication_title: Association of Type 1 Diabetes with Two Loci on 12q13 and 16p13 and the Influence Coexisting Thyroid Autoimmunity in Japanese

explanation: The authors explicitly conducted a 'replication study' of this locus in a Japanese population and concluded: 'We confirmed two loci on 12q13 and 16p13 that were identified by the independent genome-wide association studies in white populations.' The ERBB3 rs2292399 SNP showed significant association with T1D in Japanese subjects (adjusted OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.13-1.67, P = 0.001), with risk alleles consistent with white populations.

original_title: A genomewide association study identifies KIAA0350 as a type 1 diabetes gene

replication_title: Association of Type 1 Diabetes with Two Loci on 12q13 and 16p13 and the Influence Coexisting Thyroid Autoimmunity in Japanese

explanation: The authors explicitly conducted a 'replication study' in a Japanese population and confirmed this locus. The CLEC16A rs2903692 SNP showed significant association with T1D in Japanese subjects (adjusted OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.02-1.60, P = 0.030), with risk alleles consistent with white populations, leading the authors to conclude these loci 'contribute to T1D susceptibility across different ethnic groups.'

description: The minor allele of rs898611 in the HSD17B6 gene is associated with increased susceptibility to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
original_authors: Michelle R. Jones; Lisa Italiano; Scott G. Wilson; Ben H. Mullin; Robert Mead; Frank Dudbridge; Gerald F. Watts; Bronwyn G.A. Stuckey
original_title: Polymorphism in HSD17B6 is associated with key features of polycystic ovary syndrome
replication_authors: Michelle R. Jones; Ruchi Mathur; Jinrui Cui; Xiuqing Guo; Ricardo Azziz; Mark O. Goodarzi
replication_title: Independent Confirmation of Association between Metabolic Phenotypes of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome and Variation in the Type 6 17β-Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase Gene
replication_journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We did not replicate association between rs898611 and PCOS susceptibility.' No SNPs were associated with PCOS status in the replication cohort, despite the study having greater than 99% power to detect the original effect.

description: HSD17B6 variants (including rs898611) are associated with metabolic traits including BMI, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, and glucose-to-insulin ratio in PCOS subjects
original_authors: Michelle R. Jones; Lisa Italiano; Scott G. Wilson; Ben H. Mullin; Robert Mead; Frank Dudbridge; Gerald F. Watts; Bronwyn G.A. Stuckey
original_title: Polymorphism in HSD17B6 is associated with key features of polycystic ovary syndrome
replication_authors: Michelle R. Jones; Ruchi Mathur; Jinrui Cui; Xiuqing Guo; Ricardo Azziz; Mark O. Goodarzi
replication_title: Independent Confirmation of Association between Metabolic Phenotypes of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome and Variation in the Type 6 17β-Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase Gene
replication_journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
explanation: The authors conclude: 'We have successfully replicated the previously reported associations between the minor allele of rs898611 and increased BMI, increased fasting insulin, increased HOMA-IR, and reduced GIR in PCOS subjects.' Multiple SNPs showed significant associations with metabolic traits (p values ranging from 0.008 to 0.046).

description: SNPs in FEM1B (rs10152450 and rs6494730) are associated with reduced risk of polycystic ovary syndrome in a case-control study
original_authors: Mark O. Goodarzi; Joseph Maher; Jinrui Cui; Xiuqing Guo; Kent D. Taylor; Ricardo Azziz
original_title: FEM1A and FEM1B: novel candidate genes for polycystic ovary syndrome
replication_authors: Ewens KG; Stewart DR; Ankener W.; Urbanek M.; McAllister JM; Chen C.; Baig KM; Parker SC; Margulies EH; Legro RS; Dunaif A.; Strauss JF 3rd; Spielman RS
replication_title: Family-Based Analysis of Candidate Genes for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
replication_journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
explanation: The authors state 'Our results for two SNPs in FEM1B and three SNPs in SGTA confirm the findings of Goodarzi et al. (22, 24).' Both rs10152450 and rs6494730 showed the same (minor) alleles undertransmitted in the TDT analysis, consistent with the original case-control finding.

description: SGTA SNPs (rs1640262, rs2238614, rs741103) are associated with reduced risk of polycystic ovary syndrome in a case-control study
original_authors: Goodarzi MO; Xu N.; Cui J.; Guo X.; Chen YI; Azziz R.
original_title: Small glutamine-rich tetratricopeptide repeat-containing protein α (SGTA), a candidate gene for polycystic ovary syndrome
replication_authors: Ewens KG; Stewart DR; Ankener W.; Urbanek M.; McAllister JM; Chen C.; Baig KM; Parker SC; Margulies EH; Legro RS; Dunaif A.; Strauss JF 3rd; Spielman RS
replication_title: Family-Based Analysis of Candidate Genes for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
replication_journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
explanation: The authors confirm the SGTA association: 'In our analysis, rs1005556 was also significant; the minor T allele was undertransmitted, in agreement with Goodarzi et al. (24).' The most common haplotype was significant in both the original study and the replication (P = 0.015 and P = 0.008, respectively).

description: ACVR2A shows linkage and association with polycystic ovary syndrome based on microsatellite marker analysis
original_authors: Margrit Urbanek; Richard S. Legro; Deborah A. Driscoll; Ricardo Azziz; David A. Ehrmann; Robert J. Norman; Jerome F. Strauss; Richard S. Spielman; Andrea Dunaif
original_title: Thirty-seven candidate genes for polycystic ovary syndrome: strongest evidence for linkage is with follistatin
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Ewens KG; Stewart DR; Ankener W.; Urbanek M.; McAllister JM; Chen C.; Baig KM; Parker SC; Margulies EH; Legro RS; Dunaif A.; Strauss JF 3rd; Spielman RS
replication_title: Family-Based Analysis of Candidate Genes for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
replication_journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
explanation: Two SNPs in ACVR2A were nominally significant (rs1424941 χ2=6.87, P=0.009; rs3768688 χ2=5.52, P=0.019), but neither was significant after correction for multiple testing for 14 genes. The authors conclude that they 'were not able to replicate many of the other published association results.'

description: POMC shows linkage and association with polycystic ovary syndrome based on microsatellite marker analysis
original_authors: Margrit Urbanek; Richard S. Legro; Deborah A. Driscoll; Ricardo Azziz; David A. Ehrmann; Robert J. Norman; Jerome F. Strauss; Richard S. Spielman; Andrea Dunaif
original_title: Thirty-seven candidate genes for polycystic ovary syndrome: strongest evidence for linkage is with follistatin
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Ewens KG; Stewart DR; Ankener W.; Urbanek M.; McAllister JM; Chen C.; Baig KM; Parker SC; Margulies EH; Legro RS; Dunaif A.; Strauss JF 3rd; Spielman RS
replication_title: Family-Based Analysis of Candidate Genes for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
replication_journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
explanation: Reviewer: Keeping medium confidence. One of four POMC SNPs (rs12473543) survived multiple testing correction (χ²=9.09, P=0.003, Pcorrected=0.042), which supports 'success.' However, the authors are notably restrained — they call POMC a 'candidate of interest' for future studies rather than a confirmed association, unlike FEM1B and SGTA which they explicitly say they 'confirmed.' The corrected P-value is borderline (0.042), only 1 of 4 SNPs was significant, and the original used microsatellites rather than SNPs. The ambiguity between a marginal positive finding and a genuinely confirmed replication is inherent in the paper's own hedging language.

description: The TNF-376A promoter polymorphism is associated with susceptibility to multiple sclerosis in the Spanish population, independently of HLA class II gene contributions
original_authors: Fernandez-Arquero M.; Arroyo R.; Rubio A.; Martin C.; Vigil P.; Conejero L.; Figueredo MA; de la Concha EG
original_title: Primary association of a TNF gene polymorphism with susceptibility to multiple sclerosis
replication_authors: Martínez A.; Rubio A.; Urcelay E.; Fernández-Arquero M.; de las Heras V.; Arroyo R.; Villoslada P.; Montalbán X.; de la Concha EG
replication_title: TNF -376A marks susceptibility to MS in the Spanish population
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The results reported herein confirm our previous data on the TNF-376 promoter polymorphism association with MS, studying a new dataset from MS patients and control subjects.' The association was confirmed with p = 0.018 and OR = 1.87 (1.07–3.26), comparable to the original OR of 2.06.

description: The CC genotype at the ABCB1 C3435T polymorphism is associated with a higher risk of multidrug-resistant epilepsy
original_authors: Asra Siddiqui; Reinhold Kerb; Michael E. Weale; Ulrich Brinkmann; Alice Smith; David B. Goldstein; Nicholas W. Wood; Sanjay M. Sisodiya
original_title: Association of multidrug resistance in epilepsy with a polymorphism in the drug-transporter gene ABCB1
replication_authors: Tan NC; Heron SE; Scheffer IE; Pelekanos JT; McMahon JM; Vears DF; Mulley JC; Berkovic SF
replication_title: Failure to confirm association of a polymorphism in ABCB1 with multidrug-resistant epilepsy
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to replicate the association between the CC genotype of the C3435T polymorphism in ABCB1 and increased risk of drug resistance in epilepsy.' The replication showed no significant difference in genotype or allele frequencies between drug-resistant and drug-responsive groups (p = 0.21 for CC genotype comparison), and the authors conclude the initial association may have arisen by chance.

description: The A/A genotype of SNP rs1060826 in exon 22 of the NOS2A gene has a protective effect against Parkinson's disease risk (odds ratio 0.5) in French patients

replication_authors: Schulte C.; Sharma M.; Mueller JC; Lichtner P.; Prestel J.; Berg D.; Gasser T.
replication_title: Comprehensive association analysis of the NOS2A gene with Parkinson disease
explanation: The replication found no protective effect of the A/A genotype of rs1060826 in German PD patients (OR 1.064; CI = 0.704 to 1.609; p = 0.76), directly contradicting the original finding. The authors conclude 'We therefore have no evidence that common variants in NOS2A contribute significantly to PD risk.'

description: The protective association of the A/A genotype of SNP rs1060826 in NOS2A with reduced Parkinson's disease risk (odds ratio 0.5) was confirmed in Finnish patients

explanation: The replication found no protective effect of the A/A genotype of rs1060826 in German PD patients (OR 1.064; CI = 0.704 to 1.609; p = 0.76), directly contradicting the confirmed association. The authors conclude 'We therefore have no evidence that common variants in NOS2A contribute significantly to PD risk.'

description: A rare missense variant (rs75932628, R47H) in TREM2 significantly increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease with an effect size (OR ~2.9) comparable to that of the APOE ε4 allele
original_authors: Jonsson T.; Stefansson H.; Steinberg S.; Jonsdottir I.; Jonsson PV; Snaedal J.; Bjornsson S.; Huttenlocher J.; Levey AI; Lah JJ; Rujescu D.; Hampel H.; Giegling I.; Andreassen OA; Engedal K.; Ulstein I.; Djurovic S.; Ibrahim-Verbaas C.; Hofman A.; Ikram MA; van Duijn CM; Thorsteinsdottir U.; Kong A.; Stefansson K.

replication_title: The rare TREM2 R47H variant exerts only a modest effect on Alzheimer disease risk
explanation: The authors confirm the association is statistically significant (meta-analysis p=0.0029) and state their results 'serve to confirm the association between R47H and risk of AD,' but the effect size (OR=1.67, 95% CI 0.95–2.92) was substantially smaller than the original OR=2.9, and the case-control-only confidence interval barely excludes 1.0, indicating only partial replication of the original finding.

description: The HOBSCOTCH self-management program improves quality of life in people with epilepsy compared to controls
original_authors: Tracie A. Caller; Robert J. Ferguson; Robert M. Roth; Karen L. Secore; Faith P. Alexandre; Wenyan Zhao; Tor Devin Tosteson; Patricia L. Henegan; Kimberly Birney; Barbara C. Jobst
original_title: A cognitive behavioral intervention (HOBSCOTCH) improves quality of life and attention in epilepsy
