replication_title: Effectiveness of a Self-Management Program to Improve Cognition and Quality of Life in Epilepsy
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This multisite, pragmatic trial positively replicated the primary finding from the original HOBSCOTCH study by demonstrating effectiveness of the intervention in improving QoL for PWE.' The H-IP group showed a 12.4-point improvement in QOLIE-31 score vs. controls (95% CI 6.7–18.1, p < 0.001).

description: The HOBSCOTCH self-management program improves objective cognitive function in people with epilepsy
original_authors: Tracie A. Caller; Robert J. Ferguson; Robert M. Roth; Karen L. Secore; Faith P. Alexandre; Wenyan Zhao; Tor Devin Tosteson; Patricia L. Henegan; Kimberly Birney; Barbara C. Jobst
original_title: A cognitive behavioral intervention (HOBSCOTCH) improves quality of life and attention in epilepsy
replication_authors: Nicholas A. Streltzov; Samantha S. Schmidt; Lindsay M. Schommer; Wenyan Zhao; Tor D. Tosteson; Morgan T. Mazanec; Elaine T. Kiriakopoulos; Felicia Chu; Heidi L. Henninger; Keith Nagle; Robert M. Roth; Barbara Jobst
replication_title: Effectiveness of a Self-Management Program to Improve Cognition and Quality of Life in Epilepsy
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'this study failed to replicate the finding from the previous study in which HOBSCOTCH improved objective cognition.' No statistically significant group differences in objective cognition were found at any time points.

description: An interaction on the multiplicative scale between EBNA1 IgG antibody titers and smoking status increases the risk of developing multiple sclerosis
original_authors: Simon, K.C.; van der Mei, I.A.; Munger, K.L.
original_title: Combined effects of smoking, anti-EBNA antibodies, and HLA-DRB1*1501 on multiple sclerosis risk
replication_authors: Emilie Sundqvist; Peter Sundström; Magdalena Lindén; Anna Karin Hedström; Francesca Aloisi; Jan Hillert; Ingrid Kockum; Lars Alfredsson; Tomas Olsson
replication_title: Lack of replication of interaction between EBNA1 IgG and smoking in risk for multiple sclerosis
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract and discussion: 'We did not observe any interaction between EBNA1 IgG and smoking, regardless of scale used, and thus did not replicate the observations from Simon et al.' The strength of EBNA1 IgG association with MS was comparable between never and ever smokers (OR=1.97 vs OR=1.61, p for interaction=0.41), in contrast to Simon et al.'s finding of a significantly higher association among smokers (OR=3.9 vs OR=1.8, p=0.001).

description: Alzheimer's disease patients with higher levels of education have an increased risk of mortality compared to AD patients with lower levels of education
original_authors: Yaakov Stern; Ming Xi Tang; Jean Denaro; Richard Mayeux
original_title: Increased risk of mortality in Alzheimer's disease patients with more advanced educational and occupational attainment
replication_authors: Geerlings MI; Deeg DJ; Schmand B.; Lindeboom J.; Jonker C.
replication_title: Increased risk of mortality in Alzheimer's disease patients with higher education? A replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we were unable to replicate the findings of Stern et al. of an increased risk of death among AD patients with higher levels of education compared with AD patients with lower levels of education.' The replication found a non-significant trend in the opposite direction (RR=0.86, 95% CI 0.63-1.19), and concluded 'higher education is not associated with increased risk of mortality in AD patients.'

description: Housing mice in enriched environments (large cages with stimulatory objects) significantly reduces subcutaneous B16F10 melanoma tumor growth, with a 77% reduction in tumor mass and 17% of EE-housed mice showing no visible tumors compared to 0% in standard housing
original_authors: Lei Cao; Xianglan Liu; En-Ju D. Lin; Chuansong Wang; Eugene Y. Choi; Veronique Riban; Benjamin Lin; Matthew J. During
original_title: Environmental and genetic activation of a brain-adipocyte BDNF/leptin axis causes cancer remission and inhibition
replication_authors: Jennifer A. Westwood; Phillip K. Darcy; Michael H. Kershaw
replication_title: Environmental enrichment does not impact on tumor growth in mice
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to replicate these results, and found no statistical difference in tumor size between the two groups' (p=0.69 by two-tailed Mann-Whitney test). The replication used the same B16F10 tumor line, same mouse strain and sex, similar EE setup and habituation period, but found no tumor growth reduction.

description: Time-reversed priming task in which the prime is presented after participants record their response, producing longer reaction times on incongruent than congruent prime/picture pairs (evidence for precognitive priming/retroactive influence on cognition)
original_authors: Bem, Daryl J.
original_title: Feeling the future: experimental evidence for anomalous retroactive influences on cognition and affect
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Marilyn Schlitz; Arnaud Delorme
replication_title: Examining implicit beliefs in a replication attempt of a time-reversed priming task
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study failed to replicate the initial findings by Bem' and 'Overall the study failed to replicate Bem's original findings.' The primary hypothesis (shorter reaction times for congruent vs. incongruent trials) was not supported at p < 0.05 across all conditions, with the trend actually going in the opposite direction.

description: Target enhancement (faster detection when probe appears in target color) and distractor suppression (slower detection when probe appears in distractor color) concurrently and independently guide visual attention during visual search
original_authors: Seah Chang; Howard E. Egeth
original_title: Enhancement and suppression flexibly guide attention
replication_authors: Tomoya Kawashima; Kaoru Amano
replication_title: Can enhancement and suppression concurrently guide attention? An assessment at the individual level
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate the previous findings of Chang and Egeth (2019), thereby casting doubt on their claim that attention can be guided concurrently by enhancement and suppression.' The probe task showed no significant target enhancement or distractor suppression effects at the group level (F(1,45)=2.37, p=.130 for the interaction), in contrast to the original study's positive findings.

description: Distance education MSW students taught practice methods via interactive television achieve equivalent outcomes (grades, faculty evaluations, field instructor evaluations) compared to on-campus students taught in traditional classrooms
original_authors: Kleinpeter, C.; Potts, M.
original_title: Distance education: Teaching practice methods using interactive television
original_journal: Professional Development: The International Journal of Continuing Social Work Education
replication_authors: Christine B. Kleinpeter; Marilyn K. Potts
replication_title: Teaching Practice Methods Using Interactive Television: A Partial Replication Study
replication_journal: Journal of Technology in Human Services
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'a partial replication study' of their earlier first cohort work. The Discussion confirms: 'The results for the second cohort of the DE program support the findings in the first cohort (i.e., equivalent outcomes when comparing DE and on-campus groups), even with a reduction of faculty visits and an increase in the use of ITV.'

description: Rural home health care workers in Southern Illinois hold predominantly positive attitudes toward the elderly and their elderly clients, as measured by a 15-item self-report questionnaire
original_authors: Weiler, R.; Robertson, I.; Gimenez, R. J.; Ferro, M. A.; Boudreaux, D. J.; Bernstein, F. L.
original_title: Attitudes toward the elderly: An assessment of rural community care workers
replication_authors: Robert M. Weiler; Paul D. Sarvela
replication_title: Rural Home Health Care Workers' Attitudes Toward the Elderly
explanation: The authors explicitly designed this study to replicate the 1988 study (Weiler et al., 1989) using the same agencies, questionnaire, and procedure. Chi-square tests with Bonferroni correction (p < .003) found no significant differences across 15 sets of response patterns between the 1988 and 1990 data sets, and the authors conclude that 'attitudes toward the elderly among this population of home health care workers have remained relatively consistent over this two year period.'

description: The adapted Chinese 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) is valid and reliable for measuring depression in elderly Chinese immigrants, and self-rated health, living alone, and perceived satisfaction with family care are the most significant predictors of depression in this population
original_authors: Ada C. Mui
original_title: Geriatric Depression Scale as a community screening instrument for elderly Chinese immigrants
replication_authors: Daniel W. L. Lai
replication_title: Measuring Depression of Elderly Chinese Americans: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly frame the study as a replication: 'As a replication of previous research (Mui, 1996b), the findings in this study provide supporting evidence for using the adapted Chinese version of the GDS in both research and practice with the elderly Chinese. Application of the same instrument with two groups of elderly Chinese in different locations has led to similar results.' The same depression predictors (self-rated health, family care satisfaction) and two-factor GDS structure were confirmed, though in a different U.S. city (Seattle vs. Manhattan).

description: A syllable-based reading training program ('Lesen mit Willy Wortbär') improves visual word recognition (orthographic comparison processes and phonological recoding) and reading comprehension in second-grade weak readers
original_authors: Bettina Müller; Tobias Richter; Panagiotis Karageorgos
original_title: Syllable-based reading improvement: Effects on word reading and reading comprehension in grade 2
replication_authors: Bettina Müller; Panagiotis Karageorgos; Tobias Richter
replication_title: Training der Worterkennung mit Willy Wortbär: Ein silbenbasiertes Leseförderprogramm für die Grundschule
explanation: The replication succeeded in confirming the effect on orthographic comparison processes (d_corr = 0.53, significant) but failed to replicate the effects on phonological recoding and text-based reading comprehension. The authors state: 'der Befund repliziert werden, dass durch die Teilnahme am Training die Effizienz der Worterkennung durch orthografische Vergleichsprozesse gesteigert wird. Der in der Pilotierungsstudie gefundene Effekt auf phonologische Rekodierungsprozesse konnte hingegen nicht repliziert werden.'

description: Electrochemical loading of deuterium into palladium cathodes produces anomalous neutron emission and tritium, indicating cold nuclear fusion
original_authors: Martin Fleischmann; Stanley Pons
original_title: Electrochemically induced nuclear fusion of deuterium
replication_authors: Šćepan S. Miljanić; Nenad Jevtić; S. Pešić; M.M. Ninković; D. Nikolić; M. Josipović; Lj. Petkovska; Slavica Bačić; T. Šutej; S. Matić
replication_title: An Attempt to Replicate Cold Fusion Claims
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Conclusions: 'The spectacular results reported by Fleischmann and Pons and the Frascati group were not replicated.' Only marginal neutron counts of 2.5 times background were observed for 45 min in the electrolytic experiments, and excess tritium was not found.

description: Gas-loading of deuterium into titanium and palladium produces detectable neutron emission, indicating cold nuclear fusion in condensed matter
original_authors: Steven Jones; E. Paul Palmer; J.B. Czirr; D. L. Decker; G.L. Jensen; James M. Thorne; Stuart F. Taylor; Johann Rafelski
original_title: Observation of cold nuclear fusion in condensed matter
replication_authors: Šćepan S. Miljanić; Nenad Jevtić; S. Pešić; M.M. Ninković; D. Nikolić; M. Josipović; Lj. Petkovska; Slavica Bačić; T. Šutej; S. Matić
replication_title: An Attempt to Replicate Cold Fusion Claims
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Keeping 'inconclusive' at medium confidence — the ambiguity is genuine and inherent in the paper. For the gas-load experiments, the BF3 counter showed 3-4x background neutron counts during the first liquid nitrogen immersion in each of the two runs, but (a) subsequent heating/cooling cycles never reproduced the effect, (b) the more sensitive 12-in. Bonner sphere and NE-213 detector showed NO observable increase, (c) track-etch detectors showed no significant readings over 168 hours, and (d) the mass 3/mass 2 ratio change (0.53→1.66) could be explained by HD formation from hydrogen in the metal or isotopic effects from hydride decomposition. The authors themselves call these results 'inconclusive' and state the work 'warrants further work toward confirmation or refutation.' A case could be made for 'failure' since most detectors were null and the effect was non-reproducible, but the authors explicitly hedge rather than declare a negative, making 'inconclusive' the most faithful classification.

description: Causal attributions to lifestyle factors in first-time MI patients are associated with positive health behaviour change (improved diet and increased exercise) in the 6 months following myocardial infarction
original_authors: John Weinman; Keith J. Petrie; Norman Sharpe; Sarah Walker
original_title: Causal attributions in patients and spouses following first-time myocardial infarction and subsequent lifestyle changes
replication_authors: David P. French; Delyth James; Rob Horne; John Weinman
replication_title: Causal beliefs and behaviour change post‐myocardial infarction: How are they related?
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'there was no replication of the patterns of association between attributions and behaviour change across the two studies' and conclude there is 'little evidence that causal attributions for MI are predictive of changes in health behaviours, once appropriate statistical controls are in place.' The replication used identical measures in a new Brighton sample and also re-analysed the original Auckland data with corrected statistical controls, finding no significant relationship between patient lifestyle attributions and behaviour change.

description: Senior student affairs officers (SSAOs) at US colleges and universities reported on career services office (CSO) structures, staffing, and programs, finding that 51% operated a separately budgeted CSO, 83% operated a centralized CSO, and most CSOs reported to a placement office rather than student affairs

replication_authors: Bonita M. Vinson; Robert C. Reardon; Sara C. Bertoch
replication_title: Career Services at Colleges and Universities: A 30-Year Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the purpose of the present study was to replicate the earlier inquiry by Reardon et al. (1979).' Results show both consistency (centralized CSO structure remained ~83-86%; SSAOs unaware of groups studying CSO need: 66% vs. 64%) and significant change (separately budgeted CSOs: 51% vs. 84%; administrative reporting to student affairs: 21% vs. 71%), yielding a mixed pattern described as showing evolution rather than replication success or failure.

description: Three SNPs within GAD2 (−243 A>G, +61450 C>A, and +83897 T>A) are associated with class III obesity in family-based tests and case-control studies, with the −243 A>G variant showing the strongest association and functional effects on transcription and nuclear protein binding

Cavazos; Frank Geller; Raphael Merriman; Anna Ustaszewska; Mary Malloy; André Scherag; Wen-Chi Hsueh; Winfried Rief; Franck Mauvais-Jarvis; Clive R. Pullinger; John P. Kane; Robert Dent; Ruth McPherson; Pui-Yan Kwok; Anke Hinney; Johannes Hebebrand; Christian Vaisse
replication_title: Lack of Support for the Association between GAD2 Polymorphisms and Severe Human Obesity
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we found no evidence for a relationship between the three GAD2 SNPs and obesity' in family-based tests, and the pooled case-control OR for the −243 A>G SNP was 0.99 (95% CI 0.83-1.18, p=0.89). The meta-analysis including all available data also failed to support the association (OR=1.11, 95% CI 0.90-1.36, p=0.28). The authors also failed to replicate the functional findings (reporter gene and EMSA results).

description: Genetic variation in OR5A1 (D183N variant, rs6591536) is associated with differences in perceived intensity of β-ionone
original_authors: Sara R. Jaeger; Jeremy F. McRae; Christina M. Bava; Michelle K. Beresford; Denise Hunter; Yilin Jia; Sok Leang Chheang; David Jin; Mei Peng; Joanna C. Gamble; Kelly R. Atkinson; Lauren G. Axten; Amy G. Paisley; Leah Tooman; Benedicte Pineau; Simon A. Rouse; Richard D. Newcomb
original_title: A Mendelian trait for olfactory sensitivity affects odor experience and food selection
replication_authors: Bingjie Li; Marissa L. Kamarck; Qianqian Peng; Fei-Ling Lim; Andreas Keller; Monique A. M. Smeets; Joel D. Mainland; Sijia Wang
replication_title: From musk to body odor: Decoding olfaction through genetic variation
explanation: The authors explicitly replicated this association in both a Han Chinese discovery cohort and an ethnically diverse validation cohort. The Discussion states 'The N183D OR5A1 variant has now been associated with decreased intensity perception of β-ionone in several studies, as well as verified in a cell-based assay. In both the discovery and the validation cohorts, the β-ionone intensity phenotype had the highest overall effect size, showing this association is not only robust to differences in methods, but has also been replicated across multiple populations.'

description: Genetic variation in OR7D4 (RT/WM haplotype consisting of SNPs R88W and T133M) is associated with differences in androstenone perception
original_authors: Andreas Keller; Hanyi Zhuang; Qiuyi Chi; Leslie B. Vosshall; Hiroaki Matsunami

replication_authors: Bingjie Li; Marissa L. Kamarck; Qianqian Peng; Fei-Ling Lim; Andreas Keller; Monique A. M. Smeets; Joel D. Mainland; Sijia Wang
replication_title: From musk to body odor: Decoding olfaction through genetic variation
explanation: The authors replicated the OR7D4/androstenone association in the discovery cohort for both intensity (p < 9.28×10-8) and pleasantness (p < 8.64×10-6). The Discussion states 'the evidence here continues to support the role of OR7D4 in androstenone perception,' noting the meta-analysis found significant associations for both androstenone phenotypes.

description: Genetic variation in OR2J3 (T113A variant, rs28757581) is associated with the ability to detect the grassy-smelling odor cis-3-hexen-1-ol
original_authors: Jeremy F. McRae; Joel D. Mainland; Sara R. Jaeger; Kaylin A. Adipietro; Hiroaki Matsunami; Richard D. Newcomb
original_title: Genetic variation in the odorant receptor OR2J3 is associated with the ability to detect the "grassy" smelling odor, cis-3hexen-1-ol
replication_authors: Bingjie Li; Marissa L. Kamarck; Qianqian Peng; Fei-Ling Lim; Andreas Keller; Monique A. M. Smeets; Joel D. Mainland; Sijia Wang
replication_title: From musk to body odor: Decoding olfaction through genetic variation
explanation: The association was nominally replicated in the discovery cohort (p < 0.02) but not in the validation cohort. The Discussion notes 'we nominally replicated the association between cis-3-hexen-1-ol and OR2J3' but acknowledges 'this association has failed to replicate in two other studies' and presents the result as weak evidence: 'we present evidence that some OR in this LD band may be involved in perception of cis-3-hexen-1-ol.'

description: Genetic variation in OR1A1 (rs17762735) is associated with differences in caproic acid perception
original_authors: Trimmer C.; Keller A.; Murphy NR; Snyder LL; Willer JR; Nagai MH; Katsanis N.; Vosshall LB; Matsunami H.; Mainland JD
original_title: Genetic variation across the human olfactory receptor repertoire alters odor perception
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Bingjie Li; Marissa L. Kamarck; Qianqian Peng; Fei-Ling Lim; Andreas Keller; Monique A. M. Smeets; Joel D. Mainland; Sijia Wang
replication_title: From musk to body odor: Decoding olfaction through genetic variation
explanation: The authors could not examine this association in the discovery cohort due to the region not being sequenced or imputed. In the validation cohort, the association was found to be significant but in the opposite direction from the literature. The Discussion states 'The role of OR1A1, or perhaps another OR in this region, in the perception of caproic acid is still unclear.'

description: IL2RA SNP rs1570538 is associated with susceptibility to multiple sclerosis
original_authors: Fuencisla Matesanz; Alfredo Caro-Maldonado; Maria Fedetz; Oscar Fernández; Roger L. Milne; Miguel Guerrero; Concepción Delgado; Antonio Alcina
original_title: IL2RA/CD25 polymorphisms contribute to multiple sclerosis susceptibility
replication_authors: Antonio Alcina; María Fedetz; Dorothy Ndagire; Oscar Fernández; Laura Leyva; Miguel Guerrero; María M. Abad-Grau; Carmen Arnal; Concepción Delgado; Miguel Lucas; Guillermo Izquierdo; Fuencisla Matesanz
replication_title: IL2RA/CD25 Gene Polymorphisms: Uneven Association with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) and Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)
explanation: The authors explicitly state that rs1570538, 'previously reported to have a weak association with MS, is replicated here (P = 0.032)' in a larger cohort of 798 MS patients and 927 controls, showing increased statistical significance compared to the original study's P = 0.04.

description: Two IL2RA SNPs (rs2104286 and rs12722489) are associated with multiple sclerosis susceptibility identified in a genome-wide association study
original_authors: The International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium
original_title: Risk alleles for multiple sclerosis identified by a genome wide study
replication_authors: Antonio Alcina; María Fedetz; Dorothy Ndagire; Oscar Fernández; Laura Leyva; Miguel Guerrero; María M. Abad-Grau; Carmen Arnal; Concepción Delgado; Miguel Lucas; Guillermo Izquierdo; Fuencisla Matesanz
replication_title: IL2RA/CD25 Gene Polymorphisms: Uneven Association with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) and Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)
explanation: The authors replicated the association of only one (rs2104286, P=0.017) of the two IL2RA SNPs from the GWAS, while rs12722489 did not show significant association (P=0.278). The authors state: 'We replicated the association of only one (rs2104286) of the two IL2RA SNPs identified in the recently performed genome-wide association study of MS.' This is a split result — one SNP replicated, one did not — making 'inconclusive' the correct classification for the combined claim. Reviewer note: the citation sentence references '[8]' which correctly maps to the IMSGC 2007 GWAS; the consortium authorship is why no individual author name appears in the sentence text.

description: IL2RA region SNPs (including rs41295061 as the most associated SNP) are associated with susceptibility to type 1 diabetes
original_authors: Lowe, C.E.; Cooper, J.D.; Brusko, T.; Walker, N.M.; Smyth, D.J.
original_title: Large-scale genetic fine mapping and genotype-phenotype associations implicate polymorphism in the IL2RA region in type 1 diabetes
replication_authors: Antonio Alcina; María Fedetz; Dorothy Ndagire; Oscar Fernández; Laura Leyva; Miguel Guerrero; María M. Abad-Grau; Carmen Arnal; Concepción Delgado; Miguel Lucas; Guillermo Izquierdo; Fuencisla Matesanz
replication_title: IL2RA/CD25 Gene Polymorphisms: Uneven Association with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) and Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)
explanation: Reviewer verified: The most associated T1D SNP (rs41295061) was not associated with MS (P=0.135). However, another T1D-associated SNP (rs35285258) showed the strongest association with MS in this study — but with the opposite risk allele (T for MS vs C for T1D). The authors conclude there is 'a heterogeneous association between T1D and MS that suggest different immunopathological mechanisms.' Confidence remains medium because the result is genuinely mixed: the primary T1D SNP failed to associate with MS (supporting 'failure'), but other T1D SNPs did associate with MS albeit with reversed risk alleles, which complicates a clean classification. 'Failure' is the best fit since the core T1D finding (rs41295061 association) did not replicate in MS, and the associations that did appear had opposite directionality.

original_authors: Rosa Rademakers; Jason L. Eriksen; Matt Baker; Todd Robinson; Zeshan Ahmed; Sarah J. Lincoln; Nicole Finch; Nicola J. Rutherford; Richard J. Crook; Keith A. Josephs; Bradley F. Graff-Radford; Dennis W. Dickson

replication_authors: Javier Simón-Sánchez; Harro Seelaar; Zoltán Bochdanovits; Dorly J. H. Deeg; John C. van Swieten; Peter Heutink
replication_title: Variation at GRN 3′-UTR rs5848 Is Not Associated with a Risk of Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration in Dutch Population
explanation: The authors explicitly state their intent 'to replicate the results obtained by Rademakers and collaborators' and conclude: 'variation at rs5848 does not contribute to the etiology of FTLD in the Dutch population.' explanation: Reviewer kept at medium confidence: The original (Rönn et al. 2009, ref 11) found MTNR1B rs10830963 associated with both fasting glucose AND type 2 diabetes in Han Chinese. replication_authors: Matthew J. C. Crump; John V. McDonnell; Todd M. Gureckis
replication_title: Evaluating Amazon's Mechanical Turk as a Tool for Experimental Behavioral Research
explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The authors unambiguously state 'These results replicate the classic Stroop effect. Observed RT values were consistent with Logan & Zbrodoff [21].' The AMT replication found 859 ms vs. 1,152 ms (congruent vs. incongruent), F(1,39) = 179.80, p < .001, η² = .82 — a very large effect with highly significant statistics. The direction and magnitude match the original (809 ms vs. 1,023 ms). No ambiguity in either the data or the authors' interpretation.

replication_title: Evaluating Amazon's Mechanical Turk as a Tool for Experimental Behavioral Research
explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The authors state 'Task-switch costs were observed providing another demonstration that AMT can replicate classic RT effects in the attention domain.' The AMT replication found significant switch costs of 225 ms (1282 ms repeat vs. 1507 ms switch), F(1,54) = 61.56, p < .001, η² = .53. The authors explicitly note 'Our mean switch costs, RTs, and error rates fall within their reported ranges, showing qualitative replication.' Unambiguous success with large effect size.

explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The authors explicitly state 'Overall, the Flanker effect was replicated. RTs and error rates appear within in the range reported in laboratory studies.' The AMT replication found 612 ms compatible vs. 682 ms incompatible, F(1,51) = 65.78, p < .001, η² = .56. Both RT and error rate effects were significant and in the expected direction. Comparison to Wendt & Kiesel [28] shows similar magnitude. No ambiguity.

explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The authors state 'The Simon effect was reproduced and was similar to prior laboratory-based reports.' explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The critical validity × CTOA interaction was significant, F(3,147) = 12.95, p < .001, η² = .21, with the expected crossover pattern: positive cuing at 100 ms CTOA (373 vs. 387 ms, p = .028) and inhibition of return at longer CTOAs (358 vs. 334 ms, p < .001). Authors state 'the pattern of mean RTs and cuing effects are similar to those reported by Lupianez et al.' and 'visual cuing effects can be replicated using Amazon Turk shows that even small RT effects (~20 ms) can be reliably measured.' The present replication showed no significant compatibility effects for these prime durations...The fact that compatibility effects were not observed for the 16 to 64 ms prime duration conditions demonstrates important limitations in using web-browser technology.' While some positive effects were found for longer durations, the key short-duration negative compatibility effect—the theoretically critical finding—was not replicated.

The authors frame it as 'promising but also raise some interesting issues.' Reviewer note on citation mismatch flag: The citation sentence names both Shepard et al. [39] and Nosofsky et al. [40]. description: Chinese object relative clauses are easier to process than subject relative clauses at the head noun when sentences are preceded by disambiguating context, consistent with integration cost predictions of Dependency Locality Theory

replication_title: The Human Touch: Skin Temperature during the Rubber Hand Illusion in Manual and Automated Stroking Procedures
explanation: The authors set out to replicate Moseley et al.'s Experiment 3 (between-hand temperature comparison after 7 min of stimulation) using automated stroking. They found no significant interaction between hand and condition (F(1,15)=0.16, p=0.698) and no main effects for condition or hand, directly contradicting the original result.

description: During the Rubber Hand Illusion, synchronous (vs. no-hand control) stroking produces a specific relative cooling of the stimulated hand linked to illusory ownership (Experiment 2 of Moseley et al.)
original_authors: Moseley GL; Olthof N.; Venema A.; Don S.; Wijers M.; Gallace A.; Spence C.
original_title: Psychologically induced cooling of a specific body part caused by the illusory ownership of an artificial counterpart
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Marieke Rohde; Andrew Wold; Hans-Otto Karnath; Marc O. Ernst
replication_title: The Human Touch: Skin Temperature during the Rubber Hand Illusion in Manual and Automated Stroking Procedures
explanation: Using manual stroking that closely followed Moseley et al.'s Experiment 2 procedure, the authors found a main effect for hand (F(1,17)=5.9, p=0.027) indicating relative cooling of the stimulated hand, but this occurred in both the experimental and control conditions rather than being specific to synchronous stroking (hand × condition interaction was non-significant: F(1,17)=3.0, p=0.103). The authors conclude the cooling is 'not a strict correlate of the subjective feeling of hand ownership.'

description: Using the AX+/BX- conditional discrimination procedure, transfer of conditioned fear inhibition in a human fear-potentiated startle paradigm requires contingency awareness of threat and safety cues
original_authors: Tanja Jovanovic; Megan Keyes; Ana Fiallos; Karyn M. Myers; Michael Davis; Erica J. Duncan
original_title: Fear potentiation and fear inhibition in a human fear-potentiated startle paradigm
replication_authors: Merel Kindt; Marieke Soeter
replication_title: Fear Inhibition in High Trait Anxiety
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Here we replicated the original findings of Jovanovic et al. [1] by demonstrating (1) transfer of conditioned inhibition in a human fear-potentiated startle paradigm and (2) that fear inhibition is dependent on explicit knowledge of the threat and safety signals.' They used the same AX+/BX- paradigm but with minor procedural modifications (colored figures instead of colored lights; electric shock instead of air blast).

description: Males prefer self-similar facial composite images to dissimilar images in mate choice attractiveness judgments, while females show no significant preference for self-similar faces
original_authors: Ferenc Kocsor; Rita Rezneki; Szabolcs Juhász; Tamás Bereczkei
original_title: Preference for facial self-resemblance and attractiveness in human mate choice
replication_authors: Jin-Ying Zhuang; Sen Zhang; Jing Xu; Die Hu
replication_title: Discriminating Males and Unpredictable Females: Males Differentiate Self-Similar Facial Cues More than Females in the Judgment of Opposite-Sex Attractiveness
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: The authors explicitly state 'this study replicated the sex effect found previously' (Discussion) and 'replicated the sex differences found in previous researches.' The core Kocsor et al. finding — that males discriminate based on facial self-similarity in mate choice while females do not — replicated across both Experiments 1 (n=60) and 2 (n=58). In Experiment 2, males also preferred self-resemblances over other-resemblances at the same morphing degree, directly replicating Kocsor's self-vs-other comparison. However, confidence remains medium because: (1) In Experiment 1, males preferred the average composite (0% self-resemblance) over self-similar faces, suggesting inbreeding avoidance rather than the self-similarity preference Kocsor reported — the sex difference replicated but the direction of male preference partially diverged; (2) the paradigm was substantially modified (Chinese vs. Hungarian sample, multiple morphing degrees vs. binary comparison, composite images from different methodology); (3) the authors frame the divergence as complementary (optimal outbreeding) rather than contradictory, which is reasonable but could also be seen as a partial failure to replicate the specific preference pattern. Result classification kept as 'success' because the authors' claimed replication target — the sex difference in self-similarity discrimination — clearly replicated. Stats updated to the sex×self-resemblance interaction (the key replicated effect) rather than the main effect of sex.

description: Common SNPs in heterotrimeric G protein coding genes are associated with differences in human intelligence, accounting for approximately 3.3% of variance in general cognitive ability
original_authors: Ruano D.; Abecasis GR; Glaser B.; Lips ES; Cornelisse LN; de Jong AP; Evans DM; Davey Smith G.; Timpson NJ; Smit AB; Heutink P.; Verhage M.; Posthuma D.
original_title: Functional gene group analysis reveals a role of synaptic heterotrimeric G proteins in cognitive ability
replication_authors: Hill WD; de Leeuw C.; Davies G.; Liewald DC; Payton A.; Craig LC; Whalley LJ; Horan M.; Ollier W.; Starr JM; Pendleton N.; Posthuma D.; Bates TC; Deary IJ
replication_title: Functional Gene Group Analysis Indicates No Role for Heterotrimeric G Proteins in Cognitive Ability
explanation: The authors explicitly set out to replicate Ruano et al. (2010) using the same JAG software and self-contained testing approach. They found no significant associations in any of five independent cohorts, with meta-analytic p-values of 0.43 (fluid ability) and 0.98 (crystallised ability), leading them to conclude 'the original finding was likely due to sample fluctuation.'

description: The Violence Risk Appraisal Guide (VRAG) accurately predicts violent recidivism in mentally disordered offenders, both in terms of discrimination (differentiating recidivists from non-recidivists) and calibration (the probabilistic risk estimates in each risk bin matching observed recidivism rates)
original_authors: Grant T. Harris; Marnie E. Rice; Vernon L. Quinsey
original_title: Violent recidivism of mentally disordered offenders: The development of a statistical prediction instrument
replication_authors: Astrid Rossegger; Jérôme Endrass; Juliane Gerth; Jay P. Singh
replication_title: Replicating the Violence Risk Appraisal Guide: A Total Forensic Cohort Study
explanation: Reviewer verified: 'inconclusive' is correct. This is a genuinely split result. Discrimination replicated well (AUC = 0.72, 95% CI 0.63-0.81, which the authors describe as 'good' and comparable to prior studies). However, calibration clearly failed: Sanders' decomposition showed 21% average error per risk bin, the excess forecast variance ratio was 10.4 (threshold for concern is 6.0), and in 5 of 9 risk bins the Bayesian 95% credible intervals excluded the expected rates from the original study. The authors' own conclusion states: 'its poor calibration results raise questions regarding its practical usefulness.' Confidence remains 'medium' because the ambiguity is genuine — discrimination succeeded but calibration failed, and reasonable analysts could classify this as either 'inconclusive' or 'failure' depending on whether calibration is weighted as the more important metric. The authors do not use language like 'failed to replicate' overall; they describe a mixed picture.

description: Valid syllogisms elicit higher liking ratings for their conclusions than invalid syllogisms, reflecting an intuitive detection of logical status via conceptual fluency (Experiment 2 with believable/unbelievable conclusions, fixed validity assignment)
original_authors: Kinga Morsanyi; Simon J. Handley
original_title: Logic feels so good-i like it! evidence for intuitive detection of logicality in syllogistic reasoning
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Henrik Singmann; Karl Christoph Klauer; David Kellen
replication_title: Intuitive Logic Revisited: New Data and a Bayesian Mixed Model Meta-Analysis
explanation: In Experiment 1, the authors replicated MH's Experiment 2 using the original English materials with fixed conclusion validity. They found a significant main effect of validity (F(1,21)=5.94, p=.02), replicating MH's core finding of higher liking ratings for valid than invalid syllogisms.

description: Valid syllogisms elicit higher liking ratings for their conclusions than invalid syllogisms, reflecting an intuitive detection of logical status via conceptual fluency (Experiment 2 paradigm, tested with randomized conclusion-validity assignment to control for confound)
original_authors: Kinga Morsanyi; Simon J. Handley
original_title: Logic feels so good-i like it! evidence for intuitive detection of logicality in syllogistic reasoning
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Henrik Singmann; Karl Christoph Klauer; David Kellen
replication_title: Intuitive Logic Revisited: New Data and a Bayesian Mixed Model Meta-Analysis
explanation: In Experiment 2, using the same paradigm as MH's Experiment 2 but with randomly assigned conclusion validity, no effect of validity was found (both Fs < 1), showing that the original effect was driven by affective connotations of specific conclusion content rather than logical intuition. The authors conclude: 'when controlling for possible effects of content by randomly assigning the different conclusions to either valid or invalid syllogisms (Experiment 2), the validity effect disappears.'

description: Participants can accurately categorize others' political party affiliation (Democrat vs. Republican) from facial photographs alone at above-chance levels
original_authors: Nicholas O. Rule; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Democrats and Republicans can be differentiated from their faces
replication_authors: John Paul Wilson; Nicholas O. Rule
replication_title: Perceptions of Others' Political Affiliation Are Moderated by Individual Perceivers' Own Political Attitudes
explanation: Studies 1a and 1b both replicated the core finding that participants show above-chance accuracy in categorizing political affiliation from faces. The authors explicitly state: 'As predicted, participants in both Studies 1a and 1b showed above-chance accuracy in categorizing target faces according to political party affiliation. This replicates past work on the accuracy of judging political orientation from static facial information alone.' Study 1a used the same stimuli as Rule & Ambady while Study 1b used a different (politician) stimulus set and larger sample.

description: Republican faces are perceived as more dominant and facially mature than Democrat faces, and Democrat faces are perceived as more likeable and trustworthy than Republican faces
original_authors: Nicholas O. Rule; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Democrats and Republicans can be differentiated from their faces
replication_authors: John Paul Wilson; Nicholas O. Rule
replication_title: Perceptions of Others' Political Affiliation Are Moderated by Individual Perceivers' Own Political Attitudes
explanation: Study 2 partially replicated Rule & Ambady (2010): dominance and facial maturity differences between Republican and Democrat faces were significantly replicated (r=.34, p=.007 and r=.28, p=.03 respectively), but the likeability and trustworthiness differences did not reach significance (r=-.14, p=.29 and r=-.17, p=.19). The authors note: 'The lack of a significant relationship between targets' party affiliation and ratings of their likeability and trustworthiness is inconsistent with some past research [4].'

description: DRD4 C-521T genotype is associated with increased ERN (error-related negativity) amplitude during performance monitoring
original_authors: Ulrike M. Krämer; Toni Cunillera; Estela Càmara; Josep Marco-Pallarés; David Cucurell; Wido Nager; Peter Bauer; Rebecca Schüle; Ludger Schöls; Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells; Thomas F. Münte
original_title: The impact of catechol-O-methyltransferase and dopamine D4 receptor genotypes on neurophysiological markers of performance monitoring
replication_authors: Yigal Agam; Mark Vangel; Joshua L. Roffman; Patience J. Gallagher; Jonathan Chaponis; Stephen Haddad; Donald C. Goff; Jennifer L. Greenberg; Sabine Wilhelm; Jordan W. Smoller; Dara S. Manoach
replication_title: Dissociable Genetic Contributions to Error Processing: A Multimodal Neuroimaging Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated the finding that DRD4 C-521T is associated with increased ERN amplitude [7], here in a linear model of allele load.' DRD4 C-521T was significantly associated with ERN amplitude (t(90) = −1.75, p = .04), replicating the original finding in a new sample including healthy controls and clinical populations.

description: The error-related negativity (ERN) arises from the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) rather than the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), as demonstrated by multimodal neuroimaging source localization
original_authors: Yigal Agam; Matti S. Hämäläinen; Adrian K. C. Lee; Kara A. Dyckman; Jesse S. Friedman; Marlisa Isom; Nikos Makris; Dara S. Manoach
original_title: Multimodal neuroimaging dissociates hemodynamic and electrophysiological correlates of error processing
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Yigal Agam; Mark Vangel; Joshua L. Roffman; Patience J. Gallagher; Jonathan Chaponis; Stephen Haddad; Donald C. Goff; Jennifer L. Greenberg; Sabine Wilhelm; Jordan W. Smoller; Dara S. Manoach
replication_title: Dissociable Genetic Contributions to Error Processing: A Multimodal Neuroimaging Study
explanation: The authors state: 'Our prior finding of a PCC source for the ERN in 30 of the present 33 healthy participants [5] was replicated in the schizophrenia and OCD groups.' Using identical anatomically-constrained EEG/MEG source localization methods, significant PCC clusters were found bilaterally in schizophrenia and OCD groups, though ASD did not reach significance. The Discussion confirms: 'using identical anatomically-constrained EEG/MEG source localization methods, we have replicated this finding in schizophrenia and OCD.'

description: MTHFR C677T genotype (677T allele load) is associated with blunted error-related dACC activation in patients with schizophrenia and healthy individuals
original_authors: Joshua L. Roffman; Adam Z. Nitenson; Yigal Agam; Marlisa Isom; Jesse S. Friedman; Kara A. Dyckman; David G. Brohawn; Jordan W. Smoller; Donald C. Goff; Dara S. Manoach
original_title: A hypomethylating variant of MTHFR, 677C.T, blunts the neural response to errors in patients with schizophrenia and healthy individuals
replication_authors: Yigal Agam; Mark Vangel; Joshua L. Roffman; Patience J. Gallagher; Jonathan Chaponis; Stephen Haddad; Donald C. Goff; Jennifer L. Greenberg; Sabine Wilhelm; Jordan W. Smoller; Dara S. Manoach
replication_title: Dissociable Genetic Contributions to Error Processing: A Multimodal Neuroimaging Study
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Confidence kept at medium. The core MTHFR C677T → blunted dACC activation finding reached significance (t(90) = −1.75, p = .04, one-tailed), and the authors state it replicates ref [8] (independent sample) and ref [9] (subset of present sample). However, three factors warrant medium confidence: (1) the current sample partially overlaps with the original study [9] — the authors explicitly note the prior analysis used 'a subset of the present healthy and schizophrenia samples,' weakening independence; (2) the p-value is marginal at .04 on a one-tailed test; (3) the extension hypothesis (differential dissociation between dACC and ERN for MTHFR) did NOT reach significance in any model tested (Table 4, all p ≥ .11). The result classification of 'success' is maintained because the directional effect on dACC activation was statistically significant and consistent with the prior finding, but the genuine ambiguity from sample overlap and marginal significance justifies medium confidence.

description: Pupillary dilations are time-locked to stimulus onsets during attention but not during mind-wandering, suggesting that pupil dilation dynamics provide a dynamic readout of conscious information processing
original_authors: Jonathan Smallwood; Kevin S. Brown; Christine Tipper; Barry Giesbrecht; Michael S. Franklin; Michael D. Mrazek; Jean M. Carlson; Jonathan W. Schooler
original_title: Pupillometric evidence for the decoupling of attention from perceptual input during offline thought
replication_authors: Olivia E. Kang; Katherine E. Huffer; Thalia P. Wheatley
replication_title: Pupil Dilation Dynamics Track Attention to High-Level Information
explanation: The authors explicitly replicated Smallwood et al.'s paradigm while controlling for luminance changes and found the same significant Task×Time interaction (p < .002), concluding: 'We replicated Smallwood and colleagues' finding that the dynamic pupillary response discriminates trials during which participants are attending versus not attending exogenous cues.'

description: Error-Related Negativity (ERN) and Positive-Error (Pe) become internally consistent after 6 and 8 trials, respectively, in an Eriksen Flanker task
original_authors: Doreen M. Olvet; Greg Hajcak
original_title: The stability of error-related brain activity with increasing trials
replication_authors: Rietdijk WJ; Franken IH; Thurik AR
replication_title: Internal Consistency of Event-Related Potentials Associated with Cognitive Control: N2/P3 and ERN/Pe
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicate in the same sample the study by Olvet and Hajcak [1], Pontifex et al. [11], and Meyer et al. [22,23].' Their replication found approximately 8 trials required for both ERN and Pe to be internally consistent, which is 'similar to previous studies [1,11,22,23].'

description: Choosing between two similarly rated items in the free-choice paradigm produces a significantly larger spread of alternatives (choice-induced preference change) in the rating-choice-rating (RCR) sequence than in the rating-rating-choice (RRC) control sequence, providing evidence for genuine choice-induced preference change
original_authors: Keise Izuma; Madoka Matsumoto; Kou Murayama; Kazuyuki Samejima; Norihiro Sadato; Kenji Matsumoto
original_title: Neural correlates of cognitive dissonance and choice-induced preference change
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Moti Salti; Imen El Karoui; Mathurin Maillet; Lionel Naccache
replication_title: Cognitive Dissonance Resolution Is Related to Episodic Memory
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we replicated the finding reported by Izuma et al. [16], by observing a significantly larger spread in the RCR sequence than in the RRC sequence.' In Experiment 1's Reminder group (a direct adaptation of Izuma et al.'s procedure), the spread was significantly larger for Self-difficult/RCR than PostEx-Choice/RRC (t(23) = 5.1, p < 0.001), replicating the critical behavioral result.

description: Choosing between two similarly rated items in the free-choice paradigm produces a significantly larger spread of alternatives (choice-induced preference change) in the rating-choice-rating (RCR) sequence than in the rating-rating-choice (RRC) control sequence, providing evidence for genuine choice-induced preference change
original_authors: Keise Izuma; Madoka Matsumoto; Kou Murayama; Kazuyuki Samejima; Norihiro Sadato; Kenji Matsumoto
original_title: Neural correlates of cognitive dissonance and choice-induced preference change
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Moti Salti; Imen El Karoui; Mathurin Maillet; Lionel Naccache
replication_title: Cognitive Dissonance Resolution Is Related to Episodic Memory
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated in our two experiments' the finding of significantly larger spread for RCR than RRC. In Experiment 2, a significant main effect of sequence was found (F(1,2124.3) = 15.7, p < 10^-4), with larger spread for RCR than RRC, confirming genuine choice-induced preference change.

description: Self-initiated tones (triggered by voluntary key presses) are perceived as quieter than equivalent externally-triggered tones, demonstrating sensory attenuation of self-generated action effects
original_authors: Carmen Weiss; Arvid Herwig; Simone Schütz-Bosbach
original_title: The self in action effects: selective attenuation of self-generated sounds
replication_authors: John A. Dewey; Günther Knoblich
replication_title: Do Implicit and Explicit Measures of the Sense of Agency Measure the Same Thing?
explanation: Reviewer assessment: The main effect of voluntary action on sensory attenuation was NOT significant (F(1,76) = 3.07, p = .08). The effect only emerged as a significant interaction with task order (F(1,76) = 8.48, p < .05): self-initiated tones were attenuated in the TB-SA group (who performed temporal binding first) but NOT in the SA-TB group. The authors acknowledge this qualification, noting 'performing the temporal binding task somehow contributed to subsequent sensory attenuation.' While the authors' general statement 'We replicated previously reported perceptual differences' covers both effects collectively, the sensory attenuation result is a conditional success — the effect appeared only in one of two subgroups, driven by an interaction, not the primary main effect. This fits the 'inconclusive' classification under 'conditional success: effect found only in subset of conditions.' Confidence remains medium due to genuine interpretive tension between the authors' general replication claim and the qualified statistical evidence.

description: Voluntary key presses cause perceived compression of the temporal interval between action and subsequent tone (temporal binding), such that reproduced intervals are shorter in the operant condition than in the observational condition
original_authors: Gruffydd R. Humphreys; Marc J. Buehner
original_title: Temporal binding of action and effect in interval reproduction
replication_authors: John A. Dewey; Günther Knoblich
replication_title: Do Implicit and Explicit Measures of the Sense of Agency Measure the Same Thing?
explanation: Reviewer assessment: The temporal binding effect was robustly replicated. The main effect of voluntary action was highly significant (F(1,76) = 129.84, p < .05, η²G = .17), showing shorter interval reproductions in the operant condition — which the authors explicitly describe as 'the classic temporal binding effect.' There was no effect of task order on this result (F(1,76) = .19, p = .69), confirming the effect was consistent across all participants. The authors state 'We replicated previously reported effects of sensory attenuation and temporal binding.' Upgraded to high confidence: the statistical evidence is unambiguous, the effect size is large, and the authors' interpretation is clear.

description: Applying Heckman-type selection models to the 2007 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey reveals a large upward correction in male HIV prevalence (from 12% to 21%), removing the apparent gender disparity in HIV prevalence
original_authors: Bärnighausen, Till; Bor, Jacob; Wandira-Kazibwe, Sinah; Canning, David
original_title: Correcting HIV prevalence estimates for survey nonparticipation using Heckman-type selection models
replication_authors: Samuel J. Clark; Brian Houle
replication_title: Validation, Replication, and Sensitivity Testing of Heckman-Type Selection Models to Adjust Estimates of HIV Prevalence
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'independently validate the reported finding for the 2007 Zambia DHS' and report: 'Our 2007 Zambia results closely align to those found in the original paper: we find a corrected HIV prevalence for males of 20.1% compared to their 21% and a corrected prevalence for females of 18.5% compared to their 18%.' The Discussion confirms: 'We were able to validate the original findings for the Zambia 2007 DHS.'

description: Participants sitting in a warm (vs. cold) room show a greater preference for relational (vs. individual) perceptual patterns, indicating that physical warmth promotes a relational perceptual focus
original_authors: Hans IJzerman; Gün R. Semin
original_title: The thermometer of social relations: Mapping social proximity on temperature
replication_authors: Janneke D. Schilder; Hans IJzerman; Jaap J. A. Denissen
replication_title: Physical Warmth and Perceptual Focus: A Replication of IJzerman and Semin (2009)
explanation: The authors explicitly state in both the abstract and discussion that they 'successfully replicated the finding that a simple cue of physical warmth makes people more likely to adopt a relational focus.' The replication found sr=.33, t(125)=3.84, p<.01, Cohen's d=.60, confirming the original effect in a new setting (public areas using warm/cold mugs instead of warm/cold rooms).

description: BMAP-28 and its isomers (D-BMAP-28 and RI-BMAP-28) have potent anti-leishmanial activity against Leishmania major promastigotes in vitro, with D- and RI-forms showing significantly greater potency than the L-form at low concentrations (0.5 µM and 2 µM)
original_authors: Lynn MA; Kindrachuk J.; Marr AK; Jenssen H.; Panté N.; Elliott MR; Napper S.; Hancock RE; McMaster WR
original_title: Effect of BMAP-28 antimicrobial peptides on Leishmania major promastigote and amastigote growth: role of leishmanolysin in parasite survival
replication_authors: Elizabeth Iorns; William Gunn; Jessey Erath; Ana Rodriguez; Jian Zhou; Michael Benzinou
replication_title: Replication Attempt: “Effect of BMAP-28 Antimicrobial Peptides on Leishmania Major Promastigote and Amastigote Growth: Role of Leishmanolysin in Parasite Survival”
explanation: The replication confirmed the same order of potency (D > RI > L) but found substantially weaker effects at comparable concentrations, with no overlap in 95% confidence intervals between the original and replication studies. The authors state: 'the effects at 0.5 µM and 2 µM concentrations were not as large as those originally reported.' The L-BMAP-28 effect was not significant in the replication (p=0.46), whereas D- and RI-forms remained significant but at much reduced magnitudes.

description: Time pressure increases cooperation in a Public Goods Game framed as a competition (but not in the standard cooperative framing), suggesting intuitive cooperation is driven by domain-general heuristics rather than social norm compliance
original_authors: David G. Rand; George E. Newman; Owen M. Wurzbacher
original_title: Social context and the dynamics of cooperative choice
replication_authors: Jeremy Cone; David G. Rand
replication_title: Time Pressure Increases Cooperation in Competitively Framed Social Dilemmas
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These results successfully replicate the simple effects found in RNW' and the abstract confirms 'we successfully replicate these findings.' The replication found a significant interaction between time constraint and framing (F(1,747)=5.605, p=.018), and a significant positive effect of time pressure in the competitive framing (F(1,747)=6.075, p=.014), consistent with the original study.

description: STEP protein levels are significantly increased in postmortem prefrontal cortex from subjects with schizophrenia compared to controls, as measured by Western blot
original_authors: Carty NC; Xu J.; Kurup P.; Brouillette J.; Goebel-Goody SM; Austin DR; Yuan P.; Chen G.; Correa PR; Haroutunian V.; Pittenger C.; Lombroso PJ
original_title: The tyrosine phosphatase STEP: implications in schizophrenia and the molecular mechanism underlying antipsychotic medications
replication_authors: Lanz TA; Joshi JJ; Reinhart V.; Johnson K.; Grantham LE 2nd; Volfson D.
replication_title: STEP Levels Are Unchanged in Pre-Frontal Cortex and Associative Striatum in Post-Mortem Human Brain Samples from Subjects with Schizophrenia, Bipolar Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim to 'replicate the postmortem human results in a separate postmortem cohort of schizophrenic brains' from Carty et al. (2012). The Discussion section clearly concludes: 'the present data, however, failed to replicate this finding in a separate cohort of subjects,' with the CASE factor being non-significant (F = 1.09, p = 0.3611) for STEP61 protein in PFC.

description: Persons often prefer potential over achievement when evaluating others (e.g., for hiring), because uncertainty surrounding potential fosters greater interest and deeper processing, leading to more favorable evaluations
original_authors: Tormala, Zakary L.; Jia, Jayson S.; Norton, Michael I.
original_title: The preference for potential
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Xiaomin Sun; Dan Xu; Fang Luo; Zihan Wei; Cong Wei; Gang Xue
replication_title: A Cross-Cultural Perspective on the Preference for Potential Effect: An Individual Participant Data (IPD) Meta-Analysis Approach
explanation: The authors conducted 17 replications of Tormala et al.'s (2012) Experiment 3 in Chinese samples using an IPD meta-analysis. The Discussion states: 'IPD meta-analysis results showed that the preference for potential effect is replicable in the Chinese culture' — both positive assessments (ES = 0.270, 95% CI 0.178–0.361, p < .001) and five-year performance ratings (ES = 0.701, 95% CI 0.571–0.830, p < .001) showed significant preference for potential, consistent with the original.

description: Sub-threshold visual asynchronies (17ms) between two stimuli produce an implicit bias toward the location of the second stimulus, as measured by the Simon effect, even when participants cannot consciously detect the asynchrony
original_authors: Laurence Lalanne; Mitsouko van Assche; Anne Giersch
original_title: When predictive mechanisms go wrong: disordered visual synchrony thresholds in schizophrenia
replication_authors: Patrick Eric Poncelet; Anne Giersch
replication_title: Tracking Visual Events in Time in the Absence of Time Perception: Implicit Processing at the ms Level
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim was 'to replicate our earlier results showing that two stimulus presented with a stimulus onset asynchrony of 17 ms generate a bias to the side of the second stimulus,' and the Discussion confirms 'These results replicate those obtained in previous studies with the Simon effect [4,5].' Experiment 1 and subsequent experiments successfully reproduced the bias toward the second stimulus using a new priming paradigm.

description: Sub-threshold visual asynchronies (17ms) between two stimuli produce an implicit bias toward the location of the second stimulus, as measured by the Simon effect, even when participants cannot consciously detect the asynchrony
original_authors: Laurence Lalanne; Mitsouko van Assche; Weixin Wang; Anne Giersch
original_title: Looking forward: an impaired ability in patients with schizophrenia?
replication_authors: Patrick Eric Poncelet; Anne Giersch
replication_title: Tracking Visual Events in Time in the Absence of Time Perception: Implicit Processing at the ms Level
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to replicate their earlier results and confirm the bias toward the second stimulus in the current priming paradigm. The Discussion states 'These results replicate those obtained in previous studies with the Simon effect [4,5],' with refs [4] and [5] being the two Lalanne et al. 2012 papers. The effect was successfully replicated at primer-target SOAs of 75-100ms across multiple experiments.

description: Local perceptual processing style (induced via Navon letter task) improves performance on analytical reasoning tasks compared to global or control processing conditions
original_authors: Jens Förster; Markus Denzler
original_title: Sense creative! The impact of global and local vision, hearing, touching, tasting and smelling on creative and analytic thought
replication_authors: Karl Christoph Klauer; Henrik Singmann
replication_title: Does Global and Local Vision Have an Impact on Creative and Analytic Thought? Two Failed Replications
explanation: The authors explicitly describe Study 1 as a 'conceptual replication' testing GLOMO sys predictions for analytical thought using conditional syllogisms (different from FD's analytical task). No significant effects of processing style were found (largest F = 0.87, p = .49, d = -0.10), and Bayes factor analysis provided substantial evidence for the null hypothesis (BF = 4.39).

description: Local vs. global perceptual processing style (induced via Navon letter task) differentially affects performance on analytical tasks (local better) and creative tasks (global better), as tested in Experiment 6 of the original study
original_authors: Jens Förster; Markus Denzler
original_title: Sense creative! The impact of global and local vision, hearing, touching, tasting and smelling on creative and analytic thought
replication_authors: Karl Christoph Klauer; Henrik Singmann
replication_title: Does Global and Local Vision Have an Impact on Creative and Analytic Thought? Two Failed Replications
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The relatively close replication of FD's Experiment 6 was not successful.' Despite using 2.5 times the original sample size, no significant effects of processing style were found for either the analytical task (F(2,147) = 1.53, p = .22, f = 0.08) or the creative task (F(2,147) = 0.44, p = .64, f = 0.00), with Bayes factors providing substantial evidence for the null hypothesis.

description: Human defensive behaviors to written physically threatening scenarios parallel patterns of rodent defensive behavior observed to actual threats, with specific situational factors (e.g., ambiguity, escapability, distance, hiding place availability) predicting specific defensive responses
original_authors: Blanchard DC; Hynd AL; Minke KA; Minemoto T.; Blanchard RJ
original_title: Human defensive behaviors to threat scenarios show parallels to fear- and anxiety-related defense patterns of non-human mammals

explanation: Study 1 used the same date rape scenario and scrambled sentence task as the original on a Turkish sample but found no significant effect of science priming on moral sensitivity (F(1,81) = 0.54, p = .464). The authors attributed this null result to a ceiling effect rather than a definitive failure, noting that the majority of participants in both groups gave the maximum wrongness rating.

replication_authors: Marie V. Coignet; Gary Robert Zirpoli; Michelle R. Roberts; Thaer Khoury; Elisa V. Bandera; Qianqian Zhu; Song Yao
replication_title: Genetic variations, reproductive aging, and breast cancer risk in African American and European American women: The Women's Circle of Health Study
explanation: REVIEWER: Inconclusive is correct. Key SNPs from this GWAS were partially replicated: rs7759938 in LIN28B was replicated in EA (p=0.004, β=0.19 years/allele) and rs466639 in RXRG (p=0.008). However, the LIN28B SNP was not significant in AA, and overall AA replication was poor (1/37 AM SNPs significant). The authors also note rs466639 in RXRG was associated with TRLS and NRLS in both populations, a notable cross-population finding. No results survived FDR correction. The split EA success / AA failure pattern is genuinely inconclusive. Medium confidence appropriate given pooled reporting across original studies.

description: Genetic loci associated with both age at menarche and age at natural menopause identified in European populations via genome-wide association study
original_authors: Chunyan He; Peter Kraft; Constance Chen; Julie E. Buring; Guillaume Paré; Susan E. Hankinson; Stephen J. Chanock; Paul M. Ridker; David J. Hunter; Daniel I. Chasman
original_title: Genome-wide association studies identify loci associated with age at menarche and age at natural menopause
replication_authors: Marie V. Coignet; Gary Robert Zirpoli; Michelle R. Roberts; Thaer Khoury; Elisa V. Bandera; Qianqian Zhu; Song Yao
replication_title: Genetic variations, reproductive aging, and breast cancer risk in African American and European American women: The Women's Circle of Health Study
explanation: REVIEWER: Inconclusive is correct. SNPs from this and other GWAS were selectively replicated in EA women but largely failed in AA women. The authors concluded 'the overlap of genetic determinants of reproductive aging phenotypes between AA and EA populations may be limited,' and acknowledged that 'none of the SNPs for the four phenotypes passed the significance threshold after controlling for multiple comparisons via FDR correction.' The paper explicitly tests cross-population generalizability and finds population-specific results, which is genuinely inconclusive. Medium confidence appropriate given pooled reporting across 5 original studies.

description: Thresholded CT perfusion-derived cerebral blood flow (CBF) maps can substitute for diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) in measuring the ischemic core volume in acute stroke patients, with a 45% relative CBF threshold optimally identifying DWI-positive pixels
original_authors: Andrew Bivard; Patrick McElduff; Neil Spratt; Christopher Levi; Mark Parsons
original_title: Defining the extent of irreversible brain ischemia using perfusion computed tomography
replication_authors: Copen WA; Yoo AJ; Rost NS; Morais LT; Schaefer PW; González RG; Wu O.
replication_title: In patients with suspected acute stroke, CT perfusion-based cerebral blood flow maps cannot substitute for DWI in measuring the ischemic core
explanation: The authors explicitly replicated the ROC-based methodology of Bivard et al. (2011) and found that applying the 45% threshold to their data produced mean core overestimation of 137 mL (range: -63 to 254 mL) and exceeded follow-up volumes in 87% of patients, concluding: 'these data are incongruent with the conclusions drawn from the prior studies that we have replicated.'

description: CT perfusion-derived cerebral blood flow (CBF) maps optimally correlate with DWI in acute stroke, with relative CBF thresholds (16% for standard, 28% for delay-corrected) adequately identifying DWI-positive pixels and allowing CBF to serve as a DWI surrogate
original_authors: Kamalian S.; Kamalian S.; Maas MB; Goldmacher GV; Payabvash S.; Akbar A.; Schaefer PW; Furie KL; Gonzalez RG; Lev MH
original_title: CT cerebral blood flow maps optimally correlate with admission diffusion-weighted imaging in acute stroke but thresholds vary by postprocessing platform
replication_authors: Copen WA; Yoo AJ; Rost NS; Morais LT; Schaefer PW; González RG; Wu O.
replication_title: In patients with suspected acute stroke, CT perfusion-based cerebral blood flow maps cannot substitute for DWI in measuring the ischemic core
explanation: The authors replicated Kamalian et al.'s (2011) ROC methodology and found that applying its 16% and 28% thresholds to their data produced mean core overestimations of 7-90 mL and exceeded follow-up infarct volumes in 61-87% of patients, concluding that CBF-derived volumes could not substitute for DWI.

description: Cerebral blood flow is the optimal CT perfusion parameter for assessing the ischemic infarct core, with a 31% relative CBF threshold best identifying DWI-positive pixels (AUC = 0.79, sensitivity = 0.72, specificity = 0.88)
original_authors: Bruce C.V. Campbell; Søren Christensen; Christopher R. Levi; Patricia M. Desmond; Geoffrey A. Donnan; Stephen M. Davis; Mark W. Parsons
original_title: Cerebral blood flow is the optimal CT perfusion parameter for assessing infarct core
replication_authors: Copen WA; Yoo AJ; Rost NS; Morais LT; Schaefer PW; González RG; Wu O.
replication_title: In patients with suspected acute stroke, CT perfusion-based cerebral blood flow maps cannot substitute for DWI in measuring the ischemic core
explanation: The authors replicated Campbell et al.'s (2011) ROC methodology and found that applying the 31% CBF threshold to their data produced mean core overestimation of 70 mL (range: -79 to 197 mL) and exceeded follow-up infarct volumes in 83% of patients, concluding that CBF maps could not substitute for DWI.

description: Whole-brain CT perfusion with a 50% relative CBF threshold can identify the ischemic core in acute stroke with adequate accuracy (AUC = 0.75, sensitivity = 0.66, specificity = 0.81), supporting CBF maps as a DWI surrogate
original_authors: Bivard A.; Levi C.; Krishnamurthy V.; Hislop-Jambrich J.; Salazar P.; Jackson B.; Davis S.; Parsons M.
original_title: Defining acute ischemic stroke tissue pathophysiology with whole brain CT perfusion
original_journal: Journal of Neuroradiology = Journal de Neuroradiologie
replication_authors: Copen WA; Yoo AJ; Rost NS; Morais LT; Schaefer PW; González RG; Wu O.
replication_title: In patients with suspected acute stroke, CT perfusion-based cerebral blood flow maps cannot substitute for DWI in measuring the ischemic core
explanation: The authors replicated Bivard et al.'s (2014) ROC methodology and found that applying the 50% threshold to their data produced mean core overestimation of 159 mL (unilateral) and 269 mL (bilateral) and exceeded follow-up infarct volumes in 87-96% of patients, concluding that CBF maps could not substitute for DWI.

description: Gender attribution is primarily genital attribution, with the penis serving as a dominant cue such that male gender is attributed nearly universally when a penis is present regardless of other gender cues
original_authors: Kessler, Suzanne J.; McKenna, Wendy
original_title: Gender: an ethnomethodological approach
replication_authors: Frederike Wenzlaff; Peer Briken; Arne Dekker
replication_title: If there’s a penis, it’s most likely a man: Investigating the social construction of gender using eye tracking
explanation: The authors conclude: 'More than 30 years after Kessler and McKenna's foundational work, we demonstrated that gender attribution in binary forced-choice tasks is still predominately genital attribution. Moreover, we presented evidence that the penis persists as a special cue in the decision process.' The effect was less pronounced than the original (75% vs. near-100% male attribution for incongruent penis stimulus) but the core finding replicated.

description: Participants experience both egocentric and altercentric interference in a dot perspective-taking task, where an avatar's perspective affects the speed with which participants report their own perspective
original_authors: Dana Samson; Ian A. Apperly; Jason J. Braithwaite; Benjamin J. Andrews; Sarah E. Bodley Scott
original_title: Seeing it their way: Evidence for rapid and involuntary computation of what other people see
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Julia Marshall; Anton Gollwitzer; Laurie R. Santos
replication_title: Does altercentric interference rely on mentalizing?: Results from two level-1 perspective-taking tasks
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the effect documented in Samson et al. [14] that individuals make both egocentric and altercentric errors in the dot perspective-taking task.' The critical Perspective x Consistency interaction was significant, F(1, 48) = 29.76, p < .001, η_p² = .383, confirming both egocentric and altercentric interference. Result classification 'success' is unambiguous. Replication type 'close experiment' is appropriate: the study tested the same core dot perspective-taking phenomenon but used a novel continuous 'sandbox' accuracy measure instead of response times, and extended the number of dots beyond the original subitizing range. Upgraded from medium to high confidence based on the authors' explicit replication claim and strong statistical support.

description: Participants show altercentric interference only when an avatar can see (no goggles or translucent goggles), but not when the avatar is 'blind' (wearing opaque goggles), supporting the implicit mentalizing hypothesis over the attentional cueing account
original_authors: Tiziano Furlanetto; Cristina Becchio; Dana Samson; Ian Apperly
original_title: Altercentric interference in level 1 visual perspective taking reflects the ascription of mental states, not submentalizing
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Julia Marshall; Anton Gollwitzer; Laurie R. Santos
replication_title: Does altercentric interference rely on mentalizing?: Results from two level-1 perspective-taking tasks
explanation: The replication found mixed results: response time measures showed no altercentric interference in any condition (failing to replicate Furlanetto et al.'s main finding), but error/accuracy measures did replicate the pattern — altercentric interference in the seeing conditions but not in the opaque (blind) condition. The authors describe this as 'disparate findings between the two measures,' with the pattern only partially consistent with the original.

description: Intelligence (IQ) strongly correlates with motion surround suppression index (r = 0.71), such that higher-IQ participants show greater suppression of large moving stimuli relative to small ones
original_authors: Michael D. Melnick; Bryan R. Harrison; Sohee Park; Loisa Bennetto; Duje Tadin
original_title: A strong interactive link between sensory discriminations and intelligence
replication_authors: Sandra Arranz-Paraíso; Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza
replication_title: Testing the link between visual suppression and intelligence
explanation: The authors used a similar motion discrimination task but with different stimulus parameters (sizes and speed). They found a significant positive correlation between IQ and MSI (r = 0.43, p = 0.002, N = 47), which is weaker than the original (r = 0.71), but the authors state: 'These results replicate previous findings, even though the correlations are weaker than in the original study' and 'These results support the link between motion surround suppression and IQ previously found by Melnick et al.'

description: Contrast surround suppression strongly correlates with visuospatial IQ (r = 0.87), measured using a contrast matching task with first and second order gratings
original_authors: Emily Cook; Stephen T. Hammett; Jonas Larsson
original_title: GABA predicts visual intelligence
replication_authors: Sandra Arranz-Paraíso; Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza
replication_title: Testing the link between visual suppression and intelligence
explanation: The authors used a contrast detection task (rather than a matching task) and found no correlation between contrast surround suppression index and any IQ measure (general r = -0.09, p = 0.513; N = 46). The authors state their results 'do not support the link between contrast surround suppression and IQ' found by Cook et al.

description: Motion surround suppression and contrast surround suppression are not significantly correlated with each other (r = -0.19, p = 0.24), reflecting independent cortical mechanisms
original_authors: Partow Yazdani; Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza; Roger G. Whittaker; Andrew Trevelyan; Jenny C. A. Read
original_title: Two common psychophysical measures of surround suppression reflect independent neuronal mechanisms
replication_authors: Sandra Arranz-Paraíso; Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza
replication_title: Testing the link between visual suppression and intelligence
explanation: The authors computed the Pearson correlation between MSI and CSI and found r = 0.10, p = 0.47 (N = 50), a non-significant result consistent with the original. They explicitly state: 'This result replicates the main finding of Yazdani et al. (2015, r = -0.19, p = 0.24). These results suggest that motion and contrast surround suppression reflect the activation of independent cortical mechanisms.'

description: Response times and response levels show a curvilinear pattern across time frames, increasing for shorter time frames and flattening or decreasing for longer time frames, indicating a shift from episodic to semantic retrieval strategy
original_authors: Michael D. Robinson; Gerald L. Clore
original_title: Episodic and semantic knowledge in emotional self-report: Evidence for two judgment processes
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Marta Walentynowicz; Stefan Schneider; Arthur A. Stone
replication_title: The effects of time frames on self-report
explanation: The authors explicitly state that while they replicated the monotonic increase in response times and response levels with longer time frames, they failed to replicate the key effect: 'it did not replicate prior work that suggested a shift from episodic to semantic memory as time frame duration increased.' No consistent evidence was found for a flattening or decrease in slope for longer time frames, which was the central finding of the original study.

description: Familiar environmental sound cues presented during a post-encoding rest period promote autobiographical thinking and thereby interfere with episodic memory consolidation, as evidenced by reduced wordlist retention compared to quiet wakeful rest
original_authors: Michael Craig; Sergio Della Sala; Michaela Dewar
original_title: Autobiographical thinking interferes with episodic memory consolidation
replication_authors: Samarth Varma; Sander M. Daselaar; Roy P. C. Kessels; Atsuko Takashima
replication_title: Promotion and suppression of autobiographical thinking differentially affect episodic memory consolidation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We successfully replicated the results of previous studies [14, 19]' and in the conclusion: 'Replicating previous research [14], we demonstrate that this effect is exacerbated in the presence of explicit environmental cues that could trigger novel encoding/retrieval of memories.' The key comparison (rest vs. rest+sounds) was statistically significant: t(35) = 2.28, p = 0.029.
