description: Post-encoding engagement in a 2-Back task leads to the same degree of memory retention as quiet wakeful rest, demonstrating that the 2-Back task does not interfere with episodic memory consolidation
original_authors: Varma S.; Takashima A.; Krewinkel S.; van Kooten M.; Fu L.; Medendorp WP; Kessels RPC; Daselaar SM
original_title: Non-interfering effects of active post-encoding tasks on episodic memory consolidation in humans
replication_authors: Samarth Varma; Sander M. Daselaar; Roy P. C. Kessels; Atsuko Takashima
replication_title: Promotion and suppression of autobiographical thinking differentially affect episodic memory consolidation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We successfully replicated the results of previous studies [14, 19]' and in the conclusion: 'engaging in a demanding 2-Back task during the post-encoding period can reduce interference to consolidation of studied material by suppressing spontaneous autobiographical thinking, similar to our previous study [19].' The 2-Back vs. rest comparison was non-significant: t(35) = -0.22, p = 0.83, consistent with the original finding of no difference.

description: Participants accurately identify winners of music competitions when viewing silent video clips, but not when listening to audio-only or audiovisual clips, showing sight trumps sound in judgments of musical performance quality
original_authors: Chia-Jung Tsay
original_title: Sight over sound in the judgment of music performance
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Samuel A. Mehr; Daniel A. Scannell; Ellen Winner
replication_title: Sight-over-sound judgments of music performances are replicable effects with limited interpretability
explanation: The authors ran a highly-powered direct replication of Tsay (2013) Experiments 3 and 5 using 9 of the original 10 video triads. They explicitly state: 'This highly-powered direct replication demonstrated that the main findings from [1] are reliable. With nearly-identical materials, the same pattern of results emerged.'

description: Participants accurately identify winners of music competitions when viewing silent video clips, but not when listening to audio-only or audiovisual clips, showing sight trumps sound in judgments of musical performance quality
original_authors: Chia-Jung Tsay
original_title: Sight over sound in the judgment of music performance
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Samuel A. Mehr; Daniel A. Scannell; Ellen Winner
replication_title: Sight-over-sound judgments of music performances are replicable effects with limited interpretability
explanation: Using different clips from the same performances presented in pairs rather than triads, the visual-only condition was at chance (M=51.1%, p=.53), failing to replicate. The authors conclude: 'the main effect of [1] showing participants' ability to identify winners in the visual condition, while robustly replicated in Experiment 1, does not hold when different clips from the same performances are used.'

description: Participants accurately identify winners of music competitions when viewing silent video clips, but not when listening to audio-only or audiovisual clips, showing sight trumps sound in judgments of musical performance quality
original_authors: Chia-Jung Tsay
original_title: Sight over sound in the judgment of music performance
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Samuel A. Mehr; Daniel A. Scannell; Ellen Winner
replication_title: Sight-over-sound judgments of music performances are replicable effects with limited interpretability
explanation: Using different performers (winners vs. early-eliminated competitors) in pairs, visual-only performance trended below chance (M=45.2%, p=.078) while audio-only and audiovisual conditions were significantly above chance, the opposite of the original pattern. Authors state: 'in that experiment, the differences in performance quality were even more salient than in Experiment 2, but performance in the visual-only condition trended below chance.'

description: Teaching philosophy through doing philosophy (rather than just learning about it) is more effective in some lessons than others, with the lessons scalable along a single dimension from more to less effective, associated with philosophical discussions, shared guidance, and certain teaching styles
original_authors: Kienstra, Natascha; Imants, Jeroen; Karskens, Michiel; Van Der Heijden, Peter G. M.
original_title: Doing philosophy effectively: Student learning in classroom teaching
replication_authors: Natascha Kienstra; Peter G. M. van der Heijden
replication_title: Doing philosophy effectively II: A replication and elaboration of student learning in classroom teaching
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the current study appears to replicate the results of the earlier study' and 'For the first research question, the answer is positive. The one-dimensional structure can be replicated.' They found the same correspondence analysis dimensions, with the same key variables (dialogue, guidance, teaching styles, highest level of philosophy) contributing in the same direction.

description: The Conceptual Span task (clustered and non-clustered versions) measures individual differences in semantic short-term memory capacity, with the non-clustered version correlating with reading span and semantic anomaly judgment in English-speaking adults
original_authors: Henk J. Haarmann; Eddy J. Davelaar; Marius Usher
original_title: Individual differences in semantic short-term memory capacity
replication_authors: Alaitz Aizpurua; Wilma Koutstaal
replication_title: A new index of semantic short-term memory: Development and validation of the conceptual span task in Spanish
explanation: The authors explicitly call this a 'conceptual replication and extension' of Haarmann et al. (2003), developing a Spanish adaptation of the Conceptual Span task. They conclude that 'the newly developed tasks showed excellent correspondence with the English versions of those tasks both as originally developed by Haarmann and his colleagues [3],' with comparable STM capacity estimates (3.4 in replication vs. identical 3.4 in original for non-clustered version) and similar inter-task correlations.

description: Incongruent visual information increases reaction time to an auditory color-word target, and congruent visual information decreases reaction time, in an audiovisual color-word Stroop task
original_authors: Sarah E. Donohue; Lawrence G. Appelbaum; Christina J. Park; Kenneth C. Roberts; Marty G. Woldorff
original_title: Cross-modal stimulus conflict: the behavioral effects of stimulus input timing in a visual-auditory Stroop task
replication_authors: Megan C. Fitzhugh; Peter S. Whitehead; Lisa Johnson; Julia M. Cai; Leslie C. Baxter; Corianne Rogalsky
replication_title: A functional MRI investigation of crossmodal interference in an audiovisual Stroop task
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated previous behavioral AV Stroop task findings [44,45], in that congruent visual information facilitated auditory speech perception and incongruent visual information interfered with auditory speech perception.' The overall patterns of facilitation and interference coincided with those from Donohue et al., with high accuracy (>94%) and reaction time differences between incongruent and congruent conditions being the largest contrast.

description: Two-year-olds and adults show anticipatory looking toward an agent's false-belief-congruent location in implicit false belief tasks (FB1 and FB2 conditions of the anticipatory looking paradigm)
original_authors: Southgate V.; Senju A.; Csibra G.
original_title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds
replication_authors: Louisa Kulke; Josefin Johannsen; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Why can some implicit Theory of Mind tasks be replicated and others cannot? A test of mentalizing versus submentalizing accounts
explanation: In Study 1 (adults), no significant anticipatory looking was found in FB1 (p=.493), but adults showed significant positive DLS in FB2 (p=.007, d=1.208), which the authors describe as 'puzzling' and in need of clarification. The Discussion states the results were 'complex' and the original belief-consistent anticipatory looking patterns 'could largely not be replicated.'

description: Young children show anticipatory looking toward an agent's false-belief-congruent location in implicit false belief tasks (FB1 and FB2 conditions of the anticipatory looking paradigm)
original_authors: Southgate V.; Senju A.; Csibra G.
original_title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds
replication_authors: Louisa Kulke; Josefin Johannsen; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Why can some implicit Theory of Mind tasks be replicated and others cannot? A test of mentalizing versus submentalizing accounts
explanation: In Study 2 (children aged 4.5-5.5 years), DLS did not significantly differ from zero in either FB1 (p=.218, d=0.517, BF10=0.430) or FB2 (p=.748, d=0.132, BF10=0.221), providing no evidence for belief-based anticipatory looking. The authors conclude that 'children showed no gaze behavior indicating belief tracking in either FB1 or FB2, so that the study failed to replicate the original findings.'

description: Adults show anticipatory looking toward an agent's false-belief-congruent location in implicit false belief tasks (FB1 and FB2 conditions of the anticipatory looking paradigm)
original_authors: Southgate V.; Senju A.; Csibra G.
original_title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds
replication_authors: Louisa Kulke; Josefin Johannsen; Hannes Rakoczy
replication_title: Why can some implicit Theory of Mind tasks be replicated and others cannot? A test of mentalizing versus submentalizing accounts
explanation: Study 3 used animated stimuli and a modified familiarization procedure to address potential confounds. Neither FB1 (p=.334, d=0.20, BF10=0.327) nor FB2 (p=.244, d=0.24, BF10=0.302) showed significant DLS. The Discussion explicitly states 'there was no evidence for belief-tracking' in Study 3, and results 'remain largely inconclusive' with clear anticipatory looking absent.

description: Reading memory examples that include early age cues (age 1-2) causes participants to report younger ages in their earliest memories compared to reading examples with later age cues (age 5-6)
original_authors: Ineke Wessel; Theresa Schweig; Rafaële J. C. Huntjens
original_title: Manipulating the reported age in earliest memories
replication_authors: Birte Klusmann; Ineke Wessel
replication_title: Manipulating the reported age in earliest memories in a Dutch community sample
explanation: The authors confirmed the main finding: participants in the early condition reported significantly younger age estimates than control participants (d = 0.33, p = .0008). In their Discussion they state 'the present findings add to the literature showing that including age information in experimental instructions affects the reported age in earliest memories.'

description: The effect of the age instruction manipulation on reported age of earliest memories differs by memory type, such that event memories are more sensitive to the manipulation than snapshot memories
original_authors: Ineke Wessel; Theresa Schweig; Rafaële J. C. Huntjens
original_title: Manipulating the reported age in earliest memories
replication_authors: Birte Klusmann; Ineke Wessel
replication_title: Manipulating the reported age in earliest memories in a Dutch community sample
explanation: The replication found no significant condition by memory type interaction (F(2,433) = 0.091, p = .913, η²p = .0004), which the authors explicitly describe as 'a second failure to replicate the significant interaction effect between condition and memory type on age estimates reported by Wessel and colleagues.'

description: A deep learning algorithm trained on ~118,000 retinal fundus images achieves an AUC of 0.99 for detecting referable diabetic retinopathy on both the EyePACS-1 and Messidor-2 test sets
original_authors: Varun Gulshan; Lily Peng; Marc Coram; Martin C. Stumpe; Derek Wu; Arunachalam Narayanaswamy; Subhashini Venugopalan; Kasumi Widner; Tom Madams; Jorge Cuadros; Ramasamy Kim; Rajiv Raman; Philip C. Nelson; Jessica L. Mega; Dale R. Webster
original_title: Development and validation of a deep learning algorithm for detection of diabetic retinopathy in retinal fundus photographs
original_journal: JAMA-Journal of the American Medical Association
replication_authors: Mike Voets; Kajsa Møllersen; Lars Ailo Bongo
replication_title: Reproduction study using public data of: Development and validation of a deep learning algorithm for detection of diabetic retinopathy in retinal fundus photographs
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were not able to reproduce the original study's results with publicly available data.' Their reproduced algorithm achieved AUCs of 0.951 and 0.853 on the EyePACS and Messidor-2 test sets respectively, compared to 0.99 on both test sets in the original study — a substantial performance gap. They attribute this to use of public data with single grades per image rather than the original's multi-graded private data.

description: Nationalism level of the chief executive is negatively associated with government respect for the freedoms of assembly and association, electoral self-determination, and speech in partial democracies
original_authors: Emir Yazici
original_title: Nationalism and human rights
replication_authors: Joshua Holzer
replication_title: Nationalism and human rights: A replication and extension
explanation: The author explicitly states 'Consistent with Yazici's [1] results, Table 1 reports that the nationalism level of the chief executive is negatively associated with high CIRI scores for assembly and association, electoral self-determination, and speech' and that 'coefficients and the coefficients from my replication models are nearly identical, which is a testament to the reproducibility of Yazici's [1] original findings.' All three models replicated at the 99% significance level.

description: Perceptual reversals of discontinuously presented ambiguous Necker stimuli produce a characteristic chain of difference ERP components: an early occipital Reversal Positivity (~130 ms), followed by an occipital/parietal Reversal Negativity (~260 ms), and a later Parietal/Frontopolar Positivity (~340–470 ms after stimulus onset)
original_authors: Jürgen Kornmeier; Michael Bach
original_title: Early neural activity in Necker-cube reversal: evidence for low-level processing of a gestalt phenomenon
replication_authors: Jürgen Kornmeier; Evelyn. Friedel; Lukas Hecker; Stefan Schmidt; Marc Wittmann
replication_title: What happens in the brain of meditators when perception changes but not the stimulus?
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. The Discussion states unambiguously: 'These findings largely replicate previous results about both spatial and temporal features of dERP correlates of perceptual reversals.' All three core dERP components from Kornmeier & Bach (2004, ref [50]) were found in both meditators and non-meditators across both experiments: Reversal Positivity (~140 ms, occipital), Reversal Negativity (~260 ms, occipital/parietal), and Parietal Positivity (~480-540 ms). The 'largely' qualifier reflects only minor quantitative differences (e.g., the Frontopolar Positivity latency preceded Parietal Positivity by only ~6 ms vs. ~100 ms in earlier studies), not failure of any component. Classified as close extension because the study extends the original paradigm by comparing experienced meditators with non-meditating controls, finding an additional Frontal Negativity unique to meditators.

description: Low-arousal negative words are processed slower than neutral words in a lexical decision task, while positive and high-arousal negative words are processed faster than neutral words
original_authors: Markus J. Hofmann; Lars Kuchinke; Sascha Tamm; Melissa L. H. Võ; Arthur M. Jacobs
original_title: Affective processing within 1/10th of a second: high arousal is necessary for early facilitative processing of negative but not positive words
replication_authors: Larissa Lusnig; Ralph Radach; Christina J. Mueller; Markus J. Hofmann
replication_title: Zen meditation neutralizes emotional evaluation, but not implicit affective processing of words
explanation: The authors successfully replicated one of the three LDT effects from Hofmann et al. (2009) — the slow-down for low-arousal negative words — in both groups, but 'were not able to replicate their effects that high-arousal negative and (low-arousal) positive words were processed faster than neutral words.' This partial replication warrants an inconclusive classification.

description: Partition dependence in university financial aid allocation: graduate students allocated more aid to lower-income households when the low-income range was partitioned into multiple categories than when the high-income range was partitioned into multiple categories
original_authors: Craig R. Fox; Rebecca K. Ratner; Daniel S. Lieb
original_title: How subjective grouping of options influences choice and allocation: Diversification bias and the phenomenon of partition dependence
replication_authors: Chenmu Xing; Katherine Williams; Jamie Hom; Meghana Kandlur; Praise Owoyemi; Joanna Paul; Ray Alexander; Elizabeth Shackney; Hilary Barth
replication_title: Partition dependence in financial aid distribution to income categories
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Basic findings of the original study were replicated' and report a very strong partition dependence effect (F(1,119)=379.871, p<.001, η²=.76), with nearly identical values to the original (94.7% vs 49.4% in the replication; 95.9% vs 47.7% in the original).

description: Partition dependence in university financial aid allocation: graduate students allocated more aid to lower-income households when the low-income range was partitioned into multiple categories than when the high-income range was partitioned into multiple categories
original_authors: Craig R. Fox; Rebecca K. Ratner; Daniel S. Lieb
original_title: How subjective grouping of options influences choice and allocation: Diversification bias and the phenomenon of partition dependence
replication_authors: Chenmu Xing; Katherine Williams; Jamie Hom; Meghana Kandlur; Praise Owoyemi; Joanna Paul; Ray Alexander; Elizabeth Shackney; Hilary Barth
replication_title: Partition dependence in financial aid distribution to income categories
explanation: In the 'high transparency' extension (Experiment 2), participants were shown both income partitions before randomly self-assigning to one; partition dependence remained strong (F(1,96)=166.701, p<.001, η²=.63), and the authors state that 'participants demonstrated clear and strong partition dependence' even under this modified condition.

description: Application of a focal static magnetic field (tSMS) over the motor cortex for 10 minutes decreases motor evoked potential (MEP) amplitudes for up to 6 minutes after stimulation, indicating reduced motor cortex excitability
original_authors: Antonio Oliviero; Laura Mordillo‐Mateos; Pablo Arias; Ivan Panyavin; Guglielmo Foffani; Juan Aguilar
original_title: Transcranial static magnetic field stimulation of the human motor cortex
replication_authors: Sabrina Lorenz; Birte Alex; Thomas Kammer
replication_title: Ten minutes of transcranial static magnetic field stimulation does not reliably modulate motor cortex excitability
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we again did not observe any modulatory effect of tSMS on excitability, the present study confirms our previous results' (of failure). The main ANOVA showed no significant effects for SESSION (F(1,17) = 0.04, p = 0.84), TIME (F(6,102) = 1.02, p = 0.42), or their interaction (p = 0.95), confirming no tSMS modulatory effect in either condition (with or without oddball task).

description: Plasma glucocorticogenic (G) activity is positively associated with alcohol intake in women
original_authors: Laura Fejerman; Sylvia Sanchez; Reuben Thomas; Phum Tachachartvanich; Jacques Riby; Scarlett Lin Gomez; Esther M. John; Martyn T. Smith
original_title: Association of lifestyle and demographic factors with estrogenic and glucocorticogenic activity in Mexican American women
replication_authors: Phum Tachachartvanich; Sylvia S. Sanchez; Scarlett L. Gomez; Esther M. John; Martyn T. Smith; Laura Fejerman
replication_title: Plasma glucocorticogenic activity, race/ethnicity and alcohol intake among San Francisco Bay Area women
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated the previously reported positive association between G activity and alcohol intake [32].' Women drinking >10g/day had 19% higher plasma G activity than non-drinkers (P = 0.004), consistent with the original finding in Mexican women using the same CALUX assay.

description: Infants prefer prosocial agents over antisocial agents when presented with the 'opening a box to get a toy' paradigm, in which an animal puppet is helped or hindered by another puppet
original_authors: Hamlin JK; Wynn K.
original_title: Young infants prefer prosocial to antisocial others
replication_authors: Elena Vaporova; Norbert Zmyj
replication_title: Social evaluation and imitation of prosocial and antisocial agents in infants, children, and adults
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'our study did not replicate the original findings of Hamlin and Wynn [9].' None of the three age groups (9-month-olds, 14-month-olds, or 4-year-olds) showed a significant preference for the prosocial agent (Exp 1: 23/52 chose prosocial, p = .488; Exp 2: 15/32 chose prosocial, p = .860).

description: Signed reward prediction errors (SRPEs) — larger and more positive reward prediction errors — enhance declarative memory performance in a Dutch-Swahili word pair learning task
original_authors: De Loof, Esther; Ergo, Kate; Naert, Lien; Janssens, Clio; Talsma, Durk; Van Opstal, Filip; Verguts, Tom
original_title: Signed reward prediction errors drive declarative learning
replication_authors: Kate Ergo; Esther De Loof; Gillian Debra; Bernhard Pastötter; Tom Verguts
replication_title: Failure to modulate reward prediction errors in declarative learning with theta (6 Hz) frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated our earlier finding of SRPEs driving declarative learning [10]' and in the conclusion 'Previous behavioral results were replicated, with SRPEs driving declarative learning.' Frequentist statistics confirmed a significant positive SRPE effect (χ²(1, N=76) = 9.13, p = .003) with decisive Bayesian evidence (BF₁₀ > 100).

description: Symmetrical patterns (reflectional symmetry) are judged as lasting longer than random patterns in a verbal duration estimation task
original_authors: Ruth Ogden; Alexis D. J. Makin; Letizia Palumbo; Marco Bertamini
original_title: Symmetry lasts longer than random, but only for brief presentations
replication_authors: Alexis David James Makin; Afzal Rahman; Marco Bertamini
replication_title: No effect of multi-axis dot pattern symmetry on subjective duration
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a 'failed conceptual replication' of Ogden et al. [7] and Palumbo et al. [8], reporting no effect of Regularity (F < 1) — directly contrasting with the original F(2,42) = 17.114, p < .001, ηp² = 0.451. They conclude: 'there was no evidence that reflectional symmetry dot patterns were judged as lasting longer than random dot patterns.'

description: Symmetrical patterns are judged as lasting longer than random patterns in a duration estimation task
original_authors: Letizia Palumbo; Ruth Ogden; Alexis D. J. Makin; Marco Bertamini
original_title: Does preference for abstract patterns relate to information processing and perceived duration?
replication_authors: Alexis David James Makin; Afzal Rahman; Marco Bertamini
replication_title: No effect of multi-axis dot pattern symmetry on subjective duration
explanation: The authors explicitly frame their study as 'failure to replicate an effect from two of our previous papers,' including Palumbo et al. [8], which had originally found F(1,23) = 5.532, p = 0.028, ηp² = 0.194. The replication found no effect of Regularity (F < 1). The Discussion also confirms: 'it should be emphasised that what we report here is a failed conceptual replication.'

description: Individuals high in Self-Control show less avoidance of cognitive demand in the Demand Selection Task, with higher Self-Control predicting a lower proportion of low-demand choices
original_authors: Wouter Kool; Joseph T. McGuire; Gary J. Wang; Matthew M. Botvinick
original_title: Neural and behavioral evidence for an intrinsic cost of self-control
replication_authors: Alexander Strobel; Gesine Wieder; Philipp C. Paulus; Florian Ott; Sebastian Pannasch; Stefan J. Kiebel; Corinna Kührt
replication_title: Dispositional cognitive effort investment and behavioral demand avoidance: Are they related?
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to 'conceptually replicate the results by Kool et al.' and conclude that 'the direct correlation between Self-Control and Demand Avoidance was low and insignificant as well, despite adequate power to detect an effect half of the one originally reported.' Kool et al. found r = .38; this study found near-zero correlations (-.06 to .09) and a latent trait covariance that was not significant (estimate = -0.01, p = .867).

description: Objects repeatedly paired with fluent motion (smooth/predictable) are preferred over those paired with disfluent motion (sudden/unpredictable), but this preference effect is only present when objects are later rated in a moving context, not when rated in a stationary context
original_authors: Jonathan C. Flavell; Bryony McKean; Steven P. Tipper; Alexander J. Kirkham; Tim Vestner; Harriet Over
original_title: Motion fluency and object preference: Robust perceptual but fragile memory effects
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Jonathan Charles Flavell; Bryony McKean
replication_title: Motion fluency effects on object preference is limited to learned context
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'Our results supported the findings of the original study: namely, that preference effects were present when stimuli were presented moving fluently/disfluently but were absent when stimuli were presented in a stationary context.' The current paper used winged insects instead of geometric shapes to test whether more ecologically valid stimuli would change the outcome, but the same boundary condition was found.

description: Reciprocal crosses of Nasonia vitripennis and Nasonia giraulti show no parent-of-origin effects (genomic imprinting) in gene expression, suggesting a lack of epigenetic reprogramming during embryogenesis in haplodiploid wasps
original_authors: Xu Wang; John H. Werren; Andrew G. Clark
original_title: Allele-specific transcriptome and methylome analysis reveals stable inheritance and cis-regulation of DNA methylation in Nasonia
replication_authors: Kimberly C. Olney; Joshua D. Gibson; Heini M. Natri; Avery Underwood; Juergen Gadau; Melissa A. Wilson
replication_title: Lack of parent-of-origin effects in Nasonia jewel wasp: A replication and extension study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We successfully replicate the findings from Wang et al. 2016, showing a lack of parent-of-origin effects in Nasonia transcriptomes.' Both the re-analysis of the original data with new bioinformatic pipelines and the newly generated Wilson dataset with different individuals independently confirmed no parent-of-origin effects.

description: Left parietal high-density alpha tACS at 10 Hz (1 mA, 35-40 min) induces a shift in visuospatial attention away from the contralateral right to the ipsilateral left hemifield during endogenous attention tasks
original_authors: Teresa Schuhmann; Selma K. Kemmerer; Felix Duecker; Tom A. de Graaf; Sanne Ten Oever; Peter De Weerd; Alexander T. Sack
original_title: Left parietal tACS at alpha frequency induces a shift of visuospatial attention
replication_authors: Andra Coldea; Stephanie Morand; Domenica Veniero; Monika Harvey; Gregor Thut
replication_title: Parietal alpha tACS shows inconsistent effects on visuospatial attention
explanation: The authors followed the same endogenous attention task and high-density tACS montage over left parietal cortex (P3) as Schuhmann et al. (2019), but found no significant tACS effect on spatial bias (F(1,39) = .04, p = .83). They explicitly conclude: 'we failed to find a tACS effect using our parameter combinations, as there was no significant difference between 10 Hz tACS and sham.'

description: Increasing blood glucose levels via caloric intake causes people to become more future-oriented (less steeply discounting future monetary rewards)
original_authors: Wang XT; Dvorak RD
original_title: Sweet future: fluctuating blood glucose levels affect future discounting
replication_authors: Rafał Muda; Przemysław Sawicki; Michał Ginszt
replication_title: Perceived food palatability, blood glucose level and future discounting: Lack of evidence for blood glucose level’s impact on reward discounting
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'adopted virtually the same procedures as those used in previous studies of blood glucose and delay discounting (see e.g., [3])' but found 'no evidence that increases in blood glucose levels lead to changes in future discounting of monetary rewards,' adding a palatability manipulation to test a proposed moderating mechanism not present in the original study.

description: Gender disparities in obesity prevalence among racial/ethnic groups in the US, with Non-Hispanic Black women having markedly higher obesity rates than Non-Hispanic Black men — a disparity not seen to the same extent in other racial/ethnic groups
original_authors: Hales, C.; Carroll, M.; Fryar, C.; Ogden, C.
original_title: Prevalence of obesity and severe obesity among adults: United States, 2017-2018
replication_authors: Jason H. Karnes; Amit Arora; Jianglin Feng; Heidi E. Steiner; Lina Sulieman; Eric Boerwinkle; Cheryl Clark; Mine Cicek; Elizabeth Cohn; Kelly Gebo; Roxana Loperena-Cortes; Lucila Ohno-Machado; Kelsey Mayo; Steve Mockrin; Andrea Ramirez; Sheri Schully; Yann C. Klimentidis
replication_title: Racial, ethnic, and gender differences in obesity and body fat distribution: An All of Us Research Program demonstration project
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the abstract: 'Our findings replicate previous observations with respect to gender differences in BMI. In particular, we replicate the large gender disparity in obesity rates among NHB participants.' The Discussion section also confirms: 'We observed strong disparities consistent with previously published literature, including the large gender discrepancy in obesity prevalence between NHB women and NHB men.'

description: Racial/ethnic differences in abdominal obesity prevalence in the US, with prevalence highest in Non-Hispanic Black women, followed by Mexican American women, then Non-Hispanic White women
original_authors: Cheryl D. Fryar; Deanna Kruszon-Moran; Qiuping Gu; Cynthia L. Ogden
original_title: Mean body weight, height, waist circumference, and body mass index among adults: United States, 1999-2000 through 2015-2016
replication_authors: Jason H. Karnes; Amit Arora; Jianglin Feng; Heidi E. Steiner; Lina Sulieman; Eric Boerwinkle; Cheryl Clark; Mine Cicek; Elizabeth Cohn; Kelly Gebo; Roxana Loperena-Cortes; Lucila Ohno-Machado; Kelsey Mayo; Steve Mockrin; Andrea Ramirez; Sheri Schully; Yann C. Klimentidis
replication_title: Racial, ethnic, and gender differences in obesity and body fat distribution: An All of Us Research Program demonstration project
explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Our findings also replicate previous identified racial differences that exist with respect to body fat distribution. Data from NHANES has shown the prevalence of abdominal obesity to be highest for NHB women, followed by Mexican American women, and then NHW women [21].' The word 'replicate' is used directly, and Table 1 data confirms the same ordering was observed in the AoU cohort (NHB women WC=97.95cm > Hispanic women WC=93.50cm > NHW women WC=91.34cm). The replication claim is unambiguous.

description: Non-Hispanic Black women have lower alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels relative to other racial/ethnic groups despite having higher BMI, suggesting a potentially more 'metabolically healthy' obesity phenotype
original_authors: Julie-Anne Nazare; Jessica D. Smith; Anne-Laure Borel; Steven M. Haffner; Beverley Balkau; Robert Ross; Christine Massien; Natalie Alméras; Jean-Pierre Després
original_title: Ethnic influences on the relations between abdominal subcutaneous and visceral adiposity, liver fat, and cardiometabolic risk profile: the international study of prediction of intra-abdominal adiposity and its relationship with cardiometabolic risk/intra-abdominal adiposity
replication_authors: Jason H. Karnes; Amit Arora; Jianglin Feng; Heidi E. Steiner; Lina Sulieman; Eric Boerwinkle; Cheryl Clark; Mine Cicek; Elizabeth Cohn; Kelly Gebo; Roxana Loperena-Cortes; Lucila Ohno-Machado; Kelsey Mayo; Steve Mockrin; Andrea Ramirez; Sheri Schully; Yann C. Klimentidis
replication_title: Racial, ethnic, and gender differences in obesity and body fat distribution: An All of Us Research Program demonstration project
explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The authors explicitly state: 'we replicate the observation that NHB women have lower ALT despite a higher BMI, potentially suggesting a more metabolically healthy obesity phenotype in NHB women [23].' This is supported by strong statistical evidence: multivariable regression shows NHB participants have significantly lower ALT (beta = -5.24, p = 8.41x10^-60) after controlling for age, BMI, and gender, with an additional Women x NHB interaction term (beta = -1.73, p = 9.93x10^-3) indicating the effect is even more pronounced in NHB women. The authors use the word 'replicate' directly and the result is unambiguous.

description: Sleep selectively strengthens declarative memories that participants expect to be tested on in the future (future-relevant memories benefit more from overnight sleep than memories not expected to be retested)
original_authors: Ines Wilhelm; Susanne Diekelmann; Ina Molzow; Amr Ayoub; Matthias Mölle; Jan Born
original_title: Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance
replication_authors: Jennifer E. Ashton; Scott A. Cairney
replication_title: Future-relevant memories are not selectively strengthened during sleep
explanation: In Experiment 1, the authors conducted an online direct replication of Wilhelm et al. (2011) using the same verbal paired associates paradigm. They found no Delay × Expectancy interaction at the 12-hour or 7-day test (p = .786 and p = .249 respectively), with Bayesian analysis yielding BF01 = 4.00 (moderate evidence for the null). The authors explicitly state: 'we were unable to replicate the seminal finding that sleep selectively strengthens memories that are deemed relevant for the future.'

description: Sleep selectively strengthens declarative memories that participants expect to be tested on in the future (future-relevant memories benefit more from overnight sleep than memories not expected to be retested)
original_authors: Ines Wilhelm; Susanne Diekelmann; Ina Molzow; Amr Ayoub; Matthias Mölle; Jan Born
original_title: Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance
replication_authors: Jennifer E. Ashton; Scott A. Cairney
replication_title: Future-relevant memories are not selectively strengthened during sleep
explanation: Experiment 2 was a pre-registered close replication with a reduced baseline criterion (40% vs 60%) and more stimuli (100 vs 40 word pairs), designed to test whether lower encoding strength would allow the selective sleep effect to emerge. Again, no Delay × Expectancy interaction was found (p = .504, BF01 = 3.42). The authors conclude: 'memory strength at encoding does not appear to explain our failure to replicate the findings of Wilhelm et al.'

description: Adults who consume pretzels (thirst induction) show induced-state episodic foresight impairment: a minority (21%) prefer pretzels over water for tomorrow, suggesting thirst biases future predictions
original_authors: Hannah J. Kramer; Deborah Goldfarb; Sarah M. Tashjian; Kristin Hansen Lagattuta
original_title: These pretzels are making me thirsty: older children and adults struggle with induced-state episodic foresight
replication_authors: Tessa R. Mazachowsky; Katarina McKenzie; Michael A. Busseri; Caitlin E. V. Mahy
replication_title: “These pretzels are making me thirsty” so I’ll have water tomorrow: A partial replication and extension of adults’ induced-state episodic foresight
explanation: The replication found the same proportion of adults choosing pretzels after thirst induction (20% vs. 21% in original), but because the control condition showed the same pattern (21% chose pretzels without thirst induction), the authors conclude: 'we cannot conclude based on these findings that adults struggle with induced-state episodic foresight.' The effect was partially consistent but the design could not confirm the original interpretation.

description: Adults without thirst induction (control condition, lecture setting) prefer pretzels over water at rates no different from chance (66%), establishing that adults' baseline preference is for pretzels
original_authors: Hannah J. Kramer; Deborah Goldfarb; Sarah M. Tashjian; Kristin Hansen Lagattuta
original_title: These pretzels are making me thirsty: older children and adults struggle with induced-state episodic foresight
replication_authors: Tessa R. Mazachowsky; Katarina McKenzie; Michael A. Busseri; Caitlin E. V. Mahy
replication_title: “These pretzels are making me thirsty” so I’ll have water tomorrow: A partial replication and extension of adults’ induced-state episodic foresight
explanation: The replication found only 32% of adults preferred pretzels in the lecture setting, significantly below chance (p = .004), directly contradicting Kramer et al.'s finding that 66% preferred pretzels. The authors state: 'our results do not align with Kramer et al. ([1], Study 2), who found that 66% (not significantly greater than chance) of students in an undergraduate lecture reported preferring pretzels over water for tomorrow.'

description: Country-years where presidents won their previous election with an absolute majority are more likely to be associated with high government respect for human rights, compared to country-years where presidents won by a mere plurality
original_authors: Joshua Holzer
original_title: The perils of plurality rule and the major(itarian) effect of cabinet composition on human rights in presidential democracies
replication_authors: Joshua Holzer
replication_title: The perils of plurality rule in democratic presidential systems: A replication and extension
explanation: The author explicitly states: 'With this follow-up article I have replicated my previous findings and have found them to be robust to a greatly expanded dataset.' The same ordered probit model is re-estimated with an expanded dataset (1,182 observations from 55 countries over 28 years vs. the original 241 observations from 35 countries over 11 years), and the president elected with a majority variable remains positively and significantly associated with high PHYSINT scores.

description: Anodal and cathodal tDCS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex produce negatively correlated effects on attentional blink magnitude at the individual level (those who improve during anodal tDCS worsen during cathodal tDCS, and vice versa), despite no group-level effect
original_authors: Raquel E. London; Heleen A. Slagter
original_title: No effect of transcranial direct current stimulation over left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex on temporal attention
replication_authors: Reteig LC; Newman LA; Ridderinkhof KR; Slagter HA
replication_title: Effects of tDCS on the attentional blink revisited: A statistical evaluation of a replication attempt
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'all the analyses we conducted seem to support the same conclusion: that the current study is not a successful replication of the previous [20].' The original study found r(31) = -.45 (p = .009), while the replication found r(37) = .02 (p = .899), with multiple statistical measures (equivalence testing, prediction intervals, replication Bayes factor BF0r = 9.66, meta-analysis) all confirming failure to replicate.

description: Trait BAS and trait anticipatory pleasure correlate positively with the percentage of hard-task-choices in trials with low probability of reward attainment in the original EEfRT (effort expenditure for rewards task)
original_authors: Joachim T. Geaney; Michael T. Treadway; Luke D. Smillie
original_title: Trait anticipatory pleasure predicts effort expenditure for reward
replication_authors: Hanno Andreas Ohmann; Niclas Kuper; Jan Wacker
replication_title: Examining the reliability and validity of two versions of the Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT)
explanation: The authors explicitly sought to replicate the BAS and anticipatory pleasure correlations from Geaney et al. [23]. In Study 1, some correlations were found but inconsistent with the original pattern, and 'none of these correlations replicated' in Study 2 with the larger sample (N=394). The conclusion states they 'were not able to replicate previous findings linking trait BAS and trait anticipatory pleasure to effort allocation.'

description: Trait extraversion and trait BAS correlate positively with the mean number of clicks in trials with low probability of reward attainment in the modified version of the EEfRT
original_authors: Hanno Andreas Ohmann; Niclas Kuper; Jan Wacker
original_title: A low dosage of the dopamine D2-receptor antagonist sulpiride affects effort allocation for reward regardless of trait extraversion
replication_authors: Hanno Andreas Ohmann; Niclas Kuper; Jan Wacker
replication_title: Examining the reliability and validity of two versions of the Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT)
explanation: The authors sought to replicate the BAS and extraversion correlations from Ohmann et al. [24] using the modified EEfRT in Study 1. In Study 1, trait BAS did not correlate significantly with the mean number of clicks in trials with low probability of reward attainment (r = .015, ns). The conclusion states they 'were not able to replicate previous findings linking trait BAS and trait anticipatory pleasure to effort allocation within both versions of the EEfRT.'

description: Rhythm perception (detection of temporal irregularities in vocoded speech) is improved for intelligible (16-channel) compared to unintelligible (1-channel) noise-vocoded speech, despite near-identical broadband amplitude modulations
original_authors: Benedikt Zoefel; Alan Archer-Boyd; Matthew H. Davis
original_title: Phase entrainment of brain oscillations causally modulates neural responses to intelligible speech
replication_authors: Benedikt Zoefel; Rebecca A. Gilbert; Matthew H. Davis
replication_title: Intelligibility improves perception of timing changes in speech
explanation: Experiment 1 explicitly aimed to replicate the original irregularity detection finding from [26]. The authors report d-prime was significantly higher for intelligible 16-channel speech than unintelligible 1-channel speech (t(5) = 2.75, p = 0.04, Cohen's d = 1.12), confirming the original effect. In the Discussion they state: 'In Experiment 1, we replicated this effect (1) with a greater proportion of irregular trials (50% instead of 14%), (2) during a forced-choice (irregular/regular) paradigm, and (3) in the more favourable listening conditions to be found outside of an MRI scanner.'

description: Color diversity (high vs. low) can be judged for non-attended rows in a dual-task paradigm without reducing performance on the primary letter recall task ('cost-free' representation outside focal attention)
original_authors: Bronfman, Zohar Z.; Brezis, Noam; Jacobson, Hilla; Usher, Marius
original_title: We see more than we can report: 'cost free' color phenomenality outside focal attention
replication_authors: Brylee Hawkins; Dee Evans; Anya Preston; Kendra Westmoreland; Callie E. Mims; Kiara Lolo; Nicholas Rosario; Brian Odegaard
replication_title: Color diversity judgments in peripheral vision: Evidence against “cost-free” representations
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the original finding from [1] on a standard computer monitor' (Supplemental Experiment 1), confirming the cost-free color diversity phenomenon in central vision as originally reported.

description: Color diversity can be judged 'cost-free' outside focally-attended regions — specifically that attending to color diversity of non-cued regions does not impair primary task performance
original_authors: Bronfman, Zohar Z.; Brezis, Noam; Jacobson, Hilla; Usher, Marius
original_title: We see more than we can report: 'cost free' color phenomenality outside focal attention
replication_authors: Brylee Hawkins; Dee Evans; Anya Preston; Kendra Westmoreland; Callie E. Mims; Kiara Lolo; Nicholas Rosario; Brian Odegaard
replication_title: Color diversity judgments in peripheral vision: Evidence against “cost-free” representations
explanation: In Experiment 1, using the same stimuli and timing but extending the paradigm to peripheral vision (21° eccentricity on a large projector screen), the authors found that color diversity perception was NOT cost-free: letter recall accuracy was significantly lower when color diversity was judged for uncued (peripheral) regions vs. cued regions (t(20) = 2.4, p = 0.03, d = 0.53), and color diversity accuracy was also significantly lower for uncued regions, contrary to the original claim of cost-free representation.

description: Color diversity can be judged 'cost-free' outside focally-attended regions — specifically that attending to color diversity of non-cued regions does not impair primary task performance
original_authors: Bronfman, Zohar Z.; Brezis, Noam; Jacobson, Hilla; Usher, Marius
original_title: We see more than we can report: 'cost free' color phenomenality outside focal attention
replication_authors: Brylee Hawkins; Dee Evans; Anya Preston; Kendra Westmoreland; Callie E. Mims; Kiara Lolo; Nicholas Rosario; Brian Odegaard
replication_title: Color diversity judgments in peripheral vision: Evidence against “cost-free” representations
explanation: In Experiment 2, using the identical peripheral vision paradigm as Experiment 1 (with confidence judgments substituted for subjective color ratings), the authors again found that color diversity perception was NOT cost-free: letter recall was significantly lower for uncued vs. cued regions (Wilcoxon W = 202.00, p = .002), and color diversity accuracy was lower for uncued regions (t(20) = 6.85, p < .001, d = 1.50), replicating the Experiment 1 failure to find cost-free representation in peripheral vision.

description: Corrections of childhood vaccine myths presented in a myths-vs.-facts format backfire, ironically increasing false vaccine beliefs and vaccination hesitancy relative to a control condition, due to familiarity-driven and fear-driven mechanisms
original_authors: Sara Pluviano; Caroline Watt; Sergio Della Sala
original_title: Misinformation lingers in memory: Failure of three pro-vaccination strategies
replication_authors: Ullrich K. H. Ecker; Caitlin X. M. Sharkey; Briony Swire-Thompson
replication_title: Correcting vaccine misinformation: A failure to replicate familiarity or fear-driven backfire effects
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'the present study therefore replicated and extended a study by Pluviano et al. (2017), which found that fear appeals and corrections presented in a myths-vs.-facts format backfired'. They conclude: 'we found that no intervention was associated with greater misinformation belief or vaccine hesitancy than control at any timepoint', calling it a 'failure to replicate' in the abstract and title.

description: Women display more of the color red when expecting to interact with a highly attractive man compared to a less attractive man
original_authors: Daniela Niesta Kayser; Maria Agthe; Jon K. Maner
original_title: Strategic sexual signals: Women's display versus avoidance of the color red depends on the attractiveness of an anticipated interaction partner
replication_authors: Maria Agthe; Daniela Niesta Kayser; Sascha Schwarz; Jon K. Maner
replication_title: Antecedents of the red-romance effect: Men’s attractiveness and women’s fertility
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a 'conceptual replication' of Niesta Kayser et al. (2016). Results were mixed: the attractiveness effect reached significance for women on hormonal contraceptives (p = .03) but not for naturally cycling women (p = .06) when controlling for covariates, leading the authors to conclude 'mixed replicability' and 'mixed support' for the hypothesis.

description: Reading fiction (but not nonfiction) is positively correlated with IRI fantasy scores and RMET scores (theory-of-mind ability), such that habitual fiction readers are better at inferring others' mental states and more likely to transpose themselves into fictitious characters
original_authors: Raymond A. Mar; Keith Oatley; Jacob Hirsh; Jennifer dela Paz; Jordan B. Peterson
original_title: Bookworms versus nerds: Exposure to fiction versus non-fiction, divergent associations with social ability, and the simulation of fictional social worlds
replication_authors: Yuka Takahashi; Toshiyuki Himichi; Ayumi Masuchi; Daisuke Nakanishi; Yohsuke Ohtsubo
replication_title: Is reading fiction associated with a higher mind-reading ability? Two conceptual replication studies in Japan
explanation: Study 1 conceptually replicated Mar et al.'s [15] correlations between fiction reading and empathy-related constructs in a Japanese sample. The authors conclude: 'Study 1 confirmed the previously reported correlation between fiction reading and empathy-related constructs [15, 24] among a Japanese undergraduate sample.' Specifically, fiction reading time was significantly correlated with IRI fantasy score (r(315) = .21, p < .001), and with RMET score when controlling for outliers via robust regression (standardized coefficient .13, 95% CI [.01, .23]).

description: Brief exposure to literary fiction (compared to popular fiction, nonfiction, or no reading) causally improves performance on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET), a measure of theory-of-mind ability
original_authors: David Comer Kidd; Emanuele Castano
original_title: Reading literary fiction improves theory of mind
replication_authors: Yuka Takahashi; Toshiyuki Himichi; Ayumi Masuchi; Daisuke Nakanishi; Yohsuke Ohtsubo
replication_title: Is reading fiction associated with a higher mind-reading ability? Two conceptual replication studies in Japan
explanation: Study 2 explicitly failed to replicate the causal effect. The authors state: 'Study 2 failed to replicate the causal relationship reported by Kidd and Castano's experimental study [26]: In the present study, a brief exposure to literary fiction did not enhance RMET performance.' The ANOVA on ΔRMET was nonsignificant: F(2, 301) = 1.43, p = .242, η² = .009, and the mean ΔRMET was actually lowest in the literary fiction condition.

description: Americans engaged in highly dangerous cleaning practices to prevent COVID-19 infection, including approximately 4% of respondents drinking or gargling household cleaner, soapy water, or diluted bleach
original_authors: Radhika Gharpure; Candis M. Hunter; Amy H. Schnall; Catherine E. Barrett; Amy E. Kirby; Jasen Kunz; Kirsten Berling; Jeffrey W. Mercante; Jennifer L. Murphy; Amanda G. Garcia-Williams
original_title: Knowledge and practices regarding safe household cleaning and disinfection for COVID-19 prevention-United States
replication_authors: Leib Litman; Zohn Rosen; Rachel Hartman; Cheskie Rosenzweig; Sarah L. Weinberger-Litman; Aaron J. Moss; Jonathan Robinson
replication_title: Did people really drink bleach to prevent COVID-19? A guide for protecting survey data against problematic respondents
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current study was a replication of a study conducted by the CDC in May 2020... we used the identical survey design, question wording, online sample provider, and sampling methodology.' While they initially replicated the CDC's raw prevalence rates (~4% ingestion), once data quality controls were applied, 'all reports of highly dangerous cleaning practices came from problematic respondents' and 'we find no evidence that people ingested cleaning products to prevent a COVID-19 infection' — a clear failure to replicate the substantive finding.

description: People with tinnitus show an asymmetric mismatch negativity (MMN) response to intensity deviants at their tinnitus frequency — larger responses to upward deviants and smaller responses to downward deviants compared to controls, termed the Intensity Mismatch Asymmetry (IMA)
original_authors: William Sedley; Kai Alter; Phillip E. Gander; Joel Berger; Timothy D. Griffiths
original_title: Exposing pathological sensory predictions in tinnitus using auditory intensity deviant evoked responses
replication_authors: Ekaterina A. Yukhnovich; Kai Alter; William Sedley
replication_title: Nuances in intensity deviant asymmetric responses as a biomarker for tinnitus
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion: 'The current study failed to replicate the Intensity Mismatch Asymmetry as a marker of tinnitus status.' No significant group differences were found (group x direction interaction p = 0.239), and the control group showed a similar response pattern to the tinnitus group at the tinnitus frequency, contrary to the original study.

description: Intolerance of Uncertainty (IU) is negatively associated with choosing a delayed, more certain, and more valuable reward over an immediate, less certain, and less valuable reward — i.e., high-IU individuals show a greater preference for the immediate option to avoid prolonged waiting under uncertainty
original_authors: Christian C. Luhmann; Kanako Ishida; Greg Hajcak
original_title: Intolerance of uncertainty and decisions about delayed, probabilistic rewards
replication_authors: Pedro L. Cobos; María J. Quintero; Francisco J. López; David Luque; Luis F. Ciria; y. Joaquín Morís
replication_title: Intolerance of uncertainty does not significantly predict decisions about delayed, probabilistic rewards: A failure to replicate Luhmann, C. C., Ishida, K., & Hajcak, G. (2011)
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'failed to replicate Luhmann et al.'s (2011) results concerning the role of IU.' All regression coefficients for IU were negligible and non-significant (β = .01, p = .932 for the key IU predictor), and the authors conclude that 'IU is far from playing a significant role in choosing between the immediate and delayed rewards in Luhmann et al.'s task.'

description: The ETMCQ has a three-factor structure (epistemic trust, mistrust, and credulity) with acceptable psychometric properties including reliability and internal consistency
original_authors: Chloe Campbell; Michal Tanzer; Rob Saunders; Thomas Booker; Elizabeth Allison; Elizabeth Li; Claire O’Dowda; Patrick Luyten; Peter Fonagy
original_title: Development and validation of a self-report measure of epistemic trust
replication_authors: Christian Greiner; Vincent Besch; Marissa Bouchard-Boivin; Catherine Le Hénaff; Cécilia Von Rohr-De Pree; Nader Perroud; Paco Prada; Martin Debbané
replication_title: Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ) validation in French language: Exploring links to loneliness
explanation: The authors validated a French-language translation of the ETMCQ in a Francophone population and confirmed the three-factor structure with a 12-item version. The Discussion states 'our study suggest that the ETMCQ is a valid and promising instrument that can be used to assess epistemic trust in Francophone populations,' consistent with the original findings, though 3 items were removed for acceptable fit.

description: ETMCQ subscales differentially associate with distinct attachment dimensions and styles, with epistemic mistrust linked to avoidant attachment and credulity linked to anxious attachment
original_authors: Chloe Campbell; Michal Tanzer; Rob Saunders; Thomas Booker; Elizabeth Allison; Elizabeth Li; Claire O’Dowda; Patrick Luyten; Peter Fonagy
original_title: Development and validation of a self-report measure of epistemic trust
replication_authors: Christian Greiner; Vincent Besch; Marissa Bouchard-Boivin; Catherine Le Hénaff; Cécilia Von Rohr-De Pree; Nader Perroud; Paco Prada; Martin Debbané
replication_title: Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ) validation in French language: Exploring links to loneliness
explanation: The Discussion states 'We also largely replicated Campbell et al.'s [15] findings concerning attachment styles,' with EM more strongly correlated with avoidance and EC with anxiety dimensions, and differential patterns across the four attachment styles.

description: Epistemic mistrust and credulity partially mediate the relationship between childhood traumatic experiences and psychopathology
original_authors: Chloe Campbell; Michal Tanzer; Rob Saunders; Thomas Booker; Elizabeth Allison; Elizabeth Li; Claire O’Dowda; Patrick Luyten; Peter Fonagy
original_title: Development and validation of a self-report measure of epistemic trust
replication_authors: Christian Greiner; Vincent Besch; Marissa Bouchard-Boivin; Catherine Le Hénaff; Cécilia Von Rohr-De Pree; Nader Perroud; Paco Prada; Martin Debbané
replication_title: Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire (ETMCQ) validation in French language: Exploring links to loneliness
explanation: The Discussion states 'Our results regarding childhood trauma replicated those of Campbell et al. [15]. Specifically, we found that EM and EC partially mediated this link, whereas ET was not a mediator,' directly confirming replication of the original mediation findings.

description: Individuals with higher numeracy skills are more likely to correctly interpret political data when the correct interpretation is consistent with their political identity ('motivated numeracy'), with liberals and conservatives selectively using numerical skills to confirm partisan beliefs
original_authors: Kahan, Dan M.; Peters, Ellen; Dawson, Erica Cantrell; Slovic, Paul
original_title: Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government
replication_authors: Shuyuan Yu; John E. Opfer
replication_title: Cognitive support for political partisans’ understanding of policy data
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we failed to replicate motivated numeracy' using political identity as the measure. The Discussion confirms: 'we did not observe motivated numeracy [3] based on political identity, which was inconsistent with some successful replications.' The pre-registered three-way interaction among problem type, political outlook, and numeracy was not significant (χ²(3) = 4.27, p = .234).

description: Deferring feedback significantly impairs information-integration (II) category learning but leaves unidimensional rule-based (UD) category learning intact, supporting the COVIS dual-process theory of category learning
original_authors: Smith JD; Boomer J.; Zakrzewski AC; Roeder JL; Church BA; Ashby FG
original_title: Deferred feedback sharply dissociates implicit and explicit category learning
replication_authors: Charlotte E. R. Edmunds; Kathryn Carpenter; Andy J. Wills; Fraser Milton
replication_title: The effect of deferring feedback on rule-based and information-integration category learning
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Experiment 1 successfully replicated the key results from Smith et al. [11] that were taken as providing strong support for COVIS. There was a significant interaction between category structure and feedback type, with II performance significantly impaired by deferring feedback whereas UD accuracy was statistically unaffected by feedback type.' The interaction was significant (F(1,71) = 5.53, p = .021, ηg² = 0.07).

description: Deferred feedback impairs both conjunction rule-based (CJ) and information-integration (II) category learning equally, with no significant interaction between feedback type and category structure when task difficulty (number of relevant dimensions) is equated
original_authors: Mike E. Le Pelley; Ben R. Newell; Robert M. Nosofsky
original_title: Deferred feedback does not dissociate implicit and explicit category-learning systems: commentary on Smith et al
replication_authors: Charlotte E. R. Edmunds; Kathryn Carpenter; Andy J. Wills; Fraser Milton
replication_title: The effect of deferring feedback on rule-based and information-integration category learning
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This experiment successfully replicated the key result of Le Pelley et al. [17] by finding that deferred feedback similarly reduced learning performance in both the CJ and II tasks relative to the immediate feedback condition.' The interaction between category structure and feedback type was not significant (F(1,66) = .24, p = .626, ηg² = .004).

description: Women's duration estimates of briefly-viewed attractive male photographs are longer than their estimates for unattractive male photographs
original_authors: Joana Arantes; Mark E. Berg; John H. Wearden
original_title: Females' duration estimates of briefly-viewed male, but not female, photographs depend on attractiveness
replication_authors: Nuno Fernandes; Sandra Soares; Mavilde Arantes; Joana Arantes
replication_title: Time perception of attractive male faces and voices: The role of women’s menstrual cycle
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we successfully replicated previous findings in the literature, demonstrating that briefly viewed attractive faces were reproduced for longer durations than unattractive ones.' Both the ovulation and menstruation phases showed significantly longer duration estimates for attractive vs. unattractive male faces (both p<.001), confirming the original temporal dilation effect.

description: Correlations between seemingly race-neutral language-exclusive ideologies, racial essentialism, and asset-based attitudes toward African American Language among K-12 preservice teachers of science and other subjects
original_authors: Sedlacek, Quentin C.; Lemmi, Catherine; Feldman, Kimberly; Ortiz, Nickolaus; León, Maricela
original_title: African American language in science education: a translanguaging perspective
original_journal: Journal of Research in Science Teaching
replication_authors: Quentin C. Sedlacek; Nickolaus Ortiz; Catherine Lemmi; Maricela León; Kimberly C. Feldman
replication_title: Racial and linguistic ideologies and formative assessment practices of U.S. science teachers: A preregistered conceptual replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'all but one of the findings from our previous study are successfully replicated' and 'we reproduce our previous finding that seemingly race-neutral beliefs about writing pedagogy are in fact correlated with essentialist ideologies of race.' All three preregistered correlations among language-exclusive ideology, racial essentialism, and asset-based attitudes toward AAL were significant (r=0.366, -0.514, -0.409).

description: Language-exclusive ideology is associated with formative assessment behaviors among preservice teachers: grading frequency, grades assigned, inferences about student understanding, and length of written feedback in response to student science writing samples
original_authors: Sedlacek, Quentin C.; Lemmi, Catherine; Feldman, Kimberly; Ortiz, Nickolaus; León, Maricela
original_title: African American language in science education: a translanguaging perspective
original_journal: Journal of Research in Science Teaching
replication_authors: Quentin C. Sedlacek; Nickolaus Ortiz; Catherine Lemmi; Maricela León; Kimberly C. Feldman
replication_title: Racial and linguistic ideologies and formative assessment practices of U.S. science teachers: A preregistered conceptual replication and extension
explanation: The authors successfully replicated associations between language-exclusive ideology and formative assessment behaviors: it was positively related to grading mechanics/vocabulary frequency (β=0.546) and significantly related to grades and inferences for all three writing samples, as well as negatively associated with feedback length and inference length for all samples. The authors state these findings 'reproduce and extend our previous findings about the formative assessment practices of teachers.'

description: Language-exclusive ideology is associated with biased mechanics-focused feedback targeting African American Language features (habitual be) in student science writing among preservice teachers
original_authors: Sedlacek, Quentin C.; Lemmi, Catherine; Feldman, Kimberly; Ortiz, Nickolaus; León, Maricela
original_title: African American language in science education: a translanguaging perspective
original_journal: Journal of Research in Science Teaching
replication_authors: Quentin C. Sedlacek; Nickolaus Ortiz; Catherine Lemmi; Maricela León; Kimberly C. Feldman
replication_title: Racial and linguistic ideologies and formative assessment practices of U.S. science teachers: A preregistered conceptual replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Thus, our previous finding that the language-exclusive ideology scale was associated with biased responses to AAL features was not replicated.' Language-exclusive ideology was not significantly related to mechanics-focused feedback on either Writing Sample #2 (OR=1.033, 95% CI {0.991, 1.077}) or Writing Sample #3 (OR=1.042, 95% CI {0.996, 1.090}).

description: A computationally efficient beam-spread function model accurately predicts light propagation in cortical brain tissue for optogenetic applications, validated against experimental data and outperforming Monte Carlo simulations in computational speed
original_authors: Guy Yona; Nizan Meitav; Itamar Kahn; Shy Shoham
original_title: Realistic numerical and analytical modeling of light scattering in brain tissue for optogenetic applications
replication_authors: David Berling; Jan Střeleček; Tomáš Iser; Ján Antolík
replication_title: An open-source replication for fast and accessible light propagation modeling in brain tissue
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated a previously closed-source light simulation model for cortical media, originally developed by Yona et al. (2016).' They successfully re-implemented the model from scratch, resolved implementation ambiguities, corrected a bug in the original software, and validated the approach against experimental data — achieving stronger agreement with experimental data than the original software.

description: Presenting a loud acoustic probe stimulus in the 65 ms prior to an imperative stimulus causes reaction time to decrease and motor output to increase progressively, indicating that movement-related activation builds up (rather than remaining constant) in anticipation of action initiation
original_authors: Welber Marinovic; Aymar de Rugy; Ottmar V. Lipp; James R. Tresilian
original_title: Responses to loud auditory stimuli indicate that movement-related activation builds up in anticipation of action
replication_authors: Dana Maslovat; Ian M. Franks; Alexandra Leguerrier; Anthony N. Carlsen
replication_title: Responses to startling acoustic stimuli indicate that movement-related activation is constant prior to action: a replication with an alternate interpretation
explanation: The replication confirmed the original statistical pattern when all trials were analyzed (replicating Marinovic et al.'s finding of decreasing RT and increasing peak EMG), but the authors argue this was confounded by the lack of SCM measurement. When trials were separated by SCM activation (the proper startle indicator), 'the results indicate that movement-related activation is in fact constant 65 ms prior to action initiation,' directly contradicting the original study's main conclusion that activation builds up prior to action.

description: A QTL on chromosome 7 (Skmw34 locus) affects muscle weight in LG/J and SM/J mice
original_authors: Lionikas A.; Cheng R.; Lim JE; Palmer AA; Blizard DA
original_title: Fine-mapping of muscle weight QTL in LG/J and SM/J intercrosses
replication_authors: Ana I. Hernandez Cordero; Peter Carbonetto; Gioia Riboni Verri; Jennifer S. Gregory; David J. Vandenbergh; Joseph P. Gyekis; David A. Blizard; Arimantas Lionikas
replication_title: Replication and discovery of musculoskeletal QTLs in LG/J and SM/J advanced intercross lines
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The QTL on Chr 7 overlapped the position of Skmw34 locus identified in a previous mapping study (Lionikas et al. 2010)' and label it as a 'replicated' locus in Table 3. This confirms the Chr 7 muscle weight QTL found in the original F2/F34 intercross study.

description: A QTL on chromosome 1 (Lbn1.1b locus) affects tibia length in LG/J and SM/J mice
original_authors: Norgard EA; Lawson HA; Pletscher LS; Wang B.; Brooks VR; Wolf JB; Cheverud JM
original_title: Genetic factors and diet affect long-bone length in the F34 LG.SM advanced intercross
replication_authors: Ana I. Hernandez Cordero; Peter Carbonetto; Gioia Riboni Verri; Jennifer S. Gregory; David J. Vandenbergh; Joseph P. Gyekis; David A. Blizard; Arimantas Lionikas
replication_title: Replication and discovery of musculoskeletal QTLs in LG/J and SM/J advanced intercross lines
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'Two QTLs (Chr 1, 13), long bone 1.1 and 13.1 locus (lbn1.1b and lbn13.1), affecting tibia length overlapped with earlier findings in the same lineage (Norgard et al. 2011)' and designates these as 'replicated' QTLs in Table 3.

description: A QTL on chromosome 13 (Lbn13.1 locus) affects tibia length in LG/J and SM/J mice
original_authors: Norgard EA; Lawson HA; Pletscher LS; Wang B.; Brooks VR; Wolf JB; Cheverud JM
original_title: Genetic factors and diet affect long-bone length in the F34 LG.SM advanced intercross
replication_authors: Ana I. Hernandez Cordero; Peter Carbonetto; Gioia Riboni Verri; Jennifer S. Gregory; David J. Vandenbergh; Joseph P. Gyekis; David A. Blizard; Arimantas Lionikas
replication_title: Replication and discovery of musculoskeletal QTLs in LG/J and SM/J advanced intercross lines
explanation: The paper explicitly designates Lbn13.1 as a 'replicated' QTL referencing Norgard et al. (2011) in Table 3, and states these two tibia length QTLs 'overlapped with earlier findings in the same lineage (Norgard et al. 2011)'.

description: Exposure to health information in mass media is primarily interest-guided (not problem-guided), with interest and avoidance as the main determinants, and gender, preventive orientation, and socioeconomic factors as predictors of interest and avoidance
original_authors: Gerrit A. J. van der Rijt
original_title: Determinants of the consumption of health information in the media
replication_authors: Gerrit van der Rijt
replication_title: Consumption of Health Information in the Media: A Replication Study with some Contrary Results
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'although roughly the same results could be established, some additional as well as some contradictory findings emerged compared with the former study.' The core finding (interest-guided, not problem-guided) replicated, but avoidance became the primary (not secondary) predictor, and preventive orientation showed a direct negative effect on exposure contrary to the original's positive effect.

description: Students' understanding of scientific models can be assessed using a five-factor instrument (SUMS) measuring models as multiple representations, exact replicas, explanatory tools, uses of scientific models, and changing nature of models
original_authors: Treagust, David F.; Chittleborough, Gail; Mamiala, Thandi L.
original_title: Students' understanding of the role of scientific models in learning science
replication_authors: Marvin Rost; Ines Sonnenschein; Stephanie Möller; Anja Lembens
replication_title: Don’t we know enough about models? Integrating a replication study into an introductory chemistry course in higher education
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'the translated version of the SUMS inventory does not accurately reflect the original publication (Treagust et al., 2002).' The ER (exact replica) factor could not be replicated at all, and reliabilities of the remaining latent constructs were 'insufficiently low to establish generalizable measurements.'

description: Preoperative endoscopic injection of botulinum toxin into the sphincter of Oddi significantly reduces clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (grade B/C) rates after distal pancreatectomy, with no clinically relevant fistulas observed in 24 patients
original_authors: Thilo Hackert; Ulla Klaiber; Ulf Hinz; Tzveta Kehayova; Pascal Probst; Phillip Knebel; Markus K. Diener; Lutz Schneider; Oliver Strobel; Christoph W. Michalski; Alexis Ulrich; Peter Sauer; Markus W. Büchler
original_title: Sphincter of Oddi botulinum toxin injection to prevent pancreatic fistula after distal pancreatectomy
replication_authors: Andreas Volk; Marius Distler; Benjamin Müssle; Marco Berning; Jochen Hampe; Stefan Brückner; Jürgen Weitz; Thilo Welsch
replication_title: Reproducibility of preoperative endoscopic injection of botulinum toxin into the sphincter of Oddi to prevent postoperative pancreatic fistula
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the present study could not reproduce the published results of a significant lowering of grade B/C POPF.' The replication found 32% grade B/C POPF in the BTX group versus 0% in the original study, with no statistically significant difference between BTX and control groups (p = 0.737).

description: Econometric models (OLS, Tobit, Beta Regression, Fractional Logit, Probit) of the determinants of the share of exports in total sales for manufacturing firms in Lower Saxony, Germany, produce reliable and trustworthy results
original_authors: Joachim Wagner
original_title: A note on the firm size-export relationship
replication_authors: Joachim Wagner
replication_title: Anonymized Firm Data under Test: Evidence from a Replication Study
explanation: The author re-estimated all econometric models from Wagner (2001) using micro-aggregated anonymized firm data and found that 'the reported levels of statistical significance differ' and 'statistically significant coefficients sometimes differ by order of magnitude.' The paper explicitly concludes that micro-aggregated firm data 'should not be considered as a tool for empirical research.'

description: Econometric models (OLS, Probit, Ordered Probit) of the relationship between pensions and firm performance for manufacturing firms in Lower Saxony, Germany, produce reliable and trustworthy results
original_authors: Claus Schnabel; Joachim Wagner
original_title: A note on pensions and firm performance: First evidence from German micro data
replication_authors: Joachim Wagner
replication_title: Anonymized Firm Data under Test: Evidence from a Replication Study
explanation: The author re-estimated all econometric models from Schnabel/Wagner (2001) using micro-aggregated anonymized firm data and found that coefficients that were statistically significant with original data were insignificant with anonymized data and vice versa, and that point estimates differed by order of magnitude. The conclusion explicitly states that anonymized firm level data 'should not be considered as a tool for empirical research.'

description: Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is associated with higher 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) concentrations in preterm neonates, contributing to elevated false-positive rates in congenital adrenal hyperplasia newborn screening
original_authors: Frédérique Gatelais; Jacques Berthelot; Frédérique Beringue; Philippe Descamps; Dominique Bonneau; Jean-Marie Limal; Régis Coutant
original_title: Effect of single and multiple courses of prenatal corticosteroids on 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels: implication for neonatal screening of congenital adrenal hyperplasia
replication_authors: Kelli K. Ryckman; Daniel E. Cook; Stanton L. Berberich; Oleg A. Shchelochkov; Susan K. Berends; Tamara Busch; John M. Dagle; Jeffrey C. Murray
replication_title: Replication of clinical associations with 17-hydroxyprogesterone in preterm newborns
replication_journal: Journal of Pediatric Endocrinology and Metabolism
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated previous studies that observed RDS results in higher concentrations of 17-OHP (5)', referring to Gatelais et al. (2004). The replication confirmed the RDS association (p = 2 × 10⁻³ in abstract; p = 0.01 for false-positive results in Table 1) in a new cohort of 762 preterm infants, though the study also extends the finding by showing RDS is associated with higher 17-OHP independent of birth weight.

description: The number of letters used to spell a word-final obstruent is positively correlated with its acoustic duration (more letters = longer sound duration), based on corpus data from the Buckeye Corpus of Conversational Speech
original_authors: Brewer, Jordan
original_title: Phonetic reflexes of orthographic characteristics in lexical representation
replication_authors: Julia Muschalik; Gero Kunter
replication_title: Do letters matter? The influence of spelling on acoustic duration
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the present study fails to replicate a straightforward quantity effect as it was reported by Brewer (2008)' and 'we could not replicate the results by Brewer (2008) that the acoustic duration of a consonant increases with increasing numbers of letters in the corresponding graphemic realization.' The QUANT model, which directly tests Brewer's quantity hypothesis, found NUMLETSEG was not a significant predictor.

description: The Focus on Kids (FoK) HIV prevention intervention for inner-city African American adolescents increased condom use and condom intentions among intervention youth compared to controls at 6-month follow-up
original_authors: B. Stanton; Xiaoming Li; I. Ricardo; J. Galbraith; S. Feigelman; L. Kaljee
original_title: A randomized controlled effectiveness trial of an AIDS prevention program for low-income African American youth
replication_authors: Diane M. Morrison; Marilyn J. Hoppe; Elizabeth A. Wells; Blair A. Beadnell; Anthony Wilsdon; Darrel Higa; Mary Rogers Gillmore; Erin A. Casey
replication_title: Replicating a Teen HIV/STD Preventive Intervention in a Multicultural City
