explanation: The authors explicitly state this is a 'failure to replicate': 'youth in the preventive intervention condition of the replication study did not improve in attitudes, perceived norms, self-efficacy, or intentions toward sexual initiation, condom use, or abstinence compared with a carefully matched control condition.' The Discussion section is titled 'Failure to Replicate the Intervention Faithfully' and the authors conclude the most likely reason is lower rates of sexual activity among Seattle youth.

description: The Mandarin Chinese version of the OCI-R demonstrates good psychometric properties (internal consistency, factor structure, and test-retest reliability) in both non-clinical and clinical samples with OCD symptoms
original_authors: Zi-wen Peng; Wen-han Yang; Guo-dong Miao; Jin Jing; Raymond CK Chan
original_title: The Chinese version of the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory–Revised scale: Replication and extension to non-clinical and clinical individuals with OCD symptoms
replication_authors: Hengfen Gong; Tessa M. H. Nederpel; Guozhen Lin; Yingying Zhang; Yong Yang; Bin Li; Xiao Luo; Fang Fang; Bin Li; Wenjuan Liu; ChenCheng Zhang; Xirong Sun; Eric B. Lee; Eric A. Storch; Shikun Zhan
replication_title: The Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory–Revised: Replication of the psychometric properties in China
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the main study purpose was to replicate Peng et al. (2011) as the second validation of the Mandarin Chinese version of the OCI-R.' Results showed good internal consistency (α = .88 for total scale, similar to Peng et al.'s .89) and good convergent/divergent validity, with the Discussion concluding 'findings suggest that the Mandarin Chinese version of the OCI-R has good psychometric properties building on findings about...the Mandarin Chinese version (Peng et al., 2011).'

description: Patients who screen positive on the Mood Disorders Questionnaire (MDQ) for bipolar disorder are as likely to be diagnosed with borderline personality disorder (BPD) as with bipolar disorder, and MDQ-positive patients show a five- to six-fold increase in BPD diagnoses compared to MDQ-negative patients
original_authors: Mark Zimmerman; Janine N. Galione; Camilo J. Ruggero; Iwona Chelminski; Diane Young; Kristy Dalrymple; Joseph B. McGlinchey
original_title: Screening for bipolar disorder and finding borderline personality disorder
replication_authors: Mark Zimmerman; Iwona Chelminski; Kristy Dalrymple; Jacob Martin
replication_title: Screening for Bipolar Disorder and Finding Borderline Personality Disorder: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the results were 'generally consistent with the original report' and that they 'largely replicated the results of our initial report.' The replication found a four- to five-fold increase in BPD frequency among MDQ-positive patients (OR=6.0, p<.001 for full sample; OR=4.5, p<.001 for depressed subsample), consistent with the original five- to six-fold increase, and also extended findings to a depressed-only patient subsample.

description: Real-world objects benefit more from additional encoding time than simple colored squares, with behavioral performance (K) increasing at longer encoding times for objects but not for colors
original_authors: Timothy F. Brady; Viola S. Störmer; George A. Alvarez
original_title: Working memory is not fixed-capacity: more active storage capacity for real-world objects than for simple stimuli
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Colin Quirk; Kirsten C.S. Adam; Edward K. Vogel
replication_title: No Evidence for an Object Working Memory Capacity Benefit with Extended Viewing Time
explanation: Across three experiments (1a, 1b, 1c), the authors found that encoding time benefitted both simple color items and real-world objects equally, failing to replicate the key finding that objects but not colors benefit from extended encoding time. As stated: 'we failed to replicate their primary behavioral result (objects benefit more than colors from additional encoding time).'

description: CDA amplitude is higher for real-world objects than colors at set size 5 but not set size 3, indicating that working memory storage capacity is greater for real-world objects
original_authors: Timothy F. Brady; Viola S. Störmer; George A. Alvarez
original_title: Working memory is not fixed-capacity: more active storage capacity for real-world objects than for simple stimuli
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA
replication_authors: Colin Quirk; Kirsten C.S. Adam; Edward K. Vogel
replication_title: No Evidence for an Object Working Memory Capacity Benefit with Extended Viewing Time
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'failed to observe an object-specific increase in the CDA' and found 'no evidence of greater amplitudes for real-world items at higher set sizes.' They found equivalent CDA amplitude for set sizes 3 and 5 in both object and color conditions, directly contradicting the original CDA result.

description: Humans can learn the mean of a probability distribution of visuomotor shifts and perform Bayesian estimation during sensorimotor learning, integrating their learned prior with current sensory uncertainty to guide motor behavior in a statistically optimal manner
original_authors: Konrad P. Körding; Daniel M. Wolpert
original_title: Bayesian integration in sensorimotor learning
replication_authors: Christopher L. Hewitson; Paul F. Sowman; David M. Kaplan

explanation: The original study found increased hippocampal activation in noncarriers (CC genotype). replication_authors: Alexander R. Trott; Richard T. Born
replication_title: Input-Gain Control Produces Feature-Specific Surround Suppression
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Result 'success' is unambiguous — the authors explicitly state 'we first sought to replicate these findings' and confirm 'Consistent with previous reports, we found that tuned surround suppression was a common property of the multiunits recorded.' 25 of 47 multiunit sites showed significantly tuned surround suppression (p < 0.05, permutation test), and average suppression from preferred surround (46%) significantly exceeded anti-preferred surround (19%). Changed replication_type from 'direct' to 'close experiment': Sillito et al. (1995) used cat V1 with moving bar stimuli, whereas the current study uses macaque V1 with stationary sinusoidal gratings — these are deliberate methodological changes (different species, different stimulus type) while testing the same core phenomenon. The authors cite multiple papers for this established finding (Sillito 1995; Cavanaugh 2002b; Jones 2002; Shushruth 2012). Upgraded confidence to 'high' because the replication result is explicit and well-supported, and 'close experiment' correctly captures the cross-species, modified-stimulus design.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Therefore, our active-report trials replicate previous findings: independent of rivalry type, rivalry seems to be mediated by occipital, parietal, and frontal regions predominantly in the right hemisphere of the brain.' The Discussion also confirms: 'These patterns were largely consistent with earlier fMRI studies (Lumer et al., 1998)'.

replication_title: Evidence That Tetris Reduces Immediate but Not Subsequent Daily Intrusions of a Trauma Film: A Multilab Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'So we only partially replicated previous Tetris findings.' Tetris significantly reduced immediate intrusions during the task (t(335.46) = -7.8, p < .001), replicating that aspect of Holmes et al. (2009), but did not replicate the reduction in subsequent diary intrusions (p = .702) or IMS scores (p = .969) over the following week. The study included notable procedural differences: a new trauma film, online testing instead of in-person, and an active perceptual vigilance control rather than passive sitting quietly.

Only 1 of 12 chi-squared tests reached significance, and the main finding (positive condition) was not replicated (OR = 0.82, 95% CI = [0.49-1.37], p = .453 vs. original OR = 10.5). Both dimensions of perceived trustworthiness (integrity: β = 0.31, p < .001; benevolence: β = 0.19, p < .001) significantly increased with target's level of caring, consistent with original findings. The issue was changed from capital punishment to abortion and a German sample was used instead of a US sample.

original_title: Eye tracking scanpath analysis on web pages: How many users
original_journal: Proceedings of the Ninth Biennial ACM Symposium on Eye Tracking Research & Applications
replication_authors: Sukru Eraslan; Yeliz Yesilada; Simon Harper
replication_title: Less users more confidence: How AOIs don’t affect scanpath trend analysis
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the current findings are mainly consistent with the previous findings' and 'we can approximate almost the same results with a smaller group of users in scanpath trend analysis regardless of the segmentation approach used.' The results showed ~5% difference for searching tasks and ~10% difference for browsing tasks between the VIPS (original) and the two new segmentation approaches, confirming the original finding holds.

description: Directional precision of human smooth pursuit eye movements (SPEM) follows an exponential decay function reaching optimal values of 1.5°-3° within 300 ms after target motion onset, and initial saccades to moving targets show better directional precision than SPEM during the same time window
original_authors: Braun, Doris I.; Gegenfurtner, Karl R.
original_title: Dynamics of oculomotor direction discrimination
replication_authors: Jan Churan; Doris I. Braun; Karl R. Gegenfurtner; Frank Bremmer
replication_title: Comparison of the precision of smooth pursuit in humans and head unrestrained monkeys
explanation: The authors explicitly replicated Braun & Gegenfurtner (2016)'s paradigms in head-unrestrained macaque monkeys and found general agreement in the development of directional precision of SPEM over time and in the differences between directional precision of initial saccades and SPEM initiation. The Discussion states: 'Our results largely confirm previous reports on human oculomotor behavior showing that during saccades directional precision is higher than during SPEM,' though monkeys showed overall lower absolute precision likely due to differences in experimental conditions (head unrestrained vs. head-restrained).

description: Binocular reading shows shorter fixation durations than monocular reading (binocular advantage), and this advantage is attenuated by individual horizontal heterophoria (the resting state of vergence)
original_authors: Stephanie Jainta; Wolfgang Jaschinski
original_title: Individual differences in binocular coordination are uncovered by directly comparing monocular and binocular reading conditions
replication_authors: Stephanie Jainta; Joelle Joss
replication_title: Binocular advantages in reading revisited: attenuating effects of individual horizontal heterophoria
explanation: The authors explicitly describe the study as a 'large-scale replication' and state in the abstract 'we replicated (1) binocular advantages of about 25 ms for average fixation durations and (2) a reduction in binocular advantages when heterophoria increased.' The Discussion confirms: 'In the present study, we replicated binocular advantages (shorter fixation times) of about 20 ms in reading.'

description: Sighting eye dominance is dynamic and reverses as a function of horizontal gaze angle, with crossovers in eye dominance occurring when objects are aligned in the contralateral visual field, and a hand effect whereby the hand used to grasp a ring influences which eye is dominant
original_authors: Aarlenne Z. Khan; J.Douglas Crawford
original_title: Ocular dominance reverses as a function of horizontal gaze angle
replication_authors: Franziska Prummer; Ludwig Sidenmark; Hans Gellersen
replication_title: Dynamics of eye dominance behavior in virtual reality
explanation: The authors conclude: 'Our results generally agree with those of Khan and Crawford (2001), indicating that their main findings apply within a VR setting, even when targets are presented at greater depths.' The key effects (viewing angle and hand used significantly influencing eye dominance) were successfully replicated in VR, with only a narrower viewing angle range for the dominance switch.

description: Cooperation/competition priming influences perception of a Prisoner's Dilemma situation, expectations about others' cooperative behavior, and participants' own behavioral intentions, with stronger effects when situational construal precedes the decision
original_authors: Aaron C. Kay; Lee Ross
original_title: The perceptual push: The interplay of implicit cues and explicit situational construals on behavioral intentions in the prisoner's dilemma
replication_authors: Freidin, Esteban; Belaus, Anabel; Reyna, Cecilia
replication_title: Testing the effect of contextual cues on behavioral intentions in the Prisoner’s Dilemma. A replication study.
explanation: Experiment 1 found no significant priming effects on any outcome (name rating: F(1,66)=1.62, p=.207; beliefs: t(67)=-1.05, p=.299, d=.25; cooperation choice: χ²(1)=2.51, p=.113, φ=.191), and the authors concluded: 'we found no reliable evidence of an effect of priming cooperation/competition on the perception of the PD, the beliefs about other people's behavior in the game, or participants´ own cooperative decisions.' Experiment 1 differed from the original by adding monetary incentives, testing only 2 of 4 conditions, and being conducted in Argentina.

description: Cooperation/competition priming influences perception of a Prisoner's Dilemma situation, expectations about others' cooperative behavior, and participants' own behavioral intentions, with stronger effects when situational construal precedes the decision
original_authors: Aaron C. Kay; Lee Ross
original_title: The perceptual push: The interplay of implicit cues and explicit situational construals on behavioral intentions in the prisoner's dilemma
replication_authors: Freidin, Esteban; Belaus, Anabel; Reyna, Cecilia
replication_title: Testing the effect of contextual cues on behavioral intentions in the Prisoner’s Dilemma. A replication study.
explanation: Experiment 2 was a closer replication of the full 2x2 factorial design (N=200 after exclusions) with pre-registration and 95% power, but found no significant priming effects: name rating F(3,189)=.875, p=.455, ηp²=.013; behavioral intentions F(1,196)=.306, p=.581, ηp²=.001. The authors stated: 'we could not find evidence for any of the effects reported in the original study.'

description: Women report more jealousy than men when facing an attractive rival (gender × rival attractiveness interaction), and men report more jealousy than women when facing a dominant rival (gender × rival dominance interaction), as tested using vignettes depicting a partner flirting with a potential rival
original_authors: Pieternel Dijkstra; Bram P. Buunk
original_title: Jealousy as a function of rival characteristics: An evolutionary perspective
replication_authors: Pollet, Thomas V.; Saxton, Tamsin
replication_title: Jealousy as a Function of Rival Characteristics: A Replication Study - (Prolific)
explanation: Study 1 (N=339) found partial support: the gender × attractiveness interaction was significant (F(1,331)=6.55, p=.011, η²g=.02) but the gender × dominance interaction was not (F(1,331)=1.44, p=.231). The authors describe this as a mixed result: 'We replicated the first but not the second of these two-way interactions.'

description: Women report more jealousy than men when facing an attractive rival (gender × rival attractiveness interaction), and men report more jealousy than women when facing a dominant rival (gender × rival dominance interaction), as tested using vignettes depicting a partner flirting with a potential rival
original_authors: Pieternel Dijkstra; Bram P. Buunk
original_title: Jealousy as a function of rival characteristics: An evolutionary perspective
replication_authors: Pollet, Thomas V.; Saxton, Tamsin
replication_title: Jealousy as a Function of Rival Characteristics: A Replication Study - (Prolific)
explanation: Study 2 (N=456) found no support for either key interaction: gender × attractiveness F(1,448)=1.23, p=.268; gender × dominance F(1,448)=0.15, p=.694. Bayes factor analyses provided 'conclusive evidence that a null model is favoured over the three-way interaction model (factor of 87900) and both two-way interaction models.' The discussion concludes 'we found no good evidence that a rival's dominance affected men's jealousy' and only limited evidence for the attractiveness effect.

description: IS continuance intention is predicted by satisfaction and perceived usefulness, both of which are in turn predicted by confirmation, via the expectation-confirmation model (ECM) in an online banking context

replication_title: Information System Continuance Intention in the Context of Network Effects and Freemium Business Models: A Replication Study of Cloud Services in Germany
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our methodological replication confirms the validity of the proposed model on IS continuance in a modern context.' All five hypotheses were supported at p < 0.05 or better, replicating the original pattern, though path coefficients for satisfaction and perceived usefulness on continuance intention were lower than in the original.

description: Top management support for information systems influences IS performance through collective mindfulness dimensions (preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, deference to expertise)

original_title: Top management support, collective mindfulness, and information systems performance
original_journal: Journal of International Technology and Information Management
replication_authors: René Moquin
replication_title: Information and Collective Mindfulness - A Methodological Replication Study
explanation: The authors state they 'reasonably replicate Khan et al. (2013) findings with some concessions.' Results show mixed support: H1-H5 (TMS → mindfulness) were all supported in replication vs. mostly supported in original, but hypotheses H6-H10 (mindfulness → IS performance) diverged substantially — H8 (sensitivity to operations) which was supported in original was not supported here, while H9 and H10 which were not supported in original were now supported.

description: Network commonality and information dissemination (posting with or without tagging) interact to influence perceived privacy invasion and perceived relationship bonding, which in turn affect users' behavioral responses (inaction, transactional avoidance, interpersonal avoidance, approach) to embarrassing exposures in online social networks

replication_authors: Mohammadreza Ebrahimi; Juan-Manuel Martínez
replication_title: Involuntary Embarrassing Exposures in Online Social Networks: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors replicated 8 out of 12 hypotheses from the original study: the behavioral response hypotheses (H3A–H4D, involving effects of perceived privacy invasion and relationship bonding on behavioral outcomes) were successfully replicated, but the four hypotheses about network commonality effects (H1A, H1B, H2A, H2B) did not replicate, attributed to a failed manipulation of network commonality when using the original thresholds. The authors conclude: 'we could replicate 8 hypotheses out of 12 hypotheses stated in the original study.'

description: Students who take notes using longhand (rather than on a laptop) perform better on conceptual application questions but not on factual recall questions

original_title: The pen is mightier than the keyboard: Advantages of longhand over laptop note taking
replication_authors: Alanah Mitchell; Liping Zheng
replication_title: Examining Longhand vs. Laptop Debate: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication found the opposite pattern from the original: longhand participants performed significantly better on factual recall (p=.002) but not on conceptual application (p=.36), while the original found laptops harmed conceptual performance but not factual recall. The authors conclude that 'our replication of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) only partially supports some of their conclusions,' indicating mixed/inconclusive results.

description: Envy on social networking sites negatively affects users' cognitive and affective well-being and positively predicts self-enhancement behavior, with envy mediating the relationship between social information consumption and well-being outcomes
original_authors: Hanna Krasnova; Thomas Widjaja; Peter Buxmann; Helena Wenninger; Izak Benbasat

replication_authors: Benjamin M. Ampel; Steven Ullman
replication_title: Why Following Friends Can Hurt You: A Replication Study
explanation: Six of seven hypotheses were supported in the replication, but H4 (envy mediating SIC → cognitive well-being) was not supported. The authors conclude: 'Our results were largely consistent with the original study (6 of the 7 hypotheses were consistent),' but acknowledge the failed mediation hypothesis as a meaningful difference.

replication_title: Original Findings Confirmed in Replication Study: Provocation with 2.4 GHz Cordless Phone affects the Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) as measured by Heart Rate Variability (HRV)

The paper title itself states 'Original Findings Confirmed in Replication Study.' In the original, 40% (10/25) of subjects responded; in the replication, 36% reacted via altered HRV across 69 subjects.

The direction differs between populations (allele A was risk in Japanese vs. protective in Russians), but the core finding of rs893818 involvement in POAG is confirmed as stated: 'эти данные полностью согласуются с полученными нами результатами'.

explanation: Reviewer verified: All five CDKN2B-AS1 polymorphic loci (rs944800, rs4977756, rs7865618, rs2157719, rs1063192) showed no statistically significant association with POAG in the Russian male sample (n=246 POAG, n=176 controls). P-values for genotypes ranged from 0.11 to 0.93, and for alleles from 0.13 to 0.57; all OR confidence intervals included 1.0. The paper's conclusion (Заключение) mentions only the LOXL1 gene findings, implicitly acknowledging the CDKN2B-AS1 null result. This is an unambiguous failure to replicate the Burdon et al. (2011) GWAS-identified CDKN2B-AS1 associations in a different (Russian/European) population. Upgraded from medium to high confidence because the null results are clear and consistent across all five loci with no room for interpretive ambiguity.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'this study cannot represent a successful replication of the original work by Staw (1976)' and describe it as 'a well-powered failed replication attempt.' No significant main effect of personal responsibility (F(1,357)=0.05, p=0.828) and no significant interaction between feedback and personal responsibility (F(1,357)=0.15, p=0.704) were found.

description: Long-term exposure to PM2.5 and black carbon (BC) is positively associated with epigenetic age acceleration (DNAmAge) in males from the VA Normative Aging Study
original_authors: Jamaji C. Nwanaji-Enwerem; Elena Colicino; Letizia Trevisi; Itai Kloog; Allan C. Just; Jincheng Shen; Kasey Brennan; Alexandra Dereix; Lifang Hou; Pantel Vokonas; Joel Schwartz; Andrea A. Baccarelli
original_title: Long-term ambient particle exposures and blood DNA methylation age: findings from the VA normative aging study
replication_authors: Cavin K. Ward-Caviness; Jamaji C. Nwanaji-Enwerem; Kathrin Wolf; Simone Wahl; Elena Colicino; Letizia Trevisi; Itai Kloog; Allan C. Just; Pantel Vokonas; Josef Cyrys; Christian Gieger; Joel Schwartz; Andrea A. Baccarelli; Alexandra Schneider; Annette Peters
replication_title: Long-term exposure to air pollution is associated with biological aging
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Confirmed 'inconclusive' at 'medium' confidence — the ambiguity is genuine and intrinsic to the paper. The original [34] found positive associations between PM2.5/BC and DNAmAge in NAS males. This paper re-examines the NAS cohort with additional aging measures (IEAA, EEAA, TeloAA alongside DNAmAA). Key findings: (1) No association between PM2.5 and DNAmAA or EEAA — the measures most comparable to the original's DNAmAge — meaning the core original finding was not reproduced. (2) PM2.5 was inversely associated with IEAA (β = -0.37 to -0.39, p ≈ 0.04-0.05), opposite direction to original. (3) BC was inversely associated with TeloAA (β = -0.40, p<0.0001), a measure not in the original. (4) The PM2.5-IEAA result was fragile — in a slightly larger subset it reversed direction. The authors hedge heavily: 'while we did replicate both associations these results still need to be carefully considered' and call for further replication. The mixed directions, null results on the most comparable measure, and sample-sensitivity make this genuinely ambiguous — neither a clear replication nor a clear failure.

replication_title: NEURL rs6584555 and CAND2 rs4642101 contribute to postoperative atrial fibrillation: a prospective study among Chinese population
explanation: The authors set out to replicate 6 polymorphisms in 5 novel loci from Sinner et al. (2014) in the context of postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) after CABG in a Chinese population. Only 2 of the 6 original loci (NEURL rs6584555 and CAND2 rs4642101) were significantly associated in both stages, while GJA1, TBX5, and CUX2 loci were not consistently replicated. The authors state 'we replicated the previous findings' but only for two of the original five loci, representing partial replication.

explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'were only able to partially replicate results from the original study.' Native speaker findings were replicated (preference for non-hedged texts), but the key result for fluent speakers was not — in the original, fluent speakers showed weak preference for hedged texts, while in the replication they strongly preferred non-hedged texts, attributed to differences in participant type (master students vs. working professionals).

The authors state the results are 'apparently comparable' but the differences prevent a fully successful replication, and the study used Google Forms instead of the original FlexEval tool.

They could not reproduce the original correlation matrix and found substantially different correlations, even when using the original authors' own data.

description: LSTM-based PoS taggers considerably outperform CRF and HMM taggers when evaluated on corpora from the Universal Dependencies project using a coarse-grained tagset of 17 tags

replication_title: Do LSTMs really work so well for PoS tagging? – A replication study
replication_journal:
Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural
          Language Processing
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm the original finding in their conclusion: 'The replication confirmed the superior performance of the LSTM tagger reported by Plank et al. (2016) also on fine-grained tagsets.' The extension tests whether LSTM superiority over CRF/HMM taggers generalizes from coarse-grained (17 UD tags) to fine-grained tagsets across 27 corpora of 21 languages.

description: Using distributed representations of discourse units (via representation learning) substantially improves RST discourse parser performance, with a relative error reduction of up to 51% on fully-labelled structures compared to parsers using only localist (surface-form and syntactic) features
original_authors: Ji, Yangfeng; Eisenstein, Jacob
original_title: Representation learning for text-level discourse parsing
original_journal: Proceedings of the 52nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
replication_authors: Mathieu Morey; Philippe Muller; Nicholas Asher
replication_title:
How much progress have we made on RST discourse parsing? A
            replication study of recent results on the RST-DT
replication_journal:
Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural
          Language Processing
explanation: REVIEWED: The paper's conclusions are explicit and quantitative, leaving no genuine ambiguity. The authors replicated the evaluation of 9 RST discourse parsers (5 using distributed representations, including Ji & Eisenstein 2014) by re-running scoring on the same parser predictions on the same RST-DT test set. They discovered that parsers in the 'distributed representations' group had been evaluated with macro-averaged F1 scores (averaged across documents), while parsers in the 'localist features' group used micro-averaged F1 (the standard in syntactic parsing). Under standardized micro-averaged scoring, the claimed 51% relative error reduction on fully-labelled structures shrinks to at most 16% (Table 2, Table 4). On Span (S) and Nuclearity (N) metrics, parsers using distributed representations show no improvement over localist-feature parsers. The authors explicitly conclude: 'most recently reported increases in RST discourse parser performance are an artefact of differences in implementations of the evaluation procedure.' Classified as 'failure' because the primary claimed effect size (51% error reduction) was shown to be an artifact; the actual gains are dramatically smaller. Confidence upgraded to 'high' because the evidence is unambiguous — the discrepancy is fully explained by the micro/macro averaging difference, demonstrated with exact score comparisons across three evaluation tables. Discipline changed from linguistics to computer science/AI and machine learning, as this is an NLP parser evaluation paper published at EMNLP.

description: Thematic topic (TT) wa and contrastive topic (CT) wa in Japanese are prosodically distinct, with CT showing pitch suppression after the wa particle (P1>P2) while TT shows P1≈P2 or slightly higher P2, and these prosodic cues correlate with scope interpretation (CT with narrow/inverse scope reading)
original_authors: Nakanishi, Kimiko
original_title: Prosody and scope interpretations of the topic marker wa in Japanese
original_journal: Topic and Focus: Cross-linguistic Perspectives on Meaning and Intonation
replication_authors: Esposito AM; Soare AY; Patel F.; Satija N.; Chen BK; Swartz TH
replication_title: A High-throughput Cre-Lox Activated Viral Membrane Fusion Assay to Identify Inhibitors of HIV-1 Viral Membrane Fusion.
explanation: The authors replicated Nakanishi's (2007) prosodic study with native Japanese speakers and found that two participants showed starkly opposite prosodic patterns — one consistently producing TT-type F0 patterns across all conditions and one consistently producing CT-type F0 patterns regardless of the intended scope reading. The authors conclude that 'the correlation between CT/TT-reading and prosodic realization types might not be as solid as Nakanishi claims,' but acknowledge the preliminary nature of the data and the need for more participants.

description: Point rewards contingent on saving money increase savings rates among delinquent boys at Achievement Place
original_authors: Elery L. Phillips; Elaine A. Phillips; Dean L. Fixsen; Montrose M. Wolf
original_title: Achievement Place: modification of the behaviors of pre-delinquent boys within a token economy
replication_authors: Robert Paul Liberman; Chris Ferris; Paul Salgado; Jessie Salgado
replication_title: REPLICATION OF THE ACHIEVEMENT PLACE MODEL IN CALIFORNIA1
explanation: The authors explicitly state the savings replicated the procedure from Phillips et al. (1971), but found no substantial effect: 'even large point rewards did not substantially increase savings.' Mean daily savings during point-reward conditions ($0.12-$0.13) were essentially equal to baseline ($0.07) and dramatically lower than Achievement Place ($0.86-$1.00/day).

description: Response-contingent point fines reduce aggressive speech among delinquent boys at Achievement Place
original_authors: Elery L. Phillips
original_title: Achievement Place: token reinforcement procedures in a home-style rehabilitation setting for "pre-delinquent" boys
replication_authors: Robert Paul Liberman; Chris Ferris; Paul Salgado; Jessie Salgado
replication_title: REPLICATION OF THE ACHIEVEMENT PLACE MODEL IN CALIFORNIA1
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The present experiment replicated that methodology' from Phillips (1968), targeting interrupting behavior (analogous to aggressive speech). Point fines effectively reduced interruptions (average summed quotient 0.85 during fines vs. 2.65 at baseline), with similar patterns of correction and threat-no-fine conditions matching the Achievement Place results.

description: Point contingencies maintain high rates of chore/housekeeping behavior among delinquent boys, which can be faded while maintaining performance
original_authors: Elery L. Phillips; Elaine A. Phillips; Dean L. Fixsen; Montrose M. Wolf
original_title: Achievement Place: modification of the behaviors of pre-delinquent boys within a token economy
replication_authors: Robert Paul Liberman; Chris Ferris; Paul Salgado; Jessie Salgado
replication_title: REPLICATION OF THE ACHIEVEMENT PLACE MODEL IN CALIFORNIA1
explanation: The present experiment was formulated to test the effectiveness of point contingencies in housekeeping tasks at Welcome Home, replicating Phillips et al. (1971). Point rewards (100 and 1000 points) significantly increased perfect table-setting, and importantly, high performance was maintained even during the postcheck condition when points were withdrawn, suggesting faster fading is possible than implied by the original study.

description: Response-cost (point losses per minute late) produces punctual behavior at the dinner table among delinquent boys at Achievement Place
original_authors: Elery L. Phillips; Elaine A. Phillips; Dean L. Fixsen; Montrose M. Wolf
original_title: Achievement Place: modification of the behaviors of pre-delinquent boys within a token economy
replication_authors: Robert Paul Liberman; Chris Ferris; Paul Salgado; Jessie Salgado
replication_title: REPLICATION OF THE ACHIEVEMENT PLACE MODEL IN CALIFORNIA1
explanation: A baseline study of promptness was initiated as a first step toward replicating Phillips et al. (1971), but 'lateness to dinner was not a problem' at Welcome Home (mean 2.25 min, range 0-8.33 min), which was 'only half that at Achievement Place', indicating the behavior targeted in the original study was not present. The authors conclude 'deviant behaviors noted at Achievement Place in Kansas are not necessarily to be found with other delinquents living in other locales.' A point-fine contingency was nonetheless applied and did reduce lateness, but the study could not be fully evaluated as a replication of the original effect.

description: A 2-hour self-instructional training package generalized to improved on-task classroom behavior in overactive preschool boys
original_authors: Philip H. Bornstein; Randal P. Quevillon
original_title: Effects of a self-instructional package on overactive preschool boys
replication_authors: Carol Friedling; Susan G. O'Leary
replication_title: EFFECTS OF SELF‐INSTRUCTIONAL TRAINING ON SECOND‐ AND THIRD‐GRADE HYPERACTIVE CHILDREN: A FAILURE TO REPUCATE
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Failure to Replicate' and the Discussion confirms: 'This replication of Bornstein and Quevillon's (1976) self-instructional procedure did not generally produce changes in either academic or on-task behavior.' The same self-instructional training paradigm was used but with older (7-8 year old) clinically hyperactive children rather than the original's 4-year-old overactive preschool boys.

description: Self-instructional training dramatically reduces disruptive classroom behavior and increases on-task behavior in overactive preschool boys
original_authors: Philip H. Bornstein; Randal P. Quevillon
original_title: The effects of a self-instructional package on overactive preschool boys
replication_authors: Donna C. Billings; Barbara H. Wasik
replication_title: SELF‐INSTRUCTIONAL TRAINING WITH PRESCHOOLERS: AN ATTEMPT TO REPLICATE
explanation: The authors explicitly attempted a direct replication of Bornstein and Quevillon (1976) with a similar preschool population and closely matched procedures, but concluded that 'self-instructional training did not produce socially significant, durable increases in either appropriate classroom behavior or changes in teacher ratings of the children's behavior.'

description: Superimposing a schedule of continuous reinforcement (CRF) on self-stimulatory behavior and then removing it creates an extinction-like condition that produces sustained decreases in the target behavior
original_authors: Neisworth, J. T.; Hunt, F. M.; Gallop, H. R.; Madle, R. A.
original_title: Reinforcer displacement: A preliminary application of the CRF/EXT effect
replication_authors: Wylie AM; Grossmann JA
replication_title: RESPONSE REDUCTION THROUGH THE SUPERIMPOSITION OF CONTINUOUS REINFORCEMENT: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION
explanation: The authors explicitly state that their results 'differ from the results reported by Neisworth et al. (1985)' — the original study found sustained response reduction after CRF removal, while this replication found that 'response frequencies quickly returned to baseline levels following removal of CRF superimposition.' The authors conclude the original rate decreases 'may not have been the result of an extinction created by introducing and then removing a schedule of continuous reinforcement.'

description: Publicly posting feedback (percentage of drivers not speeding) on a roadside sign significantly reduced speeding behavior on an urban highway
original_authors: Ron Van Houten; Paul Nau; Zopito Marini
original_title: An analysis of public posting in reducing speeding behavior on an urban highway
replication_authors: Gloria M. Roqué; Michael C. Roberts
replication_title: A REPLICATION OF THE USE OF PUBLIC POSTING IN TRAFFIC SPEED CONTROL
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the purpose of the present study was to replicate the study of Van Houten et al. (1980)' and conclude that 'that finding was not replicated in the present study' — posted feedback produced no significant reduction in speeding compared to baseline levels.

description: A social skills training program using the 'Sorry' game format promotes acquisition and generalization of interactional behaviors in adults with developmental disabilities, with skills used most frequently in the presence of trained peers
original_authors: Richard M. Foxx; Martin J. McMorrow; Ron G. Bittle; Jayne Ness
original_title: An analysis of social skills generalization in two natural settings

replication_title: TRAINING INTERACTIONAL BEHAVIORS OF ADULTS WITH DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION AND EXTENSION
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'replication and extension' of Foxx et al. (1986). The Discussion states: 'These findings are consistent with those of Foxx et al. (1986), who found that participants' use of the skills occurred most frequently in the presence of other trained peers,' confirming the replication was successful.

description: Posting percentages of drivers not speeding on a roadside feedback sign reduces vehicle speeding on an urban highway
original_authors: Ron Van Houten; Paul Nau; Zopito Marini
original_title: An analysis of public posting in reducing speeding behavior on an urban highway
replication_authors: Ragnar S. Ragnarsson; Thröstur Björgvinsson
replication_title: EFFECTS OF PUBLIC POSTING ON DRIVING SPEED IN ICELANDIC TRAFFIC
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated a study by Van Houten, Nau, and Marini (1980)' and found significant speed reductions consistent with the original: 'The significant speed reductions add to the generality of findings of similar studies in Canada and Israel.' Average speed dropped from 69.0 km/hr during baseline to 63.4 km/hr during single posting, with a statistically significant ANOVA result.

description: Systematic preference assessment reliably identifies stimulus preferences for persons with profound multiple handicaps, whereas caregiver opinion does not coincide with the systematic assessment results
original_authors: Carolyn W. Green; Dennis H. Reid; Linda K. White; Richard C. Halford; Doris P. Brittain; Shirley M. Gardner
original_title: Identifying reinforcers for persons with profound handicaps: Staff opinion versus systematic assessment of preferences
replication_authors: Carolyn W. Green; Dennis H. Reid; Vicki S. Canipe; Shirley M. Gardner
replication_title: A COMPREHENSIVE EVALUATION OF REINFORCER IDENTIFICATION PROCESSES FOR PERSONS WITH PROFOUND MULTIPLE HANDICAPS
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Results of Experiment 1 replicated previous findings in that the assessment identified student preferences for respective stimuli, and caregiver opinion of preferences did not coincide with the systematic assessment.' The Discussion confirms: 'Results of Experiment 1 support the results of Green et al. (1988) in three ways.'

description: Stimuli assessed as highly preferred through systematic preference assessment are likely to function as reinforcers in skill-training programs, whereas stimuli not highly preferred do not function as reinforcers
original_authors: Carolyn W. Green; Dennis H. Reid; Linda K. White; Richard C. Halford; Doris P. Brittain; Shirley M. Gardner
original_title: Identifying reinforcers for persons with profound handicaps: Staff opinion versus systematic assessment of preferences
replication_authors: Carolyn W. Green; Dennis H. Reid; Vicki S. Canipe; Shirley M. Gardner
replication_title: A COMPREHENSIVE EVALUATION OF REINFORCER IDENTIFICATION PROCESSES FOR PERSONS WITH PROFOUND MULTIPLE HANDICAPS
explanation: The Discussion of Experiment 2 states: 'results of Experiment 2 support the results of Green et al. (1988) in several ways. First, stimuli assessed systematically to be highly preferred were likely to function as reinforcers when applied contingently in training programs.' A second way was also confirmed: no consistent evidence that non-highly preferred stimuli would function as reinforcers.

description: Reducing effort (via mailed parking pass) and increasing communication (via mailed and telephone appointment reminders) significantly improved appointment keeping and decreased missed appointments in a pediatric outpatient clinic
original_authors: Patrick C. Friman; Jack W. Finney; Michael A. Rapoff; Edward R. Christophersen
original_title: Improving pediatric appointment keeping with reminders and reduced response requirement
replication_authors: Linda Vance Ross; Patrick C. Friman; Edward R. Christophersen
replication_title: AN APPOINTMENT‐KEEPING IMPROVEMENT PACKAGE FOR OUTPATIENT PEDIATRICS: SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION AND COMPONENT ANALYSIS
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of the present study differ from those of the Friman et al. (1985, 1987) studies.' While interventions significantly increased cancellations, none increased appointments kept or decreased appointments not kept significantly — the main outcome of the original studies was not replicated. The key difference was the population: this study tested clinic-scheduled follow-up appointments rather than patient-scheduled or first-time appointments.

description: A follow-up replication confirming that reducing effort (parking pass) and mailed and telephone appointment reminders significantly improved appointment keeping and decreased missed appointments for additional patients in a pediatric outpatient clinic
original_authors: Patrick C. Friman; Stephen G. Glasscock; Jack W. Finney; Edward R. Christophersen
original_title: Reducing effort with reminders and a parking pass to improve appointment keeping for patients of pediatric residents
replication_authors: Linda Vance Ross; Patrick C. Friman; Edward R. Christophersen
replication_title: AN APPOINTMENT‐KEEPING IMPROVEMENT PACKAGE FOR OUTPATIENT PEDIATRICS: SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION AND COMPONENT ANALYSIS
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The results of the present study differ from those of the Friman et al. (1985, 1987) studies,' noting that in those studies 'the combined treatment package not only produced significant decreases in appointments not kept but also produced significant increases in appointments kept.' This replication failed to reproduce those effects for clinic-scheduled follow-up appointments, finding only increased cancellations but not improved appointment-keeping rates.

description: Active student response (ASR) error correction — where students repeat the teacher's model of the correct response after errors — produces better acquisition, maintenance, and generalization of sight words than no-response (NR) error correction in students with developmental disabilities
original_authors: Patricia M. Barbetta; Timothy E. Heron; William L. Heward
original_title: Effects of active student response during error correction on the acquisition, maintenance, and generalization of sight words by students with developmental disabilities
replication_authors: Gregg E. Drevno; Jonathan W. Kimball; Mwajabu K. Possi; William L. Heward; Ralph Gardner; Patricia M. Barbetta
replication_title: EFFECTS OF ACTIVE STUDENT RESPONSE DURING ERROR CORRECTION ON THE ACQUISITION, MAINTENANCE, AND GENERALIZATION OF SCIENCE VOCABULARY BY ELEMENTARY STUDENTS: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION
explanation: The authors report that ASR error correction was superior to NR error correction on all seven dependent variables for all 5 students, extending the original finding to a more complex academic task (science vocabulary definitions) and to general education (nondisabled) students. The paper concludes: 'These results add to those of Barbetta et al. (1993) and Barbetta and Heward (1993) in two important ways.'

description: Active student response (ASR) error correction — where students with learning disabilities repeat the teacher's model of the correct response after errors — produces better acquisition and maintenance of geography facts than no-response (NR) error correction
original_authors: Patricia M. Barbetta; William L. Heward
original_title: Effects of active student response during error correction on the acquisition and maintenance of geography facts by elementary students with learning disabilities
replication_authors: Gregg E. Drevno; Jonathan W. Kimball; Mwajabu K. Possi; William L. Heward; Ralph Gardner; Patricia M. Barbetta
replication_title: EFFECTS OF ACTIVE STUDENT RESPONSE DURING ERROR CORRECTION ON THE ACQUISITION, MAINTENANCE, AND GENERALIZATION OF SCIENCE VOCABULARY BY ELEMENTARY STUDENTS: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION
explanation: The authors report that ASR error correction was superior to NR error correction on all seven dependent variables for all 5 nondisabled students, replicating and extending the functional relation found by Barbetta & Heward (1993) to a more complex task and to general education students. The paper states 'this study produced the same functional relation...with general education students that was found in previous experiments.'

description: Using response cards (instead of hand raising) during whole-class instruction increases the frequency of active student responding and improves scores on quizzes over instructed content
original_authors: Janani S. Narayan; William L. Heward; Ralph Gardner; Frances H. Courson; Christine K. Omness
original_title: Using response cards to increase student participation in an elementary classroom
replication_authors: Ralph Gardner; William L. Heward; Teresa A. Grossi
replication_title: EFFECTS OF RESPONSE CARDS ON STUDENT PARTICIPATION AND ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION WITH INNER‐CITY STUDENTS DURING WHOLE‐CLASS SCIENCE INSTRUCTION
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This study replicated the findings of Narayan et al. (1990) in that response cards increased the frequency of active student response during whole-class instruction, improved students' scores on quizzes over the instructed content, and a majority of the students preferred response cards over hand raising.' The replication used the same paradigm but extended it to science instruction (vs. social studies) and added next-day and biweekly review tests.

description: Positive peer reporting (PPR) in a group-home residential care setting improves the social interactions and acceptance of a socially rejected adolescent boy
original_authors: F. E. Bowers; J. McGinnis; P. Friman; Ruth A. Ervin
original_title: Merging research and practice: The example of positive peer reporting applied to social rejection
replication_authors: Frank E. Bowers; Douglas W. Woods; William D. Carlyon; Patrick C. Friman
replication_title: USING POSITIVE PEER REPORTING TO IMPROVE THE SOCIAL INTERACTIONS AND ACCEPTANCE OF SOCIALLY ISOLATED ADOLESCENTS IN RESIDENTIAL CARE: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION
explanation: The paper is subtitled 'A Systematic Replication' and explicitly states it aims 'to experimentally replicate the results of that report with 4 adolescents in a group-home setting.' Results showed substantial improvements in social interactions for all 4 target participants, and the authors conclude the results 'extend the literature on PPR by providing experimental evidence that this classroom-based procedure can also be used successfully in family-style group homes for antisocial adolescents.'

description: An extinction analysis of separate topographies of problem behavior reveals response class hierarchies, where reinforcing milder forms of problem behavior reduces the probability of more severe topographies
original_authors: David M. Richman; David P. Wacker; Jennifer M. Asmus; Sean D. Casey; Marc Andelman
original_title: Further analysis of problem behavior in response class hierarchies
replication_authors: Jay W. Harding; David P. Wacker; Wendy K. Berg; Anjali Barretto; Lisa Winborn; Andrew Gardner
replication_title: ANALYSIS OF RESPONSE CLASS HIERARCHIES WITH ATTENTION‐MAINTAINED PROBLEM BEHAVIORS
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This investigation replicated the procedures reported by Richman et al. (1999)' and obtained consistent results: both mild and severe behaviors belonged to the same response class, and reinforcing mild behavior reduced severe behavior to near-zero levels in both participants, mirroring the Richman et al. findings. The study extended the original by adding a more precise response latency analysis.

description: A differential-reinforcement-of-low-rate-responding (DRL) schedule with response blocking and prompts reduces the rate of rapid eating in individuals with mental retardation
original_authors: David B. Lennox; Raymond G. Miltenberger; David R. Donnelly
original_title: Response interruption and DRL for the reduction of rapid eating
replication_authors: Carrie S. Wright; Timothy R. Vollmer
replication_title: EVALUATION OF A TREATMENT PACKAGE TO REDUCE RAPID EATING
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These procedures and results replicate those of Lennox et al. (1987).' The treatment package (adjusting DRL, response blocking, prompts) successfully increased interresponse times to the 15-s target level, and the initial negative side effects eventually decreased, consistent with the original findings.

description: Separate function-based interventions reduce problem behavior maintained by multiple sources of reinforcement, including automatic reinforcement, as identified via functional analysis
original_authors: Richard G. Smith; Brian A. Iwata; Timothy R. Vollmer; Jennifer R. Zarcone
original_title: Experimental analysis and treatment of multiply controlled self-injury
replication_authors: Carrie S. W. Borrero; Timothy R. Vollmer
replication_title: EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSIS AND TREATMENT OF MULTIPLY CONTROLLED PROBLEM BEHAVIOR: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION AND EXTENSION
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to 'replicate the procedures of Smith et al. (1993)' and conclude that 'results of this analysis are similar to those reported by Smith et al. (1993) in that systematic decreases in problem behavior were observed when treatments were introduced for the separate reinforcers.' The extension is that the current study applied the model to three sources of socially mediated reinforcement (attention, tangible, escape) rather than automatic reinforcement as in the original.

description: The bedtime pass (a small notecard exchangeable for one trip out of the bedroom after bedtime) combined with extinction eliminates bedtime resistance in children without producing extinction bursts
original_authors: Patrick C. Friman; Kathryn E. Hoff; Connie Schnoes; Kurt A. Freeman; Douglas W. Woods; Nathan Blum
original_title: The bedtime pass: An approach to bedtime crying and leaving the room
original_journal: Archives of Pediatric and Adolescent Medicine
replication_authors: Kurt A. Freeman
replication_title: TREATING BEDTIME RESISTANCE WITH THE BEDTIME PASS: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION AND COMPONENT ANALYSIS WITH 3‐YEAR‐OLDS
explanation: The authors explicitly label this study 'a systematic replication of Friman et al.' and the Discussion confirms: 'the results show that the pass effectively reduced bedtime resistance in 3-year-old children who were the only targets of the intervention.' Bedtime resistance was eliminated for all 4 participants and no extinction bursts were observed, consistent with the original findings.

description: Differential reinforcement of short latencies (token delivery following task completion within a preset criterion) decreased a child's latency to comply with instructions across five academic-related tasks
original_authors: Nancy Fjellstedt; Beth Sulzer‐Azároff
original_title: Reducing the latency of a child's responding to instructions by means of a token system
replication_authors: Jeffrey H. Tiger; Kelly J. Bouxsein; Wayne W. Fisher
replication_title: TREATING EXCESSIVELY SLOW RESPONDING OF A YOUNG MAN WITH ASPERGER SYNDROME USING DIFFERENTIAL REINFORCEMENT OF SHORT RESPONSE LATENCIES
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the procedures of Fjellstedt and Sulzer-Azaroff' and that 'these results are consistent with those of Fjellstedt and Sulzer-Azaroff (1973), in that the DR-short contingency was effective for decreasing the latency to Joe's question answering.' The replication applied the same differential reinforcement paradigm to a new population (a young man with Asperger syndrome) rather than a child with compliance issues, making it a close extension.

description: Experimental analysis methodology can identify the functions (mand, tact, intraverbal, echoic) of vocal behavior in children with developmental disabilities by manipulating antecedent and consequence events
original_authors: Dorothea C. Lerman; Mandy Parten; Laura R. Addison; Christina M. Vorndran; Valerie M. Volkert; Tiffany Kodak
original_title: A methodology for assessing the functions of emerging speech in children with developmental disabilities
replication_authors: Kelley ME; Shillingsburg MA; Castro MJ; Addison LR; LaRue RH Jr; Martins MP
replication_title: ASSESSMENT OF THE FUNCTIONS OF VOCAL BEHAVIOR IN CHILDREN WITH DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES: A REPLICATION
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted 'a systematic replication of the methodology developed by Lerman et al.' and conclude that 'the results replicated the findings of Lerman et al. (2005)...in that the function of at least one vocal response was identified for each participant,' though they note some differences in the proportion of mand responses observed.

description: Response interruption and redirection (RIRD) using vocal instructed responses reduces vocal stereotypy in children with autism, with appropriate vocalizations increasing as stereotypy decreases
original_authors: William H. Ahearn; Kathy M. Clark; Rebecca P. F. MacDonald; Bo In Chung
original_title: Assessing and treating vocal stereotypy in children with autism
replication_authors: Megan Duffy Cassella; Tina M. Sidener; David W. Sidener; Patrick R. Progar
replication_title: RESPONSE INTERRUPTION AND REDIRECTION FOR VOCAL STEREOTYPY IN CHILDREN WITH AUTISM: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These results replicate and extend the findings of Ahearn et al. (2007)' regarding the core RIRD effect on vocal stereotypy, but also note 'Some results obtained in the current study, however, do not replicate the findings of Ahearn et al.' — specifically, appropriate vocalizations did not increase and stereotypy did not remain low without RIRD, yielding a partial/mixed replication.

description: Response and time allocation on concurrent fixed-interval variable-interval (conc FI VI) schedules differs from conc VI VI performance, with response-rate ratios deviating from reinforcement-rate ratios and a displacement below the origin indicating preference for the VI schedule
original_authors: John A. Nevin
original_title: Rates and patterns of responding with concurrent fixed-interval and variable-interval reinforcement
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_authors: Lobb B.; Davison MC
replication_title: PERFORMANCE IN CONCURRENT INTERVAL SCHEDULES: A SYSTEMATIC REPLICATION<sup>1</sup>
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The present results on performance in conc FI VI schedules...broadly replicate previous results on response and time allocation (Nevin, 1971; Trevett et al., 1972)...But certain important details of the results are different.' Specifically, the slope (a) values differed (Nevin found ~0.5, this experiment found ~0.68), and intercept patterns diverged (Nevin found displacement for only one bird vs. consistent negative intercepts in the present study).

description: On concurrent FI VI schedules, response-rate ratios deviate from reinforcement-rate ratios with a proportional preference for the VI schedule and constant displacement below the origin; time-allocation ratios also deviate with a similar intercept displacement
original_authors: A. J. Trevett; Michael Davison; R. J. Williams
original_title: Performance in concurrent interval schedules
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_authors: Lobb B.; Davison MC
replication_title: Performance in concurrent interval schedules: a systematic replication
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors state the results 'broadly replicate previous results on response and time allocation (Nevin, 1971; Trevett et al., 1972)...But certain important details of the results are different.' Agreement with Trevett et al. was stronger than with Nevin (slope 0.62 vs 0.68, intercept -0.15 vs -0.14 for responses; -0.28 vs -0.16 for time), but the present data did not support Trevett et al.'s conclusion that conc FI VI performance differs from conc VI VI only in the c parameter.

description: Better short-term retention of pretrial unconditioned stimuli (USs) that are unexpected or 'surprising' to the subject compared to USs that are expected, attributed to greater rehearsal of surprising events
original_authors: William S. Terry; Allan R. Wagner
original_title: Short-term memory for "surprising" versus "expected" unconditioned stimuli in Pavlovian conditioning
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes
replication_authors: Sarah W. Bottjer; Eliot Hearst
replication_title: FOOD DELIVERY AS A CONDITIONAL STIMULUS: FEATURE‐LEARNING AND MEMORY IN PIGEONS<sup>1</sup>
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our failure to replicate the pattern of results reported by Terry and Wagner (1975) for differential short-term retention of surprising and expected events' — no consistent advantage for surprising over expected events was found; in fact, FP subjects showed the opposite effect on negative trials.

description: Feature-positive superiority: subjects for whom a pretrial US signals a subsequent US show better discriminative performance than subjects for whom a pretrial US signals absence of a subsequent US
original_authors: William S. Terry; Allan R. Wagner
original_title: Short-term memory for "surprising" versus "expected" unconditioned stimuli in Pavlovian conditioning
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes
replication_authors: Sarah W. Bottjer; Eliot Hearst
replication_title: FOOD DELIVERY AS A CONDITIONAL STIMULUS: FEATURE‐LEARNING AND MEMORY IN PIGEONS<sup>1</sup>
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: Across all three experiments, the authors consistently found a feature-positive superiority in their appetitive autoshaping paradigm, replicating the asymmetry reported by Terry and Wagner (1975): 'The results of these experiments indicated that, as has been shown in other situations, the presence of a unique cue correlated with subsequent reinforcement produced better discriminative performance than did the presence of that same cue correlated with the absence of reinforcement.'

description: Small thumb-twitches imperceptible to the subject can be operantly conditioned by making the contingent termination and/or postponement of aversive noise dependent on the myoelectrical response
original_authors: Ralph F. Hefferline; Brian Keenan; Richard A. Harford
original_title: Escape and avoidance conditioning in human subjects without their observation of the response
replication_authors: Lila Laurenti‐Lions; Jorge Gallego; Bernard Chambille; Guy Vardon; Charles Jacquemin
replication_title: CONTROL OF MYOELECTRICAL RESPONSES THROUGH REINFORCEMENT
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state that their Conditioning I experiment was a replication and that it 'provides, a posteriori, further support for the earlier conclusions.' 14 of 18 subjects showed operant conditioning of the myoelectrical response, demonstrating the effect was successfully replicated with an automated apparatus.

description: Reversal of AC baseline contingencies in college-student subjects produces immediate control of symmetry probe performances by the reversed contingencies, while reflexivity and transitivity/equivalence performances remain consistent with the originally established equivalence classes
original_authors: Carol Pilgrim; Mark Galizio
original_title: Relations between baseline contingencies and equivalence probe performances
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_authors: Carol Pilgrim; Lori Chambers; Mark Galizio
replication_title: REVERSAL OF BASELINE RELATIONS AND STIMULUS EQUIVALENCE: II. CHILDREN
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as 'a systematic replication of a study using college-student subjects (Pilgrim & Galizio, 1990)' but using 5- to 7-year-old children. The replication found a different pattern than the original: whereas adult symmetry was tightly controlled by baseline reversals, children showed inconsistent conditional control on all probe types, suggesting 'equivalence-class performances may be more easily disrupted in young children than in adults.' The outcomes differed substantially from the adult original, but the replication context (testing a different population) and the partial similarities make this inconclusive rather than a clear failure.

description: The extent of stimulus generalization during testing is an inverse function of the rate (schedule) of reinforcement used during training — pigeons trained with infrequent reinforcement (VI 240-s) show flat generalization gradients while those trained with frequent reinforcement (VI 30-s) show steep gradients
original_authors: Eliot Hearst; Minnie B. Koresko; Roger Poppen
original_title: Stimulus generalization and the response-reinforcer contingency
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_authors: Diana J. Walker; Marc N. Branch
replication_title: EFFECTS OF VARIABLE‐INTERVAL VALUE AND AMOUNT OF TRAINING ON STIMULUS GENERALIZATION
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the General Discussion: 'the present set of experiments failed to replicate the relation between rate of reinforcement and extent of generalization reported by Hearst et al. (1964).' Experiment 1 tested this using wavelength of light as the stimulus dimension (rather than line orientation used by Hearst et al.), and found steep gradients for all schedule groups — not the flat gradient for VI 240-s subjects predicted by the original.

description: The extent of stimulus generalization during testing is an inverse function of the rate (schedule) of reinforcement used during training — pigeons trained with infrequent reinforcement (VI 240-s) show flat generalization gradients while those trained with frequent reinforcement (VI 30-s) show steep gradients
original_authors: Eliot Hearst; Minnie B. Koresko; Roger Poppen
original_title: Stimulus generalization and the response-reinforcer contingency
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_authors: Diana J. Walker; Marc N. Branch
replication_title: EFFECTS OF VARIABLE‐INTERVAL VALUE AND AMOUNT OF TRAINING ON STIMULUS GENERALIZATION
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: Experiment 2 replicated the Hearst et al. (1964) procedure more closely using line orientation as the stimulus dimension (same as the original). The authors report that 'the inverse relation between VI mean interval and steepness of gradient slope reported by Hearst et al. (1964) was not replicated in the present study' — gradients were steep for both VI 30-s and VI 240-s subjects, and the small differences observed reflected an opposite relation to that predicted.

description: Pigeons trained on alternating concurrent schedules (VI 20s/VI 40s vs. VI 40s/VI 80s) show strong preference for the VI 40-s stimulus previously paired with the richer VI 80-s context during probe tests with the two VI 40-s stimuli presented concurrently in extinction
original_authors: Terry W. Belke
original_title: Stimulus preference and the transitivity of preference
replication_authors: Margaret A. McDevitt; Ben A. Williams
replication_title: AROUSAL, CHANGEOVER RESPONSES, AND PREFERENCE IN CONCURRENT SCHEDULES
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The discussion explicitly states: 'Experiment 1 successfully replicated Belke's (1992) pattern of results: Strong preference occurred in the probe trials for the VI 40-s stimulus paired with the VI 80-s schedule.' Six of 7 subjects showed the predicted preference with mean response proportion of .69, reliably different from .50, t(6) = 2.67, p < .05.

description: Pigeons prefer discriminative stimuli (S+) that were preceded by a high-effort response requirement (FR 20) over those preceded by a low-effort requirement (FR 1), demonstrating a work-ethic effect
original_authors: Tricia S. Clement; Joann R. Feltus; Daren H. Kaiser; Thomas R. Zentall
original_title: 'Work ethic' in pigeons: Reward value is directly related to the effort or time required to obtain the reward
replication_authors: Marco Vasconcelos; Peter J. Urcuioli
replication_title: EXTENSIVE TRAINING IS INSUFFICIENT TO PRODUCE THE WORK‐ETHIC EFFECT IN PIGEONS
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the variation in average preferences as a function of the initial-link work requirement in testing did not show a clearly discernible pattern other than a preponderance of "no preference" results,' and conclude that 'extensive overtraining is insufficient to produce the effect even using a signaled-effort procedure.' No significant overall preference for high-effort stimuli was found.

description: Starlings prefer discriminative stimuli preceded by a high-effort requirement (16 flights between perches) over stimuli preceded by a low-effort requirement (4 flights), demonstrating a work-ethic effect based on energetic cost
original_authors: Alex Kacelnik; Barnaby Marsh
original_title: Cost can increase preference in starlings
replication_authors: Marco Vasconcelos; Peter J. Urcuioli
replication_title: EXTENSIVE TRAINING IS INSUFFICIENT TO PRODUCE THE WORK‐ETHIC EFFECT IN PIGEONS
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors state that 'extensive overtraining using an adaptation of Kacelnik and Marsh's (2002) procedure for pigeons did not produce significant preferences for a high-effort S+, contrary to Kacelnik and Marsh's findings with starlings,' with none of the preferences deviating significantly from chance across all test sessions.

description: Aversively conditioned respondent elicitation (skin conductance responses) transfers to untrained equivalence class members after one stimulus in the class is paired with electric shock
original_authors: Michael J. Dougher; Erik Augustson; Michael R. Markham; David E. Greenway; Edelgard Wulfert
original_title: The transfer of respondent eliciting and extinction functions through stimulus equivalence classes
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_authors: Miguel Rodríguez Valverde; Carmen Luciano; Dermot Barnes-Holmes
replication_title: TRANSFER OF AVERSIVE RESPONDENT ELICITATION IN ACCORDANCE WITH EQUIVALENCE RELATIONS
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'this experiment failed to replicate the results of Dougher et al. (1994)'. Only 3 out of 15 participants (25%) showed the transfer of function criterion, a proportion described as 'not far from chance level', despite the majority (12/15) acquiring differential conditioning.

description: Divided stimulus control between dimensional elements of compound stimuli is graded and controlled by the relative frequency of reinforcers for correct responses to each stimulus dimension
original_authors: Timothy A. Shahan; Christopher A. Podlesnik
original_title: Divided attention performance and the matching law
replication_authors: Michael Davison; Douglas Elliffe
replication_title: DIVIDED STIMULUS CONTROL: A REPLICATION AND A QUANTITATIVE MODEL
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors confirm replication of the key finding: 'As reported by Shahan and Podlesnik (2006), the degree to which one of a pair of stimulus dimensions controlled choice depended on the degree to which reinforcers were differential with respect to stimuli on that dimension.' The paper explicitly describes itself as 'a systematic, rather than a direct, replication' using different stimuli (red-green cycle frequency and duration instead of color and line orientation) and a symbolic rather than identity matching-to-sample procedure.

description: Training an alternative response in a separate stimulus context before combining it with a target stimulus context during extinction reduces resistance to extinction of target responding, compared with concurrent (DRA) training of alternative and target responses in the same context
original_authors: Mace FC; McComas JJ; Mauro BC; Progar PR; Taylor B.; Ervin R.; Zangrillo AN

replication_authors: Christopher A. Podlesnik; John Y. H. Bai; Douglas Elliffe
replication_title: RESISTANCE TO EXTINCTION AND RELAPSE IN COMBINED STIMULUS CONTEXTS
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'The present study systematically replicated and extended the findings of Mace et al. (2010),' and in the Conclusion: 'The present study supports findings from Mace et al. (2010) that training an alternative response in a separate context before combining with a target context decreases resistance to extinction of target responding.' Key results were replicated despite additional controls addressing a confound in the original study.

description: Pigeons trained on successive AB symbolic matching plus AA oddity and BB identity show emergent BA antisymmetry — responding more to comparisons on the reverse of nonreinforced AB baseline trials than reinforced AB baseline trials
