replication_authors: Peter J. Urcuioli; Melissa Swisher
replication_title: A REPLICATION AND EXTENSION OF THE ANTISYMMETRY EFFECT IN PIGEONS
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
explanation: The Discussion states: 'it replicated in 2 of 4 pigeons the theoretically important antisymmetry effect originally reported by Urcuioli (2008, Experiment 4).' Only 2 of 4 pigeons showed significant antisymmetry (HO1 and HO4), while HO2 and HO3 showed non-significant differences, yielding a partial replication classified as inconclusive.

description: An in-class successive relearning demonstration intervention increases undergraduate students' adoption of high-utility study strategies and improves their confidence and mastery of course material
original_authors: Maurer, Trent W.; Shipp, Catelyn
original_title: Challenges of shaping student study strategies for success
replication_authors: Trent W. Maurer; Emily Cabay
replication_title: Challenges of Shaping Student Study Strategies for Success:  Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors describe their results as 'similar to those reported by Maurer and Shipp (2021) but differed in meaningful ways.' While some outcomes replicated (qualitative themes, time management barriers), key quantitative outcomes diverged notably — the current study showed much higher confidence (84%) and mastery (84%) at posttest compared to original (58% and 17%), while adoption of successive relearning remained low in both. The modified design (comparing exam-to-exam rather than pre-post within same exam) and updated course content make direct comparison difficult.

description: The proportion of correctly recalled items in short-term memory depends on the number of interfering items (not the presentation rate), indicating that interference alone accounts for forgetting in short-term memory
original_authors: Nancy C. Waugh; Donald A. Norman
original_title: Primary memory
replication_authors: Marilou Poitras; Lucie Péléja; Gardy Lavertu; Anouck Langlois; Katia Boulerice; Pauline Berthelot; Philippe Vincent-Lamarre
replication_title: A Replication of Waugh and Norman (1965) Primary Memory study
explanation: The authors describe Study 1 as 'an exact replication' and state results 'partially support Waugh & Norman's claim': the significant interference effect was confirmed, but a significant interaction between presentation rate and interference was also found (F(8,176)=2.47, p=.015), which the original study did not report. Starting accuracy was also much lower in the replication (~0.5) than the original (~1.0).

description: The proportion of correctly recalled items in short-term memory depends on the number of interfering items (not the presentation rate), indicating that interference alone accounts for forgetting in short-term memory
original_authors: Nancy C. Waugh; Donald A. Norman
original_title: Primary memory
replication_authors: Marilou Poitras; Lucie Péléja; Gardy Lavertu; Anouck Langlois; Katia Boulerice; Pauline Berthelot; Philippe Vincent-Lamarre
replication_title: A Replication of Waugh and Norman (1965) Primary Memory study
explanation: Study 2 used shorter 8-digit lists (vs. original 16-digit lists) and the authors explicitly state 'This study is not an exact replication.' Results again 'partially support' the original: interference effect was significant, but so was presentation rate and an interaction, contradicting the original's claim that only interference matters.

description: Iranian ELT instructors and content teachers show within-group inconsistencies and across-group discrepancies in their cognitions and actual practices when teaching EAP courses, with content teachers being more inconsistent than ELT instructors
original_authors: Atai, Mahmood Reza; Fatahi-Majd, Mojtaba
original_title: Exploring practices and cognitions of Iranian ELT instructors and subject teachers in teaching EAP reading comprehension
replication_authors: Fatemeh Soleimani; Ahmad Alibabaee
replication_title: Cognitions and Practices of Iranian ELT Instructors and Content Teachers in Teaching Discipline-Based EAP Courses: A Replication Study
replication_journal: IJELTAL (Indonesian Journal of English Language Teaching and Applied Linguistics)
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'The general findings supported [the original study] in all the areas under investigation where there were within group inconsistences and across-group discrepancies within and between the two groups of teachers respectively with content teachers being much more inconsistent than ELT instructors.' The Discussion section confirms the replication 'provides further evidences for what Atai and Fattahi-Majd (2014) found out.'

description: Autistic traits (ATs) are significantly more prevalent among referred children with ADHD compared to controls (18% vs. 0.87%), and children with ADHD and positive AT profiles are significantly more impaired in psychopathological, interpersonal, educational, and cognitive functioning
original_authors: Kotte A.; Joshi G.; Fried R.; Uchida M.; Spencer A.; Woodworth KY; Kenworthy T.; Faraone SV; Biederman J.
original_title: Autistic traits in children with and without ADHD
replication_authors: Joseph Biederman; Maura Fitzgerald; Stephen V. Faraone; Ronna Fried; K. Yvonne Woodworth; Alexandra Saunders; Kristina Conroy; Gagan Joshi
replication_title: Are Autistic Traits in Youth Meaningful? A Replication study in Non-referred Siblings of Youth with and without Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
replication_journal: Scandinavian Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Psychology
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These results in non-referred youth are highly consistent with the findings of previous reports (3-5) and with our findings from probands with ADHD,' confirming that this study successfully replicated the original findings in a non-referred sibling population.

description: In a principal-agent game, principals who impose a compulsory minimum transfer (control) receive lower average transfers than those who leave transfers unrestricted (trust), and most principals choose not to control — indicating that the hidden costs of control outweigh the benefits
original_authors: Armin Falk; Michael Kosfeld
original_title: The hidden costs of control
replication_authors: Matteo Ploner; Anthony Ziegelmeyer
replication_title: The Hidden Costs of Control: An Unsuccessful Replication Study
explanation: The paper explicitly titles itself 'An Unsuccessful Replication Study' and states: 'our replication reproduces as faithfully as possible the conditions of the original study...its main results support the basic premise of economics that incentives work.' The replication found 83% of principals chose to control (opposite of the original's 71% choosing not to control), and average transfers were non-significantly higher under control — directly contradicting F&K's two main findings.

description: Citizens are willing to tolerate anti-democratic behaviour by politicians who are perceived as competent, with competence not suppressing the negative effect of incremental violations of democratic principles, and respondents preferring undemocratic competent candidates over democratic incompetent ones
original_authors: Frederiksen, Kristian Vrede Skaaning
original_title: Does competence make citizens tolerate undemocratic behavior?
replication_authors: Thomas Brailey; Matthew Hepplewhite; Scott Moser
replication_title: Direct Replication and Additional Sensitivity and Robustness Analyses for Frederiksen (2022): A Replication Report from the Nottingham Replication Games
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we find that Frederiksen, 2022a's findings are replicable and remarkably robust to a battery of robustness tests.' They successfully reproduced the original Stata code and replicated the findings from scratch in R, with all main exhibits and tables replicating exactly.

description: Treatment with milnacipran (SNRI antidepressant) combined with metformin significantly improved metabolic parameters (fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, BMI, total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, triglycerides) in type 2 diabetic patients with comorbid depression who responded to antidepressant treatment, but not in nonresponders
original_authors: Abrahamian H.; Hofmann P.; Prager R.; Toplak H.
original_title: Diabetes mellitus and co-morbid depression: treatment with milnacipran results in significant improvement of both diseases (results from the Austrian MDDM study group)
replication_authors: Heidemarie Abrahamian; Hofmann; Kinzl; Toplak
replication_title: &nbsp;Diabetes mellitus and comorbid depression: improvement of both diseases with milnacipran. A replication study (results of the Austrian Major Depression Diabetes Mellitus study group)
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'The present study thus replicates some of the original findings.' The replication confirms that cholesterol and triglyceride improvements are specific to antidepressant responders, but diverges from the original in finding significant reductions in FBG and HbA1c in all patients regardless of antidepressant response — a key difference from the original pilot study.

description: MRI measurement using T2*-weighted sequences shows decreased iron concentration in the substantia nigra and putamen in patients with restless legs syndrome compared to age- and sex-matched controls
original_authors: Allen RP; Barker PB; Wehrl FW; Song HK; Earley CJ
original_title: MRI measurement of brain iron in patients with restless legs syndrome
replication_authors: Knake
replication_title: Normal regional brain iron concentration in restless legs syndrome measured by MRI
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we could not replicate the MRI findings of earlier studies' (refs 16,17) and 'failed to replicate earlier findings of reduced brain iron in the substantia nigra in patients with RLS compared to healthy controls.' No significant differences were found in any investigated brain region.

description: MRI-determined regional brain iron concentrations are significantly lower in the substantia nigra in early-onset restless legs syndrome patients but not late-onset patients compared to controls
original_authors: Christopher J. Earley; Peter B. Barker; Alena Horská; Richard P. Allen
original_title: MRI-determined regional brain iron concentrations in early- and late-onset restless legs syndrome
replication_authors: Knake
replication_title: Normal regional brain iron concentration in restless legs syndrome measured by MRI
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'could not replicate the MRI findings of earlier studies' (including ref 17) and found 'no regional brain iron deficit neither in early- or in late-onset RLS,' directly contradicting the key finding of the original study that early-onset RLS patients show reduced substantia nigra iron.

description: The UCLA Loneliness Scale Version 3 has a three-factor structure (Isolation, Relational Connectedness, Trait Loneliness) in an Italian sample, as identified using Exploratory Structural Equation Modeling (ESEM) with Geomin rotation
original_authors: M. Boffo; S. Mannarini; Cristina Munari
original_title: Exploratory structure equation modeling of the UCLA Loneliness Scale: a contribution to the Italian adaptation
replication_authors: Rossella Bottaro; Giusy Danila Valenti; Palmira Faraci
replication_title: Assessment of an Epidemic Urgency: Psychometric Evidence for the UCLA Loneliness Scale
explanation: The authors explicitly state they tested the 'replicability of the previous suggested Italian solution' and concluded their outcomes 'supported the previous findings.' The ESEM 3-factor model showed adequate goodness-of-fit (CFI = 0.942, TLI = 0.917, RMSEA = 0.062) in a broader Italian adult sample (N=1676 vs. university students in the original). They recommend Target rotation over the original Geomin rotation but report statistically significant target loadings consistent with the original. Classified as close extension because the sample is broader (general adults vs. university students) and the rotation method differs. Reviewer verified: result and type classifications are well-supported by the paper's explicit replication language and fit indices.

description: A 3-item short version of the UCLA Loneliness Scale Version 3 demonstrates good psychometric properties (CFI = 1.00, adequate reliability) and is preferable to the 10-item short version
original_authors: Azusa Arimoto; Etsuko Tadaka
original_title: Reliability and validity of Japanese versions of the UCLA loneliness scale version 3 for use among mothers with infants and toddlers: a cross-sectional study
replication_authors: Rossella Bottaro; Giusy Danila Valenti; Palmira Faraci
replication_title: Assessment of an Epidemic Urgency: Psychometric Evidence for the UCLA Loneliness Scale
explanation: Genuinely ambiguous result. The 3-item CFA produced perfect fit indices (CFI=1.00, TLI=1.00, RMSEA=0, SRMR=0) and adequate reliability (α=0.70), replicating the Japanese version's statistics. However, the authors explicitly reject the model: 'despite our findings replicating the Japanese version, this saturated model cannot be supported. Its perfect goodness-of-fit indices make the model useless due to its non-falsifiability.' The perfect fit is an artifact of a just-identified (saturated) 3-item CFA model — it always fits perfectly regardless of data, making it uninformative. The authors conclude by discouraging use of 'current short forms.' This is genuinely inconclusive: the numerical results replicated but the authors reject the methodology as non-falsifiable. A case could be made for 'failure' (authors reject the model) but 'inconclusive' is defensible since the statistical replication itself succeeded. Keeping medium confidence because the ambiguity is inherent to the paper's own conflicting conclusions.

description: Physical activity is associated with reduced depressive symptoms in adolescents, with each additional weekly exercise hour associated with an 8% reduction in depressive symptoms
original_authors: Catherine Rothon; Phil Edwards; Kamaldeep Bhui; Russell M. Viner; Stephanie Taylor; Stephen A. Stansfeld
original_title: Physical activity and depressive symptoms in adolescents: a prospective study
replication_authors: Iana Malasevskaia; Termeh Jahanbakhsh; Yusuf Adelabu; Carlos Montalván Rojas; Ana Lucia Portilla; Julia Hansen; Augusto Cesar Villar de Almeida; Valentina Ferrer Valencia; Mildred Tavarez; Igmilka Dayana Milles Dommar
replication_title: Association Between Physical Activity And Depressive Symptoms In Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional And Replication Study From ELSI-Brazil
replication_journal: Principles and Practice of Clinical Research Journal
explanation: Reviewer-verified inconclusive. This cross-sectional replication in 6,974 Brazilian older adults found genuinely mixed results: vigorous PA was protective with physician-diagnosed depression, but moderate-intensity PA showed no significant effect under either depression measure, and when depression was assessed via CES-D scale, no PA intensity at any frequency reached significance. Peer reviewers explicitly challenged the authors' claim that PA was protective 'regardless of intensity,' and the authors conceded, revising their discussion to state vigorous exercise 'may protect against depression, with moderate and low-intensity exercise showing less clear benefits.' The inconsistency across PA intensity levels and depression measures is structural, not resolvable — medium confidence is the honest classification.

description: A 24-week home-based physical activity program improves cognitive function (as measured by ADAS-Cog) in older adults aged 50+ with mild memory impairment, compared to a control group
original_authors: Nicola T. Lautenschlager; Kay L. Cox; Leon Flicker; Jonathan K. Foster; Frank M. van Bockxmeer; Jianguo Xiao; Kathryn R. Greenop; Osvaldo P. Almeida
original_title: Effect of physical activity on cognitive function in older adults at risk for Alzheimer disease: A randomized trial
replication_authors: Guilherme Luiz da Rocha; Luciane Lie Ikeda; Julia Daudt de Faro Salamonde; Faculdade São Leopoldo Mandic , Campinas, Brazil; Antonia Egert; Sacha Mukhij; Paul Warnck; Roberto Nishimura; Marcio Carlos de Freitas; Javier Grajeda; Veronica Echavarria; Dra. Veronica Echavarria Private Practice, Colombia; Laura Tam; Magdiel A. Amell Castillo; Instituto de Salud Mental y. Telepsicología, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic; Ana Beatriz Pizarro
replication_title: Association Between Physical Activity Levels and Cognitive Function in Older Adults: A Replication Cohort Analysis Using the Brazilian Longitudinal Study of Aging
replication_journal: Principle and Practice of Clinical Research Journal
explanation: The authors find a consistent positive association between moderate-to-vigorous exercise and cognitive function across all three regression models in a Brazilian cohort, stating 'The results from this analysis are consistent with the original findings.' The association persisted after adjusting for sex, race, education, and additional covariates (coefficient 1.53, p<0.001 in the emulation model).

description: Grossarth-Maticek personality Type 1 (hopelessness/depression) is associated with increased cancer risk and Type 2 (anger/hostility) is associated with increased coronary heart disease risk in prospective studies
original_authors: Grossarth-Maticek, R.; Eysenck, H.J.; Vetter, H.
original_title: Personality type, smoking habit and their interaction as predictors of cancer and coronary heart disease
replication_authors: Jun Nagano; Nobuyuki Sudo; Chiharu Kubo; Suminori Kono
replication_title: Lung Cancer, Myocardial Infarction, and the Grossarth-Maticek Personality Types: A Case-control Study in Fukuoka, Japan.
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the original type-allocation method using the SIRI failed to replicate Grossarth-Maticek et al's findings with regard to cancer and CHD proneness,' but also note that scale-level analyses showed Types 2 and 5 were positively associated with MI, 'partly supporting the GM-SPT.' The overall characterization is mixed/inconclusive, with some findings consistent with and others contradicting the original theory.

description: Daydreaming frequency, intensity, absorption, and related characteristics (as measured by the Imaginal Processes Inventory) decrease with increasing age in adult males across the life span
original_authors: Leonard M. Giambra
original_title: Daydreaming across the life span: late adolescent to senior citizen
original_journal: International Journal of Aging and Human Development
replication_authors: Leonard M. Giambra
replication_title: Adult Male Daydreaming across the Life Span: A Replication, Further Analyses, and Tentative Norms Based upon Retrospective Reports
replication_journal: The International Journal of Aging and Human Development
explanation: The abstract explicitly states: 'The characteristics of daydreaming obtained in an original sample were obtained in the replication sample thus supporting the outcomes reported earlier.' Statistical comparisons found no significant differences between sample means beyond what would be expected by chance, and factor patterns were essentially identical across original and replication samples.

replication_title: Predicting Current Glycated Hemoglobin Levels in Adults From Electronic Health Records: Validation of Multiple Logistic Regression Algorithm
explanation: The replication confirmed the general approach (73-74% accuracy vs. 77% in the original), supporting the conclusion that EHR-based logistic regression can predict HbA1c. However, the predictor importance rankings differed substantially between populations, and the authors conclude that 'direct use of the models (calculators)... may not be appropriate for all populations,' making the overall result inconclusive — the method replicates but the specific model does not transfer directly.

explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated and expanded on an earlier study [30]' and conclude: 'We replicated the positive potential of smartphone keyboard interaction monitoring for estimating rest-activity patterns among populations of regular smartphone users.' The replication found moderate to strong associations (β = .61–.78 for timing estimates) consistent with the original findings.

replication_title: Patient Preferences for Direct-to-Consumer Telemedicine Services: Replication and Extension of a Nationwide Survey
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the items used in the prior study' and 'replicated the analysis detailed in Welch et al [14]'. The Discussion confirms the replication was successful: 'Welch et al [14] found that patients became less willing to use telemedicine as they became further detached from their own health care professional in 2017, our study showed a similar trend for both willingness and comfort.' Willingness and comfort increased overall since 2017, confirming the original findings held and extended to 2022.

replication_authors: Rebecca McGrath; S. Craig Roberts
replication_title: Nosewitness Identification: A Replication Study [Conference Presentation Abstract]
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: This source is a one-page conference talk abstract (Human Ethology 2024, Suppl 1, S41) with no full paper, no statistical results, no sample sizes, no effect sizes, and no discussion section. The authors state 'we attempted to produce a replication of their study' and report that 'participants could identify the target body odour in both conditions above rates of chance, but that the rate of correct identification was higher in the violent video condition' — consistent with Alho et al. (2015)'s two key findings. Result classified as success based on the authors' verbal summary. However, confidence remains low because we have only an abstract-level claim with zero quantitative evidence to verify the strength or reliability of the reported effects. This ambiguity is irresolvable from the available source material.

description: Children's concepts of chance and probability develop through three sequential Piagetian stages (preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational), with stage-related verbal and nonverbal features forming homogeneous structures in an invariant developmental sequence

explanation: The replication found partial support: verbal performance strongly confirmed Piaget and Inhelder's stage-related descriptions and sequence, but nonverbal performance did not. The authors state: 'The results of this replication study indicate considerable agreement with Piaget and Inhelder's description of stage-related verbal features while failing to confirm their description of stage-related nonverbal features.'

explanation: The authors state findings were 'both consistent and inconsistent with the earlier studies.' Consistent findings included congruent patterns being most frequent, complementary patterns being rare, and incongruent favoritism being associated with less marital love. However, the direction of differential discipline was reversed (older siblings received more discipline rather than younger), and several family relationship correlates differed, reflecting the younger age group.

description: In preschool sibling families, parents discipline the older sibling more than the younger, and incongruent patterns of differential favoritism (one parent favoring a child while the other treats both equally) are associated with less marital love
original_authors: Brenda L. Volling
original_title: The family correlates of maternal and paternal perceptions of differential treatment in early childhood
replication_authors: Brenda L. Volling; Julie L. Elins
replication_title: Family Relationships and Children's Emotional Adjustment as Correlates of Maternal and Paternal Differential Treatment: A Replication with Toddler and Preschool Siblings
explanation: The current study found findings 'both consistent and inconsistent' with Volling (1997). Consistent with Volling, both mothers and fathers disciplined the older sibling more, parents' differential enjoyment was related to favoritism but not discipline, and incongruent favoritism was linked to less marital love. However, family patterns of differential discipline differed — the current sample of younger toddlers showed nearly all families disciplining the older sibling, whereas Volling (1997) found roughly equal rates of equal vs. older-more discipline, suggesting developmental change even within early childhood.

description: Raters from different occupational groups (students, policemen, judges) can reliably judge the seriousness of criminal offenses using a psychophysical rating scale, and the resulting scale values will show similar slopes and shapes across replications in different samples

replication_authors: Marlene Hsu
replication_title: Cultural and Sexual Differences on the Judgment of Criminal Offenses: A Replication Study of the Measurement of Delinquency
replication_journal: The Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology (1973-)
explanation: The paper found that the minimum claim (similarity of shapes) was supported cross-culturally (r=.95), but the maximum claim (similarity of slopes) was not supported (b=.60, far from 1.0). The authors conclude: 'the minimum claim of the similarity of shapes is valid in an Oriental culture, but that the maximum claim of the similarity of slopes is questionable.' Additionally, the cross-sexual comparison showed even less similarity (r=.84, b=.86), with females ranking rape as more serious than death.

description: The fertility of white Catholic and non-Catholic wives was converging and the Catholic-non-Catholic differential had all but disappeared, including the differential by frequency of communion among Catholic wives

explanation: The replication found partial agreement — both surveys confirmed convergence trends — but found a larger Catholic-non-Catholic differential (.18 vs .10 children per woman) and, crucially, found that the differential by communion frequency had NOT narrowed (.35 in 1971-1975 vs .05 in the NFS). The authors concluded 'it was premature to conclude that Protestant/Catholic fertility differentials had ended in the mid-1970s.'

description: Nursing subunit technology can be measured along three dimensions (instability, uncertainty, and variability) using a questionnaire-based factor analysis, with these dimensions differentiating among types of nursing subunits in hospitals

explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'Our replication indicated that the technological measure used in the original study is generally reliable and valid.' The same three-factor solution was found, and ranking and mean scores were similar across studies, confirming construct validity of the original measure.

description: Background knowledge (high-level schemata) constrains reading comprehension such that readers with different domain expertise interpret ambiguously written passages according to their dominant schema (e.g., music students interpret an ambiguous passage as being about music, while physical education students interpret it as being about wrestling)

The authors themselves state 'in a technical sense, this study is not a replication but an extension of the original.'

explanation: The authors tested the rs7566605 variant for association with BMI and obesity in their Italian isolated population sample and found no evidence of association: 'we did not detect association with either BMI or obesity with or without adjustment for sex and age.' Corballis; Gianvito Laera; Matthias Kliegel; Dominik Welke; Faisal Mushtaq; Yuri G. Pavlov; Heinrich R. Liesefeld
replication_title: A multilab investigation into the N2pc as an indicator of attentional selectivity: Direct replication of Eimer (1996)
explanation: Independent review confirms genuine ambiguity; confidence kept at medium. Reviewer 1 (Baykova) notes the colour N2pc 'was not replicated using the strict replication of the original pipeline and the ICA pipeline' but 'was, however, replicated using the collapsed localiser pipeline and in the additional exploratory analyses which didn't use a fixed time window.' The authors' own abstract characterises this as 'a direct replication of the more influential N2pc to color stimuli technically failed' — suggesting the primary pre-registered analysis is better classified as a failure, while alternative pipelines succeeded. The result classification of 'inconclusive' is defensible given the pipeline-dependency, but reasonable classifiers could choose 'failure' given the authors' own framing of 'technically failed.' Medium confidence is appropriate because the paper itself presents contradictory outcomes across pipelines and the authors' language sits between failure and partial success. Merged from a duplicate row extracted from the PCI RR recommendation: the colour N2pc 'did not technically replicate, though a negative deflection was found 70ms earlier than originally reported.'

original_title: The N2pc component as an indicator of attentional selectivity
replication_authors: Martin Constant; Ananya Mandal; Dariusz Asanowicz; Bartłomiej Panek; Ilona Kotlewska; Motonori Yamaguchi; Helge Gillmeister; Dirk Kerzel; David Luque; Sara Molinero; Antonio Vázquez-Millán; Francesca Pesciarelli; Eleonora Borelli; Hanane Ramzaoui; Melissa Beck; Bertille Somon; Andrea Desantis; M. replication_title: A multilab investigation into the N2pc as an indicator of attentional selectivity: Direct replication of Eimer (1996)
explanation: Independent review confirms success. Reviewer 1 (Baykova) explicitly states 'the difference in amplitude between shapes and colours' was replicated. This is stated plainly alongside the shape N2pc replication and is not qualified with pipeline caveats (unlike the colour N2pc finding). The authors' abstract does not contest this finding. Upgraded from medium to high confidence.

description: Conducting a systematic mapping study (SMS) provides educational value to students, including research skills acquisition, broad understanding of a research area, and is a useful starting point for thesis work
original_authors: Barbara Kitchenham; Pearl Brereton; David Budgen
original_title: The educational value of mapping studies of software engineering literature
original_journal: 2010 ACM/IEEE 32nd International Conference on Software Engineering
replication_authors: Jose L. Barros-Justo; Nelson Martínez-Araujo; David N. Olivieri; Alejandro González-García
replication_title: Educational value of Systematic Mapping Studies: A replication study.
replication_journal: Journal of Computer Science and Technology
explanation: The authors confirm most but not all results: 'This replication confirms all but two of the results from the original work.' Propositions P1, P2, P3 and issues I1, I4 were confirmed, while P5 (ease of documenting) yielded contradictory responses and I2 (enjoyability) showed opposite results (0% in original vs. 67% in replication), indicating partial support only.

description: Positive psychological characteristics (gratitude, satisfaction with life, forgiveness) are positively correlated with executive functioning in college students, with gratitude and satisfaction with life showing positive correlations and forgiveness showing an unexpected negative correlation with executive function
original_authors: William M. Miley; Marcello Spinella
original_title: Correlations among measures of executive function and positive psychological attributes in college students
replication_authors: Gert H. J. Kruger
replication_title: Executive Functioning and Positive Psychological Characteristics: A Replication and Extension
explanation: The paper explicitly states it is a replication and extension of Miley and Spinella (2006), using the same questionnaires. Gratitude correlations were replicated, but mixed results were obtained for forgiveness (positive vs. the original's negative correlation) and satisfaction with life (only empathy significant vs. motivational drive and strategic planning in the original). The abstract notes 'mixed results were obtained for forgiveness and satisfaction with life,' and the Discussion states 'Several of the results obtained by Miley and Spinella (2006) were replicated in this study.'

description: Different labels for unauthorized immigrants ('illegal immigrants' vs 'undocumented immigrants') do not differentially affect attitudes toward immigration policy
original_authors: Benjamin R. Knoll; David P. Redlawsk; Howard Sanborn
original_title: Framing labels and immigration policy attitudes in the Iowa caucuses: 'Trying to Out-Tancredo Tancredo'
replication_authors: Reidar Ommundsen; Knud S. Larsen; Kees van der Veer; Dag-Erik Eilertsen
replication_title: Framing Unauthorized Immigrants: The Effects of Labels on Evaluations
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors explicitly describe their study as 'a conceptual replication using slightly different methods.' Knoll et al. (2011) found no effects of labeling on attitudes; the present study found significant differences across all three label conditions (F(2)=8.96, p<.001, partial η²=0.06), directly contradicting Knoll et al.'s null result. Classification as 'failure' is correct — finding a significant effect where the original found none constitutes a failure to replicate. Confidence remains medium because: (1) the original finding was a null result, making 'replication failure' conceptually ambiguous (the original null could reflect low power rather than a true absence of effect); (2) the authors themselves describe these as 'seemingly contradictory results' without framing the outcome as a clear replication failure; (3) methodological differences (20-item attitude scale vs. policy attitudes, undergrads vs. Iowa caucus-goers, 3 labels vs. 2) are substantial enough that differences in outcome could reflect method rather than a true failure to replicate the underlying phenomenon.

description: Computer/Internet skills predict whether college students purchase books online (but not textbooks for courses)
original_authors: Bijou Yang; David Lester
original_title: Buying books online: follow-up
replication_authors: Bijou Yang; David Lester
replication_title: Buying Books Online: A Replication
explanation: The replication-only sample (n=65) showed only marginal significance for computer/Internet skills predicting other book purchases (beta=2.2, p=.09), and no significant predictors for textbook purchases. The authors combined the replication and original samples (n=137) to confirm the finding, concluding 'the analysis of the larger sample confirmed the result of the first study.' The replication alone was inconclusive due to the marginal p-value.

description: Responsiveness on a simple 5-button pressing task shows significant sex differences (males less than females), an increase in presses per minute over 10 successive 1-min. trials, and a persistent upward-bowing pattern in responses, all inconsistent with Hull's concept of reactive inhibition
original_authors: Howarth E.
original_title: A test of Hull's reactive inhibition concept: persistence of curvilinear response pattern in button pressing
replication_authors: Roy Yensen
replication_title: Replication Study of Responsiveness on a Simple Five-Button Pressing Task
explanation: The replication confirmed some of Howarth's findings (the bowing pattern persisting over trials and increase in presses per minute, supporting no reactive inhibition influence), but found contrary results on sex differences (males showed significantly HIGHER responsiveness, p < .025, vs. original males < females) and no significant relationship between responsiveness and extraversion E scores (vs. Howarth's significant relationship). The authors state: 'Some of the results of the present study support Howarth's findings...However, the remaining results are contrary to those of Howarth.'

description: Recall instructions given prior to reading material under delayed auditory feedback do not affect retention accuracy compared to no-instruction conditions
original_authors: David J. King
original_title: Immediate memory of connected meaningful material practiced under delayed auditory feedback
replication_authors: David J. King
replication_title: Replication Study of Two Unusual Findings on the Influence of Delayed Auditory Feedback on Retention
explanation: The present study replicates the finding from King (1963) that recall instructions have no significant effect on retention accuracy, using a larger sample. The authors confirm: 'The present findings confirm the previous results of a lack of influence of recall instructions.'

description: There is a large positive correlation between change in voice level under delayed auditory feedback and accuracy of retention of the material presented under DAF (for males)
original_authors: David J. King
original_title: Predicting the amount of forgetting of connected meaningful material presented under delayed auditory feedback
replication_authors: David J. King
replication_title: Replication Study of Two Unusual Findings on the Influence of Delayed Auditory Feedback on Retention
explanation: The prior study (King, in press) found r = +.55 (p < .01) between voice level change and retention accuracy. The replication found r = -.20, not significantly different from zero, which the authors describe as 'in marked contrast to a prior finding of a large and significant positive correlation.'

description: A nonvocal system for teaching children with severe mental handicaps to read by matching symbols and words to stimulus pictures, achieving 13 out of 14 children completing the training programme
original_authors: Kuntz Jb; Carrier Jk; Hollis Jh
original_title: A non-vocal system for teaching retarded children to read and write
original_journal: Quality of Life in Severely and Profoundly Mentally Retarded People--research Foundations for Improvement (Book Chapter)
replication_authors: Alan Hills
replication_title: Replication of Nonvocal System for Teaching Nonreaders to Read in an Adult Training Centre
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Nine out of 33 nonreaders completed the programme so the success rate was well short of that of the original study.' The replication used adults with mental handicaps in an adult training centre rather than children in a hospital setting, testing generalizability of the method to a different population and context.

description: Specific emotions (love, anger, grief, etc.) can be communicated through touch via characteristic finger-pressure time-displacement curves (sentograms) that are universal across cultures
original_authors: Manfred Clynes
original_title: Sentics: biocybernetics of emotion communication
original_journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Steven J. Trussoni; Anthony O'Malley; Anthony Barton
replication_title: Human Emotion Communication by Touch: A Modified Replication of an Experiment by Manfred Clynes
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude 'the definite absence of a significant correlation between our sentograms and those of Clynes,' finding no evidence for universal emotion-specific tactile expression patterns. The replication duplicated most important aspects of the original experiment but used an improved pressure-detection instrument.

description: Subjects with claimed mild head injury seeking financial compensation obtain significantly lower scores on both subtests of the Recognition Memory Test than rehabilitation inpatients with documented moderate and severe traumatic brain injuries, and a discriminant function correctly classifies group membership at above-chance rates
original_authors: Scott R. Millis
original_title: The Recognition Memory Test in the detection of malingered and exaggerated memory deficits
replication_authors: Scott R. Millis; Steven H. Putnam
replication_title: The Recognition Memory Test in the Assessment of Memory Impairment after Financially Compensable Mild Head Injury: A Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The current investigation replicated the findings reported by Millis (1992).' The discriminant function cross-validated on the new sample yielded 83% correct classification, improving on the original 76%, and the mild head-injured group again scored significantly lower on both RMT subtests.

description: Forced breathing through the right or left nostril differentially affects verbal and spatial cognition of college students, with the direction of the effect depending on gender (men showed better spatial performance during right-nostril breathing and better verbal performance during left-nostril breathing; women showed better spatial performance during left-nostril breathing with no significant verbal effect)
original_authors: Richard A. Block; David P. Arnott; Barbara Quigley; Wesley C. Lynch
original_title: Unilateral nostril breathing influences lateralized cognitive performance
replication_authors: Barbara Sanders; Clairessa Lattimore; Kirsten Smith; Lisa Dierker
replication_title: Forced Single-Nostril Breathing and Cognition
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our study thus failed to replicate their results.' The interaction of breathing condition × sex — the key finding from Block et al. — was non-significant in the replication (F=2.3, p=.80), in contrast to the original's significant interaction.

description: Hemodynamic pressure variables (e.g., right atrial mean pressure, mean pulmonary artery pressure) are inversely related to cognitive performance on measures of mental flexibility, abstract thinking, and attention among heart transplant candidates
original_authors: John D. Putzke; Mark A. Williams; Barry K. Rayburn; James K. Kirklin; Thomas J. Boll
original_title: The relationship between cardiac function and neuropsychological status among heart transplant candidates
replication_authors: Richard O. Temple; John D. Putzke; Thomas J. Boll
replication_title: Neuropsychological Performance as a Function of Cardiac Status among Heart Transplant Candidates: A Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in both the title and abstract that this is 'a replication' of Putzke et al. (1998). The discussion confirms: 'Consistent with previous findings (Putzke, et al., 1998), increasing hemodynamic pressure was related to decreased cognitive test performance.' The core finding replicated (pulmonary artery systolic pressure inversely related to Trail Making Test-Part A, r=.53, p<.01), though the relationship was more limited in scope than the original, possibly due to smaller sample size.

description: Urine-alarm signals combined with staff prompts and reinforcement promote daytime urinary continence in a student with severe intellectual disability
original_authors: Giulio E. Lancioni; Sonia Markus
original_title: Urine-triggered alarm signals and prompts to promote daytime urinary continence in a boy with severe intellectual disability
replication_authors: Lancioni GE; Van Bergen I.; Furniss F.
replication_title: Urine Alarms and Prompts for Fostering Daytime Urinary Continence in a Student with Multiple Disabilities: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The data support the findings of Lancioni and Markus (1999)', and the student 'became almost totally free from large urinary accidents, replacing them with self-initiated toileting.' The same urine-alarm and staff-prompt approach was applied to a student with multiple disabilities (Down syndrome, severe hearing loss, and visual impairment), extending the original finding to a more complex disability profile.

description: Most college students in the 1940s reported rarely or never seeing colors in their dreams, with 70.7% of 277 sophomores responding 'rarely' or 'never' to the question about color in dreams
original_authors: Warren C. Middleton
original_title: The frequency with which a group of unselected college students experience colored dreaming and colored hearing
replication_authors: Eric Schwitzgebel
replication_title: Do People Still Report Dreaming in Black and White? An Attempt to Replicate a Questionnaire from 1942
explanation: The authors found that only 17.7% of 2001 students reported 'rarely' or 'never' seeing colors in dreams, compared to 70.7% in Middleton's 1942 sample. The Mann-Whitney comparison showed a statistically significant difference (p < .0001), meaning the original finding that most people rarely dream in color was not reproduced in the modern sample.

description: Two 16-item scales measuring attitudes toward computers and toward the Internet show reliability and factorial structure
original_authors: Liaw, S. S.
original_title: An internet survey for perception of computers and the world wide web
replication_authors: Bijou Yang; David Lester
replication_title: Liaw's Scales to Measure Attitudes toward Computers and the Internet
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as 'a replication study' and conclude: 'Liaw's scales proved to have good reliability and good construct validity,' confirming the reliability of the original scales with a larger sample.

description: Anxiety and sadness differentially influence decision making such that anxious individuals are more risk averse while sad individuals are more risk taking
original_authors: Rajagopal Raghunathan; Michel Tuan Pham
original_title: All negative moods are not equal: motivational influences of anxiety and sadness on decision making
original_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
replication_authors: Wen-Bin Chiou; Ming-Hsu Chang; Chien-Lung Chen
replication_title: The Moderating Role of Personal Relevance on Differential Priming of Anxiety and Sadness on Perceived Travel Risk: A Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'These findings replicate the results obtained in the domains of risky gambles and job options employed by Raghunathan and Pham.' Anxious participants showed significantly higher perceived travel risk than sad participants, consistent with the original finding, though tested in a new domain (travel risk) with a Chinese student sample.

description: Members of different religious groups (Jews, Catholics, Protestants) differ in interaction rates and peer/self rankings, with Jews showing higher rates of interaction and assertiveness, and Protestants being more socially oriented
original_authors: John Stimson
original_title: Some religious-ethnic differences in interaction rates
replication_authors: Betty Crowther
replication_title: Note on Religious Group Differences in Interaction Profiles: A Replication Study
explanation: The replication found general agreement with Stimson's overall patterns (Jews more assertive, Protestants more socially oriented), but only one difference achieved statistical significance. Some specific findings diverged from the original (e.g., emotionality ratings). The authors conclude the consistency 'suggests that the observed relationships may be real although small in magnitude' but acknowledge the results are largely non-significant.

description: Planarians (Cura foremanii) can be trained to break a photobeam to escape strong overhead illumination, with experimental Ss demonstrating a higher response rate than yoked control Ss
original_authors: Richard M. Lee
original_title: Conditioning of a free operant response in planaria
replication_authors: F. T. Crawford; L. C. Skeen
replication_title: Operant Responding in the Planarian: A Replication Study
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: The authors state 'The present experiment was an attempt to replicate the findings of Lee (1964) and Best (1965)' and report that the light-escape contingent group made significantly more responses than yoked controls (t=1.53, df=1/15, p<.05, one-tailed), consistent with Lee's original finding. Result classified as success because the directional effect matches the original and the authors present it as confirmatory. Confidence kept at medium because: (1) the t-value of 1.53 is marginal and only significant with a one-tailed test, (2) the authors themselves acknowledge criticisms of the yoked control design (Church 1964, Beecroft 1966) and note 'potential misinterpretation of results', and (3) the authors do not use strong replication-success language — they present results matter-of-factly without explicitly claiming successful replication. Close experiment is correct: same paradigm (photobeam-breaking for light escape) but with deliberate modifications including shorter test period (4 hr vs. extended), automated recording, and higher photobeam intensity.

description: Planarians exhibit operant light-escape behavior similar to that described by Lee, including circling behavior and a reminiscence effect, with experimental Ss showing higher photobeam-breaking rates than yoked controls
original_authors: Best, J.B.
original_title: Behavior of planaria in instrumental learning paradigms
replication_authors: F. T. Crawford; L. C. Skeen
replication_title: Operant Responding in the Planarian: A Replication Study
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: The same experiment replicates both Lee (1963) and Best (1965). The authors explicitly note 'The behavior of the worms was, on the whole, very similar to that described by Best (1965)', confirming the qualitative behavioral patterns (circling, response rate differences). The statistical result (t=1.53, df=1/15, p<.05 one-tailed) supports the original finding. Confidence kept at medium for the same reasons as the Lee entry: marginal statistics (only significant one-tailed), the authors' own acknowledgment of yoked control design criticisms, and lack of strong explicit replication-success language. Close experiment is correct: same general paradigm but with deliberate modifications (shorter 4-hr test period, automated apparatus, different photobeam intensity).

description: Exposure to a stressful film causes significantly more intrusive thinking, visual images, and film references compared to a neutral film in college students
original_authors: Mardi J. Horowitz
original_title: Psychic trauma: return of images after a stress film
replication_authors: Mardi J. Horowitz; Stephanie S. Becker; Maurice L. Moskowitz
replication_title: Intrusive and Repetitive Thought after Stress: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication study using 'similar stimuli and measures with a different sample.' The core findings replicated: the stress group had significantly more intrusions (t=5.20, p<.01), higher entry ratings (t=2.26, p<.05), and more film references (t=3.97, p<.01). The authors conclude 'the replication suggests the generalizability of these two concepts across different populations,' supporting the main hypothesis.

description: Teachers' expectancies about certain randomly selected students (labeled as showing exceptional potential for intellectual gain) cause those students to show significant IQ gains over one school year, especially in first and second grade
original_authors: Robert Rosenthal; Lenore Jacobson
original_title: Teacher expectancies: determinants of pupils' IQ gains
replication_authors: William R. Fielder; Ronald D. Cohen; Stephanie Feeney
replication_title: An Attempt to Replicate the Teacher Expectancy Effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our study did not replicate these findings' after finding no significant expectancy advantage (p < .05) across grade level, sex, or minority group membership analyses. The replication used the same paradigm and test (TOGA) but was conducted over one semester rather than one full school year.

description: The presence of a rifle in an aggressive context and visibility of a victim significantly increase horn-honking in drivers obstructed at a traffic signal (the 'Weapons Effect' in a naturalistic field setting)
original_authors: Charles W. Turner; John F. Layton; Lynn S. Simons
original_title: Naturalistic studies of aggressive behavior: aggressive stimuli, victim visibility, and horn-honking
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Brent L. Halderman; Thomas T. Jackson
replication_title: Naturalistic Study of Aggression: Aggressive Stimuli and Horn-Honking: A Replication
explanation: The replication found no significant differences between weapon-present and control conditions, with horn-honking occurring in only 11% of subjects overall. The authors conclude that 'the weapons effect...has not been supported' in their study, attributing the failure partly to the common sight of rifles in pick-ups in a rural community.

description: College women with anorexic psychological profiles who have relatively thin bodies overestimate their body size (enhanced body image) compared to controls and to anorexic-profile women with fatter bodies
original_authors: Alfred B. Heilbrun; Lisa Friedberg
original_title: Distorted body image in normal women: implications for the development of anorexia nervosa
replication_authors: Alfred B. Heilbrun; Nancy Witt
replication_title: Distorted Body Image as a Risk Factor in Anorexia Nervosa: Replication and Clarification
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The singularly distorted body image of AP women with thinner bodies replicated prior results,' and the Discussion confirms: 'Prior findings indicating that thinner college women sharing anorexic characteristics (Anorexic Profile women) enhanced their body imagery relative to various comparison groups was replicated in the present study.'

description: College students rate their relationship with their mother significantly higher than with their father, with sons rating their maternal relationship significantly better than their paternal relationship while daughters rate both parents about equally
original_authors: William F. Vitulli; Brooke E. Holland
original_title: College students' attitudes toward relationships with their parents as a function of gender
replication_authors: William F. Vitulli; Wendy M. Jones
replication_title: Attitudes toward Parents: A Direct Replication
explanation: The overall finding (mothers rated higher than fathers) replicated (Z = -2.95, p = .003), but the sex-of-student interaction partially reversed: in the original, sons had higher maternal ratings and daughters rated parents equally, while in the replication daughters contributed significantly to increased maternal ratings and sons rated both parents equally. The authors describe the results as having 'partially flip-flopped,' indicating inconclusive replication.

description: Adults most often report their favorite childhood play experience occurred outdoors and involved dramatic play with friends or siblings, rarely including parents or other adults
original_authors: Michael L. Henniger
original_title: Adult perceptions of favorite childhood play experiences
replication_authors: Arielle Strudler; Charles Schaefer
replication_title: Adults' Perceptions of Favorite Childhood Play Experiences: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the findings of the Henniger (1994) study were replicated,' with results from 95 college women confirming the original finding that adults most frequently recalled outdoor dramatic play with friends or siblings as their favorite childhood play experience.

description: Male and female college students agree about what traits typify men and women in general, agree about which traits are socially desirable, attribute more socially desirable traits to men than women, and rate themselves as less different from the opposite sex than the typical man and woman are different
original_authors: Rosenkrantz, Paul; Vogel, Susan; Bee, Helen; Broverman, Inge; Broverman, Donald
original_title: Sex-role stereotypes and self-concepts in college students
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Muriel N. Nesbitt; Nolan E. Penn
replication_title: Gender Stereotypes after Thirty Years: A Replication of Rosenkrantz, et al. (1968)
explanation: The authors call this a 'partial replication' of Rosenkrantz et al. (1968). Some findings replicated (high inter-rater agreement on gender stereotypes, .89-.95 vs original .95-.96; same self-rating pattern); however, significantly fewer stereotypic items were identified (19 vs. 41 in original), and the social desirability finding reversed — current participants valued female-associated traits more than male-associated traits, opposite to the original finding.

description: Homosexuals are underrepresented in older age groups compared to nonhomosexuals, and homosexual partnering is associated with a slightly younger age of death compared to unpartnered homosexual men
original_authors: Paul Cameron; William L. Playfair; Stephen Wellum
original_title: The longevity of homosexuals: before and after the AIDS epidemic
replication_authors: Paul Cameron
replication_title: Homosexual Partnerships and Homosexual Longevity: A Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly frame their work as a replication of Cameron et al. (1994) using new datasets (1996 NHSDA, 2000 Kaiser Foundation survey, and 1999-2001 Washington Blade obituaries). The Discussion states 'as the replications in various datasets are consistent, it is increasingly certain that there is a paucity of older homosexuals in the older segments of the population' and 'as the replications appear, it is increasingly likely that homosexual partnership does not contribute to the prolongation of life for homosexuals.'

description: Homosexuals show a 20-to-30 year younger median age of death compared to nonhomosexuals, with fewer homosexuals appearing in older age groups in random sex surveys, and having a homosexual partner listed in the obituary is associated with a slightly younger age of death among male homosexuals
original_authors: Cameron, P.; Cameron, K.; Playfair, W. L.
original_title: Does homosexual activity shorten life?
replication_authors: Paul Cameron
replication_title: Homosexual Partnerships and Homosexual Longevity: A Replication
explanation: The paper explicitly states it examined new datasets 'to see if these data sets replicated previous findings' from Cameron et al. (1998), and the Discussion confirms consistent replication: 'as the replications in various datasets are consistent, it is increasingly certain that there is a paucity of older homosexuals' and 'unpartnered males who had sex with males tended, if anything, to outlive partnered males who had sex with males in the 1999-2001 series of obituaries.'

description: Leaders' anticipation of targets' zones of resistance predicts the influence tactics leaders use to persuade targets
original_authors: Barbuto, J.; Scholl, R. W.; Hickox, C. F.; Boulmetis, J.
original_title: A field study of the relation between leaders' anticipation of targets' resistance and targets' reports of influence tactics used by leaders in dyadic relationships
replication_authors: John E. Barbuto; Brent J. Coertzen; Susan M. Fritz
replication_title: Correlations for Leaders' Anticipation of Targets' Resistance and Targets' Ratings of Leaders' Influence Tactics: A Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are replicating the 2001 work and conclude: 'The weak results combined with the large sample contradict those previously reported (Barbuto, Scholl, Hickox, & Boulmetis 2001).' Only trivially small correlations (r=.09, r=-.09) were found, with r² < 1%, far short of Cohen's criteria for small effect size.

description: Memories of rejecting or nonsupportive parents are significantly correlated with self-defeating personality scores in nonclinical volunteers, with overinvolved parent memories correlating with self-defeating personality only among men
original_authors: Pezzarossa, B.; Della Rosa, A.; Rubino, I. A.
original_title: Self-defeating personality and memories of parents' child-rearing behaviour
replication_authors: Rubino IA; Pezzarossa B.; Della Rosa A.; Siracusano A.
replication_title: Self-Defeating Personality and Memories of Parents' Child-Rearing Behaviour: A Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The present study was a replication of the latter investigation, using a larger sample' and report that 'The findings were consistent with those of the previous study,' with all major correlational patterns replicated including the sex difference for overinvolved parent memories.

description: Students' use of specific language-learning strategies can be jointly predicted by knowledge about the strategy, perceived effectiveness (reason to use it), and perceived difficulty or anxiety about using it (reasons not to use it), as specified in MacIntyre's Social Psychological Model of Strategy Use
original_authors: Peter D. MacIntyre; Kimberly A. Noels
original_title: Using social-psychological variables to predict the use of language learning strategies
replication_authors: Tsung-Yuan Hsiao
replication_title: Testing a Social Psychological Model of Strategy Use with Students of English as a Foreign Language
explanation: The replication only partially supported the model: only 14 of 50 strategies (vs. 36/50 in the original) were jointly predicted by Knowledge, Effectiveness, and either Difficulty or Anxiety. The authors conclude: 'the social psychological model is incompletely supported by the present data' and 'the model requires further modification.' The study used the same paradigm but with a different population (Taiwanese EFL students vs. Canadian learners of Spanish/Italian).

description: Several artificial agents (freq, Q0, Qλ, HLQλ, MC-AIXI) achieve similar relative ordering and performance levels on the default AIQ test (BF 5 reference machine with 5 symbol action and observation space)
original_authors: Shane Legg; Joel Veness
original_title: An approximation of the universal intelligence measure
replication_authors: Ondřej Vadinský
replication_title: Towards General Evaluation of Intelligent Systems: Lessons Learned from Reproducing AIQ Test Results
explanation: The authors report that 'the AIQ estimates of freq, Q0, Qλ, and HLQλ correspond well with the results of Legg and Veness (2013)' and conclude that 'overall, the replication experiment results correspond well with the findings of Legg and Veness.' MC-AIXI results are more uncertain due to unknown configuration parameters, but the primary agents are replicated successfully.

description: Varying the action space size (2, 10, and 20 symbol tapes) in the AIQ test produces results qualitatively the same as the default 5-symbol setting
original_authors: Shane Legg; Joel Veness
original_title: An approximation of the universal intelligence measure
replication_authors: Ondřej Vadinský
replication_title: Towards General Evaluation of Intelligent Systems: Lessons Learned from Reproducing AIQ Test Results
explanation: Legg and Veness (2013) reported that varying action space gave 'qualitatively the same' results, but this replication found statistically significant differences: 'changing the action space indeed has an impact on the agents' results in the AIQ test' (F(3,72)=20.98, p=1.9×10⁻⁵), contradicting the original claim.

description: Varying the observation space size in the AIQ test produces results qualitatively the same as the default setting
original_authors: Shane Legg; Joel Veness
original_title: An approximation of the universal intelligence measure
replication_authors: Ondřej Vadinský
replication_title: Towards General Evaluation of Intelligent Systems: Lessons Learned from Reproducing AIQ Test Results
explanation: Legg and Veness (2013) reported results were 'qualitatively the same' when varying observation space. The replication found no statistically significant effect on AIQ score (F(2,48)=1.66, p=0.21), supporting the original claim. The authors conclude 'changing the observation space has no impact on the results of agents in the AIQ test.'

description: The Enhanced Model of Collaboration (EMC) framework, developed for grassroots collaborations, explains how collaboration and social capital operate in watershed restoration nonprofits, with context, process, output, outcomes, and social capital as key constructs
original_authors: John C. Morris; W. A. Gibson; William M. Leavitt; Shana Jones
original_title: The case for grassroots collaboration: Social capital and ecosystem restoration at the local level
replication_authors: Martin, Adale M.
replication_title: Enhanced Model of Collaboration and Social Capital: Hampton Roads All Hazards Advisory Committee: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'This dissertation validates that the EMC framework does not adequately explain collaboration in an agency-based setting' and that the model had 'limited generalizability for analyzing agency-based organizations.' The EMC's sub-variables did not adequately explain the political setting of agency-based collaboration, leading the authors to propose an entirely new model (EMAC).

description: Female yellow warblers approach brood parasitic cowbird models more closely than nest predator models or controls during nest defense, showing proximity-based discrimination between threat types
original_authors: Sharon A. Gill; Spencer G. Sealy
original_title: Nest defence by yellow warblers: Recognition of a brood parasite and an avian nest predator
replication_authors: Shelby L. Lawson; Janice K. Enos; Niko C. Mendes; Sharon A. Gill; Mark E. Hauber
replication_title: Responses of Female Yellow Warblers to Playbacks Signaling Brood Parasitism or Predation Risk: A Quasi-Replication Study
explanation: Independent review confirms 'inconclusive' and 'medium' confidence. The paper self-identifies as a 'quasi-replication study' that pivoted from visual model presentations to acoustic-only playbacks. Core seet-call findings clearly replicated: females seet-called specifically to cowbird chatter and conspecific seet calls, and returned to the nest after hearing/producing seets, consistent with Gill & Sealy (1996) and 15+ prior studies. However, closest approach — the specific finding in the description — did NOT replicate (F(4,83)=2.15, p=.08; no significant treatment effect), which the authors explicitly contrast with Gill & Sealy (1996). Chip call patterns were qualitatively consistent but not statistically significant. The authors attribute the closest-approach divergence to the methodological change (no visual target to approach), making it genuinely ambiguous whether this represents a failed replication or a methodological artifact. 'Inconclusive' is the appropriate classification for these mixed results. Discipline corrected from biology/physiology to environmental science/ecology, as this is a behavioral ecology study.

description: Undergraduate university students working paid employment during semester time spend on average 32.5 hours per week in paid work and 15.6 hours in class, with students managing study and paid work commitments during semester
original_authors: Robert J. Manthei; Alison Gilmore
original_title: The effect of paid employment on university students' lives
replication_authors: Edgar Burns; Noel Yahanpath
replication_title: Replication Study: Undergraduate Students Balancing Paid Semester Work and Study
replication_journal: Labour, Employment and Work in New Zealand
explanation: The authors explicitly replicate Manthei and Gilmore (2005) using the same questionnaire at a different New Zealand institution (polytechnic vs. university). The replication finds substantially different results — paid work hours increased from 32.5 to 42.1 hours per week (30% increase) — but the authors attribute this to differences in institution type, region, time period, and population rather than treating it as a straightforward failure or success.

description: MDD patients show hyperactivated oxygenated hemoglobin in the left frontal cortex in response to threat/negative emotional words during an emotional Stroop task, with no significant difference from healthy controls during the happy task
original_authors: Toshio Matsubara; Koji Matsuo; Mami Nakashima; Masayuki Nakano; Kenichiro Harada; Toshio Watanuki; Kazuteru Egashira; Yoshifumi Watanabe
original_title: Prefrontal activation in response to emotional words in patients with bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder
replication_authors: Yoshitaka Nishizawa; Tetsufumi Kanazawa; Yasuo Kawabata; Toshio Matsubara; Soichiro Maruyama; Makoto Kawano; Shinya Kinoshita; Jun Koh; Koji Matsuo; Hiroshi Yoneda
replication_title: fNIRS Assessment during an Emotional Stroop Task among Patients with Depression: Replication and Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state they aimed to 'validate Matsubara et al.'s finding in another sample set,' and in the Results section confirm: 'This finding is consistent with a previous report.' The Discussion further states: 'During the Threat task, a hyperactivated [oxy-Hb] pattern in a left frontal region...and non-significant difference during the Happy task was replicated.' The extension aspect was testing patients not in remission (vs. the original's remission patients) and adding a correlation with depression severity.

description: Interpretation of ambiguously worded passages is strongly related to participants' background knowledge (physical education vs. music education majors), such that students interpret passages in ways consistent with their academic/experiential schema
original_authors: Richard C. Anderson; Ralph E. Reynolds; Diane L. Schallert; Ernest T. Goetz
original_title: Frameworks for comprehending discourse
replication_authors: Douglas Sjogren; William Timpson
replication_title: Frameworks for Comprehending Discourse: A Replication                Study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude 'Our results were generally consistent with those of Anderson, et al.' and specifically note 'The passage by class interaction result was entirely consistent with Anderson, et al. results.' The key schema-based interpretation effect was replicated, though with smaller magnitude differences attributable to the more heterogeneous arts group used.

description: AmeriCorps volunteer one-on-one literacy tutoring (Reading Corps RTI model) produces significantly higher literacy assessment scores for at-risk kindergarten and first-grade students after a single semester of intervention compared to a business-as-usual control group
original_authors: Carrie E. Markovitz; Marc W. Hernandez; E. Hedberg; B. Silberglitt
original_title: Impact evaluation of the Minnesota Reading Corps K-3 program
original_journal: Impact Evaluation of the Minnesota Reading Corps K-3 Program
replication_authors: Markovitz, Carrie E.; Hernandez, Marc W.; Hedberg, Eric; Whitmore, Heidi W.
replication_title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Volunteer One-on-One Tutoring Model for Early Elementary Reading Intervention: A Randomized Controlled Trial Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This evaluation of the Minnesota and Wisconsin programs confirms the successful replication of the program model in a different time and location.' The replication found significant positive effects for K-1 students in both Minnesota and Wisconsin, with effect sizes in the same direction as the original study, and additionally found significant effects for 2nd-3rd grade students over a full school year.

description: Social consequences of alcoholism (but not physical or treatment consequences) are strongly related to psychiatric symptomatology in the nonalcoholic spouse, but not in the alcoholic themselves

original_title: The impact of alcoholism on the family
replication_authors: Theodore Jacob; Nancy Jo Dunn; Kenneth Leonard; Peter Davis
replication_title: Alcohol-Related Impairments in Male Alcoholics and the Psychiatric Symptoms of Their Spouses: An Attempt to Replicate
replication_journal: The American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse
explanation: Sample 1 (Davis, N=50) found only 2 of 9 SCL-90 correlations between social consequences and wife symptoms were statistically significant, with a median correlation of r=.23 compared to Steinglass' r=.49-.85. Authors explicitly stated 'this replication was not a strong one.'

description: Social consequences of alcoholism (but not physical or treatment consequences) are strongly related to psychiatric symptomatology in the nonalcoholic spouse, but not in the alcoholic themselves

original_title: The impact of alcoholism on the family
