The two lead CETP variants (rs17231520 and rs34065661) were significantly associated with HDL-C in the Ghanaian cohort (p=4.44e-09 and p=5.03e-09 respectively), replicating the overall CETP-HDL-C association in a different African population.

description: PCSK9 intronic variant rs11806638 is associated with lower LDL-cholesterol levels in African Americans
original_authors: Musunuru, K.; Romaine, S.; Lettre, G.; Wilson, J.; Volcik, K.; Tsai, M.
original_title: Multi-ethnic analysis of lipid-associated loci: the NHLBI CARe project
replication_authors: Godfred Agongo; Lucas Amenga-Etego; Engelbert A. Nonterah; Cornelius Debpuur; Ananyo Choudhury; Amy R. Bentley; Abraham R. Oduro; Charles N. Rotimi; Nigel J. Crowther; Michèle Ramsay; H3Africa
replication_title: Candidate Gene Analysis Reveals Strong Association of CETP Variants With High Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol and PCSK9 Variants With Low Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol in Ghanaian Adults: An AWI-Gen Sub-Study
explanation: The authors state 'In addition to this variant being previously associated with lower LDL-C levels in African Americans (Musunuru et al., 2012) we replicated its association in other sub-Saharan Africans from the AADM study.' The PCSK9 variant rs11806638 was significantly associated with lower LDL-C in the Ghanaian cohort (b=-0.055, p=0.027 after covariate adjustment), confirming the original finding in a new African population.

description: Young adults are more goal-directed (model-based) than older adults in the two-stage Markov decision task, indicating that aging shifts the balance from goal-directed toward habitual decision-making
original_authors: Ben Eppinger; Maik Walter; Hauke R. Heekeren; Shu-Chen Li
original_title: Of goals and habits: age-related and individual differences in goal-directed decision-making
replication_authors: Kaori L. Ito; Laura Cao; Renee Reinberg; Brenton Keller; John Monterosso; Nicolas Schweighofer; Sook-Lei Liew
replication_title: Validating Habitual and Goal-Directed Decision-Making Performance Online in Healthy Older Adults
explanation: The authors explicitly state they aimed to replicate the age-related effect and confirm success: 'we replicated the primary effect of interest: we found more goal-directed decision making in young adults than older adults across both the in-person group... and the online groups.' A significant main effect of age on the weight parameter was found [F(3,79) = 31.81, p < 0.001].

description: Brain age is greater in AD and MCI compared to healthy controls, and both AD and MCI groups show accelerated rates of brain aging over time
original_authors: Katja Franke; Christian Gaser
original_title: Longitudinal changes in individual BrainAGE in healthy aging, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease
replication_authors: Ly, Maria; Yu, Gary; Son, Sang Joon; Pascoal, Tharick; Karim, Helmet T.; The Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
replication_title: Longitudinal accelerated brain age in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current analysis replicates the results of Franke and Gaser (2012) in model 3.' The cross-sectional finding was replicated (MCI and AD had greater brain age than HC), but the longitudinal result only partially aligned: the MCI group showed faster brain aging over time, but the AD group did not — contrary to Franke and Gaser (2012) who found both groups showed accelerated aging. The Discussion notes: 'Our findings partially align with those reported by Franke and Gaser (2012).'

description: Dispositional use of reappraisal and suppression (measured via ERQ) is distinctly associated with resting-state functional connectivity between the amygdala and prefrontal cortex/insula regions
original_authors: Maria Picó-Pérez; Pino Alonso; Oren Contreras-Rodríguez; Ignacio Martínez-Zalacaín; Clara López-Solà; Susana Jiménez-Murcia; Antonio Verdejo-García; José M. Menchón; Carles Soriano-Mas
original_title: Dispositional use of emotion regulation strategies and resting-state cortico-limbic functional connectivity
replication_authors: Denise Dörfel; Anne Gärtner; Christoph Scheffel
replication_title: Resting State Cortico-Limbic Functional Connectivity and Dispositional Use of Emotion Regulation Strategies: A Replication and Extension Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'None of the hypotheses could be confirmed, that is, we could not statistically confirm associations of dispositional reappraisal and suppression use with rsFC between left and right basolateral and centromedial amygdala, respectively, and regions in the PFC (ACC and SMA) and the insula. Thus, we failed to replicate the results of Picó-Pérez et al. (2018).'

description: Task-related experiential reappraisal success (measured by affect ratings during reappraisal task) is negatively correlated with resting-state functional connectivity between the right amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex
original_authors: Mai Uchida; Joseph Biederman; John D. E. Gabrieli; Jamie Micco; Carlo de Los Angeles; Ariel Brown; Tara Kenworthy; Elana Kagan; Susan Whitfield-Gabrieli
original_title: Emotion regulation ability varies in relation to intrinsic functional brain architecture
replication_authors: Denise Dörfel; Anne Gärtner; Christoph Scheffel
replication_title: Resting State Cortico-Limbic Functional Connectivity and Dispositional Use of Emotion Regulation Strategies: A Replication and Extension Study
explanation: The authors explicitly characterize this as a conceptual replication at best and report: 'Again, none of our hypotheses could be confirmed,' finding no significant correlations of experiential reappraisal success with amygdala-PFC resting-state functional connectivity (p > 0.05, FWE-corrected). The Discussion notes 'the findings of the original study could not conceptually be replicated.'

description: Greater activation in bilateral dorsal caudate, nucleus accumbens, ventral putamen, ventral tegmental area, and prefrontal cortices when contrasting palatable vs. unpalatable foods, with greater striatal activation for obese vs. overweight individuals
original_authors: Juan Verdejo-Román; Raquel Vilar-López; Juan F. Navas; Carles Soriano-Mas; Antonio Verdejo-García
original_title: Brain reward system's alterations in response to food and monetary stimuli in overweight and obese individuals
replication_authors: Junaid S. Merchant; Danielle Cosme; Nicole R. Giuliani; Bryce Dirks; Elliot T. Berkman
replication_title: Neural Substrates of Food Valuation and Its Relationship With BMI and Healthy Eating in Higher BMI Individuals
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We were unable to replicate the findings of Verdejo-Román et al. (2017), which showed greater activation in subcortical reward circuitry, and medial and lateral portions of the prefrontal cortex when contrasting palatable vs. unpalatable foods.' The replication contrast (unhealthy > healthy) did not show similar activation patterns, and the between-group (obese > overweight) comparison also failed to replicate.

description: BALB/cByJ mice show decreased anxiety-like behavior compared to BALB/cJ mice in the light-dark conflict test
original_authors: Lady Velez; Greta Sokoloff; Klaus A. Miczek; Abraham A. Palmer; Stephanie C. Dulawa
original_title: Differences in aggressive behavior and DNA copy number variants between BALB/cJ and BALB/cByJ substrains
replication_authors: Katherine D. Sena; Jacob A. Beierle; Kayla T. Richardson; Kathleen M. Kantak; Camron D. Bryant
replication_title: Assessment of Binge-Like Eating of Unsweetened vs. Sweetened Chow Pellets in BALB/c Substrains
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the previously reported decrease in anxiety-like behavior in ByJ vs. J mice in the light-dark test (Velez et al., 2010; Sittig et al., 2014).' ByJ mice spent significantly more time in the light side (F(1,53) = 13.44, p = 0.00057, Cohen's f = 0.50), consistent with reduced anxiety-like behavior. Classified as 'close experiment' because the original Velez et al. (2010) measured anxiety in the open field test, while the current study used a light-dark conflict test with palatable food present — a different but related anxiety paradigm testing the same construct (substrain difference in anxiety-like behavior). Reviewer upgrade from medium: the explicit author replication claim, strong statistical evidence, and large effect size resolve the ambiguity. The paradigm difference justifies the 'close experiment' type but does not create uncertainty about the result itself.

description: BALB/cByJ mice show decreased anxiety-like behavior compared to BALB/cJ mice in the light-dark conflict test
original_authors: Laura J. Sittig; Choongwon Jeong; Emily Tixier; Joe Davis; Camila M. Barrios-Camacho; Abraham A. Palmer
original_title: Phenotypic instability between the near isogenic substrains BALB/cJ and BALB/cByJ
replication_authors: Katherine D. Sena; Jacob A. Beierle; Kayla T. Richardson; Kathleen M. Kantak; Camron D. Bryant
replication_title: Assessment of Binge-Like Eating of Unsweetened vs. Sweetened Chow Pellets in BALB/c Substrains
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the previously reported decrease in anxiety-like behavior in ByJ vs. J mice in the light-dark test (Velez et al., 2010; Sittig et al., 2014).' ByJ mice spent significantly more time in the light side (F(1,53) = 13.44, p = 0.00057, Cohen's f = 0.50). Classified as 'close experiment' because the original Sittig et al. (2014) measured anxiety in the open field test, while the current study used a light-dark conflict test with palatable food present — a different but related anxiety paradigm testing the same construct. Reviewer upgrade from medium: the explicit author replication claim, strong statistical evidence, and large effect size resolve the ambiguity. The paradigm difference justifies the 'close experiment' type but does not create uncertainty about the result itself.

description: Flickering auditory and visual stimuli presented synchronously at theta frequency (4 Hz) leads to enhanced recall of audio-visual associative memories compared to asynchronous or non-modulated presentation
original_authors: Andrew Clouter; Kimron L. Shapiro; Simon Hanslmayr
original_title: Theta phase synchronization is the glue that binds human associative memory
replication_authors: Louise Simeonov; Ravi Das
replication_title: The rhythm of memory. Does theta frequency audio/visual flicker improve recall?
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current study failed to replicate previous findings demonstrating improved recall for stimuli synchronously modulated at theta frequency in a multi-sensory associative learning task.' In fact, the results showed the opposite pattern: recall was significantly better in the no-modulation condition than in the theta (4 Hz) modulation condition (Cohen's d = 0.67).

description: Repeated THC exposure decreases hippocampal expression of glutathione S-transferase Mu 2 (GSTM2) and increases heat shock proteins, indicating greater oxidative stress and neurodegeneration
original_authors: Heidi R. Quinn; Izuru Matsumoto; Paul D. Callaghan; Leonora E. Long; Jonathon C. Arnold; Nathan Gunasekaran; Murray R. Thompson; Bronwyn Dawson; Paul E. Mallet; Mohammed A. Kashem; Haruka Matsuda-Matsumoto; Takeshi Iwazaki; Iain S. McGregor
original_title: Adolescent rats find repeated delta(9)-THC less aversive than adult rats but display greater residual cognitive deficits and changes in hippocampal protein expression following exposure
replication_authors: Jarrah R. Spencer; Keturah M. E. Darbyshire; Aurelie A. Boucher; Mohammed A. Kashem; Leonora E. Long; Iain S. McGregor; Tim Karl; Jonathon C. Arnold
replication_title: Novel molecular changes induced by Nrg1 hypomorphism and Nrg1-cannabinoid interaction in adolescence: a hippocampal proteomic study in mice
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our results replicate the finding that repeated THC exposure decreased the expression of GSTM2 in the hippocampus (Quinn et al., 2008).' They also replicated the effect on heat shock proteins. The study used mice instead of rats (the original used adolescent rats) and added a genetic manipulation context, making this a close extension.

description: Lipid-processing microglia (LPM) defined by marker genes MYO1E and PTPRG are expanded in individuals with Alzheimer's disease in prefrontal cortex
original_authors: Na Sun; Matheus B. Victor; Yongjin P. Park; Xushen Xiong; Aine Ni Scannail; Noelle Leary; Shaniah Prosper; Soujanya Viswanathan; Xochitl Luna; Carles A. Boix; Benjamin T. James; Yosuke Tanigawa; Kyriaki Galani; Hansruedi Mathys; Xueqiao Jiang; Ayesha P. Ng; David A. Bennett; Li-Huei Tsai; Manolis Kellis
original_title: Human microglial state dynamics in Alzheimer's disease progression
replication_authors: Jake D. Oxendine; Daniel W. Sirkis; Caroline Jonson; Jennifer S. Yokoyama
replication_title: Single-nucleus RNA-seq reveals no increase in T cells in Alzheimer’s disease prefrontal cortex or hippocampus
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully identified this cluster in our version of the dataset and confirmed its expansion in AD using a Wilcoxon Test (p = 5.17e-07) and through covariate-adjusted linear regression (p = 0.0033). This replication of a previously identified differentially abundant cell type confirmed the validity of our method.'

description: CD8+ T cells are expanded in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG) of individuals with Alzheimer's disease, as measured by single-nucleus RNA sequencing using the SEA-AD dataset
original_authors: Mai Yamakawa; Jessica Rexach
original_title: Cell states and interactions of CD8 T cells and disease-enriched microglia in human brains with Alzheimer's disease
replication_authors: Jake D. Oxendine; Daniel W. Sirkis; Caroline Jonson; Jennifer S. Yokoyama
replication_title: Single-nucleus RNA-seq reveals no increase in T cells in Alzheimer’s disease prefrontal cortex or hippocampus
explanation: The authors replicated the CD8+ T cell expansion in MTG using the same SEA-AD dataset and the same clustering method described in Yamakawa & Rexach, finding significant differences by Wilcoxon test (p = 0.010) and covariate-adjusted model (p = 0.021), though they additionally found donor age as a significant covariate not previously reported.

description: CD8+ T cells are expanded in the brains of individuals with Alzheimer's disease, as originally reported in middle temporal gyrus (MTG) using the SEA-AD dataset; tested here in prefrontal cortex (PFC) and dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC)
original_authors: Mai Yamakawa; Jessica Rexach
original_title: Cell states and interactions of CD8 T cells and disease-enriched microglia in human brains with Alzheimer's disease
replication_authors: Jake D. Oxendine; Daniel W. Sirkis; Caroline Jonson; Jennifer S. Yokoyama
replication_title: Single-nucleus RNA-seq reveals no increase in T cells in Alzheimer’s disease prefrontal cortex or hippocampus
explanation: Reviewer verified: result 'failure' and type 'close experiment' are correct. The authors clearly found no CD8+ T cell expansion in PFC (ROSMAP: Wilcoxon p=0.47, regression p=0.86) or DLPFC (SEA-AD: Wilcoxon p=0.20, regression p=0.32). Classified as 'close experiment' because Yamakawa & Rexach (2024) originally reported expansion in MTG (a different brain region), not PFC — so this tests the same biological hypothesis in a different anatomical context. Confidence remains 'medium' because the original study did not specifically claim PFC expansion; this paper frames the PFC test as addressing the broader field claim that T cells are increased in AD brains (citing both Chen et al. 2023 and Yamakawa & Rexach 2024). The authors themselves note the results 'seemingly stand in contrast to the current understanding of the field' but suggest regional specificity may explain the discrepancy.

description: Multiple excitatory inputs to CA1 pyramidal neuron radial oblique dendrites must be activated within a very narrow time window (~6 ms) to generate local dendritic spikes and supralinear responses; even slight temporal desynchronization of inputs prevents local spike initiation and results in linear integration
original_authors: Attila Losonczy; Jeffrey C. Magee
original_title: Integrative properties of radial oblique dendrites in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons
replication_authors: Gómez González JF; Mel BW; Poirazi P.
replication_title: Distinguishing linear vs. non-linear integration in CA1 radial oblique dendrites: it’s about time
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We first replicate the main findings of Losonczy and Magee (2006), including the very brief window for non-linear integration using single-pulse stimuli.' Model responses closely matched the experimental data quantitatively: average somatic depolarization at spike threshold was 146 ± 6% in the model vs. 142 ± 9% in the experimental data.

description: Emotional stimuli (negative pictures) decrease the efficiency of inhibitory control, resulting in longer stop-signal reaction times (SSRT) compared to neutral pictures
original_authors: Frederick Verbruggen; Jan De Houwer
original_title: Do emotional stimuli interfere with response inhibition? Evidence from the stop signal paradigm
replication_authors: Eyal Kalanthroff; Noga Cohen; Avishai Henik
replication_title: Stop feeling: inhibition of emotional interference following stop-signal trials
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This result replicates Verbruggen and De Houwer's (2007) findings and strengthens the claim that emotional information disrupts inhibition-related executive functions.' The replication found significantly longer SSRT for negative versus neutral trials, F(1,21) = 4.301, p = 0.05, matching the original direction and conclusion.

description: The Simon effect (slower responses when stimulus location is incongruent with response location) is significantly larger at cued (inhibited) locations in a spatial IOR paradigm than at uncued locations
original_authors: Jason Ivanoff; Raymond M. Klein; Juan Lupiáñez
original_title: Inhibition of return interacts with the Simon effect: an omnibus analysis and its implications
replication_authors: Pengfei Wang; Luis J. Fuentes; Ana B. Vivas; Qi Chen
replication_title: Behavioral and neural interaction between spatial inhibition of return and the Simon effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated that pattern of interaction at the behavioral level by showing increased size of Simon effects at the cued locations.' The interaction between cue validity and Simon congruency was significant (F(1,15) = 10.15, p = 0.006, η² = 0.40), showing a larger Simon effect at the cued (40 ms) than uncued (17 ms) location, consistent with prior behavioral studies.

description: Functional diffusion tensor imaging (fDTI) can detect task-related fractional anisotropy changes in white matter tracts (contralateral thalamo-cortical tract during tactile stimulation and optic radiations during visual stimulation) in healthy participants
original_authors: René C. W. Mandl; Hugo G. Schnack; Marcel P. Zwiers; Arjen van der Schaaf; René S. Kahn; Hilleke E. Hulshoff Pol
original_title: Functional diffusion tensor imaging: measuring task-related fractional anisotropy changes in the human brain along white matter tracts
replication_authors: Mandl RC; Schnack HG; Zwiers MP; Kahn RS; Hulshoff Pol HE
replication_title: Functional diffusion tensor imaging at 3 Tesla
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'With this study we successfully replicated our previous findings using the same types of stimuli but on a different group of healthy participants and at different field-strength.' The same white matter activation patterns were found in both the thalamo-cortical tract (tactile) and optic radiations (visual), consistent with the original study.

description: Retroactive priming (retro-priming) produces a significant effect on response times, such that participants are influenced by a prime (word/picture) they see after, rather than before, making a judgment about a stimulus
original_authors: Thomas Rabeyron; Caroline Watt
original_title: Paranormal experiences, mental health and mental boundaries, and psi
replication_authors: Thomas Rabeyron
replication_title: Retro-priming, priming, and double testing: psi and replication in a testâ€“retest design
explanation: The authors report negative and non-significant results on the retro-priming task for all groups (whole group: es = -0.25, ns; student group: es = -0.30, ns; male group: es = -0.18, ns; female group: es = -0.29, ns). In the Discussion they state: 'the results of this second study were non-significant. We also obtained overall negative effects on retro-priming results for all the groups (male, female, student, whole) and did not manage to replicate the strong effect size obtained (r = 0.41) with male participants in the first study.'

description: Using an adjective-noun word pair paradigm, concrete adjectives (vs. abstract adjectives) modifying the same noun produce a concreteness effect on the noun's N400 ERP component, reflecting differential neural processing of concretely vs. abstractly modified expressions
original_authors: Hsu-Wen Huang; Chia-Lin Lee; Kara D. Federmeier
original_title: Imagine that! ERPs provide evidence for distinct hemispheric contributions to the processing of concrete and abstract concepts
replication_authors: BÃ¡lint ForgÃ¡cs; Megan D. Bardolph; Ben D. Amsel; Katherine A. DeLong; Marta Kutas
replication_title: Metaphors are physical and abstract: ERPs to metaphorically modified nouns resemble ERPs to abstract language
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the well-known N400 lexical concreteness effect on the initial adjectives' (Discussion), confirmed by ANOVA (F(2,68)=10.65, p<.001) showing concrete adjectives (CL and MET) elicited greater N400 amplitude than abstract adjectives (AL). This adjective-level replication is unambiguous. However, confidence remains medium because: (1) the noun-level concreteness effect — the core of the original Huang et al. finding — was non-significant in the overall ANOVA (F(2,68)=1.24, p=.3), emerging only when comparing extreme subgroups (most concrete CL vs. most abstract AL, p<.05); (2) the authors themselves note 'the direction of effects for noun ERPs cannot be directly compared' due to procedural differences (central vs. half-field presentation, different task); (3) the study's main contribution is the extension to metaphorical expressions, which showed divergent patterns from both literal conditions. Classification as 'close extension' and 'success' is appropriate given the clear adjective replication and the partial noun-level convergence for literal expressions, but the genuine complexity of the noun-level results and acknowledged procedural differences prevent upgrading to high confidence.

description: The 'spreading the sparing' effect in which an attentional blink (AB) is observed when a distractor intervenes between two targets in a rapid serial visual presentation stream (Varied conditions), but not when targets are presented contiguously without intervening distractors (Uniform condition)
original_authors: Di Lollo V.; Kawahara J.; Shahab Ghorashi SM; Enns JT
original_title: The attentional blink: resource depletion or temporary loss of control?
replication_authors: Ling M. Wong; Flora Tassone; Susan M. Rivera; Tony J. Simon
replication_title: Temporal dynamics of attentional selection in adult male carriers of the fragile X premutation allele and adult controls
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In Aim 1, we replicated the spreading the sparing effect, previously observed in undergraduate students, in a sample of adults aged 18-48.' The AB was observed in both Varied conditions (both ps < 0.001) but not in the Uniform condition in controls, matching the original findings. The study tested a broader population (adults 18-48 rather than undergraduates) and added more stringent conditional accuracy analyses.

description: The COMT Met allele (associated with higher prefrontal dopamine) is associated with increased instructional bias in probabilistic reinforcement learning, such that Met carriers adhere more strongly to inaccurate instructions despite disconfirming feedback
original_authors: Bradley B. Doll; Kent E. Hutchison; Michael J. Frank
original_title: Dopaminergic genes predict individual differences in susceptibility to confirmation bias
replication_authors: Nathan Tardiff; Kathryn N. Graves; Sharon L. Thompson-Schill
replication_title: The Role of Frontostriatal Systems in Instructed Reinforcement Learning: Evidence From Genetic and Experimentally-Induced Variation
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The above results refine, but only partially replicate, the effect of COMT genotype on instructed RL. While Doll et al. (2011) found that Met carriers demonstrate greater instructional bias relative to Val homozygotes during training, we found increased bias exclusively for Met homozygotes.' Met homozygotes showed significantly increased bias, but the replication failed when using the same Met-carrier vs. Val/Val comparison used in the original.

description: Negative two-character Traditional Chinese emotion-label words take longer to break continuous flash suppression than neutral words, demonstrating unconscious emotional processing of written language
original_authors: Yung-Hao Yang; Su-Ling Yeh
original_title: Accessing the meaning of invisible words
replication_authors: Kaiwen Cheng; Aolin Ding; Lianfang Jiang; Han Tian; Hongmei Yan
replication_title: Emotion in Chinese Words Could Not Be Extracted in Continuous Flash Suppression
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their General Discussion: 'we failed to replicate the main findings reported in Yang and Yeh (2011) and found that the emotional valence of Chinese words did not modulate access to consciousness.' In Experiment 1, the main effect of emotion was not significant (F(1,19)=2.156, p>0.05), directly contradicting the original finding.

description: Negative two-character Traditional Chinese emotion-laden words take longer to break continuous flash suppression than neutral words, extending the unconscious emotional processing effect to a different word category
original_authors: Yung-Hao Yang; Su-Ling Yeh
original_title: Accessing the meaning of invisible words
replication_authors: Kaiwen Cheng; Aolin Ding; Lianfang Jiang; Han Tian; Hongmei Yan
replication_title: Emotion in Chinese Words Could Not Be Extracted in Continuous Flash Suppression
explanation: In Experiment 2 using single-character Simplified Chinese emotion-laden words, the main effect of emotion was not significant (F(1,28)=0.357, p>0.05) in the dichoptic session, and the authors conclude in the General Discussion that emotional valence did not modulate conscious access regardless of word length.

description: Anodal tDCS over the right inferior parietal lobule (IPL) decreases mind-wandering propensity during a sustained attention to response task (SART)
original_authors: Shogo Kajimura; Takanori Kochiyama; Nobuhito Abe; Michio Nomura
original_title: Challenge to unity: relationship between hemispheric asymmetry of the default mode network and mind wandering
replication_authors: Coulborn S.; Bowman H.; Miall RC; Fernández-Espejo D.
replication_title: Effect of tDCS Over the Right Inferior Parietal Lobule on Mind-Wandering Propensity
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our findings also contradict earlier reports by Kajimura et al. (2019) showing that stimulation of the right IPL via tDCS could modulate mind-wandering propensity during a SART task.' Bayesian analyses provided strong to very strong evidence for the lack of an effect of stimulation on all subjective and objective measures of mind-wandering.

description: Elderly participants can achieve high BCI performance (95.56% accuracy, 20.73 bits/min ITR) using a 4-class tactile P300-based BCI for wheelchair control in a virtual environment across five training sessions, with significant training effects on P300 amplitudes
original_authors: Andreas Herweg; Julian Gutzeit; Sonja Kleih; Andrea Kübler
original_title: Wheelchair control by elderly participants in a virtual environment with a brain-computer interface (BCI) and tactile stimulation
replication_authors: Matthias Eidel; Andrea Kübler
replication_title: Wheelchair Control in a Virtual Environment by Healthy Participants Using a P300-BCI Based on Tactile Stimulation: Training Effects and Usability
explanation: The authors confirm training effects on BCI performance (ITR and accuracy significantly increased across sessions), partially replicating key findings, but state 'our participants have not achieved the same high performance as in the Herweg et al. (2016) study' and failed to replicate significant P300 amplitude increases or age-independence of performance. The result is mixed: training effects on BCI performance were confirmed, but overall performance levels and physiological effects were not replicated.

description: German listeners show a perceptual asymmetry for place of articulation in the vowel pair /o/-/ø/ using the MMN paradigm, with a larger MMN when [ø] is the deviant (standard /o/) than when [o] is the deviant (standard /ø/), supporting underspecification of [CORONAL]
original_authors: Carsten Eulitz; Aditi Lahiri
original_title: Neurobiological evidence for abstract phonological representations in the mental lexicon during speech recognition
replication_authors: Nadine P. W. D. de Rue; Tineke M. Snijders; Paula Fikkert
replication_title: Contrast and Conflict in Dutch Vowels
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'It replicated the place asymmetry in German listeners as reported in Eulitz and Lahiri (2004) for Dutch.' The Dutch study found a significantly larger MMN amplitude and shorter latency for [ø]/o/ versus [o]/ø/, matching the German result.

description: German listeners show no perceptual asymmetry for the labiality (rounding) contrast in the vowel pair /e/-/ø/ in an MMN paradigm, treating place-sharing vowels as non-conflicting
original_authors: Carsten Eulitz; Aditi Lahiri
original_title: Neurobiological evidence for abstract phonological representations in the mental lexicon during speech recognition
replication_authors: Nadine P. W. D. de Rue; Tineke M. Snijders; Paula Fikkert
replication_title: Contrast and Conflict in Dutch Vowels
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Confidence kept at medium because the ambiguity is genuine. Eulitz & Lahiri (2004) found no asymmetry for /e/-/ø/ in German, but the current Dutch study found a significant asymmetry (larger MMN for [ø]/e/ than [e]/ø/; t(16) = -4.053, p < .001). The Dutch result directly contradicts the German null finding, supporting 'failure' as the classification. However, the authors explicitly frame this divergence as a theoretically expected cross-linguistic difference — Dutch /ø/ has stronger contrastive lexical status than German /ø/ (which arises mainly through morphological Umlaut). The abstract states: 'This study partly replicates [...] and partly presents new findings indicating cross-linguistic differences.' Because this is a close extension to a different language population, reasonable reviewers could disagree on whether a theoretically motivated cross-linguistic difference constitutes a replication failure or is simply an expected outcome of extending to a new population. Result classified as 'failure' because the specific empirical finding (no asymmetry) was not reproduced, but confidence remains medium due to the interpretive ambiguity inherent in cross-linguistic extensions.

description: East Asians (Japanese) show worse recognition memory for a central object when the peripheral background is changed compared to Westerners (Americans), who are less affected by peripheral changes — indicating that holistic processing style leads to tighter object-background binding in memory for East Asians
original_authors: Takahiko Masuda; Richard E. Nisbett
original_title: Attending holistically versus analytically: comparing the context sensitivity of Japanese and Americans
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Michael Weigl; Qi Shao; Enno Wang; Zhiwei Zheng; Juan Li; Jutta Kray; Axel Mecklinger
replication_title: Not so different after all? An event-related potential study on item and source memory for object-scene pairs in German and Chinese young adults
explanation: The authors explicitly designed their item memory task 'after the seminal study by Masuda and Nisbett (2001), Experiment 2' and predicted the same cultural difference pattern. However, the study found no cultural modulation of memory performance, and Bayesian analyses provided 'substantial evidence for H0' for all critical comparisons. The authors conclude: 'we found no evidence for a cultural modulation of memory performance, neither in our behavioral data, nor in the ERPs.'

description: Bilingual children (Spanish-English and Turkish-German) show attenuated (less positive) Ta amplitude in the T-complex auditory evoked potential compared to monolingual peers, reflecting a delayed neural commitment to language-specific speech sound patterns
original_authors: Tanja Rinker; Valerie L. Shafer; Markus Kiefer; Nancy Vidal; Yan H. Yu
original_title: T-complex measures in bilingual Spanish-English and Turkish-German children and monolingual peers
replication_authors: Theresa Bloder; Yasuaki Shinohara; Tanja Rinker; Valerie L. Shafer
replication_title: The impact of typological similarities and differences between German and Italian on the acquisition of language-specific phonetic cues in bilingual children: insights from the T-complex
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These findings partially replicated previous studies' (abstract) and 'We replicated the finding of a more negative response in the Ta-Tb latency range for bilingual compared to monolingual participants, specifically for the 0 ms VOT stimulus at the right site (T8)' (Discussion). However, the replication was only partial — the attenuation was found only for one specific stimulus and the study also revealed novel stimulus-modulation effects not present in the original, leading the authors to conclude partial rather than full replication.

description: A minimal spiking neural network model with spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) and structured synaptic delays generates polychronous groups, with approximately 5,000-6,000 such groups identifiable in network connectivity after simulation
original_authors: Eugene M. Izhikevich
original_title: Polychronization: computation with spikes
replication_authors: Robin Pauli; Philipp Weidel; Susanne Kunkel; Abigail Morrison
replication_title: Reproducing Polychronization: A Guide to Maximizing the Reproducibility of Spiking Network Models
explanation: The authors successfully reproduced the existence of polychronous groups and gamma oscillations in the network, but found substantially fewer groups than originally reported (median ~2,500 vs. the original's ~5,000-6,000), and discovered that key results were highly sensitive to implementation choices. They concluded that 'the original study significantly overstates the number of groups to be found in such networks, due to the artificial synchrony induced by these implementational (rather than conceptional) choices.' They also discovered an unreported second dynamical mode.

description: SNP rs2060546 near the NTN4 gene is associated with Gilles de la Tourette Syndrome (OR = 2.41; p = 5.8 × 10⁻⁷) in a multinational European cohort
original_authors: Peristera Paschou; Dongmei Yu; Gloria Gerber; Patrick Evans; Fotis Tsetsos; Lea K. Davis; Iordanis Karagiannidis; Jonathan Chaponis; Eric Gamazon; Kirsten Mueller‐Vahl; Manfred Stuhrmann; Monika Schloegelhofer; Mara Stamenkovic; Johannes Hebebrand; Markus Noethen; Peter Nagy; Csaba Barta; Zsanett Tarnok; Renata Rizzo; Christel Depienne; Yulia Worbe; Andreas Hartmann; Danielle C. Cath; Cathy L. Budman; Paul Sandor; Cathy Barr; Thomas Wolanczyk; Harvey Singer; I‐Ching Chou; Marco Grados; Danielle Posthuma; Guy A. Rouleau; Harald Aschauer; Nelson B. Freimer; David L. Pauls; Nancy J. Cox; Carol A. Mathews; Jeremiah M. Scharf
original_title: Genetic association signal near NTN4 in Tourette syndrome
replication_authors: Shanmukha S. Padmanabhuni; Rayan Houssari; Ann-Louise Esserlind; Jes Olesen; Thomas M. Werge; Thomas F. Hansen; Birgitte Bertelsen; Fotis Tsetsos; Peristera Paschou; Zeynep Tümer
replication_title: Investigation of SNP rs2060546 Immediately Upstream to NTN4 in a Danish Gilles de la Tourette Syndrome Cohort
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We did not find the SNP rs2060546 to be significantly associated in the Danish cohort (OR = 1.363, 95% CI 0.7188–2.675; p-value = 0.3329).' Although a subsequent meta-analysis combining all cohorts yielded significance, the authors attribute the replication failure to 'the small size of the cohort.'

description: Anodal tDCS over the left prefrontal cortex reverses the SNARC-like spatial associations of weekday stimuli (but not numerical stimuli), such that participants respond faster with their right hands to early weekdays and left hands to late weekdays
original_authors: Philipp Alexander Schroeder; Hans-Christoph Nuerk; Christian Plewnia
original_title: Prefrontal neuromodulation reverses spatial associations of non-numerical sequences, but not numbers
replication_authors: Philipp A. Schroeder; Hans-Christoph Nuerk; Christian Plewnia
replication_title: Switching between Multiple Codes of SNARC-Like Associations: Two Conceptual Replication Attempts with Anodal tDCS in Sham-Controlled Cross-Over Design
explanation: The authors found a non-significant difference in SNARC effects for weekday stimuli between anodal and sham tDCS conditions (t(23) = -0.75, p = 0.460), and explicitly state 'the conceptual replication of the reversal of the weekday sequence by anodal tDCS was not successful in the sham-controlled cross-over design and descriptively even opposite to our previous result.'

description: Anodal tDCS over the left prefrontal cortex reverses the SNARC-like spatial associations of non-numerical ordinal sequences, such that participants respond faster with their right hands to early sequence items and left hands to late sequence items
original_authors: Philipp Alexander Schroeder; Hans-Christoph Nuerk; Christian Plewnia
original_title: Prefrontal neuromodulation reverses spatial associations of non-numerical sequences, but not numbers
replication_authors: Philipp A. Schroeder; Hans-Christoph Nuerk; Christian Plewnia
replication_title: Switching between Multiple Codes of SNARC-Like Associations: Two Conceptual Replication Attempts with Anodal tDCS in Sham-Controlled Cross-Over Design
explanation: Using month names instead of weekdays, the authors found a significant difference between sham and anodal tDCS conditions (t(23) = 2.68, p = 0.013, d = 0.55), but the reversed/abolished SNARC effect during anodal tDCS was not itself significant (p = 0.175). The authors describe this as a 'partial replication' with a reduced effect size (d = 0.55 vs. original d = 0.95), stating 'we could partially replicate our previous observation.'

description: A non-linear, state-dependent interaction between tDCS current strength (1 mA vs. 2 mA) and individuals' baseline discrimination sensitivity modulates visuospatial spatial attention bias, such that high-sensitivity individuals shift rightward with low-intensity and low-sensitivity individuals shift rightward with high-intensity tDCS
original_authors: Christopher S.Y. Benwell; Gemma Learmonth; Carlo Miniussi; Monika Harvey; Gregor Thut
original_title: Non-linear effects of transcranial direct current stimulation as a function of individual baseline performance: evidence from biparietal tDCS influence on lateralized attention bias
replication_authors: Gemma Learmonth; Francesca Felisatti; Numaya Siriwardena; Matthew Checketts; Christopher S. Y. Benwell; Gesine Märker; Gregor Thut; Monika Harvey
replication_title: No Interaction between tDCS Current Strength and Baseline Performance: A Conceptual Replication
explanation: The authors explicitly label this a 'conceptual replication' and conclude it is a failed replication: Bayesian analysis yielded BF = 0.17 (< 1/3), indicating support for the null hypothesis. As stated in the conclusion: 'a within-groups design...identified no overall effects of tDCS on spatial bias, and no current × performance interaction.'

description: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) at individual alpha frequency with anterior/posterior electrode montage increases subsequent alpha power (entrains alpha oscillations) in a state-dependent manner
original_authors: Toralf Neuling; Stefan Rach; Christoph S. Herrmann
original_title: Orchestrating neuronal networks: sustained after-effects of transcranial alternating current stimulation depend upon brain states
replication_authors: Tomer Fekete; Andrey R. Nikolaev; Floris De Knijf; Aleksandra Zharikova; Cees van Leeuwen
replication_title: Multi-Electrode Alpha tACS During Varying Background Tasks Fails to Modulate Subsequent Alpha Power
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our mtACS paradigm failed to replicate previous results of tACS alpha entrainment (Neuling et al., 2013; Helfrich et al., 2014a).' No significant effect of stimulation was found (F(1,472) = 0.7, p > 0.35). The replication used a multi-electrode analog of the original anterior/posterior montage, making it a close experiment.

description: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) at individual alpha frequency with anterior/posterior electrode montage entrains brain oscillations and increases subsequent alpha power
original_authors: Randolph F. Helfrich; Till R. Schneider; Stefan Rach; Sina A. Trautmann-Lengsfeld; Andreas K. Engel; Christoph S. Herrmann
original_title: Entrainment of brain oscillations by transcranial alternating current stimulation
replication_authors: Tomer Fekete; Andrey R. Nikolaev; Floris De Knijf; Aleksandra Zharikova; Cees van Leeuwen
replication_title: Multi-Electrode Alpha tACS During Varying Background Tasks Fails to Modulate Subsequent Alpha Power
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our mtACS paradigm failed to replicate previous results of tACS alpha entrainment (Neuling et al., 2013; Helfrich et al., 2014a).' No significant effect of stimulation was found across any analysis. The multi-electrode analog of the original anterior/posterior montage was used.

description: Observation of congruent pantomimed gestures facilitates action picture naming (faster response latencies) compared to unrelated or neutral gesture primes
original_authors: Ana Murteira; Paul F. Sowman; Lyndsey Nickels
original_title: Taking action in hand: effects of gesture observation on action verb naming
replication_authors: Ana Murteira; Paul F. Sowman; Lyndsey Nickels
replication_title: Does TMS Disruption of the Left Primary Motor Cortex Affect Verb Retrieval Following Exposure to Pantomimed Gestures?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated our previous finding that observation of a congruent pantomimed gesture facilitates action-picture naming, relative to an unrelated or a neutral prime.' The significant main effect of Condition confirmed the priming effect (χ²(2) = 44.5, p < 0.001), with congruent gestures producing faster naming than neutral conditions. The extension involved adding cTBS stimulation to investigate motor cortex involvement, making this a close extension of the original behavioral paradigm.

description: Anodal tDCS over the right occipitotemporal cortex enhances perception and memory of faces and objects, with a medium effect size (ηp² = 0.20) in groups of 16 participants
original_authors: Marica Barbieri; Marcello Negrini; Michael A. Nitsche; Davide Rivolta
original_title: Anodal-tDCS over the human right occipital cortex enhances the perception and memory of both faces and objects
replication_authors: Megan L. Willis; Andrea I. Costantino; Michael. A. Nitsche; Romina Palermo; Davide Rivolta
replication_title: Anodal tDCS and High-Frequency tRNS Targeting the Occipitotemporal Cortex Do Not Always Enhance Face Perception
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate the findings of Barbieri et al. (2016), which demonstrated superior face and object perception following anodal tDCS targeting the right occipitotemporal cortex.' The main effect of tDCS condition was non-significant for both accuracy (F(1,51)=0.68, p=0.414, ηp²=0.01) and RT, and Bayesian analysis provided anecdotal to moderate evidence for the null hypothesis.

description: High-frequency tRNS applied bilaterally to the occipitotemporal cortex leads to more accurate face perception performance on the Cambridge Face Perception Task, relative to sham stimulation
original_authors: Aleksandra Romanska; Constantin Rezlescu; Tirta Susilo; Bradley Duchaine; Michael J. Banissy
original_title: High-frequency transcranial random noise stimulation enhances perception of facial identity
replication_authors: Megan L. Willis; Andrea I. Costantino; Michael. A. Nitsche; Romina Palermo; Davide Rivolta
replication_title: Anodal tDCS and High-Frequency tRNS Targeting the Occipitotemporal Cortex Do Not Always Enhance Face Perception
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we failed to replicate their finding of enhanced face perception following high-frequency tRNS targeting the occipitotemporal cortex.' The main effect of tRNS condition was non-significant for both accuracy (F(1,37)=0.64, p=0.428, ηp²=0.02) and RT. The authors acknowledge different stimulation parameters were used (different task and frequency range), and note 'Experiment 2 was not a direct replication Romanska et al. (2015).'

description: Interhemispheric asymmetry in delta (slow-wave) activity in the default-mode network during NREM stage 3 sleep is associated with the first-night effect, with the left hemisphere showing lower delta activity than the right hemisphere
original_authors: Masako Tamaki; Ji Won Bang; Takeo Watanabe; Yuka Sasaki
original_title: Night watch in one brain hemisphere during sleep associated with the first-night effect in humans
replication_authors: Masako Tamaki; Yuka Sasaki
replication_title: Surveillance During REM Sleep for the First-Night Effect
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We confirmed that interhemispheric asymmetry was present in delta activity in the DMN during stage N3 of NREM sleep [t(10) = 2.34, p = 0.042, Cohen's d = 0.70]... This result replicates previous findings (Tamaki et al., 2016).' The replication used the same nap design, same DMN regions, and same source-localized EEG methodology as the original study.

description: Right frontal goal-conflict-specific EEG rhythmicity (GCSR) in theta band is generated during an economic decision-making task involving approach-avoidance conflict (CONFLICT condition), but does not predict economic choice behavior or correlate with trait anxiety/neuroticism
original_authors: Neo, Phoebe S.-H.; McNaughton, Neil
original_title: Frontal theta power linked to neuroticism and avoidance
replication_authors: Phoebe S.-H. Neo; Jessica Tinker; Neil McNaughton
replication_title: Goal-Conflict EEG Theta and Biased Economic Decisions: A Role for a Second Negative Motivation System
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated the general findings from the economic choice task of Neo and McNaughton (2011)...we observed GCSR in the right frontal region' and 'We also replicated specific findings from Neo and McNaughton (2011), detecting GCSR only in the early phase of training and in the theta band.' The paradigm was modified from risk to ambiguity (a close experiment), but the core GCSR finding was replicated.

description: The Ego Dissolution Scale (EDS) has a two-factor structure (Ego-Loss and Unity/connectedness) with good reliability and construct validity (e.g., correlations with dissociation, depersonalization, transliminality, positive/negative affect)
original_authors: Fiona G. Sleight; Steven Jay Lynn; Richard E. Mattson; Charlie W. McDonald
original_title: A novel ego dissolution scale: a construct validation study
replication_authors: Steven Jay Lynn; Charlie W. McDonald; Fiona G. Sleight; Richard E. Mattson
replication_title: Cross-validation of the ego dissolution scale: implications for studying psychedelics
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicate key findings from our first study (Sleight et al., 2023)' and confirm this in the Results section: 'These results overall replicate the exploratory factor analyses conducted by Sleight et al. (2023).' The Discussion further confirms: 'we replicated the original factor structure (Sleight et al., 2023)' and 'As in our initial study, Ego Dissolution and Ego-Loss were associated with all measures of dissociation.' The authors added new variables (personality, mindfulness, hallucination predisposition, sleep measures) beyond the original study.

description: Performance-dependent variations in CNV amplitude at FCz (SMA) reflect the unfolding of time during interval timing, with longer produced intervals associated with higher CNV amplitudes
original_authors: Franç oise Macar; Franck Vidal; Laurence Casini
original_title: The supplementary motor area in motor and sensory timing: evidence from slow brain potential changes
replication_authors: Tadeusz W. Kononowicz; Hedderik van Rijn
replication_title: Slow Potentials in Time Estimation: The Role of Temporal Accumulation and Habituation
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'neither the analysis based on monopolar nor on Laplacian-transformed data replicated the performance-dependent variations as reported by Macar et al. (1999).' Experiment 1 found no effect of pseudo-experimental groups for FCz (F < 1 for the '3-in-a-row' group; F(2,34) = 1.2, p = 0.32 for extended group).

description: Performance-dependent variations in CNV amplitude at FCz (SMA) reflect the unfolding of time during interval timing, with longer produced intervals associated with higher CNV amplitudes
original_authors: Franç oise Macar; Franck Vidal; Laurence Casini
original_title: The supplementary motor area in motor and sensory timing: evidence from slow brain potential changes
replication_authors: Tadeusz W. Kononowicz; Hedderik van Rijn
replication_title: Slow Potentials in Time Estimation: The Role of Temporal Accumulation and Habituation
explanation: Experiment 2, which more closely matched the Macar et al. (1999) setup with an extended training block, also failed to replicate performance-dependent CNV variations. The authors state 'neither in Experiment 1, nor in Experiment 2, nor in the combined analyses of all data did we find any systematic or consistent performance-based variations in the CNV amplitude.'

description: Adults with ASD show no sex differences on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes (RME) task, in contrast to neurotypical adults who show a female advantage
original_authors: Simon Baron-Cohen; Daniel C. Bowen; Rosemary J. Holt; Carrie Allison; Bonnie Auyeung; Michael V. Lombardo; Paula Smith; Meng-Chuan Lai
original_title: The 'reading the mind in the eyes' test: complete absence of typical sex difference in 400 men and women with autism
replication_authors: Pagni BA; Walsh MJM; Rogers C.; Braden BB
replication_title: Social Cognition in Autism Spectrum Disorder Across the Adult Lifespan: Influence of Age and Sex on Reading the Mind in the Eyes Task in a Cross-sectional Sample
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The absence of sex differences in our sample of adults with ASD, when collapsed across ages, is consistent with reports from Baron-Cohen et al. (2015)' and conclude 'We replicated ASD-related impairments on a ToM task...as well as provided some evidence for an absence of sex differences in ASD.' The sex by diagnosis interaction was nonsignificant (p = 0.068), confirming no sex difference in ASD.

description: Adults with ASD perform worse than neurotypical adults on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes (RME) task, indicating reduced theory of mind abilities
original_authors: Simon Baron-Cohen; Daniel C. Bowen; Rosemary J. Holt; Carrie Allison; Bonnie Auyeung; Michael V. Lombardo; Paula Smith; Meng-Chuan Lai
original_title: The 'reading the mind in the eyes' test: complete absence of typical sex difference in 400 men and women with autism
replication_authors: Pagni BA; Walsh MJM; Rogers C.; Braden BB
replication_title: Social Cognition in Autism Spectrum Disorder Across the Adult Lifespan: Influence of Age and Sex on Reading the Mind in the Eyes Task in a Cross-sectional Sample
explanation: The authors report a significant main effect of diagnosis (t = -2.95, p = 0.004), indicating NT adults outperformed those with ASD on the RME task. The Discussion states: 'Our results confirm adults with ASD perform worse on RME than NT adults' and 'We replicated ASD-related impairments on a ToM task compared to an age- and IQ-matched NT sample.'

description: Biologically-constrained point-neuron models of CA1 pyramidal cells (strongly and weakly adapting variants) developed in the Brian simulator capture the frequency-current (f-I) profiles of these cells and exhibit rebound spiking behavior
original_authors: Katie A. Ferguson; Carey Y. L. Huh; Benedicte Amilhon; Sylvain Williams; Frances K. Skinner
original_title: Simple, biologically-constrained CA1 pyramidal cell models using an intact, whole hippocampus context
replication_authors: Shailesh Appukuttan; Andrew P. Davison
replication_title: Reproducing and quantitatively validating a biologically-constrained point-neuron model of CA1 pyramidal cells
explanation: The authors reproduced the CA1 pyramidal cell model in Brian2 and NEURON simulators and found that 'the core features of the model' were reproduced, but with 'certain unaccountable discrepancies.' The strongly adapting model was well reproduced (RMSE ≈ 0), but the weakly adapting models showed notable discrepancies in final spiking frequencies and rheobase currents (~50 pA vs. 5 pA reported in the original), making the outcome partially successful but not a full replication.

description: Vascular risk factors (diastolic blood pressure and blood cholesterol) are independently associated with a longitudinal decline in resting-state functional connectivity within higher-order brain networks (especially the default-mode network) in older adults, independent of amyloid-beta deposition
original_authors: Theresa Köbe; Alexa Pichet Binette; Jacob W. Vogel; Pierre-François Meyer; John C.S. Breitner; Judes Poirier; Sylvia Villeneuve
original_title: Vascular risk factors are associated with a decline in resting-state functional connectivity in cognitively unimpaired individuals at risk for Alzheimer's disease: vascular risk factors and functional connectivity changes
replication_authors: Miranka Wirth; Malo Gaubert; Theresa Köbe; Antoine Garnier-Crussard; Catharina Lange; Julie Gonneaud; Robin de Flores; Brigitte Landeau; Vincent de la Sayette; Gaël Chételat
replication_title: Vascular Health Is Associated With Functional Connectivity Decline in Higher-Order Networks of Older Adults
explanation: The authors explicitly state that their main goal was to 'replicate and expand earlier findings on the impact of VRF on RSFC trajectories within intrinsic brain networks (Köbe et al., 2021),' and in their Discussion they conclude: 'This finding was replicated for diastolic blood pressure' and 'we thus reproduced the previous findings (Köbe et al., 2021) in the PREVENT-AD cohort using a highly similar methodological approach in the independent IMAP+ cohort.'

description: A modular spiking neural network with reward-based learning can learn and recall temporal sequences of variable durations, preserving both order and timing of elements
original_authors: Ian Cone; Harel Z. Shouval
original_title: Learning precise spatiotemporal sequences via biophysically realistic learning rules in a modular, spiking network
replication_authors: Barna Zajzon; Renato Duarte; Abigail Morrison
replication_title: Toward reproducible models of sequence learning: replication and analysis of a modular spiking network with reward-based learning
explanation: The authors explicitly state that they 'successfully replicate the main findings of the original study' by re-implementing the model in the NEST simulator using Python instead of the original MATLAB code. In the Discussion, they confirm that 'by reimplementing the model in the NEST simulator, we were able to qualitatively replicate the main findings of the original work.'

description: Inter-subject correlations in EDA and heart rate predict the number of correctly answered questions about narrative movie clips, reflecting attentional engagement with the narrative
original_authors: Ivo V. Stuldreher; Jan B. F. van Erp; Anne-Marie Brouwer
original_title: Robustness of physiological synchrony in wearable electrodermal activity and heart rate as a measure of attentional engagement to movie clips
replication_authors: Ivo V. Stuldreher; Emma Maasland; Charelle Bottenheft; Jan B. F. van Erp; Anne-Marie Brouwer
replication_title: Physiological synchrony in electrodermal activity predicts decreased vigilant attention induced by sleep deprivation
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results: 'We replicated findings that inter-subject correlations in EDA and heart rate predicted the number of correct answers on questions about the movie clips.' The same association was confirmed using the same general paradigm (inter-subject correlations during movie clips predicting narrative comprehension), but extended to a novel context involving a sleep deprivation night protocol.

description: Rosiglitazone (RGZ) at concentrations of 0.1–5 µM upregulates LRP1 mRNA and protein levels in HepG2 cells via PPARγ activation
original_authors: Jae Hoon Moon; Hyung Jun Kim; Hyun Min Kim; Ae Hee Yang; Byung-Wan Lee; Eun Seok Kang; Hyun Chul Lee; Bong Soo Cha
original_title: Upregulation of hepatic LRP1 by rosiglitazone: a possible novel mechanism of the beneficial effect of thiazolidinediones on atherogenic dyslipidemia
replication_authors: Alejandro N. Rondón-Ortiz; Christian L. Lino Cardenas; Jimena Martínez-Málaga; Ana L. Gonzales-Urday; Kuljeet S. Gugnani; Mark Böhlke; Timothy J. Maher; Alejandro J. Pino-Figueroa
replication_title: High Concentrations of Rosiglitazone Reduce mRNA and Protein Levels of LRP1 in HepG2 Cells
explanation: The authors confirmed the mRNA upregulation of LRP1 by RGZ at 3 and 10 µM ('In agreement with the literature, we observed the transcriptional activation of LRP1 mRNA'), but were unable to replicate the protein-level upregulation: 'we did not observe increases in LRP1 protein levels following either 24 or 48 h exposures to these concentrations of RGZ.' The replication was partial — the transcriptional effect was confirmed, but the protein-level finding was not reproduced.

description: Body posture congruence with the direction of an avatar's location significantly speeds up level 2 visuo-spatial perspective taking (VPT-2), reflecting that VPT-2 is an embodied process based on movement simulation or emulation
original_authors: Kessler, Klaus; Thomson, Laura A.
original_title: The embodied nature of spatial perspective taking: embodied transformation versus sensorimotor interference
replication_authors: Kessler K.; Rutherford H.
replication_title: The two forms of visuo-spatial perspective taking are differently embodied and subserve different spatial prepositions
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We have also replicated and extended our previous VPT-2 findings (Kessler and Thomson, 2010) regarding the effect of the participants' body posture by observing significantly faster RTs with a congruent than an incongruent posture at all angular disparities, even at 60°.' The body posture effect on VPT-2 was confirmed (F(1,22) = 33.4, p < 0.00001, ηp² = 0.603), and the same effect was replicated with verbal responses in Experiment 2.

description: Level 2 visuo-spatial perspective taking (VPT-2) shows increasing reaction times with angular disparity, while level 1 perspective taking (VPT-1) reaction times remain flat across angular disparities, indicating a qualitative difference between the two types of perspective taking
original_authors: Michelon, Pascale; Zacks, Jeffrey M.
original_title: Two kinds of visual perspective taking
replication_authors: Kessler K.; Rutherford H.
replication_title: The two forms of visuo-spatial perspective taking are differently embodied and subserve different spatial prepositions
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We replicated Michelon and Zacks' (2006) findings showing that response times for VPT-2 increased with angular disparity, whereas response times for VPT-1 were not affected by angular disparity and remained constant.' The interaction between task and angular disparity was significant (F(2,21) = 26.1, p < 0.00001, ηp² = 0.658).

description: Unconscious thought (distraction before deciding) leads to better choices than conscious deliberation without information (the deliberation-without-attention effect) in complex multi-attribute decisions
original_authors: Ap Dijksterhuis; Maarten W. Bos; Loran F. Nordgren; Rick B. van Baaren
original_title: On making the right choice: the deliberation without attention effect
replication_authors: Ashby NJ; Glöckner A.; Dickert S.
replication_title: Conscious and unconscious thought in risky choice: testing the capacity principle and the appropriate weighting principle of unconscious thought theory
explanation: In Experiment 1, the UT condition outperformed the Dw/oI condition in selecting the highest EV gamble (odds = 0.18, z = -1.97, p < 0.05), which the authors explicitly describe as 'replicates the common UTE.'

description: Unconscious thought (distraction before deciding) leads to better choices than conscious deliberation without information (the deliberation-without-attention effect) in complex multi-attribute decisions
original_authors: Ap Dijksterhuis; Maarten W. Bos; Loran F. Nordgren; Rick B. van Baaren
original_title: On making the right choice: the deliberation without attention effect
replication_authors: Ashby NJ; Glöckner A.; Dickert S.
replication_title: Conscious and unconscious thought in risky choice: testing the capacity principle and the appropriate weighting principle of unconscious thought theory
explanation: In Experiment 2, the UT condition significantly outperformed the Dw/oI condition in selecting the best gamble (odds = 0.16, z = -2.18, p = 0.03), which the authors describe as 'replicating the standard UTE.'

description: Unconscious thought (distraction before deciding) leads to better choices than conscious deliberation without information (the deliberation-without-attention effect) in complex multi-attribute decisions
original_authors: Ap Dijksterhuis; Maarten W. Bos; Loran F. Nordgren; Rick B. van Baaren
original_title: On making the right choice: the deliberation without attention effect
replication_authors: Ashby NJ; Glöckner A.; Dickert S.
replication_title: Conscious and unconscious thought in risky choice: testing the capacity principle and the appropriate weighting principle of unconscious thought theory
explanation: In Experiment 3, no difference was found between the UT and Dw/oI conditions (odds = 0.47, z = -0.81, p = 0.42), and UT actually performed significantly worse than the DI condition. The authors state: 'we do not find that the UT condition does better than any of the other conditions when selecting the best gamble and in fact did significantly worse when compared to the DI condition.'

description: Orthographic consistency effects on spoken word recognition are present in ERP responses during a semantic categorization task, with inconsistent words producing more negative ERPs than consistent words around 300 ms after word onset
original_authors: Chotiga Pattamadilok; Laetitia Perre; Stéphane Dufau; Johannes C. Ziegler
original_title: On-line orthographic influences on spoken language in a semantic task
replication_authors: Laetitia Perre; Daisy Bertrand; Johannes C. Ziegler
replication_title: Literacy Affects Spoken Language in a Non-Linguistic Task: An ERP Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated the orthographic consistency effect using the same items and paradigm as Pattamadilok et al. (2009) but replacing the semantic categorization task by a simple non-linguistic noise detection task.' A significant consistency effect was observed in the left centro-posterior quadrant between 250-350 ms (F = 5.3, p < 0.05), with inconsistent words producing more negative ERPs than consistent words.

description: Multivariate pattern classification of fMRI voxel activities in frontopolar cortex can predict spontaneous left/right motor decisions up to 10 seconds before participants report their conscious decisions, with approximately 60% prediction accuracy
original_authors: Chun Siong Soon; Marcel Brass; Hans-Jochen Heinze; John-Dylan Haynes
original_title: Unconscious determinants of free decisions in the human brain
replication_authors: Martin Lages; Katarzyna Jaworska
replication_title: How Predictable are “Spontaneous Decisions” and “Hidden Intentions”? Comparing Classification Results Based on Previous Responses with Multivariate Pattern Analysis of fMRI BOLD Signals
explanation: The authors closely replicated the behavioral task from Soon et al. (2008) without fMRI and showed that response bias and sequential dependencies alone achieve comparable prediction accuracy (61.6%) to the original fMRI-based classifier. However, they explicitly state: 'our behavioral results are not sufficient to dismiss the original findings based on fMRI BOLD signals,' making the overall result inconclusive regarding the original claim about neural correlates.

description: Neural correlates of hidden intentions (addition vs. subtraction) can be decoded from voxel activities in anterior medial prefrontal cortex and left lateral frontopolar cortex with 71% and 61% accuracy respectively, before task execution
original_authors: John-Dylan Haynes; Katsuyuki Sakai; Geraint Rees; Sam Gilbert; Chris Frith; Richard E. Passingham
original_title: Reading hidden intentions in the human brain
replication_authors: Martin Lages; Katarzyna Jaworska
replication_title: How Predictable are “Spontaneous Decisions” and “Hidden Intentions”? Comparing Classification Results Based on Previous Responses with Multivariate Pattern Analysis of fMRI BOLD Signals
explanation: The authors replicated the behavioral task from Haynes et al. (2007) without fMRI and achieved 64.1% prediction accuracy from response dependencies alone (comparable to the original's 61-71% from fMRI). As with Study 1, they explicitly note their behavioral findings are not sufficient to dismiss the original fMRI findings, making the result inconclusive.

description: Participants at the Burning Man festival report less use of expressive suppression and greater use of cognitive reappraisal compared to their typical use at home
original_authors: McRae, Kateri; Heller, S. Megan; John, Oliver P.; Gross, James J.
original_title: Context-dependent emotion regulation: suppression and reappraisal at the Burning Man festival
replication_authors: Snyder SA; Heller SM; Lumian DS; McRae K.
replication_title: Regulation of positive and negative emotion: effects of sociocultural context
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We observed a replication of our previous findings (McRae et al., 2011)—a significant interaction between self-reported strategy use and context' across all four studies, with suppression decreased and reappraisal increased at Burning Man compared to home. The current study extends the original by examining valence-specific emotion regulation and additional individual difference variables.

description: Aging slows down visual processing speed (as measured by ERP 50% integration times) at the rate of approximately 1 ms/year in healthy adults

replication_authors: Magdalena M. Bieniek; Luisa S. Frei; Guillaume A. Rousselet
replication_title: Early ERPs to faces: aging, luminance, and individual differences
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'First, we replicated previous findings of Rousselet et al. (2010): aging slows down visual processing, expressed in the 50IT, at the rate of 1 ms/year' and in the Discussion: 'our data confirms previous findings of Rousselet et al. (2010), suggesting that aging slows down visual processing speed by 1 ms/year.'

description: Spaced presentation of paintings by different artists leads to better inductive learning of painting styles than massed (blocked) presentation, as measured by a yes/no recognition test (Experiment 2)

replication_authors: Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen; Samantha Bouwmeester
replication_title: Is spacing really the â€œfriend of inductionâ€?
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we think it is fair to interpret the results of the present experiment as a successful replication of Kornell and Bjork's (2008) original experiment.' The replication found d = 0.37 (95% CI [0.18, 0.55]) compared to the original d = 0.41 (95% CI [0.18, 0.64]), with highly overlapping confidence intervals.

description: Novel complex objects (random polygons) are represented with higher resolution in visual working memory than simple familiar objects (color squares), as evidenced by a higher CDA amplitude for one polygon compared to one color

replication_authors: Ayala S. Allon; Halely Balaban; Roy Luria
replication_title: How low can you go? Changing the resolution of novel complex objects in visual working memory according to task demands
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results: 'planned comparisons showed that the CDA amplitude for one polygon was higher than for one color, F(1,9)=13.54, MSE=0.06, p<0.01, replicating previous findings (Gao et al., 2009; Luria et al., 2010).' The same direction effect was successfully found.

description: When memory- and test-array similarity is low (between-category change), accuracy for novel complex items in visual working memory is equivalent to accuracy for simple familiar items (color squares)
original_authors: Edward Awh; Brian Barton; Edward K. Vogel
original_title: Visual working memory represents a fixed number of items regardless of complexity
replication_authors: Ayala S. Allon; Halely Balaban; Roy Luria
replication_title: How low can you go? Changing the resolution of novel complex objects in visual working memory according to task demands
explanation: In Experiment 2, the authors explicitly state they 'behaviorally replicated previous findings by Awh et al. (2007) by showing that when the memory and test phase similarity is low, performance for novel complex items is equivalent to performance for familiar colors.' The ANOVA showed no difference between categories (F<1).

description: Suppressing motor excitability in the lip representation via low-frequency rTMS disrupts categorical perception and discrimination of lip-articulated speech sounds (e.g., 'ba' vs. 'da') in an articulator-specific manner
original_authors: Riikka Möttönen; Kate E. Watkins
original_title: Motor representations of articulators contribute to categorical perception of speech sounds
replication_authors: Jack C. Rogers; Riikka MÃ¶ttÃ¶nen; Rowan Boyles; Kate E. Watkins
replication_title: Discrimination of speech and non-speech sounds following theta-burst stimulation of the motor cortex
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'Using cTBS, we replicated our previous findings that temporary disruption of the lip motor representation impairs the perception of speech sounds that rely on the lips for their production.' The study used a different TMS protocol (cTBS vs. low-frequency rTMS), different stimuli (natural speech vs. computer-generated), a different discrimination paradigm (AXB vs. same-different), and additional stimulus types, making this a close extension.

description: 40 seconds of continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) over motor cortex produces inhibitory suppression of motor excitability as measured by motor-evoked potential (MEP) amplitude
original_authors: Ying-Zu Huang; Mark J. Edwards; Elisabeth Rounis; Kailash P. Bhatia; John C. Rothwell
original_title: Theta burst stimulation of the human motor cortex
replication_authors: Jack C. Rogers; Riikka MÃ¶ttÃ¶nen; Rowan Boyles; Kate E. Watkins
replication_title: Discrimination of speech and non-speech sounds following theta-burst stimulation of the motor cortex
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we did not replicate findings from previous studies revealing an inhibitory effect of 40 s of cTBS on motor excitability (e.g., Huang et al., 2005, 2008; Gentner et al., 2008).' The ANOVA showed no significant effect of cTBS on MEP size for either the lip (F(3,33)=1.34, p=0.277) or hand (F(3,30)=2.11, p=0.120) representations.

description: Cathodal tDCS to the right posterior parietal cortex (P4) selectively disrupts visual working memory performance
original_authors: Berryhill ME; Wencil EB; Branch Coslett H.; Olson IR
original_title: A selective working memory impairment after transcranial direct current stimulation to the right parietal lobe
replication_authors: Berryhill ME; Peterson DJ; Jones KT; Stephens JA
replication_title: Hits and misses: leveraging tDCS to advance cognitive research
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors used the same cathodal tDCS protocol (1.5 mA, 10 min to right PPC/P4) as Berryhill et al. (2010), but applied it to a VWM grouping paradigm (from Xu & Chun, 2007) rather than the original sequential recognition/recall task — making this a close extension. The result is unambiguously a failure: no main effect of tDCS on VWM performance (F(1,32)=0.07, p=0.79), no condition × tDCS interaction (F(2,64)=0.18, p=0.83), and splitting by WM capacity did not change the pattern (F(1,31)=0.05, p=0.83). The authors state: 'Contrary to our predictions, tDCS did not modulate grouping benefits in VWM' and call these 'null results' that were 'unexpected.' While the authors speculate poor participant motivation may explain the null (low K-values vs. Xu & Chun 2007), this does not change the result classification — the replication attempt failed regardless of the suspected cause. Upgraded from medium to high confidence because the statistical evidence and authors' own characterization are unambiguous.

description: Anodal tDCS to the pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) improves response inhibition performance in healthy adults on a stop-signal task
original_authors: Tzu-Yu Hsu; Lin-Yuan Tseng; Jia-Xin Yu; Wen-Jui Kuo; Daisy L. Hung; Ovid J.L. Tzeng; Vincent Walsh; Neil G. Muggleton; Chi-Hung Juan
original_title: Modulating inhibitory control with direct current stimulation of the superior medial frontal cortex
replication_authors: Berryhill ME; Peterson DJ; Jones KT; Stephens JA
replication_title: Hits and misses: leveraging tDCS to advance cognitive research
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'failed to replicate an anodal tDCS benefit on a response inhibition task performance after stimulation to the pre-SMA (Hsu et al., 2011).' All statistical tests showed null results for Go/No-Go task accuracy (main effect of tDCS: F(2,34)=0.996, p=0.38) and reaction time (F(2,34)=0.060, p=0.942).

description: Rotating the stimulus framing 180° between two sequential Simon task trials eliminates the conflict adaptation effect (the reduction of the Simon effect after incompatible trials), demonstrating that sequential modulations depend on episodic retrieval rather than conflict monitoring
original_authors: Michiel M. Spapé; Guido P.H. Band; Bernhard Hommel
original_title: Compatibility-sequence effects in the Simon task reflect episodic retrieval but not conflict adaptation: evidence from LRP and N2
replication_authors: Michiel M. SpapÃ©; Bernhard Hommel
replication_title: Sequential modulations of the Simon effect depend on episodic retrieval
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Experiment 1 clearly replicates Spapé et al. (2011)' and describe their first experiment as 'a straight replication study.' The key findings were reproduced: conflict adaptation was significant under static conditions (t(17) = 6.17, p < .001) and completely eliminated under rotating conditions (t(17) = 0.50, p > .6), exactly as in the original.

description: Interference between holistic processing of faces and cars increases as a function of car expertise, as measured by a 2-back interleaved part-matching task with face and car composites
original_authors: Isabel Gauthier; Tim Curran; Kim M. Curby; Daniel Collins
original_title: Perceptual interference supports a non-modular account of face processing
replication_authors: Kim M. Curby; Isabel Gauthier
replication_title: Interference between face and non-face domains of perceptual expertise: a replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Consistent with previous findings, Experiment 1A provided evidence of interference between face and car processing as a function of expertise with cars (Gauthier et al., 2003). These data demonstrate that interference across different domains of perceptual expertise...is a robust and replicable effect.' The key correlation between car expertise and the interference index was replicated (r32 = 0.45, p = 0.009), though the specific pattern was unexpectedly driven by the transformed car context rather than the normal car context.

description: Feedback decisions made after a trial (Self-After) result in superior transfer performance compared to decisions made before a trial (Self-Before), suggesting that information processing activities (error estimation) rather than motivational factors drive self-controlled feedback learning advantages
original_authors: Suzete Chiviacowsky; Gabriele Wulf
