original_journal: Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport
replication_authors: Michael J. Carter; Anthony N. Carlsen; Diane M. Ste-Marie
replication_title: Self-controlled feedback is effective if it is based on the learnerâ€™s performance: a replication and extension of Chiviacowsky and Wulf (2005)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These results therefore replicate and extend the work of Chiviacowsky and Wulf (2005)' and confirm the key finding that Self-After outperformed Self-Before on transfer. The conclusion directly quotes Chiviacowsky and Wulf (2005, p. 45) approvingly, indicating the original finding was successfully replicated.

description: Retrieval practice of a subset of items from a studied category causes forgetting of the non-practiced items from that same category (retrieval-induced forgetting), as demonstrated using a category-cued recall paradigm with undergraduate participants
original_authors: Michael C. Anderson; Robert A. Bjork; Elizabeth L. Bjork
original_title: Remembering can cause forgetting: retrieval dynamics in long-term memory
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Christopher A. Rowland; Lauren E. Bates; Edward L. DeLosh
replication_title: On the reliability of retrieval-induced forgetting
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'we can conclude that the replication was successful' for Experiment 1, with RP- items recalled significantly less frequently than NRP items (t(71)=2.59, p=0.01, d=0.31), and the effect exceeded the Simonsohn d33% threshold of 0.26.

description: Retrieval practice of a subset of items from a studied category causes forgetting of the non-practiced items from that same category (retrieval-induced forgetting), as demonstrated using a category-cued recall paradigm with undergraduate participants

replication_authors: Christopher A. Rowland; Lauren E. Bates; Edward L. DeLosh
replication_title: On the reliability of retrieval-induced forgetting
explanation: The authors conclude that 'the outcome of Experiment 2 can confidently be interpreted as a successful replication,' with RP- items recalled significantly less than NRP items (t(139)=4.51, p<0.01, d=0.38), using an internet (Amazon Mechanical Turk) sample instead of undergraduates.

description: Retrieval-induced forgetting is observed using an independent cue procedure (novel cues not associated with practiced items at test), suggesting item-level inhibitory suppression rather than associative interference drives the forgetting effect
original_authors: Michael C. Anderson; Barbara A. Spellman

replication_authors: Christopher A. Rowland; Lauren E. Bates; Edward L. DeLosh
replication_title: On the reliability of retrieval-induced forgetting
explanation: No cue-independent RIF effect was observed in Experiment 3 (d=-0.05, 95% CI: -0.36, 0.27, p=0.7). The authors classify this as an 'uninformative failure to replicate' using the Simonsohn (2014) framework, as the result failed to reject both the null and the d33% threshold.

description: Repeatedly imagining eating a specific food (30 repetitions vs. 3 repetitions) reduces subsequent actual consumption of that food through habituation processes
original_authors: Carey K. Morewedge; Young Eun Huh; Joachim Vosgerau

replication_authors: Benjamin Missbach; Arnd Florack; Lukas Weissmann; JÃ¼rgen KÃ¶nig
replication_title: Mental imagery interventions reduce subsequent food intake only when self-regulatory resources are available
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Study 1 provided a replication of the initial habituation effects induced by mental imagery by Morewedge et al. (2010) and generalized these over another kind of food (gummy bears) as well as over different (smaller and larger) amount of imagery repetitions.' The habituation effect was significant: participants who imagined eating gummy bears consumed significantly less (M=24.63g) than controls (M=32.94g), F(3,95)=8.61, p=0.004.

description: Repeatedly imagining eating a specific food reduces subsequent actual consumption of that food through habituation processes
original_authors: Carey K. Morewedge; Young Eun Huh; Joachim Vosgerau
original_title: Thought for food: imagined consumption reduces actual consumption
replication_authors: Benjamin Missbach; Arnd Florack; Lukas Weissmann; JÃ¼rgen KÃ¶nig
replication_title: Mental imagery interventions reduce subsequent food intake only when self-regulatory resources are available
explanation: In Study 2 (walnuts with depletion manipulation), the habituation effect replicated only in the non-depleted condition (p=0.02) but not in the depleted condition (p=0.82). The overall main effect of imagery on food intake was not significant (p=0.16), and the interaction was only marginally significant (p=0.08). The authors describe this as 'initial evidence' that depletion moderates habituation, but characterize the interpretation as needing caution given only marginal significance of the interaction.

description: Pre-stimulus start position induces a spatially contralateral tendency of fixations (after the first ordinal fixation) during face processing, reflecting visuomotor influences on eye-movement patterns
original_authors: Joseph Arizpe; Dwight J. Kravitz; Galit Yovel; Chris I. Baker

replication_authors: Joseph M. Arizpe; Vincent Walsh; Chris I. Baker
replication_title: Characteristic visuomotor influences on eye-movement patterns to faces and other high level stimuli
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated our prior effect of starting side (left, right) to induce a spatially contralateral tendency of fixations after the first ordinal fixation' and the Discussion confirms: 'Overall fixation patterns tended contralateral to the start position (Side), replicating the effect of start position as reported in our prior study (Arizpe et al., 2012).' The replication is classified as close extension because they extended to a new unpredictable-location paradigm and added a control stimulus category (butterflies).

description: Team members' group identification (commitment) is positively associated with their emotional fit with the team (high identifiers' affective states are more closely linked to the group average than low identifiers)

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated the significant association between math anxiety and the distance effect based on RT for the symbolic number comparison task.' The key Distance × AMAS interaction was significant (t(60.99) = -2.46, p = 0.017), confirming that higher math anxiety was associated with a larger distance effect in the symbolic task.

description: High math anxious individuals show a marginally larger symbolic size effect (longer response times for larger number pairs) than low math anxious individuals during number comparison
original_authors: Núñez-Peña MI; Suárez-Pellicioni M.
original_title: Less precise representation of numerical magnitude in high math-anxious individuals: an ERP study of the size and distance effects
replication_authors: Julia F. Dietrich; Stefan Huber; Korbinian Moeller; Elise Klein
replication_title: The influence of math anxiety on symbolic and non-symbolic magnitude processing
explanation: Review confirmed: The authors explicitly state 'we did not find a significant interaction between the size effect for RT and math anxiety' (Discussion, Symbolic Number Comparison section). The Size × AMAS interaction was non-significant (t(60.85) = 0.74, p = 0.461, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15]). The original finding in Núñez-Peña and Suárez-Pellicioni (2014) was itself only marginally significant, and the authors attribute the non-replication to design differences (speed-accuracy instructions and stimulus presentation duration). Classification as failure is unambiguous.

description: Semantic interference transfers from picture naming to subsequent within-category word naming trials, but not from word naming to subsequent within-category picture naming trials, in a continuous naming task with determiner + word/picture naming
original_authors: Eduardo Navarrete; Bradford Z. Mahon; Alfonso Caramazza

replication_authors: Eduardo Navarrete; Bradford Z. Mahon; Anna Lorenzoni; Francesca Peressotti
replication_title: What can Written-Words Tell us About Lexical Retrieval in Speech Production?
explanation: The authors explicitly state their goal was to replicate Experiment 3 of Navarrete et al. (2010) and conclude: 'This pattern of results replicates the main findings of Experiment 3 in Navarrete et al. (2010).' The new experiment found transfer of semantic interference from picture to word naming but not vice versa, confirming the original findings. The paradigm was the same continuous naming task but redesigned to control for switch costs raised by Belke (2013).

description: Incorrect guesses of an upcoming task in a task-switching paradigm result in a reduction of switch costs, primarily due to an increase in task-repetition reaction times following an incorrect guess

explanation: The authors explicitly describe the Guessing condition as 'a conceptual replication of Experiment 2 of Kleinsorge and Scheil (2015)' and confirm in the Discussion that 'This procedural variation did not result in any substantial change in participants' performance. It was still observed that the presentation of an unexpected task hampered the performance of task repetitions more than the performance of task switches, which resulted in a reduction of switch costs with unexpected as compared to expected tasks.'

description: Cues in the nogo color produce cueing costs (slower responses when cue and target are congruent) in a modified spatial cueing paradigm, reflecting inhibition of locations associated with nogo-target features
original_authors: Brian A. Anderson; Charles L. Folk
original_title: Dissociating location-specific inhibition and attention shifts: evidence against the disengagement account of contingent capture
replication_authors: Caroline Barras; Dirk Kerzel
replication_title: Nogo Stimuli Do Not Receive More Attentional Suppression or Response Inhibition than Neutral Stimuli: Evidence from the N2pc, PD, and N2 Components in a Spatial Cueing Paradigm
explanation: Across three experiments with a total of 52 participants, the authors consistently failed to find cueing costs for nogo cues relative to neutral cues. The General Discussion states: 'we fail to replicate cueing costs to nogo cues in the modified cueing paradigm' and 'we were unable to find reliable cueing costs for nogo cues in three experiments.'

description: Participants show a literal interpretation facilitation effect when processing scalar quantifiers: accepting literally true but pragmatically infelicitous statements (e.g., 'Some elephants are mammals') as true is faster/more accurate than rejecting them pragmatically
original_authors: Lewis Bott; Ira A. Noveck
original_title: Some utterances are underinformative: the onset and time course of scalar inferences
replication_authors: Cécile Barbet; Guillaume Thierry
replication_title: Some Alternatives? Event-Related Potential Investigation of Literal and Pragmatic Interpretations of Some Presented in Isolation
explanation: Reviewer verification: The authors explicitly state in both the abstract and conclusion (Section 5): 'we failed to replicate a straightforward literal interpretation facilitation effect.' The result classification is unambiguous — the authors use the exact phrase 'failed to replicate.' The replication type is correctly 'conceptual' because the original Bott & Noveck (2004) used sentence verification tasks, while this study uses a fundamentally different paradigm — a single-word oddball ERP task where 'some' is presented in isolation rather than in sentences, with P3b amplitudes as the primary measure. The authors further argue (Section 4.1) that the original literal facilitation effect may reflect general task demands (match vs. mismatch context) rather than scalar inference processing per se, as their design controls for these task demands and finds no facilitation effect. Confidence upgraded to high based on the authors' explicit, unambiguous failure-to-replicate statement.

description: LSA and HAL cosine similarities (distributional semantic measures) predict lexical priming effects at the item level when item material is directly generated from those similarity measures
original_authors: Günther, Fritz; Dudschig, Carolin; Kaup, Barbara
original_title: Latent semantic analysis cosines as a cognitive similarity measure: evidence from priming studies
replication_authors: Fritz Günther; Carolin Dudschig; Barbara Kaup
replication_title: Predicting Lexical Priming Effects from Distributional Semantic Similarities: A Replication with Extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicate the pattern of results obtained by Günther et al. (2016)' and 'the results replicate the finding that priming effects can be predicted from distributional semantic similarity measures.' Methodological improvements included using a far larger corpus (~880M vs ~5M words), extended cosine range, and improved random effects structure.

description: Temporal gap detection is enhanced in near-hand compared to far-hand space, reflecting increased M-cell (magnocellular) processing near the hands as predicted by the modulated visual pathways hypothesis
original_authors: Davood G. Gozli; Greg L. West; Jay Pratt

replication_authors: Michael Wiemers; Martin H. Fischer
replication_title: Effects of Hand Proximity and Movement Direction in Spatial and Temporal Gap Discrimination
explanation: The authors state: 'our finding of enhanced temporal gap discrimination at intermediate rather than near proximity...reflects a failure to replicate Gozli et al. (2012).' In Experiment 1, temporal gap discrimination was best at intermediate proximity, not near-hand proximity as predicted, and the key near vs. far contrast was not significant.

description: Spatial gap discrimination is reduced in near-hand compared to far-hand space, reflecting increased P-cell (parvocellular) processing in far-hand space as predicted by the modulated visual pathways hypothesis
original_authors: Davood G. Gozli; Greg L. West; Jay Pratt
