replication_authors: Michael Wiemers; Martin H. Fischer
replication_title: Effects of Hand Proximity and Movement Direction in Spatial and Temporal Gap Discrimination
explanation: The authors explicitly state the 'complete absence of an effect of hand-target proximity on spatial gap discrimination, reflects a failure to replicate Gozli et al. (2012).' In Experiment 2, no proximity effect was found, conflicting with MVP's prediction of reduced spatial acuity near the hands.

description: Habit strength mediates the association between trait self-control and unhealthy snack consumption (eating behavior)
original_authors: Marieke A. Adriaanse; Floor M. Kroese; Marleen Gillebaart; Denise T. D. de Ridder
original_title: Effortless inhibition: habit mediates the relation between self-control and unhealthy snack consumption
replication_authors: Marleen Gillebaart; Marieke A. Adriaanse
replication_title: Self-control Predicts Exercise Behavior by Force of Habit, a Conceptual Replication of Adriaanse et al. (2014)
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'findings from this study conceptually replicated earlier findings by Adriaanse et al. (2014), who demonstrated similar associations between trait self-control, habit strength, and snacking behavior.' Both mediation pathways were significant (95% CIs did not include zero), confirming the mediational role of habit strength.

description: Sequential contrasting emotions (fear-then-relief or positive-then-negative) increase compliance with requests and impair cognitive processing relative to a single emotion condition
original_authors: Dariusz Dolinski; Richard Nawrat
original_title: Fear-then-relief procedure for producing compliance: beware when the danger is over
replication_authors: Magdalena C. Kaczmarek; Melanie C. Steffens
replication_title: Mindlessly Polite: A Conceptual Replication of the Emotional Seesaw Effect on Compliance and Information Processing
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Given the clear success of the present replication attempt' and in closing: 'our research conceptually replicates findings by Dolinski and Nawrat (1998)'. Both compliance and mindlessness effects were confirmed using a novel laboratory-based emotion induction technique.

description: Sequential contrasting emotions induce mindlessness and impair cognitive functioning (including simple and complex cognitive tasks), and forcing return to mindfulness reduces compliance rates to control levels
original_authors: Dariusz Dolinski; Michal Ciszek; Kacper Godlewski; Michal Zawadzki
original_title: Fear-then-relief, mindlessness, and cognitive deficits
replication_authors: Magdalena C. Kaczmarek; Melanie C. Steffens
replication_title: Mindlessly Polite: A Conceptual Replication of the Emotional Seesaw Effect on Compliance and Information Processing
explanation: The authors state 'our research conceptually replicates findings by Dolinski and Nawrat (1998) and Dolinski et al. (2002)' and confirm that the ESP impairs cognitive processing. Information recall was also found to be impaired (F(1,77)=17.69, p<0.001, ω²p=0.19), extending the cognitive deficit findings of the 2002 study.

description: Gaze discrimination shows a reversed congruency effect where responses are faster when a face looks toward the observer (direct gaze/eye contact) compared to when face location and gaze direction match (averted gaze)
original_authors: Elena Cañadas; Juan Lupiáñez
original_title: Spatial interference between gaze direction and gaze location: a study on the eye contact effect
replication_authors: Jorge Torres-Marín; Hugo Carretero-Dios; Alberto Acosta; Juan Lupiáñez
replication_title: Eye Contact and Fear of Being Laughed at in a Gaze Discrimination Task
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Replicating Cañadas and Lupiáñez (2012), a main effect of gaze direction was also found, F(1,38) = 68.02, p < 0.001' in Experiment 1, and the General Discussion confirms 'Consistent with previous research (Cañadas and Lupiáñez, 2012; Jones, 2015), we replicated a reversed congruency effect.' The study extends the original by adding emotional expression conditions and testing gelotophobia as an individual difference variable.

description: Emotional expression modulates the eye contact effect in a gaze discrimination task, with the reversed congruency effect being stronger for approach-oriented emotions (happiness and anger) than neutral faces, and non-existent for avoidance-oriented emotions (fear)
original_authors: Steve Jones
original_title: The mediating effects of facial expression on spatial interference between gaze direction and gaze location
replication_authors: Jorge Torres-Marín; Hugo Carretero-Dios; Alberto Acosta; Juan Lupiáñez
replication_title: Eye Contact and Fear of Being Laughed at in a Gaze Discrimination Task
explanation: The emotional expression × gaze direction interaction was significant in Experiment 1 (p = .035) but not Experiment 2 (p = .26). Crucially, the specific pattern Jones described was not confirmed: 'in contrast to Jones's (2015) conclusions regarding the interaction, paired t-tests showed that RTs were lower in the direct gaze than in the averted gaze condition for all emotional expressions' — the effect appeared for fearful faces too, and sadness (avoidance-oriented) showed a pattern like approach-oriented emotions. The authors conclude 'we cannot corroborate the approach and avoidance oriented emotions interpretation that Jones (2015) suggested.'

description: Morally motivated innovators (consumers who adopt a sustainable choice out of ethical concern) elicit derogation and discouragement from observers who had the opportunity to adopt the same ethical choice but declined (do-gooder derogation)
original_authors: Daniel M. Zane; Julie R. Irwin; Rebecca Walker Reczek
original_title: Do less ethical consumers denigrate more ethical consumers? The effect of willful ignorance on judgments of others
replication_authors: Jan Willem Bolderdijk; Claire Brouwer; Gert Cornelissen
replication_title: When Do Morally Motivated Innovators Elicit Inspiration Instead of Irritation?
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Zane et al. (2016) found that morally motivated innovators can elicit irritation and denigration, and discourage other consumers from imitating their sustainable choices. We replicated this phenomenon, and documented a boundary condition.' The replication used a different product (no-packaging grocery store vs. ethical apparel) and added a self-involvement manipulation, finding significant do-gooder derogation among self-involved participants (d=0.59, p=0.005).

description: Grammatical structure of Chinese compound words (subordinate vs. coordinative) interacts with semantic priming to affect compound word recognition in a lexical decision task, such that same structure boosts semantic priming for subordinate compounds but inhibits it for coordinative compounds
original_authors: Phil D. Liu; Catherine McBride-Chang
original_title: Morphological processing of Chinese compounds from a grammatical view
replication_authors: Lei Cui; Fengjiao Cong; Jue Wang; Wenxin Zhang; Yuwei Zheng; Jukka Hyönä
replication_title: Effects of Grammatical Structure of Compound Words on Word Recognition in Chinese
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we failed to find structural priming for either subordinate or coordinative Chinese compound words,' with only a semantic priming effect observed. In the General Discussion they conclude 'in contrast to Liu and McBride-Chang, no evidence for structure priming was obtained,' directly contradicting the original study's key finding of a structure priming interaction.

description: Lower empathy (as measured by the IRI and EQ) is associated with higher levels of internet use disorder, with more robust associations found in a Chinese sample than a German sample
original_authors: Martin Melchers; Mei Li; Yafei Chen; Wanqi Zhang; Christian Montag
original_title: Low empathy is associated with problematic use of the internet: empirical evidence from china and germany
replication_authors: Bernd Lachmann; Cornelia Sindermann; Rayna Y. Sariyska; Ruixue Luo; Martin C. Melchers; Benjamin Becker; Andrew J. Cooper; Christian Montag
replication_title: The Role of Empathy and Life Satisfaction in Internet and Smartphone Use Disorder
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our findings confirm earlier evidence showing a negative link between IUD and empathy (Melchers et al., 2015). As reported in Melchers et al. (2015), more robust associations between the IRI dimensions and IUD were found in the Chinese sample.' Significant correlations between IRI-PD and IUD were found in both Chinese (r = 0.32, p < 0.001) and German (r = 0.35, p < 0.001) samples.

description: Lower life satisfaction is associated with higher levels of internet use disorder
original_authors: Bernd Lachmann; Rayna Sariyska; Christopher Kannen; Andrew Cooper; Christian Montag
original_title: Life satisfaction and problematic internet use: evidence for gender specific effects
replication_authors: Bernd Lachmann; Cornelia Sindermann; Rayna Y. Sariyska; Ruixue Luo; Martin C. Melchers; Benjamin Becker; Andrew J. Cooper; Christian Montag
replication_title: The Role of Empathy and Life Satisfaction in Internet and Smartphone Use Disorder
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: Confirmed medium confidence is appropriate. The authors state they 'supported earlier findings (e.g., Shahnaz and Karim, 2014; Lachmann et al., 2016; Longstreet and Brooks, 2017)' — the 'e.g.' framing and three citations indicate a diffuse confirmation of a general finding, not a targeted replication of Lachmann et al. (2016) specifically. The result 'success' is correct: Table 3 shows significant negative correlations between IUD (s-IAT) and overall life satisfaction in both Chinese (r = -0.18, p < 0.001) and German (r = -0.15, p < 0.001) samples, consistent with Lachmann et al. (2016). However, Lachmann et al. (2016) specifically reported gender-specific effects, which this paper does not directly address for the life satisfaction-IUD link. The ambiguity about whether this is a direct replication of Lachmann et al. (2016) versus general support for the broader literature is genuine.

description: During a joint line bisection task, co-actors' attention is withdrawn away from the partner and toward themselves, producing a negative Social Influence Score (SIS), such that the perceived midpoint of a line shifts away from the co-actor's location
original_authors: Ancrêt Szpak; Michael E.R. Nicholls; Nicole A. Thomas; Simon M. Laham; Tobias Loetscher
original_title: No man is an island: effects of interpersonal proximity on spatial attention
replication_authors: Jill A. Dosso; Kevin H. Roberts; Alessandra DiGiacomo; Alan Kingstone
replication_title: The Influence of Co-action on a Simple Attention Task: A Shift Back to the Status Quo
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This work failed to replicate the effect of attentional withdrawal from the co-actor.' The replication found a mean SIS of +0.12 mm (not significantly different from zero, p=0.19, BF10=0.44), and the replication SIS was significantly different from the original -0.22 mm in the opposite direction (t(30)=3.87, p=0.0006).

description: Working at a disordered (messy) desk increases creativity as measured by the Alternative Uses Task, with participants in disorder conditions generating more creative ideas than those in orderly conditions
original_authors: Kathleen D. Vohs; Joseph P. Redden; Ryan Rahinel
original_title: Physical order produces healthy choices, generosity, and conventionality, whereas disorder produces creativity
replication_authors: Alberto Manzi; Yana Durmysheva; Shannon K. Pinegar; Andrew Rogers; Justine Ramos
replication_title: Workspace Disorder Does Not Influence Creativity and Executive Functions
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we did not find any effect of workspace clutter on cognitive performance' and conclude that 'the effect of working at a disorderly desk for a limited span of time - if true - is small and unreliable.' All Order-Disorder comparisons on creativity measures were non-significant, with none reaching the Bonferroni-corrected alpha of 0.0125.

description: Synchrony (matched movements) increases cohesion and positive affect among group members, with effects amplified when participants share a common goal (shared intentionality)
original_authors: Paul Reddish; Ronald Fischer; Joseph Bulbulia
original_title: Let's dance together: synchrony, shared intentionality and cooperation
replication_authors: Reneeta Mogan; Joseph Bulbulia; Ronald Fischer
replication_title: Joint Action Enhances Cohesion and Positive Affect, but Suppresses Aspects of Creativity When Combined With Shared Goals
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated established findings from recent studies' and 'Synchrony effects on cohesion and positive affect were replicated.' Both synchronous and asynchronous actions significantly increased cohesion and positive affect compared to passive observation (cohesion: F(2,131) = 3.84, p = .024; positive affect: F(2,131) = 3.88, p = .023).

description: Under low perceptual load conditions, instructing participants to focus on only one of two stimuli (a ring and a disk) leads to better memory for the color of the relevant than the irrelevant stimulus, demonstrating irrelevance-induced blindness
original_authors: Baruch Eitam; Yaffa Yeshurun; Kinneret Hassan
original_title: Blinded by irrelevance: pure irrelevance induced 'blindness'
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Christian Büsel; Thomas Ditye; Lukas Muttenthaler; Ulrich Ansorge
replication_title: A Novel Test of Pure Irrelevance-Induced Blindness
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'failed to conceptually replicate the findings of Eitam et al. (2013)' in their entirety. The replication found a significant congruency effect only in the disk condition (χ²(1) = 6.58, p = .009) but not in the ring condition, and the overall test just missed significance (χ²(1) = 3.17, p = .075). The implicit memory measure showed no significant effects at all, and the Discussion concludes that results 'at best partially confirmed' the original findings.

description: The trait Engagement with Moral Beauty (EmB) moderates susceptibility to experiencing state moral elevation in response to watching an elevating video clip, such that people high on EmB are more prone to experience elevation
original_authors: Rhett Diessner; Ravi Iyer; Meghan M. Smith; Jonathan Haidt
original_title: Who engages with moral beauty?
replication_authors: Rico Pohling; Rhett Diessner; Shawnee Stacy; Destiny Woodward; Anja Strobel
replication_title: Moral Elevation and Economic Games: The Moderating Role of Personality
explanation: The present study found that EmB moderated the behavioral effects of elevation (dictator game generosity) but NOT the susceptibility to experience elevation itself. As the authors state: 'Our findings corroborate Diessner et al. (2013) since we found evidence for the moderating role of EmB in moral elevation. However, in our study only the behavioral effects of elevation were moderated and not the level of state elevation ratings, as was the case in Diessner et al. (2013).' The replication was partial — the broader moderating role of EmB was supported, but the specific original finding (moderation of elevation state itself) was not reproduced.

description: A double dissociation whereby Honesty-Humility (H-H) predicts active cooperation (dictator game generosity) while Agreeableness (AG) predicts reactive cooperation (ultimatum game acceptance), with H-H correlating with dictator game but not ultimatum game behavior and AG correlating with ultimatum game but not dictator game behavior
original_authors: Benjamin E. Hilbig; Ingo Zettler; Felix Leist; Timo Heydasch
original_title: It takes two: honesty-humility and agreeableness differentially predict active versus reactive cooperation
replication_authors: Rico Pohling; Rhett Diessner; Shawnee Stacy; Destiny Woodward; Anja Strobel
replication_title: Moral Elevation and Economic Games: The Moderating Role of Personality
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'we could not replicate the double dissociation between active/reactive cooperation and H-H/AG that was found by Hilbig et al. (2013).' While H-H did correlate with active cooperation (r = 0.31, p < 0.01), AG was also positively related to active cooperation (r = 0.22, p < 0.05) rather than uniquely predicting reactive cooperation, and no significant correlation was found between AG and ultimatum game behavior (r = -0.07, p = 0.53).

description: Attentional-selection (mere-selection) effect on subsequent choice (Exp 1, no deadline, N=43): replicated, targets preferred, d=0.305.
original_authors: Chris Janiszewski; Andrew Kuo; Nader T. Tavassoli
original_title: The influence of selective attention and inattention to products on subsequent choice
replication_authors: Nadiia Makarina; Ronald Hübner; Arnd Florack
replication_title: Increased Preference and Value of Consumer Products by Attentional Selection
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Experiment 1 discussion: 'we not only replicated the attentional selection effects found by Janiszewski et al. (2013) but also generalized their results obtained with unknown products to choices between known products.' Targets were chosen on 55.2% of trials vs. 44.8% for distractors, t(42) = 2.00, p < 0.05, d = 0.305.

description: Attentional-selection effect on subsequent choice (Exp 2, 700-ms response deadline, N=47): replicated, targets preferred, d=0.440.
original_authors: Chris Janiszewski; Andrew Kuo; Nader T. Tavassoli
original_title: The influence of selective attention and inattention to products on subsequent choice
replication_authors: Nadiia Makarina; Ronald Hübner; Arnd Florack
replication_title: Increased Preference and Value of Consumer Products by Attentional Selection
explanation: The Experiment 2 discussion states: 'The results from this experiment again replicated the attentional-selection effect.' Former targets were chosen on 56.4% of trials, t(47) = 3.05, p < 0.01, d = 0.440, additionally finding that value ratings were significantly higher for former targets than distractors, extending the original findings.

description: High-confidence errors (incorrect answers a person was confident in) trigger epistemic emotions (surprise, curiosity, confusion) more strongly than achievement emotions (pride, shame), and these epistemic emotions in turn positively predict knowledge exploration behavior
original_authors: Vogl, Elisabeth; Pekrun, Reinhard; Murayama, Kou; Loderer, Kristina
original_title: Surprised-curious-confused: epistemic emotions and knowledge exploration
replication_authors: Elisabeth Vogl; Reinhard Pekrun; Kou Murayama; Kristina Loderer; Sandra Schubert
replication_title: Surprise, Curiosity, and Confusion Promote Knowledge Exploration: Evidence for Robust Effects of Epistemic Emotions
explanation: The authors explicitly state in Study 1's Discussion: 'In sum, the findings from Vogl et al. (2019, Study 3) were directly replicated by Study 1 of the present research.' Core patterns of antecedents and outcomes of epistemic emotions were confirmed, though the confusion-exploration effect was directionally consistent but marginally non-significant (p = 0.060).

description: High-confidence errors (incorrect answers a person was confident in) trigger epistemic emotions (surprise, curiosity, confusion) more strongly than achievement emotions (pride, shame), and these epistemic emotions in turn positively predict knowledge exploration behavior
original_authors: Vogl, Elisabeth; Pekrun, Reinhard; Murayama, Kou; Loderer, Kristina
original_title: Surprised-curious-confused: epistemic emotions and knowledge exploration
replication_authors: Elisabeth Vogl; Reinhard Pekrun; Kou Murayama; Kristina Loderer; Sandra Schubert
replication_title: Surprise, Curiosity, and Confusion Promote Knowledge Exploration: Evidence for Robust Effects of Epistemic Emotions
explanation: Study 2 replicated the main patterns (epistemic emotions triggered by high-confidence errors; surprise and curiosity predicting exploration) but the effect of pride after correct answers failed to replicate in terms of both direction and significance (ß = -0.114, p = 0.077), and the confusion-exploration effect again did not reach significance. The authors characterize the overall pattern as 'largely replicated' with specific noted exceptions.

description: Offering participants a monetary reward to recall to-be-forgotten (TBF) words after an initial memory test does not increase recall of TBF words, suggesting the directed forgetting effect is not driven by intentional strategic withholding of TBF memories at retrieval
original_authors: Colin M. Macleod
original_title: The item and list methods of directed forgetting: test differences and the role of demand characteristics
replication_authors: Holly J. Bowen; Sara N. Gallant; Diane H. Moon
replication_title: Influence of Reward Motivation on Directed Forgetting in Younger and Older Adults
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Replicating findings from Macleod (1999), in Experiments 3 and 4, we found little evidence of this as participants did not freely recall very many words overall, but did recall slightly more TBR than TBF words, providing evidence against the motivational prediction that participants were withholding their memory at the time of retrieval.' The recall task was directly modeled after Macleod (1999) and produced consistent results.

description: Conspiracy beliefs and conspiracy mentality are associated with negative attitudes toward vaccination science
original_authors: Stephan Lewandowsky; Gilles E. Gignac; Klaus Oberauer
original_title: The role of conspiracist ideation and worldviews in predicting rejection of science
replication_authors: Paul Bertin; Kenzo Nera; Sylvain Delouvée
replication_title: Conspiracy Beliefs, Rejection of Vaccination, and Support for hydroxychloroquine: A Conceptual Replication-Extension in the COVID-19 Pandemic Context
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are 'conceptually replicating a research by Lewandowsky et al. (2013)' regarding attitude toward vaccination science. Both Studies 1 (N=409) and 2 (N=396) found that COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs significantly and negatively predicted attitudes toward vaccination, and the Discussion confirms this 'conceptually replicates research conducted before the pandemic (Lewandowsky et al., 2013)'.

description: Exposure to anti-vaccine conspiracy theories decreases vaccination intention
original_authors: Daniel Jolley; Karen M. Douglas
original_title: The effects of anti-vaccine conspiracy theories on vaccination intentions
replication_authors: Paul Bertin; Kenzo Nera; Sylvain Delouvée
replication_title: Conspiracy Beliefs, Rejection of Vaccination, and Support for hydroxychloroquine: A Conceptual Replication-Extension in the COVID-19 Pandemic Context
explanation: The authors explicitly state they are 'conceptually replicating Jolley and Douglas (2014)' on vaccination intention. In Study 2 (N=396), COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs significantly and negatively predicted intention to be vaccinated against COVID-19, and the Discussion confirms this 'conceptually replicates research conducted before the pandemic (Lewandowsky et al., 2013; Jolley and Douglas, 2014)'.

description: Participants in the WebSurf task show economic foraging behaviors: preferring shorter delays and choosing to wait longer for more preferred video categories, with revealed preferences indexed by offer threshold correlating with video ratings and rankings
original_authors: Abram SV; Breton YA; Schmidt B.; Redish AD; MacDonald AW 3rd
original_title: The web-surf task: a translational model of human decision-making
replication_authors: Kazinka R.; MacDonald AW 3rd; Redish AD
replication_title: Sensitivity to Sunk Costs Depends on Attention to the Delay
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Data collected from Amazon mTurk users on the original version of WebSurf replicated findings of data collected in the lab (Abram et al., 2016, 2019a; Sweis et al., 2018a).' They found 93.9% of participants showed the predicted economic behaviors, and threshold correlations with ratings and rankings were significant (e.g., threshold × rating: mean r = 0.42, t(471) = 15.5, p < 0.001, d = 0.71).

description: Humans show susceptibility to sunk costs in the WebSurf task: the longer they wait in the wait phase, the more likely they are to remain and earn the video reward, but sunk costs do not accrue during the offer phase
original_authors: Sweis BM; Abram SV; Schmidt BJ; Seeland KD; MacDonald AW 3rd; Thomas MJ; Redish AD
original_title: Sensitivity to "sunk costs" in mice, rats, and humans
replication_authors: Kazinka R.; MacDonald AW 3rd; Redish AD
replication_title: Sensitivity to Sunk Costs Depends on Attention to the Delay
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'our results on the original version replicated the observation that subjects showed a susceptibility to sunk costs during the wait phase,' finding a significant interaction between time spent and time remaining (F(1,119) = 26.7, p < 0.001, η² = 0.038), and confirmed no sunk cost effect in the offer phase. The replication was conducted with an mTurk sample (online) rather than the original lab undergraduates.

description: Neutral male faces structurally resemble anger expressions more than female faces, while female neutral faces structurally resemble fear expressions more than male faces, as detected by a connectionist neural network model trained on emotional expressions
original_authors: Leslie A. Zebrowitz; Masako Kikuchi; Jean-Marc Fellous
original_title: Facial resemblance to emotions: group differences, impression effects, and race stereotypes
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Daniel N. Albohn; Reginald B. Adams
replication_title: The Expressive Triad: Structure, Color, and Texture Similarity of Emotion Expressions Predict Impressions of Neutral Faces
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The results from Study 1 replicated previous computational and behavioral work examining emotion stereotypes related to gender' and confirm that 'male neutral faces were more similar to anger expressions and female neutral faces more similar to fear expressions.' This is a close extension because the same general paradigm is used but extended to color and texture metrics beyond structure alone.

description: Structural resemblance of neutral faces to specific emotion expressions (e.g., anger, happiness) is correlated with human trait impressions of those faces (e.g., dominance, caring), as detected by a Bayesian network classifier trained on emotional expressions
original_authors: Christopher P. Said; Nicu Sebe; Alexander Todorov
original_title: Structural resemblance to emotional expressions predicts evaluation of emotionally neutral faces
replication_authors: Daniel N. Albohn; Reginald B. Adams
replication_title: The Expressive Triad: Structure, Color, and Texture Similarity of Emotion Expressions Predict Impressions of Neutral Faces
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their General Discussion: 'The present research proposed an extension of previous computer vision work that has examined the structural resemblance of neutral faces to specific expressions and personality traits (Said et al., 2009; Zebrowitz et al., 2010),' and Studies 2 and 4 confirm that emotion-resembling cues in neutral faces (anger output mediating dominance ratings) successfully replicate and extend Said et al.'s core finding. This is a close extension because the same paradigm is used but with updated models and additional face metrics.

description: Temporally-structured encoding (predictable ISI patterns between scenes) improves recognition memory for scenes compared to temporally-unstructured encoding
original_authors: Sathesan Thavabalasingam; Edward B. O’Neil; Zheng Zeng; Andy C. H. Lee
original_title: Recognition memory is improved by a structured temporal framework during encoding
replication_authors: Mrinmayi Kulkarni; Deborah E. Hannula
replication_title: Temporal Regularity May Not Improve Memory for Item-Specific Detail
explanation: Experiment 3 used identical materials (grayscale scenes) and procedure as Thavabalasingam et al. (2016) Experiment 1. The authors report: 'unlike Thavabalasingam et al. (2016), performance was not affected by timing, t(23) = 0.68, p = 0.50, d = 0.15, BF = 0.27', and conclude that temporal regularity did not improve recognition memory in any of their experiments.

description: Temporally-structured encoding (predictable ISI patterns) improves recognition memory for items, with structured timing rescuing performance from proactive interference when structured block follows unstructured block
original_authors: Sathesan Thavabalasingam; Edward B. O’Neil; Zheng Zeng; Andy C. H. Lee
original_title: Recognition memory is improved by a structured temporal framework during encoding
replication_authors: Mrinmayi Kulkarni; Deborah E. Hannula
replication_title: Temporal Regularity May Not Improve Memory for Item-Specific Detail
explanation: Experiment 1 adapted the Thavabalasingam et al. (2016) paradigm for object memory with item-specific lures (slightly modified timing parameters). No effect of temporal regularity was found on corrected recognition (t(23) = 1.61, p = 0.12, d = 0.28, BF = 0.67) or BPS scores, and contrary to the original, temporal regularity did not rescue performance from proactive interference.

description: Temporally-structured encoding (predictable ISI patterns) improves recognition memory for items, with structured timing rescuing performance from proactive interference when structured block follows unstructured block
original_authors: Sathesan Thavabalasingam; Edward B. O’Neil; Zheng Zeng; Andy C. H. Lee
original_title: Recognition memory is improved by a structured temporal framework during encoding
replication_authors: Mrinmayi Kulkarni; Deborah E. Hannula
replication_title: Temporal Regularity May Not Improve Memory for Item-Specific Detail
explanation: Experiment 2 used identical timing parameters as Thavabalasingam et al. (2016) but with objects instead of scenes. No effect of temporal regularity was found on corrected recognition (t(23) = 1.25, p = 0.22, d = 0.27, BF = 0.43), BPS scores, or d' scores (t(23) = 1.38, p = 0.18, d = 0.34, BF = 0.50). Authors concluded 'we did not find an effect of temporal expectation on memory for item detail.'

description: Insecurely attached psychotherapists differ significantly from securely attached psychotherapists in 9 out of 14 personality styles as measured by the Personality Styles and Disorder Inventory (PSDI)
original_authors: Peter, Burkhard; Böbel, Eva
original_title: Significant differences in personality styles of securely and insecurely attached psychotherapists. Data, reflections and implications
replication_authors: Burkhard Peter; Thomas G. Wolf
replication_title: Replication Studies on Significant Differences in Personality Profiles of Securely and Insecurely Attached Psychotherapists and Dentists
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'the results of the preceding attachment study of Peter and Böbel (2020b) have been replicated.' The HYP DGZH sample (dentists using hypnosis) showed significant differences between securely and insecurely attached participants in 10 of 14 personality styles, matching or exceeding the 9 styles found in the original.

description: Insecurely attached psychotherapists differ significantly from securely attached psychotherapists in 9 out of 14 personality styles as measured by the Personality Styles and Disorder Inventory (PSDI)
original_authors: Peter, Burkhard; Böbel, Eva
original_title: Significant differences in personality styles of securely and insecurely attached psychotherapists. Data, reflections and implications
replication_authors: Burkhard Peter; Thomas G. Wolf
replication_title: Replication Studies on Significant Differences in Personality Profiles of Securely and Insecurely Attached Psychotherapists and Dentists
explanation: The HYP MEG sample (mixed healthcare professionals using hypnosis/psychotherapy) showed significant differences between securely and insecurely attached participants in 10 of 14 personality styles, confirming the original finding. The authors conclude the results of Peter and Böbel (2020b) were replicated across this sample.

description: Insecurely attached psychotherapists differ significantly from securely attached psychotherapists in 9 out of 14 personality styles as measured by the Personality Styles and Disorder Inventory (PSDI)
original_authors: Peter, Burkhard; Böbel, Eva
original_title: Significant differences in personality styles of securely and insecurely attached psychotherapists. Data, reflections and implications
replication_authors: Burkhard Peter; Thomas G. Wolf
replication_title: Replication Studies on Significant Differences in Personality Profiles of Securely and Insecurely Attached Psychotherapists and Dentists
explanation: The NONHYP DENT sample (dentists not using psychological methods) showed significant differences in only 7 of 14 personality styles — roughly half the original's 9 styles. The authors interpret this partial replication as meaningful: professionals not using psychological methods show fewer attachment-related personality differences, suggesting the full pattern is specific to those using psychological methods.

description: Exposure to Mandarin-accented English syllable-final /d/ (via lexically-guided exposure) improves listeners' goodness ratings for non-native-accented /d/- and /t/-final words during test, compared to a control exposure group
original_authors: Xin Xie; Rachel M. Theodore; Emily B. Myers
original_title: More than a boundary shift: perceptual adaptation to foreign-accented speech reshapes the internal structure of phonetic categories
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Tan M.; Xie X.; Jaeger TF
replication_title: Using Rational Models to Interpret the Results of Experiments on Accent Adaptation
explanation: The Swedish experiment was explicitly designed as a replication of Xie et al. (2017) but with a different language pair (Flemish-accented Swedish instead of Mandarin-accented English). The authors report that 'Unlike Xie et al. (2017), however, the Swedish data did not yield an effect of /d/-exposure on ratings during test. In fact, the effect of exposure went numerically in the opposite direction in the Swedish data.'

description: Rats value social release of a trapped cagemate equally to high-value food rewards (chocolate chips), as evidenced by similar latencies to open food and social-release doors
original_authors: Inbal Ben-Ami Bartal; Jean Decety; Peggy Mason
original_title: Empathy and pro-social behavior in rats
replication_authors: Haoran Wan; Cyrus Kirkman; Greg Jensen; Timothy D. Hackenberg
replication_title: Failure to Find Altruistic Food Sharing in Rats
explanation: The authors found that relative preference between food and social release was not invariant but depended on motivational conditions: under low food motivation (unrestricted home cage access), food and social release were chosen about equally (consistent with the original), but under high food motivation (restricted access), rats strongly preferred food. They conclude 'relative value of social release and food are always subject to these (and other) variables, and it would therefore be premature to draw broad conclusions about their relative value from sampling only a limited range of conditions.'

description: Rats altruistically share food with a trapped cagemate, releasing the rat before consuming all available food and thus sacrificing high-value food for the benefit of their social partner
original_authors: Inbal Ben-Ami Bartal; Jean Decety; Peggy Mason
original_title: Empathy and pro-social behavior in rats
replication_authors: Haoran Wan; Cyrus Kirkman; Greg Jensen; Timothy D. Hackenberg
replication_title: Failure to Find Altruistic Food Sharing in Rats
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'we found no evidence to support the 2011 claim by Ben-Ami Bartal et al. that a rat willingly shares food with another rat.' Sharing occurred on only 1% of opportunities across all conditions, including those that closely matched the original procedure. The abstract states the results 'are therefore inconsistent with claims in the literature that rats are altruistically motivated to share food with other rats.'

description: Multilevel latent profile analysis of teacher and school demand-resource profiles (using job demands, job resources, and personal resources) identifies distinct teacher profiles and school profiles, and these profiles are associated with teacher work-related outcomes (job satisfaction and occupational commitment)
original_authors: Rebecca J. Collie; Lars-Erik Malmberg; Andrew J. Martin; Pamela Sammons; Alexandre J. S. Morin
original_title: A multilevel person-centered examination of teachers' workplace demands and resources: links with work-related well-being
replication_authors: Rebecca J. Collie; Andrew J. Martin; Alexandre J. S. Morin; Lars-Erik Malmberg; Pamela Sammons
replication_title: A Multilevel Person-Centered Examination of Teachers' Workplace Experiences: Replication and Extension With Links to Instructional Support and Achievement
explanation: The authors report that 'many of the findings from Collie et al. (2020a) were replicated' including the identification of the same two school profiles (Supportive and Unsupportive) and largely similar associations with outcomes, but a notable structural difference emerged: six rather than five teacher profiles were identified, and the relative prevalence of profiles differed greatly (Struggler profiles about half the sample vs. one-fifth in the original). The authors state 'our results generally replicated prior findings, some differences were also observed.'

description: Explanations for odd behaviors are rated as more satisfying when the behavior is given a category label (used in a circular/vitiosus explanation), compared to explanations without a label
original_authors: Carly Giffin; Daniel Wilkenfeld; Tania Lombrozo
original_title: The explanatory effect of a label: Explanations with named categories are more satisfying
replication_authors: Ivan A. Aslanov; Yulia V. Sudorgina; Alexey A. Kotov
replication_title: The Explanatory Effect of a Label: Its Influence on a Category Persists Even If We Forget the Label
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We repeated the study by Giffin et al. (2017) and replicated the explanatory effect of a label. We obtained significant differences in 7 of the 9 statements in which differences were reported by the original study's authors... Overall, the label effect was replicated.'

description: Explanations for odd behaviors are rated as more satisfying when the behavior is given a category label (used in a circular/vitiosus explanation), compared to explanations without a label
original_authors: Carly Giffin; Daniel Wilkenfeld; Tania Lombrozo
original_title: The explanatory effect of a label: Explanations with named categories are more satisfying
replication_authors: Ivan A. Aslanov; Yulia V. Sudorgina; Alexey A. Kotov
replication_title: The Explanatory Effect of a Label: Its Influence on a Category Persists Even If We Forget the Label
explanation: In a follow-up testing the label effect one week after reading, the authors found the label still significantly affected at least 4 measures (Blame, Generalization to Others, Generalization to Self, Psychological Nature), concluding 'the label effect persists over time' and 'the labeled category retains the influence of the label even when the label itself is forgotten.'

description: Learning dealbreaker traits about a potential partner reduces interest in pursuing that partner, with dealbreakers having stronger effects than dealmakers, especially in long-term mating contexts and among women compared to men
original_authors: Peter K. Jonason; Kaitlyn P. White; Laith Al-Shawaf
original_title: Should I stay or should I go?: individual differences in response to romantic dealmakers and dealbreakers
replication_authors: Peter K. Jonason; Kaitlyn P. White; Abigail H. Lowder; Laith Al-Shawaf
replication_title: To see or not to see (again): Dealbreakers and dealmakers in relation to social inclusion
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated previous research showing dealbreakers to be less appealing than dealmakers, especially in the long term (compared to short term) context and to women (compared to men).' Results in both Study 1 (N=306) and Study 2 (N=304) confirm the dealbreaker effect with large effect sizes (d=-1.41 to -3.63).

description: Americans with higher authoritarian dominance tendencies show less concern about COVID-19 and report less frequent mask wearing
original_authors: Eric C. Prichard; Stephen D. Christman
original_title: Authoritarianism, conspiracy beliefs, gender and COVID-19: links between individual differences and concern about COVID-19, mask wearing behaviors, and the tendency to blame China for the virus
replication_authors: Prichard EC; Turner KA
replication_title: Authoritarianism, psychopathy, and resistance to wearing masks during the COVID-19 pandemic: A partial replication and extension of key findings
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This represents a replication of Prichard and Christman (2020a), but in a larger sample' and confirm in the Discussion that 'The present study replicates that finding with a larger sample.' Authoritarianism was significantly negatively correlated with mask wearing (r = -0.155, p < 0.001), consistent with the original finding.

description: Job attitudes and subjective wellbeing of low-waged workers follow a sigmoidal (working poverty trap) curve relative to hourly wage, pivoting upward at the living wage threshold
original_authors: Stuart Colin Carr; Molefe Maleka; Ines Meyer; Marie-Louise Barry; Jarrod Haar; Jane Parker; James Arrowsmith; Christian Yao; Darrin Hodgetts; Harvey Jones; Amanda Young-Hausner; Emeline Afeaki-Mafile’o; Ann-Helen Rasmussen; Siautu Alefaio-Tugia; Ben Falealili; Kate Mafile’o; Tokilupe Pikula; Natassia Wolfgramm; Holika ‘Uhila; Yvonne Falealili; Arno Grueber; Leo Berlim; Emalata Hausia; Mary Ntsweng; Jafta Koza; Doutzen Groothof; Susan van Schie; Isabel Lyckholm; Abhigyan Naithani
original_title: How can wages sustain a living? By getting ahead of the curve
replication_authors: Stuart C. Carr; Jarrod Haar; Darrin Hodgetts; Harvey Jones; James Arrowsmith; Jane Parker; Amanda Young-Hauser; Siautu Alefaio
replication_title: Pandemic or Not, Worker Subjective Wellbeing Pivots About the Living Wage Point: A Replication, Extension, and Policy Challenge in Aotearoa New Zealand
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'these findings replicate earlier findings' and that 'replicability was sustained through a pandemic.' Using LOESS analysis with a new 2020 pandemic-era cohort (n=1,027) from New Zealand, they found the same sigmoidal pivot in job attitudes and wellbeing at the living wage threshold, consistent with Carr et al. (2018).

description: In a large nationwide New Zealand sample, job attitudes (satisfaction, engagement, commitment, etc.) follow a sigmoidal pattern relative to hourly wage, pivoting from negative to positive at the living wage level
original_authors: Stuart C. Carr; Jarrod Haar; Darrin Hodgetts; James Arrowsmith; Jane Parker; Amanda Young-Hauser; Siautu Alefaio-Tuglia; Harvey Jones
original_title: An employee's living wage and their quality of work life: how important household size and income?
replication_authors: Stuart C. Carr; Jarrod Haar; Darrin Hodgetts; Harvey Jones; James Arrowsmith; Jane Parker; Amanda Young-Hauser; Siautu Alefaio
replication_title: Pandemic or Not, Worker Subjective Wellbeing Pivots About the Living Wage Point: A Replication, Extension, and Policy Challenge in Aotearoa New Zealand
explanation: The authors directly state that their 2022 study 'replicated findings from Carr et al. (2019)' and extended them to subjective wellbeing during the pandemic. Results from the 2020 cohort (n=1,027) converged with the prior findings, showing the same sigmoidal pattern pivoting at the NZ living wage level.

description: A demanding 2-back working memory task following encoding produces similar memory performance to a wakeful rest condition (both better than a rest+sounds condition that promotes autobiographical thinking), suggesting the 2-back task suppresses autobiographical thinking and thereby allows consolidation
original_authors: Samarth Varma; Sander M. Daselaar; Roy P. C. Kessels; Atsuko Takashima
original_title: Promotion and suppression of autobiographical thinking differentially affect episodic memory consolidation
replication_authors: Olivia King; Jessica Nicosia
replication_title: The effects of wakeful rest on memory consolidation in an online memory study
explanation: In Experiment 1 (between-subjects, online, incidental encoding), recall was significantly better in the rest condition than the 2-back condition (d=0.50, p=0.01) and the rest+sounds condition (d=0.46, p=0.02), while 2-back and rest+sounds did not differ (p=0.88). This directly contradicts Varma et al.'s finding that rest and 2-back perform equivalently. The authors explicitly state: 'in contrast to the findings presented by Varma et al. (2018), participants' recall was worse following the 2-back condition than following the rest condition.'

description: A demanding 2-back working memory task following encoding produces similar memory performance to a wakeful rest condition (both better than a rest+sounds condition that promotes autobiographical thinking), suggesting the 2-back task suppresses autobiographical thinking and thereby allows consolidation
original_authors: Samarth Varma; Sander M. Daselaar; Roy P. C. Kessels; Atsuko Takashima
original_title: Promotion and suppression of autobiographical thinking differentially affect episodic memory consolidation
replication_authors: Olivia King; Jessica Nicosia
replication_title: The effects of wakeful rest on memory consolidation in an online memory study
explanation: In Experiment 2 (within-subjects, online, using Varma et al.'s exact stimuli), the proportional retention score was significantly better in the rest condition than in the rest+sounds condition (d=0.50, p=0.01), but the 2-back vs rest+sounds comparison was not significant (p=0.40), failing to replicate the key finding. The authors note: 'we were able to replicate the general pattern of results by Varma et al. (2018), although the pairwise comparisons did not reach significance.'

description: ADHD characteristics negatively predict engineering GPA and positively predict figural divergent thinking in undergraduate engineering students
original_authors: Christa L. Taylor; Arash Esmaili Zaghi; James C. Kaufman; Sally M. Reis; Joseph S. Renzulli
original_title: Divergent thinking and academic performance of students with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder characteristics in engineering
replication_authors: Christa L. Taylor; Arash Esmaili Zaghi
replication_title: The interplay of ADHD characteristics and executive functioning with the GPA and divergent thinking of engineering students: A conceptual replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly label this a conceptual replication and describe results as 'partially consistent with hypotheses derived from the results of that study.' The negative relationship between executive functioning difficulties and GPA was replicated, but the positive relationship between ADHD characteristics and figural divergent thinking was not, and divergent thinking unexpectedly positively predicted GPA rather than negatively.

description: University students in Hong Kong show generally positive perceptions of a law abidance leadership lecture (delivered via hybrid HyFlex mode), including satisfaction with lecture attributes, teacher attributes, and appreciation of law abidance and national security
original_authors: Daniel T. L. Shek; Xiaoqin Zhu; Xiang Li; Diya Dou
original_title: Satisfaction with HyFlex teaching and law-abiding leadership education in Hong Kong university students under COVID-19
original_journal: Applied Research in Quality of Life
replication_authors: Daniel T. L. Shek; Diya Dou; Xiaoqin Zhu; Xiang Li
replication_title: Law abidance leadership education for university students in Hong Kong: Post-lecture evaluation
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'From a replication perspective, the present findings replicated the findings reported by Shek et al. (2022b) in a new sample of students taking the subject via another mode (i.e., online teaching and learning mode) at another time.' The Conclusion reiterates: 'The present findings replicated the findings of a previous study by Shek et al. (2022b).' The current study used the same 26-item evaluation instrument but delivered the lecture via online mode rather than hybrid mode.

description: Preschool children share more food with friends than acquaintances, with girls showing a stronger preference for sharing with friends than boys; sharing is primarily driven by active elicitation from recipients; and successful prior experience as a recipient facilitates subsequent sharing behavior
original_authors: Leann Lipps Birch; Jane Billman
original_title: Preschool children's food sharing with friends and acquaintances
replication_authors: Elizabeth T. Hallers-Haalboom; Marjolijn M. Vermande; Edwin J. C. van Leeuwen; Elisabeth H. M. Sterck
replication_title: Food sharing with friends and acquaintances: A study in preschool boys and girls
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'only a small degree of agreement with the original study was found: Some significant findings could not be replicated, and some unconfirmed hypotheses of the original study were supported.' Some effects were replicated (elicited sharing more frequent with friends), some were not (preferred food shared more with friends), and the key relationship*sex interaction for non-preferred food was found in the opposite direction.

description: Processing single metaphors involves suppressing features related exclusively to the literal meaning of the metaphoric vehicle (superordinates) after 1000 milliseconds, while metaphor-related features (distinctive properties) remain activated
original_authors: Rubio Fernández, Paula
original_title: Suppression in metaphor interpretation: differences between meaning selection and meaning construction
replication_authors: Camilo R. Ronderos; Ingrid Lossius Falkum
replication_title: Suppression of literal meaning in single and extended metaphors
explanation: The authors explicitly confirm replication of the original finding: 'we found that during comprehension of single metaphors, metaphor-related features of the vehicle remain activated 1,000 milliseconds after metaphor comprehension while literal-related features show reduced activation, supporting the original findings of Rubio Fernández (2007).' The three-way interaction between CONTEXT, FEATURE TYPE and ISI was significant (t=3.3, p<0.005) for single metaphors.

description: Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping (as measured by a delayed memory test one week later)
original_authors: Jeffrey D. Karpicke; Janell R. Blunt
original_title: Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping
replication_authors: Roland Mayrhofer; Christof Kuhbandner; Katja Frischholz
replication_title: Re-examining the testing effect as a learning strategy: the advantage of retrieval practice over concept mapping as a methodological artifact
explanation: The authors explicitly state that RP+AM+AI and CM-AM-AI conditions are 'exact replications' of Karpicke and Blunt's (2011) original conditions, and they successfully replicated the original finding: 'our data replicated Karpicke and Blunt's (2011) finding that performance in a retrieval practice condition where participants additionally memorize the learning material is better compared to a concept mapping condition without additional memorization' (p < 0.001, Tukey's HSD). The replication succeeded but the paper demonstrates this is a methodological artifact driven by unequal memorization time rather than retrieval practice per se.

description: Correct and incorrect eyewitness statements occupy different semantic spaces, detectable via LSA analysis of word 5-grams
original_authors: Farhan Sarwar; Sverker Sikström; Carl Martin Allwood; Åse Innes-Ker
original_title: Predicting correctness of eyewitness statements using the semantic evaluation method (SEM)
replication_authors: Philip U. Gustafsson; Sverker Sikström; Torun Lindholm
replication_title: The semantic structure of accuracy in eyewitness testimony
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicate the finding by Sarwar et al. (2015) with both a new sample, but more importantly, with natural verbal output following an eyewitness interview, rather than written down statements.' Both LSA and BERT analyses showed significant differences in semantic space between correct and incorrect statements (LSA: t(846) = -4.35, p < .001, d = 0.37).

description: Correct and incorrect eyewitness statements occupy different semantic spaces, detectable via LSA analysis of word 5-grams
original_authors: Farhan Sarwar; Sverker Sikström; Carl Martin Allwood; Åse Innes-Ker
original_title: Predicting correctness of eyewitness statements using the semantic evaluation method (SEM)
replication_authors: Philip U. Gustafsson; Sverker Sikström; Torun Lindholm
replication_title: The semantic structure of accuracy in eyewitness testimony
explanation: Study 2 also replicated the core finding: 'Overall, we replicated the results of the first study, demonstrating that correct and incorrect statements differ in semantic content.' LSA analysis: t(1534) = -8.29, p < .001, d = 0.48. The communion/dominance differences from Study 1 did not replicate, but those were extensions beyond the original Sarwar et al. (2015) finding.

description: Fearful faces gain faster access to consciousness than neutral faces in the breaking continuous flash suppression (b-CFS) paradigm, reflecting a preconscious threat bias (meta-analytic d = 0.49)
original_authors: Nicholas Hedger; Katie L. H. Gray; Matthew Garner; Wendy J. Adams
original_title: Are visual threats prioritized without awareness? A critical review and meta-analysis involving 3 behavioral paradigms and 2696 observers
replication_authors: Ulrich W. D. Müller; Antje B. M. Gerdes; Georg W. Alpers
replication_title: Setting the tone: crossmodal emotional face-voice combinations in continuous flash suppression
explanation: The authors explicitly state their first aim was 'to replicate earlier findings that fearful faces are processed faster in b-CFS (Hedger et al., 2016).' In their results, fearful faces broke suppression significantly faster than neutral faces (F(1,34) = 8.25, p = 0.007, ηp² = 0.20), and the Discussion confirms: 'Our findings further substantiate a preconscious threat bias for fearful faces in b-CFS.'

description: Ostracism (via Cyberball exclusion) causes goal blockage of the belonging goal and triggers cognitive-affective and behavioral goal disengagement processes, including devaluation of the belonging goal, devaluation of the ostracizing group, and behavioral deprioritization of ostracizing group members
original_authors: Farina Rühs; Werner Greve; Cathleen Kappes
original_title: Inducing and blocking the goal to belong in an experimental setting: goal disengagement research using Cyberball
replication_authors: Farina Rühs; Werner Greve; Cathleen Kappes
replication_title: Goal adjustment processes as coping responses to a blocked goal: the sample case of ostracism
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'One aim of the present study was to conceptually replicate the findings of Rühs et al. (2022). In sum, almost all findings of Rühs et al. (2022) could be replicated.' The replication successfully reproduced the main effects of ostracism on goal attainability, well-being, explicit group devaluation, and behavioral deprioritization, though the implicit IAT measure showed no effect and one minor functionality correlation could not be replicated.

description: Salient color singleton distractors appearing at a high-probability spatial location produce less attentional capture than those at low-probability locations, demonstrating learned location-based distractor suppression
original_authors: Benchi Wang; Jan Theeuwes
original_title: Statistical regularities modulate attentional capture
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Catherine W. Seitz; Anthony W. Sali
replication_title: Category-like representation of statistical regularities allows for stable distractor suppression
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the General Discussion: 'In replication of a growing body of research, we found that participants learned the location a salient distractor tended to appear with higher frequency and suppressed attentional selection of this location.' Both Experiment 1 (lab) and Experiment 2 (online) successfully replicated the core learned distractor suppression effect using a variant of Wang and Theeuwes's (2018a) paradigm.

description: Abnormal inverse left-sided ventromedial prefrontal cortex-amygdala effective connectivity to happy faces in females with major depressive disorder (MDD)
original_authors: Jorge Renner Cardoso de Almeida; Amelia Versace; Andrea Mechelli; Stefanie Hassel; Karina Quevedo; David Jerome Kupfer; Mary Louise Phillips
original_title: Abnormal amygdala-prefrontal effective connectivity to happy faces differentiates bipolar from major depression
replication_authors: Jorge Renner Cardoso de Almeida; Dina Michaela Kronhaus; Etienne L. Sibille; Scott A. Langenecker; Amelia Versace; Edmund James LaBarbara; Mary Louise Phillips
replication_title: Abnormal Left-Sided Orbitomedial Prefrontal Cortical?Amygdala Connectivity during Happy and Fear Face Processing: A Potential Neural Mechanism of Female MDD
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated our previous finding of abnormal inverse left-sided OMPFC-amygdala connectivity to positive emotional stimuli in an independent group of females with MDD using a novel implicit emotion processing paradigm.' The primary analysis confirmed the vmPFC-amygdala connectivity finding at p = 0.04 in females with MDD.

description: Adults with ADHD show increased rightward EEG beta2 (16-21 Hz) asymmetry in inferior parietal brain regions (P8-P7 asymmetry index) during the Conners' Continuous Performance Test compared to controls
original_authors: Hale TS; Smalley SL; Walshaw PD; Hanada G.; Macion J.; McCracken JT; McGough JJ; Loo SK
original_title: Atypical EEG beta asymmetry in adults with ADHD
replication_authors: Hale TS; Kane AM; Tung KL; Kaminsky O.; McGough JJ; Hanada G.; Loo SK
replication_title: Abnormal Parietal Brain Function in ADHD: Replication and Extension of Previous EEG Beta Asymmetry Findings
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The current study replicated the EoI (p = 0.00003), again demonstrating that ADHD adults exhibit atypical rightward P8-P7 beta2 asymmetry during the CPT.' They also replicated the finding that beta2 asymmetry at P8-P7 and TP8-TP7 AIs were highly correlated in controls but not in ADHD subjects. The replication used a larger combined sample (84 controls, 74 ADHD) compared to the original (84 controls, 31 ADHD), with expanded analyses of additional frequency bands.

description: In ADHD adults, greater rightward beta2 asymmetry at the inferior parietal (P8-P7) asymmetry index is associated with fewer commission errors on the CPT
original_authors: Hale TS; Smalley SL; Walshaw PD; Hanada G.; Macion J.; McCracken JT; McGough JJ; Loo SK
original_title: Atypical EEG beta asymmetry in adults with ADHD
replication_authors: Hale TS; Kane AM; Tung KL; Kaminsky O.; McGough JJ; Hanada G.; Loo SK
replication_title: Abnormal Parietal Brain Function in ADHD: Replication and Extension of Previous EEG Beta Asymmetry Findings
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We did not replicate our original finding showing that rightward P8-P7 beta2 asymmetry in ADHD was associated with fewer CPT commission errors.' Table 10 also summarizes this as 'Not Replicated,' noting that in the full sample ADHD subjects did not show significant deficit for commissions, nor was EEG asymmetry associated with commissions.

description: Healthy individuals show freezing-like responses (reduced heart rate deceleration and body sway) when passively viewing unpleasant/aversive stimuli, with an initial HR deceleration in the first half of stimulus presentation sustained until the end
original_authors: Muriel A. Hagenaars; Karin Roelofs; John F. Stins
original_title: Human freezing in response to affective films
replication_authors: Iro Fragkaki; Karin Roelofs; John Stins; Ruud A. Jongedijk; Muriel A. Hagenaars
replication_title: Reduced Freezing in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Patients while Watching Affective Pictures
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated the HR pattern found by Hagenaars et al. (14) in controls, with HR deceleration in the first half and a sustained reduced HR in the second half.' The abstract also states 'Replicating previous findings, healthy controls showed decreased body sway and HR in response to unpleasant pictures.' The replication used affective pictures rather than the films used in the original, with the same passive viewing paradigm and same physiological markers.

description: Reported childhood abuse moderates psychotic and emotional reactivity to daily-life stress (activity stress and event stress) in patients with non-affective psychotic disorder
original_authors: Lardinois M.; Lataster T.; Mengelers R.; van Os J.; Myin-Germeys I.
original_title: Childhood trauma and increased stress sensitivity in psychosis
replication_authors: Jonas Weijers; Wolfgang Viechtbauer; Elisabeth Eurelings-Bontekoe; Jean-Paul Selten
replication_title: Reported Childhood Abuse and Stress Reactivity in Psychosis: A Conceptual Replication and Exploration of Statistical Approaches
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The current study did not unequivocally replicate these findings.' The primary analysis (mirroring original statistics) largely replicated findings, but the two-component analysis — argued to be better suited for the skewed data — failed to replicate the moderation effects of childhood abuse on stress reactivity, yielding mixed/inconclusive results overall.

description: Insomnia symptoms, but not sleep duration, are associated with frequency of suicidal ideation independently of depression in a nationally representative sample (NHANES 2007-2008 cycle)
original_authors: Chakravorty S.; Siu HY; Lalley-Chareczko L.; Brown GK; Findley JC; Perlis ML; Grandner MA
original_title: Sleep duration and insomnia symptoms as risk factors for suicidal ideation in a nationally representative sample
original_journal: The Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders
replication_authors: Zach Simmons; Lance D. Erickson; Dawson Hedges; Daniel B. Kay
replication_title: Insomnia Is Associated With Frequency of Suicidal Ideation Independent of Depression: A Replication and Extension of Findings From the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicated Chakravorty et al.'s findings using the NHANES 2005-2006 cycle: 'we replicated previous findings reported from the 2007-2008 NHANES cycle that showed an association between worse insomnia symptoms and a higher frequency of suicidal ideation.' The main effect was successfully replicated (OR = 1.09, p < 0.05) even after adjusting for depression and other confounds.

description: Worry, negative self-beliefs, and sleep disturbance are each associated with paranoid ideation in the general population
original_authors: Freeman D.; McManus S.; Brugha T.; Meltzer H.; Jenkins R.; Bebbington P.
original_title: Concomitants of paranoia in the general population
replication_authors: Julia M. Sheffield; Aaron P. Brinen; Daniel Freeman
replication_title: Paranoia and Grandiosity in the General Population: Differential Associations With Putative Causal Factors
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their abstract and discussion: 'We replicate previous reports that worry, negative self-beliefs and sleep quality are associated with paranoid ideation in the general population.' All three associations were statistically significant in the expected direction (worry r=0.42, p<0.001; negative self-beliefs r=0.28, p<0.001; sleep quality r=0.15, p<0.001).

description: Serotonergic antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, and mirtazapine) are associated with a markedly reduced risk of intubation or death among patients hospitalized with COVID-19 compared with those not receiving antidepressants
original_authors: Nicolas Hoertel; Marina Sánchez-Rico; Raphaël Vernet; Nathanaël Beeker; Anne-Sophie Jannot; Antoine Neuraz; Elisa Salamanca; Nicolas Paris; Christel Daniel; Alexandre Gramfort; Guillaume Lemaitre; Mélodie Bernaux; Ali Bellamine; Cédric Lemogne; Guillaume Airagnes; Anita Burgun; Frédéric Limosin
original_title: Association between antidepressant use and reduced risk of intubation or death in hospitalized patients with COVID-19: results from an observational study
replication_authors: Brian P. Brennan; Jiana Schnabel; Harrison G. Pope; James I. Hudson
replication_title: Antidepressant use and risk of intubation or death in hospitalized patients with COVID-19: A retrospective cohort study of clinical effectiveness
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We sought to replicate the results of a retrospective cohort study of hospitalized patients with COVID-19 (14), which found that a range of serotonergic antidepressant medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, and mirtazapine) was associated with a marked protective effect for the joint outcome of intubation or death... We failed to replicate these results, with hazard ratios and risk ratios little different from the null value.' The replication used a similarly designed retrospective cohort study but found hazard ratios of 1.1 (95% CI 0.83–1.5) and 1.1 (95% CI 0.86–1.5) for the primary outcome.

description: Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) patients show a paradoxical implicit motor learning curve (inverted learning pattern) on the ambidextrous serial reaction time task (SRTT), and SZ patients show more pronounced deficits when performing with the left hand
original_authors: Adrian Andrzej Chrobak; Katarzyna Siuda-Krzywicka; Grzegorz Przemysław Siwek; Anna Tereszko; Weronika Janeczko; Anna Starowicz-Filip; Marcin Siwek; Dominika Dudek
original_title: Disrupted implicit motor sequence learning in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder revealed with ambidextrous serial reaction time task
original_journal: Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry
replication_authors: Adrian Andrzej Chrobak; Katarzyna Siuda-Krzywicka; Zbigniew Soltys; Sylwia Bielak; Dominik Nowaczek; Aleksandra Żyrkowska; Magdalena Fafrowicz; Tadeusz Marek; Ewa Pęcherzewska; Jan Kużdżał; Anna Starowicz-Filip; Aleksandra Gorostowicz; Dominika Dudek; Marcin Siwek
replication_title: When practice does not make a perfect - paradoxical learning curve in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder revealed by different serial reaction time task variants
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The limited response time SRTT variant allowed us to replicate the findings of disrupted implicit motor learning in SZ and BD' and in the Discussion: 'we have replicated the results of our previous studies, indicating the presence of the paradoxical learning curve in both clinical groups and the more pronounced motor learning deficits when the task was performed with the left hand in the SZ patient group.' The new variant differs only in that response time was restricted (1.5 s limit) rather than unlimited, to enable fMRI compatibility.

description: Big Five personality traits (high Neuroticism, low Conscientiousness, low Agreeableness) are associated with both Internet Use Disorder and Smartphone Use Disorder, while low Extraversion is uniquely linked to IUD and low Openness is uniquely linked to SUD
original_authors: Bernd Lachmann; Éilish Duke; Rayna Sariyska; Christian Montag
original_title: Who's addicted to the smartphone and/or the internet?
replication_authors: Jessica Peterka-Bonetta; Cornelia Sindermann; Jon D. Elhai; Christian Montag
replication_title: Personality Associations With Smartphone and Internet Use Disorder: A Comparison Study Including Links to Impulsivity and Social Anxiety
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'replicate findings from the article by Lachmann et al.' using different questionnaires and a different cultural sample, and concluded that 'most findings were replicated which suggests that results of the work by Lachmann et al. can be considered generally valid.' The key personality-IUD/SUD associations (high Neuroticism, low Conscientiousness, and expected differential patterns for Extraversion and Openness) were confirmed, with only minor quantitative differences.

description: A temperament test for shelter dogs measuring behaviour in the kennel, sociability towards humans and other dogs, docility to leash, playfulness, cognitive skills, and reactivity, validated in an Italian shelter population
original_authors: Paola Valsecchi; Shanis Barnard; Cinzia Stefanini; Simona Normando
original_title: Temperament test for re-homed dogs validated through direct behavioral observation in shelter and home environment
original_journal: Journal of Veterinary Behavior: Clinical Applications and Research
replication_authors: Shanis Barnard; Danielle Kennedy; Reuben Watson; Paola Valsecchi; Gareth Arnott
replication_title: Revisiting a Previously Validated Temperament Test in Shelter Dogs, Including an Examination of the Use of Fake Model Dogs to Assess Conspecific Sociability
explanation: The authors state: 'The aim of the current study was to replicate and extend the Valsecchi et al. study.' In the Conclusion, they report 'there was a very good level of overlap between the outcomes of the tests that were conducted in the two different experiments when analysing traits, such as sociability towards people and other dogs and playfulness,' indicating successful replication of the core constructs, despite some inconsistencies in less robust dimensions.

description: SNP rs6811520 in the CLOCK gene is associated with increased multiple sclerosis susceptibility risk in a Slavic population (OR=1.40)
original_authors: Polona Lavtar; Gorazd Rudolf; Aleš Maver; Alenka Hodžić; Nada Starčević Čizmarević; Maja Živković; Saša Šega Jazbec; Zalika Klemenc Ketiš; Miljenko Kapović; Evica Dinčić; Ranko Raičević; Juraj Sepčić; Luca Lovrečić; Aleksandra Stanković; Smiljana Ristić; Borut Peterlin
original_title: Association of circadian rhythm genes ARNTL/BMAL1 and CLOCK with multiple sclerosis
replication_authors: Isabel de Rojas; César Martin-Montero; Maria Fedetz; Adela González-Jiménez; Fuencisla Matesanz; Elena Urcelay; Laura Espino-Paisán
replication_title: Polymorphisms in ARNTL/BMAL1 and CLOCK Are Not Associated with Multiple Sclerosis in Spanish Population
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'our study does not replicate the associations observed in the previously investigated Slavic population.' For CLOCK rs6811520, no statistically significant differences were found in the Spanish cohort (carrier OR=0.97 [0.72-1.30], p=0.82), and quality control issues in the original study (low call rate, departure from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium) are discussed as potential reasons for the original spurious association.

replication_title: Polymorphisms in ARNTL/BMAL1 and CLOCK Are Not Associated with Multiple Sclerosis in Spanish Population
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'our study does not replicate the associations observed in the previously investigated Slavic population.' description: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits and conduct problems (CP) independently predict bullying perpetration in early adolescence, with CU and CP also interacting to predict both direct and indirect forms of bullying
original_authors: Viding E.; Simmonds E.; Petrides KV; Frederickson N.
original_title: The contribution of callous-unemotional traits and conduct problems to bullying in early adolescence
original_journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
replication_authors: Gennaro Catone; Luisa Almerico; Anna Pezzella; Maria Pia Riccio; Carmela Bravaccio; Pia Bernardo; Pietro Muratori; Antonio Pascotto; Simone Pisano; Vincenzo Paolo Senese
replication_title: The Relation of Callous–Unemotional Traits and Bullying in Early Adolescence Is Independent from Sex and Age and Moderated by Conduct Problems
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their conclusion that they 'replicated in a large sample of Italian adolescent previous findings indicating that CU traits are significantly and positively associated with bullying behaviors, over and above age, sex, and general conduct problems.' The Discussion notes partial divergence: unlike Viding et al. who found CU×CP interaction for both direct and indirect bullying, this study found the interaction only for cyberbullying, not traditional bullying — but the core replication of independent CU trait effects was confirmed.

description: The Dynamic Temporal Prediction (DTP) task produces local prediction effects (faster RTs at longer SOA), global prediction effects (faster RTs in fast blocks, slower in slow blocks), and an implicit learning effect (positive delta score between slow and fast blocks) across development
original_authors: Giovanni Mento; Umberto Granziol
original_title: The developing predictive brain: How implicit temporal expectancy induced by local and global prediction shapes action preparation across development
replication_authors: Fiorella Del Popolo Cristaldi; Umberto Granziol; Irene Bariletti; Giovanni Mento
replication_title: Doing Experimental Psychological Research from Remote: How Alerting Differently Impacts Online vs. Lab Setting
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'we replicated in the online setting and across the whole age range considered (19-69 years) all the task-specific experimental effects already found in the lab (and described in [34]): (i) faster RTs and lower accuracy in trials with long vs. medium and short SOA; (ii) faster RTs in fast blocks and slower RTs in slow blocks as compared to the uniform block; and (iii) the implicit learning effect.' All three key effects from the original study were successfully replicated.

description: Performing bilateral eye movements for 30 seconds enhances subsequent episodic memory recall (the saccade induced retrieval effect, SIRE) in younger adults
original_authors: Stephen D. Christman; Kilian J. Garvey; Ruth E. Propper; Keri A. Phaneuf
original_title: Bilateral eye movements enhance the retrieval of episodic memories
replication_authors: Megan Polden; Trevor J. Crawford
replication_title: On the Effect of Bilateral Eye Movements on Memory Retrieval in Ageing and Dementia
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Results from the current study did not replicate the enhancement effect of bilateral eye movements on word memory recognition and recall.' No significant effect of eye movement condition was found for either younger adults (F(2,54) = 1.66, p = 0.20) or older adults (F(2,55) = 0.099, p = 0.91).

description: Performing bilateral eye movements for 30 seconds enhances subsequent episodic memory recall (the saccade induced retrieval effect, SIRE) in younger adults
original_authors: Stephen D. Christman; Kilian J. Garvey; Ruth E. Propper; Keri A. Phaneuf
original_title: Bilateral eye movements enhance the retrieval of episodic memories
replication_authors: Megan Polden; Trevor J. Crawford
replication_title: On the Effect of Bilateral Eye Movements on Memory Retrieval in Ageing and Dementia
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Results from experiment 2 which assessed the SIRE effect in people with AD, MCI, PD and healthy older adults failed to replicate the SIRE effect. There was no significant difference in the number of correct or false words recognised across the participants groups based on the eye movement condition.' The main effect of eye movement condition on correct words identified was non-significant (F(1,65) = 1.08, p = 0.303).

description: Authority of the speaker (mother vs. sibling) influences sarcasm comprehension in school children, with children better understanding sarcasm produced by the mother, and Theory of Mind abilities playing a key role in sarcasm comprehension
original_authors: Davide Massaro; Annalisa Valle; Antonella Marchetti
original_title: Irony and second-order false belief in children: What changes when mothers rather than siblings speak?
replication_authors: Rachele Fanari; Sergio Melogno; Roberta Fadda
replication_title: An Experimental Study on Sarcasm Comprehension in School Children: The Possible Role of Contextual, Linguistics and Meta-Representative Factors
explanation: REVIEWER: Study 1 clearly replicated the core finding from Massaro et al. [9] that children better understand sarcasm from the mother (high authority/familiarity) compared to other speakers. The Q Cochran test showed significant differences between story conditions (χ²=16.125, df=2, p<0.001), and McNemar pairwise tests confirmed children understood sarcasm better in the mother story vs. the stranger/cashier story (p<0.001). This is a close extension because the authors added a stranger-adult condition (the cashier) to test familiarity in addition to authority. Notably, unlike Massaro et al., no significant relationship between Theory of Mind (second-order false belief) and sarcasm comprehension was found, but the primary finding about contextual factors (authority/familiarity) influencing sarcasm comprehension was clearly supported.

description: Authority of the speaker (mother vs. sibling) influences sarcasm comprehension in school children, with children better understanding sarcasm produced by the mother, and Theory of Mind abilities playing a key role in sarcasm comprehension
original_authors: Davide Massaro; Annalisa Valle; Antonella Marchetti
original_title: Irony and second-order false belief in children: What changes when mothers rather than siblings speak?
replication_authors: Rachele Fanari; Sergio Melogno; Roberta Fadda
replication_title: An Experimental Study on Sarcasm Comprehension in School Children: The Possible Role of Contextual, Linguistics and Meta-Representative Factors
explanation: REVIEWER: Keeping 'inconclusive' at 'medium' confidence. Study 2 (N=180, across 1st/3rd/5th graders) produced mixed results regarding the core Massaro et al. finding.
