First graders showed the mother advantage (Q Cochran χ²=12.316, df=2, p≤0.002; McNemar mother vs. cashier p=0.002, mother vs. siblings p=0.012), replicating the original. However, this effect disappeared in third and fifth graders — no significant differences between story conditions were found in older children. The Theory of Mind–sarcasm relationship from the original was again not replicated (Fisher test non-significant at all ages). The authors' own Conclusions claim children 'at any age better understood sarcasm produced by a speaker with a high level of familiarity and authority,' but this overreaches what the Study 2 statistics actually show — the significant mother advantage was confined to first graders. This tension between the authors' framing and their data is what makes the result genuinely ambiguous: partial replication in the youngest group, failure to replicate in older groups, and no ToM replication. 'Inconclusive' accurately captures this mixed pattern.

description: Developmental prosopagnosics (N=10) show impairment in both face and object recognition, with face difficulties driven by visual similarity differences between categories rather than a face-selective deficit
original_authors: Christian Gerlach; Solja K. Klargaard; Randi Starrfelt
original_title: On the relation between face and object recognition in developmental prosopagnosia: no dissociation but a systematic association
replication_authors: Christian Gerlach; Randi Starrfelt
replication_title: Evidence for a Classical Dissociation between Face and Object Recognition in Developmental Prosopagnosia
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The present study failed to replicate the findings reported by Gerlach et al. [8,16].' The new DP group (N=21) showed no impairment in the simultaneous matching paradigm relative to controls, contrasting with the original group which was impaired across all conditions, and the new group demonstrated a classical (face-selective) dissociation rather than the strong dissociation found originally.

description: Site-specific TMS to lip or tongue motor cortex regions creates a double dissociation in phoneme discrimination accuracy and reaction times, with stimulation of the region governing articulation of a phoneme category increasing accuracy for that category and decreasing it for the other
original_authors: Alessandro D'Ausilio; Friedemann Pulvermüller; Paola Salmas; Ilaria Bufalari; Chiara Begliomini; Luciano Fadiga
original_title: The motor somatotopy of speech perception
replication_authors: Lindy Comstock; Vinícius Rezende Carvalho; Claudia Lainscsek; Aria Fallah; Terrence J. Sejnowski
replication_title: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Facilitates Neural Speech Decoding
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusions: 'This study reproduced the double dissociation between electromagnetic stimulation site and stimulus category that was reported by [D'Ausilio et al. 2009] during a phoneme discrimination task.' Bayesian analyses across both 2019 and 2021 experiments showed weak to moderate evidence for the alternative hypothesis (BF+0 between 1.188 and 2.002) in the CV conditions, consistent with the original finding.

description: Social exclusion using the cyberball paradigm reliably engages the medial default mode network (including vACC and iFG), while not reliably activating the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)
original_authors: Mwilambwe-Tshilobo L.; Spreng RN
original_title: Social exclusion reliably engages the default network: A meta-analysis of Cyberball
replication_authors: Karin Labek; Roberto Viviani
replication_title: Reassessing the Neural Correlates of Social Exclusion: A Replication Study of the Cyberball Paradigm Using Arterial Spin Labeling
explanation: REVIEWER UPGRADE: The authors explicitly state 'our findings are consistent with those reported in meta-analyses of the cyberball paradigm, confirming its replicability.' The exclusion vs. play contrast successfully replicated the meta-analytic findings: iFG activation (p=0.002, cluster-level corrected) and vACC activation (p=0.018, cluster-level corrected), while dACC showed no significant activation even at uncorrected levels — all consistent with Mwilambwe-Tshilobo & Spreng (2021). The original extraction classified this as 'inconclusive' because the same areas were also active in the watch condition, questioning specificity. However, the meta-analytic finding being tested was whether the exclusion vs. play contrast activates iFG and vACC — and it clearly did. The specificity concern is an additional interpretive finding about the cyberball paradigm, not a failure to replicate the neural activation pattern. Changed from inconclusive to success with high confidence based on the authors' own explicit replication confirmation and statistically significant results in the predicted regions.

description: Anodal tDCS stimulation of the left angular gyrus produces a significant decrease in intentional binding (sense of agency), as measured by the Wundt Clock Paradigm
original_authors: Nima Khalighinejad; Patrick Haggard
original_title: Modulating human sense of agency with non-invasive brain stimulation
replication_authors: Marika Bonuomo; Davide Perrotta; Gloria Di Filippo; Rinaldo Livio Perri
replication_title: Neurostimulation and Sense of Agency: Three tDCS Experiments on the Modulation of Intentional Binding
explanation: The authors explicitly state they failed to replicate the original: 'Despite attempting to replicate the experiment by Khalighinejad and Haggard [16] using identical methods, timing, stimulation, and tasks, our current study did not yield a significant difference between anodic and sham stimulation.' All three measures (Action Binding, Tone Binding, Intentional Binding) showed non-significant results.

description: Terminal probe (TP) schedule thinning facilitates longer periods of reinforcer unavailability compared to dense-to-lean (DTL) thinning during functional communication training for challenging behavior
original_authors: Craig W. Strohmeier; Mirela Cengher; Michelle D. Chin; John Michael Falligant
original_title: Application of a terminal schedule probe method to inform schedule thinning with multiple schedules
replication_authors: Craig W. Strohmeier; Elizabeth Thuman; John Michael Falligant; Mirela Cengher; Michelle D. Chin; Patricia F. Kurtz
replication_title: Resurgence of Severe Challenging Behavior and Schedule Thinning with the Terminal Schedule Probe Method
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Consistent with Strohmeier et al. (2024), the results of the current investigation indicate that TP schedule-thinning methods facilitate rapid transitions to practical terminal S∆ durations.' The replication used an updated cohort (17 additional participants), stricter inclusion criteria (ASD-only, structured functional analysis confirmation), and extended the resurgence analysis beyond the original.

description: Content moderators show elevated psychological distress (over a third scoring in the moderate-to-severe range on the CORE-10), a dose-response effect between frequency of exposure to distressing content and psychological distress and secondary trauma, and no significant association between wellbeing service use and mental health outcomes
original_authors: Ruth Spence; Antonia Bifulco; Paula Bradbury; Elena Martellozzo; Jeffrey DeMarco
original_title: Content moderator mental health, secondary trauma, and well-being: A cross-sectional study
replication_authors: Ruth Spence; Jeffrey DeMarco
replication_title: Content Moderator Mental Health and Associations with Coping Styles: Replication and Extension of Previous Studies
explanation: The authors state findings were 'mostly replicated': the dose-response effect and mental health rates were replicated, but the wellbeing services finding was only partially replicated (service use was not significantly associated with psychological distress or wellbeing, but was associated with reduced secondary trauma — a different pattern from the original). The abstract notes 'results pertaining to mental health, wellbeing, and the effectiveness of wellbeing services for this population were mostly replicated.'

description: Chronic stress increases deontological moral decision-making (heightens inaction preference) as measured by the CNI model's I parameter in moral dilemma scenarios
original_authors: Lisong Zhang; Ming Kong; Zhongquan Li; Xia Zhao; Liuping Gao
original_title: Chronic stress and moral decision-making: An exploration with the CNI model
replication_authors: Lemei Zou; Junhong Wu; Chuanjun Liu
replication_title: No Detectable Effects of Chronic Stress on Moral Decision-Making Are Found: A Data Reanalysis and a Pre-Registered Replication and Extension
explanation: Study 1 is a data reanalysis of Zhang et al. (2018)'s raw data using the CAN algorithm and original continuous scores. The authors state: 'there is no evidence of a correlation between chronic stress and moral decision-making, which is inconsistent with the original analysis.' The reanalysis using continuous (non-dichotomized) scores found no significant associations between chronic stress and any moral decision-making parameter.

description: Chronic stress increases deontological moral decision-making (heightens inaction preference) as measured by the CNI model's I parameter in moral dilemma scenarios
original_authors: Lisong Zhang; Ming Kong; Zhongquan Li; Xia Zhao; Liuping Gao
original_title: Chronic stress and moral decision-making: An exploration with the CNI model
replication_authors: Lemei Zou; Junhong Wu; Chuanjun Liu
replication_title: No Detectable Effects of Chronic Stress on Moral Decision-Making Are Found: A Data Reanalysis and a Pre-Registered Replication and Extension
explanation: Study 2 is a pre-registered replication using the same PSS-10 and 24-moral-dilemma materials as Zhang et al. (2018), but with a broader population sample (online adults aged 17-89 vs. undergraduates) and additional controls (social desirability, acute stress exclusion). Across all four analytical approaches (traditional, process dissociation, CNI model, CAN algorithm), no reliable correlation was found between chronic stress and moral decision-making, directly contradicting Zhang et al.'s original findings.

description: Self-reported posttraumatic growth (PTGI scores) is unrelated to actual changes in PTG domains, and is positively associated with distress and coping efforts rather than genuine positive change
original_authors: Patricia Frazier; Howard Tennen; Margaret Gavian; Crystal Park; Patricia Tomich; Ty Tashiro
original_title: Does self-reported posttraumatic growth reflect genuine positive change?
replication_authors: Adriel Boals; Lee A. Bedford; Jennifer L. Callahan
replication_title: Perceptions of Change after a Trauma and Perceived Posttraumatic Growth: A Prospective Examination
explanation: The paper explicitly states it used 'a research design very similar to the one employed by Frazier et al. (2009)' and the abstract says it attempts to 'replicate and extend previous findings.' The main hypotheses were largely supported (perceived PTG unrelated to actual PTG), but the authors acknowledge in the Discussion that 'we did not replicate all of the findings reported in Frazier et al. (2009),' citing three specific correlations that failed to replicate, making the overall result inconclusive.

description: Anticipating a stressful task after a nap leads to dynamic temporal changes in sleep parameters, with sleep depth being reduced specifically toward the end of the nap period (closer to the anticipated stressor), as compared to anticipating a relaxation task
original_authors: Jonas Beck; Erna Loretz; Björn Rasch
original_title: Stress dynamically reduces sleep depth: Temporal proximity to the stressor is crucial
replication_authors: Sandrine Baselgia; Jonas Beck; Björn Rasch
replication_title: Anticipation of Stress and Relaxation Dynamically Impacts Sleep
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'The temporal dynamic changes observed in our previous study could not be replicated.' While stress conditions across both studies showed highly similar sleep parameters, the key finding of dynamic temporal changes in sleep depth toward the end of the nap was not observed when using a neutral control condition instead of the relaxation condition used in the original study.

description: Response times decrease across prolonged lexical decision task (LDT) performance, with RT stabilizing approximately midway through the task
original_authors: Emmanuel Keuleers; Paula Lacey; Kathleen Rastle; Marc Brysbaert
original_title: The British Lexicon Project: Lexical decision data for 28,730 monosyllabic and disyllabic English words
replication_authors: Kelsey Cnudde; Sophia van Hees; Sage Brown; Gwen van der Wijk; Penny M. Pexman; Andrea B. Protzner
replication_title: Increased Neural Efficiency in Visual Word Recognition: Evidence from Alterations in Event-Related Potentials and Multiscale Entropy
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the BLP' and that their findings 'are generally consistent with those of the BLP': RT decreased significantly across the three EEG sessions. The close extension classification reflects that the study replicated the BLP's behavioral protocol (16 hours LDT, same word stimuli) but extended it with EEG recording to measure neural changes, and used a substantially smaller in-lab sample.

description: IPV perpetrators show skin conductance hyperreactivity (higher SCL) during preparatory and recovery periods to a psychosocial stressor compared to non-violent controls, and this hyperreactivity is associated with impulsivity traits
original_authors: Romero-Martínez A.; Lila M.; Williams RK; González-Bono E.; Moya-Albiol L.
original_title: Skin conductance rises in preparation and recovery to psychosocial stress and its relationship with impulsivity and testosterone in intimate partner violence perpetrators
replication_authors: Sara Vitoria-Estruch; Ángel Romero-Martínez; Marisol Lila; Luis Moya-Albiol
replication_title: Could Alcohol Abuse Drive Intimate Partner Violence Perpetrators’ Psychophysiological Response to Acute Stress?
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: REVIEWER: Confirmed 'inconclusive' at medium confidence. The current study found LA IPV perpetrators had significantly higher SCL than controls (group effect F(2,92)=3.62, p=0.030), with a significant period×group interaction (p=0.05), partially consistent with the original's SCL hyperreactivity finding. However, the stressor was changed from a psychosocial TSST (emotionally charged IPV topic) to a purely cognitive stressor with no emotional valence. The authors explicitly state 'our results partially agree with previous research' and attribute discrepancies to the different stressor. This partial agreement — directionally consistent on SCL but with a fundamentally different paradigm and only a subset of the original's findings replicated — genuinely warrants 'inconclusive.' The ambiguity is real, not resolvable by closer reading.

description: IPV perpetrators show higher heart rates, lower vagal ratios (higher NSCRs), and shorter pre-ejection period (greater sympathetic predominance) compared to non-violent controls in response to a psychosocial stressor (marital conflict version of TSST)
original_authors: Angel Romero-Martínez; Rui Nunes-Costa; Marisol Lila; Esperanza González-Bono; Luis Moya-Albiol
original_title: Cardiovascular reactivity to a marital conflict version of the Trier social stress test in intimate partner violence perpetrators
replication_authors: Sara Vitoria-Estruch; Ángel Romero-Martínez; Marisol Lila; Luis Moya-Albiol
replication_title: Could Alcohol Abuse Drive Intimate Partner Violence Perpetrators’ Psychophysiological Response to Acute Stress?
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: REVIEWER: Upgraded to 'high' confidence. The authors unambiguously state: 'our data did not support the idea of a sympathetic predominance in impulsive IPV perpetrators.' The results section confirms no significant group differences were found for any of the cardiovascular/parasympathetic markers central to the original (HR, PEP, HF, RSA) — neither in period×group interactions nor in main group effects. Only SCL and RR showed group differences, and those are electrodermal/respiratory measures, not the cardiovascular markers that were the core finding of Romero-Martínez et al. (2014). The authors attribute the null cardiovascular results to the use of a cognitive rather than psychosocial stressor, but regardless of the explanation, the failure to find the originally reported cardiovascular pattern is clear and explicitly acknowledged.

description: One year of participation in physical education classes using the Eduball method (educational balls with printed letters, numbers, and signs) improves cognitive (mathematical, reading, writing) and gross motor (locomotor and object control) skills in primary school students more than traditional PE
original_authors: Ireneusz Cichy; Magdalena Kaczmarczyk; Sara Wawrzyniak; Agnieszka Kruszwicka; Tomasz Przybyla; Michal Klichowski; Andrzej Rokita
original_title: Participating in physical classes using Eduball stimulates acquisition of mathematical knowledge and skills by primary school students
replication_authors: Sara Wawrzyniak; Marcin Korbecki; Ireneusz Cichy; Agnieszka Kruszwicka; Tomasz Przybyla; Michal Klichowski; Andrzej Rokita
replication_title: Everyone Can Implement Eduball in Physical Education to Develop Cognitive and Motor Skills in Primary School Students
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated our earlier one-year Eduball experiment' with an extension (3 experimental groups by teacher type vs. 1). Cognitive skill results clearly replicate: all Eduball groups significantly outperformed controls in math, reading, and writing with large-to-huge effect sizes (d = 1.21–2.50 vs. 0.83–1.09 for controls). Locomotor skills also replicated with significant ANCOVA differences favoring Eduball. However, object control skills showed only a non-significant trend in the Eduball vs. control ANCOVA, weaker than the original study (Section 4.1 acknowledges this). The authors attribute the discrepancy to younger participants (age 6–7 vs. older samples in prior work). Confidence remains 'medium' because the core finding is supported but with a meaningful caveat on object control skills — this is genuine ambiguity in the data, not resolvable by further reading. 'Success' is the best classification given the overall pattern, but 'inconclusive' would also be defensible if one weighted motor outcomes more heavily. The paper references multiple prior Eduball studies [15–18]; ref [15] (Cichy et al. 2020) is cited most directly in the replication statement.

description: Materialism positively predicts adolescent delinquency concurrently and longitudinally, and egocentrism mediates the relationship between materialism and delinquency in Chinese adolescents
original_authors: Daniel T. L. Shek; Xiang Li; Xiaoqin Zhu; Esther Y. W. Shek
original_title: Concurrent and longitudinal predictors of adolescent delinquency in mainland Chinese adolescents: The role of materialism and egocentrism
original_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
replication_authors: Daniel T. L. Shek; Diya Dou; Xiaoqin Zhu; Xiang Li; Lindan Tan
replication_title: Materialism, Egocentrism and Delinquent Behavior in Chinese Adolescents in Mainland China: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Discussion: 'Another contribution of the study is that we replicated the findings of Shek, Li, Zhu and Shek [7]' and in the Conclusion: 'By replicating the findings of Shek, Li, Zhu and Shek [7], this study is a positive response to the crisis of replication.' Both studies found materialism predicts delinquency and egocentrism mediates this relationship.

description: Eduball-based physical education (where students play team mini-games with educational balls) stimulates academic skill acquisition (mathematical and native language competencies) in primary school students without impairing motor development
original_authors: Sara Wawrzyniak; Marcin Korbecki; Ireneusz Cichy; Agnieszka Kruszwicka; Tomasz Przybyla; Michal Klichowski; Andrzej Rokita
original_title: Everyone can implement eduball in physical education to develop cognitive and motor skills in primary school students
original_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
replication_authors: Ireneusz Cichy; Agnieszka Kruszwicka; Patrycja Palus; Tomasz Przybyla; Rainer Schliermann; Sara Wawrzyniak; Michal Klichowski; Andrzej Rokita
replication_title: Physical Education with Eduball Stimulates Non-Native Language Learning in Primary School Students
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors explicitly state 'Replicating the Eduball experiment in a new, dual-language context, we confirmed the hypothesis that integrating PE with a non-native language stimulates L2 learning in children.' ANCOVA shows a significant group difference in non-native language skills (F=18.67, p<0.001, η²p=0.45). Result='success' is unambiguous. Replication type='close extension' is correct: the study uses the same Eduball method and parallel-group design as refs [24-28] but extends to a new outcome (L2/non-native language learning instead of L1/math). Confidence remains 'medium' because: (1) the paper replicates a family of Eduball studies [24-28] rather than one specific original, making the original somewhat diffuse; (2) the sample is very small (N=26, one class per group) as the authors acknowledge in limitations; (3) key authors overlap between the original and replication studies, reducing independence. Subdiscipline changed from 'special education' to empty — this study involves mainstream primary school students, not special education populations, and no available subdiscipline in the ontology fits.

description: A 1 µg/m³ increase in long-term average PM2.5 air pollution is associated with an 11% higher COVID-19 county-level mortality rate in the United States
original_authors: Wu X.; Nethery RC; Sabath MB; Braun D.; Dominici F.
original_title: Air pollution and COVID-19 mortality in the United States: strengths and limitations of an ecological regression analysis
replication_authors: Brandon Michael Taylor; Michael Ash; Lawrence Peter King
replication_title: Initially High Correlation between Air Pollution and COVID-19 Mortality Declined to Zero as the Pandemic Progressed: There Is No Evidence for a Causal Link between Air Pollution and COVID-19 Vulnerability
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: The authors successfully replicated Wu et al.'s results for the original study period (April–September 2020), confirming the positive association between PM2.5 and COVID-19 mortality. However, extending the analysis to May 2022 with the same methodology showed the mortality rate ratio fell sharply to near zero (0.603% increase per 1 µg/m³, 95% CI: -0.560% to +1.78%), leading the authors to conclude 'there is no long-term relationship between COVID-19 mortality and PM2.5 concentrations' and that 'short-term trends in the initial spread of COVID-19, not a long-term epidemiologic association, caused an early correlation.'

description: A half-year Eduball-based physical education intervention stimulates cognitive and motor (graphomotor) development in primary school students compared to traditional PE, without motor costs
original_authors: Sara Wawrzyniak; Ireneusz Cichy; Ana Rita Matias; Damian Pawlik; Agnieszka Kruszwicka; Michal Klichowski; Andrzej Rokita
original_title: Physical activity with Eduball stimulates graphomotor skills in primary school students
replication_authors: Ireneusz Cichy; Agnieszka Kruszwicka; Tomasz Przybyla; Weronika Rochatka; Sara Wawrzyniak; Michal Klichowski; Andrzej Rokita
replication_title: No Motor Costs of Physical Education with Eduball
replication_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
explanation: REVIEWER NOTE: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the Eduball experiment, focusing on motor development' and reference a series of prior Eduball studies [24-27,31,59-61]. The replication extends prior work by comprehensively testing space-time orientation, graphomotor, locomotor, and object control skills in a single experiment — outcomes not fully covered in any single prior study. The core finding confirms no motor costs of the Eduball intervention, consistent with original studies. However, confidence remains medium because: (1) the sample is very small (n=27, groups of 12 and 15); (2) the key results are mostly null — after ANCOVA correction, space-time orientation (p=0.256), graphomotor (p=0.554), locomotor (p=0.132), and object control (p=0.551) all showed no significant between-group differences; (3) only kicking showed a significant effect favoring Eduball (p=0.026 in ANCOVA); (4) the authors themselves extensively acknowledge limitations including short intervention period, small sample, and single-method design. The 'success' classification is retained because the prior claim was that Eduball does not harm motor development, and this null result is consistent with that claim — but interpreting null results from an underpowered study as confirmatory is inherently ambiguous.

description: People's originality judgments of their own creative ideas (in the Alternative Uses Task) are dissociated from their actual originality scores, with serial order as a reliable cue for originality judgments but manipulations that affect one measure not affecting the other
original_authors: Yael Sidi; Ilan Torgovitsky; Daniela Soibelman; Ella Miron-Spektor; Rakefet Ackerman
original_title: You may be more original than you think: Predictable biases in self-assessment of originality
replication_authors: Yoed N. Kenett; Noam Gooz; Rakefet Ackerman
replication_title: The Role of Semantic Associations as a Metacognitive Cue in Creative Idea Generation
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the General Discussion: 'Our results replicate previous findings (Sidi et al. 2020) that people consistently underestimate their originality, while also judging reliably their initial ideas as more creative than their later ones (serial order effect).' In Experiment 2 (new data, N=252), they replicate the dissociation between originality scores and originality judgments found by Sidi et al. (2020), while also adding the semantic distance as a new variable.

description: Making judgments of learning (JOLs) following retrieval practice further enhances learning of educational texts compared to retrieval practice alone (Cohen's d = 0.44)
original_authors: Ariel, Robert J.; Karpicke, Jeffrey D.; Witherby, Amber E.; Tauber, Sarah K.
original_title: Do judgments of learning directly enhance learning of educational materials?
replication_authors: Wenbo Zhao; Muzi Xu; Chenyuqi Xu; Baike Li; Xiao Hu; Chunliang Yang; Liang Luo
replication_title: Judgments of Learning Following Retrieval Practice Produce Minimal Reactivity Effect on Learning of Education-Related Materials
explanation: Experiment 1 used Chinese participants and stimuli (vs. the original's online, English, mTurk design), yielding d = 0.10 with Bayesian evidence for the null (BF10 = 0.30). The authors explicitly conclude the original finding 'is a fake phenomenon, which might result from sampling error.'

description: Making judgments of learning (JOLs) following retrieval practice further enhances learning of educational texts compared to retrieval practice alone (Cohen's d = 0.44)
original_authors: Ariel, Robert J.; Karpicke, Jeffrey D.; Witherby, Amber E.; Tauber, Sarah K.
original_title: Do judgments of learning directly enhance learning of educational materials?
replication_authors: Wenbo Zhao; Muzi Xu; Chenyuqi Xu; Baike Li; Xiao Hu; Chunliang Yang; Liang Luo
replication_title: Judgments of Learning Following Retrieval Practice Produce Minimal Reactivity Effect on Learning of Education-Related Materials
explanation: Experiment 2 used the same mTurk participant pool, English stimuli, and exact procedure as the original, yielding d = -0.03 with Bayesian evidence for the null (BF10 = 0.21). The authors confirm this 'replicated the null reactivity finding observed in Experiment 1.'

description: Making judgments of learning (JOLs) following retrieval practice further enhances learning of educational texts compared to retrieval practice alone (Cohen's d = 0.44)
original_authors: Ariel, Robert J.; Karpicke, Jeffrey D.; Witherby, Amber E.; Tauber, Sarah K.
original_title: Do judgments of learning directly enhance learning of educational materials?
replication_authors: Wenbo Zhao; Muzi Xu; Chenyuqi Xu; Baike Li; Xiao Hu; Chunliang Yang; Liang Luo
replication_title: Judgments of Learning Following Retrieval Practice Produce Minimal Reactivity Effect on Learning of Education-Related Materials
explanation: Pre-registered Experiment 3 using Prolific Academic (UK) participants with the same procedure as the original yielded d = 0.17 with Bayesian evidence for the null (BF10 = 0.47). The authors explicitly state the reactivity effect 'is a fake phenomenon, which might result from sampling error.'

description: No mathematics or physics major student with an SAT math score below roughly 600 earned an in-major GPA higher than 3.5, suggesting a cognitive threshold below which high academic performance in quantitative majors is impossible
original_authors: Hsu, Stephen D.; Schombert, James
original_title: Data mining the university: College GPA predictions from SAT scores
replication_authors: You Zhou; Nathan R. Kuncel; Paul R. Sackett
replication_title: Examining the Existence of Cognitive Thresholds in Highly Quantitative College Courses
explanation: The authors found only 2 math-major and 9 physics-major students (out of 628 and 526 respectively) who broke the SAT < 600 / GPA > 3.5 threshold, and NCA effect sizes were small (d = 0.09 for both majors). While the authors state 'we believe Hsu and Schombert's finding was replicated,' their general discussion concludes 'there does not seem to be a clear-cut and absolute cognitive threshold point,' instead characterizing quantitative ability as only a 'virtually necessary condition' — a weaker claim than the original absolute threshold.

description: The PROLOGUE score using 12 clinical variables accurately predicts poor neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest, with high discrimination (AUC 0.94) in a Korean cohort of unselected cardiac arrest survivors
original_authors: Dae Hee Bae; Hyoung Youn Lee; Yong Hun Jung; Kyung Woon Jeung; Byung Kook Lee; Chun Song Youn; Byung Soo Kang; Tag Heo; Yong Il Min
original_title: PROLOGUE (PROgnostication using LOGistic regression model for Unselected adult cardiac arrest patients in the Early stages): development and validation of a scoring system for early prognostication in unselected adult cardiac arrest patients
replication_authors: Christoph Schriefl; Christian Schoergenhofer; Nina Buchtele; Matthias Mueller; Michael Poppe; Christian Clodi; Florian Ettl; Anne Merrelaar; Magdalena Sophie Boegl; Philipp Steininger; Michael Holzer; Harald Herkner; Michael Schwameis
replication_title: Out-of-Sample Validity of the PROLOGUE Score to Predict Neurologic Function after Cardiac Arrest
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusions: 'This independent validation of the PROLOGUE score in a sample of European cardiac arrest survivors failed to replicate the high accuracy found in the original study.' The PROLOGUE score overestimated poor neurologic outcome risk in 63% of patients and demonstrated substantially lower discrimination (AUC 0.82 vs. original 0.94), with poor calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test p = 0.0024).

description: The UGT1A cluster (rs887829/rs4148325) is associated with circulating bilirubin levels in humans
original_authors: Eugene P. Rhee; Aditya Surapaneni; Zihe Zheng; Linda Zhou; Diptavo Dutta; Dan E. Arking; Jingning Zhang; ThuyVy Duong; Nilanjan Chatterjee; Shengyuan Luo; Pascal Schlosser; Rupal Mehta; Sushrut S. Waikar; Santosh L. Saraf; Tanika N. Kelly; Lee L. Hamm; Panduranga S. Rao; Anna V. Mathew; Chi-yuan Hsu; Afshin Parsa; Ramachandran S. Vasan; Paul L. Kimmel; Clary B. Clish; Josef Coresh; Harold I. Feldman; Morgan E. Grams
original_title: Trans-ethnic genome-wide association study of blood metabolites in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study
replication_authors: Chang Liu; Zicheng Wang; Qin Hui; Yiyun Chiang; Junyu Chen; Jaysingh Brijkumar; Johnathan A. Edwards; Claudia E. Ordonez; Mathew R. Dudgeon; Henry Sunpath; Selvan Pillay; Pravi Moodley; Daniel R. Kuritzkes; Mohamed Y. S. Moosa; Dean P. Jones; Vincent C. Marconi; Yan V. Sun
replication_title: Crosstalk between Host Genome and Metabolome among People with HIV in South Africa
explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The paper explicitly states 'we replicated previously reported genetic associations' and the UGT1A1/UGT1A cluster showed robust association with bilirubin. Table 3 shows rs887829 (T allele) associated with higher bilirubin in the South African HIV cohort (beta=0.31, SE=0.07, p=3.38×10⁻⁶), consistent in direction with Rhee [11] (beta=0.38, p=1.4×10⁻¹³). The replication p-value far exceeds the study's stated p<0.05 threshold for candidate replications. This extends findings from European/African American populations to Africans living in Africa with HIV, justifying 'close extension'.

description: The UGT1A cluster (rs1976391) is associated with circulating biliverdin levels in humans
original_authors: Shengyuan Luo; Elena V. Feofanova; Adrienne Tin; Sarah Tung; Eugene P. Rhee; Josef Coresh; Dan E. Arking; Aditya Surapaneni; Pascal Schlosser; Yong Li; Anna Köttgen; Bing Yu; Morgan E. Grams
original_title: Genomewide association study of serum metabolites in the African American Study of Kidney Disease and Hypertension
replication_authors: Chang Liu; Zicheng Wang; Qin Hui; Yiyun Chiang; Junyu Chen; Jaysingh Brijkumar; Johnathan A. Edwards; Claudia E. Ordonez; Mathew R. Dudgeon; Henry Sunpath; Selvan Pillay; Pravi Moodley; Daniel R. Kuritzkes; Mohamed Y. S. Moosa; Dean P. Jones; Vincent C. Marconi; Yan V. Sun
replication_title: Crosstalk between Host Genome and Metabolome among People with HIV in South Africa
explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The association of rs1976391 (UGT1A3-10) with biliverdin was successfully replicated in the South African HIV cohort (beta=0.39, SE=0.07, p=1.04×10⁻⁸), reaching genome-wide significance (p<5×10⁻⁸). This is consistent in direction and magnitude with the original finding from Luo [10] in African Americans (beta=0.42, p=3.69×10⁻¹⁷). The Discussion explicitly discusses UGT1A's role in biliverdin/bilirubin metabolism and confirms the replication. Classified as 'close extension' because it extends findings from African Americans in the US to Africans living in Africa with HIV — a different ancestry subgroup and clinical context.

description: The SLC16A9 locus (rs1171617) is associated with lower circulating carnitine levels in humans
original_authors: Eugene P. Rhee; Jennifer E. Ho; Ming-Huei Chen; Dongxiao Shen; Susan Cheng; Martin G. Larson; Anahita Ghorbani; Xu Shi; Iiro T. Helenius; Christopher J. O’Donnell; Amanda L. Souza; Amy Deik; Kerry A. Pierce; Kevin Bullock; Geoffrey A. Walford; Ramachandran S. Vasan; Jose C. Florez; Clary Clish; J.-R. Joanna Yeh; Thomas J. Wang; Robert E. Gerszten
original_title: A genome-wide association study of the human metabolome in a community-based cohort
replication_authors: Chang Liu; Zicheng Wang; Qin Hui; Yiyun Chiang; Junyu Chen; Jaysingh Brijkumar; Johnathan A. Edwards; Claudia E. Ordonez; Mathew R. Dudgeon; Henry Sunpath; Selvan Pillay; Pravi Moodley; Daniel R. Kuritzkes; Mohamed Y. S. Moosa; Dean P. Jones; Vincent C. Marconi; Yan V. Sun
replication_title: Crosstalk between Host Genome and Metabolome among People with HIV in South Africa
explanation: The G allele of rs1171617 in SLC16A9 was associated with lower carnitine in the South African HIV cohort (beta=-0.23, SE=0.07, p=0.0014), replicating the original finding from European populations (beta=-0.42, SE=0.04, p=5.9×10⁻²⁶). The Discussion explicitly states 'its association with carnitine was previously established among several studies in European populations but has not been generalized to other ancestries.'

description: The CPS1 locus (rs7422339) is associated with higher circulating creatine levels in humans
original_authors: Eugene P. Rhee; Jennifer E. Ho; Ming-Huei Chen; Dongxiao Shen; Susan Cheng; Martin G. Larson; Anahita Ghorbani; Xu Shi; Iiro T. Helenius; Christopher J. O’Donnell; Amanda L. Souza; Amy Deik; Kerry A. Pierce; Kevin Bullock; Geoffrey A. Walford; Ramachandran S. Vasan; Jose C. Florez; Clary Clish; J.-R. Joanna Yeh; Thomas J. Wang; Robert E. Gerszten
original_title: A genome-wide association study of the human metabolome in a community-based cohort
replication_authors: Chang Liu; Zicheng Wang; Qin Hui; Yiyun Chiang; Junyu Chen; Jaysingh Brijkumar; Johnathan A. Edwards; Claudia E. Ordonez; Mathew R. Dudgeon; Henry Sunpath; Selvan Pillay; Pravi Moodley; Daniel R. Kuritzkes; Mohamed Y. S. Moosa; Dean P. Jones; Vincent C. Marconi; Yan V. Sun
replication_title: Crosstalk between Host Genome and Metabolome among People with HIV in South Africa
explanation: The A allele of rs7422339 in CPS1 was associated with higher creatine in the South African HIV cohort (beta=0.19, SE=0.07, p=0.0045), replicating the original finding from European populations in the Framingham Heart Study (beta=0.24, SE=0.04, p=2.5×10⁻¹¹). The Discussion states 'The association between CPS1 and creatine was previously reported among participants of European descent in the Framingham Heart Study.'

description: Applying a phospholipid-based biofilm spray to Pinot Noir grapevines one week before smoke exposure significantly reduces the levels of smoke-derived volatile phenols absorbed into grape berries
original_authors: James W. Favell; Matthew Noestheden; Sarah M. Lyons; Wesley F. Zandberg
original_title: Development and evaluation of a vineyard-based strategy to mitigate smoke-taint in wine grapes
original_journal: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
replication_authors: James W. Favell; Osei B. Fordwour; Sydney C. Morgan; Ieva Zigg; Wesley F. Zandberg
replication_title: Large-Scale Reassessment of In-Vineyard Smoke-Taint Grapevine Protection Strategies and the Development of Predictive Off-Vine Models
explanation: The current study explicitly re-evaluates the biofilm treatment from the prior pilot study [20] and finds the opposite effect: 'In contrast with earlier studies, our results demonstrated that in all cases, the biofilm treatments led to increased concentrations of both free and total VPs in smoke-exposed grapes.' The paper notes 'a result that is in direct contrast with previous field studies, demonstrating that this product exhibited significant reductions in VPs after smoke exposure [20],' and 'The consistent failure to replicate crop protection with the biofilm was surprising.'

description: In prediabetes patients undergoing lifestyle intervention (TULIP), both low insulin secretion capacity and insulin-resistant NAFLD (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease) independently predict metabolic non-response (failure to achieve normal glucose regulation), giving a 4-fold increased risk of non-response when at least one risk factor is present
original_authors: Norbert Stefan; Harald Staiger; Robert Wagner; Jürgen Machann; Fritz Schick; Hans-Ulrich Häring; Andreas Fritsche
original_title: A high-risk phenotype associates with reduced improvement in glycaemia during a lifestyle intervention in prediabetes
replication_authors: Stefan Kabisch; Nina M. T. Meyer; Caroline Honsek; Margrit Kemper; Christiana Gerbracht; Ayman M. Arafat; Ulrike Dambeck; Martin A. Osterhoff; Martin O. Weickert; Andreas F. H. Pfeiffer
replication_title: Predicting Factors for Metabolic Non-Response to a Complex Lifestyle Intervention—A Replication Analysis to a Randomized-Controlled Trial
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We could not replicate previous data suggesting that an insulin-resistant fatty liver is a specific risk factor for treatment failure.' In their analysis, neither NAFLD, insulin resistance, nor their combination predicted non-response, directly contradicting the main novel finding of the TULIP study. The paper also notes they 'cannot replicate the TULIP finding on the high-risk potential of an insulin-resistant NAFLD.'

description: Hungarian households generate approximately 68 kg of food waste per capita annually, with avoidable food waste dominated by meals, bakery products, fresh vegetables, dairy products, and fresh fruits, as measured using the FUSIONS diary methodology
original_authors: Barbara Szabó-Bódi; Gyula Kasza; Dávid Szakos
original_title: Assessment of household food waste in Hungary
replication_authors: Gyula Kasza; Annamária Dorkó; Atilla Kunszabó; Dávid Szakos
replication_title: Quantification of Household Food Waste in Hungary: A Replication Study Using the FUSIONS Methodology
explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'a replication of the first Hungarian measurement-based research conducted in 2016' and describe 'promising results.' The 2019 study found very similar food waste quantities (65.49 kg vs. 68.04 kg per capita, a 4% decrease) and virtually identical proportions of avoidable vs. unavoidable food waste (48.82% vs. 48.70%), confirming the original study's composition findings.

description: Static emotional faces and bodies in visual artworks convey dynamic information, with specific emotions (anger, fear, disgust) rated as more dynamic ('e-motions') than others, and bodies rated as more dynamic than faces
original_authors: Rossana Actis-Grosso; Daniele Zavagno
original_title: E-motions
replication_authors: Maria Elisa Della-Torre; Daniele Zavagno; Rossana Actis-Grosso
replication_title: The Interpretation of E-Motions in Faces and Bodies Derived from Static Artworks by Individuals with High Functioning Autistic Spectrum
explanation: The authors extended the original study (conducted only with typically developed individuals) to an ASD population to see if e-motions are perceived similarly. Results were mixed: overall no significant group differences emerged for dynamicity ratings, but ASD individuals showed more missing values for bodies, more frequent negative emotion labels, and some artwork-specific differences. The authors conclude 'Contrary to our expectations, overall no difference emerged between the two groups, but the interaction Artwork x Group showed that for some images ASDs assigned a different value than TDs to perceived dynamicism.'

description: Individual differences in errors on mean length and mean orientation ensemble judgments are positively correlated (r = 0.62), suggesting a shared mechanism underlying ensemble perception of these two low-level features
original_authors: Melanie Kacin; Isabel Gauthier; Oakyoon Cha
original_title: Ensemble coding of average length and average orientation are correlated
replication_authors: Melanie Kacin; Oakyoon Cha; Isabel Gauthier
replication_title: The Relation between Ensemble Coding of Length and Orientation Does Not Depend on Spatial Attention
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated Kacin et al.'s [12] result of a correlation for errors made by participants when reporting the average length or the average orientation of arrays of 12 lines.' The replication found r = 0.65 (95% CI = [0.49, 0.76]) compared to the original Study 1's r = 0.62 (95% CI = [0.45, 0.73]), with decisive Bayes factor support (BF+0 = 1.89 × 10^8).

description: The Screening Tool for Early Predictors of PTSD (STEPP) — an 8-item brief screening tool administered during acute trauma care — can identify injured children at higher risk for persistent traumatic stress symptoms at 6 months post-injury with excellent sensitivity (0.88) and moderate specificity (0.48)
original_authors: Winston, F. K.; Kassam-Adams, N.; Garcia-Espana, F.; Ittenbach, R.; Cnaan, A.
original_title: Screening for risk of persistent posttraumatic stress in injured children and their parents
original_journal: Journal of the American Medical Association
replication_authors: Kassam-Adams N.; Marsac ML; García-España JF; Winston F.
replication_title: Evaluating predictive screening for children's post-injury mental health: New data and a replication
explanation: The STEPP showed very low sensitivity (0.16) and higher specificity (0.87) in the current sample for PTS prediction, far below the original's sensitivity of 0.88. The authors explicitly state 'poor to modest replication (STEPP)' in the Discussion, and conclude that 'evidence to date does not support the use of the current STEPP tool specifically.'

description: The Child Trauma Screening Questionnaire (CTSQ) — a 10-item screening tool of early PTS symptoms (five re-experiencing and five arousal symptoms) — can predict persistent posttraumatic stress disorder in injured children at 6 months with excellent sensitivity (0.82) and good specificity (0.74)
original_authors: Justin A. Kenardy; Susan H. Spence; Alexandra C. Macleod
original_title: Screening for posttraumatic stress disorder in children after accidental injury
replication_authors: Kassam-Adams N.; Marsac ML; García-España JF; Winston F.
replication_title: Evaluating predictive screening for children's post-injury mental health: New data and a replication
explanation: The CPSS-10 analog of the CTSQ showed moderate sensitivity (0.57) and strong specificity (0.91) for 6-month PTS prediction, compared to original sensitivity of 0.82 and specificity of 0.74. The authors characterize this as 'partial replication (CTSQ),' noting results may be limited by the use of parallel CPSS items rather than original CTSQ wording.

description: Anodal tDCS applied over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex improves the efficiency of the executive conflict network of attention in healthy volunteers
original_authors: Joanna Astrid Miler; Daniel Meron; David S. Baldwin; Matthew Garner
original_title: The effect of prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation on attention network function in healthy volunteers: TDCS and attention network function
original_journal: Neuromodulation: Technology at the Neural Interface
replication_authors: Coussement C.; de Vega MR; Heeren A.
replication_title: The Impact of Anodal tDCS on the Attentional Networks as a Function of Trait Anxiety and Depressive Symptoms: A Preregistered Double-Blind Sham-Controlled Experiment.
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'no evidence was found to support the first hypothesis,' with the Stimulation x Network interaction being non-significant (F(2,38) = 0.07, p = .93) and the executive conflict network comparison showing no effect (t(49) = .61, p = .55, d = .09), compared to the original effect size of d = .76.

description: Feeling thermometer, trait evaluation, and trust measures of affective polarization are highly correlated in the US, while social distance measures are distinct; voters rate party elites more negatively than party supporters
original_authors: James N. Druckman; Matthew S. Levendusky
original_title: What do we measure when we measure affective polarization?
replication_authors: Luana Russo; Emma Turkenburg; Eelco Harteveld; Anna Heckhausen
replication_title: This is not US: measuring polarization in multiparty systems.  A quasi-replication study
replication_journal: Quaderni dell Osservatorio elettorale QOE - IJES
explanation: The authors explicitly frame their study as following 'the logic of Druckman and Levendusky (2019)' to test how different AP measures perform relative to one another, this time in a European multiparty context. Their conclusions are broadly consistent with the original: affective scales (like-dislike, trust, thermometer) perform similarly to one another, social distance measures differ, and politicians receive lower sympathy than voters — all 'in line with previous literature (Druckman & Levendusky, 2019)'.

description: Pleasant (tonal) background music causes food to be perceived as tasting better than unpleasant (atonal) background music, with an interaction between music pleasantness and presentation order
original_authors: Ziv, Naomi
original_title: Musical flavor: the effect of background music and presentation order on taste
replication_authors: Afriza Animawan Arifin; Abdullah Azzam Al Afghani; Valendra Granitha
replication_title: The Effect of Tonal (VS Atonal) Music Background On Cookies Taste Preferences: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Hasil ini berbeda dengan penelitian Ziv (2018)' (These results differ from Ziv (2018)), reporting no significant difference in cookie taste ratings between pleasant and unpleasant music conditions (t(38) = -.269, p = 0.789), and no interaction between presentation order and background music.

description: A mechanistic mathematical model of neurovascular coupling that predicts arteriolar dilation in mice under various sensory and optogenetic stimulations in both awake and anaesthetised conditions
original_authors: Sebastian Sten; Fredrik Elinder; Gunnar Cedersund; Maria Engström
original_title: A quantitative analysis of cell-specific contributions and the role of anesthetics to the neurovascular coupling
replication_authors: Sergio Dempsey; Gunnar Cedersund; Maria Engström; Gonzalo Maso Talou; Soroush Safaei
replication_title: Reproducibility Study for a Computational Model of the Neurovascular Coupling Unit
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'All subplots agree with the primary publication' for each reproduced figure, and the Discussion confirms 'Figures illustrating the model predictions from the primary publication were produced without error.' The curation report also confirms 'Successfully reproduced all the figures presented in this manuscript.'

description: Night duty clinical placements for undergraduate registered nurse students offer diverse learning opportunities and help students appreciate the round-the-clock nature of nursing, feeling better prepared for the workforce
original_authors: Lisa McKenna; Jill French
original_title: Rethinking student night duty placements
replication_authors: Valerie Zielinksi; Denielle Beardmore
replication_title: Rethinking student night duty placements - a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly designed this as a replication study with a different student population (enrolled nurse students instead of registered nurse students), and conclude: 'The findings of this study are congruent with the findings of McKenna and French (2010)' and 'This replication study has added evidentiary support that night duty is a highly appropriate model of professional clinical practice for the enrolled nurse.'

description: Perceiving visible speech gestures (lip movements) causes perceptuomotor compatibility effects, facilitating responses when the visible gesture matches the required vocal response
original_authors: Dirk Kerzel; Harold Bekkering
original_title: Motor activation from visible speech: Evidence from stimulus response compatibility
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception & Performance
replication_authors: Bruno Galantucci; Carol A. Fowler; Louis Goldstein
replication_title: Perceptuomotor compatibility effects in speech
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Experiment 1 confirmed that the perceptuomotor effects found by Kerzel and Bekkering (2000) extend to the auditory modality' and the results section notes the voiced response latencies 'closely replicate the findings of Kerzel and Bekkering (2000).' The effect was significant (F(1,23)=17.1, p<.001, eta²=.43 for the key voiced response condition).

description: Bilingual and monolingual observers can discriminate Spanish from Catalan in visual-only speech displays, with bilinguals outperforming monolinguals, and that knowledge of at least one of the languages is necessary for successful visual-only language discrimination
original_authors: Salvador Soto-Faraco; Jordi Navarra; Whitney M. Weikum; Athena Vouloumanos; Núria Sebastián-Gallés; Janet F. Werker
original_title: Discriminating languages by speech reading
replication_authors: Rebecca E. Ronquest; Susannah V. Levi; David B. Pisoni
replication_title: Language identification from visual-only speech signals
explanation: The authors confirmed the key finding that all observer groups could identify the language from visual-only speech above chance. However, they explicitly note: 'Although we failed to replicate the effect of linguistic experience (monolingual vs. bilingual) on sensitivity, its effect was observed in response bias.' The use of different languages (English/Spanish vs. Spanish/Catalan) and a different paradigm (identification vs. discrimination) classifies this as a close extension.

description: Transient covert attention increases the apparent contrast of a stimulus, as measured by peripheral cueing of Gabor patches in a high-contrast range (6%-69% Michelson contrast)
original_authors: Marisa Carrasco; Sam Ling; Sarah Read
original_title: Attention alters appearance
replication_authors: Sam Ling; Marisa Carrasco
replication_title: Transient covert attention does alter appearance: A reply to Schneider (2006)
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted 'an exact replication of Experiment 2 in our original study' with the added manipulation of black vs. white cue luminance. The results section states 'The results with the black cue replicated what we found in the high contrast condition (Experiment 2) in Carrasco, Ling, and Read (2004)' and the discussion concludes 'The present results replicate the finding that peripherally cuing a stimulus increases its apparent contrast.'

description: Shadowing latency to words on the attended ear increases when the coincident word on the unattended ear is a synonym, and decreases when it is an associated word, demonstrating semantic processing of unattended dichotic speech
original_authors: Joe L. Lewis
original_title: Semantic processing of unattended messages using dichotic listening
replication_authors: Anne Treisman; Rosemary Squire; Joanne Green
replication_title: Semantic processing in dichotic listening? A replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This experiment confirms Lewis's finding, but also clarifies its nature and defines further the conditions under which it can be obtained.' They found a significant synonym effect at Position 3 (F(1,20) = 6.5, p < .05), consistent with Lewis's original result, though they also found the effect was limited to early list positions — a qualification not present in the original.

description: The difficulty ordering for learning six fundamental types of rule-based categorization problems follows the pattern: Type I (easiest) < Type II < Types III/IV/V (roughly equal) < Type VI (hardest), implicating selective attention to dimensions
original_authors: Roger N. Shepard; Carl I. Hovland; Herbert M. Jenkins
original_title: Learning and memorization of classifications
replication_authors: Robert M. Nosofsky; Mark A. Gluck; Thomas J. Palmeri; Stephen C. Mckinley; Paul Glauthier
replication_title: Comparing models of rule-based classification learning: A replication and extension of Shepard, Hovland, and Jenkins (1961)
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Our general patterns of results replicated those observed in the original study' and 'the ordering of task difficulty being the same as in the original study.' Pairwise t-tests confirmed the same ordering of difficulty across all six problem types.

description: Subjects presented with contextually determined homophones (e.g., taxi-FARE) in an unattended channel during selective listening show implicit memory (spelling bias toward the primed meaning) but not explicit memory for those homophones
original_authors: Eric Eich
original_title: Memory for unattended events: Remembering with and without awareness
replication_authors: Noelle L. Wood; Michael A. Stadler; Nelson Cowan
replication_title: Is there implicit memory without attention? A reexamination of task demands in Eich’s (1984) procedure
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we carried out a direct replication of Eich (1984)' and confirm 'With a slow presentation rate, we replicate the result obtained by Eich (1984).' However, they also show the effect disappears when the attended channel speed is doubled, leading them to conclude that Eich's original interpretation (implicit memory without attention) is incorrect. The replication of the narrow empirical result succeeds but the overall finding is undermined by the methodological extensions.

description: A preceding /l/ syllable shifts the identification boundary along a /da/-/ga/ synthetic continuum toward more /g/ responses relative to a preceding /r/ syllable, due to carryover coarticulatory fronting of the velar consonant
original_authors: Virginia A. Mann
original_title: Influence of preceding liquid on stop-consonant perception
replication_authors: Carol A. Fowler; Catherine T. Best; Gerald W. Mcroberts
replication_title: Young infants’ perception of liquid coarticulatory influences on following stop consonants
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In the first experiment, we replicated a portion of Mann's (1980) Experiment I, using a subset of her stimuli.' The results confirmed the identification boundary shift, with the critical item d/ga3 identified predominantly as 'ga' after /al/ (70%) but as 'da' after /ar/ (90%), consistent with Mann's original findings.

description: A preceding /l/ syllable shifts the identification boundary along a /da/-/ga/ synthetic continuum toward more /g/ responses relative to a preceding /r/ syllable, due to carryover coarticulatory fronting of the velar consonant
original_authors: Virginia A. Mann
original_title: Influence of preceding liquid on stop-consonant perception
replication_authors: Carol A. Fowler; Catherine T. Best; Gerald W. Mcroberts
replication_title: Young infants’ perception of liquid coarticulatory influences on following stop consonants
explanation: Prelinguistic 4-to-5-month-old infants showed the same context-dependent reversal in discrimination performance as adults, successfully discriminating between-category pairs but not within-category pairs. The authors conclude: 'The results suggest that prelinguistic infants disentangle consonant-consonant coarticulatory influences in speech in an adult-like fashion.'

description: Events signaling the termination of electric shock (a light signal following barpress escape) take on secondary reinforcement capability and increase resistance to extinction in a runway test
original_authors: Murray Ak; Strandberg Jm
original_title: Development of a conditioned positive reinforcer through removal of an aversive stimulus
replication_authors: Paul S. Siegel; Robert O’bannon
replication_title: Establishment of a conditioned reinforcer in relation to shock termination—an attempt to replicate
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This study fails to replicate Murray-Strandberg (1965).' No facilitating effect of the conditioned signal was found in either massed or spaced conditions (chi-square = 1.00 for experimental vs. control comparison).

description: Negative emotional distraction during a delayed working memory task causes differential modulation of dorsal frontoparietal (reduced activation) and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (increased activation) compared to neutral distraction
original_authors: Florin Dolcos; Gregory McCarthy
original_title: Brain systems mediating cognitive interference by emotional distraction
replication_authors: Alan Anticevic; Deanna M. Barch; Grega Repovs
replication_title: Resisting emotional interference: Brain regions facilitating working memory performance during negative distraction
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'In the present study, we replicated prior work showing that negative distraction differentially modulates prefrontal activity during WM when compared with other types of distraction.' The replication used the same delayed WM paradigm with negative IAPS distractors but with some methodological differences (one distractor vs. two in the original, slow event-related fMRI vs. the original design), hence classified as close experiment.

description: Resting-state amygdala functional connectivity shows significant negative coupling with main components of the dorsal frontoparietal task network
original_authors: Roy AK; Shehzad Z.; Margulies DS; Kelly AM; Uddin LQ; Gotimer K.; Biswal BB; Castellanos FX; Milham MP
original_title: Functional connectivity of the human amygdala using resting state fMRI
replication_authors: Alan Anticevic; Deanna M. Barch; Grega Repovs
replication_title: Resisting emotional interference: Brain regions facilitating working memory performance during negative distraction
explanation: Upgraded from medium to high. The authors provide explicit, unambiguous replication language in two places: (1) Results section: 'Overall, present results closely replicate prior work examining resting-state amygdala fcMRI (Roy et al., 2009), indicating significant negative coupling between amygdala and the main components of the dorsal task network'; (2) Discussion: 'We replicate prior resting-state findings by showing negative fcMRI between the amygdala and the dorsal frontal-parietal cortex.' The resting-state fcMRI results met whole-brain correction at p < .05. Replicating resting-state amygdala fcMRI was a stated goal of the study. Result classification as 'success' and type as 'close experiment' (same method, new independent sample, different broader study context) are well-supported.

description: Participants choke under pressure when performing a classification task requiring an explicit rule-based strategy, but excel under pressure when performing a task requiring an implicit information-integration strategy (with a gains reward structure)
original_authors: Markman AB; Maddox WT; Worthy DA
original_title: Choking and excelling under pressure
replication_authors: Worthy DA; Markman AB; Maddox WT
replication_title: What is pressure? Evidence for social pressure as a type of regulatory focus
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We obtained the same pattern of results as that of Markman et al. (2006)... participants who performed rule-based tasks in Experiment 2 choked under pressure, and participants who performed information-integration tasks excelled under pressure, when they were gaining points for correct responses.' The category type × pressure level interaction was significant (F(1,36) = 7.74, p < .01).

description: Selective attention to one of two interleaved colored shape streams during a one-back cover task results in learning of temporal regularities for the attended stream but not the unattended stream (Experiment 3, implicit RT measure)
original_authors: Nicholas B. Turk-Browne; Justin A. Jungé; Brian J. Scholl
original_title: The automaticity of visual statistical learning
replication_authors: Elizabeth Musz; Matthew J. Weber; Sharon L. Thompson-Schill
replication_title: Visual statistical learning is not reliably modulated by selective attention to isolated events
explanation: The authors explicitly call Experiment 2 'a direct replication of Turk-Browne et al.'s (2005) Experiment 3.' They found no Stream × Position interaction (F(2,50)<1), whereas the original found a significant interaction (F(2,22)=3.49, p=.048), leading them to conclude they 'were unable to fully replicate the findings of Turk-Browne et al. (2005).'

description: Selective attention to one of two interleaved colored shape streams results in above-chance familiarity judgment accuracy for attended shapes (77%) but not unattended shapes (49%), demonstrating that explicit VSL is gated by selective attention (Experiment 1B)
original_authors: Nicholas B. Turk-Browne; Justin A. Jungé; Brian J. Scholl
original_title: The automaticity of visual statistical learning
replication_authors: Elizabeth Musz; Matthew J. Weber; Sharon L. Thompson-Schill
replication_title: Visual statistical learning is not reliably modulated by selective attention to isolated events
explanation: Experiment 4 is explicitly described as 'a direct replication of Turk-Browne et al.'s (2005) Experiment 1B.' The original found 77% attended vs. 49% unattended (t(7)=4.06, p=.005); this replication found 62% attended vs. 55% unattended with no significant difference between streams (t(23)=1.59, p=.13), indicating failure to replicate the attentional modulation of explicit VSL.

description: Right-handers estimate objects as smaller when they intend to grasp them in their right rather than their left hand, because they believe their right hand can grasp larger objects (action-specific scaling effect)
original_authors: Sally A. Linkenauger; Jessica K. Witt; Dennis R. Proffitt
original_title: Taking a hands-on approach: Apparent grasping ability scales the perception of object size
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Elizabeth S. Collier; Rebecca Lawson
replication_title: Does grasping capacity influence object size estimates? It depends on the context
explanation: Experiment 1 tested whether leading instructions (implying body-size shrinkage, action-capacity, or objective size) would produce scaling effects using a taping manipulation on grasping capacity. No significant effects were found (Taping F(1,48)=0.416, p=.5, ηp²=.01), with Bayesian analyses providing positive to strong evidence for the null hypothesis. The authors conclude 'We found no evidence that differences in demand characteristics due to hypothesis guessing could explain why Collier and Lawson (2017) failed to replicate Linkenauger et al. (2011, Experiment 2).'

description: Right-handers estimate objects as smaller when they intend to grasp them in their right rather than their left hand, because they believe their right hand can grasp larger objects (action-specific scaling effect)
original_authors: Sally A. Linkenauger; Jessica K. Witt; Dennis R. Proffitt
original_title: Taking a hands-on approach: Apparent grasping ability scales the perception of object size
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Elizabeth S. Collier; Rebecca Lawson
replication_title: Does grasping capacity influence object size estimates? It depends on the context
explanation: Experiment 2 used explicitly directive instructions telling participants the expected outcome and found a significant scaling effect (taped hand estimates larger, p=.016, ηp²=.31), comparable to ~3% original effect. However, the authors argue this only occurred because instructions 'unrealistically' told participants the predicted direction of the effect, making it an artifact of extreme demand characteristics rather than genuine perceptual replication: 'Such extreme demand characteristics seem unlikely to explain the perceptual scaling effects reported in Experiment 2 of Linkenauger et al. (2011).'

description: Right-handers estimate objects as smaller when they intend to grasp them in their right rather than their left hand, because they believe their right hand can grasp larger objects (action-specific scaling effect)
original_authors: Sally A. Linkenauger; Jessica K. Witt; Dennis R. Proffitt
original_title: Taking a hands-on approach: Apparent grasping ability scales the perception of object size
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Elizabeth S. Collier; Rebecca Lawson
replication_title: Does grasping capacity influence object size estimates? It depends on the context
explanation: Experiment 3 reproduced the original's key procedural feature — asking participants to rate graspability immediately before estimating size on every trial — and found a significant scaling effect (taped hand estimates larger than untaped hand, p=.041, ηp²=.24). The authors conclude this replicates the original's ~3% effect: 'These results provide evidence for the suggestion by Collier and Lawson (2017) that the scaling effect reported by Linkenauger et al. (2011, Experiment 2) occurred because action capacity estimates were conflated with size estimates.' (The authors attribute the effect to demand characteristics/context effects rather than genuine perception, but the scaling effect itself was successfully reproduced.)

description: Heavy media multitaskers (HMMs) show increased susceptibility to distraction compared to light media multitaskers (LMMs) on multiple laboratory tasks of information processing, including change detection, AX-CPT, N-back, and task switching
original_authors: Ophir, Eyal; Nass, Clifford; Wagner, Anthony
original_title: Cognitive control in media multitaskers
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Wisnu Wiradhany; Mark R. Nieuwenstein
replication_title: Cognitive control in media multitaskers: Two replication studies and a meta-Analysis
explanation: In Experiment 1, only 3 of 7 targeted effects reached significance (vs. an expected 5–6 given the average replication power of .81), and a Bayesian analysis supported only 1 of those 3 effects. The authors concluded: 'the results of our first replication study did not produce a successful replication in terms of statistical tests aimed at determining the presence of an effect.'

description: Heavy media multitaskers (HMMs) show increased susceptibility to distraction compared to light media multitaskers (LMMs) on multiple laboratory tasks of information processing, including change detection, AX-CPT, N-back, and task switching
original_authors: Ophir, Eyal; Nass, Clifford; Wagner, Anthony
original_title: Cognitive control in media multitaskers
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Wisnu Wiradhany; Mark R. Nieuwenstein
replication_title: Cognitive control in media multitaskers: Two replication studies and a meta-Analysis
explanation: In Experiment 2 (conducted with Dutch university students), only 2 of 7 targeted effects reached significance, and Bayes factors supported only 1 of those. The authors concluded that 'the results of our second replication generally conform to those of our first replication study in suggesting that while HMMs may indeed perform worse than LMMs on various tests of distractibility, the magnitude of these differences is smaller than the effects found by Ophir et al.', and the overall meta-analysis turned nonsignificant after correction for small-study effects.

description: Attention effects (valid minus invalid cueing accuracy) are larger when targets are flanked by irrelevant distractors than when targets are presented alone, reflecting biased competition in which spatial attention resolves distractor interference
original_authors: Edward Awh; Antoinette Marie Sgarlata; John Kliestik
original_title: Resolving visual interference during covert spatial orienting: Online attentional control through static records of prior visual experience
replication_authors: Miranda Scolari; Edward Awh
replication_title: Object-based biased competition during covert spatial orienting
explanation: The authors explicitly state their first goal was to replicate the biased-competition pattern from Awh et al. (2005), and they successfully observed it: a significant interaction between display type and cue validity, F(1, 23) = 8.74, p = .007, d = 0.6, BF10 = 8.02, with larger attention effects in distractor-present (M = 15%) than distractor-absent (M = 6%) displays.

description: Temporal difference thresholds are lower for auditory intervals than for tactile and visual intervals, with no significant difference between tactile and visual thresholds
original_authors: Luke A. Jones; Ellen Poliakoff; Jill Wells
original_title: Good vibrations: Human interval timing in the vibrotactile modality
replication_authors: Emily A. Williams; Ezgi M. Yüksel; Andrew J. Stewart; Luke A. Jones
replication_title: Modality differences in timing and the filled-duration illusion: Testing the pacemaker rate explanation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'For Research Aim 1, we closely replicated the threshold and estimation tasks of Jones et al. (2009).' The replication found that thresholds for visual intervals were significantly higher than those for auditory and tactile intervals, consistent with the original — though this paper also found a significant auditory-tactile difference that Jones et al. did not.

description: Verbal estimation slopes are steeper for auditory intervals than for visual intervals, with tactile slopes not differing significantly from visual slopes
original_authors: Luke A. Jones; Ellen Poliakoff; Jill Wells
original_title: Good vibrations: Human interval timing in the vibrotactile modality
replication_authors: Emily A. Williams; Ezgi M. Yüksel; Andrew J. Stewart; Luke A. Jones
replication_title: Modality differences in timing and the filled-duration illusion: Testing the pacemaker rate explanation
explanation: The authors replicated Jones et al.'s estimation task (Experiment 1B) and found that 'visual slopes were significantly shallower than both auditory and tactile slopes,' consistent with the original finding. Auditory and tactile slopes did not differ significantly, also consistent with the original.

description: Verbal estimation slopes for empty intervals are approximately 35% shallower than those for filled intervals (filled-duration illusion)
original_authors: John H. Wearden; Roger Norton; Simon Martin; Oliver Montford-Bebb
original_title: Internal clock processes and the filled-duration illusion
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Emily A. Williams; Ezgi M. Yüksel; Andrew J. Stewart; Luke A. Jones
replication_title: Modality differences in timing and the filled-duration illusion: Testing the pacemaker rate explanation
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We aimed to replicate this effect' and confirmed it: slopes for empty intervals were 30% shallower than filled intervals (vs. 35% in the original), with a significant paired-samples t test (t(29) = 4.65, p < .001, d = 0.85). They state the finding 'confirms the findings of previous research (Wearden et al., 2007).'

description: High foveal load (induced by a low-frequency pretarget word) reduces parafoveal preprocessing of the upcoming word, producing a LOAD by PREVIEW interaction on fixation durations when parafoveal letter masks are used as previews
original_authors: John M. Henderson; Fernanda Ferreira
original_title: Effects of foveal processing difficulty on the perceptual span in reading: Implications for attention and eye movement control
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Eva Findelsberger; Florian Hutzler; Stefan Hawelka
replication_title: Spill the load: Mixed evidence for a foveal load effect, reliable evidence for a spillover effect in eye-movement control during reading
explanation: In Experiment 1, the authors tried to replicate Henderson and Ferreira (1990) as directly as possible using parafoveal letter masks. They explicitly state: 'This failure to replicate the original study by Henderson and Ferreira (1990) is in line with several other studies that could not (conceptually) replicate the effect.' No significant LOAD x PREVIEW interactions were found for any fixation measure.

description: High foveal load (induced by a low-frequency pretarget word) reduces parafoveal preprocessing of the upcoming word, producing a LOAD by PREVIEW interaction on fixation durations
original_authors: John M. Henderson; Fernanda Ferreira
original_title: Effects of foveal processing difficulty on the perceptual span in reading: Implications for attention and eye movement control
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Eva Findelsberger; Florian Hutzler; Stefan Hawelka
replication_title: Spill the load: Mixed evidence for a foveal load effect, reliable evidence for a spillover effect in eye-movement control during reading
explanation: REVIEWED: Experiment 2 used visual degradation of parafoveal previews (a different method from Henderson & Ferreira's letter masks). The critical Load × Preview (C1) interaction was significant for first fixation duration (t = -2.16) and gaze duration (t = -2.59), but not for single fixation duration (t = -1.62, ns). Effect sizes were small (d = 0.14 and 0.17). The authors characterize this as 'mixed evidence' (paper title) and 'some evidence' — hedging language that creates genuine ambiguity about whether to classify as success vs. inconclusive. Classified as 'success' because the key statistical interactions were significant, but medium confidence is retained because: (1) the authors themselves frame the overall findings cautiously, (2) only 2 of 3 fixation measures showed significant interactions, (3) the paper's conclusion states 'the frequency-based foveal load effect is quite small, and hence its reproducibility is uncertain.' Replication type 'close experiment' is correct: same construct (foveal load effect) tested with a different preview manipulation method.

description: Memory-driven attentional capture occurs when one item is held in visual working memory (Load 1), but disappears when two items are held (Load 2), supporting the single-item-template hypothesis
original_authors: Dirk Van Moorselaar; Jan Theeuwes; Christian N. L. Olivers
original_title: In competition for the attentional template: Can multiple items within visual working memory guide attention?
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Marcella Frătescu; Dirk Van Moorselaar; Sebastiaan Mathôt
replication_title: Can you have multiple attentional templates? Large-scale replications of Van Moorselaar, Theeuwes, and Olivers (2014) and Hollingworth and Beck (2016)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully replicated the key finding of Van Moorselaar et al. (2014): In their paradigm, memory-driven capture reliably occurs with a memory load of one item, but is completely abolished with a memory load of two items.' The task was closely modeled after the original and reimplemented by the original author (D.M.), but conducted in-the-wild by undergraduate students rather than in a laboratory setting.

description: Memory-driven attentional capture occurs even when two items are held in visual working memory, as demonstrated by the gap-location task showing stronger capture when two distractors match memorized colors versus one
original_authors: Andrew Hollingworth; Valerie M. Beck
