original_title: Memory-based attention capture when multiple items are maintained in visual working memory
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Marcella Frătescu; Dirk Van Moorselaar; Sebastiaan Mathôt
replication_title: Can you have multiple attentional templates? Large-scale replications of Van Moorselaar, Theeuwes, and Olivers (2014) and Hollingworth and Beck (2016)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully replicated the key finding of Hollingworth and Beck (2016): In their gap-location task, memory-driven capture reliably occurs with a memory load of two items.' The task was closely modeled after the original gap-location task, reimplemented based on the original script, and the same pattern of stronger capture for two matching distractors versus one was confirmed.

description: Unconsciously processed (inattentionally blind) stimuli interfere with a primary task: classification of attended stimuli is slower when the content of the undetected, task-irrelevant stimulus is incongruent versus congruent with the target
original_authors: Robert Schnuerch; Carina Kreitz; Henning Gibbons; Daniel Memmert
original_title: Not quite so blind: Semantic processing despite inattentional blindness
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Giulia Pugnaghi; Daniel Memmert; Carina Kreitz
replication_title: Loads of unconscious processing: The role of perceptual load in processing unattended stimuli during inattentional blindness
explanation: Experiment 1 successfully replicated the interference effect: 'The conducted ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of condition, with significantly higher mean reaction times in the incongruent condition than in the congruent condition, F(1, 64) = 7.40, p < .01, η²P = .10. This replicates the interference effect found by Schnuerch et al. (2016).' The authors confirm the replication in the Discussion.

description: Unconsciously processed (inattentionally blind) stimuli interfere with a primary task: classification of attended stimuli is slower when the content of the undetected, task-irrelevant stimulus is incongruent versus congruent with the target
original_authors: Robert Schnuerch; Carina Kreitz; Henning Gibbons; Daniel Memmert
original_title: Not quite so blind: Semantic processing despite inattentional blindness
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Giulia Pugnaghi; Daniel Memmert; Carina Kreitz
replication_title: Loads of unconscious processing: The role of perceptual load in processing unattended stimuli during inattentional blindness
explanation: Experiment 2 showed mixed results: the interference effect was not significant for reaction times (F(1,101) = 1.12, p = .29) but was significant for accuracy (F(1,101) = 4.26, p < .05). The authors note this was 'especially surprising' given the design was closer to the original paradigm, and describe the RT result as a failure to replicate while the accuracy result confirmed the effect.

description: A contrast effect emerges in temporally overlapping event files: when a simultaneously presented visual amplitude differs from the hand amplitude, the replication moves in the opposite direction
original_authors: Anna Schubö; Gisa Aschersleben; Wolfgang Prinz
original_title: Interactions between perception and action in a reaction task with overlapping S-R assignments
replication_authors: Oliver Simon Sack; Christine Sutter
replication_title: Temporal persistence of after-effects in the n-1 replication task
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the General Discussion: 'We replicated the contrast effect by Schubö et al. (2001) in our n-1 replication task.' The effect was observed for varying hand amplitudes in Experiment 1 (sequence 1), confirming the predicted contrast pattern.

description: Assimilation effect in the n replication task: when cursor amplitude in phase 1 is longer than hand amplitude, participants overshoot in the subsequent replication, and vice versa — reflecting short-term binding of sensory and motor codes within an event file
original_authors: Stefan Ladwig; Christine Sutter; Jochen Müsseler
original_title: Intra-and intermodal integration of discrepant visual and proprioceptive action effects
replication_authors: Oliver Simon Sack; Christine Sutter
replication_title: Temporal persistence of after-effects in the n-1 replication task
explanation: Reviewer verification: The assimilation effect was confirmed for varying hand amplitudes (sequence 2, p=.001, both over- and undershoots significantly different from zero). However, for varying cursor amplitudes, no significant after-effects were found at all — 'Contrary to [Ladwig et al.], we did not find any statistically significant after-effects for varying cursor amplitudes.' Since Ladwig et al. (2012, 2013) found the assimilation effect for both conditions, this is a genuine partial replication. The authors attribute the null finding for cursor amplitudes to internal model adjustment and their controlled gain sequences (which Ladwig et al. did not use), and call for future studies to clarify. Classified as 'inconclusive' because the core effect replicated in one condition but failed in another; medium confidence retained because reasonable reviewers could also classify this as 'success' given that the primary effect did replicate.

description: Mind-wandering during the Metronome Response Task (MRT) is associated with greater rhythmic response time variability (RRTv) compared to on-task states, with higher RRTv in the second half of the experiment
original_authors: Paul Seli; James Allan Cheyne; Daniel Smilek
original_title: Wandering minds and wavering rhythms: linking mind wandering and behavioral variability
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Thomas Anderson; Rotem Petranker; Hause Lin; Norman A.S. Farb
replication_title: The metronome response task for measuring mind wandering: Replication attempt and extension of three studies by Seli et al
explanation: The authors state they 'successfully replicated the association between MW and greater RRTv.' The ANOVA showed a significant main effect of Report Type (F(2,5386)=58.092, p<.0001) and Block (F(1,5386)=49.79, p<.0001), fully replicating the original findings, though with a modified probe design measuring intentionality rather than tuned/zoned out distinctions.

description: Motivation significantly predicts mean rhythmic response time variability (RRTv) in the Metronome Response Task, with this relationship mediated by the proportion of mind-wandering reports
original_authors: Paul Seli; James Allan Cheyne; Mengran Xu; Christine Purdon; Daniel Smilek
original_title: Motivation, intentionality, and mind wandering: implications for assessments of task-unrelated thought
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Thomas Anderson; Rotem Petranker; Hause Lin; Norman A.S. Farb
replication_title: The metronome response task for measuring mind wandering: Replication attempt and extension of three studies by Seli et al
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'findings from Seli et al. (2015a) were not replicated.' No direct correlation between Motivation and Mean RRTv was found (r(298)=-0.08, p=.187), contrary to the original study's finding that motivation significantly predicted MRT performance.

description: Confidence in self-reported mental states moderates the relationship between report type and rhythmic response time variability (RRTv) in the Metronome Response Task, such that high-confidence participants show stronger report type effects
original_authors: Paul Seli; Tanya R. Jonker; James Allan Cheyne; Kassandra Cortes; Daniel Smilek
original_title: Can research participants comment authoritatively on the validity of their self-reports of mind wandering and task engagement?
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Thomas Anderson; Rotem Petranker; Hause Lin; Norman A.S. Farb
replication_title: The metronome response task for measuring mind wandering: Replication attempt and extension of three studies by Seli et al
explanation: The authors explicitly report 'a failure to conceptually replicate the effect of confidence found in the original (Seli et al. 2015b).' Confidence did not significantly interact with Report Type as a predictor of RRTv, consistent with a prior direct replication failure by Meier (2018).

description: Attentional capture by a salient distractor singleton is reduced when the distractor frequently appears at a high-probability location (singleton-detection mode), with participants also showing less efficient target selection at the high-probability location
original_authors: Benchi Wang; Jan Theeuwes
original_title: Statistical regularities modulate attentional capture
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Yavor Ivanov; Jan Theeuwes
replication_title: Distractor suppression leads to reduced flanker interference
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'These results are completely consistent with the findings of Wang & Theeuwes (2018a)' and in the General Discussion: 'Our results are a successful replication of Wang and Theeuwes (2018a, 2018b) in an online sample of participants.' The replication used an online version of the task (Prolific), making it a close extension of the original lab-based study.

description: Even in feature-search mode, attentional capture by a salient distractor singleton is reduced when the distractor frequently appears at a high-probability location, showing statistical learning of distractor location is independent of search strategy
original_authors: Benchi Wang; Jan Theeuwes
original_title: Statistical regularities modulate attentional capture independent of search strategy
replication_authors: Yavor Ivanov; Jan Theeuwes
replication_title: Distractor suppression leads to reduced flanker interference
explanation: The authors state 'consistent with Wang and Theeuwes (2018b), even when using feature-search, there is still a reliable effect of the statistical regularity as capture was smaller in the high-probability relative to the low-probability location.' The General Discussion also confirms this as 'a successful replication' conducted online.

description: Performing a secondary tone discrimination task during the retention interval of a retro-cue working memory paradigm reduces the retro-cue benefit in memory accuracy, indicating that orienting attention in visual working memory requires central attentional resources
original_authors: Markus Janczyk; Marian E. Berryhill
original_title: Orienting attention in visual working memory requires central capacity: decreased retro-cue effects under dual-task conditions
replication_authors: Yin-ting Lin; Edyta Sasin; Daryl Fougnie
replication_title: Selection in working memory is resource-demanding: Concurrent task effects on the retro-cue effect
explanation: Experiment 1 used a paradigm nearly identical to Janczyk & Berryhill (2014) but without articulatory suppression. The authors explicitly state: 'Experiment 1 did not replicate the key finding of Janczyk and Berryhill (2014). We did not find a decrease in the retro-cue effect under dual-task interference for memory accuracy.' The interaction between cue condition and task load was not significant (F(1,33) = 0.34, p = .562, BF = 0.21 supporting the null).

description: Performing a secondary tone discrimination task during the retention interval of a retro-cue working memory paradigm reduces the retro-cue benefit in memory accuracy, indicating that orienting attention in visual working memory requires central attentional resources
original_authors: Markus Janczyk; Marian E. Berryhill
original_title: Orienting attention in visual working memory requires central capacity: decreased retro-cue effects under dual-task conditions
replication_authors: Yin-ting Lin; Edyta Sasin; Daryl Fougnie
replication_title: Selection in working memory is resource-demanding: Concurrent task effects on the retro-cue effect
explanation: Experiment 2 added articulatory suppression as in Janczyk & Berryhill's original study, and successfully replicated their key finding. The authors state: 'With the modified design we replicated Janczyk and Berryhill's finding of an interaction between cue and task load, F(1,39) = 7.30, p = .010, η²p = .158', reflecting that the retro-cue effect was reduced under dual-task conditions.

description: Sequentially presenting four colored oriented bars at the same location selectively increases the proportion of swap errors (feature binding errors) compared to presenting them at different locations
original_authors: Yoni Pertzov; Masud Husain
original_title: The privileged role of location in visual working memory
replication_authors: Sebastian Schneegans; William J. Harrison; Paul M. Bays
replication_title: Location-independent feature binding in visual working memory for sequentially presented objects
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully reproduced a key finding from the main experiment of Pertzov and Husain (2014), namely that presenting memory sample stimuli sequentially at the same location selectively increased the proportion of swap errors when using short ISIs.' The replication added an ISI manipulation as a within-subject factor but reproduced the original paradigm closely.

description: Sequentially presenting items at the same location selectively impairs binding memory (as evidenced by swap errors) compared to presenting them at different locations, when tested with color as the feature to be reported and shape as the cue
original_authors: Yoni Pertzov; Masud Husain
original_title: The privileged role of location in visual working memory
replication_authors: Sebastian Schneegans; William J. Harrison; Paul M. Bays
replication_title: Location-independent feature binding in visual working memory for sequentially presented objects
explanation: In Experiment 2, using colored shapes (shape cue, color report), the authors found decreased overall recall performance in the same-location condition but no consistent selective increase in swap errors. The Discussion states: 'we did find a consistent effect of the location condition on recall errors...However, the effect is different from the one observed in the previous experiment...no consistent increase in the proportion of swap errors.' This indicates a partial/inconclusive replication of the binding-specific effect.

description: Numbers can be processed unconsciously: masked number primes affect reaction times (indirect task) even when participants cannot consciously discriminate the prime (direct task), indicating better sensitivity in the indirect than direct task (indirect task advantage, ITA)
original_authors: Stanislas Dehaene; Lionel Naccache; Gurvan Le Clec'H; Etienne Koechlin; Michael Mueller; Ghislaine Dehaene-Lambertz; Pierre-FranÇois van de Moortele; Denis Le Bihan
original_title: Imaging unconscious semantic priming
replication_authors: Iris A. Zerweck; Chung-Shan Kao; Sascha Meyen; Catarina Amado; Martin von Eltz; Maren Klimm; Volker H. Franz
replication_title: Number processing outside awareness? Systematically testing sensitivities of direct and indirect measures of consciousness
explanation: The authors state they 'successfully replicated the results from the original studies' in terms of priming effects, but crucially found 'no evidence for an ITA' when comparing sensitivities across tasks. They conclude this 'contradicts the interpretation from the original studies,' failing to replicate the key claim of unconscious processing (ITA). The replication found similar priming effects (11.3 ms) and similar direct task performance (54.1% correct, d'=0.23), but the indirect task sensitivity (d'=0.27) did not exceed the direct task sensitivity (difference d'=0.04, p=.5).

description: Masked number primes affect reaction times in an indirect task even when participants perform close to chance on a direct prime-classification task (smaller/larger than 5), indicating unconscious semantic processing of numbers
original_authors: Lionel Naccache; Stanislas Dehaene
original_title: Unconscious semantic priming extends to novel unseen stimuli
replication_authors: Iris A. Zerweck; Chung-Shan Kao; Sascha Meyen; Catarina Amado; Martin von Eltz; Maren Klimm; Volker H. Franz
replication_title: Number processing outside awareness? Systematically testing sensitivities of direct and indirect measures of consciousness
explanation: The paper explicitly compares its Experiment 1 to Naccache and Dehaene (2001a) as one of the 'original studies' and demonstrates that when the appropriate sensitivity analysis is applied, the indirect task sensitivity does not exceed the direct task sensitivity (no ITA). The authors state that 'the study of Naccache and Dehaene (2001), the results from their Experiment 1 even showed the opposite of an ITA,' and that their own replication confirms no ITA, contradicting the claim of unconscious processing.

description: Subliminal number priming occurs within and across notations (Arabic and verbal), with indirect task showing priming effects while direct task performance is near chance, indicating unconscious number processing
original_authors: Sid Kouider; Stanislas Dehaene
original_title: Subliminal number priming within and across the visual and auditory modalities
replication_authors: Iris A. Zerweck; Chung-Shan Kao; Sascha Meyen; Catarina Amado; Martin von Eltz; Maren Klimm; Volker H. Franz
replication_title: Number processing outside awareness? Systematically testing sensitivities of direct and indirect measures of consciousness
explanation: The paper explicitly includes Kouider and Dehaene (2009) as one of the 'original studies' and compares results to it in Experiment 1. While the notation-specific priming effects (cross-notation and within-notation) replicate qualitatively (Fig. 5), the key claim of an ITA (indirect task advantage implying unconscious processing) is not supported. The authors state 'the sensitivities in our Experiment 1, Dehaene et al. (1998), and Kouider and Dehaene (2009) were quite comparable' with no ITA found in any study when sensitivity analysis is applied.

description: Listeners who expected to hear two talkers showed a multitalker processing cost (slower response times in mixed vs. blocked conditions) while those who expected one talker did not, suggesting that phonetic processing can be modulated by top-down expectations about talker identity
original_authors: James S. Magnuson; Howard C. Nusbaum
original_title: Acoustic differences, listener expectations, and the perceptual accommodation of talker variability
replication_authors: Sahil Luthra; David Saltzman; Emily B. Myers; James S. Magnuson
replication_title: Listener expectations and the perceptual accommodation of talker variability: A pre-registered replication
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted 'a well-powered, pre-registered replication of Experiment 4 from Magnuson and Nusbaum (2007)' and found no significant interaction between Expectations and Blocking (χ²(1) = 0.00, p = .97), concluding that 'the previous finding was likely spurious' and that 'the present study suggests that the previous finding by Magnuson and Nusbaum (2007) that expectations can influence talker normalization should be regarded with skepticism.'

description: Listeners who expected to hear two talkers showed a multitalker processing cost (slower response times in mixed vs. blocked conditions) while those who expected one talker did not, suggesting that phonetic processing can be modulated by top-down expectations about talker identity
original_authors: James S. Magnuson; Howard C. Nusbaum
original_title: Acoustic differences, listener expectations, and the perceptual accommodation of talker variability
replication_authors: Sahil Luthra; David Saltzman; Emily B. Myers; James S. Magnuson
replication_title: Listener expectations and the perceptual accommodation of talker variability: A pre-registered replication
explanation: Experiment 2 tested whether the expectation effect would replicate in a speeded classification paradigm (rather than word monitoring). As in Experiment 1, the authors found no influence of expectations on multitalker processing costs (interaction χ²(1) = 0.27, p = .61), concluding that 'we did not observe multitalker processing costs in either group.'

description: Targets are classified faster when presented on faces that suddenly establish eye contact (sudden direct-gaze effect), reflecting additive and parallel influences of direct gaze and sudden-onset motion on attention capture
original_authors: Böckler, Anne; van der Wel, Robrecht P. R. D.; Welsh, Timothy N.
original_title: Catching Eyes: Effects of Social and Nonsocial Cues on Attention Capture
replication_authors: Christina Breil; Lynn Huestegge; Anne Böckler
replication_title: From eye to arrow: Attention capture by direct gaze requires more than just the eyes
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'This pattern of results replicates earlier findings of attention capture by direct gaze' and in the General Discussion confirm 'results of Experiment 1 revealed a reliable direct-gaze effect for human faces, replicating prior studies (Böckler et al., 2014)'. Both the gaze effect and motion effect were significant in the same direction as the original.

description: A three-range operant discrimination paradigm reliably demonstrates octave equivalence in human adults, such that participants generalize learned pitch-chroma patterns across octaves rather than using pitch height
original_authors: Marisa Hoeschele; Ronald G. Weisman; Christopher B. Sturdy
original_title: Pitch chroma discrimination, generalization and transfer tests of octave equivalence in humans
replication_authors: Bernhard Wagner; Christopher B. Sturdy; Ronald G. Weisman; Marisa Hoeschele
replication_title: Pitch chroma information is processed in addition to pitch height information with more than two pitch-range categories
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the successful large sample size replication in this paper emphasizes the paradigm's potential as a reliable tool in documenting octave equivalence.' The three-range group (-3+6-3) showed significant octave equivalence effects during generalization testing, with participants responding to pitch chroma rather than pitch height across octaves.

description: Including pre-learnt LTM word pairs within a working memory task enhances immediate memory performance compared to lists composed entirely of new pairs
original_authors: Bartsch, Lea; Shepherdson, Peter
original_title: Freeing capacity in WM through the use of LTM representations
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Lea M. Bartsch; Peter Shepherdson
replication_title: Chunking, boosting, or offloading? Using serial position to investigate long-term memory's enhancement of verbal working memory performance
explanation: In Experiment 1, the authors report 'Performance was superior when the WM set included pre-learnt (i.e., LTM) word pairs than when it consisted entirely of new pairs (BF10 = 24.17)', directly replicating the main finding. The study extends the original by systematically varying the serial position of LTM pairs.

description: Including pre-learnt LTM word pairs within a working memory task enhances immediate memory performance compared to lists composed entirely of new pairs
original_authors: Bartsch, Lea; Shepherdson, Peter
original_title: Freeing capacity in WM through the use of LTM representations
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Lea M. Bartsch; Peter Shepherdson
replication_title: Chunking, boosting, or offloading? Using serial position to investigate long-term memory's enhancement of verbal working memory performance
explanation: In Experiment 2, the authors state 'Replicating Experiment 1 and previous findings, the results of the WM task showed that immediate memory performance was superior when the WM set included pre-learnt (i.e., LTM available) word pairs than when it consisted entirely of new pairs (BF10 = 1.33 × 10^12)'. The experiment extends the original by adding a distractor task manipulation.

description: Response repetitions aid performance when a task repeats but impair performance when a task switches, producing a crossover interaction between task repetition and response repetition in a two-choice task with univalent stimuli
original_authors: Thomas Kleinsorge
original_title: Response repetition benefits and costs
replication_authors: Iring Koch; Eliot Hazeltine; Greta Petersen; Daniel H. Weissman
replication_title: Response-repetition costs in task switching do not index a simple response-switch bias: Evidence from manipulating the number of response alternatives
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the General Discussion: 'we replicated the basic interaction between task repetition and response repetition in the two-choice task of Experiment 1A.' The interaction was significant in both RT (F(1,39) = 118.130, p < .001) and error rates (F(1,39) = 44.358, p < .001), consistent with prior findings from univalent stimuli tasks in Kleinsorge (1999) and Rogers & Monsell (1995).

description: Self-referential stimuli are automatically prioritized in working memory in a delayed match-to-sample task, such that faster responses are observed when reacting to probes at locations where self-associated (vs. other-associated) stimuli had previously appeared
original_authors: Shouhang Yin; Jie Sui; Yu-Chin Chiu; Antao Chen; Tobias Egner
original_title: Automatic prioritization of self-referential stimuli in working memory
replication_authors: Roel van Dooren; Bryant J. Jongkees; Roberta Sellaro
replication_title: Self-prioritization in working memory gating
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude across two studies: 'our results do not provide convincing evidence that self-relevance can affect distinct component processes of WM.' Using the reference-back paradigm (a different methodology from Yin et al.'s delayed match-to-sample), they found null effects of self-relevance on all WM component processes (updating, gate opening, gate closing).

description: In the reference-back paradigm, a repetition benefit occurs on consecutive gate-opening trials (consecutive reference trials), reflecting a behavioral cost associated with switching the WM gate from closed to open
original_authors: Rachel Rac-Lubashevsky; Yoav Kessler
original_title: Dissociating working memory updating and automatic updating: The reference-back paradigm
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Roel van Dooren; Bryant J. Jongkees; Roberta Sellaro
replication_title: Self-prioritization in working memory gating
explanation: The authors report in both Study 1 and Study 2: 'Overall, these observations replicate previous findings in the literature (Rac-Lubashevsky & Kessler, 2016b).' The basic reference-back effects (repetition benefit on consecutive reference trials, updating cost, gate-opening and gate-closing costs) were successfully replicated in both studies.

description: Proactive regulation of cognitive stability (congruency effects) and flexibility (switch costs) are independent of each other: high proportions of switch trials reduce switch costs but do not increase congruency effects (LWPS effect), and high proportions of incongruent trials reduce congruency effects but do not increase switch costs (LWPC effect)
original_authors: Raphael Geddert; Tobias Egner
original_title: No need to choose: independent regulation of cognitive stability and flexibility challenges the stability-flexibility trade-off
replication_authors: Raphael Geddert; Tobias Egner
replication_title: Contextual control demands determine whether stability and flexibility trade off against each other
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'The results supplied a clear replication of our previous findings that proactive stability and flexibility modulations (i.e., LWPS and LWPC effects) are independent of each other.' Experiment 2 used the same parity-magnitude task switching paradigm with independently varied switch and incongruent trial proportions, but added embedded diagnostic trial sequences to control for local trial-sequence confounds.

description: Direct face/gaze and sudden onset motion independently capture attention, with the fastest responses occurring when both cues coincide (a suddenly moving face with direct gaze)
original_authors: Anne Böckler; Robrecht P. R. D. van der Wel; Timothy N. Welsh
original_title: Catching eyes: Effects of social and nonsocial cues on attention capture
replication_authors: Jens Kürten; Christina Breil; Roxana Pittig; Lynn Huestegge; Anne Böckler
replication_title: How eccentricity modulates attention capture by direct face/gaze and sudden onset motion
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the finding that social attention towards the participant and sudden onset motion presented at 4.3° eccentricity capture attention (Böckler et al., 2014)' and used the same paradigm. Both the face/gaze direction effect (F(1,156)=51.02, p<.001) and motion onset effect (F(1,156)=58.37, p<.001) were successfully replicated across eccentricity groups.

description: Successive and concurrent presentation of tones and colors yield similar working memory outcomes for item recognition, including similar single-task performance and dual-task costs across modalities
original_authors: Cowan, Nelson; Guitard, Dominic
original_title: Encoding colors and tones into working memory concurrently: A developmental investigation
replication_authors: Nelson Cowan; Dominic Guitard
replication_title: Similar working memory outcomes with successive versus concurrent presentation of tones and colors
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicate the finding' of Cowan and Guitard (2024). The Discussion confirms: 'The present results confirm this surprising outcome in a larger sample of adults.' Experiments 1 and 2 both show no difference between successive and concurrent presentation methods in item memory, replicating the original.

description: Successive and concurrent presentation of tones and colors yield similar working memory outcomes for item recognition, including similar single-task performance and dual-task costs across modalities
original_authors: Cowan, Nelson; Guitard, Dominic
original_title: Encoding colors and tones into working memory concurrently: A developmental investigation
replication_authors: Nelson Cowan; Dominic Guitard
replication_title: Similar working memory outcomes with successive versus concurrent presentation of tones and colors
explanation: Experiment 3 extends the original finding to serial position memory, finding the same null effect of presentation schedule. The authors state: 'The near-equivalence of successive and concurrent presentation methods in Experiment 3, in which position tests were given' supports the original conclusion that storage rather than encoding limits working memory capacity.

description: Learned distractor rejection: after gaining experience with a salient color singleton distractor, attentional capture costs are large in the first half of a block but eliminated or reversed in the second half, demonstrating feature-dependent learned rejection
original_authors: Daniel B. Vatterott; Shaun P. Vecera
original_title: Experience-dependent attentional tuning of distractor rejection
replication_authors: Isaac Savelson; Christopher Hauck; Mei-Ching Lien; Eric Ruthruff; Andrew B. Leber
replication_title: Learned distractor rejection: Robust but surprisingly rapid
explanation: Experiment 1 failed to replicate the conventional split-block learned distractor rejection effect (block half × singleton presence interaction, p = .08, η²p = .05, with only ~16 ms vs. the original ~106 ms difference). However, finer-grained moving RT analyses revealed significant capture only in the first two to three encounters, supporting the existence of the effect on a shorter timescale than Vatterott and Vecera assumed.

description: Learned distractor rejection: after gaining experience with a salient color singleton distractor, attentional capture costs are large in the first half of a block but eliminated or reversed in the second half, demonstrating feature-dependent learned rejection
original_authors: Daniel B. Vatterott; Shaun P. Vecera
original_title: Experience-dependent attentional tuning of distractor rejection
replication_authors: Isaac Savelson; Christopher Hauck; Mei-Ching Lien; Eric Ruthruff; Andrew B. Leber
replication_title: Learned distractor rejection: Robust but surprisingly rapid
explanation: Experiment 2 (online replication) failed to replicate the split-block learned distractor rejection effect (block half × singleton presence interaction not significant, F(1,59) = 2.61, p = .112, η²p = .04). However, a finer-grained 8-trial bin analysis revealed significant attentional capture only in the first bin, supporting the effect on a shorter timescale.

description: Learned distractor rejection: after gaining experience with a salient color singleton distractor, attentional capture costs are large in the first half of a block but eliminated or reversed in the second half, demonstrating feature-dependent learned rejection
original_authors: Daniel B. Vatterott; Shaun P. Vecera
original_title: Experience-dependent attentional tuning of distractor rejection
replication_authors: Isaac Savelson; Christopher Hauck; Mei-Ching Lien; Eric Ruthruff; Andrew B. Leber
replication_title: Learned distractor rejection: Robust but surprisingly rapid
explanation: Experiment 3 (in-lab replication) failed to replicate the split-block learned distractor rejection effect (block half × singleton presence interaction not significant, F(1,59) = 0.21, p = .652, η²p = .003). However, a finer-grained 8-trial bin analysis revealed significant singleton presence costs only in the first bin, again supporting the effect on a very short timescale.

description: An item-cueing intervention highlighting the positions of all potential targets (letters) in a noisy visual search display reduces miss errors while increasing reaction times
original_authors: Aoqi Li; Johan Hulleman; Jeremy M. Wolfe
original_title: Errors in visual search: Are they stochastic or deterministic?
replication_authors: Aoqi Li; Jeremy M. Wolfe; Johan Hulleman
replication_title: Errors in visual search: How can we reduce them?
explanation: The authors explicitly say Experiment 2 'partly replicated the RT pattern in our previous online experiment 3c (Li et al., 2024) where the cue slowed down the search.' The error reduction was replicated (cue reduced miss rates for low-contrast targets), but the RT increase was only partially replicated — it occurred only on high-contrast targets in Experiment 2, not across all target contrasts as in the original online experiment.

description: ERP components reflecting structural face encoding speed (N170 latency) and access to structural representations in memory (ERE/N250r amplitude) are linked to individual differences in face cognition accuracy and speed, above and beyond established cognitive abilities
original_authors: Grit Herzmann; Olga Kunina; Werner Sommer; Oliver Wilhelm
original_title: Individual differences in face cognition: Brain-behavior relationships
replication_authors: Laura Kaltwasser; Andrea Hildebrandt; Guillermo Recio; Oliver Wilhelm; Werner Sommer
replication_title: Neurocognitive mechanisms of individual differences in face cognition: A replication and extension
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated the results of Herzmann et al. (2010), showing that both the N170 latency and the ERE amplitude for learned faces predicted the accuracy of face cognition as well as the speed of face cognition.' The Conclusions also confirm: 'the present study replicated and extended several previously established brain-behavior relationships (Herzmann et al., 2010).' The replication used a modified paradigm with backward masking of primes, reversed experimental sequence, new stimulus materials, and LDS modeling technique.

description: Monetary incentive cues enhance cognitive control in a response conflict task, reducing conflict-related interference effects and increasing transient cue-related activations in fronto-parietal regions, ventral striatum, and caudate
original_authors: Srikanth Padmala; Luiz Pessoa
original_title: Reward reduces conflict by enhancing attentional control and biasing visual cortical processing
replication_authors: Yu Sun Chung; Deanna Barch
replication_title: Anhedonia is associated with reduced incentive cue related activation in the basal ganglia
explanation: The authors replicated the neural activation findings (increased sustained and transient activity in bilateral DLPFC and basal ganglia as a function of reward), but explicitly acknowledged a failure to replicate the behavioral reward × conflict type interaction: 'These results are somewhat in contrast with those of Padmala and Pessoa (2011)' and 'may have resulted in a failure to replicate some aspects of their work.' The summary states the neural findings were replicated, but the behavioral conflict reduction effect was not.

description: The anticipation of immediate (versus preference-matched delayed) rewards increases go responding in an intertemporal go/no-go learning task, reflecting an intertemporal Pavlovian bias that facilitates instrumental approach and interferes with instrumental inhibition
original_authors: Floor Burghoorn; Anouk Scheres; John Monterosso; Mingqian Guo; Shan Luo; Karin Roelofs; Bernd Figner
original_title: Pavlovian impatience: The anticipation of immediate rewards increases approach behaviour
replication_authors: Floor Burghoorn; Anouk Scheres; Karin Roelofs; Bernd Figner
replication_title: Intertemporal Pavlovian biases and links with mental health in the general population
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Results: 'We replicated all go/no-go task effects reported in Burghoorn et al. (2024)' and in the Discussion: 'we replicated the intertemporal Pavlovian bias effect on go responding...The magnitude of this effect (b = 0.19) was highly similar to Burghoorn et al., (2024; b = 0.17), supporting the reliability of this effect.'

description: Processing words for their relevance to a grassland survival scenario enhances subsequent free recall compared to processing for a non-survival control scenario (moving scenario)
original_authors: James S. Nairne; Sarah R. Thompson; Josefa N. S. Pandeirada
original_title: Adaptive memory: Survival processing enhances retention
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Chelsea M. Stillman; Jennifer H. Coane; Caterina P. Profaci; James H. Howard; Darlene V. Howard
replication_title: The effects of healthy aging on the mnemonic benefit of survival processing
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the survival advantage in two separate groups of younger adults' using the identical paradigm from Nairne et al. (2007, Exp. 2), with full-attention younger adults showing a significant survival advantage (t(21) = 2.17, p = .04) and divided-attention younger adults also showing the advantage (t(26) = 2.33, p = .03).

description: Processing words for their relevance to a grassland survival scenario enhances subsequent free recall compared to processing for a non-survival control scenario (moving scenario)
original_authors: James S. Nairne; Sarah R. Thompson; Josefa N. S. Pandeirada
original_title: Adaptive memory: Survival processing enhances retention
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Chelsea M. Stillman; Jennifer H. Coane; Caterina P. Profaci; James H. Howard; Darlene V. Howard
replication_title: The effects of healthy aging on the mnemonic benefit of survival processing
explanation: Across three separate experiments with older adults (Experiments 1, 2, and 3 with pooled N=57 and N=56), no survival advantage was found; the authors conclude 'we did not find evidence for a survival advantage in three separate samples of older adults and with both within- and between-subjects manipulations,' and a power analysis indicated >93% power to detect the effect if it existed.

description: When sentences imply a certain color, pictures mismatching that color are verified faster than matching pictures (mismatch advantage), suggesting color is represented differently than other visual features in mental simulations
original_authors: Louise Connell
original_title: Representing object colour in language comprehension
replication_authors: Lara N. Hoeben Mannaert; Katinka Dijkstra; Rolf A. Zwaan
replication_title: Is color an integral part of a rich mental simulation?
explanation: The authors explicitly frame Experiment 1 as a 'conceptual replication of Connell's (2007)...experiments on color, using the same paradigm but a different stimulus set.' The original found a mismatch advantage; the replication found the opposite — a significant match advantage of 104 ms (d = 0.26, p = .003) — directly contradicting Connell (2007). The authors conclude: 'These findings support the results of Zwaan and Pecher (2012), rather than those of Connell (2007).'

description: When sentences imply a certain color, pictures matching that implied color are verified faster than mismatching pictures (match advantage), with color showing a larger effect size than shape or orientation
original_authors: Rolf A. Zwaan; Diane Pecher
original_title: Revisiting mental simulation in language comprehension: Six replication attempts
replication_authors: Lara N. Hoeben Mannaert; Katinka Dijkstra; Rolf A. Zwaan
replication_title: Is color an integral part of a rich mental simulation?
explanation: The authors explicitly frame Experiment 1 as a 'conceptual replication of Connell's (2007) and Zwaan and Pecher's (2012) experiments on color.' The replication found a significant match advantage of 104 ms (d = 0.26, p = .003), consistent with Zwaan and Pecher (2012). The authors state: 'These findings support the results of Zwaan and Pecher (2012)...and suggest that color, like shape and orientation, is an object property that is simulated during language comprehension.'

description: Making judgments of learning (JOLs) leads to significantly better final recall accuracy compared with making retrospective confidence judgments (RCJs) or no explicit metacognitive judgment
original_authors: Michael R. Dougherty; Petra Scheck; Thomas O. Nelson; Louis Narens
original_title: Using the past to predict the future
replication_authors: Michael R. Dougherty; Alison M. Robey; Daniel Buttaccio
replication_title: Do metacognitive judgments alter memory performance beyond the benefits of retrieval practice? A comment on and replication attempt of Dougherty, Scheck, Nelson, and Narens (2005)
explanation: Four replication attempts all failed to find the JOL memory enhancement effect. The main experiment yielded BF10 = 0.05 (20:1 odds in favor of the null), and a meta-analysis across all four studies (N=600) yielded BF10 = 0.0184. The authors conclude: 'the original finding observed in Dougherty et al. (2005) persisted seemingly unchallenged for over 12 years, yet in our view it appears to be nothing more than a Type I error.'

description: Memory accuracy is impaired for imagined unethical relative to ethical actions (participants who imagined unethical behaviors correctly remember fewer details than those who imagined ethical behaviors)
original_authors: Maryam Kouchaki; Francesca Gino
original_title: Memories of unethical actions become obfuscated over time
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Matthew L. Stanley; Brenda W. Yang; Felipe De Brigard
replication_title: No evidence for unethical amnesia for imagined actions: A failed replication and extension
explanation: Study 1 directly replicated Kouchaki and Gino's (2016) fifth study using identical materials and procedure. No significant effect was found (p=.06), and the pattern was actually in the opposite direction. Authors explicitly state: 'These results fail to replicate the effect reported by Kouchaki and Gino.'

description: Memory accuracy is impaired for imagined unethical relative to ethical actions (participants who imagined unethical behaviors correctly remember fewer details than those who imagined ethical behaviors)
original_authors: Maryam Kouchaki; Francesca Gino
original_title: Memories of unethical actions become obfuscated over time
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Matthew L. Stanley; Brenda W. Yang; Felipe De Brigard
replication_title: No evidence for unethical amnesia for imagined actions: A failed replication and extension
explanation: Study 2 attempted to replicate Kouchaki and Gino's (2016) fifth study again, adding covariates for ease of imagining the vignette and perceived moral wrongness to increase chances of finding an effect. No significant difference in memory accuracy was found (p>.78, d=.04), and even subset analyses failed to produce any significant effect.

description: Memory accuracy is impaired for imagined unethical relative to ethical actions (participants who imagined unethical behaviors correctly remember fewer details than those who imagined ethical behaviors)
original_authors: Maryam Kouchaki; Francesca Gino
original_title: Memories of unethical actions become obfuscated over time
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Matthew L. Stanley; Brenda W. Yang; Felipe De Brigard
replication_title: No evidence for unethical amnesia for imagined actions: A failed replication and extension
explanation: Study 3 used the same paradigm as Kouchaki and Gino (2016) but with a new vignette describing a different moral violation (damaging a parked car and driving away). No significant difference in memory accuracy was found (p>.20, d=.17). Authors conclude they 'were unable to directly or conceptually replicate Kouchaki and Gino's (2016) memory accuracy effect.'

description: Working memory period shows card-order effects such that short-final (long-first) trial sequences yield higher working memory performance than long-final sequences, and this effect extends beyond end-position manipulations to central positions
original_authors: John N. Towse; Graham J. Hitch; Zoë Hamilton; Kirsty Peacock; Una M. Z. Hutton
original_title: Working memory period: The endurance of mental representations
replication_authors: John N. Towse; Graham J. Hitch; Neil Horton
replication_title: Charting the trajectory of forgetting: Insights from a working memory period paradigm
explanation: The authors replicated the original card-order effects for three of four sequence permutations (end positions, middle positions, and first-half positions showed significant short-late advantages), but found no significant advantage for the second-half permutation, stating 'previous card-order phenomena have been replicated and extended, but interestingly, a short-late advantage is not found under all circumstances.'

description: Working memory period is a reliable predictor of children's scholastic attainment (reading and number skills) and shows test-retest reliability
original_authors: John N. Towse; Graham J. Hitch; Zoë Hamilton; Kirsty Peacock; Una M. Z. Hutton
original_title: Working memory period: The endurance of mental representations
replication_authors: John N. Towse; Graham J. Hitch; Neil Horton
replication_title: Charting the trajectory of forgetting: Insights from a working memory period paradigm
explanation: The authors found that working memory period robustly correlated with scholastic attainment (r = .544, composite BAS) and showed stable test-retest reliability (r = .514), successfully replicating the individual differences findings from Towse et al. (2005): 'working memory period robustly correlated with a composite ability measure from BAS tests, and this relationship remained significant once partialing out children's age.'

description: Verbal labeling improves visual working memory in younger adults by activating categorical visual long-term memory (LTM) knowledge, boosting both categorical and continuous memory representations as well as precision of continuous representations
original_authors: Alessandra S. Souza; Zuzanna Skóra
original_title: The interplay of language and visual perception in working memory
replication_authors: Alicia Forsberg; Wendy Johnson; Robert H. Logie
replication_title: Cognitive aging and verbal labeling in continuous visual memory
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'For younger adults, we replicated these observations' regarding the labeling benefit (improved categorical K, continuous K, and precision). The study extends the original to older adults with a slightly longer stimulus presentation time (930ms vs 250ms), making it a close extension to a new population.

description: Older adults are more susceptible to false hearing (perceiving contextually predicted words instead of the actual presented word in noise) than young adults
original_authors: Chad S. Rogers; Larry L. Jacoby; Mitchell S. Sommers
original_title: Frequent false hearing by older adults: The role of age differences in metacognition
replication_authors: Eric Failes; Mitchell S. Sommers; Larry L. Jacoby
replication_title: Blurring past and present: Using false memory to better understand false hearing in young and older adults
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the findings of past studies that older adults are more susceptible to false hearing than are young adults (Rogers et al., 2012; Sommers et al., 2015)' and in the General Discussion confirm 'We were able to successfully replicate the findings of Sommers et al. (2015, Experiment 2) and Jacoby et al. (2005, Experiment 2) using their respective hearing and memory tasks.'

description: Older adults show greater susceptibility to false hearing (reporting contextually predicted words instead of the actually presented word in noise) compared to young adults
original_authors: Sommers, M. S.; Morton, J.; Rogers, C.
original_title: You are not listening to what I said: False hearing in young and older adults
original_journal: Remembering: Attributions, Processes, and Control in Human Memory (Essays in Honor of Larry Jacoby)
replication_authors: Eric Failes; Mitchell S. Sommers; Larry L. Jacoby
replication_title: Blurring past and present: Using false memory to better understand false hearing in young and older adults
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we replicated the findings of past studies that older adults are more susceptible to false hearing than are young adults (Rogers et al., 2012; Sommers et al., 2015)' and in the General Discussion: 'We were able to successfully replicate the findings of Sommers et al. (2015, Experiment 2) and Jacoby et al. (2005, Experiment 2) using their respective hearing and memory tasks.'

description: Older adults are more susceptible to false memory (incorrectly completing word fragments with contextually-primed but unstudied words) than young adults, and more frequently rate these false memories as 'remembered'
original_authors: Larry L. Jacoby; Anthony J. Bishara; Sandra Hessels; Jeffrey P. Toth

replication_authors: Eric Failes; Mitchell S. Sommers; Larry L. Jacoby
replication_title: Blurring past and present: Using false memory to better understand false hearing in young and older adults
explanation: The authors state 'This replicates the findings of Jacoby et al. (2005, Experiment 2), who reported that older adults were more likely to falsely remember having studied the prime word in the incongruent condition than young adults' and 'the results of Experiment 2 replicated those of Jacoby et al. (2005, Experiment 2).' They used the exact same task as Jacoby et al. (2005, Experiment 2).

description: Listeners show more willingness to interact, more social support, and a more positive attitude towards narrators who share autobiographical memories in a coherent manner compared to an incoherent manner
original_authors: Lauranne Vanaken; Patricia Bijttebier; Dirk Hermans

replication_authors: Lauranne Vanaken; Dirk Hermans
replication_title: Be coherent and become heard: The multidimensional impact of narrative coherence on listeners’ social responses
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'we could replicate the effect of coherence on listeners' social responses that was described in Vanaken et al. (2020).' The effect was confirmed significantly for positive narratives (F(1, 106) = 29.34, p < .001, ηp² = .22), though only for positive and not negative narratives, which the authors consider consistent with an interaction effect already observed in the original study.

explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'the behavioral results of Experiment 1 confirmed the conclusions previously reached by Bhatia et al. (2019b)' and in the general discussion that 'the present study successfully replicated the results already reported by Bhatia et al. (2019b).' replication_title: Effects of pointing movements on visuospatial working memory in a joint-action condition: Evidence from eye movements
explanation: The authors explicitly state that 'Experiment 2 replicated the behavioral findings reported by Bhatia et al. (2019b), in that the passive observation of the pointing movements performed by the experimenter did not enhance recognition memory for move arrays.' The null effect of Condition was confirmed with a Bayes factor of 5.19 in favor of the null hypothesis.

description: When proactive interference is minimized by having participants study a single DRM theme per list (content change method), the forward testing effect is eliminated — tested and control participants recall the same proportion of target list words
original_authors: Ludmila D. Nunes; Yana Weinstein
original_title: Testing improves true recall and protects against the build-up of proactive interference without increasing false recall
replication_authors: Dahwi Ahn; Jason C. K. Chan
replication_title: Does testing enhance new learning because it insulates against proactive interference?
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed to 'directly replicate Nunes and Weinstein's Experiment 2' (Experiment 3 of the current paper). In contrast to the original null finding (d ≈ 0), the replication found a robust forward testing effect (d = 0.75, p = .005), contradicting Nunes and Weinstein's key result. The authors conclude they 'failed to replicate Nunes and Weinstein's (2012) finding.'

description: When proactive interference is minimized by having participants study a single DRM theme per list (content change method), the forward testing effect is eliminated — tested and control participants recall the same proportion of target list words
original_authors: Ludmila D. Nunes; Yana Weinstein

replication_authors: Dahwi Ahn; Jason C. K. Chan
replication_title: Does testing enhance new learning because it insulates against proactive interference?
explanation: Experiment 4 is a second direct replication of Nunes and Weinstein (2012) Experiment 2, adding full counterbalancing of word assignments. Again, a robust forward testing effect was found (d = 1.42, p < .001), directly contradicting the original null effect. The authors conclude 'we failed to replicate Nunes and Weinstein's (2012) finding.'

description: Switching between tasks that differ only in response modality (vocal vs. manual) yields significant switch costs, suggesting response modality is an integral component of a task set
original_authors: Andrea M. Philipp; Iring Koch
original_title: The role of response modalities in cognitive task representations
replication_authors: Mareike A. Hoffmann; Iring Koch; Lynn Huestegge
replication_title: Are some effector systems harder to switch to? In search of cost asymmetries when switching between manual, vocal, and oculomotor tasks
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that Experiment 2 'replicated...a central result reported in Philipp and Koch (2011): An alternation of the response modality (while keeping other task features constant) yielded effects similar to those observed in more typical task switching settings, namely significant mixing costs and switch costs.' The present study extended to oculomotor responses and used auditory stimuli instead of visual.

description: Switching to a vocal response yields greater switch costs than switching to a manual response (switch-cost asymmetry), indicating vocal tasks are more dominant than manual tasks in a task-switching context
original_authors: Andrea M. Philipp; Iring Koch
original_title: The role of response modalities in cognitive task representations
replication_authors: Mareike A. Hoffmann; Iring Koch; Lynn Huestegge
replication_title: Are some effector systems harder to switch to? In search of cost asymmetries when switching between manual, vocal, and oculomotor tasks
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'none of the present experiments revealed any significant switch-cost asymmetries when switching between tasks involving different effector systems.' In Experiment 2, while there was a 'numerical trend towards such an effect' (vocal 75 ms vs. manual 55 ms switch costs), 'this trend failed to reach statistical significance.' The 95% CI of the vocal-manual asymmetry in Experiment 2 was [-3; 35], which did not include the 70 ms effect size reported in Philipp and Koch (2011).

description: People show a valence dissociation in thinking about their personal versus collective futures: a positivity bias for personal future but a negativity bias for their country's future
original_authors: Sushmita Shrikanth; Piotr M. Szpunar; Karl K. Szpunar

replication_authors: Will Deng; Alexa K. Rosenblatt; Thomas Talhelm; Adam L. Putnam
replication_title: People from the U.S. and China think about their personal and collective future differently
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the data replicated the personal versus collective dissociation shown in prior studies' and in the Discussion note 'we replicated past work demonstrating a personal/collective valence dissociation in future thoughts for Western samples (Shrikanth et al., 2018).' U.S. participants showed the predicted Valence × Domain crossover interaction (F(1,39) = 49.21, p < .001).

description: Delayed memory for faces encoded with a distractor face in the retention interval is better than for faces encoded without distraction (the McCabe effect for complex visual stimuli)
original_authors: Zanto TP; Clapp WC; Rubens MT; Karlsson J.; Gazzaley A.
original_title: Expectations of task demands dissociate working memory and long-term memory systems
replication_authors: Lea M. Bartsch; Philipp Musfeld
replication_title: Delayed memory for complex visual stimuli does not benefit from distraction during encoding
explanation: Experiment 1 tested faces (and doors) with picture-distraction and math-distraction conditions. Authors conclude: 'Overall, our findings did not replicate the results and conclusions obtained by Zanto et al. (2016).' For faces, BF analysis provided inconclusive evidence tending against the McCabe effect; the benefit found for doors was attributable to extended maintenance duration rather than distraction itself.

explanation: Experiment 2 tested pure vs. mixed blocks to investigate whether blocked design (as in Zanto et al. 2016) was a boundary condition. Authors state: 'our results neither replicate the findings by Zanto et al. (2016), nor the original McCabe effect (McCabe, 2008).' BF analyses showed clear evidence against a difference between simple span and distraction in delayed memory for both blocking types.

For delayed memory, BF analyses showed clear evidence against a difference between simple span and distraction condition for both set size conditions.

description: Delayed memory for faces encoded with a distractor (incidental encoding, as in original surprise delayed test) is better than for faces encoded without distraction

Authors report: 'delayed memory performance was better for the simple span condition compared to the distraction condition' and explicitly note this is 'opposite to the predictions of the McCabe effect.' The BF for Simple vs. Distraction in delayed memory was 1043 (strong evidence), indicating a significant effect in the opposite direction.

The Age × Emotional Valence interaction was significant in the replication (F(2,406) = 5.97, p = 0.003, ηp² = 0.03), consistent with the original finding, though the study extended from online to controlled laboratory settings.

Specifically, no-go trial accuracy was worse preceding negative TUTs for both age groups (Welhaf et al., 2024c), but neutral and positive TUTs did not differ in their associated no-go performance.' The replication study found negative TUTs predicted unique variance in no-go accuracy (p = 0.019), consistent with the original.

description: Memory for an object's location is more accurate and precise in gaze-centered (retinotopic) than world-centered (spatiotopic) coordinates, with greater accumulation of error for spatiotopic than retinotopic memory across saccades
original_authors: Julie D. Golomb; Nancy Kanwisher

replication_authors: Anna Shafer-Skelton; Julie D. Golomb
replication_title: Memory for retinotopic locations is more accurate than memory for spatiotopic locations, even for visually guided reaching
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our mouse response results replicate Golomb and Kanwisher's (2012b) findings. First, we found a main effect of number of saccades... Importantly, we found larger overall error in the spatiotopic condition than the retinotopic condition... as well as a greater accumulation of error in the spatiotopic compared to the retinotopic condition.' The Discussion confirms: 'In addition to replicating Golomb and Kanwisher's original (2012b) findings that memory for retinotopic locations is more accurate than memory for spatiotopic locations.'

description: Memory for an object's location is more accurate and precise in gaze-centered (retinotopic) than world-centered (spatiotopic) coordinates, with greater accumulation of error for spatiotopic than retinotopic memory across saccades
original_authors: Julie D. Golomb; Nancy Kanwisher

original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Anna Shafer-Skelton; Julie D. Golomb
replication_title: Memory for retinotopic locations is more accurate than memory for spatiotopic locations, even for visually guided reaching
explanation: Using a touchscreen reaching response (rather than mouse click), the authors found the same pattern: 'we also still found greater spatiotopic error and steeper accumulation of spatiotopic error in the touchscreen task.' The authors conclude: 'we found no evidence that engaging the motor system improves spatiotopic memory across saccades,' confirming the retinotopic advantage extends to visually-guided reaching.

description: Working memory performance declines after longer retention intervals, and forgetting is due to probabilistic loss of individual item representations rather than gradual decay of all items
original_authors: Weiwei Zhang; Steven J. Luck
original_title: Sudden death and gradual decay in visual working memory
replication_authors: Nicole Hakim; Megan T. deBettencourt; Edward Awh; Edward K. Vogel
replication_title: Attention fluctuations impact ongoing maintenance of information in working memory
explanation: Reviewer upgrade from medium to high. The authors explicitly state in the abstract: 'we replicated the finding that performance declines after long (10 s) retention intervals, as well as past observations that forgetting was due to probabilistic dropping of individual items rather than all-or-none losses.' Both Experiment 1 (t(19)=4.35, p<.001, d=0.62) and Experiment 2 (t(19)=3.73, p<.001, d=0.34) show significant performance decline at longer retention intervals, and the partial drop model (item-level probabilistic forgetting) was strongly preferred over the complete drop model in both experiments. The replication language is explicit and the statistical evidence is unambiguous. Description was corrected: the original entry described the Zhang & Luck finding as 'sudden all-or-none loss,' but what this paper actually replicates is probabilistic item-level forgetting (partial drop), consistent with the broader Zhang & Luck finding about item-level loss rather than gradual decay. Replication type 'close experiment' is appropriate: same general paradigm (visual WM with retention intervals) but different task (discrete whole-report vs. change detection) and different computational models.

description: Perceptual coupling between two simultaneously viewed bistable kinetic-depth effect (KDE) rotating sphere displays is reduced when one of the spheres is disambiguated via stereoscopic depth cues
original_authors: Jon K. Grossmann; Allan C. Dobbins
original_title: Differential ambiguity reduces grouping of metastable objects
replication_authors: Alexander Pastukhov; Claus-Christian Carbon

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'In our first experiment, we sought to replicate and extend earlier work on perceptual coupling, particularly the reduced perceptual coupling when one of the spheres is disambiguated (Grossmann & Dobbins, 2003).' They further report: 'Our results were in complete agreement with the earlier work, as the spheres were strongly perceptually coupled... Also, as in the original report, the proportion of time the participants reported corotation decreased significantly for strongly disambiguated primes.'

replication_authors: Colleen M. Parks; Kevin D. Mohawk; Laura L. S. Werner; Christopher Kiley

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated this finding: in the 3-day condition there was a significant and credible difference between the reminder groups for number of List-2 intrusions into Day 1 memory, but only null effects were found in the 2-day condition.' The abstract similarly concludes 'We replicated these results, thereby bolstering the reconsolidation theory of memory updating.'

description: Memory updating (List-2 intrusions into List-1 recall) is absent in a 2-day paradigm when reconsolidation does not have time to complete (reminder vs. no-reminder conditions show no significant difference)

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Thus, the null effect in the 2-day conditions found by Hupbach et al. (2007) was replicated.' There was no significant difference between reminder and no-reminder groups in intrusions, t(42) = .86, p = .198, d = .26.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the classic between-participant hindsight bias in the hypothetical design.' At M1, probability judgments under hindsight instructions (M = 58.85%) were significantly higher than under foresight instructions (M = 49.83%), b = 8.60, t(88.37) = 2.25, p = .01, d = .36.

description: Within-participants (memory design) hindsight bias: probability judgments of the actual outcome increase from foresight instructions (M1) to hindsight instructions (M2) within the same participants
