explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The classic within-participant finding in the memory design was also replicated.' After foresight judgments at M1 (M = 49.83%), participants judged the actual outcome as more likely under hindsight instructions at M2 (M = 62.79%), b = 12.60, t(89) = 5.92, p < .001, d = .52.

description: Objects initially paired with a semantically congruent sound are better recognized (higher accuracy on 'old' trials) than objects paired with an incongruent sound, demonstrating a multisensory memory advantage
original_authors: Sandra Lehmann; Micah M. Murray
original_title: The role of multisensory memories in unisensory object discrimination
replication_authors: Shea E. Duarte; Simona Ghetti; Joy J. Geng
replication_title: Object memory is multisensory: Task-irrelevant sounds improve recollection
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'aimed to conceptually replicate previous studies showing generally improved recognition memory for congruent multisensory pairs' and in the Discussion confirm: 'Our results replicated previous findings (Lehmann & Murray, 2005; Thelen et al., 2015).' Experiment 1 found a significant main effect of auditory condition on recognition confidence scores (F(2,130) = 8.41, p < 0.001, η_p² = 0.12), with congruent items recognized with higher confidence than incongruent items.

description: Participants continue to refer to corrected misinformation when making inferential statements about an event (the continued-influence effect), even after an unambiguous correction has been presented
original_authors: Hollyn M. Johnson; Colleen M. Seifert
original_title: Sources of the continued influence effect: When misinformation in memory affects later inferences
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Saoirse Connor Desai; Stian Reimers
replication_title: Comparing the use of open and closed questions for Web-based measures of the continued-influence effect
explanation: Experiment 1A replicated the CIE online with open-ended questions using the same stimuli as Johnson and Seifert (1994, Exp. 3A). The omnibus test was significant (F(2,75)=10.73, p<.001, ηp²=.22), and the authors conclude that 'both open-ended and closed-ended questions can successfully be used in online experiments with AMT to measure differences in references to misinformation in a standard continued-influence experiment.'

description: Participants continue to refer to corrected misinformation when making inferential statements about an event (the continued-influence effect), even after an unambiguous correction has been presented
original_authors: Hollyn M. Johnson; Colleen M. Seifert
original_title: Sources of the continued influence effect: When misinformation in memory affects later inferences
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Saoirse Connor Desai; Stian Reimers
replication_title: Comparing the use of open and closed questions for Web-based measures of the continued-influence effect
explanation: Experiment 1B replicated the CIE online using closed-ended questions adapted from the Johnson and Seifert (1994, Exp. 3A) stimuli. The omnibus test was significant (F(2,72)=9.39, p<.001, ηp²=.21), showing a clear continued-influence effect in the closed-ended format. The authors conclude these findings show 'both open-ended and closed-ended questions can successfully be used in online experiments.'

description: Participants continue to refer to corrected misinformation when making inferential statements about an event (the continued-influence effect), even after an unambiguous correction has been presented
original_authors: Hollyn M. Johnson; Colleen M. Seifert
original_title: Sources of the continued influence effect: When misinformation in memory affects later inferences
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Saoirse Connor Desai; Stian Reimers
replication_title: Comparing the use of open and closed questions for Web-based measures of the continued-influence effect
explanation: Experiment 2A, the preregistered open-ended question replication with a larger sample, found a non-significant omnibus test (F(2,154)=0.62, p=.54, ηp²=.01). The authors note this is consistent with findings from other labs that 'a correction sometimes reduces references to misinformation relative to no correction, and sometimes it does not,' and that 'any effect of a correction for the open-ended questions...is relatively small.'

description: Participants continue to refer to corrected misinformation when making inferential statements about an event (the continued-influence effect), even after an unambiguous correction has been presented
original_authors: Hollyn M. Johnson; Colleen M. Seifert
original_title: Sources of the continued influence effect: When misinformation in memory affects later inferences
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Saoirse Connor Desai; Stian Reimers
replication_title: Comparing the use of open and closed questions for Web-based measures of the continued-influence effect
explanation: Experiment 2B, the preregistered closed-ended question replication with a larger sample, found a significant effect of correction information (F(2,163)=26.90, p<.001, ηp²=.25). The authors conclude 'Experiments 2A and 2B again showed clear evidence of a CIE' and that the continued-influence effect can be replicated online.

description: Younger adults outperform older adults in route learning tasks using egocentric navigation strategies, with both groups showing learning improvement across sessions
original_authors: Denise Head; Marlisa Isom
original_title: Age effects on wayfinding and route learning skills
replication_authors: Jan M. Wiener; Denise Carroll; Stacey Moeller; Iram Bibi; Dima Ivanova; Peter Allen; Thomas Wolbers
replication_title: A novel virtual-reality-based route-learning test suite: Assessing the effects of cognitive aging on navigation
explanation: The authors state 'We were able to replicate earlier findings (Head & Isom, 2010). Specifically, whereas both our young and our older participant group showed learning over the course of the experiment, the young participant group performed better than the old participant group.' The tasks were adapted with a more ecologically valid virtual environment while preserving the core route-learning paradigm.

description: Younger adults outperform older adults in route retracing tasks, with younger but not older adults showing learning improvement over experimental sessions
original_authors: Jan M. Wiener; Hana Kmecova; Olivier de Condappa
original_title: Route repetition and route retracing: Effects of cognitive aging
replication_authors: Jan M. Wiener; Denise Carroll; Stacey Moeller; Iram Bibi; Dima Ivanova; Peter Allen; Thomas Wolbers
replication_title: A novel virtual-reality-based route-learning test suite: Assessing the effects of cognitive aging on navigation
explanation: The authors state 'the exact procedure was slightly different from the one we used earlier, we were able [to] replicate the main findings: First, our young participants outperformed our older participants; second, we found that our young, but not our old, participant group improved over the course of the experiment.'

description: Older adults show greater declines than younger adults in allocentric spatial processing tasks requiring perspective shifts when approaching intersections from different directions than during encoding
original_authors: Jan M. Wiener; Olivier de Condappa; Mathew A. Harris; Thomas Wolbers
original_title: Maladaptive bias for extrahippocampal navigation strategies in aging humans
replication_authors: Jan M. Wiener; Denise Carroll; Stacey Moeller; Iram Bibi; Dima Ivanova; Peter Allen; Thomas Wolbers
replication_title: A novel virtual-reality-based route-learning test suite: Assessing the effects of cognitive aging on navigation
explanation: Despite notable methodological differences (participants not required to learn a full route, only a single intersection), the authors found the same age-related decline and the same interaction with approach direction: 'Despite these methodological differences, we found an age-related decline in participants' ability to solve the task. Importantly, we found an interaction between approach direction and age group, with older adults showing stronger performance decrements when the approach direction in the test phase was misaligned with the encoding situation by 180° instead of 90°.'

description: Semantic diversity (computed via LSA on the British National Corpus) has a facilitatory effect on visual word recognition (lexical decision and reading aloud latencies)
original_authors: Paul Hoffman; Matthew A. Lambon Ralph; Timothy T. Rogers
original_title: Semantic diversity: a measure of semantic ambiguity based on variability in the contextual usage of words
replication_authors: Benedetta Cevoli; Chris Watkins; Kathleen Rastle
replication_title: What is semantic diversity and why does it facilitate visual word recognition?
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated previously observed effects of semantic diversity on lexical decision and reading aloud latencies' using the English Lexicon Project and British Lexicon Project, and report significant facilitatory effects of semantic diversity across all megastudy datasets (all p < 0.001).

description: In a regression design, words with multiple meanings are recognised more slowly while words with multiple senses are recognised more quickly in visual lexical decision
original_authors: Jennifer Rodd; Gareth Gaskell; William Marslen-Wilson
original_title: Making sense of semantic ambiguity: semantic competition in lexical access
replication_authors: Benedetta Cevoli; Chris Watkins; Kathleen Rastle
replication_title: What is semantic diversity and why does it facilitate visual word recognition?
explanation: The authors report that 'Rodd et al.'s (2002) data were perfectly captured in the BLP and ELP', with significant effects of number of meanings (slowing) and number of senses (speeding) in both datasets (all p < 0.05), replicating the pattern from Rodd et al.'s Experiment 1.

description: In a factorial design, number of senses significantly affects lexical decision response time but number of meanings does not
original_authors: Jennifer Rodd; Gareth Gaskell; William Marslen-Wilson
original_title: Making sense of semantic ambiguity: semantic competition in lexical access
replication_authors: Benedetta Cevoli; Chris Watkins; Kathleen Rastle
replication_title: What is semantic diversity and why does it facilitate visual word recognition?
explanation: Both BLP and ELP showed a significant main effect of number of senses on response time (BLP: F1(1,4735)=18.86, p<0.001; ELP: F1(1,3763)=7.23, p<0.01) and no significant effect of number of meanings, replicating the pattern from Rodd et al.'s Experiment 2.

description: Polysemous words are recognised faster than unambiguous controls in standard (low task difficulty) lexical decision, while homonymous words do not show a significant disadvantage relative to unambiguous controls
original_authors: Blair C. Armstrong; David C. Plaut
original_title: Disparate semantic ambiguity effects from semantic processing dynamics rather than qualitative task differences
replication_authors: Benedetta Cevoli; Chris Watkins; Kathleen Rastle
replication_title: What is semantic diversity and why does it facilitate visual word recognition?
explanation: The authors found faster recognition of polysemous words in both BLP (t=-2.66, p<0.01) and ELP (t=-2.70, p<0.01), with no significant homonymy disadvantage in either dataset, which is fully consistent with Armstrong & Plaut's (2016) predictions for standard (low difficulty) lexical decision conditions.

description: Semantic interference effect in the picture-word interference paradigm: naming latencies are slower when distractor words are semantically related (vs. unrelated) to the target picture, observed for both overt naming and manual button-press classification responses
original_authors: Rasha Abdel Rahman; Sabrina Aristei
original_title: Now you see it . . . and now again: Semantic interference reflects lexical competition in speech production with and without articulation
replication_authors: Anne Vogt; Roger Hauber; Anna K. Kuhlen; Rasha Abdel Rahman
replication_title: Internet-based language production research with overt articulation: Proof of concept, challenges, and practical advice
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude 'we replicated the semantic interference effect in both tasks, classification and overt articulation in three pre-registered experiments.' The key extension was moving the paradigm online. While SoSciSurvey never reached significance for naming and jsPsych1 required post-hoc outlier correction, jsPsych2 showed clear pre-registered success (naming p = .035, button-press p = .008), and the pooled jsPsych1+jsPsych2 analysis confirmed the effect (relatedness p = .008; naming nested p = .02, button-press nested p = .008). The inconsistencies across individual experiments reflect increased noise from online data collection—the very challenge the paper set out to characterize—rather than genuine ambiguity about the replication outcome.

description: Semantic diversity (C20_SemD) and its interaction with word frequency, age of acquisition, and word length predict word recognition performance (lexical decision and naming latencies) in the British Lexicon Project and English Lexicon Project datasets
original_authors: Benedetta Cevoli; Chris Watkins; Kathleen Rastle
original_title: What is semantic diversity and why does it facilitate visual word recognition?
replication_authors: Paul Hoffman; Matthew A. Lambon Ralph; Timothy T. Rogers
replication_title: Semantic diversity is best measured with unscaled vectors: Reply to Cevoli, Watkins and Rastle (2020)
explanation: The authors replicated Cevoli et al.'s word recognition analyses using their own H13_SemD measure and found 'similar results to those reported by Cevoli et al. using C20_SemD data', with H13_SemD also showing a positive effect of semantic diversity modulated by word frequency. H13_SemD additionally provided better model fit (lower AIC/BIC) than C20_SemD.

description: Semantic diversity (C20_SemD) does not co-vary with polysemy or homonymy in stimuli from published studies that manipulated lexical ambiguity (Rodd et al. 2002; Armstrong & Plaut 2016), implying semantic diversity is unrelated to ambiguity in word meaning
original_authors: Benedetta Cevoli; Chris Watkins; Kathleen Rastle
original_title: What is semantic diversity and why does it facilitate visual word recognition?
replication_authors: Paul Hoffman; Matthew A. Lambon Ralph; Timothy T. Rogers
replication_title: Semantic diversity is best measured with unscaled vectors: Reply to Cevoli, Watkins and Rastle (2020)
explanation: When Hoffman et al. replicated Cevoli et al.'s lexical ambiguity analyses using H13_SemD, they found the opposite result: 'H13_SemD, conversely, reliably covaried with polysemy in every stimulus set', while Cevoli et al. had found no relationship. The authors explicitly state this reverses Cevoli et al.'s key conclusion that semantic diversity is unrelated to word meaning ambiguity (though the null finding for homonymy was consistent across both measures).

description: Firm characteristics (size, physical capital intensity, wage per employee, R&D expenditure share) are systematically related to export participation and export share among German manufacturing enterprises
original_authors: Joachim Wagner
original_title: Exports and firm characteristics in German manufacturing industries
original_journal: University of Lüneburg Working Paper Series in Economics
replication_authors: Joachim Wagner
replication_title: The Quality of the KombiFiD-Sample of Enterprises from Manufacturing Industries: Evidence from a Replication Study
replication_journal: Journal of Contextual Economics – Schmollers Jahrbuch
explanation: The replication yields highly similar results for West Germany ('the KombiFiD sample can be regarded as a sound data base for empirical studies on West German firms'), but fails for East Germany where 'the KombiFiD sample is too small and differences between the results based on this sample and the original data are too large to suggest the use of the KombiFiD data in empirical investigations.' The mixed regional outcomes make the overall result inconclusive.

description: Combined high stromal CAIX (sCAIX hi) and low tumoral Ki-67 (Ki-67 lo) expression is associated with significantly reduced disease-specific survival in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma (HR=7.2, 95% CI: 2.5-20.4)
original_authors: Alexander C. Klimowicz; Pinaki Bose; Stephanie Petrillo; Anthony M. Magliocco; Joseph C. Dort; Nigel T. Brockton
original_title: The prognostic impact of a combined carbonic anhydrase IX and Ki67 signature in oral squamous cell carcinoma
replication_authors: Nigel Brockton; Pawadee Lohavanichbutr; Emeka Enwere; Melissa Upton; Elizabeth Kornaga; Steven Nakoneshny; Pinaki Bose; Chu Chen; Joseph Dort
replication_title: Impact of tumoral carbonic anhydrase IX and Ki‑67 expression on survival in oral squamous cell carcinoma patients
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the previously proposed functional hypoxia signature was not replicated in the current FHCRC study' and 'The current study did not replicate this proposed functional hypoxia signature according to our original definitions of low Ki-67 and high sCAIX.' The combined sCAIX hi/Ki-67 lo group showed no significant association with reduced DSS (HR=1.43, 95% CI: 0.69-2.97), compared to the original HR of 7.2.

description: SNPs rs2736340 and rs13277113 in the C8orf13-BLK region are associated with rheumatoid arthritis in a European population
original_authors: Gregersen, P.K.; Amos, C.I.; Lee, A.T.; Lu, Y.; Remmers, E.F.; Kastner, D.L.
original_title: REL, encoding a member of the NF-kB family of transcription factors, is a newly defined risk locus for rheumatoid arthritis
replication_authors: Harshal A. Deshmukh; Amit K. Maiti; Xana R. Kim-Howard; Adriana Rojas-Villarraga; Joel M. Guthridge; Juan-Manuel Anaya; Swapan K. Nath
replication_title: Evaluation of 19 Autoimmune Disease-associated Loci with Rheumatoid Arthritis in a Colombian Population: Evidence for Replication and Gene-Gene Interaction
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the genetic association with rs13277113 (p = 0.0009, OR 1.46) and rs2736340 (p = 0.0001, OR 1.63) from C8orf13-BLK' in a Colombian population. The Discussion also notes 'a study [18] reported an association between rs2736340 and RA in a European population (p = 5.69 × 10-9, OR 1.19)' — this is the reference being replicated.

description: The rs763361 SNP in CD226 (18q22.3) is associated with susceptibility to multiple autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis
original_authors: Maiti AK; Kim-Howard X.; Viswanathan P.; Guillén L.; Qian X.; Rojas-Villarraga A.; Sun C.; Cañas C.; Tobón GJ; Matsuda K.; Shen N.; Cherñavsky AC; Anaya JM; Nath SK
original_title: Non-synonymous variant (Gly307Ser) in CD226 is associated with susceptibility to multiple autoimmune diseases
replication_authors: Harshal A. Deshmukh; Amit K. Maiti; Xana R. Kim-Howard; Adriana Rojas-Villarraga; Joel M. Guthridge; Juan-Manuel Anaya; Swapan K. Nath
replication_title: Evaluation of 19 Autoimmune Disease-associated Loci with Rheumatoid Arthritis in a Colombian Population: Evidence for Replication and Gene-Gene Interaction
explanation: Reviewer assessment: The authors claim replication of the CD226 rs763361 association 'under the dominant model (p = 0.03).' However, the primary allelic association test in Table 1 shows p = 0.122 with OR 1.21 (95% CI 0.94–1.54) — non-significant, with the confidence interval crossing 1.0. The p = 0.03 comes from a secondary dominant genotype model, not the allelic model used for the other replicated SNPs. Additionally, no correction for multiple testing of 19 SNPs was applied (Bonferroni threshold would be ~0.0026). The authors explicitly use the word 'replicated,' so result is coded as 'success,' but the statistical evidence is genuinely borderline. Confidence remains medium due to: (1) allelic test non-significance, (2) reliance on a secondary genetic model, (3) no multiple testing correction, and (4) the reported replication p-value (0.03, dominant model) and 95% CI (0.94–1.54, allelic model) come from different statistical tests. The original study's effect sizes for RA specifically are not reported in this paper.

description: U.S. registered nurses routinely use only approximately 30 physical assessment techniques in clinical practice out of a larger set of possible assessment skills
original_authors: Jean F. Giddens
original_title: A survey of physical assessment techniques performed by RNs: Lessons for nursing education
replication_authors: Cindy Kohtz; Suzanne C. Brown; Ryan Williams; Patricia A. O'Connor
replication_title: Physical Assessment Techniques in Nursing Education: A Replicated Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they used 'a replicated survey tool concerning physical assessment skills developed and shared by Dr. Jean Giddens (2007)' and found 'a surprising overlap' with the original study: 'Both studies reported a median score of 4 or 5 for the same 27 of 30 physical assessment skills.' The Limitations section notes 'a strong similarity exists between the findings of this study and the Giddens (2007) study conducted nearly a decade earlier.'

description: Nurses and health professionals hold measurable attitudes toward suicide/attempted suicide that can be assessed using the ATAS-Q instrument, with psychometric support for eight subscales (positiveness, acceptability, religiosity, professional role and care, manipulation, personality traits, mental illness, discrimination)
original_authors: Ouzouni, C.; Nakakis, K.
original_title: Attitudes towards attempted suicide: The development of a measurement tool
replication_authors: Kathleen Neville; Nora M. Roan
replication_title: Suicide in Hospitalized Medical-Surgical Patients: Exploring Nurses’ Attitudes
replication_journal: Journal of Psychosocial Nursing and Mental Health Services
explanation: The authors explicitly call this a 'descriptive replication study' of Ouzouni and Nakakis (2009), using the same ATAS-Q instrument in a U.S. population. They found general psychometric support for the tool and confirmed age and religion effects, but four subscales did not reach acceptable reliability and specific findings (e.g., Protestant vs. Catholic attitudes) differed from the original — producing mixed results rather than a clear success or failure.

description: Contingency management (CM) interventions improve retention and compliance (abstinence from heroin) in patients enrolled in methadone maintenance treatment (MMT) programs
original_authors: Kenzie L. Preston; Annie Umbricht; David H. Epstein
original_title: Methadone dose increase and abstinence reinforcement for treatment of continued heroin use during methadone maintenance
replication_authors: Jiang H.; Du J.; Wu F.; Wang Z.; Fan S.; Li Z.; Hser YI; Zhao M.
replication_title: Efficacy of contingency management in improving retention and compliance to methadone maintenance treatment: a random controlled study.
explanation: Reviewer verification: The authors are unambiguous — the abstract states 'Prize-based CM is not effective in improving the retention and compliance of heroin abusers to MMT in Shanghai,' the Discussion states 'The original hypothesis... was not confirmed,' and crucially: 'We believe the main reasons our study failed to replicate western studies that have demonstrated the efficacy of CM as an adjunctive treatment for MMT [7-9] were the very high baseline retention rates... and the relatively weak incentives.' No outcome measure showed significant group differences (retention: 87.5% vs 86.2%, p=0.819; mean days on methadone: 70 vs 71; urine tests and ASI scores also non-significant). Classification as 'close extension' is correct: this tests CM (validated in Western settings) in a different country/culture (Shanghai, China) with a different population and adapted incentive structure. The paper targets refs [7-9] collectively (Petry 2005, Preston 2000, Robles 2002); Preston 2000 is used as primary reference as it directly concerns MMT abstinence reinforcement and has a DOI. Upgraded to high confidence because the authors explicitly use 'failed to replicate' and every outcome supports this classification.

replication_authors: Zongqi Xia; Qingquan Liu; Christoph T. Berger; Brendan T. Keenan; Anna Kaliszewska; Patrick C. Cheney; Gyan P. Srivastava; Irene Wood Castillo; Philip L. De Jager; Galit Alter
replication_title: A 17q12 Allele Is Associated with Altered NK Cell Subsets and Function
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the finding by Ferreira et al. (7) in our cohort of 96 healthy adult subjects: rs9916629 C is associated with a lower frequency of CD3-CD56+ NK cells (p = 0.015 unadjusted; p = 0.036 after adjusting for age and sex)'. The replication is classified as close extension because it was conducted in an adult population whereas the original study used predominantly adolescent subjects.

description: Socioeconomic development (SED index) is positively and curvilinearly associated with young adults' propensity to live alone in China, with compositional effects of internal migration (rather than singlehood) largely explaining the concentration of one-person households in developed regions
original_authors: Adam Ka-Lok Cheung; Wei-Jun Jean Yeung
original_title: Socioeconomic development and young adults' propensity of living in one-person households: Compositional and contextual effects
replication_authors: Xin Wang; Chenyu Yan; Che Deng; Hong He
replication_title: Socioeconomic development and Chinese young adults’ propensity to live alone: An extended replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'conceptually and methodologically replicated Cheung and Yeung's (2021) work' using 2020 census data (vs. 2005 data). In the Discussion they confirm: 'Consistent with the conclusions of Cheung and Yeung (2021), we found a positive curvilinear relationship between prefecture-level socioeconomic development and living alone' and confirmed the role of migration and single status, while also extending findings on migration duration and education effects.

description: RNA hairpins designed via hybridization chain reaction (HCR) can selectively kill cancer cells expressing a specific target transcript (tpc/hpr fusion) by triggering PKR-mediated apoptosis, while sparing cells lacking that transcript
original_authors: Suvir Venkataraman; Robert M. Dirks; Christine T. Ueda; Niles A. Pierce
original_title: Selective cell death mediated by small conditional RNAs
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Kalpesh Patel; Scott E. Kern
replication_title: “Selective cell death mediated by small conditional RNAs” is not selective
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'when repeating the work described in the publication, we could not replicate the results using the methods described.' They found that the HCR hairpins caused non-selective killing of both target-expressing and control cells, and their own designed mesothelin-targeting hairpins also failed to show selectivity.

replication_authors: Dorra Bouzid; H. Fourati; A. Amouri; Isabel Marques; O. Abida; N. Tahri; C. Penha-Gonçalves; H. Masmoudi
replication_title: Replication of Identified Inflammatory Bowel Diseases Genetic Associations: A Case–Control Study in the Tunisian Population
explanation: Reviewer assessment: The paper explicitly states it is 'a replication study' of GWAS-identified IBD susceptibility loci in a Tunisian cohort. The WTCCC (ref [53] in paper, ref 54 in parsed references) originally found PTPN2 rs2542151 associated with CD. In this Tunisian replication, rs2542151 was significantly associated with UC (p=0.013, Pcorr=0.039, OR=6.23) but NOT with CD — a partial replication in a different IBD subtype. Most other tested genes (TNFα, IL23R, PTPN22, IL2, IL10) showed no significant single-SNP associations, though some haplotype-level associations emerged (PTPN11 ATG haplotype in CD, TNFα AG haplotype in CD). The authors conclude 'These results reveal limited replication in Tunisian population' and note 'apparent genetic/allelic heterogeneity at UC/CD loci.' Result classified as 'inconclusive' because the key PTPN2 finding partially replicated (same SNP, same disease family, but different subtype), while the majority of tested loci did not replicate. Confidence remains 'medium' because the paper tests multiple original findings simultaneously and the overall picture is genuinely mixed — reasonable readers could classify this as either failure (most loci not replicated) or inconclusive (some partial replication). Replication type is 'close extension' because the same SNPs were tested in a novel population (Tunisian/North African vs. European), adding a cross-ethnic dimension.

description: Motor activity in childhood and mental vitality, sociability, and positive emotionality in adolescence are associated with apolipoprotein E (apoE) gene polymorphism in a Finnish population sample
original_authors: Keltikangas-Järvinen L.; Räikkönen K.; Lehtimäki T.
original_title: Dependence between apolipoprotein E phenotypes and temperament in children, adolescents, and young adults
replication_authors: Aino M. Pitkänen; Päivi Merjonen; Liisa Keltikangas-Järvinen; Ilkka Seppälä; Terho Lehtimäki; Jorma Viikari; Olli T. Raitakari; Mirka Hintsanen
replication_title: Is There an Association between Temperament  and Apolipoprotein E?  &lt;br&gt;A Replication of a 1993 Young Finns Study&lt;/br&gt;
replication_journal: Journal of Behavioral and Brain Science
explanation: Most original findings replicated (adolescent mental vitality, sociability, and positive emotionality significantly associated with apoE, p<0.001 to p=0.005), but the original significant finding for children's motor activity did not replicate (original p<0.05; replication p=0.145), and self-rated mental vitality dropped from p<0.01 to borderline p=0.052. The authors conclude overall confirmation but acknowledge 'the weakest association of our original article, that between motor activity and apoE, was no longer found.'

description: Autologous cultured fibroblast cell (Azficel-T) injections improve facial contour deformities including nasolabial folds, with 42% of patients achieving a 2-point improvement on a 7-point standardized severity scale as assessed by investigators
original_authors: Robert A. Weiss; Margaret A. Weiss; Karen L. Beasley; Girish Munavalli

replication_journal: Journal of Cosmetics, Dermatological Sciences and Applications
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'clinical replication study' and directly compare their primary endpoint result (22% achieving ≥2-point improvement) to the original Azficel-T trial's 42%, concluding: 'Our results however did not compare favourably to the original ACF.' The replication failed to meet its pre-specified 45% success threshold and underperformed the original study.

description: Nontraditional nursing students perceive environmental factors as the most restrictive and friend support as the most supportive in relation to retention, as measured by the Student Perception Appraisal-Revised (SPA-R) instrument
original_authors: Marianne R. Jeffreys

replication_authors: Brelinda Kern
replication_title: Factors That Restrict or Support Retention among RN-to-BSN Nursing Students: A  Replication Study
explanation: The replication partially confirmed the original findings: it mirrored Jeffreys' (2007) finding that friend support was the most supportive and environmental factors the least supportive, but the rankings of the three middle factors differed. The authors note the study was 'congruent with previous studies' but acknowledge significant limitations including small sample size, low statistical power (0.58), and poor subscale reliability.

description: Current electronic cigarette use is associated with 2.5-fold higher odds of chronic kidney disease, with CKD risk positively correlated with frequency of EC use, in a cross-sectional analysis of NHANES 2017-2020 data

original_title: Electronic cigarette use and risk of chronic kidney disease: a dose-response analysis with propensity score matching in a nationally representative cohort
replication_authors: Gal Cohen; Sooyong Kim; Arielle Selya
replication_title: Association of Electronic Cigarette Use with Chronic Kidney Disease in NHANES 2017-2020: A Cross-Sectional Replication Study
explanation: The replication authors explicitly state: 'We could not replicate the results of Li et al.' Using the same NHANES 2017-2020 dataset but with improved segmentation by CC use history and more careful handling of skip patterns, the replication found no evidence of an association between EC use and CKD across all segments (all ps > 0.05 in CC current and former users; only 1 CKD event among CC never-user EC users).

description: A food education program based on Ribes's (1990) behavioral complexity model affects preference and selection of natural versus industrialized foods in Mexican schoolchildren
original_authors: Assol Cortés-Moreno; María del Refugio López-Gamiño; Martha Elba Alarcón-Armendáriz; Xochitl Karina Torres-Beltrán

explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication of Cortés et al. (2009), testing the same behavioral complexity model with a different, larger sample (298 vs. 116 schoolchildren). The Discussion notes that 'Children in this study reported more preference for natural foods, but selected industrialized ones; this is consistent with the study conducted by Cortés, et al. (2009)', but effects on preference and selection were mixed across grades and programs, with significant changes appearing mainly in fourth grade and not consistently across all groups.

explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'a replication of the Highfill, Spencer, Fad, and Arnold (2016) study,' and their conclusion reports that 'the results of the current study suggest that African and Asian elephants perform similarly on this type of task.' Adults passed conditions A and B (as in the original), directly mirroring the original findings, supporting the success classification.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'In this study, the results of Tice (1992) were not replicated.' No main effects or interaction effects were significant; extraversion scores did not change from before to after self-presentation in any condition.

description: Stigma and gender are independent predictors of professional psychological help-seeking attitudes among university students, with higher stigma and male gender associated with more negative attitudes toward counseling
original_authors: Taniguchi, Hirokazu
original_title: カウンセリングに対する抵抗感を規定する要因の検討（2）
replication_authors: Hirokazu Taniguchi
replication_title: Predictors of attitudes toward seeking counseling among Japanese college students (3): A replication study using a measure of attitudes toward emotional experiences
replication_journal: The Proceedings of the Annual Convention of the Japanese Psychological Association
explanation: Reviewer verification: This is a conference poster abstract (PD-067, Japanese Psychological Association). The author (Taniguchi) explicitly frames this as a 追試研究 (replication study) of his own 2018 work, adding new data to the original dataset and re-examining. The multiple regression found stigma (β=−.28, p<.01) and gender (β=.14, p<.05) had unique contributions to help-seeking attitudes, consistent with the original. Result classified as 'success' based on the replication framing and consistent direction of effects. Confidence kept at 'medium' because: (1) the abstract is very brief and does not explicitly compare the new results to the 2018 findings point by point; (2) we cannot confirm whether all original findings replicated or only the stigma/gender effects; (3) two other predictors (unconditional acceptance of emotional experience, psychological/physical distress) are not discussed in the results, leaving ambiguity about whether they were also significant in the original. Citation mismatch flag resolved: 谷口 is the Japanese reading of Taniguchi — the citation correctly identifies the original author.

explanation: The current study explicitly states it is 'a modified replication of Harvey and Wandersee's original study' and found a statistically significantly lower publication rate of 21.8% versus the original 27.6% (X²=4.73, p=0.03), indicating the original publication rate finding did not hold for the 2012 and 2014 MLA conferences.

This suggests that the findings of the earlier study were accurate and robust.' The replication used five consecutive years of data (vs. single year), a more recent dataset, and added two additional proxy measures of adversity.

description: Cubic spline methods combined with hourly temperature data can reduce product basis risk in weather index insurance for winter wheat and winter rapeseed producers in Eastern Germany

explanation: The authors explicitly state in their Conclusion: 'The direct replication at farm level successfully reproduced the key findings of the original study, achieving statistical significance for similar temperature-yield effect sizes.' Regression coefficients and risk reduction magnitudes closely matched the original findings.

description: Cubic spline methods combined with hourly temperature data can reduce product basis risk in weather index insurance for winter wheat and winter rapeseed producers in Eastern Germany

explanation: The extended replication using different crops (winter barley replacing winter wheat) and a different region (Saxony only) 'did not achieve the same level of risk-reducing capabilities as the original findings.' Risk reduction capacities were substantially lower (e.g., 10.46–17.37% vs. 18.46–19.62% in the original for comparable strike levels), though the non-linear temperature-yield relationship was confirmed, yielding mixed results overall.

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'We replicated the finding of Dixon et al. (2006) of steeper discounting in gambling vs. neutral environments in gamblers.' The effect was confirmed via both model-agnostic analyses and computational modeling (softmax and DDM), with strong Bayesian evidence (BF = 1688 for softmax model discount rate increase in gambling context).

description: Episodic geomorphic events (erosion and deposition) significantly affect archaeological deposit formation and bias radiocarbon chronologies toward the present, creating gaps in the record not attributable to demographic change

Results confirm the findings of the original model.' The qualitative patterns replicated were relationally equivalent to those in the original study, validating its core conclusions.

description: Semantically constraining verbs (e.g., 'eat') cause listeners to make anticipatory eye movements toward the thematically compatible target object before it is named, compared to neutral verbs (e.g., 'move')

explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Study 1 discussion: 'this is a replication of the critical effect in Altmann and Kamide (1999),' and found a significant effect of verb condition on target fixation latency (estimate = -0.19, 95%-CI = [-0.28; -0.10], p(<0) = 1.00) and fixation probability (estimate = 0.46, 95%-CI = [0.18; 0.73]).

description: Semantically constraining verbs (e.g., 'eat') cause listeners to make anticipatory eye movements toward the thematically compatible target object before it is named, compared to neutral verbs (e.g., 'move')

explanation: Study 2 explicitly 'replicated the effect of condition on latency' (estimate = -0.18, credible interval = [-0.30; -0.07], p(<0) = 0.999) and also replicated the condition effect on fixation probability; the Study 2 discussion states 'Study 2 replicated the pattern of results from Study 1: across subjects, there was strong evidence for an effect of verb condition on eye movements.'

description: Adults who encounter novel words after a highly predictive sentence context (generating a stronger prediction error when the novel word appears) show better retention of novel word-object associations compared to adults who encounter novel words in non-predictive contexts (prediction error boost effect in adults)
original_authors: Gambi, Chiara; Pickering, Martin; Rabagliati, Hugh
original_title: Prediction error boosts retention of novel words in adults but not in children
replication_authors: Chiara Gambi; Jaroslaw R. Lelonkiewicz; Davide Crepaldi
replication_title: Do Children (and Adults) Benefit From a Prediction Error Boost in One-Shot Word Learning?
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'One important limitation to our findings is the failure to replicate the prediction error boost effect in Italian adults' and in the abstract: 'we also failed to replicate previous evidence for such an effect in adults.' The follow-up analyses showed all p's >= .034 for adults, failing the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of .0125. The study used Italian-translated materials (close extension) rather than the original English materials.

description: Young children (ages 2-4) do not benefit from a prediction error boost in one-shot word learning: novel words encountered after highly predictive sentence contexts are not better retained than those encountered in non-predictive contexts
original_authors: Gambi, Chiara; Pickering, Martin; Rabagliati, Hugh
original_title: Prediction error boosts retention of novel words in adults but not in children
replication_authors: Chiara Gambi; Jaroslaw R. Lelonkiewicz; Davide Crepaldi
replication_title: Do Children (and Adults) Benefit From a Prediction Error Boost in One-Shot Word Learning?
explanation: Reviewer verification: The current study tested Italian children aged 5-10 (vs. original English children aged 2-4) and found no evidence for a prediction error boost in any child age group (all p's >= .034, Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of .0125), consistent with the original null finding. Result classified as 'success' because the original null result (no prediction error boost in children) was replicated. However, confidence remains 'medium' for two reasons: (1) replicating a null finding is inherently ambiguous — it could reflect a true absence or insufficient power; the authors themselves note 'it is possible that our analyses for children were underpowered'; (2) pooled analyses across both studies found a marginal effect (p = .024, odds ratio 1.39) with only 'anecdotal' Bayes Factor support, suggesting the null may not be as clean as it appears. The extension to older children and different language makes this a close extension.

description: Letters and words are perceived as taller than pseudoletters and pseudowords of the same objective height (the word/letter height superiority illusion), a perceptual consequence of lexical feedback activation
original_authors: Boris New; Karine Doré-Mazars; Céline Cavézian; Christophe Pallier; Julien Barra
original_title: The letter height superiority illusion
replication_authors: Boris New; Clément Guichet; Elsa Spinelli; Julien Barra
replication_title: Listening to Foreign Languages: Pump Up the Volume!
explanation: The authors set out to test whether the visual 'word height superiority illusion' could be found in the auditory modality (words perceived as louder than pseudowords). In Experiment 1, native French speakers judged words as louder than pseudowords in both their L1 (t(70)=6.35, p<.001, d=0.75) and L2 (t(70)=2.4, p=.02, d=0.28), replicating the illusion in a new modality. The Discussion concludes: 'we demonstrated that the phenomena underlying the word height superiority effect also applied in the auditory modality.'

description: Letters and words are perceived as taller than pseudoletters and pseudowords of the same objective height (the word/letter height superiority illusion), a perceptual consequence of lexical feedback activation

replication_title: Listening to Foreign Languages: Pump Up the Volume!

The authors conclude: 'This illusion was proven to be robust as it was found every time we tested it (four times across our two experiments).'

The interaction effect was statistically significant when using SIMs (F(1, 327) = 7.94, p = .005, η²p = .024), the same measure as the original, though not significant when using CSIMs. The effect was described as 'somewhat smaller than in Vorms and colleagues' original work.'

description: Numerical distance and masked priming effects in a digit comparison-to-standard task: comparison distance effect, congruity-priming effect, and priming distance effect

original_title: Dissecting the symbolic distance effect: Comparison and priming effects in numerical and nonnumerical orders

explanation: The author explicitly states this is 'a direct replication of part of a study by van Opstal and colleagues' and concludes in the discussion that 'all expected effects in a comparison to the given standard task were observed in a direct replication of van Opstal et al.' All three effects (comparison distance, congruity-priming, priming distance) were significant and in the same direction as the original, with comparable effect sizes.

description: Dissociative disorders (hysteria) occur at a frequency of approximately 5.1% among psychiatric outpatients in Eastern Saudi Arabia, with a characteristic symptom profile dominated by fits and a female-to-male ratio of approximately 1.8:1
original_authors: Hassan B. Hafeiz; Maher M. Al-Maghraby; Sayed M. El-Sayed

explanation: The replication found a significant decrease in the frequency of dissociative disorders (2.5% vs. 5.1%, p<0.0006), and statistically significant differences in symptom profiles (dyspnea and tremors changed significantly). However, the authors conclude that 'dissociative disorder seems to have stood the test of time and its unique clinical presentation has bred true,' suggesting the core phenomenon persists even as specific rates and symptoms shifted — yielding mixed/inconclusive overall results.

explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicate Hartley and Trueman (1997) using the same institution, same four modules, and same matching procedure. replication_title: The U-Shaped Curve in the Low Countries: A Replication Study
explanation: Reviewed paper's Discussion and Table 1. The authors explicitly state 'our outcomes confirm the latter, more relativistic position' — that aesthetic judgment patterns vary by judge background rather than reflecting universal graphic development. Key patterns replicate: few/no U-curves among 8- and 14-year-old judges and adult nonartists; many inverted U-curves among 8-year-olds (44% vs 46% in original). Dutch expert artists produced even more U-curves (41% vs 29%), which strengthens rather than undermines the original finding that art-trained judges hold modernist views. Differences in upward-slope and zigzag percentages are attributed by the authors to stricter operational definitions, not substantive disagreement. Classification as 'close extension' is correct: same paradigm applied in a new cultural context (Dutch art education) to test generalizability.

original_title: Confidence matching in group decision-making
replication_authors: Jamal Esmaily; Sajjad Zabbah; Reza Ebrahimpour; Bahador Bahrami
replication_title: Interpersonal alignment of neural evidence accumulation to social exchange of confidence
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated the emergence of confidence matching' (Introduction). Confidence matching was observed in both their discovery study (N=12) and their pre-registered replication study (N=15), with linear regression p<0.001 for both (Figure 1b). A permutation test confirmed the effect was not a statistical artifact. The replication type is close extension: the authors used the same dyadic paradigm and computer-generated partners as Bang et al. (2017), but added EEG, pupillometry, and a neural attractor model. The pre-registered within-paper replication, the explicit verbal claim of successful replication, and the highly significant statistics across two independent samples provide unambiguous evidence for a successful replication. Upgraded from medium to high confidence on review.

The replication extended the original (which was only in older adults) to both younger and older adults, using the same HMAX model and houses-vs-faces fMRI paradigm.

Contrary to prediction, the TD group showed significantly more right lateralisation than the DLD group (19.90% vs. 9.30%). explanation: Reviewer verification: The paper is anchored on Rogaeva et al 2007 (reference 1) — the SNP numbering scheme used throughout follows Rogaeva (footnote a of Table 1: 'SNP numbers are reported according to Rogaeva et al.'), and the 13 genotyped SNPs are drawn from the 5' and 3' clusters originally reported by Rogaeva. The Discussion concludes: 'Our results replicate in an Italian population the findings that SORL1 genetic variants may modify the LOAD risk, although with a marked allelic heterogeneity.' Concretely, SNP 4 (rs661057), SNP 7, SNP 10, and the 5' CGC haplotype were associated with LOAD (SNP 4 OR=1.47, 95%CI 1.15-1.89, P=.002), but the 3' cluster SNPs and haplotypes — also associated in Rogaeva — did NOT replicate ('we could not replicate, in our case-control sample, the reported association of haplotypes at the 3' region of SORL1'). Result is genuinely mixed: the broad SORL1-LOAD association replicates, but at a different locus within the gene than in the original. 'Inconclusive' with medium confidence honestly reflects this partial/heterogeneous replication; reasonable reviewers could also call it 'success' (broad finding replicated) — the ambiguity is real and stems from the paper itself.

explanation: Reviewer verified the verbatim citation sentence ('This study confirms and extends observations of the chemopreventive impact of, and actions triggered, by dietary b-ionone during DMBA-initiated mammary carcinogenesis in Sprague-Dawley rats.' — body.md line 27). Result classification 'success' is strongly supported: dose-dependent inhibition of tumor incidence (82.1% control vs. 53.3/25.9/10.0% at low/medium/high doses, p<0.01) and tumor multiplicity. Ambiguity that justifies keeping confidence at medium: the authors simultaneously claim 'These results demonstrate for the first time that supplementation with b-ionone has potent anticarcinogenic activity in mammary cancer induced by DMBA in a rat model' (Discussion), which is in tension with the abstract-level 'confirms and extends' framing. Yu 1995 (ref 16) is discussed as comparing b-ionone potency vs. monoterpenes on HMGR/tumor multiplicity rather than as a directly matched DMBA-Sprague-Dawley protocol, so the exact degree of methodological overlap with Yu 1995 is unclear from this paper alone. 'close extension' is reasonable given the explicit confirm-and-extend claim plus substantial new IHC endpoints (PCNA, cyclin D1, Bcl-2, Bax, TUNEL), but a 'conceptual' classification could also be defended if Yu 1995 used different methodology.

The one exception (PADI4-92) showed a statistically significant genotype distribution difference but in the OPPOSITE direction from Fan et al. — the minor G allele appeared protective (OR<1), not a susceptibility factor. The Discussion concludes: 'Our study indicated there was no association between PADI4 and RA... the overall results suggested that PADI4 polymorphisms might not play an important role in the etiology of RA in Chinese Han population.' description: Article. The annotation covers OCs of (in)definite articles (a(n)/the). Given that the ‘zero article’ was disregarded in previous MOS, it was also disregarded here for comparative purposes. The non-suppliance of an article in an (in)definite OC was tagged as omission. Also, given that both definite and indefinite articles were analysed as a single morpheme in previous MOS, we analysed them similarly, even if we are aware that they are better analysed separately as they do not emerge simultaneously (cf. the discussion in Section 4.4). Selection of one article for the other was tagged as ‘mis-selection’. The forms a/an were understood as spelling variants, so selection of one when the other was expected was not tagged as NTLU. Importantly, determining the OC of the/a(n) is based on information-status distinctions deriving from discourse, i.e., on whether the entity has been previously mentioned in the discourse (i.e., discourse-old, topic) or not (i.e., discourse-new, focus), and therefore whether or not the referent is known to the reader. Articles were annotated independently of the appearance of characters in the picture story, which could give the sense of old information, but technically introduce discoursenew information when retelling the story to a reader. Therefore, ILA considers hearer/reader knowledge (and not speaker knowledge) to determine discourse-old/discourse-new distinctions (cf. Hawkins, 2001). [Original Study 1.]

description: "Table 1 shows the average amount allocated (amount given in the GG, or (£10—amount taken) in the TG) for both the aggregated data and for males and females by treatment. In the GG, an average of £2.066 is given to the recipients. In the TG, the dictators take on average £7.87 and as a result, the amount left to the recipient is £2.13. A Mann-Whitney test shows no significant difference in final amount allocated to recipients between the two treatments (p-value = 0.583).", "Both nonparametric tests and regressions reaffirm the observations from existing studies (Dreber et al. 2013; Grossman and Eckel 2015) that overall there is no framing effect within the dictator game and giving is indeed equivalent to “not taking.” However, further investigations by gender show that framing has opposing effects for females and males. Females take less in a taking game compared to what they give in a giving game; but the males do just the opposite. Furthermore, we find that this occurs as the male dictators are significantly more likely to be selfish in the taking frame compared to the giving frame. Conversely, the female dictators are significantly more likely to be egalitarian in the taking frame compared with the giving frame."

description: "In column 1, I estimate multinational wage spillovers by pooled ordinary least squares. The results are consistent with multinational spillovers, though without controls for individual and establishment heterogeneity, the result is difficult to interpret.", "This is the main contribution and new result of this paper. When multinational workers leave multinational establishments and are rehired at domestic establishments, the wages of continuing domestic workers increase. This avenue for multinational spillovers, to my knowledge, has not previously been explored. At the average wage for a typical domestic worker of $3,841 (R$6,522 at average annual exchange rates during the 1996–2001 period), this is an increase of approximately $23 per year per worker, equivalent to one more month of job tenure within the establishment. While this may seem to be a small impact, it is also an appropriately sized impact for the average worker. More important, these estimates are worker-level wage spillovers and not plant-level productivity spillovers, as in previous studies. For the average domestic stablishment in Brazil, with a workforce of approximately sixty, the total implied wage effect from 10 percentage point increase in the share of former multinational workers is roughly $1,400 per year. According to RAIS, in 1998 there were 1,795,798 establishments in Brazil, approximately 98% of which were domestically owned. Therefore, this average impact has the potential to generate $2.5 billion in wage spillovers across all of Brazil (in the range of 0.3% of GDP)." [N=1.21256e+06; test statistic=γM - γD ]

description: "In column 1, I estimate multinational wage spillovers by pooled ordinary least squares. The results are consistent with multinational spillovers, though without controls for individual and establishment heterogeneity, the result is difficult to interpret.", "This is the main contribution and new result of this paper. When multinational workers leave multinational establishments and are rehired at domestic establishments, the wages of continuing domestic workers increase. This avenue for multinational spillovers, to my knowledge, has not previously been explored. At the average wage for a typical domestic worker of $3,841 (R$6,522 at average annual exchange rates during the 1996–2001 period), this is an increase of approximately $23 per year per worker, equivalent to one more month of job tenure within the establishment. While this may seem to be a small impact, it is also an appropriately sized impact for the average worker. More important, these estimates are worker-level wage spillovers and not plant-level productivity spillovers, as in previous studies. For the average domestic stablishment in Brazil, with a workforce of approximately sixty, the total implied wage effect from 10 percentage point increase in the share of former multinational workers is roughly $1,400 per year. According to RAIS, in 1998 there were 1,795,798 establishments in Brazil, approximately 98% of which were domestically owned. Therefore, this average impact has the potential to generate $2.5 billion in wage spillovers across all of Brazil (in the range of 0.3% of GDP)." [N=1.39605e+06; test statistic=γM - γD ]

Incumbent domestic workers’ wages increase with the proportion of coworkers in the establishment who have experience in foreign owned establishments (γM > 0).", "This is the main contribution and new result of this paper. When multinational workers leave multinational establishments and are rehired at domestic establishments, the wages of continuing domestic workers increase. This avenue for multinational spillovers, to my knowledge, has not previously been explored. At the average wage for a typical domestic worker of $3,841 (R$6,522 at average annual exchange rates during the 1996–2001 period), this is an increase of approximately $23 per year per worker, equivalent to one more month of job tenure within the establishment. While this may seem to be a small impact, it is also an appropriately sized impact for the average worker. More important, these estimates are worker-level wage spillovers and not plant-level productivity spillovers, as in previous studies. For the average domestic stablishment in Brazil, with a workforce of approximately sixty, the total implied wage effect from 10 percentage point increase in the share of former multinational workers is roughly $1,400 per year. According to RAIS, in 1998 there were 1,795,798 establishments in Brazil, approximately 98% of which were domestically owned. Therefore, this average impact has the potential to generate $2.5 billion in wage spillovers across all of Brazil (in the range of 0.3% of GDP)." [N=1.39605e+06; test statistic=γM - γD ]

source: Manual entry. ACX Grants 2024 replication by Alexander Putilin, published as a guest post on Astral Codex Ten 2026-06-16. Preregistration https://osf.io/mjpxw (registered 2025-10-11); code and per-block data https://github.com/eleweek/EEG_entrainment . Original study data from the University of Cambridge Apollo repository https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.89519 .
explanation: Effect sizes computed by MO from primary data; neither write-up reports a usable effect size for this claim. ORIGINAL: from groupLR_forLMM.csv (Cambridge Apollo, doi:10.17863/CAM.89519), which holds the Day-1 per-participant learning rates for the three entrainment groups (the arrhythmic control is not released; groupLR_postLMM.csv is the Day-2 file). T-match (phase=2, match=1) mean 3.271 SD 2.941 n=20 vs P-match (phase=1, match=1) mean 0.945 SD 4.134 n=20 -- ratio 3.46, the paper's '3x faster' claim. Coding confirmed by locating the LR=-7.129 outlier the replication write-up attributes to P-match. Student t(38)=2.050, p=0.047; pooled SD 3.587; Cohen d=0.648; raw-difference 95% CI [0.029, 4.622], scaled to d CI [0.008, 1.288]. The paper reports the same contrast as the LMM main effect of phase, t(57)=2.05, P=0.045, which is the p-value recorded here. REPLICATION: the preregistered confirmatory H1 (OSF mjpxw) is the within-subject difference in log-block learning-rate slope, T minus P, N=12. Recomputed from published_replication_data/block_accuracy.csv by OLS fit of accuracy = a + b*ln(block) over 8 blocks per participant-day, matching the author's scripts/analyze_data.py. Mean difference -0.050 slope units, SD 7.113; t(11)=-0.024; one-sided p=0.5095, two-sided p=0.9809; Cohen dz=-0.0071, dz 95% CI [-0.642, 0.628]. dz is not auto-convertible, so replication_es_r was supplied directly as dz/sqrt(dz^2+4) = -0.0035. CAVEAT ON 'failure' -- the replication is a weak test and does not statistically exclude the original effect. At N=12 it had only 28 percent power against the original effect (dz 0.327 on the replication's own SD; the smallest dz detectable at 80 percent power is 0.77), and its 95% CI for the raw difference, [-4.57, 4.47], contains the original difference of +2.33. The crossover design compounds this: because the original's Day 2 was an entrainment-free, feedback-free retention test while the replication's Day 2 delivered the opposite entrainment condition, half of every participant's data comes from a session in which the task had already been largely learned. Day-2 slopes are strongly attenuated (mean 1.351 vs 6.205 on Day 1, paired t(11)=3.369, p=0.0063) and Day-2 starting accuracy is 11.2 points higher, so the within-subject contrast is both noisier and biased toward the null even though condition order was randomised 1:1. 'failure' follows the replication author's own stated conclusion, not a demonstration that the effect is absent. Exploratory H2 (Day-1 between-groups, the design the original actually used, n=6 per group) also failed and pointed the other way: T 4.79 vs P 7.62, Welch t(8.73)=-1.31, two-sided p=0.224, Hedges g=-0.70. A non-preregistered Day-1 initial-accuracy difference favoured T-match (58.3 vs 46.2 percent, Welch t(10)=2.911, p=0.0155) but is absent in the original. Deviations from the original: within-subject crossover instead of four independent groups, so the T-nonMatch and arrhythmic-control arms are absent and Day 2 is a second entrainment session rather than a retention test; consumer 8-channel OpenBCI Ultracortex Mark IV instead of a 63-channel research system; a variable-refresh-rate monitor (48-165 Hz) instead of a fixed 120 Hz panel, which the author argues gives more faithful flicker at frequencies that do not divide the refresh rate; IAF band widened from 8-12 Hz to 7-14 Hz with SpecParam aperiodic-adjusted spectra; 7.5-minute instead of 5-minute resting recording, in a dark room; trial feedback shown for the full inter-trial interval instead of 100 ms; breaks every 100 rather than 200 trials, with the participant's per-block accuracy displayed at each break.

source: Manual entry 2026-08-12 from the full text of Reaves et al. 2012 (doi:10.1126/science.1219861; preprint arXiv:1201.6643), growth results and Figure 1. Bibliographic fields verified against Crossref.
explanation: Reaves et al. obtained the GFAJ-1 strain from Wolfe-Simon et al.'s co-authors and confirmed its identity by 16S rRNA PCR and sequencing with the primers specified in the original paper, obtaining a sequence identical to that reported for GFAJ-1. They could not grow the strain in basal AML60 medium with the specified trace elements and vitamins at all, even with 1500 uM sodium phosphate added. Adding small amounts of yeast extract, tryptone or individual amino acids restored growth, and 1 mM glutamate was therefore added to AML60 for every experiment (doubling times 90-180 min, versus the ~12 h reported originally). That glutamate supplement is the single deliberate deviation from the original protocol. Growth yield then tracked phosphate supplementation: ~2x10^8 cells/ml at 1500 uM phosphate (similar to Wolfe-Simon et al.'s own -As/+P yield), ~2x10^7 cells/ml with 3 uM phosphate added, and ~5x10^6 cells/ml unsupplemented. The four-fold difference between the last two implies ~1 uM contaminating phosphate in the base medium, so AML60 + 3 uM phosphate reproduces the original's '-P' condition (whose own contaminating phosphate was ~4 uM, itself enough to support moderate growth in other low-phosphate microbes). Decisively, these growth analyses were run in the ABSENCE of arsenate, showing that GFAJ-1 does not require arsenate to grow under phosphate limitation - the observation on which the original claim rested. +As and -As cultures grew to similar densities and the authors 'never observed cases where +As cultures grew but -As cultures did not.' Coded failure: the arsenate requirement was not observed again. No effect size is entered because neither paper reports a statistic that converts to a comparable standardized effect; the comparison is between growth-yield curves and a detection limit. The original paper was retracted by Science on 2025-07-24 (retraction notice: H. Holden Thorp, Science 389(6758):357, doi:10.1126/science.adu5488), the editors citing that the nucleic acids were not sufficiently purified before spectra were acquired and that the key conclusion rests on contamination; there was no finding of fraud or misconduct and the authors dissented. Eight Technical Comments had already been published in Science on 2011-06-03 (Redfield doi:10.1126/science.1201482; Cotner & Hall .1201943; Borhani .1201255; Benner .1201304; Csabai & Szathmary .1201399; Foster .1201551; Oehler .1201381; Schoepp-Cothenet et al. .1201438), but none of them reported new experiments on GFAJ-1 and they are not entered as replication rows. No published study has ever reproduced arsenate substitution for phosphate in GFAJ-1 macromolecules.

source: Manual entry 2026-08-12 from Erb et al. 2012 (doi:10.1126/science.1218455), growth characterisation. Bibliographic fields verified against Crossref.
explanation: Erb et al. grew GFAJ-1 under controlled phosphate concentrations rather than the original's AML60 formulation - the deliberate change that makes this a close experiment rather than a direct one, and the change that matters, since the original's '-P' medium carried ~4 uM contaminating phosphate. GFAJ-1 grew at phosphate concentrations as low as 1.7 uM even in the presence of 40 mM arsenate, but was unable to grow in phosphorus-depleted (<0.3 uM) arsenate-containing medium. The organism is therefore arsenate-RESISTANT but still phosphate-DEPENDENT: the arsenate tolerance the original observed is real, but it does not substitute for phosphorus, and the apparent 'growth without phosphate' reflects residual phosphate in the medium. Coded failure against the substitution claim. No effect size is entered; the comparison is between growth/no-growth thresholds in phosphate concentration. The original paper was retracted by Science on 2025-07-24 (retraction notice: H. Holden Thorp, Science 389(6758):357, doi:10.1126/science.adu5488), the editors citing that the nucleic acids were not sufficiently purified before spectra were acquired and that the key conclusion rests on contamination; there was no finding of fraud or misconduct and the authors dissented. Eight Technical Comments had already been published in Science on 2011-06-03 (Redfield doi:10.1126/science.1201482; Cotner & Hall .1201943; Borhani .1201255; Benner .1201304; Csabai & Szathmary .1201399; Foster .1201551; Oehler .1201381; Schoepp-Cothenet et al. .1201438), but none of them reported new experiments on GFAJ-1 and they are not entered as replication rows. No published study has ever reproduced arsenate substitution for phosphate in GFAJ-1 macromolecules.

explanation: High-resolution mass spectrometry of GFAJ-1 extracts showed that phosphorylated central metabolites and phosphorylated nucleic acids predominated. source: Manual entry 2026-08-12 from the full text of Basturea, Harris & Deutscher 2012 (doi:10.1074/jbc.C112.394403, PMC3436571), Figures 1-3 and Discussion. Bibliographic fields verified against Crossref.
explanation: CODED CONCEPTUAL, AND THE REASON MATTERS: these authors never cultured GFAJ-1. The only strain in their Experimental Procedures is Escherichia coli MG1655 (an rph+, RNase I- derivative). They tested the original's causal claim in a surrogate laboratory organism, and the GFAJ-1 figures they cite (~40 h doubling time, ~20-fold growth) are quoted from Wolfe-Simon et al., not measured here. What they showed: cells prelabelled with [3H]uridine and shifted into medium with 40 mM arsenate released almost 70% of their total label into the acid-soluble fraction within 20 h - massive ribosome degradation - versus less than 10% in medium lacking phosphate or containing 1.5 mM phosphate without arsenate. Paper chromatography identified uracil as the terminal product, meaning rRNA breakdown liberates free phosphate internally. In +As/-P medium E. coli first died (>99% of cells eliminated within 24 h by viable count), then a small arsenate-tolerant subpopulation grew out after a lag of ~80 h; pre-exposing cells to arsenate abolished the lag, confirming selection rather than adaptation. This reproduces the original's growth pattern - long lag, very slow growth, 4-5 doublings - in an ordinary bacterium with no capacity for arsenic substitution, and the authors calculate that ribosome degradation alone supplies more than enough phosphate for the ~20-fold increase reported. Their own summary is precise: 'although we agree with the experimental observations of Wolfe-Simon et al., we disagree with their interpretation of the data.' The growth observation therefore stands; the arsenic-instead-of-phosphorus explanation for it does not, which is why this row is coded failure against the substitution claim described. Included because it empirically re-tested the causal claim; excluded from a 'direct' or 'close' label because the organism is different. source: Manual entry 2026-08-12 from primary text on both sides. Original: Gino & Desai (2012) published JPSP version, Experiment 1, Moral purity paragraph, via the Harvard DASH green open-access copy (nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:10996789, OpenAlex oa_status=green). Replication: Shin (2021) Study 1, section 3.2.3, doi:10.14695/KJSOS.2021.24.1.73 (Korean, open access via koreascience.kr). Identified from the co-author transparency page manycoauthors.org/gino/105.
explanation: ORIGINAL. Gino & Desai (2012) published Experiment 1: 113 undergraduates at a southeastern US university, 110 analysed after excluding 3 who voiced suspicion; childhood-memory essay vs last-visit-to-the-supermarket essay. Moral purity M=3.73 (SD=1.79) vs M=2.38 (SD=1.41), t(108)=4.42, p<.001, d=0.86 (d reported by the authors). The paper gives no CI and does not report the per-condition n; the CI entered here is computed from d=0.86 with N=110 and is insensitive to the split (50/60 through 60/50 all give [0.468, 1.252] to three decimals). IMPORTANT for anyone re-checking these numbers: the freely circulating HBS working paper 11-079 has FOUR experiments and is NOT the published article. The published JPSP version has FIVE: 1 Helping Others, 2 Donating Money to a Good Cause, 3 Manipulating Moral Purity (new, absent from the working paper), 4 Judging and Punishing the Actions of Others (= working paper Exp 3), 5 Good and Bad Childhood Memories (= working paper Exp 4). Working-paper Exp 2 is also a DIFFERENT donation study from published Exp 2 (N=103 with a grocery-store control vs N=87 with a high-school control). All original-side values in this row were read from the published version (Harvard DASH accepted manuscript, nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:10996789), whose Experiment 1 is identical to working-paper Experiment 1. REPLICATION DESIGN. Shin (2021) Study 1: 117 undergraduates at a Korean four-year university (M_age 20.03, 40 men / 77 women), recruited via a campus board, randomly assigned to recall childhood experiences (n=58) or recent everyday experiences (n=59), online, ~15 min, paid a 5,000-won coffee voucher. Both conditions first wrote a disguising essay about their morning routine, exactly as in Gino & Desai. Shin states the childhood-condition prompt follows Gino & Desai (2012) and uses their two-item moral purity scale, citing their alpha of .84 (alpha = .74 here, on a 9-point rather than 7-point scale). Manipulation check t(115)=7.42, p<.001. Affect was measured to rule out a mood account and, as in Gino & Desai Experiments 1-3, did not differ: positive affect 6.36 (1.49) vs 5.93 (1.43), t(115)=1.586, p=.116; negative affect 4.60 (1.23) vs 4.38 (1.86), t(115)=.624, p=.534. Shin's Study 2 is NOT a replication and is deliberately not entered here: it manipulates construal level with childhood recall in BOTH arms, so it contains no childhood-vs-control contrast. REPLICATION RESULT. Moral purity was higher after childhood recall, M=6.14 (SD=1.98), than after recent-everyday recall, M=5.70 (SD=1.57), t(115)=2.06, p=.041, giving d=0.381, 95% CI [0.015, 0.747], r=0.187. Same direction as the original at roughly half the magnitude (original d=0.86, r=0.395); the replication CI excludes zero but also excludes the original point estimate. DISCREPANCY IN THE REPLICATION REPORT, recorded rather than smoothed over: Shin's reported means and SDs are not consistent with the reported test. The pooled SD implied by 1.98 and 1.57 is 1.785, giving d=0.247 and t(115)=1.33 (p=.185), not t=2.06 (p=.041). The reported t and p ARE mutually consistent (t=2.06 at df=115 is p=.0417 two-tailed), so the SDs are the suspect element. This row is therefore entered from the test statistic, which is the quantity the two reported values agree on. Note this is specific to the moral-purity measure: the three other Study 1 contrasts all reconcile to within d=0.01 (prosocial motivation d=0.402 from F vs 0.403 from means/SDs; informal prosocial 0.468 vs 0.468; formal prosocial 0.104 vs 0.095). If the SDs rather than the t are correct, this row becomes a failure rather than a success, so it is worth writing to Shin. EFFECT-SIZE DERIVATION. Replication d computed from the reported test statistic as d = t * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) with n1=58, n2=59; 95% CI as d +/- 1.96*SE with SE = sqrt((n1+n2)/(n1*n2) + d^2/(2*(n1+n2))) (Hedges & Olkin). Left original_es_r/replication_es_r blank for the ingestor to compute. The original paper's data provenance is documented at manycoauthors.org/gino/105: co-author Sreedhari Desai reports that Gino was involved in data collection for all five experiments, that co-authors never held the raw data, and that no data for reproducing the results of any experiment is available. The paper is NOT retracted and carries no expression of concern (checked PubMed 22181000, 2026-08-12). Recorded here because it bears on what a replication of this paper can and cannot settle, not as a claim about the original's validity.
