source: Manual entry 2026-08-12 from the full dissertation text, CUNY Academic Works academicworks.cuny.edu/gc_etds/4092 (advisor Sankar Sen; committee Ana Valenzuela, Stephen J. Gould, Gita Venkataramani Johar). Study 2, the first of two studies measuring actual lending behavior. Original side: Gino & Desai (2012) published JPSP version, Experiment 1, via the Harvard DASH copy. Identified from the co-author transparency page manycoauthors.org/gino/105.
explanation: WHY THIS IS CODED INCONCLUSIVE, AND WHY EFFECT-SIZE CELLS ARE BLANK. Across all five studies the dissertation reports ONLY an interaction between the childhood-memories manipulation and trait rebelliousness. No unconditional main effect of childhood memories on lending is reported anywhere in the document, so there is no quantity that can be set against Gino & Desai's main effect, and no comparable Pearson r exists to enter. Same treatment as the arsenic-life and Betatrophin rows: the numbers live here instead. THIS ROW'S STUDY. Study 2, N=93 undergraduates (46 female, M_age 22.05) who had been asked by email to bring their own calculator to the lab; after the essay manipulation they were asked whether they would lend it to another student, a yes/no choice - real behavior, not intention. Logistic regression (PROCESS model 1): childhood-memories x rebelliousness b=-.69, SE=.31, z=-2.22, p=.027. Johnson-Neyman: a significant POSITIVE effect only at or below 1.32 on the 5-point rebelliousness scale, which is 5.38% of the sample (b=.96, SE=.49, z=1.96, p=.05), and a significant NEGATIVE effect at or above 4.06, a further 6.45% (b=-.93, SE=.47, z=-1.96, p=.05). For roughly 88% of participants the manipulation did nothing, and among the most rebellious it significantly REDUCED lending. THE OTHER FOUR STUDIES, all the same shape and all consistent with each other: Study 1, N=114 MTurk, lending intentions on a mock sharing website, interaction b=-.45, SE=.19, t=-2.37, p=.019, positive simple effect only at or below 2.20 (28.07% of the sample); number of items willing to lend, b=-.21, SE=.045, z=-4.56, p<.01. Study 3, N=242 MTurk, interaction on willingness to lend a vacuum cleaner b=-.55, and on general app-based lending b=-.52, SE=.25, t=-2.08, p=.039, positive simple effect at or below 2.29 (32.23%); interaction on self-community connectedness b=-.38. Study 4, N=197 MTurk, interaction on lending intentions b=-.34. Study 5, N=133, calculator lending again, interaction b=-1.03, SE=.45, z=-2.31, p=.021, with the same two-tailed crossover. RELATION TO THE ORIGINAL. The manipulation is described as 'created based on the manipulations used by Wildschut et al. (2006), Gino and Desai (2012), and Lasaleta, Sedikides, and Vohs (2014)' - an adaptation drawing on three sources, not a reuse of the original protocol. The dependent variable is lending one's own possessions rather than helping or donating. The proposed mechanism is self-community connectedness, and MORAL PURITY IS NEVER MEASURED, so the original's mediator goes untested. Study 4 does run the same nostalgia-as-mediator test that Gino & Desai ran, citing them, and likewise finds no mediation by nostalgia. Desai's statement on manycoauthors.org/gino/105 describes this dissertation as having 'findings that align with Gino and Desai (2012)'. That holds only for the less-rebellious portion of each sample; in the behavioural studies the aligned region is a small minority of participants and the effect reverses at the other tail. WHY THE THIRD WORK CITED ON THAT PAGE IS NOT IN THE DATABASE. Laguna, Kedra & Mazur-Socha (2021), Front. Psychol. 12:661336, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.661336, was assessed on 2026-08-12 and deliberately NOT entered. Both of its arms are active - a 'Three Good Things for Others' intervention versus a childhood-memories placebo - with no inert control, so no contrast in the design isolates childhood-memory recall. The between-group tests are flat: Time x Group F(3,264)=0.25, p=0.844; Group F(1,88)=0.80, p=0.778. The claim that it supports Gino & Desai rests entirely on an uncontrolled within-arm pre-post rise in the placebo group (SVO M=5.96 at T0 to 6.67 at T1, p=.041, and 6.96 at T3, p=.011) across four measurement points, in a study where 89 of 303 recruited participants (29.4%) completed all four. It can adjudicate the original effect in neither direction. Do not add it later without reading this note. explanation: Study 1 found a significant main effect of time constraint on cooperation (F(1,195)=4.00, p<0.05), replicating the direction of the original time-pressure effect, with no significant interaction with group membership; the authors state this 'successfully increased cooperation through time pressure...as predicted based on past research,' concluding the effect generalizes to both in-group and out-group partners.

description: In economic games, forcing participants to decide quickly under time pressure increases cooperation relative to allowing time for deliberation (time delay); Study 2 tests whether this time-pressure effect generalizes to a four-person public goods game framed as a competition versus one framed as a collaboration.

explanation: Independent review confirms the ambiguity is genuine, not an artifact of incomplete reading, so confidence stays medium. The paper makes a global claim of success: the abstract states time pressure 'increased cooperation to a similar extent' in both the competition and collaboration framings, and the Study 2 'Results and discussion' section argues the non-significant time-constraint x context interaction, 'together with both significant main effects, replicated the results of Study 1'; the General Discussion goes further, concluding the effect 'extends even to two social contexts that are "hostile" toward cooperation.' But the paper's own disaggregated (simple-effects) results are mixed, not uniform: time pressure significantly increased cooperation in the competition condition (F(1,737)=4.38, p<0.05) but not in the collaboration condition (F(1,737)=0.67, p=0.41) -- the condition that most closely matches the original Rand et al. (2012) paradigm's neutral framing. The authors themselves flag this null result as 'surprising given prior work (Rand et al., 2012)' and offer a post hoc explanation (MTurk pool familiarity with the standard design) rather than treating it as a failed replication. Per the rule that a global claim of support does not override a paper that also reports a differing/partial pattern, and that only one of the two named sub-conditions (competition vs. collaboration) independently replicated the original effect, this remains inconclusive rather than success. No new evidence resolves the tension between the authors' framing and their own simple-effects breakdown either way, so this is a case of genuine authorial ambiguity, not reviewer uncertainty.

description: In a choice between two mutually exclusive events on which unequal amounts of money had already been (non-recoverably) spent, individuals disproportionately choose to consume the option with the larger sunk cost even when they would enjoy the cheaper, less-costly alternative more (the sunk-cost effect).
original_authors: Arkes, Hal R.; Blumer, Catherine
original_title: The psychology of sunk cost
replication_authors: Dilip Soman
replication_title: The mental accounting of sunk time costs: why time is not like money
explanation: The author explicitly frames the monetary version of Experiment 1 as adapted from Arkes and Blumer's (1985) Experiment 1 and reports that it reproduces the classic sunk-cost finding: 'a significantly lower fraction of the respondents (38.3%, p<0.001) made a choice consistent with their anticipated enjoyment and a majority of the respondents fell prey to the sunk-cost effect,' concluding 'the sunk-cost effect was observed when the costs are monetary.' The paradigm (forced choice between two mutually-exclusive events with unequal sunk costs) is the same as the original, but it was run on a different population (Hong Kong Univ. of Science and Technology students, in HK$) with a different cover story (theater/rock-concert tickets vs. the original ski-trip scenario), so it is scored as a close extension rather than a direct replication.

description: Children with specific language impairment (SLI) aged 7-11 show weaker/less lateralized hand preference than age-matched typically-developing children on a reaching test (the quantification of hand preference, QHP, task) that requires crossing the body midline, despite showing no group difference on a conventional handedness-inventory measure.
original_authors: Elisabeth L. Hill Dorothy V.M. Bishop
original_title: A reaching test reveals weak hand preference in specific language impairment and developmental coordination disorder
replication_authors: Dorothy V. M. Bishop
replication_title: Handedness and specific language impairment: A study of 6-year-old twins
explanation: Reviewed independently: the Abstract states plainly that in this 6-year-old TEDS sample 'Hand preference (HP) assessed by inventory did not distinguish SLI, TD, or GD groups' while 'the quantification of hand preference (QHP) measure ... did show weaker HP in those with SLI compared to the other two groups' -- an unhedged restatement of exactly the two sub-findings named in this entry's description. The Results section backs this with statistics: QHP slope differed by language status, F(2,375)=4.95, p=.008, with post-hoc Scheffe tests confirming SLI < control, while the EHI inventory score was uncorrelated with QHP slope in both groups (both p>.4), i.e. the inventory again showed no group effect. The Discussion explicitly frames this as 'consistent with previous data from our research group in three respects,' first among them being the QHP-vs-inventory dissociation. The only caveat ('these relationships were small in magnitude') concerns effect size, not direction or significance, and does not qualify as the 'mixed/partial' language that would force inconclusive -- both named sub-measures replicated cleanly and concordantly. Upgraded to high confidence on this direct evidence.

description: In a twin sample aged 7-13, genetic analysis found no evidence of heritability for either a conventional handedness inventory or a hand-preference reaching (QHP) measure, used as evidence against a genetic link between handedness and specific language impairment; the QHP heritability test in that study was based on only a small subsample of twins who had completed the task.
original_authors: Dorothy V. M. Bishop
original_title: Individual differences in handedness and specific language impairment: Evidence against a genetic link
replication_authors: Dorothy V. M. Bishop
replication_title: Handedness and specific language impairment: A study of 6-year-old twins
explanation: Reviewed independently against the Discussion and genetic-analysis Results: the current, much larger twin sample confirms Bishop (2001)'s null result for the conventional inventory ('there was no evidence of any heritable influence on HP assessed by inventory', a2=.25, CI 0-.408, and dropping the genetic term did not worsen fit), but for the QHP slope measure it finds a2=.43 (95% CI .02-.56), a significant genetic effect (chi-sq(1)=4.28, p=.038) -- explicitly called a 'novel finding' of heritability where the original reported none. That is a direct hit on one of the two sub-measures the entry describes as originally null, and a miss on the other, matching the codebook's 'mixed signals within one experiment: significant on one measure but not another' -> inconclusive. The genuine ambiguity: the authors never characterize this as confirming or contradicting Bishop (2001) in replication terms -- they frame the QHP heritability finding as a new discovery enabled by much greater power, not as a failed/mixed replication per se, and the original's QHP test is explicitly flagged (by both the original authors and this entry) as underpowered rather than a confident null. Reasonable readers could therefore call this either 'this extends beyond what the original could detect' or 'this is a mixed/partial replication' -- the paper itself does not resolve which framing is correct, so confidence stays medium.

description: Recognition of a previously viewed scene declines in accuracy as the perspective at test increasingly departs from the viewpoint experienced at encoding (viewpoint-dependent scene recognition).
original_authors: Vaibhav A. Diwadkar; Timothy P. McNamara
original_title: Viewpoint dependence in scene recognition
replication_authors: Veronica Muffato; Christopher Hilton; Chiara Meneghetti; Rossana De Beni; Jan M. Wiener
replication_title: Evidence for age‐related deficits in object‐location binding during place recognition
explanation: Reviewed against Table 1 and the Discussion: the LME on d' shows two significant, unhedged perspective coefficients (30° vs. 0°: β=-0.29, SE=0.07, t=-4.36; 60° vs. 30°: β=-0.13, SE=0.07, t=-2.07), and the independently-run response-bias LME also finds a significant main effect of perspective (main text, 'perspective shift from 0° to 30°, and from 30° to 60° significantly predicts a reduction bias scores'). The Discussion states plainly, with no hedging language, 'we found that performance declined with increasing perspective shifts,' confirming the viewpoint-dependence effect from Diwadkar & McNamara (1997). The paper's one perspective-related null result is unrelated to this entry: the absence of an age × perspective interaction, i.e. no evidence that perspective-taking itself degrades with age ('we did not find an interaction between age and perspective shifts'). That does not qualify the main effect being reviewed here. The paradigm was extended to a 3D virtual-environment place-recognition task and to an older-adult sample not present in the 1997 study, so this is a conceptual/contextual extension rather than a strict direct replication. Upgraded to high confidence based on this specific quantitative evidence (both LMEs, unambiguous Discussion statement).

description: Failures of object-location binding produce 'swap' errors (objects believed to have occupied a location held by a different object) that are harder to detect than simple object-substitution errors, because substitutions can be resolved by object-identity memory alone whereas swaps require correctly bound object-location associations.
original_authors: Yoni Pertzov; Mia Yuan Dong; Muy-Cheng Peich; Masud Husain
original_title: Forgetting what was where: The fragility of object-location binding
replication_authors: Veronica Muffato; Christopher Hilton; Chiara Meneghetti; Rossana De Beni; Jan M. Wiener
replication_title: Evidence for age‐related deficits in object‐location binding during place recognition
explanation: Reviewed against Table 1 and the abstract: the pooled LME on d' does show a significant main effect of condition (Substitute vs. Swap: β=-0.17, SE=0.03, t=-5.42), which is the number the first-pass explanation cited. But that average effect is driven almost entirely by the older groups: the age(60-69 vs 20-29) x condition interaction is itself significant and large (β=-0.23, SE=0.07, t=-3.21), and the abstract states this plainly in non-technical terms -- 'older adults were less sensitive to object swapping than to object substitution, while young participants did not show any difference.' Pertzov et al. (2012), the original study being tested, was a binding-fragility study in a non-aging (predominantly young/general) sample, not an aging study -- so the age group most comparable to the original showed NO swap-vs-substitute difference at all, while the effect that did replicate cleanly is a new, age-specific phenomenon this paper itself frames as a novel contribution ('our older age groups were less likely to detect that two objects had been swapped than that one object had been substituted... a specific age-related object-location binding deficit'). This is a global claim of support (significant pooled main effect) sitting alongside the paper's own explicit report of a subgroup showing no such effect -- a 'differing results' pattern per the review rules, not a clean success. Left at medium confidence per the rule that a changed label is not one the evidence made obvious.

description: Among the linked, functionally related alcohol-metabolism gene polymorphisms, the genetic effect on alcoholism susceptibility is attributable to specific causal loci (centered on ADH1B His47Arg) rather than distributed equally across all associated polymorphisms.
original_authors: Chiao-Chicy Chen; Ru-Band Lu; Yi-Chyan Chen; Ming-Fang Wang; Yue-Cune Chang; Ting-Kai Li; Shih-Jiun Yin

replication_title: Scanning of genetic effects of alcohol metabolism gene (ADH1BandADH1C) polymorphisms on the risk of alcoholism
explanation: Reviewed the full Results and Discussion. The current paper's own subgroup analysis (Table 3, individuals carrying ADH1B*47His) is a complete, not partial, null: the Results section states 'No significant associations were detected in any polymorphisms' once conditioned on ADH1B*47His carrier status -- every other ADH1B/ADH1C site's association vanished. The unhedged Conclusion states 'Our results provide strong evidence that ADH1B His47Arg might be the only locus responsible for the susceptibility to alcoholism among ADH1B and ADH1C polymorphisms,' and neither the abstract nor the conclusion contains any 'differing/mixed/partial' hedge, so 'success' (not inconclusive) is the right label for this claim. What remains genuinely uncertain is the citation correspondence, not the result direction: Chen et al. 1999 is co-cited with Osier et al. 1999 for this exact 'ADH1B*47Arg is sufficient' finding, but elsewhere in this Discussion Chen et al. 1999 is cited separately for a distinct claim (ALDH2/ADH1B genetic-effect independence), and the title of Chen et al. 1999 points toward an ADH1B-ALDH2 interaction focus rather than the ADH1B-vs-ADH1C causal-locus question described here. Without the original Chen et al. 1999 text, this correspondence can't be confirmed beyond the current paper's own characterization, so confidence moves from low to medium rather than high.

description: Linkage disequilibrium between the ADH2 (ADH1B) and ADH3 (ADH1C) loci means that the ADH1C association with alcoholism risk is a passive consequence of LD with the causal ADH1B His47Arg polymorphism, rather than an independent genetic effect.

replication_title: Scanning of genetic effects of alcohol metabolism gene (ADH1BandADH1C) polymorphisms on the risk of alcoholism
explanation: Reviewed the full Results and Discussion. Osier et al. 1999's title ('Linkage disequilibrium at the ADH2 and ADH3 loci and risk of alcoholism') matches this entry's description exactly and unambiguously -- unlike the Chen et al. 1999 co-citation in Entry 0, whose title points to a different (ADH1B-ALDH2 interaction) focus. The current paper's Results confirm the replication is complete, not partial: the subgroup analysis stratified on ADH1B*47His carrier status found 'No significant associations were detected in any polymorphisms' -- i.e., the ADH1C (and other ADH1B) associations vanished entirely once the LD confound with ADH1B His47Arg was removed, exactly the passive-LD mechanism Osier et al. proposed for the ADH2/ADH3 loci. The unhedged Conclusion states 'ADH1B His47Arg might be the only locus responsible for the susceptibility to alcoholism among ADH1B and ADH1C polymorphisms,' with no 'differing/mixed/partial' language anywhere in the abstract or conclusion. The exact title match, the completeness of the null subgroup result, and the unhedged conclusion together resolve the original ambiguity, so confidence is upgraded to high.

In fact, in opposition to the claim of Van Hiel and De Clercq (2009) that RWA should be considered a protective factor against distress, results suggest that, over time, RWA constitutes a risk factor for depression.'

replication_authors: Bart Duriez; Theo A. Klimstra; Koen Luyckx; Wim Beyers; Bart Soenens
replication_title: Right–Wing Authoritarianism: Protective Factor against Or Risk Factor for Depression?
explanation: Study 3 tested, in a high-school sample (N=590, 1-year longitudinal, with parent- and friend-reported RWA), whether family and friend RWA levels moderate the longitudinal authoritarianism-depression relation, using a different outcome (depression rather than life satisfaction) and a continuous interaction term rather than Peterson and Duncan's categorical match/mismatch design. The result is unambiguous and stated three separate times with no hedging: in Results, 'adolescent RWA interacted with neither family nor friend RWA in the prediction of depression' (the interaction model also fit worse than the no-interaction model by BIC: 29398.67 vs. 27533.83); in the Study 3 Discussion, using the same (mis)match framing as the original claim, 'the effects of RWA on depression do not seem to depend on the degree of (mis)match in RWA between the adolescent and either his parents or his best friends'; and in the General Discussion, 'authoritarianism is not more adaptive among people who grew up in a speciﬁc family, among a particular type of friends or in a speciﬁc socio-political climate.' No partial or mixed-support language appears anywhere for this test, so despite the conceptual (not direct) mapping to Peterson and Duncan's design, the null finding itself is clear-cut.

That comparative claim did not hold up. Table 3 shows fasting insulin (p[add]=0.12, p[dom]=0.058) and HOMA-S (the insulin-sensitivity measure inverse to HOMA-IR; p[add]=0.17, p[dom]=0.10) were NOT significantly associated with rs1260326 at all -- the exact traits DESIR highlighted as showing stronger rs1260326 effects. For several other traits (T2DM, obesity, BMI, waist circumference) rs780094 was as strong or stronger than rs1260326 (e.g. T2DM dominant model: rs780094 p=0.0038 vs rs1260326 p=0.031; verified against both body.md and the raw PDF text). The authors state this explicitly and twice: 'no evidence suggests that GCKR rs1260326 is more informative than GCKR rs780094' (Results) and 'we found no evidence here to suggest that rs1260326 is more informative than GCKR rs780094' (Discussion). rs1260326's general direction of association with T2DM, dyslipidaemia and glucose did replicate, but the specific comparative claim named in the description was explicitly refuted, so this is scored as a failure for that comparative claim rather than a partial success.

replication_title: Choice of alcohol over a natural reward: an experimental study in light and heavy social drinkers
explanation: Reviewed against body.md Results/Discussion and abstract.md. The severity-preference sub-measure clearly replicated: AUDIT and group both significantly predicted percentage alcohol choice (F1,56=12.5, p<.001; F1,56=8.3, p=.006), and the authors explicitly state 'We replicate the significant association between alcohol use severity and preference for alcohol across all relative point levels.' However, the second sub-measure (no association between severity and cost/price sensitivity) is NOT cleanly replicated. While the formal interaction tests were non-significant (AUDIT x point level F1,116=0.4, p=.5; group x point level F2,112=0.10, p=.90), a separate group-level comparison of fitted slopes found non-overlapping 95% CIs between heavy (0.76 [0.71,0.82]) and light drinkers (0.98 [0.91,1.06]), which the authors themselves describe as heavy drinkers showing significantly lower cost sensitivity. This is stated as a headline finding in the Abstract's Conclusions: 'price sensitivity was lower in heavy compared to light drinkers' -- and in the Discussion as 'a modestly attenuated price elasticity of alcohol demand' in heavy drinkers. This directly contradicts the entry's claim (drawn from the original Hogarth & Hardy 2018 study, restated in this paper's Introduction) that severity is 'not associated with increased discounting of costs.' Per the scoring rule that a global 'replicate' framing does not override a reported difference elsewhere in the same paper, this is a mixed/partial result: one sub-measure replicated, the other did not (the study instead found a severity-related difference in cost sensitivity where the original found none). Changed from 'success' to 'inconclusive' for this reason; confidence kept at medium since the change is not obvious from a single unambiguous statement but from reconciling conflicting statistical framings within the same paper.

description: Swiss elementary/secondary students confronted with standard 'problematic' word problems (e.g., a bus task requiring rounding up a remainder, a plank-sawing task, a running-speed extrapolation task) predominantly give 'unrealistic' answers that ignore relevant real-world considerations rather than solutions consistent with the realities of the described situations.
original_authors: Kurt Reusser; Рита Стеблер
original_title: Every word problem has a solution – the social rationality of mathematical modeling in schools
replication_authors: Torulf Palm
replication_title: Impact of authenticity on sense making in word problem solving
explanation: Verified against the actual Table 2 numbers (RR% = 'realistic written reactions' on the less-authentic task variants): Reusser & Stebler WP2(balloon)=75, WP3(bus)=49, WP4(plank)=14, WP6(running)=5, WP7(bowl)=0, vs. Palm's Swedish sample WP2=67, WP3=63, WP4=24, WP6=5, WP7=2. The across-task ordering replicates (balloon/bus tasks draw far more realistic responses than plank/running/bowl tasks in both datasets), and the paper's unhedged conclusion is that the Swedish students 'share the same tendencies to provide "unrealistic" solutions as their counterparts in the other three countries.' But this is a purely descriptive comparison (no cross-study significance test), and two of the five tasks drift meaningfully toward MORE realistic responses in Palm's sample than in Reusser & Stebler's: WP3/bus 63% vs 49% (14-point gap, flipping the bus task from roughly even to majority-realistic) and WP4/plank 24% vs 14%. That sub-task-level drift is real ambiguity in how closely the replication actually matches, not just an absence of formal testing, so confidence stays medium rather than being upgraded.

description: Exposure to news media frames that use explicit ethnic cues (featuring Latino rather than European immigrants) produces a substantially larger shift toward more conservative/restrictive immigration policy preferences than cues based on economic cost or skill level, an effect driven by anxiety.
original_authors: Brader, Ted; Valentino, Nicholas A.; Suhay, Elizabeth
original_title: What triggers public opposition to immigration? anxiety, group cues, and immigration threat
replication_authors: Benjamin R. Knoll; David P. Redlawsk; Howard Sanborn
replication_title: Framing Labels and Immigration Policy Attitudes in the Iowa Caucuses: “Trying to Out-Tancredo Tancredo”
explanation: The authors test Brader et al.'s ethnic-cue finding with a narrower design (framing immigrants as 'Mexican' vs. unspecified; they do not include Brader's economic/skill-cue arms or test the anxiety mechanism, and note their data 'do not allow us to conclusively prove which theoretical mechanism is correct'). Verified against Table 2's actual regression coefficients (checked the PDF page image directly, since significance daggers are stripped from the plain-text rendition): in the full-sample model the ethnicity-frame main effect is only marginally significant (b=0.383, p<0.10) and its interaction with issue importance 'just misses' significance (b=-0.474, ns); split by party, the effect is concentrated entirely in Republicans (main effect b=0.959, p<0.01; interaction with importance b=-1.194, p<0.01) with no effect whatsoever for Democrats (b=0.258, ns). This confirms the Discussion's own summary: the ethnic cue 'did influence policy preferences in the expected direction, but only among Republicans, especially for those who viewed immigration as particularly important.' Per the result rules, this subgroup-only support is inconclusive, not success.

description: Framing unauthorized Latino immigrants using the label 'undocumented aliens' rather than 'foreign workers' increases respondents' likelihood of expressing support for a policy of mass deportation.

replication_authors: Benjamin R. Knoll; David P. Redlawsk; Howard Sanborn
replication_title: Framing Labels and Immigration Policy Attitudes in the Iowa Caucuses: “Trying to Out-Tancredo Tancredo”
explanation: Using a similar survey-experiment design with an expanded set of policy response options (improving on McAdams et al.'s binary deportation measure) but a different wording pair ('illegal' vs. 'undocumented' rather than McAdams's 'undocumented aliens' vs. 'foreign workers'), the authors found no significant effect of the legal-status frame in any specification. Verified directly against Table 2: the illegal-framing-label coefficient is non-significant in the pooled model (b=-0.099, ns), the model with interactions (b=-0.277, ns), the Republicans-only model (b=0.045, ns), and the Democrats-only model (b=-0.378, ns), and its interaction with issue importance is likewise non-significant everywhere it's estimated. Text confirms: 'we also confirm that receiving the illegal frame has no effect for members of either party,' and the Discussion states 'framing the immigration policy issue in terms of "undocumented" vs. "illegal" did not influence policy preferences among Iowa caucus-goers in the 2008 primary season.' This is an unambiguous null result across every model in the paper.

replication_title: ARHGAP21 is a RhoGAP for RhoA and RhoC with a role in proliferation and migration of prostate adenocarcinoma cells
replication_journal: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Molecular Basis of Disease
explanation: Testing the same manipulation (ARHGAP21 silencing) and the same GTPase pull-down readout in new cell contexts (prostate cancer PC3 and HEK293T cells, vs. the original glioblastoma line), the authors report a clean failure to replicate, corroborated by two independent experimental designs. Results (3.4): 'ARHGAP21 silencing increased RhoA and RhoC activity compared to control cells but, surprisingly, no difference in Cdc42 activity was observed... Corroborating these findings, ARHGAP21 overexpression decreased RhoA and RhoC activities, but not Cdc42' -- i.e. no Cdc42 effect in either the loss-of-function or the reciprocal gain-of-function experiment. The Discussion explicitly contrasts this with the original finding: 'Surprisingly, we observed no changes in Cdc42 activity in PC3 or HEK293T cells. Previous studies from our group showed an increase in Cdc42 activity upon ARHGAP21 silencing in a glioblastoma cell line [11]. We hypothesize that the ARHGAP21 specificity for different Rho GTPases may vary according to the cell type.' No hedging language is present; both the silencing and overexpression assays, in two cell lines, converge on the same null result, making this an unambiguous failure to replicate.

replication_title: ARHGAP21 is a RhoGAP for RhoA and RhoC with a role in proliferation and migration of prostate adenocarcinoma cells
replication_journal: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Molecular Basis of Disease
explanation: Using two independent methods -- immunofluorescence and biochemical subcellular fractionation -- in two new prostate adenocarcinoma cell lines (PC3, LNCaP), the authors confirm the earlier localization pattern without qualification. Results (3.1): 'ARHGAP21 was expressed and had a nuclear and cytoplasmic localization in both cell lines, with prominent perinuclear localization... ARHGAP21 nuclear and cytoplasmic localization in PC3 and LNCaP cells was confirmed by cell fractionation and western blotting.' The Discussion draws the direct comparison to the same original (glioblastoma-line) work: 'We observed that ARHGAP21 localizes in the nucleus, cytoplasm and cell protrusions of both PC3 and LNCaP cells, with a prominent localization in the perinuclear region. Previous work from our group showed a nuclear and perinuclear localization of ARHGAP21 in different cell lines [11].' The core pattern (nuclear + perinuclear) matches cleanly across two cell lines and two assay types, with no hedging language; the additional cytoplasmic/protrusion localization noted is an extension, not a contradiction.

description: Suvak et al. (2011) found that, relative to nonclinical controls, females with borderline personality disorder (BPD) demonstrated poorer differentiation of negative emotions (lower emotional granularity), using an experience-sampling/diary-based measure of within-person negative-emotion correlations.

replication_authors: Landon F. Zaki; Karin G. Coifman; Eshkol Rafaeli; Kathy R. Berenson; Geraldine Downey
replication_title: Emotion Differentiation as a Protective Factor Against Nonsuicidal Self-Injury in Borderline Personality Disorder
explanation: Independently verified against the Results section: 'As predicted, we found... The BPD group also evidenced significantly lower negative emotion differentiation scores (M = 0.55, SD = 0.15)... relative to the HC group (M = 0.81, SD = 0.13), t(78) = 8.32, p < .001.' This is a clean, unhedged, significant result in the predicted direction, and it is the only sub-measure this entry's description names (BPD < HC negative emotion differentiation, the specific claim carried over from Suvak et al., 2011). The paper's other, unrelated hypotheses — a main effect of rumination on NSSI (not supported: 'this prediction was not supported') and a novel rumination x differentiation interaction on NSSI (a new finding, not part of the Suvak replication) — are separate analyses that don't bear on this entry's claim, so there is no 'mixed results' hedge attached to the specific measure being reviewed here. Replication_type close extension is confirmed: the diary-based AIC methodology matches Suvak et al. almost exactly, but the context differs — this sample restricts to BPD participants with NSSI histories (84% female, mixed gender) rather than Suvak's general female BPD sample without an NSSI requirement.

replication_title: Infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 is associated with cognitive deficits in bipolar disorder
explanation: Using the identical serologic assay and RBANS cognitive battery methodology as their prior schizophrenia study, but in a new population (bipolar disorder patients), the authors found the same pattern: HSV-1 seropositivity was an independent predictor of decreased RBANS total score (F = 20.5, p < .0001) driven mainly by immediate verbal memory deficits. In both patient groups, the significant relationship between cognitive functioning and serologic evidence of HSV-1 infection remained after controlling for variables that could contribute to cognitive level.'

explanation: For the Model-Building Group, the authors report: 'All five hypothesis-driven brain regions ... were significantly activated, consistent with our prior two studies (Kozel et al 2004a, 2004b)'. Independently verified against the paper's own data: Table 2 marks exactly these five regions (right anterior cingulate, right orbitofrontal, right inferior frontal, right middle frontal, left middle temporal) with footnote 'a', 'Regions indicate brain areas of significant activations replicated from prior two studies' -- a data-level confirmation, not just narrative. The Discussion states this unqualifiedly: 'we have replicated the five regions of significant activation for Lie-minus-True at the group level for the third and fourth time (MBG, MTG).' No partial/mixed/differing-results language appears anywhere in Results or Discussion, so this is a clean full replication for the MBG sample.

description: In a symbolic number comparison task (Experiment 2 of the original: simultaneous presentation of two single-digit Arabic numbers, judge which is larger), high math-anxious individuals show a larger numerical distance effect (greater response-time cost for numerically close vs. far pairs) than low math-anxious individuals, indicating a less precise representation of numerical magnitude in high math-anxious individuals.

replication_title: Less precise representation of numerical magnitude in high math-anxious individuals: An ERP study of the size and distance effects
explanation: The authors state directly in the Discussion: 'Concerning the Distance x Group and Size x Group interactions, we not only reproduced the result reported by Maloney et al. (2011), finding a larger distance effect in the more anxious group, but also found a larger size effect in HMA than in LMA individuals.' The behavioral RT distance effect analysis also showed a marginally significant Distance x Group interaction (p = .056) with the distance effect larger for the HMA group, consistent with the original.

description: Using matched 'prime control' stories that share the same content words but lack a strong message-level bias toward a specific noun, discourse-based lexical anticipation of upcoming words (probed via gender-marked material) was shown to depend on the precise message conveyed by the discourse, and could not be reduced to low-level word-word (lexical) priming between content words.
original_authors: Otten, Marte; Nieuwland, Mante S.; Van Berkum, Jos J. A.
original_title: Great expectations: specific lexical anticipation influences the processing of spoken language
replication_authors: Marte Otten; Jos J.A. Van Berkum
replication_title: Does working memory capacity affect the ability to predict upcoming words in discourse?
explanation: Verified against the Results and Discussion sections: 'In the prime control condition, the expectancy effect is absent in both the low WMC and the high WMC group' (p.95) shows the null word-word-priming finding held uniformly across BOTH WMC subgroups, not just on average -- so this specific sub-claim is not undermined by the paper's other WMC-related mixed findings (e.g. the late-negativity effect that appears only in low-WMC readers, which concerns a separate measure). The Discussion then explicitly ties this to the earlier studies: 'As in our two earlier ERP experiments with a word-word prime control condition (Otten et al., 2007; Otten and Van Berkum, 2008), the current study reveals that the discourse-based lexical predictions observed in this gender-dependent paradigm depend on the precise message developed in the preceding discourse, and not on lower-level word-word priming.' The authors do add a caveat ('the absence of a differential effect in prime control stories does not provide compelling evidence that additional word-based priming plays no role at all') but this is a generic epistemic caution about interpreting a null result, not a report of mixed/partial replication for this specific claim -- so 'success' is the correct label with no residual ambiguity.

description: Theta EEG power increases when human subjects recall previously explored haptic information, compared to a resting baseline.
original_authors: Martin Grunwalda; Thomas Weissb; Werner Krausec; Lothar Beyerd; Reinhard Roste; Ingmar Gutberletb; Hermann-Josef Gertza
original_title: Power of theta waves in the EEG of human subjects increases during recall of haptic information
replication_authors: Martin Grunwald; Thomas Weiss; Stephanie Mueller; Lysann Rall
replication_title: EEG changes caused by spontaneous facial self-touch may represent emotion regulating processes and working memory maintenance
explanation: Reviewed body.md Results §2 and Discussion §3.1 directly. The baseline-vs-aHE comparison is reported with no hedging: 'Comparisons of the EEG of the resting period (baseline) and after haptic exploration (aHE) showed significant increases of the spectral power of all frequency bands except for alpha. Theta power increased mainly above central-parietal regions.' Table 1a confirms significant theta increases at C3 (p=.028) and P3 (p=.028, both centro-parietal) plus FP2, F8, T3 -- consistent with the authors' own description, and not contradicted by any 'differing/mixed/partial' language, so 'success' is the correct label, not inconclusive. The remaining ambiguity is attribution, not outcome: this finding is cited jointly to (Grunwald et al., 1999, 2001b) in both places it appears in the paper (Discussion §3.1 and Methods §4.1, 'The same haptic tasks and procedures have been used as part of other psychophysiological studies (Grunwald et al., 1999, 2001b)'); no passage anywhere in the paper distinguishes the two citations or separately addresses 1999's 'recall' framing vs. 2001b's 'ongoing processing' framing. This is a genuine gap in the source paper, unresolvable from this text alone, so confidence stays medium rather than high.

replication_title: Cognitive confidence in obsessive-compulsive disorder: Distrusting perception, attention and memory
explanation: Authors state 'The results replicate and extend the previous findings from our lab... In line with the findings of Hermans et al. (2003), the difference from the nonclinical control group was most evident for the attention factor,' confirming the original MCQ-based pattern; the design was extended with an added psychiatric control group and a novel behavioural (BCCQ) measure.

replication_authors: Dirk Hermans; Ute Engelen; Luc Grouwels; Els Joos; Jos Lemmens; Guido Pieters
replication_title: Cognitive confidence in obsessive-compulsive disorder: Distrusting perception, attention and memory
explanation: Using idiographically selected compulsive actions (performed 5 times, in a clinical OCD sample) instead of the original gas-stove paradigm, the authors explicitly report 'In contrast with other studies (e.g. Van den Hout & Kindt, 2003a), we did not observe a significant effect of repeated checking on confidence in memory,' though they attribute this to the smaller number of trials used.

description: In a prospective study of 45 firefighters, reduced fear extinction learning measured before trauma exposure (using a de novo conditioning paradigm with physiological/skin conductance measures) predicted greater posttraumatic stress symptoms up to two years later.
original_authors: Rachel M. Guthrie; Richard A. Bryant
original_title: Extinction learning before trauma and subsequent posttraumatic stress
replication_authors: Miriam J.J. Lommen; Iris M. Engelhard; Marit Sijbrandij; Marcel A. van den Hout; Dirk Hermans
replication_title: Pre-trauma individual differences in extinction learning predict posttraumatic stress
explanation: Verified against the Results and Discussion of this close extension (N=249 Dutch soldiers) of Guthrie & Bryant (2006, N=45 firefighters). The primary regression showed reduced pre-trauma extinction learning significantly predicted higher post-deployment PTSD symptom severity even after controlling for baseline PSS, neuroticism, and stressor exposure, explaining unique variance (23% of variance accounted for, Table 2). The Discussion states unhedged: 'Consistent with the preliminary study of Guthrie and Bryant (2006), the current study suggests that reduced extinction learning before trauma puts people at risk of later PTSD symptoms.' Neither the abstract nor discussion use 'mixed'/'partial'/'differing results' language about this finding — the only caveats are that the effect was 'modest' relative to other predictors (e.g., neuroticism), and a footnoted sensitivity check using later extinction trials (6-8) as an alternate measurement definition lost significance while the direction of the pattern remained similar (a robustness probe on operationalization, not a separate sub-measure that failed). This supports 'success' with high confidence.

description: A multi-method, multi-source composite measure of self-discipline (from student and teacher questionnaires) strongly predicts adolescents' grade point average and performance on a standardized achievement test.
original_authors: Duckworth, Angela L.; Seligman, Martin E. P.
original_title: Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents
replication_authors: Barry J. Zimmerman; Anastasia Kitsantas
replication_title: Comparing students’ self-discipline and self-regulation measures and their prediction of academic achievement
explanation: Independently verified against the abstract and Discussion (5.1-5.5). Using hierarchical regression with three of the original five self-discipline (SD) scales in a larger, older (grades 9-12 vs. 8th grade) sample, the SD composite alone significantly predicted 34% of GPA variance and 10% of VSOL variance, paralleling the original's strong prediction. But the paper's own abstract reports the opposite once SD is tested as a latent factor alongside self-regulation (SR) in SEM: 'the SR latent factor predicted both measures of students' achievement significantly, but the SD factor did not predict either achievement measure significantly.' The Discussion confirms this split is method-dependent ('when SR composite was included as a predictor, the role of SD greatly diminished') and the authors themselves flag it as unresolved, asking 'why did the SD measures predict so poorly in the present study?' This is a genuine paper-internal split (significant under regression, non-significant under SEM), not an artifact of unclear reporting, so it remains inconclusive relative to the original finding.

description: Girls exhibit significantly higher self-discipline than boys, and self-discipline mediates the relationship between gender and GPA, giving girls higher grades than boys (though not better standardized achievement test scores).
original_authors: Duckworth, Angela L.; Seligman, Martin E. P.
original_title: Self-discipline gives girls the edge: Gender in self-discipline, grades, and achievement test scores
replication_authors: Barry J. Zimmerman; Anastasia Kitsantas
replication_title: Comparing students’ self-discipline and self-regulation measures and their prediction of academic achievement
explanation: The authors state directly: 'no significant gender differences were found with students' SD, SR, or achievement measures,' and that 'this absence of gender findings regarding the SD composite or two measures of academic achievement contrasts with the composite results reported by Duckworth and Seligman (2006),' who had found girls' superior self-discipline mediated their higher GPA than boys.

description: In human embryonic stem cells, c-Myc binds the core promoter region of a large fraction of actively transcribed genes and functions to enhance transcription elongation by recruiting the P-TEFb complex, thereby stimulating RNA polymerase II pause release.
original_authors: Rahl, Peter B.; Lin, Charles Y.; Seila, Amy C.; Flynn, Ryan A.; McCuine, Scott; Burge, Christopher B.; Sharp, Phillip A.; Young, Richard A.
original_title: c-Myc regulates transcriptional pause release
replication_authors: Charles Y. Lin; Jakob Lovén; Peter B. Rahl; Ronald M. Paranal; Christopher B. Burge; James E. Bradner; Tong Ihn Lee; Richard A. Young
replication_title: Transcriptional Amplification in Tumor Cells with Elevated c-Myc
explanation: Reviewed body.md Results (lines 481-539, 'High c-Myc Expression Causes Transcriptional Amplification in Tumor Cells') and the SCLC confirmation (lines 1017-1035) and Discussion (lines 1068-1071). The paper explicitly set out to test whether the P-TEFb recruitment/Pol II pause-release mechanism established by Rahl et al. (2010) in embryonic stem cells also occurs in c-Myc-overexpressing tumor cells ('We therefore investigated whether the elevated levels of c-Myc have these effects at active genes in P493-6 tumor cells'). Every sub-measure named replicated with statistical support and no hedging language ('differing', 'mixed', 'partial') anywhere near this result: Cdk9 (P-TEFb catalytic subunit) occupancy increased significantly at genes with increased c-Myc binding while the initiation mark H3K4me3 was unchanged (Figure 3A); elongation-associated Ser2-phosphorylated Pol II rose 2-fold while initiation-associated Ser5 was largely unchanged (Figure 3B); genome-wide traveling ratio increased significantly (p < 1e-5, Figure 3D). The same pattern (increased Ser2 ratio, increased ChIP-Seq elongation signal, increased traveling ratio) was independently confirmed in a second tumor model, SCLC cell lines with differing endogenous c-Myc levels (Figure 5D-F). The paper's own conclusion is unhedged: 'these results indicate that increased c-Myc binding at active genes stimulates RNA Pol II elongation,' and the Discussion restates it as established fact ('increased recruitment of the pause release factor P-TEFb, increased transcriptional elongation'). Upgraded from medium to high based on this specific, unambiguous, multiply-replicated (two independent cell models) quantitative evidence.

description: Images initially encountered as auditory-visual (multisensory) pairs are later discriminated as repeats significantly more accurately than images initially encountered only visually.
original_authors: Micah M. Murray; Christoph M. Michel; Rolando Grave de Peralta; Stephanie Ortigue; Denis Brunet; Sara Gonzalez Andino; Armin Schnider
original_title: Rapid discrimination of visual and multisensory memories revealed by electrical neuroimaging
replication_authors: Sandra Lehmann; Micah M. Murray
replication_title: The role of multisensory memories in unisensory object discrimination
explanation: Experiment 1's auditory (pure-tone) condition re-tested whether AV pairing enhances later discrimination (as in Murray et al., 2004) and found the opposite: repetition-discrimination accuracy was significantly WORSE for images initially paired with a tone than for unisensory images (76.6% vs. 79.3%; t(15)=2.235; P=0.041). The abstract states accuracy 'was significantly impaired by auditory-visual... multisensory memory traces' and frames the results as showing 'opposing effects of purely episodic versus semantic information from auditory-visual multisensory events,' which supports reading this as a direction-reversal. However, the Discussion never states in so many words that this specific finding reverses ref [17]; it instead folds the impairment into an extended model alongside the (replicating) semantically-congruent-pairing enhancement of Exp. 2, describing all of it together as work that 'replicate[s] and extend[s] our previous work.' Whether the authors themselves explicitly characterize this result as a reversal of the original effect, versus a qualification/extension of it, remains genuinely ambiguous from the text -- confidence stays at medium.

description: Images initially encountered as multisensory pairs are later discriminated as repeats significantly more accurately than images initially encountered only visually, tested here by substituting a somatosensory (vibration) pairing for the original's auditory pairing.
original_authors: Micah M. Murray; Christoph M. Michel; Rolando Grave de Peralta; Stephanie Ortigue; Denis Brunet; Sara Gonzalez Andino; Armin Schnider
original_title: Rapid discrimination of visual and multisensory memories revealed by electrical neuroimaging
replication_authors: Sandra Lehmann; Micah M. Murray
replication_title: The role of multisensory memories in unisensory object discrimination
explanation: Experiment 1's somatosensory (vibration) condition tested whether the AV-pairing enhancement (Murray et al., 2004) generalizes to somatosensory-visual pairing. The result is an unambiguous null: accuracy was virtually identical for paired versus unisensory images (77.8% vs. 77.8%; t(15)=0.004; P=0.997), one of the cleanest non-significant results reported in the paper. The Discussion states outright, without hedging, that 'the effect of episodic multisensory memories on later unisensory discrimination would appear to be limited to auditory-visual experiences' -- i.e., it does not generalize to touch. The near-perfect equivalence of the two conditions plus the authors' own unambiguous interpretation leaves little room for a different reading, so confidence is upgraded to high.

description: Images initially encountered as meaningful, semantically-corresponding auditory-visual pairs are later discriminated as repeats significantly more accurately than images initially encountered only visually.
original_authors: Micah M. Murray; Christoph M. Michel; Rolando Grave de Peralta; Stephanie Ortigue; Denis Brunet; Sara Gonzalez Andino; Armin Schnider
original_title: Rapid discrimination of visual and multisensory memories revealed by electrical neuroimaging
replication_authors: Sandra Lehmann; Micah M. Murray
replication_title: The role of multisensory memories in unisensory object discrimination
explanation: Experiment 2's semantically congruent auditory-visual condition, which most closely parallels the original study's meaningful AV pairing, replicated the original enhancement effect: repetition-discrimination accuracy was significantly higher for congruently-paired images than for unisensory images (83.6% vs. 78.0%; t(10)=4.013; P=0.002), and the authors state these effects 'replicate and extend our previous work.' A semantically incongruent control condition (not present in the original) showed no such enhancement, supporting the semantic specificity of the effect.

description: In a magnitude comparison task performed during the retention interval of a working memory task, a spatial (visuospatial) working memory load — but not a verbal working memory load — abolishes the SNARC-effect (the spatial-numerical association of response codes).

replication_authors: Jean-Philippe van Dijck; Wim Gevers; Wim Fias
replication_title: Numbers are associated with different types of spatial information depending on the task
explanation: The authors explicitly frame Experiment 2 as a replication attempt ('we tried to replicate the findings of Herrera et al. (2008)') using a magnitude comparison task, and report the same pattern found by Herrera et al.: the magnitude-weight (SNARC effect) 'differed from zero under verbal load [t(34) = 4.34, p < .01], but not under spatial load [t(35) = 1.25, p = .22]', with the General Discussion stating 'In Experiment 2 the opposite pattern was found: during a magnitude comparison task the SNARC-effect was abolished by spatial load but not by verbal load' — matching the original finding.

description: Chinese-English bilinguals judging the semantic relatedness of English word pairs showed implicit activation of their L1 (Chinese) translations while reading L2 (English) words: the N400 ERP response was reduced when the Chinese translations of the two English words shared a character (form overlap), even though the task was performed entirely in English and monolingual English speakers showed no such effect.
original_authors: Guillaume Thierry; Yan Jing Wu
original_title: Brain potentials reveal unconscious translation during foreign language comprehension
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Jill P. Morford; Erin Wilkinson; Agnes Villwock; Pilar Piñar; Judith F. Kroll
replication_title: When deaf signers read English: Do written words activate their sign translations?
explanation: Deaf ASL-English bilinguals (Experiment 1) showed a significant semantics x phonology interaction on the same semantic-relatedness judgment paradigm, faster to accept semantically related pairs and slower to reject unrelated pairs when the ASL translations shared phonological form; the authors state 'these results provide compelling evidence that deaf bilinguals activate signs while processing written words' and describe the pattern as 'similar to those reported by Thierry and Wu (2007) for unimodal Chinese-English bilinguals.'

description: Bi-parietal tDCS with a Left Anode/Right Cathode montage over posterior parietal cortex causes a rightward shift in subjective midpoint during line bisection performance in healthy participants (relative to sham).
original_authors: Giuseppe Giglia; Paola Mattaliano; Angela Puma; Silvia Rizzo; Brigida Fierro; Filippo Brighina
original_title: Neglect-like effects induced by tDCS modulation of posterior parietal cortices in healthy subjects
replication_authors: Christopher S.Y. Benwell; Gemma Learmonth; Carlo Miniussi; Monika Harvey; Gregor Thut
replication_title: Non-linear effects of transcranial direct current stimulation as a function of individual baseline performance: Evidence from biparietal tDCS influence on lateralized attention bias
explanation: Authors state in Discussion 'we replicated the polarity specific effect of bi-parietal tDCS with a LA/RC electrode montage leading to a rightward shift in subjective midpoint (Giglia et al., 2011)', and the Abstract opens with the identical claim -- but both immediately qualify it: the Abstract itself says the effect was 'weak over our entire sample (n=38), but ... substantial in a subset of participants' via 'a complex, nonlinear interaction', which is exactly the global-claim-plus-partial/mixed-language pattern that the scoring rules say must not be overridden by the headline 'we replicated' framing. The whole-sample sham-corrected t-test for LA/RC was only a non-significant trend (t(37)=2.003, p=.052, d=.66); the reversed LC/RA montage showed nothing (t(37)=.664, p=.511, d=.22). Significance appeared only via a post-hoc 3-way tDCS-polarity x tDCS-intensity x baseline-performance interaction (F(1,34)=7.221, p=.011) and its subgroup splits (1mA, high-discrimination-sensitivity: t(9)=2.866, p=.019, d=1.91; 2mA, low-discrimination-sensitivity: t(7)=3.274, p=.014, d=2.47) -- conditional support in specific subgroups, not a clean overall replication. This is correctly inconclusive. Confidence stays medium: the ambiguity is genuine (the authors' own 'we replicated' headline sits against their own 'weak/trend, significant only in subsets' qualifiers, in both Discussion and Abstract), not something further reading resolves.

description: A short daytime nap containing only NREM sleep enhances performance on a virtual maze-navigation learning task, relative to remaining awake during an equivalent retention interval.
original_authors: Wamsley, Erin J.; Stickgold, Robert
original_title: Virtual maze learning is enhanced by a short daytime nap containing only NREM sleep
replication_authors: Erin J. Wamsley; Matthew Tucker; Jessica D. Payne; Joseph A. Benavides; Robert Stickgold
replication_title: Dreaming of a Learning Task Is Associated with Enhanced Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation
explanation: The authors explicitly frame the wake-vs-sleep comparison as a replication of their own prior finding with the same task ('As previously observed with the same task [11]...') and report a significant main effect of condition favoring the nap group (F1,95 = 5.34, p = 0.02), consistent in direction and magnitude with the original observation.

description: Speakers of languages that grammatically mark the future tense (strong future-time-reference languages) save less, retire with less wealth, smoke more, and are less healthy than speakers of futureless (weak-FTR) languages, because obligatory grammatical marking of the future causes the future to feel more psychologically distant and hence induces less patient, future-oriented behavior (the 'linguistic-savings hypothesis').
original_authors: Keith Chen
original_title: The effect of language on economic behavior: evidence from savings rates, health behaviors, and retirement assets
replication_authors: Josie I. Chen; Tai-Sen He; Yohanes E. Riyanto
replication_title: The effect of language on economic behavior: Examining the causal link between future tense and time preference in the lab
explanation: The authors ran a controlled lab experiment (multiple-price-list intertemporal choice task) manipulating whether the auxiliary 'will' appeared in the description of delayed rewards to Chinese-speaking subjects in Singapore and Taiwan, as a causal test of Chen's (2013) linguistic-savings hypothesis; they conclude explicitly that 'our results do not lend further empirical support for the linguistic-savings hypothesis' and that repetitive exposure to 'will' 'does not induce subjects to behave less patiently,' with the (statistically insignificant) qualitative pattern in both sites trending opposite to the LSH prediction.

description: Children who have a greater number of older siblings (higher birth order), and therefore greater exposure to childhood infections, have a lower prevalence of hay fever (allergic rhinitis), a finding taken as key evidence for the hygiene hypothesis.

original_title: Hay fever, hygiene, and household size

explanation: Table I reports the unadjusted OR for AR given >=1 older sibling separately for all four cohorts: B58C (a later, age-42 sweep of the same 1958 British birth cohort as the original study) 0.667 (0.581-0.765); ECRHS2 0.885 (0.732-1.069); NFBC1966 0.875 (0.771-0.992); SAPALDIA 0.776 (0.600-1.000); pooled 0.792 (0.731-0.857). Every cohort's point estimate is protective (OR<1) in the same direction as Strachan 1989, and the pooled estimate is clearly significant; only ECRHS2's individual CI crosses 1, which is what the authors mean by 'despite finding a consistent protective effect of increasing birth order on AR in all 4 participating cohorts' (Discussion) -- a claim the per-cohort table substantiates rather than just asserts. This is a single sub-measure (birth order vs AR prevalence), not a multi-measure claim, so there is no partial-replication concern; the paper's negative finding is about a separate question (whether SNPs modify this effect), which the description does not claim was replicated. Reproduces the original 1989 finding in new, larger, and more geographically diverse adult samples, as a secondary/background confirmation supporting the paper's main gene-environment interaction aim rather than its primary focus.

description: Thematically (in)congruent ambient scents (e.g., a grass scent) have no significant effect on retail sales of congruent versus incongruent products (e.g., nature/soccer magazines versus women's magazines).
original_authors: Schifferstein HN, Blok ST.
original_title: The signal function of thematically (in)congruent ambient scents in a retail environment
replication_authors: Doucé, Lieve; Poels, Karolien; Janssens, Wim; Backer, Charlotte De
replication_title: Smelling the books: The effect of chocolate scent on purchase-related behavior in a bookstore
explanation: The authors explicitly build on and critique Schifferstein and Blok (2002), noting that study 'did not take gender into account' and 'only the sales of the magazines were measured, and no other data on approach behavior were collected,' and design their field study (in a bookstore with chocolate scent and book genres) to extend it by observing actual behavior, controlling for gender, and using popular product categories. In the Discussion they state directly: 'In contrast with Schifferstein and Blok (2002), we found that the chocolate scent positively affects the sales of the store' -- confirmed on independent review of the Discussion/Conclusion (body.md lines 447-476). Caveat found on review: the sales figures backing that sentence (total sales +5.07%; congruent-genre sales +40.07% vs. incongruent +22.19%) are explicitly labeled 'indicative support' in the text, i.e. descriptive, not significance-tested -- the paper's actual statistically significant results (logistic regression / odds ratios, e.g. congruent books bought 5.93x more often with scent) are for approach/buying BEHAVIOR, an outcome the original study never measured, not for sales per se. So the authors' explicit contrast claim is directionally consistent with the (weak, untested) sales data but not itself backed by a significance test against the original's null. Authors' explicit statement is given priority per the classification rules since it doesn't contradict the reported stats, keeping this a failure to reproduce the original's null sales finding -- but the reliance on merely 'indicative' evidence for the specific sales claim is a genuine source of residual ambiguity, so confidence stays medium rather than high.

description: Under self-activation (induced by flashing self-related words prior to the prime), priming participants with a low-intelligence category (hussy) versus a high-intelligence category (professor) produces a contrast effect on a subsequent knowledge test, with professor-primed participants performing worse than hussy-primed participants.
original_authors: Schubert, Thomas; Häfner, Michael
original_title: Contrast from social stereotypes in automatic behavior
replication_authors: Bry, Clémentine; Follenfant, Alice; Meyer, Thierry
replication_title: Blonde like me: When self-construals moderate stereotype priming effects on intellectual performance
explanation: Verified against Study 1's own 'Results and discussion' section: the 2x2 ANOVA interaction was significant, F(1,82)=5.77, p<.02, but the independence-Blonde vs. independence-control contrast that maps onto Schubert & Häfner's contrast effect was non-significant, F(1,82)=1.38, ns ('Performance was equivalent with those in the control condition') — a clean null for this sub-effect in this study specifically. Confidence stays medium (not upgraded) because the ambiguity is structural, not textual: the paper's own General Discussion aggregates across both studies and headlines 'We replicated their contrast effect' even though it explicitly notes the effect 'occurred only in the second study' — i.e., the authors' global success claim is only true at the two-study aggregate level, not for Study 1 alone. This entry is scored correctly as a Study-1-specific failure (paired with the Study-2 success in the sibling entry), but reasonable coders could instead read the paper as reporting one aggregate (mixed) replication rather than two independent ones. Self-activation was also operationalized very differently from the original (chronic self-construal priming vs. flashed self-related words), and the prime domain differed (Blonde stereotype vs. professor/hussy), supporting the 'conceptual' typing.

description: Under self-activation (induced by flashing self-related words prior to the prime), priming participants with a low-intelligence category (hussy) versus a high-intelligence category (professor) produces a contrast effect on a subsequent knowledge test, with professor-primed participants performing worse than hussy-primed participants.

replication_title: Blonde like me: When self-construals moderate stereotype priming effects on intellectual performance
explanation: In Study 2 (lab sample), 'the expected contrast eﬀect occurred under independence priming: Performance was higher in the Blonde condition than in the control condition,' and the authors explicitly conclude: 'We replicated their contrast effect following independence priming in a paradigm that included a control condition.' The self-activation manipulation (self-construal priming) and stereotype domain (Blonde vs. professor/hussy) differ substantially from the original, making this a conceptual rather than direct replication.

description: Among participants who spontaneously self-activate (adopt an 'I' perspective) while being primed with a negative (Black) versus positive (White) racial stereotype, priming produces a behavioral assimilation effect, with negatively-stereotype-primed participants performing worse on a subsequent math test.
original_authors: S.Christian Wheeler; W.Blair G. Jarvis; Richard E. Petty
original_title: Think unto others: The self-destructive impact of negative racial stereotypes
replication_authors: Bry, Clémentine; Follenfant, Alice; Meyer, Thierry
replication_title: Blonde like me: When self-construals moderate stereotype priming effects on intellectual performance
explanation: Verified against both studies' results sections: unlike the contrast effect, the assimilation effect was fully consistent, with no partial/mixed language attached to it. Study 1: interdependence-Blonde (M=1.14) < interdependence-control (M=1.93), F(1,82)=4.82, p<.04. Study 2: interdependence-Blonde (M=1.52) < interdependence-control (M=2.17), F(1,69)=5.33, p<.03. General Discussion states plainly: 'In both experiments, only participants primed with interdependence demonstrated an assimilation effect.' So the result label itself (success) is not in doubt. Confidence stays medium because the residual uncertainty is about paradigm correspondence, not outcome: Wheeler et al.'s original effect arose from spontaneous, unmanipulated adoption of an 'I' perspective while writing an essay about a Black/White-stereotyped student, whereas this paper experimentally induces interdependent self-construal via a questionnaire before an unrelated hair-color/Blonde-stereotype task — a substantially different operationalization of both the self-activation moderator and the stereotype domain, which the paper itself does not attempt to bridge beyond the one-sentence claim.

description: Self-consciousness/self-activation moderates behavioral assimilation to primes, such that self-activated individuals show greater prime-congruent (assimilative) behavior.
original_authors: Jay G. Hull; Laurie B. Slone; Karen B. Meteyer; Amanda R. Matthews
original_title: The nonconsciousness of self-consciousness
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Bry, Clémentine; Follenfant, Alice; Meyer, Thierry
replication_title: Blonde like me: When self-construals moderate stereotype priming effects on intellectual performance
explanation: Confirmed by a full-text search: Hull et al. (2002) is cited only twice in this paper, both in passing (once as 'see also Hull et al., 2002' with no description of its design, once in the single-sentence General Discussion claim), plus the reference-list entry itself ('The nonconsciousness of self-consciousness,' JPSP 83, 405-424). At no point does the paper describe Hull et al.'s manipulation, measures, sample, or effect size. The current paper's own assimilation result (interdependence-primed participants underperform after Blonde priming, replicated in both studies, e.g. F(1,82)=4.82, p<.04 and F(1,69)=5.33, p<.03) is unambiguous, so 'success' is the right call for what this paper found — but whether that finding actually corresponds to what Hull et al. reported cannot be assessed from this text at all, which is genuine, irreducible ambiguity rather than a gap I can close by re-reading. Confidence stays low.

description: Using Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) data on disposable household income for ten countries with two time points of inequality data each, Judge, Mulligan and Benzeval (1998) found no significant relationship between changes in income inequality and changes in either life expectancy or infant mortality.
original_authors: Ken Judge; Jo-Ann Mulligan; Michaela Benzeval

replication_authors: Andrew Leigh; Christopher Jencks
replication_title: Inequality and mortality: Long-run evidence from a panel of countries
explanation: Footnote 10 (body.md) gives the exact replication statistics: using their own top-10-percent income-share inequality measure for the same seven overlapping countries and the same before/after time intervals as Judge et al.'s Table 5, the correlation between the change in life expectancy and the change in Share 10 was 0.227 (95% CI: -0.635 to 0.837), and the correlation between the change in infant mortality and the change in Share 10 was 0.663 (95% CI: -0.945 to 0.180). Both 95% CIs span zero, so neither correlation is statistically significant, matching Judge et al.'s original null finding for both sub-measures named in this entry (life expectancy and infant mortality). The paper's Conclusion (Section 5) independently corroborates this: 'This finding is consistent with a number of other careful cross-country papers, such as Judge et al. (1998) and Deaton and Paxson (2001).' No hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'differing') qualifies this specific comparison, so 'success' is confirmed for both sub-measures.

The authors report 'Results of the study indicate that the LBG was effective in reducing disruptive behavior in the lunchroom during each lunch period and across all grade levels,' with an immediate and sustained decrease in disruptive behavior upon implementation in all three lunch periods.

explanation: The authors state explicitly: 'we were not able to replicate previous findings, which reported differences of evoked GBRs between meaningful and meaningless objects (Herrmann et al., 2004a)'; the current study's evoked gamma peak (30-50 Hz, 70-170 ms) analysis showed no significant effect of stimulus type, which the authors attribute to differences in stimulus material (bold vs. faint line drawings) between the two studies.

explanation: The authors state: 'Replicating findings from a previous study (Gruber and Muller, 2005), the L1 ERP component from 200 to 400 ms after stimulus onset revealed higher amplitudes for unfamiliar as compared to familiar objects,' and report this effect as statistically significant and topographically consistent with the original.

description: Perception of a coherent, meaningful visual stimulus is accompanied by a denser pattern of significant long-distance phase-locking (synchronization) between EEG electrode sites than perception of an incoherent, meaningless stimulus.
original_authors: Rodriguez, Eugenio; George, Nathalie; Lachaux, Jean-Philippe; Martinerie, Jacques; Renault, Bernard; Varela, Francisco J.
original_title: Perception's shadow: long-distance synchronization of human brain activity
replication_authors: Thomas Gruber; Nelson J. Trujillo-Barreto; Claire-Marie Giabbiconi; Pedro A. Valdés-Sosa; Matthias M. Müller
replication_title: Brain electrical tomography (BET) analysis of induced gamma band responses during a simple object recognition task
explanation: Reviewed and upgraded on independent verification. Two new pieces of evidence resolve the prior ambiguity. (1) The Results section (not just the Discussion citation sentence) reports the effect directly for both analyses the paper ran: in electrode space, familiar/meaningful stimuli produced 'a dense pattern of significant phase-locking values predominantly among posterior but also temporal and frontal electrode sites,' while for unfamiliar/meaningless pictures 'the number of significant phase-locking values is approximately half as many as for familiar material.' The authors then specifically cross-validated this in source space to rule out volume-conduction artifacts (the standard confound for scalp phase-locking, citing Lachaux et al., 1999): using reconstructed ROI forward-solution signals, they found 'five pairs of significantly phase-locked recording sites related to familiar object presentations. In contrast, unfamiliar objects did not elicit any significant phase-locking values' - the same direction, more starkly (5 vs. 0). (2) The Introduction explicitly names Rodriguez et al. (1999) as one of the specific studies whose finding is being tested: 'it was demonstrated that the establishment of unequivocal object representations is mirrored in dense patterns of significant phase-locking values as opposed to control stimuli (Gruber and Muller, 2005; Gruber et al., 2002; Rodriguez et al., 1999)' - so the 'e.g.' list in the Discussion sentence is not evidence of an ambiguous target; Rodriguez et al. (1999) is a genuine, explicitly-named comparison study, not an incidental example. No hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'differing results') appears anywhere regarding this specific finding. Replication_type remains 'conceptual' since the original Rodriguez et al. (1999) study used a face-perception paradigm, whereas the present study used familiar/unfamiliar line drawings.

description: When presented out of context (i.e., not embedded in a supportive sentence), concrete nouns elicit larger (more negative) N400 and sustained frontal negativity ERP responses than abstract nouns.

explanation: The Results 'Adjectives' subsection (not just the Discussion summary) reports the dedicated ANOVA on the initial, out-of-context adjectives: a significant main effect of concreteness on the posterior N400 (300-500ms) [F(1,31)=39.23, p<.001, ηp2=.56] and on the frontal negativity at both 300-500ms [F(1,31)=34.05, p<.001, ηp2=.52] and 500-900ms [F(1,31)=18.07, p<.001, ηp2=.37], all more negative for concrete than abstract items -- matching both sub-measures named in this entry's description (N400 and sustained frontal negativity). The Discussion explicitly frames this as replicating the noun effect documented by Holcomb et al. (1999), now extended to adjectives. No hedging language ('mixed', 'partial') appears anywhere near this specific out-of-context finding; the paper's genuine complexity is confined to the separate lateralized-noun analysis.

explanation: The authors state their 'primary purpose' was 'replicating and extending' their original 6 Hz RSVP study (Bekhtereva & Müller, 2015), and in the Discussion report: 'Replicating our recent 6 Hz RSVP results..., we found that changing a task-irrelevant 6 Hz background RSVP stream from neutral to unpleasant content elicited a significant reduction in SSVEP amplitude,' confirming the original effect even when embedded within a new active foreground detection task.

replication_title: Neural Mechanisms of Sustained Attention Are Rhythmic
explanation: The Results section (not just the Discussion's qualitative summary) gives the direct quantitative evidence for this specific behavioral finding: in every one of 7 participants, the FFT of the target-detection accuracy time course showed a theta-band peak (3.99 Hz ± 0.88 Hz, mean ± SD) exceeding the 1/f background estimate (mean + 3 SD; p < 0.001), independently confirmed by a permutation test (Z = 2.20 ± 0.55, combined p < 0.0001) and reproduced under an alternate 1/f-correction method and a shorter averaging window. The authors state the conclusion directly: 'these findings suggest that attention does not sample the cued location continuously but periodically at 4 Hz.' No caveats, non-significant sub-measures, or partial/mixed results are reported for this behavioral finding, and the abstract independently states the effects 'were robust at the single-subject level.' This is a close extension rather than a direct replication (modified cue-target-interval and other parameters, intracranial epilepsy patients rather than healthy adults, ~11% of the original trial count per subject), but the core behavioral result itself is unambiguously and robustly confirmed, so 'success' is correct.

description: During spatial attentional allocation, the 2-5 Hz theta phase significantly modulates high-frequency band (HFB) cortical activity in the frontoparietal network, indicating theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling.
original_authors: Szczepanski, Sara M.; Crone, Nathan E.; Kuperman, Rachel A.; Auguste, Kurtis I.; Parvizi, Josef; Knight, Robert T.
original_title: Dynamic changes in phase-amplitude coupling facilitate spatial attention control in fronto-parietal cortex
