replication_title: Neural Mechanisms of Sustained Attention Are Rhythmic
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'it had previously been reported that only the 2-5 Hz phase significantly modulated HFB activity during attentional allocation (Szczepanski et al., 2014). We replicate and extend this finding using the peak-triggered method,' and report a significant group-level theta-band (~4 Hz) modulation of HFB activity (permutation test p = 0.0230) using the new peak-triggered analysis approach, but no comparable alpha-band effect, consistent with the original finding.

description: Using electron microscopy, Pullen and Athanasiou (2009) found that the presynaptic territory (size) of C-terminals (cholinergic C-boutons) on lumbar motoneurons increases in G93A SOD1 mutant ALS-model mice as disease progresses.
original_authors: Pullen AH, Athanasiou D.
original_title: Increase in presynaptic territory of C-terminals on lumbar motoneurons of G93A SOD1 mice during disease progression
replication_authors: Herron, Lissa R.; Miles, Gb
replication_title: Gender-specific perturbations in modulatory inputs to motoneurons in a mouse model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
explanation: Re-reviewed against the Results and Discussion text. The authors explicitly designed an experiment to test, using immunohistochemistry and confocal microscopy instead of electron microscopy, 'whether, as suggested by recent electron microscopy data (Pullen and Athanasiou, 2009), the size of C-boutons might be perturbed in SOD1 mutant animals,' and their Discussion states a global claim of support: 'Our demonstration of larger C-boutons in SOD1 mutant versus control animals is consistent with recent electron microscopy (EM) data.' However, that claim is immediately undercut by differing/partial results reported in the same paper: the pooled comparison across both sexes and all ages only trended toward significance and did not reach it (main effect of genotype: F(5,55)=2.976, P=0.052). The effect only became statistically significant after splitting by sex, and only in adult males (F(5,24)=6.775, P=0.01; genotype x age interaction in males F(4,24)=5.097, P=0.003; post hoc P<0.05 vs. wildtype adult males, wildtype neonate males, and SOD1 neonate males); females and neonates of both sexes showed no significant change at any age. The abstract itself flags this qualification directly ('Interestingly, we found that C-boutons are only enlarged in male mice'). The paper also reports the enlargement emerging much earlier developmentally (P8-30, persisting to P120-140) than the original EM study's later (~42-day/10-week) timepoint. Per the rule that a global claim of support does not override an abstract/conclusion that also reports differing or partial results, this is a sex-restricted, partial replication (confirmed in males only, not in the unstratified sample or in females) rather than a clean success -- hence inconclusive. This remains a judgment call the paper itself does not resolve (the authors' own framing leans toward 'consistent with' the original), so confidence stays medium rather than moving to high.

description: New episodic learning shortly after the reactivation of a previously encoded (autobiographical) memory interferes with the reconsolidation of that original memory, reducing its subsequent accessibility.
original_authors: Schwabe, Lars; Wolf, Oliver T.
original_title: New episodic learning interferes with the reconsolidation of autobiographical memories
replication_authors: Sonja Wichert; Oliver T. Wolf; Lars Schwabe
replication_title: Changing memories after reactivation: A one-time opportunity?
explanation: Confirmed on review by cross-checking the abstract and General Discussion in addition to the Experiment 1 Discussion cited by the first pass. The abstract states the Experiment 1 finding plainly and without hedging: 'We found that new learning after reactivation reduced the subsequent memory of the original pictures; new learning alone or reactivation alone, however, had no effect on memory.' No 'partial'/'mixed'/'some differences' qualifier is attached to this claim anywhere -- those qualifiers appear only later, regarding whether repeated reactivation is a boundary condition (Experiments 2-3), which is a separate question from the interference effect replicated in Experiment 1. The predicted Reactivation x New Learning interaction was significant for both accuracy, F(1,52)=4.30, p=.04, and hits, F(1,52)=8.19, p=.006, with post hoc tests confirming impairment occurred only in the retrieval/new-learning condition (p=.01/p=.001) and not without prior retrieval (p=.75/p=.61) -- exactly the predicted pattern, and this held after controlling for a Day-2 retrieval-performance confound (p<.05). The General Discussion explicitly identifies Schwabe & Wolf (2009), not Hupbach et al. (2007), as the matching original: 'we observed impaired memory for the initially learned material in participants who learned new information after retrieval of the older memory, which is in line with the results of other studies (Schwabe & Wolf, 2009; Strange, Kroes, Fan, & Dolan, 2010).' Hupbach et al.'s (2007) distinct intrusion/incorporation mechanism was explicitly not seen here (false alarm rates 'virtually absent'), confirming Schwabe & Wolf (2009) as the closer original and that its specific mechanism (impairment, not intrusion) is the one that replicated.

description: In a step-level public goods dilemma, outcome variance in the value of the public good has little to no effect on individuals' contributions when the distribution of possible outcomes offers only gains prospects (no possibility of a real loss).
original_authors: Eric van Dijk; Henk Wilke; Marieke Wilke; Linda Metman

replication_authors: Matthew W. McCarter; Kevin W. Rockmann; Gregory B. Northcraft
replication_title: Is it even worth it? The effect of loss prospects in the outcome distribution of a public goods dilemma
replication_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
explanation: The authors explicitly label this Hypothesis 1 as a 'Replication of van Dijk et al., 1999' and report: 'There was no difference in the mean contribution for the no variance condition (M = 66.52) as compared to the outcome variance with gains-only condition (M = 66.54)... This result replicates van Dijk et al. (1999), and provides support for Hypothesis 1.'

description: In a public goods dilemma, outcome variance in the value of the public good has little to no effect on individuals' willingness to contribute when the distribution of possible outcomes offers only gains prospects (no possibility of a real loss).
original_authors: Eric van Dijk; Henk Wilke; Marieke Wilke; Linda Metman
original_title: What information do we use in social dilemmas? Environmental uncertainty and the employment of coordination rules
replication_authors: Matthew W. McCarter; Kevin W. Rockmann; Gregory B. Northcraft
replication_title: Is it even worth it? The effect of loss prospects in the outcome distribution of a public goods dilemma
replication_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
explanation: CONFIRMED on review. Study 2 restates Hypothesis 1 for a structurally different assurance-dilemma paradigm (all-or-nothing dichotomous contribution, analyzed with GEE/Wald tests) rather than Study 1's continuous step-level game, and reports: 'there was no significant difference in the contribution rate between the gains-only conditions (76%) and the no variance conditions (72%); Wald χ2(1) = 0.10, p > .74' -- consistent with the prediction that gains-only outcome variance does not affect contribution likelihood. This is the only sub-measure named in the description, and it replicated cleanly, so 'success' is warranted (not a partial/mixed result). The immediate citation sentence for Study 2's Hypothesis 1 does not name van Dijk by author/year (it only says 'As with step-level public goods dilemmas...', pointing back to Study 1's explicit 'Replication of van Dijk et al., 1999' framing), but the paper's General Discussion resolves the attribution directly: 'The empirical results reported here extend previous research (van Dijk et al., 1999) by demonstrating when outcome variance influences contribution behavior and when it does not' -- confirmed verbatim in the PDF text. This establishes van Dijk et al. (1999) as the correct original target for this conceptual replication, not a misattribution. Bibliographic fields (title/journal/volume/pages/year) were checked against the paper's reference list entry ('van Dijk, E., Wilke, H., Wilke, M., & Metman, L. (1999)... Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 35, 109-135') and match exactly. Upgraded to high confidence based on this direct textual link, which the original pass had not located.

replication_title: A case-control study of the relationship between the metabotropic glutamate receptor 3 gene and schizophrenia in the Chinese population
explanation: Testing the same SNP in a much larger Chinese sample (752 cases, 752 controls), the authors state in the abstract 'We did not detect any association between rs1468412 and schizophrenia' (p=0.216 vs. Fujii's p=0.011), attributing the discrepancy to differing genetic backgrounds between the ethnic groups and the small size of the original Japanese sample.

description: A GRM3 haplotype constructed from three SNPs including rs1468412 shows a significant association with schizophrenia in a Japanese case-control sample (p=0.00083).
original_authors: Fujii, Yasue; Shibata, Hiroshi; Kikuta, Ryota; Makino, Chihiro; Tani, Akiko; Hirata, Noriko; Shibata, Aya; Ninomiya, Hitoshi; Tashiro, Nobutada; Fukumaki, Yasuyuki

replication_authors: Qi Chen; Guang He; Qingying Chen; Shengnan Wu; Yifeng Xu; Guoyin Feng; Yucheng Li; Lijun Wang; Lin He
replication_title: A case-control study of the relationship between the metabotropic glutamate receptor 3 gene and schizophrenia in the Chinese population
explanation: Reviewed: the Chinese haplotype (rs2237562/rs1468412/rs2299225) shows a significant global association (chi2=26.33, p=0.0017) with the specific haplotype C/T/C more prevalent in cases (p=0.008, OR=1.62), and the Discussion explicitly links this to Fujii et al.'s prior positive haplotype finding. However, the exact SNP composition match to Fujii's original haplotype remains unverified: this paper's own results section shows the three-SNP grouping was derived from the authors' own LD analysis of their Chinese sample (blocking SNPs by D'>=0.75 into two triads), not from deliberately re-testing Fujii's specific triplet, and Fujii's paper (not in this folder) never has its exact 3-SNP composition spelled out here beyond 'includes rs1468412'. The Discussion also contains an ambiguous aside -- 'the haplotype study with different combination of rs2237562, rs1468412 and rs2299225' -- that could be read as flagging the SNP set as different from Fujii's, but the grammar is equally consistent with contrasting the haplotype analysis against the single-SNP comparisons discussed in the same paragraph. This is a genuine, paper-level ambiguity that cannot be resolved without consulting Fujii et al. (2003) directly, so confidence stays medium.

description: First-time blood donors who make an explicit, written commitment/pledge to give blood are much more likely to actually go on to donate blood than those who do not make such a commitment.
original_authors: Anne Wevers; Daniël Wigboldus; Katja van den Hurk; Rick van Baaren; I.J.T. Veldhuizen
original_title: Increasing first-time blood donation of newly registered donors using implementation intentions and explicit commitment techniques
replication_authors: Cécile Sénémeaud; Camille Sanrey; Nathalie Callé; Candice Plainfossé; Alexandra Belhaire; Patrice Georget
replication_title: The watching-eyes phenomenon and blood donation: Does exposure to pictures of eyes increase blood donation by young adults?
explanation: Verified against the Results section (Table 1): participants who gave a pledge donated blood at 50.62% (41/81) vs. 2.68% (10/373) for those who did not pledge, Wald(1)=83.86, p<.001, OR=37.21 — a single, clean, strongly significant result with no hedging or mixed-result language attached to this specific comparison, and the Discussion states plainly 'our results support Wevers et al.'s [10] finding that first-time donors who provide a written pledge to give blood are much more likely to actually give blood.' That supports 'success' for this single described sub-measure. Genuine ambiguity remains, however, about how much weight this comparison carries as a replication: pledge status here was self-selected by participants (not experimentally manipulated, as it was via Wevers et al.'s implementation-intention/explicit-commitment conditions), and the comparison was secondary to this paper's primary watching-eyes hypothesis, run on a different population (French first-year university students vs. Wevers et al.'s newly registered Dutch donors). These are limitations inherent to the paper's own design, not something further re-reading resolves, so 'close extension' and medium confidence stand. Citation check: reference [10] in the bibliography reads in full 'Wevers A, Wigboldus DHJ, van den Hurk K, van Baaren R, Veldhuizen IJT. Increasing first-time blood donation of newly registered donors using implementation intentions and explicit commitment techniques. Vox Sang 2015;108(1):18-26, http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/vox.12189' — this exactly matches the extracted original_authors, original_title, original_journal, original_volume, original_issue, original_pages, original_year, and original_url. The flagged 'citation mismatch' was a false positive of the automated year-in-sentence check (the citation sentence cites Wevers et al. by bracket number [10] only, without an inline year); no changes to the original-study fields were needed.

description: Using an oculomotor capture task with a short (~1300 ms) stimulus onset asynchrony between prime and probe displays, saccade latencies were increased (inhibition-of-return) when a target appeared at the location of either a previously attended target or a previously presented distracter.
original_authors: Jan Theeuwes; Richard Godijn
original_title: Inhibition-of-return and oculomotor interference
replication_authors: Trevor J. Crawford; Sarah Hill; Steve Higham
replication_title: The inhibitory effect of a recent distracter
explanation: Verified against body.md Section 6 (Experiment 5) and Section 8.2 (General discussion). Crawford et al. explicitly re-ran their own saccadic distracter paradigm at the 1300 ms SOA used by Theeuwes and Godijn (2004) because the absence of IoR in their Experiments 1-2 'appeared to conflict with recent work (Theeuwes & Godijn, 2004).' At the matched SOA they found a significant main effect (F(1,12)=21.2, p=0.001), with SRT increased on both T1->T2 (232 ms vs. 221 ms, p<0.05) and T1->D2 (243 ms vs. 221 ms, p<0.001) relative to T1->N2, i.e., inhibition at both the previous-target and previous-distracter locations -- the same pattern T&G reported. The paper's own words ('These results provide support for the idea that the IoR and IRD emerge relatively early') and the General discussion ('These ideas were supported by the emergence of inhibition-of-return when a shorter SOA was introduced [Experiment 5]') both frame the outcome as consistent with T&G, with no hedging language ('differ', 'partial', 'mixed') attached to this specific comparison. No sub-measure named in the description failed. Kept at medium rather than raised to high: Experiment 5 uses Crawford's own LED-based saccadic distracter task (single stimulus per display), not T&G's oculomotor-capture-task paradigm (multi-item colour-change display) -- only the 1300 ms SOA parameter is matched -- so whether this counts as a genuine conceptual replication of T&G versus an internal parameter check within the authors' own paradigm is a defensible judgment call the paper itself does not resolve.

description: Chronic exposure to a high physiologic (10%) dose of 17β-estradiol via Silastic implants impairs performance on an operant delayed spatial alternation (DSA) working-memory task in ovariectomized young adult female rats.
original_authors: Victor C. Wang; Helen J. K. Sable; Young H. Ju; Clinton D. Allred; William G. Helferich; Donna L. Korol; Susan L. Schantz
original_title: Effects of chronic estradiol treatment on delayed spatial alternation and differential reinforcement of low rates of responding
replication_authors: Victor C. Wang; Steven L. Neese; Donna L. Korol; Susan L. Schantz
replication_title: Chronic estradiol replacement impairs performance on an operant delayed spatial alternation task in young, middle-aged, and old rats
explanation: The authors state in the Discussion 'a similar impairing effect of estradiol was observed in rats with either a 5% or a 10% estradiol implant' and in the abstract 'These data confirm our earlier finding that chronic estradiol treatment has an impairing effect on working memory as measured on DSA task.' The extension to middle-aged and old rats and to a lower (5%) dose found the same impairing effect, though the added hypothesis that older rats would show larger deficits was not supported (no significant age x estradiol interaction).

Goodall; Willem H. Ouwehand; Heribert Schunkert; John R. Thompson; Tim D. Spector; Christian Gieger; David-Alexandre Trégouët; Panos Deloukas; Nilesh J. Samani
replication_title: DNA methylation and body-mass index: a genome-wide analysis
explanation: As 'a form of overall validation of our discovery analysis,' the authors tested the known smoking-cg03636183 (F2RL3) association in their own discovery cohort (n=459) using the newer HumanMethylation450 array (successor to the 27K array used in the original) and 'recorded a similarly highly significant association (p=3.8x10-33) between methylation at cg03636183 and smoking, with reduced methylation in smokers,' matching the original finding's direction and strength. This is the only mention of this association in the paper (verified via full-text search), with no hedging or partial-support language elsewhere, so the single sub-measure is unambiguously successful. Citation review: body.md's numbered reference marker '22' (Lancet uses Vancouver-style numeric citations, not author-year) immediately follows this sentence, and bibliography entry 22 reads 'Breitling LP, Yang R, Korn B, Burwinkel B, Brenner H. Tobacco-smoking-related differential DNA methylation: 27K discovery and replication. Am J Hum Genet 2011; 88: 450-57' -- an exact match to the extracted original_authors/title/journal/volume/pages/year, so the earlier 'no author/year in citation' flag was a false positive from the numeric citation style, not an actual mismatch.

description: Analyzing citation patterns in Canadian politics textbooks (1995-2005), Rocher found that references to French-speaking scholars were systemically absent from English-speaking scholars' scientific production, showing the field of Canadian politics is neither inclusive nor comprehensive due to the underrepresentation of francophone scholars.
original_authors: Rocher, François
original_title: The end of the 'two solitudes'? the presence (or absence) of the work of French-speaking scholars in Canadian politics
original_journal: Canadian Journal of Political Science/Revue canadienne de science politique
replication_authors: Jean-François Daoust; Alain-G. Gagnon; Thomas Galipeau
replication_title: Language Matters: The Study of Canadian Politics through an Exploration of Syllabi and Comprehensive Exams
explanation: Independently reviewed body.md's Study 1 Findings: across 351 syllabi (9,388 coded readings), 38% of courses (133/351) had zero francophone-authored readings and the median was 5%; the paper states 'we have a strong case that francophones are underrepresented (when not totally absent)' and concludes 'a clear and substantial underrepresentation.' Every cut of the data (institution language, region, undergrad vs. grad) points the same direction -- no 'mixed'/'partial'/'differing' language undermines this single-study result, so 'success' holds. Confidence stays medium (not upgraded): this is confirmation of the same evidence the original explanation already cited, not new evidence, and the underlying ambiguity is structural rather than result-based -- Study 1 measures assigned course readings, a different operationalization from Rocher's (2007) citation-pattern analysis of published textbooks/scientific production, so it corroborates the broader underrepresentation phenomenon in a new domain rather than directly re-running Rocher's method.

description: Analyzing citation patterns in Canadian politics textbooks (1995-2005), Rocher found that references to French-speaking scholars were systemically absent from English-speaking scholars' scientific production, showing the field of Canadian politics is neither inclusive nor comprehensive due to the underrepresentation of francophone scholars.

explanation: Independently reviewed body.md's Study 2 Findings/Discussion: across 16 universities' comprehensive-exam reading lists (2,894 readings), mean francophone representation is .198 (median .155); even excluding the 3 highest outlier universities, 13 of 16 still fall below the paper's own 20% inclusivity threshold. The paper states the Study 1 conclusion 'still applies,' and the French abstract confirms representation is only 'légèrement meilleure' (slightly better) while francophones 'demeurent systématiquement sous-représentés à tous les niveaux' (remain systematically underrepresented at all levels) -- i.e. the smaller gap versus Study 1 is a difference of magnitude in the same direction, not a contradictory/mixed result, so it does not meet this benchmark's bar for downgrading to inconclusive. Confidence stays medium rather than high: as with Study 1, this is a conceptual replication using a different operationalization (doctoral reading lists, not Rocher's 2007 citation-pattern analysis of textbooks), and the smaller-but-still-present gap leaves room for reasonable disagreement about how strongly this counts as 'success' versus a more qualified partial confirmation.

description: Using a modified CANTAB attentional set-shifting task that dissociates 'perseveration' from 'learned irrelevance' conditions at the extra-dimensional shift stage, patients with frontal lobe excisions show a selective impairment in shifting attentional set under the perseveration condition, while unmedicated Parkinson's disease patients show milder deficits under both conditions.
original_authors: Adrian M. Owen; Angela C. Roberts; John R. Hodges; Trevor W. Robbins
original_title: Contrasting mechanisms of attentional set-shifting in patients with frontal lobe damage or Parkinson's disease
replication_authors: Rebecca Elliott; Peter J. McKenna; Trevor W. Robbins; Barbara J. Sahakian
replication_title: Neuropsychological evidence for frontostriatal dysfunction in schizophrenia
explanation: Independently verified against the Results/Discussion. The authors apply the identical modified CANTAB attentional set-shifting paradigm from Owen et al. (1993) to a new clinical population (chronic medicated schizophrenics, N=32) tested against age/IQ-matched controls (N=24). At the EDS stage patients differ significantly from controls in the perseveration condition (F(1,74)=50.25, P<0.001) but not the learned irrelevance condition (F(1,74)=0.54, P>0.45) -- a clean dissociation mirroring the selective frontal-lobe deficit pattern from Owen et al. (1993), and it holds up in the IQ-preserved subgroup too (F(1,62)=41.1 vs F(1,62)=0.43). The authors overlay their data on Owen et al.'s published frontal and Parkinson's disease patient data (Fig. 7) and conclude schizophrenics show 'a much more pronounced deficit even than the frontal patients' and that 'the performance of schizophrenics more closely resembles that of patients with frontal lobe damage than of patients with Parkinson's disease.' The summed EDS+EDR measure in Fig. 7 superficially also suggests a learned-irrelevance-condition deficit (resembling the Parkinson's pattern), but the authors directly resolve this: EDR-stage-specific data show that effect is a reversal-learning deficit, not a true learned-irrelevance deficit, so the summed metric is misleading. Neither the synopsis nor the Discussion hedges with 'mixed'/'partial' language -- the frontal-like selective perseverative dissociation is presented as clear and robust, so the selective perseverative EDS deficit pattern generalizes to, and is even amplified in, the new population. One caveat noted by the authors themselves: the schizophrenic-vs-Owen-et-al. comparison groups are not age-matched (schizophrenics significantly younger); however the core dissociation (perseveration vs. learned irrelevance) is established within-study against matched controls, independent of that cross-study overlay.

description: In elderly depressed and demented patients, cognitive test performance (recall, learning, psychomotor speed) is positively correlated with measures of cerebral arousal (barbiturate sensitivity and rate of salivary secretion), and cognitive/arousal deficits that appear during depressive illness are later restored after recovery in depressed patients while remaining unaltered in demented patients.
original_authors: L. K. Hemsi; Antonia Whitehead; F. Post
original_title: Cognitive functioning and cerebral arousal in elderly depressives and dements
replication_authors: Robert H. Cawley; Felix Post; Antonia Whitehead
replication_title: Barbiturate tolerance and psychological functioning in elderly depressed patients
explanation: The authors describe this as a self-replication with an improved, more carefully standardized barbiturate-threshold procedure: 'The present investigation was therefore planned in order to re-examine some of the psychophysiological correlates of clinical improvement in elderly depressed patients.' Results were mixed: the correlation hypothesis was rejected ('Our data do not support the first hypothesis' — physiological and psychological measures were uniformly low-correlated), while the hypothesis that thresholds and (more weakly) psychological scores rise with clinical improvement was supported ('Hypotheses 2, 3 ... are largely supported by our data ... however, the effects were much weaker for the psychological than for the physiological measures'). Reviewed: the flagged 'citation mismatch' is a false alarm, not a real error. The paraphrased citation_sentence doesn't itself contain 'Hemsi', but it is the very next sentence after the paper explicitly writes '... were discussed in an earlier communication (Hemsi, Whitehead, and Post, 1968) and subsequently by Savage (1970)' (body.md line 19), and the paper later confirms it again: 'Results of the earlier investigation (Hemsi et al., 1968) indicated that some depressed patients still had low scores...' (line 139). Two of that 1968 paper's three authors (Whitehead, Post) are also authors of the present paper, which explains the first-person 'our earlier investigation.' original_authors/title/year were already correct; only citation_sentence has been widened below to include the explicit name-year mention.

description: Barbiturate (sedation) thresholds rise to a greater extent after clinical recovery in more severely ill ('endogenous'/psychotic) than in mildly ill ('neurotic') depressed patients.
original_authors: Perris, Carlo; Brattemo, Carl-Erik
original_title: The sedation threshold as a method of evaluating anti-depressive treatments. A preliminary report
replication_authors: Robert H. Cawley; Felix Post; Antonia Whitehead
replication_title: Barbiturate tolerance and psychological functioning in elderly depressed patients
explanation: Reviewed against body.md/PDF (Results secs. 5-6, Tables 4-5, Discussion). Narrowed the description: the original two-part claim as framed in the Introduction has a baseline-level component ('lower barbiturate thresholds in severely ill than in mildly ill') and a recovery-change component. This paper's own Hypothesis 4 ('Changes in barbiturate thresholds ... will be greater for patients ... nearer to the endogenous type ... than for those with more neurotic features') tests only the change component, and Table 3 (correlations with initial threshold) never includes clinical severity or the Newcastle endogenous/neurotic score, so the baseline-level claim is not independently re-tested here — it is only the finding being extended, not itself replicated. The change component, however, is clearly and quantitatively supported: 'Hypotheses 4 and 5 receive substantial support ... from our data' (p. 47); Table 5 shows initial severity and the Newcastle (endogenous) score both significantly correlated with the CHANGE in sedation threshold (r=0.51, P<0.01 and r=0.53, P<0.001 respectively); and p.45 states plainly 'The increase in thresholds was greatest among patients who showed the most symptomatic improvement, and absent for those who showed no improvement' (r=0.59, P<0.001 for proportionate change vs. degree of improvement). The Discussion explicitly credits this pattern to the source being extended: 'Increases in sedation thresholds after recovery from endogenous or psychotic, and to a smaller extent from neurotic depressions, have previously been reported by Perris and Brattemo (1963) and by other writers.' Confidence stays medium: Shagass and Jones (1958), Perris and Brattemo (1963), and Perris (1966) are cited together throughout as converging prior evidence rather than one single named target, and the paper itself never disambiguates which of the three its own hypothesis is 'the' replication of — a genuine ambiguity in the text, not resolved by this review.

description: In a sample of Korean patients with major depressive disorder, 5-HTT (SLC6A4) promoter methylation (with a trend at CpG2 toward higher methylation) was associated with poorer response to naturalistic antidepressant treatment after 12 weeks.
original_authors: Hee-Ju Kang; Jae-Min Kim; Robert Stewart; Seon-Young Kim; Kyung-Yeol Bae; Sung-Wan Kim; Il-Seon Shin; Myung-Geun Shin; Jin-Sang Yoon
original_title: Association of SLC6A4 methylation with early adversity, characteristics and outcomes in depression
replication_authors: Katharina Domschke; Nicola Tidow; Kathrin Schwarte; Jürgen Deckert; Klaus-Peter Lesch; Volker Arolt; Peter Zwanzger; Bernhard T. Baune
replication_title: Serotonin transporter gene hypomethylation predicts impaired antidepressant treatment response
explanation: Confirmed on review of the Discussion (body.md ll.833-841): authors state their finding 'is somewhat in contrast to the only other pharmaco-epigenetic study in this respect by Kang et al. (2013), who observed a trend toward increased 5-HTT methylation at CpG2 -- the same CpG most significantly associated with treatment response in the present study -- to confer less improvement.' This study's CpG2 effect is significant (p=0.002, Bonferroni-corrected) and opposite in direction to Kang et al.'s finding at the same site. Caveat kept in view: per the Introduction (body.md ll.130-136), Kang et al.'s own CpG2 result was itself only a non-significant trend after correction for multiple testing, not a significant effect -- so this is a significant reversal of a non-significant original trend, and the authors' own hedge ('somewhat in contrast', not 'reversed') leaves room for reasonable disagreement with a softer label. Confidence held at medium for that reason, not upgraded.

description: Framing an identical decision outcome as gains versus losses changes risk preferences in the Asian disease problem: participants prefer the risk-free option when the outcome is framed as lives saved (gains) but prefer the risky option when framed as lives lost (losses).
original_authors: Tversky, Amos; Kahneman, Daniel
original_title: The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice
replication_authors: Jonathan Corbin; Todd McElroy; Cassie Black
replication_title: Memory reflected in our decisions: Higher working memory capacity predicts greater bias in risky choice
explanation: Using the verbatim Asian disease problem, the authors found a significant overall framing effect in the predicted direction (t(82) = -2.67, p = .009: more risk-seeking in the loss frame, M=4.28, than the gain frame, M=3.33). But this unconditional effect is not robust: entering OSPAN (working memory capacity) as a covariate made the main framing effect non-significant, F(1,84)=1.336, n.s., while the frame-by-WMC interaction was significant, F(1,84)=5.35, p=.023. The regression-based high/low-WMC model (+/-1 SD from the OSPAN mean) shows why: high-WMC participants replicate the classic pattern (Gains=3.06, Losses=4.80), but low-WMC participants show the OPPOSITE pattern (Gains=4.81, Losses=3.67) -- a reversal of the framing effect, not merely its absence, even though the Discussion downplays this as the effect being 'absent among those with low WMC.' Because the effect only holds for part of the sample and inverts for the rest, this is a partial/conditional replication of the framing effect, not a clean success across the described sample.

description: In a fictional warehouse-fire scenario, providing an alternative causal explanation for the event (e.g., arson) displaces reliance on discredited misinformation (e.g., improperly stored flammable chemicals) about its cause, whereas simply denying the false claim does not eliminate its continued influence on subsequent inferences.
original_authors: Hollyn M. Johnson; Colleen M. Seifert
original_title: Sources of the continued influence effect: when misinformation in memory affects later inferences
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Brendan Nyhan; Jason Reifler
replication_title: Displacing Misinformation about Events: An Experimental Test of Causal Corrections
explanation: Verified against Results/Conclusion: on both dependent measures central to this entry (favorability, belief Swensen took bribes), the denial condition remained significantly different from control (p<0.01 in both IPW and survey-weighted models), i.e. denial did NOT eliminate the innuendo's continued influence; the causal-correction condition was statistically indistinguishable from control on both measures (the authors explicitly report they 'cannot reject the null hypothesis of no difference' vs. control for both favorability and bribery belief), i.e. the alternate explanation fully displaced reliance on the discredited claim. The Conclusion states this unhedged, without any 'mixed'/'partial'/'differing results' language: 'our results demonstrate that findings from the psychology literature on the continued influence effect apply to politics... it is necessary to provide an alternate causal explanation that displaces inferences made from the false information.' The only weighting-scheme-dependent (non-robust) significance is on secondary pairwise comparisons (denial vs. innuendo; causal vs. denial) not named in this entry's description, so it does not create genuine ambiguity for the described effect. Both sub-claims in the description (causal explanation displaces the misinformation's influence; mere denial does not) replicated on every measure tested.

description: Women rate a potential short-term sexual partner's current involvement in another relationship (e.g., being 'already in another relationship,' promiscuous, unfaithful, 'sleeps around a lot') as undesirable, consistent with women using short-term mating to identify and secure a long-term partner.
original_authors: David M. Buss; David P. Schmitt
original_title: Sexual strategies theory: An evolutionary perspective on human mating
replication_authors: Todd K. Shackelford; Aaron T. Goetz; Craig W. LaMunyon; Brian J. Quintus; Viviana A. Weekes-Shackelford
replication_title: Sex Differences in Sexual Psychology Produce Sex-Similar Preferences for a Short-Term Mate
explanation: Using an entirely different measure (imagined-scenario likelihood ratings rather than abstract desirability ratings of listed traits), the authors found women's willingness to pursue a short-term partner rose as his relationship involvement decreased, and state in the Discussion: 'These results concur with Buss and Schmitt's (1993) demonstration that women rate as undesirable in a potential short-term partner current long-term romantic involvement with another woman.'

description: Men are far more likely than women to accept and pursue a casual, short-term sexual encounter with an attractive opposite-sex stranger.
original_authors: Russell D. Clark
original_title: Gender differences in receptivity to sexual offers
original_journal: Journal of Psychology and Human Sexuality
replication_authors: Todd K. Shackelford; Aaron T. Goetz; Craig W. LaMunyon; Brian J. Quintus; Viviana A. Weekes-Shackelford
replication_title: Sex Differences in Sexual Psychology Produce Sex-Similar Preferences for a Short-Term Mate
explanation: Independently re-checked against body.md: Prediction 3 (men > women likelihood of pursuing the imagined short-term encounter, at all three relationship-status levels) was confirmed with a clean, unambiguous statistical result and no mixed/partial component: significant main effect of Sex, F(1,466)=254.34, p<.001, and men scored higher than women at every level with large effect sizes (married: t(466)=13.55, d=1.27; not married w/ casual partners: t(466)=14.93, d=1.40; not married, no casual partners: t(466)=11.69, d=1.10; all p<.01), with no Sex x Relationship-Status interaction complicating the pattern. The Discussion explicitly claims this 'replicate[s], using a different paradigm, the finding that a short-term sexual strategy looms larger in male than in female psychology,' naming Clark & Hatfield (1989) first among five works cited together for that general finding -- confirmed this is the only place in the paper Clark & Hatfield is mentioned (searched full body.md). So the result label itself (success) is well-supported by the data; the residual uncertainty is attributional rather than evidentiary: Clark & Hatfield is not cited in the Introduction among the studies motivating Prediction 3 (only Ellis & Symons, Schmitt et al. 2003, and Trivers are cited there), and appears only in this bundled 'e.g.' list in the Discussion, so it is genuinely unclear whether the authors intend a dedicated replication of Clark & Hatfield's specific field-study finding versus a general supporting citation. No further reading resolves this, so confidence remains medium.

description: Depression is a prominent, though not exclusive, form of psychopathology associated with bulimia.
original_authors: Katzman, Melanie A.; Wolchik, Sharlene A.
original_title: Bulimia and binge eating in college women: A comparison of personality and behavioral characteristics
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Donald A. Williamson; Mary Lou Kelley; C. J. Davis; Laurie Ruggiero; David C. Blouin
replication_title: Psychopathology of eating disorders: A controlled comparison of bulimic, obese, and normal subjects.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: Verified against body.md Discussion: the authors state explicitly and without hedging, 'These data replicated the findings of Katzman and Wolchik (1984), who reported that depression is a prominent though not exclusive form of psychopathology associated with bulimia,' immediately after reporting that a majority of bulimics (87%) showed clinical psychopathology, the MMPI Depression scale was clinically elevated, and BDI mean was 15.4 (moderate depression) -- data that directly support the single claim being replicated. No 'differing results'/'mixed'/'partial' qualifier is attached to this specific claim anywhere in the paper (the one hedge in the Discussion, about not substantiating overfeminization, concerns a different original study, Hatsukami et al., not Katzman and Wolchik). Reference list entry (Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 52, 423-428, 1984) matches the cited original exactly. Classified as conceptual because the current study used a different assessment battery (MMPI, SCL-90, BDI, body image) and a clinically-diagnosed bulimic sample rather than replicating Katzman and Wolchik's exact instruments/population of college women binge eaters.

description: The dose-effect curve linking the number of psychotherapy sessions clients receive to their symptomatic improvement is negatively accelerated, similar in shape to that of many effective pharmacological treatments (e.g., 14% of clients improved before an initial session, 53% by 8 sessions, 63% by 13 sessions, and 83% by 52 sessions).
original_authors: Kenneth I. Howard; S. Mark Kopta; Merton S. Krause; David E. Orlinsky
original_title: The dose-effect relationship in psychotherapy
replication_authors: Michael Barkham; Anne Rees; William B. Stiles; David A. Shapiro; Gillian E. Hardy; Shirley Reynolds
replication_title: Dose–effect relations in time-limited psychotherapy for depression.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The authors state their results were 'a curious mixture of contradiction of and support for Howard et al.'s (1986) conclusion': session-by-session plots of clinically significant change looked linear rather than negatively accelerated, but when comparing outcomes of clients randomly assigned to 8 vs. 16 total sessions, the shorter dose produced more than half the effect of the longer dose, which the authors say is 'consistent with negative acceleration.'

description: Different classes of depressive symptoms, arrayed along a continuum from acute to chronic to characterological, show differential rates of response to psychotherapy: acute distress symptoms (e.g., crying, hopelessness) abate quickly, chronic distress symptoms respond well but more slowly, and characterological/interpersonal symptoms (e.g., 'never close to others') respond much more slowly, if at all.
original_authors: Stephen Mark Kopta; Kenneth I. Howard; Jenny L. Lowry; Larry E. Beutler
original_title: Patterns of symptomatic recovery in psychotherapy
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_authors: Michael Barkham; Anne Rees; William B. Stiles; David A. Shapiro; Gillian E. Hardy; Shirley Reynolds
replication_title: Dose–effect relations in time-limited psychotherapy for depression.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: The Discussion states 'several features of our results support the continuum from quickly to slowly responding classes of symptoms, consistently with Kopta et al.'s (1994) findings': far more clients improved on the BDI (acute/chronic distress) than the IIP (interpersonal problems), BDI items previously classed as acute changed faster than characterological ones, and PQ symptom domains had steeper slopes than self-esteem/relationship domains, though the authors also note qualifications (e.g., appetite/weight-loss items changed fastest despite being a 'vegetative' symptom expected to change slowly).

description: In unpublished pilot treatment-development work comparing cognitive therapy (CT) and supportive-expressive (SE) dynamic therapy, cognitive therapy was somewhat more effective for patients with elevated avoidant personality features, whereas SE dynamic therapy was somewhat more effective for patients with elevated obsessive-compulsive personality features (a personality-by-treatment matching effect assessed dimensionally).
original_authors: Barber, Jacques P.
original_title: Change in obsessive and avoidant personality disorders following dynamic therapy
original_journal: Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Psychiatric Association, Miami, FL
replication_authors: Jacques P. Barber; Larry R. Muenz
replication_title: The role of avoidance and obsessiveness in matching patients to cognitive and interpersonal psychotherapy: Empirical findings from the Treatment for Depression Collaborative Research Program.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: Using the full TDCRP completer sample (n = 84, CT vs. IPT substituted for SE) and dimensional avoidance/obsessiveness scores, the authors found the predicted significant Avoidance x Treatment and Obsessiveness x Treatment interactions on both the HRSD and BDI, and state in the Discussion that 'the results of the present study support the predicted hypothesis that there is a significant interaction between type of treatment and dimensions of personality... These results were replicated across self-report and clinician-rated assessments of depression.'

description: In unpublished pilot treatment-development studies specifically designed to examine change in patients diagnosed with avoidant personality disorder (AVPD) or obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD), AVPD patients improved more with cognitive therapy (CT) while OCPD patients improved more with supportive-expressive (SE) dynamic therapy, i.e., a diagnosis-by-treatment matching effect.
original_authors: Barber, Jacques P.
original_title: Change in obsessive and avoidant personality disorders following dynamic therapy
original_journal: Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Psychiatric Association, Miami, FL
replication_authors: Jacques P. Barber; Larry R. Muenz
replication_title: The role of avoidance and obsessiveness in matching patients to cognitive and interpersonal psychotherapy: Empirical findings from the Treatment for Depression Collaborative Research Program.
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
explanation: Among the 32 completers who met PAF diagnostic criteria for AVPD or OCPD and received CT or IPT (substituted for SE), the predicted Diagnosis x Treatment interaction was significant for the HRSD but not for the BDI ('There was no significant interaction between diagnostic group and treatment... ns, p = .37'); the authors explicitly note 'we did not replicate the findings across the two measures of depression (BDI and HRSD),' though the averaged effect size was of medium magnitude.

description: Among children in Grades 1-3, cognitive variables including nonverbal reasoning, processing speed, short-term memory, and working memory each accounted for unique variance in concurrent arithmetic word-problem-solving performance, with working memory and nonverbal problem solving emerging as significant correlates.
original_authors: H. Lee Swanson; Margaret Beebe-Frankenberger
original_title: The relationship between working memory and mathematical problem solving in children at risk and not at risk for serious math difficulties
replication_authors: Fuchs, Lynn; Compton, Donald L.; Fuchs, Douglas; Paulsen, Kimberly; Bryant, Joan D.; Hamlett, Carol L.
replication_title: The Prevention, Identification, and Cognitive Determinants of Math Difficulty.
explanation: The authors report partial corroboration: 'Our findings do, however, corroborate Swanson and Beebe-Frankenberger's (2004) results where nonverbal reasoning accounted for variance in arithmetic word problem performance,' and their working-memory beta for story problems was 'a figure identical to our estimate.' But other predictions diverged: attention (not tested by the original) emerged as the most robust predictor, working memory for calculation skill only partially replicated, and the authors state their findings together with Swanson and Beebe-Frankenberger's 'raise questions about the role of processing speed' rather than confirming a clean replication.

description: Buss's (1989) cross-cultural study of mate preferences across 37 cultures found that, consistent with evolutionary theory, men place greater value than women on a mate's youth and physical attractiveness, while women place greater value than men on a mate's earning potential/resource-acquisition ability; the gender difference in age preferences was the largest gender difference observed in that study.
original_authors: Buss, David M.
original_title: Sex differences in human mate preferences: Evolutionary hypotheses tested in 37 cultures
replication_authors: Susan Sprecher; Quintin Sullivan; Elaine Hatfield
replication_title: Mate selection preferences: Gender differences examined in a national sample.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Verified against the paper's Results, Discussion, and Conclusion. Table 1 reports significant (p < .001) gender differences, in the predicted direction, for all three Buss (1989) sub-measures: youth ('younger by 5 years', F = 394.17, the single largest gender difference in the study), physical attractiveness ('not good-looking'), and earning potential (multiple items). The Discussion states unhedged: 'We found clear support that the gender differences found in previous studies replicate in a national probability sample... All of these gender differences were fairly large in magnitude.' The Conclusion reiterates: 'consistent with those predicted by both evolutionary theory and the sociocultural perspective and consistent with those secured in previous research... their results were essentially correct.' The only hedging in the paper ('sociodemographic groups differed slightly in the magnitude of gender differences for some of the mate preferences', from the abstract) refers to a separate research question (whether effect size varies by race/age subgroup), not to whether the core Buss sub-measures replicated, and does not qualify the replication claim itself. All three named sub-measures replicated with no mixed/partial language attached to them, so 'success' is well-supported.

description: Grouping by proximity in dot lattices produces a proximity attraction function—the log odds of perceiving one lattice orientation over another—that is a linear function of relative interdot distance (a 'pure distance law').
original_authors: Michael Kubovy; Alex O. Holcombe; Johan Wagemans
original_title: On the lawfulness of grouping by proximity
replication_authors: Michael Kubovy; Martin van den Berg
replication_title: The whole is equal to the sum of its parts: A probabilistic model of grouping by proximity and similarity in regular patterns.
explanation: The authors state explicitly in the Discussion, 'The experiments replicated those of Kubovy et al. (1998): The attraction functions were linear,' confirming the pure distance law for proximity attraction held across all three new experiments before they extended the paradigm to add a similarity (dissimilarity) manipulation and test additivity of the two conjoined grouping principles.

description: When observers directed covert spatial attention toward a location with a high prior probability of distractor interference, target discrimination benefits at that location were substantially larger than when the location had a low probability of interference, but only when distractors were actually present in the display (with no probability effect in distractor-absent displays), indicating that distractor probability selectively modulates top-down distractor exclusion rather than the spatial distribution of attention.
original_authors: Edward Awh; Michi Matsukura; John T. Serences
original_title: Top-down control over biased competition during covert visual orienting
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Edward Awh; Antoinette Marie Sgarlata; John Kliestik
replication_title: Resolving Visual Interference During Covert Spatial Orienting: Online Attentional Control Through Static Records of Prior Visual Experience.
explanation: Using the same distractor-probability cueing paradigm as Awh et al. (2003) but with a much shorter 59-ms cue-target SOA, the authors found the same significant three-way interaction of attention, distractor presence, and distractor probability and concluded 'Experiment 1 therefore replicated the key results from the Awh et al. (2003) studies.'

description: When observers directed covert spatial attention toward a location with a high prior probability of distractor interference, target discrimination benefits at that location were substantially larger than when the location had a low probability of interference, but only when distractors were actually present in the display (with no probability effect in distractor-absent displays), indicating that distractor probability selectively modulates top-down distractor exclusion rather than the spatial distribution of attention.
original_authors: Edward Awh; Michi Matsukura; John T. Serences
original_title: Top-down control over biased competition during covert visual orienting
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Edward Awh; Antoinette Marie Sgarlata; John Kliestik
replication_title: Resolving Visual Interference During Covert Spatial Orienting: Online Attentional Control Through Static Records of Prior Visual Experience.
explanation: Experiment 2 added a second cued location/target and cue-adjacent invalid trials to test an attentional-breadth alternative, but reproduced the same distractor-probability by display-type interaction found by Awh et al. (2003) with the brief 59-ms SOA; the authors state 'In addition to replicating the observations of Awh et al. (2003), Experiments 1 and 2 demonstrate that these probability effects can be observed with a cue-target SOA of only 59 ms.'

description: Using the Hassles Scale administered over a nine-month period, Kanner et al. (1981) found that the frequency (but not intensity) of daily hassles was significantly related to psychological symptomatology, more strongly than major life events were.
original_authors: Kanner, Allen D.; Coyne, James C.; Schaefer, Catherine; Lazarus, Richard S.
original_title: Comparison of two modes of stress measurement: Daily hassles and uplifts versus major life events
replication_authors: Anita DeLongis; James C. Coyne; Gayle Dakof; Susan Folkman; Richard S. Lazarus
replication_title: Relationship of daily hassles, uplifts, and major life events to health status.
explanation: On close reading, the paper's own comparison to Kanner et al. is explicitly qualified rather than a clean confirmation: 'the overall findings of the present study with somatic health are similar to those of Kanner et al. (1981) for psychological symptoms, [but] there were some differences, too. Kanner et al. found that hassles frequencies, but not intensities, were correlated with psychological symptoms. In the present study, both frequencies and intensities of hassles were related to illness.' The granular data (Table 4) show a split picture: for Somatic Symptoms specifically (the closest analog to Kanner's outcome), the original frequency-not-intensity pattern DOES hold (frequency r=.27**/.35** vs. intensity r=.08/.15 n.s.), but for Overall Health Status and Energy Level, intensity is also significant (e.g., r=-.38**/-.29** for health status) -- a divergence from Kanner's single-measure result that the authors themselves flag as a difference, additionally noting the two studies drew on the same HPL sample. Per the rule that a global 'similar' claim combined with an explicit 'some differences, too' acknowledgment is inconclusive rather than success, and since not every sub-measure in the description (frequency AND intensity's differential pattern) replicated across all three health outcomes, this is reclassified as inconclusive.

description: Kanner et al. (1981) found a positive association between frequency of daily uplifts and psychological symptoms in women, but no relationship between uplifts and symptoms in men, leaving the role of uplifts in adaptational outcomes uncertain.
original_authors: Kanner, Allen D.; Coyne, James C.; Schaefer, Catherine; Lazarus, Richard S.
original_title: Comparison of two modes of stress measurement: Daily hassles and uplifts versus major life events
replication_authors: Anita DeLongis; James C. Coyne; Gayle Dakof; Susan Folkman; Richard S. Lazarus
replication_title: Relationship of daily hassles, uplifts, and major life events to health status.
explanation: The authors directly equate their finding to Kanner's: 'the obtained relationship of uplifts to somatic health was weak, as was true in the case of psychological symptoms in the Kanner et al. (1981) study.' Table 4 shows this in more detail: uplifts frequency WAS significantly, positively correlated with somatic symptoms at the final assessment (r=.25, p<.01) -- echoing Kanner's positive zero-order finding -- but was not significantly related to overall health status or energy level, and this symptoms correlation became nonsignificant once variance shared with hassles frequency was partialled out. So the present study reproduces a weak, inconsistent, largely hassles-confounded uplifts effect, matching the qualitative 'uncertain role' conclusion from Kanner et al. Confidence stays medium rather than high: the present study does not break results out by sex, so the specific women-positive/men-null contrast in the description was not directly re-tested, only the broader 'weak and inconsistent' characterization of uplifts.

description: Generating keywords for a text after a delay (rather than immediately after reading) dramatically improves metacomprehension accuracy, whereas immediate keyword generation is no more accurate than not generating keywords at all.
original_authors: Keith W. Thiede; Mary C. M. Anderson; David Therriault
original_title: Accuracy of metacognitive monitoring affects learning of texts
replication_authors: Keith W. Thiede; John Dunlosky; Thomas D. Griffin; Jennifer Wiley
replication_title: Understanding the Delayed-Keyword Effect on Metacomprehension Accuracy.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 1 retained Thiede et al.'s (2003) original immediate- and delayed-keyword conditions (adding new groups to isolate the keyword-judgment lag) and found metacomprehension accuracy was again significantly higher for RK-delayed groups on inference questions, F(1,128)=12.86, p<.001; the authors state 'These results replicate the delayed-keyword effect reported by Thiede et al. (2003).'

description: Generating keywords for a text after a delay (rather than immediately after reading) dramatically improves metacomprehension accuracy, whereas immediate keyword generation is no more accurate than not generating keywords at all.
original_authors: Keith W. Thiede; Mary C. M. Anderson; David Therriault
original_title: Accuracy of metacognitive monitoring affects learning of texts
replication_authors: Keith W. Thiede; John Dunlosky; Thomas D. Griffin; Jennifer Wiley
replication_title: Understanding the Delayed-Keyword Effect on Metacomprehension Accuracy.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 2 again retained Thiede et al.'s (2003) original immediate- and delayed-keyword groups (adding filler texts to isolate the keyword-keyword lag) and found a significant main effect of the RK lag, F(1,96)=12.25, p=.001; the authors note 'these results revealed the delayed-keyword effect and implicate the longer RK interval as critical.'

description: Delayed keyword generation, in which readers actively produce keywords capturing the essence of a text after a delay, dramatically improves metacomprehension accuracy relative to no generation task.
original_authors: Keith W. Thiede; Mary C. M. Anderson; David Therriault
original_title: Accuracy of metacognitive monitoring affects learning of texts
replication_authors: Keith W. Thiede; John Dunlosky; Thomas D. Griffin; Jennifer Wiley
replication_title: Understanding the Delayed-Keyword Effect on Metacomprehension Accuracy.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 4's generate group reproduced Thiede et al.'s (2003) delayed-keyword procedure exactly and, when compared to a new yoked group who merely read others' keywords, showed significantly higher metacomprehension accuracy, t(57)=2.64, p=.01; the authors conclude 'the act of generating keywords is critical to improving metacomprehension accuracy,' extending the original finding by testing whether active generation itself (versus exposure to the same cues) is necessary. Confirmed on independent review: the General Discussion explicitly reiterates and generalizes this specific result ('the metacomprehension accuracy of delayed judgments was relatively low compared to keyword generation... delayed activities like vaguely thinking about the text or reading other people's keywords does not require the same process and representation access as delayed generation, thus does not provide diagnostic feedback about comprehension'), and the abstract states without hedging that 'the third and fourth experiments show that not all delayed tasks will produce improvements.' No qualifying language ('partial', 'mixed', 'some differences') appears anywhere in connection with this finding.

description: Delaying metacomprehension judgments until after all texts have been read and studied (without any intervening generation task) does not improve metacomprehension accuracy relative to making judgments immediately after reading; accuracy for delayed judgments was not reliably different from zero.
original_authors: Ruth H. Maki
original_title: Predicting performance on text: Delayed versus immediate predictions and tests
replication_authors: Keith W. Thiede; John Dunlosky; Thomas D. Griffin; Jennifer Wiley
replication_title: Understanding the Delayed-Keyword Effect on Metacomprehension Accuracy.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Experiment 3 used the same immediate-versus-delayed-judgment design as Maki (1998b) but added explicit instructions to think about the text's essence during the delay, and still found no accuracy difference between the delayed and immediate groups, t(52)=.20, p>.10; the authors conclude the extra time thinking about the texts 'did not improve metacomprehension accuracy in an analogous manner to the delayed generation of keywords,' consistent with Maki's original null finding for delayed judgments alone. Confirmed on independent review: the General Discussion explicitly names this as a replication of the original result rather than just a parallel finding: 'Delaying comprehension judgments alone does not improve metacomprehension accuracy. This is supported both by our data and previous finding of Maki and Dunlosky (Maki, 1998b; Dunlosky et al., 2005).' No hedging language ('partial', 'mixed', 'some differences') is attached to this conclusion anywhere in the paper.

description: Using manipulations of a single real database to compare the Hedges-Olkin, Rosenthal-Rubin, and Hunter-Schmidt methods for meta-analyzing correlation coefficients, Johnson, Mullen, and Salas (1995) found that the Hunter-Schmidt method produced conservative (overly cautious, low Type I error rate) significance tests of the mean effect size relative to the other two methods.
original_authors: Blair T. Johnson; Brian Mullen; Eduardo Salas
original_title: Comparison of three major meta-analytic approaches
replication_authors: Andy P. Field
replication_title: Meta-analysis of correlation coefficients: A Monte Carlo comparison of fixed- and random-effects methods.
explanation: Independently verified in both the Conclusion and General Discussion. Conclusion: 'unlike Johnson et al. (1995), who found that the Hunter-Schmidt method was too conservative, this study showed that the Hunter-Schmidt method (using their revised formula) was too liberal—too many null results were significant.' The General Discussion restates the same opposite-direction finding even more plainly: 'Contrary to Johnson et al. (1995), the present results indicate that the Hunter-Schmidt method is too liberal in the homogeneous case (not too conservative).' Two independent, unhedged statements of the reversal (not just one) leave no genuine ambiguity, so confidence is raised to high.

description: Strube (1988), extending a critique of Silver and Dunlap (1987), showed that once more than a few studies are included in a meta-analysis, the upward bias in mean effect-size estimates from using Fisher-z-transformed correlations is equal in magnitude (but opposite in direction) to the downward bias from using untransformed correlations.
original_authors: Michael J. Strube
original_title: Averaging correlation coefficients: Influence of heterogeneity and set size
replication_authors: Andy P. Field
replication_title: Meta-analysis of correlation coefficients: A Monte Carlo comparison of fixed- and random-effects methods.
explanation: Reconsidered on closer reading of both studies, not just the Conclusion's headline sentence. In the homogeneous case (Study 1), the match to Strube's equal-and-opposite-bias claim is clean: 'the Hedges-Olkin and Rosenthal-Rubin method tends to slightly overestimate the population effect size whereas the Hunter-Schmidt method underestimates it ... The degree of bias appears to be virtually identical when rounded to two decimal places.' But in the heterogeneous case (Study 2), Table 4 shows the two biases are NOT generally equal: at rho=.1/.3/.5 the Hedges-Olkin overestimate (~.03-.21) is several times the Hunter-Schmidt underestimate (~.001-.026), and the two only converge to roughly equal magnitude at the single largest effect size tested, rho=.8 (~.10-.14 vs ~.08-.09). The Conclusion itself flags this: after saying 'Prediction 2 was also substantiated,' it immediately qualifies that the Hunter-Schmidt bias 'was less severe than the Hedges-Olkin method in the heterogeneous case' — i.e., not equal there except at the extreme. This is a global claim of support paired with an explicit 'less severe'/differs-by-condition qualifier, so per the inconclusive-vs-success rule this is partial (clean in Study 1, condition-dependent in Study 2), not a full replication of the general 'equal in magnitude once more than a few studies are included' claim in the description.

explanation: REVIEWED: verified against body.md Results/Discussion and the PDF. The three-way interaction (BDNF genotype x PA x stress) was significant for social stress (chi-sq(1)=6.3, p=.012): PA's buffering of the genotype's effect on NA reactivity strengthened as hypothesized, weakening the Val/Met-vs-Val/Val difference from a large effect at low PA to a small/negligible one at high PA. The authors attribute the event-stress null to an already-weak BDNF-event-stress association rather than a failed replication, but that is a post-hoc rationalization, not independent confirmation. Per the rule that partial support across sub-measures is inconclusive rather than success, and given the original description named event-related stress specifically (the domain that did not show the effect), the result label was changed from success to inconclusive; confidence is kept at medium because this is a changed-label case, not a newly obvious one.

replication_title: Genome-wide association study identifies common variants at four loci as genetic risk factors for Parkinson's disease
explanation: Verified on review. Results text is unhedged: 'the association with MAPT was not replicated in our study' (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 2) — a single-locus finding with no qualifying language ('partially', 'mixed', etc.) that would soften it toward inconclusive. The Discussion explicitly reiterates the failure and offers a mechanistic explanation rather than walking it back: the MAPT region's H2 haplotype, common in Europeans, is absent in East Asians, so 'the differences observed between our study and the findings in populations of European descent reflect population differences in the genetic heterogeneity of PD etiology.' Methods confirm this isn't an artifact of poor genotyping: the six MAPT SNPs (four genome-wide significant in the European GWAS) all had call rates >95% and PHWE >0.001 in the replication samples. Citation mismatch resolved: the numbered citation '17' in the text resolves via the paper's own reference list (ref. 17: 'Simon-Sanchez, J. et al. Genome-wide association study reveals genetic risk underlying Parkinson's disease. Nat. Genet. advance online publication, doi:10.1038/ng.487 (15 November 2009)'), which matches the extracted original_authors/title/year/url exactly — not a mismatch, just a footnote-number citation that the flagging heuristic couldn't resolve without the bibliography.

explanation: Reviewed body.md and the reference list: reference 1 (Meyre, D. et al., 'A genome-wide scan for childhood obesity-associated traits in French families shows significant linkage on chromosome 6q22.31-q23.2', Diabetes 53, 803-811, 2004) exactly matches the original_authors/title/journal/volume/pages/year already recorded; the citation_sentence cites it as a bracket number rather than inline year, so the flagged 'year not found in citation' is a false mismatch and no fields needed correction. On the result classification: the authors re-test the D6S1656 marker (identified via linkage in ref. 1) in an independent replication set of 68 families and report only 'modest evidence of linkage' (MLS = 0.83, P = 0.04) plus a marginal, uncorrected undertransmission signal (P = 0.02). MLS = 0.83 is far below conventional linkage significance thresholds (Lander-Kruglyak suggestive ~1.9, significant ~3.3), and the authors' own 'modest evidence' hedge, rather than a claim of confirmed linkage, indicates this specific sub-finding was only marginally and partially supported, not clearly replicated. The paper's global 'strongly supports' conclusion addresses the broader ENPP1-obesity/T2D association findings elsewhere in the paper, not this linkage replication specifically. This is a genuinely borderline result (directionally consistent, only marginally significant, no correction for multiple testing) rather than a case the paper itself resolves clearly, so inconclusive at medium confidence remains the correct call.

description: In cocaine-naive rhesus monkeys, the dopamine D2/D3 agonist quinpirole produces a dose-dependent, inverted U-shaped yawning response curve.
original_authors: Martelle, J.L.; Claytor, R.; Ross, J.T.; Reboussin, B.A.; Newman, A.H.; Nader, M.A.
original_title: Effects of two novel D3-selective compounds, NGB 2904 and CJB 090, on the reinforcing and discriminative stimulus effects of cocaine in rhesus monkeys
original_journal: Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics
replication_authors: Blaylock BL; Gould RW; Banala A.; Grundt P.; Luedtke RR; Newman AH; Nader MA
replication_title: Influence of Cocaine History on the Behavioral Effects of Dopamine D3 Receptor-Selective Compounds in Monkeys
explanation: Independently verified against body.md. Discussion states explicitly: 'We had previously reported a similar shape of the quinpirole-elicited yawning dose-response curve in cocaine-naive rhesus monkeys (Martelle et al, 2007; Hamilton et al, 2010), which was replicated in this study,' immediately followed by 'An extensive history of cocaine self-administration did not alter the shape, potency, [...]' — no hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'differing') attaches to this specific measure. The Results section independently corroborates this with quantitative data: 'Quinpirole (0.03-1.0 mg/kg) significantly (F(4,20)=9.45, p<0.001) elicited yawns in a dose-dependent manner as characterized by the inverted U-shaped function of dose... There were no differences between groups, with peak yawns elicited by 0.1 mg/kg quinpirole.' This is a clean, unambiguous 'success' for the quinpirole sub-measure specifically (distinct from the more mixed PG 619/CJB 090 findings discussed elsewhere in the paper, which do not bear on this entry). Confidence remains medium rather than high: the ambiguity is not about the result label (which is unambiguous) but about which prior paper is 'the' original being replicated — the sentence jointly cites Martelle et al (2007) and Hamilton et al (2010) (the latter a study of monkeys with prenatal cocaine exposure, per the reference list: 'Characterization of the dopamine receptor system in adult rhesus monkeys exposed to cocaine throughout gestation,' Psychopharmacology 210:481-488). Martelle et al (2007) is retained as the primary original because it is independently and repeatedly cited elsewhere (e.g., in the Introduction: 'full agonists such as quinpirole elicit yawning... (Martelle et al, 2007)') specifically for this behavioral fact, whereas Hamilton et al (2010) is cited only jointly. This dual-citation is a genuine feature of the source paper (Hamilton et al 2010 is not available for review to resolve which contains the original inverted-U dose-response curve report), so confidence is not upgraded.

description: In rats, midbrain dopamine neurons respond with prediction-error-like signals to violations in the expected sensory identity (features) of a reward, even when reward value is held constant, indicating that dopamine error signals are not restricted to cached value.
original_authors: Yuji K. Takahashi; Hannah M. Batchelor; Bing Liu; Akash Khanna; Marisela Morales; Geoffrey Schoenbaum
original_title: Dopamine neurons respond to errors in the prediction of sensory features of expected rewards
replication_authors: James D. Howard; Thorsten Kahnt
replication_title: Identity prediction errors in the human midbrain update reward-identity expectations in the orbitofrontal cortex
explanation: Verified: reference 17 in this paper's bibliography (Takahashi, Y. K. et al., 'Dopamine neurons respond to errors in the prediction of sensory features of expected rewards,' Neuron 95, 1395-1405, 2017) exactly matches the cited original study. Using a human fMRI transreinforcer reversal-learning task with olfactory rewards (a conceptual replication across species/paradigm rather than a direct replication of the rodent single-unit recordings), the authors found significant midbrain responses to value-neutral identity prediction errors (iPEs): whole-brain t(22)=4.05, pFWE=0.033, and ROI t(22)=1.69, p=0.050 (Fig. 3b,c), corroborated by converging control analyses ruling out value confounds (positive correlation between iPE_SW->SV and iPE_SV->SW, r=0.49, p=0.0087, Fig. 3e) and linking midbrain iPE to OFC identity updating (r=0.48, p=0.0097, Fig. 6a). The Discussion explicitly states 'our results directly parallel recent findings in rodents, which demonstrate that the same dopaminergic neurons respond to errors in the value and identity of expected rewards,' and no hedging language ('mixed,' 'partial,' 'some differences') is applied to this specific identity-PE finding anywhere in the abstract or Discussion (the paper's only caveat -- failing to observe a striatal value PE, unlike other studies -- concerns a different measure and does not bear on this entry). This is a single, clearly-stated positive finding, not a multi-measure result with partial support, so 'success' is well supported.

replication_title: Genetic and Environmental Influences on Disordered Gambling in Men and Women
explanation: Reviewed and confirmed. The paper's COMMENT (Discussion) section makes an explicit, unhedged numeric comparison: Eisen et al.'s (1998) Vietnam Era Twin Registry estimates (48% additive genetic, 0% shared environment, 52% nonshared environment, using the same >=1-symptom liability-threshold cutoff) are stated to be 'nearly identical to the estimates for men in the present study' (48.5%, 0.01%, 51.4% in Table 3). The paper also states 'neither the Vietnam Era Twin Registry study nor the present study obtained evidence of shared environmental influences' and 'the univariate model-fitting results for men were similar to the results obtained from the all-male Vietnam Era Twin Registry study.' No hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'differing') applies to this specific comparison; the paper's novel findings on women and sex differences are an extension beyond Eisen et al., not part of the replicated claim. All three sub-measures named in the description replicated closely, so 'success' is correct.
