description: Human observers can accurately estimate men's physical strength and fighting ability by viewing their bodies and faces.
original_authors: Aaron Sell; Leda Cosmides; John Tooby; Daniel Sznycer; Christopher von Rueden; Michael Gurven
original_title: Human adaptations for the visual assessment of strength and fighting ability from the body and face
original_journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
replication_authors: Samuele Zilioli; Aaron N. Sell; Michael Stirrat; Justin Jagore; William Vickerman; Neil V. Watson
replication_title: Face of a fighter: Bizygomatic width as a cue of formidability
explanation: Using a new rating task (composites of experienced vs. inexperienced UFC fighters), the authors found experienced-fighter composites rated as significantly more formidable than inexperienced-fighter composites (t(35)=4.692, P<.001), and state explicitly: 'This result replicates previous work establishing the ability to estimate formidability from the face (Sell, Cosmides et al., 2009; Trebicky et al., 2013).' This is a single, decisive test with no countervailing result elsewhere in the paper. Confidence remains medium (not upgraded) because the match is still conceptual rather than direct: the original tested faces AND bodies via individual assessments, whereas this study tested only faces via composite-average ratings of a formidability construct that blends strength and fighting-ability judgments — a genuine, unresolvable method gap rather than an unclear result.

description: Perceived aggressiveness/fighting ability judged from photographs of mixed-martial-arts fighters' faces predicts their actual fighting performance.
original_authors: Třebický, Vít; Havlíček, Jan; Roberts, Craig; Little, Anthony C.; Kleisner, Karel
original_title: Perceived aggressiveness predicts fighting performance in mixed-martial-arts fighters
replication_authors: Samuele Zilioli; Aaron N. Sell; Michael Stirrat; Justin Jagore; William Vickerman; Neil V. Watson
replication_title: Face of a fighter: Bizygomatic width as a cue of formidability
explanation: Revised after checking Study 2b, the more directly relevant individual-level test (the prior pass cited only the Study 2a composite comparison, which addresses formidability-estimation generally rather than performance-prediction specifically). Study 2b found raters' perceived-formidability judgments correlated significantly with total number of fights (r=.456, P=.001) and total number of wins (r=.445, P=.002), but explicitly did NOT correlate with win/loss record (r=.061, P=.680) -- the measure most analogous to 'fighting performance' in the original claim. The authors themselves frame this null result as showing win/loss record is 'an inferior measure of fighting ability,' and Table I's summary omits it entirely, but per the scoring rules a global claim of confirmation does not override a specific null sub-result on the very measure ('performance') the entry describes. This is genuine partial support (experience measures replicate, the performance/win-rate measure does not), so the label is inconclusive rather than success.

description: Caucasian mixed-martial-arts fighters with wider bizygomatic facial features (identified via geometric morphometrics) have higher combat success.
original_authors: Třebický, Vít; Havlíček, Jan; Roberts, Craig; Little, Anthony C.; Kleisner, Karel
original_title: Perceived aggressiveness predicts fighting performance in mixed-martial-arts fighters
replication_authors: Samuele Zilioli; Aaron N. Sell; Michael Stirrat; Justin Jagore; William Vickerman; Neil V. Watson
replication_title: Face of a fighter: Bizygomatic width as a cue of formidability
explanation: Correcting a miscitation from the prior pass, which quoted the whole-sample statistic (wins: r=.203, P=.001) even though this entry's claim is specifically about Caucasian fighters. The actual Caucasian-specific analysis ('Similar analyses were performed in our database'): fWHR correlated significantly with percentage of wins (r=.206, P=.019; partial r=.234, P=.008 controlling for number of fights) but NOT with total number of fights (r=.058, P=.511) or total number of wins (r=.134, P=.129) among Caucasians. Because 'combat success' in this literature is standardly operationalized as win rate/percentage (consistent with how entries 2 and 3 both use this framing), the significant, robust percentage-of-wins correlation supports 'success' -- but it is a narrower match (direct fWHR measurement vs. Trebicky's geometric-morphometric approach) and two of three Caucasian-specific measures did not replicate, so confidence stays medium rather than being upgraded.

original_journal: Paper presented at The Nordic Evolutionary Psychology Meeting 2013, Tartu, Estonia (unpublished conference presentation)
replication_authors: Samuele Zilioli; Aaron N. Sell; Michael Stirrat; Justin Jagore; William Vickerman; Neil V. Watson
replication_title: Face of a fighter: Bizygomatic width as a cue of formidability
explanation: Narrowed the description after checking what Zilioli et al.'s own 'similar analyses' actually tested: the original unpublished study's claim has two parts (fWHR predicts both proportion of fights won AND perceived aggressiveness), but the paper's replication attempt ('Among Caucasian fighters, fWHR correlated with the percentage of wins, r=.206, P=.019') only covers the win-proportion half -- there is no corresponding Caucasian-specific perceived-aggressiveness rating task anywhere in this paper, so that component was never actually tested and has been dropped from the description rather than scored as replicated or failed. For the narrowed win-proportion claim, the match is direct and significant. Confidence remains low because the original source is still an unverifiable unpublished conference presentation with no DOI or journal to check against.

original_authors: David A. Greenberg; Martina Durner; Mehdi Keddache; Shlomo Shinnar; Stanley R. Resor; Solomon L. Moshe; David Rosenbaum; Jeffrey Cohen; Cynthia Harden; Harriet Kang; Sibylle Wallace; Daniel Luciano; Karen Ballaban-Gil; Livia Tomasini; Guilian Zhou; Irene Klotz; Elisa Dicker
original_title: Reproducibility and complications in gene searches: linkage on chromosome 6, heterogeneity, association, and maternal inheritance in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
replication_authors: Martina Durner; Mehdi A. Keddache; Livia Tomasini; Shlomo Shinnar; Stanley R. Resor; Jeffrey Cohen; Cynthia Harden; Solomon L. Moshe; David Rosenbaum; Harriet Kang; Karen Ballaban‐Gil; Sharon Hertz; Douglas R. Labar; Daniel Luciano; Sibylle Wallace; David Yohai; Irene Klotz; Elisa Dicker; David A. Greenberg
replication_title: Genome scan of idiopathic generalized epilepsy: Evidence for major susceptibility gene and modifying genes influencing the seizure type
explanation: Reviewed: the Results section states 'For chromosome 6 we were able to reconfirm the previously observed linkage to the HLA region in JME families,' with a two-point lod score of 4.2 and multipoint heterogeneity lod score of 2.3, and the paper directly supports both remaining sub-claims in the description: 'These results suggest evidence for heterogeneity and possible maternal inheritance in JME at the chromosome 6 locus.' The Discussion section independently reinforces the result with an unambiguous, unhedged statement: 'The results for chromosome 6, on the other hand, represented confirmation of a previous finding and need no correction for multiple testing.' No caveats, partial-support language, or contradicting sub-measures appear anywhere in the paper for this claim, so 'success' is well supported. Confidence stays medium (not upgraded) because the genuine open question is not whether the paper reports success -- it unambiguously does -- but whether the 91-family sample analyzed here is independent of the family sample underlying Greenberg et al. (2000). The Methods describe 20 additional chromosome-6 markers typed as fine-mapping on top of the existing panel, not a newly, separately ascertained cohort, and the paper never states the degree of family overlap with the 2000 study. That ambiguity is not resolved by anything in the text, so it is left as a genuine unknown rather than resolved in either direction.

The authors' summary line ('would confirm a role for ASPN in susceptibility to knee OA... in Caucasians') is a gene-level global claim that papers over this D14/D13 split; per the review rule that such a claim does not override reported differing results, and since the specific sub-measure named in this entry's description (D14) failed to replicate while a distinct allele succeeded, this remains a genuine mixed result -- correctly inconclusive, not success or failure. On the result label: the original study found no significant association between 6 COMP polymorphisms and knee/hip OA in Japanese patients. Taken alone, the current (Caucasian) cohort found the opposite of a clean replication of that null result -- COMP haplotypes WERE associated with knee OA, but with different haplotypes implicated in men versus women (Table 3: 'Association in both sexes, but different haplotypes'). This three-way split (original null -> single-study positive -> pooled meta-analysis null), explicitly acknowledged by the authors themselves with no overall verdict offered, is a genuine mixed result rather than a resolvable one, so inconclusive remains correct and confidence stays medium.

description: In preschool children, native-to-foreign (N-F) intraverbal training, despite requiring more sessions to master, was more likely than foreign-to-native (F-N) intraverbal training to produce emergence of untrained foreign tacts and reverse intraverbal relations.

original_title: A comparison of four strategies for teaching a small foreign-language vocabulary
replication_authors: Katerina Dounavi
replication_title: Tact training versus bidirectional intraverbal training in teaching a foreign language
explanation: Partial replication, confirmed by two independent pieces of evidence in the current adult study beyond the directional comparison itself. (1) The core comparison did reproduce the original's direction: N-F intraverbal training produced emergent tacts and the reverse (F-N) intraverbal at mastery level, while F-N intraverbal training produced only below-mastery emergent responses (RESULTS AND DISCUSSION). (2) But the 'despite requiring more sessions to master' tradeoff attributed to N-F in the original does not replicate -- it reverses. Here N-F intraverbal training was the MOST efficient condition (17 sessions for Pedro, 18 for Carlota, reaching mastery in one phase; Figure 1, Set 3/Set 4 single-phase panels), while F-N intraverbal training was the LEAST efficient because its below-mastery emergence required a second, follow-up phase of direct N-F ('reverse intraverbal') training to reach full mastery-level emergence (~33 total sessions; Figure 1, two-phase panels). (3) The authors themselves explicitly flag the study as not a clean confirmation: 'The present results differ from those obtained in studies that have examined transfer of stimulus control in children ... in which no or few emergent responses have been found (Miguel et al., 2005; Petursdottir & Haflidadottir, 2009; Petursdottir et al., 2008),' attributing the much stronger overall emergence to using verbally more competent adult participants. Given a replicated main-effect direction alongside a reversed efficiency finding and an author-acknowledged difference in overall emergence magnitude, 'inconclusive' (not 'success') is the correct label -- this is a textbook partial replication.

description: Extinguished free-operant behavior renews (returns) when animals are returned to the context in which the response was originally reinforced, despite continued extinction of the response.

explanation: The authors state their ABA renewal design (MTurk workers clicking a moving button for points, extinguished then tested back in the original context) produced a significant increase in responding upon return to Context A (paired t-test, p < .0001) and conclude: 'These data were similar to those produced in basic research (Bouton, Todd, Vurbic, & Winterbauer, 2011) ... evaluating renewal.' The species, apparatus, and reinforcer differ substantially from Bouton et al.'s rodent lever-press studies, so this is a conceptual test of the same renewal effect rather than a procedural repetition. Independently reviewed the PDF's Results/Discussion and Figure 2: Phase 3 shows a clear transient renewal burst (first trial M = 21.2 rpm vs. Phase 2's near-zero M = 1.41) that gradually re-extinguishes across the remaining Phase 3 trials — the standard renewal-then-re-extinction pattern, not a caveat on the finding — and the Discussion contains no hedging ('differing', 'mixed', 'partial') language. That confirms 'success' is unambiguous; confidence stays medium because the residual uncertainty is about the replication_type call (Bouton et al. used rats in operant chambers, a categorically different paradigm), which this paper's text cannot resolve.

description: Prior test experience in the elevated plus-maze (EPM) abolishes the anxiolytic-like effect of GABAA-related anxiolytic drugs (e.g. the benzodiazepine chlordiazepoxide) on trial 2, a phenomenon the authors termed 'one-trial tolerance' (OTT), even though the drug produces a clear anxiolytic effect in maze-naive animals on trial 1.

explanation: Verified against the full text. The abstract states unambiguously: 'All drugs increased open arms exploration, indicating an anxiolytic effect, in maze-naive but not in maze-experienced rats, in which increased open arms avoidance was observed.' Table 2's post-hoc pairwise comparisons confirm this per-drug: HA-966 (3.0 mg/kg), MK-801 (0.06 mg/kg) and memantine (8.0 mg/kg) each significantly increased open-arm exploration versus saline in maze-naive rats, while in maze-experienced rats 'drugs failed to produce any effect ... as compared to controls' (the one exception, an MK-801-driven rise in a minor risk-assessment measure, does not touch the anxiolytic measure itself). The Discussion/Conclusion state plainly, without hedging ('mixed'/'partial'/'some differences' language is absent throughout), that 'the OTT phenomenon may also be observed for drugs that reduce the activity of the NMDA/glycine-B receptor complex' and that 'the present findings extend the OTT phenomenon to drugs that reduce the NMDA/glycine-Breceptor activity.' All three drug classes tested show the identical qualitative pattern (anxiolytic in maze-naive rats, abolished in maze-experienced rats), so this is a uniform, unambiguous extension of the File et al. explanation: Verified against the Results and Discussion text. The 'Comparison of Domain Means' section reports concrete numbers showing the original norming means held up closely in the much larger sample: e.g. Module 2 Autism social-communication combined totals were 18.38 (N=21, norming) vs. 18.11 (N=171, new sample), and Module 2 non-autism ASD totals were 11.83 (N=18, norming) vs. 11.94 (N=83, new sample) -- differences that are clinically negligible despite statistically significant age/IQ differences between samples. Table 3 (sensitivity/specificity of the existing 2000-norms algorithm by module and diagnostic group in the new 1,139-participant sample) likewise shows sensitivity/specificity in the same range as the original 94% figure for most cells (e.g. Module 2: 96-98% sens/93-97% spec; Module 3: 86% sens/89% spec), with the one clear exception -- low specificity (19%) for Module 1 no-words children with non-verbal mental age <=15 months -- explicitly attributed by the authors to the inclusion of a lower-functioning PL-ADOS subgroup not present in the original norming sample, not framed as a failure to replicate. The Discussion's global claim ('both domain means and sensitivity and specificity remained similar to the original norming data, indicating that the ADOS continues to be a valid and reliable measure') is not undercut by any 'differing results/some differences/partially/mixed' hedge attached to this specific comparison -- the hedging language elsewhere in the Discussion ('sensitivity ... lower than desired', specificity 'remained weak' for low-functioning children) concerns the performance of the NEW revised algorithm on non-autism ASD distinctions, a separate question from whether the original norming results (domain means, ~94% classification) replicated in the larger sample. Both sub-measures named in this entry's description (domain means, ~94% correct classification) are supported as replicated. This is a close extension because the same ADOS paradigm and classification approach were tested in a substantially expanded, more heterogeneous sample and set of clinical sites/examiners rather than an exact repetition of the original conditions.

description: Among neurotypical adults from the general population (AQ score below 32), the number of self-reported autism traits (measured with the Autism-Spectrum Quotient) was positively and significantly associated with the number of self-reported gender dysphoric traits.
original_authors: Rita George; Mark A. Stokes
original_title: Gender identity and sexual orientation in autism spectrum disorder
replication_authors: Aimilia Kallitsounaki; David Williams
replication_title: Mentalising Moderates the Link between Autism Traits and Current Gender Dysphoric Features in Primarily Non-autistic, Cisgender Individuals
replication_journal: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
explanation: The authors state in the Discussion, 'To our knowledge, this is the first study to replicate George and Stokes (2018) findings of a significant relation between autism traits and current gender dysphoric traits in adults from the general population,' and Table 1 shows a significant correlation between AQ and GIDYQ (r = -.32, p < .01), consistent in direction and significance with the original finding.

description: The Five Cs second-order confirmatory factor model of positive youth development (PYD) — with Competence, Confidence, Connection, Character, and Caring loading on a common second-order PYD factor — is a valid, configurally invariant measurement structure for youth in early adolescence (Grades 5-7), as established using 4-H Study of PYD data by Phelps et al. (2009).
original_authors: Phelps, Elizabeth; Zimmerman, Sara; Warren, Amy A.; Jelicic, Helena; von Eye, Alexander; Lerner, Richard M.
original_title: The structure and developmental course of positive youth development (PYD) in early adolescence: Implications for theory and practice
replication_authors: Edmond P. Bowers; Yibing Li; Megan K. Kiely; Aerika Brittian; Jacqueline V. Lerner; Richard M. Lerner
replication_title: The Five Cs Model of Positive Youth Development: A Longitudinal Analysis of Confirmatory Factor Structure and Measurement Invariance
explanation: The authors directly fit the hypothesized second-order Five Cs model 'first identified by Lerner et al. (2005) and then confirmed by Phelps et al. (2009)' to new 4-H Study data from Grades 8-10, but report inadequate fit at all three grades (chi-square = 938.65/1090.15/1359.84, RMSEA = .093/.102/.115 for Grades 8/9/10), requiring modification before adequate fit and strict longitudinal invariance could be established; Fig. 2's caption confirms the specific change ('Athletic competence was removed from revised model and physical appearance now loads on confidence'), and the Discussion states plainly that 'the initial Five Cs model verified for Grades 5-7 should be modified for middle adolescents.' This is a genuine mixed outcome: the core second-order structure and all second-order loadings remained significant even in the unmodified model, and the revised model then achieved strict invariance, but the specific measurement model as validated by Phelps et al. (2009) did not hold as-is — notably, the abstract omits the modification entirely, framing the result more positively than the Discussion does.

description: States with higher per capita representation in the U.S. Senate receive higher per capita federal expenditure, reflecting the overrepresentation of small states in the Senate.
original_authors: Atlas, C. M.; Gilligan, T. A.; Hendershott, R. J.; Zupan, M. A.
original_title: Slicing the federal government net spending pie: who wins, who loses, and why
replication_authors: Gary A. Hoover; Paul Pecorino
replication_title: The Political Determinants of Federal Expenditure at the State Level
explanation: The authors state: 'We confirm the most important result of Atlas et al., which is that state-level federal expenditure is positively related to per capita senate representation for that state. The effect is strongest for procurement spending,' with SENATE significant (mostly at the 1% level) across nearly every spending category in all three model specifications.

description: States with higher per capita representation in the U.S. House of Representatives receive higher per capita federal expenditure.
original_authors: Atlas, C. M.; Gilligan, T. A.; Hendershott, R. J.; Zupan, M. A.
original_title: Slicing the federal government net spending pie: who wins, who loses, and why
replication_authors: Gary A. Hoover; Paul Pecorino
replication_title: The Political Determinants of Federal Expenditure at the State Level
explanation: The authors state: 'By contrast, we find evidence against their result that per capita representation in the House is positively related to per capita federal expenditure' and, in the conclusion, 'In contrast to Atlas et al., we do not find a positive relationship between house representation per capita and spending per capita.' HOUSE is insignificant in the main specification and only becomes significant (and negative, i.e., not supporting the original positive relationship) in a robustness check omitting ELECTORAL.

description: Victim sensitivity's negative effect on cooperative/forgiving responses toward a transgressor is mediated by a 'suspicious mindset', specifically hostile (mistrustful) interpretations of the other person's intentions and self-protective legitimizing cognitions justifying one's own uncooperative reaction.
original_authors: Tanja M. Gerlach; Mathias Allemand; Dmitrij Agroskin; Jaap J. A. Denissen
original_title: Justice sensitivity and forgiveness in close interpersonal relationships: the mediating role of mistrustful, legitimizing, and pro-relationship cognitions
replication_authors: Merle Buchholz; Mario Gollwitzer; Zoe Magraw-Mickelson; Christopher Stolz; Philipp Süssenbach
replication_title: Taking Back Control: Findings on the Cognitive, Behavioral, and Motivational Consequences of Victim Sensitivity
explanation: Reviewed against the full Study 1 Results/Discussion: this is a clean failure to replicate, not a mixed result. The base relationship the mediation was built to explain was itself absent — VS had no total effect on trust behavior at all (r=.09, p=.40). Of the two named mediators, legitimizing cognitions was not even correlated with VS (r=.14, p=.21); VS did significantly predict hostile interpretations (β=.27, p=.04), but hostile interpretations (like the other mediators) did not in turn predict trust behavior, and bootstrapped 95% CIs for ALL indirect effects (social distancing, hostile interpretations, legitimizing cognitions) contained zero — the model explained only 10% of trust variance. The authors state plainly: 'we were unable to replicate the established negative relationship between victim sensitivity and trust, and we also did find no support for the assumption that social distancing, hostile interpretations, and legitimizing cognitions ... mediated this hypothesized relation,' and conclude Study 1 by saying they 'were not able to demonstrate that this bias actually mediated behavioral trust and cooperation.' The one surviving finding — VS correlating with hostile-interpretation *perceptions* of the partner — never connects to the cooperative/forgiving-behavior outcome that Gerlach et al.'s mediation claim was actually about, so it does not rescue the hypothesis; it is a tangential aside, not partial support for the mediation being tested.

description: When cues of untrustworthiness activate a suspicious mindset, victim sensitivity (fear of exploitation) is associated with reduced trust and cooperation toward an interaction partner in a trust game.
original_authors: Gollwitzer, Mario; Rothmund, Tobias
original_title: What exactly are victim-sensitive persons sensitive to?
replication_authors: Merle Buchholz; Mario Gollwitzer; Zoe Magraw-Mickelson; Christopher Stolz; Philipp Süssenbach
replication_title: Taking Back Control: Findings on the Cognitive, Behavioral, and Motivational Consequences of Victim Sensitivity
explanation: Reviewed against the full Study 2 Results/Discussion/Limitations: the ambiguity here is genuine and does not resolve cleanly either way. Study 2 explicitly used Gollwitzer & Rothmund (2011, Study 2) as the basis for its trust-game paradigm and its a-priori power analysis ('f2 = 0.03, as in Gollwitzer & Rothmund, 2011; Study 2'), while extending it with a novel control- vs. self-affirmation manipulation. Arguing for failure/inconclusive: the pooled base VS × suspiciousness interaction (across all affirmation conditions) was not significant (t=-1.64, no marginal marker in Table 3), and the authors' own Limitations section calls the Study 2 effect 'smaller than expected.' Arguing for success: in the specific cell most comparable to the original study's design (suspicious mindset, no affirmation applied), the simple slope of VS on trust was significant and in the predicted direction (B=-1.834, p=.015) — a cleaner result than merely marginal. The theoretically novel three-way VS × suspiciousness × affirmation interaction (testing whether control-affirmation attenuates the effect) reached only the 10% level (B=0.913, SE=0.505, p=.072). Because the paper's own narrative treats the base effect as established enough to be 'attenuated' by affirmation, while simultaneously downplaying its size, reasonable readers could code this either as a conditional success (replicated in the no-affirmation baseline) or as inconclusive (non-significant when pooled, and the moderation itself only marginal) — kept as inconclusive/medium since no decisive new evidence emerged on review.

description: A pilot mixed-methods evaluation found that a bespoke six-week online Mindfulness-based Social Work and Self-Care (MBSWSC) programme improved social work students' stress, emotional exhaustion, personal achievement, anxiety, and well-being, as well as mindfulness-based mechanisms of action (attention regulation/decentering, mindfulness, acceptance, self-compassion, non-attachment, and aversion), plus non-judgement, empathy and observation in practice.
original_authors: Alan Maddock; Pearse McCusker; Carolyn Blair; Audrey Roulston
original_title: The Mindfulness-Based Social Work and Self-Care programme: a mixed methods evaluation study
original_journal: The British Journal of Social Work
replication_authors: Alan Maddock; Karen McGuigan; Pearse McCusker
replication_title: A randomised trial of Mindfulness-based Social Work and Self-Care with social workers
explanation: Confirmed via the paper's own Results (Table 2 ANCOVA) and Discussion that this is a genuine partial/mixed replication of the Maddock et al. (2021) pilot, not a clean success. Only 10 of the 17 outcome measures assessed showed a significant MBSWSC-vs-active-control effect at follow-up. Among the sub-measures named in this entry's description: stress, emotional exhaustion, anxiety, mindfulness, attention regulation (decentering), acceptance, non-attachment, and non-judgement replicated with significant between-group effects (the authors call emotional exhaustion 'in line with' the pilot), but personal achievement, self-compassion, well-being, and aversion showed NO significant between-group difference (only within-group change, similar in size to the pilot's own uncontrolled pre-post design), and mindful observation (the practice-observation outcome from the pilot) likewise did not reach significance versus control. The authors explicitly flag personal achievement and depersonalisation as diverging from the pilot ('This study did not see changes on the burnout-personal achievement subscale... This diverges from Maddock et al. (2021)') and state plainly for self-compassion/well-being, 'There were no significant differences between the MBSWSC and the active control ... however both groups experienced significant within group effects.' Because only some of the named sub-measures replicated with a between-group effect while others explicitly diverged, 'inconclusive' is the correct label; the abstract's global claim that MBSWSC was 'significantly superior' does not override this measure-by-measure mixed pattern.

description: Using a word-fragment completion task, some amnesic patients showed evidence of learning and remembering new word-pair associations (larger repetition priming when a word fragment appeared with the same word it was paired with at study than with a different word), despite impaired explicit recall/recognition of those associations.
original_authors: Graf, Peter; Schacter, Daniel L.
original_title: Implicit and explicit memory for new associations in normal and amnesic subjects
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Nissen, Mary Jo; Bullemer, Peter
replication_title: Attentional requirements of learning: Evidence from performance measures
explanation: In Experiment 4, Korsakoff's syndrome patients showed clear performance-based (reaction time) learning of a repeating sequence on a nonverbal serial reaction time task despite having no awareness of the pattern; the authors state directly, 'The results from this experiment confirm Graf and Schacter's (1985) finding that some amnesic patients can learn new associations, and extend them to a nonverbal task that presumably does not involve elaborative processing.'

description: Using a progressive-ratio schedule requiring increasing effort to obtain money, melancholic depressed patients who responded to antidepressant treatment showed an increase in the number of responses needed to obtain reward, whereas nonresponders did not, indicating that improved mood is associated with increased responsiveness to monetary reinforcement.
original_authors: John Hughes; Carol N. Pleasants; Roy W. Pickens
original_title: Measurement of reinforcement in depression: a pilot study
original_journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
replication_authors: Diego A. Pizzagalli; Allison L. Jahn; James P. O’Shea
replication_title: Toward an objective characterization of an anhedonic phenotype: A signal-detection approach
explanation: In a Discussion subsection titled 'Approach-Related System Abnormalities in Depression: Replication and Extension,' the authors state their findings 'replicate and extend earlier reports in depression of blunted hedonic responses,' summarizing Hughes et al (1985)'s finding as converging evidence. Independent review: the original study is unambiguously identified (authors/journal/volume/pages match the reference list exactly), and the full abstract (Background/Methods/Results/Conclusions, checked against the PDF since abstract.md is truncated) contains no 'differing results'/'mixed'/'partially' language anywhere that would trigger the inconclusive-override rule, so 'success' is well supported by the authors' own explicit statement and not contradicted elsewhere. Confidence raised from low to medium but not to high: this remains a fundamentally different paradigm (progressive-ratio effort task on a 6-participant pilot sample vs. the present signal-detection response-bias task) identified as converging evidence in the Discussion rather than a study the current authors designed specifically to replicate Hughes et al., so it qualifies as a conceptual replication (explicitly includable per the taxonomy) but the evidentiary weight of a single-sentence citation is a genuine judgment call.

description: On a verbal recognition memory task in which correct 'old' responses were monetarily rewarded, nondepressed control participants developed a more liberal response bias to maximize earnings, whereas dysphoric and clinically depressed participants failed to shift their response bias in the reward condition, indicating blunted reward responsiveness in depression.
original_authors: Jeffrey B. Henriques; Jeanne M. Glowacki; Richard J. Davidson
original_title: Reward fails to alter response bias in depression
replication_authors: Diego A. Pizzagalli; Allison L. Jahn; James P. O’Shea
replication_title: Toward an objective characterization of an anhedonic phenotype: A signal-detection approach
explanation: The authors state their findings 'replicate and extend' prior work (Discussion subsection 'Approach-Related System Abnormalities in Depression: Replication and Extension'), describing Henriques et al (1994; also Henriques and Davidson 2000) as reporting that 'dysphoric and clinically depressed subjects displayed a more conservative bias during the reward condition' of a verbal memory task, paralleling the present study's finding that high-BDI participants failed to develop a response bias toward the more frequently reinforced stimulus. Independent review: the original study is unambiguously identified (authors/journal/volume/pages match the reference list exactly), and the full abstract (checked against the PDF since abstract.md is truncated) plus the rest of the Discussion/Conclusions contain no 'differing results'/'mixed'/'partially' language for this comparison, so 'success' is well supported. Confidence raised from low to medium but not to high: the paradigms differ substantially (verbal recognition memory vs. perceptual signal-detection), and this is a conceptual replication identified only as converging evidence in the Discussion rather than a study the current authors designed to directly replicate Henriques et al., so the evidentiary weight of a single-sentence citation is a genuine judgment call even though it is includable per the taxonomy's conceptual-replication category.

description: A connectionist network trained to parse complex structures containing embedded subordinate clauses succeeded only when the training input was organized incrementally by complexity ('starting small'/staged input), but failed when exposed to the entire input as a whole from the outset.
original_authors: Elman, Jeffrey L.
original_title: Learning and development in neural networks: The importance of starting small
replication_authors: Jun Lai; Fenna H. Poletiek
replication_title: The impact of adjacent-dependencies and staged-input on the learnability of center-embedded hierarchical structures
explanation: Independently verified against body.md: Experiment 1 compared an SS (staged-input) group and a random-input group, both trained on the same set of 0-, 1-, and 2-LoE items. The SS group significantly outperformed the random group overall (d'=1.51 vs .08, t(26)=3.94, p=.001), and only the SS group performed above chance (t(13)=4.21, p=.001), while the random group never exceeded chance across 12 blocks. This directly parallels Elman's original claim that staged input enables learning of embedded structure while random/whole exposure does not. Confidence kept at medium rather than upgraded to high because two genuine, paper-inherent ambiguities remain (rereading does not resolve them): (1) this is a human artificial-grammar-learning behavioral study, not a re-run of Elman's connectionist simulation, so how tightly it maps onto his original claim is a judgment call; (2) the paper's own abstract conclusion is conditional -- 'learning was observed only when the training set was staged and contained 0-LoE exemplars' -- and since both Experiment 1 arms already included 0-LoE items, staged input was not tested in full isolation from basic-exemplar availability here.

description: A connectionist network trained to parse complex structures containing embedded subordinate clauses succeeded only when the training input was organized incrementally by complexity ('starting small'/staged input), but failed when exposed to the entire input as a whole from the outset.
original_authors: Elman, Jeffrey L.
original_title: Learning and development in neural networks: The importance of starting small
replication_authors: Jun Lai; Fenna H. Poletiek
replication_title: The impact of adjacent-dependencies and staged-input on the learnability of center-embedded hierarchical structures
explanation: Independently verified against body.md: Experiment 2 removed all 0-LoE learning items; the SS group no longer differed from the random group (d'=.05 vs .18, t(16)=1.11, n.s.), and both groups stayed at chance from the first to the last block. The General Discussion states explicitly: 'The facilitation effect of SS disappeared, as Experiment 2 further revealed, when participants were deprived of exposure to the 0-LoE exemplars... no matter whether the stimuli were presented incrementally or randomly.' This is an unambiguous failure of the staged-input advantage under this specific condition. Confidence kept at medium rather than upgraded to high: Experiment 2 is not a literal re-run of Elman's staged-vs-whole manipulation but layers on a second, novel manipulation (removing the simplest items entirely) that Elman's original design did not isolate, so whether this counts as a direct failure to replicate Elman specifically -- versus a boundary-condition finding about a compound design -- is a genuine interpretive question the paper itself does not resolve.

description: Cognitive load imposed by a concurrent secondary task does not reduce the overall frequency of utilitarian judgments on high-conflict moral dilemmas (Greene et al.'s original load manipulation raised response latencies but left frequency unaffected).
original_authors: Greene, Joshua D.; Morelli, Sylvia A.; Lowenberg, Kelly; Nystrom, Leigh E.; Cohen, Jonathan D.
original_title: Cognitive load selectively interferes with utilitarian moral judgment
replication_authors: Bastien Trémolière; Wim De Neys; Jean-François Bonnefon
replication_title: Mortality salience and morality: Thinking about death makes people less utilitarian
explanation: Reviewed against body.md's Experiment 2 Results and Discussion (Section 7). Only the frequency half of Greene et al.'s finding is re-tested here: reaction times are never re-measured anywhere in this paper (checked full text; 'latency'/'reaction time' occur only when summarizing Greene et al.'s original result), so the entry's description has been narrowed to that single sub-measure rather than bundling in an RT claim this study never examined. Using a different cognitive-load manipulation (a spatial Dot Memory Task at three graded levels: low, high, very high) and a French student sample, the authors found a significant main effect of cognitive load on the frequency of utilitarian responses to conflict problems, F(2,109)=6.03, p=.003, but post hoc tests found no difference between low and high load, only between low load and very high load (p=.023) and high load and very high load (p=.005) -- i.e., the effect appears only at the most extreme load level rather than scaling with load overall. The Discussion frames this as confirming that Greene et al.'s original null finding on frequency was due to 'too weak a manipulation of load,' a fairly confident global claim of success, but the actual pattern is a threshold effect present in only 2 of 3 pairwise comparisons, not a uniform effect of load. Per the rule that a global claim of confirmation does not override an underlying partial/level-contingent result, and that a single significant contrast does not settle a multi-level comparison, this remains inconclusive rather than success. This is a genuine judgment call the paper's own confident framing does not resolve, so confidence stays medium.

description: Visual-form synesthetes report significantly more vivid visual imagery on the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) than non-synesthete matched controls.
original_authors: Kylie J. Barnett; Fiona N. Newell
original_title: Synesthesia is associated with enhanced, self-rated visual imagery
replication_authors: Mary Jane Spiller; Clare N. Jonas; Julia Simner; Ashok Jansari
replication_title: Beyond visual imagery: How modality-specific is enhanced mental imagery in synesthesia?
explanation: Checked both independent group splits in Results 3.1.1-3.1.2. Concurrent-based split: significant group effect on VVIQ (F(2,202)=7.06, p=.001); synesthetes with visual concurrents scored higher than controls (p=.001), while synesthetes WITHOUT visual concurrents did not differ from controls (p=.502) and did not differ from the visual-concurrent synesthetes either (p=.605) -- i.e. the effect is specific to the visual-concurrent subgroup, exactly as the entry's description is scoped. Inducer-based split independently replicates the same pattern: significant group effect (F(2,202)=8.98, p<.001), driven entirely by synesthetes with visual inducers scoring higher than controls (p<.001), with no significant difference for synesthetes without visual inducers vs. controls (p=.928) or vs. the visual-inducer group (p=.068). Two large, independent group splits (N=74 vs 102, and N=66 vs 102) both single out the visual-form synesthetes as the source of the effect, which is a materially stronger basis than the single concurrent-based comparison originally cited. (A finer 5-way split in 3.1.3, with much smaller cells of N=15 and N=7, only reached significance for synesthetes with BOTH a visual concurrent and inducer -- consistent with a power issue in the smaller subgroups rather than a contradicting result, as the paper's own footnotes attribute similar underpowered non-significant follow-ups elsewhere to small cell sizes.) The Discussion explicitly frames this as replicating Barnett & Newell (2008): 'Previous studies have found that visual synesthetes have higher self-reported visual imagery than non-synesthete controls with the VVIQ (Barnett & Newell, 2008)... This study therefore provides a useful contribution to our understanding.'

description: Synesthetes with visual concurrents (a broad visual-synesthesia sample, not isolated by subtype) report using mental imagery more frequently in everyday life (measured by the Spontaneous Use of Imagery Scale, SUIS) than non-synesthete controls.
original_authors: Price, Mark C.
original_title: Spatial forms and mental imagery
replication_authors: Mary Jane Spiller; Clare N. Jonas; Julia Simner; Ashok Jansari
replication_title: Beyond visual imagery: How modality-specific is enhanced mental imagery in synesthesia?
explanation: Corrected the population in the description: the paper explicitly states it did NOT break its sample down by synesthesia subtype ('The number of particular forms of synesthesia (e.g. grapheme-color) has not been listed as this was not the focus', Participants section) -- so this study never isolates sequence-space synesthetes the way Price (2009) did; the original description's 'sequence-space' label was not something this paper actually tested. What it does test -- synesthetes with visual concurrents, a broader group -- replicates the SUIS effect robustly and by two independent routes: concurrent-based split (F(2,201)=25.84, p<.001; visual-concurrent group vs. controls p<.001) and inducer-based split (F(2,201)=27.00, p<.001; visual-inducer group vs. controls p<.001). Notably the SUIS effect is even broader than the VVIQ one: synesthetes WITHOUT a visual concurrent, and those WITHOUT a visual inducer, also scored significantly higher than controls (p=.043 and p=.011 respectively), so elevated everyday visual-imagery use looks close to a general synesthete trait in this sample, not confined to the visual-concurrent/inducer subgroup. The authors explicitly link this to Price: 'they report a greater everyday use of visual imagery with the SUIS (following Price, 2009).' Net effect: the underlying SUIS finding replicates with high confidence, but it does so for a broader population than the original description claimed, so the description was narrowed to match what was actually measured.

description: Contrast-discrimination perceptual learning is retinal-location specific: practice-induced improvement at a trained retinal location does not transfer to an untrained retinal location.
original_authors: Yu, Cong; Klein, Stanley A.; Levi, Dennis M.
original_title: Perceptual learning in contrast discrimination and the (minimal) role of context
replication_authors: Lu-Qi Xiao; Jun-Yun Zhang; Rui Wang; Stanley A. Klein; Dennis M. Levi; Cong Yu
replication_title: Complete Transfer of Perceptual Learning across Retinal Locations Enabled by Double Training
explanation: Before introducing their novel double-training manipulation, the authors state 'We first replicated the common finding of location specificity in a conventional perceptual-learning paradigm,' finding significant contrast-discrimination learning at the trained location (MPI = 24.6% ± 2.7, p < 0.001) but no significant transfer to an untrained location (MPI = 5.7% ± 3.4, p = 0.102). The citation for this claim groups four references together [1, 6-8], but checking each in references.json shows only one studies contrast discrimination: ref 6, Yu, Klein, and Levi (2004), 'Perceptual learning in contrast discrimination and the (minimal) role of context.' The other three test different tasks (Shiu & Pashler 1992: line orientation; Karni & Sagi 1991: texture discrimination; Fahle 1994: pattern recognition). This paper's replicated experiment uses the identical task (V-Gabor contrast discrimination at 5° eccentricity) as ref 6, and three of ref 6's authors (Klein, Levi, Yu) are co-authors of this 2008 paper too, confirming Yu, Klein, and Levi (2004) as the specific self-replicated target rather than an interchangeable member of the citation cluster. Both components of the location-specificity finding (significant learning at the trained location, non-significant transfer to the untrained location) replicated cleanly and are reported without hedging, supporting 'success.'

description: Using a within-subjects, trial-by-trial design, higher occipital alpha power is associated with a lower probability of perceiving the sound-induced double-flash illusion, indexing momentary visual cortex excitability.
original_authors: Joachim Lange; Julian Keil; Alfons Schnitzler; Hanneke van Dijk; Nathan Weisz
original_title: The role of alpha oscillations for illusory perception
replication_authors: Roberto Cecere; Geraint Rees; Vincenzo Romei
replication_title: Individual Differences in Alpha Frequency Drive Crossmodal Illusory Perception
explanation: Reviewed body.md in full (Results and Discussion). The correlation reuses Experiment 1's n=22 sample ('back to experiment 1, we differently analyzed our data...assessing the relationship between the proneness to the illusion...and...alpha power'), and is reported as significant and in the same direction as Lange et al.: 'In line with the findings of Lange and colleagues [16], we found that higher levels of alpha power were inversely correlated with the proneness to perceive the illusion (r = 0.52, p < 0.015, see Figure 4)'. The Discussion independently reaffirms this with no hedging: 'we further confirm (and extend previous findings from a within-subjects design [16] to a between-subjects design) the role of alpha power as a momentary index of visual cortex excitability.' No qualifying language ('partial', 'mixed', 'differing results') appears anywhere near this specific finding, it is the only sub-measure in this entry, and it is corroborated in two independent passages (Results and Discussion) rather than only a single summary sentence. Upgraded from medium to high on this basis.

description: Dick et al. (2006) found that adolescents/children carrying at least one A allele of GABRA2 SNP rs279871 (from alcohol-dependent COGA families and community control families) were twice as likely to meet a three-symptom DSM-III-R threshold for conduct disorder (CD) (OR 2.0; 95% CI = 1.02-3.90).
original_authors: Danielle M. Dick; Laura Bierut; Anthony Hinrichs; Louis Fox; Kathleen K. Bucholz; John Kramer; Samuel Kuperman; Victor Hesselbrock; Marc Schuckit; Laura Almasy; Jay Tischfield; Bernice Porjesz; Henri Begleiter; John Nurnberger; Xiaoling Xuei; Howard J. Edenberg; Tatiana Foroud
original_title: The role of GABRA2 in risk for conduct disorder and alcohol and drug dependence across developmental stages
replication_authors: Joseph T. Sakai; Michael C. Stallings; Thomas J. Crowley; Heather L. Gelhorn; Matthew B. McQueen; Marissa A. Ehringer
replication_title: Test of association between GABRA2 (SNP rs279871) and adolescent conduct/alcohol use disorders utilizing a sample of clinic referred youth with serious substance and conduct problems, controls and available first degree relatives
explanation: A case-control test in the replication sample found a significant CD association (p=0.02) but in the opposite direction to Dick et al. (2006) (association with the GG genotype rather than the A allele), and this result did not survive Bonferroni correction (α=0.05/3=0.017); all family-based tests were non-significant (p=0.48 for CD) despite adequate power under most models. The paper itself is not internally consistent about how to characterize this: the Abstract states flatly that 'our results also do not support an association between rs279871 and CD' (reading like a failure to replicate), while the Discussion/Conclusion instead hedges, 'while our results do not definitively support nor refute the previously reported association between GABRA2 and CD, they offer another important piece of information on this topic.' Given one significant-but-reversed, uncorrected case-control finding alongside null family-based tests, and the authors' own unresolved framing, 'inconclusive' is the correct label and the ambiguity is genuine (originating in the paper, not in this review) rather than something further reading resolves.

description: Dutch-French bilinguals show greater cross-language agreement in how they name common household objects (bottles, jars, dishes, etc.) than corresponding Dutch-speaking and French-speaking monolinguals show between languages, indicating that bilingual naming patterns converge on a common pattern rather than paralleling each monolingual group separately.

replication_authors: Eef Ameel; Barbara C. Malt; Gert Storms; Fons Van Assche
replication_title: Semantic convergence in the bilingual lexicon
explanation: Reviewed body.md in full, including both studies and the General Discussion (not just Study 1, which is all the prior explanation cited). Study 1 (prototype convergence, new typicality-rating paradigm) found bilinguals' cross-language correlations significantly higher than monolinguals' both at the aggregate level (t(5)=3.514, p<.01) and for every one of the 6 category pairs individually, and at the individual-pairing level for both stimulus sets (t(1090)=29.3, p<.0001 bottles; t(1090)=18.6, p<.0001 dishes) -- unanimous support, no exceptions. Study 2 (boundary convergence, LINSEP dimensionality + outlier proportion, an independent paradigm using Ameel et al.'s original naming/MDS data) also came out confirmatory: bilingual categories needed fewer dimensions to separate linearly overall (t(13)=-2.59, p<.05; only the bottles subset reached significance alone, with 3/14 category pairs going the other direction, but the authors do not hedge the overall conclusion), and bilinguals showed a smaller outlier proportion than monolinguals in 11/14 (79%) category names, significantly more than chance (p<.05). The General Discussion states both results plainly as confirmed ('we found...', 'together these results indicate...') with no 'mixed'/'partial'/'some differences' hedging anywhere in the paper. Both independent tests of the underlying convergence claim from Ameel et al. (2005) succeeded, which is stronger and more specific evidence than the original review (which only checked Study 1) had considered, so I'm raising confidence to high. The residual reason this is 'conceptual' rather than a closer replication type stands: neither study re-runs the original naming task itself, instead testing typicality ratings and category-boundary structure as new manifestations of the same theoretical convergence claim.

explanation: Verified against the abstract, Results (3.2-3.3, Table 1-2) and Discussion. The abstract itself states the extension's outcome in the same terms as the description: '91% (n=20) were classified as responders at post-treatment... Remission rates were 73% (n=16) at post-treatment... OCD-related impairment and symptoms of anxiety and depression were significantly reduced.' The primary outcome (CY-BOCS) showed a significant time effect (F(3,19.7)=91.54, p<.001) with large within-group effect sizes at every assessment point (d=4.67 post, 4.98 at 3-month, 5.20 at 6-month follow-up), and gains were maintained at follow-up (no significant post-vs-follow-up differences). All three sub-measures named in the description -- large symptom reduction, high response rate, high remission rate -- are directly confirmed by these numbers, and the Discussion explicitly frames this as replicating the adult cET findings ('As for adults (Havnen et al., 2014; Havnen et al., 2016), the results demonstrate that concentrated Exposure Therapy (cET) is a promising treatment approach also for adolescents'). No hedging language ('differing results', 'mixed', 'partially') appears anywhere in the Discussion or Conclusion regarding this core claim; the stated limitations concern study design (no control group, small sample, self-report secondary measures) rather than the outcome itself. The only minor non-significant sub-result is the child-rated (not parent-rated) COIS-R impairment score at post-treatment (p=.09, though significant by 6-month follow-up, p=.002) -- a secondary functional-impairment measure not named in the description's claim about OCD symptom reduction and response/remission rates.

description: Using a dual perfusion-threshold approach with CT perfusion (CTP) imaging (rather than a single threshold) increases the accuracy of measuring the acute ischemic core in acute ischemic stroke patients.
original_authors: Bivard, Andrew; Spratt, Neil; Levi, Christopher; Parsons, Mark

replication_title: Defining acute ischemic stroke tissue pathophysiology with whole brain CT perfusion
explanation: Verified independently against body.md and references.json. Reference [25] is confirmed to be exactly this original study (Bivard, Spratt, Levi, Parsons; Brain 2011;134:3408-16; DOI 10.1093/brain/awr257) — all cited fields match. The Discussion states verbatim: 'Previous methods to improve the accuracy of measurement of the acute ischemic core using perfusion CT have used a duel [sic] threshold approach [25]. This study is a natural extension of the work showing that multiple thresholds are able to increase the accuracy and decrease the variability seen when measuring the acute core on CTP.' The Results/Discussion report the probability model was 'significantly closer in volume to the corresponding reference DWI volumes for both ischemic core or penumbra than single thresholds (P = 0.031)', with higher AUC (core 0.799 vs. single-threshold 0.73; penumbra 0.85 vs. 0.79) and lower variability (sensitivity 0.75/specificity 0.81 vs. 0.69/0.85). The Discussion concludes without hedging: 'In any event, the novel probability approach was more accurate than the single threshold approach to define both core and penumbra.' No 'mixed'/'some differences'/'partially' language qualifies this specific comparison anywhere in the Discussion; the paper's only caveats concern unrelated methodological choices (absolute CBF threshold value vs. other studies, reperfusion definition, AIF selection). This is an unambiguous success, and the method/context both changed (new cohort, whole-brain 320-slice scanner, multi- vs. dual-threshold model), consistent with the 'close extension' typology.
