explanation: Independently verified against Results/Discussion: source-strength (amplitude) Hemisphere x Group ANOVAs for the two overlapping rates the current MEG study tested (10 Hz and 20 Hz) found 'No significant main effects or interactions...(all F-values<3.68, p-values>0.10; see Fig. 5)' (Results, p.2957), and the Discussion confirms this directly against this citation: 'On the basis of the prior EEG literature, we expected that the two groups would show processing differences at all 4 modulation rates, however this was not the case', attributing the discrepancy to the prior single-electrode EEG measurement 'lacking the power of whole-head MEG'. This supports 'failure'. Confidence stays medium because genuine ambiguity remains: only the 20 Hz point of McAnally and Stein's original 20-80 Hz range was re-tested here, and the comparison crosses modality (raw single-electrode scalp AMFR amplitude vs. MEG source-localized dipole strength) — the authors themselves treat the null result as possibly a power/sensitivity artifact rather than a clean refutation.

description: Using single-electrode EEG, adults with dyslexia show significantly smaller amplitude modulation following response (AMFR) amplitude to AM white noise than controls, across modulation frequencies of 10-160 Hz.
original_authors: Peter Menell; Ken I. McAnally; John F. Stein
original_title: Psychophysical sensitivity and physiological response to amplitude modulation in adult dyslexic listeners
original_journal: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
replication_authors: Jarmo A. Hämäläinen; André Rupp; Fruzsina Soltész; Denes Szücs; Usha Goswami
replication_title: Reduced phase locking to slow amplitude modulation in adults with dyslexia: An MEG study
explanation: Narrowed the description: the original entry conflated two separate Menell et al. measures (a psychophysical AM-detection-threshold task, 10-320 Hz, and the AMFR amplitude, 10-160 Hz), but the current paper's Methods show no psychophysical/behavioral AM task at all -- its 'Behavioral assessments' are diagnostic IQ, reading/spelling and phonology tests used only for group classification, and the MEG procedure is passive (participants watched a silent movie). So the detection-threshold claim was never tested here and is removed from the description; only the AMFR-amplitude claim was actually assessed. For that claim, the overlapping rates (10 Hz, 20 Hz) were re-tested via whole-head MEG source-strength ANOVAs, which found 'No significant main effects or interactions...(all F-values<3.68, p-values>0.10; see Fig. 5)', directly contradicting Menell et al.'s reported significantly smaller AMFR in dyslexics at these same rates. The Discussion confirms this was an explicit, failed expectation ('we expected... processing differences at all 4 modulation rates, however this was not the case'). Confidence raised to high: the narrowed claim is now clean (no untested sub-measure folded in) and the null result is unambiguous and directly attributed by the authors to this exact prior finding.

description: In a Go/NoGo response inhibition task with healthy adults, greater response variability (intra-individual coefficient of variation of reaction time) was positively correlated with false alarm error rates, indicating that less behaviorally consistent participants were less successful at inhibiting prepotent responses.
original_authors: Mark A. Bellgrove; Robert Hester; Hugh Garavan
original_title: The functional neuroanatomical correlates of response variability: evidence from a response inhibition task
replication_authors: Diane Swick; Nikki Honzel; Jary Larsen; Victoria Ashley
replication_title: Increased response variability as a marker of executive dysfunction in veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder
explanation: Verified independently against body.md. The authors explicitly predicted and then confirmed this correlation in a new population (combat veterans with PTSD and veteran controls), stating in the Discussion 'More variable RTs were in turn associated with a greater number of errors, replicating previous findings in adult controls (Bellgrove et al., 2004)' and in the Conclusion 'RT variability was strongly correlated with false alarm errors, replicating previous results in controls (Bellgrove et al., 2004; Simmonds et al., 2007)'; the Pearson correlations were significant in both task conditions (50/50: r=.56, p<.0001; 90/10: r=.49, p<.0001), matching Bellgrove's original direction. This is the only sub-measure named in the entry's description and it fully replicated, so 'success' is warranted. Confidence kept at medium rather than raised to high because of a genuine interpretive wrinkle the paper itself does not address: the text introduces this analysis with 'the relationship between RT variability and error rate was examined across groups' (i.e., the correlation appears to be computed on the pooled patient+control sample, n=79), and no table reports it separately within the control group alone. Since PTSD patients independently show both higher ICV and more false alarms than controls (both group main effects significant), part of the pooled correlation could reflect a between-group mean shift rather than the purely within-person relationship Bellgrove demonstrated in a single homogeneous healthy-adult sample. The paper does not report or rule this out, so whether the replication is as clean as the authors' own framing suggests is not fully resolvable from the text.

description: Depressed patients show reduced (blunted) heartbeat-evoked potential (HEP) amplitude compared to healthy individuals, reflecting altered bodily/interoceptive perception associated with depression.
original_authors: Filipa Campos Viola; Janneke Terhaar; Karl-Jürgen Bär; Stefan Debener; Terhaar, Janneke; Viola, Filipa Campos; Bär, Karl-Jürgen; Debener, Stefan; Ishii, Ryouhei; Canuet, Leonides
original_title: Heartbeat evoked potentials mirror altered body perception in depressed patients
replication_authors: Lampros Perogamvros; Hyeong-Dong Park; Laurence Bayer; Aurore A. Perrault; Olaf Blanke; Sophie Schwartz
replication_title: Increased heartbeat-evoked potential during REM sleep in nightmare disorder
explanation: Verified against Results §3.4 and Discussion §4.2. Perogamvros et al. tested Terhaar et al. (2012)'s blunted-HEP-in-depression finding as an a priori hypothesis in nightmare patients whose depression scores were all subclinical (BDI < 17 was an exclusion criterion), and found a significant negative correlation between frontal HEP amplitude and BDI in the nightmare group (Kendall's τ = −0.50, p = .03) but not in controls (τ = −0.05, p = .84). Critically, the direct test of whether these two correlations actually differ from each other was only a one-tailed statistical trend (p = .059), and the authors explicitly state: 'we cannot draw any strong conclusion in this regard because the difference of correlations between groups showed only a statistical trend for significance' (§4.2). This is the authors' own stated hedge, not an artifact of ambiguous reporting: a significant within-group correlation exists, but the group-comparison test needed to actually parallel Terhaar's depressed-vs-healthy contrast did not reach significance. The ambiguity is genuine, so inconclusive/medium is the correct call.

description: Both musical novices and professional musicians can identify the individual winners of live music performance competitions from silent video alone, but not from audio-only or audio-plus-video recordings, even though both groups report that sound matters most to their judgments of an individual musician's performance quality.
original_authors: Tsay, Chia-Jung
original_title: Sight over sound in the judgment of music performance
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Chia-Jung Tsay
replication_title: The vision heuristic: Judging music ensembles by sight alone
replication_journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
explanation: Across a program of six experiments the author (the same researcher who conducted the original study) extended the 'vision heuristic' from judgments of individual musicians to judgments of musical groups/ensembles and symphony orchestras, keeping the same video-only/audio-only/video-plus-sound paradigm and comparison to chance. As in the original, participants overwhelmingly said sound mattered most (e.g. 80.7% in Exp 1, 81.3% in Exp 6) yet identified competition winners above chance from silent video in most experiments while audio-only performance was at or below chance; the General Discussion concludes 'people appear to overweight visual information in their evaluation of music performances. This vision heuristic rapidly guides people, even domain experts, toward judgments.' Results for professional musicians (Experiment 6) were weaker and only reached significance in one of four conditions, which the authors themselves note as a caveat, but the overall pattern across experiments is framed by the authors as confirming and extending the original effect.

description: Using a microswitch-linked computer system that presents brief stimulus samples, persons with multiple (intellectual, motor and sensory) disabilities can actively choose among environmental stimuli (selecting preferred ones, bypassing non-preferred ones) and request repetitions of preferred stimuli, demonstrating purposeful choice behavior.
original_authors: Giulio E. Lancioni; Mark F. O’Reilly; Nirbhay N. Singh; Jeff Sigafoos; D. Oliva; Laura Severini
original_title: Enabling persons with multiple disabilities to choose among environmental stimuli and request stimulus repetitions through microswitch and computer technology
replication_authors: Giulio E. Lancioni; Nirbhay N. Singh; Mark F. O’Reilly; Jeff Sigafoos; Francesca Buonocunto; Valentina Sacco; Fabio Colonna; Jorge Navarro; Crocifissa Lanzilotti; Doretta Oliva
replication_title: Post-coma persons with motor and communication/consciousness impairments choose among environmental stimuli and request stimulus repetitions via assistive technology
explanation: The Abstract explicitly states 'All participants asked for the repetition of preferred stimuli and showed minimal responding in relation to non-preferred stimuli' — confirming that Edith, despite comparatively 'modest' response frequency (mean 18 responses vs. ~116 and ~94 for Alfred and Becky), still exhibited both target sub-measures (repetition requests and selective avoidance of non-preferred stimuli). The Discussion attributes her lower magnitude to her more severe clinical status (lower Rancho/CRS-R levels, fluctuating wakefulness) rather than to a failure of the choice paradigm, and states she showed 'positive engagement and presumably purposeful choice behavior.' No language in the paper ('mixed', 'differing results', 'partially') qualifies the 'support and extend' conclusion; the variation across the three participants is one of degree (magnitude of responding) rather than kind, so all sub-measures named in the description — choosing preferred over non-preferred stimuli, requesting repetitions, and demonstrating purposeful choice — replicated for all three participants.

description: Microsatellite markers in the CAPON region of chromosome 1q22 show linkage disequilibrium (association) with schizophrenia susceptibility, as found in a Canadian family sample.
original_authors: Linda M. Brzustowicz; Jaime Simone; Paria Mohseni; Jared E. Hayter; Kathleen A. Hodgkinson; Eva W.C. Chow; Anne S. Bassett
original_title: Linkage disequilibrium mapping of schizophrenia susceptibility to the CAPON region of chromosome 1q22
replication_authors: Ana Miranda; Jenny García; Carlos López; Derek Gordon; Carlos Palacio; Gabriel Restrepo; Juan Ortiz; Gabriel Montoya; Carlos Cardeño; Jorge Calle; María López; Omer Campo; Gabriel Bedoya; Andrés Ruiz-Linares; Jorge Ospina-Duque
replication_title: Putative association of the carboxy-terminal PDZ ligand of neuronal nitric oxide synthase gene (CAPON) with schizophrenia in a Colombian population
explanation: Reviewed body.md in full (Letter to the Editors, single-page report). In 110 Colombian family trios, the CAPON-region marker D1S1679 (23.5 kb from CAPON's 3' end) had TDTae p_corr=0.019, described by the authors as 'still significant after Bonferroni correction' -- but the very next sentence states 'When correcting for multiple test across all markers, none marker showed significance.' The paper never reconciles these two corrections for the same marker/data, and its own conclusion is hedged as providing only 'further evidence for the existence of a schizophrenia susceptibility locus in 1q21-22,' not a confirmed replication of the CAPON association. This is a genuine ambiguity in the source itself (contradictory correction outcomes, non-committal author language), not a gap in extraction, so inconclusive/medium is the correct call and is not being upgraded absent new evidence.

description: Using survival analysis in a Kentucky sample, schizophrenia patients showed an age at onset of daily smoking (AODS) that was significantly different from both healthy controls and mood-disordered patients, with schizophrenia patients continuing to show a high hazard of smoking initiation through their 20s when controls' initiation rates had already declined.
original_authors: Jose de Leon; Francisco J. Diaz; Thea Rogers; Debra Browne; Lori Dinsmore
original_title: Initiation of daily smoking and nicotine dependence in schizophrenia and mood disorders
replication_authors: Francisco J. Diaz; Diana M. Velásquez; Margaret T. Susce; Jose de Leon
replication_title: The association between schizophrenia and smoking: Unexplained by either the illness or the prodromal period
explanation: Verified against the paper's Results/Discussion. The new, larger Kentucky sample (N=258 schizophrenia, 166 mood disorders, 381 controls) replicated a significant 3-way difference in AODS hazard curves (log-rank chi2=86.5, df=2, pb0.001), and after adjusting for gender/education both schizophrenia (chi2=36.5, df=1, pb0.001) and mood-disordered (chi2=27.4, df=1, pb0.001) patients differed significantly from controls, with schizophrenia patients' hazard staying elevated through their 20s after controls' initiation had already declined -- so that portion of the original finding replicated cleanly. But schizophrenia and mood-disordered patients did NOT differ significantly from each other (p=0.8), directly contradicting the original 2002 study's significant schizophrenia-vs-mood-disorder difference; the authors state this explicitly: 'These survival analyses did not find significant differences between schizophrenia and mood disorders as did our first Kentucky study.' Per the rule that every named sub-measure must replicate for a 'success' label, this mix of one replicated and one non-replicated sub-claim is correctly scored 'inconclusive.'

description: After excluding schizophrenia patients whose smoking initiation could plausibly be attributed to the prodromal period (using a cutoff of at least 5 years before schizophrenia onset), schizophrenia patients still showed a significantly higher hazard of starting daily smoking than controls, indicating the prodromal period does not explain the increased smoking initiation in schizophrenia.
original_authors: Manuel Gurpegui; José M. Martínez-Ortega; Mariano Aguilar; Francisco J. Díaz; Hernando M. Quintana; José de León
original_title: Smoking initiation and schizophrenia: a replication study in a Spanish sample
replication_authors: Francisco J. Diaz; Diana M. Velásquez; Margaret T. Susce; Jose de Leon
replication_title: The association between schizophrenia and smoking: Unexplained by either the illness or the prodromal period
explanation: Verified against the paper's Introduction/Methods/Results. The original Gurpegui et al. (2005) prodromal-exclusion analysis, described in this paper's introduction, compared 107 Spanish schizophrenia patients who started smoking >=5 years before schizophrenia onset against 290 controls and found a significantly higher hazard for schizophrenia even after exclusion (chi2=20.7, df=1, pb0.001, adjusting for gender/education). This paper's new Kentucky sample applied an analogous proxy cutoff (>=5 years before starting psychiatric medication, since exact schizophrenia-onset dates were unavailable; N=111 schizophrenia patients vs N=172 ever-smoker controls) and found the same pattern: hazard curves significantly different (chi2=9.4, df=1, p=0.002), remaining significant after adjustment (chi2=4.8, df=1, p=0.03). The paper states this directly supports 'our main conclusion: neither schizophrenia illness, nor treatment, nor the prodromal period appears to explain the association between schizophrenia and daily cigarette smoking.' No caveats or contrary findings are reported anywhere for this specific schizophrenia-vs-controls comparison, so this single, narrowly-defined sub-measure replicated cleanly.

description: Training improves direction discrimination of moving dots at the trained direction, but this learning does not transfer to an untrained opposite direction, demonstrating strict direction specificity of motion direction learning.
original_authors: Karlene Ball; Robert Sekuler
original_title: Direction-specific improvement in motion discrimination
replication_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Yu-Xiang Yang
replication_title: Perceptual learning of motion direction discrimination transfers to an opposite direction with TPE training
explanation: Verified against body.md Section 3.1: the authors state 'We first replicated direction specificity in a foveal motion direction discrimination task' and found significant learning at the trained direction (MPI=40.0%, t=7.21, df=5, p<0.001) but no significant transfer to the opposite direction (MPI=5.7%, t=1.06, df=5, p=0.17), 'showing very strong direction specificity of motion direction learning.' This part of the classification (success) is unambiguous and well-supported. The residual uncertainty is citation attribution only: Ball & Sekuler (1982, Science, 'A specific and enduring improvement in visual motion discrimination') and (1987, Vision Research, 'Direction-specific improvement in motion discrimination') are cited jointly everywhere in this paper's text for the specificity claim, and both papers are by the same authors on the same general topic. I attempted to check the 1987 paper's own abstract independently (PubMed/ScienceDirect/Science.org) but could not retrieve reliable primary-source text (paywalled/blocked). The 1987 title is the closer semantic match to 'direction-specific,' so it remains the better-supported guess for original_title/journal/volume/pages, but this is inference from title wording rather than confirmed abstract content, so confidence stays medium.

description: Using a training-plus-exposure (TPE) method in which participants are trained on one orientation and later exposed to an orthogonal orientation via an irrelevant contrast-discrimination task, orientation discrimination learning that is normally specific to the trained orientation transfers completely to the orthogonal orientation.
original_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Gong-Liang Zhang; Lu-Qi Xiao; Stanley A. Klein; Dennis M. Levi; Cong Yu
original_title: Rule-based learning explains visual perceptual learning and its specificity and transfer
replication_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Yu-Xiang Yang
replication_title: Perceptual learning of motion direction discrimination transfers to an opposite direction with TPE training
explanation: Re-examined body.md Section 3.1 (Experiment I) against the original claim being extended, which is specifically COMPLETE transfer via successive TPE. Applying the successive design (train then later expose) to motion direction, transfer to the untrained opposite direction was statistically significant (MPI=20.3%, t=3.60, df=5, p=0.008; overall TPE effect MPI=24.6%, p=0.010) but only partial: the transfer index was TI=0.62, not the 1.0 that would indicate complete transfer, and the paper itself says the overall effect was 'about two thirds of the 40.0% improvement due to direct training,' concluding only that 'a majority' of learning transferred -- language the authors reserve for this experiment, in explicit contrast to the simultaneous-TPE design (Experiment II, TI=1.2) which they describe as 'complete transfer.' The authors also report that two of the six participants showed no transfer effect at all and treat them as outliers, i.e. the effect did not hold uniformly across the sample. Since the entry's description asserts transfer that is 'complete,' and the actual successive-TPE finding is significant-but-partial with non-uniform individual results, this is partial support rather than a full replication of completeness, so it is reclassified from success to inconclusive per the rule that partial support is inconclusive, not success (contrast with the simultaneous-TPE entry, which genuinely achieved complete transfer and stays 'success').

description: Using a training-plus-exposure (TPE) method in which participants are trained on one orientation while simultaneously exposed to an orthogonal orientation via an irrelevant contrast-discrimination task (alternating staircases), orientation discrimination learning transfers completely to the orthogonal orientation.
original_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Gong-Liang Zhang; Lu-Qi Xiao; Stanley A. Klein; Dennis M. Levi; Cong Yu
original_title: Rule-based learning explains visual perceptual learning and its specificity and transfer
replication_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Yu-Xiang Yang
replication_title: Perceptual learning of motion direction discrimination transfers to an opposite direction with TPE training
explanation: Applying the simultaneous TPE design to the motion direction domain (Experiment II), learning transferred to the untrained opposite direction by a similar amount as at the trained direction (MPI=26.9% vs 28.0%, not significantly different, p=0.44), yielding a transfer index of 1.2, which the authors describe as 'indicating complete transfer of motion direction learning.'

description: When the order of TPE training is reversed (exposure to the orthogonal orientation via an irrelevant task precedes rather than follows/accompanies orientation discrimination training), the learning transfer to the orthogonal orientation disappears.
original_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Gong-Liang Zhang; Lu-Qi Xiao; Stanley A. Klein; Dennis M. Levi; Cong Yu
original_title: Rule-based learning explains visual perceptual learning and its specificity and transfer
replication_authors: Jun-Yun Zhang; Yu-Xiang Yang
replication_title: Perceptual learning of motion direction discrimination transfers to an opposite direction with TPE training
explanation: The authors explicitly state their aim to 'replicate an interesting finding with TPE-enabled orientation learning transfer in motion learning tasks' regarding reversed order, and found that with reversed-order TPE, motion direction learning trained at one direction (MPI=29.3%, p=0.002) failed to transfer to the opposite direction (MPI=3.5%, p=0.39), concluding 'the transfer of motion direction learning also disappeared with a reversed-order TPE procedure,' matching the original orientation-domain finding.

description: Semantically related prime and target words facilitate (positively prime) one another in lexical processing of Chinese compound words, a 'pure' semantic priming effect reported in prior work on morphology, orthography, and phonology in reading Chinese compounds.
original_authors: Xiaolin Zhou; William Marslen-Wilson; Marcus Taft; Hua Shu
original_title: Morphology, orthography, and phonology in reading Chinese compound words
replication_authors: Phil D. Liu; Catherine McBride-Chang
replication_title: Morphological processing of Chinese compounds from a grammatical view
explanation: Reviewed body.md Results/Discussion in full. The paper's own test of the 'pure' semantic priming effect (SMDS vs. DMDS: shared meaning only, no shared morphological structure) was NOT significant when collapsed across compound types (t1(20)=1.53, p>.10; t2(29)=1.46, p>.10). Broken down by structure, it was significant only for coordinative compounds (t1(20)=2.78, p<.05; t2(12)=2.09, p<.10, marginal by items — 'semantic information alone could activate the lexical representation of targets') and absent for subordinate compounds (omnibus F1(3,60)=0.85, ns; F2(3,25)=0.55, ns — 'the single activation of semantic information only was not sufficient to prime'). This confirms a genuine partial/mixed replication across the two structure conditions of the same experiment, correctly scored inconclusive rather than success. The original target remains hedged ('e.g., Zhou et al., 1999; Zwitserlood, 1994') with no other passage in the paper separately attributing the replication to one cited study over the other, so which specific finding each entry maps to is a genuine, irresolvable ambiguity in the source text itself, not an extraction artifact.

description: Semantically related prime and target words facilitate (positively prime) one another in lexical processing of compound words, a 'pure' semantic priming effect reported in prior work on semantic transparency in the processing and representation of Dutch compounds.
original_authors: Pienie Zwitserlood
original_title: The role of semantic transparency in the processing and representation of Dutch compounds
replication_authors: Phil D. Liu; Catherine McBride-Chang
replication_title: Morphological processing of Chinese compounds from a grammatical view
explanation: Reviewed body.md Results/Discussion in full. Using a Chinese-compound paradigm quite different from Zwitserlood's Dutch compound-transparency design, the paper's own test of the 'pure' semantic priming effect (SMDS vs. DMDS) was NOT significant when collapsed across compound types (t1(20)=1.53, p>.10; t2(29)=1.46, p>.10). By structure, it was significant only for coordinative compounds (t1(20)=2.78, p<.05; t2(12)=2.09, p<.10, marginal by items — 'semantic information alone could activate the lexical representation of targets') and absent for subordinate compounds (omnibus F1(3,60)=0.85, ns; F2(3,25)=0.55, ns). This confirms a genuine mixed result across the two structure conditions, correctly scored inconclusive. The specific target study is still hedged with an 'e.g.' citing Zhou et al. (1999) and Zwitserlood (1994) jointly, with no other passage separately identifying Zwitserlood (1994) as a discrete replication target rather than general background — a genuine, irresolvable ambiguity in the source text.

description: The MAOA-L allele interacts with childhood maltreatment (abuse/neglect) to increase depressive symptomatology among adolescents.
original_authors: Cicchetti, Dante; Rogosch, Fred A.; Sturge-Apple, Melissa L.
original_title: Interactions of child maltreatment and serotonin transporter and monoamine oxidase A polymorphisms: depressive symptomatology among adolescents from low socioeconomic status backgrounds
replication_authors: Philippe A. Melas; Yabin Wei; Chloe C. Y. Wong; Louise K. Sjöholm; Elin Åberg; Jonathan Mill; Martin Schalling; Yvonne Forsell; Catharina Lavebratt
replication_title: Genetic and epigenetic associations of MAOA and NR3C1 with depression and childhood adversities
explanation: The authors state: 'In accord with these [Cicchetti et al., 2007] findings, and by using a much larger study group, we were able to show that MAOA-L females with childhood adversities had a higher risk of developing depression compared to those with the MAOA-H genotype' (interaction Wald=16.4, p=0.006 in females; combined sexes Wald=26.8, p<0.001). Correction on re-review: the male interaction was in fact also statistically significant (Wald=13.4, p=0.02), not a 'non-significant trend' as previously stated -- it was merely weaker than in females and, unlike females, showed no clear dose-response across adversity-count subgroups. A more consequential caveat found on review of the Methods ('Definition of childhood adversities'): this study's adversity measure is early parental death, parental divorce, financial problems, and other familial constraints -- it does NOT include abuse or neglect, the specific maltreatment Cicchetti et al. (2007) studied. Population (adults vs. adolescents) and outcome (clinical diagnosis vs. symptom scale) also differ. The authors nonetheless explicitly present the result as confirmatory of Cicchetti et al., consistent with a 'close extension' rather than a direct replication, but the adversity-type mismatch means the specific abuse/neglect claim was not itself tested -- genuine ambiguity remains about how much weight to give this as a replication of that claim.

description: Childhood abuse is associated with hypermethylation of the NR3C1 (glucocorticoid receptor) exon 1-F promoter region, particularly near NGFI-A transcription-factor binding sites, in postmortem human hippocampus.
original_authors: McGowan, Patrick O.; Sasaki, Aya; D'Alessio, Ana C.; Dymov, Sergiy; Labonte, Benoit; Szyf, Moshe; Turecki, Gustavo; Meaney, Michael J.
original_title: Epigenetic regulation of the glucocorticoid receptor in human brain associates with childhood abuse
replication_authors: Philippe A. Melas; Yabin Wei; Chloe C. Y. Wong; Louise K. Sjöholm; Elin Åberg; Jonathan Mill; Martin Schalling; Yvonne Forsell; Catharina Lavebratt
replication_title: Genetic and epigenetic associations of MAOA and NR3C1 with depression and childhood adversities
explanation: The authors write: 'In the present report we analysed the same region as in the study by McGowan and colleagues and found an association of EPD with hypermethylation of CpGs located near NGFI-A binding sites,' and the one CpG unit reaching significance (CpG 35: EPD 19.1% vs. non-EPD 13.7%, p=0.005 by both linear regression and Mann-Whitney) 'belongs to the site that is closest to a canonical NGFI-A binding region (McGowan et al., 2009)' -- the same specific site emphasized in the original study, and this core finding is not hedged as preliminary (unlike the separate three-way MAOA-mediation analysis, which the authors do call exploratory given small subgroup sizes). Important caveat confirmed on review of the Methods: childhood abuse itself was never measured in this cohort -- the adversity variable here is early parental death (EPD), parental divorce, financial problems, and familial constraints, and only EPD (not abuse, which was not assessed) showed the hypermethylation association. The authors themselves caution that 'the association of EPD only (and not of the other adversities...) gives support to the recent recommendation of not treating childhood maltreatment as a unitary construct... but trying to distinguish and study each adversity subtype independently' -- i.e. they do not claim this generalizes to abuse. This is a same-region, same-site conceptual extension to a different early-life adversity (also differing in tissue: saliva vs. postmortem brain) with a positive result, but it is not a direct test of the abuse-specific claim, so genuine ambiguity remains about how strong a replication this counts as.

description: Barro's (1990) cross-country endogenous growth model found that government spending and taxation have opposing effects on economic growth: productive government expenditure raises the marginal productivity of capital and growth, while the taxation needed to fund non-productive expenditure lowers it, implying a growth-maximizing tax rate; in cross-country regressions non-productive spending was significantly negatively related to growth while productive spending was positively but insignificantly related to growth.
original_authors: Barro, Robert J.
original_title: Government spending in a simple model of endogenous growth
replication_authors: Gerald W. Scully
replication_title: Optimal Taxation, Economic Growth and Income Inequality
explanation: Re-estimating Barro's model with U.S. time-series (rather than cross-country) data, the authors obtain a point estimate of the growth-maximizing tax rate (25.1%) whose 't-value is well below the 90 percent confidence level,' and when spending is split into productive/non-productive components the non-productive coefficient is significant (matching Barro's cross-country pattern) but the residuals are non-stationary, so 'the regression result needs to be taken with reservation' — a mixed, qualified outcome rather than a clean confirmation or failure. Checked the paper's Conclusions section (Section 5) directly: it restates the identical qualifications without resolving them ('one does not have much confidence in the estimate'; 'caution is warranted over these regression results'), and footnote 11 additionally finds the relationship between the productive/non-productive spending series and growth is bicausal, so 'no direction of causality... can be inferred.' This confirms the hedge is the paper's own consistent framing end-to-end, not an isolated caveat — the ambiguity is genuine, so confidence stays medium rather than being upgraded on a second read.

description: Scully's model relates total government taxation as a share of GDP to the economic growth rate, positing that growth rises with taxation at low tax levels (productive spending) and falls at high tax levels (non-productive spending), implying a specific growth-maximizing tax rate; the model was originally estimated using New Zealand data.
original_authors: Scully, Gerald W.
original_title: Taxation and economic growth in New Zealand
replication_authors: Gerald W. Scully
replication_title: Optimal Taxation, Economic Growth and Income Inequality
explanation: Applying Scully's growth-tax model (whose derivation the authors attribute to Scully, 1996) to United States time-series data 1960-90 with unit-root and cointegration corrections, the authors report 'there is empirical confidence in the result that the optimal or growth-maximizing tax rate for the United States, over this period, is 19.3 percent,' with a highly significant coefficient and stationary residuals. Verified against the paper's Conclusions section (Section 5), which restates this identically with no hedge ('The coefficient is highly significant, and the residuals are stationary') — a sharp contrast to the qualified Barro result in the same paper. Footnote 12 adds a robustness check not previously noted: substituting the actual tax rate (T/Y) for the anticipated rate (G/Y) used in the main specification changes the estimate only slightly, and 'the conclusions about the optimal size of the fiscal state are not materially affected by this choice of the tax rate.' This specification-robustness evidence resolves the flagged ambiguity, supporting an upgrade to high confidence.

description: Masked (subliminal) number primes influence speeded classification of visible target numbers as smaller or larger than 5, with faster responses when prime and target are congruent (same side of 5) than incongruent, demonstrating semantic-level processing of subliminal numerical stimuli, alongside neural evidence (fMRI/ERP) of motor and parietal involvement.
original_authors: Stanislas Dehaene; Lionel Naccache; Gurvan Le Clec'H; Etienne Koechlin; Michael Mueller; Ghislaine Dehaene-Lambertz; Pierre-FranÇois van de Moortele; Denis Le Bihan
original_title: Imaging unconscious semantic priming
replication_authors: Sid Kouider; Stanislas Dehaene
replication_title: Subliminal Number Priming Within and Across the Visual and Auditory Modalities
explanation: Experiment 1 reproduced the original masked congruity effect (and repetition priming) for both masked and unmasked trials, with the masked-priming regression intercept significant (49 ms, p<.0005) even when extrapolated to zero prime visibility; the authors state 'this first experiment suggests that both repetition and congruity priming occur not only for visible but also for subliminal number stimuli.'

description: Subliminal (masked) congruity priming for numbers generalizes from practiced primes to novel, unpracticed primes that were never presented as targets, indicating that subliminal number priming has a genuinely semantic locus rather than being restricted to overlearned stimulus-response associations.
original_authors: Lionel Naccache; Stanislas Dehaene
original_title: Unconscious semantic priming extends to novel unseen stimuli
replication_authors: Sid Kouider; Stanislas Dehaene
replication_title: Subliminal Number Priming Within and Across the Visual and Auditory Modalities
explanation: Across three successive, progressively refined experiments (Experiments 2-4) testing generalization to unpracticed primes, none individually showed a robust, significant congruity effect for novel primes ('none of the three experiments containing novel primes (Experiments 2-4) showed a robust and significant effect of generalization'), though small trends in the expected direction were consistently observed and became significant only when experiments were pooled (6 ms, p<.02); the authors call the outcome 'ambiguous' and 'difficult to interpret'.

description: Initial exertion of self-control (a depleting task) impairs performance — specifically accuracy, not response time — on a subsequent, unrelated task requiring self-regulation (the 'ego depletion' effect).
original_authors: Roy F. Baumeister; Ellen Bratslavsky; Mark Muraven; Dianne M. Tice
original_title: Ego depletion: Is the active self a limited resource?
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Junhua Dang; Ying Liu; Xiaoping Liu; Lihua Mao
replication_title: The Ego Could Be Depleted, Providing Initial Exertion Is 					Depleting
explanation: Reviewed the full Results/Discussion (not just the summary sentence). The authors explicitly designate accuracy on the antisaccade task as the sole preregistered primary DV ('The primary dependent variable was the accuracy of the antisaccade task'). Depletion-condition accuracy (M = 0.60, SD = 0.18) was significantly worse than control (M = 0.68, SD = 0.15), t(174) = 2.92, p = .004, Hedge's g = 0.48, 95% CI [0.18, 0.78] — and this held controlling for age/gender, F(1,172) = 7.52, p = .007, and controlling for RT as a covariate, F(1,173) = 12.45, p = .001, which the authors note rules out a speed-accuracy tradeoff account. All four manipulation-check items (effort, difficulty, fatigue, frustration) differed significantly between conditions, confirming the Stroop manipulation was experienced as more depleting than the congruent control task. A secondary measure, RT, showed no significant group difference (t(174) = 0.66, p = .508) — but the paper is explicit that RT was not the primary confirmatory outcome, so this null does not qualify the main finding; the description has been narrowed to reflect that only accuracy (not RT) replicated. Exploratory interaction tests with three individual-difference moderators (action orientation, willpower beliefs, trait self-control) were all non-significant, but these concern moderation, not the core replication claim in this entry. Critically, neither the Abstract nor the Discussion contains any hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'some differences', etc.) — both state the effect unqualified ('The results demonstrated a significant ego depletion effect'; 'the current preregistered experiment demonstrated a significant ego depletion effect ... comparable to that found in Dang's (in press) meta-analysis'). This is an unambiguous, robustly-checked success on the specific (accuracy) claim, so confidence is upgraded from medium to high.

description: Using taxometric analysis (MAXCOV) of BDI items reflecting distress/discouragement (e.g., dissatisfaction, self-blame, suicidal ideation, indecisiveness) in clinical samples, the original study found these depression indicators are dimensional rather than taxonic.
original_authors: Ruscio, John; Ruscio, Ayelet Meron
original_title: Informing the continuity controversy: A taxometric analysis of depression
replication_authors: Steven R. H. Beach; Nader Amir
replication_title: Is depression taxonic, dimensional, or both?
explanation: The authors explicitly state they replicate the original finding: 'the taxometric analysis using the eight distress items is broadly consistent with that of Ruscio and Ruscio (2000)... we conclude as did Ruscio and Ruscio (2000) that the distress indicators do not show evidence of taxonicity,' and in the Discussion note 'our replication of their results for the distress indicators adds considerable strength to their conclusion that the distress item set is truly dimensional.'

description: Kerpelman and Himmelfarb (1971) found that greater consistency of initial reinforcement about a target person's behaviors (100% vs. 80% or 70% of trials reinforcing the same valence) produced a larger, more dramatic shift in attitudes toward that target when subsequent counterattitudinal information was presented.
original_authors: Kerpelman, Jonathan A.; Himmelfarb, Samuel
original_title: Partial reinforcement effects in attitude acquisition and counterconditioning
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Robert J. Rydell; Allen R. McConnell
replication_title: Understanding implicit and explicit attitude change: A systems of reasoning analysis.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: The authors modeled Experiment 1 directly on Kerpelman and Himmelfarb's (1971) attitude-learning paradigm (computerizing it, adding an implicit attitude/IAT measure, and using 100%/75% rather than 100%/80%/70% reinforcement) and explicitly state the interaction 'reflects the much larger effect of counterattitudinal condition on explicit attitude extremity in the 100% reinforcement condition than in the 75% reinforcement condition (replicating Kerpelman & Himmelfarb, 1971)'; the same pattern was again confirmed for explicit attitudes in Experiments 2 and 3.

description: Rydell, McConnell, Mackie, and Strain (in press) found that when a target person's subliminally primed valence was paired with consciously presented (supraliminal) behavioral information of the opposite valence, explicit attitudes toward the target reflected the valence of the supraliminal (consciously available) information, whereas implicit attitudes reflected the valence of the subliminal primes.
original_authors: Rydell, Robert J.; McConnell, Allen R.; Mackie, Diane M.; Strain, Laura M.
original_title: Of two minds: Forming and changing valence-inconsistent implicit and explicit attitudes
replication_authors: Robert J. Rydell; Allen R. McConnell
replication_title: Understanding implicit and explicit attitude change: A systems of reasoning analysis.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Experiment 5 used a modified version of the subliminal-priming paradigm ('similar to Rydell et al., in press') with neutral (rather than counter-valent) supraliminal behavioral information. Results were unambiguous, not merely partial: explicit attitudes showed no significant effects whatsoever (F(1,48)=1.66, ns, and no other significant effects), while implicit attitudes showed the single predicted significant Condition x Time interaction (F(1,48)=10.02, p<.005), with clean simple effects in the expected direction for both prime orders (p=.03 and p=.02). The Discussion states plainly: 'Experiment 5 demonstrated that implicit, but not explicit, attitudes were sensitive to the subliminal presentation of the priming words' -- reproducing the implicit/explicit dissociation Rydell et al. (in press) reported, with no hedging language in the paper's own account. Verified the citation is not a mismatch: the reference list (body.md line 1749-1751) confirms 'Rydell, R. J., McConnell, A. R., Mackie, D. M., & Strain, L. M. (in press). Of two minds: Forming and changing valence inconsistent implicit and explicit attitudes. Psychological Science.' -- authors, title, and journal all match exactly; the year is genuinely absent because the source paper cites this work only as '(in press)' throughout (7 occurrences), never with a year, so 'in press' is the correct and complete year value.

description: University students who attempted to answer prequestions about upcoming textbook material before reading it recalled more of the passage content than students who were shown the same prequestions but were not asked to try to answer them (instead judging whether the questions were well written).
original_authors: Pressley, Michael; Tanenbaum, Rebecca; McDaniel, Mark A.; Wood, Eileen
original_title: What happens when university students try to answer prequestions that accompany textbook material?
replication_authors: Lindsey E. Richland; Nate Kornell; Liche Sean Kao
replication_title: The pretesting effect: Do unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance learning?
explanation: Experiment 5 added a 'question learning' condition explicitly modeled on Pressley et al.'s (1990) no-answer exposure condition. Reviewed the paper's overview of the five experiments (preceding Experiment 1, not previously quoted in this entry), which states in advance: 'Experiment 5 sought to differentiate between reading potential test questions and attempting to answer test questions before studying. Similar to Pressley et al. (1990), we manipulated whether participants memorized the pretest questions versus produced an answer to the same questions.' Combined with the Experiment 5 section's explicit directional prediction 'in agreement with Pressley et al. (1990),' this shows the authors deliberately designed the manipulation to test Pressley et al.'s finding, even though they never use the word 'replicate.' The test-and-study condition significantly outperformed the question-learning condition (t(48) = 2.04, p = .02, one-tailed, d = 0.59), matching the direction of Pressley et al.'s original finding, and the Discussion states plainly: 'Attempting to answer a prequestion was significantly more effective than reading the same question and attempting to memorize it without making an attempt to retrieve the answer.' This is the only sub-measure named in the description and it replicated cleanly (a control check on untested/non-italicized items showed no group differences, consistent with the intended contrast, not a partial result). Differences in materials (science essay vs. textbook passage) and question format (fill-in-the-blank vs. dichotomous) keep this a conceptual rather than direct replication. Confidence raised to high based on the newly located 'Present Experiments' passage, which resolves the previous uncertainty about whether the design correspondence was deliberate.

description: Using 20 dichotomous items from a mental status questionnaire and Bayes' theorem to classify 841 older individuals as having dementia or not, and comparing these taxometric classifications against clinical diagnosis, Golden (1982) found high concordance and concluded that dementia has a categorical (taxonic) rather than dimensional latent structure.
original_authors: Golden, Robert R.
original_title: A taxometric model for the detection of a conjectured latent taxon
replication_authors: Glenn D. Walters
replication_title: Dementia: Continuum or distinct entity?
explanation: Confirmed against the paper's own Abstract (body.md lines 6-15, not quoted in the prior pass), which states unhedged that the study 'found results more consistent with dementia as a dimensional ... than categorical ... construct' -- no 'partial'/'mixed'/'some' qualifier anywhere. Using validated neuropsychological indicators (episodic memory, attention/concentration, executive function, language) and the MAMBAC/MAXCOV/L-Mode taxometric procedures with CCFI consistency testing (a fundamentally different approach from Golden's Bayes-theorem clinical-concordance method), Study 1 (N=10,775 adults 65+) found a mean CCFI of .251, well below both the .500 single-threshold and .450 narrow-dual-threshold cutoffs for dimensional structure. The Discussion's own tally across both studies (34 of 36 individual tests fell below the dimensional threshold; the 2 remaining 'indeterminate' scores still fell below .50, i.e. still leaned dimensional, not contradictory) rules out an internal split that would instead call for 'inconclusive.' The Discussion states these results 'run counter to Golden's (1982) earlier conclusion that dementia has a categorical latent structure.'

description: Using 20 dichotomous items from a mental status questionnaire and Bayes' theorem to classify 841 older individuals as having dementia or not, and comparing these taxometric classifications against clinical diagnosis, Golden (1982) found high concordance and concluded that dementia has a categorical (taxonic) rather than dimensional latent structure; the current authors extended a test of this claim to adults younger than 65 (a population not covered by Golden's original older-adult sample).
original_authors: Golden, Robert R.
original_title: A taxometric model for the detection of a conjectured latent taxon
replication_authors: Glenn D. Walters
replication_title: Dementia: Continuum or distinct entity?
explanation: Confirmed against the paper's own Abstract (body.md lines 6-15, not quoted in the prior pass): 'A second study conducted with a group of 2,375 adults whose ages ranged from 21 to 64 years produced similar results' -- unhedged, no 'partial'/'mixed'/'some' qualifier. In Study 2, using the same four neuropsychological indicators and taxometric procedures as Study 1, the mean CCFI (.408) and two of three individual procedures (MAMBAC .376, MAXCOV .373) favored dimensional structure; L-Mode alone was 'indeterminate' (M = .475) but the Discussion notes even this indeterminate score still fell below .50, i.e. it too leaned dimensional rather than contradicting the other two measures -- so this is not the 'mixed signals within one experiment' pattern that would call for 'inconclusive.' The Discussion concludes 'the results of both studies support a dimensional interpretation of the latent structure of dementia and run counter to Golden's (1982) earlier conclusion that dementia has a categorical latent structure,' explicitly extending the failure to replicate Golden's taxonic conclusion to this younger sample.

description: In Experiment 5, a memory item captured attention in visual search (slowed RTs to a matching distractor) only when it was the sole item held in visual working memory across trials (constant search target, load 1); when observers additionally had to remember a new search target on every trial (raising memory load to two items), the memorized color no longer captured attention, suggesting memory load abolishes memory-driven attentional capture.
original_authors: Olivers, Christian N. L.
original_title: What drives memory-driven attentional capture? The effects of memory type, display type, and search type
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Dirk van Moorselaar; Jan Theeuwes; Christian N. L. Olivers
replication_title: In competition for the attentional template: Can multiple items within visual working memory guide attention?
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
explanation: The authors note that in Olivers's (2009) Experiment 5, the load manipulation was confounded with whether an item's role in memory (target vs. accessory) changed, so Experiment 1 here reuses the same memory-driven-capture paradigm but isolates load (1-4 items, constant search target) from that role confound. The abstract states without hedging: 'Consistent with earlier findings, we observed increased attentional capture by memory related distractors when VWM was filled with a single item. However, memory related capture was no longer present for memory loads beyond a single item.' The Results section gives clean statistics: significant slowing from a memory-matching singleton at Load 1 only (t(14)=2.862, p=.013 location match; t(14)=3.367, p=.005 location mismatch), completely absent at Loads 2-4 (all ts<1.302, all ps>.21), with no correlation to individual VWM capacity at any load. The General Discussion states plainly that 'Results support the distinction between two different states of memory representations within VWM.' No mixed/partial/differing-results hedging is attached to this specific finding anywhere in the paper (the paper's hedged discussion of Beck et al. 2012 and Soto & Humphreys 2008/Zhang et al. 2011 concerns a separate debate about simultaneous multi-item templates, not this experiment's own result). This is a clean, single-measure confirmation of the original Olivers (2009) Exp 5 pattern with the confound explicitly removed and capacity controlled for.

description: Institutionalized retarded children are more motivated by (responsive to) social reinforcement than noninstitutionalized normal children of comparable mental age.
original_authors: Zigler, Edward
original_title: Rigidity and social reinforcement effects in the performance of institutionalized and noninstitutionalized normal and retarded children
replication_authors: Edward Zigler; David Balla
replication_title: Developmental course of responsiveness to social reinforcement in normal children and institutionalized retarded children.
explanation: The present study used the same Marble-in-the-Hole social-reinforcement task from Zigler's earlier work and found retarded children played significantly longer (more responsive to reinforcement) than normals at every mental-age level (F = 41.89, df = 1/72, p < .001; retarded X = 944s vs. normal X = 314s). Critically, the Groups x MA interaction was not significant (F < 1), and the Discussion explicitly rules out a partial or age-limited effect: 'The difference between the two types of subjects was striking at every age... the disparity in motivation for social reinforcement between deprived retarded children and nondeprived normal children was just as great at the upper as at the lower developmental levels.' The Discussion also states this was 'also consistent with earlier findings (Green & Zigler, 1962; Zigler, 1961, 1963; Zigler et al., 1968)... that socially deprived retarded children were more motivated for social reinforcement than were normal children,' with no hedging language anywhere in the paper's discussion of this specific finding.

description: The degree of social deprivation institutionalized retarded children experienced prior to institutionalization is positively related to their motivation for social reinforcement.
original_authors: Edward Zigler; David Balla; Earl C. Butterfield
original_title: A longitudinal investigation of the relationship between preinstitutional social deprivation and social motivation in institutionalized retardates
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Edward Zigler; David Balla
replication_title: Developmental course of responsiveness to social reinforcement in normal children and institutionalized retarded children.
explanation: Verified against Table 2: for the total retarded group (N=39), only the subjective score (r=.30*) and Richness factor correlated significantly with total time; the objective score and the Continuity, Attitude, and Harmony factors did not. The MA 7.0 subgroup alone showed significant correlations on all four of subjective, objective, Richness, and Harmony scores. The authors themselves attribute the total-group relationship to this one subgroup ('This relationship was due to the performance of the youngest MA group'), so although they describe it as 'consistent with the general findings of earlier studies (Zigler, 1961; Zigler et al., 1968),' the support is partial and concentrated in one subgroup rather than a clean full-sample confirmation.

description: Using 5-, 10-, 20-, and 40-word lists all presented at a slow rate of 2.5 sec/word, the primacy effect in free recall was consistently more marked than the recency effect.
original_authors: Bousfield, W. A.; Whitmarsh, G. A.; Esterson, J.
original_title: Serial position effects and the "Marbe effect" in the free recall of meaningful words
replication_authors: Bennet B. Murdock
replication_title: The serial position effect of free recall.
explanation: The authors ran an additional experiment matching Bousfield et al.'s slow 2.5 sec/word presentation rate on a 20-word list to test whether that rate explained the earlier study's primacy-dominant finding; instead they found 'the recency effect is more pronounced than the primacy effect,' concluding 'the results of Bousfield et al. (1958) are not due to the slower presentation rate per se' -- i.e., the specific finding did not reproduce even when the suspected causal parameter was matched.

description: In a laboratory obedience paradigm, participants were more willing to inflict harm (deliver electric shock) on a victim when mutual visibility between subject and victim was reduced (i.e., when they were less likely to see and be seen by the victim).
original_authors: Stanley Milgram
original_title: Some conditions of obedience and disobedience to authority
replication_authors: Charles W. Turner; John F. Layton; Lynn S. Simons
replication_title: Naturalistic studies of aggressive behavior: Aggressive stimuli, victim visibility, and horn honking.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Study 2's Contrast A found closing the curtain (reducing mutual visibility) significantly increased honking versus the open curtain, F(1,86)=4.43, p<.05, and the authors explicitly draw the parallel: 'Similarly, Milgram (1965) found in a laboratory setting that subjects were more likely to harm a victim who was not visible.' But the authors themselves offer a live, unresolved rival explanation for this same effect: 'there is another interpretation possible for effects of the curtain manipulation... subjects... might have used their horns to signal that the light had changed... This alternative interpretation of the horn honking measure cannot be dismissed.' Because the authors cannot rule out that honking reflects attention-signaling rather than dehumanization-driven aggression, and their own study-specific conclusion is hedged ('tentatively suggest'), this is a 'significant but questionable' case rather than a clean success. (Citation check: 'Milgram (196S)' is an OCR misread of 'Milgram (1965)' -- confirmed against the reference list entry 'Milgram, S. ... Human Relations, 1965, 18, 57-76,' which exactly matches the extracted original_authors/title/journal/volume/pages/year, so no field change is needed; the flagged mismatch was an OCR artifact, not a real citation error.)

description: The mere presence of a weapon (a pistol and a shotgun) in the environment increased participants' aggressive behavior (shock delivered to a confederate) in a laboratory setting — the 'weapons effect.'
original_authors: Leonard Berkowitz; Anthony Lepage
original_title: Weapons as aggression-eliciting stimuli
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Charles W. Turner; John F. Layton; Lynn S. Simons
replication_title: Naturalistic studies of aggressive behavior: Aggressive stimuli, victim visibility, and horn honking.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Verified directly against the text: Study 2's Contrast B shows the rifle/vengeance combination significantly increased honking only when the curtain was closed, F(1,86)=5.98, p<.02 (ns when curtain open, Contrast D: F(1,86)=1.37, p>.20), while the rifle alone (paired with the non-aggressive 'friend' sticker) never differed from the no-rifle control in either visibility condition (Contrasts C and E, both F<1.0). This is a textbook 'conditional success' pattern (effect found only in a subset of conditions), and the present data explicitly reject a 'mere presence' weapons effect (rifle alone had no effect regardless of visibility) -- inconclusive is correct with no genuine residual ambiguity.

description: The mere presence of a weapon (a pistol and a shotgun) in the environment increased participants' aggressive behavior (shock delivered to a confederate) in a laboratory setting — the 'weapons effect.'
original_authors: Leonard Berkowitz; Anthony Lepage
original_title: Weapons as aggression-eliciting stimuli
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Charles W. Turner; John F. Layton; Lynn S. Simons
replication_title: Naturalistic studies of aggressive behavior: Aggressive stimuli, victim visibility, and horn honking.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Verified directly against the text: in Study 3 the rifle/vengeance combination produced a significant INCREASE in honking for male drivers of new vehicles, F(1,129)=4.03, p<.05, but a significant DECREASE for male drivers of old vehicles, F(1,129)=5.23, p<.05, and no significant effect for female drivers (F<1.0). Per the taxonomy, an opposite-direction effect confined to a subset of conditions is 'inconclusive,' not 'reversal' -- the authors themselves attribute the old-vehicle decrease to inhibition in lower-status subjects rather than describing it as a true reversal of the weapons effect, and they call the overall pattern 'somewhat weaker' than Study 2. Inconclusive is correct with no genuine residual ambiguity.

description: The context in which an aggression-relevant stimulus is presented (e.g., labeling a filmed football game as a 'grudge match' rather than a routine sporting event) determines whether observers perceive it as having an aggressive meaning, which in turn increases their subsequent aggressive behavior (shock given to a partner who had angered them).
original_authors: Leonard Berkowitz; Joseph T. Alioto
original_title: The meaning of an observed event as a determinant of its aggressive consequences
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Charles W. Turner; John F. Layton; Lynn S. Simons
replication_title: Naturalistic studies of aggressive behavior: Aggressive stimuli, victim visibility, and horn honking.
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
explanation: Verified directly against the text: the authors explicitly frame the vengeance bumper sticker as 'somewhat analogous' to Berkowitz and Alioto's grudge-match framing manipulation. The aggressive-framing effect appeared for new-vehicle males (F(1,129)=4.03, p<.05) and when the victim was not visible in Study 2 (F(1,86)=5.98, p<.02), but reversed for old-vehicle males (F(1,129)=5.23, p<.05) and was absent for females (F<1.0), and the authors conclude only that the sticker 'might have modified' honking 'because its aggressive meaning was more salient,' explicitly noting alternative explanations cannot be ruled out. This hedged, subgroup-dependent pattern matches the taxonomy's 'authors explicitly hedge' and 'mixed signals' rules for inconclusive with no genuine residual ambiguity.

description: The revised Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) yields two underlying components—Cognitive-Affective and Somatic-Performance—with the specific symptom compositions described by Beck and Steer (1987), based on data from clinical (including heroin-addict) populations.
original_authors: Beck, Aaron T.; Steer, Robert A.
original_title: Manual for the revised Beck Depression Inventory
replication_authors: Robert A. Steer; Martin Y. Iguchi; Jerome J. Platt
replication_title: Use of the revised Beck Depression Inventory with intravenous drug users not in treatment.
explanation: Independently verified against the Results and Discussion sections. The principal-components analysis on 1,290 not-in-treatment IV drug users found exactly two eigenvalues >1.00, with Items 1-13 loading on Component 1 and Items 14-21 on Component 2 — the paper states these are 'identical to those symptoms summed by Beck and Steer (1987) to yield the Cognitive-Affective and Somatic-Performance subscales.' Unlike the paper's other findings (mean severity, background correlates), where the Discussion adds explicit hedges ('the 2-3-point mean difference is not clinically meaningful,' equivocal interpretation of health correlates), the component-structure claim carries no hedging anywhere in the paper: the Discussion states flatly that 'the principal-components structure of the BDI supports the scoring system for the Cognitive-Affective and Somatic-Performance subscales that had been described by Beck and Steer (1987)' with no adjacent language of partial, mixed, or differing results. This is an unambiguous success for the narrow claim described here (the two-component structure and its specific item composition), which is distinct from — and does not extend to — the paper's other, more qualified findings about symptom severity levels and demographic correlates.

description: Using a correlational design, individual differences in attentional control (a latent variable drawn from working memory capacity and attention tasks) were positively related to forward-associate (FA) priming but not to backward-associate (BA) priming in a lexical decision task, indicating that prospective expectancy generation (EG) requires cognitive resources whereas retrospective semantic matching (RSM) is relatively effortless; the data also showed underadditivity of symmetric-pair priming relative to the sum of FA and BA priming.
original_authors: Hutchison, Keith A.; Heap, Stacey J.; Neely, James H.; Thomas, Melvin A.
original_title: Attentional control and asymmetric associative priming
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_authors: Tom Heyman; Bram Van Rensbergen; Gert Storms; Keith A. Hutchison; Simon De Deyne
replication_title: The influence of working memory load on semantic priming.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Instead of correlating attentional control with priming, the authors directly manipulated working memory load with a dual-task procedure and found FA priming disappeared under high load while BA and SYM priming remained stable, and the low-load data showed the same underadditivity pattern as the original; the Discussion states 'these findings are in line with those from Hutchison et al. (2014) and indicate that EG, a prospective process, depends on working memory capacity ... whereas RSM, a retrospective process, is relatively effortless.'

description: After learning a linear rank order (A>B>C>D...), test queries about pairs spanning wider distances on the order (e.g., AD) are responded to more quickly and accurately than queries about pairs spanning narrower distances (e.g., AB) — the symbolic distance effect (SDE).
original_authors: George R. Potts
original_title: Storing and retrieving information about ordered relationships
replication_authors: Ulrich von Hecker; Karl Christoph Klauer; Lukas Wolf; Masoud Fazilat-Pour
replication_title: Spatial processes in linear ordering.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Independently verified: Experiment 1's Results section reports pair distance effects on accuracy and latency in the predicted direction ('were responded to with greater speed and accuracy than those of narrower distances,' body.md ~line 480), Experiment 3 reports 'The SDE replicated both in terms of accuracy and response time' (~line 1132), and the General Discussion states 'the SDE replicated in seven consecutive experiments, confirming that this effect counts amongst the most robust and replicable effects in experimental psychology' (~line 1588) — an unambiguous, uniformly positive result with no hedging language across experiments, so 'success' is well supported. The confidence-limiting issue is attribution, not the result: every statement of the specific replicated claim (the pair-distance effect on accuracy/RT) cites Potts (1974), Smith & Foos (1975), and Pohl & Schumacher (1991) jointly (lines 101, 319, 481), and this joint citation never varies for that specific claim — although Potts (1974) does appear alone elsewhere for related but distinct points ('end anchor processing strategies,' 'ease of mental model construction,' lines 533/535/558), while Smith & Foos and Pohl & Schumacher never appear without Potts anywhere in the paper. That asymmetry favors Potts as primary but does not resolve the joint citation of the actual tested claim, so the attribution ambiguity is genuine; confidence remains medium.

description: In comparative size judgments, left- or right-hand response facilitation depends on the instructed salient pole (searching for 'smaller' vs. 'larger'), and this facilitation effect reverses (from a left-hand to a right-hand advantage, or vice versa) as the queried pair's ordinal position moves from the salient/anchored pole toward the opposite pole of the dimension.
original_authors: Samuel Shaki; William M. Petrusic; Craig Leth-Steensen
original_title: SNARC effects with numerical and non-numerical symbolic comparative judgments: Instructional and cultural dependencies
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
replication_authors: Ulrich von Hecker; Karl Christoph Klauer; Lukas Wolf; Masoud Fazilat-Pour
replication_title: Spatial processes in linear ordering.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Independently verified in body.md's General Discussion (~lines 2020-2030): the authors confirm the general moderation-by-ordinal-position pattern ('In the majority of our experiments, we did observe an interaction between side of dominant element and average ordinal position of the pair... germane to Shaki et al.'s (2012)'), but explicitly deny the specific sub-measure this entry names — a full left-to-right reversal — for the horizontal dimension that actually parallels Shaki et al.'s design: 'we do not, in our horizontal experiments, replicate Shaki et al.'s (2012) conversion of a left-side- into a right-side-facilitation.' They report only an analogous reversal in a different modality (top-to-bottom, vertical dimension, Experiments 5-6), which is not the pair described here. Per the result rules, since the named reversal did not replicate in the tested (horizontal) modality while a weaker, related moderation effect did, and only an analogous effect emerged in a different (vertical) design, this is genuinely mixed/partial support and 'inconclusive' (not 'success') is correct — cannot be upgraded to success since not every element of the described effect replicated. No new evidence resolves this beyond what the original explanation already cited; the ambiguity is genuine, so confidence stays medium.

description: Responses on incongruent Stroop trials are facilitated when participants use response keys located relatively far apart rather than close together.
original_authors: Daniël Lakens; Iris K. Schneider; Nils B. Jostmann; Thomas W. Schubert
original_title: Telling things apart: The distance between response keys influences categorization times
replication_authors: Ulrich von Hecker; Karl Christoph Klauer; Lukas Wolf; Masoud Fazilat-Pour
replication_title: Spatial processes in linear ordering.
replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
explanation: Independently verified in body.md's Experiment 1 Discussion (~lines 499-505): 'Response key distance made no difference in the present experimental setting. Whether the two keys used to indicate the side of the dominant element were close together or far apart on the keyboard did not matter by itself, nor did it interact with the SDE or the left-anchoring effect... are not likely to influence the observed spatial anchoring phenomenon, at least not in the sense as observed by Lakens et al. (2011).' This is an unambiguous null result with no hedging, so 'failure' is correct. Note this is a conceptual replication in a different paradigm (a spatial-anchoring/ordering task, not a literal incongruent-Stroop task) and the manipulation was tested only once, in Experiment 1, then dropped from all six subsequent experiments — the clarity of the null finding is not in question, but it rests on a single manipulation check rather than a dedicated, repeated test, which is a reasonable basis for medium rather than high confidence. No new evidence beyond what the original explanation already quoted, so confidence stays medium.

description: Using a coordinated multi-site meta-analytic pipeline (ENIGMA consortium, 15 cohorts, 2028 patients / 2540 controls), patients with schizophrenia show smaller bilateral hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus and accumbens volumes and smaller intracranial volume, but larger globus pallidus and lateral ventricle volumes, with a characteristic rank order of effect sizes across regions.
original_authors: Van Erp, T. G. M.; Hibar, D. P.; Rasmussen, J. M.; Glahn, D. C.; Pearlson, G. D.; Andreassen, O. A.; Agartz, Ingrid; Westlye, L. T.; Haukvik, Unn K.; Dale, A. M.; Melle, I.; Hartberg, C. B.; Gruber, O.; Kraemer, B.; Zilles, D.; Donohoe, Gary; Kelly, S.; McDonald, C.; Morris, D. W.; Cannon, D. M.; Corvin, Aiden; Machielsen, M. W. The flagged 'mismatch' was a false positive: this journal cites via superscript reference numbers without inline years, so no citation sentence in the paper will ever contain a literal year, and that check cannot discriminate a real error here. On the result label itself: the single Discussion sentence (line 811-816) unambiguously states 'We successfully replicated ... That is why confidence moves from low to medium rather than to high.

explanation: Citation mismatch resolved: the citation marker (14) in the Introduction -- 'The empirical observation that even these three transdiagnostic latent factors are positively correlated (13) has given rise to a more radical hypothesis... (14). The work that first confirmed this hypothesis reported a single factor in psychopathology data (14)' -- maps in the paper's own reference list to reference 14: Lahey BB, Applegate B, Hakes JK, Zald DH, Hariri AR, Rathouz PJ. 'Is there a general factor of prevalent psychopathology during adulthood?' J Abnorm Psychol 2012;121:971-977. The previously extracted original (Caspi et al. 2014) is reference 15, which the same sentence cites only for the 'p factor' label and its analogy to the 'g factor,' not as the study that first identified the general factor. Lahey 2012 is the correct replication target -- it is explicitly named as 'the work that first confirmed this hypothesis' -- and notably shares co-author Hariri with the present paper, consistent with this being the lab's own earlier finding being extended into neuroimaging. On the result: the Results subsection 'Replication of the p factor' reports, without qualification, that a bi-factor model with one general factor plus specific factors for internalizing and externalizing symptoms (there was no separate 'thought disorder' specific factor in this winning model, so the description has been narrowed accordingly) fit the data well, and that 'the general factor replicated the presence of a shared liability for common mental illness... This alone is important as it further suggests the p factor is relatively robust to different samples and measures of psychiatric symptoms.' The abstract states plainly, 'we first replicate the p factor.' Neither passage contains hedging language ('partially,' 'mixed,' 'some differences'); the Discussion's caveats (small effect sizes, cross-sectional design, non-exhaustive symptom assessment) apply to the exploratory neuroimaging-correlate findings, not to the p-factor replication itself. Confidence raised to high on this specific new evidence (correct reference-list match plus unhedged replication language).

That is nominally significant and survives Bonferroni correction across the 15-locus family in Table 2 (alpha=0.05/15=0.0033), so it is a genuine, if modest, independent replication, not a failed one. The Discussion's 'P<=0.001' phrasing for T1D loci is a loose approximation rather than a strict rule the paper itself applies: the two T2D loci elsewhere in this same table, PPARG and KCNJ11 (both P=1.3x10^-3, likewise above that literal threshold), are described in the text as 'detected...with effect-sizes consistent with previous reports' and are treated as clean successes in this dataset's other entries. By that same standard, IFIH1 belongs among the 'five of these previously identified associations...detected in this scan' (HLA-DRB1, CTLA4, PTPN22, IL2RA, IFIH1); INS is the only T1D locus in Table 2 the authors call a non-replication, and that is explicitly attributed to the SNP failing study-wide QC filters, not to a null result for IFIH1.

replication_title: Phantom pain is associated with preserved structure and function in the former hand area
explanation: The Introduction explicitly ties this test to Flor et al. (1995), cited as ref. 5, stating the maladaptive plasticity model 'is most clearly supported by expansions or shifts in cortical lip representations towards the deprived hand area: the greater the remapping, the more severe the pain5.' The authors test this via fMRI activation during lip movement (in place of Flor's MEG-based dipole mapping) and find a clean double null: no significant increase in lip-related activation in amputees versus 2-handed controls in the phantom hand ROI (t(37)=0.122, P=0.904), and no significant correlation between lip activation and phantom pain magnitude (r(15)=0.17, P=0.512). The Discussion explicitly frames this as 'contrary to the reorganization model' and reframes the whole study as 'a reassessment of the link between phantom pain and brain reorganization.' No hedging language (mixed/partial) attaches to this specific lip-representation measure -- it is the only sub-measure named in this entry and it failed on both tests applied to it, so 'failure' is unambiguous. (The paper separately reports an unexpected positive correlation between phantom-hand, not lip, activation and pain magnitude -- a distinct finding not part of the Flor et al. claim being tested here.)

replication_title: Rare coding variants in PLCG2, ABI3, and TREM2 implicate microglial-mediated innate immunity in Alzheimer's disease
explanation: Verified against the text: the authors reanalyzed the same eight AD-associated pathway clusters (originally identified from common variants) using rare-variant data (MAF < 1%). The paper states explicitly: 'After correction for multiple testing, we observed enrichment for immune response (P = 8.64 x 10^-3), cholesterol transport (P = 3.84 x 10^-5), hemostasis (P = 2.10 x 10^-3), clathrin-AP2 adaptor complex (P = 9.20 x 10^-4), and protein folding (P = 0.02)' -- exactly 5 of the 8 named clusters, meaning the remaining 3 of the original 8 did not reach significance in the rare-variant reanalysis. Per the partial-support rule, this is a genuine partial replication (5/8), not a full success, so 'inconclusive' is correct and not genuinely ambiguous once the exact count is checked. Confirmed the citation number '36' resolves via the paper's numbered bibliography to Cruchaga, C. et al., 'GWAS of cerebrospinal fluid tau levels identifies risk variants for Alzheimer's disease,' Neuron 78:256-268 (2013) -- exactly matching the already-extracted original citation fields.
