On the result: the combined P value for rs10260404 was 1.5x10-3 -- nominally below 0.05, but rs10260404 is not among the three SNPs the authors report as meeting the replication phase's own Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold (P<0.05/60=8.33x10-4), and the paper states explicitly that it, along with ITPR2 (P=0.08) and FGGY (P=0.11), 'did not approach genome-wide significance' (the study's threshold, P<5.0x10-8). explanation: This was the initial, flawed attempt at Study 5 (N=879): a scale-labeling error gave some participants inconsistent response-scale information. Two independently reported statistics agree the effect was nominally significant in the original's direction: the preregistered covariate-adjusted regression, b=-3.46, t(872)=-2.26, p=.024, and the paper's disclosure table (Table 1), whose analysis format matches the original's primary hypothesis test directly: F(1,876)=6.71, p=.009, r=.09 (about half the original's r=.19). Despite this convergent significance, the authors explicitly disavow a causal reading: differential attrition by condition (52% of quitters from the God-prime arm vs. 32% from control) 'undermines random assignment, and therefore the validity of the experiment' and 'impairs our ability to draw confident causal conclusions.' Because the authors themselves reject causal interpretation of an otherwise-significant, direction-consistent result, this specific attempt is genuinely ambiguous rather than a clean success or failure -- the confidence is kept at medium rather than raised, since the paper itself does not resolve it. (The correctly-administered attempt, this entry set's plain 'Study 5', is the one that cleanly failed to replicate, b=-0.39, t(872)=-0.25, p=.800.)

explanation: Because Norris et al.'s (2006) sentences confounded contrastive accent with syntactic/lexical presupposition triggers, the authors designed two new cross-modal priming experiments in Dutch with syntactically and semantically neutral sentences to test whether contrastive pitch accent per se facilitates recognition of contextual alternatives; Experiment 1a found the predicted intonation x prime-type interaction (facilitation for contrastive associates only after contrastive intonation) and the control Experiment 1b showed no such interaction for non-contrastive associates (a specificity check, not a failed replication measure), leading the authors to conclude the findings 'support and extend the conclusion drawn by Norris et al. (2006) that prosody alters the interpretation of the sentence.' Independent review confirmed this: neither the abstract nor the General Discussion uses any hedging language ('partially', 'mixed', 'some differences'), so the inconclusive-override rule does not apply. The citation-mismatch flag is a false positive: the extracted authors/title/journal/volume/pages match the paper's own References-list entry verbatim ('Norris, D., Cutler, A., McQueen, J., & Butterfield, S. (2006). Phonological and conceptual activation in speech comprehension. Cognitive Psychology, 53, 146-193'), and the year 2006 appears in the sentence immediately preceding the extracted citation_sentence span ('...priming effects (Norris et al., 2006). In Experiment 4C, Norris et al. presented sentences...') -- it was just outside the narrow snippet chosen. references.json for this paper is garbled/incomplete and has no usable Norris entry, so original_url is left blank rather than fabricated. Confidence is kept at medium (not upgraded) because this is a close extension with new stimuli, a new paradigm, and a different language (Dutch) rather than a literal repetition of Norris et al.'s Experiment 4C, so 'success' reflects the authors' own global framing rather than a directly comparable quantitative replication of Exp 4C itself.

description: In a good-outcome psychotherapy case (the client 'Gabriel'), two configurations of therapist activity preceding client assimilation setbacks were identified — a challenging configuration (Looking for an extensional orientation + Defying the dominant voice) and an exploratory configuration (Exploring + Empathizing with the nondominant voice) — and when balance-strategy setbacks were preceded by the challenging configuration, the setback was almost always to a high APES level (≥3), while exceeding-the-therapeutic-zone-of-proximal-development (TZPD) setbacks were comparatively rare (25% of setbacks) and mostly to low APES levels regardless of preceding activity.

explanation: Verified against the Discussion (paper's own explicit Gabriel-vs-Santi comparison, lines ~860-920): of the three sub-claims in the description, only one held. (1) The two configurations recurred — 'These two patterns replicated, respectively, the challenging configuration and exploratory configuration observed in the good-outcome case of Gabriel' (replicated). (2) The specific responsiveness finding did not hold: for Gabriel, challenging activity preceding balance-strategy setbacks was 'almost always only to APES level 3 or higher,' but for Santi the same setbacks were 'more-or-less evenly split between ≥3 and <3' (did not replicate). (3) TZPD setbacks, 'relatively rare' for Gabriel at 25%, were the majority for Santi at 59.3% (214/361; did not replicate — reversed in direction, not merely attenuated). Because the authors themselves state these contrasts explicitly and quantitatively rather than leaving them ambiguous, this is a clear-cut case of partial/mixed replication (1 of 3 sub-measures held), which the scoring rules require to be labeled 'inconclusive' rather than 'success.' Confidence raised to high: the divergence is stated in the paper's own numbers, not inferred.

replication_title: How to Make a 29% Increase Look Bigger: The Unit Effect in Option Comparisons
explanation: The authors explicitly frame study 2 as a replication of Burson et al. (2009) 'using a different methodology' (an attraction-effect, three-option choice task rather than Burson's original two-option task). Table 2 (body.md lines 457-503) shows the core preference-reversal measure -- probability of choosing the superior (target) option -- rose significantly with the expanded (1,000-unit) vs. contracted (10-unit) quality scale in both sub-studies: study 2A 19%->46%, LR chi2(1)=5.95, p=.02; study 2B 14%->43%, LR chi2(1)=10.59, p=.001. The General Discussion states unqualifiedly that these changes in perception 'lead to an increased preference for the option that is superior on the focal attribute (study 2)', with no hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'differing results') anywhere regarding this finding. The paper's one boundary condition (lines 700-717) concerns study 3 (a separate real-choice apple/Twix task), not study 2, so it does not qualify this result. This is a clean, twice-replicated significant confirmation of Burson et al.'s preference-reversal finding.

replication_title: Neural signatures of experimentally induced flow experiences identified in a typical fMRI block design with BOLD imaging
explanation: The authors, largely the same research group as the original study, explicitly state in the Discussion: 'Except for one specific region (left putamen) the present BOLD imaging study replicated our previous findings (Ulrich et al., 2014) of invU-shaped neural activation in the IFG, and U-shaped response profiles in the MPFC, the lateral temporoparietal cortex, the HC and amygdala.' They used a fundamentally different fMRI acquisition (BOLD with 30s blocks vs. the original's perfusion imaging with 3-min blocks) to test the same paradigm and hypotheses in the same lab/population, and reported successful replication of nearly all regions.

description: Psychotic women can estimate the phase of their menstrual cycle by self-report as accurately as non-psychotic control women, with no significant difference in agreement between the two groups when compared against an objective criterion.
original_authors: Katherine Thompson; Anthony de Castella; Jayashri Kulkarni
original_title: Psychotic women can estimate cycle phase as well as controls
replication_authors: Enrique Baca-García; Carmen Díaz-Sastre; Jose de Leon; Jeronimo Saiz-Ruiz
replication_title: The Relationship Between Menstrual Cycle Phases and Suicide Attempts
explanation: Citation check: reference #21 in this paper's bibliography reads 'Thompson K, de Castella A, Kulkarni J. Psychotic women can estimate cycle phase as well as controls. Schizophr Res 1997; 23:185-6' -- an exact match to the extracted original_authors/title/journal/volume/year. The 'mismatch' flag was a false positive from a truncated preview of the citation_sentence; the full sentence (and the Discussion paragraph immediately after) names Thompson et al. explicitly, so no fields were changed. On the result: in the Discussion (Assessment of Menstrual Cycle Phases), the authors recompute agreement k-values between self-reported and hormonally-assessed cycle phase separately for their patients (suicide attempters) and controls, and state the group difference was not statistically significant (overlapping 95% CIs) -- 'patients were not significantly worse than control subjects in providing accurate information about their menstrual cycles... Although our results are similar to Thompson et al.'s results, our interpretation is different.' This directly replicates the specific sub-measure named here (no significant patient-vs-control difference in agreement against the hormonal/objective criterion), supporting 'success'. Confidence stays medium rather than high because of that same 'our interpretation is different' caveat: the authors found BOTH groups' self-reports agreed only moderately (~two-thirds) with the hormonal gold standard, undercutting Thompson et al.'s characterization of self-report as 'extremely accurate' in an absolute sense. That absolute-accuracy caveat falls outside the narrow sub-measure extracted here (patient-vs-control comparison, not absolute accuracy), but it means the paper's overall stance toward Thompson et al. is more qualified than a clean replication, so some genuine interpretive ambiguity remains.

description: Fear conditioning of one stimulus category retroactively and selectively strengthens memory for conceptually related items that were incidentally encoded before the conditioning ever occurred, an effect evident at a delayed (6-24 h) memory test but not at an immediate test, indicating dependence on post-encoding consolidation.
original_authors: Dunsmoor, Joseph E.; Murty, Vishnu P.; Davachi, Lila; Phelps, Elizabeth A.
original_title: Emotional learning selectively and retroactively strengthens memories for related events
replication_authors: Anuya Patil; Vishnu P. Murty; Joseph E. Dunsmoor; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Lila Davachi
replication_title: Reward retroactively enhances memory consolidation for related items
explanation: Extending the aversive-domain effect to reward, the authors found that at a 24-h delayed test 'there was better memory for stimuli that shared the same category as high versus low reward stimuli (t(23)=2.98, P=0.007)', and explicitly state the study 'complements prior work from our laboratory demonstrating a similar pattern of results in the aversive domain (Dunsmoor et al. 2015)... fear facilitated retroactive memory benefits for related items during a delayed memory test,' confirming the retroactive, consolidation-dependent enhancement generalizes to a reward manipulation.

description: At an immediate memory test, no retroactive memory enhancement is observed for items conceptually related to a subsequently fear-conditioned category, showing that the retroactive benefit requires post-encoding consolidation time rather than reflecting an immediate/attentional effect.
original_authors: Dunsmoor, Joseph E.; Murty, Vishnu P.; Davachi, Lila; Phelps, Elizabeth A.
original_title: Emotional learning selectively and retroactively strengthens memories for related events
replication_authors: Anuya Patil; Vishnu P. Murty; Joseph E. Dunsmoor; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Lila Davachi
replication_title: Reward retroactively enhances memory consolidation for related items
explanation: Experiment 2 (n=25) tested memory immediately (~5 min) after the reward phase and, mirroring the original's dissociation, 'found that there was no difference in immediate memory for stimuli that were related to the category subsequently rewarded (t(24)=0.003, P=0.99)'; the authors conclude these 'effects were evident only on a long-term memory test, as no differences in memory were evident at an immediate test,' replicating the original's finding that retroactive enhancement is consolidation-dependent.

description: U.S. corporations exhibited a trend toward increased corporate focus, i.e., declining industrial (business-segment) diversification, over the 1978 to 1989 period.
original_authors: Comment, Robert; Jarrell, Gregg A.
original_title: Corporate focus and stock returns
replication_authors: David J. Denis; Diane K. Denis; Keven Yost
replication_title: Global Diversification, Industrial Diversification, and Firm Value
explanation: Using industrial diversification measures (fraction of firms with multiple segments, average number of segments, sales-based Herfindahl index) over a later, largely non-overlapping 1984-1997 sample, the authors state directly: 'These results confirm and extend those of Comment and Jarrell (1995), who document increases in industrial focus over the 1978 to 1989 time period,' with all three measures changing significantly at the 0.01 level in the same direction as the original.

description: Firm value is positively related to the degree of internationalization specifically for firms with substantial firm-specific intangible assets, as proxied by R&D and advertising intensity interacted with multinationality.
original_authors: Morck, Randall; Yeung, Bernard
original_title: Why investors value multinationality
replication_authors: David J. Denis; Diane K. Denis; Keven Yost
replication_title: Global Diversification, Industrial Diversification, and Firm Value
explanation: The authors explicitly replicate Morck and Yeung's interaction test in their own excess-value regression framework using a larger, more recent (1984-1997) panel, and report: 'Unlike Morck and Yeung, we find no evidence that the value of global diversification increases with R&D and advertising expenditures,' a direct failure to reproduce the original interaction effect.

description: Hazard education programs significantly increased children's awareness, knowledge of hazards and protective behaviors, and led to more realistic (increased) risk perceptions compared with uneducated children.
original_authors: Ronan, K. R.; Johnston, D. M.; Daly, M.; Fairley, R.

original_journal: Australasian Journal of Disaster and Trauma Studies
replication_authors: Kevin R. Ronan; David M. Johnston
replication_title: Correlates of Hazard Education Programs for Youth
explanation: The current study replicated the original knowledge/risk-perception findings with a larger, separate sample: Table I shows significant knowledge advantages for educated children, and the Discussion states 'findings of the current study are the first to provide empirical support for the value of hazard education programs' and that programs help children achieve 'increased awareness... more realistic risk perceptions... more knowledge of risk mitigation.'

description: Children involved in hazard education programs reported lower fear levels than uneducated children (in the original study, 12% versus 28% reported being 'often scared'), reflecting more adaptive emotional functioning without negative side effects.
original_authors: Ronan, K. R.; Johnston, D. M.; Daly, M.; Fairley, R.
original_title: School children's risk perceptions and preparedness: a hazards education survey
original_journal: Australasian Journal of Disaster and Trauma Studies
replication_authors: Kevin R. Ronan; David M. Johnston
replication_title: Correlates of Hazard Education Programs for Youth
explanation: Reviewed independently against Sec. 3.6 and the Sec. 4 Discussion. The direction matches the original (7.73% vs 8.80% 'often scared') but the difference is essentially null, t/chi-square well below significance (chi2(2,436)<1, p>.10), and the authors state the programs conferred 'not... any significant emotional advantage.' This alone would support 'failure' (Table III's own significance key requires p<=.05; this result is far from that), but the authors do not use failure language: in Sec. 4 they instead describe the null result as 'supported by our previous research in which education programs were related to more adaptive emotional functioning,' folding a non-significant result into a supportive narrative. Per the codebook's failure criterion (non-significant result AND authors frame it as a failure), the second condition is not met, so inconclusive remains the better fit — this is genuine ambiguity in how the authors themselves characterize a null result, not an extraction error.

description: Using children's reports of a limited number of home-based adjustments, the original study found no difference in home-based hazard adjustments between children involved versus not involved in hazard education programs.
original_authors: Ronan, K. R.; Johnston, D. M.; Daly, M.; Fairley, R.
original_title: School children's risk perceptions and preparedness: a hazards education survey
original_journal: Australasian Journal of Disaster and Trauma Studies
replication_authors: Kevin R. Ronan; David M. Johnston
replication_title: Correlates of Hazard Education Programs for Youth
explanation: Reviewed independently against Table I and Sec. 3.4. Using a broader battery (child AND parent reports of 23 adjustments) the current study found a significant education-group difference in child-reported total adjustments (t(431)=4.19, p<=.005), but the parent-reported total difference fell short of Table I's own significance threshold (t(340)=1.03, flagged only at the loose p<=.15 level, not p<=.05), with conventional significance (p<=.05) recovered only for an 11-item subset (t(436)=1.70). So relative to the original's clean null finding, the pattern is genuinely mixed across reporters/measures rather than a uniform success or failure, matching the codebook's guidance to classify as inconclusive when results differ across measures. The authors explicitly note the original study's measurement limitation ('that study relied solely on children's reports of a limited range of home-based hazard adjustments') as the motivation for adding the parent-report and expanded-item extension.

description: Using 1986 Australian data, Beggs and Chapman (1988) estimated that having a first child was associated with a lifetime after-tax earnings loss of about $435,000 (in 1997 dollars) for women with average education levels, with second and third children associated with smaller additional lifetime earnings losses of about $75,000 and $55,000 respectively.
original_authors: Beggs, J. J.; Chapman, B. J.
original_title: The foregone earnings from child-rearing in Australia
original_journal: Discussion Paper no. 190, Centre for Economic Policy Research, Australian National University
replication_authors: Bruce Chapman; Yvonne Dunlop; Matthew Gray; Amy Liu; Deborah Mitchell
replication_title: The Impact of Children on the Lifetime Earnings of Australian Women: Evidence from the 1990s
explanation: Independently verified. The paper explicitly re-estimates 1997 forgone earnings 'using the same specifications as Beggs and Chapman' for direct comparison (Section 4.2, Table 10) and finds the same qualitative pattern as the 1986 original for all three sub-measures: a statistically significant negative effect of children on women's lifetime earnings ('ever had a child' t=-4.44 in the earnings equation; permanent 7.0-point reduction in employment probability) that diminishes with each successive child. The magnitude is far smaller than the original, though -- $160,000 vs. $435,000 for a first child (-63%) and $12,000-$15,000 vs. $75,000/$55,000 for the second/third child (-73% to -80%). The authors do not frame this as a failure of Beggs and Chapman's estimate: the abstract states 'the impact of having children on women's lifetime earnings decreased over the period 1986-1997,' and the Conclusion attributes the gap to a real rise in mothers' labour force participation (employment probability for a 26-year-old with one child under 5 rose from 15.4% to 39.5%), not to a replication failure. Per the rule that a same-specification comparison with a significant same-direction effect counts as success even when weaker than the original, and since all three sub-measures show the same qualitative pattern, 'success' is retained. But a 60-80% smaller effect size is a large quantitative departure, and the paper's own framing emphasizes the decrease rather than confirmation -- so genuine ambiguity remains about whether this reads as a full or only partial success; confidence is kept at medium rather than upgraded. Citation check: the flagged citation_sentence omits the year, but the paper unambiguously dates the original to 1988 elsewhere -- Section 1 ('Beggs and Chapman (1988)... suggested that in 1986...'), endnote 18 ('The 1986 figure is from Beggs and Chapman (1988)'), and the References list entry ('Beggs, J. J. and Chapman, B. J. 1988, "The foregone earnings from child-rearing in Australia", Discussion Paper no. 190, CEPR, ANU'). original_authors/title/year/journal are all correct as extracted; no change was needed.

description: Infants habituated to displays of items (e.g., pictures of household objects that varied in size) dishabituated to displays with a novel numerosity, which was interpreted as evidence that infants can discriminate small numerical sets (discrete number) independent of item size.
original_authors: Starkey, Prentice; Spelke, Elizabeth S.; Gelman, Rochel
original_title: Numerical abstraction by human infants
replication_authors: Melissa Wechsler Clearfield; Kelly S. Mix
replication_title: Number Versus Contour Length in Infants' Discrimination of Small Visual Sets
explanation: Verified against body.md and the PDF directly: the authors deliberately re-used Starkey et al.'s (1990) stimulus positioning and standard habituation criterion (explicitly cited twice in Method), then systematically varied contour length independent of number to deconfound the two. Results are clean and unhedged, not mixed: infants dishabituated to the contour-length change, t(15)=3.58, p<.01 (13/16 infants individually, p<.01 binomial), but showed no dishabituation to the number change, t(15)=0.51, n.s. The Discussion states without qualification, 'Our results clearly indicate that when these features are separated, infants attend to contour length, rather than number, to discriminate between sets,' and explicitly reinterprets prior number-discrimination findings, naming Starkey et al. (1990) among them, as likely driven by the uncontrolled contour-length confound. There is no 'partially'/'mixed'/'some differences' language here — this is a single, well-powered, statistically clear null result on the number dimension paired with a significant confound-driven effect, so 'failure' (of the original's number-discrimination interpretation) is the correct label, not 'inconclusive'.

description: In a preliminary fMRI study on a small subsample of the cohort followed for 3 months, non-alcohol-related (money) Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer (PIT) was associated with increased nucleus accumbens activation specifically in patients who later relapsed, but not in those who remained abstinent.
original_authors: Maria Garbusow; Daniel J. Schad; Miriam Sebold; Eva Friedel; Nadine Bernhardt; Stefan P. Koch; Bruno Steinacher; Norbert Kathmann; Dirk E. M. Geurts; Christian Sommer; Dirk K. Müller; Stephan Nebe; Sören Paul; Hans-Ulrich Wittchen; Ulrich S. Zimmermann; Henrik Walter; Michael N. Smolka; Philipp Sterzer; Michael A. Rapp; Quentin J. M. Huys; Florian Schlagenhauf; Andreas Heinz
original_title: Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer effects in the nucleus accumbens relate to relapse in alcohol dependence
replication_authors: Christian Sommer; Julian Birkenstock; Maria Garbusow; Elisabeth Obst; Daniel J. Schad; Nadine Bernhardt; Quentin M. Huys; Friedrich M. Wurst; Wolfgang Weinmann; Andreas Heinz; Michael N. Smolka; Ulrich S. Zimmermann
replication_title: Dysfunctional approach behavior triggered by alcohol‐unrelated Pavlovian cues predicts long‐term relapse in alcohol dependence
explanation: Verified against the Results section (money-PIT model, body.md ~L675-689): 'Relapsers showed a stronger PIT effect compared with abstainers, as documented by a significant interaction of money CS x instrumental condition x group (Estimate = 0.28, z = 4.04, P < .001). When comparing controls and relapsers, we found the same significant interaction (Estimate = 0.27, z = 4.87, P < .001), indicating a stronger PIT effect in relapsers compared with controls. When comparing controls and abstainers, there was no significant interaction indicating no differences in the PIT effect between those groups (Estimate = -0.006, z = -0.09, P = .93).' This reproduces the exact relapse-specific pattern reported for the original fMRI NAcc finding (effect present in relapsers, absent in abstainers, abstainers indistinguishable from controls), now in the full sample with 1-year follow-up using behavioral PIT accuracy instead of the original BOLD signal. Only one sub-measure is named in the entry's description (money/non-alcohol-related PIT specific to relapse status) and it fully replicated, so 'success' is warranted at high confidence.

description: In an early fMRI subsample of the same cohort followed for 6 months, alcohol-related background pictures inhibited instrumental approach behavior specifically in the n=13 abstinent patients, with no such inhibiting effect found in patients who later relapsed.
original_authors: Daniel J. Schad; Maria Garbusow; Eva Friedel; Christian Sommer; Miriam Sebold; Claudia Hägele; Nadine Bernhardt; Stephan Nebe; Sören Kuitunen-Paul; Shuyan Liu; Uta Eichmann; Anne Beck; Hans-Ulrich Wittchen; Henrik Walter; Philipp Sterzer; Ulrich S. Zimmermann; Michael N. Smolka; Florian Schlagenhauf; Quentin J. M. Huys; Andreas Heinz; Michael A. Rapp
original_title: Neural correlates of instrumental responding in the context of alcohol-related cues index disorder severity and relapse risk
original_journal: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience
replication_authors: Christian Sommer; Julian Birkenstock; Maria Garbusow; Elisabeth Obst; Daniel J. Schad; Nadine Bernhardt; Quentin M. Huys; Friedrich M. Wurst; Wolfgang Weinmann; Andreas Heinz; Michael N. Smolka; Ulrich S. Zimmermann
replication_title: Dysfunctional approach behavior triggered by alcohol‐unrelated Pavlovian cues predicts long‐term relapse in alcohol dependence
explanation: Restricting the full sample to match Schad et al.'s 6-month follow-up window (abstainers vs n=32 patients who relapsed within 6 months), the authors 'found no significant group difference, similarly to the data from the 1-year follow-up,' and concluded 'the different result of Schad et al [33] might be attributed to the smaller sample size' -- i.e., the claim that only abstainers (not relapsers) show the alcohol-picture inhibition effect did not reproduce, in either the full 1-year sample or the 6-month-matched subsample. Narrowed the description to this relapse-status sub-claim only: the original passage also reported alcohol pictures inhibiting approach 'more strongly in patients compared with controls,' and that direction WAS corroborated by this study's own full-sample finding ('[b]everage PIT effects...were stronger in patients compared with controls,' body.md ~L841-843) -- so the original Schad et al. finding is only a partial failure to replicate (patients>controls direction holds, relapser/abstainer subgroup distinction does not), and the paper does not evaluate these two components separately. Kept at medium confidence: this is genuine ambiguity in how a compound original finding should be scored, not something a closer read resolves. Citation check: reference 33 in the bibliography (Schad DJ, Garbusow M, Friedel E, et al., Eur Arch Psychiatry Clin Neurosci, 2018, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00406-017-0860-4) exactly matches the extracted original_authors/title/journal/year/url, confirming the flagged 'year not found in citation' was a false positive -- the year is carried by the numbered reference (33), not stated inline in the citation sentence itself. No field changes needed.

description: Kearney and Fleischer (1979) developed the 43-item Exercise of Self-Care Agency (ESCA) instrument and established its reliability (split-half reliabilities of 0.80 and 0.81, test-retest 0.77) and normative self-care agency mean scores (approximately 120-126) among American associate degree nursing students and undergraduate psychology students.
original_authors: Barbara Y. Kearney; Barbara J. Fleischer
original_title: Development of an instrument to measure exercise of self-care agency
replication_authors: William R. Whetstone
replication_title: Perceptions of self‐care in East Germany: a cross‐cultural empirical investigation
explanation: Independently verified against the PDF (pp. 170-171): the German-translated ESCA administered to 17 East German adults showed markedly poorer split-half reliability (0.31 vs. the original 0.80/0.81) -- a clear failure on that sub-measure -- and a mean score 7-12 points lower than the American norms, significantly so vs. the nursing student sample (P<0.02) but not vs. the psychology student sample (P>0.10). Notably, the paper's own Discussion asserts 'Cross-culturally, both instruments demonstrated reliability' immediately after reporting the 0.31 coefficient -- a global claim of support that contradicts the underlying data, exactly the pattern that keeps a mixed result inconclusive rather than success. Since reliability, one of the two named sub-measures, clearly did not hold up, success is ruled out; since the paper's own framing is supportive despite mixed/failed statistics, inconclusive (not failure) is the better fit. This ambiguity is intrinsic to the paper, not an extraction gap.

description: For a highly ego-involving persuasion issue, manipulating source credibility (high vs. low credibility communicator) has no significant effect on attitude change among field-independent (FI) subjects, who are naturally inclined to differentiate message content; a newly examined field-dependent (FD) subgroup showed the opposite pattern.
original_authors: Homer H. Johnson; John A. Scileppi
original_title: Effects of ego-involvement conditions on attitude change to high- and low-credibility communicators
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Martin Heesacker; Richard E. Petty; John T. Cacioppo
replication_title: Field dependence and attitude change: Source credibility can alter persuasion by affecting message‐relevant thinking
explanation: This was an a priori prediction, not a post-hoc reading: the Introduction states 'Both of the cognitive response formulations would expect FI subjects (who are naturally differentiating the message) to show no effects for credibility, replicating previous research employing high involvement issues (Hass, 1981; Johnson & Scileppi, 1969; Petty, Cacioppo, & Goldman, 1981).' That prediction was then confirmed in Results (no Source Credibility x Message Quality interaction for FI subjects, F(1,158) < 1; only a significant message-quality main effect, F(1,158) = 11.08, p < .002) and explicitly declared replicated in Discussion: 'source credibility failed to affect the attitudes of FI subjects... data from the FI subjects replicated the failure of previous researchers to find source credibility effects for highly involving issues (Johnson & Scileppi, 1969; Petty, Cacioppo, & Goldman, 1981).' The null result is specific to the FI subgroup: FD subjects in this same study did show a source credibility effect (SC x message-quality interaction, F(1,187) = 3.30, p < .08, with credibility affecting differential persuasion only for FD subjects) — a novel extension finding about a subgroup the original studies never tested, not evidence against the FI-specific replication.

description: For issues of high personal involvement, source credibility (high vs. low) has no significant effect on persuasion among field-independent (FI) subjects; message argument quality, rather than source credibility, drives their attitude change. A newly examined field-dependent (FD) subgroup showed the opposite pattern (credibility increased their message scrutiny).
original_authors: Richard E. Petty; John T. Cacioppo; Rachel Goldman
original_title: Personal involvement as a determinant of argument-based persuasion
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Martin Heesacker; Richard E. Petty; John T. Cacioppo
replication_title: Field dependence and attitude change: Source credibility can alter persuasion by affecting message‐relevant thinking
explanation: Using the same high-involvement 'comprehensive exams' persuasion paradigm associated with this research group (the Petty/Cacioppo line), the authors state in the Introduction, as an a priori prediction, that 'Both of the cognitive response formulations would expect FI subjects (who are naturally differentiating the message) to show no effects for credibility, replicating previous research employing high involvement issues (Hass, 1981; Johnson & Scileppi, 1969; Petty, Cacioppo, & Goldman, 1981).' Results confirmed this for field-independent subjects (a new individual-difference subgroup not examined in the original study): no Source Credibility x Message Quality interaction, F(1,158) < 1, with only a significant message-quality main effect, F(1,158) = 11.08, p < .002. The Discussion explicitly declares this 'replicated the failure of previous researchers to find source credibility effects for highly involving issues (Johnson & Scileppi, 1969; Petty, Cacioppo, & Goldman, 1981).' The null finding is scoped to FI subjects only: FD subjects in this same study showed a significant SC x message-quality interaction (F(1,187) = 3.30, p < .08), the paper's novel extension result, which does not contradict the FI-specific replication since the original study never tested an FD subgroup.

description: In a case-control study of predominantly non-Hispanic White subjects, ADORA2A (rs3032740/rs5751876) and CYP1A2 (rs762551) polymorphisms did not modify the association between caffeine/coffee consumption and Parkinson's disease risk.
original_authors: Maurizio F. Facheris; Nicole K. Schneider; Timothy G. Lesnick; Mariza de Andrade; Julie M. Cunningham; Walter A. Rocca; Demetrius M. Maraganore
original_title: Coffee, caffeine-related genes, and Parkinson's disease: a case-control study
replication_authors: Popat RA; Van Den Eeden SK; Tanner CM; Kamel F.; Umbach DM; Marder K.; Mayeux R.; Ritz B.; Ross GW; Petrovitch H.; Topol B.; McGuire V.; Costello S.; Manthripragada AD; Southwick A.; Myers RM; Nelson LM
replication_title: Coffee, ADORA2A, and CYP1A2: the caffeine connection in Parkinson’s disease
explanation: The larger, more ethnically diverse PEGASUS consortium found the same null ADORA2A x coffee interaction as Facheris et al. ('consistent with two other reports that did not find any effect modification of caffeine-PD association with these SNPs [8,9]'), but diverged for CYP1A2 rs762551, where Popat et al. did find a significant coffee-genotype interaction (Pinteraction=0.05) that Facheris et al. did not detect, so the two studies' findings only partly agree.

description: In an ethnically homogeneous Asian sample, ADORA2A polymorphisms (rs3032740/rs5751876) showed no association with Parkinson's disease risk and no interaction with coffee or tea intake on PD risk.
original_authors: Eng‐King Tan; Eng‐King Tan; Zejun Lu; Stephanie Fook‐Chong; E. Tan; E. Tan; Hui Shen; E. Chua; Y. Yih; Yik‐Ying Teo; Yi Zhao
original_title: Exploring an interaction of adenosine A2A receptor variability with coffee and tea intake in Parkinson's disease
original_journal: American Journal of Medical Genetics Part B: Neuropsychiatric Genetics
replication_authors: Popat RA; Van Den Eeden SK; Tanner CM; Kamel F.; Umbach DM; Marder K.; Mayeux R.; Ritz B.; Ross GW; Petrovitch H.; Topol B.; McGuire V.; Costello S.; Manthripragada AD; Southwick A.; Myers RM; Nelson LM
replication_title: Coffee, ADORA2A, and CYP1A2: the caffeine connection in Parkinson’s disease
explanation: Testing the same ADORA2A variants (rs3032740/rs5751876) in a larger, multi-ethnic US consortium, Popat et al. found no overall association with PD risk and state this 'is consistent with two other reports that did not find associations of rs3032740 (or rs5751876...) with PD risk [8,9]' -- reference [9] in this paper's own bibliography is Tan et al. (2006), confirmed via references.json. For the interaction, the rs3032740-coffee (cups/day) interaction was non-significant (Pinteraction=0.08) and is likewise described as 'consistent with two other reports that did not find any effect modification of caffeine-PD association with these SNPs [8,9]'; the paper separately reports 'No interactions of ADORA2A genotypes were observed with caffeinated tea or soda (data not shown),' directly confirming the tea-intake half of the original null finding too. Both sub-measures named in the description (no main association; no coffee/tea interaction) are thus explicitly and specifically matched to Tan et al. (2006) by citation number, which is why confidence is upgraded to high.

description: Among Asian subjects, the inverse association between caffeine intake and Parkinson's disease risk was directionally stronger in slow CYP1A2 (rs762551) metabolizers than in fast metabolizers, though the gene-caffeine interaction was not statistically significant.
original_authors: Eng-King Tan; Eva Chua; Stephanie M. Fook-Chong; Yik-Ying Teo; Yih Yuen; Louis Tan; Yi Zhao
original_title: Association between caffeine intake and risk of Parkinson's disease among fast and slow metabolizers
replication_authors: Popat RA; Van Den Eeden SK; Tanner CM; Kamel F.; Umbach DM; Marder K.; Mayeux R.; Ritz B.; Ross GW; Petrovitch H.; Topol B.; McGuire V.; Costello S.; Manthripragada AD; Southwick A.; Myers RM; Nelson LM
replication_title: Coffee, ADORA2A, and CYP1A2: the caffeine connection in Parkinson’s disease
explanation: Popat et al. explicitly write 'Similar to our results, Tan et al. [10] found that among Asian subjects, the caffeine-PD association was also stronger in slow compared to fast metabolizers (OR 0.19 vs. 0.40); however, the caffeine-genotype interaction was not statistically significant in multivariable analysis [10]' -- confirming the directional pattern named in this entry's description. However, Popat's own version of the same interaction, unlike Tan's, reached nominal significance (Pinteraction=0.05), which they immediately caveat as 'not adjusted for multiple comparisons and hence must be interpreted with caution'; they also note the effect was 'somewhat weaker for heterozygotes, who are also considered physiologically to be slow metabolizers,' i.e. not a clean monotonic dose-response across genotype. Since the description specifically characterizes the original finding as non-significant, and the replication diverges on exactly that point (while matching direction) plus shows an inconsistent genotype dose-response, this remains a partial rather than a clean confirmation.

description: Speakers converge in speech rate toward an interviewer even when the interviewer's speech is pre-recorded and delivered from a separate room, showing that convergence is driven by the interlocutor's speech properties rather than by shared conversational factors.
original_authors: James T. Webb
original_title: Interview synchrony: An investigation of two speech rate measures
replication_authors: Uriel Cohen Priva; Lee Edelist; Emily Gleason
replication_title: Converging to the baseline: Corpus evidence for convergence in speech rate to interlocutor's baseline
replication_journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
explanation: Study 2's mixed-effects regression found a significant positive effect of interlocutor's baseline speech rate on the speaker's own speech rate in conversation (b = 0.054, SE = 0.019, t = 2.804, p < 0.01, FDR-adjusted p < 0.05; Sec. IV.C) -- a single, clean, unambiguous effect, not a mixed or partial result across sub-measures. This is the only sub-measure named in the entry's description (convergence to the interlocutor driven by the interlocutor's speech properties rather than conversational factors), and it held up. Sec. VI (Conclusion) explicitly credits this as supporting Webb's design: 'This provides strong support for previous findings on convergence, especially those on convergence in speech rate (Kendall, 2009; Putman and Street, 1984; Webb, 1972).' No hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'some differences') appears near this finding anywhere in the abstract or discussion.

description: Speakers increase their speech rate to match a fast-speaking virtual interlocutor in a virtual reality environment, showing convergence to the interlocutor's controlled baseline speech rate independent of conversational dynamics.
original_authors: Staum Casasanto, L.; Casasanto, Daniel; Jasmin, Kyle; Casasanto, D.; Jasmin , K.; Staum Casasanto, Laura; Casasanto, Laura Staum
original_title: Virtually accommodating: Speech rate accommodation to a virtual interlocutor
original_journal: Proceedings of the 32nd Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society
replication_authors: Uriel Cohen Priva; Lee Edelist; Emily Gleason
replication_title: Converging to the baseline: Corpus evidence for convergence in speech rate to interlocutor's baseline
replication_journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
explanation: Same Study 2 regression result (b = 0.054, SE = 0.019, t = 2.804, p < 0.01, FDR-adjusted p < 0.05; Sec. IV.C) is the specific evidence: a single, unambiguous significant convergence effect to interlocutor baseline speech rate, not a mixed or partial finding. Sec. VI (Conclusion) explicitly names Staum Casasanto et al. (2010), alongside Webb (1972), as one of the 'certain notable exceptions' that had already isolated interlocutor-driven convergence from shared conversational factors, and states 'The present results demonstrate that at least for speech rate, speakers do converge with their interlocutor's baseline behavior in an ecologically valid setting' -- directly generalizing Staum Casasanto's virtual-interlocutor finding to a naturalistic corpus. No hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'some differences') appears near this finding.

description: In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (the Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study, 4S) of 4444 patients with coronary heart disease, simvastatin treatment significantly reduced all-cause mortality relative to placebo over a median follow-up of 5.3 years.
original_authors: Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study Group
original_title: Randomised trial of cholesterol lowering in 4444 patients with coronary heart disease: the Scandinavian simvastatin survival study (4S)
replication_authors: Hippisley-cox, Julia
replication_title: Effect of statins on the mortality of patients with ischaemic heart disease: population based cohort study with nested case-control analysis
explanation: Confirmed on independent review of the Discussion/Conclusion. The Discussion states explicitly: 'Both the cohort and nested case-control analyses in our study confirm that the benefits of statins extend to unselected patients in a non-trial setting including the elderly, those with diabetes, and women,' and the Conclusion restates 'The benefits of statins found in randomised controlled trials extend to unselected community based patients' -- unhedged confirming language with no 'differing results', 'mixed', or 'partially' language anywhere in the abstract, results, or discussion. The cohort analysis found a 53% lower mortality risk with statin use (adjusted HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.53); the case-control analysis found a 39% lower risk (adjusted OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.72, p<0.001); and the simvastatin-specific analysis (most directly comparable to 4S, which tested simvastatin only) showed adjusted OR 0.62 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.76, p<0.001), comparable in magnitude to the 30% reduction reported in 4S. Every sensitivity analysis reported (excluding diabetes/CCF/MI, excluding cancer, restricting to >=1-year survivors, restricting to complete BMI/smoking records) gave 'similar results,' and subgroup interaction tests by age, sex, and diabetes were all non-significant (p>=0.43), i.e. no subgroup diverged from the overall finding. This is a consistently confirmatory result with no caveats undermining it, so 'success' is well supported.

description: In lung transplant recipients, the TGF-β1 high producer genotype for codon 10 was significantly associated with histological evidence of pulmonary fibrosis (graft fibrosis).
original_authors: Mohammed R. Awad; Ahmed El-Gamel; Philip Hasleton; David M. Turner; Paul J. Sinnott; Ian V. Hutchinson
original_title: Genotypic variation in the transforming growth factor-β1 gene
replication_authors: Arkwright, Peter D.
replication_title: TGF-beta 1 genotype and accelerated decline in lung function of patients with cystic fibrosis
explanation: In cystic fibrosis patients, the TGF-β1 codon 10 high producer genotype was again significantly associated with more rapid pulmonary decline (hazard ratio 1.74 for FEV1, p<0.02; 1.95 for FVC, p<0.005), consistent in direction and significance with the original lung transplant fibrosis study, though the authors note the association was numerically weaker than the original (p<0.004) because spirometry is a less precise fibrosis measure than histology. Verified against the Discussion, which states explicitly: 'In this study we have shown that, in patients with cystic fibrosis, the TGF-β1 codon 10 high producer genotype is associated with a more rapid deterioration in lung function. This is in agreement with studies of patients following lung transplantation[5,13]...' Reference 5 in the bibliography ('Awad MR, El-Gamel A, Hasleton P, et al. Genotypic variation in the transforming growth factor-β1 gene. Transplantation 1998;66:1014-20') matches the extracted original study exactly, confirming both the citation identity and the success classification for codon 10.

description: In lung transplant recipients, the TGF-β1 high producer genotype for codon 25 was significantly associated with histological evidence of pulmonary fibrosis (graft fibrosis), albeit less strongly than codon 10.
original_authors: Mohammed R. Awad; Ahmed El-Gamel; Philip Hasleton; David M. Turner; Paul J. Sinnott; Ian V. Hutchinson
original_title: Genotypic variation in the transforming growth factor-β1 gene
replication_authors: Arkwright, Peter D.
replication_title: TGF-beta 1 genotype and accelerated decline in lung function of patients with cystic fibrosis
explanation: In cystic fibrosis patients, no significant association was found between the TGF-β1 codon 25 genotype and either FEV1 or FVC decline (hazard ratios 1.05 and 1.40, both NS), and the authors explicitly state 'No correlation was found between the TGF-β1 codon 25 genotype and measures of survival or lung function,' contrasting with the significant codon 25 finding in the original lung transplant study. Verified against reference 5 in the bibliography ('Awad MR, El-Gamel A, Hasleton P, et al. Genotypic variation in the transforming growth factor-β1 gene. Transplantation 1998;66:1014-20'), which matches the extracted original study exactly (cited as ref. 5 immediately after the codon 25/10 comparison sentence in the Discussion) and confirms the original reported a significant codon 25 association (p<0.02) that failed to replicate here.

description: Using a loud acoustic stimulus (LAS) to probe the startle-mediating pathways in a simple reaction-time task with a fixed 1-s warning foreperiod, response-related activation shows a uniform increase from stimulus onset up to 100 ms after the imperative stimulus (IS), with no further gradual buildup of excitability as the moment of movement initiation approaches.
original_authors: Hatice Kumru; Josep Valls-Solé
original_title: Excitability of the pathways mediating the startle reaction before execution of a voluntary movement
replication_authors: Welber Marinovic; Aymar de Rugy; Ottmar V. Lipp; James R. Tresilian
replication_title: Responses to loud auditory stimuli indicate that movement-related activation builds up in anticipation of action
explanation: Review confirms this with a second, independent Discussion passage plus the underlying statistics, beyond the single sentence originally cited. Experiment 2 used the same fixed 1-s warning foreperiod as Kumru and Valls-Sole (2006) and probed LAS at intervals after the IS spanning their range. The paper reports no significant effect of probe time on peak FCR EMG when comparing across probe trials only [F(3,21)=0.11, P=0.949] and no effect on EMG duration [F(3,21)=0.33, P=0.800] -- i.e., activation rose to a plateau by the earliest post-IS probe and did not build up further. The Discussion states this explicitly in two places: right after the experiment 2 results ("The results obtained in experiment 2 are similar to those reported by Kumru and Valls-Sole (2006), who found evidence of increased response-related activation in probe trials compared with control trials but no evidence for a gradual buildup of excitability as the moment of movement initiation approached") and again in the general discussion ("we found no evidence for further increase of peak FCR muscle EMG as a function of time. This pattern of results is similar to that reported by Kumru and Valls-Sole (2006) and indicates that in RT tasks the response-related excitability level is close to peak at about the time of the IS, and it does not increase further as the time of movement initiation approaches"). The one measure that did change further after the IS -- peak torque, which declined gradually from 15 ms after the IS -- is a distinct mechanical-output measure the entry's description does not claim replicated, so it does not create ambiguity for the excitability/EMG plateau finding that is being scored here.

description: OXTR exon III DNA methylation, measured in blood-derived DNA, is elevated (hypermethylated) in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder relative to healthy controls.
original_authors: Carolina Cappi; Juliana Belo Diniz; Guaraci L. Requena; Tiaya Lourenço; Bianca Cristina Garcia Lisboa; Marcelo Camargo Batistuzzo; Andrea H. Marques; Marcelo Q. Hoexter; Carlos A. Pereira; Euripedes Constantino Miguel; Helena Brentani
original_title: Epigenetic evidence for involvement of the oxytocin receptor gene in obsessive-compulsive disorder
replication_authors: Miriam A. Schiele; Christiane Thiel; Leonie Kollert; Lena Fürst; Lisa Putschin; Rebekka Kehle; Walter Hauke; Marina Mahr; Elena Reinhold; Michael G. Gottschalk; Markus Heinrichs; Michael Zaudig; Götz Berberich; Katharina Domschke
replication_title: Oxytocin Receptor Gene DNA Methylation: A Biomarker of Treatment Response in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'This pilot finding thus replicates and extends a previous observation of increased OXTR exon III methylation in OCD [12]', and report a significantly higher average OXTR methylation in OCD patients than controls (p < 0.001), consistent in direction with the original finding. The replication used a new, independently recruited German case-control sample (vs. the original study's different population) and embedded the case-control comparison within a larger longitudinal treatment-response design, so context differs from the original while the core measure and paradigm (blood-based OXTR exon III methylation, case-control comparison) are preserved.

description: A sustained induced gamma-band response (approximately 400-1000 msec post-stimulus, 35-80 Hz) is observed during recognition memory retrieval and predicts successful encoding/retrieval of declarative memory.
original_authors: Daria Osipova; Atsuko Takashima; Robert Oostenveld; Guillén Fernández; Eric Maris; Ole Jensen
original_title: Theta and gamma oscillations predict encoding and retrieval of declarative memory
replication_authors: Thomas Gruber; Dimitris Tsivilis; Claire-Marie Giabbiconi; Matthias M. Müller
replication_title: Induced Electroencephalogram Oscillations during Source Memory: Familiarity is Reflected in the Gamma Band, Recollection in the Theta Band
explanation: Confirmed as a clean single-measure failure to replicate. The Methods section confirms the authors deliberately targeted the identical time window and frequency band used by Osipova et al. (2006) ('a time window from 400 to 1000 msec in a frequency range from 35 to 80 Hz'). The Results section reports the underlying statistical outcome directly: 'The examination of the time window from 400 to 1000 msec revealed no significant effects' — a plain null result, not a mixed or partial one. The Discussion reiterates this in explicit comparison to the original study: 'we found no evidence of a sustained gamma effect similar to that reported by Osipova et al. (2006).' The authors' speculation about task differences (source discrimination added, no confidence-based withholding) is offered as a post hoc explanation for why the effect might be absent, not a qualification suggesting the effect was partially found — no significant sustained gamma effect was detected. Since this entry targets a single, specific sub-finding (not a multi-measure claim with some parts replicating), and the outcome for that finding is an unambiguous null, 'failure' is the correct label.

description: Individual differences in attentional blink (AB) magnitude are large and represent a stable, reliable individual trait across testing occasions.
original_authors: Gillian Dale; Paul E. Dux; Karen M. Arnell
original_title: Individual differences within and across attentional blink tasks revisited
replication_authors: Raquel E. London; Heleen A. Slagter
replication_title: No Effect of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation over Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex on Temporal Attention
explanation: Reviewed body.md in full (Individual Differences results section and Discussion). Both sub-claims in the description are explicitly and unambiguously confirmed with statistics: large individual differences in AB magnitude are reported ('Replicating previous reports, large individual differences in AB magnitude (Dale et al., 2013)... were observed'), and test-retest stability is separately confirmed (baseline AB magnitude correlated between sessions, r(31) = .583, p < .001, 'replicating previous reports that AB performance is stable over time'). No countervailing statement appears anywhere in the paper regarding this specific claim. Confidence is kept at medium rather than raised to high because this is a secondary, incidental analysis in a paper whose primary focus and abstract are entirely about tDCS effects -- the AB-magnitude replication is never mentioned outside this one paragraph -- and no additional resolving evidence beyond what was already identified was found on review.

description: Distractor inhibition ability -- indexed by the degree to which a subliminal prime of the second target (T2) impairs its later identification (T2 priming) -- shows large individual differences that predict individual differences in recovery from the attentional blink.
original_authors: Heleen A. Slagter; Katerina Georgopoulou
original_title: Distractor inhibition predicts individual differences in recovery from the attentional blink
replication_authors: Raquel E. London; Heleen A. Slagter
replication_title: No Effect of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation over Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex on Temporal Attention
explanation: The AB task, including the priming manipulation, was 'identical to the task used by Slagter and Georgopoulou (2013)' (a self-replication, as Slagter co-authored both), and large individual differences in distractor inhibition were again observed. However, checking the Methods (Analyses/Individual Differences section) confirms this study never actually recomputed the specific 'distractor inhibition predicts AB recovery' correlation: only 'AB magnitude' (Lag10 vs. Lag2) and 'T2 priming' (Lag4 prime-present vs. prime-absent) were calculated from the new data -- 'AB recovery' (Lag10 minus Lag4) is not a measure this study computed. The paper's doubt is therefore built from two things that are NOT a direct empirical re-test of the original correlation: (1) a newly measured, genuinely null test-retest reliability of the T2 priming measure itself (r(31) = -.089, ns), and (2) a statistical/mathematical argument (shared-variable nonindependence, citing Archie, 1981) that the original correlation could be a coupling artifact. On that basis the authors conclude this 'casts serious doubt on the previously reported relationship... (Slagter & Georgopoulou, 2013; Dux & Marois, 2008)'. Because the specific predictive relationship named in the description was never directly retested with new data -- only critiqued and undermined via reliability/artifact arguments -- 'inconclusive' remains the more defensible label than 'failure', but genuine ambiguity remains: a reader could reasonably argue the authors' own strong skepticism ('casts serious doubt') tips this toward failure rather than a neutral inconclusive.

description: Distractor inhibition ability, indexed by T2 priming, shows large individual differences that predict individual differences in attentional blink performance.
original_authors: Paul E. Dux; René Marois
original_title: Distractor inhibition predicts individual differences in the attentional blink
replication_authors: Raquel E. London; Heleen A. Slagter
replication_title: No Effect of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation over Left Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex on Temporal Attention
explanation: The AB/priming task used was 'modeled after the task designed by Dux and Marois (2008)' rather than identical to it. Large individual differences in distractor inhibition were again observed. As with the Slagter & Georgopoulou (2013) entry, checking the Methods confirms this study never recomputed 'AB recovery' (Lag10 minus Lag4) at all -- only 'AB magnitude' (Lag10 vs. Lag2) and 'T2 priming' (Lag4 present vs. absent) were calculated. The doubt cast on Dux and Marois's original priming-predicts-AB relationship rests on (1) a newly measured null test-retest reliability of the T2 priming measure (r(31) = -.089, ns) and (2) a statistical argument that the original correlation could reflect shared-variable nonindependence rather than a true effect -- not on a direct re-test of the correlation itself. The authors conclude this jointly 'casts serious doubt on the previously reported relationship between distractor inhibition and AB recovery (Slagter & Georgopoulou, 2013; Dux & Marois, 2008)'. 'Inconclusive' remains defensible since the specific relationship was not directly retested with new data, but the ambiguity is genuine: the authors' skepticism is strongly worded, and a reasonable reader could argue for 'failure' instead given how pointed the reliability failure and critique are.

description: Currently depressed patients, relative to healthy individuals, show a perturbed (reduced) pattern of cerebellar neural response to facial emotional expressions during fMRI.
original_authors: Surguladze, Simon; Brammer, Michael J.; Keedwell, Paul; Giampietro, Vincent; Young, Andrew W.; Travis, Mick J.; Williams, Steven C.; Phillips, Mary L.
original_title: A differential pattern of neural response toward sad versus happy facial expressions in major depressive disorder
replication_authors: Fabrice Jollant; Natalia S. Lawrence; Vincent Giampietro; Michael J. Brammer; Miguel A. Fullana; Dominique Drapier; Philippe Courtet; Mary L. Phillips
replication_title: Orbitofrontal Cortex Response to Angry Faces in Men With Histories of Suicide Attempts
explanation: Verified against the paper's structured Results and Table 3. The abstract's own Results section states plainly: 'Relative to healthy comparison subjects, both patient groups showed reduced activity in the right cerebellum to neutral faces and to mild happy versus neutral faces' -- no hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'some differences'). Table 3's post hoc between-group analysis confirms this with statistics: HC > SA and HC > AC (both significant, and both survive exclusion of medicated patients, footnote b) for neutral-vs-fixation, and HC > AC > SA (both significant) for mild happy vs. neutral -- i.e., both patient groups were significantly lower than healthy comparison subjects on both contrasts named in the abstract's Results. (A third cerebellar contrast, prototypical happy vs. neutral, showed only a significant omnibus group effect with no significant pairwise post hoc differences -- weaker, but not contradictory: no contrast showed patients elevated relative to healthy.) The Discussion (body.md line ~997-1004) repeats the same unqualified claim: 'Healthy individuals showed significantly greater activity than both patient groups in the right cerebellum in response to neutral faces and to mild happy expressions. These findings parallel our previous results (27) in currently depressed patients compared with healthy individuals. Together, they provide replicable evidence of perturbed cerebellar function...' This is a self-replication (3 overlapping authors, incl. senior author Phillips) extending the effect to a euthymic, previously-depressed/suicide-attempter sample using a related but not identical facial-expression fMRI paradigm (angry/happy vs. neutral, rather than sad vs. happy), so it is correctly classified as a close extension rather than direct replication. Citation check: the numbered citation '(27)' was cross-referenced against references.json entry id 27 -- 'Surguladze S, Brammer MJ, Keedwell P, Giampietro V, Young AW, Travis MJ, Williams SC, Phillips ML: A differential pattern of neural response toward sad versus happy facial expressions in major depre[ssion]', DOI 10.1016/j.biopsych.2004.10.028 -- which exactly matches the extracted original_authors/original_title/original_url. The earlier 'citation mismatch' flag was a false positive of an author/year-in-text checker: this paper cites numerically rather than by author-year, so the name and year do not appear literally in the citation sentence, but the numbered reference resolves unambiguously to the correct original study. No changes needed to original_authors/original_title/original_year/original_url.

description: The CW-FIT (Class-Wide Function-related Intervention Teams) group contingency intervention, implemented in six urban classrooms in three schools, improved classwide on-task behavior, and adding a self-management component for children who continued to be disruptive further decreased their disruptive behavior and improved on-task behavior.
original_authors: Kamps, Debra; Wills, Howard; Heitzman-Powell, Linda; Laylin, Jason; Szoke, Corina; Hobohm, Tanya; Culey, Angela
original_title: Class-wide function-based intervention teams: Effects of group contingency programs in urban classrooms
replication_authors: Howard Wills; Debra Kamps; Kandace Fleming; Blake Hansen
replication_title: Student and Teacher Outcomes of the Class-Wide Function-Related Intervention Team Efficacy Trial
explanation: The Discussion explicitly states: 'Findings also confirm results in prior CW-FIT intervention studies with smaller numbers of students with EBD risk (Kamps et al., 2011; Wills et al., 2010).' Both sub-measures named in the description are independently confirmed with unambiguous, unqualified quantitative results (no 'mixed'/'partial'/'differing' hedging anywhere in the Discussion for these outcomes): (1) classwide on-task/disruptive improvement — Group x Time interactions were significant for both on-task (F(1,313)=85.37, p<.001; CW-FIT rose 65%->87% vs. control 65%->67%) and disruptions (F(1,315)=35.38, p<.001; CW-FIT fell from a mean of 17 to 6 vs. control's 16 to 14); (2) the self-management add-on for still-disruptive students — the Results section reports disruptive behavior for the 35 self-management students fell further from 11.9 (CW-FIT alone) to 7.2 (CW-FIT + self-management), with on-task rising from 80.8% to 86%. Every sub-measure in the description replicated with statistically significant, unqualified support.

description: The CW-FIT group contingency intervention improved on-task behavior in 16 urban elementary classrooms across three schools.
original_authors: Wills, Howard P.; Kamps, Debra; Hansen, Blake D.; Conklin, Cyrus; Bellinger, Susan; Neaderhiser, Jenny; Nsubuga, Betty
original_title: The class-wide function-based intervention team (CW-FIT) program
replication_authors: Howard Wills; Debra Kamps; Kandace Fleming; Blake Hansen
replication_title: Student and Teacher Outcomes of the Class-Wide Function-Related Intervention Team Efficacy Trial
explanation: The Discussion explicitly states: 'Findings also confirm results in prior CW-FIT intervention studies with smaller numbers of students with EBD risk (Kamps et al., 2011; Wills et al., 2010).' The single sub-measure named in the description — improved on-task behavior under CW-FIT — is confirmed unambiguously and quantitatively: the on-task Group x Time interaction was significant, F(1,313)=85.37, p<.001, with the CW-FIT group's time-on-task rising from 65% at baseline to 87% during intervention while the control group was flat (65% to 67%). No hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'differing') appears in the Discussion regarding this outcome.

description: An earlier version of the Transitions mental health literacy life-skills resource was positively received by postsecondary students, who reported that reading it improved their knowledge about mental health/mental illness, decreased stigma, and increased help-seeking efficacy and intentions (including discussing what they read with friends and others).
original_authors: Jacqueline Potvin-Boucher; Magdalena Szumilas; Tabinda Sheikh; Stan Kutcher
original_title: Transitions: A mental health literacy program for postsecondary students
replication_authors: Stan Kutcher; Yifeng Wei; Catherine Morgan
replication_title: Mental health literacy in post-secondary students
explanation: Reviewed the paper's own Results/Discussion directly, not just the Discussion's summary sentence. The Discussion does say 'These results are similar to those reported in an earlier study using an earlier version of the resource (Potvin-Boucher et al., 2010),' but the paper's own abstract qualifies this: 'Reading Transitions (2nd edition) improved student knowledge about and decreased stigma towards mental health and mental illness and increased help-seeking efficacy. There were sex differences in response regarding discussion of the resource with others and help-seeking intentions.' The Results section shows this caveat is substantive, not cosmetic: only 24.0% of women vs 0% of men said they were planning to seek help for a mental health concern (p=.006), and men were significantly more likely than women to say they would NOT seek help despite having a concern (p=.018); discussing the resource with friends also differed sharply by sex (68.0% women vs 29.6% men, p=.001). The entry's description bundles 'help-seeking efficacy and intentions (including discussing what they read with friends and others)' as one outcome from the original 2010 study. In this replication, knowledge, stigma, and general help-seeking-efficacy items were broadly positive across the whole sample, but the help-seeking-intentions and discuss-with-others sub-measures were not a clean replication -- they were essentially null for men. Per the rule that a global claim of support does not override an abstract/conclusion that also reports differing results, and that partial support on a multi-measure entry is inconclusive rather than success, this is best labeled inconclusive rather than success.

description: Using the Militarized Compellent Threat (MCT) data, Downes and Sechser (2012) found no significant relationship between a challenger's audience-cost/democratic capacity and whether its compellent threat achieved full compliance, contradicting the audience cost proposition.
original_authors: Downes, Alexander B.; Sechser, Todd S.
original_title: The illusion of democratic credibility
replication_authors: Chungshik Moon; Mark Souva
replication_title: Audience Costs, Information, and Credible Commitment Problems
explanation: The authors reanalyze the MCT data with a base model that modifies Downes and Sechser's specification in minor ways (different audience-cost measure, dropped/replaced covariates; see note 10) and state: 'The estimates from this model support Downes and Sechser's (2012) central findings. Specifically, consistent with Downes and Sechser, we do not find a significant influence of audience costs on threat success (model 1).'

description: Using a censored selection model of militarized interstate dispute (MID) initiation and escalation, Uzonyi, Souva, and Golder (2012) found that challengers with greater audience cost capacity are less likely to have their militarized threats reciprocated by targets.
original_authors: Uzonyi, Gary; Souva, Mark; Golder, Sona N.
original_title: Domestic institutions and credible signals
replication_authors: Chungshik Moon; Mark Souva
replication_title: Audience Costs, Information, and Credible Commitment Problems
explanation: The authors state their MID research design 'mirrors that of Uzonyi, Souva, and Golder (2012)' and report base models (4 and 7) that 'mimic the research design of Schultz (1999), Weeks (2008), and Uzonyi, Souva, and Golder (2012)'; they find 'the coefficient on Audience Costs is negative and statistically significant... This result conforms to extant research.'

description: Using International Crisis Behavior (ICB) project data, Gelpi and Griesdorf (2001) found that democratic challengers and challengers with a relative audience-cost/resolve advantage are more likely to prevail (avoid losing) in international crises.
original_authors: Gelpi, Christopher; Griesdorf, Michael
original_title: Winners or losers? Democracies in international crisis, 1918-94
replication_authors: Chungshik Moon; Mark Souva
replication_title: Audience Costs, Information, and Credible Commitment Problems
explanation: The authors rerun Gelpi and Griesdorf's ordered probit model on the ICB data and report: 'The first column (model 10) of Table 4 shows the estimates for the Gelpi and Griesdorf model on all cases. Democratic Challenger and Audience cost x Resolve are significant and positive, just as Gelpi and Griesdorf find.'

description: When personal death is made salient (mortality salience), participants in a minimal group paradigm display greater levels of ingroup bias than when death is not made salient.
original_authors: Eddie Harmon-Jones; Jeff Greenberg; Sheldon Solomon; Linda Simon
original_title: The effects of mortality salience on intergroup bias between minimal groups
replication_authors: Emanuele Castano; Vincent Yzerbyt; Maria-Paola Paladino; Simona Sacchi
replication_title: I Belong, therefore, I Exist: Ingroup Identification, Ingroup Entitativity, and Ingroup Bias
explanation: Castano et al. found a significant condition x target-group interaction, F(1,46)=4.11, p<.05, with mortality-salient participants showing stronger ingroup bias than controls, and explicitly write in the Discussion that 'the effect obtained by Harmon-Jones et al. (1996) ... is of the same nature. Indeed, it is the judgment of the ingroup that is affected by MS and not that of the outgroup.' Follow-up t-tests confirm this precise pattern: MS raised ingroup ratings specifically, t(24)=3.24, p<.01, while leaving outgroup ratings unaffected, t(24)=1.03, p>.29 (ingroup bias was reliable in both conditions, but markedly stronger under MS: MNS t(23)=2.20, p<.05 vs. MS t(23)=5.28, p<.0001). This ingroup-specific localization independently verifies the qualitative match to the original finding, not merely a general claim of support, and no hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'some differences') appears anywhere regarding this comparison. The replication extends the original minimal-group paradigm to a real, established national ingroup/outgroup (Italians vs. Germans).

description: Manipulating group members' interaction in a laboratory small-group setting (a proximal factor) increases perceived ingroup entitativity, which in turn increases the level of ingroup bias.
original_authors: Lowell Gaertner; John Schopler
original_title: Perceived ingroup entitativity and intergroup bias: An interconnection of self and others
replication_authors: Emanuele Castano; Vincent Yzerbyt; Maria-Paola Paladino; Simona Sacchi
replication_title: I Belong, therefore, I Exist: Ingroup Identification, Ingroup Entitativity, and Ingroup Bias
explanation: Using mortality salience (a distal factor) rather than interaction (a proximal factor) to vary perceived ingroup entitativity, Castano et al. found MS significantly raised perceived entitativity, F(1,46)=4.15, p<.05, and the authors state directly: 'the findings of Gaertner and Schopler and our study are entirely consistent,' testing the same entitativity-to-ingroup-bias link via a fundamentally different manipulation. Figure 1a's mediation model shows entitativity remained a significant predictor of ingroup bias after controlling for condition (corrected coefficient .27, p<.05). However, the formal mediation test itself was only marginal, Sobel Z=1.71, p<.08 (not conventionally significant); the authors instead lean on convergent structural equation modeling (chi2(1)=2.05, p=.15, GFI=.97) and stepwise Baron & Kenny criteria to call the mediation supported. That marginal Sobel result is a genuine wrinkle in the paper's own statistics -- not an extraction artifact -- so confidence stays medium rather than high despite the authors' unambiguous 'entirely consistent' framing.

description: Video prompting was more effective than static picture prompting in enabling students with moderate intellectual disabilities to independently complete a greater percentage of cooking-related tasks.
original_authors: Mechling, Linda C.; Gustafson, Melissa R.
original_title: Comparison of the effects of static picture and video prompting on completion of cooking related tasks by students with moderate intellectual disabilities
replication_authors: Linda C. Mechling; Melissa R. Gustafson
replication_title: Comparison of Static Picture and Video Prompting on the Performance of Cooking-Related Tasks by Students with Autism
explanation: The authors state 'Results are consistent with the replicated study of Mechling and Gustafson (in press), which indicated that video was more effective than static pictures in prompting task completion by students with disabilities,' and in the Discussion: 'Results support the findings of Mechling and Gustafson...and extend the results to students with ASD.' The same 20 identical cooking tasks and AATD design were used, but the population was changed from students with moderate intellectual disabilities to students with autism spectrum disorder.

description: Individuals with higher reappraisal ability reported fewer depressive symptoms when exposed to uncontrollable stressors, but more depressive symptoms when exposed to controllable stressors, indicating that reappraisal is adaptive in uncontrollable contexts but maladaptive in controllable contexts (the strategy-situation-fit hypothesis).

description: Using fixed arrays of 12 faces expressing anger shown for 1 s, participants' estimates of a crowd's average emotion were biased toward more extreme values than the true average, providing initial evidence of a crowd-emotion-amplification effect.
original_authors: Goldenberg, Amit; Sweeny, Timothy D.; Shpigel, Eran; Gross, James J.

replication_authors: Amit Goldenberg; Erika Weisz; Timothy D. Sweeny; Mina Cikara; James J. Gross
replication_title: The Crowd-Emotion-Amplification Effect
explanation: Study 1 explicitly builds on Goldenberg et al. (2020, Study 2), which found initial amplification evidence using fixed 12-face anger arrays, and extends it by varying set size (1-12 faces) and adding positive-valence arrays; the amplification effect was confirmed (estimated mean crowd emotion 2.87 points higher than actual, b = 2.87, 95% CI [2.53, 3.21], t(14533) = 16.8, p < .001), consistent with the original finding. Verified against the General Discussion, which states without hedging that 'we found that participants tended to overestimate the intensity of a crowd's average emotion'; no 'mixed/partial/differing results' language is attached to this hypothesis anywhere in the paper (that hedge applies only to the separate valence hypothesis, which held in Studies 1-2 but not Study 3, and is unrelated to this entry).

description: When estimating the mean size of a set of circles varying in diameter, perceivers overestimated the average size (overweighting the largest, most salient items), and this amplification bias grew larger as more circles were added to the set.

replication_authors: Amit Goldenberg; Erika Weisz; Timothy D. Sweeny; Mina Cikara; James J. Gross
replication_title: The Crowd-Emotion-Amplification Effect
explanation: Hypothesis 2 explicitly tested, 'following Kanaya et al. (2018),' whether Kanaya's set-size-amplification finding (obtained with circles varying in size) generalizes to emotional face arrays; number of faces significantly predicted increased amplification in Study 1 (b = 0.42, 95% CI [0.21, 0.64], t(7233) = 3.86, p < .001) and was independently replicated in Study 2 (b = 0.28, p = .01), matching the original pattern in a fundamentally different (social/emotion) paradigm. Verified against the General Discussion ('amplification grew as the number of faces within an array increased,' stated without hedging) and the paper's Notes: Note 2 flags a surprising single-face amplification visible in Fig. 3, but the authors attribute this to a carryover artifact from preceding trials, ruled out by a dedicated pilot study, so it does not undermine the set-size finding.
