original_journal: The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology
replication_authors: Mateusz Woźniak; Günther Knoblich
replication_title: Self-prioritization of fully unfamiliar stimuli
explanation: The authors state directly in the Discussion: 'In our study, we replicated the results reported by Payne et al. (2017) showing an SPE for unfamiliar faces in the conventional version of the matching task.' The standard task's own one-way ANOVA also showed the predicted self > friend > stranger pattern in matching trials (p < .001).

description: After briefly associating three identities (self, friend, stranger) with three arbitrary geometric shapes presented alongside familiar verbal labels, participants are faster and more accurate at recognising self-associated matching pairs than friend- or stranger-associated pairs (the self-prioritization effect, SPE), which the original authors argued does not depend on higher familiarity of self-related information.
original_authors: Sui, Jie; He, Xun; Humphreys, Glyn W.

replication_title: Self-prioritization of fully unfamiliar stimuli
explanation: Using a modified 'no-labels' matching task that replaced the original's familiar verbal labels with unfamiliar abstract symbols (and geometric shapes with avatar faces) to test whether SPE depends on label familiarity, the authors report a significant self-prioritization effect for symbols and conclude: 'we provide conclusive evidence of facilitated processing of rapidly self-associated fully unfamiliar stimuli, and hence confirm and strengthen the main finding from the original study by Sui et al. (2012)... our study provides conclusive evidence of a genuine SPE supporting the claims of Sui et al. (2012).'

description: Presenting a train of auditory clicks (~5 Hz) before a to-be-judged stimulus speeds up the internal pacemaker, increasing the subjective/perceived duration of that stimulus relative to silence, with the size of the effect growing multiplicatively with actual stimulus duration and being distinctly larger than the (null) effect of white noise.
original_authors: Penton-Voak, Ian; Edwards, Helen; Percival, Andrew; Wearden, J. H.
original_title: Speeding up an internal clock in humans? Effects of click trains on subjective duration
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes
replication_authors: Letizia Palumbo; Ruth Ogden; Alexis D. J. Makin; Marco Bertamini
replication_title: Does Preference for Abstract Patterns Relate to Information Processing and Perceived Duration?
explanation: Independently verified against body.md Experiment 2 results and Discussion (lines ~373-375, 428-430, 479-485, 553-558) and the reference list (Penton-Voak et al., 1996, JEP:ABP, 22, 307-320 -- bibliographic fields confirmed correct). Click trains significantly increased judged duration relative to silence (t(23)=3.31, p=.003), and the authors' framing sentence is a global success claim: 'This replicates all previous work in this area (Droit-Volet, 2010; Jones et al., 2011; Penton-Voak et al., 1996; Treisman et al., 1990)'. But the paper's own later Discussion is explicit that two of the three sub-measures named in this entry's description did not replicate: no slope/multiplicative effect ('we did not find these slope effects on duration estimates in Experiment 2'; 'Duration estimates in our Experiment 2 were not consistent with either claim [white-noise-null and multiplicative-slope]') and no distinct clicks-vs-white-noise difference (t(23)=0.732, p=.472, vs. silence-vs-white-noise t(23)=1.699, p=.103). The authors themselves call these 'apparent anomalies' relative to Penton-Voak et al. (1996) and argue they don't undermine their preference conclusions, but that is a defense of the paper's own (different) research question, not a claim that the click-train duration paradigm was fully replicated. Per the mixed-results rule, a global claim of replication does not override an explicit report that specific sub-measures diverged, so only the basic clicks>silence direction (1 of 3 named sub-measures) replicated; the label stays inconclusive. This is a case of the paper itself asserting both 'replicates all previous work' and detailed non-replication of that same work's signature findings in the same Discussion section -- confidence stays medium since resolving this requires weighing the authors' own conflicting framing rather than new documentary evidence.

description: Examining the relationship between democratic presidential elections and government respect for human rights, presidential elections (treating all presidential systems as essentially the same) are associated with lesser levels of government respect for human rights, reflecting the winner-take-all, zero-sum structure of presidentialism.
original_authors: Richards, David L.; Gelleny, Ronald D.
original_title: Good things to those who wait? National elections and government respect for human rights
replication_authors: Joshua Holzer
replication_title: The perils of plurality rule and the major(itarian) effect of cabinet composition on human rights in presidential democracies
explanation: Independently verified against the Results (p.4-5) and Conclusion (p.7). The author's first model is 'nearly identical' to Richards and Gelleny (2007) but uses updated/expanded datasets (newer CIRI version, newer electoral-systems dataset, newer conflict data, newer World Bank data), a different serial-correlation correction, and an extended, non-overlapping 2001-2011 time window, while also replacing R&G's undifferentiated 'presidential election' variable with a majority-vs-plurality split. Both of the author's own (refined) hypotheses are fully confirmed by his data: majority-elected presidents are associated with significantly (p<0.01) greater government respect for human rights than plurality-elected ones (Model 1), and a higher share of cabinet posts held by other parties is likewise associated with greater respect (p<0.05, Model 2); predicted-probability plots (Figures 1-2) show the same direction across best/average/worst scenarios. But this is not a like-for-like replication of R&G's original, undifferentiated claim that 'presidential elections' as a class are associated with lower respect for human rights - Holzer's result implies the effect is conditional on election type (plurality drives it; majority does not), which the author himself frames as only a partial confirmation: 'My findings partially confirm their observation that some presidential elections lead to lower levels of respect for human rights. My results, however, add nuance to our understanding of this relationship.' Given the result rule that a global claim of support does not override an author's own 'partial'/'differs' language, and that only some (not every) part of the original undifferentiated claim carries over unchanged, inconclusive is the correct label; the ambiguity is genuine (it lies in how a refined-IV extension maps onto the original blanket claim, not in any lack of clarity about Holzer's own findings) so confidence remains medium.

description: In a nested case-control study of HIV-positive persons within the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study (49 cases, 135 controls), elevated baseline serum soluble CD30 (sCD30) concentration was associated with increased subsequent risk of AIDS-related non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).

replication_title: A prospective study of serum soluble CD30 concentration and risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
explanation: The authors extend Breen et al's finding from severely immunocompromised HIV+ patients to a healthy, immunocompetent population, and report the same dose-response association ("our findings suggest that chronic B-cell stimulation may be an important mechanism involved in B-cell lymphomagenesis among severely immunocompromised and healthy populations alike"), which persisted even 6-10 years after blood draw, longer than the original's <3 year window.

description: Depressed patients living with spouses/relatives who made two or more critical remarks (high expressed emotion, EE) during a research interview were significantly more likely to relapse over a nine-month follow-up than patients living with low-EE or non-critical relatives.
original_authors: Vaughn, Christine E.; Leff, Julian P.

replication_authors: Jill M. Hooley; John Orley; John D. Teasdale
replication_title: Levels of Expressed Emotion and Relapse in Depressed Patients
explanation: Authors explicitly frame the study as 'the first full replication' and conclude 'The results thus replicate the earlier work of Vaughn & Leff (1976) and suggest strongly that EE is a variable which is of predictive utility in both schizophrenic and depressed populations'; relapse rates (51% vs 53% original) and the critical-comments/relapse association (t=2.51, P<0.02) closely matched the original.

description: Patients' total psychiatric symptom severity score is significantly correlated with the frequency of critical comments made about them by relatives (original correlation of 0.48).
original_authors: Vaughn, Christine E.; Leff, Julian P.
original_title: The influence of family and social factors on the course of psychiatric illness: a comparison of schizophrenic and depressed neurotic patients
replication_authors: Jill M. Hooley; John Orley; John D. Teasdale
replication_title: Levels of Expressed Emotion and Relapse in Depressed Patients
explanation: Verified against body.md: the Results section states directly 'Whereas Vaughn & Leff found a correlation of 0.48 between total symptom score of the patients and the frequency of criticisms made by relatives, there was no such significant correlation within the present study (r=0.01, P>0.1)' -- an unambiguous numeric contrast (significant 0.48 vs. non-significant 0.01) explicitly framed by the authors as a non-replication of this specific secondary measure. The symptom score is the same PSE-derived total score used elsewhere in the paper, so the description matches the original claim being tested. I checked the Discussion section for any later reinterpretation or softening of this point and found none: the Discussion revisits only the main EE-relapse finding (labeled a successful replication) and the criticism-threshold comparison, never returning to the symptom-severity/criticism correlation. Confidence kept at medium per review policy, since this conclusion rests on the same passage the prior pass already quoted rather than on newly surfaced evidence -- though on the merits the failure classification for this narrow, single-measure claim is well supported and not genuinely ambiguous.

description: In rats, hippocampal Gh mRNA is elevated by estradiol treatment after ovariectomy.
original_authors: Christine P. Donahue; Kenneth S. Kosik; Tracey J. Shors

original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Melisande L. Addison; Emilie F. Rissman

explanation: Verified against the Results section: in gonadectomized mice, estradiol significantly increased Gh mRNA in females in both the MPOA [F(1,30)=19.01, P<0.001] and ARC [F(1,31)=19.89, P<0.001], with no significant estradiol effect in males in either region — directly paralleling Donahue et al.'s rat finding that ovariectomy lowers and estradiol restores hippocampal Gh mRNA. The Discussion states unqualified agreement ('our data are in agreement with the findings of Donahue et al. (11)...') with no hedging language ('however', 'in contrast', 'partial', 'mixed') anywhere near that passage, and the sex-specificity of the current study's effect matches the female-only framing of the original. Narrowed the description to drop the primary-cortical-neuronal-cell-culture sub-finding of Donahue et al.: the current paper only ran in vivo qRT-PCR (MPOA/ARC), never a cell-culture assay, so that part of the original two-part finding was cited as consistent background rather than independently tested, and per the result rules an untested sub-measure should not be folded into a 'success' label.

description: Using serial analysis of gene expression (SAGE) on mouse hypothalamus, GH transcripts were found to be expressed at dramatically higher levels in females than in males.
original_authors: Yuichiro Nishida; Mayumi Yoshioka; Jonny St-Amand

replication_authors: Melisande L. Addison; Emilie F. Rissman
replication_title: Sexual Dimorphism of Growth Hormone in the Hypothalamus: Regulation by Estradiol
explanation: Verified against the Results section: in gonad-intact mice, Gh mRNA was significantly higher in females than males in both hypothalamic nuclei tested — MPOA [F(1,26)=125, P<0.001, females higher than all three other groups] and ARC [females different from all other groups, P<0.05] — matching the direction of Nishida et al.'s SAGE finding of dramatically higher hypothalamic GH transcripts in females. The Discussion states this plainly ('Our findings confirm a serial analysis of gene expression study that reported GH gene expression was dramatically higher in the hypothalamus and cortex... (15)') with no hedging nearby. Narrowed the description to drop the cortex and pituitary sub-measures: the current study never quantified Gh mRNA sex differences in cortex or pituitary (only in MPOA, ARC, NAc, VP), so those parts of Nishida et al.'s three-tissue finding were cited as background, not independently tested, and per the result rules an untested sub-measure should not be folded into a 'success' label. Because the original used untargeted transcriptomic profiling (SAGE) and the current study used targeted qRT-PCR on microdissected nuclei, this remains a conceptual replication (same theoretical claim, different measurement paradigm) rather than a direct or close one.

description: Patients with idiopathic restless legs syndrome (RLS) show abnormally reduced CSF ferritin and elevated CSF transferrin compared to normal controls, suggesting an underlying brain iron insufficiency in RLS.
original_authors: Earley, C.J.; Connors, J.R.; Allen, R.P.
original_title: RLS patients have abnormally reduced CSF ferritin compared to normal controls
replication_authors: Allen RP; Barker PB; Wehrl FW; Song HK; Earley CJ
replication_title: MRI measurement of brain iron in patients with restless legs syndrome
explanation: Using an MRI-based regional brain iron measure (R2'), the authors found significantly lower iron in the substantia nigra (t=-2.17, p=0.031) and only marginally/non-significantly lower iron in the putamen (t=-1.69, p=0.065) of RLS patients vs. controls, with no significant group difference in the caudate (p=NS) or in any of the five secondary regions of interest (globus pallidus, dentate nucleus, pons, red nucleus, thalamus; all p=NS). Severity correlations (Spearman) were significant for substantia nigra (rho=-0.69, p=0.02) and putamen (rho=-0.64, p=0.03) but not caudate. The paper's own abstract states the results 'indicate that brain iron insufficiency may occur in patients with RLS in some brain regions' (not all), and the Discussion calls this 'a limited initial study' with results 'consistent with,' not confirming, the prior CSF iron-insufficiency finding. With only 1 of 3 primary ROIs (and 0 of 5 secondary ROIs) reaching significance on the direct group comparison, and the authors' own explicit region-limited framing, this is a partial/mixed replication of the iron-insufficiency hypothesis, correctly labeled inconclusive rather than success.

description: Framing an intertemporal choice so that both options explicitly show a $0 payoff at the time the alternative option pays off (the Explicit zero frame) increases patience (choices of the larger, later reward) relative to the standard Hidden zero frame that omits these zero outcomes.

replication_authors: John Weinman; Keith J. Petrie; Norman Sharpe; Sarah Walker
replication_title: Causal attributions in patients and spouses following first‐time myocardial infarction and subsequent lifestyle changes
explanation: Reviewed Table 4 and the stepwise regressions in the Results section directly rather than relying on the Discussion's global 'confirm and add to' framing. Patients' lifestyle-cause attribution factor score was significantly correlated with dietary change (r=.42, p<.01) and exercise change (r=.29, p<.01), and regression confirmed it as the sole significant predictor of dietary change (beta=.43, F(1,65)=14.90, p<.001, 17% variance explained). However, the same lifestyle attribution factor was NOT significantly associated with reduced smoking (r=.24, ns) or reduced alcohol consumption (r=.15, ns), and did not enter the regression equations predicting either behaviour. The original description covers smoking, diet and exercise collectively as 'lifestyle behaviours', but this prospective replication only held for diet (strongly) and exercise (moderately, via the composite factor score, though not the individual-item Bonferroni-corrected analysis); it explicitly failed for smoking, one of the named examples. Per the partial-support rule, this is a mixed/partial finding rather than a clean success, so the label is changed to inconclusive. Confidence stays medium: this is a genuine partial pattern in the paper's own data, not a case the evidence made obvious in either direction.

explanation: Verified against Table 6 and the Results/Discussion (body.md ~455-465, 990-1004; confirmed in the PDF's Table 6). STK39 showed excess nominally-significant SNPs (p<0.05) for BOTH traits tested, versus this study's own ~7/136 chance expectation: SBP 9/136 (top SNPs rs2063958 p=0.010, rs2390639 p=0.012) and DBP 33/136 (top SNPs rs11890527 p=1.02e-4, rs2203703 p=2.17e-4). Critically, ALL 9 SBP-associated SNPs and 24/33 DBP-associated SNPs fall within the same LD bins (chr2:168,699,002-168,788,544) reported in the Amish discovery study -- a positional, not merely count-based, replication for both traits, strongest for DBP. This contrasts sharply with CDH13 (see Entry 1), whose SNP counts are statistically indistinguishable from the ~51/1020 expected by chance, with no comparable LD-bin concordance reported anywhere. The Discussion explicitly singles out STK39 ('especially regarding STK39... provide strong supporting evidence') as the stronger of the two candidate-gene follow-ups. Upgraded to high confidence because the original explanation cited only the DBP numbers; confirming that all of the (count-wise weaker) SBP hits also map onto the identical Amish LD region resolves the prior ambiguity over whether this was really a DBP-only finding, and supports the general 'blood pressure' success label for both sub-traits.

explanation: Verified against Table 6 and the Results/Discussion (body.md ~455-465, 990-1004; confirmed in the PDF's Table 6). Of 1020 CDH13 SNPs tested, 49/1020 (SBP) and 51/1020 (DBP) reached p<0.05 -- essentially identical to the ~51/1020 (5%) expected by chance, with top nominal p-values no stronger than 5.71e-4, and (unlike STK39, see Entry 0) no LD-bin or other positional concordance with the original European loci is reported anywhere in the paper. The ambiguity is genuine, not an artifact of a shallow read: the Discussion's positive claim ('Our findings... provide strong supporting evidence that these two genes may indeed be good candidate genes') nominally covers CDH13 too, but is explicitly qualified as applying 'especially' to STK39, and the authors never separately state whether CDH13 did or did not replicate. Per the rule that a global support claim does not override data showing no enrichment above chance, this stays inconclusive rather than a clear success or failure; confidence remains medium because the paper itself never resolves this, not because the review was incomplete.

description: Free recall: behavioral descriptions studied in spatial locations congruent with the GOOD is UP metaphor (positive material placed higher, negative material placed lower) are later recalled better than descriptions studied in metaphor-incongruent locations.

replication_title: "Good Is Up” Is Not Always Better: A Memory Advantage for Words in Metaphor-Incompatible Locations
explanation: Experiment 1 (free recall of isolated valenced words, without the stereotype/impression-formation framing of the original) found a significant valence x location interaction (F(1,17)=5.69, p<.05) in the opposite direction from Palma et al.'s congruency advantage; the authors write 'unlike previous studies, here it produces an advantage for information that was incongruent with the GOOD is UP metaphor.' However, the within-valence follow-up comparisons driving that interaction do not independently reach significance (negatives: t(17)=2.05, p=.056; positives: t(17)=-1.29, ns), and the General Discussion narrows the claim to 'at least for negative stimuli' rather than a general incongruency advantage. The reversal framing is the authors' own and is unhedged in the General Discussion (contrasted explicitly with Palma et al. [16]), but rests on a significant omnibus interaction rather than clean significant simple effects and is valence-specific, so confidence stays medium.

description: Recognition memory (location manipulated at encoding): material studied in spatial locations congruent with the GOOD is UP metaphor at encoding is later recognized more accurately than material studied in metaphor-incongruent locations.
original_authors: Tomás A. Palma; Margarida V. Garrido; Gün R. Semin

replication_authors: L. Elizabeth Crawford; Stephanie M. Cohn; Arnold B. Kim
replication_title: "Good Is Up” Is Not Always Better: A Memory Advantage for Words in Metaphor-Incompatible Locations
explanation: Experiment 2 (recognition memory, location varied at encoding) reproduced the pattern from Experiment 1 (significant valence x location interaction, F(1,32)=4.48, p<.05): negative words studied in the metaphor-incongruent top position were somewhat better recognized, though that simple effect is only marginal (t(32)=1.94, p=.061) and positive words showed no location effect (ns) — so, as in Experiment 1, the reversal is driven specifically by negative stimuli. The authors state the results are 'consistent with those of Experiment 1 in showing that the effect of studied location on memory for words depends on word valence, and that the advantage is for words that were studied in locations incongruent with the GOOD is UP metaphor' — the opposite pattern from Palma et al.'s congruency advantage — and the General Discussion confirms this generalizes across free recall and recognition 'at least for negative stimuli.' Confidence stays medium because this rests on a significant omnibus interaction rather than an independently significant simple effect, and is valence-specific rather than general.

description: Combining accurate scientific-consensus information with an inoculation that explains the misleading argumentation technique used by climate misinformers (or presenting consensus information alone) neutralizes the negative effect of misinformation on perceived scientific consensus, restoring it to the level of no-misinformation controls.
original_authors: van der Linden, Sander L.; Leiserowitz, Anthony A.; Rosenthal, Seth A.; Feinberg, Gabrielle D.; Maibach, Edward W.
original_title: Inoculating the public against misinformation about climate change
replication_authors: John Cook; Stephan Lewandowsky; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
replication_title: Neutralizing misinformation through inoculation: Exposing misleading argumentation techniques reduces their influence
explanation: Verified against Table 1 (group means) and Table 2 (ANOVA) for Experiment 1. Perceived consensus—explicitly named by the authors as 'the dependent variable of greatest interest'—showed a significant Consensus main effect (F=89.27, p<.001) and a significant Consensus x Inoculation interaction (F=4.60, p=.033); means show the Misinformation-only group at 63.5% vs. Consensus+Misinformation at 86.1% and Consensus+Inoculation+Misinformation at 83.9%, i.e. both fully neutralized the misinformation's negative effect on perceived consensus, matching the paper's own summary ('an inoculation message was effective in neutralizing the effect of misinformation on perceived consensus'). However, the original (medium-confidence) description also claimed the combined intervention 'increases ... acceptance of climate change' (mirroring van der Linden et al.'s headline AGW-acceptance finding). Table 2 shows this did NOT replicate in Experiment 1: Consensus (p=.066), Inoculation (p=.356), and Consensus x Inoculation (p=.276) were all non-significant for AGW acceptance—free-market support was the only significant predictor, and it is a covariate, not an intervention. Per the multi-measure rule, I narrowed the description to the sub-measure that actually replicated (perceived consensus) and dropped the unsupported 'acceptance of climate change' and 'consensus alone gets cancelled out' claims (the latter also contradicted: consensus alone was NOT cancelled out here, unlike the original). The narrowed claim is unambiguously supported by specific reported statistics, so confidence is raised to high.

description: Presenting images of children sick with vaccine-preventable diseases as a fear-based corrective message paradoxically increases (rather than decreases) parents' belief in the discredited vaccine-autism link, a backfire pattern the original authors called the 'danger-priming effect'.
original_authors: Nyhan, Brendan; Reifler, Jason; Richey, Sean; Freed, Gary L.
original_title: Effective messages in vaccine promotion: a randomized trial
replication_authors: Sara Pluviano; Caroline Watt; Sergio Della Sala
replication_title: Misinformation lingers in memory: Failure of three pro-vaccination strategies
explanation: The Discussion explicitly frames the Fear Correction condition's effect on autism belief as replicating Nyhan et al.'s danger-priming backfire ('the exposure to fear appeals through images of sick children led to more increased misperceptions about vaccines causing autism'), but the paper's own inferential statistics for this specific measure are more equivocal than that sentence suggests. At both Time 1 (immediately post-intervention) and Time 2 (7-day follow-up), the Fear condition's autism-belief level is reported as significantly higher only versus the Myths-vs-Facts and Visual corrections -- never versus the Control condition, which is the comparison that would most directly parallel Nyhan's original fear-vs-control finding. The 'simple main effect of time' analysis found a significant within-condition increase in autism belief only for the Myths-vs-Facts and Visual conditions, not for Fear, and the omnibus post-hoc on the autism-belief change score (Fig 6A) states the effect was 'driven by the myths vs. facts condition,' whose increase was significantly larger than Fear, Visual, AND Control alike (implying Fear's own change score did not differ from Control's). Fig 6A's bar chart confirms this visually: the Fear Correction bar for autism-belief change is low, similar to Visual and Control, while Myths-vs-Facts stands out as elevated. So the fear images produced a higher absolute misperception level than the other two active corrections, but the paper does not establish this differed from doing nothing (Control), and it was Myths-vs-Facts, not Fear, that drove the significant backfire increase in autism belief over time. This is a partial/mixed result for the autism-belief sub-measure specifically named in this entry, not a clean replication of the danger-priming effect -- reclassified from success to inconclusive. (The Fear condition's backfire IS robustly established, vs. all three other conditions, for the separate 'vaccines side effects' belief measure -- but that measure is not what this entry's description names.) The population (Italian/Scottish university students vs. Nyhan's US parents), specific images (drawn from the Illinois Department of Public Health rather than Nyhan's materials), and addition of a 7-day delayed measurement differ from the original, so this is a context/methodology extension rather than a direct replication.

description: In a small, non-randomized pilot study (N = 39), solution-focused (but not problem-focused) coaching questions about a personal problem increased positive affect.
original_authors: Anthony M. Grant; Sean A. O'Connor
original_title: The differential effects of solution-focused and problem-focused coaching questions: a pilot study with implications for practice
replication_authors: Anthony M. Grant
replication_title: Making Positive Change: A Randomized Study Comparing Solution-Focused vs. Problem-Focused Coaching Questions
explanation: Narrowed from the prior draft, which also credited the pilot with 'improved goal approach, while problem-focused questions did not' -- a claim the paper never makes. The only specific pilot finding this paper states is on positive affect: 'Past research supports this study's findings ... Grant and O'Connor (2010) also found that solution-focused, but not problem-focused, coaching questions enhanced positive affect.' That is unambiguously confirmed by this study's own results: a significant Time x Group interaction for positive affect, F(1,138.04) = 11.03, p < .001, with the solution-focused group's positive affect rising by 1.94 (significant) versus a non-significant -0.28 drop for the problem-focused group -- the exact asymmetric pattern described. Goal approach is a different story in this larger, randomized study: 'Both the problem-focused and the solution-focused coaching conditions were effective at enhancing goal approach' (significant main effect, F(1,223) = 72.65, p < .001), with solution-focused only showing a significantly larger increase, not an exclusive one. Had the removed goal-approach clause been attributed to the pilot, this study would have contradicted rather than replicated it, so it was dropped rather than marked as replicated.

description: Using measures of neuroticism and extraversion over a 5-week pharmacotherapy trial, personality traits showed both relative stability (high test-retest correlations) and absolute mean-level change, but this change was not, or only modestly, accounted for by concurrent change in depression scores, leading the authors to conclude that claims of state-dependent instability in personality scores were premature.
original_authors: Darcy A. Santor; R. Michael Bagby; Russell T. Joffe
original_title: Evaluating stability and change in personality and depression
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_authors: Lee Anna Clark; Jeffrey Vittengl; Dolores Kraft; Robin B. Jarrett
replication_title: Separate Personality Traits From States To Predict Depression
explanation: Independently verified against body.md's Results section (no contradicting 'mixed'/'partial' language appears near this passage, and the Discussion/Conclusion do not revisit Santor et al. further). Using a different personality inventory (SNAP temperament/trait scales) and a different clinical context (cognitive therapy rather than pharmacotherapy), the authors explicitly and quantitatively corroborate Santor et al.'s claim: partialling out depression change increased trait stability only modestly (r increase = .07-.12) for the four scales with a theoretical affective/depression link (Negative Temperament, Positive Temperament, Self-harm, Detachment), very slightly (.01-.05) for five more scales, and not at all for the remaining seven theoretically depression-unrelated scales -- i.e., state-dependent instability was present only where predicted and even then was modest, never overriding trait stability. The authors state this 'speak[s] directly to Santor et al.'s (1997) contention that claims of depression state-dependent instability in personality scores needed to be reconsidered.' This is a genuine (if secondary) conceptual replication embedded in a paper whose primary aim is a broader state/trait model, not a dedicated replication study, which is why confidence remains medium despite the clear textual support -- there is no new evidence beyond the already-quoted citation sentence to justify upgrading to high.

description: Erickson and Mattson (1981) found that when people are asked a semantically distorted trivia question with high feature overlap between the true and substituted term (e.g., 'How many animals of each kind did Moses take on the Ark?' instead of Noah), most respondents fail to detect the distortion and answer with their spontaneous association (e.g., 'two'), a phenomenon known as the Moses illusion.
original_authors: Thomas D. Erickson; Mark E. Mattson
original_title: From words to meaning: A semantic illusion
original_journal: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
replication_authors: Hyunjin Song; Norbert Schwarz
replication_title: Fluency and the Detection of Misleading Questions: Low Processing Fluency Attenuates the Moses Illusion
explanation: Using the identical Moses question from Erickson & Mattson (1981), the easy-to-read baseline reproduced the classic illusion (88% answered 'two'), and, as predicted, a difficult-to-read print font significantly attenuated it (53% vs. 88%, z = 2.5, p < .02) while increasing correct 'can't say' responses (z = 2.66, p < .01); the authors state the difficult font 'attenuated the Moses illusion' as predicted.

description: Erickson and Mattson (1981) also showed the semantic illusion effect with other distorted trivia questions relying on high feature overlap, such as asking what Joshua (instead of Jonah) was swallowed by, with respondents defaulting to the expected answer (e.g., 'whale' or 'fish') without noticing the substitution.
original_authors: Thomas D. Erickson; Mark E. Mattson
original_title: From words to meaning: A semantic illusion
original_journal: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
replication_authors: Hyunjin Song; Norbert Schwarz
replication_title: Fluency and the Detection of Misleading Questions: Low Processing Fluency Attenuates the Moses Illusion
explanation: Using a second distorted question from Erickson & Mattson (1981) about Joshua/Jonah, the baseline illusion was present (47% answered 'whale'/'fish' vs. only 23% correctly said 'can't say' in the easy-to-read condition, matching E&M's phenomenon, albeit weaker than Experiment 1's 88%, which the authors attribute to the Jonah story being less well known), and the illusion rate was significantly reduced by a difficult-to-read font (47% vs. 23%, z = 2.09, p < .04) -- the basis for the authors' claim that 'the results replicate the earlier findings.' However, that global claim of replication sits alongside non-significant secondary measures within this experiment: the predicted increase in correct 'can't say' answers (23% vs. 40%, z = 1.41, p = .16) and the parallel undistorted-question effects (z = 1.48, p = .14; z = 1.02, ns) did not reach significance on their own -- the full four-measure pattern (as seen cleanly in Experiment 1) only became significant after the authors pooled Experiments 1 and 2 in the Combined Analysis. Since only the primary distorted-question measure clearly replicated while the secondary measures showed non-significant directional trends, this is a partial/mixed result rather than a clean success.

description: In a single human patient with central scotomas from atrophic macular degeneration, retinotopic fMRI mapping found that cortical areas corresponding to the pericentral scotoma location were silent, showing no evidence of visual cortical reorganization.
original_authors: Sunness, Janet S.; Liu, Tianjiao; Yantis, Steven
original_title: Retinotopic mapping of the visual cortex using functional magnetic resonance imaging in a patient with central scotomas from atrophic macular degeneration
replication_authors: Chris I. Baker; Eli Peli; Nicholas Knouf; Nancy G. Kanwisher
replication_title: Reorganization of Visual Processing in Macular Degeneration
explanation: Independently verified against the Discussion (and confirmed the disease-duration/bilaterality figures against the Results/Subjects section): Baker et al. tested two MD subjects (MD1, MD2) with extensive bilateral central scotomas of >20 years' duration, versus the single Sunness et al. (2004) patient with a 3-year-old scotoma with foveal sparing. Where Sunness et al. reported silent, non-reorganized cortex, Baker et al. found robust, highly significant activation (p<10^-10) of the scotoma-corresponding foveal confluence in both subjects -- a direct contradiction of the earlier null finding. The Discussion explicitly attributes the discrepancy to Sunness et al.'s methodological limitations ('the conclusion in this previous study is based on data from one hemisphere in a single 8 min imaging run') and to differences in disease duration and foveal sparing, i.e. the original null finding did not hold up under more extensive testing. 'Failure' (rather than 'reversal') is the correct label: the original was a null/no-effect finding rather than a signed effect, so there is no directionally 'opposite' effect to reverse, and the authors never use reversal/opposite-direction language for this comparison -- per the taxonomy's tiebreaker, ambiguity between reversal and another category should default away from reversal. Confidence stays medium: this determination rests on my own reading of the same passages the original extraction already cited, not on new evidence, and treating a single-case-study citation embedded in a Discussion (rather than an explicit designed replication) as a codeable 'close extension/failure' entry retains some genuine interpretive latitude.

description: Using fMRI during a flanker attentional-control task, COMT Val158Met genotype showed a linear relationship with dorsal anterior cingulate cortex activity, with Val/Val homozygotes showing the highest ACC activity and, at the same time, the poorest task performance (more errors), interpreted as less efficient prefrontal processing in Val carriers.
original_authors: Giuseppe Blasi; Venkata S. Mattay; Alessandro Bertolino; Brita Elvevåg; Joseph H. Callicott; Saumitra Das; Bhaskar S. Kolachana; Michael F. Egan; Terry E. Goldberg; Daniel R. Weinberger
original_title: Effect of catechol-O-methyltransferase val158met genotype on attentional control
replication_authors: Ulrike M. Krämer; Toni Cunillera; Estela Càmara; Josep Marco-Pallarés; David Cucurell; Wido Nager; Peter Bauer; Rebecca Schüle; Ludger Schöls; Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells; Thomas F. Münte
replication_title: The Impact of Catechol-O-Methyltransferase and Dopamine D4 Receptor Genotypes on Neurophysiological Markers of Performance Monitoring
explanation: Independently verified against the Results and Discussion. The authors explicitly derived their hypothesis for enhanced ERN/N2 in COMT Val homozygotes from Blasi et al. (2005)'s fMRI finding (linear COMT-genotype relationship with ACC activity, highest in Val/Val, who also showed the poorest performance/most errors). The paper's own ANOVA on the N2 incompatibility (conflict-monitoring) effect found no COMT main effect and no COMT×condition interaction (all p>0.1), matching the prose claim that 'no differentiation between the groups could be detected in these markers of conflict monitoring.' On the behavioral side, error rates were not elevated in Val/Val homozygotes as in Blasi et al.; if anything there was a nonsignificant trend toward higher error rates in Met/Met — the opposite pattern. Both sub-measures named in the description (the ACC-linked conflict-monitoring marker and the Val/Val error-rate pattern) failed to replicate, with no partial confirmation on either, so 'failure' is unambiguous for the specific claims tested. The authors' own alternative explanation (lower overall task demand than Blasi's 'more demanding' flanker task) accounts for the discrepancy but does not soften the failure classification of the effects actually measured here.

description: The COMT Val158Met polymorphism affects the behavioral flanker incompatibility (interference) effect in an attention-network task, with Met allele carriers showing a tendency toward greater distractibility and a larger incompatibility effect.
original_authors: John Fossella; Tobias Sommer; Jin Fan; Yanhong Wu; James M. Swanson; Donald W. Pfaff; Michael I. Posner
original_title: Assessing the molecular genetics of attention networks
replication_authors: Ulrike M. Krämer; Toni Cunillera; Estela Càmara; Josep Marco-Pallarés; David Cucurell; Wido Nager; Peter Bauer; Rebecca Schüle; Ludger Schöls; Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells; Thomas F. Münte
replication_title: The Impact of Catechol-O-Methyltransferase and Dopamine D4 Receptor Genotypes on Neurophysiological Markers of Performance Monitoring
explanation: Independently verified: the Discussion explicitly contrasts the study's null COMT effect with Fossella et al. (2002)'s behavioral incompatibility-effect finding ('This is somehow surprising, because Fossella et al. (2002) reported a COMT polymorphism impact on the incompatibility effect even on the behavioral level'). However, the paper's reported inferential statistics test this only via the neurophysiological N2 incompatibility marker (COMT main effect and COMT×condition interaction both p>0.1); no COMT×condition interaction on reaction time is reported anywhere in the Behavioral Results or Table 1, so the specific behavioral claim from Fossella (an attention-network task, not the present flanker/stop-signal task) was never formally tested in this paper. Table 1's descriptive per-genotype 'RT difference' (incompatibility cost) values are close across groups (Met carriers average ~28 ms vs Val carriers ~24 ms, collapsing across DRD4) — a small trend in the same direction Fossella predicted (larger cost in Met carriers) but untested and too small to count as either confirmation or disconfirmation. Confidence remains low: this is a post hoc Discussion comparison to a different paradigm, without a matching formal statistical test of the behavioral measure in the present data.

description: Social skills/vocational training delivered through a modified table game (the precursor to 'Stacking the Deck') generalizes to a natural social setting, but the design could not rule out whether the observed post-training improvements (which only appeared weeks after training ended) were actually caused by the training.
original_authors: Richard M. Foxx; Martin J. McMorrow; Mark Mennemeier
original_title: Teaching social/vocational skills to retarded adults with a modified table game: An analysis of generalization
replication_authors: Richard M. Foxx; Martin J. McMorrow; Ron G. Bittle; Jayne Ness
replication_title: AN ANALYSIS OF SOCIAL SKILLS GENERALIZATION IN TWO NATURAL SETTINGS
explanation: Independently verified against the paper's Results/Discussion: using a matched contrast group (a design refinement absent from the 1984a study) and a narrower population of long-term elderly residents, the authors found the predicted delayed generalization effect in the 'group only' setting (training group rose to 81% appropriate interactions at follow-up vs. contrast group's stable 67.1%, close to its own 69.0% baseline), but found no such effect in the 'group plus untrained peers' (lunchroom) setting, where 'there were no apparent effects in the contrast group' and training-group gains were 'virtually nonexistent (S2 and S3) or sporadic (S1).' The authors themselves conclude generalization 'is more likely in some situations... than others,' explicitly framing the test of the original hypothesis as situation-dependent rather than a clean confirmation. This mixed pattern is the paper's own stated conclusion, not an extraction ambiguity, so 'inconclusive' is correct; confidence remains medium because no new evidence resolves the paper's deliberately mixed framing to a single clean result.

description: Gottman et al. (1995) classified intimate partner violence (IPV) perpetrators into subtypes based on their cardiovascular (heart rate) reactivity to marital conflict, with reactive (type II) perpetrators expected to show a distinct baseline cardiovascular profile (lower resting heart rate, higher pre-ejection period and vagal tone) and heightened cardiovascular reactivity to conflict-related stress compared to controls.
original_authors: John M. Gottman; Neil S. Jacobson; Regina H. Rushe; Joann Wu Shortt
original_title: The relationship between heart rate reactivity, emotionally aggressive behavior, and general violence in batterers
replication_authors: Angel Romero-Martínez; Rui Nunes-Costa; Marisol Lila; Esperanza González-Bono; Luis Moya-Albiol
replication_title: Cardiovascular reactivity to a marital conflict version of the Trier social stress test in intimate partner violence perpetrators
explanation: Checked against the paper's Results section (not just the Discussion prose): both effects named in this entry's hypothesis were null. (1) Baseline profile: 'no differences were found in baseline values of cardiovascular variables' (Results), confirmed in Discussion as 'IPV perpetrators and controls did not differ in HR, PEP or vagal tone in the resting period.' (2) Stress-reactivity magnitude: 'No significant effects were detected in the magnitude of the response (AUCi) in any cardiovascular measure.' Instead, the authors found a different, non-hypothesized pattern: a significant HR time x group interaction (F(2.05,65.58)=3.17, p=.047) with higher HR in IPV perpetrators specifically during recovery; a significant vagal-ratio time x group interaction (F(1.92,61.49)=3.08, p=.050) with lower vagal ratio in IPV during recovery; and a significant overall PEP group main effect (F(1,32)=3.93, p=.050) with SHORTER PEP in IPV perpetrators, which is the opposite direction from Gottman's predicted profile (higher/longer PEP in reactive type II men). So neither hypothesized sub-measure (baseline profile, reactivity magnitude) replicated, and the one directionally-relevant significant finding (PEP) ran counter to the predicted direction; only the recovery-phase HR/vagal findings are loosely consistent in direction with a 'hyper-reactive' profile, just at an unhypothesized timepoint. The abstract/conclusion frame this positively ('supporting the validity of cardiovascular measures as diagnostic indicators') without reconciling the null baseline/reactivity results, which per the scoring rules does not override the mixed pattern. This is inconclusive, not success or failure: real group differences exist, but not the ones the entry's hypothesis specified.

description: Using a 'double pairs' comparison of driver-to-child-passenger fatality ratios in restrained versus unrestrained cases, Hertz (1996) estimated that child safety seats reduce fatalities of infants by 71% (cars) and 58% (light trucks/vans), and of children aged 1-4 by 54% and 59% respectively, implying safety seats are more protective than the roughly 47-48% effectiveness estimated for seat belts.
original_authors: Hertz, Ellen
original_title: Revised estimates of child restraint effectiveness
replication_authors: Steven D. Levitt; Steven D. Levitt; Steven D. Levitt
replication_title: Evidence that Seat Belts are as Effective as Child Safety Seats in Preventing Death for Children Aged Two and Up
explanation: Independently verified against the PDF (this passage is in the Introduction/footnotes 4-5, which are entirely absent from the body.md rendition, so it had to be checked against raw PDF text rather than the markdown). The quote is exact. Levitt states he replicated Hertz's (1996) double-pairs analysis, adds bootstrapped standard errors Hertz never reported (.06 on the child-seat estimate, .05 on the seat-belt estimate for 1-4 year-olds), cannot reject the null hypothesis of equal coefficients on seat belts vs. child safety seats, and states 'in all cases, I obtain slightly smaller gaps between child safety seats and seat belts' -- a clear failure to replicate Hertz's implied conclusion that safety seats are meaningfully more protective than belts. Confidence held at medium rather than raised: Levitt's own regression sample is restricted to ages two to six ('children under the age of two are almost exclusively in child safety seats or unrestrained'), and the only specific replicated numbers he reports (the .06/.05 SEs) are for the 1-4 year-old comparison. No infant-specific (under-1) replicated figures appear anywhere in the paper, even though Hertz's infant estimates (71%/58%) are part of this entry's description -- so the 'failure' verdict is well-supported for the 1-4 year-old sub-measure but not independently confirmed for the infant sub-measure. That gap is inherent to the source text, not resolvable by further reading.

description: Using data from 1982-1987 and a 'double pairs' comparison method, Partyka (1988) estimated that child safety seats are 69% effective at reducing fatalities of infants and 47% effective for children aged 1-4, versus seat belts estimated to be only about 36% effective for children aged 4 and under, implying child safety seats outperform seat belts.
original_authors: Partyka, Susan
original_title: Lives saved by child restraints from 1982 through 1987
replication_authors: Steven D. Levitt; Steven D. Levitt; Steven D. Levitt
replication_title: Evidence that Seat Belts are as Effective as Child Safety Seats in Preventing Death for Children Aged Two and Up
explanation: Independently verified against the PDF (this passage is in the Introduction/footnotes 4-5, entirely absent from the body.md rendition -- had to be confirmed against raw PDF text). Partyka (1988) is explicitly named, alongside Kahane (1986) and Hertz (1996), in the sentence introducing the replication claim ('the point estimates on seat belts suggest they are less effective than child safety seats (Kahane 1986, Partyka 1988, Hertz 1996) ... When I replicate their analyses, I cannot reject the null hypothesis of equal coefficients on seat belts and child safety seats due to substantial standard errors'), and again in 'I have been unable to precisely replicate the findings of these earlier papers; in all cases, I obtain slightly smaller gaps between child safety seats and seat belts.' Both statements textually cover Partyka, supporting 'failure' as the correct result direction. Confidence held at low rather than raised, however: I searched the full paper text and found no Partyka-specific number, standard error, or point estimate anywhere -- the only worked example with reported figures is Hertz's ('for instance, in replicating Hertz (1996), I obtain bootstrapped standard errors of .06...'). Whether Levitt's replication of Partyka's specific 69%/47% (child seat) vs. 36% (belt) estimates was quantitatively as clean as the Hertz example, or just qualitatively similar, is genuinely unresolvable from the text as written.

description: Images morphed between a tomato and a strawberry received the lowest food-likability ratings at the point of greatest categorization ambiguity, an Uncanny-Valley-like effect for non-human food stimuli.
original_authors: Yuki Yamada; Takahiro Kawabe; Keiko Ihaya
original_title: Can you eat it? A link between categorization difficulty and food likability
replication_authors: Anne E. Ferrey; Tyler J. Burleigh; Mark J. Fenske
replication_title: Stimulus-category competition, inhibition, and affective devaluation: a novel account of the uncanny valley
explanation: Using a wholly different paradigm (bistable animal-animal line drawings rated on an affect scale, rather than food-morph categorization), the authors conclude 'the results of Experiment 1 replicate and expand upon the important preliminary findings of Yamada et al. (2012, 2013) to confirm that Uncanny Valley-type effects can occur with distinctly non-human stimuli.'

description: Images morphed between pairs of dog types (real dog vs. cartoon dog, real dog vs. stuffed-toy dog, cartoon dog vs. stuffed-toy dog) received the most negative affective ratings at the point of greatest categorization ambiguity, an Uncanny-Valley-like effect for non-human stimuli.
original_authors: Yuki Yamada; Takahiro Kawabe; Keiko Ihaya
original_title: Categorization difficulty is associated with negative evaluation in the "uncanny valley" phenomenon
replication_authors: Anne E. Ferrey; Tyler J. Burleigh; Mark J. Fenske
replication_title: Stimulus-category competition, inhibition, and affective devaluation: a novel account of the uncanny valley
explanation: Using bistable animal-animal line drawings rather than dog-type morphs, the authors state 'the results of Experiment 1 replicate and expand upon the important preliminary findings of Yamada et al. (2012, 2013) to confirm that Uncanny Valley-type effects can occur with distinctly non-human stimuli,' explicitly framing Experiment 1 as converging support for both 2012 and 2013 Yamada findings.

description: Ambiguous morph-stimuli near the midpoint of a human-likeness continuum of digitally created faces were associated with heightened negative affect (eeriness), producing a non-linear (cubic/quadratic) Uncanny Valley function best fit using AIC-based curve-fitting analysis.
original_authors: Tyler J. Burleigh; Jordan R. Schoenherr; Guy L. Lacroix
original_title: Does the uncanny valley exist? An empirical test of the relationship between eeriness and the human likeness of digitally created faces
replication_authors: Anne E. Ferrey; Tyler J. Burleigh; Mark J. Fenske
replication_title: Stimulus-category competition, inhibition, and affective devaluation: a novel account of the uncanny valley
explanation: Verified against Experiment 2's Results section (not just the summary sentence): both sub-measures named in this entry replicated with explicit statistics. (1) Non-linear function: Table 2's AIC-based curve-fit analysis put quadratic/cubic models inside the confidence set and excluded linear models, for both the human-robot continuum and each human-animal continuum. (2) Midpoint = most negative affect: paired-samples t-tests showed the continuum midpoint rated significantly lower than endpoints for human-robot stimuli (t(68)=12.95, p<0.001) and human-animal stimuli (t(68)=9.83, p<0.001), with the affective low-point located at the midpoint for all five stimulus sets. The only caveat in the text is individual-level variability (a minority of participants did not show a personal valley shape), which the paper treats as expected noise rather than a qualifier on the group-level result, and there is no 'partial'/'mixed'/'some differences' language attached to Experiment 2. Using the same AIC curve-fitting approach ('as in Burleigh et al., 2013') but extending the paradigm to new stimulus domains (human-robot and human-animal 3D morphs rather than digitally created human faces), the authors conclude 'the results of Experiment 2 replicate previous findings (e.g., Burleigh et al., 2013)' and confirm that affective low-points occur near continuum midpoints rather than consistently on the human side.

description: In a live-fire field study, an intervention training focused on situational awareness, tactical gaze control, and visual attention led police cadets to bring their handgun to eyesight level later, keep both eyes open longer, make more correct shoot/don't-shoot decisions, and respond faster in shoot scenarios than an active control group, although the control group improved marksmanship more.
original_authors: Heusler, Benedikt; Sutter, Christine
original_title: Shoot or don't shoot? Tactical gaze control and visual attention training improves police cadets' decision-making performance in live-fire scenarios
replication_authors: Joshua Olma; Christine Sutter; Sandra Sülzenbrück
replication_title: When failure is not an option: a police firearms training concept for improving decision-making in shoot/don’t shoot scenarios
explanation: Verified against the Introduction's hypothesis list (body.md lines 377-398, explicitly mapped to measures at lines 771-823) and the Discussion/Conclusion (lines 1252-1420) plus the abstract. The authors designed a new video-based, 4C/ID-grounded version of the training for experienced officers in a lab setting and tested five hypotheses directly derived from Heusler and Sutter (2022)'s findings: H1 (muzzle position raised later) rejected as differences were marginal; H2 (both eyes open longer) could not be evaluated, since only a fraction of participants ever closed an eye; H3 (more correct decisions) rejected due to a ceiling effect (almost all participants in both groups decided correctly); H4 (faster response time) was the only one confirmed ('This is in line with the findings of Heusler and Sutter, 2022'); H5 (marksmanship/Hit Factor manipulation check) was rejected/opposed ('the improvement in marksmanship skills over Time did not depend on Group'). The abstract corroborates this: 'Both groups did very well regarding decision-making, the optimal muzzle position, and the tactical conduct to keep both eyes open... the intervention group significantly improved their response times and time until the first hit.' So only 1 of 4 evaluable sub-measures (response time) replicated the original field study's pattern, with the others showing ceiling effects or no group difference — a genuine mixed, partial-replication pattern per the paper's own framing, not an artifact of unclear reporting.

description: Spellman and Bjork (1992) theorized, and Kelemen and Weaver (1997) supported, that having participants make a delayed judgment of learning (JOL) itself increases subsequent final recall for the judged items, rather than merely predicting recall.
original_authors: Spellman, Barbara A.; Bjork, Robert A.
original_title: When predictions create reality: Judgments of learning may alter what they are intended to assess
replication_authors: Michael R. Dougherty; Petra Scheck; Thomas O. Nelson; Louis Narens
replication_title: Using the past to predict the future
explanation: Verified against the Results and Discussion of Experiment 2. Using a between-participants JOL vs. RCJ vs. no-judgment design with prejudgment recall forced for all groups, Dunnett's tests (control = no-judgment condition) showed the JOL condition had reliably higher rates than the no-judgment control on all three named recall measures -- p(prejudgment recall), p(final recall), and p(final recall|correct prejudgment recall) -- and this held in both the 3- and 12-sec study-time conditions; the RCJ condition never differed from the no-judgment control on any of the three. The authors' own verdict sentence names only the two studies in this entry: 'The pattern of results illustrated above is consistent with Spellman and Bjork (1992) and Kelemen and Weaver (1997) insofar as JOLs appear to alter what they assess' -- resolving the earlier concern that the effect was attributed jointly to a third co-cited study (Kimball & Metcalfe, 2003), which does not appear in this specific verdict sentence. Upgraded to high confidence on this new evidence: a clean, multi-measure, statistically significant replication of the core claim plus an explicit author statement scoped to exactly the two cited studies. Note a caveat not part of this entry's claim: the paper's own data argue against the specific 'covert retrieval practice' mechanism Spellman and Bjork proposed for the effect -- forcing prejudgment recall in all conditions did not eliminate the JOL advantage, leading the authors to conclude 'JOLs appear to alter retrieval for more reasons than mere retrieval practice.' The description was narrowed to drop that mechanism clause accordingly; the behavioral finding (JOL increases actual recall, not just its prediction) is what replicated.

description: Words with many semantic features (high number-of-features, NOF) are processed faster than words with few semantic features in a lexical decision task, an effect attributed to semantic feedback activation.
original_authors: Pexman, Penny M.; Lupker, Stephen J.; Hino, Yasushi
original_title: The impact of feedback semantics in visual word recognition: Number-of-features effects in lexical decision and naming tasks
replication_authors: Penny M. Pexman; Gregory G. Holyk; Marie-H. Monfils
replication_title: Number-of-features effects and semantic processing
explanation: Experiment 2B re-tested the NOF effect in a lexical decision task but with a regression design across the full set of 190 McRae et al. norm concepts rather than the original's matched extreme-groups design; NOF remained a significant unique predictor of both RT and errors ('the predictor variables that had significant, unique relationships with RT were NOF, word frequency, and word length', R2=.17, F(4,185)=9.31, p<.001 for RT; R2=.11, F(4,185)=5.89, p<.001 for errors). Verified against Table 4's zero-order correlations that the direction matches the original: NOF is negatively correlated with both RT (r=-.25) and errors (r=-.23), i.e., high-NOF words were faster and more accurate, consistent with Pexman et al.'s (2002) original LDT finding.

description: Words with many semantic features (high-NOF) are processed with a facilitation advantage relative to low-NOF words, reflecting greater semantic (feedback) activation for those words.
original_authors: Pexman, Penny M.; Lupker, Stephen J.; Hino, Yasushi
original_title: The impact of feedback semantics in visual word recognition: Number-of-features effects in lexical decision and naming tasks
replication_authors: Penny M. Pexman; Gregory G. Holyk; Marie-H. Monfils
replication_title: Number-of-features effects and semantic processing
explanation: Using virtually the same word sets as Pexman et al. (2002) in a self-paced reading task (a paradigm different from the original LDT/naming tasks), the NOF x context interaction was significant [F_s(2,72)=3.20, p<.05], and the NOF effect was significant only in the incongruent-context condition and not in the highly or moderately congruent conditions: 't s (36) = 2.59 ... p < .05' for incongruent versus 't s < 1' for highly congruent and 't s (36) = 1.69, p = .10' for moderately congruent, so the facilitation effect was conditional on context rather than general. There was also a significant overall main effect of NOF [F_s(1,36)=5.44, p<.05], and the paper's own General Discussion frames the effect as present 'particularly when context information was minimal or nonexistent' -- i.e., the authors themselves treat this as a genuinely conditional/partial effect rather than a general facilitation effect, so 'inconclusive' is the correct label and the ambiguity is real, not an artifact of underspecified reporting.

description: High-NOF words are processed faster than low-NOF words due to greater semantic (feedback) activation.
original_authors: Pexman, Penny M.; Lupker, Stephen J.; Hino, Yasushi
original_title: The impact of feedback semantics in visual word recognition: Number-of-features effects in lexical decision and naming tasks
replication_authors: Penny M. Pexman; Gregory G. Holyk; Marie-H. Monfils
replication_title: Number-of-features effects and semantic processing
explanation: In Experiment 2A, a semantic categorization (concrete vs. abstract) task -- a paradigm entirely different from the original LDT/naming tasks -- NOF was a significant unique predictor of both RT and errors ('the predictor variables that had significant, unique relationships with RT were NOF and word length', R2=.18, F(4,185)=9.82, p<.001 for RT; R2=.09, F(4,185)=5.52, p<.001 for errors). Verified against Table 4's zero-order correlations that the direction matches the original: NOF is negatively correlated with both RT (r=-.31) and errors (r=-.28), i.e., high-NOF words were reliably faster and more accurate, cleanly extending the original facilitation effect to a new semantic task with no conflicting sub-result.

replication_authors: Penny M. Pexman; Gregory G. Holyk; Marie-H. Monfils
replication_title: Number-of-features effects and semantic processing
explanation: Experiments 3A, 3B, and 3C tested the NOF effect on a controlled, single-category (bird) item set across three semantic categorization contexts of varying specificity; the NOF effect was significant in all three (all ps < .001), with authors noting 'the size of the NOF effect roughly doubled as the task was made less specific,' extending and confirming the original facilitation effect under new stimulus and task-context conditions. Verified against Table 8's descriptive means that high-NOF words were faster and more accurate than low-NOF words in every one of the three contexts, with no exception: 3A (bird/nonbird) 586 vs. 639 ms RT and 7.00% vs. 15.00% errors; 3B (living/nonliving) 574 vs. 664 ms RT and 6.00% vs. 13.00% errors; 3C (concrete/abstract) 643 vs. 747 ms RT and 4.00% vs. 15.00% errors. Every sub-measure named in the description replicated cleanly.

description: Spatially precuing a single letter position and coloring that letter differently from the rest (making it the 'odd man out' in color), rather than cuing/coloring all letters in the display uniformly, significantly reduces — but here does not fully eliminate — the Stroop interference effect produced by an incongruent color-word distractor.
original_authors: Besner, Derek; Stolz, Jennifer A.
original_title: What kind of attention modulates the Stroop effect?
replication_authors: Laurie A. Manwell; Martha Anne Roberts; Derek Besner
replication_title: Single letter coloring and spatial cuing eliminates a semantic contribution to the Stroop effect
explanation: Reviewed against the Results section (not just the Discussion sentence). The classic Stroop effect (incongruent color-word vs. neutral) shrank significantly from 149 msec (all-letters cued/colored) to 49 msec (single-letter cued/colored) [interaction F(1,15)=38.88, p<.001], replicating the direction of the original Besner & Stolz (1999)/Besner et al. (1997) manipulation. But the specific claim under test in those originals was full elimination of the effect, and here the residual 49-msec effect remained itself statistically significant [t(15)=5.86, SEM=8.33, p<.001] — i.e., the effect was reduced, not eliminated, in this replication. This is not a wording quibble: the paper's own Introduction describes the originals as reporting 'elimination of the Stroop effect,' but when characterizing their own result in the Discussion the authors deliberately downshift to 'a reduction in the size of the Stroop effect' and add the hedge 'though it should be noted that the manipulations used here are combinations of ones used in previous work' — an implicit acknowledgment that full elimination was not reproduced. Since the qualitative pattern (attenuation via single-letter cuing) replicated but the specific quantitative claim (statistical elimination) did not, this is partial support, which the review rules classify as inconclusive rather than success.

description: In a change-detection task, scrambling the spatial locations of colored objects between sample and test arrays did not significantly impair performance, leading to the conclusion that object representations in visual working memory are maintained independently of each other and are not tightly bound to absolute or relative location.
original_authors: Geoffrey F. Woodman; Edward K. Vogel; Steven J. Luck
original_title: Flexibility in visual working memory: accurate change detection in the face of irrelevant variations in position
replication_authors: Yoni Pertzov; Masud Husain
replication_title: The privileged role of location in visual working memory
explanation: Using a continuous-report orientation-recall task (a conceptual replication, not the original's change-detection paradigm), the authors found a significant, robust effect of shared location on memory errors and explicitly state in the General Discussion: 'Both of these conclusions would be inconsistent with the recent claim that items in WM are maintained independent of each other and need not be tightly bound to their perceived locations (Woodman et al., 2012)... the proposal that items in WM are divorced from their perceived location (Woodman et al., 2012) is based on a null effect.' This is not a hedged or partial finding: the abstract reports the location effect without qualification ('participants exhibited a higher tendency to report features of the wrong object'), and the paper's final 'In conclusion' paragraph restates it the same way with no mention of mixed or partial results. The authors offer possible reasons for the discrepancy (greater sensitivity of continuous-report measures; orientation vs. color as the reported feature) but never walk back the claim that their result contradicts Woodman et al.'s conclusion. This consistency across abstract, discussion, and conclusion — with no hedging language anywhere in the paper regarding this specific finding — resolves the ambiguity in favor of 'failure'.

replication_authors: Tzvi Ganel
replication_title: Smiling makes you look older
explanation: Using a counterbalanced between-subjects design intended to avoid a confound in Voelkle et al.'s repeated-presentation procedure, the author found smiling faces rated significantly older than neutral faces; the discussion states this is 'contrary to what has been suggested in a previous study (Voelkle et al. 2012), smiling makes people look older rather than younger.'

description: Task-evoked pupil dilation (a marker of phasic arousal) during a visual yes-no contrast-detection task reflects and predicts the direction of an individual's upcoming choice and their intrinsic conservative decision bias.
original_authors: de Gee, Jan Willem; Knapen, Tomas; Donner, Tobias H.
original_title: Decision-related pupil dilation reflects upcoming choice and individual bias
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_authors: Jan Willem de Gee; Olympia Colizoli; Niels A. Kloosterman; Tomas Knapen; Sander Nieuwenhuis; Tobias H. Donner
replication_title: Dynamic modulation of decision biases by brainstem arousal systems
explanation: Verified against body.md: the authors state the negative TPR-bias relationship 'was present in two independent data sets using an analogous contrast detection task: the newly collected fMRI data set, and a re-analysis of an existing data set (de Gee et al., 2014)', calling the effect 'robust and consistent.' Figure 2's reported statistics confirm this quantitatively for the specific claim in this entry: the TPR-criterion correlation was significant and negative in both the new fMRI sample (r=-0.662, p<0.001, N=14) and the reanalyzed de Gee et al. (2014) sample (r=-0.339, p=0.015, N=21); the yes-choice-fraction contrast between high/low TPR bins was likewise significant in both data sets (p<0.001 and p=0.022). The Discussion reaffirms this as the paper's dominant, most consistent finding ('the dominant and most consistent link was a monotonic and approximately linear relationship between phasic arousal and decision bias'), and the abstract states plainly that 'large pupil responses generally predicted a reduction in decision bias,' with no hedging language ('mixed', 'partial', 'differing') attached to this specific TPR-bias claim. The one measure that WAS inconsistent across data sets — a non-monotonic (inverted-U) relation between TPR and perceptual sensitivity (d') — is a separate claim not covered by this entry's description (which concerns choice/bias, not sensitivity), so it does not weaken the success classification here. The new fMRI experiment used essentially the same yes-no contrast-detection paradigm but in a different setting (concurrent MRI scanning) and with new subjects, so 'close extension' remains the appropriate replication_type rather than a strict direct replication.

description: Learning a set of semantically related second-language vocabulary words together (e.g., words from the same semantic field such as 'fruits' or 'furniture') impedes learning compared to learning an unrelated set of words, because of confusion stemming from semantic overlap.
original_authors: Tinkham, Thomas M.
original_title: The effect of semantic clustering on the learning of second language vocabulary
replication_authors: Tomoko Ishii
replication_title: Reexamining semantic clustering: Insight from memory models
explanation: Verified against Results and Discussion (body.md): the semantic-vs-unrelated comparison — the direct re-test of Tinkham's (1993) impeding effect — was non-significant on both administrations (Test 1, immediate: unrelated M=13.42 vs semantic M=14.00, p=0.273; Test 2, after a 20-min delay: unrelated M=5.06 vs semantic M=5.59, p=0.336), and in both cases the semantic-set mean was numerically slightly higher than the unrelated-set mean, i.e. the opposite direction from the originally claimed impairment. The two administrations agree with each other (no mixed pattern within this comparison), and the authors state their own conclusion plainly: the study 'did not observe any advantage or disadvantage of the semantic sets,' proposing instead that visual similarity, not semantic relatedness per se, drives the effect Tinkham reported. This is an unambiguous failure to replicate the specific claim in the description (that semantic clustering impedes learning relative to unrelated sets); it is a separate condition (physically-related sets) that gave the significant impediment.
